**COMPLETE COURSE OF PATROLOGY, OR A UNIVERSAL LIBRARY, COMPLETE, UNIFORM, CONVENIENT, ECONOMICAL, OF ALL THE HOLY FATHERS, DOCTORS, AND ECCLESIASTICAL WRITERS WHO FLOURISHED FROM THE APOSTOLIC AGE TO THE TIMES OF INNOCENT III; A CHRONOLOGICAL REPRINTING OF ALL THE MONUMENTS OF CATHOLIC TRADITION THAT HAVE SURVIVED THROUGH THE FIRST TWELVE CENTURIES OF THE CHURCH, MOST CAREFULLY CORRECTED BY COLLATION WITH THE MOST ACCURATE EDITIONS AND WITH CERTAIN MANUSCRIPT CODICES; CONTINUALLY ILLUSTRATED WITH DISSERTATIONS, COMMENTARIES, AND VARIANT READINGS; ENLARGED BY ALL WORKS DISCOVERED AFTER THE MOST COPIOUS EDITIONS COMPLETED IN THE THREE MOST RECENT CENTURIES; PROVIDED WITH SPECIAL ANALYTICAL INDEXES FOLLOWING EACH VOLUME OR EACH AUTHOR OF SOME IMPORTANCE; ARRANGED WITH CHAPTERS PROPERLY SET WITHIN THE TEXT ITSELF, AND WITH TITLES DISTINGUISHING THE UPPER MARGIN OF INDIVIDUAL PAGES AND INDICATING THEIR SUBJECT MATTER; EXPANDED WITH WORKS BOTH DOUBTFUL AND APOCRYPHAL, YET POSSESSING SOME AUTHORITY IN RELATION TO ECCLESIASTICAL TRADITION; ENRICHED WITH TWO GENERAL INDEXES: ONE OF SUBJECTS, BY CONSULTING WHICH WHATEVER EACH of the Fathers wrote on any topic may be seen at a glance; THE OTHER OF HOLY SCRIPTURE, FROM WHICH THE READER MAY READILY LEARN WHICH FATHERS COMMENTED ON INDIVIDUAL TEXTS OF INDIVIDUAL BOOKS OF SCRIPTURE, AND IN WHAT PLACES IN THEIR WORKS. A MOST ACCURATE EDITION, EASILY TO BE PREFERRED TO ALL OTHERS, if one considers: the clearness of the type, the quality of the paper, the completeness of the text, the perfection of the correction, both the variety and number of works reprinted, the highly convenient format of the volumes, consistently uniform throughout the course of the entire work, the low price, and especially this one, methodical, chronological collection of six hundred fragments and short treatises hitherto scattered here and there, but now for the first time gathered in our library from works belonging to every age, place, language, and form.**

[Col. 0009]

**IN THE YEARS OF THE LORD 1165–1168: ECKBERT, OR EGBERT, ABBOT OF SCHÖNAU, AND SAINT ELIZABETH, HIS NATURAL SISTER**

[Col. 0009]

**HISTORICAL NOTICE ON ECKBERT**

(Fabricius, *Bibliotheca medii et infimae Latinitatis*, II, 78)

Eckbert, otherwise Egbert, priest and canon of Bonn, in the diocese of Cologne, and finally a monk and, after Hildelin, abbot of Schönau [Note: [Col. 0009] Vossius, p. 430; Oudin, vol. III, p. 1548; and others, incorrectly make the abbey of Schönau distinct from the abbey of St Florin.] of St Florin in the diocese of Trier, of the Benedictine Order, about the year 1160. His short work *On the Praise of the Cross*, and the *Soliloquy*, or *Meditations* and *Spur of Love*, occur in the most celebrated Bernard Pez’s *Ascetical Library*, vol. VII, pp. 13, 21, 37, Regensburg, 1725, octavo. His work *On the Death of His Natural Sister, St Elizabeth*, virgin abbess of Schönau, who died in 1165, addressed to her female relatives, appeared in the *Acts of the Saints*, vol. III for June, June 18, p. 607, together with the five books of this Elizabeth’s *Visions*, as it had previously appeared under the editorship of Jacques Lefèvre of Étaples, Paris, 1500, and subsequently at Cologne, 1628, etc. Thirteen sermons against the heresies of the Cathars, who renewed the heresy of the Manichaeans (with an extract on the Manichaeans from Augustine), addressed to Reginald, archbishop of Cologne, Cologne, 1530, octavo [Note: [Col. 0009] Hermann von der Hardt’s autographs, vol. III, p. 195.], and in vol. XII of the Cologne edition and vol. XXIII of the Lyons edition of the *Library of the Fathers*, p. 601. Other works attributed to this Eckbert by Trithemius, ch. 403, *On Ecclesiastical Writers* and *Illustrious Benedictines*, II, 121, are: *On the Beginning of the Gospel of John*; *On the Magnificat*; *On “The Angel Was Sent”*; *Meditations*; *Sermons through the Year*; *Praises of the Saviour*; and *Letters to Various Persons*.

[Col. 0009]

**SECOND NOTICE**

(R. P. D. Bernard Pez, *Ancient and Modern Ascetical Library*, vol. VII, Preface, no. 2.)

The name of Eckbert occurs among most cataloguers of ecclesiastical writers. John Trithemius celebrates him in remarkable terms both in the *Annals of the Hirsau Chronicle*, St Gall edition, vol. II, p. 450, and in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, ch. 403, where his words are these:

“Eckbert (Egbert in the Hirsau Chronicle), second abbot of the monastery of St Florin, of the Order of the holy father Benedict, in the diocese of Trier, a German by nation, a man diligent and learned in the divine Scriptures, and no less venerable for his manner of life than for his learning, was brother of the blessed virgin Elizabeth, abbess of Schönau. Formerly he was a canon of the church of Bonn; called to Schönau by his holy sister, he first became a monk and afterwards an abbot. He wrote short works not unworthy of reading, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Among these I have found the following:

*Against Heresies*, one book: ‘Long ago in the time of the prophets.’  
*On the Beginning of the Gospel of John*, one book: ‘The mysteries of the divine discourse.’  
*On the Magnificat*, one book: ‘The Spirit of the Lord is upon thee, Ma[ry].’  
*On “The Angel Was Sent”*, one book: ‘An evangelical sermon: “To every…”’ [Col. 0011]  
*On the Death of His Sister*, one book: ‘To virgins consecrated to God.’  
*Meditations*, one book: ‘A word is mine for thee.’  
*Sermons through the Year*, two books: ‘There shall be signs,’ etc.; Advent.  
*Praises of the Saviour*, one book.  
*Letters to Various Persons*, one book.”

He also published several other things which have not come to my knowledge. For he was an outstanding speaker, learned and eloquent, so much so that he overcame in a single disputation a certain heretic whom no one had been able to refute. He flourished in the aforesaid monastery of St Florin, called Schönau, in the diocese of Trier, under Emperor Frederick I, in the year of the Lord 1160, and was highly esteemed for both religious devotion and learning.

This is what Trithemius says concerning the life and writings of Eckbert. Of these, the *Book against Heresies*, that is, the thirteen *Sermons against the Cathars*, was published at Cologne in 1530, in octavo, and later inserted in vol. XII of the Cologne edition of the *Library of the Fathers*. The *Book on the Death of His Sister* is found among the Bollandists on 18 June, and had already been published at Paris in 1500 by Henri Estienne, Robert’s father, together with the *Revelations of St Elizabeth*, and at Cologne in 1628, according to the testimony of Casimir Oudin, vol. II of *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, col. 1549. Yet Oudin is seriously mistaken when, in the same place, he attributes to Eckbert, abbot of Schönau, the *Life of Blessed Heimerad, Priest and Confessor*, published by Leibniz among the writers of Brunswick affairs. For Egbert, the biographer of St Heimerad, was never abbot or monk of Schönau, but belonged to Hersfeld, as is clear even from the title of the *Life of St Heimerad*.

In the most recent edition of the works of St Bernard, John Mabillon, vol. II, col. 687, denies to St Bernard of Clairvaux a panegyric sermon to the Blessed Virgin Mother of God, which appears under Bernard’s name in more recent editions, and restores it to our Eckbert among the contents of vol. V. Nor do I know of any further works hitherto committed to print under the name of Abbot Eckbert. But it is possible to add three further short works to these.

The first is taken from a small folio parchment codex of the renowned Premonstratensian monastery of Windberg, of the Order of Regular Canons, written about five hundred years ago. No title other than this is prefixed to the work: “Praise of the Cross, words of Eckbert.” Hardly anyone could reasonably doubt that this heading concerns our Eckbert. It is a little composition as sober as it is devout. In section 5, it explains in few and clear words nearly everything that more recent scholastic theologians debate in several chapters concerning the reasons and modes of worshipping the Lord’s cross.

The second short work of Eckbert, now, I believe, for the first time brought to light and printed, is his *Soliloquy*, or, as Trithemius calls it above, *Meditations*. It survives in nine codices of the Melk Library, though none is older than the fifteenth century. A paper codex marked letter B, no. 29, attributes it to Richard of St Victor in these words at the end: “Here ends the Soliloquy of Richard, on the special commendation of Jesus.” But that it is not Richard’s but Eckbert, abbot of Schönau’s, we learn, among other evidence, from the aforementioned Trithemius, who expressly attributes to Eckbert the *Meditations* beginning: “A word is mine for thee.” In order that the work might reach the devout reader in a more correct form, we have corrected it according to the testimony of different codices and have added variant readings at the foot of the pages.

The third short work which I now for the first time make public under Eckbert’s name is his *Spur of Love*, which until now has occupied a place among the works of St Bernard of Clairvaux. Mabillon also reprinted this little book, or sermon, among Bernard’s works, in the most recent edition, vol. V, col. 649; yet he there learnedly observes that it is attributed to St Anselm by Trithemius, Bellarmine, and others under the title *Spur of Love*. “Certainly,” he says, “it does not savour of Bernard’s style, nor is it found in ancient manuscripts or in the first Lyons edition under Bernard’s name.” Thus speaks that most learned man correctly. But the excellent Windberg codex cited a little above teaches us that this composition, full of piety and spirit, is neither Anselm’s: besides the *Praise of the Cross*, it contains the same work expressly under Eckbert’s name, with this title: “The Spur of Love of Eckbert.” Two codices of St Peter’s at Salzburg agree with the Windberg codex, one paper and one parchment, both written in the fifteenth century. The former calls it “the book of Lord Eckbert, entitled *Spur of Charity*”; the latter says that it is by Abbot Eckbert.

It seems to me highly probable that this *Spur of Love* is not different from the *Praises of the Saviour*, which Trithemius mentioned above as having been written by Eckbert. For what else does the author do in it than urge us to glory in the name of the Son, the Redeemer, and to give honour to our Saviour, who has done great things in us, etc.? Moreover, the variant readings that I have added at the bottoms of the pages arose from my comparison of Mabillon’s edition with Melk codex E. 42, which seems to have been written from an exemplar of good quality.

[Col. 0011]

**THE SERMONS OF ECKBERT OF SCHÖNAU** against the condemned, pestilential, and utterly foul errors and heresies of the Cathars, who revived the heresy of the Manichaeans.—There is added a brief extract on the Manichaeans from Augustine, made by Eckbert himself. A work of the greatest value, truly worthy of cedarwood, and never sufficiently to be commended to students of theological matters, both because of the clarity of its style and because of the most orderly method and force of its arguments.

(Galland, *Library of the Ancient Fathers*, XIV, 447.)

**ECKBERT’S PREFACE TO REGINALD, ARCHBISHOP OF COLOGNE**

To the most illustrious lord Reginald, governor of the episcopal see at Cologne: Brother Eckbert, monk of the monastery of Schönau, offers this small gift from his meditations.

In your diocese it has frequently happened that certain heretics have been discovered, who in these days are especially conspicuous [Col. 0013] for their errors. These are those whom people commonly call Cathars: a people exceedingly destructive to the Catholic faith, which they undermine and corrupt like moths, proceeding with great craftiness. They are armed with words of Holy Scripture which seem in some way to accord with their sects; from these they know how to defend their errors and bark against Catholic truth. But they are utterly lacking in that sound understanding which lies hidden in the sacred words and is recognized only with great discernment.

I have therefore thought it worthwhile to set out their errors, to note the authorities from Scripture by which they defend themselves, and to show how those authorities should rightly be understood; at the same time, to state the parts of our faith against which they set themselves, and, with heavenly assistance, to show by what authorities of Scripture and by what refutations these may be defended. Thus those who take care to read and remember these matters may be somewhat readier to dispute with them, should they, as often happens, be discovered among the people. For they are very talkative, and always have something at hand which they can say against us. And it is no small disgrace to our own learned people that they should be mute and tongue-tied in the presence of such persons.

When I was a canon in the church at Bonn, I and my close companion Bertolph often disputed with people of this kind, and I carefully observed their errors and their defences. Much concerning them also became known through persons who had left their conventicles and recovered their senses from the devil’s snares. Therefore, at the urging of my abbot, Lord Hildelin, I have collected more abundantly in this book both what concerns them and what can be said against them; and, because of our former friendship, I have sent it to Your Excellency. Thus, if persons of this kind should happen to be examined before you, your prudence may be armed by these sermons to stop the mouths of those speaking wickedness and to strengthen the wavering minds of impressionable people, who, deceived by their crafty speeches, suppose that they walk according to truth. I ask, moreover, that, if you judge the composition of this book perhaps reasonable and discern it to be in some respect useful to Christian religion, you arrange for it to become public, so that it may be a scandal to that most wicked generation for all days.

**FIRST SERMON**

[Col. 0013A]

**On the heresies against which the disputation is undertaken**

I. The virgin Church received from her Bridegroom, Christ Jesus, one precious pearl as her dowry: the Catholic faith. This pearl, grievously, suffers many assailants in these days who labour to crush it. The perils of the last times, I think, have begun to come, of which the Saviour prophesied in the Gospel. Speaking to his disciples, as Matthew writes, about the signs which would precede the day of judgment, he said among other things:

> “Then if anyone says to you, ‘Behold, here is Christ,’ or ‘There,’ do not believe it. For false Christs and false prophets will arise and give great signs and wonders, so that, if possible, even the elect may be led into error. [Col. 0013B] Behold, I have foretold it to you. Therefore, if they say to you, ‘Behold, he is in the wilderness,’ do not go out; ‘Behold, he is in inner chambers,’ do not believe it” (Matt. 24).

Indeed, we have not yet heard of anyone so insane as to come forward claiming to be Christ himself. But we now learn much concerning the false prophets who say that Christ is in inner chambers. For certain perverse and corrupting men, lurking in concealment, who for a long time lay hidden and secretly corrupted the Christian faith in many people of foolish simplicity, have multiplied throughout all lands to such a degree that the Church of God suffers great danger from the most wicked poison which they pour out against her on every side. For their speech creeps like a cancer, and like spreading leprosy [Col. 0013C] runs far and wide, contaminating Christ’s precious members. In our Germany they are called Cathars; in Flanders, Piphles; in Gaul, *Texerant* [“weavers”], named from the practice of weaving.

As the Lord foretold concerning them, they say that Christ is in inner chambers, because they say that the true faith of Christ and the true worship of Christ exist nowhere [Col. 0014A] except in their own conventicles, which they hold in cellars, weaving-shops, and similar subterranean houses. They claim to live the life of the apostles; but they are opposed to the holy faith and sound doctrine handed down to us by the holy apostles and by the Lord Saviour himself. For they are those of whom the apostle Paul spoke in this way in his letter to Timothy:

> “Now the Spirit expressly says that in the last days some will depart from the faith, giving heed to spirits of error and doctrines of demons, speaking lies in hypocrisy, and forbidding marriage, and abstaining from foods which God created to be received with thanksgiving” (1 Tim. 4).

**On marriage. First heresy**

[Col. 0014B] These are indeed the very people to whom this statement applies, since they reject and condemn marriage, so that they promise nothing but eternal damnation to those who remain in married life to the end. Some of them say that they approve the marriage of those who unite with virgins; yet they say that even these cannot be saved unless they separate from one another before the end of their lives. In this way they also forbid such marriage.

**Second: on avoiding the use of meat**

All those who have fully entered their sect avoid every kind of flesh. They do so not for the reason that monks or other people living spiritually abstain from it, but because they say that eating flesh must be avoided since all flesh is born from sexual intercourse; and for this reason they judge it [Col. 0014C] unclean.

**Third: on the creation of flesh**

They state this reason more openly, but, worse still, say it in their secret gatherings: namely, that every kind of flesh is the work of the devil. [Col. 0015A] Therefore, not even in the greatest necessity do they taste it in any circumstances.

**Fourth: on the baptism of little children**

They speak variously concerning baptism. They say that baptism is of no benefit to children who are baptized, because they cannot seek baptism for themselves and cannot profess any faith.

**Fifth: on baptism in water**

There is another matter which they speak of more commonly, though more secretly: namely, that no baptism in water avails for salvation. Accordingly, they rebaptize those who pass over to their sect by a certain secret rite of their own, which they call baptism in the Holy Spirit and fire.

**Sixth: on the souls of the dead**

[Col. 0015B]

They hold the following view about the souls of the dead: at the very hour of their departure, they pass either to eternal blessedness or to eternal damnation. For they do not accept the belief of the universal Church, namely, that there are certain purgatorial punishments, in which the souls of some elect persons are examined for a time because of sins from which they have not been fully purged in this life by adequate satisfaction. Therefore they judge it superfluous and vain to pray for the dead, to give alms, or to celebrate masses; and they mock the ringing of bells which we practise. Yet this is done in churches for a devout reason: that the living may be moved to pray for the dead and roused to remember their own [Col. 0015C] death.

**Seventh: on contempt for the Mass**

They wholly despise and regard as nothing the masses celebrated in churches. If, perhaps, they attend Mass with the people among whom they live, or even approach to receive the Eucharist, they do so entirely hypocritically, lest their unbelief be detected. For they say that the order of priesthood has utterly perished in the Roman Church and in all churches of the Catholic faith, and that true priests are found nowhere except in their sect.

**Eighth: on the body and blood of the Lord**

They believe that the Lord’s body and blood cannot in any way be made through our consecration or received by us in communion; but they say that they alone make the Lord’s body at their own tables. Yet there is deceit in those words. They do not mean that true body of Christ which we believe was born of the Virgin and suffered on the cross; rather, they call the flesh of their own selves the Lord’s body. And when they nourish their own bodies with the foods of their table, they say that they make the Lord’s body. Nor shall I pass over what I heard from a trustworthy man who, after recognizing their treachery and certain secret indecencies, left their fellowship.

**Ninth: on the Saviour’s humanity**

He affirmed that they err concerning the Lord Saviour to such an extent that they say he was not truly born of the Virgin, nor did he truly possess human flesh, [Col. 0016A] but only an apparent form of flesh; nor did he rise from the dead, but feigned death and resurrection. Consequently, when Christians celebrate Easter, they either celebrate it carelessly if they are among them, or seek opportunities to leave those with whom they live, so that they may not be obliged to keep the feast with them.

Instead, they celebrate another festival, at which their heresiarch Manichaeus was killed, whose heresy they undoubtedly follow. Blessed Augustine says that it was called *Bema*; but the man who recounted this to me said that those among whom he had lived called it *Malilosa* [reading uncertain], and that it was celebrated in the autumn. Besides these matters, we have learned that they hold a new and hitherto unheard-of madness, which certain of them openly [Col. 0016B] confessed when they were examined by the clergy in the city of Cologne, where they were also burned by a populace fervent with zeal.

**Tenth: on human souls**

For they said that human souls are nothing other than those apostate spirits who were cast out of the kingdom of heaven at the beginning of the world; and that in human bodies they can earn salvation by good works, but only among those who belong to their sect.

For a long time they have whispered such things in secret, going about everywhere through the houses of impressionable people; and in these times, as we have heard, they lead many wretched souls captive in the snares of their most wicked whispering. They compass, so to speak, sea and land to make one Cathar, and with impious slander they defile every religious way of life. They assert that no one can be saved unless he has crossed over to their sect. Therefore all who have zeal for God and have their senses trained in the holy Scriptures must keep awake with every diligence to capture these most wicked foxes which destroy the vineyard of the Lord of Hosts. Their errors are indeed many, so that no one could set them all forth by enumeration. But I have distinguished and arranged in one sequence those which seemed to me most dangerous, since, God permitting, I have undertaken to speak specifically against them.

**On the origin of the sect of the Cathars**

[Col. 0016D]

III. It must be known, and not concealed from the ears of the people, that the sect of those of whom we speak undoubtedly took its origin from the heresiarch Manichaeus, whose doctrine was accursed and wholly poisonous, and took root in this perverse people. Yet they have mingled in many things with the doctrine of their master which are not found among his heresies. They are also divided against one another, since certain things said by some of them are denied by others.

Now this Manichaeus, to say a few things about him, was Persian by origin. At first he was called Manes, but later he was called Manichaeus by his disciples, lest he seem insane; and he was called Manes from *mania*, the name for madness. [Col. 0017A] He was so insane that he said that he himself was the Holy Spirit and had been sent by Christ into the world, as Christ had promised when he was about to ascend into heaven. Thus he also called himself Christ’s apostle, as though sent by Christ himself. For this reason his disciples gloried that Christ’s promise concerning the Paraclete Spirit had been fulfilled in their master.

From the number of his disciples he chose twelve, whom he regarded as his apostles, so that in this he might possess the pattern of Christ, who chose twelve apostles for himself from his disciples. His imitators observe that number to this day: from among their elect they have twelve whom they call masters, and a thirteenth who is their chief; seventy-two bishops ordained by the masters; and priests [Col. 0017B] and deacons ordained by the bishops. These persons are called “the elect” among them. From all of them, those considered suitable are sent out either to maintain and increase their error where it already exists, or to sow it where it does not.

The doctrine of Manichaeus and his followers opposes the Christian faith at its very root, as I shall now show.

IV. We believe and confess that there is one God alone, who made heaven and earth and all things in them; and this is the root of our faith. But they teach that there are two creators, one good and the other evil: namely, God and a certain monstrous prince of darkness, whom I do not know by what more fitting name we can call the devil. They say that there have existed from eternity two natures contrary to one another, [Col. 0017C] one good and the other evil, and that the universe was created from them. They say that the souls of human beings, the life-giving spirit of every living creature, and the power that gives life to trees, herbs, and all seeds have their origin from God and were created from that good nature. Indeed, they insist that each such thing is some part of God.

But they say that the flesh of all living things upon the earth, both human beings and other living creatures, derives from that monstrous prince of darkness—that is, the devil—and was created from the evil nature. For this reason, as was said above, they avoid eating flesh. It is a horrible doctrine, wholly alien to human reason, which the children of the devil have devised concerning such matters for the destruction of all [Col. 0017D] who believe them and turn their minds away from the chaste truth found in the holy Scriptures.

V. This also is plainly read among the errors of Manichaeus and his disciples: they said that the Son of God never truly assumed a human body in the Virgin, but had only the likeness of a human body; and that he was never truly made to suffer, die, or rise again, but merely deceived human senses in all these matters, so that all things said concerning his humanity seemed true to human beings, although there was no truth in any of them. Before Manichaeus, two magi in Persia, Zaroc and Arphaxat, taught the same thing.

And, as we have said, all these matters have been reliably established for us concerning all those now called Cathars. [Col. 0018A] They themselves originated from certain disciples of Manichaeus who were once called Catharists. For the Manichaeus from whom this entire error proceeded had many disciples, and while he still lived they belonged to one sect. After his death, however, they disagreed among themselves and divided into three parties. Some of them were called Mattharii, others Catharists, and others were called Manichaeans in a special sense, because they followed their master more particularly than the rest. Yet they all shared the common name Manichaeans, because the error of all originated from Manichaeus.

Those called Catharists were considered more shameful than all the others because of certain secret abominations which they alone especially practised. [Col. 0018B] The people of whom we are now speaking undoubtedly follow their doctrine and way of life. But why the Catharists were first called “purifiers” (*Catharistae*) I have determined to say elsewhere, lest anyone be disgusted by the beginning of this book if I immediately recount all their depraved practices.

I have collected in summary and briefly what Blessed Augustine wrote concerning the Manichaeans from three of his books: namely, from the work entitled *Against the Manichaeans*, from that entitled *On the Morals of the Manichaeans*, and from the book *On Heresies*. I intend to append the same collection at the end of this book, so that those who read it may more fully recognize this entire heresy, as though from its foundation, and understand that this heresy is the cesspool of all heresies.

They betray themselves as belonging to the error [Col. 0018C] of Manichaeus by their usual statement that Blessed Augustine disclosed their secrets. It is established that before receiving baptism he took part for some time in the discipline of the Manichaeans, and afterwards plainly described and refuted their errors and secrets in the books I have named.

**SECOND SERMON. On the fact that Christian doctrine ought not to be concealed.**
I. Therefore I now address you, O Cathars, angular folk, who think that Christ is to be sought nowhere except in your own inner chambers. Tell me: when did the Lord adopt this plan, that he should wish to be hidden in your corners? You say [Col. 0018D] that the truth of the Christian faith is known to you alone and hidden among you alone. But we know that the Lord and Savior himself did not hide it, as is evident from his own words, spoken before the high priest of the Jews when his Passion was imminent: “I have spoken openly to the world; I have always taught in synagogues, where all the Jews assemble, and I have said nothing in secret” (John 18). For he did not speak anything in such a way as to wish it to remain concealed. For although at times he spoke privately to his disciples, apart from the crowds, of matters not suitable to be made public at that time, he nevertheless said to them: “What I tell you in darkness, speak in the light; and what you hear in the ear, proclaim upon the housetops” (Matt. 10). And after his resurrection he commanded them, saying: [Col. 0019A] “Go into the whole world; preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark 16). Of them the Evangelist adds: “But they went forth and preached everywhere, the Lord working with them and confirming their word by the signs that followed” (ibid.). They preached not in corners, not in cellars or weaving-shops, but, as Scripture says, “they preached everywhere”: not only before the common people, but also before kings and rulers of all lands, as it is written of them: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth” (Rom. 10). The Lord did not wish his teaching to be concealed by Paul when he said: “This man is a vessel of election to me, to bear my name before kings and rulers and the children of Israel” (Acts 9). Paul himself likewise judged that [Col. 0019B] the truth of the Gospel should be hidden from no class of people, when he said: “I am debtor to Greeks and barbarians, to the wise and the foolish; so, as far as lies in me, I am ready to preach the Gospel also to you who are in Rome” (Rom. 1). As I have said, the holy apostles preached openly the doctrine of salvation; they performed signs by raising the dead, giving light to the blind, and driving away every sickness in Christ’s name; and they endured crucifixion, death by the sword, and being led to death through diverse sufferings, for the testimony of truth.

II. But if you are, as you say, Christ’s apostles, why have you lain hidden for so long? If you are God’s Church, as you say, why have you always walked in concealment until these times? The Lord says in the Gospel concerning his Church: “A city set upon a mountain cannot [Col. 0019C] be hidden; nor do people light a lamp and put it under a bushel, but upon a lampstand, that it may shine upon all who are in the house” (Matt. 5). The mountain itself is Christ; the city set upon the mountain is the Church, whose foundation is Christ. The Lord says of it that it cannot be hidden. But you have always been hidden, and you have concealed your teaching; thus you keep your lamp under the bushel of fear, and never disclose it to anyone whom you fear may expose you. For even from those who come to you, you conceal your faith—by which you hope that you will be saved—and your secret practices for a long time, as they say, for fifteen years, [Col. 0019D] until you have tested them long enough that you may hope they will not betray you. The holy apostles did not do this, nor did their successors known to us. They did not hide the lamp under a bushel, because neither from fear nor for temporal advantage did they conceal the light of evangelical truth which they had received from Christ. Rather, they set it upon the lampstand—that is, upon the Church—so openly that it shone upon all who were in the house, that is, in the world. For the Lord wished every person, both good and evil, elect and reprobate, to know what the faith and religion of Christians was, so that no one might excuse himself through ignorance.

III. Perhaps you take refuge in that saying which [Col. 0020A] the Lord spoke to his disciples: “Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor cast pearls before swine” (Matt. 7). You base rustics, do not take up these words in your defense, for you do not discern them correctly. The words of salvation, without knowledge of which no one can be saved, must be spoken openly to all people; nor is anyone to be judged so much a dog or a pig that they should be withheld from him. For, as the Apostle says: “God wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (1 Tim. 2). But if someone, after hearing and recognizing the truth, obstinately and incorrigibly contradicts it, and strives to defile the truth through foul slander and mockery, then preaching of the truth should rightly be suspended for such a person. This is to withhold what is holy and [Col. 0020B] pearls from swine and dogs. The holy apostles had found the Jews to be such persons, after laboring sufficiently among them through the word of preaching, when at last they said to them: “Since you have rejected the word of God from yourselves and judged yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13). They turned to the Gentiles and openly preached to them the doctrine of salvation, though they knew them to be idolaters and defiled by every kind of uncleanness. Yet you judge people to be dogs and swine in such a way that you never openly preach your doctrine among them, although you believe that no one can be saved without it, whereas the Lord says: “Whoever confesses me before people, I too will confess before my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 10).

[Col. 0020C] IV. If it should happen that one of you is apprehended on account of his error and brought before the judges of the Church, either you wholly deny your faith, or only then for the first time confess some of your errors, when you have no further hope of life. But such confession brings you no glory; it is like the confession of a thief who, when he despairs of his life, shamelessly admits his robberies beneath the noose. And the executions which some of you sometimes suffer at the hands of a people zealous for the law of their God are not like the sufferings of apostles, but like the punishments of thieves and robbers. For you are those of whom the Lord says in the Gospel: “All who came before me are thieves and robbers” (John 10). For [Col. 0020D] only furtively, and as though by robbery, do you gain for your party the souls of wretches whom you draw after yourselves. All your business walks in darkness, because, as the Savior says: “Everyone who does evil hates the light and does not come to the light, lest his works be reproved” (John 3). O what apostles! O what evangelists! For you well fulfill what the Lord commanded the preachers of his word through the prophet: “Go up upon a high mountain, you who bring good tidings to Zion; lift up your voice, you who bring good tidings to Jerusalem; lift it up, do not fear” (Isa. 40). Certainly you do not fulfill this; rather, you observe Priscillian’s command: “Swear, forswear; do not betray the secret.” You now say, “Our time to be made manifest has not yet come; [Col. 0021A] but now we are beginning to speak openly to the world, and there will yet be a time when God exalts his Church—that is, us—and that saying which the Lord speaks of his Church will be fulfilled in us: ‘A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden’” (Matt. 5). But tell me: if this city—that is, your association—has always been set upon the mountain, namely Christ, how could it have remained hidden for so long? For already more than eleven hundred years have passed since the time of the Lord’s Ascension, and your religion has never been exalted. Or, if it has been exalted, tell us—if you know—in what times and under what kings of the earth this happened, so that the faith of the Cathars was heard preached [Col. 0021B] throughout the world. When did it happen that all rulers and lords of the lands who were neither pagans nor Jews were Cathars and governed their subjects according to the law of the Cathars? Certainly, if you could show this to us, we would believe you that your city had at some time been set openly before the world. But by God’s grace this has never happened.

## SERMON III. On the Growth and Public Manifestation of the Catholic Faith

I. Hear now concerning the faith and grace which we profess and preach openly: how it came down to us, and how God’s Church, of which by his grace we are members, was exalted and set in public view. After the Lord’s Ascension, the great city of Antioch received the faith of the blessed apostle Peter, [Col. 0021C] which he himself possessed and preached. He taught there for seven years, not secretly or in underground houses, but as bishop of the whole city. On his account, the royal hall that stood in the city was, by the people’s devotion, converted into a church, in which he taught the people publicly, celebrated Masses, and arranged matters belonging to the Christian religion. There, for the first time, those who received Christ’s faith were given the name Christians. When blessed Peter had established the Christian faith and divine law there, he appointed the blessed Evodius bishop in his place for the city. Ignatius, that most illustrious martyr, disciple of Saint John the Evangelist, succeeded Evodius. [Col. 0021D] Peter himself then departed for Rome. There also he taught the Christian faith, converted the greater part of the city to Christ, and governed Christ’s Church there for twenty-five years. There he openly confessed Christ’s faith before the Emperor Nero; converted to the faith his wife Libya and Agrippina, wife of Agrippa the prefect; and because he preached that same faith, Nero commanded him to be crucified and ordered Paul, who was preaching there with him, to be killed by the sword.

II. From that time onward, therefore, the Christian faith always increased in the city of Rome. The faith that Peter had possessed and preached never failed in the Roman Church, as the Lord had promised him when, with his Passion imminent, he said to him: “I [Col. 0022A] have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail” (Luke 22)—that is, the faith of the Church entrusted to you. When blessed Peter knew that his Passion was approaching, he appointed as bishop Saint Clement, whom he had converted to the faith and baptized, and committed to his governance his own see and the Church he himself had ruled. Clement thus became successor to blessed Peter in that see and in the end likewise suffered martyrdom for the testimony of the Christian faith. As for the statement that Linus and Cletus are read to have been Peter’s successors, it must be understood that while Peter himself was still alive they acted as his fellow-workers in governing God’s people at Rome, and were ordained bishops by him for that purpose, as a certain one of the apostolic Fathers writes to the bishops of Germany and Gaul. [Col. 0022B] The faith Clement received from blessed Peter was also possessed and preached by Clement’s successors in the city of Rome. They caused it to be preached in other lands through those whom they sent out to preach. Thus the Church gradually grew in that faith and advanced more and more day by day, although many kings and rulers strove to crush it with severe persecutions, until the time of Pope Saint Sylvester, under whom great peace and freedom were granted to the Church; then Christian faith and religion began to be exalted and advanced to the highest honors.

III. For, as ancient writings recount to us, by preaching the word of God and displaying great miracles, Sylvester converted to the faith Emperor Constantine, [Col. 0022C] son of Queen Helena, who found the Lord’s cross. The emperor descended from his royal throne, set blessed Sylvester upon it, and humbled himself at his feet. He also had him ride on his own horse and, walking on foot before him, served him like a servant, led him by the bridle, and assigned to him dominion over the city. Moreover, he built a royal palace for him there, granted to Sylvester and his successors all royal honor and authority which he possessed at Rome and in the western regions, and transferred the dignity of the entire senate to the clergy who were with him. He himself, departing the city with all the senators, moved to Byzantium and built the city named after himself, Constantinople; [Col. 0022D] he retained only the name of emperor for himself and his successors. In this manner God’s Church, and the faith which blessed Peter taught and which his successors received from him and handed down to these times, grew, was strengthened, and was advanced to the highest honors under Roman power.

IV. In like manner, through the other apostles, Christ’s faith was spread and exalted in other kingdoms throughout the whole world. It reached these regions on this side of the Alps in the following order. While blessed Peter governed God’s Church at Rome, he sent three of his disciples—Eucharius, Valerius, and Maternus—to preach Christ’s Gospel to the German people. Arriving in the city of Trier, they preached there [Col. 0023A] and, with God’s help, converted it to Christ’s faith; they baptized all the people in the river of that city, called the Olevia. Eucharius was the first of them to be bishop of the city; after his death Valerius succeeded to the episcopate, and after Valerius’s death Maternus became bishop. Maternus had been raised from death by Peter’s staff. He became bishop not only at Trier, but also at Cologne, anciently called Agrippina, and likewise in the city of Tongeren, which was destroyed in the persecution of the Huns. This, then, is the faith of blessed Peter which these saints preached to the Churches that they governed, and which their successors possessed and preached down to the present day. Finally, Crescens, disciple of the apostle Paul, preached the faith in the city of Mainz. Blessed [Col. 0023B] Boniface also, a man of outstanding holiness, who was its first archbishop and received martyrdom for Christ, together with his successors down to the present day, possessed and taught this faith in the Church of Mainz; and it is still held and preached in all Churches subject to it.

V. The first bishop of the Church of Metz was Saint Patiens, disciple of Saint John the Evangelist. He taught and established our faith there, and it remains there to this present day. Saint Clement, successor of the apostle Peter, sent into Gaul to preach God’s word the blessed Dionysius, a man of most illustrious holiness, who had been converted at Athens through the preaching of the apostle Paul; and he sent with him three eminent men: Marcellus, Saturninus, and Lucian. [Col. 0023C] When they had arrived at the harbor of Arles, blessed Dionysius sent Saint Marcellus into Spain, Saint Saturninus into Aquitaine, and Saint Lucian to the city of Beauvais. Each filled the region and cities assigned to him with the teachings of the faith, which is still held and preached there. Saint Dionysius himself, with his two companions Rusticus and Eleutherius, went to Paris. There he preached the faith which he had learned through blessed Paul, spread it through all France, and suffered martyrdom for that faith, together with his companions Rusticus and Eleutherius. God honored Dionysius’s martyrdom with a unique and unheard-of miracle: [Col. 0023D] after his beheading, he carried his own head in his hands from the place of martyrdom for the distance of a mile to the place where his body was buried. This was a great testimony to his most perfect holiness, sound faith, and the holy religion which he had taught and established there.

VI. Saint Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, an outstanding teacher and most noble lamp of God’s Church, held and taught by word, writings, and example the same faith which blessed Dionysius left in Gaul. Saint Martin, bishop of Tours, likewise possessed, taught, and promoted that faith in every manner. His holiness shines most brilliantly throughout all regions of the world even to the present day and is held in the highest reverence. Divine power bore witness to his faith and teaching [Col. 0024A] by the raising of three dead persons and the performance of other exceedingly wondrous works. Blessed Remigius, archbishop of the city of Rheims, likewise held and taught the same faith and confirmed it by remarkable miracles. He converted Clovis, illustrious king of France, and with him a great multitude of the Frankish people, to Christ’s faith, and baptized them in the city of Rheims, having received chrism sent to him from heaven. From that time, therefore, the kings of the Franks and the rulers of Gaul began to be Christians. Throughout all France the Christian religion began to be publicly observed in common, and Christian faith to be held in reverence in every city. It is preached to this present day in the whole Gallican Church.

VII. From Clovis’s line came Charlemagne, [Col. 0024B] the greatest and most glorious among the kings of the Franks. He was baptized in the same faith which King Clovis had received from blessed Remigius and which the other kings descended from Clovis had held. He was summoned to Rome by Pope Saint Leo, consecrated as emperor, and made advocate of the Roman Church and most faithful defender of the whole Christian people. Through him the Christian religion was greatly increased, extended, and strengthened; through his diligence the faith of the Roman Church was spread through many lands that did not know the Lord. The same faith which the Roman Emperor Charles professed was held and confessed by all emperors or Roman kings, and by all [Col. 0024C] kings of the Franks after him and their rulers, down to the present time of Frederick, Roman emperor, and Louis, king of France.

Therefore we hold and confess the same faith which blessed Peter first planted at Rome; which his successors held in the Roman city; which holy bishops and other holy Fathers obedient to the Roman Church taught in every land; and which emperors, kings, and rulers of the lands received from them along with their subject peoples. We mean the clergy, monks, and laity who have been baptized in Christ’s Church, and who assemble in Churches consecrated to God to pray and praise God, and to partake of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ with [Col. 0024D] unfeigned faith and hope for the salvation of our souls. We are certain that we possess the same faith as the holy Fathers before us because we possess, and believe, the same Gospels of Christ and the same apostolic Scripture which they possessed and taught publicly in the Church. We also possess their holy writings, in which they made known what their faith was and what interpretation they held of the books of the Old Law and prophets, the Gospels, and the apostolic writings; and we follow them in that same understanding. From what has been said, therefore, it is clear that the foundation of our faith is the teaching of Peter, who belonged to Christ, who belonged to God—indeed, who was God. But the foundation of your error is the teaching of Manichaeus, who belonged not to God [Col. 0025A] but to the devil; not to Christ but to Antichrist. Every sensible person can know, therefore, that our Catholic faith ought to be obeyed rather than your hidden unbelief, which, together with its foundation, is cursed by all who love truth and condemned under eternal confinement.

## SERMON IV. On the Text: “Faith without Works Is Dead”

I. Perhaps, O holy Cathars who cannot sin, you reproach us with our sins and say, as we read: “Faith without works is dead” (Jas. 2). Yet you do not have works belonging to faith. Therefore your faith is dead; and because your faith is dead, it is nonexistent. Therefore [Col. 0025B] your sacraments have no effect, and you cannot baptize, consecrate the Lord’s body, or perform anything of that kind in the Church which benefits yourselves or others. This is your objection against us. Go first and learn by inquiry why God struck down Uzzah, who stretched out his hand to support God’s ark when it swayed as though about to fall, at the time when David wished to bring it back from Beth-shemesh to Jerusalem. When you have learned this, construct your accusations against God’s Church. We ought not to answer your accusations concerning our faith, because you are outside the Catholic faith, as we shall show by God’s will. Nor ought we to answer your accusations concerning our evil works, because your works are worse and more criminal; but there will be another place for speaking of those. Nevertheless, we answer you here, lest we seem to let the matter pass through ignorance.

II. We do indeed confess that we are sinners, because, as the apostle James says: “We all offend in many things” (Jas. 3). Yet there is a difference among those who offend. Many commit lesser sins daily in a venial manner; by daily satisfaction they appease the Lord, and they perform praiseworthy works belonging to the faith we profess. Of such persons, I hope, you cannot reasonably say that their faith is dead or that the sacraments of such priests are empty. Such persons [Col. 0025D] through God’s grace are neither lacking from the Church nor have ever ceased to exist in it from the beginning. Yet there are some, to our grief, who commit greater sins called mortal sins and do not make satisfaction to God for them with worthy repentance. Of such persons we confess that the faith which they possess is dead, because it is without works of justification in them. It is dead, I say, not in the sense that what they believe has been annihilated because of them or is of no benefit at all; rather, their faith is dead to them and does not benefit them for salvation unless they repent of the evil works which in them kill faith.

III. But as for what you say about our priests whose conduct is so evil that their faith may be called dead—namely, that their sacraments are of no [Col. 0026A] benefit whatsoever—we wholly deny this, because it is plainly false. You say: their faith is dead, and therefore it can benefit neither themselves nor others. This is false, because it benefits others. The faith which they openly profess can benefit others through their ministry and can have a good effect in others, though not in themselves. I demonstrate this to you by an analogy. It sometimes happens that a wise physician falls into a most serious illness. He possesses knowledge, because he knows how to heal himself; he has medicine effective against his disease. Yet he is so fastidious that he cannot taste his antidotes. He gives them to another person suffering the same illness, and that person is cured; but he himself remains in his illness until death. We may truly say of such a physician [Col. 0026B] that his knowledge is dead to himself but alive to another. So I speak to you concerning Church priests who live badly: they do believe, but believing does not benefit them for salvation if they remain in their wickedness. For “even the demons believe and tremble” (Jas. 2), as Scripture says. Certainly the demons believed who, as the Evangelist says, declared to the Lord Jesus: “What have you to do with us, Son of God? Have you come before the time to torment us?” (Matt. 8). Enormously sinful priests, I say, believe and possess faith; but as I said of the wisdom of the sick physician, their faith is dead to themselves yet alive to others, while they baptize in Christ’s name and perform the other sacraments according to the ordinances of the holy Fathers. Such was the person of whom Luke [Col. 0026C] the Evangelist relates, saying: “John answered and said: ‘Master, we saw someone casting out demons in your name, and we forbade him, because he does not follow us.’ And Jesus said to him: ‘Do not forbid him. No one who performs a mighty work in my name can quickly speak evil of me. For whoever is not against you is for you’” (Mark 9). Certainly, whoever that person was, he had faith dead to himself, since he did not follow Jesus; yet his faith lived for those from whom he cast out demons in Jesus’ name. He could not have done this at all if he had possessed no faith whatever in his name. So, without doubt, evil priests also cast out demons in Christ’s name when they baptize in his name—that is, according to what he instituted—and the faith which they profess with words but not works benefits those baptized. [Col. 0026D] But this matter must be discussed more fully elsewhere; now I turn my discourse back to your hidden faith and your corner-bound doctrine.

## SERMON V. Concerning the First Heresy about Marriage

I. I speak to you, teachers and leaders—not in holiness, indeed, but in error and perversity. Observe and see that in the testimony introduced at the beginning of this sermon the Apostle calls you not human beings but demons: “In the last times,” he says, “some will depart from the faith, attending to spirits of error and doctrines of demons, speaking lies in hypocrisy, forbidding marriage,” and so forth [Col. 0027A] (1 Tim. 4). You are these demons of whom he speaks, and those who heed you depart from right faith. For your teaching forbids marriage, in that you say that no one can be saved who remains with his or her spouse to the end. O demons, where does this teaching of yours come from? It is not from Christ’s Gospels; it is not from the apostles’ writings; it plainly comes from spirits of error. Look at the Gospel of the apostle Matthew, which is read in Churches throughout the whole world. If you do not trust Greek and Latin manuscripts, go to your enemies the Jews and examine the Hebrew text in which they have the Gospel of Matthew written; you will find this written in it: “The Pharisees came to Jesus, testing him and saying, ‘Is it lawful for a man to dismiss his wife [Col. 0027B] for any cause whatsoever?’ He answered them: ‘Have you not read that he who made humankind from the beginning made them male and female? Therefore a man shall leave father and mother and cleave to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh. Thus they are no longer two, but one flesh.’ They say to him: ‘Why then did Moses command that a bill of divorce be given and that she be dismissed?’ He said to them: ‘Because Moses, on account of the hardness of your hearts, permitted you to dismiss your wives. But from the beginning it was not so’” (Matt. 19). Certainly, if you possess any sound understanding, you can observe in this answer that the Lord does not approve that all men should leave their wives, as you teach must be done. If no one could be saved while remaining with his or her spouse, [Col. 0027C] a short reply would have sufficed him: when they asked, “Is it lawful for a man to dismiss his wife for any cause whatsoever?” he could have said: “It is lawful, it is good, and otherwise they cannot be saved.”

II. But he did not say this. Rather, by divine authority he established that the bond of fellowship created by God’s law between a man and his wife ought to be stronger than the natural bond between a man and his parents. But you say that man and woman must separate from each other and cannot otherwise be saved. He, on the contrary, says: “What God has joined, let no human being separate” (Matt. 19; Mark 10). God joins man and woman who enter into a marital covenant before the Church in accordance with the ordinances of divine laws, and such persons ought not to be separated by human action. It does sometimes happen that such persons jointly enter the monastic life and choose dwellings separated from one another so that they may serve God more freely. But God accomplishes such separation, not man; indeed, they do not wholly depart from one another, nor is the marital bond broken between them, because the unity of their minds remains undivided. For the more freely they devote themselves to divine love, the more purely and firmly they can love each other. But we urge no married persons to a separation of this sort, as you do, on the ground that they cannot be saved while remaining together in the world and [Col. 0028A] in married life. The Lord specified one ground for separation, by which a man may, if he wishes, leave his wife and break the marital bond by which he is bound, when, after the reply mentioned above, he added: “But I say to you that whoever dismisses his wife, except on account of fornication, and takes another, commits adultery” (Matt. 5). By adding “except on account of fornication,” he indicated that divorce may take place for the cause of fornication alone. If you think we have not rightly understood the Lord’s words just quoted, hear the apostle Paul and see how he agrees with us in interpreting the same words, where he says to the Corinthians: “To those already joined in marriage I command—not I, but the Lord—that a wife [Col. 0028B] not depart from her husband; but if she departs, she should remain unmarried or be reconciled to her husband. And a husband should not dismiss his wife” (1 Cor. 7). Then, adding on his own authority, he says: “But to the rest I say—not the Lord: if any brother has an unbelieving wife, and she consents to live with him, let him not dismiss her. And if a woman has an unbelieving husband, and he consents to live with her, let her not dismiss her husband. For the unbelieving husband is sanctified through the believing wife, and the unbelieving wife is sanctified through the believing husband; otherwise your children would be unclean, but now they are holy. But if the unbeliever departs, let him depart” (ibid.). In the time of the early Church, it often happened that a husband was a believer and his wife an unbeliever; and conversely that a husband was an unbeliever and [Col. 0028C] his wife a believer. The Apostle urged even such people not to separate from one another, which he certainly would not have done if he knew that both would perish in such a marriage. Your teaching, therefore, differs greatly from his teaching, since you compel those who are plainly subject to divine laws to separate from one another, while declaring that they cannot be saved if they remain together. Hear also the apostle Peter speaking similarly to married persons in his Epistle: “Wives,” he says, “be subject to your husbands, so that, if any do not believe the word, they may be won without a word through the conduct of their wives, as they observe your chaste conduct in the fear of God” (1 Pet. 3). He adds: “Likewise, husbands, live with them according to knowledge, giving honor to the woman as to the weaker vessel, as fellow-heirs of grace” (ibid.).

[Col. 0028D] III. Perhaps you say: “A man and woman who remain together can indeed somehow be saved, but only if they abstain from marital intercourse.” Hypocrites! What are you saying? If the Lord and Savior knew, and if the holy apostles knew, that a man and woman who carried out the act belonging to marriage could in no way be saved, were not their words, by which they so carefully urged married people not to separate from one another, full of perfidy and deceit? Far be that thought. Human frailty was certainly known to them, and they knew that not all men and women were so iron-like that they could live [Col. 0029A] together and observe continence. Therefore know that it is not they, but you, who must be accused in this respect also of the worst deceit. Perhaps, O Cathar, you raise against me the saying of the Apostle: “It is good for a man not to touch a woman” (1 Cor. 8 [sc. 7:1]). I grant that it is good for a man not to touch a woman; but I am not thereby required to grant that it is evil and unlawful for a man to touch a woman. Likewise, in order to avoid temptations, it is good for a man not to see a woman. Must it therefore be maintained as necessary that it is evil for a man to see a woman? If you concede that it is evil to touch a woman because it is good not to touch a woman, concede also that it is evil to see a woman because it is good not to [Col. 0029B] see a woman. And if you concede that it is evil to see a woman, pluck out your eyes so that you never see a woman. Hypocrite! It is lawful for a man to touch his own wife, because it is lawful for each person to have his own wife, according to the words of that same Apostle. And because it is lawful, it is not evil. But it is better for a man, and more advantageous for salvation, to have no woman at all and not to touch one.

> **[Note on Col. 0027D / 0028A]** This is Greek chaff. For dissolution of the bond on account of fornication—and indeed only on that ground—was permitted by the Mosaic law to the Jews; the Gospel, however, is not speaking about Christian marriage.

IV. Again, perhaps you will take refuge in what the Apostle says in the same place: “The time is short; it remains that those who have wives should be as though they had none” (1 Cor. 7). “Behold,” you say, “he says that, even if they remain together, they should nevertheless abstain from marital intercourse.” And I say that, if they can do this, it is good for them; yet no sensible person has commanded it of them, but recommends it. [Col. 0029C] It may nevertheless happen that a man lives with his wife and performs the marital act, while being as though he had no wife. This happens if he is with her soberly and temperately, and preserves reverence for God in all things concerning her. Sensible people know how this ought to be done. But if marital intercourse brought condemnation upon all married persons, the Apostle would by no means have said: “Let the husband render the due to the wife, and likewise also the wife to the husband. The woman does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does; likewise also the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does. Do not deprive one another, except perhaps by agreement for a time, that you may devote yourselves to prayer; and return again to the same, lest Satan tempt you because of your lack of self-control. But I say this by [Col. 0029D] concession, not by command” (ibid.).

I know, moreover, that you stumble over this expression also, where he says: “But I say this by concession.” For you say that if this concession—that is, pardon—applies to their rendering the due to one another, then marital intercourse is evil. For if it were not evil, pardon would not be necessary for it. If you say this, I have already gained something on this very point: you acknowledge that the Apostle grants pardon for marital intercourse. For if the Apostle grants it pardon, it is pardonable; and if it is pardonable, then not all who remain in marriage are condemned because of it, as you preach. Yet we must consider more carefully what the Apostle says: “But I say this by concession, not by command.”

V. It should be known that this word *indulgentia* (“concession,” “indulgence”) is commonly used in three senses. [Col. 0030A] For it signifies absolution, by which the punishment owed by a sinner is remitted; and in this sense the term “pardon” is properly applied to it. It also signifies a concession by which lesser goods are granted to those who cannot carry out greater ones; and in this sense the term “pardon” does not apply to them. It also signifies permission, by which lesser things are allowed to be done in order that greater evils may be avoided; and in this sense too it may be called pardon.

Among greater goods is continence. Since not everyone can preserve it, the lesser good—namely marriage—is granted. It is granted, I say, not commanded; for if it were commanded, everyone not in marriage would be considered a transgressor. Among greater evils is homicide; and in order to avoid it, the lesser evil was formerly permitted to the Jews—namely retaliation in kind and the repudiation of wives—so that they might restrain themselves from the crime of homicide.

Now marital intercourse too must be distinguished for us, so that it may become clear what kind of concession applies to what kind of intercourse. Marital intercourse which occurs simply with the intention of begetting offspring and rearing them for God is not in itself a sin, because the goods of marriage prevent it from being sinful: namely, the hope of offspring, fidelity, and sacrament. It belongs among the lesser goods which have an *indulgentia* called concession. That it can occur without sin may be understood from the Apostle’s statement: “And if a virgin marries, she does not sin” (1 Cor. 7).

I said that it is not in itself a sin, because it can sometimes happen that, even with that good intention, some sin arises [Col. 0030C] when carnal pleasure exceeds the reasonable measure. Then it is indeed a sin, but a slight one, and is excused by the aforesaid goods of marriage. If, because of such a sin, the marital duty ought to be avoided—as you are accustomed to whisper—then for the same reason the duty of eating and drinking ought altogether to be avoided, in which a similar sin sometimes slips in even upon wise persons.

But marital intercourse which occurs not with the intention of begetting offspring, but solely for satisfying lust, is indeed sinful in itself, but pardonable, because it is excused by the other goods of marriage. It has an *indulgentia* called permission, because this evil is permitted in order that the greater evil may be avoided—that is, [Col. 0030D] fornication. Therefore let that saying of the Apostle be understood concerning such intercourse: “But I say this by concession, not by command” (1 Cor. 7:29).

VI. I know one of your whispered teachings; I know the saying of your hidden wisdom which is the foundation of your heresy concerning marriage. It became known to me through certain men who left your fellowship and came to their senses from words of falsehood through the word of God and through the ministry of His servant.

For you say that the fruit concerning which God commanded the first man in Paradise not to taste was nothing other than the woman whom He had created. You say that the Lord commanded Adam not to unite with her, and that he united with her against the Lord’s command; and that this was to taste of the forbidden tree. From this, then, you prove [Col. 0031A] that the whole human race propagated from them was born from fornication, and that no one can be saved unless purified through the prayers and sanctifications of those who among you are called “perfect.” This is the reason for which you are accustomed to blame marriage and say that all who are married and perform the marital act commit fornication and are guilty of the same disobedience through which Adam fell. Therefore they are all condemned unless they separate from one another, join themselves to you, and are purified by you.

For this reason too your first teachers took this name for themselves: they called themselves *Catharists*, that is, “purifiers,” and *Cathars*, that is, “pure ones.” And behold: by God’s just judgment, the very name which you assumed for your glory has in popular speech been turned into disgrace for you. And now, my lords, purifiers and pure ones, like whitewashed tombs, I proceed to answer your hidden wisdom.

VII. Tell me: where have you read that the Lord forbade the first man to eat of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil? I suppose in the book of Genesis. Peasants, return to the same book; open your eyes, if you know how to read; examine the recapitulation of the work of the sixth day, and read what it says: “Therefore the Lord formed man from the mud of the earth, breathed the breath of life into his face, and man became a living soul” (Gen. 2).

After this it adds, concerning what had been done before the formation of man: “But the Lord God had planted a paradise of delight from the beginning, in which He placed the man whom He had formed” [Col. 0031C] (ibid.). After this it adds a description of Paradise and shows what God had made it like, saying: “And the Lord God brought forth from the ground every tree beautiful to look upon and pleasant for food: also the tree of life in the midst of Paradise, and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil” (ibid.). After describing also the four rivers of Paradise, it finally adds: “Therefore the Lord God took the man and placed him in the paradise of delight, to cultivate and guard it; and He commanded him, saying: ‘Eat from every tree of Paradise; but from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil do not eat’” (ibid.).

Do you not understand from these words that, before Adam was created, the paradise of delight had been planted with all its adornment, and that the two trees were in it—[Col. 0031D] namely, the tree of life and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil? Therefore, if the tree of the knowledge of good and evil was created before God formed Adam and placed him in Paradise, it is evident that the tree which God prohibited to Adam was created before God created Eve; and if it existed before Eve’s creation, it follows that it was not Eve.

Observe also the order in which Scripture speaks of the prohibition of the tree and the formation of the woman. “He commanded him,” it says—that is, Adam—“saying: ‘Eat from every tree of Paradise; but from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil do not eat. On whatever day you eat from it, you shall die by death’” (ibid.). And it adds: “God also said: ‘It is not good for man to be alone; let us make him a helper like himself’” (ibid.). And [Col. 0032A] after this it adds how He formed her from his rib. From this sequence of speech also we are given to understand that the tree of the knowledge of good and evil was prohibited to Adam before God formed Eve.

And how was God so rash in His command that He could not wait until He had formed the woman and brought her to Adam, and only then forbid him intercourse with her? Tell me also: if that tree of which Adam tasted against the Lord’s command was nothing other than the woman, what tree was it of which the woman ate and gave to her husband to eat?

VIII. Perhaps you say: “The woman ate of the forbidden tree insofar as she desired the man”; and you maintain that, just as God had forbidden the woman to the man, so He had forbidden the man to the woman. But I ask you still: [Col. 0032B] what was it that the woman first ate in part, and afterwards gave the man to eat, as Scripture says? You have nothing, unless I am mistaken, to answer, unless you choose to answer some absurd folly.

And now, since you have fixed your line of battle against us from the Scripture of Genesis, you must also answer us from it. Tell me: what assistance did God intend a woman to give Adam when He said, “It is not good for man to be alone; let us make him a helper like himself” (ibid.)? For what purpose did he need her help? Did he need her to wash and comb his head? Did he need her, in the manner of a servant, to prepare and provide food for him? Did he have [perhaps: any need] for her to supply him with clothing by spinning, weaving, shaping, sewing, [Col. 0032C] washing, and mending? Certainly you cannot say any of these things or anything similar, if you have any soundness of mind, because no assistance was necessary for man in Paradise, where he suffered no deficiency.

Perhaps God made the woman as his helper in order that she might help him praise his Creator? Certainly Adam could sufficiently sing praises to the Lord in a loud voice without Eve, so that he would never become weary or hoarse. Or if God did not wish that this one man should praise Him alone, but that someone else should do so with him, there was no need to create a woman for the sake of praising and singing hymns, because He could sufficiently have created other men to praise God with him.

Perhaps you say: “God knew that Adam was going to fall into sin and suffer bodily deficiencies; therefore He made the woman as his helper, so that [Col. 0032D] after his fall she might provide him with such assistance as has now been mentioned.” But I say that, in these same matters, a man of his own sex could have helped him, if he had needed help. Why then did He make a woman as his helper rather than another man to serve him?

Now, if you wish to appear wise and interpreters of Holy Scripture, you must name some such duty in which Adam would have needed a woman’s help, and in which another man could not have helped him. Certainly you cannot find anything reasonable to say here unless you agree with me in what I am about to say. God wished to create the human race for the praise and glory of His name, but not in the way in which He had made the angelic creation. For He had created all angelic [Col. 0033A] spirits at once, so that no angel might be born from another. But He intended to create the human race so that people should succeed one another and some should be born from others, in order that the bond of charity among them might be stronger because of kinship. Yet He wished all to have one head and one origin, the first man, so that the whole human race might be propagated from him; and in this he would have a certain likeness to God, who is the head and beginning of every creature.

IX. But Adam had not been made such that the human race could proceed from him alone; for God had not given him the capacity to give birth or to suckle. Therefore He made a woman for him, so that through her he might have assistance in increasing and multiplying the human race: namely, that he might beget children from her as a father, while she might bear and nurse his children as a mother. [Col. 0033B]

Tell me further, foolish and senseless people: if, as you teach, God prohibited the woman to the man and the man to the woman, how could what He said to them be accomplished: “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth” (Gen. 1)? What should or could they have done in order to increase and multiply if they were to abstain altogether from one another? If God willed Adam to beget children from Eve, and thus for their race to multiply through them and fill the earth, yet in accordance with this forbade him to touch the woman, then He was contradictory to Himself in His will and commands and could be accused of foolishness—which it is impious to say.

If I were altogether to forbid my farmer the work of sowing, and nevertheless said to him, “See that my field bears fruit well, and that I may have many crops through you,” would I not be contradicting myself and open to an accusation of foolishness? Indeed I would.

I can say similar things about Noah, who was saved through the ark at the time of the Flood. If, as you say, God abominates marriage and marital intercourse, why, when He wished to save Noah and his sons so that they should not perish in the Flood, did He save their wives together with them? For when He commanded Noah to make the ark, He said to him: “You shall enter the ark—you, your sons, your wife, and your sons’ wives” (Gen. 6). And again, when he had made the ark, He said to him: “Enter, you and your household; for I have seen you righteous before Me in this generation” (Gen. 7). Behold: [Col. 0033D] God bears witness concerning a man who has a wife and three sons that he is righteous before Him. With what audacity, then, do you condemn all men who have wives?

And why, as I said, did He save their wives together with the men? If every marriage was offensive to God, He would better have saved the men alone and drowned all the women in the water; or He would have saved the women alone and destroyed all the men. And if it was against God’s will that husbands should unite with their wives, why did He conceal this from Noah, whom He loved, and from his sons when He brought them out of the ark? If He loved them, why did He not say: “Adam sinned against Me in having intercourse with the woman whom I had forbidden to him; his son Seth sinned against Me because he had a wife and begot children, and his son likewise; all who [Col. 0034A] after them took wives and begot children sinned against Me, and therefore I destroyed them. But do not commit this evil, nor unite with your wives, lest I likewise destroy you”?

But He said nothing of the kind to them. Rather, He said: “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth.” I do not know how this could be done unless they united with their wives. Or if you know how they could otherwise increase, multiply, and fill the earth, tell us.

X. Again, I also wonder how God, if He abominates marriage as you say, could have shown Himself so intimate with the holy patriarchs—namely Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—that He Himself spoke with them, sent holy angels to them, and promised them so much concerning the future propagation of [Col. 0034B] their race: how He would multiply, enlarge, and fill it with blessings. We know from Scripture that the first of them was married to three women, the second to one, the third to four; and yet God did not abominate this in them. Rather, He very frequently called them His beloved servants and, on account of their merits, bestowed many great blessings upon their descendants and upon imitators of the holy faith which they had toward the Lord.

XI. I shall come also to what some of you mutter—namely, the followers of Hartuvinus: that only the marriage in which virgins are joined is just; that they ought to beget only one child; and that immediately afterward they must separate from one another and never thereafter come together in the marriage bed. [Col. 0034C]

I see that you are foolish and undiscerning in every respect, both because your error does not agree with itself and because you cannot establish what you say either by reason or by any authority of Holy Scripture. Your error truly [read: “your error”] does not agree with itself: for if, as you say, God forbade the woman to the first man and that prohibition still remains, then neither the marriage of virgins nor that of persons joined after their virginity has been violated is lawful or just.

Again, I judge you foolish because you contradict the manifest testimonies of Holy Scripture. For the Apostle Paul says: “A woman who is under a husband is bound by the law while her husband lives. But if her husband has died, she is released from the law of her husband” (1 Cor. 7). Therefore, while her husband lives, she will be called an adulteress [Col. 0034D] if she is with another man. But if her husband has died, she is free from the law of her husband, so that she is no longer an adulteress if she is with another man. “Let her marry whom she wishes,” he says, “only in the Lord. But she will be happier if she remains as she is, according to my counsel” (ibid.). Again he says: “I desire younger widows to bear children and to be mothers of households” (1 Tim. 5).

What he says concerning women must be understood likewise concerning men.
