Therefore, if it is lawful, as the Apostle says, for widowed women to marry other men again and for widowed men to take other wives, it is clearly established that not only marriages of virgins are lawful and just, but also those of people who were not virgins before their marriage.

XII. I know, however, that in this matter also you oppose us and object to us certain words of John [Col. 0035A] Chrysostom, which he writes in his exposition of Matthew, saying: “To take a second wife is according to the Apostle’s counsel; according to the principle of truth, it is true fornication. If it is committed openly and freely, with God permitting it, it is honorable fornication.”

And I tell you: if John Chrysostom’s teaching is to be believed, then surely the teaching of Saint Augustine and Jerome, and of the other holy Fathers, must also be believed. Their life was holy, their teaching agreed with the holy Gospels and writings of the Apostles, and it possesses the strongest authority in the Roman Church, to which we look with respect in matters of Christian religion. Hear what these men also say concerning second marriages.

Augustine writes in the book *On Widowhood* as follows: [Col. 0035B] “The Apostle grants second marriages to be entirely lawful. But concerning third, fourth, and still more numerous marriages, people are accustomed to raise a question. Yet who would dare to define what I do not hear the Apostle himself defining? For he says: ‘If her husband sleeps [dies], let her marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord’ (1 Cor. 7). He does not say first, second, third, or any numbered husband; nor ought we to define it. Therefore, to answer briefly: I ought neither to condemn any marriages nor to strip them of the modesty belonging to their number.”

Jerome also testifies, saying: “I now cry out in a free voice that bigamy is not condemned in the Church—indeed, not even trigamy—and that it is as lawful to marry a fifth or sixth husband as a second husband.”

Let the testimonies of these two now suffice, for they affirm that second marriages are lawful—which they certainly would not do if they knew that such marriages involved the disgrace of fornication. And because these writers agree, in the words cited, with the words of apostolic teaching more than does that Greek teacher Chrysostom, these statements are accepted, while his are neither approved nor received as authoritative. Consider it yourselves. Does it seem reasonable to you that he should say a second marriage is fornication, and that it is according to the Apostle’s counsel? Certainly the Apostle dissuades from every fornication and frightens people away from it when he says: “The Lord will judge fornicators and adulterers” (Heb. 13).

XIII. How, then, can it be said that any fornication is according to his counsel? We certainly praise that Chrysostom and his golden mouth, but we do not praise him in these words. Yet I judge that John did not, in those words, favor the heresy which you hold—namely, that second marriages are altogether unlawful, like fornication. Rather, perhaps he said what you object to us because in second marriages one departs from the sacrament of unity which ought to exist between God and the human soul, and whose signification lies in monogamy; and perhaps also because second marriages are less within the bounds of chastity than first marriages, and he wished very earnestly to persuade them of this.

XIV. I return again to your assertion that spouses who [Col. 0036A] came together as virgins ought to beget only one child. Where do you get this? What Scripture has determined this for you? Does it not appear from the Apostle’s words which I have just cited that not only monogamous persons but also those in a second marriage may lawfully beget several children? And are they, as you say, to separate from each other immediately once they have had one child? I ask: why? If, as you say, this marriage alone is just, why must it be dissolved? Or if it must be dissolved for those people to attain salvation, how is their marriage just?

If, therefore, every marriage, as you say, must be dissolved, who are those who ought to keep the Apostle’s command: “Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek release” (1 Cor. 7)? O senseless Cathars! Who has bewitched you so that you do not believe the truth of so many testimonies of the divine word, and so that you wish to destroy [Col. 0036B] all lawful marriages, which from the beginning of the world until the present day have been held in honor throughout the world, among every class of human beings, believers and unbelievers alike?

I suppose that you say all this out of love for chastity. I suppose that it is out of love for chastity that you have among yourselves this custom: in your gatherings, as I heard from one of your heresiarchs, two men sleep together in one bed, and likewise two women in one bed, so that they may guard one another in turn and each may have from the other testimony of his chastity. The man who told me this considered the practice a matter of great religion. But this religion is undoubtedly from the counsel of the Evil One; and shame has not so restrained my mouth that I cannot speak of the things said concerning your wretched chastity by those [Col. 0036C] who have experienced it.

You reject the marital union instituted by God and consonant with the law of nature. Take care lest, because of this rashness, you have perhaps been given over by God’s just judgment to a disgrace at variance with the law of nature. Let this much discussion of marriage suffice; now let us speak of that holiness of yours by which you abstain from eating meat.

## SERMON VI. Against the Second Heresy concerning the Eating of Meat

I. I speak to you whom, as I have said, the Apostle calls not men but demons, when he says: “Giving heed to doctrines of demons, speaking lies in hypocrisy, forbidding marriage” (1 Tim. 4)—and one must understand: [Col. 0036D] “teaching abstinence from foods which God created to be received with thanksgiving by the faithful and by those who know the truth; for every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected which is received with thanksgiving. For it is sanctified by the word of God and prayer” (ibid.).

Tell me: of what class of foods does the Apostle speak here? If you do not know, I will tell you. He meant meats, and he spoke about you, who speak lies in hypocrisy—namely, that it is not lawful for people to marry or eat meat. You speak this in hypocrisy because you wish to appear chaste and holy before people in this matter; but your doctrine is false. For it is lawful to marry, as the Apostle himself shows here when he abominates and calls demons those who forbid these things. And it is lawful to eat meat for those who have not made a vow to abstain from it.

Your reason why meat should not be eaten is that all flesh is born from intercourse and therefore is unclean and defiles the eater.

II. I wonder whether the Lord, creator of all things, when He granted human beings permission to eat meat, was unaware of this holy reasoning of yours—namely, that all who ate meat would become unclean because all flesh was born from intercourse. Alas, that He did not have one Cathar to whisper this wisdom into His ear at the hour when He gave Noah and his sons authority to eat meat, saying: “Increase and multiply; and let your fear and dread be upon all animals of the earth and all birds [Col. 0037B] of heaven, together with everything that moves upon the earth. All fish of the sea have been delivered into your hand; and every moving, living thing shall be food for you. As the green herbs, I have given you all things, except that you shall not eat flesh with its blood” (Gen. 1).

Is it not evident from these words that God made it lawful for human beings to eat meat? With what face, with what audacity, then, do you say it is unlawful? Certainly, if He knew all flesh to be so polluted that no one could taste it without being defiled, God was not sufficiently faithful when He granted people such food, which they could not eat without defilement. But if God did not know this and you do, I suppose you are wiser than God and great lovers of purity. But you yourselves know how false this is.

Are you wiser and holier than the holy patriarchs, who considered eating meat lawful and themselves ate it? The holy patriarch Abraham, who was judged worthy to speak familiarly with God, is read to have received God’s angels as guests in the form of three men; he made them a meal and set before them to eat a very tender and excellent calf which he had cooked. Certainly that holy and most wise man would not have done this if he had known there was impurity in such food.

His son Isaac also asked his son Esau for a dish made from game, and ate the food made from kids and offered by Jacob. Moreover, the priests of the people Israel and all who belonged to the priestly line were commanded by the Lord to eat the meat of the legal sacrifices in the holy place. If all flesh were as unclean as you think, God would never have commanded so many sacrifices of animal flesh to be offered to Him upon His altar. He would never have given His priests any command in His holy law concerning eating it, nor have permitted their holiness to be defiled by it.

III. Perhaps you answer this by saying that many things were lawful during the time of the old Law which are not lawful during this time of the Gospel Law, and that God demands greater purity from the people of the New Testament than from the people under the former covenant. Therefore those of the New Testament must avoid meat, although those under the former covenant did not abstain from it.

But I say in reply that, if, as you say, there is some natural impurity in animal flesh [Col. 0038A] which defiles the eater, it existed then too, since animals were then of the same creation and constitution as they are now. Again, if eating meat is not lawful, show us some commandments of Gospel or apostolic Scripture, or traditions of any orthodox Fathers, in which abstinence from it is generally commanded, and we shall believe you.

When the Lord and Savior sent His disciples out to preach, among other things He said to them: “Into whatever house you enter, first say, ‘Peace to this house.’ And if a son of peace is there, your peace will rest upon him. But remain in the same house, eating and drinking what they have; for the laborer is worthy of his wages” (Luke 10). You see that He did not exclude the use of meat from their food by saying: “If meat is set before you, do not eat it.” He certainly would have said this if He had judged eating meat dangerous to their holiness.

Tell me: if all flesh is unclean and defiles the eater, how can the Savior’s saying be true: “Not what enters the mouth defiles a person, but what proceeds from the mouth defiles a person. For,” He says, “evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false testimonies, and blasphemies proceed from the heart. These are what defile a person” (Matt. 15). Therefore, O Cathars, it is not meat that defiles you if you eat it, but your lies, by which you call God’s good creation unclean.

IV. Yet I do not say this as though I cared whether you ever eat or drink anything good, you who everywhere offer the people of God the deadly cup of so perverse a teaching. Hear now what our Apostle says in writing to the Corinthians: “Eat whatever is sold in the meat market, asking no questions for conscience’ sake. For the earth is the Lord’s and its fullness” (1 Cor. 10). Do you not know that meat is customarily sold in the meat market? If, therefore, everything that comes into the market—that is, is sold—may be eaten, then according to the Apostle’s word Christians may also eat meat.

Why he added, “asking no questions for conscience’ sake” (ibid.), was that in that time meat sacrificed to idols was also sold in the market, and the Apostle did not wish Christians who bought it to ask whether it had been sacrificed to idols or not. Otherwise another Christian, still weak in faith, knowing that they deliberately ate idol-sacrifices, might think they ate them in veneration of the idol to which they had been sacrificed, and thus might himself begin to worship idols.

Similar is what he adds: “If one of the unbelievers invites you to supper and you wish to go, eat whatever is set before you, asking no questions for conscience’ sake. But if anyone says, ‘This has been sacrificed,’ do not eat it, for the sake of the one who informed you and for conscience’ sake. But I mean not your conscience, but that of the other” (ibid.)—that is, understand, of the weak person, as stated above.

Therefore, if the meats which had been sacrificed to demons could not defile one who ate [Col. 0039A] them—namely, one to whom it had not been disclosed that they were idol-sacrifices—much less could meats which had never been used in such sacrileges.

V. Perhaps you object to me what the Apostle says in writing to the Romans: “It is good for a person not to eat meat and not to drink wine” (Rom. 14). I too grant the same: it is good for a person. Why is it good? Because one who abstains from eating meat and drinking wine is further from the sin incurred through the concupiscence of gluttony than one who uses these things. For they are pleasant to taste and easily provoke the concupiscence of gluttony, so that the person tasting them takes pleasure in them beyond what is proper; and that is indeed a sin.

Again, it is good because the body is afflicted by abstinence from these things, [Col. 0039B] and through the body’s affliction a greater reward is acquired from the Lord. These, indeed, are the reasons why monks and penitent faithful men abstain from them.

Nevertheless, even though it is granted that, as the Apostle says, “It is good for a person not to eat meat and not to drink wine,” it must not therefore be granted, as seems right to you, that eating meat and drinking wine are evil; for it is possible for someone to use these things so temperately that he does not sin. For the Savior drank of the fruit of the vine with His disciples, and yet never sinned.

That this argument is not necessary—“It is good for a person not to eat meat and not to drink wine; therefore it is evil for a person to eat meat and drink wine”—I shall show by a similar statement. We know that silence [Col. 0039C] is good and is greatly commended by spiritual men, because one who keeps silent is further from the sin of the tongue than one who speaks. For the person who does not sin in word is a perfect man. Therefore, if silence is good, is speaking evil? Does this necessarily follow? Not at all. For these things are both true together: namely, it is good to be silent, and it is good to speak.

Thus, not eating meat and not drinking wine, when called good, is called so as a precaution, not as a virtue. It ought not therefore to be called evil to eat meat and drink wine, because that would immediately imply that it was a fault and a sin.

VI. Nevertheless, it is not very necessary for us to pursue this argument here; for if we [Col. 0039D] rightly attend to the tenor of the Scripture from which these words are taken, it is clear that it was not said simply: “It is good for a man not to eat meat or drink wine.” For, after speaking above about foods and saying, “All things indeed are clean, but it is evil for the man who eats with offence,” he immediately added: “It is good for a man not to eat meat or drink wine,” and at once appended: “Nor anything by which your brother is offended, or scandalized, or made weak” (ibid.). The meaning is this: since it is evil for a man to eat anything so as to cause offence, so that by his food he scandalizes another, it is good for a man not to eat meat or drink wine—that is, you must understand something of such a kind, by which your brother is offended or scandalized. [Col. 0040A]

Thus these words contain a general inclusion of every sort of food, so that the same may be understood of beans and vegetables. For if someone, by eating these, scandalized his brother, it would be good for him not to eat them. But he expressly named the more agreeable foods, from which it is harder to abstain, in order to urge that even desirable foods be relinquished for the sake of brotherly love. He considered it necessary to give this counsel at that time because some had faith so perfect that they regarded no food as unclean, as the Apostle also said: “All things indeed are clean”; while others were still so weak in faith that they thought certain foods must be avoided—for example, Jews recently converted, who abhorred those who ate pork or food offered to idols [Col. 0040B] before them, and were thereby scandalized. Therefore, on account of such persons, he said: “If your brother is grieved because of your food, you no longer walk according to charity” (Rom. XII). And of himself he said: “If food scandalizes my brother, I will never eat meat, lest I scandalize my brother” (I Cor. VIII). Thus, whatever objection you had in these cited words of the Apostle has been emptied of force.

VII. Tell me further: You do not eat meat because it comes from sexual intercourse. Why then do you eat fish, which likewise come from sexual intercourse? Here you have no reasoning at all. I suppose you hold that the intercourse of land animals and birds is sinful, but not that of swimmers; that every animal is conceived and born in sin, [Col. 0040C] and that therefore their flesh cannot be eaten without sin. This is all false, O Cathars—false; for they have never received, nor could they have received, any command to avoid intercourse. Therefore what you say—“We do not eat beef because it was born from intercourse”—is no more rational than if you said, “We do not eat beef because it has horns.” For being born from intercourse is no more sinful than having horns.

## Against the Third Heresy: concerning the creation of flesh

VIII. We know that Manes, the prince of your error, had this reason for avoiding flesh: he said that all flesh was created by the devil, and he attributed the formation of the human body also to him. [Col. 0040D] But he affirmed that the soul was created by God. And, as I have learned, you too whisper in your secret meetings this same reason for avoiding flesh. But this too is a most deceitful lie—unless, far be it, the Scripture of truth is lying, which says: “God also said: Let the earth bring forth the living creature according to its kind, cattle and creeping things and beasts of the earth according to their kinds; and cattle and every creeping thing of the earth according to its kind. And God saw that it was good” (Gen. I).

But if the Scripture of the Old Testament is not enough to prove to you that God made all flesh, hear the Gospel Scripture, which says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. The same was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him [Col. 0041A] nothing was made” (John I). If, therefore, all things were made through the Word of God, then all flesh too was made through him. O mad Manes, with your insane followers! May he assist you as befits him—the one whom you have made God’s helper in the creation of things. Accursed race! Why did God need the devil’s assistance, so that he could not complete the creation of the universe unless the devil aided him? Or do you not know that the devil is of such great malice that, if he could, in a single moment he would destroy and reduce to nothing everything in the world that is for God’s praise, rather than create it?

IX. I now pass over the bodies of irrational creatures; I speak of the human body, which was especially created to serve the living God and in every respect to resist the devil’s will. Surely, if the devil had created [Col. 0041B] man’s body, he would never have arranged its members so honorably, so orderly, or so conveniently as they are. For, if they are rightly considered, all things are arranged according to wonderful wisdom and goodness, as is evident to everyone.

The other animals were so formed that they walk with their bodies bent toward the earth and their faces cast downward; but man alone is so constituted bodily that he walks upright and has a face suited to look up toward heaven, to which he ought to direct the whole intention of his mind. Do you think that, if human limbs had been arranged according to the choice of the devil, who bears boundless hatred toward us all and envies all our goods, he would have granted us such an honor above the other living creatures? Not at all. Rather, he would have preferred [Col. 0041C] to create us so that we crawled over the earth with our whole bodies, or walked—as might be possible—with our feet lifted upward and our head turned toward the earth, using our hands as feet.

How little he loves the honor and convenience of the human body he frequently shows in those whom God permits him to afflict for certain offences: as in that woman whom Satan bound for eighteen years, so that she could not look upward; and in the man whom he repeatedly cast into fire and water in order to destroy him; and in very many others. It is therefore evident from what has been said that, if you abstain from meat because animals are born from intercourse, you are foolish. But if you do so because they are the devil’s workmanship, as your leader Manes lied, it is clear that you are mad along with him. And now let us move on to other matters.

# SERMON VII: Against the Fourth Heresy, concerning the Baptism of Infants

I. Concerning the baptism of infants, you say that it is empty: that it benefits neither them for salvation nor anyone who is not of an age of discernment, so as to be able to believe or to ask for the grace of baptism on his own behalf. You support this error, I suppose, by the authority of the Gospel saying uttered by the Lord when he sent his disciples to baptize, saying: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. XXVIII). “He who believes and is baptized shall be saved; but he who does not believe shall be condemned” [Col. 0042A] (Mark XVI).

From this, unless I am mistaken, you form an argument of this sort: No one can believe unless he has discernment of good and evil; but infants, when baptized, do not have discernment of good and evil; therefore they do not believe; therefore, when they die before reaching the years of discernment, they are condemned. If you say this, you should know that you do not rightly understand the words of truth. For when the Lord says, “He who does not believe shall be condemned,” this is not to be taken as though it were said of all who do not believe, but only of those who can believe and refuse to do so. Infants, because they are baptized and cannot yet believe, are excused by the weakness of their understanding, so that they are not included in that sentence by which unbelievers are condemned.

Holy Scripture often speaks in many [Col. 0042B] places as though it included a certain universality, whereas the universality is not actually to be understood, but something must be excepted from it. This is clear in the earlier part of the same Gospel saying which I cited, where he says: “He who believes and is baptized shall be saved.” For this appears to be said of all who believe and are baptized, that they shall be saved; but it is not so. Many believe and are baptized, yet will not be saved, because they believe for a time and in time of temptation fall away from the faith, or through an evil life render their faith useless. Therefore, as I said, something must be excepted from that apparent universality of believers, so that this is understood as said not of all believers but of those [Col. 0042C] who have faith working through love and persevere in it: whose love does not grow cold in temptation and whose hearts do not turn away from God. Therefore, if that earlier part of the saying, which seems to be stated generally, cannot stand unless something is excepted from the whole, it should not seem inappropriate if we explain its latter part likewise, saying that it too is not to be understood universally.

II. Similar is what the same Savior declared in the Gospel concerning the sacrament of his body and blood, saying: “He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life” (John VI). This appears to be said of all who eat and drink the body and blood of the Lord; [Col. 0042D] but it must be understood only of those who worthily eat and drink the Lord’s body and blood. For many eat and drink the Lord’s body and blood unworthily, and do not thereby have eternal life; rather, as the Apostle says, “they eat and drink judgment upon themselves, not discerning the body of the Lord” (I Cor. XI).

Thus, as I said, the statement, “He who does not believe shall be condemned,” does not apply to all unbelievers, but to those who, although they have the possibility of believing, do not believe. Infants who are baptized and cannot yet believe are excepted.

III. Perhaps it still seems to you that we do violence to the letter of the Gospel, which appears to concern only those who have the possibility of believing. [Col. 0043A] But, I ask you, answer me from a similar expression found in Holy Scripture. The Apostle James writes in his Catholic Epistle: “He who does not sin with his tongue is a perfect man” (James III). Does this apply universally to all who do not sin with the tongue? Certainly, if all who commit no sin of the tongue possess perfect holiness, then all infants and all mute persons must be judged holy and perfect—which no one doubts to be false. Therefore the saying, “He who does not sin with his tongue is a perfect man,” must be understood thus: he is perfect who, though able and knowing how to sin with his tongue, abstains through fear of God from sinning with it.

Similar too is the Apostle’s saying: “He who does not work, let him not eat” (II Thess. III). It appears [Col. 0043B] to be pronounced universally concerning all who do not work, but it is not so. For if no one who does not work is to be excepted from that statement, then neither children, nor old people, nor the sick—who do not work—ought to eat. Therefore this saying concerns those who can work but do not, instead devoting themselves to idleness.

Similar is: “Those who have done evil, unto the resurrection of judgment” (John V). This too appears to be said generally of all who do evil; but excepted from this judgment are those who do evil and afterwards repent and persevere in goodness. Many similar statements are found in Holy Scripture, but there is no need at present to introduce more examples. And now, if you have another defence of your error, bring it forward; for the defence of which we have now spoken [Col. 0043C] will not help you.

IV. Foolish and senseless people! Do you not recognize the time? Do you not know that Holy Scripture calls this whole period, running from Christ’s birth until the end of the age, the time of grace? It is called the time of grace because in it the Lord’s mercy has been extended over humankind, and the bosom of God has been opened to receive human souls, more than in all the ages that preceded Christ’s coming.

But if matters are as your impiety proclaims—namely, that all who die before the years of discernment are condemned, and that God has established no remedy for them by which they may be helped through the Church of God, so that they must necessarily pass away into [Col. 0043D] eternal perdition—then God is surely harsher and less merciful in this age than he was in the times preceding Christ’s coming, and less concerned for human salvation. For from the time of Abraham until Christ, God had established among the Jewish people descended from Abraham that every male infant should be circumcised on the eighth day from his birth in the flesh belonging to generation, so that he might thereby be delivered from original sin, with which every human being is born and for which every soul is condemned unless it has been cleansed from it by some remedy.

V. That this command was given for the salvation of souls may clearly be known from the Lord’s words to Abraham when he gave him the commandment of circumcision: “An infant eight days old shall be circumcised among you. Every male in your generations, both one born in the household and one bought, shall be circumcised. The soul of the male whose flesh of the foreskin has not been circumcised shall be cut off from his people” (Gen. XVII). Behold: [Col. 0044A] in this threat it can plainly be known that he commanded them to be circumcised for the preservation of their souls.

Observe also that he did not say that it should be delayed until a person reached the years of discernment and could then ask for circumcision on his own behalf. Rather, he commanded that the infant be circumcised on the eighth day, because he knew the frailty of the human body and that, through a slight misfortune, a person may die before reaching mature [Col. 0044B] years. Therefore, because he wished circumcision to be performed so promptly, he did this in order that souls might be saved and might not fall into eternal condemnation through the stain of original sin, which all of us contracted from our first parents.

Indeed, the same circumcision could even be performed before the eighth day if infants appeared to be in danger of death. So also, for the same reason, we sometimes baptize infants before the prescribed time, although it has been established by the apostolic Fathers that we baptize either at Easter or at Pentecost. And just as male infants were cleansed from original guilt through circumcision, so female infants were cleansed from it through legal offerings, so that their souls also might not perish from among their people.

VI. [Col. 0044C] Before the time of circumcision, from Adam until Abraham, who first received the commandment of circumcision, those who maintained the worship of God customarily made offerings to God, through which original sin and the other sins arising from human frailty could be removed in God’s elect, both little and great, so that their souls might be saved. For God’s mercy never wholly abandoned the human race.

Behold how great was God’s care for infants in the earlier ages, that their souls might be preserved from perdition. And do you think, impious people, that God has forgotten that same mercy in this age, which is called the time of grace and the year of goodwill? Or do you think that he loves the sons and daughters of Christians less than the infants of the Jews, for whom he established [Col. 0044D] circumcision so that their souls should not perish from among their people?

VII. After Christ’s ascension, he commanded circumcision to cease through the teaching of the apostles, one of whom said: “If you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing” (Gal. V). In place of circumcision he willed baptism in water, so that every person, small or great, who was immersed in it in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit might be cleansed from sins.

And indeed, if it is as you say—namely, that baptism benefits only adults and not infants for salvation—then baptism now does not have as great a power as circumcision had when it was observed in its own time. Answer me, therefore, concerning this: [Col. 0045A] when the Lord established baptism in the Church and caused circumcision to cease, either he willed but could not give baptism the power that circumcision had possessed, namely, that souls of infants should be preserved through it; or he could do this and would not; or he neither would nor could. If he willed and could not, he was not as powerful as he formerly was, when he established circumcision and through it preserved the souls of infants from condemnation. How, then, can the Scripture be true which says: “Whatever the Lord willed, he did in heaven and on earth” (Ps. CXXXIV)?

But if he could and would not, then in this age of grace he is neither as abundantly gracious nor as faithful toward the Christian people as he had been toward the Jewish people: he removed [Col. 0045B] circumcision, by which the souls of infants could be preserved, and established nothing in its place through which they might be helped. But if God neither willed nor could extend through baptism to infants the mercy he had extended through circumcision, it follows that he is neither as powerful nor as gracious in this age as he was in ancient days. This is as far from the truth as a Cathar is from salvation.

And if your teaching is true, it would surely have been better and happier for the world if the Jewish law—which in its own state could help both little and great—had remained, and all nations had flocked to it, than that the Christian law should have entered the world, which, as you whisper, cannot benefit anyone except those who reach the years of discernment. [Col. 0045C] Hardly half of humankind lives to attain the days in which they can know what they ought, or ought not, to believe. If all such persons must necessarily perish, then the whole Church ought rightly to suffer intolerable grief over the change God made in it: that he forbade circumcision, established baptism in its place, and permits so many thousands of souls to go into perdition—souls for whom baptism is thought to be beneficial but is not, according to your heresy.

VIII. What else, then, will Rachel do but weep for her children without ceasing and refuse consolation, because they are not? (Matt. II). How, then, can this age rightly be called a time of grace and not rather [Col. 0045D] a time of wrath? Rather, O son of wrath, O evil seed of Cathars, criminal children: now is the time of grace, not of wrath: “Now is the acceptable time; now is the day of salvation” (II Cor. VI), because, as I have said, God’s mercy has been extended over this world more than in earlier ages.

For before the Savior’s coming death and perdition reigned in humankind; God’s wrath oppressed the whole world; and very few souls in that time were saved from eternal death. All nations, except the Jewish nation, were ignorant of their Creator and served idolatry. In that nation God was known, and it was devoted to the laws and service of the true God. But in this age God has shown his mercy throughout the world and willed to be known in every region of the earth. He established the grace of baptism not for one nation, as circumcision was for the Jews, but for every kind of human being, [Col. 0046A] so that whoever is baptized in his name—Jew or Greek, Latin or barbarian, small or great, male or female, slave or free—obtains in it so full a remission of all sins that, if immediately after baptism he departs this life, the gate of the kingdom of heaven is open to him.

Circumcision did not possess such power of salvation among the ancient people. Through circumcision, or through any observances of the ancient law, entrance into God’s kingdom was opened to no one, small or great, however innocent or holy. Rather, the souls of all who were chosen for God’s kingdom among that people were kept in places appointed for them [Col. 0046B] by God, awaiting the time when, through Christ’s power, access to the glory of perfect blessedness would be opened to them.

IX. For these reasons which I have now stated, this time of Christianity is rightly called the time of grace, the acceptable time, and these days the days of salvation—days which might rather be called days of perdition if matters were as you impiously whisper. Yet do not suppose that I mean that all who are baptized in the Church according to the Lord’s institution receive remission of sins in such a way that, however they subsequently live, they will nevertheless reach God’s kingdom.

But this I say, and our faith firmly holds it: Whatever infants are baptized in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit—whether by a good person or a bad one, even if he is a heretic—and are overtaken by death before they mature, are saved through baptism and through the faith of the Holy Trinity held by the Catholic Church, which invokes the Lord’s name for the salvation of those baptized in her, just as they were formerly saved through circumcision and the faith of the fathers. Those who reach mature years, if their lives accord with the grace received in baptism, are brought to salvation by baptism, Catholic faith, and upright works. But those who stain their lives with wicked deeds and, contrary to God’s commandments, serve the devil’s pomp, certainly extinguish within themselves the grace of the Holy Spirit received in baptism; baptism profits them nothing for salvation, [Col. 0046D] just as circumcision profited many Jews who walked perversely nothing toward attaining salvation.

This is our Catholic faith concerning those who are baptized: a faith always preached openly in God’s Church in the times of the apostles and of the holy Fathers who succeeded them in the Roman Church and in other churches down to our own times. They are read to have preached publicly and baptized in Christ old people and young people, women and infants.

X. I return now to what I said: that infants are saved through baptism and through the faith of the Holy Trinity held by the Church, which invokes the Lord’s name for the salvation of those baptized in her. You say it is incredible that one person’s faith can benefit another before God. Why is it incredible to you? If you know the Gospels, turn them over and you will find that, while the Lord Savior lived among human beings and performed divine miracles, he showed mercy to many who were ill, not because of their own merits but because of the faith of others who prayed to him for them.

We read of the Canaanite woman that she begged the Lord for her daughter, grievously afflicted by a demon. Having heard the mother’s pitiable cries, he finally had mercy on her and said: “O woman, great is your faith; let it be done to you as you wish.” And her daughter was healed from that hour (Matt. XV). [Col. 0047A] Behold: in saying, “Great is your faith,” he plainly declared that, through the faith which the mother had in him, she merited that her daughter should be healed, though the daughter had neither faith nor [Col. 0047B] a sound mind.

We also read of the centurion, who begged the Lord for the health of his paralyzed servant. When the Lord said to him, “I will come and heal him,” the centurion replied, “Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof, but only speak the word and my servant shall be healed.” The Lord marveled at his faith and said: “Amen, I say to you, I have not found such great faith in Israel.” Then he said to him: “Go, and as you have believed, let it be done to you.” And the servant was healed that hour (Matt. VIII). Do not these words also make it plain that the faith of the man who made the request benefited the person for whom he made it, so that he was healed?

XI. Perhaps you will reply that in the cases now mentioned—the possessed girl and the paralyzed servant—the faith of those who asked for them did indeed benefit their bodies, [Col. 0047C] but not the health of their souls; and you say that, for attaining the salvation of the soul, each person can be helped only by his own faith, not by another’s faith, however much that other may cry out for him. I shall now bring forward another example against you on this point.

It is written in the Gospel of Luke that, on one of the days, Jesus was sitting and teaching; Pharisees and doctors of the law were sitting there, who had come from every village of Galilee and Judea and from Jerusalem; and the power of the Lord was present to heal them. And behold, men were carrying on a bed a man who was paralyzed, and they sought to bring him in and place him before Jesus. But, finding no way to bring him in because of the crowd, they went up upon the roof and lowered him through the tiles with his bed into the midst, before Jesus. “When he saw their faith, he said: ‘Man, your sins are forgiven you’” (Luke V). [Col. 0047D]

Behold: when the Evangelist says, “When he saw their faith” (ibid.), he plainly indicates that the faith which they had in Christ’s power was pleasing to the Lord, and that especially on account of it the man was first granted the forgiveness of sins, which concerned the salvation of his soul; and afterwards bodily health, when he said to the same paralytic: “I say to you, arise; take up your bed and go to your house” (ibid.). For if the Lord had shown this mercy to the paralytic because of the merit of his own faith and not because of their faith, the Evangelist would by no means have said, “When he saw their faith,” but rather, “When he saw his faith.” [Col. 0048A]

Observing this, we too trust that the Lord Jesus will regard our faith when we present our sick person to him for healing. We also carry a paralytic on a bed and place him before Jesus when we carry an infant to baptism, asking him to baptize and save the child. For a rational soul still bound by original sin, as yet able to exercise none of its natural powers in its infant body—to what can it better be compared than to a person inwardly bound by sin and outwardly disabled in his limbs by paralysis, lying on a bed?

The friends of that paralytic asked for nothing but his bodily healing. But Christ, out of gratuitous goodness, first gave what was greater, healing him from sins in his soul; and then [Col. 0048B] he added what was sought, restoring his bodily health. Thus the faith of those who believed that he could do the lesser thing was approved. Yet unquestionably our faith, with which we present our paralytic to the Lord, is greater than theirs, and our petition more spiritual than theirs. For we believe that, just as he can through baptism cleanse the souls of adults from every sin, both actual and original, so he can free the souls of infants from original sin without their own merits, just as he healed that aforesaid paralytic without his merits, both in soul and body. We believe this, I say, and faithfully ask it of him whenever we offer infants to him for baptism; for he is invisibly present there with them, [Col. 0048C] and he himself invisibly baptizes all who are immersed in water with the invocation of the Holy Trinity.

XII. Do not be surprised at what I have said, that he himself invisibly baptizes those who are baptized. For it is written that John the Baptist gave this testimony concerning him: “He who sent me to baptize in water said to me: ‘He upon whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining, this is he who baptizes.’ And I saw and bore witness that this is the Son of God” (John I). He also said to the crowds concerning Christ: “He who is to come after me is mightier than I, whose shoes I am not worthy to carry. He will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire” (Matt. [Col. 0048D] III).

From these words we are assured that the Lord Jesus Christ himself is the common baptizer of all who are baptized in the Catholic Church in the name of the Holy Trinity: namely, that he himself invisibly sanctifies their spirit in the Holy Spirit and cleanses it from every sin. Hence we say that whether the person through whose hands the body of the baptized person is visibly immersed in water is good or bad, the power of baptism does not thereby work more or less remission of sins and invisible sanctification in the soul of the person regenerated.

For this reason the Apostle Paul, writing to the Corinthians, who boasted of their respective baptizers, rebuked them: “It has been reported to me by those of Chloe that there are contentions among you. Now I mean this: each one of you says, ‘I indeed am of Paul; I am of Cephas; I am of Apollos; I am of Christ’” (I Cor. I). [Col. 0049A] For each believed himself holier according as the person by whom he had been baptized was holier. But this is not at all so. The one who visibly baptizes grants no holiness to the baptized; rather, the highest priest, the Lord Jesus Christ himself, grants there through the power of the Holy Spirit all the spiritual grace conferred in baptism.

He admits to that grace every kind of person who wishes to turn to him, however burdened with sins they may be; but, as you say, he repels only infants, who have the least sin. Most wicked people, why do you say this? Did he not call all without distinction when he said: “Come to me [Col. 0049B] all who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you”? (Matt. XI). Surely, when that most merciful guardian of human salvation said this, he saw every human being laboring under the penalty which original guilt had brought into the world. He saw as well that, apart from himself, no human being then alive or thereafter to live on earth had a soul not burdened by the weight of sins—so that not even an infant of one day was free from sin.

XIII. Understanding this, the Apostle Paul said: “God has shut up all things under sin, that he might have mercy on all” (Gal. III). “All things,” he says—that is, human beings of every kind and every age—he “shut up,” that is, permitted to be shut up under sin, so that he might have mercy upon all by granting all remission of sins. [Col. 0049C] If, therefore, you grant that all infants too are shut up under sin, you must grant that God’s mercy extends to them, and that they too, together with the rest, are invited into the wide bosom of his goodness by that call in which he says: “Come to me, all who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. XI).

“I will refresh you,” he says. This refreshment which he promised is granted to our spirit in this life, when through the Holy Spirit it is relieved of the burden of sins, and when, with grace added, it is helped to resist the tinder of sin and to persevere in good works. It is granted also after this life, when a person is allowed to rest from all labors. He promised all this refreshment to all [Col. 0049D] who come to him. On what ground do you think that he refuses it to infants coming to him? Do you suppose that the Lord says: “Let all come to me, however sinful they may be; only infants, who do not yet have enough sin, must remain outside”?

“They do not come,” you say, “but are carried by others; and therefore he does not grant them the grace he grants to other sinners.” But was not that paralytic of whom we spoke above carried by others? He did not come on his own, yet he did not receive less grace from Christ on that account. Likewise, those infants of whom Matthew speaks did not come on their own, nor did they themselves ask Jesus for blessing: “Then infants were offered to him, that he might lay hands on them and pray. But the disciples rebuked them. Jesus, however, said: ‘Allow the little children to come to [Col. 0050A] me, for of such is the kingdom of heaven.’ And when he had laid his hands upon them, he departed from there” (Matt. XIX).

XIV. Behold how gracious the Lord was at that time: he deigned to receive unformed little children who did not come of themselves or know how to ask for any grace, when others presented them to him and petitioned for them; and he deigned, with prayer, to lay his blessed hand upon them. How then has it happened that in these times he does not have the same graciousness toward little children, whom the Church is accustomed to offer to him, asking that he lay his hand upon them—that is, the power of his Holy Spirit—by which their sins may be forgiven and they may be filled with spiritual gifts? How has he changed that sweet voice in which he says, “Allow the little children to come to me, for the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these” [Col. 0050B] (ibid.), into a bitter voice, as though he said, “Take the little children away from me, for the kingdom of heaven does not belong to such as these”? For according to the tenor of your teaching, though not in plain words, he nevertheless says this by the very fact of the matter, if he allows all who die before the years of discretion to perish in the original sin with which they were born.

We know indeed that in the words, “The kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these” (ibid.), those of mature age are also included who resemble children in innocence and simplicity. Nevertheless, those who are children in innocence and simplicity and, moreover, in age, and who are offered by the Church to the Lord, like those little children upon whom he once laid his hand, cannot reasonably be excluded from the same declaration—unless perhaps, after they reach maturity, they lose through evil conduct the grace received [Col. 0050C] in baptism.

XV. Are you still without understanding, and do you not perceive from these words which have been spoken that what you affirm concerning the baptism of little children is false and heretical? Tell me: what reason have you for such language, when you have neither a firm argument nor any evident testimony from the Holy Scriptures to confirm this error? If you are ashamed to say it, I shall say it for you. The pride of your hearts and the envy of the devil have put this word in your mouths. For, in order that you may be regarded as somehow singular above others and seem to know many things not found in ordinary human knowledge, you [Col. 0050D] whisper such things into the ears of simple and easily deceived people, to whom stolen waters are sweeter.

Therefore I said that the pride of your hearts, which is the mother of vain glory, has caused you to sow this error, as it has many others. The envy of the devil likewise inspired this teaching in you. For when he saw innumerable thousands of souls being saved through baptism in their infant years, and none of his will being done in those whom God, after their regeneration, hastens to transfer to his kingdom so innocent and pure from every stain; when, I say, he saw this, he envied their innocence; he envied the swiftness of their blessedness; he envied the fact that God would perfect his praise even from the mouths of such infants and nursing children (Ps. VIII), because of his enemies, the apostate [Col. 0051A] spirits, who through their own wickedness had fallen from his court and diminished the number of those praising him.

He therefore sought some device by which he might prevent all the souls of infants from sharing the grace bestowed by God in baptism. He found instruments especially suited to this work: namely, the tongues of the Cathars, which are the quivers of his most wicked arrows, with which they shoot upright-hearted persons in darkness (Ps. X). Among them he placed this wicked saying: that the washing of baptism contributes nothing to the salvation of little children, and that they ought to be reserved until they reach the years of discretion, and only then baptized, when they are able to profess their faith with their own mouths.

The devil devised this so that he might introduce [Col. 0051B] this custom into the world: people would not bring their little children to baptism, and thus he would draw over to his own side all souls that depart this life in their infant years and keep them far from the kingdom of God. But, by God’s grace, this teaching has not yet been believed so far that this custom has been received among God’s people. Little children are still offered to the Lord for baptism; he lays his hand upon them and receives them. O Cathars! O Piphles! I do not know what praise I could more rightly give you than this: diabolical wickedness has been poured out upon your lips; therefore God has cursed you for ever.

## SERMON VIII. Against the Fifth Heresy concerning Water Baptism

I. Yet I am not unaware that you hold no less a heresy concerning those who are baptized at a more advanced age [Col. 0051C] than that which has now been discussed concerning the baptism of little children. For you say that a person ought indeed to be baptized upon reaching the years of discretion, but not in water—in fire; and that water baptism benefits no one. You derive your defence of this error from the words John uttered concerning the Lord and Savior: “He will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire” (Matt. III). Hence, as I have heard from someone who had experienced your secrets, you rebaptize those whom you receive into the fellowship of your Cathar community in the following manner.

II. When you gather together in some dark inner room, the first and most careful precaution is that no one outside may perhaps, through some window or door, perceive by sight or hearing what is being done within; for it is written, “Whoever does evil hates the light” (John III). Lamps are placed abundantly on every wall. You stand in an orderly circle with great reverence, because a holy thing is being done—yet one more pleasing to the devil than to God. In the middle is placed that wretched person who is to be baptized, or “made Cathar”; and the arch-Cathar stands beside him, holding in his hand a little book assigned to this rite. Placing it upon the candidate’s head, he pronounces blessings—though they ought rather to be called curses—while the others standing around pray; and they make him a son of Gehenna rather than of God’s kingdom. Thus that baptism is completed.

This baptism is said to be performed in fire [Col. 0052A] because of the fire of the lamps burning around them. Not so, you ungodly ones; not so ought you to follow the words of the holy Gospel in which it is said, “He will baptize you in Spirit and fire” (Matt. III). Attend more carefully to the words themselves: “He will baptize,” it says, “in fire,” not beside fire, as you do. Listen to me, and I shall teach you how to fulfill these same words more correctly. I shall speak to fools according to their folly, lest they seem wise to themselves.

III. Build a great fire in the middle of your synagogue. Take your novice, whom you wish to make a Cathar, and place him amid the fire. Then you, arch-Cathar, lay your hand upon his head, as you are accustomed, and so bless him. If then you do not burn your fingernails, and if he escapes unharmed, I shall certainly confess that your Cathar has been well baptized. But if he does not escape, does he not immediately go, so hot, to heaven? Did Cologne not recently baptize your arch-Cathar Arnold and his accomplices in this way, and Bonn likewise Theoderic and his companions, who, as you say, immediately flew up to heaven? Rather, to speak more truly, they descended into the depths of hell, from temporal fire to the burning of eternal fire—and deservedly so. For in order to empty water baptism, established by the Lord Savior himself, of its force, they taught that baptism must be administered in fire. Therefore, by God’s most just judgment, it came about that they were baptized in fire in such a way that they were irrevocably devoured by it.

O most foolish of men, whence comes this presumption by which you exalt yourselves against everything evangelical and Catholic? Truly that singular beast finds in you food most pleasing to itself, since you seek such singularity in every part of the Catholic faith that those miserable people whom you deceive may revere in you a certain singular holiness. I postpone to another place the explanation of how the saying concerning the Savior—“he will baptize in Spirit and fire”—is to be understood. I now address you concerning water baptism, against which you speak.

IV. Tell me: with what audacity do you contradict it, when the Lord himself instituted it and taught that it should be observed? For he himself, as each of the four holy evangelists testifies in his writings, came to the Jordan, where John was baptizing, and there was baptized by him [Col. 0052D]—not because he, who was free from every sin, needed the sanctification of baptism, but so that he might sanctify waters for us to wash away sins, and provide in himself an example of receiving the water baptism which he intended to establish in his Church for the remission of sins.

There too the Holy Spirit manifested himself above him in the form of a dove, as John bore witness concerning him: “For I saw the Spirit descending from heaven like a dove and remaining upon him” (John I). This too happened for our instruction and consolation, so that we might believe all the more certainly that the grace of the Holy Spirit comes to all who receive Christ’s baptism, so that they may become members of that head which is Christ.

We call our baptism Christ’s baptism because he himself principally baptizes in it, as we said above, granting remission of sins through the Holy Spirit [Col. 0053A]; because, as has been said, he initiated it for us by his example; and because in the words of his holy teaching he appointed that it be observed, determining in what material and according to what form it should be performed. He determined the material in which baptism was to be performed when he showed that a person must be regenerated in water, saying: “Unless one is born again of water and Spirit, he cannot see the kingdom of God” (John III).

Because every person has two substances, body and soul, he said that two things belong to our baptism: water and the Holy Spirit. From his words we most certainly believe that at the very hour when our visible body is washed in visible water, our invisible substance, the soul, is also washed in an invisible washing—namely, in the Holy Spirit—and cleansed from every sin. He also determined the form of words in which he wished us to be baptized when he said to his disciples: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. XXVII).

V. These, then, are the Lord’s words from which the Church of God has testimony concerning the baptism that has come down to us. It also has testimony from the sign that occurred during the Savior’s passion, when blood and water flowed together from his side after he had already died. For John, the most faithful witness of the Lord’s [Col. 0053C] passion, writes thus concerning his crucifiers:

“Then the soldiers came, and broke the legs of the first, and of the other who was crucified with him. But when they came to Jesus, and saw that he was already dead, they did not break his legs. But one of the soldiers opened his side with a spear, and immediately blood and water came out” (John XIX).

If this did not concern something greatly to be wondered at, if it were not the sacrament of a great matter, the evangelist would not have affirmed it so carefully when he added: “And he who saw it has borne testimony, and his testimony is true; and he knows that he speaks the truth, so that you too may believe” (ibid.).

It should therefore be observed thoughtfully that before death came upon the Lord on the cross, he shed pure blood without water from his wounds, but after he had yielded up his spirit, he brought forth from his side blood mingled with water [Col. 0053D]. In these things he gave us a fitting and rational signification: namely, that by his blood he redeemed not only those who for many ages before his death had faithfully awaited the grace of redemption and had departed this life without water baptism, which had not yet been instituted, but also those whom he wished to regenerate through baptismal water and who would devoutly worship his death until the end of the age.

That mixture of blood and water which came forth from Christ’s side was for us both the price of redemption and the sacred sign of our regeneration, by which we are born again through water and faith in the Lord’s blood. For neither water without faith in the passion [Col. 0054A] nor faith without water is sufficient for regeneration.

VI. Thus in two ways that blessed side of Christ built up the Church of God: by pouring out the price of redemption and by showing us the form of regeneration. Therefore the Apostle, writing to the Romans, said that the old Adam was “a figure of the Adam to come” (Rom. V), that is, of Christ. For just as Eve was formed from the side of the sleeping man, so from the side of this one, who slept in death, was built his bride, the Church.

If this is not the matter in which that ancient Adam was a figure of the one to come, tell us, O Cathar, in what matter was he so? I should like to hear your hidden wisdom on this point. I suppose that your answer will arrive at its usual conclusion: you will say, “I do not know.” If you do not know, sit down, be silent, do the work customary for you; make the shuttle run with its weft through the middle of the warp, and let those deal with the mysteries of God to whom the divine ordinance has entrusted the teaching of the Holy Scriptures [Col. 0054B].

VII. As has been said, the Lord Jesus Christ invited us to water baptism both living and dead. What other baptism, then, do you seek, O unbelieving Cathar? If you can be content with one God, let one baptism likewise suffice you, since it is written: “One Lord, one faith, one baptism” (Eph. IV). Let such a baptism suffice you as the holy apostles administered to those baptized by them. If you do not know with what baptism they baptized, read the writing of Luke the evangelist entitled *The Acts of the Apostles*, which is no less trustworthy than the Gospel written by him.

Read, I say, the place in which he writes thus concerning the conversion of Cornelius and his friends:

“While Peter was still speaking, the Holy Spirit fell upon all who heard the word. And the faithful of the circumcision who had come with Peter were astonished, because the grace of the Holy Spirit had been poured out also upon the Gentiles. For they heard them speaking in tongues and magnifying God. Then Peter answered: ‘Can anyone forbid water, that these should not be baptized who have received the Holy Spirit as we have?’ And he commanded them to be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ” (Acts X).

Hear, senseless man: the Prince of the Apostles had water, not fire, provided for baptizing those people. The same Scripture likewise reports concerning Philip, one of Christ’s disciples, that while he was preaching Jesus to the eunuch of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians, sitting with him in the chariot as the angel of the Lord had directed, they came to some water. The eunuch said, “Behold water; what prevents me from being baptized?” Philip said, “If you believe with all your heart, it is permitted.” He answered, “I believe that Jesus is the Son of God.” He ordered the chariot to stop, and both Philip and the eunuch went down into the water, and he baptized him. “When they had come up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord caught Philip away, and the eunuch saw him no more” (Acts VIII).

What do you think of this too? I suppose Philip also erred when he baptized a man in water. Certainly, if he had possessed your [Col. 0055A] wisdom, when the eunuch asked him to baptize him in water, he ought to have answered: “No, no. Rather, we must delay until we come to an inn and enter a dark chamber. We shall light many lamps, and there I shall baptize you amid fire, O son of error!” Would that you did not err worse than Philip! Would that an angel worse than that angel who led Philip to this work did not lead you!

VIII. “What then,” you ask, “does it mean that John the Baptist said that we are to be baptized in Spirit and fire?” I intend to speak of this in the following chapter, in such a way that it will be a stumbling-block to you and will appear more against you than for you. However this is to be understood, it is certain and evident from what has already been said that one single baptism was established by God for the cleansing and sanctification of the whole Church: namely, water baptism with invocation of the Holy Trinity. The Apostle expresses this briefly when, writing to the Ephesians, he says: “Husbands, love your wives, just as God loved the Church and gave himself for her, in order to sanctify her, cleansing her with the washing of water in the word of life” (Eph. V). At last give glory to God, O Cathar, and confess that you have been defeated in this matter also. Now let us pass from here to another contest.

## SERMON IX. Against the Sixth Heresy concerning the Souls of the Dead

I. You say that the care performed by the Church for the dead [Col. 0055C] is vain and superfluous. You assert that each soul of the departed, in the very hour of its departure from this life, is placed according to its merits either in eternal blessedness or handed over to eternal punishments. On this basis you maintain that prayers offered for them, masses celebrated, and alms given neither benefit the wicked nor are necessary for the good.

For you refuse to admit in your faith that, besides the eternal fire prepared for the devil and those to be damned with him for ever, there are any purgatorial punishments in which the souls of believers who have not in this life been completely cleansed from their sins through adequate satisfaction may be tried for a time, and then freed by the remedies just described [Col. 0055D] and transferred to rest. Let us now discuss this also according to the Scriptures of truth, of which you boast that you possess great knowledge.

II. First tell me: do you believe that the Lord Jesus Christ, in the passion of the cross, yielded up his spirit and was buried in body, but in soul descended into the lower regions and despoiled the princes of darkness of the souls of the elect who had departed this life either before the Law or under the Law of Moses—which could save no one—and had faithfully awaited the grace of their redemption, promised from former ages and accomplished through Christ?

If it is to be believed that those souls were freed by Christ from the punishments in which they were held, it is certain that you are preachers of falsehood when you say that there are no punishments for souls except the eternal torments of the damned, and that no one can be freed from punishments who is not taken immediately after death into eternal blessedness. But if you do not believe that Christ descended into hell after his passion, you reject both the Athanasian Creed, in which this is contained, and the Catholic Creed publicly chanted in the service of God, in which the Church likewise confesses it. Therefore testimonies from Scripture on this point must be brought against you from both the Old and the New Testament.

III. David in the psalm gives voice to the angels going before Christ into hell and commanding the rulers of Tartarus thus: “Lift up your gates, O rulers, [Col. 0056B] and be lifted up, eternal gates, and the King of glory shall enter” (Ps. XXIII). Again, the same David, rejoicing in Christ’s victory by which he led out to heaven with himself souls rescued from hell, says elsewhere to him: “You ascended on high; you took captivity captive” (Ps. LXVII).

Likewise, through the prophet Hosea, the very person of the Son of God says: “O death, I shall be your death; I shall be your bite, O hell!” (Hos. XIII). That bite of hell was fulfilled when the Savior, descending into hell, cut his elect away from it by his invincible power and justice, while leaving the reprobate there—just as one who bites an object holds part of it in his mouth and leaves another part outside.

And the apostle Paul, writing to the Colossians, says: “Despoiling principalities and powers, he displayed them openly, triumphing over them in himself” (Col. II). Let these now suffice for the affirmation of our faith on this point.

IV. You will now, I think, resort to this answer: “We do grant that before the Redeemer’s coming, souls ordained for life were delayed from the joys to come in places of punishment. But after the way of life was opened through Christ, this was bestowed upon all who are to be saved without distinction: after the course of this life has been completed, they are in no way further delayed after death from entering the kingdom.” This, you say, is made clear by what was once said by the Savior to the penitent thief on the cross: “Truly I say to you, today you shall be with me in paradise” (Luke XXIII).

You judge that this must be understood universally of every sinner [Col. 0056D]: if, at the end of his life, he repents from the heart in Christ himself, however criminal he may have been throughout his entire life, all his sins are forgiven him so perfectly that he immediately departs this life for the heavenly kingdoms without any examination whatever. To confirm this error you cite certain testimonies of Scripture which appear contrary to us. One is from Ezekiel: “The righteousness of the righteous shall not deliver him in whatever day he sins; and the wickedness of the wicked shall not harm him in whatever day he turns from his wickedness” (Ezek. XXXIII). Again, the following passage there is similar:

“If I say to the wicked, ‘You shall surely die,’ and he turns from his sin and does penance, and performs judgment and righteousness, restores the debtor’s pledge, returns what he has taken by robbery, and walks in the commandments [Col. 0057A] of life, doing nothing unjust, he shall surely live and shall not die; none of the sins that he committed shall be imputed to him” (ibid.).

You think Scripture has caught us in these nets, and you say mockingly: “See, Scripture is with us: it affirms that the wickedness of the sinner who turns from his wickedness shall not harm him. And again it drives home the same point, saying that none of the sins he committed shall be imputed to him. It is therefore false that, after repentance and contrition of heart, in which the sinner’s sins are forgiven, he should thereafter be handed over after death to any punishments to be tormented and purified. For if this is to happen to him after his conversion, then surely his wickedness will still harm him and his sins will be imputed to him.”

Such, O Piphles, is your objection [Col. 0057B] against us. Hear now what we answer to this before we say anything concerning your other objections.

V. The words of Holy Scripture must be considered with great discernment; otherwise in many places they can greatly confuse the reader and become vessels of death to him, because often several meanings can be understood in one and the same saying, one of which pertains to truth and another to falsehood. Thus we understand the prophet’s words now under discussion, lest they lead us into error as they have led you, with the following qualification: on whatever day the wicked person turns, his wickedness will thereafter not harm him in such a way that he is eternally condemned on its account, nor will his sins be imputed to his destruction.

For even if, after his conversion, a sinner suffers some distress in his soul from purgatorial fire because of sins for which he did not undergo sufficient correction in this life, that distress, being temporary and passing, ought to be considered virtually no harm in comparison with the eternal punishment which he would have suffered in hell had he not turned from his wickedness before death. I shall show you a similar Scripture that requires a similar qualification.

VI. Blessed Peter, in his Epistle, said to certain persons newly converted to faith in Christ: “And who is he that will harm you, if you are imitators of good?” (1 Pet. III.13). This question signified the same as if he had affirmatively said: “There is no one who can harm you, if you are imitators of good—that is, of goodness.” Yet the Lord Jesus Christ announces to his disciples, together with all other imitators of good: “They will deliver you up to tribulation and kill you, and you will be hated by all for my name’s sake” (Matt. XXIV). Likewise: “In the world you shall have tribulation; but in me, peace” (John XVI).

Here also, as above, you could reason against us in the following fashion: if imitators of good are handed over to tribulation, killed, hated by all, and suffer many similar things for righteousness’ sake, then surely many people harm them precisely because they are imitators of good. Peter therefore does not speak truly [Col. 0058A] when he promises that no one will harm them if they are imitators of good. Yet I suppose you are not so mad as openly to dare say that either Peter or Christ lied, or that they contradicted one another.

Know that we understand Peter’s words which we cited in this way: he did not promise God’s servants who imitate good that they would suffer no distress at all on the path of righteousness. For immediately after those words he added: “But even if you suffer anything for righteousness’ sake, you are blessed” (1 Pet. III). In those words, however, he meant that no one would harm them so as to be able to draw them away from eternal blessedness. For he was certain that neither death nor life, neither sword nor hunger, nor any adversity—indeed, no creature whatever—could separate true imitators of good from Christ’s love (Rom. VIII).

He did not consider temporal hardships to be harms, but rather helps toward attaining blessedness for God’s elect. Just as a person who tests gold in fire does not harm it, but rather helps it shine more brightly, so the persecutors of believers, while afflicting them, do not harm them as they suppose; rather, they cooperate toward their shining in eternal blessedness. In accordance with what has now been said, then, consider also that the wickedness of a wicked person turned away from wickedness will not harm him; and do not let that saying lead you astray from the way of truth.

VII. You also cite against us another passage from Ecclesiastes [Col. 0058C], of this kind: “If a tree falls toward the south or toward the north, in whatever place it falls, there it shall be” (Eccles. XI). You likewise bend this to support your error, saying that it should be understood thus: when a soul departs from the body, if it turns toward rest, it will remain there for ever; if toward punishment, it will likewise remain there for ever.

I say that if Ecclesiastes intended his words to signify only what you say, “in whatever place it falls” would have been introduced superfluously. To convey your opinion it would have sufficed for him to say: “If a tree falls toward the south or toward the north, there it shall be.” But now attend to my argument, and it will become clear what force belongs to the added words, “In whatever place it falls.”

Consider the preceding text, and you will find that he exhorts his hearer to give alms, saying: “Cast your bread upon the waters, for after many days you shall find it” (ibid.). Again: “Give portions to seven, and also to eight, for you do not know what evil may come upon the earth” (ibid.). In what follows he exhorts to perseverance in good work, saying: “In the morning sow your seed, and in the evening do not let your hand cease” (ibid.). With these he fittingly inserts: “If a tree falls toward the south or toward the north, in whatever place it falls, there it shall be” (ibid.); as if he said: While you live, diligently strive to increase your merits by almsgiving and good works. For after death, whether a person comes into the condition belonging to those [Col. 0059A] who are to be saved—which is to fall toward the south—or comes into the condition belonging to the damned—which is to fall toward the north—in whatever place he falls, that is, in whatever degree of merits, good or evil, he then is when he falls, there he shall remain: he will neither rise from it by meriting better things nor sink from it by meriting worse. Henceforth neither the good nor the reprobate will be given an opportunity to merit good or evil; thereafter it will be a time for receiving good or evil recompense.

VIII. A tree falls toward the south in two ways: either when, immediately after death, a righteous man is placed in blessedness—which belongs only to the most perfect, who will judge the world with God—or when he enters that way through which some of those to be saved must pass, those who must proceed through purgatorial punishments to refreshment: namely, those who will be judged unto life. Likewise, the wicked fall toward the north in two ways: either when, immediately after death, they are carried off to the utmost punishments, like those of whom it is said that they have been judged, namely unbelievers and the supremely wicked; or when they are handed over to those punishments [Note: [Col. 0059D] Understand this conveniently as referring to the punishments and miseries of this life, into which, by divine justice, many wicked persons fall who are soon to be consigned to eternal punishments. They do not emerge from these punishments, but use them as a kind of prelude [Col. 0060D] to Gehenna until the day of death or of the last judgment. Compare also below, no. 15.] in which they are to be kept until the Last Judgment, like those reprobate who are to be judged unto death.

This is a frequent mode of speech in Holy Scripture: the south is called heavenly blessedness because of the divine brightness that is in it; the north, the dwelling-place of the reprobate, dark and covered by the gloom of death.

IX. You also object to us another passage, similar to that now discussed, as though spoken in the person of the Lord [Col. 0059C]: “Where I find you, there I shall judge you” (Ezek. XXXIII). You judge this too to have been said as though he had said: “At your end, when I demand your soul from you, in whatever manner of life I find you, in that manner I shall immediately judge you, either to perpetual rest or to eternal damnation.”

But we distinguish these matters differently. These words briefly sum up what he says more fully through Ezekiel: “When the righteous turns away from his righteousness and commits iniquity, he shall die in the iniquity that he has done; and when the wicked turns away from the wickedness that he has done and performs judgment and righteousness, he shall give life to his own soul: he shall surely live and shall not die” (ibid.)—that is understood to mean, not die the eternal death.

The brief meaning of this entire chapter is: “Where I find you, there I shall judge you”—or “in whatever condition I find you” (which is the same) [Note: [Col. 0060D] These words appear redundant.]—“in that condition I shall judge you.” That is to say: If I find you turned away from injustice and converted to righteousness, you need not despair because of past evils, because there—that is, in the state of your conversion—I shall judge you, that is, distinguish you from those who are to be damned. But if I find you turned away from righteousness, you must not put confidence in past righteousness, because there—that is, in that condition—I shall judge you, that is, distinguish you from those who are to be saved.

God distinguishes the good from the evil when he either brings the good immediately after death into blessedness, or places them in that purification in which he prepares them for future glory [Col. 0060A].

X. Moreover, we are answering you beyond what is necessary regarding the testimonies you cite from the Old Scripture to confirm your error concerning the souls of the dead. For if you admit what you necessarily must admit—namely, that the souls of the ancients who lived before the time of grace were delayed from entering the kingdom of heaven until the time of redemption—you contradict yourselves when you suppose that the writings of the ancient Fathers attest that every soul, when it departs from the body, immediately passes either to eternal blessedness or to eternal damnation. For the testimonies you take from them concern not only people of these times, but also people under the ancient Law, while entry into the kingdom of heaven was still closed.

XI.
