Yet I am not unaware that you also confirm your error from the New Testament, objecting to us that Gospel saying spoken by the Savior: “Truly I say to you: whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life, and shall not come into judgment, but will pass from death to life” (John V). From these words you say that salvation is promised to everyone believing in God: immediately after bodily death each person passes into eternal life, so that after death there comes no other judgment than what he experiences in death itself. You insist that the Lord undoubtedly meant by this statement [Col. 0060C] that there are no punishments in which the souls of believers undergo God’s judgment after death.

You ought rightly to be compared to unclean animals which neither chew the cud nor divide the hoof: you turn God’s teaching over in your mouths, but have in it no discernment of right understanding. Therefore words of life are not life to you but death. Your teachers were blind, became guides of the blind, and caused you to fall with them into the pit of falsehood and destruction. Hear, therefore, rebels and unbelievers, how you may more rightly consider the Lord’s words which you strive to pervert. Unless they are explained otherwise than you understand them, they contradict other words of Holy Scripture, which [Col. 0060D] we shall bring forward in their proper place.

XII. “Amen, I say to you,” he says, “that whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me,” namely God the Father—for to hear the word of God without believing is useless—“has eternal life.” The saints who reign with God have eternal life, so that they already enjoy his blessedness. The faithful also, while placed in this world, have eternal life: not as a possession which they already enjoy according to their desire, but as something most certainly prepared and kept for them by God, to be given in its proper time; “and shall not come into judgment” [Col. 0061A], “but shall pass from death to life.” The term *judgment* is known to bear such meanings in Holy Scripture. It signifies chastisement, by which human beings are scourged by the Lord; it signifies the final separation of good and evil, which takes place on the last day; and it also signifies condemnation, which belongs especially to the reprobate.

That it signifies affliction may be understood from what the Apostle says: “When we are judged, we are corrected by the Lord,” that is, when we are scourged, we are corrected by the Lord, “so that we may not be condemned with this world” (1 Cor. 11). What these scourges are, he specifies where he says: “Therefore among you many are weak and infirm, and many sleep” (ibid.). But if you say that the term *judgment* should be taken in this sense when it is said that whoever believes “shall not come into judgment,” the statement cannot stand; for believers too are often scourged by the Lord, just as unbelievers are: “For God scourges every son whom he receives” (Heb. 12).

But if you say that it should be understood to mean that believers will not, after death, undergo any other chastisement besides that which they suffer in this life, you do violence to the letter, which does not say this, but simply says that whoever believes “shall not come into judgment.” The term *judgment* signifies the final separation of good and evil where the Savior says of himself: “And he gave him authority to execute judgment, because he is the Son of Man” (John 5). Nor can it be taken in that sense here, because both good and evil will come to judgment, according to that saying: “We must all [Col. 0061C] be made manifest before the tribunal of God, so that each may receive the things proper to the body, according to what he has done in the body, whether good or evil” (2 Cor. 5).

But the term *judgment* signifies condemnation, as immediately follows when it is said: “Those who have done evil, unto the resurrection of judgment” (John 5). So too in the Apostle: “Whoever eats the body of the Lord unworthily eats and drinks judgment to himself, not discerning the body of the Lord” (1 Cor. 11). In this sense, beyond doubt, *judgment* must be understood in the present saying, where the Lord says: “Whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life, and shall not come into judgment” (John 5), that is, into condemnation. It follows: “But shall pass from death to life” (ibid.), namely from that death which had been a cause of condemnation for him, and through which he would have passed into perdition [Col. 0061D] if he had remained in it.

What was that death? Without doubt, the death of the soul, produced in it by unbelief. Such was the death of those of whom Peter says in his Epistle: “For this reason the Gospel was preached also to the dead” (1 Pet. 4). So likewise those to whom Paul wrote, saying: “You were buried with Christ in baptism, in whom you also rose through faith in the working of God, who raised him from the dead. And when you were dead in sins, he made you alive together with him, forgiving you all your sins” (Rom. 6).

XIII. It is therefore plain that through faith one passes to life, so as not to come into judgment, that is, condemnation. This happens in two ways. In one way, each person passes through faith from death to the life of the soul [Col. 0062A], when one who had been an unbeliever is justified in the soul through faith. To this applies the saying: “The just person lives by faith” (Rom. 1). God’s elect attain this life during the time of their mortality.

In another way, the elect must pass through faith to life when, by the merit of faith and of those virtues which have their origin in faith, eternal life is to be granted to them alike in body and soul. This will be on the day of the final resurrection, when they shall be freed from every power of death and transferred to blessed immortality. The Lord showed that these two modes of passing from death to life would occur in his elect immediately after the words now under discussion. For he declared the first mode of passing to life when he said: “Amen, I say to you, the hour is coming, and now is, when the dead shall hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear shall live” (John 5). He declared the second mode of passing to life when he later added: “Do not marvel at this, for all who are in the tombs shall hear his voice, and those who have done good shall come forth unto the resurrection of life; but those who have done evil, unto the resurrection of judgment” (ibid.).

Now, if there is anything of uncorrupted understanding in you, you perceive that I have led you quite directly to the truth. But if you are without understanding, the lyre sings in vain to asses.

XIV. I shall bring forward one further objection of yours, with which you are accustomed to oppose us. It is written: “Each shall receive his own reward according to his labor” (Rev. 2). Again: “Each shall bear his own burden” (Gal. 5). Again: “I shall judge each according to his ways, says the Lord” (Ezek. 18): that is, I shall repay each according to his good or evil works. From these texts, therefore, you take occasion to say that it cannot happen that the souls of the dead should be helped by the good works of the living, so as to be freed from their punishments and transferred to rest. For you say that, if God has mercy on them because of the good works which others have done for them, then they are repaid not according to their own works but according to the works of others; and they do not bear their own burden—that is, the punishment which they themselves deserved by their sins—if they are released from their burdens on account of others’ labors. To this we reply as follows.

[Col. 0062D] XV. If faithful persons pray, fast, give alms, celebrate masses, or have them celebrated for their dead, they perform good works; and they themselves shall in due time receive a reward for these things according to their labor. But those for whom they do these things, if in their lifetime they were guilty of mortal sins and neither repented of them nor took care to make confession, cannot be helped toward salvation by these good works.

But if they fell into certain sins during their lifetime, repented of them before their end, departed this world in the Catholic faith, and, being overtaken by death, could not complete all the satisfaction which they owed for their sins, we say that they shall bear their own burden—that is, they shall undergo punishment for their sins as long as God permits [Col. 0063A]. Yet, for their repentance at the end, for the Catholic faith in which they remained until death, and for the other good things which they did in this life, they shall receive this reward: that eternal life shall be given to them, in soul and body, on the last day.

Very many of these shall also receive this as a reward: that before the last day they are freed from their punishments through the aforementioned good works of living believers—some sooner, others later, according as their merits were greater or lesser in this world. Thus we may truly say both of these things concerning them: that they shall bear their own burden, because they endure punishment for their sins for the time appointed to them by God; and that they are repaid according to their own good works [Col. 0063B], by which they have merited that assistance may be given them by the Church of God.

God could indeed liberate souls from their punishments without the intervention of any human beings. But he wills them to be liberated in this order: that the living may serve him on their behalf, so that by this very fact the living may be more strongly reminded to reverence God and avoid offending him, and so that their merits may likewise be increased through the works of mercy which they do out of love for their neighbors. Therefore the Scriptures mentioned above are in no respect contrary to us; rather, they support us. If those who put the divine words so raw into your mouths, O foolish wise men, had cooked them with careful reflection, they would have fed you more wholesomely and would not have vainly puffed up your hearts with such windy pride.

[Col. 0063C] XVI. I judge that your objections, in which you placed most trust, have been sufficiently answered; they have been burst like swollen bladders, and no truth has been found in them. Let us now examine the Scriptures which are with us on the side of truth, in whose defense we have girded ourselves. And, to begin with Paul, let us first consider the words which he wrote to the Corinthians:

“If anyone builds upon this foundation gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, stubble, each person’s work shall be made manifest; for the day of the Lord shall reveal it, and fire shall test what kind of work each person’s is. If anyone’s work shall be burned, he shall suffer loss; but he himself shall be saved, yet so as through fire” (1 Cor. 3).

It is not for our people, to whom the writings of the holy Fathers are known, but because of your error, that I must now explain the sense of this discourse. The foundation of the spiritual building which we construct inwardly in the soul is faith in Christ. Whoever truly possesses it bears Christ in the mind; he is the beginning and completion of every good in his elect, and is therefore himself called the foundation. Faith is called our foundation because we begin the good life from faith. For if right faith is not in us, nothing whatever that we do, whether good or evil, can be pleasing to God. But once faith begins to be in us, we begin to please God; and then we may safely perform good works, because henceforth they shall receive their reward.

We build precious stones upon the foundation [Col. 0064A] when, in addition to right faith, we are adorned with good dispositions: namely, kindness, patience, temperance, justice, mercy, and other such dispositions, which we call virtues of the soul. Whenever we do works proceeding from such virtues, we build precious stones upon the foundation. Such things are fittingly compared to precious stones because, as precious stones commonly adorn gold and other things beautiful in themselves, so virtues and good works confer great beauty upon the rational soul, which is formed according to God and is more precious than all gold. This beauty cannot be dissolved in the soul even if it is sent into purgatorial fire for certain lighter faults, just as precious stones cannot melt if cast into fire.

Those also build silver upon the foundation who make it their pursuit to understand the divine Scriptures and instruct others with words of wisdom. Sacred Scripture is commonly compared to silver, which has a sweet and piercing sound, as in the passage: “The words of the Lord are pure words, silver tried by fire” (Ps. 11). For what sounds sweeter than Holy Scripture, in which the joys of eternal life are promised? What is sharper than the divine word, which is more penetrating than every two-edged sword and reaches even to the dividing of soul and spirit?

Likewise, the person places gold in his building who gives his heart over to such perfect contemplation that he can meditate continually upon God, draw from hidden things the wisdom by which God’s sweetness is tasted [Col. 0064C], pray to him without ceasing, and embrace him with the unbroken ardor of charity. Such contemplation is rightly compared to gold, because it excels all virtues as gold is more precious than other metals; and it produces works of the highest perfection, which themselves are like gold in the building of the soul when compared with other good works. For it causes a person, for God’s sake, to abstain even from things whose use is lawful; to despise the world and all its glory; to preserve unstained chastity; to lay down one’s soul for God and for the brethren; and to do other such things.

XVII. But those heap wood, hay, and stubble upon their foundation who, although they have right faith, occupy their hearts too greatly with cares and thoughts [Col. 0064D] pertaining to this world, and have greater love than is fitting for things not forbidden them, such as wives, sons and daughters, secular friends, houses and possessions, dignities, and the like. These, I say, are said to build wood, hay, and stubble upon the foundation in their souls, because they occupy their minds with things combustible like wood, hay, and stubble. For the things mentioned make the soul dark and heavy, so that it cannot freely contemplate the things of God or love him as it ought.

But all this darkness and heaviness must be burned away in purgatorial fire, so that the foundation itself suffers no destruction, provided that God is held above all things, so that, if necessary, these things are abandoned rather than God denied [Col. 0065A]. They also heap combustible things in their souls who do not guard themselves against lighter faults, such as idle speech, laughter and jesting, anger, vain merriment, excess in food and drink that is not too frequent, and similar daily sins, which are not called capital sins. These, I say, accumulate wood, hay, and stubble upon their foundation, and these too must be purified by fire.

I have spoken of lighter sins; for if mortal sins are committed, it cannot be said that they are in any way placed upon the foundation. They destroy the foundation and faith itself, because they kill it; and on account of them faith is called dead. But if a person repents of these sins and does not make satisfaction to God for them in this life, they shall be reckoned like the things [Col. 0065B] compared to wood, hay, and stubble, and shall be destroyed by fire on the day of the Lord, just as the lighter sins mentioned above.

XVIII. The “day of man” is called this period in which God permits each person to do according to his own will what he chooses, and in which he can earn good or evil according to his works. But the “day of the Lord” is that time which comes upon each person when his soul is separated from the body and can no longer proceed according to its own will, but is led according to God’s judgment either to rest or to punishment, to receive the recompense it has earned. Then things previously hidden in that person, good or evil alike, are made manifest. Hence it is said: “Each person’s work shall be made manifest; for the day of the Lord shall reveal it [Col. 0065C], and fire shall test what kind of work each person’s is” (1 Cor. 3).

The fire is that punitive condition which God has ordained so that in it the souls of the elect may be afflicted and purified from the stains which they contracted in this life. It can cause no loss at all to the building of those who built gold, silver, and precious stones upon the foundation, even if they happen to pass through its midst. Therefore he says of them: “If anyone’s work which he built upon it remains, he shall receive a reward” (ibid.), namely the reward which he has earned by his superstructure.

But of those who built wood, hay, and stubble upon it, he says: “If anyone’s work shall be burned, he shall suffer loss” (1 Cor. 3): namely, so that he will receive no reward for his building, but rather bitter affliction. “But he himself shall be saved, yet so as through fire,” that is, only through the testing of fire. By the different names wood, hay, and stubble he designated those things which must be burned in each person, because of their diversity: accordingly, some will endure the fire longer than others, as wood burns longer than hay, and hay longer than stubble.

This fire is the same thing that the Psalmist calls wrath when he says: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury, nor correct me in your wrath” (Ps. 6), or “amend me,” as another translation has it. In fury, those will be rebuked and not amended to whom it shall be said: “Depart, you cursed, into eternal fire” (Matt. 25). But in wrath, those will be corrected and amended who shall be saved through fire. Fearing both, he prays, saying: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury,” as though saying: May I not be among those to whom you will say, “Depart, you cursed, into eternal fire”; “nor amend me in your wrath” [Col. 0066A], but burn and cut me in this life, and make me such that corrective fire may not be necessary for me.

XIX. This is the fire, O Cathars, which John the Baptist signified when he preached concerning the Lord Savior, saying: “He shall baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire” (Matt. 3). For in this life he baptizes in the Holy Spirit: externally, indeed, through visible ministers he baptizes us in water in baptism; inwardly, however, by his own operation he baptizes our souls in the Holy Spirit, granting us remission of all sins. But he baptizes us in fire when, after this life, he purifies our souls in purgatorial punishments from the stains of sins which they contracted in the dwelling-place of the corruptible body; for he wills to receive into that utterly pure city of his nothing that has not been cleansed of every defilement.

XX. We may also take testimony from the Lord’s words in confirmation of the position now under discussion. We read in the Gospel that, among other things, he said this to the Pharisees who blasphemed his works: “Whoever speaks a word against the Holy Spirit shall not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come” (Matt. 12). What that sin is by which a person is said to sin against the Holy Spirit, I need not determine here, because it does not concern the present matter. But what does concern the present matter [Col. 0066C] is that this indicates some sin which shall not be forgiven either in this age or in the age to come.

If your assertion is true, no sin can be forgiven anyone in the age to come. For, as you say, every soul, as soon as it departs from the present world, is either established in eternal blessedness, to which no one comes bearing the stain of sin and where no one contracts a stain of sin; or it is assigned to eternal punishments, where there is no remission and no exercise of mercy. Therefore the Savior made this distinction superfluously when he said that the sin against the Holy Spirit shall be forgiven neither in this age nor in the age to come. For if no sin were forgiven in the age to come [Col. 0066D], he would not have said so particularly of that sin that it would be forgiven neither in this age nor in the age to come; it would have sufficed simply to say that it would not be forgiven.

But just as it is wicked to say that any falsehood is found in the Savior’s words, so beyond doubt it is wicked to say that there is in them anything superfluous or useless. For it is written of him in the Psalm: “And his leaf shall not fall, and all things whatsoever he does shall prosper” (Ps. 1). His leaf would fall if anything in his words were superfluous, and whatever he did would not prosper if he had said anything without usefulness. Therefore it must necessarily be conceded that in the age to come there is some remission of sins. Since we cannot say that it is granted either to those who are eternally condemned [Col. 0067A] or to those who are saved, we must say that sins are forgiven in the other age to certain persons who are placed neither in eternal condemnation nor in eternal blessedness. There are no persons intermediate between eternal blessedness and eternal condemnation except those of whom we say that they are in purgatorial punishments.

XXI. See now in what way we say sins are forgiven them. God forgives a sinful person’s sins in two ways in this life: by softening the hardness of the heart through inward grace unto conversion, and by freeing the convert, turned to himself, from the debt of Gehenna’s punishment which was due for sins. But when he forgives sins in these ways in this life to persons who depart this life without having made full satisfaction to God for their sins [Col. 0067B], he permits them to be punished for a time in certain punishments which he has established so that his elect may be purified in them. When he remits those punishments to them and leads them into refreshment, he is said then to forgive them their sins, because the punishments of sins are also called “sins,” according to the Apostle’s saying: “Christ bore our sins in his body upon the wood” (1 Pet. 2). But he bore our sins in no other way than by enduring the punishments due to us for our guilt.

We may bring forward one more quite evident testimony in confirmation of our position, from the history of the Maccabees, which possesses such authority in the Church that it is publicly read in the divine service. It is written in the second book of this history that, while Judas Maccabaeus was fighting against Gorgias, governor of Idumaea, a few Jews happened to fall. But after Gorgias had been put to flight through God’s help, Judas gathered his army and came to the city of Odolla. When the seventh day arrived, they observed the Sabbath in that place according to custom; and on the following day Judas came with his men to take up and bury the bodies of the fallen. But beneath the tunics of the slain they found votive offerings of idols from Jamnia, forbidden to the Jews by the Law. Thus it was made manifest to all that they had fallen for this reason; and so, turning to prayers, they asked God that the offense might be consigned to oblivion. After this Scripture continues as follows [Col. 0067D]:

“After a collection had been made, Judas sent twelve thousand drachmas of silver to Jerusalem, to be offered for the sins of the dead, thinking justly and religiously concerning the resurrection” (2 Macc. 12), and so forth.

And at the end it concludes thus: “It is therefore a holy and healthful thought to pray for the dead, that they may be released from sins” (ibid.).

XXII. What do you now say to these things, O Piphles? As you hear, the Gospel Scripture is for us; and who is against us? Apostolic Scripture stands in defense of our side; and who is there to condemn us? The example of Maccabaeus, a warrior of the Lord, is in our battle line; and who will fight against us? I have still a few things to discuss with you concerning the present question.

[Col. 0068A] XXIII. If a person is overtaken by more serious sins, turns away from his iniquity, and repents from the heart for the evils he has committed, does he need, in addition to that inward repentance of heart, to render God some outward satisfaction for his sins—namely by giving alms, fasting, and afflicting his body for God’s sake in other ways? If things are as I have learned from certain persons acquainted with your teachings, you say that after a person has repented from the heart for sins and ceased from iniquity, he has no need of that outward satisfaction of which I spoke, because every sin has already been forgiven him in repentance of heart.

But that this is not so is demonstrated by clear testimonies of Holy Scripture. For the Lord says through the prophet Joel: “Turn to me with all your heart, in fasting and weeping and mourning; and rend your hearts, not your garments” (Joel 2). Behold: besides inward conversion of heart, he plainly demands outward satisfaction as well. John the Baptist likewise, as we read in the Gospel, exhorted to both when he said: “Do penance” (Matt. 4). And a little later he adds: “Therefore produce fruits worthy of repentance” (Luke 3). The fruits of repentance are good works by which God is appeased for sins, and various bodily chastisements.

What effect these have in appeasing God is clear from the history recounting the repentance of the Ninevites, and from the Scripture which says how Ahab, king of Israel, when rebuked by Elijah for the killing of Naboth [Col. 0068C], tore his garment, covered his flesh with sackcloth, fasted, slept in sackcloth, and walked with bowed head. And the word of the Lord came to Elijah, saying: “Have you not seen Ahab humbled before me? Since therefore he has humbled himself for my sake, I shall not bring evil in his days, but in the days of his son I shall bring evil upon his house” (3 Kings 21). From these things it is plain that God requires not only inward compunction of heart but also outward satisfaction appropriate to sins; when it is rendered, he is appeased, but when neglected, he is moved to vengeance.

XXIV. Therefore, if you concede that this is so, what will you say concerning one who has grown old in every kind of crime [Col. 0068D], and is pierced with compunction and converted to righteousness only at the very point of death? Is he not indebted to God for some satisfaction for his sins? Certainly he is indebted; but because, owing to the shortness of time, he cannot fulfill it, satisfaction together with sins is forgiven him, and immediately after death he is snatched up to eternal blessedness. Is this what you say? This doctrine is fine indeed, and greatly contributes to the correction of many people.

What sort of correction? If this teaching were publicly preached before vain and wicked people, each would defer conversion as long as possible, saying to himself: “I shall do every desire of my heart, and at the end of my life I shall be converted and repent; then, without any labor at all, I shall immediately pass to the kingdom of heaven.” Do you not see how your doctrine [Col. 0069A], if believed and accepted, would become an occasion for every vanity and every wickedness? Most foolish of people! What reason or usefulness is there in this doctrine which you maintain? None whatever, except that you may appear uniquely wise above other people if you say something distinctive which is not held by others.

But in our teaching concerning the souls of the dead there is unquestionably great benefit, because many works of mercy are daily performed for the poor which would in no way be done if people did not believe that through such works they could help the souls of those dear to them.

XXV. It is therefore manifest that that purgatorial fire of which we have spoken is altogether necessary. In it, the souls of those who in this life did not render full satisfaction to God for their sins are tested until they become fit to be admitted into that heavenly city of God, which receives nothing that is not perfect and fully tested [Col. 0069B]. For what is more absurd than to believe that a soul freshly drawn from the sewer of foulness, still in some fashion reeking with the memory of such things, should so suddenly burst into that utterly clear light and be mingled with assemblies of most pure spirits—so that on one and the same day it might be in the morning in the foulest mire of sins and in the evening in the most pure heaven of angels?

Should it not at least have been covered with the shame of seven days because of many criminal excesses, when Miriam, Moses’ sister, was struck by the Lord with the worst leprosy merely for a contentious word and set apart from the camp of the children of Israel for seven days [Col. 0069C]? All the vessels of the sanctuary, through which the corruptible sacrifice in the wilderness was to be administered, were commanded to be made from the purest gold. How much more fitting is it that the vessels into which the incorruptible glory of the most pure divinity will deign to pour itself should be proved by every kind of testing before they are brought into the Holy of Holies?

XXVI. Perhaps you object to me the thief, who was in paradise with the Lord Jesus on the same day on which he confessed. To this we reply that this was specially granted to him above other penitents because of the marvelous power of his faith: he was able to believe to be God the man whom he saw as having neither form nor beauty, and as the very last of men, delivered to an ignominious death [Col. 0069D], saying: “Lord, remember me when you come into your kingdom” (Luke 23). This faith, I judge, was accounted of greater merit before the divine judgment than the severe penance of many years. Give glory to God now, and come over to the truth by which you have been overcome; or, if you do not come over, flee, you opposing party, together with your teacher, who is a liar from the beginning and the father of lies.

## SERMON X. Against the Seventh Heresy: Concerning the Priesthood

I. Let us proceed to examine also that claim of yours that the order of priesthood has failed among us, and that true priests are found nowhere except among you. I speak now for ourselves, who in matters pertaining to the Christian religion look to the Roman Church. We received the priestly order from the Roman Church; the Roman Church received it from the apostle Peter; Peter from Christ; and Christ from God the Father, who anointed him with “the oil of gladness” (Ps. 44), that is, with the Holy Spirit, above his companions, and swore, saying to him: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. 109).

The Lord Jesus Christ was a true priest, who publicly offered his most holy body and blood to God the Father upon the altar of the cross, in order to establish peace and reconciliation between himself and the human race which had been lost. If a priest (*sacerdos*) is so called from the giving of a sacred thing, this name never belonged more fittingly to anyone than to him who gave the most sacred sacred thing—that is, himself—so that we might be saved through him [Col. 0070B].

He also invisibly gave his body and blood when, before his disciples, he blessed bread and wine at supper with a heavenly blessing and by his marvelous power caused them, under the appearance of that same bread and wine, to receive from his hands his body and blood. Likewise, as he promised, he is with his Church “until the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28), and daily, invisibly, through the hands of the Church, offers his body and blood under the appearance of bread and wine to God the Father for the salvation of the world. For this reason he was called a priest according to the order of Melchizedek, who was king of Salem and priest of the Most High God, and who made an offering to God from bread and wine.

II. The Lord Jesus Christ made his disciples true priests in that he anointed them with the Holy Spirit and gave them authority to preach the divine word and to baptize, when he said: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you” (ibid.) [Col. 0070C]. He gave them authority to bind and loose when he said: “Receive the Holy Spirit. Whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them; and whose sins you retain, they are retained” (John 20). He gave them authority to consecrate his body and blood under the appearance of bread and wine when he said to them: “This is my body, which shall be given for you. Do this in remembrance of me” (Luke 22). In short, they received from him every authority pertaining to the priestly office and episcopal dignity.

Each of them, moreover, left the same authority to successors in those lands and churches which the Lord had entrusted to them for conversion and governance. And, to say nothing now of the others, blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, ordained presbyters and bishops in the city of Rome and gave them every authority pertaining to their offices, just as he himself had received it from the Lord Jesus Christ. And I think you cannot deny that he was able to do this.

When he knew that the end of his life was at hand, he appointed his disciple, blessed Clement, to preside over the Church in his place, and handed over to him the authority which he himself possessed in the primacy of the apostolate. By the same consecration through which Clement was ordained presbyter and bishop by blessed Peter [Col. 0071A], other bishops and presbyters were ordained at Rome by Clement; by it Clement’s successor was ordained, and he in turn ordained other bishops and presbyters by it. Thus, from successors to successors, the priestly office and episcopal dignity descended in due order down to him who at the present day is the supreme pontiff of the Church.

III. If you now say that the priestly order has failed in the Roman Church, you must show us under which pope this failure occurred, and for what reason it occurred. But if you do not know how to say this, you may be charged with great folly and rashness, because you have dared to defame so great a matter which you have not ascertained to be true, but merely [Col. 0071B] hold as an opinion. Perhaps you say: “We do not know under which pope this failure occurred, but we know that for many ages all who were called Roman pontiffs and cardinals have always been avaricious and proud, and, for many reasons, unworthy of Christ’s priesthood; and from this we are certain that true priesthood is not among them.” Granted that they are unworthy: is it impossible for someone to be unworthy of the priesthood and yet truly possess the order of priesthood? It is by no means impossible.

For we know that the priesthood which existed under the old Law was instituted by God. Aaron, Eleazar, and Phinehas, the first priests of God, holy men, had many successors in the priesthood who were not pleasing to God and were unworthy of priestly [Col. 0071C] dignity; yet God tolerated them in their offices and permitted the priestly blessing in them to remain valid. The priests of the Jews at the Savior’s coming were hypocrites, avaricious, proud, and sellers and buyers of spiritual things, as is clear from the Lord’s words, by which he often reproved them. Yet he himself said of them to the people: “The scribes and Pharisees have sat on Moses’ seat; therefore do what they say, but do not do what they do” (Matt. XXIII). Behold: although he knew their vices inwardly, he nevertheless did not draw the people away from them, but wished the honor due to priests and spiritual teachers to be shown to them.

Likewise, when ten lepers came to him wishing to be cleansed by him, [Col. 0071D] he said to them: “Go, show yourselves to the priests” (Luke XVII). And to one, after he had been cleansed of leprosy, he said: “Go, show yourself to the priest, and offer the gift which Moses commanded, as a testimony to them” (Matt. VIII). See how he honored those whom he knew to be wicked. What, I ask, did he honor in them? Not their persons, but their office, which was holy and instituted by God. Certainly, if that office had failed in them because they were unworthy of it, he would not have called them priests, nor commanded that the gift be offered to them which by divine law was to be offered to God’s priests.

IV. It is written of Caiaphas, the high priest of the Jews, who was one of Christ’s chief crucifiers, that when the chief priests and Pharisees had assembled a council against Jesus to determine how they might destroy him, [Col. 0072A] he said: “It is expedient for you that one man should die for the people, lest the whole nation perish” (John XI). The Evangelist then adds: “But he did not say this of himself; rather, being high priest that year, he prophesied that Jesus would die for the nation, and not for the nation only, but that he might gather into one the children of God who were scattered abroad” (ibid.).

From this statement of the Evangelist it is understood that Caiaphas, although not holy, nevertheless possessed, because of the holiness of his high-priestly office, some particular grace from God by which he prophesied the redemption that was to come through Christ. Yet he was unworthy of the dignity of that office, not only because of the wickedness by which he opposed the Savior, but also because of avarice, pride, and the other vices in which [Col. 0072B] all the priests of that time were entangled, as is clear from the words of John the Baptist, who often rebuked them.

For, as the histories relate, they were so avaricious and eager for honor that every year they changed the high priests, and each hastened to obtain the dignity of the high priesthood before another through money given to the Gentiles who ruled over them at that time, although according to the Law each high priest ought to have remained in office until the end of his life. This changing of high priests may also be understood from the Evangelist’s statement concerning Caiaphas, that he was high priest “in that year” (John XVIII); for Annas, his father-in-law, had been high priest the preceding year, as the histories report. These things have been said because you claim that the priestly [Col. 0072C] office cannot remain valid among those who are unworthy of the priesthood.

V. Who was more criminal, who more unworthy to administer the mysteries of God, than Judas Iscariot, who was both a thief from the Lord’s treasury, harbored the Savior’s death in his mind for a long time, and killed him in intention? Yet the Lord, like the other apostles, sent him forth to administer his spiritual grace by preaching, baptizing, and carrying out all that belonged to the apostolic office; and he permitted the things done by Judas to remain valid, just as those done by the other apostles in their ministries.

We read of many who were baptized by John the Baptist, a holy and perfect man, that they were rebaptized by [Col. 0072D] the apostles; but of those baptized by Judas we do not read that any were rebaptized. Yet it would have been necessary for them to be rebaptized if that sacrament could not have had its efficacy under his hands because he himself was unworthy to administer baptism. The Lord permitted this for our instruction: that one unworthy to be numbered among God’s ministers should nevertheless distribute his grace to people, just as the other apostles did, so that, when we see unworthy priests handling and distributing spiritual things, we should not distrust God’s grace because of their wickedness, nor suppose that spiritual things established by God’s grace for salvation have no power because those who hold office over them are evil. Therefore do not rashly affirm [Col. 0073A] that the priestly order has failed in the Roman Church because those who rule in it are unworthy of it.

VI. Certainly, we would confess what you say to be true if you could prove that the Catholic faith had failed in it. For if faith had been emptied out, undoubtedly the sacraments of faith would also be empty. And if the sacraments were empty, the office of priests who administer them would be empty and of no use. Regarding the other vices for which you blame the Roman Church, perhaps we cannot sufficiently excuse it; but that the Catholic faith has failed in it, you certainly cannot prove by any reasoning.

For the same faith which from the beginning was planted in it through blessed Peter, and which was preached by [Col. 0073B] his successors who suffered martyrdom for the confession of the Catholic faith—such as Clement, Sixtus, Marcellus, and many others too numerous to enumerate—and who greatly illuminated the Church by holiness of life and heavenly teaching—such as Sylvester, Gregory, Leo, and very many others—that same faith, I say, is preached and held in it to this present day, aided by that intercession of our Lord Jesus Christ with the Father, concerning which he himself said to Peter: “I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail” (Luke XXII).

Certainly he was not speaking spiritually of the faith which was in Peter’s own mind, but of the faith of the Church which he wished to be governed by Peter. Hence, whenever it happened that one of the apostolic Fathers erred from the Catholic faith, [Col. 0073C] the Lord did not allow him to remain long, lest perhaps the Church should be corrupted through him. For in the time of the Arian heresy a certain pope called Leo, as is read in the Life of blessed Hilary, assented to the Arians in their heresy and was struck by sudden death. It is also read of another that he departed from the true faith and was deposed for that reason.

VII. But if you still cling to that assertion and say that the Roman Church has been so corrupted that something other is now believed and taught in it than what blessed Peter and those of his successors, whose sanctity is beyond doubt, believed and taught there, then you must show us by rational argument what that thing is in which it disagrees with their faith and [Col. 0073D] preaching; and what they believed which is not now received in faith by their successors. But we are certain that, for demonstrating this, you lack both argument and language.

As I have said, our Lord Jesus, because of his love for the prince of the apostles, has amid the many storms of persecutions and the barking assaults of heretics preserved the Catholic faith uncorrupted to this day in that apostolic see; and together with it he has preserved there the dignity of the priestly order—more because of the steadfastness of faith than because of the merits of the priests who govern it. I say, because of the steadfastness of faith: for it would undoubtedly already have fallen into neglect and failure if the office of preaching, baptizing, confirming, binding and loosing, offering the saving sacrifice, [Col. 0074A] praying for the people of God, consecrating churches, conferring orders, and performing the other such acts belonging to bishops and priests had been rendered void.

And from the Roman Fathers, just as knowledge of the sacred faith, so also the order of priesthood has come down to us through holy men who were sent from there to these western regions for the sake of the Christian religion.

VIII. For when the apostle Peter sent his three disciples Eucharius, Valerius, and Maternus to preach the word of God in Gaul and Germany, he ordained the first of those Fathers, namely blessed Eucharius, a priest and raised him to episcopal dignity. He promoted Valerius to the rank of deacon. He consecrated Maternus a subdeacon. Blessed Eucharius, while bishop in the city of Trier, promoted holy Valerius to the rank of priesthood and, when he was dying, entrusted the Church to him to govern in his place. Likewise Valerius, when he was about to depart this life, ordained blessed Maternus a priest and entrusted to him the episcopal administration.

Thus from these three pontiffs the sacred orders of the Fathers, together with the Catholic faith, were planted and rooted in the provinces of Trier and Cologne, both of which Saint Maternus is known to have governed, and likewise Tongeren, [Col. 0074B] while it was still an episcopal see. By the authority and grace of God by which they ordained bishops and priests and conferred the other orders, all their successors in episcopal dignity—remaining in the same faith which they had taught and obedient to the master of the apostolic see—likewise ordained bishops, priests, and the other ministers of God’s altar down to the present day.

IX. I say the same concerning the province of Mainz. By the authority by which Saint Boniface was ordained priest and bishop—he who, being a cardinal of the Church of the Roman see, was sent by Pope Zachary to Mainz and made its first archbishop—by that authority, I say, he himself ordained bishops, priests, and other ministers of God; [Col. 0074D] and by that same authority his successors and their suffragans have, each in their own cities, conferred orders upon ministers of God down to the present time.

Therefore, from what has now been said, know that in these three archbishoprics, which are chief among the German people, and in the bishoprics subject to them, the priestly office has its root and foundation from the head of the holy Catholic Church—that is, from the see of the blessed apostle Peter, which is in the city of Rome. Moreover, all the metropolitan cities of the Roman Empire plainly demonstrate, by requiring pontifical pallia from the Roman Fathers, obeying them, receiving and observing the decrees of Roman pontiffs, and conducting divine service according to their institutions, that they possess the episcopal and [Col. 0075A] priestly office and the other orders of divine ministry from the Roman Church.

X. We may say the same of the cities of the other western kingdoms. Blessed Dionysius the Areopagite, ordained bishop by Saint Clement, successor of the apostle Peter, brought the priestly office to the kingdom of the Franks. He was the first to convert the Gallic people in the city of Paris and its territory to the faith by preaching the word of God; he built churches and, as is read, consecrated priests and ordained other ministers of God’s altar from approved persons. For the same purposes he sent from himself to Spain, Aquitaine, and the district of Beauvais three distinguished men: Saint Marcellus, Saturninus, and Lucian, [Col. 0075B] whom Pope Saint Clement had given him as companions on his journey.

Likewise, in the kingdom of the English, blessed Augustine the bishop, sent by the venerable holy Pope Gregory, extended both the observance of Christian religion and the priestly office. Therefore, just as the same faith disseminated from the Roman see through the holy men sent from it still remains today in all the cities of the western kingdoms mentioned above, so too the priestly office planted through them remains there to this day.

XI. Perhaps you answer this: “We indeed admit that those first preachers of the Christian faith, of whom mention has been made, were truly priests of God and could ordain [Col. 0075C] others to the priesthood. But they had many successors in episcopal sees whose lives were so depraved and abominable that they themselves could neither possess the priestly office nor ordain others to it; and through them the priesthood entirely perished.”

To this I answer the very point stated above concerning Roman pontiffs: it is not impossible for rulers of churches to possess certain spiritual gifts directed toward the benefit of those whom they must govern, while they themselves are unworthy before God of those same gifts and receive no benefit from them for salvation. Thus the prophetic spirit of Balaam and Caiaphas, of whom we have also spoken above, and the apostolic power of Judas, did not benefit them but others.

Therefore, from your statement that the pontiffs succeeding the holy men mentioned above lived wickedly and without reason, you cannot, I say, thereby necessarily prove that they could not possess the authority to perform the office of priests and ordain priests—a power that is undoubtedly holy and a spiritual gift of God. Many in the primitive Church possessed this gift of the Holy Spirit, so as to speak in diverse tongues which they had never learned from anyone, and yet did not possess God’s charity, because this gift was given not for merit but for the honor of God. Many possessed this gift of the Holy Spirit so as to prophesy in Christ’s name, cast demons out of possessed bodies, and perform other signs, yet did not truly follow Christ, as is apparent from the words [Col. 0076A] of the Savior himself, who said: “Amen, I say to you, many will come on that day, saying: ‘Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, cast out demons, and perform many mighty works?’ And then I shall confess to them: ‘I never knew you; depart from me, workers of iniquity’” (Luke XIII).

If you knew how to consider such statements, you would certainly not judge so rashly that the office of priest or bishop could not exist among those whose life is not praiseworthy before God.

XII. Again, perhaps you will resort to such an objection as this: “Even if not through the evil conduct of bishops, it could nevertheless happen through their unbelief that priestly dignity was made void. For there were certain times in which heresies multiplied and grew so greatly in the Church [Col. 0076B] that even bishops of many cities were led into error, especially in the days of Arian unbelief, to which many bishops are read to have assented. In those times many were ordained to the priestly order, and many also to episcopal dignity, by heretical bishops. But the ordinations of heretics could have no efficacy, so that one ordained by them might truly perform the office of bishop or priest, or promote another to it. Those ordained by heretics, thinking themselves bishops when they were not, ordained other bishops and priests; and those ordained by them likewise did not truly possess the office which they thought they had received. They in turn ordained others, [Col. 0076C] and thus down to these times ecclesiastical orders have descended from those heretical bishops by whom they were first corrupted, and have been so annihilated that where they are thought to exist, they do not truly exist.”

If you frame such an objection against us, know that we are not without an answer. We indeed read that it often happened that even bishops of various cities were led into error and assented to heretics who attempted to overthrow the Catholic faith. If some assented to heresies in such a way that they nevertheless did not openly oppose the Church, were not cut off from the Church by the excommunication of orthodox Fathers, and thus still remained, at least outwardly, within the Church, we do not deny that they truly possessed [Col. 0076D] sacred orders and could truly confer them upon others, though not for their own benefit. For it is not impossible that the sacraments of the Church are sometimes administered even through heretics, as Augustine’s words also testify:

> The sacraments of Christ and of the Church are not therefore not sacraments because they are used unlawfully not only by heretics but by all the impious. The latter must be corrected and punished; the former must be acknowledged and venerated.

But if any were so corrupted by heresies as openly to dare defend them and attack the Catholic faith, the Roman rulers and orthodox Fathers, who under them upheld the Catholic faith, strove, so far as possible, to expel them from episcopal sees and cut them off from the Church of God by excommunication.

XIII. If, while they were cut off from the Church of God, they presumed to confer any orders, [Col. 0077A] those orders, together with the heresies, lay under excommunication, so that they had no saving efficacy as long as the heresies remained in those who assented in heresy to their ordainers. Hence Cyprian the martyr says in his letter that all things done by heretics are carnal, empty, and sacrilegious; that their altars are false, their priesthoods unlawful, and their sacrifices sacrilegious; and that, like apes which, though not human, imitate the human form, they claim for themselves the appearance and authority of the Catholic Church although they themselves are not the Church.

But after, with God’s help, the heresies began to fail, so that those excommunicated because of them either died or gradually returned [Col. 0077B] to the Catholic Church and were reconciled to it, then those ordained by heretical bishops outside the Church were indeed received into communion with the Church, though not all in one and the same manner. Some were received in such a way that, through the laying on of hands, they possessed lay communion only and existed in the Church altogether without clerical order, as we understand from the words of Pope Innocent. For he is read to say that Arian clerics are not to be received with the dignity of priesthood or of any ministry; he allows only their baptism, received in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, to remain valid. He also directs that such persons receive lay communion only through the laying on of hands, and that none of them be appointed to any rank, however slight, of the clerical order.

This was first established generally concerning heretics; but later, as various circumstances intervened, this rigor was moderated by the counsel of orthodox Fathers. By their decree, some of those ordained by heretics were received, for reasons of dispensation, in such a manner that they remained in the orders which they had received from heretics outside the Church. This is clear from a decree of Innocent, in which he says:

> The chief deliberation of the priests was this: that those whom Bonosus had ordained should be received, lest they remain with him and no small scandal arise. But, he says, the necessity of the time urgently required this to be done.

Therefore, if such persons lacked any spiritual grace which they ought to have received in their ordination, it is clear that it was conferred upon them [Col. 0077D] when they received from Catholic Fathers permission to minister in the Church. Again, some ordained by heretics were received in such a way that, upon receiving the laying on of hands, they were ordained and so remained in the clergy—perhaps because they had not been ordained according to the form of the Church. This is read to have been decreed only concerning the Novatians in the canons of the Council of Nicaea.

XIV. Some thought that all who had been ordained by heretics outside the Church ought to be ordained a second time when they returned to the Catholic Church. But Pope Gregory shows in a letter to John, bishop of Ravenna, that this should not be done, writing thus: “What you say—that those who have been ordained should be ordained again—is very ridiculous. For just as one baptized once ought not to be baptized again, so one consecrated once cannot validly be consecrated again in the same order” [Col. 0078A].

Again, certain persons coming from heretics were received with rigor tempered by mercy, so that they ministered in whatever orders they then held but were never advanced to any others. Pope Urban is read to have ordered Gebhard, bishop of Constance, concerning this matter:

> Permit those ordained formerly by excommunicated, though Catholic, bishops, if their more religious life and distinction in doctrine appear to merit it, after imposing such penance as you judge appropriate, to remain in the orders they have received. But we do not grant them permission to ascend to higher ranks unless the greatest necessity and usefulness demand it, and their [Col. 0078B] holy conduct has deserved it. Even this, however, is to be granted more rarely and with especial caution.

Some others are read to have ordered the same without any exception.

XV. Know that I have recalled these things in this manner so that from them you may perceive with what diligence the Fathers who held the helm of God’s Church made provision and took care that what you allege should not occur—namely, that ecclesiastical orders should be rendered void through heretics. For they did not perish through those received into the communion of the Church; nor were they rendered void through those who remained outside communion. For once the Catholic Church prevailed over them, they no longer ministered openly in the Church or conferred orders publicly. And if they did so secretly, and any Catholic, knowing them to be heretics, received ordination [Col. 0078C] from them, he was not received in the Church. Thus it is read in the seventh session of the synod held at Nicaea: “If anyone goes voluntarily to a heretic and receives ordination, let him not be received.”

And what more should I say about heretics? We certainly know that when the Lord and Savior spoke to the prince of the apostles about the building of the holy Church, he said among other things: “The gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Matt. XVI). By the gates of hell he meant heretics, who open the entrance of hell to those who follow them. Yet, according to the Lord’s promise, they have not prevailed against the Church, because he entrusted it to the prince of the apostles so that they could never destroy the Catholic faith in it. If they had prevailed over it to such an extent that [Col. 0078D] all ecclesiastical orders in it had already been emptied out through them, and all the Church’s sacraments thus weakened, they would indeed have prevailed over it excessively, and the Savior’s promise—which cannot be made void—would not have been properly fulfilled.

XVI. Perhaps you make against us concerning simoniacal bishops the same objection introduced above concerning heretics. We answer concerning them as follows. So long as a bishop’s simony is not so manifest that he is accused, convicted, and sentenced canonically for it before his superiors, we believe that his office retains its efficacy in the ecclesiastical sacraments which he administers, as we gather from the words of blessed Gregory, who, [Col. 0079A] speaking of the sacrament of the Lord’s body, says:

> And what is better than the body and blood of Christ? Therefore, whether it is administered within the Church through good or bad ministers, it is nevertheless holy, and the Holy Spirit gives life; it is neither increased by the merits of good administrators nor diminished by those of bad ones.

But there are simoniacs within the Church who have not yet been condemned by it. Since both consecrating the Lord’s body and ordaining God’s ministers belong to their office, if their office is not invalid in the greater sacrament on account of their sins, it is probable that it is not invalid in the lesser either. For although their life is reprobate and their prayers unacceptable to God, we nevertheless believe that, through the merits and prayers of the Church to which they still adhere in some manner, [Col. 0079B] they are aided so that their offices remain valid in the sacraments which concern the Church’s use.

For no one says in the consecration of the Eucharist, “I offer,” but “We offer”; this is said on behalf of the whole Church. Nor does any bishop, in performing his office, say, “I pray that this or that may be done,” but each says, “Let us pray,” whereby he numbers himself with the whole Church, by whose merits and prayers he is aided in obtaining from God the things for which he asks—things which perhaps he would be unworthy to obtain by himself.

XVII. Perhaps you object to me again, saying: “What then is meant by the Lord’s threat to priests or bishops displeasing to him: ‘I will curse your blessings’?” (Mal. II). Understand this [Col. 0079C] as though he said: “I shall cause your blessings to become a curse upon yourselves.” For it may happen that someone’s blessing benefits the person blessed, whereas that same blessing results in evil for the one who blesses. So it was with those who, though they did not follow Christ, nevertheless in his name blessed persons possessed by demons. The possessed were indeed set free; but those who freed others by their blessings, and thereby sought glory and profit among men, were rejected by God, as is clear from the Gospel words cited above.

You say, I think, in response to what I have already said about simoniacal ordainers: “How can they give the Holy Spirit when they do not have the Holy Spirit?” Consider what you say and what you ask. [Col. 0079D] I tell you that, apart from Christ—who is both true man and true God—no human being can give the Holy Spirit to another. Blessed Augustine testifies to this when speaking thus of Christ: “He received the Holy Spirit as man and poured him out as God.” We can indeed receive this gift according to our measure, but we certainly cannot pour it out upon others; rather, we invoke upon them the God from whom it is effected, so that this may occur.

Again he says: “No disciple of Christ gave the Holy Spirit. They prayed that he might come upon those upon whom they laid hands; they did not themselves give him. The Church still observes this custom even now among its leaders.” Finally, Simon Magus, offering money to the apostles, did not say: “Give me also this power, that I may give the Holy Spirit”; but: “That whoever, [Col. 0080A] he said, I lay hands upon may receive the Holy Spirit” (Acts VIII). For Scripture had not previously said, “Simon saw that the apostles gave the Holy Spirit”; rather, it said: “Simon saw that through the laying on of the apostles’ hands the Holy Spirit was given” (ibid.).

But if any of the Catholic Fathers is found to have stated in writing that the apostles gave the Holy Spirit, or that those who ordain God’s ministers give the Holy Spirit, it should be understood that they had no other sense in such a statement than that expressed in Augustine’s words now cited. Therefore you ask in vain how those who do not have the Holy Spirit can give him. What is possible for them, therefore, both bad and good bishops do: namely, they pray [Col. 0080B] and, according to their office, pronounce the appointed blessings over those whom they ordain; and God grants this gift of the Holy Spirit to each person ordained, not for the bishops’ own merits, but for love of his Church, of which they are still, however deficiently, members. He grants them the grace belonging to their order, a grace which each may use either for good or for evil.

Nor is it surprising if, in answer to the invocation of God made by an evil person, he grants some grace of the Holy Spirit to one who is ordained, since at the invocation of the holy Trinity—sometimes made over one baptized in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit by any criminal Christian or even an unbeliever—the baptized person receives that [Col. 0080C] grace of the Holy Spirit through which all sins are forgiven and by which he becomes a member of Christ.

XVIII. Now put to me also this objection: when Simon Magus offered the apostle Peter money for the power by which, whomever he laid hands upon, that person might receive the Holy Spirit, Peter said to him: “May your money be with you unto destruction, because you thought that the gift of God could be possessed with money” (Acts VIII). From this construct the following argument against me: because Simon thought to obtain God’s gift through money, he was cursed, rejected from it, and did not obtain it. Therefore the simoniacal imitators who offer and give money for the episcopal office, which is a spiritual gift of God, are likewise cursed by God and do not obtain what they seek; and if they do not obtain it, they are not truly bishops and cannot perform what belongs to the episcopal office. Is this your objection?

You will not find me without an answer even now. It is true that Simon was rejected from the spiritual gift for which he had wickedly bargained, and did not obtain it; this was the judgment of an angry God. But these men obtain the spiritual gift for which they too bargain wickedly—namely, the episcopal office—and this is a benefit partly from an angry God and partly from a merciful God. It is a benefit from an angry God because he truly grants it to them so that they may become all the more condemnable for having bargained wickedly for it. It is as though he said in the words concerning Saul, who, when he was about to give his daughter to David in marriage while plotting David’s death, said: “I will give him my daughter as wife, that she may be a snare to him” [Col. 0081A] (1 Sam. XVIII).

Those of whom the Apostle says, “Although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God, but became vain” (Rom. I), received a benefit from an angry God; so too did those of whom the Psalmist says: “Yet because of their deceit you set them in slippery places; you cast them down while they were being raised up” (Ps. LXXII). I say that it is in part a benefit from a merciful God, because for the use of his Church he grants them the spiritual grace which they employ in their offices, lest through their occasion the sacraments of the Church, without which she cannot be, should perish.

XIX. Nevertheless, there seems to be a difference between the sin of these men and Simon’s sin. Simon did not see that the apostles, through that power which they had from God and which he himself wished to possess, had acquired [Col. 0081B] any riches or worldly dominion; nor did he therefore offer them money so that they might help him attain such things. Rather, he chiefly sought to obtain that very spiritual gift of God which he saw that they possessed: namely, that upon whomever he laid his hand, that person might receive the Holy Spirit with some visible miracle—so that he might speak in various tongues, or something similar might happen in him by which the Holy Spirit could be plainly recognized. In this he desired to become like the holy apostles, whom he envied because they surpassed him in so eminent a gift. His envy was undoubtedly indicated by the words Peter said to him: “I see that you are in the gall of bitterness” (Acts VIII).

He wished to obtain this not in order to use it for good, but for evil—[Col. 0081C] to win glory for himself before men—just as the Jews bought Christ, not in order to enjoy him for good, but in order to carry out their wicked will against him. And since his heart was not right before God, he made no effort to be reconciled to God’s grace, so that he might obtain His gift. Rather, as though he could secure it against God’s will, he irreverently and openly demanded that men sell him, at a price, the priceless grace which God alone could give.

His presumption was therefore like that of a servant of some powerful man who is despised and hateful to his master, and who has no concern to gain his master’s favor, yet openly offers money to his master’s counselors in order that they may procure for him the master’s daughter, so that he may abuse her in fornication.

But now, if someone becomes so forgetful of his salvation [Col. 0081D] that he desires the honor of a see not according to God, he first considers the riches, honors, and similar temporal advantages attached to that prelacy, which are objects of desire; and he chiefly desires these and deliberates how to acquire them. Alongside these, he considers the spiritual requirements without which he cannot possess those things: namely, the priestly office, which requires him to devote himself to divine contemplation, praying for others and meditating upon the things of God; that he may be learned and teach others; that he may be chaste, sober, modest, serious, and altogether beyond reproach in conduct. Reflecting on these things, he is greatly afraid and judges himself unworthy of the dignity to which he aspires.

Placed therefore between desire and fear, he is overcome by desire. He begins to negotiate [Col. 0082A] through petitions, gifts, and promises, both personally and through friends, conducting the business now secretly, now openly. Indeed, he does everything chiefly for the worldly things he desires; only secondarily for spiritual things—not because he loves them or thinks himself worthy of them, but because he knows that he cannot obtain those worldly things without them. He completes the transaction, gives what is demanded, and receives, under the hand of the ecclesiastical father by whom he is ordained, the spiritual power belonging to the dignity to which he is ordained.

God confers this upon him not because He loves him or because he is worthy of it, but, as I said above, partly because of His mercy: so that the elect of God in the people belonging to His kingdom may not, through that man’s sin, lack the ecclesiastical sacraments which pertain to [Col. 0082B] the salvation of their souls. Partly also, in His wrath, God grants it to him so that He may have a greater ground for condemning him in the future, if he does not repent—he who by money intruded himself into enjoying, according to his own will, the alms of the faithful, which they contributed to the churches for Christ’s honor and for the needs of His poor.

God also partly permits such men in this manner to hold ecclesiastical dignities because of the sins of certain people in the community, who are not worthy to have good prelates, as Scripture testifies when it says: “Because of the sins of the people, God permits a hypocrite to reign.”

XX. Often those who negotiate thus in the Church, because their principal intention is not [Col. 0082C] to purchase spiritual things but temporal things, which they love more, and because all their conversation with sellers and buyers concerns such things, say that they are not buying spiritual things but temporal ones. Yet in saying this they deceive themselves. It is reckoned to them as a purchase that they approach those things by means of money, which, out of desire for temporal goods, they give for things established so that they may possess those temporal goods together with spiritual things.

Concerning merchants of this kind the pope says as follows: “If any allege that they are not buying consecrations but the things themselves which arise from consecration, they are shown to be completely foolish. For whoever sells either of two things, without which the other cannot be possessed, fails to refrain from selling either.”

I see a comparison for this transaction in the following example. If the guardian of an orphan fraudulently [Col. 0082D] sells a mill, which belongs to the orphan’s inheritance, to a man who knows of his fraud, the buyer is unjust no less than the seller. Although in their agreement he made no mention of the water of the mill-race belonging to the mill, nonetheless that water is said to be possessed by the same purchase. Yet God alone, as governor of nature, supplies this water to the mill: both to meet the needs of those who use it, and also so that He may hold its unjust possessor all the more guilty, the more abundantly he enjoys its benefits, to which he came unjustly.

Those mentioned above are called Simoniacs because, in negotiating by money concerning ecclesiastical prelacies, which joined together contain God’s spiritual gifts and temporal goods, they imitate Simon, [Col. 0083A] who thought that God’s gift could be acquired with money. For this reason they shall share the curse by which Peter cursed him, saying: “May your money perish with you, because you thought that the gift of God could be acquired with money” (Acts VIII).

XXI. As may be observed from what has been said, Simon’s transaction was more wicked and more presumptuous than theirs. It was more wicked because he envied the apostles, with whom he wished to make himself equal, for the grace of God; and he was in the gall of his bitterness (ibid.), as he later demonstrated by his deeds. But these men seek no such equality with the saints, nor do they envy their holiness; rather, they venerate them.

It was more presumptuous because he openly and shamelessly offered money directly for God’s grace, as though it were merchandise [Col. 0083B] offered in a market. These men, however, do not direct their payment immediately toward the spiritual gift but toward worldly advantage—although they are still guilty in this, that they know neither can be approached through money, yet they approach both through it. Thus what Simon thought to possess principally, these men think to possess secondarily in their transaction.

By “thought,” I mean that he deliberated it in his mind. For the word “supposition” (*existimatio*) must not here be taken to mean an uncertain opinion, just as it is not in the place where the Apostle says: “For I reckon that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that shall be revealed in us” (Rom. VIII).

We have said these things concerning Simoniacs who are neither manifest nor convicted, in order to show that they can confer ecclesiastical orders and [Col. 0083C] that their ordinations are held valid. Even if they are at some time convicted of simony, those ordained by them remain in their orders if they were ordained before it became known to them that those men were Simoniacs. Certainly this would not be permitted if the Simoniacs could confer no orders.

For Pope Urban says thus concerning such persons: “Those who are ordained by Simoniacs whom, at the time of their ordination, they do not know to be Simoniacs and who are then held to be Catholics—their ordination is mercifully tolerated.” He says “mercifully,” because according to the strictness of justice they could be deposed—not because they do not possess orders, but for the greater shame of those by whom they were ordained, and as a terror to others who do not fear to engage in simoniacal dealings. The same mercy is also granted [Col. 0083D] to those who, knowing from another person’s report that their ordainers are Simoniacs, nevertheless cannot prove it and ought not to do so, and do not dare withdraw from ordination.

XXII. But if some have been ordained by Simoniacs who have been convicted and condemned, their ordinations have been annulled by the Fathers, and they have been ordered to cease from their ministries.

O Cathars, I want you to know that the various things I have said concerning what has been done in the Church, and what has been established and said in it by the Fathers, I have said not only because of you, but even more because of our unlearned people, who sometimes hear both our sermons and yours. They may thus know that reasonable arguments are not lacking to us, but that an account must be given of what we believe and do in God’s Church. Concerning you, however, [Col. 0084A] I know that whatever we say, however reasonable it may be, you will chatter on with your errors, as the common saying has it: “The wolf cries, ‘Sheep, sheep,’ whatever you say to him.”

## SERMON XI  
### Against the Eighth Heresy: Concerning the Body and Blood of the Lord

I. My mouth is still open against you, O Antichrists, and I have no small discourse against your unbelief. You are also accused of this: that concerning the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ you do not hold the faith confessed by the Catholic Church. That faith is as follows.

The people of God, in all parts of the world to which the Christian religion has spread, believe and confess that whenever priests [Col. 0084B] of the Church—whether of good conduct or bad—perform the divine office at God’s altar and pronounce over the offering of bread and wine the sacred words which our high priest, that is Christ, and our holy Fathers left for us to say there, a change undoubtedly takes place: beneath the appearance of bread and wine are the flesh of Christ, which was uninjured upon the cross, and the living blood which flowed from His wounds. They also believe that this same flesh is received by the priest himself and by all who come to communicate with him.

This is our faith. And, as they say, you altogether refuse to believe that the body of the Lord can be made by any consecration performed by any priest, good or bad, or that it can be received by any human being for eating. I do not doubt that you are already in this error, [Col. 0084C] since you hold in contempt all the priests of the Church who administer the Lord’s sacraments, and value none of their ministry.

I remember once seeing, in the presence of Arnold, archbishop of Cologne, a man of no small reputation who had returned to his own people from the school of the Cathars. When we carefully asked him what their heresies were, he answered thus: “I shall state briefly the matters about which you ask: everything you believe, everything you do in the Church, they judge false and empty.” When he had said this, the answer satisfied the archbishop, and he judged that nothing further needed to be asked of him. Hence I find it credible that the unbelief of which I spoke is not absent from your wickedness.

[Col. 0084D] But whether you believe what we believe or not, so that you may recognize in this matter also that our faith has a reasonable foundation, we must bring forward the words of evangelical and apostolic Scripture which bear manifest witness to it.

II. When the holy evangelists speak of the Lord’s supper which He had with His disciples before His passion, they say that when evening had come the Lord reclined with His disciples; and while they were eating, Jesus took bread, blessed it, broke it, gave it to His disciples, and said: “Take and eat; this is my body, which shall be given for you. Do this in remembrance of me.” And taking the cup, He gave thanks and gave it to them, saying: “Take and drink from this, all of you; for this is my blood of the New [Col. 0085A] Testament, which shall be shed for you and for many for the remission of sins” (Matt. XXVI).

Observe all these words carefully. He blessed the bread, gave it to them, and said: “This is my body.” And to make more certain to them and to us which body, or what kind of body, was signified by those words, He specified it when He added: “Which shall be given for you.” Likewise, concerning the blood He specified it when He said: “This is my blood, which shall be shed for you and for many.”

From these words we believe without doubt that He gave them to eat the same body in which He then appeared present before them while speaking, and which afterwards hung on the cross and suffered death there; and that He gave them to drink the same blood which flowed from His wounds. It is indeed impossible for human understanding [Col. 0085B] to comprehend how this could take place. Yet it has a right and firm reason why it ought to believe this without doubt. What is that reason by which one should believe that what outwardly appeared to be bread was the very body of the Lord? It is that the Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, said it—and He could not lie. Truly He could not lie, because He was God, because He was Truth, as He Himself testifies of Himself, saying: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV).

III. I believe without doubt that He could do whatever He wished with His body, because it is written of Him: “The Lord has done whatsoever He pleased in heaven and on earth” (Ps. CXXXIV).
