He was Lord of all nature; and therefore I believe that by His heavenly blessing He could cause that bread which He blessed [Col. 0085C] to pass into the substance of His body, and could cause it, in an invisible and inconceivable manner, to enter Peter’s mouth and pass into the inmost part of his spirit, and of the other disciples to whom He offered it. For that food was spiritual and properly belonged to the soul.

I believe that He could do with His body this, just as He could do many other things with it which seem impossible to one who does not believe and does not consider that the Lord was dwelling in that body. He took that body from the Virgin’s womb and brought it into the world while His mother’s womb remained closed. He Himself bore that body upon the waters of the sea, so that it was not submerged where Peter was sinking; but Peter was not drowned because he was aided by Him. He displayed heavenly brightness [Col. 0085D] in His body while it still remained for Him to suffer and die: namely, when He was transfigured before His disciples on the mountain and His face shone like the sun (Matt. XVII). By His own power He raised that body from death and brought it forth while the tomb remained closed. Where the disciples were gathered in a house, He entered with the same body while the doors were shut and stood in their midst. He also powerfully lifted that same body from the earth and placed it in the highest heaven, above all the choirs of angels.

All these things are written in the Gospels, and we believe them, although they seem unbelievable according to the ordinary nature of things, and although we do not know how to consider and discover the manner in which they could have happened. But we believe that the Lord truly could do, and did do, all these things, because He was God, to whom nothing is impossible. For the same reason [Col. 0086A] we must believe that He could also do with His body what we stated above: namely, that He gave it to His disciples to eat when He said: “Take and eat of this, all of you; this is my body, which shall be given for you.”

IV. Where the Evangelist says that the Lord broke the bread which He gave to His disciples, and which He told them to eat, “breaking” and “eating” must not be understood in the same sense as when ordinary bread is said to be broken and eaten. For in the breaking and eating of ordinary bread, one part is entirely separated from another, so that no wholeness remains in the bread which is broken and eaten.

[Col. 0086B] But after the Lord had blessed that bread, there was no longer the true substance of bread there, but the appearance of bread, and beneath that appearance the true body of Christ. The breaking was not in the substance of the Lord’s body, but in that visible appearance of bread, which remained unchanged. Thus they ate Christ’s body, while it remained whole and unconsumed. Therefore the eating by which they ate Christ’s body was not like the eating by which they ate other ordinary foods. What they received by the mouth, they inwardly ate in their soul by faith and love, and there they were sanctified by the power of that bread.

[Col. 0086C] Consider a certain comparison for this matter. When a spiritual teacher instructs the people in church, he sometimes speaks one proposition which each person receives through the bodily ear, and it passes in its entirety into the hearts of individuals. In a sense it is divided among them, yet it remains whole with the one who teaches. In the same way, the Lord’s disciples received the holy food with their bodily mouths, and it passed wholly into each of their hearts; thus it was divided among them, yet remained whole with the one who gave it.

V. Observe also this: when the Lord had given His body to His disciples and said, “Take; this is my body, which shall be given for you,” He added: “Do this in remembrance of me.” If you are instructed in the Holy Scriptures as you think you are, and as you customarily boast, say what the Lord intended by these words [Col. 0086D] and what He commanded His disciples to do in His remembrance when He said: “Do this in remembrance of me.”

You cannot, I think, deny that by saying “Do this,” He indicated what He was handing to them in His hand, which had the form of bread. But if that thing was nothing but bread, do you say that He commanded them to make bread in remembrance of Him? To say this is foolish. Yet beneath the appearance of bread there was something other than bread—namely, His body, as is clear from His words: “This is my body.” And He commanded them to make that in remembrance of His passion and death.

Thus, in saying, “Do this in remembrance of me,” He gave both them and all those to whom the priestly office would come through them the power to make [Col. 0087A] His body and blood with prayer and blessing. When priests are said to “make” or “prepare” (*conficere*, which has the same sense in ordinary language) the body of the Lord, we do not understand this to mean that they create the Lord’s body anew or give it its essence. Their “making” means nothing other than that, over the visible sacrifice upon the altar, they perform their office, say prayers and blessings, and make the appointed signs; then, by divine power, it is granted that the true body and true blood of the Lord are there, where previously there was nothing but bread and wine.

VI. The work which priests then perform is customarily described in this way: they are said to make the body of the Lord. Perhaps this manner of speaking derives from the Lord’s words: [Col. 0087B] “Do this in remembrance of me.” Or if anyone thinks that “Do this in remembrance of me” should be understood as though He had said, “Eat my body in remembrance of me,” so that He repeats for a second time what He had said above, “Take and eat,” I shall not oppose him, although this interpretation fits the continuous wording of the text less aptly than the interpretation given above.

Nonetheless, by the very fact that He commanded them to eat His body and drink His blood—and to do so after His passion in remembrance of His death—He gave them power to prepare His body and blood through the blessing which He taught them by His own example. They afterwards used this in consecrating the Eucharist and handed it down to others to whom the priestly [Col. 0087C] office came from them. For unless He had given them this power, how could they have had His body to eat and His blood to drink even after His resurrection?

VII. Perhaps you will utter this madness: it could indeed in some way happen that the Lord, before His passion, gave His disciples His body to eat and His blood to drink in remembrance of Himself—that is, in order that afterwards they might remember Him. But after His passion and resurrection, there could in no way be a blessing by which they could have His body to eat or His blood to drink.

To this I first say that, if you interpret that remembrance in this way, [Col. 0087D] you do not understand Scripture correctly. For how it is to be understood appears from the Apostle’s words, when, explaining that word “remembrance” to the Corinthians, he says: “For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes” (I Cor. XI). From these words it is understood that the eating of the Lord’s body under the appearance of bread and the drinking of the cup—that is, of the Lord’s blood—is a proclamation, that is, a testimony, of the Lord’s death which He suffered on the cross.

In adding “until he comes,” the Apostle means: until the Lord comes for judgment. By this he signifies that this proclamation of Christ’s death through participation in His body and blood will not be absent from the Church until the day of judgment. It is therefore clear from the Apostle’s words that [Col. 0088A] even after the Lord’s passion Christ’s faithful could eat the Lord’s body and drink His blood.

It is also clear from Paul’s words that the holy apostles and their followers pronounced blessings over the Lord’s sacrifice in order to fulfill the Lord’s command which He had given them concerning the preparing and receiving of His body and blood in remembrance of Him. For he says in the Epistle to the Corinthians: “The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not a communion of Christ’s blood? And the bread which we break, is it not a participation in Christ’s body?” (I Cor. X). That is: is it not Christ’s body, of which we partake?

[Col. 0088B] And in saying “which we bless,” he signified not only that he and the other apostles possessed power to pronounce blessings over the sacrifice of the altar, but also that the presbyters of Corinth, to whom he wrote and gave many instructions concerning the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood, possessed it—how they ought worthily to administer it. He would have given those instructions to them in vain if it could in no way happen that the Lord’s body should be eaten or His blood drunk in the Church.

VIII. On one occasion in my house at Bonn I disputed concerning these matters with a man whom we suspected of belonging to the sect of the Cathars. It happened that we began speaking of wicked priests, and he said this about them: “How can men who live so irrationally distribute the Lord’s body in the Church?” I said to him: “Do we not read that Pilate, who crucified the Savior and was an unbeliever, had the power to give His body to whomever he wished, and gave it to Joseph, a just man?”

[Col. 0088C] The Lord is still in that same patience, tolerating wicked priests and allowing them to possess authority in the Church and to distribute His body and blood to both good and wicked persons. Immediately he added: “After the time of His passion, He Himself did not come into their hands.” From these words I sufficiently understood the unbelief which I had suspected in him: namely, that he did not believe the Lord’s body and blood could be handled or received in the Church by any human being.

I said to him indignantly: “O Cathar, I shall now plainly convict you.” I turned through the epistles of Paul, which I had before me, and showed him the passage in which Paul, writing to the Corinthians, says: “Whoever [Col. 0088D] eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord unworthily shall be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord. But let a person examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread and drink of that cup. For whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself, not discerning the Lord’s body” (I Cor. XI).

When I had explained these words to him, I pressed him with this argument: “If it is as you say—namely, that since the time when the Lord departed from this world His body has not come into anyone’s hands—it follows that since that time no one has been able either worthily or unworthily to eat His body or drink His blood. And if no one can receive it unworthily, no one can receive judgment upon himself in it. In vain did the Apostle say that whoever [Col. 0089A] receives the Lord’s body and blood unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself.” When I had said this, he fell silent: he neither denied the unbelief for which I reproved him nor assented to the truth by which he had been convicted.

IX. And now I address you also, my adversaries, concerning the same Scripture. If it is not as we believe—that the Church’s priests consecrate the Lord’s body and blood—and if it cannot happen that it should be received by any human being, can you tell us what that bread or cup of the Lord is in which one who eats and drinks it unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself, and from which many have even been afflicted bodily and have died while communicating unworthily? What is that body of the Lord which, the Apostle shows, must be discerned? And what is it to discern the Lord’s body? [Col. 0089B]

Certainly all these things are said superfluously and vainly if Christ’s true body itself is not communicable to human beings. I shall explain to you the sense of the Scripture now under discussion, although I know you are unworthy; yet I do this especially for our simple people.

The Apostle calls the Lord’s bread and cup the Lord’s body and blood because these are under the appearance of bread and wine upon the altar. Although the true substance of bread and wine is not there after consecration has taken place, the taste, color, and form of bread and wine are there. If indeed there were no substance in that sacrifice except bread and wine themselves, no one would eat judgment—that is, his own condemnation—in that food more than in [Col. 0089C] any other food; nor would some become sick or die through that eating, since mere bread and wine are harmless food.

Perhaps, you may say, because the bread is blessed and the wine is blessed, whoever unworthily eats that bread and drinks that wine eats and drinks judgment upon himself, and perhaps becomes sick or dies because he did not duly honor the holy blessing. If you say this, I ask why Paul said: “Whoever unworthily eats that bread and drinks the cup shall be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord” (I Cor. XI). If there is nothing there except plain blessed bread and plain blessed wine, he would more rightly have said: “He shall be guilty of blessed bread and blessed wine unworthily received.” But he said: “He shall be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord”—understand, received unworthily [Col. 0089D] and, so far as lies in him, in some manner destroyed.

X. Observe also that he says that the one who unworthily eats that bread of the Lord or drinks the cup does not discern the Lord’s body. If someone lives wickedly and foully and, without fear on account of his sins, boldly comes to partake of the Lord’s body and blood as though it were another food, that person communicates unworthily and does not discern—that is, does not distinguish—the Lord’s body from other foods by fear and reverence for God.

Likewise, if a man lives chastely and soberly but does not believe that what is consecrated by the Church’s priests upon the altar through prayer and blessing is truly the Lord’s body—[Col. 0090A] if he comes to holy communion for the sake of some pretense—he unworthily eats the Lord’s body, does not distinguish it from other foods by Catholic faith, and eats and drinks judgment, that is, condemnation, upon himself.

This is what you do, unhappy Cathar: secretly you deny that Christ’s true body is on the altar; in your workshop (*textrina*) you mock everything done by our priests in church; yet when Easter comes, you hurry to church with the people, reverently smooth your beard, bend your knees before the altar far more humbly than the rest, and open your mouth wider to receive holy communion—namely, your eternal condemnation—in order to appear to men a good Catholic and religious person, and so that those whom you hire with [Col. 0090B] money to protect you may say in your defense: “What do we require of these people? They are good and just; they do everything that belongs to Christians. Would that we were such as they!”

XI. From one man who had come out of your corners I heard this one piece of your wisdom: “Your body is the Lord’s body, and you make the Lord’s body when you bless your bread and restore your body from it.” You deceitfully imply this teaching when you are asked whether you truly hold the faith concerning the Lord’s body and reply to those questioning you that you have a sound faith concerning the Lord’s body.

If, then, this is the case, and this is the saying of your hidden wisdom, know that [Col. 0090C] this wisdom is not from the Lord God. Rather, your prince, the devil, devised it so that through such language he might give your unbelief some coloring by which it would resemble the Catholic faith, and so that the foolish people whom you draw after yourselves might be less repelled by it.

Do not deceive yourselves with empty words, wretched people! We confess that it is true that every body and all flesh belong to the Lord, whose are “the earth and its fullness”; and not only the souls of righteous people but also their bodies are called members of Christ, as in Paul, who says: “Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ?” (I Cor. VI). Yet nowhere in the Scriptures is this manner of speaking found: that the body of any human being, however holy, is called the Lord’s body, or anyone’s flesh Christ’s flesh, [Col. 0090D] except that one body which is united to divinity in the Lord and Savior.

This alone is distinctively called the Lord’s body and Christ’s flesh in the Scriptures. Wherever Scripture says anything of this kind—that the Lord’s body is to be eaten by the faithful—it says it in such a way that the statement cannot be understood of anyone other than that unique body of Christ’s person.

See that the Lord says thus in the Gospel: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink His blood, you shall not have life in yourselves” (John VI). Do you think this can truthfully be understood of the son of any human being other than that one Son of Man, Christ, the Virgin’s son? Do you think that some human being must be slaughtered, [Col. 0091A] cooked, or roasted and thus eaten, in order that eternal life may be obtained? Certainly God did not command this in His law, when He said: “You shall not kill” (Exod. XX). Even if a human being could be killed and eaten without sin, human flesh nevertheless does not possess such power that, by tasting it, it can grant anyone eternal life.

Therefore know from this that the Lord spoke uniquely of His own body, united to divinity, when He said: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink His blood,” etc. The Savior customarily called Himself the Son of Man, and nowhere in the Gospels is anyone besides Himself designated by this title. Hence we know that here also, when He spoke of the flesh of the Son of Man, He uniquely meant Himself.

[Col. 0091B] XII. But so that it might be made more certain of which Son of Man he was speaking here, and what kind of life he promised to those who ate his flesh and drank his blood, he later said elsewhere as well: “He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life.” Christ’s flesh is indeed true flesh, but in many respects it is unique among all other flesh, and it is eaten in such a manner as no other food is eaten, as has also been shown above. It is united to divinity, and from this it has the power that whoever worthily eats it eats eternal life in it, because it is sanctified by the power of the deifying Spirit joined to the flesh. But whoever eats unworthily receives no benefit from that flesh, as the Lord himself also testified when he said: “It is the Spirit that gives life; the flesh profits nothing” (John 6). That flesh not only does not benefit one who eats unworthily, but actually harms him, because in it he eats judgment upon himself. For God, who dwells in that holy flesh, destroys him and avenges the injury done to his dwelling.

Just as that flesh is unique among all other flesh, so God ordained that it should be eaten uniquely, and otherwise than any other food. For under the appearance of bread it is presented to us on the altar by divine power, and is seen and touched; it is tasted and eaten with the taste of bread. Likewise the Lord’s blood is presented to us under the appearance of wine and is tasted and drunk with the taste of wine. The breaking is seen there, but it belongs only to the sacrament—that is, to the visible form of bread. [Col. 0091D] The sharing of portions is perceived in eating, but likewise belongs only to the sacrament. The very substance of the Lord’s body, which lies hidden in the sacrament, remains whole and incorrupt. This food is eaten, but is not consumed as other food is: it passes into the soul, strengthens and illumines the soul, and leads it to eternal life.

This uniqueness belongs to that holy flesh which the Son of God assumed from the Virgin’s womb and set apart for himself from all flesh under heaven, in order to work in it these wonders for the salvation of his elect. Therefore, do not find it difficult to believe that the statement quoted above from the Gospel was spoken specifically of this flesh: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and [Col. 0092A] drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves”; and: “My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink” (ibid.); and other similar sayings.

XIII. Certain disciples of Christ, having heard him say such things, murmured: “How can this man give us his flesh to eat? This saying is hard; who can hear it?” And they turned back, departed from him (ibid.), and no longer walked with him. For they thought that he was telling them that he was to be eaten by them in the appearance in which he appeared among them: that he would be cut into pieces and torn by their teeth, and that his blood would be drunk by them in the appearance of blood. But he did not mean this manner of eating. Rather, he meant that manner of eating in which Christ’s flesh is truly eaten, yet the eater seems to himself to be eating not flesh but bread; and the drinker of his blood seems to himself to be drinking not blood but wine.

God truly ordained that it should be so, in order that the merit might be greater for one who receives both with such faith as to believe that God’s power is so great that he can do this, and his goodness so great that he deigns to do it out of love for humankind. Moreover, the Lord wished his flesh to be eaten and his blood to be drunk under an appearance other than their own, lest anyone be too greatly horrified at eating that flesh and drinking that blood if he saw both in their proper appearance; and so that Jews or pagans might have less occasion to mock Christians [Col. 0092C] and say that they ate their Lord and drank the blood of a slain man.

XIV. A man of our time, who had been accused of having tasted of your Catharism, is remembered to have said, when he was questioned at his end whether he wished the body of the Lord to be given to him: “If that were the Lord’s body, of such a size as the rock of Erembert [note: Hermelstein, opposite Confluence/Koblenz; Col. 0091D], it would long ago have been consumed, since it first began to be eaten.” This was a mocking remark and proceeded from unbelief, in which, as they say, you too are engulfed. Therefore I confront you with the same saying.

Do you believe it true that the Lord Jesus Christ satisfied five thousand people with five loaves, and that when they had been satisfied, [Col. 0092D] twelve baskets of fragments remained? You cannot deny this unless you wish to contradict the Gospels, in which it is plainly written. And do you not believe that, by the same power with which he performed this miracle, he could have satisfied still more people than those five thousand from the same loaves? There is no doubt that he could have done so. For there was more bread in the twelve baskets of fragments which remained after the people had eaten than there had initially been in those five loaves before he began to distribute them to the crowds. Perhaps those loaves which one boy carried there could have been contained in one or two of the twelve baskets. The Lord wished more to remain than had been distributed, so that [Col. 0093A] it might be understood that his power had not yet been so restricted that he could not still have satisfied many more thousands from the same loaves.

And the very miracle that he performed with five loaves he could undoubtedly have performed with one; nor only with one whole loaf, but he could have done this even with a morsel of bread. With every doubt removed, we may believe that by the same power through which he could make all things from nothing, he could multiply a crumb of bread so as to satisfy countless thousands of people from it. On what grounds, then, can we distrust that by the same power he can perform this miracle with his body: that it is daily eaten in the sacrament by many in his Church, yet is never consumed by being eaten?

Certainly, just as Christ of old sat before his disciples at his supper with his body unconsumed and whole at the very hour when they ate his body, he himself saying, “Take and eat: this is my body, which will be given for you” (1 Cor. 11); so too now, at the same hours and moments at which his body is eaten in churches throughout different regions of the world, he sits at the right hand of the Father in heaven with his body unconsumed. We do not possess this faith from our own human perception, but from the Scriptures of truth, which are from the Holy Spirit and in which the whole Church of Christ possesses the foundation of the entire Catholic faith.

XV. But you, Cathar, mock this faith in your secret assemblies as utter folly. Unhappy man! How dare you count as folly what the wisdom of God does? Is it impossible—or is it not permitted—to Christ, who is God’s power and God’s wisdom, to do with his body what he wishes? Is your eye evil because he is good? He is truly good, because for the sake of his elect he has done, and still does, many things which his enemies—namely Jews and pagans, and those like you—regard as folly and weakness. But, as the Apostle says: “What is foolish in God is wiser than human beings, and what is weak in God is stronger than human beings” (1 Cor. 1).

“You say: I cannot believe what is said of Christ’s body, because I do not at all understand how it can be.” Foolish man! Do you suppose that God can do nothing which you cannot understand? And among all things that we must believe, what is there that a human being living on earth can wholly penetrate or understand by his own intellect—how it is, or how it came to be? At last, then, lay aside your obstinacy, enemy of truth, and confidently believe the things I have said. You will suffer no danger from this faith; indeed, you will find much benefit in it. But if you do not believe, you will perish eternally in your unbelief.

I say “confidently” because you will suffer no danger from the faith that I preach: holy men who lived before us, whose holiness is proclaimed and glorified throughout the world, were saved in this faith. We read that the holy apostles and apostolic Fathers celebrated in the faith by which they believed that they consecrated and received the body and blood of the Lord, and gave them to others.

XVI. It is recorded that this unbelief concerning Christ’s body, in which you are ensnared, once increased even among the Roman people and occupied a great part of the city in the time of Pope Gregory. As he prayed for the people’s unbelief, and during the solemn rites of Mass, according to custom, offered bread and wine upon God’s altar and pronounced the customary blessings, he obtained this from God through prayer: that the Lord’s flesh should appear there as it was, and that what had previously been there in the appearance of bread should be shown to those present in the appearance of flesh. Thus the people were freed from this unbelief.

We read of Saint Martin, bishop of Tours, who was held to be no less than the holy apostles, that while he offered in church the sacraments of the body and blood of the Lord, a ball of fire appeared above his head. This sign was unquestionably from God: in it God showed the merit of the holy man and honored the holiness of his office. He would by no means have done this if Martin’s faith had been false and empty—the faith with which he stood at the divine altar and believed the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ to be present in his hands.

You may therefore confidently follow such men in the faith in which they went before us and which we have in the books they left behind. Your Manes remains in hell; they remain in heaven. Flee Manes and hell; follow these men with us, that together with them we may remain forever. May Jesus Christ deign to grant this—he who lives and reigns as God with God the Father and the Holy Spirit, through all ages of ages.

## SERMON XII. Against the Ninth Heresy, concerning the Savior’s Humanity

[Col. 0094C]

I. I think I have built an edifice without a foundation. For those who know you well say that you deny the Savior’s humanity. If this is so, I have wasted my labor in disputing with you about the body and blood of the Lord. Yet it is not incredible to me that mad teachers have mad disciples. For Manes, the chief source of your error, taught that our Savior appeared in such a way in humanity that he seemed to be a man but was not truly a man; that he was neither truly born of the Virgin, nor truly suffered, nor truly died, nor was truly raised from death. The two magicians Zoroe and Arphaxat are likewise recorded to have taught this before him in Persia.

If in this error you follow him rather than the holy Gospels—of which you boast that you alone know and observe them—you are unquestionably either blind or mad. You are blind if you do not understand in them Christ’s humanity, which is plainly proclaimed there; but you are mad if you do understand it truly and yet dare, with stubborn mind, to contradict the evangelists. If you were Jews, perhaps I would undertake a lengthy argument with you on this matter from the Law and the Prophets. But since you profess to be Christians and, as you say, read and know the Gospels, indignation does not allow me to labor against you in a lengthy discourse on this point.

For you plainly read there that he endured in his flesh the same weaknesses of human nature that other people naturally suffer. He hungered and thirsted, was weary from the journey, slept, wept, and was sorrowful, as the evangelists testify—whom, I suppose, you do not dare to call liars. But if he did not truly possess the substance of flesh, but only some shadowy semblance of a human body, these things could in no way have been true of him.

II. Perhaps you say that, because he made himself seem to hunger, thirst, and undergo all the other things we have mentioned, the evangelists spoke of him in this way in order to express those gestures of his simulation in such words. Sons of Belial! With what audacity do you impute the duplicity of pretence to the simple Lamb, falsehood to the Truth that is God? He testified that he possessed a true body and soul; with what recklessness do you say that he had neither, and judge the deceitful Manichaean more worthy of belief in this matter than the truthful God?

He testified that he had a true body when he said to his disciples: “See my hands and my feet, that it is I myself. Touch me and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have.” And when he had said this, he showed them his hands and feet (Luke 24). After this, when they offered him a piece of broiled fish and a honeycomb to eat, he ate before them. He also showed that he possessed a soul in saying, when his passion was imminent: “My soul is sorrowful unto death” (Matt. 26). Likewise when he said: “I have power to lay down my soul, and power to take it up again” (John 10).

Why then do you doubt, unhappy Cathar, that he possessed true humanity, when from his own words you can understand that he possessed a true human body and soul? If you doubt that he assumed a body from the Virgin’s womb, run, wretched man, to Luke’s Gospel, where the angel’s words to Mary are read in this form: “Behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son” (Luke 1). “In your womb,” he says, so that you may understand that he assumed flesh from the very flesh of the virginal womb and not from elsewhere.

You can likewise understand this from the words which, as Matthew writes, the angel spoke to Joseph: “Joseph, son of David, do not fear to take Mary your wife; for what is born in her is from the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 1). “In her,” he says, lest you should think that he brought forth something shadowy rather than true flesh from his mother’s womb, or that he assumed a body from some source other than her. Thus the unhappy Valentinian said that Christ brought a body from heaven into his mother’s womb and passed through her into this world as through a pipe; or, as the heretic Apelles said, that he assumed a body not from heaven but from the air, which he brought forth from the Virgin.

The Apostle’s statement also pertains to this same point: “God sent his Son, made from a woman, made under the Law” (Gal. 4). “Made from a woman,” he says, so that you may understand that the substance of his body was fashioned from the substance of virginal flesh.

III. From the testimonies already cited, if you possess any soundness of mind, you can understand that Christ was born in true flesh. That he suffered and died in true flesh is most evident from many testimonies of Scripture; for the present, one passage from John’s Gospel, offered in place of many, will suffice. At the end of the Lord’s passion he says: “One of the soldiers pierced his side with a lance, and immediately blood and water came out. And he who saw it has borne witness, and his testimony is true; and he knows that he speaks the truth, so that you too may believe. For these things happened so that the Scripture might be fulfilled: ‘You shall not break a bone of him.’ And again another Scripture says: ‘They shall look on him whom they pierced’” (John 19).

Observe that he says blood and water came out; he testifies that he saw this, and emphatically affirms that he knows he speaks the truth of the matter, so that there can be no doubt whatever that Christ possessed the reality of bodily substance. For if he had had a phantom body—if there had been in him no true flesh, but only an empty and shadowy likeness of flesh, as your Manichaean lied—blood and water could no more have flowed from his body when pierced by the lance than from a struck wind.

That he also rose in the same flesh in which he was born and suffered is clear from the words I cited above, which he said after his resurrection while showing his hands and feet to his disciples, and from what he said to doubting Thomas. If what I have said can suffice to prove to you the truth of the human nature that was in Christ Jesus, let it suffice. But if not, let the unhappy Cathar remain with his Manes in his lies: “Let him who is filthy be filthy still” (Rev. 22), and let him flow onward into the destruction of those who speak falsehood.

## SERMON XIII. Against the Tenth Heresy, concerning Human Souls

[Col. 0096C]

I. I do not know whether the heresy that I ranked above as the tenth among the others is general among the people of this sect, because in many matters they disagree among themselves, so that what is asserted by some of them is denied by others. I speak of the heresy by which they say that human souls are nothing other than those apostate spirits who fell from God’s kingdom at the beginning of the world, and that these spirits can merit salvation in human bodies—but only among those who belong to their sect.

This is not read among the errors of Manichaeus, though another no less serious error concerning souls is found there. For this reason I am uncertain, as I said, whether these people generally hold this error or not. But whether this is so or not, although this discourse pertains to great mercy and ought rightly to be restrained by no arguments other than rod and staff, it nevertheless befits us to give rational answers even to madmen. This error, however, is so abominable and so contrary to human reason that I have no great fear that the simpler people could easily be led into it. Therefore I do not propose to undertake much labor in this part, but shall bring a brief refutation against these senseless people.

II. Since ancient times it has belonged to the common faith, and the sacred writings testify, that God created the human race in order to restore from it the number of angels in the heavenly court who fell from it at the beginning of the world. But after the human race too fell into sin through the devil’s envy and was expelled from paradise in its first parents, the Son of God became man in these last times in order to free the human race from its sins and from the devil’s power, and thus still accomplish in it what he had proposed: namely, to restore the heavenly court from it and fill the number of his angels, diminished by the fall of those who had been cast from heaven because of their pride.

Do you who are from paradise believe this? If you do not, behold, I shall cite to you words of the apostle Paul from which you may understand that it is as I have said. In the epistle he wrote to the Ephesians, he says at one point concerning God the Father: “He made us acceptable in his beloved Son, in whom we have redemption through his blood, and forgiveness of sins, according to the riches of his grace, which abounded in us in all wisdom and prudence, that he might make known to us the mystery of his will, according to his good pleasure which he purposed in him: in the dispensation of the fullness of times, to restore all things in Christ, things in heaven and things on earth in him” (Eph. 1).

Observe, then, in this discourse that he says God the Father purposed to restore in Christ all things that are in heaven and all things that are on earth. “All things on earth in him,” that is, in his predestination and election—all elect human beings—God purposed to restore in Christ, that is, through Christ. Likewise, “all things in heaven,” that is, the entire number of angels, diminished by the fall of the fallen spirits, he purposed [Col. 0097C] to restore through Christ: so that the human race might be redeemed through him, and the number of elect human beings might be placed in the place of angels, and thus the heavenly court might return to the wholeness of its fullness in which it was first established.

For if that number of God’s servants, which he created at the beginning for the praise of his name, is not restored through Christ, then not all things in heaven are restored through Christ. But if that number is filled through him, so that as many people are saved as angels fell—or more, as some assert—and if souls are nothing other than those spirits that fell, it must necessarily be granted that all fallen angels and all human beings are to be saved. Who, then, will be the angels to whom the Lord will say at the last day, and who will be the human beings to whom he will say: “Go, cursed ones, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25)? Do you not recognize here too that you are liars?

III. Now understand, you senseless ones, your foolishness; and you foolish people, at last become wise (Ps. 93). Recognize that the Son of God did not descend from heaven to redeem demons from eternal death, but human beings, who are not demons, though their struggle is “against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavens”—that is, against malignant spirits. These spirits do not, as you say, govern our bodies; rather, they continually strive to destroy us both in body and soul. He did not come to save malignant spirits, but to torment them, as they themselves confessed when they cried out to him from the bodies of possessed people: “What have we to do with you, Son of God? Have you come before the time to torment us?” (Matt. 8).

IV. Let it suffice that I have argued this far concerning these matters. If I have said anything insufficiently, let a prudent defender of truth add whatever seems fitting to him for the defense of the Catholic faith, so that the most wicked little foxes which destroy the Lord’s vineyard may be driven away from it. And if I seem to have said anything simply and somewhat roughly, the reader should not despise me for this, because I did so in order that the discourse might everywhere be intelligible to simple people. Their edification was my chief concern in writing these things, to the praise and honor of Jesus Christ, our God and Lord, to whom belong enduring glory and power in heaven and on earth, unto ages of ages. Amen.

Whoever copies this book for the defense of the Catholic faith and carefully corrects the writing, may God write his name in the book of life. I ask the copyist also to add these words to his text and not neglect to append at the end of his book the extract which follows.

[Col. 0097]

## EXTRACT CONCERNING THE MANICHAEANS FROM ST AUGUSTINE

[Col. 0097D] I. Manes, who was also called Manichaeus by his disciples in order to avoid the name of madness, was Persian by nation. Coming into Greek regions, he asserted that he was the Paraclete Spirit whom the Lord Jesus promised to send to the apostles. He chose twelve of his disciples and called them apostles, in imitation of the Lord Jesus. The Manichaeans still preserve this number today. For among their Elect they have twelve whom they call masters, and a thirteenth who is their chief; seventy-two bishops, who are ordained by the masters; and presbyters, who are ordained by the bishops. They have their deacons, and all these are called Elect among them. The rest, who have not yet risen to these ranks, are merely Hearers. From all of them, those considered suitable are sent out to sustain and enlarge their error where it exists, or to sow it where it does not.

[Col. 0099A] II. The doctrine that they received from their heresiarch is as follows. They deny that God is the creator of all things, but maintain that there are two principles of things, one good and the other evil, coeternal with and opposed to one another. They affirm that the good principle is God; but the evil principle, they believe, is a certain monstrous prince of darkness, from whom every body derives its origin.

They say that human souls, the vital spirit of all living creatures, and the force that gives life to trees, plants, and seeds originate from God—indeed, they insist that each such thing is a part of God. For they believe that the divine substance is mixed into every kind of body. They assert that this mixture occurred for the following reason.

[Col. 0099B] III. At the beginning, Manichaeus says, there were two substances separated from each other: namely, two distinct, opposed, and coeternal kingdoms, the kingdom of light and the kingdom of darkness. The Father God possessed the kingdom of light. Manichaeus also called this the good substance, or good, unchangeable, and altogether inviolable nature; and he confessed that it was nothing other than God.

But, he says, beside one side of that bright and holy land there was an immeasurable expanse of darkness. He called this the evil substance, or evil smoke, or evil nature. He divided it into five elements: smoke, darkness, fire, water, and wind; and called these five evil natures. He said that in each were born deadly and utterly evil monsters: bipeds in smoke, from whose inhabitants he also said human beings originate; crawling creatures in darkness; quadrupeds in fire; swimming creatures in waters; and flying creatures in wind. He said that each kind remained in its own element, and called all these the race of darkness.

IV. In this land, he says, there lived a certain monstrous prince, with countless princes around him; he himself was the leader and source of them all. He places his seat in the element of smoke. Since this land with its inhabitants was exceedingly destructive and opposed to God’s kingdom, lest it perhaps inflict some injury upon God’s kingdom, God determined to conquer it and restrain its malice by some counterbalancing measure. Therefore he sent from his own kingdom five other elements which he had fashioned from his own substance, and mixed these five with those five evils, one with one: air with smoke, light with darkness, good fire with evil fire, good water with evil water, and good wind with evil wind.

[Col. 0099D] V. When this mixture of good nature with evil had occurred, there arose from those five kinds of living beings, distinguished above, all the kinds of living beings that we see on earth, so that individual kinds came from individual kinds. From that time, they say, all animals possess a part of the good nature and a part of the evil nature, because they were born after the mixture of good and evil.

By this reasoning they assert that Adam and Eve were born from the princes of smoke, [Col. 0100A] and that their father, named Saclas, as they say, devoured the offspring of all his companions. Because a great part of the divine substance was mixed into those offspring, they say that he possessed a very great part of the good nature and a small part of the evil. Since he lived holily because of the overflowing abundance of good, nevertheless the adverse part of evil was stirred in him and inclined him to sexual intercourse. Thus he fell and sinned, but afterwards lived more holily.

They say that certain heavenly powers have been appointed by God for this purpose: that, traveling throughout the whole world, they gradually cleanse that good nature from the evil with which it is mixed; and when cleansed, place it upon two ships and convey it to its own kingdoms. They say that these ships are fashioned from the pure substance of God, and that they are the sun and moon. They say that the moon is made from good water, and the sun from good fire. Therefore they pray to the sun by day, wherever it travels in its course; but to the moon by night if it appears, and, if it does not appear, to the north, because the sun, when it sets, returns to the east.

VI. In imitation of the heavenly spirits, their Elect likewise say that they cleanse that good nature from the evil while they eat or drink. For whatever of the good nature is mixed into foods and drinks, they say, is liberated in their stomach, and they themselves convey it to the heavenly regions with prescribed rites. Whatever of the evil nature is there goes to the privy.

They do this with all grains, fruits, and seeds. For they say that a portion of that good nature is also mixed into the earth. When it exhales and strives to return upward to its proper seats, it enters plants and trees through their roots; and thus it happens that it is held and prevented in them from ascending. This is why they do not farm: they regard uprooting or cutting plants or trees as a kind of homicide. They likewise consider it unlawful to pluck leaves or fruits. For they assert that certain holy souls possessing intelligence are in these things; that they suffer severely when these are injured, and are expelled when they are cut off.

They suppose that the souls of their Hearers pass into the Elect or into trees. Consequently they venerate all trees so greatly that they do not dare even pull thorns from fields. Yet they allow their Hearers to do these things, so that they may obtain their livelihood through them. They consider lending at interest far more permissible than cultivating fields.

VII. They are so intent, as stated, upon carefully cleansing that good nature in every seed by eating that they do not shrink from tasting human semen mixed into the flour of their bread; but they conceal this most vigorously. Yet this shamefulness of theirs was discovered at Carthage through two girls in separate places, at the compulsion of the tribune Ursus, so that neither knew the other had revealed it. One, named Margareta, not yet twelve years old, confessed that she had been violated for the sake of this supposedly heavenly mystery. The other, named Eusebia, a Manichaean and apparently a woman religious, at first denied it; but at last, with difficulty compelled, confessed the same of herself and exposed the whole of that most disgraceful crime.

Not all are said to do this, however, but certain of those called Catharists—that is, “purifiers.” The sect is divided into three parts: Catharists, Mattharians, and those who are specifically called Manichaeans, although all observe Manichaeus’ teaching. They judge all meats unclean and do not eat them. For they say that when any animal is killed, the part of the divine substance which was in its body immediately flies away, and that all which remains is unclean, because it came from sexual intercourse, is the handiwork of the race of darkness, and defiles the eater.

They nevertheless permit their Hearers to eat meat, but entirely forbid them to kill animals. For they say that the individual princes of the race of darkness possess their own animals on earth, descended from their own race and stock; they hold the animals’ killers guilty and do not permit them to depart this world until they have first crushed them, insofar as possible, with punishments. They do not consume even eggs, on the ground that when these too are broken, they expire; nor do they use milk as nourishment, although it is milked from the body of a living animal.

VIII. They do not drink wine, saying that it is the gall of the princes of darkness. They do, however, drink *carenum*, which is nothing other than concentrated wine. They eat grapes and abominate must, saying that the divine substance is put to flight when grapes are pressed—though they say that it flees from things in many ways. It flees, they say, when grain and fruit are gathered; it flees when they are crushed, ground, cooked, or eaten; it flees in every movement of animals, whether they frolic or labor; it even flees in digestion itself. They invent many exceedingly shameful things about such matters.

They forbid giving alms from anything which they themselves eat to a begging non-Manichaean, so that they will not even offer water to one in the utmost necessity, lest the member of God mixed into these things pass into that person and, defiled by that person’s sins, be hindered from returning. Consequently they are often compelled to eat beyond measure, and to kill their own little children by excessive gluttony, lest their foods either be given to others or perish in their own possession—both of which they consider unlawful.

[Col. 0102A] IX. Wives are forbidden to their Elect but permitted to their Hearers. The Hearers, however, are most earnestly warned that, if they have intercourse with their wives, they must by whatever art they can avoid conception and generation, lest the divine substance, which enters them through food, be bound by fleshly bonds in offspring. For they believe that the soul descends into every fetus through the food and drink of its parents. Thus they unquestionably condemn marriage, since they forbid generation, the purpose for which marriages are contracted.

They say that the Lord Jesus came to earth to free souls, not bodies; that he was not born of the Virgin and was not in true flesh, but displayed a simulated appearance of flesh to deceive human senses, in which he feigned not only death but also resurrection. Therefore they celebrate our Pascha either carelessly or not at all. Instead, they observe a certain feast which they call the *Bema*, that is, the day on which their Manichaeus was killed.

They say that the God who gave the Law through Moses and spoke through the prophets was not the true God, but one of the princes of darkness. They say that our Lord Jesus Christ’s promise concerning the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, was fulfilled in their heresiarch Manichaeus—namely, that he himself was the Paraclete Spirit. Hence in his writings he calls himself an apostle of Jesus Christ. They say that baptism in water benefits no one unto salvation. They attribute the origin of sins not to the free choice of the will, but to the substance of the hostile race, which they say is mixed with human beings.

They say that there are two souls in one person, a good and an evil, which contend with one another when the flesh desires against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh. They further assert that at the end of this age souls that are good by nature but have been unable to be cleansed from the contamination of evil nature will gather, as it were, into a single mass and be eternally condemned together with evil nature.

Here end the words gathered from Augustine’s books, which I promised at the beginning of this book to append to this work.

[Note: [Col. 0103C] Thus the codex.]

[Col. 0103]

## Eckbert, Abbot of Schönau: A Little Work in Praise of the Cross

(Dom Bernard Pez, *Bibliotheca ascetica antiquo-nova*, vol. VII, p. 13, from a manuscript codex of the illustrious Premonstratensian monastery of Windberg.)

# Praise of the Cross: Words of Eckbert

## I

[Col. 0103A]

Hail, Cross, sign of the living God, banner of the right hand of the Most High; hail, triumphant sign, saving sign, mighty and wondrous sign; hail, sign honorable to the heavenly beings, beloved by those on earth, terrible to those below. Hail, Cross, blessed sign, precious and chosen wood, fruitful wood above all the trees of the forests and above all the spices that have sprung from the earth since the world’s beginning. Blessed the root that bore you, but more blessed she who blessed you! O Cross, the root of your nobility is in the land of the living; it imparted divine power to you and caused you to surpass every dignity of trees. O splendid and noble wood, before whose dignity cedar and cypress, laurel and plane tree, [Col. 0103B] palm and olive, vine and fig tree and apple tree, cinnamon and balsam, myrrh and frankincense, storax and galbanum, stacte, cassia and terebinth, acacia woods, precious thyine wood from Ophir, and every tree beautiful to see, delightful in fragrance, sweet and health-giving in fruit, yield place. No tree of the paradise of God is comparable to you; no refined gold, no precious stone, can be compared with you.

## II

O Cross, more radiant than the sun, brighter than all the stars of the world to those who behold you with the gaze of faith and charity! O glorious and most holy sign! What a miracle is this which has occurred in you! Long ago your name was accursed and dreadful, and [Col. 0103C] you were a sign of condemnation and disgrace, assigned to thieves and murderers; but now you are a sign of glory and blessing. And behold: by a great and wondrous leap you have risen from the lowest of humankind to the highest heavens, so that you possess even the heads of kings, which ought to be honored. [Col. 0104A] Let impious Nero see and envy: behold, amid gold and precious stones the diadems of emperors admit you, O Cross, as their noblest ornament. Let jealous Judaea see, let stiff-necked paganism behold and waste away: behold, the necks of the proud and the knees of the lofty bend before you. O Cross, all God’s angels honor you on high; and among them only he is acceptable who comes marked with your stigma. O precious coin, known and loved only in the city of God! You possess worth in every way, for through you even the kingdom of God is acquired.

## III

Who, then, emptied you of disgrace? Who made you worthy of such great honors? Surely that man who is called Jesus is also the author of this miracle: he who alone works wonders—he himself, indeed he himself, did this thing, and no other: Jesus Christ, Son of the living God, Lord of heaven and earth. The sinful earth cast him out from itself; he mounted upon you, and you received him and bore the precious weight of his body. Then you were sanctified by the touch of his naked flesh and by the sprinkling of his most holy blood. For the nails which fastened his innocent hands and venerable feet to you drove that precious liquid into you; and the soldier’s lance, which opened that virginal side, sprinkled you with the stream of sacred blood and mystical water. Behold with what oil God, your consecrator, Jesus, the true and supreme high priest, anointed you: he anointed you, I say, above your companions, above all the trees [Col. 0104C] of the forests, so that you might be the holy altar of the true sacrifice wholly offered and most pleasing to the Lord. Truly you are a holy altar, because upon you was first offered for the salvation of the world the true sacrifice, the holy sacrifice, the unspotted and peace-making sacrifice, which alone could reconcile earthly things with heavenly. [Col. 0105A] You are the altar of precious incense, whose most sweet odor penetrated to heaven’s innermost places, delighted the heart of God Most High, and by its sweetness caused him to incline down to earth and be appeased concerning the wickedness of those who dwell upon it.

## IV

Your disgrace has in every respect been turned into its opposite, O Cross! You were an instrument of destruction, and have become an instrument of salvation. You ought to have taken life away, and you destroyed death. The prince of this world went forth armed through you to wage war against the Author of life; but Christ Jesus, our strong-handed champion, turned you back upon his head, struck down the sinner’s neck, and divided between him and the mass of humankind, of which he boasted that he was the head. [Col. 0105B] Thus his fall was great, and reproach was removed from Israel.

## V

Therefore, O instrument of great exultation and salvation, blessed Cross, chosen Cross, exceedingly pleasant and beloved Cross: the whole Church of the saints, sanctified through you in the name of Christ—who deigned to bear you on his own shoulders and to be borne by you—rightly honors you and exalts you with splendid praises. For if it is fitting that subjects honor kings’ thrones, scepters, or crowns out of reverence for those who are earth and ashes, how much more worthy are you, the scepter of the eternal King, to be honored and adored, to Christ’s glory, by every people of his possession, since through you he subjected the world to himself. [Col. 0105C] You are worthy, I say, to be adored—not indeed as God, but as the wondrous sign of power. If the footprints of the feet of our King and Lord are to be adored, why should you not rightly be adored, O Cross, which bears impressed upon you the traces not only of his feet, but also of his hands and of his whole sacred body? Truly we rightly raise suppliant hands before your holy sign, bow [Col. 0106A] our necks, bend our knees, and cast ourselves wholly upon the ground, in honor of him who, stretching out bloodied hands upon you, drew all things to himself; who, bowing his head upon you, gave up his spirit; whose lifeless knees were folded upon you in a mournful manner; whose little sacred body was stretched out wholly upon you.

## VI

O Cross, glory of the Christian brow; O T of propitiation, marked upon us by God’s hand! O unconquerable banner of Christian warfare! May Christ make you a faithful protection for me and for every believing person against every danger of soul and body. By the Lord’s grace, be for me an unconquerable shield [Col. 0106B] against the enemy’s fiery darts, against all his wiles; and mightily overcome on my behalf all the power of demons. Guard all the windows of my body, lest death enter through them into my soul; and may your power extinguish everything that is deadly to me.

## VII

At whatever hour, in whatever work, my hand raises you in the name of my Lord Christ, may he who sanctified you, the Lord Jesus, grant you swift effectiveness. Be, O Cross, a strong protection to my sinful soul on the day when it must be stripped of this mortal flesh, against the dreadful assaults of the most wicked spirits. Be for it a sweet shade against the burning fire of Gehenna’s flame, so that [Col. 0106C] unharmed it may be able to pass with free step to behold its Lord God in heaven: through him who was crucified upon you, Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns as God with God the Father and the Holy Spirit for ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0105]

# The Same Eckbert’s Soliloquy, or Meditations

(Dom Pez, ibid., p. 21, from Melk codices.)

## I

[Col. 0105D]

I have a word for you, O Jesus Christ, King of the ages: I, the work of your hands, longing for your beauty and eagerly desiring, with my heart’s desire, to draw near to you, presume in the boldness of charity to address you. How long shall I endure your absence? For how long shall I bear the waiting for your face? How long shall I groan [Note: [Col. 0105D] another codex: “he will groan” (*ingemiscet*)], and my eye drip after you? Beloved Lord, where do you dwell? [Col. 0106D] Where is your lodging, where you recline at table among your dearest ones and satisfy them with the manifestation of your glory? O how happy, how bright, how holy, how greatly to be desired is that place of divine delight, the place of everlasting pleasures! My eye has not reached it, nor has my heart approached the abundance of your sweetness, which you have hidden within for your children. By its fragrance alone, [Col. 0107A] outside, [Note: [Col. 0107] an ancient codex: *fortis* (“strong”), which is wholly absent from another, more recent codex.] I am somehow sustained. Its breath of sweetness [Note: [Col. 0107] another codex: “your sweetness.”] comes to me from afar; it is to me beyond the scent of balsam and the fragrance of frankincense and myrrh, and every kind [Note: [Col. 0107] another codex: “sweet perfumes.”] of sweet perfumes, and it produces in me pure desires, whose tasting is sweet, though scarcely drinkable. For what have I in heaven? Who is my treasure in that heavenly chamber? What is my inheritance in the land of the living? Is it not Christ, my Lord, my only salvation, my entire good, my full joy? And how, Lord, shall I restrain my heart from loving you? If I do not love you, what shall I love? If I transfer my love away from you, where shall I worthily place it? Desirable Lord, where outside you shall my desires rest? If my love stretches a foot anywhere [Col. 0107B] outside you, it will be defiled; if my desires turn away from you [Note: [Col. 0107] another codex: “if they do not turn toward you.”], they will be vain. Are you not lovable and desirable above everything that can be loved or desired?

## II

For every creature has from you whatever beauty and value it possesses. And what wonder if you alone surpass all things? [Note: [Col. 0107] another codex: “excel.”] You clothed the sun among the stars with surpassing brightness, and you are brighter than the sun. Indeed, what are the sun, all creation, even light itself, except darkness [Note: [Col. 0107] another codex: “shadow.”] in comparison with you? You adorned heaven with stars, the Empyrean with angels, the air with birds, the waters with fish, the earth with lilies [Note: [Col. 0107] another codex: “the earth with flowers.”], flowers, and shrubs. Yet no form or beauty belongs to all these things in comparison with you. [Col. 0107C] O Jesus, fountain of all beauty! You gave honey its sweetness, and you are sweeter than honey; you gave oil its pleasantness, and you are more pleasant than oil; you breathed their fragrances into all spices, and, O Jesus, your fragrance is sweeter and more pleasing than all spices.

## III

Among metals gold was created by you beautiful in price and in unique excellence; but what is it in comparison with your inestimable and immeasurable brightness, Lord, into which angels long to look? Every precious and desirable stone is the work of your hands: sardius and topaz, jasper and chrysolite, onyx and beryl, sapphire and carbuncle and emerald. And what [Col. 0107D] are these except straws in comparison with you? O King exceedingly beautiful and greatly to be loved, your works are living and immortal gems, with which, O wise architect, at the beginning of the ages you beautifully adorned the super-aetherial hall for the praise and glory of the Father. Through you, thousands of thousands continually move in eager course to fulfill the Father’s ministries; and, between heaven and earth, like busy bees among [Note: [Col. 0107] another codex: “within.”] hives and flowers, they order all things sweetly—a girded people [Col. 0108A] knowing no stain, knowing no delay of disobedience. Through you, a hundred times ten thousand thousands stand in the sanctuary of the heavenly temple, directing their clear and unturned [Note: [Col. 0107] another codex: “unreflected.”] gaze toward the face of your Majesty and sounding the harmony of an unceasing hymn to the glory of the triune and simple Divinity [Note: [Col. 0107] another reading: “Deity.”].

## IV

Through you the seraphim burn; through you the cherubim shine; through you the thrones judge. You, our God, are a fire that burns harmlessly; and the holy order of seraphim is wholly kindled with charity and clothed in flaming radiance through immediate nearness to your divinity. It also scatters the fragrant sweetness of its pleasing fire over the other ministering ranks who serve you below it, from whose abundance we too somehow taste. [Col. 0108B] You, our God, are true light, and from you the mountains receive light for your people. The treasures of wisdom and knowledge hidden in you, you yourself pour abundantly into the eyes of the cherubim that behold you closely; and through them you cause these treasures to be conveyed to illuminate the subordinate electrum lamps of your wondrous tabernacle, which shine unquenchably before your face, Lord. You, King of kings and Judge of judges, great and terrible, sit upon the lofty and exalted thrones, which have only your own height above them—living, sweet, utterly peaceful seats, joined together in the uniformity of supreme tranquility. Through you they discern hidden truths; through you they judge with righteous judgment.

## V

[Col. 0108C]

O Lord, ruler over rulers, the holy eminence of the ruling orders adores you, extending its mind with singular freedom into the divine; and among the very noble heroes of your court, through you exercising primacy of high lordship without the loftiness of pride. Noble splendor of the principalities: through you the exalted order of Principalities rules with no envious superiority over the host of heaven, to which, for carrying out divine ministries in accordance with the dispensation conceived inwardly in your heart, it provides the leadership of gentle mastery. Yours is the power of the Powers, Lord, who with fiery zeal press down the necks of Tartarean princes; and in them these princes fear you, lest they be able to accomplish as much evil for our destruction as they wish. [Note: [Col. 0107] other codices: “that they may not be able to accomplish whatever evil they wish.”]

## VI

[Col. 0108D] Yours, O power of the Father, is all the wonder-working might of the blessed Virtues, by whose ministry it comes about that every age marvels and, astonished at your wonders, cries out and says: “Whatever the Lord willed, he did in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the deeps” (Psalm 134). Yours, O Jesus, is the magnificence of the archangels, in whom your kindness works a deed of great condescension, since you do not disdain to send such glorious satraps of your palace to the farthest bounds of this [Col. 0109A] world to aid our littleness—we who are compared with mud and likened to ash and dust. For by these, at your command, the greatest concerns of our salvation are administered; through them the deepest secrets of the heavenly counsel are brought to us; through them the healing of mortals is procured; through them the kingdoms and empires of the world endure. Among them we recognize as preeminent your Michael, the noble standard-bearer of heaven, who stands for the battle-line of the living God, extending the sword of defense and thundering in a terrifying voice: “Who is like God?” against those who stand opposed.

## VII

And is not that lovely innocence of the blessed angels a precious work of your fingers, O Wisdom of God? With it you adorned them as with incorruptible clothing on the day you created them for the work of your sacred ministry. These are the living stars of the higher heaven, the lilies of the inner paradise, roses planted above the waters of Siloam, which flow silently, fixed immovably in minds [Note: [Col. 0109] another codex: “in mountains.”]. O river of peace! O field of delights! O Wisdom alone, encompassing heaven’s circuit! From you they shine, gleam, and glow [Note: [Col. 0109] the words “in” are lacking in the manuscripts.] in abundant wisdom, in virginal chastity, in the everlasting ardors [Note: [Col. 0109] another codex: “in everlasting ardor.”] of charity. This is your flowering youth, Lord, faithfully serving you in our weakness: while amid these world-darknesses it directs our steps with pedagogical [Note: [Col. 0109] another codex: “guiding.”] guidance; while it repels hostile assaults from us; while it announces the secrets of your will; while it strengthens minds loosened from every good; while [Col. 0109C] it carries the incense of our prayers to the golden altar and continually entreats the countenance of the merciful Father for us.

## VIII

Thus, Father, you still have some care even for us who remain far off. And if this tenth drachma, once slipped from your bosom and now at last sought amid labors, has any value, that comes from your merciful gift, good Jesus. If this tenth string has any sweet-sounding voice for the Lord’s praise, your pleasant touch produces it in that string, while you play the Father’s glory upon the ten-stringed psaltery. Play, as you play, Lord; make sweet melody to the Father with the swift fingers of manifold graces. Touch those nine most pure strings in heaven, which never sounded anything sad. [Col. 0109D] Touch also this heavy tenth one, whose upper part, indeed, now touched, resounds joy to you, while its lower part, still bound to earth, knows how to yield mournful sounds.

## IX

When I consider with attentive mind all the works of your power, O Only-Begotten of God, I am amazed and afraid, because in them you appear glorious in every way. They are great, beautiful, and very good; but in comparison with you they are reckoned as almost nothing and emptiness. Heaven and earth and all their adornment subsist through you as author and governor, and all proclaim you mighty and [Col. 0110A] terrible, wise and beautiful, good and lovable. And as light surpasses darkness, so you alone surpass all things. You are kept for me in heaven, my Lord; you are your servant’s reward, yourself both the giver and the gift of salvation, for which my soul waits from you. And what did I desire from you upon earth except you alone? What did I judge better and more lovable than you, so that I might draw my heart away from you to desire anything in the world apart from you? Woe is me, miserable man! Why did I love, why did I desire during all my life anything besides Christ Jesus my Lord? Why did I delay, why did I at any time fail to keep you, Jesus, dwelling in my heart, to embrace you with my whole mind, and to delight all the inner parts of my spirit in your sweetness? Where was I [Note: [Col. 0109] another codex: “were.”] when I was not with you in mind? Into what did my desires flow away when they heard not you alone? [Col. 0110B]

## X

God of my life, how vainly my times have been spent, how fruitlessly they have slipped away from me—the times you gave me in order that I might do your will in them, and I did not! How many years, how many days and hours have perished for me, in which I lived fruitlessly before you! And how shall I stand? How shall I be able to raise my eyes to your face in that great examination of yours, when you command all my times to be recalled and demand the fruit of each one? Most patient Father! Let this not happen; rather, let my times—alas, far too many—which I wasted vainly pass into oblivion before you. And if I have, with your help, preserved any usefully—whose number, O Lord, is brief—let them remain in everlasting remembrance. [Col. 0110C] Make, beloved Father, at least this remainder of my time fruitful and sanctified in your grace, so that it may find a place in the days of eternity and be reckoned forever before you.

## XI

Now henceforth, all my desires, grow warm and flow forth into Jesus, my Lord; run! You have delayed long enough until now. Hasten where you are going; seek him whom you seek. Do you seek Jesus of Nazareth, crucified? He has ascended into heaven; he is not here. He is not where he was; he is not where he had no place in which to lay his noble head. He is not where he walked amid tribulation, much filled [Col. 0110D] with contempt. He is not where he stood to be judged before Pilate’s face. He is not where he stood despised and mocked before Herod. He is not where he went forth spat upon, beaten, wounded, and drenched with blood. He is not where he hung among criminals. He is not where he lay shut beneath a stone and guarded by a soldiery of the Gentiles. But where is the most loving Lord? He dwells in confidence, and scourge shall not come near his dwelling-place. By his own power he has ascended above the height of the heavens, above every excellence of angels; he sits upon the throne of unique glory at the right hand of the Father, with whom he is coeternal and consubstantial, clothed in divine [Col. 0111A] light, crowned with glory and honor—as is fitting for the Only-Begotten Son of God—serene [Note: [Col. 0111] another codex: “second.”] in joy, full of omnipotence, ruling in heaven and on earth.

## XII

There all God’s angels and the whole multitude of citizens of heavenly Zion adore him. In him the hearts of all rejoice with one accord; upon his desirable face the eyes of all the blessed feed. Toward him the desires of every individual flow from every side; to him the whole heavenly court gives jubilation and applause; him it magnifies—the glorious city, in every respect amid the splendors of his glory. Rejoice and praise, dwelling-place of Zion, because the Holy One of Israel is great in your midst. Rejoice in Jesus, your noble son, illustrious patriarchs, because in him all your expectation has been fulfilled. And [Col. 0111B] behold, he is exceedingly exalted, and in him—that is, in your seed—all nations are blessed, as the divine word promised you long ago. Rejoice in the great Prophet, you prophets, truthful men, because you see all that you announced concerning him in the Holy Spirit wonderfully and gloriously fulfilled, and because through him you have been found faithful in all your sayings. Rejoice in Jesus, your Lord and Master, illustrious princes of heaven, blessed apostles. Rejoice in him and with him in intimate gladness. For behold: him whom you saw among yourselves hungry, thirsty, weary, and enduring similar weaknesses of flesh; him whom you saw reproached [Note: [Col. 0111] another reading: “rejected.”] by human beings and numbered with criminals—see how he conquered, how he reigns, how all things are beneath his feet, how [Col. 0111C] gloriously he shines in his divine light, and how he now has you as companions of his joy and ineffable glory, you who once remained with him in his temptations and shared his afflictions. Adore now those sweet knees which bent down before you to the ground while you sat at the most sacred supper. Adore now those most sacred hands with which the King of kings deigned to wash and wipe away the dust from your feet.

## XIII

Rejoice in Jesus, the commander of your warfare, victorious martyrs, because behold, you possess Jesus himself, the Son of God, for whose sake you surrendered your souls to death—Jesus himself, I say, the reward of your contest. Rejoice in Jesus, teacher [Note: [Col. 0111] another codex: “ornament.”] of truth, venerable confessors, because he whom you once confessed before humankind by sacred teachings and righteous deeds now confesses you before his Father and his holy angels. Rejoice in Jesus, the Virgin and sanctifier of virgins, you virgins dwelling in paradise, you most like the angels, because behold, him whom you loved, whom you desired, whom you sought with burning longings, and for whose love you despised earthly spouses and every adornment [Note: [Col. 0111] another codex: “all adornments.”] of the world—the Son of the supreme King—you now see, now hold, now rest in his chaste embraces, and no deceitfulness of the deceiver can [Col. 0112A] tear him away from you.

## XIV

But to whom among the inhabitants of heaven belongs more abundant joy than to you, O Mary ever-virgin, Virgin of virgins, unique Virgin, rose of heavenly loveliness, radiant image (*agalma*) among the primeval lights able to receive the divine light? Therefore in your Jesus rejoice alone above all others with exceedingly great joy, because him whom you bore as a human being and nourished at your own breasts, you now adore as the living [Note: [Col. 0111] another codex: “one.”] and true God with the angels and all the citizens of heaven. Rejoice, blessed Mary, because him whom you saw hanging on the wood, you see reigning in heaven with great glory; you see every height of heavenly beings, earthly beings, and beings below bowing to [Col. 0112B] his majesty, and all the strength of his enemies crushed.

## XV

May the joy of joys be yours, all fullness of the saints, O blessed Jerusalem, our mother who are above. Celebrate a joyful and unfailing feast in the vision of your peace-making Jesus Christ, the author of your freedom.

## XVI

And now, my soul, raise yourself upward with whatever effort you can, and join yourself to the sacred thousands rejoicing in the Lord Jesus. Go there by the vehicle of faith and hope; dwell continually there through charity’s ardor, where Christ sits at God’s right hand. Direct the eye of your mind toward his lights. Survey and kiss with thankful devotion [Col. 0112C] each place [Note: [Col. 0111] another codex: “wounds.”] of his blessed wounds, from which flowed those precious liquids of sacred blood by which God’s Only-Begotten both purchased you at a price and sanctified you for eternal life. O Jesus, let him who does not love you be accursed; let him who does not love you be filled with bitterness. Your love, Lord, is chaste and admits no impurity; the savor of your love is sober and estranges no mind from what is right; your love is sweet and has nothing bitter in it [Note: [Col. 0111] another codex: “with no admixture of bitterness.”]. For it sweetens even the world’s bitter things [Note: [Col. 0111] another reading: “makes sweet.”], and renders its sweet things bitter. It is not constrained amid narrowness, not crushed amid pressures; it does not perish under want, nor is it contracted by sorrow; in labors it remains even-tempered, amid threats secure, in persecution [Col. 0112D] most secure, amid flatteries incorrupt, amid torments it persists unconquered, and in death it is always alive.

## XVII

As the greedy person rejoices in hidden treasure, and as a mother delights in the love of an only son, so there is joy and grateful delight for the soul to embrace you, Jesus, in your charity. O Jesus, to one who loves you, sweetness of honey, pleasantness of milk, intoxicating savor of wine: all delights do not please the palates of those who taste them as your love pleases the minds of those who taste you. O Jesus, living bread, [Col. 0113A] desirable cluster of grapes, sweet wine, gentle lamb, strong lion, beautiful panther, simple dove, swift eagle, morning star, eternal sun, angel of peace, fountain-light of everlasting lights: may every good sense, fitting to your praise, love you, seek you, delight in you, and marvel at you. God of my heart and my portion, Christ Jesus! Through you may my heart fail from its own spirit, and my flesh from its own desires; and may you live in me. May the glowing coal of your love grow warm in my spirit and grow into a perfect fire. May your grace cherish and nourish it within me, so that it may burn continually upon my heart’s altar; may it boil in my marrow, blaze in the hidden places of my soul, so that on the day of my consummation [Note: [Col. 0113] another codex: “death.”] it may be found perfected before you.
