On the day when you command me to strip off this mortal tunic [Col. 0113B] which I now bear about, may your visitation guard me; may your love [Note: [Col. 0113] another reading: “delight.”] surround me, and become for my soul as a garment of your beauty, so that it may be found not naked but clothed, so that its weaknesses may have something under which to be hidden from your eyes.

## XVIII

May the ardor of your love remove far from me the alien fire—the fire which consumes your adversaries; may it raise my soul [Note: [Col. 0113] another codex: “may it raise my soul as it runs upward toward you.”] to its Creator and, insofar as is permitted, immerse it in your divine light. Lord Jesus, may all who love you be filled with your blessings; may those who draw near to you be written in heaven, and may peace be theirs in the shelter of your wings forever. But to you, Only-Begotten of God, with the eternal Father and the Holy Spirit, be unceasing praise, unshaken splendor, and enduring kingdom, remaining for ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0113]

# The Same Eckbert’s *Stimulus of Love*

(It appears among the works of St Bernard. See *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXXIV.)

# Concerning Saint Elizabeth, Virgin and Mistress of the Sisters of the Order of St Benedict at Schönau in the Diocese of Trier

(*Acta Sanctorum* of the Bollandists, June, vol. III, 18 June, p. 604.)

[Col. 0113]

The age, visions, and life of the holy virgin; Eckbert as her writer; Emicho is also praised; the origin of her cult in the present Roman [Martyrology].

[Col. 0113C] 1. The little river Millus skirts the western boundary of the county of Cattimillebocensis in Rhenish Germany, commonly called Catzenelleboghen. This boundary looks toward the Rhine at a distance of about two leagues. The river received part of its name from the remnants of the ancient Chatti who lived there; flowing into the Lahn near Nassau, it loses its name before it is carried into the Rhine by that river and together with it. At the source of this little river, five and a half centuries ago, a noble abbey of the Benedictine order was founded. From the beauty of its situation it received the German name Schönau. Concerning its origin, our Brower writes thus in his annals under the year 1125:

> “At this time the diocese of Trier was enlarged by the new and celebrated monastery of Schönau. Begun on the estate of the counts of Laurenburg, beyond the Rhine and sixteen Roman miles opposite Bingen, by a wealthy man named Hilduin, it was later completed by Count Robert of Laurenburg and dedicated to Blessed Florinus, whose sacred ashes distinguish it. Hildelin was the monastery’s first superior. At a stone’s throw away he likewise established another monastery of the same name for virgins, in which Elizabeth of Schönau later became famous: a virgin fruitful in holiness and heavenly inspirations, and celebrated for the praise of her wondrous piety.”

She herself describes herself as “a humble nun and mistress of the sisters who are at Schönau.” More recent writers incorrectly call her an abbess, though she lived subject to an abbot.

[Col. 0115A] 2. Her full brother Eckbert, while he was still a cleric of the church of Bonn, was summoned to his sister, who had already begun to be visited by God and illuminated by frequent visions. In 1152, as she dictated, he wrote down these visions in two books. Later, once a monk at Schönau, he similarly committed to writing a third book entitled *The Ways of God*. Then—leaving aside a fifth book of doubtful authority—he wrote the final book concerning her death, as an eyewitness of a large part of the events then occurring. Later he became the second abbot of Schönau, according to Trithemius, who praises him among notable men as “a man distinguished no less by devotion and religious life than by learning.” In the *Chronicle of Hirsau*, however, he says that Eckbert succeeded the first abbot, “Hildelin, who died on the Nones of December, 1167.”

At the end of the final book the virgin is said to have been buried “on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of July, on Friday, at the ninth hour.” Since this concurrence of the Kalends and weekday indicates the year of the Lord 1175, rather than the preceding fourth year, an error must be recognized in the manuscript from which the aforesaid material was published. It must be corrected from Trithemius, who, using a more accurate manuscript, places her death “in the year of the Lord 1165, in the thirteenth indiction.”

3. Nevertheless, in the *Chronicle of Hirsau*, before his lengthy eulogy of “Saint Elizabeth, the virgin beloved of God,” as he calls her, the same Trithemius has not only been corrupted by careless scribes who wrongly record MCLXII and 1162, when MCLXV and 1165 had appeared previously, but he might also seem to have forgotten himself when, after noting in that year the election of Rupert, abbot of Hirsau, made “on the second day after the feast of St Peter in Chains, which was the fourth day before the Nones of August,” he added that the Virgin died “in the first current year of Abbot Rupert.” Nor should anyone consider him excusable on the supposition that he perhaps wrote “in the last current year”; for he immediately continues that “in the aforementioned year in which the holy virgin Elizabeth departed from the body, which was the first of Abbot Rupert, the winter was [Col. 0115C] most severe, and a great famine followed, with pestilence and many evils.”

But here again I detect the fault of a bold scribe. For Trithemius customarily divides between dying and succeeding abbots the years common to both, begins the following years from the beginning of the civil year, and sometimes passes over years marked by no memorable event—just as, in this case of Rupert, he omitted his second and fifth years, corresponding to the years of Christ 1166 and 1169. The editor therefore placed the date of the preceding year where it did not belong, making it seem that what Trithemius had assigned to the aforementioned year 1165 concerning the winter and pestilence was assigned to the following year. I think that something similar occurred in the same Trithemius’s *Chronicle of Sponheim*, where, between the years 1153 and 1157, the numbers of three years were lacking: the year 1164 was prefixed to the death of St Elizabeth—as she is there called—instead of 1165.

4. After the body of the deceased had for a full three days been honored, amid eager rivalry, by the crowds flocking to the sisters, it was borne, as was customary with the others, to the church [Col. 0115D] sacred to the aforesaid St. Florinus, belonging to the brethren, and placed “in a coffin beside the altar dedicated to the Lord and to all holy virgins.”

As to whether, and what kind of, cult St. Elisabeth had there from ancient times, or may still have there, I can meanwhile say, upon inquiry among the neighboring people, that the Carthusians of Cologne were the first to enter her name in the public calendar of the Martyrology formerly published by Usuard, on the aforesaid day. They followed either the above-mentioned Ekbert, or the records of the sanctuary at Schönau itself, or at least the necrology of the place. This enlarged Usuard was printed at Cologne in 1515 and reprinted in 1521, with these words appended to 18 June:

> “Of blessed memory, Elisabeth, a consecrated virgin at Schönau, to whom many secrets were revealed by the Lord, about the year 1161.”

Molanus inserted the same words—found in no manuscript of Usuard enlarged in any place, but only among the Carthusians of Cologne—in the first edition of his *Additions*, published in 1568, [Col. 0116A] in small type. But in the two other editions, of 1573 and 1583, although he lived two years longer still, omitting the title “Of blessed memory” and the erroneous year, he wrote only:

> “At Schönau died Elisabeth, a consecrated virgin, to whom many secrets were revealed by the Lord.”

Meanwhile, the first edition—which perhaps alone was seen by Baronius, who treated it almost as an oracle—had this effect at Rome: her commemoration was added to the Martyrology revised and enlarged by authority of Gregory XIII and published in 1584, with the title “Saint,” in this form, which is still read today:

> “At Schönau, St. Elisabeth, virgin, renowned for the observance of monastic life.”

This was prudently done, in omitting mention of the revelations, concerning which there was good reason for doubt—especially because the matters concerning St. Ursula’s martyrdom read in Book IV are wholly unworthy of belief.

5. We embrace the judgment of the Apostolic See concerning the Roman Martyrology proposed to the faithful, as having been [Col. 0116B] “corrected by learned men according to the truth of history, which comprises the diversity of deeds, persons, places, and times, and enlarged in many places,” as Gregory declares in his preface. Yet, until every particular has been examined to its foundation—as we are attempting to do—Franciscus Maria Florentinius rightly judged, in his preface to the most ancient Martyrology of the Western Church, that there would always remain something to correct. But this is not the work of the few years during which the Gregorian revision was prepared, perhaps not even of one or two centuries.

Whatever may be true in other cases, here at least the procedure seems prudent: the mention of revelations was omitted, since among the uninstructed it would have carried the force of express approval. But the more prudently we judge that the revisers of the Roman Martyrology acted in this matter, the more highly we value their judgment in assigning the title “Saint,” which no one before Trithemius had used, as though founded upon the merits of her life, confirmed by a most holy death. For such a judgment seems to possess something of the character of canonization and cannot lightly be called into doubt. We have therefore followed it in the title, as also have all the compilers of monastic calendars: Menard, Wion, Dorganius, Bucelinus, and others.

6. After the much-praised Ekbert, Schönau was governed, according to Trithemius, by Emicho—called Einicho in Molanus’s notes and thence in Baronius—formerly a hearer and disciple of the aforementioned Ekbert: a man diligent and learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant also of secular literature, quick in intellect and distinguished in speech, eminent no less for life than for learning. He wrote many excellent little works in both verse and prose, of which, however, “few,” says Trithemius, “have come into our hands. I have read his little work on the praises of the holy virgin Elisabeth of Schönau, and some others.”

Would that we too had happened to find it, or that posterity might obtain an addition to the writings. Meanwhile, we shall be content with those things [Col. 0116D] which she herself dictated while alive, and which Ekbert wrote after her death. Molanus says that these were “published by Faber”—commonly called Lefèvre of Étaples, Jacob by first name, a man most renowned throughout France in the preceding age for publishing books—“in a book entitled *The Book of Three Men and Three Spiritual Women*.” This book is not found among the many books of Lefèvre enumerated by Gesner, but we possess it: printed at Paris in 1513 and dedicated

> “To Adelaide, devout servant of Christ, and mother of the convent of virgins consecrated to God, Hildegardis.”

Moreover, so that such an ancient edition should not now be greatly missed, the diligence of the Brigittines of Cologne provided this: when in 1628 they had arranged for the *Revelations* of their holy mother Bridget to be reprinted by the heirs of Antonius Boetzer, in the same year and by the same press, though without naming themselves, they published

> “from ancient monuments, as the title announces, the Revelations of the holy virgins Hildegard and Elisabeth, [Col. 0117A] entered in the Roman Martyrology.”

From this work it is our pleasure to reprint, dividing in our own manner into chapters, those portions concerning the life of the latter: namely, the first and second books, part of the third, and the whole sixth book; passing over the others only briefly, because they contribute less to history.

7. By the same diligence of the Brigittines, among the encomia bestowed upon Elisabeth by the Church and learned men and prefixed to the work, there is presented to us a certain praise-song, or rhythmical hymn, by Abbot Emicho. If it were established that this had at any time been used among the divine offices, it would suffice to prove an immemorial cult. They profess to have received it from a book of the library of Schönau. It is pleasing to append this hymn here; for I strongly suspect it to be the very work read by Trithemius, and that no other need be wished for as surviving.

> Hail, happy Elisabeth, fragrant rose,  
>   
> [Col. 0117B] Virgin greatly renowned among God’s wonders.  
>   
> Hail, devoted contemplator of the Lord’s ways,  
>   
> And lover also of the undivided Trinity.  
>   
> Hail, singular daughter of the Virgin Mary,  
>   
> For in ecstasy you were often visited by her.  
>   
> Hail, fountain full of streams of divine knowledge,  
>   
> Distilling honey-sweet drops of deifying teaching.  
>   
> Hail, flowering little tree of Schönau’s forest,  
>   
> Surrounded by countless branches of visions.  
>   
> Hail, to whom heaven’s gates seemed opened,  
>   
> And heavenly secrets were there shown.  
>   
> Hail, mirror without blemish, into which  
>   
> The citizens of heaven longed to look, for they loved you greatly.  
>   
> Hail, you who secretly saw, enclosed in the pyx of the sacrament,  
>   
> The appearance of the true flesh of the body of Jesus Christ.

8. Come now, most gracious one, exalted in heaven,

> Who are in heaven, as we devoutly believe, be our advocate.  
>   
> Defend this convent and us who dwell within it;  
>   
> Remember me, I pray, and acknowledge those who love you.  
>   
> [Col. 0117C] O Virgin, bring it about that religious life may continually increase  
>   
> In our monastery, and that its progress may not decline.  
>   
> Drive away, I pray, every deception of demons,  
>   
> And obtain for us the protection of angels.  
>   
> Cause all things hostile to us to be softened;  
>   
> Obtain for us every season of prosperity.  
>   
> O most devoted virgin, adorned with virtues,  
>   
> We ask you, plead with God Most High  
>   
> That he may receive us to himself when we depart hence,  
>   
> And grant us the reward in which we may rejoice forever.  
>   
> Glory be to God the Father and to his holy Son,  
>   
> And glory to the equal and blessed Spirit. Amen.

9. O noble bride of Christ, O venerable Mother, intercede for us with the Lord, King of angels, whom you have always loved with a pure heart and in whose embrace you remain without end; that he may forgive us whatever sins we have committed against him, grant us the ardor of his most holy love, and, after the exile of this most brief life, a dwelling in the heavenly habitation. Amen.

[Col. 0117D]

> Aid us, Elisabeth, most holy virgin, most noble bride of the eternal King, in whose court you shine like a most radiant star. Be a refuge to the wretched in every need and tribulation. Amen.

Besides these, no trace of ancient cult is to be found at Schönau. But after Elisabeth’s name was admitted to the Roman Martyrology, as I said above, her feast began to be celebrated with double rite, together with an office and Mass from the Common of Virgins. Exactly the same happened to St. Poppo, abbot of Stavelot, after Baronius judged him worthy of similar honor because of the life printed among the lives of saints by Surius, as was said under 25 January.

10. Father John Helm, who travelled there from our residence at St. Goar in October 1690, by direction of the most serene Prince Ernest, Landgrave of Hesse, recently deceased in piety, and of his superior Father Nicholas Grass, reports to us:

> “The men’s monastery survives; the women’s monastery was destroyed by the Swedes because women lived there. On the right side of the church is a chapel now called that of St. Elisabeth, with two altars. Set partly into the wall of this chapel is an ancient tomb, once broken by heretics and rejoined with iron hooks. It is held in honor, as is one of the altars, named after her. In the tomb itself no bones remain; only a few bones together with the head escaped the sacrilegious hands of those who searched, and these, wrapped in silk, are displayed for veneration.”

Likewise, no trace of the old epitaph survives; but someone sent it to us [Col. 0118B] as he had found it written after the Life, in this form:

> A virgin like the prophets, who, cleaving to God,  
>   
> Had beheld in mind the heights of heaven, here has her bones laid.  
>   
> Elisabeth lives, rejoicing in the light of life,  
>   
> Which she tasted beforehand by Christ’s special gift.

Furthermore, there is preserved at Schönau a little book called the prayers of Blessed Elisabeth, in old parchment. On its first folio are written these words:

> “This book belongs to the monastery of the Blessed Virgin Mary at Schönau, of the Order of St. Benedict . . . . on the day of the venerable sacrament, which was the third day before the Nones of June, under Pope Julius II and Maximilian, King of the Romans.”

Thus it belongs to the year 1507, when Easter was celebrated on 4 April. From this one might suspect that one or two words indicating that the book was then completed or finished by the copyist were intentionally erased, in order more easily to persuade readers that it had been used by the saint herself—whereas perhaps it was copied then from the one she had used, [Col. 0118C] after that original had already worn out.

11. Henriquez, Libanorius, and certain others who assigned this Elisabeth, together with St. Hildegard, to the Cistercian Order were deceived by the ambiguity of a name common to several monasteries elsewhere because of a common etymological basis. One such monastery of virgins was in Franconia; another, of men, in the diocese of Mainz. There Blessed Hildegundis, commemorated in this work on 20 April, concealed herself under male attire and the name Joseph. In the same place, half a century after her death, Blessed Daniel was abbot, having been taken from the monastery of Himmerod; he will be mentioned by us on 29 June.

Jongelinus observed the error in his *Notice of the Abbeys of His Order*, recognizing no monastery except Himmerod in the diocese of Trier. Chalemotus likewise observed it, though silently passing over both this Elisabeth and St. Hildegard of Bingen. Hildegard’s case had long been certain to us, since we had been at Bingen in 1160 and had there seen her sacred objects, [Col. 0118D] bones, writings, and hood—not white, like that of the Cistercians, but reddish-black, like that of the Benedictines.

Manrique, in treating of Elisabeth and her admirers under the year 1221, chapter 6, wonders how she could have been assigned to the Cistercians: “for the Cistercian Order has hitherto had no double monasteries, as there were at Schönau under one abbot.” He adds that “I have wished to state this in passing, lest we, who possess so many and such great things of our own, seem to stretch out our hands toward what belongs to others, or to connive with those who do so.”

[Col. 0119]

# THE LIFE OF SAINT ELISABETH

Partly dictated by herself, partly written by her brother Ekbert.

## PROLOGUE OF EKBERT, WITH THE VIRGIN’S LETTER TO SAINT HILDEGARD

[Col. 0119A]

1. In the days of Pope Eugenius, within the boundaries of the diocese of Trier, in the monastery named Schönau, under the rule of Abbot Hildelin, there was a young woman of monastic profession named Elisabeth. In the eleventh year that she spent in the monastery among the religious women, when she was twenty-three years old, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1152, she was visited by the Lord. His hand was with her, performing in her, according to his ancient mercies, works of great wonder and worthy of remembrance.

For she was granted to be carried beyond her ordinary mind and to see visions of the Lord’s secrets, hidden from the eyes of mortals. This did not occur without an evident miracle. Frequently, indeed almost habitually, on Sundays [Col. 0119B] and other feast days, at the hours when the devotion of the faithful burns most fervently, she was rapt into an ecstasy of mind. As her spirit gradually returned, she would suddenly utter certain divine words in Latin, which she had never learned from another and could not discover by herself, being uneducated and possessing no, or only very slight, knowledge of Latin speech.

She also frequently uttered, without any prior meditation, testimonies from the canonical Scriptures and other words of divine praise appropriate to what she had seen in the spirit. Therefore, all that occurred in connection with her and seemed to pertain to God’s glory and the edification of the faithful has in large part been written down in this little book, according to her account. She explained every matter to one of her brothers [Col. 0119C] of the clerical order, with whom she was more intimate than with the others. For although she concealed much from inquirers, since she was very fearful and most humble in spirit, she was compelled, by the bond of siblinghood and affection and by the abbot’s command, to recount everything familiarly to him, as he diligently investigated all things and wished to commit them to memory. The beginning of the account was as follows.

2. Thus far speaks Egbert, the virgin’s brother, the same cleric who is said to have written everything in the third person. Before we proceed to let the virgin herself speak, Elisabeth’s letter to St. Hildegard must be presented, since it wonderfully serves to illuminate the whole argument that follows. We would now seek it in vain, had Abbot Trithemius not inserted it in his *Chronicle of Hirsau* under the year—1165, as we have noted it should be read. St. Hildegard, moreover—to say this in passing from the same Trithemius’s *Sponheim Chronicle*—the virgin of Christ, founder and mistress of the monastery of St. Rupert near Bingen, died on 17 September, in the eighty-third year of her age, in the year of the Lord 1179, in the thirteenth indiction, only just begun, in September. Thus, being born in 1097, she was thirty-three years older than Elisabeth, who was born only in 1130, and survived her by eighteen years.

They were indeed remarkably alike. For Elisabeth, as the same Trithemius says in the previously cited chronicle, deserved from her youth to be visited by divine revelations, from which she wrote down many things by divine command for the benefit of posterity. Although ignorant of Latin speech and having learned from human beings nothing beyond simple psalmody, taught inwardly by the Holy Spirit, she correctly understood all Scripture and the arrangement or construction of the work. She expressed her revelations and heavenly visions partly in Latin and partly in German.

The letter, reproduced word for word by Trithemius for a definite purpose—one which, it is not difficult to infer, concerned establishing belief in Elisabeth’s revelations—and written under the year 1162, or even 1160, when Elisabeth was already set over the virgins, is as follows.

## LETTER TO HILDEGARD

3. Elisabeth, humble nun and mistress of the sisters at Schönau, sends devout prayers with every affection to Lady HILDEGARD, venerable mistress of the brides of Christ at Bingen. [Col. 0120C] May the grace and consolation of the Most High fill you with joy, because you have compassionately sympathized with my tribulation, as I learned from the words of my comforter, whom you diligently urged to comfort me.

For, as you said had been revealed to you concerning me, I confess that recently I conceived in my heart a certain cloud of disturbance because of the foolish talk of people saying many things about me that are untrue. Yet I could easily endure the talk of the crowd, if those too who walk in the habit of religion did not grieve my spirit more bitterly. For they too, driven by I know not what goads, mock God’s grace in me and do not fear rashly to judge matters of which they are ignorant.

I hear also that certain letters, written out of their own spirit, are being circulated under my name, alleging that I have prophesied concerning the day of judgment. This I certainly have never dared to do, since knowledge of its coming escapes every mortal. But I shall disclose to you the occasion of this report, so that you may judge whether I have done or said anything presumptuously in this matter.

4. As you have heard from others, the Lord has magnified his mercy toward me beyond what I have deserved or could in any way deserve, so greatly that he has frequently deigned to reveal certain heavenly mysteries. Through his angel he has also frequently signified to me what would come upon his people in these days unless they repented of their iniquities, and he commanded me to announce these matters openly. [Col. 0121B]

But, in order to avoid arrogance and not appear an author of novelties, I strove, as far as I could, to conceal all these things. Therefore, when on a certain Sunday, according to my usual manner, I was in ecstasy, an angel of the Lord stood by me and said:

> “Why do you hide gold in mud? This is the word of God, which has been sent through your mouth to the earth because of distorted faces: not so that it may be hidden, but so that it may be made manifest, for the praise and glory of our Lord and the salvation of his people.”

Having said this, he raised above me a scourge and, as though in great anger, struck me five times most bitterly, so that for three days my whole body was weak from the blow. After this, he put his finger upon my mouth, saying:

> “You shall be silent until the ninth hour, when you shall make known what the Lord has done with you.”

Accordingly I remained mute until the ninth hour. Then I indicated to the mistress that she should bring me a certain little book which I had hidden in my bed, containing in part what the Lord had done with me. When I offered it into the hands of Lord Abbot Hildelin, who had come to visit me, my tongue was freed with these words:

> “Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but give glory to your name” (Psalm 113).

After this, when I had also revealed to them certain other matters which I had not wished to commit to writing—namely, concerning the great vengeance of the Lord which, I had learned from the angel, would shortly come upon the whole world—I most earnestly begged him to keep that word hidden.

[Col. 0121D]

5. But the lord abbot himself commanded me to devote myself to prayer and ask the Lord to grant me understanding whether he wished those things which I had said to be covered in silence or not. Having for some time afflicted myself by persevering in prayer on this matter, in the Advent of the Lord, on the feast of St. Barbara, at the first watch of the night, I fell into ecstasy. The angel of the Lord stood by me and said:

> “Cry aloud and say, ‘Alas!’ to all nations, because the whole world has been turned into darkness. And you shall say: ‘Come forth: he who formed you from the earth calls you.’ And say: ‘Repent, for the kingdom of God is near.’”

Moved by this saying, the lord abbot began to publish the word among the rulers of the Church [Col. 0122A] and religious men. Some of them, however, spoke not rightly but maliciously about the angel familiar to me, saying that he was a deceiving spirit transformed into an angel of light. Therefore the lord abbot himself bound me under obedience, commanding that, when he appeared to me again, I should adjure him in the name of the Lord to tell me whether or not he was truly God’s angel.

Considering this presumptuous, I accepted the command with great fear. Therefore, one day, when I was in my ecstasy, he appeared to me in his accustomed way and stood before me. Trembling, I said to him:

> “I adjure you by God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit to tell me rightly whether you are truly God’s angel, whether the visions which I saw in my ecstasy are true, and whether the things I heard from your mouth are true.”

He answered and said:

> “Know with certainty that I am truly God’s angel; the visions you have seen are true; what you have heard from my mouth is true; and it shall truly come to pass unless God is reconciled to humankind. I myself am he who has long labored with you.”

6. After this, while I was praying on the vigil of Epiphany, my Lord again appeared to me, but he stood far off and had his face turned away from me. Understanding his indignation, I said to him fearfully:

> “My Lord, if I offended you in adjuring you, do not, I pray, charge it against me. Turn your face toward me and be gracious to me, for I did it because I was bound by obedience and did not dare to transgress my superior’s command.”

After I had shed many tears [Col. 0122C] in such words, he turned to me and said:

> “You have shown contempt to me and my brethren, because you distrusted me. Therefore know certainly that you shall no longer see my face or hear my voice, unless the Lord and we are appeased.”

And I said:

> “My Lord, how may you be appeased?”

And he said:

> “Tell your abbot to celebrate the divine office devoutly in memory of me and my brethren.”

Therefore, after the solemnities of Mass had been celebrated not once but many times, both by the lord abbot and by the other brethren, in honor of the holy angels, and after the sisters had likewise honored them with readings of psalms, my Lord again appeared to me with a serene countenance and said:

> “I know that what you did was done in charity and obedience; therefore you have obtained forgiveness. Henceforth I shall visit you more frequently than before.”

7. After this, the lord abbot planned to go to a certain place at the request of clerics dwelling there, in order to preach to the people the Lord’s word of warning, in case they might repent and God’s anger be turned away from them. First he began, together with us all, to beseech the Lord that he might deign to reveal to his handmaid whether the message which had already begun to be made public should be spread further or not.

While he was celebrating the divine mysteries and we were praying most devoutly, suddenly the joints of my limbs were relaxed, [Col. 0123A] I grew faint, and I entered into ecstasy. And behold, the angel of the Lord stood before me, and I said to him:

> “Remember, my lord, that you told your handmaid: ‘My word has been sent through your mouth to the earth, not that it may be hidden but that it may be made manifest, for God’s glory and the salvation of his people.’ And now tell me what ought to be done concerning the message of warning which you spoke to me. Has it now been made sufficiently public, or must it still be preached further?”

But he looked severely at me and said:

> “Do not put God to the test; for those who test him shall perish. And say to the abbot: ‘Do not fear, but complete what you have begun. Truly blessed are those who hear the words of your prophecy and keep them and are not scandalized by you.’ Further, suggest this to him: that he should not alter the form he has followed thus far in preaching, for I have been his counselor in it. Tell him not at all to heed the words of those who out of envy speak doubtingly of the things said through you, but to heed what is written, that nothing is impossible with God.”

8. Encouraged by this saying, he went to the place he had intended. He exhorted the people, who had been awaiting his arrival, to repentance, announcing that God’s wrath would come unless they strove to avert it by fruits of repentance. But he never described in any of his sermons what scourges threatened the world, as rumor falsely alleged.

It therefore happened that many persons among whom this report [Col. 0123C] circulated afflicted themselves through repentance in great fear throughout the whole season of Lent and diligently applied themselves to almsgiving and prayer. At that time, someone, led by I know not what zeal, sent letters to the city of Cologne in the person of the lord abbot, without his knowledge—God knows—in which certain terrible warnings were read aloud before all the people. Thus, although fools made a mockery of us, the people nevertheless, as we heard, prudently and reverently took heed of the message and did not disdain to honor God by fruits of repentance.

Then, on the Wednesday before Easter, when after great bodily suffering I had entered ecstasy, the angel of the Lord appeared to me. I said to him:

> “My Lord, what will become of the word which you spoke to me?”

He replied:

> “Do not grieve or be disturbed if what I foretold does not happen on the day I specified to you, for the Lord has been appeased by the satisfaction of many.”

9. After this, on Friday after the third hour, I entered into ecstasy of mind amid severe suffering, and he again stood by me, saying:

> “The Lord has seen the affliction of his people and has turned away the wrath of his indignation from them.”

I said to him:

> “Then, my Lord, shall I not become an object of ridicule to all among whom this report has spread?”

He said:

> “Bear patiently and willingly everything that may happen to you on this occasion, carefully considering him who, though he was the Creator of the whole world, endured the mockery of human beings. Now the Lord tests your patience for the first time.”

Behold, my lady, I have explained to you the whole course of the matter, so that you may know my innocence and that of our abbot, and may be able to make it known to others. I beg you also to make me a participant in your prayers and, as the Spirit of the Lord shall suggest to you, to write back some words of consolation to me. May the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen.

Thus far she speaks. Since none of these matters is contained in the following books, it may be understood that very many other revelations were granted to the virgin and many letters written by her, of which no account is taken here. Now receive the titles of the old division, with an indication of our numbering in the margin.

# CHAPTER ONE

Address to her brother; diabolical temptations dispelled by a divine visitation; beginnings of the visions.

10. You ask me, brother—and this is why you have come—to recount to you the mercies of the Lord, which according to the good pleasure of His grace He has deigned to work in me. Indeed, brother, I am ready in every respect to satisfy your affection; for my soul itself has long desired that I might be granted to speak with you concerning all that the Lord has wrought magnificently in me, and to hear your judgment. But, I pray you, beloved, bear with me a little and consider the manifold [Col. 0126C] distresses of my heart, which constrain me beyond belief. If that matter of which you have heard should become public, as through certain incautious brethren—God knows—against my will it has already in part become public, what talk do you suppose there will be about me among the people? Perhaps some will say that I possess a certain holiness, and will ascribe God’s grace to my merits, thinking that I am something when I am nothing. Others, however, will think to themselves: “If she were God’s handmaid, surely she would keep silent and would not allow her name to be magnified upon earth,” not knowing by what goads I am usually pressed to speak. Nor will there be lacking those who say that everything they have heard about me is womanish invention, or perhaps judge that Satan has deceived me. [Col. 0126D] In these and other ways, dearest brother, I must be tossed about in human mouths. And why should this befall me: that I should become known to any human being—I who chose to remain hidden, and who certainly do not consider myself worthy that anyone should lift up his eyes to look upon me? My distresses are also greatly increased by the fact that it has pleased the lord abbot that my words should be committed to writing. For what am I, that things concerning me should be handed down to memory? Might not this too be imputed to arrogance?

11. But certain wise persons tell me that the Lord has done these things for me not for my sake alone, but has also provided through them for the edification of others, since they seem in some measure to pertain to the strengthening of faith and to the consolation of those whose hearts are [Col. 0127A] troubled for the Lord’s sake. Therefore, for causes such as those stated, they do not think that God’s works ought to be passed over in silence. And I partly believe that this is so, as they say, because of certain things which I shall now relate to you. It has happened several times that, when I had resolved in my heart to conceal what the Lord had shown me, such a torment of my innermost being seized me that I thought myself near to death; but as soon as I disclosed to those about me what I had seen, I was immediately relieved. Yet I confess that even thus I am not altogether certain what I ought chiefly to do; for I understand that it is dangerous for me to keep silent concerning God’s mighty works, and I fear still more that it will be dangerous to speak. For I know that I have less discernment than would suffice to distinguish which of the things revealed to me [Col. 0127B] ought to be spoken and which ought to be honored by silence. And behold, amid all this I am placed in danger of sinning. For this reason, my beloved, tears do not cease from my eyes, and my spirit is continually anxious within me. But behold, at your arrival my soul has begun to be consoled, and great tranquility has come upon me. Blessed be the Lord, because He has deigned to receive the prayer of His handmaid, by which for many days I entreated Him concerning your coming.

12. And now, since by the Lord’s will you have been sent to me from afar, I shall not conceal my heart from you; but I shall disclose to you the good and evil things concerning me. Thereafter, let what should be done rest in your discernment and that of the lord abbot. I give thanks to the Lord, [Col. 0127C] I the least of His poor ones, because from the day when I began to live under regular observance until this very hour, the hand of the Lord has been so firmly laid upon me that I have never ceased to bear His arrows in my body. My illnesses, various and prolonged, have tormented not only me but also all the sisters around me. May the Lord grant them mercy, because with a motherly affection they have borne with me the burden of my affliction. At times they also applied remedies to my infirmities; but I became the more ill, and in a vision by night I heard a voice saying to me: “But our God is in heaven; He has done whatsoever He has willed” (Psalm 113). From this I understood that I was being admonished to entrust my body not to human remedies but to the will of my Creator; and [Col. 0127D] so I did. And although I was often overwhelmed by such severe weakness that I had control of no limb except my tongue, I may say without arrogance that I remained no less diligent in meditating upon the Psalms; and when paralysis deprived me even of my tongue, I supplied the tongue’s office with my mind. It would be long to enumerate how great a lack of necessary things I have endured together with my illnesses. You yourself know that our house’s possessions are slight, and that those who ought to have shown compassion toward me have withdrawn far from me. Yet the Lord, Father of orphans, is solicitous for me; through whose grace all [Col. 0128A] my affliction is great joy to my heart. In all things blessed be God, the comforter of the lowly. But lest I detain you longer, I shall now turn my discourse to those matters about which you principally inquire.

13. It happened on the holy day of Pentecost [Note: [Col. 0127D] In the year 1152 from the Incarnation of Christ, with dominical letters F and E, Easter was celebrated on 30 March; [Col. 0128D] and therefore Pentecost fell on 18 May. Thus the mental darkness described below lasted until the twenty-fifth of the same month.], when the sisters assembled for the Lord’s Supper, that I was detained by some circumstance and did not partake of that divine and life-giving sacrament. Therefore the solemnity of that day did not make me joyful as it usually did; rather, I remained all day in a certain darkness of mind. The next day also, and throughout that whole week, I went sorrowfully in the same darkness of mind, unable to shake sadness from my soul. All my sins rose into my heart more than usual; I magnified each one within myself, and so accumulated pains for myself. As this evil sorrow gradually increased within me, my mind was so darkened that, wherever I turned, I thought that I walked in darkness in comparison with the light which I had formerly felt within me. Amid these things I was also afflicted by such weariness that there was nothing which my soul did not find distasteful. Even the prayers which had been my greatest delight were burdensome to me. The Psalter, which had always been pleasant to me, I sometimes flung far from myself after scarcely reading one psalm. Then, reflecting again and wondering within myself what had happened to me, I took it up and read; but again my mind collapsed.

14. For my adversary poured out all his strength against me; that faithless one even caused me to waver in faith, [Col. 0128C] so that I thought doubtfully concerning our Redeemer, saying within myself: “Who, then, was He who humbled Himself so greatly for humankind? Could all that is written about Him really have been true?” I turned elsewhere and said: “Yet He was good, whoever He was, of whom so many good things are proclaimed.” I thought similarly and doubtfully of our most blessed advocate when the sisters celebrated her commemoration. And what wonder, brother? Almost all my understanding had been overturned within me. At times, however, returning to myself, I understood that I was being tempted and resisted strongly; and I urged those close to me to pray for me. But my adversary pressed all the more strongly, disturbing me so that I was even weary of living. Because of this weariness I could take food and drink only in the smallest quantity, and I went about [Col. 0128D] failing and wasting away throughout my body. Finally that faithless one suggested to me that I myself should put an end to my life, and thus end the miseries which I had long endured. But in this most wicked temptation He who keeps Israel did not slumber over me. For He did not permit this greatest iniquity to rule over me; rather, He made me understand the malice of my ambusher and suddenly turned me away from this thought. How abundant in mercy You are, Lord, who deliver those who trust in You from such great dangers! I confess to You, Father, that unless You had helped me, my soul would almost have dwelt in hell.

[Col. 0129A] 15. And these things continued thus with me until the feast of Maximinus [Note: [Col. 0129D] St Maximinus, bishop of Trier, is commemorated on 29 May, which then fell on Thursday.], the fourth day before the Kalends of June [Note: [Col. 0129D] That is, certainly Friday, and consequently 30 May.]. On that day at Compline I saw in our chapel a small apparition, as though clothed in a monk’s cowl. Immediately after Compline had been said, a most severe illness came upon me; and I asked the mistress to take the sisters and come with me into the chapter house, where they might pour out prayers over me. When I wished to prostrate myself before the crucifix, my bones became so rigid that I could not bend my knees at all. Therefore, forcing myself, I threw myself heavily upon the ground. When I rose from prayer, the Gospel book was brought, and they made me read the Passion of the Lord; they assisted me because I was too weak to read. But as we read, [Col. 0129B] the same apparition appeared to me as before; and when we were reading that place where the Evangelist says, “Now Satan entered into Judas, who was called Iscariot” (Luke 22), it began to leap about and make laughter. I told the sisters to drive that most evil being away, and they wondered of whom I was speaking. When the Gospel had been read through, it vanished. Afterward, at Matins, it stood before me in human form: short of stature, thickset, and dreadful in appearance; its face fiery, its tongue flaming and stretched far out from its mouth, its hands and feet like the claws of very rapacious birds. In this form it appeared to me seven times that day, and once in the form of a most hideous dog. The next morning [Note: [Col. 0129D] The morning, as is said shortly afterward, of Saturday; and thus [Col. 0130D] everything follows in correct order.] it stood by my bed and, with some oath of its own, threatened me that it would strike me in the teeth with the shoe which it seemed to hold in its hand. After this, shortly before Mass, it presented itself to me again in the form of a great and dreadful bull, opening its mouth over me as though to swallow me, and it seemed to wear a cymbal about its neck.

16. Then, when the Mass of our most blessed Lady the Virgin was begun—for it was Saturday—I fell into ecstasy. My heart was opened, and I saw in the air a wheel of great light, like the full moon but as though twice as large. Looking through the middle of the wheel, I saw the likeness of a royal woman standing on high, as though clad in garments of purest white and surrounded by a purple mantle. Immediately I understood that she was the exalted Queen of heaven, [Col. 0129D] the Mother of our Savior, whose sight I had always desired. As I looked upon her with utmost longing, she fell upon her face three times, worshipping before a certain divine light which was before her. But the fourth time that she humbled herself, she seemed to remain lying down for a long while. When she rose, she turned her face toward me and, advancing a little into the lower air opposite me, had two glorious companions, one at her right and one at her left. He who was on the right seemed clothed in a monk’s cowl, most white, and he appeared to hold in his hand the staff of a monastic [Col. 0130A] father. Hence it came into my mind that this was our venerable father, blessed Benedict. He who was on the left appeared a handsome young man, notable for white, curling hair. Then my Lady, standing, signed me with the sign of the cross and in some manner I do not know impressed these words upon my mind: “Do not fear, because these things shall not harm you.” I did not hear the sound of a voice, but only saw distinctly the movement of her lips. After this she returned to the interior of her light, and I, worshipping most devoutly, followed her with the praises of thirteen verses which I customarily use. Having said these, I returned from ecstasy and immediately refreshed my spirit with the saving Host. Then I asked the priest to invoke the name of the Lord over me; [Col. 0130B] and when he began the Litany, I again fell into ecstasy and saw my Lady standing beside the altar, clothed in a garment like a priest’s chasuble. She had upon her head a glorious diadem, as though adorned with four precious gems, and that angelic salutation was inscribed around her: “Hail, Mary, full of grace; the Lord is with thee” (Luke 1).

17. That same day at Vespers I again saw that evil one in the form of a bull, hanging in the air before me; and shortly afterward I beheld my comforter in heavenly light as before, fortifying me with the sign of the cross. On the following day, which was Sunday, my ambusher again [Note: [Col. 0130D] Namely, 1 June; and consequently the following Monday and Thursday, on which the saints were seen.] presented himself to me in the form of a bull, as before. Then, since that dreadful vision had tormented [Col. 0130C] me greatly, I said to him confidently: “If you truly are that evil one, I command you in the name of the Lord to change your form quickly, and not to appear to me again in this form.” He immediately disappeared; and I beheld a horrible valley full of smoke and black flame, from which there came a most filthy herd of goats. That day at Vespers a great light appeared to me in heaven, and from its midst a dove, beautiful with snow-white brightness and a kind of fiery splendor, flew forth, displaying something red in its mouth. After it suddenly wheeled in the air, it returned into the light. Following it reverently, I recited prayers to the Holy Spirit, because I had heard that He had appeared in the form of a dove. After this, at Compline, as I stood before the cross and greeted it most devoutly, [Col. 0130D] a great cross of golden radiance was shown to me in heaven, so resplendent that it dazzled the eyes of my heart with which I beheld it.

18. The next morning, while I stood alone in the chapter house and prayed, my adversary again presented himself to me, standing before me in the guise of an elegant cleric, as though dressed in a white shirt. I was frightened, indeed; yet persevering in prayer, I acted with no less diligence in order to confound him the more. When the prayer was completed, I went up to the dormitory, and he followed me there. [Col. 0131A] I left it for the chapel and came to stand between two sisters who were praying. He followed me there too, and stood before me, mocking me with a shameful gesture; nor could I turn from him the eye of my mind with which I beheld him. Then, unable to endure his wickedness any longer, I said to him boldly: “I command you in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit to cease quickly from such behavior and never again show me such wickedness.” Immediately he abandoned his former appearance and stood reverently, as though dressed in religious habit. Then I went out to sit among the assembly of sisters, and he followed me there and stood smiling at me. When he then disappeared, he did not appear to me again. After I had heard Mass and communicated, and had gone to the meal, I scarcely touched food because of the excessive torment. [Col. 0131B] But after the meal I suddenly became weak; no strength remained in me, and I was so constricted on every side that none of my limbs was free from suffering. Then, with the sisters standing around me, I scarcely moved my tongue to signify that, when relics had been brought, they should say over me the Passion of the Lord and prayers. While they prayed, I felt my throat as though strongly gripped by someone’s hand, so that my breath was almost cut off. When that hour had passed, thereafter I had greater peace from my tempter, by the Lord’s grace, who knows how to deliver His own from temptation; and this, I think, was obtained from the Lady.

19. The sisters and the lord brethren, seeing the distress of my soul, assembled and decreed that for seven consecutive days [Col. 0131C] they should offer common prayers and afflict themselves before the Lord for me, and that each day they should celebrate a Mass for my afflictions. Since among the seven Masses one to the Holy Spirit was to be sung on Thursday, I awaited that day with great longing, hoping that I should then receive some consolation. The desired day came; and while the brethren celebrated the divine rites, they lay in prayer together with the sisters. My heart was enlarged, and I saw a great light in heaven; and behold, a dove of great beauty, such as I had seen before, came forth from the light and reached me. It circled my head three times with wings outspread, then immediately flew upward. After this, [Col. 0131D] on Friday, when the Mass of the Holy Cross was said and I had prostrated myself in prayer, the glorious sign of the cross was shown to me in heaven, as though at the left of the divine Majesty.

20. On Saturday, when the office of the most glorious Virgin was celebrated, I again saw her in heavenly brightness, worshipping before the great Majesty. While the ministers of the altar devoutly sang her praises and had proceeded in the sequence *Ave praeclara* (“Hail, illustrious one”) to the verse, “Pray, Virgin, that we may be made worthy of that bread of heaven,” she fell upon her face and prostrated herself wholly in prayer; and so she remained until the Gospel was begun. From that day until these [Col. 0132A] times, on almost every Saturday, and sometimes on other days when her office was celebrated, I have customarily seen the same vision. On that same day after None, while I stood in the chapter house and wept most bitterly because of certain dreams in which the wickedness of my ambusher had sorely troubled my soul, I most devoutly begged my Lady that, if those troubles were perhaps not going to harm me, she might deign to grant me some consolation. And behold, suddenly that heavenly light flashed forth and my comforter came from it. When she had descended a little, she stood opposite me; and, looking upon her, I carefully observed the movement of her lips, and I knew that she called me by my name, Elizabeth, and added nothing further. Receiving this as consolation, [Col. 0132B] I gave her thanks, and she departed from me.

## CHAPTER II. Saints Seen, from 23 June 1152 to 14 September 1153

21. It happened once, when that snowy dove of which I have spoken had frequently presented itself to me, that I doubted concerning it and asked the lord abbot whether Satan could transform himself into a dove. Since he denied ever having read this, and I remained doubtful, one day I beheld the cross which I am accustomed to see; that dove came from the opposite side and settled upon it. Thus I was made certain that this was not Satan, because he is the enemy of the cross.

22. On the vigil of blessed John the Baptist [Note: [Col. 0131D] The vigil of St John the Baptist, 23 June, then falling on Monday.], while the divine office was being celebrated, I was in prayer and reciting [Col. 0132C] fifty psalms and certain other prayers in praise of that venerable Forerunner of the Lord. When I had almost completed the prayers, a great light suddenly shone in heaven, and in the midst of it was, as it were, the figure of a glorious man. He appeared standing toward the rising of the sun in white clothing. Shortly afterward he turned toward me a gentle and most lovely face, as though wishing to be seen by me. He wore on his head a crown of golden splendor, exceedingly radiant and marked in its front part with a kind of purple color. In his right hand appeared a palm branch of such brilliance that, because of its excessive brightness, I could scarcely distinguish the other things near it. Therefore I understood this to be that glorious martyr whom we were serving. After this, at Matins, [Col. 0132D] when we said, “We praise Thee, O God,” he appeared to me in the same manner; and this was without ecstasy, although I was near to falling into ecstasy. When the light in which I had seen him disappeared again, it suddenly seemed to split into two parts and flashed like lightning altogether unbearable for me to see. I said: “Your grace is sufficient for me, Lord; spare my weakness and lessen this excessive brightness for me, because I cannot bear it.” Immediately it was removed, and in its place a most brilliant star appeared. Again, during the day, at the time of the divine sacrifice, the man of God appeared to me in like manner.

23. On the third day after this [Note: [Col. 0132D] SS John and Paul, 26 June.], at the feast of the most blessed [Col. 0133A] martyrs John and Paul, at the time of Matins, while I read fifty psalms in their honor, I saw them in an exceedingly great light, standing very closely together toward the East and turning their backs to me. When I had completed the prayers and added: “Behold how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity, like ointment upon the head, which runs down upon the beard, upon Aaron’s beard. This is the true brotherhood, which conquered the crimes of the world, followed Christ in glory, and holds the kingdoms of heaven.” And, further: “If they suffered torments before men, God tested them, proved them like gold in a furnace, and received them as whole burnt offerings.” When, I say, I had completed these things, I begged them most earnestly to deign to turn their faces toward me; and they turned [Col. 0133B] to me. They too bore the signs of victory and martyrdom: namely, shining palms in their hands, crowns upon their heads most radiant and marked with red upon the forehead. For holy martyrs appear adorned with such emblems whenever they deign to appear to me. When I had delighted in the sight of them, they were suddenly taken from my eyes.

24. On the feast of the most blessed apostles Peter and Paul, at First Vespers, carried away in ecstasy, I saw those glorious princes in the splendor of a great light, standing with the signs of victorious martyrdom. Turning their faces toward me, they descended into the region of our air, with the most blessed Virgin, mother of our Lord Jesus Christ, going before them. Peter, standing there, made the sign of the cross over me, and I greeted [Col. 0133C] him, saying: “You are shepherd of the sheep, prince of the apostles.” Looking also upon Paul, I took up these words: “I have fought the good fight; I have finished the course” (2 Timothy 4). When they returned to the region of light, I came out of ecstasy. During the day at Mass, while the office was being intoned, I saw a dove descend from heaven and come as far as the right horn of the altar, where it settled. It was the size of a turtledove, and its whiteness exceeded snow. While the lord abbot among the other prayers said that Collect which begins, “God, unto whom every heart is open,” and had proceeded to the words, “purify by the infusion of the Holy Spirit the thoughts of our hearts,” it flew up, circled his head three times, and returned to the place where [Col. 0133D] it had previously settled. When the *Sanctus* was said, it came and settled upon the corporal, and something red seemed to hang from its mouth. When Mass was ended and I approached with the sisters to communicate, I could not see it when I turned the eyes of my body toward it. But with my eyes turned away I saw it; and immediately after I had communicated, I fell into ecstasy and soon recovered myself. [Col. 0134A] From that time onward, every saint whose feast we celebrate among us has appeared to me on his or her feast day in heavenly light, through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ: namely, the martyr Quintilianus [Note: [Col. 0133D] St Kilian, martyr with his companions at Mainz, celebrated throughout Germany, 8 July.], with his companions; then the seven brothers [Note: [Col. 0133D] The seven brothers, sons of St Felicitas, 10 July.].

25. After these came our venerable father Benedict [Note: [Col. 0133D] Translation of St Benedict, in the Mainz and Trier calendars, 11 July.], who likewise seemed to come out into the air opposite me. Then blessed Margaret [Note: [Col. 0133D] St Margaret, Virgin and Martyr, there on the 13th, according to the Roman calendar on 20 July.], conspicuous for immense brightness and glorious in the signs of victory. At the Division of the Apostles [Note: [Col. 0133D] The Division of the Apostles is celebrated widely throughout Germany on [Col. 0134D] 15 July.] all appeared to me, though Peter and Paul seemed to stand apart from the others. After this I saw Alexius [Note: [Col. 0134D] St Alexius, 17th.], the confessor, having some great adornment from his chest down to below his navel. On the vigil of blessed Mary Magdalene [Note: [Col. 0134D] St Mary Magdalene, 22nd.], at [Col. 0134B] Vespers, I saw her with a most shining crown, and with her the Mother of our Lord Jesus Christ. They stood facing one another, as though conversing with each other; shortly afterward they turned toward the East.

26. During the day at Mass, while I prayed with knees bent upon the ground, I saw in the air, as though near the earth, two splendid men [Note: [Col. 0134D] The Brigittine editors here name in the margin Sts Nicodemus and Joseph; but I think angels are understood better, in accordance with Luke 24:4, “Behold, two men,” and John 20:11, “She saw two angels sitting.”] seated facing one another, and between them something luminous having, as it were, the form of a tomb. And behold, a woman like her whom I had seen in the evening approached and stood examining closely that form of the tomb. As she stood there, a young man came up behind her, clad in a garment of purest white, with black hair and a soft beard, and a face exceedingly beautiful. Immediately she turned toward him and went to meet him, standing [Col. 0134C] as though asking him something. Then I began anxiously to consider within myself who that young man might be. As I burned with great desire to know this, a golden cross suddenly appeared in his right hand. Hence I immediately inferred that he was the one who, rising from the dead, first appeared to Mary. That same day at Vespers, because I could not attend the assembly on account of illness, I sat in the chapter house with the mistress; and we were at the evening psalms—it was rainy weather—and I saw a bright rainbow by the sight of the mind alone, for from where I was I could not look upon the face of heaven with my outward eyes. I said to the Lord in my heart: “I beseech You, Lord, that what I now see with the mind alone I may also behold with the eye of the body, so that [Col. 0134D] I may be made more certain of this spiritual vision.” For I did not sufficiently trust myself. Shortly afterward, the sisters came out of the chapel and stood in the cloister looking at the sky. When the mistress wondered what they were looking at, I said: “They are seeing, I think, the rainbow which I too have already seen by the sight of the mind.” Going out to them, we saw it as well.

[Col. 0135A] 27. On the vigil of St James [Note: [Col. 0135D] The vigil of St James, together with the feast of St Christina, Virgin and Martyr, 24 July.], after the meal, without ecstasy, I saw the light which I am accustomed to see, as though above the church of St Florinus [Note: [Col. 0135D] St Florinus, patron of Schönau, 17 November.], where our lord brethren dwell. On the following day a feast of its dedication was to be celebrated there [Note: [Col. 0135D] Perhaps one should read “on the following Sunday”; for who could believe that the anniversary of a dedication was fixed upon the feast of an apostle, whose office would for that reason have to be deferred? Thus the event would have occurred on 27 July.]. I saw, as it were, a ladder, bright like radiant gold, descending from that light as far as the high altar in the sanctuary. Looking, I saw two youths descend by it as far as the altar; the one who went before seemed to carry a golden censer in his hand. Then two others descended after them; finally, a great multitude descended and in turn ascended. They ascended and descended from None on the previous day until None on the following day; for I remained continuously [Col. 0135B] in this vision for so long. Blessed James also appeared, standing near the summit of the ladder, with the blessed virgin Christina and the Virgin of virgins with them; and on that day, about the time of the Lord’s sacrifice, he seemed to descend into these lower regions of our dwelling. On that day I saw great brightness about the aforementioned altar and all that was done there; for I knew what kind of altar covering there was and told our mistress. She sent a messenger there and found it to be as I had said.

28. On the feast of St Peter in Chains [Note: [Col. 0135D] St Peter in Chains, 1 August.] I again saw him in the same form in which he had appeared before. After this, Stephen the protomartyr [Note: [Col. 0135D] The Finding of St Stephen, 3 August, then also [Col. 0136D] Sunday.] on the day of his finding; then Oswald [Note: [Col. 0136D] St Oswald, king of England, 5 August; on that day St Afra, martyr of Augsburg, is also commemorated with her companions Digna and Merita, but in the Mainz and Trier calendars her feast is deferred to 7 August.] the king; then Afra [Col. 0135C] the martyr with her two maidservants; then blessed Cyriacus [Note: [Col. 0136D] Cyriacus, Martyr, 8 August, and consequently the vigil and then the feast of St Lawrence.]; then blessed Lawrence on his vigil. I saw them all in light, bearing the signs of victorious martyrdom. The light surrounding blessed Lawrence on every side was so dense that it seemed almost touchable. The brightness of his palm and crown was so great that it in some way dazzled the eyes of my heart, just as the brightness of shining gold is accustomed to strike the eyes of the body. He wore a splendid stole stretched from his left shoulder to his right side. I asked the mistress what this meant; and she told me that it was the sign of his diaconate. The most blessed Virgin stood with him, as with all those mentioned above; and he kept his face gently turned toward me until my desire was fulfilled, [Col. 0135D] for all are accustomed to grant me this favor.

29. In the following year [Note: [Col. 0136D] The year 1153 had dominical letter D. The Sunday immediately after the feast of St James, which then fell on Saturday, was 26 July.], on the Sunday night which was the first after the feast of blessed James, I was withdrawn from my body and carried away in ecstasy. Behold, a great flaming wheel flashed in heaven, the sight of which struck [Col. 0136A] great terror into me, and it immediately disappeared. After this, as it were a door opened in the same place, and I looked through it. I saw a light far surpassing that which I was accustomed to see, and many thousands of saints within it, standing around a great Majesty, arranged in the following order. Along one side of that circle stood certain men, very magnificent and eminent, adorned with palms and crowns shining abundantly and marked on their foreheads with the title of their passion. From both their title and the distinctive glory they possessed beyond the others, I understood these to be the venerable apostles of Christ. At their right stood a great host, glorious with the same emblems. After these stood other splendid men, but no sign of martyrdom appeared upon them. At the apostles’ left the sacred order of virgins shone, adorned with the emblems of martyrdom. After them came another choir of distinguished maidens, crowned indeed but without the signs of martyrdom. Then other venerable women appeared with white veils; and thus that whole circle was completed from all these. Below it appeared another circle of great brightness, which I understood to be that of the holy angels.

30. In the midst of all I saw the glory of the immeasurable Majesty, which I am utterly unable to describe, whose glorious throne a shining rainbow surrounded. At the Majesty’s right I saw One like the Son of Man, seated in supreme glory; at its left appeared the sign [Col. 0136C] of the cross, most powerfully radiant. As I beheld all these things with a trembling heart, the Lord also deigned to add this: to signify somehow to me, a most unworthy sinner, concerning the glory of His ineffable Trinity—by a manner which I cannot explain and do not dare to explain—how there is truly one Godhead in three persons and three persons in one divine substance. At the right of the Son of Man sat the Queen of angels and Lady of kingdoms, upon a throne as though starry, surrounded by immeasurable light. At the left of the aforesaid cross, twenty-four honorable men sat in one row, their faces turned toward it. Not far from them I saw two rams, great and splendid, before the sign of the cross, bearing on their shoulders a wheel of excessive brightness and marvelous size. [Col. 0136D] Having thus viewed all these things, I burst forth in these words: “Lift up the eyes of your hearts to the deifying light; attend and behold the glory and majesty of the Lord.” The next morning, at the third hour, one of the brethren came to the window, and I asked him [Col. 0137A] to celebrate a Mass of the Holy Trinity; he consented. Immediately when he began the Mass, I fell into ecstasy and saw the aforesaid vision again, but more clearly. At the same hour I saw the aforesaid brother, who was serving at the altar, surrounded by much light; and his breath, in the form of white smoke, ascending upward from his mouth.

31. On the following Sunday, namely the Finding of St Stephen [Note: [Col. 0137D] It seems altogether necessary to read *before* the Finding of St Stephen, for this feast (as is evident) fell on the same Monday.], I saw the same vision, but more fully than then; for I now saw before God’s throne the Lamb standing, most lovely, and having a golden cross as though fixed into his back. I also now saw the four Evangelists, in those forms which Holy Scripture assigns to them. They stood arranged on the right of the most blessed Virgin, so that their faces were turned toward her.

[Col. 0137B] I concealed such visions within myself for more than seven days. And when I had firmly resolved in my heart to reveal them to no one, I was seized by a most grievous twisting of the heart, so that I thought I would die. The sisters therefore pressed me, earnestly demanding that I disclose to them what I had seen; and when they had drawn it from me, I immediately recovered from my suffering. And, lest I repeat what has already been said, know that such visions as I saw on the Sundays mentioned above, I was accustomed to see on each Sunday that afterward occurred—twice, three times, or even more often—though first falling into ecstasy, as you yourself have now seen with your own eyes.

[Col. 0137C] 32. But on the Wednesday before the Assumption of the most blessed Mary [Note: [Col. 0138D] That is, 12 August, for the Assumption was to fall on Saturday.], after Compline, I was standing in the chapel; and I prayed to the Lord with all my inmost heart, saying:

> “Lord my God, behold, I commit my soul and body to your unconquered right hand, to your holy and undivided Trinity. To you, Lord, I commit all my anxieties, since my spirit is greatly troubled by the things you have worked in me, because I know that I am altogether unworthy of so great a grace. You know, my Lord, that I never presumed to ask such things of you. But now, since out of your freely bestowed goodness you have so magnified your mercy toward me, I beseech you henceforth so to preserve me that through no sin of mine may I deserve to fall away from your grace; nor may that spirit of [Col. 0137D] sorrow seize me again, by which I would already have been swallowed up had you not, Lord, come to my aid.”

When I had finished this and similar prayers, and was already returning to my bed, these words suddenly came upon my lips: “O virgin, take care not to fall again, lest something worse happen to you, because the good shepherd has care for his sheep.”

On the following day at noon, my heart was suddenly struck by an impulse, and I received these words: “Do not fear, daughter, for the Lord your comforter chastises every son whom he receives.” That same day, toward evening, after I had poured out my heart before my lady with many tears, it happened again that [Col. 0138A] I suddenly found these words turning on my lips: “Rejoice and be glad, daughter of Zion, for divine mercy has rescued you from danger to body and soul.”

33. After this, on the vigil of the Assumption, when I had prayed most devoutly, it suddenly came upon my lips to say: “These are words of consolation which a new tongue speaks, because it is necessary to console a troubled soul.” And I fell into ecstasy and saw the vision which I am accustomed to see on Sundays.

Among other things, I saw my lady rising from her glorious throne and coming forth from that great light which I saw as if through a door. She was accompanied by that threefold multitude of women which I had seen standing about her. Closest after her came those who bore the title of martyrdom on their foreheads; after these, those whom I had seen [Col. 0138B] crowned without a title; and in the third place, those adorned with white veils. On her right walked a certain man, most glorious and lovable, distinguished by a priestly robe. And after she had appeared thus for a short time in the lower air with this sacred host, she was received back into the light from which she seemed to have come forth, with immense praise and glory.

When I awoke from this vision, I immediately took up these words:

> “O glorious light, in which all the saints continually stand, clothed in white robes, and give glory for their reward to him who sits upon the throne and lives for ages of ages.”

Again, during the day at Mass, while I was in the spirit and saw the same things as before, I turned over in my mind these words:

> “O glorious Trinity, who, sitting on the throne of your majesty, behold the abysses [Col. 0138C] and number the thoughts of every human being.”

To this I added: “Hail Mary, glory of virgins, lady of nations, Queen of Angels.” Afterward, waking, I burst forth in these words: “You, holy Lord,” and the remainder with the verse. And I added: “The Lord opens to us the gate of life if we are willing to strive against the most cruel devil.”

I likewise saw all the things that have been related on the Nativity of our Lady.

34. On the Saturday after the Assumption [Note: [Col. 0138D] Thus, on the very day of the Octave.], I suddenly took up these words:

> “The Lord is our lawgiver; the Lord is our king. He himself has called us into his marvelous light, so that, if we are willing to repent of evil deeds, we may receive the prize which is gained in the race-course. Do not neglect these words, for they are profitable to your souls. Attend carefully to the way in which the Creator admonishes his creature.”

After this I added:

> “I will comfort you, says the Lord, and in place of sorrow I will give you spiritual joy; and I will place in your hearts both fear and love. If you fear me and keep my commandments, you will be my true disciples.”

Likewise:

> “I admonish you to love one another. You ought to reflect how God first loved you, when he did not spare his only-begotten Son but gave him up for you as an offering, so that the drachma which had been lost might be found.”

[Col. 0139A] 35. Therefore this proverb applies to us:

> “If we love God and possess perfect charity and brotherly love toward one another, we shall find that drachma which was lost.”

Again I admonish you to have perfect love of God and neighbor, because charity is the highest gift, a great good upon which the whole order of the perfect depends. But above all have charity, which is the bond of perfection; and let the peace of Christ rejoice in your hearts, to which also you were called in one body. And be thankful; let the word of Christ dwell in you abundantly.

Likewise, all who wish to live here according to the world, and do not withdraw their bodies from carnal desires but wish to fulfill everything that belongs to this world, must greatly fear [Col. 0139B] what is said:

> “Do not love the world or the things that are in the world, but repent of evil deeds, for behold, the time is near. Watch therefore, because you do not know the day or the hour when the Lord will come.”

36. On the Beheading of St John the Baptist [Note: [Col. 0139D] The Beheading of St John the Baptist: 29 August.], I began to see that great light which I am accustomed to see as though through a door. Anxious because of this, I cast myself wholly down in prayer, was caught up into ecstasy, and saw Blessed John in the same way in which I had seen him before. And I said in my spirit:

> “May God the Father bless us; may Jesus Christ guard us; may the Holy Spirit enlighten us.”

And I added: “O Key of David.” And I added:

> “This is John, whom the hand of the Lord consecrated in his mother’s womb; we humbly beseech that we may be aided by his prayers.”

Returning again to myself, I uttered these words: “Help me, O Lord my God”; and I added: “By the grace of God I am what I am.” They also say that I said: “Lest the greatness of the revelations exalt me,” and nothing further.

During the day at Terce, again caught up into ecstasy, I looked inward as though through a door and saw that great light which I am accustomed to see, and my lady rising from her throne and coming toward me into this outer light. And with her was that blessed Forerunner of the Lord. I prayed most devoutly and earnestly entrusted myself, all those close to me, and our community to their patronage. At the same time I requested that, if they heard me, they would provide me with some [Col. 0139D] sign that I had been heard.

Immediately they returned to the light from which they had come, and before the great majesty fell upon their faces as though praying, together with them innumerable hosts standing around. Then, waking from ecstasy, I said freely these words:

> “To you be praise, to you glory, to you thanksgiving, O blessed, blessed, and glorious Trinity. Pray for us, most blessed Virgin Mary, that we may be made worthy of Christ’s promises. May all the holy angels of God pray for us in [Col. 0140A] the presence of the Lord. Among those born of women none has arisen greater than John the Baptist. Make wonderful your mercies, O God, who save those who hope in you.”

## CHAPTER III. Other Visions up to the Feast of the Annunciation, in the Year 1154

37. On the Exaltation of the Holy Cross [Note: [Col. 0139D] The Exaltation of the Holy Cross, 14 September, then a Monday.], having often entered ecstasy, I saw that glorious sign of the cross, of excessive splendor. It was shown openly to me not only in that hidden realm of light, but also outside, in a certain lower light.

On the feast of St Michael [Note: [Col. 0139D] St Michael, 29 of the same month, then a Tuesday.], at First Vespers, while I was in ecstasy, I saw three exceedingly glorious men standing before the throne of the Lord’s majesty. The one in the middle appeared more eminent than the others, and seemed to hold a golden censer in his right hand. [Col. 0140B] When I returned to myself, I said: “An angel stood beside the altar of the temple, having a golden censer in his hand” (Rev. 8).

During the day at Mass, I again saw the same more eminent man advancing with a distinguished banner, accompanied by a great multitude. And when they came around the throne before the presence of the Majesty, they fell upon their faces; and this happened three times.

38. At the same Mass, when the sisters approached to receive communion and I still sat at a distance because of weakness, I looked into the chalice and saw the true appearance of blood. And when wine was poured in, I clearly saw the difference between the blood and what was added, until they were mixed and [Col. 0140C] a single color of blood appeared.

On another day—I do not know which—a similar thing happened to me. And I saw, as is my custom, everything taking place outwardly around the altar during Mass. And while the priest blessed the chalice, behold, the dove which I am accustomed to see on the altar approached slowly, dipped its head into the chalice, and immediately the appearance of blood was seen. Even now it is not rare for me to see such things.

It also happened one day that one of the brethren came bearing in a pyx the divine sacrament of the Lord’s body, as seemed necessary for a sick sister.
