The sceptre in his left hand is royal power, which he testified that he had received even according to his human nature, saying: “All power in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matt. 28).

The hyacinth tunic signifies the power of heavenly contemplation, which possessed the Saviour’s mind wholly and perfectly. For unlike other human beings he had not received the Spirit by measure, he in whom “all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Col. 2). The white belt signifies in him the brightness of inviolable innocence. He appeared upon the path signifying the contemplation of his divinity, [Col. 0166C] because he wills it to remain thus forever, whereas the others are not to remain. He did not appear in all the paths, and yet he was in all of them (Matt. 28), because they severally signify the virtues through which righteous people come to the high mountain, where they receive individual rewards for individual virtues; and in all the paths of truth God is to be contemplated.

90. The mystery of the second vision is as follows. The three paths that appeared to the left of the man standing on the mountain, alongside the green path, express the character of three orders in the Church: namely, married persons, the continent, and rulers. The path enclosed by brambles is the life of married persons. This path appeared pleasant because this way of life was instituted by God from the beginning; and [Col. 0166D] if it is lawfully observed, it is beautiful and pleasing in the Lord’s sight, and those who walk upon it doubtless ascend the mountain of God. But the countless thorns of worldly cares press in upon it on every side, so that its travellers must be pricked by them unless, through restrained living, they bind themselves in every way and always proceed bowed down, humbling themselves before God and human beings.

The path free from brambles and bordered on both sides by pleasant flowers is the life of the continent. For it is characteristic of these persons to withdraw their minds from the cares and anxieties of the present life and to think only upon the things of the Lord, that they may be holy in body and spirit. This path is narrow because, if it is to be observed lawfully and wisely, the steps of those walking on it must be constrained by the safeguard of great discipline, [Col. 0167A] lest, perhaps, living according to their own will, they fall into fornication, or be reckoned with the foolish virgins or the self-indulgent widows who are dead while they live. It is little trodden because, in comparison with others, few enter it and fewer persevere in it. It is delightfully bordered everywhere with flowers of diverse kinds because every kind of virtue adorns the life of the continent.

The middle path, wider than the two just described, is the way of rulers. Since it was instituted for governing the lives of married persons, continent persons, or both alike, it is less restricted than theirs and has freer scope for exercising its own will; consequently, the feet of those walking upon it slip more easily, as its flatness appropriately signifies. Therefore it was called dangerous, because so many slip upon it that very few are found firm upon it. [Col. 0167B] Its seeming pavement of red bricks, which are made from earth baked by fire, signifies the care of prelates, by which their minds must continually be fired in concern for their subjects, to whom they owe care of both soul and body.

91. When I asked my instructing angel concerning the interpretation of the third vision, he said to me: “Behold, you have begun the Book of the Ways of God, as had been proposed to you.” He said this because in the preceding year, on a certain day when I was in the spirit, he had led me, as it were, into a meadow in which a tent was pitched; and we entered it. He showed me [Col. 0167C] a great heap of books laid there and said: “Do you see these books? All are still to be dictated before the day of judgment.” Then, lifting one of them, he said: “This is the Book of the Ways of God, which is to be revealed through you when you have visited Sister Hildegard and heard her.”

And indeed it began to be fulfilled immediately after I had returned from her [Note: [Col. 0167D] That is, between Easter and Pentecost of the year 1156; Pentecost was to be celebrated on 3 June that year, and this event had occurred on 15 April, when the letter G indicated the Sundays after leap-year.].

92. The meaning of the four paths shown in the third vision is as follows. The first, nearest the purple path, rough with thickets in its lower part but open and flowered in its upper part, signifies the life of those who live lawfully in the world, spend half their days in worldly concerns, and then pass to the flowered and open life of the continent. Binding themselves by the latter’s rule, [Col. 0167D] they ascend the mountain of God with them.

The dry path, rough with clods, is that most severe form of life in which holy hermits walk, as do some who maintain a way of life in human society and mortify and dry out their flesh beyond human measure by fasts, vigils, genuflections, scourges, haircloth, and every kind of most grievous affliction. All such things are like the harshest clods; and those who walk this path need much effort and vigilance lest they stumble in its excessive harshness and fall more grievously than others.

Of the two paths which appeared together with those [Col. 0168A] described, one—as was said—seemed more worn and easier. Of it my instructor said: “The holy souls of children walk this path: those sanctified in holy baptism who depart this life before their seventh year. Since they have not experienced the wickedness of the world, they attain the kingdom of God with a swift and utterly unencumbered step.”

Of the other he said: “This is the path of youths, who proceed a little more slowly than those children; and for that reason their path appears less trodden and easy.” These, then, are the visions and their interpretations. He who opened my eyes that I might see the visions of God undoubtedly showed through his angel that, as was pleasing in his sight, they were to be understood in this manner.

## CHAPTER VII. A summary selection of the first five discourses, dictated by the angel for the individual Ways

[Col. 0168B]

93. It happened on the feast of Blessed James that, while I was in the spirit and saw the vision of the Ways of God, I was caught up on high and contemplated, as though on a nearby mountain, the mountain of God. Behold, that immeasurable light which occupied the summit of the mountain seemed to be split through the middle; and I looked through it and saw a multitude of saints whose number could not be reckoned. My guide said to me:

“Here you see martyrs, holy bishops and confessors of the Lord, virgins, cenobites, widows of both sexes, secular married persons and continent persons, nobles and persons of low rank, all [Col. 0168C] reigning with Christ. They walked the ways of the Lord, the holy ways which you saw, and received unfading glory from Christ the Lord with his angels. Let each person now consider his or her own way. If one has walked unjustly, let that person correct himself or herself with humility, charity, and obedience, and make the way straight. If one reaches the end, one shall receive the eternal reward.”

94. After this I was resting on my bed and had not yet begun to sleep, when suddenly the Spirit of the Lord visited me and filled my mouth with words of this kind:

“Therefore now give heed, you who have renounced worldly desires and have chosen to follow in his footsteps . . . . Consider within yourselves how you live with humility and obedience and charity, [Col. 0168D] without murmuring, detraction, and envy, and without pride; and refrain from other vices . . . . .”

The angel who spoke to me in turns had not yet finished these words when a certain doubt occurred to me concerning the distinction of the ways of God that had been described. I asked, saying: “My lord, are we cenobites on the way of contemplation when we are on the way of continence? Or can we be on both?”

And he said: “The way of contemplation is common to you and to clerics, just as the way of continence is common to them and to you. Yet know that many are on the way of continence who are not on the way of contemplation. And there are many clerics who walk neither on the way of contemplation [Col. 0169A] nor on the way of continence; and these are unhappy . . . .”

When these discourses had been completed, on the day when we kept the commemoration of St. Michael, he again appeared to me. I addressed him, saying: “My lord, can we safely affirm that all these discourses have proceeded from you?” I said this because he had partly uttered these words in such a manner that I did not see his face, while partly they had been pronounced through my mouth in the spirit.

Then he, looking upon me with great severity, said: “Believe with all your heart these words which have been written down and which proceeded from my mouth. Blessed is he who reads and hears the words of this book, for they are true and never depart from truth.”

Immediately he began another [Col. 0169B] discourse in these words:

“I admonish those who are oppressed by worldly cares to reflect sometimes upon the commandments of life—that is, to love God, etc. . . . If they cannot raise themselves to the height of contemplation, let them strive to fulfill the duties of lawful actions . . . . . This is the straight and beautiful way of the Lord, the way of holy actions. Whoever walks in it to the end shall find life and rest upon God’s holy mountain, and his lot shall be with the children of light.”

95. A feast day was being celebrated, and we were present at the divine office, when the angel appeared before me according to his custom. Reproaching my sins before him because of his delay, longer than usual, I said to him: “May it now please you, my lord, to impart to us the discipline of that third [Col. 0169C] way, which is the way of the holy martyrs; and do not let yourself be restrained from this goodness of yours because of any sins of mine.”

Then he opened his mouth and spoke, saying:

“The Lamb of Christ goes before the holy martyrs, and they follow him with palms and crowns, rejoicing with him in noble triumph . . . Hear these things and receive them in your heart, you who suffer persecution for righteousness: go rejoicing by the noble way, the way of the Lord’s warriors, the way made purple by the blood of the saints and of the Lamb . . . . .”

But before the angel speaking with me had finished these words, the feast of the Blessed Virgins Ursula and her eleven thousand companions arrived. [Col. 0169D] Then, at the morning vigil, that divine saying was sung in which it is said: “God shall render the reward of the labors of his saints and lead them by a wondrous way.” Taking occasion from this, when my instructor appeared to me as usual amid the silences of the Mass, I asked him: “Lord, show me what that wondrous way is . . . . .”

He immediately replied: “This is the way of the holy martyrs . . . . . and it may rightly be called wondrous . . .”

After this, when the feast of St. Martin was at hand, around midnight before the morning vigil, I suddenly awoke and sleep fled from my eyes. And behold, the angel of the Lord stood before me. I addressed him, saying: “I pray, my lord, that you now complete [Col. 0170A] the exhortation of your discourse concerning the holy martyrs and bring it to a fitting conclusion.”

After causing me to behold certain sublime things, whose sight I was unworthy to receive, he fulfilled my request . . . . .

96. I was in prayer, and my lord appeared to me as usual. I asked him for the discipline of that way which was said to belong to the order of married people. He immediately assented to my request and began thus:

“Behold, I speak and admonish worldly married persons: refrain from your wicked deeds . . . namely avarice, lust, fornication, adultery, homicide . . . for it is impossible to enter by your way while burdened with such vices.”

Having said this, he departed. When he appeared again, I asked him to continue the exhortation of the discourse he had begun. He said:

“Were it not that the Lord is gracious and merciful, [Col. 0170B] he might be wearied because he admonishes the inhabitants of the world in so many ways, while they make nothing of his warnings . . . Give honor, O man and woman, to your order, which God has deigned to honor . . . Let fear of the Lord bind your hearts, so that in the work permitted to you, you may impose a bridle upon yourselves . . . Honor feast days, the days of lawful abstinence, and times of purification by continence; and if you add anything beyond this, the Lord shall add grace to you and to your offspring . . . . .

“But know this: the principal cause of your mutual union ought to be the propagation of offspring. If there is another cause, it belongs to infirmity and receives indulgence, provided it has the restraint of the fear of the Lord and the remedy of almsgiving . . . . . Again I say to you [Col. 0170C] who live under the yoke of marriage: fear God; preserve unblemished faith and love toward one another; bring up your sons, daughters, and household in the fear of the Lord and in chastity . . . This is the delightful beauty of your way, which was shown in mystery . . . Yet those who walk in it must endure the tribulation of the flesh and worldly anxieties, which those who are continent do not experience, just as this was expressed by the image of thorns . . . .”

97. My brother asked me to inquire of the angel why, at the beginning of this discourse, he had included the name of fornication among the other names of iniquities, since it did not seem to pertain to the married persons to whom he was speaking.

When I began to ask my lord concerning this doubt, [Col. 0170D] he spoke to me, saying . . . :

“The world is full of the uncleanness of fornication, and scarcely anyone is found who does not hurl himself into its pit . . . But I included the name of fornication in the rebuke of married persons because, before they undertake the law of marriage, they too defile themselves excessively in it and provoke God’s wrath against themselves. Hence, when they enter lawful marriages, they are deprived by the Lord of the fruit of generation; and they wonder why this happens to them, not knowing the cause of their sterility. But those to whom offspring is granted are divinely afflicted in many ways, either in the offspring itself or in other necessary matters, and everything turns out unhappily for them . . .”

Then I asked him, saying: “My lord, what do you say about those [Col. 0171A] whom they call Cathars, who are said wholly to reject the life of married persons?”

He replied: “The life of those concerning whom you ask is abominable before the Lord . . .”

Again I addressed him, saying: “Lord, as I have heard, some among them assert that marriage cannot be lawful unless it is between persons who have both preserved virginity until the time of lawful union. What do you say to this?”

He replied: “Where such a marriage can exist, it is pleasing to the Lord; but it is very rare for this to occur. Nevertheless, among those who have not remained continent, many are acceptable to the Lord: they have lawful marriages and walk in the commandments of the Lord. Otherwise the number of God’s people would be excessively reduced.”

[Col. 0171B] 98. As we celebrated the solemnity of Blessed John the Evangelist, I was intent on prayer after the morning vigils. With earnest intention of heart I besought the Lord, according to his customary kindness, to deign to reveal to me the discipline of the way of the continent which I had seen in the spirit. I also invoked the divine Evangelist and my angelic teacher to assist me.

When I had grown weary in prayer, I relaxed my eyes a little into sleep; and soon afterward I suddenly awoke. Behold, the angel stood by me and began the discourse I desired in these words:

“I say to you, O children of God, O children of light: behold your way, how it blossoms and how delightful it is to run in it. Therefore run and [Col. 0171C] hasten to meet your Bridegroom, who awaits you. Love chastity, and preserve for him the integrity of your virginity. A virgin adorned with chastity, charity, prudence, and humility runs well.”

Having said this, he added nothing further.

99. On the following day, while the Mass office of the blessed Innocents was being celebrated, I took occasion from the reading of the Apocalypse that was read and besought my lord, who again stood beside me, saying: “Lord, if I have found favor before you, tell me, I beseech you: what is this song which these blessed martyrs sing before the throne of God and of the Lamb, as today’s reading testifies? Or how do they follow the Lamb wherever he goes?”

He answered: “Why do you question me? No tongue on earth knows this [Col. 0171D] song; I shall tell you nothing of it. But as to your question, ‘What does it mean that they follow the Lamb wherever he goes?’—it means that they imitate him in all the virtues that may be considered in the Lamb . . . .”

Again, at the Circumcision of the Lord, when my lord presented himself to me, I said to him: “My lord, teach me, I beseech you, concerning the integrity of virginity. Can it be lost through unclean lust such as occurs in temptation, if the lust is not carried through to the act?”

He said: “It is not lost, but it is defiled . . . . It is not acceptable to God and is deprived of its due reward.”

When, however, on the Octave of Blessed John he again presented himself to me, he anticipated my words, cheerfully addressing me thus: “You wish to question me: ask, and I shall answer you.”

And I said, as [Col. 0172A] I had been forewarned by my guide: “Lord, can the statement written, ‘The will shall be accounted as the deed,’ conflict with the discourse that you spoke recently?”

He replied: “Not at all.” He added:

“What you cite from Scripture is certainly true: when a person has the will to perform some deed, such that nothing remains in him but to bring to completion what he desires, and he so persists to the end, this is accounted before the Lord as though done. Yet it can be erased through the power of true repentance. For whatever a person has done in thought or will can be annulled before the Lord as though it had never been. . . . But the integrity of one who does not wash away a wicked will by the fruit of repentance, although it remains, is useless and obtains no [Col. 0172B] fruit.”

100. Again I added, saying: “Lord, there are persons who unwillingly experience stirrings of the flesh in temptation, who are distressed by the ardor that opposes the purity of their bodies, yet are unable to avoid it by any resistance. Shall this be imputed to them as sin?”

He said: “If they are distressed by temptations of this kind and do not consent to them in their minds, by a lighter penance they shall obtain pardon for the guilt which they thus contract, and they shall gain a great reward.”

He told me of a person intimate with Christ—who or what person it was, God knows—who was enduring an assault against chastity from the adversary and afflicting his soul with excessive distress because of it. [Col. 0172C] He said: “Announce consolation to that person. Tell that person to spare the affliction. Let that person recall what is written of the Lord’s elect: ‘He tested them as gold in a furnace.’ Let it be a joy, yet not without sorrow: joy because the Lord has deigned to impose such a thing, by which that person is prepared for a great reward; but not without sorrow, because in such temptation guilt is not altogether avoided.”

And I said: “Lord, how should that person resist the adversary, and by what weapons shall that person overcome him?”

He said: “Let that person fight by prayer, confession, and scourging of the flesh, and shall overcome. But let that person not persist in asking the Lord to be freed from this goad; rather, let that person pray that the Lord may have mercy during this time of temptation. If that person is in a more secluded place, let that person bend the knees [Col. 0172D] three times before the Lord; but if the circumstances of the place do not permit it, let that person mark the heart three times with the sign of the cross and say: ‘Savior of the world, save us, who redeemed us through the cross and blood; assist us, we beseech you, our God.’”

101. After this, one day he raised his voice in these words:

“O virgins, behold, the divine voice cries out to you; the voice of your Bridegroom knocks upon your ears. Open to him, bring him into the palace of your hearts, and embrace him, for he is more beautiful and more lovable than every creature . . . . .”

There follows a long exhortation to virgins, and after it another. In the course of it Elizabeth asked the angel: “Lord, what are those wedding garments of which you spoke?”

He answered: “Virgins ought to go into the [Col. 0173A] inner chamber of their hearts and purchase there three kinds of adornment. First, they must have a white and spotless garment, which is innocence of the flesh. They also need a second covering with which they ought to be clothed: charity, by which they must love Christ the Bridegroom. Their third ornament is a golden necklace, which is modesty, by which the virgin ought to restrain herself, so that she may be modest in speaking, hearing, seeing, and doing everything that is not indecent. This is the sign of which it is said: ‘He set a sign upon my face.’”

He added this, I think, because at the feast of Blessed Agnes I had questioned him about this very phrase, and he then gave me no answer concerning it.

Again I said: “Lord, at what [Col. 0173B] price are these ornaments to be purchased by virgins?”

He said: “By the chastening of their own bodies, and by one denarius, which is contemplation of the Bridegroom’s modesty; this they ought to store in the midst of their hearts . . . . .”

When these discourses had been completed, on the second Sunday of the sacred Fast, the feast day of St. Matthias the apostle—for in the year 1157 the dominical letter was F, and Ash Wednesday fell on 11 February—during the time of the divine office or sacrifice, the blessed one of the Lord, the holy angel, appeared to me and gave a fitting end to the discourse addressed to the Lord’s virgins.

## CHAPTER VIII. Synopsis of the five remaining discourses

102. When the preceding discourse had been brought to its end, the angel of the Lord delayed longer than usual to visit me. I attributed this to my sins, was troubled within myself, and more diligently devoted myself to tears and prayers; our community also assisted me with common prayer.

When seventeen days had passed since he had completed the words already mentioned—after the feast of Pope St. Gregory, 12 March—I was standing alone in the oratory around the third hour, pouring out my heart before the Lord and saying:

“Lord, you did not regard my merits in all that you have thus far done with me, but have done all these things in your mercy. Therefore I beseech you: do not let my sins, or those of anyone else, restrain you from bringing, through your goodness, to a good completion those things which you have now deigned to begin with me. Deign to reveal to us fitting instruction concerning the way of the rulers [Col. 0173D] of the Church which you showed me in mystery, so that some fruit of correction may arise from it, as you know to be necessary for your people.”

While I was still speaking these and similar things in prayer, behold, the angel of my desire suddenly appeared before me and began the discourse I desired in these words:

“Thus says the Lord: Behold, I send my angel to announce to you who are imitators in exalted authority. But I say to you that the iniquity of the land, which you conceal for gold and silver, rises before me like smoke from fire . . . Behold the great high priest, the Lord Jesus, exalted above all things: how, in the days of his obedience, he walked among his disciples [Col. 0174A] not in the loftiness of one who dominates but in the humility of one who serves, as one more zealous for his flock, even to the consummation of death on its behalf. Look upon his blessed seed, the holy apostles, ministers of your calling: were their ways like your ways? . . .”

103. As we celebrated the feast day of Easter (31 March), during the divine office after the reading of the Gospel, the angel of the Lord appeared to me standing before me. I asked him to deign to ensure that no negligence occurred in that sacred communion which we were awaiting; I added the request that he deign to continue his discourse concerning the rulers of the Church, as he had begun it.

To this he gave me a brief answer, [Col. 0174B] saying: “If they were worthy, the Lord would reveal many great things concerning them.”

Having said this, he immediately went swiftly to the altar and, with two angels who had come at the beginning of Mass, stood there with great attentiveness until we had all communicated. On the following day, coming at about the same time, he repeated similar things. On the next day he added:

“Thus says the Lord to the great prelates of the Church: Remember what an account you shall render at my dreadful judgment concerning my sheep, whom you have undertaken to govern and guard . . .”

After this, as if in a spirit of gentleness, he said: “I, the Lord, cry out and admonish my shepherds . . . For there are some who seem good and peaceable to me—alas, how few!—and many others [Col. 0174C] wicked and perverse . . . Therefore the good must be admonished to make progress toward better things; but the wicked and perverse, to be converted, lest they perish from the righteous way.”

When he visited me again, he added: “With every care of mind attend to your way . . . For if you love me and render honor to my name, I shall honor you before my holy angels.”

104. While the angel was still speaking these discourses to me about the shepherds of the Church, some thought it opportune that I should ask concerning matters in which certain doubters take an occasion for their error. Therefore I asked, not as one doubting in faith but as desiring that our faith be confirmed by angelic authority. I said:

“Lord, in the Church’s [Col. 0174D] sacraments, do the ministrations of those bishops who entered their episcopacy improperly and not according to God possess equal truth with those of bishops whose entry was good?”

He replied: “Many persons, by probing such things too deeply, are made worse rather than better; and the Lord would reveal such things, if those to whom they pertain would not thereby sin more freely.”

Having said this, he immediately vanished from my sight. But when he returned to me on another day, I asked him again, repeating the same question written above. He said: “They have equal power; but God is better pleased with the ministrations of those who entered rightly.”

Again I added: “Is it so, my lord, that priests ordained by those whose entry was bad [Col. 0175A] have the same power to consecrate the body and blood of the Lord upon the altar as those ordained by persons who entered lawfully?”

He said: “Let doubt concerning this matter never enter your heart; but be certain that all who have received the priesthood in ecclesiastical ordination have the same power in consecrating the Lord’s sacrament, whether their ordainers entered rightly or wrongly . . . . .”

105. Since this entire discourse seemed to concern our Fathers, who exercise spiritual judgments in the Church, I asked the angel of the Lord, saying: “I pray, lord, that as you have thus far given words of admonition to spiritual rulers, so too you may announce from the Lord some admonitions to those who hold secular judgments, [Col. 0175B] by which they too may be corrected.”

He immediately granted my request and began the discourse concerning them in these words:

“Behold, the Lord has appointed princes and judges over his people, that they might exercise judgment and justice and establish truth and peace between man and man, so that all the people might be pleasing before the living God. But now . . . . . Therefore, as I live, says the Lord, if you do not heed the voice of my admonition and turn to me, I shall cast you down from your height, which you have used wickedly, into the depths of hell; and you shall be companions of those to whom you have made yourselves like, in the living fire for ever.”

On the holy day of Pentecost (19 May), at the first hour before the celebration of the divine office, while I was [Col. 0175C] in prayer, the angel appeared before me and completed the discourse thus far stated . . .

106. On the feast of St. Martin [Note: [Col. 0175] I read and correct this to: Maximinus, bishop of Trier, 29 May; for this is required by the sequence of the following feasts.], amid the silences of the Mass, I addressed the angel, saying:

“May it now please you, lord, to give us instruction suited to that way whose one part appeared occupied by brambles, while the other was pleasant with flowers and narrow, containing no brambles or impediments.”

I had scarcely finished the words of my request when he immediately said:

“Behold, I say to you who have been widowed in the world, living in the flesh amid labors and many straits: refrain from the vices of this world and walk on the way of the continent . . .”

He added on the Vigil of the Apostles (28 June):

“And what more shall I add in admonishing you? Behold, I have shown [Col. 0175D] the way and instructed you in discipline. Feel your way here and there, consider the words, retain the examples, love chastity, run toward the brightness of our Lord Jesus Christ, which may he deign to grant you—he who lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.”

When all these discourses were almost completed, on the feast of the apostles Peter and Paul, before the hour of the divine office, I was praying in private. The angel of the Lord appeared before me and spoke these words in my hearing:

“Let it be announced to the bishop of Trier (Hillinus), and to the bishops of Cologne and Mainz (Arnold II and Radulf), by the Lord God, great and dreadful, and by the Angel of the Covenant of this book, [Col. 0176A] that they are to announce to the Roman Church, to the whole people, and to the entire Church of God these words which they shall find in this present book. Correct yourselves and turn away from your errors. Do not receive this sacred and divine admonition unworthily, for these things have not been invented by human beings. I speak to you by name because in this province you bear the name of religion. Read and hear the divine admonitions and receive them with a tranquil mind. Do not suppose that these are women’s fictions, for they are not; rather, they are from God the almighty Father, who is the fountain and origin of all goodness. And what I say to you, I say to all others.”

107. I wished to receive the beginning of the eighth discourse on the feast of the translation of our holy father Benedict (11 July), [Col. 0176B] but on that day my prayers were hindered by the presence of guests, and my desire was deferred until the next day.

Then too, as I stood in prayer after the chapter hour, the angel of the Lord presented himself to me. I asked him to begin a discourse addressed to those whose way had appeared in the vision as though covered with clods of earth. Immediately opening his mouth, he spoke these words:

“Give heed, you who have chosen to live in the wilderness, to the discretion you possess . . . so that you do not quickly follow every impulse of your zeal, which drives you to the height of perfection, nor exceed the measure of your strength by immoderate labors . . . Therefore remember, O man, your frailty, that you may walk cautiously on [Col. 0176C] the hard way which you have entered and proceed patiently in your haste, lest you suffer a fall . . . Moreover, receive the instruction and discipline of contemplation, and console your lowliness in it.”

As we sat in chapter to hear the reading of the Rule, on the feast of St. Mary Magdalene, my lord stood before me and brought the present discourse to a fitting conclusion. When it was the feast of Blessed James at First Vespers, the angel of the Lord appeared before me. Therefore I did as the writer of these discourses had suggested to me, and asked him to pronounce the title that ought to be written at the head of this book. Immediately assenting to my request, he said: “This is the book,” etc., no. 86.

108. In August, on the fifth day of the month, after the morning vigils, [Col. 0176D] while I lay on my bed and had not yet begun to sleep, the angel of the Lord suddenly appeared before me and began the ninth discourse of the present book in these words:

“Behold, I have something to say to you who are in youth, like a lily which was closed before the sun’s rising and, when the sun shines, opens itself in its power and delights in the sun’s warmth . . . Learn first to fear the Lord . . . Behold, in your bosom is a desirable and precious treasure: the jewel of virginity. You shall be blessed if you preserve it . . . If your soul is pleased to preserve it, take heed that you do not defile it by the careless frivolities [Col. 0177A] of your youth. Turn away with fear in your heart from inducements to impurity; flee the conversations and playful familiarities of young women, and do not associate with their seducers. Keep your mouth from indecent speech; restrain your eyes and hands from every shameful thing . . .”

After this he added again:

“I shall further speak to my brothers and fellow servants the admonitions of their Father. Children, make habits of holiness customary to yourselves in your flowering age, habits which you may practice in the time of your maturity . . . O unblemished adolescents and young men . . . walk in the beauty of your way, and you shall be children beloved by the Lord and like the angels of God in heaven, into whose fellowship may our Lord Jesus Christ deign to lead you.”

[Col. 0177B] 109. When the preceding discourse had been completed by the angel, on the Vigil of the Assumption of Mary, holy Mother of God, and again on the feast day itself during the divine office, he visited me and said:

“Behold, I still wish to complete my discourses, for there is still room, and I have something briefly to say concerning children who do not know how to guard themselves because of ignorance. Their mothers must therefore be admonished to keep them chaste and spotless in the fear of God, lest perhaps they perish.”

To this I added, asking: “Lord, what did you mean when you said, ‘Chaste and spotless’? What can children do by which they may defile their chastity? And if they commit any fault, does not ignorance excuse them?”

He said: “They often defile their chastity by unclean [Col. 0177C] words and by deeds which they themselves can perform. Although they do these things in ignorance, they are nevertheless not without guilt; and if they depart this life, they cannot altogether escape punishment, because they have been chastised by no one, nor did they know how to have repentance for their sin on their own account. Therefore they ought to be chastised by their parents for their sins, because just as they become accustomed to doing evil, so they would learn to do good if they were brought up toward this end through charity.

“But when I said, ‘spotless,’ I said it concerning those who have passed a little beyond their seventh year. Then they defile themselves more by wicked deeds, because they know better how to think of evil, since they are not prevented from it; for they too, to the extent they are able, perform works of indecency, not knowing what they do. If such persons depart this life, they endure great punishments until they are purified, since absolutely no stain can enter the kingdom of God. This, then, [Col. 0178B] is their perishing, of which I spoke above. They are punished all the more severely and for a longer time because they are less aided by the prayers and alms of friends, since they are not thought to need them.

“I say to you parents, and to all who have charge of little children: take heed how you keep them with great care, because their sins shall recoil upon you . . .”

He completed this discourse on the Octave of the Assumption . . . . . .

This is the adjuration of the writer of these discourses:

“I adjure everyone who copies this book, by the Lord and by his angel, to correct it diligently and to append this adjuration to that person’s copy.”

[Note: [Col. 0177C]

The Book IV which follows in the printed editions, divided into five chapters, prefixes to them a vision concerning the Assumption of the Virgin Mary, Mother of the Lord. This vision was promised on her feast day in 1156, was shown in 1157, and was ordered to be published two years later. There it is affirmed that the Mother of God did indeed fall asleep on 15 August, but was raised again and assumed bodily into heaven on the fortieth day afterward, 23 September—a day which the sisters then began to keep solemnly in Elizabeth’s chamber. There too the Mother of God herself is represented as informing the questioning virgin that she lived on earth for only one year after the Lord’s Ascension, together with the interval from the feast of the Ascension to 15 August.

All these things are of such a kind that we may rightly doubt whether Elizabeth truly dictated them. Still more so is the discourse concerning the eleven thousand virgins, which forms the principal part of this book. Whoever wishes to learn something from us in advance concerning them should read our dissertation inserted into the attempted historical Chronicle on the Roman pontiffs after the pontificate of St. Pontian, and the Supplement to the same dissertation. That person should also remember the *Parergon*, placed among the Lives of St. Mary Magdalene de’ Pazzi, whose teaching would derive from this another new argument for excluding from the determination of historical controversies the sayings and deeds of ecstatic holy women. For, since—as is there reported—the Mother of God, speaking to Elizabeth, restricts her own age to less than fifty years, the same Mother of God may be set against this statement, as asserting to St. Birgitta, Book VII, chapter 26, that after her Son ascended into heaven she lived in the world for fifteen years; while others nevertheless maintain that she departed this life much later.]

[Col. 0178C] Our Cancellottus, in his *Marian Annals* for the year of Christ 46, adduces in support of Elisabeth’s opinion “testimony from secrets revealed to the blessed man Bertram the Cistercian,” cited in the eighth book of a certain Massaeus’s *Chronicle*, under the year of Christ 36; and he admits that the holy Ildephonsus of Toledo likewise favors them, when in Sermon 6, *On the Assumption*, he says that “after Christ’s triumph the Virgin did not remain long among the living.” But the objections which he brings against both Elisabeth and Birgitta will not carry great weight with one who has sifted these matters by critical examination. Cancellottus might have answered Elisabeth as he answers Birgitta in no. 7: that “the Virgin spoke according to the opinion then very common in the Church”; but I doubt whether such an answer will satisfy many. Brower [Col. 0178D], in the *Annals of Trier*, book IV, no. 104, discussing the Ursulans and admitting that “it cannot easily be determined whether Elisabeth’s revelations concerning them are distinguished by such careful marking of times and detailed narration of events that a historical foundation lies hidden in them” (the subject being difficult and ancient), finally thinks that in this very knowledge of so remote and obscure an antiquity which Elisabeth drew concerning the virgins, something may have proceeded partly from a free mind and partly from some signification granted from above; for, he says, since many eagerly demanded it, as commonly happens from curiosity, she received no more than the divine power judged it expedient for them to know. Let each abound here in his own opinion. For Elisabeth, thus far—at least with respect to the Ursulans—I see nothing more advantageous than to doubt whether she truly dictated such things herself. We shall explain the rest more fully under 21 October, and likewise the year of the Mother of God’s death under 15 August. Yet that day began first to be assigned to her Dormition under the Emperor Marcian [Col. 0179D], in the year 450, for an altogether different reason than that she was thought to have died then: this is shown by the dedication, then performed with great solemnity, of the church at Blachernae; and by the fact that the most ancient copies of the Hieronymian Martyrology do not mention her in August, but on 18 January record: “The deposition of the holy and glorious Blessed Mary, mother of our Lord Jesus Christ.” On this passage see Florentinius’s learned dissertation among his notes on the most ancient Martyrology of the Western Church, which we commonly call the Hieronymian. Learn also that the more ancient Greeks observed the same day and handed it down for observance to the Egyptians or Copts. In the *Sermon on the Ursulans* she entitles herself “the servant of the handmaids of the Lord who are at Schönau”; for this seems to coincide with the title *Magistra*, “Mistress” or “teacher,” which she employs in writing to St Hildegard, similarly calling her “the mistress [Col. 0180D] of the convent of St Rupert near Bingen,” not abbess. But when she was elected mistress, there is no basis on which I can determine. Yet conjecture leads me to believe that this occurred in 1157, after she had heard the eighth discourse from the angel, or perhaps after the completion of the *Book of the Ways of God*, or after the virgin had reached thirty years of age. Together with book IV we omit book V also, which consists of letters irrelevant to history, and pass to book VI, which properly belongs to Egbert alone; and it deserves all the credit due to an eyewitness and to a man of integrity, learning, and prudence.

.

## CHAPTER IX. The virgin’s final illness, and what occurred in it until her brother’s return from Mainz.

[Col. 0178C]

**110.** Brother Egbert, from the monastery of Schönau, sends the service of his prayers and the affection of devotion to the virgins consecrated to God in the congregation of Anturnac [Col. 0179A]—Buda, Hadevig, Redelind, his kinswomen and intimates.

> [Note: [Col. 0180D] The Anturnac congregation: neither where it was situated nor from what place it took this name have I thus far been able to discover. Elisabeth’s sixth letter is addressed to them, but contributes nothing to history.]

**111–112.** Allow me, my dearest ones, to lament my sorrow a little among you, and receive the words of my mourning with the sweetness of compassion. I shall lament a little, grieve only moderately, in proportion to the greatness of my wound, lest I be thought disturbed by carnal affection and it be reckoned to me as folly. Behold, our Elisabeth—that chosen lamp of heavenly light, illustrious and honored virgin, the radiant jewel of abundant divine grace in our convent, leader of our virginal company—alas, has been taken from this life before reaching more mature years. She who gave me birth into the light of an unfamiliar newness [Col. 0179B], who drew me into the familiar service of Jesus my Lord, who with honey-sweet mouth was accustomed to bring me consolations and instructions from God out of heaven, and made my heart taste the first-fruits of that sweetness hidden for the saints in God—she has gone by the path from which there is no return. And behold, the sweetness of my soul, the consolation of my poverty, and the sweet seasoning of all my labors is no longer found upon earth. Rightly, then, I gird my heart with the belt of mourning; rightly, my beloved, do I take up lamentation for you: gracious virgin, most lovable virgin, richly endowed with the holy sweetness with which the Spirit of God had anointed you. The inward parts of my soul mourn your untimely departure, O daughter of grace, and the strings of my heart sound a mournful song to my spirit.

[Col. 0179C] **113.** Yet my sorrow is not like the sorrow produced by flesh and blood, as though I were now mourning carnal things because of our kinship; rather, it is the shared loss of spiritual delights that grieves me, delights which you, in God’s service, were accustomed to dispense to many in an unheard-of manner. Through you heaven stood open to the world, and God’s mysteries hidden from the ages flowed through the instrument of your voice to us; your speech was more precious than gold and sweeter than honey. Through you angels spoke familiarly with us and we with angels; through your mediation the exalted princes of heaven were graciously accessible to us. O happy woman! How many kings and prophets desired to see what you saw and did not see it (Luke 10)! For the sublime palace of heaven lay open to your blessed eyes [Col. 0179D], and before the time of the common vision you beheld beforehand the inaccessible brightness of the immortal kingdom. You made known to us the glory of heaven’s citizens [Col. 0180A] and set it, as it were, before the eyes of our minds; and your blessed prayers greatly kindled our hearts with longing for the homeland for which we wait. Your words of admonition often strengthened wavering souls in God’s service, and by holy fervor you made us multiply the praises of the Lord greatly.

**114.** O how many works of mercy have been done far and wide throughout the lands through your exhortations! For many souls of the elect obtained the consolations they longed for through your mediation. Blessed daughter, you are blessed by the Lord, because you dealt fruitfully between God and human beings. O woman happily born, how our unhappy times have lost you! Lamp of God, how have you been extinguished to the world! [Col. 0180B] How have you been shut, O bright window, through which the Lord’s eyes looked upon us! It is fitting, O chosen one of God, that we weep over the loss of your sweet presence, for you fought the good fight and happily completed the course of your martyrdom. Indeed, your whole life from your tender years onward, if we observe rightly, may truly be called a martyrdom. For from your youth you bore the Lord’s yoke, always walking under religious discipline, in poverty and manifold tribulation. The hand of the Lord was always heavy upon you, nor at any time did heavenly visitation fail you, pressing your spirit and crushing your pitiable body with afflictions and hardships. May he alone who considers toil and sorrow deign to know and number them. Cheerful and patient [Col. 0180C], you showed yourself under every chastisement of the Lord; and upon the pain of the wounds which his hand inflicted on you, you always added the sacrifice of voluntary affliction.

**115.** May the streams of your innumerable tears, lady, the weariness of your knees, the tearing of your tender flesh which you endured from the harshness of the stone, the cuts in your sides inflicted by the hardness of your girdle, your unbelievable sparing use of food, and your countless holocausts of prayer, remain in remembrance before the eyes of the merciful God, to whom all things are naked and open. May the fountain of life now satisfy the ardor of your holy longing for himself, for whom you thirsted with your whole heart. May God, the raiser of the humble, look upon and honor the humility of your spirit, by which, beyond all whom I have known [Col. 0180D], you always regarded yourself as small and lowly in your own eyes. May divine goodness acknowledge the kindness [Col. 0181A] which you were accustomed to show to those opposed to you, and bring it to worthy recompense. Wearied soul, contrite soul, sated with the miseries of a troubled life, go now into the rest long desired. May the bosom of eternal peace receive you; may the right hand of your faithful Bridegroom embrace you, cherish and bind up all your wounds, and give you the oil of joy instead of mourning, a crown of beauty instead of the ashes of contempt, and a mantle of praise instead of a spirit of sorrow.

How far I have wandered from my purpose! I had intended, O my beloved ones to whom I began to address this discourse, to describe for you the blessed consummation of our dearest sister; but from the abundance of my sorrowful heart I took up this lament before the narrative I had proposed. And now, with the Lord’s favor, I shall carry out what I intended [Col. 0181B], since I do not doubt that it will be welcome to your charity.

**116.** The handmaid of the Lord was still, on the day of Pentecost,

> [Note: [Col. 0181D] Pentecost in the year 1165—when Easter had been celebrated on 4 April—fell on 23 May.]

as was her custom, cheerful; and, as it was her habit to give us joy, throughout the whole solemn day she gladdened us with holy revelations, relating among other things how and at what hour each person present at divine service was visited by the Holy Spirit. But on the third day after this, about evening, she suddenly fell into a very severe illness and began to be afflicted throughout her body so grievously that the whole community immediately gathered around her, invoking God’s aid over her. She remained in this suffering through almost the entire night. On the next day [Col. 0181C], namely Wednesday, when the solemn fast was observed, the community of brothers made a procession in albs to the cell,

> [Note: [Col. 0181D] “Cell” means the monastery of the virgins—as is clearer below in no. 242—to whose entrance they themselves, arranged in procession, received the monks and led them into their church.]

and we carried with us in shrines all the relics of the company of holy Queen Ursula: namely, fourteen bodies, which we possess, as it were, whole, apart from many portions of different bodies. While we were there celebrating the first Mass solemnly of the Holy Spirit, she was caught up in ecstasy and for a long time, as the sisters reported to us, remained still, as was her custom during her trances, when something was divinely revealed to her. But afterward, when she returned to herself, we asked how she had been and whether she had received any consolation from the Lord. She told us [Col. 0181D]:

> “In a vision of my spirit I saw our most holy Lady, and immediately beside her blessed Queen Ursula and St Verena,

> [Note: [Col. 0181D] The *Sermon on the Ursulans*, right at its beginning, treats of the body of St Verena, brought to Schönau [Col. 0182D] in the year 1156. Verena, appearing to Elisabeth, is said to have narrated all those things concerning the history of the martyrdom which, when carefully weighed, will never gain credence. Yet this does not prevent her truly having appeared to Elisabeth, and thus giving rise to an occasion for inventing things said and not said alike.]

> whose body is with us; and likewise all the holy virgins whose relics had been brought here—a very great multitude—all wondrously crowned, clothed in immense brightness, and holding palms of victory in their hands.”

[Col. 0182A] **117.** “I addressed our Lady, who stood in the midst of that holy company, and said to her: ‘To you, dearest Lady, I make complaint from my whole heart concerning all my tribulation. Have mercy upon the fact that I, broken and afflicted, have endured so many labors and innumerable hardships from my youth until this day, and now suffer so intolerable a martyrdom in this miserable body of mine.’

“And she answered me with great sweetness: ‘My beloved, our Lord has ordained this life for you in such a way that you must suffer in it many troubles, many afflictions, and great lowliness. But he will have mercy on you and will console you well in all things. It is his will to purify you by these things and make you such that, when you pass from the world, you will suffer no distress thereafter. Therefore have patience in all the evils you endure, and do not murmur against the Lord in your heart, because he will turn all things to your good. Look at these who stand around me: see how they are crowned, and how great is their beauty. They endured many hardships and very cruel martyrdoms for the Lord; and therefore they not only have honor before God, but are also greatly honored by human beings, and are widely venerated in the world.’

“She added and said: ‘Truly I tell you that, if it were possible for you to be burned to ashes thirty times in a single day, and as often restored again to bodily wholeness, you could not by such suffering [Col. 0182C] merit that grace and glory which the Lord has reserved for you in heaven.’

“Again I said to her: ‘Lady, I fear lest people perhaps be scandalized by my illnesses and suppose that I am thus tormented for certain graver sins; and lest, on this occasion, they wish to disparage God’s grace in me and distrust those things which the Lord has wrought with me.’

“And she again said to me: ‘No one of the wise will do this.’”

**118.** From that time day by day the illnesses of the handmaid of the Lord grew more severe, and every day some new distress befell her. Above all, she was oppressed by pains in her vital organs, against which we could offer no help. During the days of her illness she took so little nourishment that it would seem incredible that a human body could be sustained by it for any length of time; and even what she did take was driven out by the violence of her coughing. Throughout all those days until her death she remained so unmoved in mind that not even once could the lamentations of her sisters and intimates, fearing for her death, move her to tears—although, when she was still well [Col. 0183A], she would readily burst into tears for a slight cause. Even when she seemed somewhat relieved, and the sisters about her rejoiced and spoke words of gladness, she did not at all relax the severity of her expression. The violence of the pain did not permit her to lie in bed or rest in sleep; rather, sitting almost night and day, with her mind undisturbed, she prudently considered many matters

> [Note: [Col. 0183D] The printed text has *jactabat*, “was tossing about”; I have emended it to *tractabat*, “was considering,” since the former makes no sense.]

which we scarcely thought she could even think about.

**119.** Before the days of this illness, she had told us that on a certain feast day, while she was still well, she saw our blessed Lady in the spirit; and in her prayer she most devoutly commended to her both her life and the end of her life, saying: “I pray you, most holy Lady, by your mercy, help me [Col. 0183B] that the ending of my life may be fitting; and that I may never pass from this world without everything being done for me that belongs to the death of a Christian person.” And she answered her with great kindness: “You must be certain that your death will be not merely like that of a Christian person, but like that of a holy person.” And indeed, by God’s grace we saw this promise fulfilled in her. For all the sacraments belonging to the passage of Christians were fully administered to her; moreover, God so blessed her last days that his singular grace in her was plainly recognized and glorified by many.

For when she saw her illness increasing and considered that her bodily strength was entirely failing, she asked that our spiritual father, the lord abbot, be summoned to her [Col. 0183C].

> [Note: [Col. 0184D] Hildelin, still living at the time, according to Trithemius.]

In his presence she had the entire congregation of sisters gathered before her; and amid the most extreme pains, sitting as though she felt no suffering, she addressed them with great strength of spirit in a long and fitting discourse. Although I was present, only these few words have remained in my memory.

**120.** “Do not, dearest sisters, marvel at my illnesses as ignorant people do; nor distrust God’s grace in me because of his chastisements, which I endure and have often endured in your midst. My conscience is good before the Lord, and I know with complete certainty that through what I suffer the Lord is preparing and adorning my crown in his kingdom. [Col. 0183D] He, not because of my merits but because of his mercy, has now for many years wrought in me great things unheard of in our times. I know that there are many among the people who have received these things faithfully and kindly, and have been built up by them for good; but many others, distrustful, have been scandalized by what they heard concerning me. May God not impute this to them.

“But I tell you, and confidently, by that journey by which I hope to proceed to the kingdom of God: these things which you have seen in me and heard from me are true, and I have never added to them anything of pretense or deceit. The Lord is my witness. Keep these things [Col. 0184A] always before your eyes, and be reformed by them more than other people, lest perhaps the Lord impute more to you than to others who have not received these things so truly. Always give thanks to the Lord, and praise him together in all his wonders which he has wrought with me in your sight, because by these he has granted you a singular honor above other enclosed religious communities. Be harmonious, love one another, and preserve your order with great diligence. Bear your poverty patiently. Faithfully and earnestly care for my soul; do not neglect anything belonging to my due, on the assumption that I do not need the aid of your prayers. I say this because those who appear religious are often neglected [Col. 0184B], while those who have known their good way of life think that they do not greatly need their help.”

**121.** While she was speaking these things anxiously, the lord abbot added this to her words: “We trust that the promise of our Lady will be fulfilled in you—the promise by which she assured you of perpetual rest after this tribulation. Nevertheless, we shall in no way neglect what you request.” She answered: “I do not in the least distrust the promise of our dearest Lady; yet, nonetheless, I must do what is mine to do and carefully provide for my soul.” And she said also to the sisters: “If, dearest sisters, you have ever offended God in anything concerning me, may he forgive you; and I forgive every offense from my heart. And if I have done anything to you which I ought not to have done, I beg you to forgive me. I have not yet received from the Lord any certainty concerning the end of my life; nonetheless, it is right that I should be concerned for the safeguarding of my soul and make arrangements for what belongs to my end. Therefore I ask for the sacrament of anointing.” When she had spoken these and many similar things beyond her strength, she asked the lord abbot to summon several of the elder priests and anoint her; and so it was done. After she had made confession, we deliberately delayed giving her the sacrament of the Lord’s body because of her stomach illness and the violence of her cough.

**122.** On the following night her illness became so severe [Col. 0184D] that she thought she would die at once. Anxious because the Lord’s body had been delayed, she raised her hands to heaven and prayed to the Lord:

> “Savior of the world, Lord Jesus Christ, I beseech you, by that holy passion in which you stretched yourself out fully upon the wood of the cross, to redeem the world and embrace everything that you redeemed: do not ever suffer me to pass from this world before I receive your most holy body for the consolation and protection of my soul. Remember, Lord, that I have often received it with the deepest devotion [Col. 0185A] of my heart and with much shedding of tears; and do not allow me in my last moments to lack this blessing.”

One of the sisters keeping vigil with her said: “Remember, lady, that in one of your visions the divine voice said to you: ‘I have begun, and I shall complete.’ Therefore I trust that the Lord will not permit you to pass away so suddenly without first receiving from him some manifest consolation and greater certainty of your end.”

She received this answer gratefully. “And the Lord heard her desire, because her passing was then delayed; afterward, before the end, she communicated.” But I, thinking that she might be helped by medical skill and fearing lest it perhaps be imputed to me as folly and inhumanity if I neglected to attempt this, hurried to the city of Mainz [Col. 0185B]

> [Note: [Col. 0185D] Mainz is only six hours distant from the monastery. Egbert appears to have gone there on Monday after Trinity Sunday. For it is evident from no. 131 that Wednesday night was the tenth day before her death, on which, upon his return, Egbert found the virgin assured of her death; yet he must have spent at least one day consulting doctors and seeking medicines [Col. 0186D].]

to consult physicians and obtain medicines. But since it was the Lord’s will to take her from this world, I found none of all the things I sought.

**123.** That very night, while I was there, our sick sister sat in bed as usual, with the sisters keeping vigil beside her. About midnight, after she had prayed most diligently to the Lord and commended her end to him, she began to suffer grievously and changed so much from her former condition that she was thought to be dying. After much anguish she entered into ecstasy. The sisters standing around and looking at her from every side were exceedingly astonished, and, thinking that the end was at hand, some began running to fetch the hair-shirt [Col. 0185C] upon which she might be laid, while others went to awaken the community of sisters. When they had come, she began again to draw breath and to return to herself. Quietly she said to one of the sisters lying close beside her and holding her in her arms: “I do not know what is happening to me: that light which I customarily behold in heaven is dividing itself.” She added nothing more.

Then each of the sisters, prostrating herself before her, begged forgiveness, asking her to pardon every offense. She did this with great goodwill and prudence; and in return, as far as she could, she humbled herself before them, using such discernment in all things that they clearly perceived the grace of the Holy Spirit in this. Then one of the sisters secretly asked her [Col. 0185D]: “Dearest, has the Lord yet shown you any sign, or have you received any voice, by which you may know your end?” She said: “I have not yet received anything of that kind.” After this she told the sisters that the community should go to sing Matins, for it was already time.

**124.** While the sisters around her began to chant the psalms, she again entered into ecstasy. When they had completed the Office of Matins, she drew breath and returned to herself. She told some of them [Col. 0186A] to go and rest. As those most intimate with her remained, one of them said: “Dearest, tell us, if you can, how you were in this ecstasy; and if anything has been revealed to you by the Lord, disclose it to us.” She said: “I cannot yet; wait a little.” When she had gathered a little strength, she said:

> “The holy visions which I was formerly accustomed to see on the highest feast days, and concerning which the angel of God told me many years ago that I would not see them until the time of my death—the Lord has now shown them to me. This, therefore, is a most certain sign to me of my end. Yet I ask you still to keep silence about it and not spread it abroad widely.”

After the community of sisters had finished chanting Matins, one of the older sisters came [Col. 0186B] and said to her: “Tell us, dearest, whether you have received any consolation from the Lord.” She answered: “Oh, what good consolation I have received!” Since she lacked the strength to speak, the sisters who had heard from her told, in her hearing, both her and the others now gathering together what vision she had seen. And there was great weeping among them. Then, strengthened in spirit and sitting upright, she addressed them all thus:

**125.** “My dearest ones, in this matter have certainty of my end, and true testimony to all that the Lord has wrought with me. I ask and urge you to give firm faith to those things which the Lord has done in me before you, and never to distrust. I too believe his works and bear them testimony by my death. He has worked in me until now, and works even to the end; always give him particular thanks for all these things. Satan has always lain in wait for me and set many snares for me. I know that even after my death he will not cease to oppose me, corrupt my reputation, and obscure what the Lord has done with me. From my youth I have suffered many things among you which were hard and unbearable to my body: many illnesses, lack of my necessities, and labors that I undertook. And after the Lord began to place his singular grace in me, I suffered things more grievous than before—not especially because of any wrongdoings of mine, but so that through my labors, which you saw outwardly in me, those things which the Lord showed me secretly might be confirmed, and thus become more credible both to you and to other people who would receive them [Col. 0186D].”

**126.** Then the sisters said to her unanimously: “Dearest lady, since we can no longer have you yourself, we ask you to name for us someone among us who, with God’s will, can exercise authority over us; and we shall receive her with every goodwill and the greatest gratitude [Col. 0187A].” She said:

> “My counsel is that you take in my place the very woman who, after me, has held the priorate

> [Note: [Col. 0187D] They commonly called her prioress, or perhaps subprioress; for the same woman was called both mistress and prioress. We should wish to learn the designation used at Schönau.]

> among you, and who has done well and competently everything belonging to her office. Honor her, love her, and support her for the Lord’s sake as long as he leaves her to you. The Lord knows that I say this not because of the kinship between her and me, nor because of any special affection; but because I trust that it is pleasing to the Lord and will be expedient for you. May the Lord henceforth console you and teach you in all things that are pleasing to him.”

They gratefully accepted her counsel and afterward asked the lord abbot to give the woman whom she had named to them as mistress; he consented to their request.

[Col. 0187B] **127.** When she had finished the words with which she addressed the sisters, she said to those ministering familiarly to her: “Alas! What will happen because of my brother’s absence? Alas for the medicines which he is procuring for me! What have medicines to do with me? I beg you, send a messenger with all haste to call him back.” And so they did. It was Wednesday. When morning came, the lord abbot was immediately summoned; as he sat before her, the sisters related to him the vision by which she had been assured of her death, since she herself lacked the strength to tell it. When he had heard their account, he said to her: “Are these things so?” She said: “They are, my lord; and from this I have the most certain testimony [Col. 0187C] of my death.”

Immediately, therefore, he proceeded to divine service and celebrated the Office of the Holy Trinity, because the handmaid of the Lord testified that the mystery of the Holy Trinity had been revealed to her in the aforesaid vision, in the manner in which it had been shown her ten years before in the same vision. When the divine office was completed, he fortified her with holy communion; and a litany was said with much devotion by both brothers and sisters, who wept abundantly over her.

## CHAPTER X. The final stage of her holy life and death, and the salutary admonitions given during it.

**128.** After this, about the ninth hour, I arrived. I was received amid the tears of all, so that I thought she had already died. When I asked those who met me weeping, and they said that she still lived, I still hoped for her life. When I was admitted, I found her sitting and speaking; and I wondered greatly at the cause of the many tears around her, seeing as yet no likeness of death in her. After I had sat before her a little while, she addressed me, saying: “Behold, dearest [Col. 0188A] brother, I am dying and shall in no way recover for this life.” Struck to the heart by these words, I said to her: “How do you know this, dearest?” She said:

> “That great vision which I saw many years ago, concerning which I was told that I would not see it until the end of my life, the Lord showed me this night. From it I am certain that the end of my life has come.”

On hearing this, I recognized the vision and recalled the angel’s words which had foretold the end of her life. Since I had written everything down in my own hand after her,

> [Note: [Col. 0187D] Yet nothing of this appears in the two preceding books of visions. Egbert must therefore have written it down but judged it not to be made public while she was alive, as with many other things; here it was enough for him to mention this vision only in passing [Col. 0188D].]

I immediately abandoned all hope for her recovery and life. As I wept before her from the deepest pain of my heart, she showed no sign whatever of sorrow; but, remaining unmoved in spirit, she said to me [Col. 0188B]:

> “Know, dearest, that I have no sadness at my departure, and that I part from you without any pain. Although you have been dearer to me than all other people, still above all food and drink I hunger and thirst for the kingdom of God.”

I said: “I do not now presume, after the manner of the prophet, to pray that your spirit may be doubled in me; but if the Lord were willing simply to give me your spirit, that would suffice me.” She said: “Dearest, may the Lord’s will be done in you.”

**129.** After the ninth hour of prayer had been completed, the lord abbot again arrived with the whole community of brothers; and again, at his beginning, a litany was said with many tears. After blessings had been pronounced over her [Col. 0188C], she asked to be heard by them all. Sitting with steadfast spirit, she addressed us and thanked us all for every kindness bestowed on her and for all the labors we had undertaken around her. Most wisely she urged us to concord, endurance of poverty, and unfailing service to the Lord.

> “Let each of you,” she said, “be diligent for himself, lest the Lord’s service fail in him. I know—and it has often been revealed to me by the Lord—that the Lord has blessed this place with a singular blessing, and that his praise and worship shall not fail in it until the last time.

> [Note: [Col. 0188D] At least up to the present, even under a non-Catholic prince, after the devastation of so many monasteries in the preceding century, discipline still flourishes at Schönau among the men; although scarcely any traces can now be seen of the nunnery, separated only by an intervening street, except such as may here and there be recognized from rare ruins.]

> Therefore always render him special thanksgiving because he has particularly honored this place above other cloisters [Col. 0188D] by the grace which he has deigned to work in me.”

After she had given many exhortations in this manner, she added an exhortation also to me, asking and urging me to preserve perseverance in stability, and never to wish to leave the place, even if I should happen to be called to a more honorable and wealthier place. We all received her words of admonition with the greatest gratitude [Col. 0189A], because we plainly perceived the Spirit of the Lord at work in her.

And the lord abbot said to her: “Dearest, we receive your admonitions gladly. But we ask that, after you have departed to the Lord, you diligently commend us to him and always pray to him for this place, that he may keep it in his protection and peace.” She likewise assented to his request.

130. After this she joined her hands together, stretched them out toward him, and said: “To the Lord my Creator I commend my soul, and after him to you, most beloved Father; and I ask that on the last day you present it to him, for I am your spiritual daughter, and I have loved you as I ought and kept the obedience due.” Receiving her with tears, he said: “I hope that I shall joyfully offer you to the Lord.” After this she again said: “[Col. 0189B] Do not wonder that I deal so anxiously with everything pertaining to my departure, for I must do this while I still retain some strength, lest, when my powers utterly fail, I be found unprepared in some respect.”

When the lord abbot was leaving her, she said: “May that blessing remain upon you all, most beloved Father, with which the Lord and Savior blessed his disciples when he ascended from them into heaven.” She also addressed each of the brethren with untiring spirit, exhorting them to advancement in virtues and commending herself to their prayers. She appealed not only to the priests concerning the offering of the saving sacrifice for her, but also to the deacons, when they should have ascended to a higher rank. As each person asked her to assign certain psalms to be said [Col. 0189C] in her memory, she asked one of them to say, for the sake of the consolation which she hoped to obtain from the Lord amid her tribulations, the psalm, “When the Lord restored the captivity of Zion”; to another she assigned, “Praise the Lord, O Jerusalem”; to another, “Praise the Lord, O my soul”; to another, “Praise the Lord, for a psalm is good”; to another, “A hymn befits you, O God, in Zion”; to another, “Its foundations are in the holy mountains”; to another, “O God, in your name”; and to another, “The Lord reigns; let the earth rejoice.”

131. Meanwhile they greatly marvelled at the strength of her mind and the fullness of her faculties, when they considered the severity of her illness and the failure of her bodily strength. For from the beginning of her illness [Col. 0189D] she had scarcely eaten any food which was not shaken from her stomach by the violence of coughing. From that Wednesday on which she was assured of her death until the tenth day, on which she died, she took no nourishment whatsoever except cold water alone. On one day, compelled by us, she took a few strawberries and a little of one apple, but did not retain even these.

After this she addressed at length the sisters assembled about her, carefully admonishing them concerning all things necessary. Having kissed them all individually, she added at the end of her discourse: “My dearest ones, the angel of the Lord [Col. 0190A] assigned to guard me has always watched over me with great care. He has shown me many good things and, through me, has often consoled both you and others with great kindness. Therefore I ask you always to give him thanks, and that each of you render him special service and say daily in his honor the psalm: ‘The Lord reigns; let the earth rejoice.’”

On Thursday, during the divine office, she earnestly invoked the Lord and Savior, whom she testified that she saw in that vision [Note: [Col. 0189D] Namely, Vision I, no. 86.] described in the Book of the Ways of God. She asked him mercifully to release her from the intolerable bond of her sickness. He answered her: “I come swiftly, and I shall release you.”

132. On the Saturday following [Note: [Col. 0189D] That is, 12 June.], while the divine [Col. 0190B] office of our Lady was being celebrated, she beheld her in the heavenly places and likewise implored her for release. She said to her: “This illness of yours is unto temporal death; and the vision which you see shall not be taken from you, but you shall continue seeing it until the hour when I come to you with an honorable retinue, receive your soul, and lead it to the place of refreshment, where it may rest from all its labors.”

That entire day she was in extreme weakness, continually gazing toward our blessed Lady as though she were present, and incessantly calling upon her in a faint and pitiful voice. But on Sunday night her spirit was somewhat strengthened after the long-desired arrival of one of our sisters, a God-fearing woman, whom I had summoned from afar to her funeral [Note: [Col. 0189D] Thus below, no. 140, a brother too is said to have been summoned “from afar”; whence it may be inferred that the homeland of them all was at some distance from Schönau, though it is remarkable that it is nowhere named.].

Then, [Col. 0190C] with the sisters assembled around her, as she sat on her bed with eyes lifted upward and with the entire intention of her heart, she prayed to the Lord in an abundant flow of holy words:

“Lord, my Creator, my Deliverer, my Savior, my Receiver: to your holy majesty, to your undivided Trinity, I commend my soul, that you may receive it, console it, and save it. I beseech you, Lord, by your holy incarnation, by your holy birth, circumcision, presentation, baptism, passion, resurrection, ascension, by the coming of the Holy Spirit, and by your future judgment, that you may deign to release me from these bonds of mine and bring my soul to that place where it may receive consolation [Col. 0190D] for all its tribulations.”

133. Having prayed much in this manner, she added the customary praises of the Lord:

“You, God the unbegotten Father; you, the only-begotten Son; you, the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete—we confess, praise, and bless with all heart and mouth, holy and undivided Trinity; glory be to you for ever. Blessed be the holy and undivided Trinity, creatress and governess of all things, now and always and through infinite ages of ages.”

She added likewise:

“I commend my soul to my Lady Saint Mary, ever-virgin, that she may receive, console, [Col. 0191A] and preserve it; to Saint Michael and the whole host of heaven; to Saint John the Baptist and all the holy prophets; to Saint John the Evangelist, Saint Peter, and all the holy apostles; to Saint Stephen and all the holy martyrs; to Saint Nicholas and all the holy confessors; to Saint Margaret and all the holy virgins; to all the saints of the Lord: that they may be intercessors for me with the Lord, and, when my soul has departed from this life, may receive it and assist it before the Lord, so that it may be placed there where it deserves to enjoy everlasting consolation with the holy souls.”

134. When all the sisters had said Amen, she greeted our Lady, saying:

“Hail, Queen, mother of mercy, sweetness of life and our hope, [Col. 0191B] hail. To you we cry, exiled daughters of Eve. To you we sigh, groaning and weeping in this valley of tears. Come then, our advocate: turn toward us those merciful eyes of yours, and after this exile show us Jesus, the blessed fruit of your womb. O clement, O loving, O sweet Mary.

“Nurturing mother of the Redeemer,
who remain the open gate of heaven and star of the sea,
aid your fallen people striving to rise;
you who, to nature’s astonishment, bore your own holy begetter,
virgin before and afterward,
receiving that ‘Hail’ from Gabriel’s lips:
have mercy on sinners.”

“All the angels praise you, the holy Lord on high, saying: ‘Praise and honor are fitting for you, O Lord.’ The cherubim and seraphim likewise proclaim you holy, [Col. 0191C] and every heavenly order says: ‘Praise and honor are fitting for you, O Lord.’ Savior of the world, save us all. Holy Mother of God, ever-virgin Mary, pray for us.
