By the prayers of the holy apostles, martyrs, and confessors, and of the holy virgins, we humbly ask that we may be delivered from every evil and may deserve always to enjoy every good.”

135. To these she added the Lord’s Prayer, the Creed, and a confession to those standing around. Finally she added: “Lord my God, deign to receive all my words which you have given me, for I could by no means have possessed them unless you had granted them to me.”

When she had said all these things, her strength utterly failed, so that she seemed already to be dying; and she remained for a long time [Col. 0191D] in that state of exhaustion. Yet, as our Lady had promised her, she was—as she told us—continually seeing the vision which had appeared to her on the aforementioned Wednesday; though at some times more clearly than at others. At times she saw a great light poured down upon her from heaven; and she saw our Lady with many other saints draw so near to her that she thought herself already about to be taken away. Whenever this happened, her entire consciousness and all her strength turned thither. She could neither speak nor give us any attention, so that we thought her end had arrived.

136. But when, after one or two days, she had recovered speech, she began piteously to complain: “Alas, what will happen? Alas, what will happen?” And she repeated this often. When we asked why she said this, she replied: “Those whom I saw drawing near to me, and of whom I thought that they would now take my soul, go upward again and withdraw from me; they do not take me away.” This happened frequently during those ten days.

One day she saw the angel of the Lord who was familiar to her, standing by her and saying: “The reason why the Lord so prolongs your passage is that he may thereby be glorified in you by so many more people.” And so it indeed happened. For many, both from near and from afar, who knew the Lord’s grace in her, hearing the report which had spread of her imminent end, came daily in great numbers, longing to see her. Although we have no custom of admitting [Col. 0192B] strangers to our sick persons, nevertheless, by counsel, several persons who pressed us were admitted for edification’s sake, since we feared that they might conceive some suspicion from this very fact if she were carefully hidden from all eyes.

She bore this most patiently; and, concealing the bitterness of her illness by strength of spirit, she did not weary of sitting before them and admonishing them, as was appropriate to each, concerning their salvation.

137. She exhorted clerics who were priests to live blamelessly and to build up the people by good examples. To them she said: “It is yours, beloved ones, to show yourselves more familiar with the Lord than other people through good conduct [Col. 0192C] and your holy ministry, so that after this life he may join you more intimately to himself in his kingdom.”

Those not in that order she urged not to withdraw themselves from familiarity with the Lord, but willingly to make themselves available for promotion to God’s sacred ministry and to be diligent concerning the things of God. She exhorted persons of the military estate also to protect the common people, assist the oppressed, give tithes from their goods, refrain from robbery, from slashing and perforating garments, and also from fornication. She affirmed that fornicators are punished not only by the penalties of Gehenna after this life, but in this world by barrenness of offspring or by extreme misfortune.

She urged ordinary people to keep faith with their lords and with one another, patiently to endure their poverty, [Col. 0192D] give alms according to their ability, be devout in visiting churches, and invoke the Lord their Creator. Nor did she exhort only those present to good: she sent counsels of salvation also to certain absent persons, and forgave the offense of detraction to persons far away. She entreated all alike to remember her after her death in prayers and almsgiving.

138. Finally, if I wished to recount individually every word of her reasonable discourses and the holy prayers which she made during those days, I should certainly produce no small volume. All marvelled greatly at her wisdom and glorified the power of God in her. By his operation alone could it happen that the handmaid of the Lord, in so frail a body, [Col. 0193A] endured for so long without any food, and nevertheless sat speaking with such an abundance of words marked by such discernment.

The Lord granted her request in this matter. For, as she told us, she had often asked the Lord in her prayers that at the end he would grant her a sober illness, one free from appetite. Every day she reached such extreme weakness that we expected nothing but her end; and the Litany was said over her twice or more, while the Gospels of the Lord’s Passion were also recited. Just as she had always had great devotion to the Lord’s Passion, so the Lord appointed both the day and hour of his Passion for her death.

For on Friday morning she said to those around her: “Today [Col. 0193B] all who are dear to me must keep careful watch over me, for my hour is near.” When she had caused the bed to be moved away, she sat upon a cushion, leaning upon one of the sisters, and spoke familiarly of many wonderful things with those present until the sixth hour. Thereafter her breathing began to be labored.

139. Then the lord abbot arrived with the priests and again strengthened her with blessings and the Litany. When I suggested holy communion to her, she signalled to me that she did not have strength to swallow. I did not think it dangerous for her to abstain from it, since on the preceding day she had communicated through my administration.

After we [Col. 0193C] had left, the sister upon whose breast she reclined said to her: “You used to tell us, dearest one, concerning our sisters who were dying, at what time their end was near and when we ought to lay them upon the haircloth. But now we cannot know this concerning you unless you yourself tell us.” To this she was silent; and shortly afterward she had me summoned in haste.

140. While for a little while I, together with our brother—a cleric of religious life whom I had summoned from afar for this very purpose—waited before her to see what would happen, she began to fail in the use of her voice, though she continued to turn over prayers in her customary manner, gazing devoutly upward with uplifted eyes.

Finally, as if mindful of the word [Col. 0193D] spoken by the aforesaid sister concerning indicating the hour at which she should be laid down, she stretched out her hand and with great quickness signalled to us three times that she should be laid upon the haircloth spread before her. When we had done this, and as she lay in a gentle agony, the Litany was said once by the sisters and a second time [Col. 0194A] by the lord abbot and the community of brethren. Then, about the ninth hour, as though gently falling asleep, she surrendered her spirit to the Lord, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of July.

141. Then one of the priests assisting there, who loved her in Christ, burst into tears and said:

“Depart now, holy soul, into your rest. Ascend like a little column of smoke, from the spices of myrrh and frankincense and every powdered perfume. Enter into the joy of your Lord. Lord Jesus Christ, Savior of the world, receive the soul which you created, the soul which you redeemed by your blood. O Mary, mother of mercy, receive now your handmaid. O Virgin of virgins, acknowledge now your virgin. Holy angel, receive the soul entrusted to you and lead it in peace where it may rest from its labors.”

[Col. 0194B] The Lord looked upon the humility of his handmaid, who had always held herself in contempt in every respect for his sake. God honored her latter end by the magnificent services of our people, who voluntarily came together from every surrounding quarter until the third day, Sunday, on which she was buried.

Even while she was alive and well, she often spoke of the approach of her death and piously wished, saying: “Would that it might befall me to depart from this life at such a time that no one might suffer inconvenience or discomfort from inclement weather.” And this indeed happened, for the weather had not passed more gently during the whole summer than it did during those three days.

142. Although we all mourned her [Col. 0194C] departure, every heart nevertheless enjoyed a certain gracious joy, rejoicing for her blessed manner of life. Although an unchangeable custom among us provides that the community of sisters never goes outside the bounds of its cell, nevertheless, in reverence for the singular grace of the Lord which he had visibly wrought in his handmaid, it pleased our venerable Father and all the brethren alike that all the women disciples together should be allowed to attend the venerable body of their teacher and render her service at the burial.

Accordingly, by the hands of those whom she herself had named for this purpose, and also of Countess Beatrice, who had devotedly attended both her illness and funeral, she was laid in a coffin beside the altar dedicated to the Lord and to all holy virgins in [Col. 0194D] the church of Blessed Florin [Note: [Col. 0193D] From no. 70 it appears that the sisters were customarily buried in the cemetery together with the brethren and carried to their church.].

She died in the thirty-sixth year of her age, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of July, Friday, at the ninth hour, in the year of the Lord 1165 [Note: [Col. 0193D] “The fourth” is printed by an evident error; see the preceding commentary.], in the thirteenth year of her visitation [Note: [Col. 0194D] That is, completed; for she began to be visited in the year 1152, on 31 May. Thus, reckoning up to the year 1165 and 18 June, one obtains the aforesaid thirteen years and eighteen days.]—from the time when the fatherly grace of our Lord had visited her. May he be blessed in all his mercies for ever and ever. Amen.

## In the Year of the Lord 1166: Blessed Aelred, Abbot of Rievaulx, in England

[Col. 0195]

# The Life of Blessed Aelred by an Anonymous Author

*(Acta Sanctorum of the Bollandists, January, vol. I, 12 January, p. 748)*

## Preliminary Commentary

1. In the province of York there is a river, the Rye, which, as Camden says concerning the Brigantes, “carries with it into the Derwent the waters of many torrents.” From it “a certain pleasant, delightful, fertile valley, adorned with twenty-three parish churches, is called Rydal,” because the Rye cuts through it. There was formerly there a celebrated Cistercian monastery, founded in the lifetime of Saint Bernard himself by Walter Espec. William of Newburgh says of it, book I, chapter 14:

“Indeed, a little before this, monks of Clairvaux, invited by the nobleman Walter Espec and sent by Abbot Bernard of blessed memory, had come into the province of York and had taken up residence in the place now called Rievaulx—then a place of horror and vast solitude—through the grant of the aforesaid man and with the venerable Archbishop Thurstan offering episcopal favor with fatherly affection.”

Harpsfield, century 12, chapter 43, records nearly the same things.

2. Its first abbot was William, Saint Bernard’s disciple, a praiseworthy man, called “Blessed” by Chrysostomus Henriquez and listed in the Cistercian Menology on 2 August. He was succeeded by Blessed Aelred, and Aelred by Silvanus, whom the same work commemorates on 16 April. John Picard, in his notes on Newburgh, reports the following verses of Nicholas of Rievaulx concerning them:

> William received the first fruits; next after him  
> Aelred bore greater things; Silvanus increased them.  
> Three men, pre-eminent in merit and scarcely unequal:  
> the first, his successor, and this last one.  
> William shone in office thirteen years;  
> pious Aelred was shepherd at Rievaulx three times six years;  
> Silvanus presided thirty-three years in all.  
> Here you may reckon fifty-four years.  
> Under these Fathers and patrons  
> the pleasant valley of the Rye flourished and shone—  
> a holy valley, a rich valley.  
> England shines illustriously through such a sun.

Robert of Torigni, continuator of Sigebert, reports that this monastery was begun in 1131: “Clairvaux,” he says, “produces two monasteries on one day, namely Longpont and Rievaulx, and after a few months Vaucelles.” In the same year, the supplement to Sigebert from Vaucelles has this: “In this year the monastery of Saint Mary of the Church of Vaucelles, in the territory of Cambrai, was begun.” Miraeus agrees in his Cistercian Chronicle.

If this is so, then either Nicholas reckons William’s years not from the beginning but from the completion of Rievaulx monastery, or some error has entered the text. For from 4 March 1131 until 12 January 1166, when Aelred died, there are about thirty-five years; yet he assigns to William and Aelred together only thirty-one. Chrysostomus Henriquez discusses in various ways the year in which that monastery was founded in his notes to the Menology for 16 April.

3. Blessed Aelred died on the day before the Ides of January. On that day Chrysostomus Henriquez says of him:

“In England, Saint Aelred, abbot of Rievaulx, distinguished by knowledge of sacred letters and integrity of character. After humbly scorning the dignities offered him, adorned with every kind of virtue, he departed from the world and was enrolled after death among the number of the saints.”

John Bale himself acknowledges that he was entered in the catalogue of saints, although Bale was an enemy of monks and of the Catholic Church. On 5 January he is listed in the Cistercian Calendar published at Dijon in these words: “Aelred, doctor, abbot of Rievaulx.” In Ferrarius’s general catalogue: “In England, Saint Ealfred, abbot of Rhievaulx.”

But Ferrarius is greatly mistaken when he adds in his notes that Rhovallum, or the town of Rhyum, where he believes Aelred was abbot, “is in Kent, forty-eight Roman miles distant from London.” For Rievaulx lies far from London and the borders of Kent. Another town, Rye, is in Sussex, near Kent’s borders. Hugh Menard, however, has on 11 January: “In the district of York, Saint Aelred, abbot of the Cistercian order.” [Col. 0197] Finally, the English Martyrology lists him on 16 March. There one must first correct the statement that he belonged to the Benedictine order, and then that he presided over the ancient monastery of Rievaulx; for how can that be called ancient which was built in his own sight and perhaps even with his assistance? Ferrarius likewise has on the same day: “In England, Saint Altred, abbot.”

4. Aelred’s name is rendered in various ways: Aelredus, Alredus, Aelredus, Elredus, Adelredus, Adilredus, Altredus, Athelredus, Ealredus, Hailredus, Eleredus, and Ethelredus; by some also Aluredus, by Ferrarius Ealfredus, and by Miraeus Valredus. The first twelve derive from the same root, *athel*, *ethel*, *edel*, *eel*, or *ael*, meaning “noble,” and *rad* or *red*, “counsel”; thus Aelred means “noble in counsel.” Or it derives from *al*, meaning “all” or “entirely,” so that Alred means “all counsel,” or “one who excels altogether in counsel.” But Ealfred and Alvred mean “altogether peaceful,” from *fred* or *ured*, that is, “peace.”

5. We have transcribed the Life of Blessed Aelred from John Capgrave’s *Legend of the Saints of England*, composed by an anonymous author. Trithemius mentions it in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, calling Aelred “a man exercised by continual study in the holy Scriptures, not ignorant of secular philosophy, gentle in disposition, sweet in speech, and outstanding in devotion.” For the year 1164, William Eysengren says he was “a man illustrious in learning and eloquence, taught in the studies of sacred letters and especially well educated.” Under the year 1200—though he seems to have considered Alred and Ethelred different persons—he calls him “a most eloquent man, esteemed no less for his life than for his eloquence.”

There survives a letter of William of Newburgh to Aelred himself, in which he declares that he writes history at Aelred’s exhortation, although he did not complete it during Aelred’s lifetime. John Picard, in his notes on Newburgh, quotes a poem which Nicholas of Rievaulx composed in Aelred’s praise:

> Illustrious Aelred, steeped in the perfume of virtues,  
> was a honeycomb and sweetness to monks.  
> In the flower of youth, the court of the king [Note: [Col. 0197] In John Picard’s manuscript, “of Scotland” was added in the margin.] cherished him  
> and removed whatever was harmful, far from his heart and hand.  
> Led by Christ, he came from Jericho to Jerusalem.  
> There may he swiftly bear fruit; he turns thorns into lilies;  
> he gathered what was scattered and reunited what was broken.  
> Raised higher thence, and having attained heavenly rewards—  
> if it is pleasing and lawful to say so—I shall unfold the truth.  
> Nor do I think I begin anything woven from falsehood.  
> He was a Maurus in mature character, and a Benedict  
> in example; like Bernard in his celibate life;  
> a pattern of virtues, a broom for vices, an honor  
> and mirror of the Order, a way of peace, a clasp of the law.  
> Jerome preferred Paul’s cast-off clothing to Croesus’s gold;  
> our jewel is adorned with equal brightness.  
> Many encomia give others their titles; but he himself  
> was peaceful Solomon and gentle as a lamb.  
> I do not rehearse much from ancient counsel.

## The Life Begins

### Chapter I. The youth of Blessed Aelred; his entry into religious life

[Col. 0197A]

1. When the venerable Aelred lay as an infant in the cradle, a certain archdeacon named William came to his father’s house. He was a man illustrious in birth and Aelred’s kinsman according to the flesh [Note: [Col. 0197B] Pitseus, Chrysostomus Henriquez in *Phoenix*, chapter 7, and in *Fasciculus*, book II, distinction 26, chapter 23, also report that Aelred was of noble birth.]. Looking at the infant, he saw his face changed into the likeness of the sun and flashing with most splendid rays, so that the shadow cast by his outstretched hand fell across it. The child’s countenance appeared so serene that it could be seen perfectly, as in a mirror. The archdeacon therefore declared that he would become great in God’s eyes, since such grace had smiled upon him in infancy.

2. When the boy had returned home from children’s play, his father looked at him and said: “Come, my son, what news do you bring us?” He replied: “The Archbishop of York died today, father.” At hearing this, his father and the whole household laughed and said: “Truly, my son, he is dead who lives badly [Note: [Col. 0197B] Three bishops are found to have held York during Aelred’s youth: Gerard, who died in 1108; Thomas, who died in 1114; and Thurstan, who voluntarily resigned the office he had held for a long time. Yet Thomas and Thurstan are widely praised for piety, while Gerard was notorious for various vices. But if we suppose that Gerard is meant here, Aelred, who died in 1166, must certainly have been more than fifty-seven years old—indeed at least sixty-seven—if he made this pronouncement as a boy in 1108.].”

But the boy said: “This man is dead in another sense, father; released from the flesh, today he bade his final farewell to mortals.” On the third day afterward, what the boy had foretold was shown to all to be true concerning the bishop’s death.

3. While he was at the guest-house of Rievaulx, in the diocese of York and of the Cistercian order, on the day before he was received into the habit, a fire broke out in the novices’ house. It raged so fiercely up to the joints of the ceiling that the roof of the building was thought likely to be consumed in a moment. While Aelred sat at table with the others, he took a cup and, stretching out his hand, confidently threw the cider it contained into the midst of the flames; immediately he extinguished the fire’s blaze.

4. As a young man he was so greatly loved by David, king of the Scots [Note: [Col. 0199D] He succeeded his brother Alexander in 1125, according to Westminster, who calls him “a man of great holiness and generosity.” He died in 1152. Accordingly, correct Pitseus’s assertion that Aelred first became known to King David after he had already been made abbot.], that, having become almost second in his court, he would have promoted him to a bishopric had Aelred not hastened first to the Cistercian order.

He showed himself so devout and gentle in all things that injury did not stir him to anger, nor did abuse provoke him to revenge. He always strove to return love for hatred, good for evil, and service for envy. A certain knight, seeing that the king loved and honored him above all others, began to persecute him and pursue him with bitter hatred, sometimes even attacking him with insulting words before the king. Aelred said to him: “You speak well, knight; you speak excellently; all that you say is true, and you hate falsehood. And, I think, you love me.”

At last the knight, seeing that Aelred was not disturbed or drawn away from virtue in any respect, was moved to repentance, asked forgiveness, and promised that henceforth he would be his steadfast friend. Aelred said to him: “I confess that I rejoice at your repentance, and therefore I shall love you all the more; because through your hatred I have increased in love for my Lord, and because my patience, stirred and tested by this, has perhaps made some little progress before God.”

5. After this, when he came to Rievaulx monastery, received the monks’ habit, and advanced in the religious life, the care of the novices was entrusted to him. A certain cleric entering the order became very unstable, tossed about like a changeable reed. Troubled by this, Aelred said to God in his heart: “Give me this man’s soul; and what he lacks in salvation, deign to grant by your grace, Lord my God, though I am unworthy.”

Not long afterward, that brother, desiring to return to the world, informed his master and explained the desire of his corrupt mind. Aelred said to him: “Do not perish, brother; for you cannot, even if you wish it. And it is most foolish to wish this very thing, the opposite of which all the saints desire; for all desire to be saved.”

But he did not heed the counsels of salvation and left the monastery. Wandering all day through the byways of a wood, shortly before sunset he returned to the road and suddenly found himself transported within the monastery wall. Aelred met him, embraced his neck, kissed his face, and said: “Son, what have you done to me thus? Behold, I have wept much for you today; and I trust in God that, as I asked of the Lord and promised you, you shall not perish.”

[Col. 0200A] 6. In the novitiate he made an earthen chamber like a small underground cistern, into which water flowed through hidden channels. To avoid discovery, he closed its mouth with a very broad stone. Entering it often, he quenched within himself by the coldest water the heat of every vice by the very cold water.

### Chapter II. Offices, virtues, miracles

7. The same brother, for whose soul he had asked the Lord that it might be given to him, again burned with the fire of his former instability and wished to leave the monastery. Coming to Aelred, then made abbot of Revesby [Note: [Col. 0199D] Others write “Renesby.” It was a monastery in the diocese of York, founded by the monks of Rievaulx.], he said: “Lord, my weakness cannot bear the rigors of the Order. Everything is contrary to [Col. 0200B] my nature. I cannot endure prolonged labor; I am distressed and tormented by long vigils; I often succumb to manual work; the roughness of garments pierces my flesh; my will seeks worldly delicacies and longs for the loves and pleasures of the world.”

“And I,” said the abbot, “will prepare more sumptuous food and softer clothing for you, and will make all things required of a monk more bearable.”

“I do not want them,” he replied, “even if you gave me all the wealth of this house.”

The abbot said: “Nor shall I taste food until the Lord brings you back, willing or unwilling.”

One ran to the gate to depart; the other entered his chamber and prayed. The pious abbot lamented for his son, mourned the wanderer with the deep sighs of his heart, and rejected consolation. But when the fugitive came to the gate and found its doors open, he felt as though there were an iron wall before him. Trying repeatedly to go out, and unable by any effort to accomplish his purpose, he returned contrite to the abbot, asked forgiveness, and promised stability. The abbot said to him: “Well done, my son; you have come well. Truly my God has had mercy on me, in restoring you sound.”

8. Not long afterward, by the sign of the cross he drove away the swelling from the arm of a brother which had been inflated by a tumor, and restored it to health.

9. When afterward he was made abbot of Rievaulx, he was so sparing in food that one would have thought him not a man but a spirit. He increased the number in his monastery to one hundred and forty monks and five hundred brethren. Though for ten years before his death he was afflicted by stone and gout [Col. 0200D], he nevertheless persevered in humility and patience and often said to the brethren: “My little sons, say what you will, provided no shameful word, detraction against a brother, or blasphemy against God proceeds from your mouth.”

10. He wrote the *Life of Saint Edward, King and Confessor* [Note: [Col. 0200D] We published a Life of Saint Edward on 5 January; but from what we said there, it may be inferred that Aelred wrote another work on Saint Edward, and perhaps that the Life found there is not the genuine one written by Aelred.], the *Life of David, King of the Scots* [Note: [Col. 0200D] Pitseus cites the beginning of that Life, “The religious and pious King David,” and adds that Aelred also wrote “a lament for his death.”], and the *Life of Saint Margaret, [Col. 0201A] Queen of the Scots* [Note: [Col. 0201D] David’s mother. We shall treat of her on 10 June.]; thirty-three homilies on the burden of Babylon in Isaiah [Note: [Col. 0201D] Only thirty-one, published by Gibbon, survive.]; three books *On Spiritual Friendship*; two books *On the Nature, Quantity, and Subtlety of the Soul* [Note: [Col. 0201D] Pitseus has: “One book On the Nature of the Soul; one book On the Endowments of the Soul.”]; and many letters [Note: [Col. 0201D] Pitseus: “One book of three hundred letters.”]. What he commended in writing, he took care to fulfill in life.

He placed his finger in the mouth of a certain mute brother and commanded him to speak: “Speak, my brother, in the name of the Lord.” Immediately, to the astonishment of all, the man replied: “I gladly speak with you, blessed lord.” At once, healed through Aelred’s merits, he gave praise to the Lord.

11. A certain brother was severely afflicted by a syncopal attack [Note: [Col. 0201D] Syncope is a most serious collapse of strength, involving danger of imminent death. It is commonly called *syncops* by physicians.], so that neither voice nor consciousness appeared in him. The abbot approached him and said: “Beloved son, may the Son of God [Col. 0201B] save you.” Without delay, all his pain subsided.

12. An abbot subject to him, heaping many insults, reproaches, and blasphemies upon Aelred, unjustly provoked him and deservedly stirred his spirit against himself. Bearing his malice heavily, Aelred raised his eyes and hands to heaven and said: “Lord, King of eternal glory, I pray that this man may swiftly experience the end of his malice, for you know that the things he strives to ascribe to my name are false.” When that abbot had entered his monastery, he fell into bed and on the seventh day ended his life amid great torments.

13. Going down into Galloway [Note: [Col. 0201D] It is called by some Gallwallia and Gallovidia, “from the Irish,” says Camden, “who once occupied it and call themselves, in an abbreviated form in their language, Gael.” It is a region of Scotland, bordering Ireland and England [Col. 0202D], which rebels once held.], Aelred found the petty king [Note: [Col. 0202D] This was Fergus, who later became a canon at Holyrood in Edinburgh. His son Uhtred was defeated in battle by his younger brother Gilbert and, his tongue cut out and his eyes gouged out, was miserably deprived of life and principality. Nevertheless Roland, Uhtred’s son, later succeeded him.] of that land angry with his sons, the sons raging against their father, and brothers against one another. That land is fierce, wild, and barbarous; its people are brutish, and everything it produces barbarous. Truth is not found there; wisdom has no place there. For neither faith nor charity endures long in it. Chastity suffers shipwreck as often as lust wishes, nor is there any distinction between a chaste woman and a prostitute: women change husbands by the month. Yet among the religious, some are sufficiently devout through another’s counsel and direction, though they are rarely perfect through their own effort. For they are naturally dull and, possessing an animal spirit, always attend to the pleasures of the flesh.

Aelred therefore found the princes of the province disturbed by anger and dissension. Neither the king of Scotland [Note: [Col. 0202D] Camden nevertheless writes: “After the many disturbances he had caused, Fergus was brought by Malcolm to give his son Uhtred as a hostage.” But it is more likely that this was achieved by the counsel of Blessed Aelred under Malcolm IV, David’s grandson, rather than by arms.] [Col. 0201D] could humble their hatreds and resentments, nor the bishop mitigate them; and they polluted the land with much blood. Aelred not only made them peaceable, but persuaded the father of the sons to assume the religious habit; and he taught one who had deprived many [Col. 0202A] thousands of people of life to become a sharer in eternal life.

14. He placed his fingers in the mouth of a man who had swallowed a frog while drinking water, and, raising his eyes to heaven, said: “Lord, almighty King, I beseech you through your Son, the Lord Jesus: look upon this creature of yours, and do for him what you will and know.” Without delay, the frog climbed up to his fingers and, with much fluid and putrefaction following, fell to the ground.

15. For four years before his death, he freed his body from every pleasure of the present life. Because of the excessive emaciation of his body and wasting of his face, his skin clung to his bones. Eating little and drinking less, by incredible [Col. 0202B] abstinence he extinguished his appetite for food. He spurned physicians’ advice and, despising bodily remedies for God’s sake, strove to provide for the health of his soul.

16. He read books whose reading commonly draws forth tears and builds up character, and he continually carried Augustine’s *Confessions* in his hands. He often sat in a hollow made in the floor of his oratory, reflecting that he was dust. There the light of an angelic visitation shone over his head; and as he spoke with men, so he spoke with heavenly spirits. Though he was often alone, the voices of very many were heard with him.

17. He also shone with the spirit of prophecy. Before certain brothers had confessed, he ordered them to confess their sins [Col. 0202C] and foretold what they had committed in secret, adding place and time. One night, when two brothers cried out in the dormitory and the brethren were awakened by their dreadful voice, a brother reported this to Aelred on the next day. He said: “Truly, son, this night the devil came among our brothers and planned to seduce someone; but he was compelled, his attempted malice having failed, to depart very quickly in confusion. Nevertheless, someone gave him a little consent.”

18. After a sermon delivered in chapter, he said among other things to the brothers: “Look to your lives, brothers; amend your conduct; attend to your salvation. For I state with certainty that one of you approaches the Body of Christ to his own condemnation. I do not wish to expose him publicly [Col. 0202D]: I desire his correction and spare his shame.” When they heard this with great astonishment, those who knew themselves guilty hastened to come and disclose to him the secrets of their hearts.

## CHAPTER III. Outstanding gentleness; illness; death.

[Col. 0203A]

19. A certain brother beheld a vision in the night and saw before him a lofty building, artfully constructed, spacious and beautiful, showing only one doorway for entrance. It had no windows, no openings, no light there, except for a small ray of the sun that streamed in when the door was open. All the timbers of the house were fragrant and sweet-smelling. The nearer he came, the more he delighted in the sweetness of its scent. Looking through the doorway, he saw a bed placed on the floor and his abbot lying upon the roof.

When he entered and saw the abbot dead, he began to lament and weep abundantly. Raising his eyes to the roof of the house [Col. 0203B], he saw an image of a man shining more brilliantly than anything a bodily eye has seen in this world; and the whole building shone as though illuminated by a thousand lamps. He saw through the midst of every limb of the image as clearly as if he were present on its other side. In the middle of the house the image appeared in the air, supported neither below nor above by any aid. Yet a certain somewhat dark cloud was visible near its navel; it did not adhere to the light of the figure, but hung there, moving slightly.

And behold, a man standing at his side, pleasing in face and bearing, said to the brother, who was marveling beyond expression: “What are you wondering at? Why do you not rather look at your Father, who lies before you and whom you think dead?” [Col. 0203C]

He replied: “Lord, the glory of this image has made me forget the death of my most sweet Father.”

The other said: “Your Father is not dead. For this figure which you see is his soul. Only so much remains to be illumined in his deeds as that little cloud which moves about the image’s navel. When it has been illumined, he will pass to the Lord. And, so that you may know,” he said, “that this image is his soul, behold: it enters his body.”

In the twinkling of an eye, that figure slipped through his mouth into the body. At once he saw the abbot move, as though he wished to rise from his place. The brother began to cry out so loudly for joy that he forced the other brothers, rising from their beds, to awaken him.

20. Throughout the whole year before his death, a dry cough [Col. 0203D] shaking his chest, together with other kinds of infirmity [Col. 0204A], so weakened him that he often, after celebrating the solemnities of Mass and returning to his cell, lay motionless on his bed for an hour, unable either to speak or to move himself. At last, having summoned the brethren together, he said among other things:

“I call God as witness that, since I received the religious habit, I have never been inflamed by anyone’s malice, detraction, or quarrel in a way that could await the day’s end in my heart with any disturbance; always loving peace and brotherly well-being and my own tranquillity. By God’s grace I so ruled my mind that the patience of my soul, once disturbed, should not outlast the setting of the sun.”

21. The sick abbot appeared to a certain sleeping brother and said: “When, brother, do you think that I shall depart?”

“I do not know, lord,” he replied.

And the abbot said: “On the day before [Col. 0204B] the Ides of January, the soul of the handmaid of the Lord—my soul—will pass from its earthly house, which it has inhabited until now.”

And so it happened. For on the second day after this, about the fourth watch of the night, on the day before the Ides of January, he passed to the Lord [Note: [Col. 0203D] Others subscribe to this date: Pitseus, Gibbon, and Henriquez in the *Phoenix* and the *Fasciculus*. Yet the latter, in the *Menology* which he published last, writes that he died in the year 1200, at the age of fifty. Trithemius writes that he flourished about the year 1200; Menard dates him to 1161. John Picard [Col. 0204D] says that he was present at the translation of St Edward in 1164. This may indeed seem probable, although he is not listed among the other abbots who were then present. Yet that translation took place not in 1164 but in 1163, on 13 October, a Sunday, as we said above under 5 January.] in the year of the Lord 1166, and in the fifty-seventh year of his life.

22. While this abbot was still alive, he was greatly afflicted by colic and the twisting pain of a stone. Sitting on a mat beside the fire, he seemed to have his head wholly between his knees. A certain brother came upon him, roaring and gnashing his teeth cruelly, seized the abbot together with the mat in his hands, and hurled him with all his strength into the fire, crying out: “Wretch, now I kill you; now I destroy you by a harsh death. [Col. 0204C] Why are you lying here, most deceitful man? From now on there will be nothing for you to lie about, for you will certainly die now.”

As this was happening, the monks came and pulled their Father from the fire; inflamed with zeal, they wished to lay hands on the son of pestilence. But forgetting his infirmity and mindful of charity, the abbot commanded them: “Do not, I beg you, do not, my sons, strip your Father of the garment of patience. I am not moved; I am not hurt; I am not troubled, because it is my son who cast me into the fire, and by this purified me, not destroyed me. He is my son—but he is sick. I myself am not sound in body, but that sick man has healed me in soul.”

Taking hold of his head, he kissed him, blessed him, embraced him, and—as though he had felt or suffered no harm—endeavoured gently to soothe [Col. 0204D] the rage of one who was angry with him without cause.

[Col. 0203]

## HISTORICAL-LITERARY NOTICE

(FABRICIUS, *Bibliotheca mediae et infimae Latinitatis*, I, 14.)

Aelred—also Adilred, Aethelred, Ailred, Ealred, Elered, Alured, Edilred, Ethilred—was educated with Henry, son of David king of Scots; later, from the year of Christ 1150, he was abbot of Rievaulx, or Rhienvaulx (Riedval), in the diocese of York in England, of the Cistercian Order. He died in 1166. On him see Charles de Visch, pp. 9 ff. of the *Bibliotheca Cisterciensis*; George Mackenzie, vol. I of his English work *Lives of Scottish Writers*, pp. 123 ff.; *Acta Sanctorum*, 12 January, vol. I, p. 748; and, more extensively, Oudinus, vol. II, pp. 1487 ff.

His published historical works include those printed in Roger Twysden’s *Ten English Writers*, London, 1652, folio: *On the Battle of the Standard*, A.D. 1138, in the time of King Stephen, or *On the Valour of Walter Espec, Who Defeated the Scots*, p. 337; *Genealogy of the Kings of England*, p. 347; and *History of the Life and Miracles of St Edward, King and Confessor* (more complete than that in Capgrave and Surius under 5 January), p. 369. Also: *History of the Nun of Watton*, p. 415. Surius, under 10 June, has a shortened *Life of St Margaret, Queen of Scotland*; the *Acta Sanctorum* for that day has a fuller version. A fragment from *On the Affairs of England*, addressed to Henry II, duke of the Normans and later king, containing King Edgar’s address to bishops and heads of monasteries, occurs in Nicholas Harpsfield, chapter 3 of the tenth century of his *English History*, and in vol. XXIII of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, 1677, p. 164 ff.

The following unpublished works are mentioned by John Leland, chapter 199; Pitseus, p. 229; Bale, II, 99; and others: a book *On the Miracles of the Church of Hexham*; *Life of St Ninian, Bishop*; a *Life of St Edward* written in elegiac verse for Laurence, abbot of Westminster; two books *On the Life of David, King of Scots*, addressed to Henry II, king of England; the latter of which briefly treats the lives of English kings from Æthelwulf, father of Alfred the Great, to Henry II; and a *Chronicle from Adam to Henry I*.

The works of moral and ascetical subject-matter edited by Richard Gibbon, S.J., at Douai in 1631, reprinted in vol. V of the *Bibliotheca Cisterciensis* and in vol. XXIII of the Lyons 1677 edition of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, are these: thirty-one sermons on Isaiah 13, 14, 15, and 16, addressed to G., bishop of London, *On the Burden of Babylon*. Of these, the first sermon, *On the Advent of the Lord*, is in vol. II of Bernard’s *Works*, p. 568, Paris, 1719, folio. The *Mirror of Charity*, first set out in summary and then more fully in three books. Three books *On Spiritual Friendship*, for composing which he testifies that he was prompted by reading Cicero’s *Laelius*. *On Jesus at Twelve Years Old*, on Luke 2:42, vol. II of Bernard, p. 590; here a lacuna of five pages is supplied from the Paris edition of 1609 among Bernard’s works, and from David Camerarius, III, 41, *On Scottish Courage*, ibid., 1631. A volume of homilies addressed to Gilbert, bishop of London, or twenty-five sermons for the seasons and saints, omitted from the *Bibliotheca Patrum* but found in the Douai edition and in Bertrand Tissier’s *Cistercian Library*, Bonfontaine, 1662, folio, vol. V, p. 162. A *Rule for Enclosed Nuns*, addressed to his sister, in Holstenius’s collection of Rules, part III, p. 110, Rome, 1661, and Paris, 1663, quarto; and in the appendix to vol. I of the Benedictine edition of St Augustine’s works, Amsterdam edition, p. 640, under the title *On the Eremitical Life, to a Sister*. A portion also occurs among the works of Anselm of Canterbury, Meditations 15, 16, and 17.

Also mentioned among the unpublished works are: *Jonathan’s Arrow*; *On Three Men*; *On Various Virtues*; *On the Song of Songs*; *On the Bond of Perfection*; *Dialogue on the Nature and Endowments of the Soul*, in two books; *On the Twelve Abuses of Cloistered Persons*; *On Gospel Reading, to Ivo*; *Dialogue between Man and Reason*; three hundred letters; *Flowers of Sentences*; *On the Conduct of Prelates*; *On the Duties of Ministers*; one hundred synodal sermons; *On Christian Knighthood*; *On the Virginity of Mary*; *On the Foundation of the Monasteries of St Mary of York and of Fountains*. In Leland, p. 200, and Bale, p. 209, appears *On the Burdens of Isaac*, wrongly printed for *On the Burdens of Isaiah*.

[Col. 0205]

## ANOTHER NOTICE

(D. B. TISSIER, *Bibliotheca Patrum Cisterciensium*, Bonfontaine, 1662, folio, vol. V, p. 160.)

Who this Ailred, or Aelred, was may be learned from Pitseus, book *On the Illustrious Writers of England*, the twelfth age, under the year 1166, where he writes as follows:

“Aelred, born of noble parents in England, was carefully educated from his earliest age in the fear of God and in good studies. From the first years of his youth he learned to bear the Lord’s yoke, always innocent in life and free from crime. As piety and learning grew with his years, he became a monk of the Cistercian Order. In its way of solitary life he gave himself so wholly to contemplation of heavenly things that among his own he stood forth like the moon among lesser stars. Yet meanwhile he did not neglect the study of sacred literature, nor lose the knowledge of other disciplines. Thus distinguished by so many ornaments of virtue, he was first elected abbot of Rievaulx by the common vote of his brethren; this place is in the diocese of York. Not long afterwards the fame of the man reached the ears of David, king of Scots, and the king made him his most intimate friend. Yet Aelred gladly fled worldly honours and refused various ecclesiastical dignities, even a bishopric on one occasion, so that he might be freer for contemplation of divine things and devote himself more freely to preaching the Gospel. He frequently turned over the books of St Augustine; among them, Augustine’s *Confessions* pleased him wonderfully above all others. In writings, words, deeds, and the whole pattern of life, he was a most diligent imitator of St Bernard. Gentle, meek, humble, modest, devout, temperate, chaste, he loved, fostered, and brought about peace and concord within himself, with others, and among all, beyond what can be said or thought. So peaceful in all things and with all people was he that he might deservedly be called blessed on that account, and most rightly be called a son of God.”

Thus Pitseus, who immediately afterwards lists his minor works, of which we too shall presently speak. From Aelred’s own preface to the *Mirror*, however, it is apparent that before his conversion he had been steward or seneschal to a king or some prince, or had discharged some similar office. For he says that, coming from kitchens to the hermitage, he changed place, not occupation—because, evidently, when writing this he acted, as may be inferred, as steward or administrator of his monastery.

He passed from this world at Rievaulx in the year of human salvation 1166, on the day before the Ides of January, in the fifty-seventh year of his life, under Henry II, king of the English; and was eventually enrolled among the number of saints, as Molanus in his notes on Usuard reports, as does the compiler of the old Cistercian Missal, who give him a place among the blessed and saints of the Order; likewise Abbot John in his *Catalogue of Saints*; Trithemius in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*; Arnold de Wion, *Tree of Life*, book I, chapter 47; Peter Calzelius; William Eisengrein; Pitseus; Richard Gibbon; Miraeus; and, most recently, Fr Chrysostom Henriquez in the *Fasciculus of Saints of the Cistercian Order* and in the *Menology*.

Manrique reports these words concerning Aelred from a Cistercian manuscript: “His feast is solemnly celebrated during the octave of the Epiphany, according to the decree of the general chapter of 1276; I myself read this also in an old Clairvaux manuscript. But I wonder that Fr Henriquez himself, in the aforementioned *Menology*, assigns this author’s death to the year 1220, whereas in the *Fasciculus* he correctly assigned it, with others, to 1166 and noted that he is sometimes confused with another author called Edilbred, who died in 1220. Certainly our Aelred succeeded William, the first abbot of Rievaulx and disciple of St Bernard, in the abbacy. This William wrote the first, in the order of Bernard’s letters, in the midst of rain without rain, and died in the year of the Lord 1148. Gilbert, Aelred’s contemporary, speaks of Aelred’s passing from this world in Sermon 41 on the *Song of Songs*; he is in turn praised by Aelred in Sermon 2, *On the Burdens*.

“Pitseus, Henriquez, and others list Aelred’s works, but confusedly. For they give some three or four times under different titles and headings, such as the sermons on Isaiah and the sermons *On the Burdens*, although they are the same work. After I had copied out the works of this saint himself, I found that they had been published by Fr Gibbon, theologian of the Society of Jesus, though with a large portion omitted—namely the sermons throughout the year, both for the seasons and for saints—which I copied from the Clairvaux manuscript. These sermons will be followed by the sermons *On the Burdens*, and the homily on the twelve-year-old boy Jesus falsely attributed to St Bernard; then the *Mirror of Charity*, divided into three books; and lastly the book *On Friendship*, which is found mutilated among Augustine’s works in volume IV.

“As writers testify, this holy man’s eloquence was almost equal to Bernard’s. Above all, Nicholas, monk of Rievaulx, sang this of him:

> Renowned Aelred, enriched with the perfume of virtues,  
> Was honeycomb and sweetness to the monks.  
> The royal court of a king nourished him in youth’s flower,  
> And he removed whatever was harmful, far from mind and hand.  
> From Jericho he came to Jerusalem, with Christ as guide.  
> There he quickly bore fruit, changing thorns into lilies.  
> What was scattered he gathered; what was broken he restored into one.  
> Raised higher from this, he was born anew after heavenly rewards.  
> If it is pleasing and permitted to say it here, I shall unfold the truth:  
> Nor do I think to begin anything from a thread of falsehood.  
> He was a Maurus in mature character, a Benedict  
> In example, like Bernard in celibate life.  
> A pattern of virtues, a broom for vices, the glory  
> And mirror of the Order, the way of peace, the clasp of the Law.  
> Jerome preferred Paul’s relics to Croesus’ gold;  
> Our jewel is adorned with equal brightness.  
> Many praises give others their titles, but he himself  
> Was a peaceful Solomon and meek as a lamb.  
> I do not rehearse much from the ancient counsel.

In another epigram, the same author says this of the first three abbots of Rievaulx, of whom Aelred was the second:

> William takes the first fruits, but Aelred, next after him,  
> Brought forth greater things; Silvanus increased them.  
> The three are especially worthy, scarcely unequal in merit: he  
> The first, his successor the second, and this man the last.

Another:

> Who envied Aelred to Bernard and believed  
> The two so alike beneath a single pen?

Likewise:

> Aelred surpasses Attic honey; he surpasses sugar.  
> Not even Sicilian bees make honey so well.  
> Something sweeter than sweetness itself distils,  
> And as quickly as he is read, so quickly is he reread.  
> No desire for satiation comes; hunger, provoked by eating, increases;  
> What has been read delights when read again.  
> This is Aelred’s, that is Bernard’s, and the same  
> Voice is believed to sound, the same honeycomb to speak.  
> Each joyfully sings chaste and devout loves;  
> Each, learned, plays with sacred subtleties.  
> I think honeyed Mary cherished each client,  
> And each drew honey from her virgin breast.  
> He flows almost equal to Bernard and vies with him in sweetness;  
> Each wonderfully fashions honeyed combs.  
> Let us grant Bernard first place; let Aelred take second;  
> Rightly, the one nearest the first should be read next.  
> Their age was alike; the same times bore them both;  
> Their Order alike, their love of piety alike.  
> France bore Bernard, England ours—but England then  
> Was unlike, alas, the England of our times.  
> England then poured forth sweet honey for the lands;  
> She was Europe’s sweet Hybla, sweet Hymettus.  
> Now almost whatever crosses the sea from there becomes Colchis,  
> Carrying baneful aconite in pestilent books.

I think these matters sufficient for the commendation of our Aelred. Those who proceed to read his works will discover that these praises are not false. Moreover, the following sermons for the Seasons and Saints have a style different from his other works; but for that reason they should not be denied to our author or judged spurious. For he delivered those sermons before the lay and unlettered brothers whom we call *conversi*: they attended the sermons delivered in the chapter-house of the monks on feast days and Sundays, but not those delivered on other days. Therefore the Fathers who were abbots, and others, sometimes used humbler and more familiar speech in these addresses, accommodating themselves to their hearers’ ignorance.

# PART ONE OF THE WORKS OF BLESSED AELRED, ABBOT OF RIEVAULX—ASCETICAL WRITINGS

[Col. 0209]

## SERMONS FOR THE SEASONS AND SAINTS

(D. TISSIER, *Bibliotheca Patrum Cisterciensium*, vol. V, p. 162.)

## SERMON I. ON THE ADVENT OF THE LORD

[Col. 0209A]

You ought to know, dearest brothers, that this blessed season, which we call the Advent of the Lord, represents two things. Therefore our joy ought to concern two things, because it must confer upon us a twofold benefit. This season represents for us both comings of our Lord: namely, that most sweet coming in which he who is beautiful beyond the sons of men (Psalm 44), he who is desired by all nations (Haggai 2), the Son of God, manifested to this world his visible presence in the flesh—long awaited and ardently desired by all the Fathers—that is, when he came into this world to save sinners [Col. 0209B]; and likewise that coming which we are to await in firm hope and indeed recollect often with tears, when this same Lord of ours, who first came hidden in the flesh, will come manifest in his glory, as is sung of him in the Psalm: “God will come manifestly” (Psalm 49)—that is, on the day of judgment, when he will come openly to judge.

His first coming became known to very few righteous persons. At his second coming he will appear openly both to the righteous and to the reprobate, as the Prophet more plainly declares: “All flesh shall see the salvation of God” (Psalm 97). Yet, properly speaking, just as the day which we are shortly to celebrate in memory of his Nativity represents him as born—that is, more expressly signifies that day and hour [Col. 0209C] when he came into this world—so this season, which we celebrate before that day, represents him as desired: that is, it represents the longing which the holy Fathers who lived before his coming had for him.

The Church has therefore wisely provided that at this season their words should be recited and their longings recollected—those who preceded the Lord’s first coming. We do not celebrate their longing on one day only, but as it were over a long period; for it commonly happens that what we greatly desire, if it is delayed for some time, seems sweeter to us when the thing we love arrives.

It is therefore for us, dearest brothers, to follow the examples of the holy Fathers, to recall their longings, and thus kindle our minds in love and desire for Christ. You ought therefore to know that this season was instituted for us for this reason: that we should consider the longing which our holy Fathers had for our Lord’s first coming, and by their example learn to have great longing for his second coming. We ought to consider how many good things our Lord did for us through his first coming, and that he will do far greater things for us through the second; and by this consideration to love that first coming [Col. 0210B] greatly and desire the second greatly.

If we do not have a conscience good enough to dare to desire his coming, we should at least fear his coming; and through that fear amend ourselves from our vices, so that, if perhaps we cannot avoid fear here, at least when he comes we may then not fear, but be secure.

Indeed, brothers, those who are now watchful concerning themselves and fear that day of judgment before it comes will undoubtedly not fear when it comes. Who is so hard that he cannot fear that day, when our Lord shall come in his majesty; when heaven and earth shall burn; when all the evils which people have done in this life shall be laid open before God and his angels, before the devil [Col. 0210C] and his angels, and before the whole human race from Adam to the last person who will be in the world? Without doubt, every vice and sin which confession has not covered in this life will there be made public.

Who cannot fear that day in which each person must receive that which he shall possess without end? It is very good, brothers, to think often upon these things, especially when temptations arise. Then everyone who has chosen a more perfect life than that of those [Col. 0211A] who are in the world should strive further, through good conduct, to acquire such a conscience that he need not fear punishment on that day, but may desire the glory and joy that the righteous will have on that day.

And just as the holy Fathers desired the day on which they were to be redeemed, so should he desire the day on which all the saints are to be glorified. For Christ first came to free us from our sins; but at his second coming he will heal all our infirmities. Therefore someone exhorts his own soul to bless the Lord and gives the reason: “Who forgives,” he says, “all your iniquities; who heals all your infirmities” (Psalm 102). One clause belongs to the Lord’s first coming, the other to the second: through the first coming he erased our sins, but we still suffer great infirmities as punishment for those sins.

Who can enumerate all the infirmities of this life—hunger, thirst, labours, pains, sicknesses, sluggishness, weariness? Yet these concern the body. How many are the infirmities of the soul, how many its desires, how many its temptations!

All these infirmities, and every other infirmity that we cannot mention, the Lord will heal by his second coming, when what the Apostle says shall be fulfilled: “This corruptible must put on incorruption,” and so forth (1 Corinthians 15). Through the first coming our Lord raised us only in soul; through his second coming he will raise us in body, so that, just as now we serve God by both—that is, by soul and body—so then we may have perfect blessedness with God in both [Col. 0211C].

At this coming he gave us faith, so that we might know how to believe in him. At his second coming he will bring us to the point where we can see him—not as the ungodly will see him on the day of judgment. For on the day of judgment all, good and evil alike, will see him in that likeness in which he suffered for us, rose again, and ascended into heaven. But we shall see him in the manner in which those who have a pure heart can see him. For the Lord says: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5). That is, we shall also see his divinity: that excellence and beauty [Col. 0211D] which angels now see. For we shall be like angels in heaven—provided that we now love and desire him, and despise every pleasure and honour of the world.

Then undoubtedly we shall see him securely in that likeness in which he will judge the living and the dead; and happily we shall see him in that likeness in which he will show himself only to the good, whom he will lead with himself from judgment to the kingdom. Let us now consider as much as we can how great will be our joy and happiness if, on that day when heaven and earth burn, when the Lord comes with such might and power, we can be secure: not merely not fearing him when he comes, but loving him greatly and looking upon him with confidence.

Therefore, brothers, if we wish then to have this joy [Col. 0212A] and security, let us earnestly strive to love our Lord greatly. Whom ought we to love so much as him who is our Creator and Lord, and moreover our Redeemer? Nor is there anything else that we can love so safely. For whatever else we love, we shall undoubtedly have to lose; and if we take delight in things that we must lose, then, when the time comes for us to lose them, we shall certainly feel as much sorrow afterwards as delight we felt beforehand.

Let us therefore safely love him who always is, who is always good in the same way, and always delightful in the same way. Thus, brothers, let us now love him so that, when we see him coming from heaven with his angels, we may not fear his coming, but immediately run to him with great desire [Col. 0212B], as to our most intimate friend.

Let us see how all the saints who lived before His first coming longed for Him, and let us follow their example—not that of those who love the world, for Scripture says: “The world is passing away, and its desire” (1 John 2). Therefore, those who love the world will perish with the world when the world perishes. And that we may know how greatly the ancient fathers desired to see our Lord, let us hear what the Lord Himself says in the Gospel: “Truly I say to you, many kings and righteous persons wished to see what you see, and did not see it,” etc. (Luke 10). In this sense Scripture says of Solomon: “All the kings of the earth desired to see [Col. 0212C] Solomon’s face and to hear his wisdom” (3 Kings 10). For without doubt only those ought to be called kings who desire to see Solomon’s face and hear his wisdom. They are those who rule themselves well and preserve their members from the stain of sin. For those who possess much land and many people under them are not truly kings, but servants of sins; since, as our Lord says, “Everyone who commits sin is the servant of sin” (John 8). And certainly he ought not to be called a king who is a servant—and such a vile servant that sin rules over him.

Therefore, brethren, let us strive to govern ourselves well and guard our members well. Thus we too shall be kings, and shall begin to desire to see [Col. 0212D] the face of the true Solomon, that is, our Lord Jesus Christ. It is unnecessary, brethren, to tell you why our Lord is called Solomon. You have often heard that Solomon in our language means “peaceful,” and our Lord Himself is our peace: He made peace between us and God and reconciled us to His Father by His own blood.

Saint David himself was surely one of those kings who desired to see the face of the true Solomon. He plainly showed this once, when he desired water from the fountain which was at Bethlehem. For, as Scripture relates, the king desired it and said: “Oh, that someone would give me water from the cistern of Bethlehem, which is by the gate” (2 Kings 13). Certain men were there who thought that he desired [Col. 0213A] the visible water from that cistern; and, at great danger, they crossed the camp of their enemies, drew that water, and carried it to the king. But because he wished to show that he had spoken this through the spirit of prophecy, not on account of that carnal and worthless water, he immediately poured it out upon the ground. For he did not desire water from that bodily cistern, but water from that fountain which was born at Bethlehem. Hence elsewhere he said: “My soul thirsted for God, the living fountain,” etc. (Psalm 41).

This is the true fountain, our Lord Jesus Christ, who was born in Bethlehem of Judah, and who says: “If anyone thirsts, let him come and drink; and from his belly shall flow living waters” (John 7). Saint David desired this water; to this fountain he ran with great longing, [Col. 0213B] as he at once explained in the verse itself. For after saying, “As the stag desires,” etc., he immediately added: “When shall I come and appear before the face of God?” (Psalm 41).

Behold, brethren, we now see what he then desired. That fountain was born at Bethlehem, and waters from that fountain run through the whole world. Such, without doubt, is the water by which those wash themselves who have any defilement in themselves; by which those drink who thirst; and by which those who hunger also cook their raw food. This water, brethren, which flows from this fountain, is Christ’s teaching, which He Himself taught in the Gospel. By it all who are bound and defiled by their sins wash themselves, as did those to whom the Lord said: [Col. 0213C] “Already you are clean because of the word which I have spoken to you” (John 15). Behold, these were cleansed through Christ’s teaching. By this water also those who thirst for knowledge of our Lord drink and become intoxicated; for in Christ’s teaching we can know Him.

For if our heart does not turn over carnal thoughts, if we gladly hear and understand the word of God, then a certain fire will arise in us, so that we think only of those things which pertain to love of our Lord. When Saint David, like a stag, desired that water so intensely before He was born, certainly it is a great shame if we, who see this fountain born and have already tasted something of the water flowing from it, do not greatly desire and love Him. For we see [Col. 0213D] that what the prophet Isaiah greatly desired has now been fulfilled, when he said: “Would that, Lord, you would rend the heavens and come down; before your face the mountains would melt away” (Isaiah 64).

What do we think that the holy prophet desired in these words? Without doubt, first of all His coming, and that with great longing. He immediately gave the reason why he desired Him so ardently: “Before your face,” he says, “the mountains would melt away” (ibid.). For that holy man saw how the devil, who fell from heaven through his pride, possessed the whole human race. He saw how the devil swelled and exalted himself because kings and princes of this world worshipped him, and because almost all people in the world followed his pride. The prophet saw this [Col. 0214A] and was greatly grieved; and, as I think, could scarcely endure that pain—especially because the Lord delayed so long, He who was to destroy all the devil’s pride. Therefore he said with great longing: “Would that, Lord, you would rend the heavens and come down,” etc.

He knew that the time when He was to come had been appointed; but the prophet endured so great a delay with profound distress. Therefore he desired that, if it were possible, He might forestall that hour which He had fixed, signifying this in the words: “Would that, Lord, you would rend the heavens and come down!” As though he said: “I know, Lord, that You await the time which You provided from the beginning; You await the fulfilment first of all those things which the saints said must be fulfilled before Your coming. But would that, Lord, [Col. 0214B] You would rend the heavens—that is, interrupt, if possible, that purpose of Yours which You revealed to the heavens, that is, to Your saints—and come! I see such pride in the devil, who draws the entire human race into his power; and behold, he stretches out his hand against that nation which You chose. Already among these Jews, who used to be Your people, pride, lust, and every vice reign. Why do You delay any longer? Why do You wait any longer? We threaten them and say: ‘Our Lord will come; Christ will come, who will judge the evil and honor the good.’ And they mock and deride us: ‘Command upon command’ [*manda remanda*] (Isaiah 28). Behold how many years have passed since You first promised us that He would come, and still [Col. 0214C] He has not come. It appears that You do nothing but deceive us.”

These wretches said this and, as though secure, gave themselves over to the service of idols and to every sort of pride and lust. Thus they acted; but the holy prophets were sorrowful, grieved, and wept, and with wondrous longing longed for His coming. Hence comes this utterance of Isaiah: “Would that, Lord, You would rend the heavens and come down.” But what did Christ’s mercy do? Surely it did not allow His holy prophet to remain long in so great a sorrow without great consolation. Hear what the same prophet says a little later: “You came down, and before Your face the mountains melted away.” Here you may hear a wondrous thing. First he said, “Would that, Lord, You would come down,” etc.; and now he says: “You came down, and before Your face the mountains melted away,” [Col. 0214D] as though what he so greatly desired had already taken place.

Why is this? I think that when holy Isaiah was in that sorrow, both over the devil’s pride and human wickedness, our Lord, to console him, showed him in the Spirit what we now see: namely, that the whole world would believe in Him, that kings and princes would worship Him, that all idols would be destroyed, and that those who were proud would become humble through the Lord’s coming. Seeing these things in the Spirit, the prophet surely rejoiced and exulted; and through excessive exultation, as though he already saw fulfilled what he truly saw would be fulfilled, he said: “You came down, Lord, and before Your face the mountains melted away.”

O dearest brethren, would that we who now see this fulfilled felt as great a joy [Col. 0215A] as he felt when he saw that it would be fulfilled! We now see it; we can turn to our Lord and say with great joy: “Lord, You came down, and before Your face the mountains melted away.” This has now been fulfilled, as David also desired when he said: “Touch the mountains, and they shall smoke” (Psalm 143). Our Lord came down; by the grace of the Holy Spirit He touched the mountains, that is, the proud of this age; and behold how they melted away—that is, how they were humbled. They begin to weep for their sins; they cannot bear the smoke, that is, the darkness and obscurities of their sins.

Do you not see this daily, brethren? Do you not daily see the proud of this age, with great shame and [Col. 0215B] great fear, turn to the Lord, humble themselves, and weep for their sins? Certainly, brethren, this happens daily. Even if it does not happen daily before us, it nevertheless happens daily in the holy Church. Therefore, dearest brethren, we see much better and more clearly that what holy Isaiah says elsewhere has been fulfilled than the Jews suppose. For in one place, showing what was to happen at the Lord’s coming, he says: “The wolf shall dwell with the lamb, and the leopard shall lie down with the kid; calf and lion shall feed together, and a little child shall lead them” (Isaiah 11).

What great thing would it be if God did this with many beasts, when human beings often accomplish the same through their own ingenuity—namely, that beasts naturally opposed to one another should be together? Certainly, let us say with the apostle Paul: [Col. 0215C] “Is God concerned about oxen?” (1 Corinthians 9). If God, brethren, is not concerned for oxen in such a way that He gives a command in the law on their account, much less is He concerned for lions or leopards so as to speak such great things about them through His prophet. Yet if we wish to see and consider this assembly, we can see that this prophecy has been fulfilled much more beautifully and excellently than if those beasts were together.

Consider how God has assembled you here—from how many different regions and customs. What was one of you in the world, by comparison, but a lion, when through his pride and riches he despised others and exalted himself above them? Was not another of you [Col. 0215D] like a wolf, when he lived by plunder and strove to seize another’s goods? The leopard is an animal full of variety: such were some of you through cunning, deception, and fraud.

Again, many in this assembly were foul through lust. Those who were such resembled a kid, because a kid is a foul-smelling animal. There are also some who, while they were in the world, lived innocently and may rightly be compared to a lamb. Again, others, because of the simple life they led, were like sheep. See now, brethren, in what great harmony and peace God has assembled all these into one fellowship. Here the wolf dwells with the lamb: he eats and drinks with the lamb, [Col. 0216A] does it no harm, and loves it greatly. For undoubtedly the one who was a wolf while he was in the world is now in great harmony with the one who was innocent as a lamb. The one who was proud as a lion now lives in great peace and quiet with the one who was, and still is, a sheep through simplicity.

Here the lion not only remains together with the calf; more wonderfully still, the lion becomes a calf. You know that long ago, under the old law, calves used to be offered in sacrifice. Therefore, in a spiritual sense, he becomes a calf who offers himself to God in sacrifice. Thus many lions become calves, because many who were formerly cruel and rapacious now sacrifice themselves to God through labors, vigils, and other such exercises. Likewise, not only does the wolf dwell here with the lamb, [Col. 0216B] but this wolf has become a lamb. How beautiful it is to see some among you who were so wise in the world, so powerful, so proud and cunning, now become so simple and unlearned, as though they knew nothing.

Why has all this happened except because our Lord came down and the mountains melted before His face? Even if we could not show this in this assembly, would it therefore not have occurred through the Lord’s coming? Consider how Paul raged like a wolf, how he seized Christ’s Christian sheep, despoiled them, and stoned them. Consider how suddenly he was changed and made a sheep; how gently, sweetly, and kindly he afterward dwelt with Christ’s other sheep; and how he not only did not seize them, but gave himself over to death for Christ’s sheep. [Col. 0216C] Surely, brethren, if we consider this change, the Lord performed a greater wonder in it than if He had made those beasts—the wolf and the sheep—exist together.

“And a little child shall lead them.” Who is this little child, except He of whom Isaiah says: “A child is born to us and a little one is given to us” (Isaiah 11)? He is surely the one who led Paul and made him go to Ananias. He also leads these wolves and lions in this fellowship who have come from the world; He still leads them before Him in all that we do. Therefore, brethren, He must lead us before Him until we become such that we can follow Him.

These, brethren, are two matters which we ought to consider in our condition: the beginning, which belongs to [Col. 0216D] the leading by which He drives us before Him; and the other, which belongs to the following by which we follow Him. For an earthly shepherd drives before him those animals which do not know or do not wish to follow him; we also see that some are so tame that they know how to follow the shepherd. Let each person now consider himself: does he follow this Shepherd of ours, or does He still drive him before Himself?

For without doubt He first drove Saint Paul before Him, when He struck him down and, as it were, compelled him to go to Ananias so that he might be baptized by him. But afterward Paul followed Him with great joy when he said: “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ,” etc. (Philippians 1). This driving, brethren, pertains to fear; following pertains to love. He drove us before Him when He caused us [Col. 0217A] to consider our sins and our evil manner of life; when He caused us to fear the punishment of hell and, through this fear, made us leave the world and come here.

And still, brethren, whoever is here, obedient and humble, and keeps his rule—and does this from fear, lest he be condemned, because he knows that one who abandons what he has begun cannot be saved—whoever does the things commanded and pertaining to his order for this reason, our Shepherd still drives before Him. But he who has often tasted how sweet our Lord is, who has begun to love Him, and finds his heart such that, even if no other punishment followed except the offense of his Lord or the slightest diminution of His love, [Col. 0217B] he would not abandon what he has begun—such a person now follows. His Shepherd need not drive him, but only go before him and show him the way along which He wishes him to follow.

Such a person can say: “I ran in the way of Your commandments, when You enlarged my heart” (Psalm 118); not as he did then, when he needed to cry: “Pierce my flesh with Your fear” (ibid.). He had not yet received that broad commandment by which his heart was enlarged when he ran. Brethren, those who were before the Lord’s coming, because they were as it were before Him, He rightly drove; therefore He gave them a law which signified fear. All whom He still drives undoubtedly belong to that law, because so long as they do good through fear, they belong to the law.

But since this is our beginning, [Col. 0217C] we must strive to pass beyond this state and arrive at such a condition that we follow with joy. For this belongs to charity, which especially suits us who are after the Lord’s coming and see where He has ascended before us. And whom should we follow so willingly as this Child, who is a child for our sake? Certainly, brethren, we ought not merely to follow Him, but also to run after Him. For even if His sweetness did not draw us and in some fashion compel us to follow Him, nevertheless desire for that blessedness, that joy which is in the place to which He has gone before us, ought greatly to make us eager to run after Him. For we do not follow Him to fading and transient joys, but to that which “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man” (1 Corinthians 2): that is, to that blessed homeland of which the Prophet says: “My portion, Lord, is in the land of the living” (Psalm 141).

Therefore, dearest brethren, if we wish to attain that blessedness, we must not only follow our Lord in the way of which we have spoken, but also both follow and go before Him in the manner of those who went before and followed Him, concerning whom today’s Gospel relates that they led Him into Jerusalem. For when the Lord came to Jerusalem, as the Gospel says: “A very great multitude spread their garments in the way; others cut branches from the trees and cried: Hosanna to the Son of David; blessed is He who comes [Col. 0218A] in the name of the Lord” (Matthew 21).

You have often heard, brethren, of our Lord’s coming—how and in what manner He came to Jerusalem, that is, to His Church. Therefore it is not necessary to tell you the manner in which He came, especially since the day is short, and on this day we are much occupied because it is Sunday, because of holy Communion, and because of the two meals. Yet, for the sake of the Gospel read today in the holy Church, we wish briefly to say how the Church herself received His coming.

Without doubt some members of the Church went before His coming, while others follow after it. For God’s Church is not only this congregation of believers which believed in Him after His coming, but all the saints from Abel to the last righteous person who shall be in this [Col. 0218B] world belong to the holy Church. That one Church consists of all of them, and to it is said: “My dove is one” (Song of Songs 6). But one part went before His coming—namely, the saints Abel, Noah, Abraham, David, and so forth; after His coming came the apostles, martyrs, confessors, and all believers, among whom we also are through His mercy.

But among all these, some spread garments before Jesus’ feet; others spread branches of trees, who cast away all worldly glory for Christ. For what are the riches and glory of this world but leaves and branches of trees, which are green in summer and wither in winter? Certainly all worldly glory, as it were, blooms in prosperity, but in adversity—especially in the death of a person, when [Col. 0218C] the winter storm comes upon him, that is, final condemnation—it becomes worthless and foul. But blessed is he who spreads these things before Jesus’ feet by distributing them to the poor, who are as it were His feet, that is, His weak members.

Yet far more blessed is he who is able also to despise his own garment for Christ and spread it beneath His feet. For what is our garment except our body, by which the soul itself is in some way covered and clothed? Blessed is he who can despise his own members, his very body, for Christ and devote every deed of his body to God’s service.

Both were done by those who went before the Lord’s coming and by those who followed. For the holy [Col. 0218D] fathers in the Old Testament counted the riches and glory of the world as nothing because of the faith they had in Christ’s coming. Many also subjected their very bodies to martyrdom, such as Abel, the first martyr, Isaiah, and the Maccabean martyrs, whose wonderful passion you heard a few days ago. And after His coming, who can enumerate not merely individuals, but the thousands upon thousands of people who did all these things? For you too belong to their number.

For you have cast down the branches of trees—that is, all worldly pomp—for Christ’s service and honor. You, what is greater, have despised your very bodies; you have expended even your souls, which is greater still, for Christ’s honor, because you have relinquished the proper will of your souls.
