[Col. 0219A] Moreover, all who went before and all who followed cried, saying: “Hosanna to the Son of David; blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord.” Great faith, great confession, great praise.

*Hosanna* is the cry of one asking for salvation, as though one said, “Save [us].” Certainly, by asking salvation from Him they confess Him to be Savior, which properly belongs to God. They call Him another David because they confess Him to be a true man. They bless Him because He comes in the name of the Lord; by this they plainly show that He is the one whom God the Father promised through His prophets would come. In this faith the holy Church receives the coming of the Son of God. It believes Him to be true God, true man, true Savior of the world: promised by God the Father and foretold by the holy prophets.

In [Col. 0219B] this faith those who go before His coming and those who follow it meet, are joined together, and are one Church. In this faith both are saved. Whoever are without this faith are outside the Church; Christ does not come to them, and therefore they are not saved in Christ. This concerns the first coming.

But we ought to know, brethren, that in the very same form in which He first came to redeem His Church, He will come a second time to glorify His Church. For thus the angels said to the apostles after the Lord’s Ascension: “He will come in the same way as you saw Him going into heaven” (Acts 1). This, brethren, will add to the condemnation of the ungodly. For they will not be able, without great shame and sorrow, to see in such glory and power Him whom they despised [Col. 0219C] in human weakness.

The second coming of the Lord is aptly represented by what other Evangelists likewise relate in that history. For when Jesus came to Jerusalem, the children of the Hebrews took branches of olive or palm and came to meet Him. So it will be at the Lord’s second coming. For when He comes in that form in which He redeemed the Church, in order to glorify it and present it to Himself without spot or wrinkle or anything of the kind, then indeed the children of the Hebrews will come to meet Him with palms or branches of olive.

And who are these children except those of whom the Prophet says: “Praise the Lord, children” (Psalm 112); and elsewhere: “The Lord preserves little ones” (Psalm 114)? For He does not preserve those who are great, lofty, and proud, but little ones—that is, the humble. These praise the Lord, provided they are Hebrews, that is, “those who pass over.” For if they are now humble, if they now pass beyond the works and vices of the flesh, if they now know how to make spiritual leaps of contemplation and good thoughts, then surely, on the day of judgment, when Jesus comes in His power, they will come to meet Him with palms—that is, with signs of the victories which they have won here over the devil, for palms signify victory. Then they will be able, as it were, to glory with palms and say: “Where is your victory, O death? Where is your sting, O death?” (1 Corinthians 15).

Then they will come with olives, which signify peace. For now they have no peace, while they fight with the devil, while they fight [Col. 0220A] against vices and against their flesh. But then there will be perfect peace and perfect tranquillity: the flesh will not be able to resist the spirit, nor will the spirit resist God; nor will the devil be able to attack, nor death or infirmity weigh us down. But if we wish to have this peace at the Lord’s second coming, let us strive first to receive His first coming with faith and love, and to persevere in those works which He showed and taught us through His first coming. Let us nourish His true love, and through love, desire, so that when He comes—the Desired of all nations—we may be able to see Him with all confidence: Him who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON II. ON THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD

[Col. 0220B]

“Do not fear: behold, I announce to you great joy, which shall be for all people, because today a Savior has been born to you, who is Christ the Lord, in the city of David” (Luke 2). The report which the angel proclaims to the world I ought rightly today to commend to your charity.

An edict has now gone forth from our Emperor, God, that the whole world should be enrolled. The world has been made subject to our Emperor, namely God. His envoys have been sent throughout the whole world, that it may be enrolled and declare its census. These envoys are the apostles and holy preachers, whose “sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Romans 10), so that the whole world might be enrolled.

Just as that earthly emperor wished and commanded the whole world to be enrolled, [Col. 0220C] so that all might know that they belonged to that metropolitan city, Rome, and might all pay him tribute—that is, the coin bearing his image—so our Emperor, who has now won the whole world, wishes all to be registered in that city which is above and free, and is the mother of us all. Of it the Prophet says: “Glorious things have been said of you, city of God” (Psalm 86). This city may rightly be called Rome, that is, “lofty.” Blessed is he who receives this edict of his Emperor, so that he may be registered in that city. For he shares in the joy which the angel announces today. “The Lord gave joy and gladness to his hearing” (Psalm 50). For he is a companion of, and is found in the lot of inheritance of, those who heard from Him who was born today as Savior of the world—the fountain and source of every true joy—“Rejoice, because your names are written in heaven” (Luke 10).

[Col. 0220D]

But what is the coin which our Emperor requires from us? Without doubt, it is our soul, which bears His image within itself. For God made us in His image, but in the soul. Blessed is he who pays Him this tribute, who renders this coin, who restores His image to Him.

You see, brethren, people throughout the world running to the envoys of our Emperor, so that they may be deemed worthy to be registered in that glorious and lofty city and render Him His image—that is, their souls. Each does this in his own city. There is one city toward which we all journey and in which we all wish [Col. 0221A] to be registered; but, so long as we are in the body, we are “away from the Lord” (2 Corinthians 5), keeping watch against our enemies. We are not all in one city, nor do all keep themselves in one place.

For although the holy Church is called and is one city, it nevertheless contains diverse orders, like different cities, in which each makes his profession. There are many who either do not wish or are unable to keep chastity. Therefore, lest through lusts, fornications, or uncleannesses they be carried off by their enemies, they need to be in some city where they may protect themselves. The city in which such persons guard themselves from those vices is marriage. This city has many inhabitants, though they are weak.

But among the continent, those who resolve to preserve chastity choose different cities. Some choose [Col. 0221B] solitude; others, the cloister. Some give greater attention to fasting; others especially to vigils. Some tame the pride of the flesh by daily labors; others extinguish vices through contrition of heart and an outpouring of tears. Let us consider ourselves and our own city. Our order is a most strongly fortified city, enclosed on every side by good observances, as though by walls and towers, lest our enemy deceive us or turn us away from our Emperor’s army. What a wall poverty is—how it defends us against worldly pride, against harmful and condemnable vanities and superfluities! What a tower silence is, repressing the assault of contention, quarrelling, discord, and detraction! What of obedience, humility, plainness of clothing? What of the austerity [Col. 0221C] of food? They are walls; they are towers against vices and against the assaults of our enemies.

In this city we profess ourselves not Romans but angelic beings. For these observances show that we belong to the fellowship of angels, not to the servants of Romans. At the time of this profession Isaiah’s saying is fulfilled: “They shall beat their swords into ploughshares and their spears into sickles” (Isaiah 2). And he adds: “Nation shall not lift sword against nation, nor shall they train any longer for war” (ibid.).

Without doubt, brethren, although wars abound, seditions become frequent, and killings multiply, what the prophet promises is now fulfilled: “Nation shall not lift sword against nation.” There are two nations of which Scripture often speaks: one of the elect, the other of the reprobate. That nation of the reprobate is [Col. 0221D] certainly the devil’s kingdom; and this kingdom is divided against itself. Therefore that nation never has peace within itself: they always fight and destroy one another, either bodily or spiritually.

And that nation once raised the sword against the other nation, when the earthly city of the reprobate persecuted God’s Church and killed and slaughtered the holy Christian martyrs. This does not happen now; that open persecution, in which many did not dare from fear to profess themselves Christians, has ceased. Those who belong to that heavenly city now go securely toward it and declare the census which their great Emperor, their God, requires from them; because at this time [Col. 0222A] nation does not raise sword against nation.

You freely see many beat their swords into ploughshares and their spears into sickles. This is daily fulfilled literally—not in that faithless nation which has no peace, never has had it, and never will have it, but in that generation of the righteous which shall be blessed. Do you not see noble worldly people coming to conversion, laying aside their spears and swords and, like peasants, working with their own hands for their food? But this is understood to be fulfilled much better, more clearly, and more fully in a spiritual sense among every class of persons: poor and rich, clergy and laity.

Let us consider the sword of which the Lord says: “Everyone who takes the sword shall perish by the sword” (Matthew 26), and that ploughshare by which the earth of our heart is cut, according to the saying: “Rend your hearts and not your garments” (Joel 2). [Col. 0222B] Then we shall see an innumerable multitude in this time changing their swords into ploughshares. The sword is iniquity. By this sword each person harms himself before he harms another, as blessed Augustine says: “Every person is first unjust toward himself before he is unjust toward another; for as soon as he conceives the will to harm another, even before harming the other he harms himself,” whom he kills by the sword of iniquity. Of this sword the Lord says to Peter: “Everyone who takes the sword shall perish by the sword.”

How many, brethren, in this time beat this sword of iniquity into the ploughshare of compunction! Many who previously killed their souls with the sword of sin now cut their hearts through the compunction of repentance. They also change [Col. 0222C] their spears—that is, the subtlety of their own intellect, by which they used to draw many with them into sin—into sickles, by which they gather spiritual fruits, so that they may meet the Lord bearing sheaves of righteousness and salvation.

Therefore, rightly on this day and at this time we commend the report which the angel announces to us. And what is this report? “Today a Savior of the world has been born to you,” he says, “in the city of David.” He rightly commends joy who proclaims that the Savior has been born. For true joy is the joy of salvation; and the Savior’s birth truly bestows upon us the joy of salvation.

Therefore we ought to rejoice with great joy at what is said to us today by the angel, namely, [Col. 0222D] that a Savior is born today. But, dearest brethren, this report is not pleasing to everyone. It did not please Herod, nor the scribes and Pharisees; indeed, when they heard it, they were troubled, and many with them. Nor does it please everyone now. To many today the corruptible delights of the belly are more pleasing than these incorruptible delights of the mind. Many today rejoice more in drinking than in Christ’s Nativity. These hear this report with their ears, but do not understand it. For they do not have the inward ears required by him who said: “He who has ears to hear, let him hear” (Luke VIII). But this report is rightly addressed to you, who have both ears for hearing and a sound palate for tasting. For you keep watch and observe the watches of the night over your flock. But those who devote themselves to draining cups [Col. 0223A] so as to become drunk and indulge in lust do not keep watch in the night: they are weighed down by the sleep of sloth and the wine of drunkenness. “Those who sleep,” as the Apostle says, “sleep at night; and those who are drunk are drunk at night” (I Thess. V). Their day is night because of the works of darkness which they perform. “Their foolish heart was darkened” (Rom. I); but you are surrounded by God’s brightness, as children of the day, imitating those blessed shepherds of whom the Gospel speaks. For, as I have said, you keep watch and observe the watches of the night over your flock, keeping yourselves cautiously on guard everywhere and directing all your actions so that they may please God. And indeed it must be so. For it is night, in which that roaring lion prowls round Christ’s sheepfolds, seeking someone to devour (I Pet. V). If he finds the shepherds asleep, he carries off [Col. 0223B] from their flocks; and what he carries off he drags to death. Therefore let us, being watchful, guard our flock.

Our flock is our good affections and good thoughts. Over these flocks we must keep watch, lest at any time the enemy prevail against them and take them from us, scattering and destroying them. They keep watch over their flock who carefully preserve all their thoughts, words, and deeds, lest they incur any offense in any respect. Likewise, one guards one’s senses—that is, sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch—lest that most wicked thief steal or snatch them away. He steals sight when through negligence we sin incautiously by sight; he snatches it when by the force of pleasure he compels us to sin. [Col. 0223C] So too he steals hearing when, almost without our knowing it, he lures us to listen to vanities and idle words; he snatches it when he impels us through pleasure to do vain things. He steals taste when through the desire of gluttony he deceives us unawares; he snatches it when, through desire for gluttony, he overcomes us knowingly.

The same must also be understood concerning the other senses. Of these flocks the bridegroom says in the Song of Songs to his bride—Christ, that is, to the Church or to any holy soul: “Your hair is like a flock of goats” (Song IV). The hair of our soul is the subtle thoughts which proceed from the rational mind, the head of the soul. Just as, without our knowing it, hairs grow from the head and again, without our knowing it, fall away, so too thoughts often come and depart even without our knowing it. And as no pain is felt when the hair is cut, so, when we cast away superfluous thoughts, we rejoice rather than suffer. In holy souls these hairs are compared to a flock of goats, feeding in the mountains with heads raised high, because the thoughts of the saints always feed themselves upon heavenly things and raise themselves toward heaven, fulfilling the Apostle’s command: “Seek the things which are above,” etc. (Col. III). Moreover, that we ought to understand the senses of the flesh under the name of kids is said in the same Song of Songs: “If you do not know yourself, O fairest among women, go forth and follow after your kids” (Song I). For without doubt, whoever turns his eyes away from himself, unwilling to attend to himself—that is, to his own weakness—but rather to scrutinize and judge the lives of others, will plainly go forth [Col. 0224A] from the fellowship of Christ’s sheep and will feed his carnal senses upon the most evil delight of sin.

But because, following the example of those shepherds, you watchfully guard your flock, what was then said to them by the angel, and what we set before you at the beginning of this sermon, is still said to you today. Hear it, therefore, and receive it with special joy: “Do not be afraid.” You are indeed rightly told, “Do not be afraid.” But what then? Rather, love: for you have a just and evident reason why you ought to love rather than fear. Before this day it was necessary to fear; before this day we had the Creator as Lord, God as judge, and we rightly feared him—for we, his creature, committed such an injury against our Creator that in the first man we despised him, [Col. 0224B] refusing to be subject to him; rather, at the devil’s counsel, we attempted to become his equals. “You shall be,” he said, “as gods, knowing good and evil” (Gen. III). We could rightly fear our Lord, whom we offended like evil servants. We could rightly fear God’s judgment, since we had nothing by which we could make expiation for so great a sin.

Before this day there was nothing from which a human being could rejoice securely, except insofar as he knew or believed that this day would come. But today you are told: “Do not be afraid, but love; do not be sad, but rejoice.” Behold, an angel from heaven is present, announcing to you great joy. Rejoice, then, for yourselves; rejoice also for others, because this joy is not for you alone but [Col. 0224C] for all people. O what joy—how great, how sweet, how desirable! Until now you grieved because you were dead; but now rejoice, because life has come to you, that you may live. You grieved because of the darkness of your blindness; but rejoice, because today “light has risen in darkness for the upright in heart” (Ps. CXI). You grieved because you were miserable; but for us the merciful and compassionate one has been born, so that you may pass into blessedness. You grieved because you were oppressed by the weight of sins; but rejoice now, because today the Savior has been born, who will save his people from their sins. This is the joy announced by the angel: “A Savior is born today.” Until now you feared him who created you; henceforth love him who will heal you. Until now you feared your judge; [Col. 0224D] henceforth love your Savior. “A Savior,” he says, “is born to you today.” Who is he, and of what kind? Hear: “who is Christ the Lord.” *Chrisma* is Greek, *unctio* Latin: hence *Christus*, that is, “anointed.” See what kind of Savior comes: our Christ comes, he comes anointed. For “he went forth as a bridegroom from his bridal chamber” (Ps. XVIII); and he went forth anointed, that he might be more pleasing to his bride. But with what was he anointed? Hear: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions. Myrrh, and stacte, and cassia are from your garments” (Ps. XLIV). Behold the stone which holy Jacob anointed with oil. This very stone, today cut from the mountain without hands—that is, born of a Virgin without the work of a man—went forth anointed with the oil of exultation. And rightly with the oil of exultation, because “he rejoiced as a giant to run [Col. 0225A] his course” (Ps. XVIII): he rejoiced and ran. What he commanded us through his Apostle, he himself first displayed. The Apostle says: “Not out of sorrow or necessity, for God loves a cheerful giver” (II Cor. IX). Thus he himself, first anointed with the oil of exultation, entered upon the way by which he saved us not out of sorrow or necessity, but by his own good will and with great rejoicing. Rightly, therefore, is he Christ, because he was anointed with the oil of gladness above his companions. By his companions he means all the saints who share his name, being called Christians from Christ.

Likewise, the saints of the Old Testament, though they were not called by this name, are not deprived of the reality signified by the name. All are anointed [Col. 0225B] with the oil of gladness, of whom the Apostle says: “Rejoicing in hope” (Rom. XII). But because all find some sin in themselves over which they ought to grieve, he who had no sin is rightly said to have been anointed with the oil of gladness above his companions. “Myrrh,” he says, “and stacte and cassia are from your garments.” O Christ, O Anointed One, how fragrant are these garments of yours! His garments are the members of the body assumed for us: “The Word was made flesh” (John I). There is myrrh, there is stacte, there is cassia. O sweet ointments of our Anointed One! He who is in himself immortal life was made mortal for us: therefore myrrh. He who by the presence of his divinity fills all things emptied himself for us, becoming like [Col. 0225C] water poured out: therefore stacte. He whom angels fear humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross (Phil. II): therefore cassia. Myrrh, by which dead bodies are usually anointed, signifies mortality. Stacte, which is gathered drop by drop, signifies emptying; therefore he was made a little lower than the angels for us. Cassia, a lowly but fragrant herb or tree, signifies his humility, whose fragrance has been diffused throughout the whole world. Rightly, therefore, is he Christ; rightly anointed; rightly “your name is oil poured out.” Therefore the young maidens, sensing the fragrance of these ointments of yours, loved you whom they had previously feared.

Therefore, brethren, let us grind these ointments in our hearts by diligent meditation. Let us consider how sweet [Col. 0225D] to us ought to be the myrrh of his mortality, by which we are freed from all mortality; how sweet his abasement, by which we are raised to heavenly things; how sweet his humility, by which we are exalted. Let us consider how far Christ stooped for us. See these marvels. As death approaches, Christ is sorrowful (Matt. XXVI), while Paul rejoices (Phil. I). At the death of his friend Lazarus, Christ weeps (John XI); and that Maccabean woman does not weep at the dreadful death of her seven sons (I Macc. VII). John the Baptist came neither eating nor drinking; Christ came eating and drinking, and is called a glutton and a drinker of wine (Matt. XI). These things have no savor for you, O Jew or pagan; they have no savor for you, and you perceive no fragrance from them. Indeed, from them the pagan charges us with folly, and from them the Jew takes offense. Why do these things have no savor for you, why do they not smell sweet? Certainly not because they are not savory and fragrant, but because you are tasteless and foul. To me, surely, your sorrow, Lord Jesus, is more savory than all the world’s joy. Your tears, which you shed at the death of your friend, are sweeter to me than the fortitude of the philosophers, who would have the wise person moved by no emotion. More sweetly, surely, does your eating and drinking among sinners and tax collectors smell to me than the rigid abstinence of the Pharisees. Surely the fragrance of your ointments is above every spice. How sweet is it to me that I see the Lord of majesty presenting himself, in bodily practices and human affections, not according to [Col. 0226B] the manner of the strong but according to the manner of the weak! How greatly this strengthens me in my weakness!

This weakness of my Lord is surely, without doubt, the strength and support of my weakness. Hence you who are strong in religious observance and most ready for every austerity must be admonished not rashly to judge those whom you see sometimes tempering their rigor in accordance with the condition of the weak. For if I see my brother, for whose body and soul I have care—for I do not love the whole person if I neglect anything belonging to either—if, therefore, I see him suffering need through the harshness of food, labor, or vigils; if, I say, [Col. 0226C] I see him tormented in body and assailed in heart—for it is very difficult, when the flesh is excessively afflicted, for the mind not to be tempted—if, therefore, I see him so afflicted, and possess this world’s goods, yet close my heart against him, how does God’s love remain in me? (I John III). Certainly, if I always conduct myself according to the rigor of the strong and do not sometimes condescend to the condition of the weak, I do not run in the fragrance of Christ’s ointments, but in the harshness of the Pharisees, who boasted of the rigor of their abstinence and judged the Lord’s disciples—indeed, the Lord himself—calling him a glutton and drinker of wine. One must certainly beware lest, under the appearance of condescension, the softness of laxity be nourished; but one must hold to Blessed Gregory’s principle: that neither should strictness be rigid nor compassion lax. [Col. 0226D] Therefore let us run, brethren, let us run in the fragrance of these ointments with which Christ was anointed. Let us run with the shepherds to our Anointed One, because what was said to them is said also to us: namely, “Today there is born to us the Savior of the world, who is Christ the Lord.” And “Lord” is appropriately added. If anyone, because of the stench of carnal vices, cannot perceive this fragrance and therefore cannot love the Anointed One, that is, Christ, let him at least fear the Lord; for today there is born to us, in the city of David, the Savior of the world, who is Christ the Lord. This is Bethlehem, to which we must run, as the shepherds did when they heard this report. As you are accustomed to sing: “They sang glory to God; they ran to Bethlehem.” “And this,” he says, “shall be [Col. 0227A] a sign to you: you shall find an infant wrapped in swaddling clothes and laid in a manger” (Luke II). Behold what I said: that you ought to love. You fear the Lord of angels, but love the little infant; you fear the Lord of majesty, but love him wrapped in swaddling clothes; you fear him reigning in heaven, but love him lying in a manger. But what sign did the shepherds receive? “You shall find an infant wrapped in swaddling clothes and lying in a manger”: the sign that he himself is Savior, that he himself is Christ, that he himself is Lord. But what is great about being wrapped in cloths or lying in a stable? Are not other infants also wrapped in cloths? What kind of sign, then, is this? Great indeed—provided that we understand it. We understand it if we do not merely hear this love, but also possess in our hearts the light that appeared with the angels. The light appeared when it first announced this report, so that we might know that only those truly hear who have spiritual light in their minds.

Much may be said of this sign; but since the hour has passed, I shall say a little about it, and briefly. Bethlehem, the house of bread, is the holy Church, in which the body of Christ, the true bread, is ministered. The manger in Bethlehem is the altar in the church. There Christ’s animals are fed, of whom it was said: “Your animals shall dwell in it” (Ps. LXVII). Of this table it is written: “You have prepared a table before me” (Ps. XXII). In this manger Jesus is wrapped in swaddling clothes. The wrapping of the cloths is the covering of the sacraments. In this manger, under the form of bread and [Col. 0227C] wine, are the true body and blood of Christ. Christ himself is believed to be there, but wrapped in cloths—that is, invisibly in the sacraments themselves. We have no sign of Christ’s birth so great and manifest as our daily receiving at the holy altar his body and blood, and seeing him, who was once born for us of a virgin, daily offered in sacrifice for us. Therefore, brethren, let us hasten to the Lord’s manger; but, as far as we can, let us first prepare ourselves by his grace for this approach, so that, joined to the angels, with a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith (I Tim. I), we may sing to the Lord in all our life and conduct: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke II). Through the same [Col. 0227D] our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be honor and glory for ever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON III. ON THE EPIPHANY OF THE LORD

A few days ago, brethren, we made known to you the light that “has risen in darkness for the upright in heart” (Ps. CXI): that dawn which God the Father anointed with the oil of exultation above his companions (Ps. XLIV). But our speech could not express the sweetness and power of that anointing. Such is Christ’s power that no tongue can express it, and no heart conceive it as worthily as it deserves. But what a human being cannot show in words, God shows in deeds. It pleased his kindness today to make his power known to us [Col. 0228A] by a manifest display of events. The wise people of this world describe very small matters—victories of kings, battles of the brave, or indeed the courses of stars, even the disposition of the world itself—in fine and ornate discourse. But our fishermen set forth in few and simple words the great and marvelous things they learned concerning God, confirmed by the testimony of mighty deeds. For they knew that they were debtors not only to the wise but also to the foolish, not only to the ingenious but also to the unlearned; and therefore they spoke simply, so that all might understand. They proved what they said by facts so plain that all might see. We ought to imitate them, adapting our words to the benefit of the simple, for Christ’s glory and for their advancement. We told [Col. 0228B] you on another occasion that Christ came into this world to save sinners. Now Christ is called “anointed,” and today the power of this anointing became openly known. Christ was born in Judaea, and immediately those who were in Chaldaea perceived the fragrance of his anointing. And in our Lord himself was fulfilled what the Apostle later said of himself and those like him: “We are a sweet fragrance to God in every place: to some a fragrance of life unto life, to others a fragrance of death unto death” (II Cor. II).

This was accomplished today in Christ himself, from whom all good fragrance comes. For what does a good fragrance signify except a good reputation? And what report is better or sweeter than that he who lay as a little child in a manger was God, and Lord, and the salvation of the whole world? [Col. 0228C] The pagans heard this report, and the Jews heard it too. The Jews had formerly lived, while the pagans were dead; but immediately when both perceived this fragrance, the pagans came to life and the Jews died. To the pagans it was a fragrance unto life; to the Jews, unto death. For as soon as those kings of whom the Gospel speaks learned the Lord’s birth through the star they had seen in the East, they came with gifts to worship him; and as soon as Herod heard the report of him, he devised a plan with the Jews to kill him. Then began that blindness in Israel of which the Apostle says: “A partial blindness has happened to Israel” (Rom. XI). Then also began to rise that light which the Lord promised through the prophet to his Church, which he would gather from the nations, saying: “Arise, [Col. 0228D] be enlightened, Jerusalem, for your light has come” (Isa. LX). This is the Jerusalem which the Lord Jesus—who is true and highest peace—builds from living stones: it tends toward his vision, most certainly believing that in his vision it will be blessed. It is the holy Church; it is every holy congregation; it is every holy soul. “Arise,” he says, “be enlightened, Jerusalem.” Rightly is “arise” said to her who lay fallen; rightly is “be enlightened” said to her who was blind. She lay blind in darkness, in errors, in iniquities. Therefore she is told, “Arise,” because he who would raise her had already stooped down; she is told, “Be enlightened,” because he who would enlighten her was already present. What else does the new star from heaven proclaim today except, “Arise, be enlightened”? The sign of the Lord’s birth appeared in heaven so that we might rise from love of earthly things to heaven. And this sign appeared in a star so that we might know that through his birth we are to be enlightened. But to whom did that star cry this? Certainly not to the Jews, who were blind; not to bloodthirsty Jerusalem, which, as soon as it heard of peace’s presence, was troubled and sought to kill peace itself, having lost peace; but undoubtedly to that queen Jerusalem who hastened from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, whose name is interpreted “peaceful.” That queen is therefore Jerusalem—whose name is interpreted “vision of peace”—because she came to see the Peaceful One. This queen signifies the Church from among the pagans, for that queen herself was pagan. And the Church is undoubtedly the queen who rules so many nations and peoples, of whom [Col. 0229B] David says: “The queen stood at your right hand, clothed in gold” (Ps. XLIV). This Church began to be born today in those pagans who saw this star and understood its meaning. Therefore today this queen came from the ends of the earth to behold the face of him of whom it is said: “Behold, here is more than Solomon” (Matt. XII). Truly more than Solomon, because he is only Solomon—that is, peaceful—whereas this one is so peaceful that he is peace itself, as the Apostle says: “He is our peace, who made both one” (Eph. II). Therefore our queen is rightly called Jerusalem, that is, “vision of peace,” because she was hastening to Peace itself. And our queen is also beautifully called the queen of Sheba. For Sheba is interpreted “captivity.” The Church is plainly the queen of Sheba, because it rightly orders and rules this [Col. 0229C] captivity in which it lives as a pilgrim away from that kingdom where there is no captivity and no misery. That kingdom it will receive on the day of judgment, when the Lord says: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you,” etc. (Matt. XXV). This queen—that is, the holy Church from the nations—lay fallen before this day; before this day she was blind; but today she is told: “Arise, be enlightened.”

Today, in these three pagan kings, she arose from that most evil custom, from that unclean bed in which she committed fornication with demons, because she worshipped idols, images, and demons; and she began to desire him “fair in beauty above the children of men” (Ps. XLIV), that is, the face of the true Solomon. [Col. 0229D] She was blind before this day; but today, raising her eyes toward that wonderful star, as though hearing, “Draw near to him and be enlightened” (Ps. XXXIII), she began to seek that true light “which enlightens every person coming into this world” (John I). It seems to me that today God says: “Let there be light,” and there was light (Gen. I). He had first created heaven and earth; but the earth was empty and void, and darkness lay over the face of the deep. Heaven was Saint Simeon, who recognized the Lord as an infant; heaven was Saint Anna the prophetess; heaven was Zacharias and Elizabeth, and the other spiritual people who were among the Jews. These three kings, in whom we said the holy Church was signified, were still earth. They were earth: they savored nothing but earth. [Col. 0230A] But this earth was empty and void: empty of truth, void of every good work. Darkness too was upon the face of the deep. The deep is the soul because of the exceeding depth of its nature; the face of the deep is the mind itself. Darkness was upon this face of the deep: darkness of error, darkness of paganism, darkness of dreadful unbelief. But today they are told, “Arise,” who were earth; “Be enlightened,” they whose face of the deep was covered by darkness. That is, “Let there be light” means “Be enlightened.” When the Gentiles are enlightened by faith and knowledge of God, they become light and hear Paul say: “You were once darkness, but now light in the Lord” (Eph. V). But whence comes this light to them? “Arise,” he says, “be enlightened, Jerusalem, because your light has come.” This is the whole reason why the holy Church is enlightened: [Col. 0230B] first in those three kings and afterwards among all the nations. This is the entire reason why it is said to her through the prophet: “Because your light has come.” For it has arisen in darkness. But for whom? Not for those perverse in heart, remaining in their darkness, but for the upright in heart, who, recognizing the light itself, desired to worship it. The empty and void earth is told to arise, that is, to prepare itself to desire heavenly things. And as if it replied, “I do not see which heavenly things, which spiritual things, I ought to desire,” there is added: “Be enlightened.”

And observe how beautifully, in these two readings—the prophetic and the evangelical—which are recited in the Church today, the two Testaments accord. We see the Gospel plainly in prophecy, and prophecy [Col. 0230C] in the Gospel, like a wheel within a wheel. In prophecy the holy Church from among the nations is told: “Arise, be enlightened, for your light has come”; in the Gospel is recounted the time when, for that very Church from the nations, a new star appeared in heaven, to admonish her to rise from earthly works and invite her to the true light newly born. In the prophecy it is added: “And the glory of the Lord has risen upon you” (Isa. LX). In the Gospel is recounted the time when that very star, in which the Lord’s great glory appeared, visibly rose over the three kings themselves, in whom the holy Church then existed. But this is according to the letter. According to the spiritual sense, what does it mean that the holy Church is told: “Because the glory of the Lord has risen upon you”? Before [Col. 0230D] this time the carnal Jews glorified the Lord; but all that glory was beneath them, not above them. For all earthly and transitory things, all riches, all worldly honor, are undoubtedly beneath a human being, not above one. The reason those carnal Jews glorified the Lord was that the Lord promised them earthly goods. Therefore they had, as it were, beneath them that glory of the Lord by which they glorified him, because they sought nothing but a temporal reward. But today the holy Church is told: “Arise, because the glory of the Lord has risen upon you,” so that the children of the holy Church may direct their hearts from earthly things to heavenly ones and serve and glorify God not for earthly things but for heavenly. But let us see what follows in the prophecy and in the Gospel. “For behold,” says the prophet, [Col. 0231A] “darkness shall cover the earth, and a mist the peoples” (ibid.). But these words are now said to her as though the Church from the nations, amazed that God should take thought for her, had responded to what came before: “Why do you call me now? In the beginning you rejected me and chose the Jews for your work, as it is written: ‘When the Most High divided the nations,’ etc., ‘the Lord’s portion is his people; Jacob the lot of his inheritance’” (Deut. XXXII). Among that people were prophets, righteous persons, and saints pleasing to you. “Why, then,” she says, “do you call me now?” Hear why: “For behold, darkness shall cover the earth.” He calls the Jews earth because they savored only earthly things and desired nothing but the earthly. Darkness covers this earth because, as the Apostle says, “A partial blindness has happened to Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter in” (Rom. XI).

[Col. 0231B] Today the pagans receive the true light, at whose presence the Jews are blinded. Hear how the Gospel displays this darkness and describes the Jews themselves as blinded in accordance with this prophecy. These three kings of whom we have spoken came to Jerusalem and said: “Where is he who is born King of the Jews?” (Matt. II). As soon as Herod heard this saying, he was troubled. Why, except because he was earth and darkness covered the earth? He feared to lose his earthly kingdom; therefore, when he heard that the King of the Jews had been born, he was troubled and blinded, because he sought nothing but an earthly kingdom and thought that he who had been born would seek nothing but an earthly kingdom. And not only was Herod troubled, but all [Col. 0231C] Jerusalem with him (Matt. II), because darkness covered the earth and a mist the peoples. That earthly Jerusalem was troubled, she who killed the prophets and stoned them. But our mother Jerusalem—the spiritual Jerusalem, namely the holy Church from among the nations—was not troubled but rejoiced. Therefore the prophet added: “But the Lord shall rise upon you, and his glory shall be seen in you” (Isa. LX). Between these two statements he placed that blinding of the carnal Jews. See how beautifully the Gospel agrees with all these things. Thus the holy Church, which this prophet addresses, first in those three pagan kings saw God’s glory rise over itself when that new star announcing the Lord’s birth appeared to them. Then, as soon as they came [Col. 0231D] to Jerusalem, there appeared such blindness among the Jews that they supposed the one who had been born to be Christ, yet sought to kill him. And again, as soon as the kings left Jerusalem, the star which they had seen in the East went before them until it came and stood over where the child was (Matt. II). Perhaps therefore, after the prophet had said of the Jews, “For behold, darkness shall cover the earth, and a mist the peoples”—which undoubtedly happened when King Herod was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him—he immediately turned to our queen and said: “But the Lord shall rise upon you.” Undoubtedly this star, which these pagans saw above themselves, signifies that our Lord, who had been born, would reign over the holy Church drawn from [Col. 0232A] the pagans. “And his glory,” he says, “shall be seen in you.”

Today, brethren, today the Lord’s glory was certainly seen by the Church from the nations. Was not God’s glory great when kings worshipped and offered gifts to him who was little and poor, the son of a poor girl? Yet, brethren, this is little in comparison with the further thing signified in those kings and gifts. Let that queen mentioned before now come to mind, who came from the ends of the earth to see Solomon’s face and hear his wisdom (III Kings X). She did not come empty-handed, but offered Solomon very precious gifts. Behold, in these three pagans is that which the queen signifies, namely the holy Church from among the pagans. There were gifts there, and there are gifts here. Why? [Col. 0232B] Because it was undoubtedly signified that throughout the whole world the holy Church would offer spiritual gifts to our Lord Jesus Christ. Hence the prophet continues: “And nations shall walk in your light, and kings in the brightness of your rising” (Isa. LX). You see that nations everywhere walk in the light of the holy Church. What is the Church’s light except that which enlightens every person coming into this world? The holy Gospel too is the Church’s light, because it is a most bright star by which she is enlightened and walks from strength to strength, so that she may come to Jerusalem and offer him gold, frankincense, and myrrh. Gold signifies faith in his divinity; myrrh, in his humanity; frankincense, in the sacrifice that he himself offered for us to reconcile God the Father to us. These are the gifts; [Col. 0232C] these are the spices which our queen, coming from the ends of the earth—that is, from every part of the world—offers to the true Solomon.

Each one of us was in Sheba, that is, in captivity. Certainly we were in captivity when we were in the world. We were captives in vices, in sins, in the devil’s power; bound in the chains of the worst habits, we were among the Chaldaeans, a name interpreted as “like demons.” Those are like demons who do not wish to go to destruction alone, but deceive and draw into the vices in which they themselves are entangled as many people as they can. We were among such people; indeed, many of us were such people. But there our soul heard: “Arise, be enlightened, Jerusalem.” There we heard the report of the true Solomon and began to desire to come [Col. 0232D] to him. But because we were blind and paralytic, lying in the desires of our flesh as if on a bed, enfeebled, infirm, unfit for any good work, and ignorant of the way that leads to life, it was necessary that he say to each of us: “Arise,” so that you may be able to walk; “Be enlightened,” so that you may recognize the straight way. When God awakened you by the grace of his visitation, so that you were indignant at your sins, then he said: “Arise.” When he inspired in you the affection of good zeal, then he said: “Be enlightened.”

But why is the soul that exists in darkness, lying in sins, called Jerusalem, unless because it was destined to pass from confusion to peace? He called her Jerusalem so that, on hearing this name, she might be prompted by a hidden inspiration [Col. 0233A] as to what she had been created for and what she was like; so that, observing this, she might blush at the stench of her vices and faithfully turn herself to Him who is the peace and glory of all His saints. A guiding star leads us to Him: the star announces Him and shows Him. By appearing, it announces Him; by going before and standing over the house where He is, it shows Him. The star, brothers, the star that leads us to Jesus, is Holy Scripture. Behold, now our light has come; for our sake and for our salvation God became man, was seen on earth, and lived among human beings (Baruch 3), so that by the power of the Word and by the example of His life He might enlighten those sitting in darkness and guide them in the way of peace (Luke 1).

It was not surprising that before the Lord’s coming the pagans [Col. 0233B] lay in their sins and in the darkness of errors, when they had heard nothing about God, when they did not know the light of the Scriptures. But now it is a great disgrace to lie in carnal desires and in the darkness of iniquities, because the true light has now come, which enlightens every person coming into this world (John 1): Jesus Christ. We can no longer have an excuse for our sins, since Christ, who takes away the sins of the world and justifies the ungodly, speaks plainly to us. “Whoever follows me does not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life” (John 8).

And what is the way by which He Himself walks, and which leads to Him? Let Him say it; let Him say: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Luke 9). The Apostle also points out [Col. 0233C] the way leading to Christ: “Through many tribulations,” he says, “we must enter the kingdom of God” (Acts 14). Again the Lord says in the Gospel: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5). This is the way by which Jesus walked and by which we shall come to Him: namely, the denial of one’s own will, imitation of Christ’s Passion, the adversities of this life, and voluntary poverty. Holy Scripture shows us this way, signified by that star which, as we said, appeared to the three kings.

Therefore be kings, and let your soul be queen—the queen of Sheba. For you are still in Sheba, that is, in captivity; and see what kind of captivity it is: “I see another law in my members, resisting [Col. 0233D] the law of my mind and making me captive under the law of sin” (Romans 7). Behold Sheba. But restrain the carnal impulses within yourselves, lest sin reign in your mortal body (Romans 6); then you are kings, and your soul is the queen of Sheba. Yet because, under the guidance of the Gospel of peace, as though led and preceded by a star, you travel the paths that lead to Christ, you will without doubt come to Him and worship Him.

But since one ought not come to Christ, or worship Him, empty-handed, prepare your gifts for Him. Offer Him gold, that is, true charity; offer incense, that is, pure prayer; offer myrrh, namely the mortification of your flesh. By such gifts God will be appeased toward you, so that He Himself may rise over you and His glory may be seen in you. For He will be glorified in [Col. 0234A] you and will make you participants in His glory—may He deign to grant this, He who lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON IV. ON THE PURIFICATION OF SAINT MARY

Brothers, I see that you have assembled in order to be fed with the food that endures, the nourishment of God’s saving word. As the Lord says, “Heaven and earth shall pass away, but the word of the Lord shall remain forever” (Matthew 24; Luke 21). This is the bread that came down from heaven (John 6) and gives life to the world. You seek this bread as the little children of the Lord Jesus, concerning whom He Himself says: “Allow the little children to come to me, for of such is the kingdom of heaven” (Mark 10). But lest you fail on the way, you wish to come and be fed—fed, indeed, with that bread which fills the mind rather than [Col. 0234B] the stomach.

May the Lord grant that there be someone to break it for you, lest it be said of us: “The little children asked for bread, and there was none to break it for them” (Lamentations 4). As it is yours to ask for bread, so it is ours to break it. We must break the bread which God granted you on the journey of your pilgrimage, so that you may be able to reach that bread which He keeps whole for you with the angels in your homeland. The bread of your pilgrimage is the mystery of Christ’s Incarnation, the truth of His teaching, and the example of His humility and that of His faithful ones. The bread of your homeland, on which angels feed, is the face of God: participation in divinity and possession of that joy which “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart” (1 Corinthians 2).

So that you may desire this bread of angels more eagerly [Col. 0234C] and hasten toward it more ardently, the Gospel today serves you bread that will give strength to your spirit on this path of exile. It sets before you the purification of the holy Mary, Mother of God and our Lady, and the offering of the Savior Himself. This bread must be broken so that it may be eaten, for these matters must be expounded if they are to be understood. She is purified who bore Him who had no sin at all—indeed, who was sufficient to purify the whole world. He offered sacrifice for Himself who was the sacrifice for the whole world.

Why was all this done? First, because the time had not yet come for the Law of Moses to be set aside. Next, because He wished to show that the Law of Moses was good when He Himself fulfilled it. Finally, [Col. 0234D] He wished to teach us to seek something spiritual in those bodily observances which the Jews observed.

Why was it commanded that an infant be circumcised on the eighth day, and that its mother enter the Temple after forty days, and then with her son and sacrifice? Why, too, was it commanded that all should cut away a part of their flesh—and that part from which a person is usually most ashamed? Someone might think such an observance shameful rather than holy, unless the Lord Himself had first commanded it and later observed it. Yet this observance was holy, because through it a person was cleansed from original sin, and because it signified the faith that we have in the Lord Jesus, through which faith we are cleansed from all sins.

But although there were many who did not descend from Abraham’s loins, as Saint Job did, the command of circumcision was given especially to Abraham’s children. And the fact that those of Abraham’s race cut away one part of that member (Genesis 17) through which human beings generate and are generated in carnal corruption and pleasure signifies that the Lord Jesus would be born from his stock, but without all corruption and fleshly pleasure. And as those children of Abraham cut away from themselves that part of the flesh in which pleasure rules most strongly, so we, Abraham’s spiritual children, ought to cut away every carnal pleasure—and this on the eighth day. Why? Because, just as they were cleansed on the eighth day by this sacrament from the sin in which they had been born through corruption, [Col. 0235A] so our Lord, who was born of Abraham’s race, by His resurrection—which took place on the eighth day, that is, after the seventh, called the Sabbath—having laid aside every weakness of mortality and corruption, raised immortal and incorruptible that very nature of flesh which He had taken from us and for us. Likewise, through faith in our Lord’s resurrection we are cleansed from all sins.

Purification follows circumcision. Before circumcision the woman was unclean, and the infant unclean; after circumcision they were neither wholly clean nor wholly unclean. For if they were wholly clean, they would not need purification, nor would they be forbidden to enter the Temple. But if a greater uncleanness were not present in them before circumcision, it would not have been commanded [Col. 0235B] that, if a woman had borne a child, she should be regarded as unclean when the child was to be circumcised.

Retain what we have said about circumcision, and then let us break this bread so that it may have flavor. It seems to me that this woman signifies human nature, which, made unclean by vices and sins, was cast out of Paradise. There were some who thought that without faith in Christ they could justify themselves by their own power and come to God. Many and very eminent philosophers believed this; but they were deceived. They bore sons—that is, they performed manly deeds in abstinence, contempt of the world, and continence of the flesh. They bore sons because they had many disciples; but because they did not know circumcision and the eighth day, both those who bore and those who were born remained in uncleanness. Thus among them the mother—that is, human nature—and the son—that is, their works—could have no cleanness.

Therefore the Lord taught us through Moses how this woman and her son ought to be cleansed. First, she is unclean until the circumcision of the eighth day. The circumcision of the eighth day is faith in Christ, which pertains especially to His resurrection. For He died openly before all. Therefore it is no merit to believe that He died; rather, the merit lies in believing what was done secretly. Through this faith we have righteousness; through this righteousness, cleansing. Therefore the Apostle says: “Christ was delivered up for our offences and rose again for our justification” (Romans 4). Before [Col. 0236A] a person has this faith, he is unclean, and whatever he does is unclean, as the Apostle openly says: “Whatever is not from faith is sin” (Romans 11). If it is sin and unclean, then the woman—whatever she bears, whatever she does—will be unclean until the eighth day; for human nature is always in sin, both itself and whatever it does, until it comes to faith in Christ.

On the eighth day the woman receives cleansing, and human nature, in faith in Christ’s resurrection, receives forgiveness of sins. Then the boy is circumcised, because the work is cleansed from sin. For example, before faith in Christ someone possessed chastity, but that chastity was unclean because it existed in the sin of unbelief. Therefore the boy is circumcised on the eighth day because, in faith in Christ, this chastity [Col. 0236B] is cleansed from the sin of unbelief.

But why is the woman, as if still unclean, cleansed through this cleansing? There are many kinds of uncleanness. One uncleanness comes from nature, another from the will, another from weakness. From nature comes the uncleanness we have when we are born. Hence Saint Job says: “No one is clean from defilement, not even an infant whose life upon earth is one day old” (Job 14). Therefore David says: “Behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother conceived me” (Psalm 50). Saint Job had this uncleanness in view when he said: “Who can make clean one conceived from unclean seed?” (Job 14). Because of this uncleanness all human beings, when they are born, are children of Gehenna and children of wrath. [Col. 0236C] Because of this uncleanness there was circumcision in the old Law; it cleansed a person from this uncleanness because it signified faith in our Lord Jesus Christ. This uncleanness alone was sufficient for a person’s condemnation.

But who is there that has not added another uncleanness to this one by his own will? Scripture says of this uncleanness: “There is no righteous person on earth who does good and does not sin” (Ecclesiastes 7). And if a righteous person increases this uncleanness, how much do adulterers, fornicators, murderers, and thieves increase it! Yet baptism cleanses all these uncleannesses, and after baptism, penance does so; and this occurs on the eighth day, in faith in the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ.

There is still another uncleanness arising from weakness. Of it the Apostle says: “I see another law in my members, resisting the law of my mind and making me captive under the law of sin” (Romans 7). Who, brothers, can boast that he does not have this uncleanness in himself? From it come evil desires and evil delights; from it, disordered impulses in our members; from it, vanities and wanderings of the human heart. Now see, brothers: you have been cleansed from those great uncleannesses, that is, condemnable vices. Your works have been cleansed, like sons circumcised on the eighth day. Yet can you immediately enter that Temple—namely, the Temple above, in the heavenly Jerusalem? But who, so long as he remains in this flesh, can enter that Temple? David says: “I shall pass into the place of the wonderful tabernacle, even to the house of God” (Psalm 41). [Col. 0237A] Yet one might suppose that he said this would happen after death. But hear what follows: “Why are you sad, O my soul, and why do you trouble me?” (ibid.). Why, then, was his soul sad, unless because he had descended again from that Temple into himself, where he found misery and sorrow?

Hear another who continually remained in that Temple: “Our citizenship,” he says, “is in heaven” (Philippians 3). Therefore, brothers, we cannot immediately ascend to that Temple when we are cleansed from our sins through baptism or confession. Why not? Certainly because of certain uncleannesses that accompany us. For who will boast that he has a pure heart? When we wish to lift our heart upward and strive [Col. 0237B] to ascend to that Temple, certain thoughts come into our heart concerning those vices we committed and those vanities we pursued. They have not yet been erased from our memory, and they draw our heart downward so that we cannot ascend to that Temple.

Therefore we must endure forty days and seek the sacrifice through which we may be so cleansed as to be able to enter the Temple of which we speak. This number, forty, signifies the labors and temptations which we must patiently endure as long as we are in this life. Because of this signification, the children of Israel spent forty years in the wilderness, where they endured many temptations and many labors, and thus came into the land of promise. [Col. 0237C] Because of this signification Elijah also fasted for forty days and thus came to the mountain of God. For without doubt, whoever desires to enter that heavenly Temple, signified by the land of promise, and to ascend the mountain of the Lord and stand in His holy place (Psalm 23), must fast, labor, and endure the temptations and hardships of this life, so that he may thus be cleansed from every defilement of flesh and spirit (2 Corinthians 7), and be among those of whom it is written: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5).

Therefore, dearest brothers, after the cleansing of baptism or confession, if we wish with a pure heart to search out heavenly things and visit God’s Temple, we must endure the purification [Col. 0237D] of forty days—that is, patiently bear the labors and temptations of the present life.

We must also seek a sacrifice. What kind? “A pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons.” Both these birds are accustomed to mourn and never to sing; they signify tears and mourning, through which we can be cleansed from all our vices. Tears are usually produced in those still needing purification by two things: fear and shame. For there is a third kind of tears which does not so much cleanse as enriches and refreshes; that kind arises from love. But we must speak of those two kinds through which we can be cleansed.

In the mourning of the dove, understand those tears that come from fear. For the dove lives among people, [Col. 0238A] where it always has snares and traps. In the mourning of the turtledove, understand those tears that shame provokes. The turtledove is said to be a certain modest bird that can have only one mate, because of a certain natural modesty, as I think. Therefore the Bridegroom says to the holy soul in the Song of Songs: “Your cheeks are like those of a turtledove” (Song 1). You know that shame is displayed in the cheeks. The holy soul has cheeks—that is, the modesty of the turtledove—because she is ashamed of every other love except the love of God.

He offers a dove who, through fear of God, is pierced with sorrow for his sins and sheds tears. He offers a turtledove who, out of shame for his sins, weeps before God. But why was it commanded to offer a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons? Because [Col. 0238B] we must have a double fear and a double shame: fear lest we be condemned for the sins we have committed, and fear lest we yet fall into sins. For although it is true that the Lord forgives all sins to those who turn to Him and do penance, we must nevertheless always fear, because we do not know whether our satisfaction is worthy. Again, although a person feels himself to be in good condition, nevertheless, so long as he lives, he can fall into evil. Therefore we must always fear and weep before God in this double fear; and then we offer two young pigeons.

Again, we must have a double shame: shame because we have defiled [Col. 0238C] and corrupted ourselves by sins and vices; shame because we have been ungrateful for all the good things God has done for us. He created us, nourished us, and gave us sense and understanding; He—who is above all—offered His death for us. Yet we were ungrateful for all these things and, beyond this, returned evil for good and hatred for His love. Therefore, brothers, whoever is affected by this double shame and weeps offers a pair of turtledoves. By this sacrifice we can without doubt be cleansed. With this sacrifice we ought to offer our children to God in the Temple: that is, commend all our works to the Lord with tears and transfer the whole treasure of our works, as though it were our son, to that lofty Temple, as the Lord commanded, saying: “Lay up treasures for yourselves in heaven” (Matthew [Col. 0238D] 6).

He lays up treasure on earth—where rust and moth, that is, pride and vain glory, are present—who performs his works not in God’s Temple but before human eyes. Therefore let us raise all our works to God, so that, as He was presented for us today in the Temple, we too may be presented to Him with pure minds and deeds in that heavenly Temple. May He deign to grant this to us, He who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON V. ON THE FEAST OF SAINT BENEDICT

I know that you are accustomed to receive with every joy the feasts of the saints whenever they occur, and through remembrance and representation of their life and perfection to stir yourselves to spiritual fervor. Yet I think that this feast of our holy father Benedict is sweeter to you than the others and in some way more welcome—not because his feast is higher than the others, but because he, our father, is nearer to us than the other saints. For in Christ Jesus he begot us through the Gospel.

Whatever purity you possess in chastity, whatever spiritual sweetness you possess in charity, whatever glory you possess in your conscience from contempt of the world, labors, vigils, fasts, voluntary poverty—all comes from his teaching. Whatever progress you make in meditations, prayers, compunction, devotion, and other spiritual matters: did not God’s grace supply it all to you through his ministry and example? [Col. 0239A] Therefore he is nearer to you than the other saints, so that not undeservedly his feast ought to be more joyful to you.

Look at Israel according to the flesh, that is, the carnal Jews. Although they descend from the great patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, concerning whom the Lord says, “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (Exodus 3)—which the Lord plainly said because of their excellence—yet the Jews themselves boast more of Moses, saying, “We are Moses’ disciples” (John 9). And the Apostle James says in the Acts of the Apostles: “Moses has those who preach him in the synagogues every Sabbath” (Acts 15). Why then do these carnal Jews have such affection for Moses? I think it is because through Moses’ ministry the Lord led them [Col. 0239B] out of Egypt, brought them through the Red Sea, and because through his prayers they received manna from heaven and water from the rock; because, while he prayed, they overcame their enemies; and because, by his giving, they received the Law, which, if they kept it, would enable them both to receive and possess the land of promise.

Certainly, brothers, if we rightly see and understand the benefits the Lord has conferred upon us through our holy father Benedict, we shall plainly see that monks ought to love him no less than the carnal Jews love Moses. Through Moses’ ministry the Lord led them out of Egypt; through Saint Benedict’s ministry He led us out of the world. They were under Pharaoh, a most wicked king; we were under the devil. They [Col. 0239C] were in slavery to the Egyptians; we were under the dominion of vices. Pharaoh’s ministers scourged them and required bricks of mud.

Perhaps you have forgotten what scourges you suffered in the world. One person strove after some worldly honor or riches: what scourges did he suffer in those desires? How fear and envy scourged him; how he was scourged when he could not acquire what he wanted; when someone else acquired what he himself had so ardently coveted! But if he acquired it, how fear scourged him lest he lose it, and sorrow when he lost it! Another rushed with his whole purpose toward fulfilling all his wishes and lusts: how did most evil love, jealousy, and suspicions scourge such a person? What when someone exposed his vices? How he grieved, how [Col. 0239D] his mind was scourged! And over all these things, how each person’s own conscience scourged him!

What when each began to consider his life and his sins? How often, because of the very scourges of his own heart, did he resolve and say: “I will never do this again; I will never again plunge myself into that vice”? Yet Pharaoh’s ministers—that is, unclean spirits—drove us almost against our will to make muddy bricks, that is, unclean and filthy works, and thus to build a city for Pharaoh, that is, for the devil, in our heart. Whoever can remember the violence he suffered from his evil habit, and sees himself now freed through God’s grace and the teaching of blessed Benedict, sees that through him God has granted us greater things [Col. 0240A] than He granted the Jews through Moses.

If you compare the spiritual sweetness that you are accustomed to feel from Christ with the manna the Jews ate in the wilderness; if you compare the victories that you often gain over your spiritual enemies, through the merits and teaching of blessed Benedict, with the victories they gained over human enemies—you will surely see that these things are much greater, because they are spiritual. Moses established and taught them a law so that they might enter the land of promise and possess it so long as this world endures. Blessed Benedict established a law for us: if we keep it, we shall enter heaven itself—the land of the living—and possess it eternally. This law, brothers, is his Rule. In it he teaches us [Col. 0240B] to offer spiritual sacrifice to God, observe a spiritual Sabbath, and build a spiritual tabernacle for Christ in our hearts. If we keep this law, we shall be, as he himself says, heirs of the kingdom of heaven.

But since we have mentioned Moses and Pharaoh, let us speak something from their words for our edification on this feast of our father.

As you know, when the children of Israel were captives in Egypt under Pharaoh, Moses was sent to tell that wicked Pharaoh on God’s behalf to let the Lord’s people go. When Pharaoh refused to do this, he and his people were struck with many great plagues. At last, because of the plagues he was suffering, he said to Moses: “Go and sacrifice to the Lord your God in this land” (Exodus 8). Moses replied: “By no means; it cannot be done in that way.” And he gave the reason why: “We shall sacrifice to our God the abominations of the Egyptians” (ibid.).

Therefore they could not sacrifice to God in Egypt, because they were to sacrifice the abominations of the Egyptians to God. For although it is read in interrogative form, “Shall we sacrifice the abominations of the Egyptians to our God?”, it has the same sense. For Pharaoh had said, “We shall sacrifice the abominations of the Egyptians to our God,” with “in this land” understood; and it must be understood: “It cannot be done in that way.” But Moses shows where this ought to be done, for he added: “We shall go a three days’ journey into the wilderness, in order that we may sacrifice to the Lord” (ibid.).

You know, brothers, what Egypt is, who Pharaoh is, and who the Egyptians are. Yet I shall say it briefly: Egypt is the world; [Col. 0241A] Pharaoh is the devil; the Egyptians are vices and sins. Understand it thus. You were in this Egypt, under these Egyptians, under this Pharaoh. The devil held you captive through love of the world and love of relatives; he bound you with your own desires; he held you through your evil habits. Brothers, when would he have released you if the Lord had not struck him? But how did He strike him? Certainly by the good will He gave you; by the good desires He inspired in you; by the good thoughts He put into your hearts. By all these things the Lord struck the devil; by all these things the spiritual Egyptians—that is, vices and sins—were crushed.

Yet Pharaoh held you by your evil habit and did not allow you quickly to break those bonds of habit. [Col. 0241B] But when he saw that your resolve prevailed, what did he say? “Go, and sacrifice to the Lord in this land” (Exodus 8). I wonder, brothers, I wonder if you have not all heard this voice—either secretly in your hearts through the devil, or openly through one of his members. “Do you wish,” he says, “to serve the Lord? Good. Must you therefore leave your possessions, your churches, your riches? Serve God here; do penance here; serve God from your own resources; give alms.”

I think you recognize what I am saying. Brothers, we know, and have experienced, how many have been deceived by this voice. We know some who conceived a good purpose, firmly resolved to leave the world, and had almost done so. But they heard this voice of Pharaoh; they heard it and consented. They began to wish to live in a seemingly religious manner in the world, but they were deceived. For they fell back into their former vices and added hypocrisy. Nor is this surprising. It is a great, brothers, a great presumption to wish to do penance amid the very riches, pleasures, and honors through which they fell into those dreadful crimes.

Not so, brothers, not so. One must go a three days’ journey into the wilderness, in order that we may sacrifice to the Lord our God the abominations of the Egyptians. Perhaps penance itself belongs among the abominations of the Egyptians; therefore they could not offer this sacrifice among the Egyptians. But first let us see what these three stages of the journey are. The first stage is [Col. 0241D] to leave the world; the second, to leave vices and sins and change one’s habits for the better; the third, to leave one’s own will. Whoever completes these three stages can sacrifice the abominations of the Egyptians to the Lord.

And see, brothers: many abandon riches and worldly honors and, as it were, remove themselves from the world by a one-day journey. But because they still refuse to abandon their evil habits, remaining proud as before, lustful as before, bitter as before, angry as before, they do not at all complete two stages and therefore are not fit to sacrifice to God. There are others who do both things: they forsake riches and honors and abstain from their former crimes. Yet because they withdraw by themselves into some forest or other place and eat when they wish, fast when they wish, keep vigil when they wish, sleep when they wish, work and rest when they wish, they undoubtedly do not complete the third stage.

Even those who are in a community and seem to have left their own will behind do not complete the third stage if they still seek certain freedoms: to leave the cloister when they wish, speak when they wish, work when they wish, attend reading when they wish; and if, in whatever and as much as they can, they draw things toward their own will. I do not mean everyone who possesses this freedom, but those who seek it and delight in it. For some occasionally go out, speak, and do certain things for whom all these things are more burdensome [Col. 0242B] than delightful; they would more gladly remain at peace.

Therefore he has perfectly gone out of Egypt who has completed these three stages: first, as he once outwardly left the world’s riches, so he daily and continually casts them out of his mind, and always shows the Lord a mind free from every desire and ambition, saying with blessed Peter, “Behold, we have left all things” (Matthew 19); next, he reforms his life and manfully resists the vices to which he was subject in the world; finally, he wholly mortifies his own will and depends upon his elder’s judgment concerning whatever he must do.

Certainly, brothers, Saint Moses taught the children of Israel those three bodily stages, through which they came [Col. 0242C] to the place where they bodily sacrificed to the Lord. But blessed father Benedict teaches you these three spiritual stages and shows quite plainly the way by which you can complete them. For, as it seems to me, the first stage is completed by the way of mortification, the third by the way of obedience. Hear blessed Benedict showing us this way (Rule, ch. 7): “The first degree of humility,” he says, “is fear of the Lord.”

And as it seems to me, the first indication of humility is contempt for riches and possessions. For while a person preserves and holds worldly riches and honors, he may perhaps be humble, but his humility does not appear as clearly. Therefore, through the first degree of humility a person comes to the first indication of humility. And surely each of you can see this in himself: how could you have abandoned your riches and possessions, how could you have completed this stage, unless the fear of the Lord urged you? The fear of the Lord, therefore, is the way by which this first stage is completed.

But someone says: “How have I completed this stage, since I left nothing? For I possessed nothing in the world and left nothing.” Whoever thinks this should answer me whether, when he was in the world, he desired any riches and whether he acquired, according to his means, what he could. If, then, he has also left desire behind, he has indeed completed the first stage well.

Now let us see the way of the second stage and gladly walk in it. It is the mortification of the flesh. Blessed Benedict says (ibid.): “The second degree of humility is that a person, not loving his own [Col. 0243A] will, should not delight in fulfilling the desires of the flesh.” This plainly is the way by which we can complete the second stage—that is, avoid former vices—if, namely, by vigils, fasts, and labors we mortify the desires of the flesh. Let no one say: “I am strong, I am chaste, I am wise; I have no need to labor, keep vigil, or fast.” Are you wiser than Paul? Are you stronger than blessed Benedict? Paul chastises his body and brings it into slavery, as he himself says: “In hunger and thirst, in labor and hardship” (2 Corinthians 6); and yet he sees another law in his members, resisting the law of his mind.

Saint Benedict too spent several years of his life on bread and water, and yet scarcely escaped the temptation of lust. For he was almost overcome; this was read tonight, as you heard. He thus lived, and you, intent on I know not what luxuries and vanities, think that you can escape the filth of the flesh? Therefore whoever wishes to complete the course of abstinence does not take delight in fulfilling the desires of the flesh. Now let us hear what Saint Benedict says concerning the way of the third course (ibid.): “The third degree of humility,” he says, “is that, for the love of God, a man submit himself in all obedience to his superior.” In this way a person wholly leaves himself and gives himself over to God: if he submits himself in all obedience to another, so that he neither eats according to his own arrangement, nor fasts, nor works when he himself wishes, but when another commands; and thus in all other matters follows not his own will but another’s. He who has completed these three courses must sacrifice to God the abominations of the Egyptians—that is, the things which the Egyptians abominate and hate.

The Egyptians are lovers of the world, worldly and vicious people: “who rejoice when they have done evil, and exult in the worst things” (Prov. 2). When they have fulfilled their evil desires, they rejoice, grow proud, do not know how to blush, and do not wish to repent. The abominations of the Egyptians, therefore, are the bitterness of repentance, sorrowful mourning, voluntary poverty, and contempt for oneself. We must offer these abominations of the Egyptians to the Lord our God. Let us repent of our sins; let us mourn and weep for the sins which we have committed and continue to commit, so that our vices and sins may be drowned, perish, and be blotted out in the tears of repentance, as it were in the bitter and salty waters of Egypt. Let us also embrace poverty; let us be lowly and contemptible in our own eyes; and thus, as those who have perfectly gone out from Egypt, we shall truly sacrifice the abominations of the Egyptians to the Lord our God, and our sacrifice will please him.

Yet there are some who, after leaving the world, grow proud either of their property, their clerical standing, or even of the riches, vanities, nobility, and worldly honour which they have left behind; and they think that they ought to be honoured more than others. They want their superior to call them into his counsels and honour them more than the rest; they wish to involve themselves in all his decisions. If anything is ordered or arranged without their counsel, they are offended and angry, thinking that their superior despises them out of envy. Such persons do not yet offer the abominations of the Egyptians to the Lord.

But see how Saint Benedict teaches us to offer these abominations of the Egyptians.
