Having taught us, through those three degrees of humility, the way by which we may complete those three courses, he immediately added concerning these very abominations of the Egyptians which we must offer (ibid.): “The fourth degree of humility is that, in obedience itself, amid hard and adverse things, or even injuries of any kind inflicted upon him, he embrace patience with a silent conscience.” And again in the same place: “When struck on one cheek, they offer the other; when compelled to go one mile, they go two; they endure false brethren and persecution.” These plainly are the abominations of the Egyptians, because the Egyptian—that is, the worldly mind—abominates all these things. For it considers it very shameful not merely to endure injuries patiently, but even not to avenge oneself as far as one can.

These are sacrifices pleasing to God, in which those things are slain which the world worships and loves. Saint Moses rightly says: “If we sacrifice before their eyes the things which the Egyptians worship, they will stone us” (Exod. 8). What do the Egyptians worship? Certainly riches, honours, gold, silver, the pleasures of the belly, and gluttony. These are what the Egyptians worship. Whatever Egyptian possesses such things grows proud and exalts himself above others. Those who do not possess them honour, worship, and as it were adore those who do possess them, calling them blessed. Hence it is said in the Psalm: “Their sheep are fruitful, abundant in their goings forth; their oxen are fat. There is no breach in the wall, no passage through it, and no outcry in their streets” (Ps. 143). This is the happiness of the Egyptians; and other Egyptians, who do not possess these things, call such persons blessed and say what the Prophet adds: “They called blessed the people to whom these things belong” (ibid.).

Whoever wishes to kill all these things in his own mind while living among worldly people—that is, to despise riches, honours, and pleasures, and to live sparingly, soberly, chastely, and religiously—will immediately be stoned by the Egyptians, that is, assailed with harsh abuse. One calls him a deceiver, another a hypocrite. Therefore you acted wisely in leaving Egypt and, through the aforesaid three courses, coming into the wilderness. But what is it to have come into the wilderness? It is to regard this entire world as a desert; to desire one’s homeland; to have from this world only as much as suffices for completing this journey, not as much as the flesh desires.

Offer sacrifices, then, to God. Slay within yourselves what the world loves. Love to be lowly for Christ, poor for Christ, despised for Christ. This is what our blessed father Benedict teaches. Follow his footsteps and his teaching, so that he may deign to recognize you among his own—as a shepherd recognizes sheep, a father his children, a master his disciples—and so that, through the intervention of his merits, you may reach the pastures of eternal happiness, the inheritance of God’s servants, and the joys of Christ’s disciples; through the grant of the same Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON VI. ON THE SAME FEAST, II

Since today we celebrate the passing of our holy father Benedict, we ought to say something about him, especially because we see that you eagerly desire to hear. You have also gathered together for this purpose, as good sons, that you may hear about your father, who begot you in Christ Jesus through the Gospel. Since, then, we know that he has passed away, let us consider from where and to where he passed. He passed from the place where we still are, to the place where we have not yet arrived. Yet although we are not bodily in the place to which he has passed, we are there in hope and love, according to the saying of our Redeemer: “Where your treasure is, there your heart also is” (Matt. 6). Hence too the Apostle says: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3).

For Saint Benedict himself, while bodily living here, dwelt in that heavenly homeland in thought and longing. Therefore today our father Saint Benedict passed from earth to heaven, from prison to kingdom, from death to life, from misery to glory; he happily migrated from this life, which should more rightly be called death, to the land of the living. I rightly say that he passed to the land of the living, because this life is not the life of the living but of the dying. For all the things mentioned above—namely death, prison, and misery—are found in this life; indeed, the present life itself is all these things. For if it were not death, the Apostle Paul would never say: “I die daily, by your glory, brethren” (1 Cor. 16). And: “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?” (Rom. 7). He most plainly calls this life death and says that to live in the body is to die.

That this is called a prison, the Psalmist testifies, saying: “Bring my soul out of prison” (Ps. 141). And although our daily experiences teach us that this life is miserable—indeed, misery itself—blessed David calls it “the pit of misery and the mire of dregs”; and, knowing that he was to be delivered, he cries out with great joy as though already delivered: “He heard my prayers and brought me up out of the pit of misery and the mire of dregs” (Ps. 39).

[Col. 0245D] But since we know from where and to where he passed, let us also see by what way he passed. For it profits those who desire to follow him nothing to know from where and to where he passed unless they also know by what way he passed. He passed through Christ to Christ; through faith in Jesus Christ, working in him through love, he passed to the sight and contemplation of Jesus Christ, in which the desire for every good is satisfied. His way, then, was Christ, who says of himself in the Gospel: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14). Through him he passed to him, because he is life, because he is the way.

The most upright way of this same father of ours was his excellent manner of life. The way of his life was holiness. For, as blessed Gregory says, the present life is nothing other than a certain road. Therefore whoever lives well and commendably passes to God and eternal life; but whoever leads a reprobate life moves through it toward Gehenna and everlasting death. This is the way of sinners, of which the first Psalm speaks, David saying: “Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly, nor stood in the way of sinners” (Ps. 1). By this evil way one goes to the most evil death of sinners, of which the same Prophet says elsewhere: “The death of sinners is most evil” (Ps. 33).

He rightly calls the death of sinners most evil, since their way is plainly evil. For, as the Apostle says: “The wicked always advance from bad to worse, deceiving and being deceived” (2 Tim. 3). Thus the death of sinners is called most evil because by living wickedly they proceed so far in malice that, having become utterly wicked, they deserve to be cut down and cast into the fire. But blessed father Benedict did not keep this way, because he did not lead a reprobate life; rather, he kept that way of which it is said: “The way of the righteous is straight” (Isa. 26). Though narrow, it nevertheless leads to life.

This way is indeed narrow at its beginning; afterwards, however, as blessed Benedict himself teaches in his Rule, one runs “in the ineffable sweetness of love along the way of God’s commandments.” It is narrow for beginners, as it was for David when he said: “Because of the words of your lips, I have kept hard ways” (Ps. 16). But because the Prophet found it narrow at the beginning, did he therefore abandon it or judge that it should be abandoned? Far from it! Rather, he held it until he could utter a saying quite unlike this: “I have run in the way of your commandments, when you enlarged my heart” (Ps. 118).

Blessed Benedict too found this way narrow at the beginning of his conversion and found it very broad at the end. Was it not narrow for him when, as we read in his Life, he threw himself into thorns lest he consent to lust? But when he found it narrow, what did he do? Did he turn aside from it? Rather, he held to it and stood manfully upon it. He first did what he taught, so that he might teach us, his followers, what he had done. For, as Saint Pope Gregory says of him (*Dialogues*, ch. 36), he lived as he taught, nor could he teach otherwise than he lived.

How manfully he stood in the way of God may be gathered from his own words. For in his Rule he warns that no one, frightened by fear, should flee the way of salvation; and experience itself had taught him that it cannot be begun except by a narrow path. For he knew that, however narrow it might be, it nevertheless led to life, as our Lord himself says: “Narrow is the way that leads to life, and few are those who walk by it” (Matt. 7). To what life this way leads, the Lord himself teaches elsewhere, saying: “This is eternal life: that they may know you, the true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17).

This is therefore the way by which we read that Isaac journeyed, which leads to the well of the One who sees and lives. Of this way it is likewise said in the book of Wisdom: “The path of the righteous, like a shining light, grows unto the perfect day” (Prov. 4). Hellish fear, also called servile fear, makes this way narrow; perfect love makes it broad. For as long as a person fears while on God’s way, he suffers difficulty and feels harshness. But when he comes to perfect love, which “casts out fear,” then with great joy he proclaims those apostolic words: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith” (2 Tim. 4); and David’s words: “I have run in the way of your commandments, when you enlarged my heart” (Ps. 118).

He who has Christ in such a manner desires with Paul “to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Phil. 1); indeed, he bears most grievously being separated from Christ any longer, saying daily with tears the words of the Psalm: “How long, O Lord, will you forget me utterly?” (Ps. 12), and with Habakkuk: “How long, O Lord, shall I cry and you will not hear? Shall I cry out to you, suffering violence, and you will not save?” (Hab. 1). By this way Saint Benedict passed, as we have said, from death to life, from Egypt to the promised land—that is, from the darkness of this world to Jerusalem, which is the vision of peace. And certainly he passed happily, because he lived praiseworthily.

For he passed with Moses to see that great vision: not how the bush burned and was not consumed, but how the blessed angels and God’s saints, made equal to angels, always burn with love and in them love never grows cold. Let us also pass over, dearly beloved, to behold this great vision. Let us follow in the footsteps of our holy father Benedict. We have a most straight road by which to arrive there: namely, his Rule and teaching. If we hold to this as we ought and persevere in it, we too shall undoubtedly arrive where he is. May the grace of our Redeemer Jesus Christ grant this to us through the merits and intercession of Saint Benedict; he who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON VII. ON THE SAME FEAST, III

Your charity, dearest brethren, has often heard that Saint Moses, after bringing the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt, constructed the tabernacle in the wilderness from the offerings of the children of Israel (Exod. 35). Some offered him gold, others silver, others precious stones, and others animals, which need not now be enumerated individually. [Col. 0247D] But this must be considered: since, as the Apostle says, all these things happened as a figure (1 Cor. 10), we were in a kind of spiritual Egypt when we were living in the world. Egypt, indeed, means “darkness.” Iniquities and sins, and the obstinacy of the mind within them, are thick darkness. We were once in these things, and by participating in them we ourselves became darkness, as the Apostle says: “You were once darkness” (Eph. 5).

But so that we might be light in the Lord, he appointed for us a certain Moses, a lawgiver—namely, our holy father Benedict, whose feast we celebrate today. By his knowledge and skill we pass through the wilderness of this world, so that we may come to the promised land: not that which the carnal children of Israel carnally desired, but that for which the Prophet hoped, saying: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. 26); and of which the Lord says: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth” (Matt. 6).

He, filled not only with the spirit of Moses but also, in some sense, as someone has said, with the spirit of all the righteous, constructed this spiritual tabernacle from the offerings of the children of Israel. In his Rule shines the gold of most blessed Augustine, the silver of Jerome, and Gregory’s scarlet dyed twice over; and likewise the sayings of the holy Fathers, like precious stones, adorn this heavenly edifice. For you, brethren—you are God’s tabernacle, you are God’s temple, as the Apostle says: “The temple of God is holy, which temple you are” (1 Cor. 3). You are a temple because the Lord will reign in you eternally. Yet you are still a tabernacle because he journeys in you, hungers in you, and thirsts in you.

This tabernacle is still carried by the ministry of Levites. Some carry it on their own shoulders; others with the aid of oxen and carts. Those carry the tabernacle who earnestly fulfil the command of our Moses (Rule, ch. 72): “Let them bear their infirmities, whether of body or character, with the greatest patience; let them vie in showing obedience to one another.” But those carry it on their own shoulders who, expecting no aid from any earthly advantage, diligently weigh what follows in the same verse: “Let them prefer absolutely nothing to Christ” (ibid.). Those carry it, but not on their own shoulders, who observe the Rule’s practices indeed, but hope here for something transitory—rank, honours, or something of that kind. Disappointed in this hope, they lay down the tabernacle and depart, as though deprived of the aid of carts. For the cart signifies temporal honour.

Others likewise carry it, but not on their own shoulders; rather, with the aid of oxen, that is, of prelates. For they want their prelates always to flatter them and show them some temporal favour. If, perhaps, it happens that they hear some harsh word from them, then, as though deprived of their support, they either lay down the tabernacle altogether or carry it with grumbling. Of such persons the Apostle says: “The time will come when they will not endure sound doctrine, but, according to their own desires, will heap up teachers for themselves, having itching ears” (2 Tim. 4). For just as adulterers seek the itch of lust, so these seek the itch of flattery.

This, my brethren, this tabernacle suffers while it is carried through the wilderness of this age, until it is brought into the land of promise, and from a tabernacle becomes a temple, and is dedicated by the true Solomon for seven days and seven days—that is, with a double rest and a double perfection—when each is given two robes: namely, the immortality of the body and the blessedness of the soul. But now, brethren, if we are spiritual children of Israel, if we have spiritually departed from the land of Egypt, let each of us offer—let all of us offer—for the construction of this tabernacle, each from that in which he abounds. For “each has his own gift from God, one in this way and another in that” (1 Cor. 7). One can offer more labour, another more vigils, another fasts, another prayers, another more readings or meditations.

Let one tabernacle be made from the offerings of all, so that, according to the command of our lawgiver, no one may call or presume anything his own, but all things may be common to all. This, brethren, must not be understood only of cowl and tunic, but much more of virtues and spiritual gifts. Let no one glory individually in some grace bestowed on him by God as though it were his own. Let no one envy his brother for a grace as though it belonged exclusively to him; rather, let him regard as belonging to all his brothers whatever is his own, and let him not doubt that whatever belongs to his brother is also his own.

Almighty God could indeed immediately advance anyone he wished to perfection and bestow every virtue upon each person. But in a merciful dispensation he deals with us so that each person needs another and has in another what he does not have in himself, so that humility may thus be preserved, love increased, and unity made manifest. Therefore each thing belongs to all, and all things to each; and the fruit of virtues is usefully gathered while humility is preserved through consideration of one’s own weakness. Therefore let our lay brethren not complain that they do not sing psalms and keep vigils as much as monks do. Let monks not complain that they do not work as much as lay brethren. For I say most truly that whatever one person does belongs to all, and whatever all do belongs to each one.

For just as the members of one body do not all have the same activity, so, as the Apostle says: “Though many, we are one body in Christ, and individually members of one another” (Rom. 12). Therefore let the weak person say, “I am strong,” because just as another has in him patience under weakness, so in another there is for him the strength of fortitude.

Let us beware, then, lest dying flies destroy the sweetness of the oil. The sweetness of the oil is the sweetness of brotherly love, which dying flies—namely covetousness, envy, and suspicion—destroy. For no one loves perfectly who desires anything in this world. Envy is born from covetousness. For whatever a person desires for himself, he envies in another; and often the mind strives to think ill of the one whom it envies.

But let us now compare certain ordinances of that ancient Moses with the ordinances of this modern Moses of ours. Moses appointed six cities of refuge for the children of Israel: three outside the promised land and three in the promised land itself, so that whoever committed homicide unwittingly might be saved by fleeing to them (Num. 35). There is bodily homicide, and there is spiritual homicide. Sin, indeed, is the death of the soul; and this is the worst kind of homicide: to kill either oneself by vice or another by example.

While the children of Israel were in Egypt, they had no cities of refuge, not because they did not kill, but because they killed more from pride than from ignorance. We too, while in spiritual Egypt, sinned not because we were weak but because we were proud; we delighted in sinning, and therefore had no cities of refuge. Now, although we have gone out from Egypt, “if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1). For “in many things we all offend” (Jas. 3). But it matters whether this happens through weakness and ignorance, or through pride. As long as anyone lies proudly in some sin, although he may seem to have gone out of Egypt, no city of refuge will benefit him. As the Apostle says: “If we sin willingly after receiving the knowledge of truth, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins” (Heb. 10).

These six cities seem to me able to signify the six general exercises established for us: three bodily ones—labours, vigils, and fasts. These belong particularly to those who are still assailed by carnal passions and are, as it were, still outside the promised land; those of whom it cannot be said, “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3). There are also three spiritual exercises: reading, prayer, and meditation. These belong particularly to those who, having conquered their passions, have passed into the love of virtues, tasting in these cities how sweet the Lord is (Ps. 33), namely the fruits of the promised land.

We flee to these cities because of those who pursue us on account of homicide. Who are they? The devil, certainly, or concupiscence itself. For as the Apostle James says: “Each person is tempted when drawn away and enticed by his own concupiscence” (Jas. 1). The more one sins, the more the very desire for sin increases. Hear the Apostle greatly fearing this enemy: “I see another law in my members,” he says, “warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive in the law of sin which is in my members” (Rom. 7). Hear him fleeing to these cities: “I chastise my body and bring it into servitude” (1 Cor. 9). How? Plainly as he says elsewhere: “In labours, in vigils, in fasts” (2 Cor. 6). Hear Peter urging us toward these cities: “Be sober and watch in prayers” (1 Pet. 4), and so forth.

As for the command in the Law that one should flee to one of these cities (Num. 35), although it had to be prescribed thus in order that it might be fulfilled literally, we must nevertheless observe that no one has equal grace in every exercise. Therefore in temptation each person ought to flee to that exercise in which he finds that he has greater grace. We must also consider the command that he not leave these cities until the death of the high priest. And who is our high priest but Jesus? Therefore we must persist in labours, fasts, and vigils until “our members which are upon the earth” are mortified; until we bear about in our flesh the death of Jesus, so that we may say with the Apostle: “I am crucified with Christ” (Gal. 2), and: “I bear the marks of the Lord Jesus in my body” (Gal. 6).

But there is also a mortification of the spirit as well as of the flesh. Thus it is written: “Sing to God with harp and harp” (Ps. 147), that is, with a double harp. We must therefore also persevere in spiritual exercises, so that, as the flesh dies to its worst passions, so the spirit may die to evil thoughts. If we have thus been planted together in the likeness of this death, we shall also be united with his resurrection, walking in newness of life (Rom. 6); and when Christ, our life, appears, we too shall appear with him in glory (Col. 3). May our Lord Jesus Christ deign to grant this through the merits and prayers of our blessed father Benedict; he who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON VIII. ON THE ANNUNCIATION OF THE BLESSED MARY

When our Lord and Saviour Jesus departed from us bodily, he promised us the presence of his divinity [subkahens: uncertain reading] the presence of his grace, saying: “Behold, I am with you all days, even unto the consummation of the age” (Matt. 23). But because it was expedient for us always to remember the benefits which he bestowed on us through his bodily presence; because he knew that our memory is corrupted by forgetfulness, our understanding by error, and our zeal by desire, he mercifully provided that his benefits should not only be recounted to us through the Scriptures but also represented to us through certain spiritual actions.

Therefore, when he handed to his disciples the sacrament of his body and blood, he said to them: “Do this in remembrance of me” (1 Cor. 11). For this reason, brethren, these feasts were established in the Church: so that, by now representing his Nativity, now his Passion, Resurrection, and Ascension, that mercy, sweetness, and pure love which he showed in us through all these things may always remain fresh in our memory. Our faith too ought to profit greatly from these things, when we hear with our ears and see, as it were, before our eyes what Christ suffered for us, what he gives us in this life, and what he promises us after this life. He suffered death for us; in the present life he gives us forgiveness of sins; after this life he promises us eternal happiness.

All this deliverance of ours, all this hope of ours, all this blessedness of ours began on this present day. Before this day there was nothing in the world but misery and darkness; but today the Dayspring from on high visited us, and light arose for those who sat in darkness and in the shadow of death (Luke 1). Today our Joseph clothed himself in his many-coloured tunic—that is, a varied and beautiful tunic—in which he was sent by the Father to visit his brothers and sheep. Today he fulfilled what was foretold through Isaiah the prophet, which we set forth at the beginning of this sermon: “Behold, the Lord shall ascend upon a light cloud and enter Egypt” (Isa. 19).

Saint Moses greatly desired this, as we can understand from his words. As you have often heard and read, when the children of Israel endured that harsh bondage in Egypt under Pharaoh, God appeared to Moses and commanded him to go down into Egypt and bring his people out of that misery. But although Moses greatly grieved over the captivity suffered by the children of Israel in Egypt, he grieved still more for the misery which the whole world endured under the devil. Therefore he desired and sought the one who would be able not merely to bring that people out of Egypt, but also to deliver the whole world from hell. Hence he said with intense feeling: “I beseech you, Lord, send whom you will send” (Exod. 4). He knew indeed that God would send him, but did not want the sending to be delayed so long. It is as if he said: “I know, sweet Lord, that you will send your beloved Son, who is to free us from that great misery and that unhappy captivity; and perhaps you wish to send this beforehand as a sign of that deliverance. But what need is there of such great preliminaries? Let him himself rather come; let him himself descend; let him himself illumine spiritual Egypt—that is, the darkness of the whole world—with his sweet presence.” This desire of Saint Moses was fulfilled today.

Let us consider, then, brethren, how great our exultation ought to be, since we see fulfilled what Saint Moses so ardently desired to be fulfilled. For today he ascended upon a certain light cloud and entered Egypt. Egypt, brethren, means “darkness.” And what was the entire world before Christ’s coming but darkness? Thus it was altogether necessary for this wondrous light to arise amid this darkness—that is, for Christ to be born in the world. But, as the Evangelist says: “The light shines in darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it” (John 1). For without doubt human minds were so enwrapped and blinded by the darkness of sins that they could not direct the inner eye toward that divine light.

Therefore he—that is, Mercy itself—acted mercifully and tempered the brightness of his divinity for the world through a certain cloud. That most holy flesh, brethren, which he today assumed from the Virgin’s flesh, is called a cloud because through it the divinity was veiled. But it is called light because no iniquity weighed it down. Iniquity is heavy and draws down to the depths. Therefore the prophet saw it sitting upon a talent of lead (Zech. 5). His flesh too is quite fittingly called a tunic, signified by Joseph’s tunic, which was many-coloured, varied, and reaching to the ankles, because it extended down to the heels.

This Joseph, brethren, as you have learned from sacred history, was Jacob’s son, whom Jacob loved more than the others and begot in his old age. He was Rachel’s son; after long barrenness she finally bore this son (Gen. 37). All these things most clearly suit our Lord Jesus Christ. He is the one whom the Father loved more than all others, in whom he was pleased in every respect, as he himself says: “You are my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Luke 3). Joseph means “increasing.” No one does this name suit so properly as Christ. He is that stone cut from the mountain without hands, which grew into a great mountain and filled the whole world. Hence his father says in his blessing: “Joseph, a growing son; a growing son, and fair in appearance” (Gen. 47).

Truly fair in appearance, he upon whom the angels desire to look (1 Pet. 1), whose beauty sun and moon marvel at. Truly fair in appearance: for he is the wisdom of God, concerning which it is written: “She is more beautiful than the sun and above every arrangement of the stars” (Wis. 7). That Joseph is born of a barren woman; ours, of a virgin. There is a certain correspondence between barrenness and virginity. For although virginity has a certain spiritual fruitfulness, it nevertheless has bodily barrenness. But because the privilege of being born from a virgin was reserved for the true Joseph, that Joseph is born from a barren woman, because barrenness is in a certain way near to virginity.

Therefore the prophecy of the book of Wisdom applies fittingly to blessed Mary: “Blessed is the undefiled woman who has not known a bed in sin; she shall have fruit at the visitation of holy souls” (Wis. 3). Blessed Mary was indeed blessed: in order to avoid the defilement of the flesh, she chose bodily barrenness. Nor was she much concerned about that curse of the Jews: “Cursed is the barren woman in Israel.”

See, brothers, a most beautiful harmony between the Son and the mother. It is written in the Law of Moses: “Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree” (Deut. 21). The Son did not avoid the curse of the cross; the mother did not avoid the curse of barrenness. But he, by the cross, having become a curse for us, redeemed us from the curse of the Law; and she, because she chose such virginal barrenness, deserved fruitfulness and bore the Son of God. Therefore Saint Joseph was not without reason born of a barren woman [Col. 0253C]. For Rachel’s barrenness, the mother of the Joseph of old, prefigured virginity. Nor is it without significance that Rachel is interpreted as “sheep.” Far more fittingly may the mother of our Joseph be called a sheep, upon whose fleece that heavenly rain descended, as Saint David says: “He shall descend like rain upon the fleece” (Ps. 71).

The fleece, as someone has said, though it is from the body, does not know the body’s passions. So virginity, though it is in the flesh, does not know the vices of the flesh. “He shall descend like rain upon the fleece.” The fleece can receive the moisture that comes down from above, but cannot feel the moisture of fleshly pleasure. Thus the virginity of blessed Mary received that dew which came from heaven, but could experience no fleshly pleasure. Moreover, what could be more fitting for a lamb than to have a sheep for its mother? See, then, how fittingly she is called a sheep, from whom arose that heavenly Lamb who takes away the sins of the world (John 1); who “was led as a sheep to the slaughter,” and “as a lamb before its shearer was silent and did not open his mouth” (Isa. 53; Acts 8).

Further, Scripture says of Rachel: “She was beautiful and comely in appearance” (Gen. 29). Although it is pleasant to suppose of the most blessed Mary that she was also, in body, most graceful and most beautiful, we ought nevertheless to refer these words to her inward beauty. But who can worthily speak of her inward beauty, whom he who is “fairer in form than the sons of men” (Ps. 44) loved, desired, and sanctified above all creatures to such a degree that he not only dwelt in her mind, but also prepared for himself a dwelling in her body? “While the king was at his reclining, my nard gave forth its fragrance” (Song 1) [Col. 0254A]. Without doubt, while he was in the bosom of the Father, there he perceived the fragrance of her virginity; there he considered the beauty of her soul. And therefore today his angel was sent to announce his coming, not only into her heart, but also into her flesh.

See, brothers, what nuptials these are, and how heavenly: in them God is the bridegroom, a virgin the bride, and an angel the bridal attendant. By these nuptials the virgin did not lose her virginity, God did not lose his divinity, and the angel did not lose his dignity. Yet there is a greater miracle in these nuptials. The bridegroom is the Son; the bride is the mother [Col. 0254B], because the Son united the soul of that most holy Virgin to his divinity; because God himself, having become man, came forth from her womb as a bridegroom from his chamber. Rightly, therefore, did the angel greet her, saying: “Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you; blessed are you among women” (Luke 1).

Consider, brothers, what gifts the Son of God sent to his bride. Let those gifts come now to mind which Abraham’s son sent through his father’s servant to Rebecca, his bride; she too, like Rachel, was a most beautiful virgin who had not known a man. Abraham’s servant found her beside water, spoke to her there, and there gave her gifts (Gen. 24). Likewise, our most beautiful Virgin, of whom I speak, gladly remained beside spiritual waters, that is, the Holy Scriptures [Col. 0254C]. She often resorted to these waters, so that she could say with the Prophet: “He has led me beside the waters of refreshment” (Ps. 22). Indeed, there the angel found her: the servant, namely, of Abraham—not of that earthly and mortal Abraham, but of the heavenly and eternal one. For so the Evangelist says: “The angel entered to her and said: ‘Hail, full of grace; the Lord is with you’” (Luke 1).

Where did he enter to her? Without doubt, where she had hidden herself from the vanities of the age; where, withdrawing from worldly cares, she had entered her private chamber, shut her door, and prayed privately to her Father. She was drawing for herself waters with joy from the springs of the Savior (Isa. 12), that is, from the Holy Scriptures, where she had read both of a virgin’s childbirth and of the Savior’s coming. Perhaps at the time when the angel came she had Isaiah in her hands; perhaps she was then studying that prophecy: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel” (Isa. 7) [Col. 0254D].

I think that Scripture had, in that hour, stirred up a most beautiful conflict in her heart. For I think that, when she read that a virgin was to bear the Son of God, she secretly and with a certain fear wished that she herself might be that virgin; yet again she thought herself wholly unworthy for so great a gift to be granted her. Love contended with fear; devotion with humility. She was almost despairing through excessive fear; but again, because of the immense desire she had for this, she could not help hoping. Again devotion made her dare to hope, but again her great humility made her hesitate [Col. 0255A]. Therefore, while she was in this hesitation, this fluctuation, this longing, the angel entered to her and said: “Hail, full of grace.”

Abraham’s servant, as Scripture says, gave Rebecca golden earrings and bracelets (Gen. 24). Of these earrings speak the friends of the true bridegroom, one of whom is this Gabriel who speaks to Mary; and they say to the bridegroom: “We shall make for you little ornaments of gold” (Song 1). The little ornaments and the earrings are one and the same. They are adornments for the ears, just as bracelets are adornments for the arms. And indeed this servant of the great Abraham—that is, the angel Gabriel—adorned the ears of this Virgin of ours with a beautiful ornament when he said: “Hail, full of grace.” He adorned her arms with a beautiful golden bracelet when he said: “The Lord is with you” [Col. 0255B].

For he whose coming the angel announced may rightly be called a bracelet, because, just as a bracelet has neither beginning nor end, so he, according to his divinity, neither begins to be nor ceases to be. With this bracelet the arms of this Virgin of ours were adorned, because she often carried in her embrace and arms the Son of God whom she bore from herself. Amid all these riches and delights, blessed Mary remained most chaste not only in body but also in mind. Therefore it is said in the Song of Songs: “You are beautiful and comely, most chaste amid delights” (Song 7).

The corruption of the flesh is lust; the corruption of the mind is pride. It is no great thing to preserve chastity amid poverty, or humility without virtues. For no one can be subject to fleshly vices and be spiritually proud. We are not now speaking of that pride in which fleshly and worldly people are accustomed to take pride, but of that which is accustomed to assail perfect and holy men [Col. 0255C]. Therefore, just as it is a great thing to preserve bodily integrity amid bodily riches and pleasures, so beyond doubt it is supreme not to experience this pride amid spiritual graces. This indeed is true chastity of mind, which was present in full measure in blessed Mary.

And so, amid all these spiritual graces, which she possessed above all human beings, hear how humble she was. Mary said to the angel: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord” (Luke 1). Hear also the Evangelist: “Mary, rising,” he says, “went with haste into the hill country to the house of Zachariah and greeted Elizabeth” (ibid.). Let us add this also: “Joseph too went up to Bethlehem with Mary, his betrothed wife, who was pregnant” (Luke 2) [Col. 0255D].

Consider in all these things her wondrous humility. She who was full of God, greater than the world, higher than heaven, more fruitful than paradise; the adornment of virgins, the glory of women, the praise of humankind, the joy of angels; she whom the Son of God chose as his mother, called herself a handmaid. She whom the angel greeted subjected herself in great obedience to a craftsman. She, the Queen of Heaven and Lady of the angels, who carried God in her womb, humbly greeted her kinswoman because she was older in age. Most fittingly, then, was it said of blessed Mary: “You are beautiful and comely, most chaste amid delights.” If we can rightly appraise this beauty, we shall see that what was said of Rachel is fitting for no one more than for the mother of our Joseph [Col. 0256A]: “She was beautiful in face and comely in appearance” (Gen. 29).

Scripture further says that Jacob loved Joseph more than his other sons, because he had begotten him in his old age. Moses was a son of God; every prophet was a son of God; and all the saints are sons of God. But “who among the clouds shall be equal to the Lord? Who shall be like God among the sons of God?” (Ps. 88). All are beloved, but none is beloved as our Joseph is. He was begotten in his Father’s old age by that very Ancient of Days of whom Daniel says: “I watched until thrones were set in place, and the Ancient of Days sat down” (Dan. 7). God’s antiquity, old age, or long duration is nothing other than his eternity. In this eternity, the eternal Father begot this our Joseph as coeternal and consubstantial with himself. For he is “the radiance of eternal light, the spotless mirror of the majesty of God, and the image of his goodness” [Col. 0256B].

It is therefore not surprising if God the Father does not love those who are his sons by grace as much as the one who is his Son by nature. Moreover, although our Joseph according to the flesh is later born than many other sons of God, he is nevertheless the firstborn of all, as the Apostle says: “Who is the firstborn of every creature” (Col. 1). The only-begotten from God; the firstborn from the dead.

Because of this signification, Scripture says of the typological Joseph that, though Reuben was firstborn according to the flesh, the rights of the firstborn were reckoned to Joseph. Therefore John the Baptist says of our Joseph: “After me comes a man who was made before me” (John 1) [Col. 0256C]. It is as though he said: “Although I was born earlier according to the flesh, he is nevertheless the firstborn.” So far as human beings are concerned, God grows old in those hearts in which love of God becomes lukewarm and charity grows cold. In a certain way God had already grown old to this world, because “all had turned aside; together they had become useless; there was none who did good” (Ps. 52).

But his father made Joseph a many-colored tunic. This is that cloud of which we spoke a little earlier: the most holy flesh of our Savior. It is a cloud because through it he tempered for us the brightness of his divinity. It is a tunic because, as though clothed in flesh, he appeared in this world; and as though it were a tunic, he laid aside that very flesh when he wished and took it up again when he wished [Col. 0256D]. Long ago he had made a tunic for disobedient Adam, but one of skins; for our Joseph, who obeyed him in all things, he made a tunic, but one of many colors. That tunic of skins, which is usually made from dead and earthly animals, showed Adam to be earthly. This many-colored tunic, which by its lovely diversity possessed a certain likeness to heaven, signifies that this Joseph is heavenly. Hence the Apostle says: “The first man is from earth, earthly; the second man is from heaven, heavenly” (1 Cor. 15).

That tunic is also most beautifully called *talaris*, that is, reaching down to the ankles, where the body ends, because that holy flesh remained incorrupt to the end, as the Psalmist says: “You will not give your Holy One to see corruption” (Ps. 15) [Col. 0257A]. Let us then put off, brothers, Adam’s tunic of skins—that is, the works of darkness—and because the true day has dawned upon us today: “Let us walk honorably as in the day, not in feasting and drunkenness, not in beds and indecencies, not in strife and jealousy” (Rom. 13). For all these things belong to that tunic which we must put off if we wish to put on the many-colored tunic of which the Apostle immediately adds: “But put on the Lord Jesus Christ” (Col. 3). Elsewhere he exhorts us concerning the diversity of this tunic, saying: “Put on, as God’s chosen, holy and beloved, bowels of mercy, kindness, humility, gentleness, patience” (ibid.) [Col. 0257B]. This is that lovely diversity of virtues with which our Lord Jesus Christ was preeminently clothed, and which every Christian must also put on.

But because the tunic of our Joseph was not only many-colored but, as it is written in the Gospel, “woven from above throughout,” after the Apostle had enumerated that lovely diversity in different virtues, he immediately added concerning the weaving itself: “Above all these, have charity, which is the bond of perfection” (ibid.). Yet, as that diversity signifies that he was full of every virtue, so the light cloud signifies that he was entirely empty and free from every vice.

We may also understand blessed Mary by that light cloud [Col. 0257C], through whom our Lord came into Egypt, that is, into this world. She may rightly be called a cloud because she was full of the rain of spiritual grace. She is light because no burden of the world weighed her down. The Lord ascended upon this cloud and entered Egypt, that is, the lowest parts of the world, according to that prophecy of which we have spoken: “Behold, the Lord shall ascend upon a light cloud and shall enter Egypt. And the idols of Egypt,” he says, “shall be shaken at his presence” (Isa. 19).

Thanks be to God: it has now been accomplished. The idols of Egypt have been shaken; idols have been removed from the world. Few, if any, remain who worship stones and wood, as almost the whole world did before Christ’s coming. But would that, brothers, just as people have thrown idols out of their houses, so they would wish to cast all idols out of their hearts! Yet whoever loves money more than God neglects God and worships idols. For what is money but an idol bearing the image not of God but of a human being? But this does not concern us. What then? Must we fear nothing from these images? Would that it were so! But although Jacob departed from Syrian Mesopotamia and went up to Bethel, he nevertheless had in his company a wife who had stolen Laban’s idols (Gen. 31) [Col. 0257D].

So too, although we have departed from the world, as Jacob did from Mesopotamia, we nevertheless still have sensuality and carnality: like a woman who retains memories of the world and images of that life which we have abandoned. Thus these Egyptian images occupy and claim for themselves that part of our memory which God alone ought to inhabit [Col. 0258A]. Because of these images, Laban—that is, the devil—pursues us; and because he cannot claim us for himself through the world’s riches, luxurious banquets, drunkenness, lusts, discords, and enmities, he strives as far as he can at least to bring an accusation against us through the illusions of these images.

What then must be done? Even if we cannot expel them altogether, we must cover them as far as we can. For “blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven and whose sins have been covered” (Ps. 31). Whatever sins we commit through this instability and wandering of the mind, and through such memories, let us cover with vigils, fasts [Col. 0258B], and diligent prayers. And because charity covers a multitude of sins, let us practice it with every effort. Thus the devil will find nothing of his own in us. Through these virtues we shall become one with him in whom he finds nothing.

Let us strive with all our attention that we too may become spiritual clouds, abounding in the dew of heavenly teaching. Let us be light, so that, freed from the dregs of desires, we may fly above this world on certain wings of virtues. For if our soul is such, the Lord will deign to ascend upon it as upon a light cloud, to enlighten our Egypt—that is, the darkness of our heart—to expel each of the things of which we have spoken, and alone to possess and inhabit our soul.

But because these images are accustomed to arise through a kind of curiosity by which we direct our attention to outward things, let us enter the chamber with blessed Mary, hide ourselves as much as possible, and, with the door shut, beseech our Lord Jesus Christ that he who today deigned to assume our nature may dispose it according to his will and our benefit, and so preserve our life that he may always remain in our hearts: he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON IX. ON PALM BRANCHES

Although the observance of this day, which all Christians celebrate with such earnestness [Col. 0258D], is sufficient to stir our hearts to devotion, both because of the recitation of the Lord’s Passion and because of the remembrance of our salvation, we must nevertheless also render to you the service of our sermon. Thus provision has been made for us in every respect, so that no means may be lacking by which our minds can be inflamed with the love of God.

First, see, brothers, that two things concerning our Lord Jesus Christ are commended to us today: namely, the great glory which the Jewish people showed him in this world, and the great outrage which that same people inflicted upon him. For, as you heard a little while ago from the Gospel, and will hear again shortly, when the Lord came to Jerusalem seated upon an ass, a great crowd went out to meet him. Some spread their garments in the road; others cut branches from the trees and spread them in the road; and those who went before and those who followed cried out: “Hosanna to the Son of David; blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Matt. 21) [Col. 0259A]. It is also narrated in the Gospel itself—which you did not hear then but, God willing, will hear shortly—what an outrage that same people inflicted upon the Lord. For they bound him, struck him with fists, spat upon him, and finally condemned him to a most shameful death, in their estimation.

But consider more attentively what I have said: the same people, not the same persons. For Jews were those who received the Lord with such honor, and Jews were those who treated him with such contempt. Yet these were one group, and those another. Long ago the Lord showed both groups to Jeremiah the prophet by a comparison, saying to him: “What do you see, Jeremiah?” And he said: “Figs—good figs, very good; and bad figs, very bad, which cannot be eaten because they are bad” (Jer. 24) [Col. 0259B].

Those are called good figs who displayed to the Lord such sweetness of love and such pleasantness of service that they were worthy to be eaten by him as sweetest figs—that is, to be joined to his body, namely the holy Church. Therefore Jeremiah says of those good figs: “They were such as figs are at the first season” (ibid.). For these were, as it were, the first fruits of the holy Church, of whom the Apostle says: “You have come to the Church of the firstborn, who are enrolled in heaven” (Heb. 12) [Col. 0259C]. Those very bad figs, likewise, may most fittingly be called those who retained within themselves no sweetness of charity and no pleasantness of devotion, but had become utterly bitter through envy, hatred, and malice; and therefore were not at all worthy to be eaten by him—that is, to be brought into his body.

This was the vineyard of which he himself says through Isaiah: “I expected it to bear grapes, and it brought forth thorns” (Isa. X). It indeed produced thorns so bitter and piercing that they even drew blood from that most holy body. Thus, when the prophet spoke of both good and bad figs, he called both figs; yet he made a division between them, calling some good and others bad. So too, those who today cried, “Hosanna to the Son of David” (Matt. 21) [Col. 0259D], and those who cried, “Crucify, crucify him” (John 19), were Jews indeed, but there was a great division between them.

This division, brothers, is signified quite clearly in the book of Joshua. When the children of Israel were about to cross the Jordan in order to enter the promised land, according to the Lord’s command the Levites first entered the Jordan carrying the ark of the Lord (Josh. 4). As soon as the ark of the Lord entered the water, the waters themselves were divided: the upper part stood like a wall, while the lower part flowed down into the sea. That ark, brothers, signified our Lord. In the ark were Aaron’s rod, which had budded, the tablets of the covenant, and a golden jar containing manna (Heb. 9) [Col. 0260A]. All these are found most beautifully in our Lord.

In him is Aaron’s rod—that is, the priestly power—which first withered among the Jews but blossomed eternally in the Lord Jesus Christ, as the Psalmist says to him: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. 109). In him are the tablets of the covenant, namely perfect knowledge, as the Apostle says: “In him are hidden the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Col. 2). The Apostle says in one place: “The head of Christ is God” (Eph. 5). And in the Song of Songs it is written of him: “His head is finest gold” (Song 5). By the golden jar, therefore, his divinity itself may be understood. Hence the Apostle says: “For in him dwells all the fullness of divinity bodily” (Col. 2) [Col. 0260B]. In it, indeed, manna is contained: the bread of angels, the nourishment of holy souls. He is the bread of which it is written: “Blessed is he who shall eat bread in the kingdom of God” (Luke 14). This is the bread which the Lord himself, passing by after the day of judgment, will serve to all his own.

These three things are fittingly said to be in that tabernacle: rod, tablets, manna. The rod, by which he disciplines us; the tablets, by which he instructs us; the manna, by which he feeds us. The rod scourges us lest we become proud; by the tablets he teaches us to love him; the manna of his sweetness feeds us lest we fail on the way. He threatens some with this rod, saying: “I will visit their iniquities with a rod, and their sins with stripes” (Ps. 88). The prophet desired this rod when he said: “Correct me, O Lord, but in judgment and not in justice” (Jer. 10) [Col. 0260C]. The Lord promises us these tablets, saying: “I will give my law into their minds, and I will write it in their hearts” (Jer. 31). He desired these tablets who said: “Teach me the way of your justifications” (Ps. 118). The Lord promises us this manna, saying: “Come to me, all who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. 11). He rejoiced in this spiritual food who said: “The Lord feeds me, and I shall lack nothing” (Ps. 22).

Therefore, the ark was in the Jordan, Christ in Judea. For by the Jordan, which was in the promised land that the Lord himself promised and gave to the Jews, the Jews themselves were signified. Just as the water was divided at the presence of this ark, consider those of whom you sang a little while ago: “As the Lord entered the holy city,” and so forth. This is the upper part of the water, which stood firm [Col. 0260D]. It stood firm in the law of the Lord, in the way of his commandments, in the exultation of his praise, in the sweetness of his love. And it was rightly the upper part, for it belongs to the Jerusalem above, which is free and which is our mother. Rightly upper, for it does not incline its heart to earth, and therefore cries: “Hosanna in the highest.”

They are called children, as it were, because they are pure: pure from malice, pure from envy, pure from greed. The Prophet exhorts them, saying: “Praise the Lord, children; praise the name of the Lord” (Ps. 112). These are the true Hebrews, that is, those who pass over. They had passed over all things perishable and transitory [Col. 0261A], and rejoiced and exulted only in the praises of their Creator and Savior. It was fitting indeed for them to bear palms in their hands, the sign of victory and the sign of peace. For they recognized their unconquered king, who, as is said in the Apocalypse, “went forth conquering, that he might conquer” (Rev. 6). They recognized the true Solomon, son of David, in whose kingdom are perpetual peace and everlasting rest.

These are the waters of the Jordan which, at the presence of this ark, retained without any admixture of bitterness the sweetness and pleasantness which they had drawn from their springs—that is, from the stock of the prophets and patriarchs. Therefore they deserved to taste the power of eternal sweetness and pleasantness, and to display in their deeds the glory of the resurrection. For, meeting the Lord with palms [Col. 0261B], they proclaimed the resurrection of life, since the saints will come with exultation bearing the sheaves of their works (Ps. 125), bearing the palms of their victories won over the devil.

Then—that is, in that resurrection—the Lord will enter the holy city, the heavenly Jerusalem. He will enter with the Hebrew children, who in that resurrection will go out to meet him, as the Apostle says: “We who are alive shall be caught up in clouds to meet Christ in the air; and so we shall always be with the Lord” (1 Thess. 4). Then they will truly be children, because perfectly pure, not only from the contagion of sin but also from all corruption. Then they will truly be Hebrews, that is, those who have perfectly passed over not only the danger of death [Col. 0261C], but also the fear of death. Then they will safely bear palms of victory with great exultation and security, saying: “Where is your victory, O death? Where is your sting, O death?” (II Cor. XV.)

And truly, brothers, it was fitting that they should proclaim the resurrection of life, since the Lord himself was set for them not for ruin but for resurrection, as Simeon had prophesied of him: “Behold, this one is set for the ruin and resurrection of many in Israel, and for a sign that shall be contradicted” (Luke 2). He says three things: ruin for some, resurrection for others, and also a sign of contradiction. Now, in this division of which he speaks, see how Jesus is resurrection for some and ruin for others. For those, certainly, who proclaimed the resurrection, who displayed the future resurrection in their deeds, who most clearly declared themselves already raised in soul, and who hoped to be raised by him on the day of judgment—for them Jesus was without doubt set for resurrection.

See now that other part of the Jordan which flowed down into the sea at the presence of the ark of the Lord. When on this day this holy ark, which we have just commended to your charity, appeared in the waters of the Jordan—that is, in the Jewish people—the good part thereby advanced and increased itself in a better and stronger condition [Col. 0261D]; but from the same source the other part, namely the scribes and Pharisees, hurled themselves into greater bitterness as into a sea. Whatever they had brought with them from the natural spring from which they had arisen was swallowed up by the salt of the sea. The bitterness of their envy and malice consumed within them all knowledge of the Scriptures, all understanding of the Law, all comprehension of prophecy [Col. 0262A].

Therefore, hearing the cry of the people who praised him and seeing the marvelous glory shown him, they were stung with excessive envy. Since they could not restrain the people, they rebuked him who endured these things, saying: “Do you hear what these people are saying?” To them he answered most fittingly: “Amen I say to you, if these are silent, the stones will cry out” (Luke 19). This, brothers, has now been fulfilled most plainly. The Jews are silent; the stones cry out. That prophetic saying has been fulfilled: “The bricks have fallen, but we shall build with squared stones” (Isa. 9). Who are these bricks but those muddy and earthly Jews who fell from that holy edifice of patriarchs and prophets? These are those for whom Jesus was set for ruin. From the very place where they might have been built up most firmly, they fell miserably.

But as they fell, having rejected the firm and solid foundation, Jerusalem is built from living stones, squared stones. Clinging to that most solid stone, Christ, who “was made the head of the corner” (Acts 4) [Col. 0262B], they also receive their name from him. Come then, Jews, what have you gained? What you wished has come to pass. The Hebrew children according to the flesh no longer cry out, “Hosanna to the Son of David.” But does this mean that the cry is no longer made? Kings cry out, emperors cry out, men cry out, women cry out, young people cry out, virgins cry out, indeed children cry out, old people cry out. See, wretches; see, blinded ones, how many thousands upon thousands of people today go out to meet him with palms. See how many thousands today spread before him not garments but their own bodies. Hear, if indeed you are not deaf, from how many thousands of mouths today it is cried, sung, jubilantly proclaimed, and invoked: “Hosanna to the Son of David; blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Matt. 21) [Col. 0262C]. But what Saint David said has been fulfilled: “The sinner shall see and be angered; he shall gnash his teeth and waste away” (Ps. 111).

See, brothers, what the Jews can do today amid Christ’s many praises. They can be angry; they can gnash their teeth; they can waste away in envy. But “the desire of sinners shall perish” (ibid.). Christ is adored, praised, and proclaimed because living stones cry out in place of those muddy bricks. Thus our Jesus was set for the ruin and resurrection of many: for the ruin of bricks, for the resurrection of stones. “And for a sign,” he says, “that shall be contradicted” (Luke 2) [Col. 0262D].

This is the sign which he has now raised in the midst of the nations: the sign, namely, of his Passion, the sign of his cross. This is the sign which the whole world contradicted: a stumbling block to Jews and folly to Gentiles. “We,” says the Apostle, “preach Christ crucified: to Jews indeed a stumbling block, but to Gentiles foolishness” (1 Cor. 1). See, brothers, how quickly this sign was contradicted. On the very day on which this sign was raised, as you heard in the Gospel itself, Pilate wrote a title for him: “Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews” (John 19). It was immediately contradicted, for they said: “Do not write, ‘King of the Jews.’” The cross of Christ overcame this contradiction [Col. 0263A]; and where the wicked thought they had more completely conquered Christ, there Christ appeared the greater victor.

The sign of his victory was fixed upon the cross itself—and, more wonderfully still, fixed there by his very enemies. His enemies, who had agreed upon his death, now contend among themselves over his glory. “Do not write,” says the Pharisee. “What I have written, I have written,” says Pilate. And behold: Pilate and the Pharisee have now perished, yet what Pilate wrote has not been erased. Does not a certain wondrous joy arise in your hearts, my brothers, when you see before you the sign of the cross, still glorious with that title? Still one may read upon Christ’s cross: “Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews.” So completely did that contradiction of the wicked accomplish nothing.

The contradiction of the Jews was followed by the contradiction of the pagans. Emperors too armed themselves against the cross of Christ; philosophers disputed; orators raised their clamor; even the most contemptible rabble barked against it. What shall I say? Against one piece of wood the whole world everywhere was fighting.

But now, brethren, consider the omnipotence of our Lord Jesus Christ; consider his wisdom. By that wood than which nothing was more rejected, more vile, more hateful, more dreadful—for what was more vile than the cross, on which thieves were hanged, sacrilegious persons put to death, parricides slain?—by that wood, I say, he subdued emperors, made the wise foolish, instructed the simple and unlearned, glorified the poor, and made all of them alike worshippers of the wood. Behold, brethren: on the foreheads of kings nothing is more glorious; nothing more conspicuous in the hand; nothing more salutary upon the breast. All that contradiction has now perished—but would that it had perished from conduct as it has from speech! Many, however—and, what is more grievous, even professors of Christ’s cross—contradict Christ’s cross. Not indeed by words, but by conduct. Hear the Apostle: “Many walk, of whom I have often told you, but now tell you even weeping, that they are enemies of the cross of Christ” (Phil. 3). Who are those who contradict Christ’s cross, if not the enemies of Christ’s cross? And who are they? “Whose god,” he says, “is their belly” (ibid.).

I address you, my brethren, my children: not only worshippers of Christ’s cross, but also its confessors, indeed lovers of the cross itself. I address you: let each feel as he pleases, judge as he pleases, flatter himself as much as he pleases. In Christ’s cross there is nothing tender, nothing soft, nothing luxurious, nothing sweet to flesh and blood. Let Christ’s cross itself now be, as it were, the Christian’s mirror. Let him look into Christ’s cross, so that in his life his conduct may conform to Christ’s cross; and insofar as he shares in Christ’s cross, so far may he presume upon Christ’s glory. But whoever rejects the bitterness of Christ’s cross should fear lest perhaps he be shut out from the sight of the Crucified One.

Now, my brethren, observe how greatly you ought to rejoice, you who have crucified yourselves with Christ himself. I speak the truth, brethren; I do not lie. Our order is Christ’s cross. Therefore, brethren, carefully observe these two things: neither depart from Christ’s cross, nor, while set upon the cross, do anything against the cross. That is, to say it more plainly, persevere in your order; and, persevering in that order, knowingly do nothing against that order itself. Thus, without any doubt, you shall follow where Christ has gone before you by his cross.

I delight, brethren, to speak at greater length concerning Christ’s cross, which is our glory and our way; but moderation is necessary, especially because we must remain longer at the divine offices themselves. Therefore let us turn to our Lord Jesus Christ himself, and beseech his mercy that he may deign to look upon this his household, for which he did not hesitate to be delivered into the hands of the guilty and to undergo the torment of the cross: he who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON X. ON PALM BRANCHES, II

[Col. 0264B]

You have heard, dearest brethren, in the Gospel reading how our Lord, when he had drawn near to Jerusalem, caused an ass and a colt to be brought to him. You have heard also the devotion of the people of Israel: how they went out to meet him with palm branches, and how those who went before and those who followed cried out, saying, “Hosanna to the Son of David.” But someone says: “It is true indeed; we have heard these things, and heard them with great rejoicing. But what do they have to do with this day, on which we represent not the Lord’s Passion but his coming?”

So it is, brethren. This undoubtedly occurred, as the other Evangelists plainly show, a few days before his Passion. For because of this glory the Pharisees and chief priests [Col. 0264C] were tormented with the greatest envy, and, having assembled a council, deliberated concerning his death. Yet I think that this history is not recited today in the whole Church without cause, nor was it so established by the holy Fathers without cause.

You know that the wheel which Ezekiel saw had four faces. That wheel signifies Holy Scripture. Hence the Psalmist says: “The voice of your thunder is in the wheel” (Ps. 46). This wheel has four faces: sometimes we consider only one of its faces, sometimes two, sometimes three, and sometimes all four. Its first face is history; the second, morality; the third, allegory; the fourth, anagogy—that is, a sense concerning things above.

To some who cannot grasp deeper things, Scripture displays [Col. 0264D] only its first face, that is, simple history; and they delight in the beauty of this face. Thus some, seeing only this face of Scripture, because in a certain part that face is less beautiful—as in the deed of the patriarch Judah, who lay with his daughter-in-law (Gen. 38), and likewise in the deed of David, who, after killing Uriah, took his wife (2 Kings 11)—and being unable to see the other, beautiful face of this Scripture, despised the Scripture because of the one face which they saw.

Therefore, brethren, we have heard this Gospel Scripture and considered one of its faces, namely its simple history; and it appears sufficiently beautiful to us. For what Scripture is more beautiful than this, which recounts the glory of our most sweet [Col. 0265A] Lord and the devotion of a faithful people? Yet according to this face it does not show us how this reading pertains to the present season. [lacuna] Let us consider, therefore, its other face and see whether it reveals to us some mystery of this season.

And therefore it must briefly be indicated what sacramental meaning this season contains. This season, brethren, was established so that we might call to mind the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ: how he whom the holy fathers of the Old Testament had long awaited and greatly desired came humbly in order to redeem us; and so that we might not forget his second coming, in which he whom all the saints await and desire will come [Col. 0265B] with great power and glory, to judge the whole world and render to each according to his works. These are principally the two things—namely, the remembrance of both his comings—for which this celebration was instituted, and necessarily so. For it is very good always to retain these two things in memory: the Lord’s first coming and his second; because from the first the love of God is born in our hearts, and from the second fear.

Let us therefore consider the Gospel which has just been read, that we may see what mysteries it contains: “When the Lord had drawn near to Jerusalem” (Matt. 21).

You know, brethren, that according to the letter Jerusalem was a certain city which holy David acquired and built, and in which Solomon also made that wonderful [Col. 0265C] Temple of which you have often heard. According to this face—that is, according to history—nothing is shown us that pertains to this celebration. Therefore it is necessary that we attend to another face of this Scripture.

Jerusalem, as you are accustomed to hear, is interpreted “vision of peace.” This name belongs first to those who abide in the perfect vision of God, who is true peace and true tranquility of mind, and who therefore feel true peace and tranquility within themselves. This is that blessed society of angels, which is indeed called Jerusalem, and properly so, as the Apostle Paul says: “The Jerusalem above is free, which is our mother” (Gal. 4).

But how is Jesus said to draw near to this city, when he is always in it and that city has never departed from him? [Col. 0265D] This is that other face of Scripture, namely anagogy, the sense concerning things above. Let the face which we called allegory now appear to us. For according to this sense Jerusalem signified the holy Church among human beings, to which Isaiah says: “Arise, be enlightened, O Jerusalem, for your light has come” (Isa. 60). It is called Jerusalem not because it perfectly sees that peace which the angels see, but because it tends toward that peace by believing rightly, acting well, and ardently loving him who is our peace, Jesus Christ our Lord.

And how did God draw near to this Jerusalem, when he is present everywhere and absent nowhere? Yet through the prophet he says: “Draw near to me, and I [Col. 0266A] will draw near to you.” And how do we draw near to him in whom “we live and move and are” (Acts 17)? Yet the prophet says: “Draw near to him and be enlightened” (Ps. 33). For the Lord reproves certain persons and says: “Woe to them, because they have departed from me” (Hos. 7). What kind of approach and departure is this? It does not occur from place to place, but from affection to affection. If you love the world, you have departed from God. If you withdraw from love of the world and begin to love God, you have already drawn near to God.

Thus we draw near to him when we make progress in his love; he draws near to us when he deigns to have mercy upon us. In this way Adam departed from God, namely by loving him less and the world more. For he loved private preeminence, which pertains not to God but to the world. In this way the whole human race departed from God. Therefore the Church of God which now exists likewise departed from God in this way, and so far that by itself it could in no way draw near to God or come to him. It was therefore necessary that, because it could not come to God its salvation, God, its salvation, should come to it.

But first he drew near. He came indeed when he showed that wonderful mercy by which, hanging on the cross, he shed his blood for it and, by opening his side, joined and united it to himself, so that the two might be one flesh (Eph. 5). If, therefore, he came then, he certainly drew near when he promised, proclaimed, and began to show it this mercy. Jesus drew near to Jerusalem, [Col. 0266C] the salvation of the Church, salvation to the world, salvation to wretched humanity expelled from Paradise, when he foretold that he would become human and promised Abraham himself the mercy which he afterwards fulfilled, saying: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 22).

Christ was to be born from Abraham’s seed, through whom that curse pronounced in Adam was to be abolished and that blessing bestowed which Isaiah prophesied, saying: “For he shall call his servants by another name” (Isa. 65). First his servants were called Jews, but now they are called Christians: “And he shall call his servants by another name, in which he who is to be blessed upon the earth shall be blessed in the Lord.” For without doubt no one can avoid the curse or possess the blessing who does not have this name.

Therefore Jesus then drew near [Col. 0266D] to Jerusalem, that is, to the Church, when through holy Abraham he promised his coming to the Church. He plainly signified the holy Church when he named all nations, because the holy Church consists of all nations. Thus he began to draw near then, but had not yet come to Bethphage. Bethphage is interpreted “house of the cheek” or “house of the mouth.” Perhaps he had come to Bethany, but not yet to Bethphage. For, as the other Evangelists clearly show, he first came to Bethany and then, when he had drawn near to Jerusalem, came to Bethphage, to the Mount of Olives. Bethany is interpreted “house of obedience.” And what was that holy soul of Abraham but a house of obedience, he who, in order to preserve the good of obedience, thought that even his own son—such a son—was not to be spared? [Col. 0267A] (Gen. 22).

Jesus therefore first came to him, because to him was first made the promise concerning the coming of our Lord Jesus. But that promise, that future mercy of the Lord, he and his sons alone—and, if any others, still only a few—knew; yet they did not disclose it to others. They did not disclose it by preaching of the mouth, but through certain hidden and wonderful signs. Therefore the Lord had not yet come to Bethphage, that is, to the house of the mouth.

For without doubt he showed holy Abraham the Incarnation of the Lord through a certain hidden sign when, sending his servant to take a wife for his son, he said: “Put your hand under my thigh and swear by the God of heaven” (Gen. 24). [Col. 0267B] What is this? Was the God of heaven in Abraham’s thigh? He certainly showed beautifully, though secretly, why he wished his son to take a wife: not in order to satisfy his lust, but in order to beget that seed from which the God of heaven would be born. Therefore he commanded him to put his hand under his thigh and swear by the God of heaven, because without doubt the God of heaven was to be born from his thigh, that is, from his generation.

For that “thigh” is used for generation is common enough in Scripture, according to the words: “All the souls that came forth from Jacob’s thigh were seventy” (Exod. 1); and: “The scepter shall not be taken from Judah, nor a ruler from his thigh” (Gen. 49). But this sign of the Lord’s coming was hidden, because Jesus had not yet come to the house of the mouth: that is, his Incarnation was not yet openly preached [Col. 0267C] to any household, that is, to any people.

But when the children of Israel had already been led out of Egypt, had received the Law, celebrated sacrifices, and constructed the tabernacle, then Jesus began to come to the house of the mouth, because his coming began to be openly revealed to all the people. For Moses openly said concerning him before all the people: “God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brethren; you shall hear him as myself. Every soul that does not hear that prophet shall be exterminated from his people” (Deut. 18). The apostles themselves showed that this was prophesied concerning the Lord Jesus, for they often used this testimony against the Jews.

The Lord came to Bethphage when Isaiah the prophet prophesied the Lord’s very coming and the virgin’s [Col. 0267D] childbirth, saying: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel” (Isa. 7). When did he come to the Mount of Olives? *Oleos* in Greek means “mercy.” Therefore the Mount of Olives signifies that excellence and, so to speak, the height of the mercy of which we are speaking. He came then to the Mount of Olives when the time was already drawing near in which he wished to show that wonderful and outstanding mercy which he had first promised to obedient Abraham and afterwards preached through his prophets to all the people.

Therefore, when Jesus had drawn near to Jerusalem and had come to Bethphage at the Mount of Olives, he then sent two disciples, saying to them: “Go into the village opposite you, and immediately you will find an ass tied, [Col. 0268A] and a colt with her. Untie them and bring them to me” (Matt. 21).

What do these two disciples, whom the Lord sends ahead, signify? They are those who go before his face into every place and village to which he himself is to come. For thus you have in Luke’s Gospel: “The Lord appointed another seventy-two disciples and sent them two by two before his face into every city and place to which he himself was to come” (Luke 10). Perhaps, therefore, these two signify the two things that everywhere precede his face, of which the Psalmist says: “Mercy and truth shall go before your face” (Ps. 88). His face signifies his presence: the presence of his mercy, the presence of our salvation through his coming. Mercy and [Col. 0268B] truth precede this face, this coming, in order to bring him the ass and colt.

I think that by the ass and colt we may not inappropriately understand the whole human nature, that is, flesh and soul: by the ass, flesh, because of its slowness and heaviness; by the colt, soul, because of its lightness and mobility. Mercy and truth bring the ass and colt to the Son of God because, in order that the Word might become flesh and dwell among us, “mercy and truth met together” (Ps. 84). Mercy and truth bring the ass and colt to the Son of God because, in order that the Son of God might assume the whole human being—that is, both flesh and soul—mercy and truth without doubt accomplished this. Mercy alone would not accomplish it, because it could not do so without truth. Truth alone would not accomplish it, because it would not will to do so without mercy.

Again, mercy and truth accomplished this—that the Son of God should have the ass and colt, that is, flesh and soul: truth, because he promised this to the Jews; mercy, because he wished to show it to the Gentiles. Therefore he fittingly sends these two ahead, because before his coming he promised this to the Jews, as it were, by an oath in truth, and proposed to show this mercy to the Gentiles. The Apostle plainly shows this when he says: “I say that Christ Jesus was a minister of the circumcision for the truth of God, to confirm the promises of the fathers; but that the Gentiles should glorify God for mercy” (Rom. 12).

Therefore mercy and truth met together, and truth sprang up from the earth; and, taking to himself the ass and colt, body and soul, he came to Jerusalem, [Col. 0268D] came to visit his Church, came to save her. This he certainly would not have done except by mounting the ass and colt in the manner we have described.

Nor should it disturb you that he says, “Untie them.” For although the flesh and soul which the Son of God assumed were never bound by sin—because from the moment that man was created, he was certainly perfect God—nevertheless, because human nature itself had always previously been bound by the chains of sins in all human beings, it is not unfittingly said to have been untied in our Lord himself, inasmuch as it was always free. Or, if we wish to say that mercy and truth absolved the most blessed Mary, from whom he was born, from every bond of sin before he was conceived in her—so that “to untie the ass and colt and bring them to Jesus” means to cleanse from every sin the flesh and soul of his most blessed [Col. 0269A] mother, and thus make her pregnant with the Son of God—whether this or the former is said, I think this passage is not inappropriately expounded.

We have heard the manner in which Jesus came to his Church, namely according to the flesh and soul which he assumed. For according to his divinity he neither comes nor departs, because he is present everywhere. But what do these garments signify, with which the disciples cover these animals upon which the Son of God sits? The Evangelist says that they brought the ass and colt and made him sit upon them (Matt. 21). How could he sit upon both? Drawn away from the letter, we are compelled to investigate the spiritual sense.
