Therefore, without prejudice to another interpretation, in which these two [Col. 0269B] animals signify, by another symbolism, the two peoples, Jewish and Gentile—without prejudice, I say, to that interpretation also—we say that he came to Jerusalem upon both these animals, because in the human nature which he wholly assumed, namely rational soul and flesh, he appeared to his Church, that is, to his faithful people.

But what do these garments signify? Perhaps they are those with which the elder and younger sons of Noah covered their father’s shame, turning their faces away. A great mystery, brethren. But because this day keeps us occupied with many matters, I shall say briefly that these garments signify the faith and teaching of the apostles and prophets, through which Christ’s humanity, as a certain weakness, is covered by the knowledge of his divinity. Those who believed and preached that he was only a human being and not God left naked the ass and colt [Col. 0269C] upon which Jesus sat. They left his humanity naked. But the faith and teaching of the apostles and prophets did not leave it in that condition, because, by preaching the strength of his divinity, they covered the weakness which unbelievers despised.

For Isaiah says: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son” (Isa. 7). Behold, a human being. But lest this human being be thought weak and small, he immediately added: “And his name shall be called Emmanuel,” which means “God with us.” But when Paul had spoken of his weakness—“He became obedient unto death” (Phil. 2)—a little later he said: “That the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (ibid.).

[Col. 0269D] But a very great crowd spread their garments on the road. Others cut branches from the trees and cried: “Hosanna to the Son of David” (Matt. 21). It has been said how the Lord came to Jerusalem; now it is said how Jerusalem itself, that is, the holy Church, received his coming. The Church goes before and the Church follows his coming. For the Church is not only this congregation of the faithful which believes in him after his coming; rather, all the saints from righteous Abel to the last righteous person who will be in this world belong to the holy Church. From all these is formed the one Church to which it is said: “My dove is one” (Song 6).

One part goes before his coming: Abel, Noah, Abraham, David, and the other saints. The other part follows: the apostles, [Col. 0270A] martyrs, confessors, and all the faithful, among whom we too are through his mercy. Of all these, some lay their garments before Jesus’ feet, and others branches of trees. Those lay down branches of trees who cast aside all worldly glory for Christ. For what are the riches and glory of this world but like the leaves and branches of trees, which are green in summer and wither in winter? Without doubt all worldly glory, as it were, flowers in prosperity; but in adversity, especially in a person’s very death, when the winter storm comes upon him—that is, final condemnation—it becomes worthless and foul.

But blessed is the person who lays them at Jesus’ feet by distributing them to the poor, who are, as it were, his feet, namely his weak members. Yet far more blessed is the one who can even despise his own garment for Christ and lay it beneath his feet. For what is our garment but our body, by which the soul itself is in some way clothed and covered? Blessed is the one who can despise his own limbs, his very body, for Christ, and devote all the acts of his body to God’s service.

Both things were done both by those who went before the Lord’s coming and by those who followed it. For the holy fathers in the Old Testament regarded the riches and glory of the world as nothing because of the faith which they had in Christ’s coming. Many also subjected their bodies to martyrdom: the first martyr Abel, Isaiah, and the Maccabean martyrs. But how many persons, not only individually but [Col. 0270C] how many thousands, have done all these things after his coming—who can enumerate them? You too are among their number. You have cast down the branches of trees—that is, all worldly pomp—in the service and honor of Christ. You have, what is greater, despised your own bodies for him. You have, what is greater still, expended your very souls in honor of Christ, because you have relinquished your soul’s own will.

Moreover, all who went before and followed him said: “Hosanna to the Son of David; blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.” Great faith, great confession, great praise. *Hosanna* is the cry of one asking for salvation, as though it said, “Save, I pray.” Without doubt they confess him to be the Savior from whom they ask salvation, which properly belongs to God. They call him Son of David because they confess him to be truly human. They bless him because he comes in the name of the Lord, whereby they plainly show that he is God, whom God the Father promised would come.

In this faith the Church receives the coming of the Son of God. It believes him to be true God and true human being, the true Savior of the world, promised by God the Father and foretold by the holy prophets. In this faith those who go before his coming and those who follow it meet and are joined, and are one Church; in this faith both are saved. Whoever are without this faith are outside the Church: Christ does not come to them, and therefore they are not saved.

This concerns the first coming. But you should know, brethren, that in the same form in which [Col. 0271A] he first came to redeem his Church, he will come a second time to glorify his Church. For after the Lord’s Ascension the angels said to the apostles: “He will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven” (Acts 1). This, brethren, will add to the condemnation of the ungodly. For they will not be able, without great shame and grief, to see in such glory and power him whom they despised in human weakness.

What the other Evangelists also relate from this history is quite suited to the Lord’s second coming. When Jesus came to Jerusalem, the Hebrew children took branches of olives or palms and came out to meet him. So it will be at the Lord’s second coming. For when he comes to glorify his Church, presenting her altogether perfect, without spot or wrinkle, then indeed the Hebrew children will come out to meet him with palms or olive branches.

These are the children to whom David says: “Praise the Lord, children” (Ps. 112); and again: “The Lord preserves little ones” (Ps. 114). The Lord does not preserve the great, exalted, proud; but the little ones, that is, the humble. They praise the Lord, provided that they are Hebrews—that is, “those who cross over.” For if humble persons now pass beyond the vices and works of the flesh, and make leaps through contemplation and good thoughts, then without doubt on the day of judgment, when Jesus comes in his power, they will come out to meet him with palms—that is, with the signs of the victories which they have won here over the devil. For palms signify victory. Then they will be able, as it were, to glory with palms and say: “Where, O death, is your victory? Where, O death, is your sting?” (1 Cor. 15).

Then they will also come with olives, which signify peace. For now they have no peace, while fighting with the devil, the world, vices, and their own flesh. But then there will be perfect peace and true tranquility, when flesh will not resist spirit, nor spirit God; when the devil will not attack, nor death or any infirmity ever burden them. If we wish to have that peace at his second coming, let us receive his first coming with faith and love. Let us persevere in the works which he showed and taught us, nourishing within ourselves his love and true desire, by which we may meet him as perfect human beings when [Col. 0271D] he comes to judge the world: he who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XI. ON THE HOLY DAY OF EASTER

“Like newborn infants, desire the reasonable milk without deceit, that by it you may grow unto salvation, if indeed you have tasted that the Lord is sweet” (1 Pet. 2).

The Apostle exhorts you, brethren, to desire milk, and such milk as can enable you to grow—indeed, to grow unto salvation. But hear what he adds: “If indeed you have tasted that the Lord is sweet.” And what should that milk signify except the sweetness of Jesus Christ? What, then, does it mean that he exhorts us to desire milk, if we have tasted that [Col. 0272A] the Lord is sweet?

It seems, therefore, brethren, that the Apostle here makes mention of two kinds of sweetness. Perhaps one is that which you have tasted during these days; and therefore he confidently exhorts you to desire that other kind of sweetness which is signified by milk. For it is credible that in these days you have tasted how sweet the Lord is—especially you who have seen and considered, as though in your presence, Jesus Christ on the cross; who have seen those holy arms stretched out as though to embrace you; who have considered those sweet breasts uncovered as though to refresh you.

All these things, brethren, although they occurred only once—for, as the Apostle says, “Christ was offered once to exhaust the sins of many” (Heb. 9)—yet you have seen them far better and more clearly with the eyes of the heart than many then saw them with the eyes of the body when they occurred. In all these things you have tasted that the Lord is sweet: sweet, humble, gentle, merciful, gracious, and loving.

For how great a sweetness he displayed in that supper which he celebrated with his disciples before his Passion! At this supper he said to his disciples: “With desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer” (Luke 22). This is that most sweet food into which the Jews mixed gall, as holy David cries out: “They gave me gall for my food” (Ps. 68). This was fulfilled according to the letter when they gave him wine mixed with gall to drink. But because that gall was given him as drink, not food, it seems that the Prophet wished in these words to direct us not only to the letter but also to the signification.

Into this most sweet food, therefore, which he received so sweetly and humbly with his disciples, the Jews mixed gall: they corrupted with money that disciple himself who had come with the others to this food, took love from him, and made him exceedingly bitter with the gall of malice. And what were his good disciples but his food, in whom he delighted and upon whose love and devotion he fed? And what was that traitor Judas among them but like gall in good food?

At that supper the old Passover, which the Jews were accustomed to celebrate, ended; and the new Passover which we celebrate [Col. 0272D] began. And how could he show us a greater sweetness than by leaving us, in memory of himself, his body and blood? For he wished that the price which he once gave for us should always be before our eyes. By a certain wonderful affection he wished his body and blood to be not only our price but also our food.

Does it not seem to you, my brethren, that at supper he most plainly fulfilled what the prophet David said: “A cup of pure wine is in the Lord’s hand, full of mixture; and he inclined it from this to that” (Ps. 74)? For after he had celebrated that old Passover which the Jews used to celebrate through the flesh and blood of a lamb, Jesus took bread and, giving it to his disciples, [Col. 0273A] said: “This is my body” (Matt. 26); and afterwards the cup, saying: “This is my blood” (ibid.).

See how the cup is in the Lord’s hand. What is this cup except the institution of the Law? This cup was full of pure wine—that is, unmixed wine. This wine is the spiritual understanding contained in those ordinances which belonged to the old Law. It is wine because it gladdens the human heart. It is wine because it intoxicated those who understood it. It intoxicated them with love of God; it intoxicated them so greatly that they forgot themselves and loved God alone.

Was David not intoxicated with this wine when, as though drunk, he stripped and uncovered himself in order to dance before the ark of the Lord? (2 Kings 6). Was Isaiah not intoxicated with this wine when, as he himself testifies, he walked [Col. 0273B] naked and barefoot before all the people? (Isa. 10). Although this wine was pure in itself, still, because certain carnal observances were intermixed with it, the cup in the Lord’s hand was “of pure wine, full of mixture.”

Consider the lamb itself which our Lord had in his hands at this supper. See there the institution of the Law, as it were a cup in the Lord’s hand. In this cup—that is, in this ordinance—was pure wine, namely spiritual understanding. On the other side, see bread and wine, as it were another cup. In this cup that spiritual wine was not previously present. Now see how he poured the wine which was in one cup into another.

What was the wine in that ancient institution? That lamb signified Christ’s body; the lamb’s blood, Christ’s blood. Behold the wine in that former cup. But “he inclined it from this to that.” Hear how. He took bread and said: “This is my body”; he took wine and said: “This is my blood.” The change was made: that lamb, in which was the signification of Christ’s body and blood, remained empty; the other cup was filled, because bread became Christ’s body and wine Christ’s blood.

Let us consider further. In that lamb was the signification of the Lord’s Passion; therefore it was commanded that, in remembrance of the same Passion of the Lord, that lamb should be slain every year. The commemoration of the Lord’s Passion was therefore in the lamb like wine in a cup. But God “inclined it from this to that,” because he transferred the commemoration [Col. 0273D] of his Passion, which had formerly been in that lamb, into the sacrament of his body and blood, which he then gave to his disciples, saying: “Do this in remembrance of me” (1 Cor. 11).

There was a certain mixture there because of the carnal observances: for although that lamb signified Christ’s body, it was not truly Christ’s body, but a lamb. In our sacrament there is no mixture, because after consecration our sacrament is no longer the substance of an animal, nor even of the bread and wine which it previously was, but truly Christ’s body and blood. But because the prophet foresaw in the Spirit that carnal Jews would not wish to leave the dregs of carnal observances, he therefore added: “Yet its dregs have not been emptied” [Col. 0274A] (Ps. 74). The wine has been removed, but the dregs still remain. Therefore he says: “All sinners of the earth shall drink” (ibid.). But some drink dregs, others wine.

Before the Lord’s coming and Passion, only the Jews drank from this cup; but they drank mixed, not pure, wine. The Gentiles did not drink from it, and therefore not all sinners drank. Christ came, suffered for us, rose again, and ascended into heaven; and behold, all the sinners of the earth drink: all, that is, Jews and Gentiles. But the Jews drink only dregs; we drink only wine. They have the lamb, in which there is now no savor of signification; we have that Lamb who took away the sins of the world (John 1), in whom is the full expression of truth.

See still further how he has inclined from one thing to another. [Col. 0274B] In the old Passover, according to the commandment of the Law, they ate unleavened bread with wild lettuces along with the flesh of the lamb. Behold the cup in the Lord’s hand. The wine in this mystical cup is certainly the sign of sincere humility. For what is leaven but pride? Therefore the Apostle exhorts us: “Purge out the old leaven” (1 Cor. 5). Pride is truly the old leaven. For it began to exist when the angels were first created. This leaven puffed up one of them so greatly that he wished to be like God; it corrupted him so greatly that from an angel he became the devil. This leaven puffed up man so greatly that he desired to be like God; it corrupted him so greatly that he became like senseless beasts. In the unleavened breads—which were, as it were, wine to the fathers—were exercises of humility, because this is what they [Col. 0274C] certainly signified.

Now see how our Lord rises from supper, girds himself with a linen cloth, and washes the disciples’ feet. Thus he has now taken that signification of humility which was in the unleavened breads and transferred it into this sacrament. For he says: “Do you know what I have done to you? You call me Teacher and Lord, and you say well, for so I am. If therefore I, the Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet” (John 13). This washing is not only the sign of a great reality, of which it is not now the time to speak; it is also a clear exercise of humility.

Hear, brothers, how at that supper he set before you not wild lettuces but wine—that is, the signification which was in those lettuces. For what do wild lettuces signify except the bitterness of this life and persecutions? Wild lettuces are bitter. Therefore, among the many other things which the Lord said in that final discourse, he also added this: “If they persecuted me, they will persecute you also” (John 15). And again: “In this world you will have tribulation” (John 16). Why should we further seek those wild lettuces bodily, when we are daily exercised in the very bitter things of this life? It would take long, brothers, to unfold all those things which they performed bodily in those old observances and which the Lord has appointed us to celebrate spiritually. For our Lord commended these and many other sacraments to you during these last three days, in all of which [Col. 0275A] you have undoubtedly been able to taste that the Lord is sweet, so that you should now desire that other sweetness which the Apostle Peter signified.

What, finally, could the very remembrance of the Lord’s Passion not accomplish in your hearts? What was it like to see our most sweet Lord bound, spat upon, struck with blows? How Isaiah fed himself upon this vision! He did not indeed see it as accomplished, yet he narrated it as though accomplished: “As many were astonished at you, so his appearance shall be without glory among men, and his form among the sons of men” (Isa. 52). Many indeed were astonished when he fed five thousand men with five loaves and two fish (John 6); many were astonished when he gave sight to the man born blind (John 9); many were astonished [Col. 0275B] when he raised Lazarus (John 11). They were astonished, praised, and glorified him. Great was that glory; yet no less was the indignity which they afterward inflicted upon him. Therefore the Prophet says: “So his appearance shall be without glory among men” (Isa. 52). “Without glory,” that is, without glory. Truly his appearance was without glory when his face was veiled and spat upon. His form was without glory when they crowned him with thorns, when they scourged him and struck his head with a reed. It was without glory—but, as the Prophet says, among the sons of men (ibid.). For among the sons of God all this indignity is great glory.

Indeed, in the truth of the matter it was all glory, so that the same prophet says: “And we saw [Col. 0275C] him, and there was no comeliness; and we desired him, despised” (ibid.). Isaiah desired him thus. Why? He saw that all that contempt was the salvation of the human race and Christ’s own glory. The Apostle plainly shows this when he says: “He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death—even death on a cross” (Phil. 2). Behold the contempt. But hear what follows:

“Therefore God also exalted him,” and so forth. The holy prophet David proclaimed this same thing: “He shall drink from the torrent on the way; therefore he shall lift up his head” (Ps. 109). He drank from the torrent because he tasted the bitter things of this life; but “on the way,” that is, in passing through. For his sufferings were quickly ended; his death was quickly changed. “Therefore he shall lift up his head.” Because he [Col. 0275D] died, he rose again; and because he rose again, he was glorified.

Moreover, what sweetness could your heart draw when, with its inward eye, you saw the Lord himself carrying his cross? Who can estimate this humility, this gentleness, this patience? “Like a sheep he was led to slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer he was silent and did not open his mouth” (Isa. 53). What sweetness it was to contemplate Christ’s wounds as though fresh; to stand as though beside his cross; to see the tears of his mother; to hear that sweet voice: “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke 23). What hope for the forgiveness of our sins could arise in us when we heard him praying so sweetly even for his enemies? Yet this [Col. 0276A] sweetness was not like milk, but like wine. On one side it was sweet, but on the other it bit. It was sweet through affection and devotion; yet it bit again through a certain sweet sorrow and compassion. For not without a certain sweet sadness could you see those sweet hands pierced by such hard nails, those feet likewise pierced with iron, that most gracious side wounded by a lance; nor, though it was sweet, could you behold the most sweet tears of our Lady without compassion.

Therefore, you who have tasted this biting wine—that is, the remembrance of the Lord’s Passion—now desire milk, that is, the sweetness of his resurrection. And rightly milk, because it contains no admixture of sorrow. The angels exult, the apostles glory, the holy women delight in that blessed vision; everywhere is alleluia, everywhere praise, everywhere joy. What a thing it is now to see him eating and drinking with his disciples, whom you formerly saw hanging on the cross; to kiss with great joy those sweet wounds for which, a little before, you wept with such compassion. “This is the day which the Lord has made; let us exult and rejoice in it” (Ps. 117).

Blessed Abraham saw this day in the Spirit; he saw it and rejoiced. For thus the Lord says in the Gospel: “Your father Abraham exulted to see my day; he saw it and rejoiced” (John 8). As the holy Fathers explain, Abraham saw the Lord’s day when, in the figure of the Holy Trinity, he received three angels as guests. He received them, as Scripture says, beneath a tree, and ministered certain things for their service, [Col. 0276C] in which he himself saw this day: he saw and rejoiced. For their use he killed the best and most tender calf, and set before them a hearth-baked bread with milk and butter. See, brothers, a great sacrament. These things seem to have little savour. They are obscure; yet in them our Lord Jesus Christ lies as though hidden. He lies covered.

But let us go with those holy women of whom the Evangelist speaks today (Mark 16); let us go to the tomb of the Scriptures; let us go with the spices of devout affection. Let us seek our Lord here; let us seek him with faith, devotion, and charity. For these are the ointments which we must bring to this [Col. 0276D] tomb if we wish to find Jesus. But who will roll away for us the stone from the door of the tomb (ibid.)—that is, the covering of this Scripture—so that we may find what we seek? May his angel, may his grace, be present.

What is this tree? It is that upon which hung the most sweet cluster, from which flowed that wine which today gladdens the whole world. Consider that cluster which the children of Israel carried on a piece of wood. And what is a cluster upon wood except Christ upon the cross? Today, my brothers, the whole world is nourished by the wine which flowed from it. For what Christian is there who does not today drink Christ’s blood? And what did Abraham see in that excellent calf except the sacrifice offered for the salvation of the whole world? Certainly an excellent calf: by his death he redeemed the whole world; by his flesh he refreshes the whole world; with his horns he defeated the devil and his angels; with his hooves he never ceases to dig earthly desires out of our hearts.

But what shall we say now about the hearth-baked bread? What is bread in ashes? Who is this bread? Perhaps it is he of whom the Jews said, as is written in the prophet Jeremiah: “Come, let us put wood into his bread” (Jer. 11). Behold again the wood, again Christ’s cross. And what is the bread except Christ’s body? “The bread,” he says, “which I shall give is my flesh for the life of the world” (John 6). What then is bread in ashes? Certainly hearth-baked bread, when it is baked, is covered with ashes. And what are ashes except earth? Does it not seem to you that Christ’s burial is most fittingly signified here? Bread, then, in [Col. 0277B] ashes is Christ’s body in the heart of the earth.

But why is the number three mentioned here? Abraham commanded that hearth-baked breads be made from three measures. Why this, except because he saw in the Spirit that, just as Jonah was in the belly of the whale three days and three nights, so Christ’s flesh was in the earth three days and three nights? Therefore, as the Lord’s Passion was signified in the calf which he killed, and burial in the hearth-baked bread, so the sweetness of his resurrection is understood in the milk.

And it was necessary, brothers, that his disciples, who were still little children, should be nourished by this milk. They were so little that in his Passion they fled and left him. Peter was so little that at [Col. 0277C] the voice of one serving-woman he denied him. It was therefore necessary that, like little children, they should see his resurrection even with the eyes of the flesh and thus be nourished, as it were, with milk, so as to be fit to believe invisible things and contemplate invisible things.

How beautiful it is that he willed women to announce his resurrection to the disciples! For it belongs to women to give milk to little children. This too has another signification. Those who govern little children and the weak must, with great compassion and condescension, offer this milk to them like mothers to their children; and before they are nourished by that milk, they ought not to show them solid bread—that is, profound matters concerning the divinity. Such was Paul, who says: “As to little children in Christ, I gave you milk to drink, not solid food” (1 Cor. 3).

Rightly did Abraham [Col. 0277D] exult, who saw these things. And you, brothers, who see them, exult. Desire this milk; desire it and taste it. Grow in this milk, and grow unto salvation. For the Apostle Paul says: “If you confess with your mouth the Lord Jesus, and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you shall be saved” (Rom. 10). But here we must understand the faith which works through love.

Gather from this milk—that is, from this remembrance of the Lord’s resurrection—the richness of Christ’s love. This is what that butter of which we spoke a little earlier signified. For as butter is gathered from milk, so from the remembrance which we ought to have of the Lord’s resurrection—from that intercourse in which he lived with his disciples, from that touching by which they touched [Col. 0278A] his wounds, and from those tears which the women shed beside his tomb—we ought, as it were, to be made rich in his love.

Let us be like newborn infants: infants in innocence and simplicity, so that, having put off the old man according to whom we formerly lived, who was crucified with Christ, as Christ rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we also, crucified with him and buried from all the desires of this world, may deserve to rise here to a new life and in the resurrection to come rejoice with him without end. May our Lord Jesus Christ deign to grant this, he who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XII. FOR THE SAME FEAST

[Col. 0278B]

It was commanded in the Law that, at the time when the children of Israel departed from Egypt, a lamb should be sacrificed and eaten. This feast was called Passover. Then there was a command that for seven days they should eat unleavened breads, that is, without leaven; and this feast was called the Feast of Unleavened Bread, but also Passover. The Evangelist shows this when he says: “The feast day of unleavened bread, which is called Passover, was drawing near” (Matt. 26). That first feast, when they killed the lamb, was called Passover alone; this one was both Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread.

As it seems to me, that feast signifies the Lord’s Passion, and this one his resurrection. And it is sufficiently well known that [Col. 0278C] the former feast signifies the Lord’s Passion, in which that true Lamb was slain, by whose blood we were saved from the hand of the spiritual Pharaoh, that is, the devil. Therefore that feast is called *pascha*, which is “passing,” because Christ himself in his Passion passed from this world, as the Evangelist says: “Before the feast day of the Passover, Jesus, knowing that his hour had come to pass from this world to the Father” (John 12).

But let us see how this other feast signifies the Lord’s resurrection. First consider how greatly that majesty humbled itself, and how far it descended for us. He who was Creator made himself a creature; he who was Lord made himself a servant; he who was rich made himself poor; he who was great made himself little; and “the Word was made flesh” [Col. 0278D] (John 1). He was bread, and fed the angels, but did not feed us; and therefore we were wretched, because a rational creature is always in misery unless it is fed by that bread. But we were so weak that we could in no way taste that bread in its purity.

For we had within us a certain leaven which had corrupted us and removed the first strength that we possessed; and we had become so unlike that pure and clean bread that we could taste none of it. This leaven which we had in ourselves was twofold: we had in ourselves a leaven of mortality, and we had in ourselves a leaven of iniquity. You see now how greatly we have exulted in that bread in which neither was present: neither mortality nor iniquity. How could we ascend there? How could we taste it? What things are as contrary as mortality and immortality, iniquity and righteousness? We are mortal and sinful; he is immortal and righteous. How could we come together?

That compassionate and merciful one saw this: because we could not ascend to him, he descended to us. He took up one part of our leaven and so adapted himself to our weakness. He did not take up all the leaven that was in us, but a certain part. For if he had taken up nothing, he would have been so far from us that we could in no way approach him, and so would always have remained in misery. We said that the leaven in us was twofold: mortality and iniquity. He took up one, by which he became like us. He therefore took up the leaven of [Col. 0279B] our mortality and remained in the purity of his righteousness, so that he might be such as could descend to us and yet remain such that we ought to ascend to him.

You see now, brothers, how that pure bread was leavened for our sake. Hunger, thirst, sorrow, and misery belong to this leaven of mortality; our Lord had all this in himself. He willed to take up these leavens, but he ought not to remain in the leaven. First he showed this leaven in himself through wonderful compassion, and afterward he purified himself from it through wonderful charity, because he purified himself from this leaven in such a way as, in that very act, to show his marvellous charity toward us.

He knew that we had not only this leaven, which is very evil, but also another, most wicked and deadly, which prevented us from being joined to that bread which is truly pure and clean. Therefore he willed in that way to purify himself from the leaven of iniquity. But we must know that our iniquity is the cause of our mortality; and therefore, when we have been fully purified from iniquity, we shall afterward undoubtedly also be purified from this mortality.

We must further know that our iniquity is twofold. It arises from the nature in which we were born; and it arises from the evil will which we afterward added. God purified us from both kinds of iniquity. He gave a sacrifice for us, namely his own flesh and blood; and through that sacrifice we were purified. Therefore whatever [Col. 0279D] we suffer from the corruption of our nature is no longer iniquity but weakness. From the corruption of our nature come movements of concupiscence which we suffer unwillingly: movements of lust, movements of anger, movements of pride, movements of ambition. But if we do not consent, he does not impute these to us, because that pure sacrifice was offered for the corruption of our nature.

But behold: through the compassion which worked in us, we were purified in baptism from all sins, both those arising from nature and those which we had added by our will. Yet did we afterward preserve ourselves in that purity? What then shall we do? He has taught us how we ought to be purified. Therefore, in the very manner in which he was purified from [Col. 0280A] the leaven of mortality, we ought to be purified from the leaven of iniquity.

Without doubt he could have purified himself from this mortality without suffering any punishment. But because we cannot be purified from this iniquity except through temporal punishments, he willed to give us an example of this. Now remember what we said: our Lord Jesus Christ is bread. Consider him before the Passion, and see that he was like bread with leaven. He hungered, thirsted, wept, slept, and was weary. All these belong not to the leaven of iniquity but to the leaven of weakness and mortality; through all of them he showed the compassion and charity which he had toward us.

All these are certain forms of medicine suited to our weakness. Because they suited us and he did not have them in himself, he took them from us. But in us all these are mixed with sin. For evil concupiscence is accustomed to associate itself with our hunger and thirst; murmuring, despair, or bitterness with our sorrow; dissipation with our sleep; and lukewarmness and dullness with our weariness. But our Lord separated and divided these things: he left behind sin and took up weakness. For a short time he concealed what was his own and assumed what was ours. Therefore Isaiah said: “That he may do his work, his work is strange; that he may do his work, his act is foreign to him” (Isa. 28).

“That he may do,” he says, “his work.” What [Col. 0280C] work? There are many works of our Lord; but here he speaks of a certain special work which belongs above all to him. His work is the angels, archangels, and all the powers of heaven. His work is heaven, earth, sea, and all that is in them (Ps. 145). But we know how he made those works: he did not take up foreign works in order to make them. “He spoke, and they were made” (Ps. 32). What then is this work of his, so special, so singular, so wonderful, so unheard-of? Let us accordingly hear what Scripture says:

“His mercies are over all his works” (Ps. 144). I see three kinds of God’s works. There is the work of his wisdom, the work of his mercy, and the work of his judgment. The work of his wisdom is heaven and earth and all that is in them; the work of his judgment is to render to each according to his works. But “his mercies are over all his works.” Therefore the work of his mercy is his special work: his own work, his proper work, in which his goodness, charity, and kindness appear most fully.

His work corresponds to his name. To which name? You know his name. What does his name sound like, taste like, smell like? Oil: “Your name is oil poured out” (Song 1). Why oil? Because his name tastes of charity and of mercy. For what does that sweet name Jesus signify? It signifies our salvation, because he is my God and my Jesus, that is, my Saviour. He had made the work of his wisdom when he created the world; but he had not yet [Col. 0281A] made the work of his mercy. For the work of mercy concerns the wretched. He had also made the work of judgment when he cast the devil from heaven for his pride. He had also made the work of judgment when he cast man from Paradise for disobedience. But in these works he showed his wisdom and power. He willed also to show his mercy, because “his mercies are over all his works.” Therefore the work of his mercy is properly called his own work.

But how could he accomplish this work except by saving the wretched? Therefore the work of our salvation is the work of his mercy; it is properly his own work. What is so proper to the Saviour—that is, to Jesus—as saving? But what does the prophet say? “That he may do his own work, his work is strange” (Isa. 28).

As you know, brothers, our Lord Jesus Christ is wisdom; he is life. What is contrary, and as it were foreign, to wisdom? Certainly folly. And what is contrary to strength? Certainly weakness. Likewise, nothing is contrary to death except life. Consider now how our Lord took up a certain work foreign to himself, so that he might accomplish his own work—that is, the work of his mercy. He who was wisdom willed to be as though foolish; he who was strength willed to be weak. Therefore the Apostle says: “What is foolish in God is wiser than men, and what is weak in God is stronger than men” (1 Cor. 1).

“That he may do his own work, his work is foreign to him.” Bread hungers; the fountain thirsts; strength grows weary; life dies. But how does he accomplish his own work through this foreign work? His hunger feeds us; his thirst gives us drink; his weariness refreshes us; his death gives us life. Our spiritual fullness, our spiritual inebriation, our spiritual refreshment, our spiritual enlivening: all this is the work of his mercy. Through this foreign work he accomplishes it all. Wisdom accomplishes this through folly, as the Apostle says: “Since the world did not know God through wisdom, it pleased God through the folly of preaching to save those who believe” (ibid.).

Therefore, as we have said, wisdom accomplishes this its own work through folly; strength accomplishes it through weakness; bread through hunger; the fountain through thirst; strength through weariness; life through death. [Col. 0281D] “That he may do his own work, his work is foreign; that he may do his own work, his act is foreign to him” (Isa. 28). In order to accomplish the work of his mercy, the work of his wisdom and the work of his judgment became foreign to him.

We said that the angels are the work of his wisdom; and hear what he himself said when he was seized by the Jews. Peter wished to defend the Lord and struck someone with his sword. And the Lord said to him: “Do you think that I cannot ask my Father, and he will furnish me with more than twelve legions of angels?” (Matt. 26). He could have had with him all the angels to destroy those who wished to seize him, but he did not will it. For, in order that he might accomplish his own work, that marvellous work which he had purposed, [Col. 0282A] he willed that the angels themselves should be as though foreign to him and should not fight against his enemies.

Human beings also are the work of his wisdom. And hear what he himself said to Pilate: “If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would surely fight that I should not be delivered to the Jews” (John 19). He did not will to have with him angels, men, or any creature. Therefore, in order that he might accomplish his own work, his own work was foreign to him. Hence he himself said: “I have trodden the winepress alone” (Isa. 63). “Alone,” he says. Alone, because his own work was foreign to him. The angels were foreign, because they were not present. Men were foreign, because they did not fight. Heaven was foreign, because it did not strike his enemies with lightning. Earth was foreign, because it did not swallow them up. The sea was foreign, because it did not drown them. [Col. 0282B] The work of his judgment was likewise foreign to him, as he himself said: “I judge no one” (John 8). And again: “God did not send his Son into the world to judge the world” (John 3).

“That he may do his own work, his work is foreign.” In order to do the work of his mercy, he took up the leaven of our mortality, which was certainly foreign to the purity of his divinity. At last the time came when he willed to remove this leaven from himself: he applied fire, that is, the Passion. In his Passion all that leaven perished—all corruption, all mortality—and today unleavened bread, pure bread, rose from the earth.

You see now why it was commanded that, after the lamb had been sacrificed, the bread on which the Jews fed should be without leaven. For before the Passion of that Lamb, our Lord Jesus Christ, the flesh of the same Lord—which flesh is our refreshment and our bread, as you know, because we eat that flesh in the likeness of bread—before the Passion, I say, was mortal. It could hunger, thirst, grieve, and die. But after the Passion it rose immortal, incapable of suffering, incorruptible.

Come then, brothers: let us celebrate the Feast of Unleavened Bread. Let us eat this bread without leaven. Our bread is the body of our Lord. It is without leaven because, as the Apostle says, “Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more” (Rom. 6). If we wish to eat this bread which is without leaven, we must ourselves be [Col. 0282D] without leaven, as the Apostle commands. A little earlier you heard what he says: “Purge out the old leaven” (1 Cor. 5). This leaven, as we said above, is sin. But our Lord undoubtedly taught us how we ought to purge ourselves of this leaven. In the manner in which he laid aside the leaven that he had taken up for us, we must lay aside the leaven which corrupts us. Through reproaches, insults, scourges, the cross, and death, he came to the resurrection. In the resurrection he laid aside the leaven and now offers us his flesh, pure and immortal.

What do we think, my brothers? Can we come to the resurrection by any other way than that by which he came? Whoever thinks so deceives himself. But you ask: to which resurrection? We read in the Scriptures of two resurrections. Thus John says in the Apocalypse: “Blessed is he who has a part in the first resurrection” (Rev. 20). The first resurrection is of souls; the second, of bodies. Our Lord accomplishes these two resurrections in us through his one resurrection. For he could not rise in soul, because he was not dead in soul; he rose in body because he was dead in body. We, who have had death in body and soul, must rise in body and soul—but first in soul, afterward in body. In the resurrection of his body our Lord laid aside the leaven of mortality. Through the resurrection of the soul we lay aside the leaven of iniquity.

But if he came through the tribulations [Col. 0283B] of life to the resurrection of the flesh, much more must we come through the tribulations of this life to the resurrection of the soul, so that through the resurrection of the soul we may lay aside the leaven of sin and, as the Apostle says, become “a new dough” (1 Cor. 5). The old dough was sin, with which we were all sprinkled and leavened. The new dough is the blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, with which we were sprinkled and through which we were purified from that evil leaven. Just as flour, when it is moistened with water, is united and becomes one mass, so we, when we were sprinkled in baptism, became as it were one mass with Christ, as the Apostle says: “Because we who are many are one bread, one body in Christ” (1 Cor. 10).

Because through our negligence [Col. 0283C] we defile ourselves after that purification, nevertheless let us flee to Christ’s blood—that is, let us imitate his Passion—so that we may be sharers in his resurrection: here in soul, and on the day of judgment in body and soul together. Since this cannot come about through ourselves, let us pray for his mercy, that our Lord Jesus Christ himself may deign to work this in us—he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XIII. ON THE ASCENSION OF THE LORD

For some time now we have represented the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ and that second [Col. 0283D] period during which he was in this world after his resurrection. Today we represent the day on which he showed us openly that all that he did and suffered in this world he did in order to lead us from the death into which we fell through Adam to true life, and to raise us from this exile to our homeland, for which we were created—that is, to heaven. For he died because of our sins, rose because of our justification, and ascended into heaven because of our glorification.

Through his merits we have received forgiveness of our sins. For what we could not do, he accomplished on account of our sins. Through faith in his resurrection we are justified. For unbelievers, pagans, and Jews knew and believed his death, although they did not wish to believe in his death. But because they could not see his resurrection, they refused to believe it. Yet our faith merits justification and awaits a great reward because we believe what we could not see. Hence the Lord said to Thomas: “Because you have seen me, you have believed. Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed” (John 20).

That blessedness which we await, he willed today to show in himself by ascending into heaven, so that we may be certain that we, who are his members, will ascend where he ascended, who is our head. Therefore, dearest brothers, we ought to celebrate this day with great joy, because on this day there was displayed so great a glorification of human nature that none greater can be. For this nature of ours, [Col. 0284B] which had been so cast down and corrupted that it was even compared with brute animals, as the Prophet says, “Man, though he was in honour, did not understand; he was compared with senseless beasts” (Ps. 48), has in our Lord Jesus Christ been so exalted that it has every creature beneath it, and even angels adore it above themselves.

As you have often heard, after his resurrection our Lord wished to remain bodily in this world for forty days, for many reasons. For after his resurrection he wished to confirm, and to demonstrate in many ways, that he had truly risen from the dead according to the flesh; and therefore he often ate and drank with his disciples, and showed them his wounds. And when the apostle Thomas [Col. 0284C] refused to believe the other apostles that they had seen him, he allowed him to touch his side and his hands (Luke XXIV; John XX). He wished, by his bodily presence, to strengthen his disciples, who had been exceedingly saddened at his passion and had almost despaired; and by the authority of the Scriptures to prove to them that it was necessary for him to die and rise again. Moreover, he opened their understanding, that they might understand the Scriptures.

But we should also note that, before his passion and resurrection, he fasted for the same length of time that after his resurrection he wished to be bodily with his disciples. By his fasting he commended to us the bodily affliction which we must endure in this life; [Col. 0284D] by the bodily presence which he showed to his followers after his resurrection, we may understand the consolation of his most sweet presence which we shall have after our own resurrection. Yet both are commended by the same number, because according to the measure in which we are afflicted for Christ in this life, we shall receive consolation in the life to come.

Besides this, after his resurrection our Lord wished by certain bodily signs to commend great mysteries to us. During these days he appeared to his disciples as they were fishing, and at his command they drew to shore a net full of one hundred and fifty-three large fish (John XXI). In this was signified the blessedness of those who, in the future resurrection, will be presented to the Lord by Christ’s ministers. [Col. 0285A] And the meal which he wished to share with his disciples signified that banquet when we shall eat and drink at his table in his kingdom. During these days he gave the Holy Spirit to his disciples while they were still on earth (John XX), whom he afterwards sent from heaven; and by giving the same Holy Spirit twice (Acts I), he commended love of God and of neighbour. Yet this number of forty days also signifies profound mysteries. But you who are accustomed to read the expositions of the holy Fathers have no need to hear much about this; and, as I think, my lay brothers would more gladly hear something else. Therefore we do not wish to speak further of it.

Therefore, after he had fulfilled everything for which he had wished to remain on earth for so long, on this present day, [Col. 0285B] when he wished to ascend into heaven, he appeared to them and ate with them, as Luke says in the Acts of the Apostles: “And while eating with them, he commanded them not to depart from Jerusalem” (Acts I). O how blessed were those who were at that meal! Yet, as the Evangelist says, he reproached their unbelief and hardness of heart, because they did not believe those who had seen him risen (Mark XVI). He had often appeared after his resurrection, and had eaten and drunk with his disciples. But at this final appearance, when he wished to ascend into heaven, there were, I think, many who had not seen him before, but had only heard from those who had seen him, and were somewhat doubtful. Therefore the Lord reproached [Col. 0285C] their unbelief, and acted most fittingly. On the one hand he rebuked them; on the other he strengthened them. And he rebuked them especially when he promised them such great things, as it is written: “He commanded them not to depart from Jerusalem, but to wait for the promise of the Father, which,” he said, “you have heard through my mouth; for John indeed baptized with water, but you shall be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days hence” (Acts I).

We read in the Book of Kings that, when Elijah was taken up in a fiery chariot, he left his cloak to Elisha, and Elijah’s spirit became double in Elisha. The prophet Elijah signifies our Lord, and Elisha signifies the Lord’s apostles and disciples. Elijah’s being taken up into the aerial heaven signifies [Col. 0285D] the Ascension of our Lord. But because Elijah was only a human being, he required another’s help. Our Lord, who was true God, ascended into heaven by his own power, as the Evangelist says: “And it came to pass, while he blessed them, that he withdrew from them and was carried into heaven” (Luke XXIV).

Elijah’s cloak signified the holy Church, as the holy patriarch Jacob said concerning our Lord: “He shall wash his robe in wine, and his cloak in the blood of grapes” (Gen. XLVIII), because by his own blood he cleansed his Church. When Elijah ascended the chariot, he left his cloak to Elisha; and when our Lord ascended into heaven, he entrusted his Church to his disciples. For he said: “Go into the whole world; preach the Gospel to every [Col. 0286A] creature” (Mark XVI), that is, to every class of people: Jews and Gentiles, wise and foolish, rich and poor—of all of whom the holy Church consists.

But what does it signify that Elijah’s spirit became double in Elisha? Our Lord said somewhere to his disciples: “He who believes in me will also do the works that I do; and he will do greater works than these” (John XIV). Indeed, our Lord did many things in person while he was bodily on earth. Yet, after he ascended into heaven, he in some sense did far more through the apostles and his other disciples. In person he converted few Jews; through the apostles he made the whole world believe in him. Many sick people were healed by touching the fringe of his garment; and, what seems greater, through Peter’s shadow alone he cured many of their illnesses. [Col. 0286B] Therefore it may be said that Elijah’s spirit became double in Elisha, because, as regards the conversion of people, he converted far more through the apostles than through himself.

For Elisha himself, of whom it is written that Elijah’s spirit became double in him, came to the Jordan and struck the river, but it was not divided. As soon as he invoked Elijah, saying, “Where is now the God of Elijah?” (IV Kings II), the water was divided. Thus, although the apostles appear to have done more than the Lord did in person on earth, they did not do these things in their own name or by their own power, as our Lord did, but in the name and by the power of their master.

It may also be understood thus: Elijah’s spirit [Col. 0286C] became double in Elisha after he was taken up, because the Spirit of God, who was in the apostles before his Ascension, became double in them after his Ascension. For they possessed a greater grace of the Holy Spirit after his Ascension than they had before. Again, the grace said to have been possessed by Elisha may be understood in this way: the holy apostles received the spirit of our Elijah—that is, of our Lord Jesus Christ, namely the Holy Spirit—twice, as we said shortly before: first on earth, when he appeared to them, breathed upon them, and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John XX); and afterwards from heaven, when divided tongues as of fire appeared to them and rested upon each of them. The anniversary of that day [Col. 0286D] we shall celebrate, God willing, in a few days.

After that sweet meal had ended, the Evangelist says: “He led them out as far as Bethany” (Luke XXIV). Bethany is a small town, situated on the Mount of Olives. Bethany is interpreted “house of obedience.” Note here the beautiful significance: first he ate with them, and afterwards he led them out to Bethany, because he makes those truly obedient whom he is accustomed to refresh with spiritual food. Nor should we pass over his words: “He led them out.” For that person truly ascends to Bethany whom the Lord leads out.

First, he leads them out of this world, when he causes them not to love the world nor the things that are in the world; and also [Col. 0287A] out of their evil deeds and habits, when he makes a lustful person chaste, an impatient person patient, and a proud person humble. He also leads one out of oneself—that is, out of one’s own will—so that one may always keep in heart what the Lord said: “I came not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John V). The one whom he has thus led out, he surely leads to Bethany, which is upon a mountain—and not just any mountain, but the Mount of Olives.

There is a certain Bethany in the valley. Bethany, as we have said, is interpreted “house of obedience,” and signifies a heart obedient to God’s commands. The house of obedience is in the valley when someone appears obedient in order to obtain earthly things. Again, just as there are good mountains, of which it is written: “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from which help shall come to me” (Ps. CXX), so there are evil mountains, of which it is said where the Lord speaks of the devil: “For him the mountains bear herbs” (Job XL). There is a mountain of pride, upon which sits the one who sees every lofty thing and is king over all the children of pride. [Col. 0287B] Some have their Bethany upon this mountain—that is, their heart, which appears to be a house of obedience—because whatever they do, they do in order to be glorified by people. Jesus, the teacher of humility, does not approach this Bethany, but the one situated upon the Mount of Olives.

The Mount of Olives is interpreted “richness of oil.” “A mountain of God, a fat mountain” (Ps. LXVII). The Mount of Olives signifies charity, because it excels the other virtues. In it abounds the spiritual oil by which the wounds of our souls are healed and through which the light of truth is made known to us. The nature of oil is that, if it is placed in other liquids, it floats above them all. Therefore the Apostle, after speaking of other virtues, prefaced his discussion of charity by saying: “And I show you a still more excellent way” (I Cor. XII). [Col. 0287C]

Therefore, dearest brothers, if we wish to see Jesus ascending into heaven with spiritual eyes, and if we wish to reach heaven with him and through him, we must depart from this world in mind and contemplation. We must also, if we can, lift our heart above the senses of the flesh; take up the splendid arms of obedience; and place the reward of our obedience neither in valleys—that is, in earthly things—nor on the mountain of pride, lest the Lord say of us: “Amen, I say to you, they have received their reward” (Matt. VI). Rather, our obedience must be upon the mountain of oil, that is, the mountain of charity, so that whatever we do, we may do for love of God.

“He led them out as far as Bethany, and, lifting up his hands, he blessed them” (Luke XXIV). O how blessed were those who were in that company and deserved to be blessed by those hands! “And lifting up his hands, he blessed them.” See, my brothers, what an inheritance our Lord left us when he departed from this world: not gold, not silver, not any earthly thing, but [Col. 0288A] his blessing. And lest we be too saddened that he withdrew bodily from us, let us hear what he himself said to them according to another Evangelist: “Behold,” he says, “I am with you until the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXVIII). How, then, did he withdraw from us? Certainly as to his bodily presence. As to his divinity, he is always with us; as to his loving providence, he is always concerned with us. “And it came to pass, while he blessed them, that he withdrew from them and was carried into heaven” (Luke XXIV).

“If God is for us, who is against us? God who justifies—who is there that condemns? Christ Jesus, who died—indeed, who also rose again—who also intercedes for us?” (Rom. VIII). Therefore, dearest brothers, we must resist manfully the devil and his snares, [Col. 0288B] and place great hope in our Lord Jesus Christ. For how can those perish for whom Christ stands, for whom he presents before the sight of his Father those wounds which he suffered for us? Therefore our hope must be firm in him.

We read in the Old Testament that, after the children of Israel had gone out of Egypt under Moses, Amalek—a certain barbarous people—came and fought against them. Moses sent an army against them, while he himself went up the mountain to pray for them, lifting his hands to the Lord. And it came to pass that, when he lifted up his hands, the children of Israel prevailed; but whenever he lowered his hands, [Col. 0288C] Amalek prevailed (Exod. XVII). Why do we think that the raising of his hands had such grace? Without doubt, God is accustomed to attend more to the disposition of the mind than to the movement of the body. What then? Did his prayer have no effect before God unless he raised his hands? Such was the effect of raising his hands that Israel’s enemies could not resist the children of Israel.

This raising had such power because it signified the raising of the hands of him who said in the Psalm: “The lifting up of my hands is the evening sacrifice” (Ps. CXL). For, now that the world was drawing toward evening, those most sweet hands were stretched out upon the cross, and that evening sacrifice was offered which bore away the sins of the whole world. Thus Moses’ lifting up of his hands signified the passion [Col. 0288D] of our Lord, who went up the mountain to pray because he ascended into heaven to intercede with the Father for us. There he lifts up his hands, so that Amalek—that is, the devil—may not conquer us; for there he appears before the face of God for us and presents his passion, which he underwent for us.

And we, brothers, so long as we are in this wretched life, which is a trial upon earth; so long as our struggle is against the principalities and powers of this darkness, against the rulers of the world, against spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places (Eph. VI), need our Lord to have his hands raised up within us—that is, we need the continual remembrance of his passion to be in our minds. And let us be certain, my brothers, that so long as the memory [Col. 0289A] of his passion is in our hearts, so long as our hope is fixed where Christ intercedes for us at the Father’s right hand, spiritual Amalek—that is, the devil—will not be able to overcome us. Therefore, my brothers, let us see to it that through our negligence this affection and remembrance do not grow lukewarm within us; for immediately we shall fail, and our enemy will overcome and afflict us.

On this present day, then, our Lord ascended to the Father while his disciples watched, wondered, and rejoiced—but sorrowed amid their rejoicing. They rejoiced because they had placed their hope in one endowed with such power that he could penetrate heaven by his own strength. They rejoiced, knowing that where he had ascended, they too would be, as before his passion he said to the Father: “I will that where I am, they too may be with me” (Matt. X). [Col. 0289B] They rejoiced because the pride of the Jews had been confuted: they saw ascending into heaven the one whom the Jews, blaspheming and shaking their heads beside the cross, had thought unable to come down from the cross. They rejoiced because, according to his promise, they would shortly receive the Holy Spirit and be strengthened by his consolation against every temptation. Moreover, they rejoiced at seeing angels in white garments, who said: “Men of Galilee” (Acts I), and so forth.

They are aptly called Galileans, that is, “those who pass over,” those who were passing from the carnal observances of the Law to spiritual things. Before the Lord’s passion [Col. 0289C] they had heard: “Do not go into the way of the Gentiles, and do not enter into the towns of the Samaritans” (Matt. X). Now a kind of passing-over is enjoined upon them, as the Lord says: “Go into the whole world and preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark XVI). “Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven?” (Acts I).

Certainly, although they rejoiced in all the things we have mentioned, they still felt no slight sorrow at his recent departure. For his bodily presence was very dear to them, and they took great delight in it. Hence they could not lose without sorrow what they had possessed with such love; and so they did what they could. They looked into heaven, to which he had ascended, following with their eyes, at least, the one they loved. And the angels said to them: “Men of Galilee, [Col. 0289D] why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven.” A great consolation: “He will come in the same way.” How? In the same flesh, in the same form, with those scars and wounds which he bore up into heaven. “They shall look upon him whom they pierced”; the Jews shall see the face which they veiled; they shall see the one whom they scorned and at whom they shook their heads.

We too, beloved, shall see our Lord, whom we poor follow—but not poor, not veiled, not hidden, not silent. For “our God shall come openly; our God shall not keep silence” (Ps. XLIX). He was hidden from the Jews who veiled his face; he was silent before the Pharisees who blasphemed him. [Col. 0290A] But “our God shall come openly; our God shall not keep silence.” And we, my brothers, should hear blasphemers without fear, endure persecutors patiently, and remain silent under reproaches. “Our God shall come openly.”

Let us ponder this one thing with anxious minds: that we may cling to him with our whole heart, whole mind, and whole strength, remembering that he is our head—truly our head. Let us live as the members of that head ought to live, setting our mind not here, where the lower part of us is, but there, where our head ascended on this day. Let us beseech the Lord, the almighty Father, to deign to grant us his grace, so that all the yearning of our devotion may tend where our substance is with him: Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns with him through [Col. 0290B] all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XIV. ON SAINT JOHN THE BAPTIST

One who speaks God’s word to others ought not to aim at displaying his own learning, but at building up his hearers. Therefore he ought to adapt his speech to the capacity of his audience and, compassionating weak understandings with a kind of maternal affection, to descend, if I may so say, to childlike words by stammering. But the slenderness of my own ability requires my hearers rather to incline their ears to the smallness of my discourse.

Therefore, my brothers, I confess that I am not a little ashamed. Yet I regain some confidence when I consider the blessed [Col. 0290C] Zechariah, father of this holy man whose feast we celebrate today. When he wished to pronounce the name John, at the very utterance of the name he who had formerly been mute became most eloquent. Perhaps, if we begin to speak of John, we too shall not be altogether mute. But what shall we say of him, or what shall we declare in his praise—he who, before he was born, was praised by angelic authority, and who through ineffable grace became a most worthy dwelling-place of the Holy Spirit even in the womb into which he had come through the contagion of sin?

Nor should this be passed over: the priest from whom he would be born was chosen; the Temple in which his birth would be foretold was chosen; the name to be given to him was chosen. Not even the hour is to be omitted. For it was the hour of incense. Would that, my brothers, [Col. 0290D] we too might be among those priests to whom the apostle Peter says: “But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood” (I Pet. II). Would that our heart might become God’s Temple, as the Apostle says: “The holy Temple of God is what you are” (I Cor. III). Perhaps at the hour of incense, the hour of saving compunction, when our prayer is directed like incense before the Lord (Ps. CXL), an angel too—the messenger, that is, of divine grace—will appear to us.

For John is interpreted “the grace of God,” and this name is expressly imposed upon him at the angel’s command. While still within his mother’s womb, he recognized that unutterable grace by which “the Word became flesh” (John I); afterwards he pointed out with his finger the Word made flesh; and, as a wonderful preacher of God’s grace, he opened by his preaching [Col. 0291A] the entrance to the kingdom of heaven even to tax collectors and prostitutes, bringing a kind of force upon heavenly purity through their conversion. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel, in the words you have just heard: “From the days of John, the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matt. XI).

From the days of John, indeed, force was brought against the kingdom of heaven—a force which the kingdom of heaven certainly did not suffer before John’s days. For the cherub with the turning sword was still driving unhappy Adam, hiding as it were beneath fig leaves, from entrance into Paradise (Gen. III), and was in a sense frustrating the effort of one bringing force. Those seven women were still suffering reproach: though they ate their own bread and wore their own garments, they nonetheless suffered reproach, going around and seeking some one man whom [Col. 0291B] all of them might take hold of for themselves. For one seized one man, another another, and all together no one who could take away the reproach of human beings—until that one man, because he was unique, because he was singular (“for he was singular until he should pass over”); that one man, I say, whom a woman encompassed, whose wife was human flesh, and to whom divinity, which had long remained barren in the other sons of Adam, was joined in marriage by a wonderful dispensation in a virginal womb as in its bridal chamber, brought forth in the Lord’s [Note: [Col. 0291] “Lord’s” is an improper word here, which Augustine retracted.] man the seven—that is, he fulfilled all the operations of the Holy Spirit.

In the Lord himself the fullness of divinity dwelt wonderfully, because bodily. Those seven women all together laid hold of this one man: namely, the seven graces of the Holy Spirit, not indeed needing [Col. 0291C] bread or garments. What is the food of the Holy Spirit? The Lord says in the Gospel: “My food is to do the will of my Father” (John IV). Thus the food of the Son is to do the Father’s will; therefore it is also the food of the Holy Spirit. He delights in this food: namely, in inspiring people to do the Father’s will. His garments too are holy people, in whose hearts that divine fire is accustomed to be nourished and, as it were, cherished. Hence it is said: “With all these you shall clothe yourself as with a garment” (Isa. XLIX). Even before John’s days the sevenfold Spirit was clothed with these garments and delightfully fed with this bread. Some shone with the spirit of wisdom, others of understanding, others of counsel, others of fortitude, others of piety, others of knowledge, others of fear, by the cooperating grace of the Holy Spirit.

What reproach, then, did the Holy Spirit suffer in these seven gifts? He bestowed righteousness upon humanity but did not render righteousness’ reward. What is the reward of righteousness? The kingdom of heaven. Thus righteousness by a kind of force demanded the kingdom of heaven for itself, but the kingdom of heaven did not admit this force until he came who removed this reproach. To those who acquire righteousness for themselves by a kind of force—namely, by crucifying their flesh with its vices and desires—he opened entrance into Paradise, removing the cherub and the turning sword (Gen. III). But what does this mean: “Let your name be invoked over [Col. 0292A] us” (Isa. IV)? Let this man be wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety, and fear. For this too is written: “Our fear.” Let Jesus then be such, and by his wonderful wisdom remove the cherub and the turning sword.

The cherub seems to me to be divine justice, which excluded proud and disobedient humanity from Paradise until equal humility was paid for its pride and equal obedience for its disobedience. Since this payment was made through Jesus Christ our Lord, the excluding justice was removed and an admitting justice succeeded it. But what was that turning sword? I hear the Lord call something a sword in the Gospel: “I have not come to bring peace, but a sword” (Matt. X). By “sword,” then, he intended to signify something contrary to peace. And what is so contrary to peace [Col. 0292B] as discord? There he expressed a good discord, if indeed it may be called good. But this sword, as it seems to me, signifies that discord which came about through the sin of the first human being: between God and humanity, between angelic and human nature, between the heavenly and earthly creation. This sword is called turning because at some time it was to be removed through God’s grace. For the true Solomon came, the true peacemaker, making peace through the blood of his cross with the things in heaven and the things on earth (Col. I). And this is the wonderful grace: from the days of John the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it (Matt. XI).

The kingdom of heaven is also understood as purity of heart, which we cannot attain except by bringing a kind of force upon ourselves. Of this kingdom the Lord says: [Col. 0292C] “The kingdom of God is within you” (Luke XVII); and the Apostle: “The kingdom of God is not food and drink, but righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit” (Rom. XIV). This kingdom the same Apostle eagerly sought to seize by a kind of force when he said: “I chastise my body and reduce it to slavery” (I Cor. IX). John first taught this violence in the Gospel by the example of his manner of life, then by the word of his preaching, saying: “Produce fruits worthy of repentance” (Matt. III).

We produce fruits worthy of repentance if, in the same manner in which we presented our members to serve injustice and iniquity, we present our members to serve righteousness and sanctification, and if sin does not reign in our mortal body (Rom. [Col. 0292D] VI), but rather righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit—that is, the kingdom of God. We produce fruits worthy of repentance if, rejecting the works of the flesh through which the devil reigns in a human being, we plough open the soil of our heart with the ploughshare of compunction, so that the fruits of the Spirit may spring from it: charity, joy, peace, and the rest enumerated by the Apostle. The same Apostle immediately shows in the following verse the way by which they reach these fruits, saying: “Those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires” (Gal. V).

Does not John show this same thing by his example? From infancy itself, if I may so say, fearing that he might be defiled by the filth of clamorous crowds, like a most chaste dove he took for himself the borrowed wings of purity and innocence and flew away to the secret place of the desert, showing that the first step toward this heavenly kingdom is contempt for the world. [Col. 0293A] “For whoever loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him” (I John II). But where love is absent, the kingdom of God certainly cannot be. Thus it is fittingly said of John: “And he was in the desert until the day of his manifestation” (Luke I).

And we, brothers, if we desire to have the kingdom of God within us, let us fly to a certain spiritual desert, and let our heart be a desert, pathless, and waterless land (Ps. LXII), so that the Lord may appear there and establish his kingdom there. Let it be desert from the occupations of this world, so that the world may be crucified to us [Col. 0293B] and we to the world. Let it be pathless to spiritual beasts, namely unclean spirits, lest they say to our soul: “Bend down, so that we may pass over” (Isa. LI). Let it be waterless, devoid of the flow of harmful pleasure, so that our soul may pass through water in which there is no substance.

What need I say now of contempt for one’s own flesh? The Gospel says: “He had a garment of camel hair” (Matt. III). Behold the clothing in which Christ’s soldier walks arrayed. This man seems to me to cry from his dwelling-place: “Alas for me, for my sojourn has been prolonged” (Ps. CIX), and: “I am a stranger with you and a sojourner, as all my fathers were” (Ps. XXXVIII). Hair-shirts are made from camel hair; this is the dress of penitents. What he later taught in word, he first showed in example: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand” (Matt. III). [Col. 0293C]

Let us also hear of his remarkable abstinence. His food was locusts and wild honey. By his bodily dress he had trampled softness; by this food he had trampled the greediness of the belly. This is the violence by which the kingdom of heaven is seized; it suffers this force from the days of John. For henceforth our conflict is not against fleshly Canaanites and Perizzites, in order that we may possess their earthly kingdom by force; rather, it is against the most savage enemies of carnal passions, so that, driving them out from the dwelling-places of our hearts, we may prepare in the land of our heart a temple and kingdom for the true Solomon, crucifying our flesh with its vices and desires (Gal. V).

Those of whom Paul said, “Many walk, of whom I often told you, but now say even weeping, that they are enemies of the cross of Christ” (Phil. III), had neglected to possess these things in the kingdom of heaven. [Col. 0293D] What it means to be enemies of Christ’s cross he makes clear when he adds: “Their god is the belly, and their glory is in their shameful parts” (ibid.). Thus to pursue the belly’s greediness and the flesh’s softness is to be an enemy of Christ’s cross. In these words he expressed all those vices to which nearly the whole world has given its hand: gluttony and lust. If pride and avarice are added to them, there will be the four wheels by which the devil penetrates nearly the entire world.

As for the heavenly flight of the locusts and the sweetness of spiritual honey, since we have prolonged [Col. 0294A] the sermon, let us leave them to your meditations. I had almost passed over that leather girdle, which signifies the virtue of chastity; in the excellence of this virtue purity of heart especially consists. Although chastity, like the other virtues without it, is of little or no benefit without the others, it is nevertheless more tolerable to lack any other virtue for a time than to lack this one. Finally, among the other virtues it shines with a special privilege: it has not only, as the other virtues do, a quality pertaining to the soul, but also brings the corruptible flesh itself to a kind of incorruption, making it taste beforehand something of the sweetness of that future resurrection in which “they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are as the angels of God.”

This is the virtue which, among the others, merits fellowship with angels, the approach of the Holy Spirit, [Col. 0294B] and a more intimate embrace of him who is “fair in beauty beyond the children of men” (Ps. XLIV). “John,” it says, “had a leather girdle around his loins” (Mark I). Thus he became a most vigorous practitioner of evangelical perfection before he became its hearer. May the Almighty grant us to walk by the way which he himself showed, so that, following the exhortations of so great a forerunner, we may come safely to him whom John foretold, our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns through endless ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XV. ON THE DAY OF SAINTS PETER AND PAUL

When the rich of this world engage in some war, they are accustomed to encourage their soldiers to fight well, not [Col. 0294C] only with words but also with promises. When they see them acting with insufficient wisdom and prudence, they usually show them the strength of their enemies; when they see them giving way under excessive labour, they usually spur them on with promises. So our Lord, because he knows how cunning and powerful our enemy is, exhorts us to be strong, saying: “Be strong in battle” (Heb. XI). Though the labour is very great, he promises us a great reward, saying: “And you shall have a great reward.” This battle is great, this enemy is strong, but the reward is great. Therefore, be strong in battle.

It is a great duel, a great war. Let no one be secure. So long as one lives—provided one lives well—it is war. Hence holy Job says: “Human life upon earth is warfare” (Job VII). [Col. 0294D] For one who is not here in spiritual warfare ought not to be called a human being, but a beast. If one does not fight against the pleasures and desires of the flesh, but consents to them, one certainly does not live as a human being but as a beast. Know, brothers, that from the day you came here and began to serve Christ, you entered the place of battle. Hence Solomon says: “Son, when you come to the service of God, stand firm and prepare your soul for temptation” (Ecclus. II). This is the battle. Therefore, be strong in battle.

The saints whose feast we celebrate today had a double battle, inner and outer. We have only one, the inner. For Saint Peter, as you know, had a battle not only spiritual, against that lion who [Col. 0295A] prowls about seeking whom he may devour (I Pet. V), but also external: against Simon Magus, against the most wicked Nero, against tortures and the persecutions of evil people. Likewise Paul says of external battle: “Without, conflicts; within, fears” (II Cor. VII). And again: “If I fought with beasts at Ephesus” (I Cor. XV).
