Of the inner battle he says: “I see another law in my members, resisting the law of my mind and leading me captive in the law of sin” (Rom. VII). But they had well heeded the voice of their leader, who had said: “Be strong in battle.” Therefore they fought well, conquered well, and today received the reward of victory.

And you, brothers, be strong in battle. Do not abandon the place of combat. For this is the place of combat. Hold your ground in this your fortress, in this your house, [Col. 0295B] and let each one hold and defend his own place well. For in this fortress there are different posts, and it is appointed who ought to keep one post and who another. Therefore let no one permit the enemy to enter through that part in which he himself is stationed. The cloistered monks have one post, those assigned to obediences another, the prelates another; let each carefully guard his own place. Let him watch as far as he can, lest the enemy enter.

The place of the cloistered, which they themselves must defend and protect against enemies, is regular observance. They must take care lest the enemy find some opening in that observance through which he may enter. They must see that there is no negligence in work, lest through it the enemy enter and demolish [Col. 0295C] that great wall by which they customarily keep the worst enemies away from us—namely, sloth and sadness. They must diligently take care lest some excess destroy our abstinence, lest excessive sleep diminish our vigils. These are two excellent towers by which we are defended against the fiery darts of lust; therefore they must be well guarded, lest the enemy find some opening in them. They must also diligently preserve silence; if it is pierced and worn away, the enemy immediately enters through quarrels, disputes, and discord.

The place of those assigned to obediences is charity, mercy, the care of guests and of the poor, and other such things. It is therefore necessary that they guard their place and do not allow the enemy to enter, whether through cruelty or avarice. Let them provide [Col. 0295D] what is good not only before God but also before all people, so that in all things God may be glorified. But the place of prelates is judgment and discipline. They must guard this place so that judgment is not cruel and discipline not lax; rather, they must order all things in such a way that the enemy finds no opening for murmuring in the community because of their less-than-right governance, nor again any opening for harmful licence because of their indulgence.

But because in all these things there is warfare, the Lord therefore exhorts all, saying: “Be strong in battle.” For the cloistered are commonly attacked by the vice of curiosity and pleasure. Because, when they see themselves free from external business, they are apt to scrutinize too curiously the actions of those who concern themselves with outside affairs; [Col. 0296A] and so to judge all their deeds and words. Thus they begin to despise those whom above all they ought to honour, while esteeming themselves. Then they devise and imagine things in their hearts, saying: “Oh, if I were abbot, or prior, or cellarer, or porter, I would not entangle myself in earthly matters; I would do this and that.” And they consume almost all their time in such thoughts. From this begin envies against prelates, and from this slanders. And if at any time they see, or suppose, that prelates exceed in some matter, they publicize it wherever they dare. Such persons unquestionably incur that curse by which Noah cursed his son who mocked his father’s nakedness (Gen. IX). This vice especially attacks those who think themselves of some consequence.

[Col. 0296B] There are others who, because they are lax concerning themselves, do not care greatly about others. Since they themselves are free from external concerns, they give themselves over to idleness and lukewarmness; and, though they cannot do so in body, they roam in mind through worldly desires and pleasures of the flesh. They care for nothing except to remain bodily in the monastery. Of them the prophet says: “The enemies saw her and mocked her Sabbaths” (Lam. I). The Sabbath, as you know, is rest; but enemies mock the rest of those who seem to rest in the outward person while inwardly they do not cease to entertain worldly and shameful matters.

Certainly the manner of such thoughts must be considered here. For one who experiences all these thoughts within himself, if he is strong in battle and fights [Col. 0296C] against the ancient serpent that instils such thoughts, loses nothing by them; indeed, he will gain a crown. For sin lies not in suggestion but in consent. Yet because thoughts of this sort are exceedingly violent and greatly afflict those who endure them, we must listen to the Lord saying: “Be strong in battle.”

Those assigned to obediences—for example cellarers, porters, and guest-masters—are commonly attacked by avarice, sadness, and covetousness. For many such officers, either excessively timid or naturally avaricious, when they see that the things in their hands are diminishing a little, either desire too greatly what they do not possess, or keep what they possess miserly, or give it away with a certain sadness. Against all these temptations they must be strong, fight steadfastly, and take up firm [Col. 0296D] faith against covetousness, generosity against avarice, and cheerfulness against sadness. Let them take God’s commandments and promises as certain darts against the ancient serpent, their enemy, who suggests these things. Against fear and covetousness let them set what the Lord says: “Do not be anxious, saying, ‘What shall we eat? What shall we drink? Or with what shall we be clothed?’” (Matt. VI).

Here it must certainly be observed what the Lord has allowed us: without doubt, the things we need—namely necessities, that is, food and clothing.

You see, therefore, that the Lord has not promised us superfluities. Let us then be secure: so long as we seek not superfluities but necessities, God will provide them. And if at times he withholds bodily necessities, he certainly does [Col. 0297A] this for the greater benefit of the soul. Against that sadness also let them hear the Apostle: “Not out of sadness,” he says, “or compulsion; for God loves a cheerful giver” (II Cor. IX). Let them too be strong in battle; let them fight against temptations as far as they can, provide necessities honourably, and lay aside anxiety.

Prelates, who are in a higher position, must especially beware of two temptations: pride and vanity. Pride is when they think themselves better because they are superiors. Vanity is when they delight and glory in their very prelacy. Let these also, then, be strong in battle and fight against the ancient serpent. Against pride, let them set the saying of Scripture: “The higher you are, the more humble yourself in all things” (Ecclus. III). And again: “Have they appointed you leader? Be as one of them” (IV Kings XIV). Against vanity, by which the mind delights in prelacy, let them consider what is written: “A most severe judgment will be made upon those who rule; the powerful shall suffer powerful torments” (Wis. VI). [Col. 0297B]

Since, therefore, there is no one who serves God—in whatever place, order, or rank—against whom the ancient serpent does not fight, let us all hear: “Be strong in battle, and fight against the ancient serpent.” As I said at the beginning, when worldly commanders see their soldiers acting less wisely, they show them the strength and cunning of their enemies. So here he tells us two things about our enemy: he calls him ancient, and a serpent. By his antiquity he shows us that he has long experience [Col. 0297C] in this kind of warfare, and is therefore exceedingly shrewd. Hence we must watch over ourselves cautiously and vigilantly. He has no other concern—neither food nor sleep—but only to deceive human beings. He has practised this from the beginning of the world until the present time. Brothers, he has learned much of this art; therefore we must keep watch.

The serpent also, as you know, is very slippery; wherever it can first put in its head, it easily enters wholly. Such is this our enemy: wherever he can first put in his head—that is, an act of sin. Therefore we must always examine every movement of the heart, so that this serpent may not instil anything unclean or contrary to reason. For, as our Lord says, in the heart [Col. 0297D] is the root and, as it were, the head of all our actions: “From the heart,” he says, “come evil thoughts, fornications, adulteries, blasphemies” (Matt. XV).

We ought to consider what we have been called to. We must see that the people of this world give us their lands and possessions so that they may be protected by our prayers and reconciled to God. Therefore it is necessary that we surpass those who place such trust in us in purity of life and the practice of good works, lest it be said of us: “Be ashamed, Sidon, says the sea” (Isa. XXIII). This undoubtedly occurs when those called religious become worse than secular people. For then, in comparison with the sea—that is, the world—Sidon, that is, religion, is put to shame.

But because it is exceedingly laborious to fight daily—indeed, without interruption—against the flesh, thoughts, and the other spiritual wickednesses, it is necessary always to look to the reward promised us. Therefore, after exhorting us to battle and disclosing the cunning and malice of our enemy, he immediately consoles us with the reward, saying: “And receive his kingdom.” We must understand the kingdom of God in two ways: in this life and in the life to come. For in this life we undoubtedly can and ought to have the kingdom of God within us. The Apostle says: “The kingdom of God is not food and drink, but righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit” (Rom. XIV). If we persevere in this battle and do not consent to vices, we shall have God’s kingdom within us in this life, and also righteousness, peace, [Col. 0298B] and joy: righteousness from virtues; peace from the agreement of flesh and spirit, when both agree together in what is good; and joy from the testimony of a good conscience.

This kingdom is also followed by that ineffable kingdom which “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man” (I Cor. II). Hence the Lord will say on the day of judgment: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. XXV). May he who promised it deign to bring us there: Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XVI. ON THE SAME FEAST

You know, brothers, that among all the apostles and [Col. 0298C] martyrs of our Lord, these two whose feast we celebrate today appear to possess a particular dignity. Nor is this surprising. For these are the men to whom the Lord entrusted the holy Church more specially. When Saint Peter confessed that the Lord himself was the Son of God, the Lord answered him: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church. And I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. XVI). Again, the Lord in a certain way made Saint Paul his equal, as Paul himself says: “He who worked in Peter for the apostleship worked also in me among the Gentiles” (Gal. I).

These are those whom the Lord promised to the holy Church through the Prophet, saying: “In place of your fathers, sons have been born to you” [Col. 0298D] (Ps. XLIV). The fathers of the holy Church are the holy patriarchs and prophets, who first taught God’s law and prophesied the coming of our Lord. Before the Lord’s coming, prophets ceased because of the people’s sins. But our Lord came; and in place of the prophets he chose the holy apostles, and what the Prophet said was fulfilled: “In place of your fathers, sons have been born to you.”

And observe how he shows that the dignity of the apostles is greater than that of the prophets. The prophets were leaders of one people and belonged to one nation, in one part of the earth; but of the apostles he says: “You shall appoint them over all the earth” (ibid.). What land, brothers, is there in which the authority and dignity of these apostles is absent? Kings, counts, rich and poor alike, all today praise and glorify these holy friends of God. Why, unless the Lord has appointed them rulers over all the earth? And we, brothers, as far as we can, should praise these holy apostles, friends of God, our fathers and rulers. Let us praise them, and make ourselves such that we may be able worthily to praise them. Then we shall be able worthily to praise them if we strive to imitate their life. Let us imitate their strength, their most holy life, and their good perseverance.

They undoubtedly possessed great strength, brothers. They are those pillars which the Lord established, as it is written: “The earth was melted, and all who dwell in it; I established its pillars” (Ps. LXXIV). When was the earth melted? See, brothers: before our Lord came to earth, all the earth was frozen, because it had no warmth of charity but was in the cold of iniquity. It was hardened, because it had no softness of piety and kindness. But our Lord came and sent fire into the earth against that cold, as he himself says: “I came to cast fire upon the earth; and what do I desire but that it burn?” (Luke XII). This fire dissolved the cold, and the earth began to melt and flow in tears.

But what does he mean when he says, “All who dwell in it”? (Ps. LXXIV). All, brothers, were melted; but some like her who says in the Song of Songs: “My soul melted” (Cant. V); others, as the Prophet says: “As wax melts before fire, so let sinners perish before God” (Ps. LXVII). Some were melted through repentance, others through envy. Here we may understand the earth as the holy Church, which says what we mentioned shortly before: “My soul melted,” in the presence of our Lord, “and all who dwell in it.” One must dwell in the Church in another manner, that is, in true faith and charity. All such persons were indeed melted by the fire of divine love: “The earth was melted, and all who dwell in it; I established its pillars.”

The pillars of this earth are the holy apostles, especially these two whose feast we celebrate today. They are the pillars that sustain the holy Church by their teaching, their prayers, and the example of their patience. Our Lord established these pillars. [Col. 0299D] At first they were very weak, unable to sustain either themselves or others. This was a great dispensation of our Lord. For if they had always been strong, someone might have thought that they possessed this strength from themselves. Therefore our Lord wished first to show what they were of themselves and then to strengthen them, so that all might know that all their strength came from God.

Again, because they were to be fathers of the Church and physicians for healing the weak, they would not have known how to have compassion on others’ weaknesses unless they had first felt weakness in themselves. Thus he established the pillars of the earth, that is, of the holy Church. For that pillar, Saint Peter, was very weak when the voice of a single maidservant cast him down. Afterwards he established [Col. 0300A] that pillar: first, when he questioned him three times, “Peter, do you love me?” and Peter answered three times, “I love you” (John XXI). For as, when he denied him three times, he had in some sense diminished within himself his love for our Lord, and therefore had failed and that pillar was broken; so, by confessing his love three times, the pillar was strengthened.

And it should be noted that when Peter answered, “I love you,” the Lord immediately said to him: “Feed my sheep” (ibid.), as though he were saying: “Show your love for me in this: feed my sheep.” Therefore, brothers, the person who is unwilling to feed Christ’s sheep falsely says that he loves God.

But someone says: “What has this to do with us? It concerns bishops, abbots, and priests who have the care of souls.” This is true, brothers, concerning [Col. 0300B] them; but it also concerns you. For Christ’s sheep are fed in two ways: by word and by example. Certainly, brothers, many prelates in the Church can adequately feed Christ’s sheep by word; but because they live badly, they would feed them better if they kept silent, or withdrew bodily and thereby gave them an example of humility, poverty, abstinence, chastity, and the other virtues. Yet the one who does both acts better; and one who cannot do both does better to feed by example than by word. For if by word alone he can benefit them, he harms himself; if he cannot do both, by example he benefits them and does not harm himself.

Therefore, brothers, if you love our Lord, live in such a way that Christ’s sheep may be fed by your example, as the Lord says: “Let your works so shine before people that they may glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. V). In every holy soul our Lord also has certain sheep—that is, virtues—which whoever loves Christ must feed. These sheep are charity, humility, spiritual joy, and other such things. We feed these sheep when we perform such deeds as make these virtues grow within us. Each of us must also feed these virtues in another. We do this if we conduct ourselves before our brothers in such a way that, by our example, their charity, their joy, their humility, and their patience increase.

For how do I feed humility in my brother if I am proud before him, if I speak [Col. 0300D] proudly, answer proudly, and walk proudly? How do I feed obedience in my brother if he sees me rebellious and disobedient? How do I feed his patience if I murmur, grow angry, speak harshly, or make signs before him? Whoever does these things before his brother does not feed Christ’s sheep in him; rather, so far as lies in him, he destroys and kills them, because he causes him to stumble. Whoever causes his brother to stumble sins against his brother. But whoever sins against his brother, as the Apostle says, sins against Christ (I Cor. VIII). And whoever sins against Christ does not love Christ. Therefore, if you love Christ, feed Christ’s sheep, and you will belong to that pillar strengthened by Christ’s love.

After this strengthening, it was strengthened again [Col. 0301A] when the Holy Spirit was sent. Then that pillar was so strong that blows, stones, threats, and finally death itself could not move it from its place. Again, that other pillar too was undoubtedly weak at first. For sins are the weakness of the soul. Hear how weak he was: “I was formerly a blasphemer, a persecutor, and an injurious man” (I Tim. I). Likewise, when he was struck down, blinded, and led into the city, and when Ananias came to him and instructed him, then he was weak. But hear how strong he afterwards became: “I am certain,” he says, “that neither death nor life, nor angels nor any other creature shall be able to separate me from the charity of God” (Rom. VIII).

Therefore, brothers, all strength is in charity, as it is written: “Love is strong as death” (Cant. [Col. 0301B] VIII). What does death do in a human being? It extinguishes every vice and every evil passion, closes the eyes, and makes the whole body insensible, so that the spirit alone lives. Charity does this as well: it extinguishes lust, removes anger, casts down pride, and drives out every vice. It closes the eyes so that they are not curious, and it extinguishes all carnal senses so that a person may say with Paul: “I live, yet no longer I; rather, Christ lives in me” (Gal. II). He himself does not live, because charity mortifies in him whatever was his own. Christ truly lives in him, because only the love of Christ has power in him.

Therefore, brothers, let us imitate the strength of these pillars. But what can we say of the holiness of these fathers? All holiness consists in purity of heart and the testimony [Col. 0301C] of a good conscience. Contempt for the world produces purity of heart. For every impurity of heart comes from love of the world. Love of the world defiles the heart; and therefore, when a person perfectly despises the world, he has no defilement in his heart.

The good testimony of conscience arises from two things: good work and right intention. For if a person does not act well, he cannot have a good conscience. Again, if he performs praiseworthy works without right intention, but either from love of praise or in order to acquire some temporal thing, he cannot have a good conscience. Who despised the world more perfectly than he who spoke so confidently to the Lord, saying: “Behold, we have left all things”? (Matt. [Col. 0301D] XIX). What testimony did he have to his own conscience, who said: “Lord, you know that I love you” (John XXI). Likewise, how perfectly Paul despised the world, since he reckoned all carnal things as dung in order to gain Christ! Likewise, concerning his works he himself said: “I laboured more than all of them” (I Cor. XV). And again: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith” (II Tim. IV). Concerning the testimony of his conscience, he again said: “This is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” (II Cor. I).

Therefore, brothers, let us imitate these holy fathers of ours. Let us strive to work well, despise the world, and possess a good conscience, so that we may attain their fellowship. But since it profits nothing to begin [Col. 0302A] all these things unless we strive to persevere in them, we must imitate the perseverance of these holy fathers. Perseverance is known only in death. However quickly a person begins to serve God, it profits him nothing if, even shortly before death, he abandons the good he began. And although a person may live badly for a long time, if while still healthy he turns to God, even if he lives only a short time thereafter, he has nevertheless persevered. Therefore, as it seems to me, perseverance is nothing other than ending one’s life commendably.

Thus, brothers, while we live, no one can be secure and no one can presume upon himself. For if, as is said, every praise is seen at the end, our salvation rests in perseverance alone. Yet no one can be secure of this perseverance before death. [Col. 0302B] Therefore nothing is better than to listen to the Apostle saying: “Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling” (Eph. VI). We should know, moreover, that the more a person suffers tribulations and pains in the Lord’s service, the more praiseworthy is that person’s perseverance.

For this reason these holy fathers of ours are greatly to be praised, since they endured so much for Christ and persevered so perfectly. It is no great thing to persevere with Christ in joy, prosperity, and patience; but this is altogether great: to be stoned, beaten, and struck for Christ, and in all these things to persevere with Christ. It is great, with Paul, to be cursed and to bless; to endure persecution and bear it; to be blasphemed and to entreat; to be as the refuse of this world and to glory in it. [Col. 0302C] How worthy of praise is Paul’s perseverance, which persevered amid such things! He was almost always either in prisons, chains, hunger, cold, or nakedness; and in all these things he persevered with Christ. He did not murmur or become sad; rather, he was pleased when he suffered such things, as he himself says: “I take pleasure in my weaknesses, in insults, in beatings, in tribulations, in distresses for Christ” (II Cor. XII). Finally, on this present day he perfectly commended his perseverance when he did not hesitate to endure death for Christ.

What shall I say of Peter’s perseverance? Even if he had suffered nothing else for Christ, this would suffice: that today he was crucified for Christ. And how praiseworthy is this: that he was unwilling to be crucified as our Lord was, but wished his feet to be above and his head below. He knew well where the one whom he loved, desired, and longed for was. Where, except in heaven? Why then did he wish his feet to be turned upward, unless to show openly that through that suffering he would go to God? That cross was, as it were, a road.

And truly, brothers, let us set before our eyes the life and death of these saints, and their reward; and let us consider that, if here we imitate their sufferings as far as we can, we shall undoubtedly come to their fellowship. May our Lord Jesus Christ grant this to us through their merits—he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XVII. ON THE ASSUMPTION OF THE BLESSED MARY

[Col. 0303A]

“Jesus entered a certain fortress-town; and a woman named Martha received him into her house. And she had a sister named Mary” (Luke XI). You have heard in the Gospel of the great blessedness of two women. Great indeed, brothers, was Martha’s blessedness: she received so great a guest, ministered to him, and was occupied with his service. Great was Mary’s blessedness: she recognized the excellence of this guest, heard his wisdom, and tasted his sweetness.

For the Evangelist relates that our Lord Jesus Christ entered a certain fortress-town, and that a woman called Martha received him into her house [Col. 0303B] and ministered to him. She had a sister called Mary, who, as soon as Jesus entered, ran to his feet, sat there, and listened to his sweet words. She attended so intently to the Lord’s words that she cared nothing about what was happening in the house, what anyone might say, or even how much her sister was working.

For which one of you, if our Lord were on earth and wished to enter his house, would not rejoice in a marvellous and ineffable way? What then shall we say, brothers? Since he is not now bodily on earth and we cannot receive him bodily, ought we therefore to despair of his coming? Far from it: let us prepare our houses, and without doubt he will come to us for our benefit better than if he had come bodily. Those women were undoubtedly blessed because they received him bodily; but they were altogether more blessed because they received him in mind. For at that time many received him bodily and ate and drank with him; yet because they did not receive him in mind, they remained wretched. Who was more unhappy than Judas? Yet he too ministered bodily to the Lord.

I shall say more. The Blessed Virgin Mary herself, whose glorious Assumption we celebrate today, was undoubtedly blessed because she received the Son of God in her body; nevertheless, she was more blessed because she had received him in mind. I should be lying if the Lord himself had not said this.

Yesterday it was read how a certain woman said to [Col. 0303D] our Lord: “Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts which you sucked” (ibid.). And the Lord said to her: “Rather, blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it” (ibid.). Therefore, brothers, let us prepare a certain spiritual fortress so that our Lord may come to us. For I say boldly that unless Blessed Mary had prepared this fortress within herself, the Lord Jesus would not have entered either her womb or her mind, nor would this Gospel be read today on her feast.

Therefore let us prepare this fortress. Three things are made in a fortress so that it may be strong: a ditch, a wall, and a tower. First comes the ditch, then the wall above the ditch, and then the tower, which is stronger and loftier than the rest. The wall and ditch guard one another: for unless the ditch lay before it, people could by some contrivance approach the wall to undermine it; and unless the wall stood above the ditch, they could approach the ditch and fill it in. The tower guards everything because it is higher than all.

Let us now enter our own soul and see how all these things ought spiritually to be made within us. What is a ditch but deep earth? Let us therefore dig our heart, down to where the earth is lowest. Let us remove the earth that is within and throw it upwards: thus a ditch is made. The earth which we ought to take up and throw above is our earthly frailty. Let it not remain hidden within, but let it always be before our eyes, so that there may be in our heart a ditch—that is, humble and deep earth. Therefore, brothers, this ditch is humility.

Remember what the vine-dresser says in the Gospel concerning the tree which the lord of the vineyard wished to cut down because he found no fruit on it: “Lord, let it alone this year also, until I dig around it and put manure upon it” (Luke XIII). He wished there to make a ditch—that is, to teach humility. Thus, brothers, let us begin to build this fortress. For unless this ditch first exists in our heart—that is, true humility—we shall be able to build nothing but ruin upon our own head.

How well Blessed Mary had made this ditch for herself! Certainly she considered her own frailty more than all her dignity and holiness. She knew indeed that her frailty was from herself, whereas her holiness, her being the Mother of God, the Lady of Angels, the temple of the Holy [Col. 0304C] Spirit, were assuredly only from God’s grace. Therefore she humbly confessed what was from herself, saying: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it done to me according to your word” (Luke I). And again: “He has regarded the humility of his handmaid” (ibid.).

After the ditch we must make a wall. This spiritual wall is chastity: altogether a strong wall, preserving the flesh whole and undefiled. It is the wall that preserves the ditch of which we have spoken, so that enemies cannot fill it in. For if anyone loses chastity, the whole heart is immediately filled with filth and uncleanness, so that humility—that is, the spiritual ditch—wholly perishes from the heart. But just as this ditch is guarded by the wall, so the wall must be guarded by the ditch. For one who loses humility will certainly be unable to preserve chastity of the flesh. Hence it happens that virginity, preserved from infancy to old age, is sometimes lost; because when the soul is defiled by pride, the flesh too is defiled by lust.

Holy Mary possessed this wall within herself more perfectly than anyone else. She is the holy and untouched virgin whose virginity, like a most firm wall, could never be penetrated by any battering-ram or other instrument—that is, by the devil’s temptation. She was a virgin before childbirth, a virgin in childbirth, and a virgin after childbirth.

But if you now imitate the most blessed Mary and possess this ditch of humility and wall of chastity, it is necessary that [Col. 0305A] we build the tower of charity. Charity is a great tower, my brothers. As a tower is ordinarily higher than every other structure of a fortress, so charity is above all the other virtues present in the soul’s spiritual building. Therefore the Apostle says: “I show you a way still more excellent” (I Cor. XII). He said this of charity, because it is the more excellent way that leads to life. Whoever is in this tower does not fear enemies, because “perfect charity casts out fear” (I John IV).

Without this tower, the spiritual fortress of which we speak is weak. For someone may have a firm wall of chastity and yet perhaps despise or judge his brother, failing to show him the charity he owes him; because he lacks the tower, his enemy passes the wall and kills his soul. Likewise, if someone appears humble in dress, food, and bows, yet inwardly bears a bitter spirit toward prelates and brothers, that ditch of humility cannot defend him from his enemies.

Who can tell how perfectly the most blessed Mary possessed this tower? If Peter loved his Lord, how greatly did Blessed Mary love both her Lord and her Son! And how greatly she loves her neighbours—that is, humankind—is shown by many miracles and visions, through which the Lord himself has deigned to show that she especially prays to her Son for the entire human race.

Brothers, it is superfluous for me even to attempt to set forth [Col. 0305C] her charity, which is so great that no mind suffices to conceive it. This is undoubtedly the castle into which Jesus deigns to enter. And undoubtedly happier are those who receive him spiritually in such a castle than were many who then received him bodily into their homes. But why does the Evangelist withhold the castle’s name, saying only that Jesus entered into a certain castle? (Luke XI.) “Certain” denotes a singularity; therefore this properly belongs to our most blessed Lady. For she is a singular castle: in no human being is there such humility, in none such perfect chastity, in none such surpassing charity. Undoubtedly a singular castle [Col. 0305D] which the Father established, which the Holy Spirit sanctified, which the Son entered, and which the whole Trinity chose as its own singular dwelling. This is the castle which Jesus entered. He entered while the gate remained shut; he departed while the gate remained shut, as Saint Ezekiel prophesied: “And he brought me,” he says, “to the gate which looked toward the east, and it was shut” (Ezek. XL). The eastern gate is the most holy Mary. For a gate customarily set toward the east first receives the sun’s brightness. Thus the most blessed Mary, who always looked toward the east—that is, toward God’s brightness—first received into herself the ray, indeed the whole fullness of the brightness, of that true sun, namely the Son of God, of whom the prophet Zechariah says: “The Dayspring from on high has visited us” (Luke I).

This gate was shut [Col. 0306A] and well fortified. The enemy found no entrance, no opening whatever. It was shut and sealed with the seal of chastity, which was not broken by the Lord’s entrance but rather made still more solid and secure. For he whose gift virginity is did not take virginity away by his presence, but rather confirmed it. Therefore Jesus entered this castle. And if we, brothers, have within ourselves this spiritual castle of which we speak, Jesus will undoubtedly enter us spiritually. But he entered blessed Mary not only spiritually, but bodily also, because in her and from her he assumed a body. “And a certain woman named Martha received him into her house. And she had a sister named Mary” (Luke XI).

[Col. 0306B] If then, brothers, our soul has become a castle, as we have said, two women must dwell in it: one who sits at Jesus’ feet to hear his word, and another who ministers to Jesus in order to feed him. Consider, brothers. If Mary alone had been in that house, no one would have fed the Lord. If Martha alone, no one would have delighted in the Lord’s words and presence. Therefore, brothers, Martha signifies that activity by which a person labors for Christ; Mary, however, that repose by which one is free from bodily works and delights in God’s sweetness, whether through reading, prayer, or contemplation. Therefore, brothers, so long as Christ is poor, walks on earth on foot, hungers, thirsts, and is tempted, it is necessary [Col. 0306C] that these two women should be in one house—that these two activities should be in the same soul. So long as you and I and that other person are on earth—provided that we are his members—he is on earth. So long as those who are his members hunger and thirst and are tempted, Christ hungers, thirsts, and is tempted. Therefore he will say on the day of judgment: “As long as you did it to one of my least ones, you did it to me” (Matt. XXV).

Therefore, brothers, in this wretched and laborious life Martha must be in our house: that is, our soul must apply itself to bodily actions. For as long as we need to eat and drink, so long must we tame the flesh by vigils, fasts, and bodily labor. This is Martha’s part. [Col. 0306D] Mary too must be in our soul—that is, spiritual activity. We ought not always to attend to bodily exercises, but at times to be still and see how gracious and sweet the Lord is (Ps. XXXIII); to sit at Jesus’ feet and hear his word. You must by no means neglect Mary for Martha’s sake, nor Martha for Mary’s sake. For if you neglect Martha, who will feed Jesus? If you neglect Mary, what benefits you that Jesus has entered your house, when you taste nothing of his sweetness?

Know, brothers, that in this life these women must never be separated. When that time comes in which Jesus will be neither poor, nor hungry, nor thirsty, nor any longer capable of being tempted, then Mary alone—that is, spiritual activity—will occupy this entire house, namely our soul. Saint Benedict saw this; indeed, the Holy Spirit in Saint Benedict saw it. Therefore he did not merely say and ordain that we should attend to reading, as it were to Mary, while omitting labor, as it were Martha; rather, he commended both to us, assigning fixed times for Martha’s work and fixed times for Mary’s work. These two activities existed perfectly in Blessed Mary, our Lady. That she clothed our Lord, fed him, carried him, and fled with him into Egypt—all this belongs to bodily activity. But that she pondered all these words, keeping them together in her heart (Luke II); that she considered his divinity, contemplated his power, and tasted [Col. 0307B] his sweetness—all this belongs to Mary. Hence the Evangelist aptly says: “Mary, sitting at Jesus’ feet, heard his word” (Luke X).

According to Martha’s part, Blessed Mary was not sitting at Jesus’ feet. Rather, as I suppose, the Lord Jesus himself sat at the feet of his most sweet Mother. For, as the Evangelist says—and he himself says—“He was subject to them” (Luke II), namely Mary and Joseph. Yet inasmuch as she saw and knew his divinity, she undoubtedly sat at his feet, for she humbled herself before him and regarded herself as his handmaid. According to Martha’s part she ministered to him as to one weak and small, hungry and thirsty; she grieved at his sufferings and at the insults which the Jews inflicted upon him. Thus he says to her: “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and [Col. 0307C] troubled about many things” (Luke X). According to Mary’s part, she supplicated him as Lord, worshipped him as her Lord, and, as far as she could, longed after his spiritual sweetness.

Therefore, my brothers, while we are in this body, in this exile, in this place of penitence, let us know that what the Lord said to Adam is more proper and more natural to us: “In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread” (Gen. III). For this belongs to Martha. Whatever we taste of spiritual sweetness is only, so to speak, a small extra portion by which God sustains our weakness. Therefore, dearest brothers, let us diligently do what belongs to Martha; and with all fear and care let us practice what belongs to Mary, abandoning neither one’s part for the other’s. It will sometimes happen that Martha wishes to have Mary in her labor, but she must not be yielded to. “Lord,” she says, “do you not care that my sister has left me alone to minister? Tell her, therefore, to help me” (Luke X). It is a temptation.

See then, brothers: when, in the time in which we ought to devote ourselves to reading and prayer, our thought suggests that we should go to this or that task, as though it were necessary, then in a certain way Martha calls Mary to help her; but the Lord judges well and justly. He does not command Martha to sit with Mary, nor does he command Mary to rise and minister with Martha. Mary’s part is indeed better, sweeter, and more pleasant; nevertheless [Col. 0308A] he does not wish Martha’s work to be abandoned on its account. Martha’s part is more laborious; nevertheless he does not wish Mary’s repose to be disturbed. He wishes, therefore, that each should perform her own part. Whoever understand this to mean that some people in this life ought to follow Martha’s part alone, while others ought to apply themselves to Mary’s part alone, undoubtedly err and do not understand. Both women are in one castle, both in one house; both are pleasing and acceptable to the Lord, both beloved by the Lord, as the Gospel says: “Jesus loved Mary and Martha and Lazarus” (John XI). Or let them say which of the holy Fathers ever came to perfection without both activities.

Since both these parts must be practiced by each one of us, we must undoubtedly at fixed times do what belongs to Martha, and at fixed times what belongs to Mary, unless necessity intervenes, which knows no law. Therefore we must diligently keep the times appointed for us by the Holy Spirit: namely, at the time for reading, we must be steadfast and quiet, neither yielding to idleness or sluggishness nor withdrawing ourselves from Jesus’ feet, but sitting there and hearing his word. At the time for labor, we must be energetic and ready, and must in no way omit the service of truth under the pretext of repose. Nor should we ever mingle these two, except through obedience, before which we must prefer neither repose nor labor, neither action nor contemplation, nor anything whatever—if it compels us, so to speak, even to leave Jesus’ feet. For certainly, though it would have been sweeter for Mary to sit at Jesus’ feet, if the Lord had commanded her, she would without any doubt have risen and ministered with her sister. But the Lord did not command this, in order in this action to commend both activities, and in order that we might carefully observe these two at all times, unless something else is commanded us, and not abandon one for the other.

We should consider what the Lord says: “Mary has chosen the best part, which shall not be taken away from her.” In these words the Lord gives us great consolation. Martha’s part shall be taken from us, but Mary’s part shall not be taken away. Who would not grow weary of these [Col. 0308D] labors and miseries if they were always to remain with us? Therefore the Lord consoles us. Let us act manfully, then; let us endure these labors and miseries manfully, knowing that they will have an end. Again, who would greatly value these spiritual consolations if they endured no longer than this life lasts? But Mary’s part will not be taken from us; rather, it will be increased. What here we begin to taste in certain very tiny drops, after this life we shall drink unto a kind of spiritual intoxication, as the Prophet says: “They shall be intoxicated with the abundance of your house, and you shall make them drink from the torrent of your delight” (Ps. XXXV). Therefore let us not be overcome by these labors, because they will be taken from us. Let us eagerly desire the taste of divine sweetness, because it indeed begins here, but after this life [Col. 0309A] it will be perfected in us and will remain in us forever. May blessed Mary assist us in attaining that blessedness through her Son, our Lord, who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XVIII. ON THE ASSUMPTION OF BLESSED MARY

Our Lord does not wish us to suffer weariness. Therefore he visits us, sometimes in person, sometimes through Holy Scripture, sometimes through our sermons, in which we recount something about him, sometimes also through the sweetness of the good things which he has done for us through himself, and sometimes through what he has done through his own servants. These are our dishes, with which he [Col. 0309B] feeds our soul, so that we may suffer neither hunger nor any weariness in eating. But just as among all the saints she is more excellent, more blessed, and sweeter, who tastes his sweetness more familiarly and delightfully; and just as she is not merely his creature, handmaid, friend, or daughter, but also his mother: so it is fitting that we receive her feast with greater sweetness and joy, and that at her festival we feed ourselves more abundantly with spiritual banquets.

And certainly, brothers, although we should always praise and honor her and rehearse her sweetness with every devotion, today we ought to rejoice with her more fully, because today her joy was perfectly fulfilled. She had great joy when the angel greeted her. She had great joy when she felt the coming of the Holy Spirit, when that wondrous union was made in her womb between the Son of God and her flesh, so that he who was the Son of God might be her son. She had great joy when she held such a son in her arms, kissed him, ministered to him, heard his words, and saw his miracles. And because she had been greatly saddened in his Passion, she again had wondrous joy in his resurrection, and greater joy still in his ascension. But the joy which she received today surpassed all these joys.

You know well, my brothers, that in our Lord Jesus there are two natures, divine and human. These two [Col. 0309D] natures are so perfectly in him that the divine nature was not changed on account of the human, nor the human annihilated on account of the divine. Thus he is both equal to the Father and less than the Father: equal according to divinity, less according to humanity. Certainly, brothers, it is a great good and a great joy to know our Lord Jesus Christ according to his humanity, to love him and think of him; as it were to behold within one’s heart his birth, passion, wounds, death, and resurrection. Yet much greater is the joy of one who can say with the Apostle: “Even though we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him so no longer” (2 Cor. V).

It is a great thing to see how our Lord lay in the manger; but it is a far greater joy to see how he reigns in heaven. It is a great joy to see how he suckles at the breast; but far greater to see how he feeds all things. It is a great joy to see him in the arms of one maiden, but a greater joy to see how he contains all things in heaven and earth. Until this day, brothers, the blessed Mary, Mother of God, knew her most sweet son according to the flesh. For although, after that most beloved son and Lord of hers ascended into heaven, all her desire and love were where he was, still, so long as she remained in this corruptible flesh, what she had seen of him according to the flesh could not pass from her memory. His deeds and words always came to her mind, and above all the image of the beauty of his face dwelt [Col. 0310B] in her heart.

But today she passed from this world and ascended to the heavenly kingdoms, where she began to contemplate his brightness and the divinity of the Father; and her joy and desire were fulfilled, so that she could deservedly say: “I have found him whom my soul loves” (Song III). She holds him and does not let him go. Earlier she had found him whom her flesh loved, since the flesh still savored flesh, and a human being another human being; she held him, yet let him go. She held him according to the flesh, and therefore through death lost him in some measure—according to the flesh. Today she has found him whom her soul loves. For although, as some believe, she was also assumed bodily into heaven, nevertheless that body was surely made spiritual, so that all the love by which she loves her Lord, her son, is not according to the flesh but according to the spirit. Today she has found him whom her soul loves; she has found him according to the spirit, loves him according to the spirit, and holds him according to the spirit; and therefore she will never lose him again. Today she has found him because today the shadow of death departed and the light of light arose for her. In the night she sought him but had not found him; therefore she says: “Upon my bed by night I sought him whom my soul loves; I sought him and did not find him” (ibid.).

As long as she lived this life, it was night; yet in this night she did not cease to seek, and therefore, when the night passed, she found him. “Upon my bed,” she says, “I sought him whom my soul loves.” What is this bed? Who can say what this bed is and was like? If it were bodily, it would not be necessary to seek long. Suppose that this is the bed of which she elsewhere says: “Our bed is flowering” (Song I). And what was that bed? It was where her heart was, where were the flowers of every virtue. It was rightly called a bed because of the wondrous repose and tranquillity which she possessed there. There was no tumult of vain thoughts there; no desires of this world, no carnal passions or longings. Where these are, there is no bed, for no one can have repose and tranquillity who has such tumults in the heart. Many make themselves a bed, not in the heart but in the flesh, because they have no repose in the heart on account of an evil conscience; but they lie in the flesh—that is, in fleshly desires—and there rest as if upon a bed. To such persons the Apostle says: “Awake, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ shall enlighten you” (Eph. V).

But blessed Mary had her repose not in the flesh but in her mind and good conscience. There she rested, and did not rest. She rested from every worldly care, every tumult of vices, every noise of vain thoughts; yet she did not rest, because she desired and sighed, and with groaning and tears sought him whom she loved. “Upon my bed by night I sought him whom my soul loves.” But let us see when she began to seek.

First, before the Lord’s coming, she sought and desired him. She sought that he might come to earth as he had promised, redeem the world, and free her with the rest from that wretched captivity. She sought him not in the marketplace or at the fairs, but upon her bed, in the secret chamber of her heart. This is the bed in which Abishag the Shunammite warmed King David. We read in the Books of Kings that David the king, because of extreme old age, had become so cold that he could in no way be warmed. He was covered with garments, as Scripture says, and was not warmed. Then the king’s servants said to him: “Let us seek for our lord the king a young maiden, a beautiful virgin, to minister to him, sleep in his bosom, and warm our lord the king.” And they found a certain virgin named Abishag the Shunammite; she was with the king, ministering to him and warming him. “But the king did not know her” (3 Kings I).

You know well that King David signifies our Lord Jesus Christ, who was born from his seed. He had, spiritually speaking, a certain infancy and childhood, a certain youth, and a certain old age. His infancy was, as it were, when he first began to be born in the hearts of the holy Fathers who lived before his coming. He was born in their hearts in two ways: through knowledge and through love. He began to be born in Abraham’s heart when Abraham was told that one would be born from his seed in whom all nations would be blessed (Gen. XXVI). We see this now fulfilled, because all nations are now blessed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was born from Abraham’s seed. Likewise, he began, as it were, to be born in Isaac’s heart when his coming began to be made known to him; likewise in Jacob’s heart and in those of the other patriarchs. But this was still, as it were, his infancy. Infancy is that age at which a child cannot yet speak. Knowledge of our Lord had already, as it were, been born, but it did not yet speak, because the holy Fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob did not openly preach his coming to all people. Yet although they did not speak openly of him, they nevertheless warmed him—that is, embraced him with ardent love.

Afterward came, as it were, his childhood, when the Law was given, when this knowledge of him began to speak to all through the various ordinances and sacrifices of the old Law. In all these Christ undoubtedly spoke and made himself known to them, but in some manner through childish words—that is, through carnal observances and ceremonies. Afterward he began to show his youth, when he began much more openly to show his strength—which is customarily greater in a person’s youth: that strength which was to conquer the devil, despoil hell, redeem the world, rise from the dead, condemn the wicked on the day of judgment, and crown the saints. All this our Lord himself spoke through his prophets.

We could show you all this plainly in the writings of the prophets, but we would make too great a digression. These spiritual powers which our Lord Jesus Christ exercised are signified by David’s bodily powers, battles, and victories in his youth. For without doubt, whoever could investigate and examine David’s battles and victories spiritually would find that Holy Scripture contains not empty fables or simple narratives, but would see all things full of great mysteries. In this, as it were, his youth, our David was warmed all the more as there were more who knew, loved, and desired him.

Afterward holy David began, as it were, to grow cold. For iniquity abounded and the charity of many grew cold, so that, with the Lord’s coming now approaching, the Prophet says because of the multitude of evils: “They have all turned aside; together they have become useless. There is none who does good, not even one” (Ps. XIII). Then our David was covered with garments but was not warmed. His garments were, as it were, the high priests, priests, and Jews generally, whom our Lord had spiritually joined to himself as garments. In a manner, he was already covered with these garments before his coming: for they frequented the Temple; the high priests and priests offered sacrifices; they celebrated their feasts, Sabbaths, new moons, and other things of that sort. But all this did not warm our Lord, because the warmth of true love was not in their hearts. They did all these things not from love but from hypocrisy, as our Lord showed plainly enough. It was therefore necessary to provide a virgin maiden in whose embrace that true David might rest, in whose bosom he might sleep, and who might warm him, now grown cold and old, upon her bed.

Our David himself provided, knew—indeed, himself made ready for himself—this virgin, purer than every virgin, holier than every woman, stronger than every man, fairer than the sun, more fervent than fire; nevertheless, he wished her to be sought through his servants. Solomon sought her, saying: “Who shall find a strong woman?” (Prov. XXXI). Isaiah sought and found her, and therefore said: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel” (Isa. VII). Jeremiah sought and found her, and marvelled, saying: “The Lord has created a new thing upon the earth: a woman shall encompass a man” (Jer. XXXI). Finally Saint Gabriel sought her; he sought, found, recognized, greeted, [Col. 0313A] and invited her to the embrace of the true David. She alone was found in whose bosom the true David would rest more familiarly, by whose embrace he would be warmed more sweetly, and with whom he would sleep more tranquilly in bed: namely, our Lady Saint Mary. In her most sacred breast the flame of charity had not grown lukewarm; and as she loved more than all others, so she desired more than all others, and therefore sought more diligently.

But him whom her flesh still loved, her soul now loves. Therefore she says: “Upon my bed I sought him whom my soul loves” (Song III). She does not say, “whom my soul loved,” but “whom my soul loves.” For then her flesh loved him in a certain manner. Although the power of divine love wholly possessed her most holy soul, so that she could rightly be called Shunammite—for *Shunammite* means “scarlet,” and scarlet is the color of fire—displaying the flame of charity and glowing with the fire of divine love; although, therefore, she loved God with her whole soul, still, because she was concerned for her own salvation and that of the whole world, which he had yet to accomplish, desiring him through his flesh—that is, his very humanity—she still thought of him according to the flesh, sought him according to the flesh, and her very soul loved him according to the flesh. She indeed sought him whom her soul loved, but in a certain manner according to the flesh, not altogether according to the spirit.

“Upon my bed by night I sought him whom my soul loves.” In this first seeking of hers it was undoubtedly night, because the night of unbelief then occupied the whole world. “I sought,” she says, “and did not find.” What shall we say? Did she not find him? Did not this our Shunammite embrace the true David, not only upon the bed of her heart but upon the bed of her flesh? What then means, “I sought him and did not find him”? Consider, then, that these words do not fit her in that time when she savored the Son of God according to the flesh, but rather in the present time, when she has ascended into heaven. Therefore she recounts the matter as past, saying: “Upon my bed I sought him whom my soul loves.” And see how subtly she places the seeking itself in the past tense: “Upon my bed,” she says, “I sought”; but she places the loving in the present tense, as though saying: Then I sought him whom my soul now loves. And she adds: “I sought him and did not find him.” But how did she not find him—she who conceived him in her womb, bore him from her chaste body, fed him from her breasts, and cherished him in holy embraces; she who, a virgin, conceived him, a virgin bore him, and after giving birth, still a virgin, nourished him?

Therefore Scripture rightly says of Abishag the Shunammite: “But the king did not know her” (3 Kings I). Nowhere do we read that Abishag was anything but a virgin. Indeed, Adonijah, Solomon’s brother, who with rash daring wished to violate her, received a sentence of death. Therefore Abishag was a virgin before the king’s embrace, a virgin in the king’s embrace, and a virgin after the king’s embrace. Do you see how clearly the virginity of this most holy virgin, most blessed Mary, is commended? Before the king’s conception—when the Son of God, in the wondrous embrace of union, joined flesh from the virgin’s flesh to himself—she was a virgin; nor did she lose the seal of that virginity in conception, unseal it in childbirth, or fail to preserve it wholly intact after childbirth. Do you wish to hear further what the wisest Solomon thought of the excellence of Abishag the Shunammite? When Bathsheba asked that Abishag be given to Adonijah, Solomon replied: “Why do you ask Abishag the Shunammite for Adonijah? Ask the kingdom for him also” (3 Kings II). O virgin of wondrous excellence, whose embrace he who merits also merits the kingdom! Why? Because the embrace of a king alone was fitting for this our Shunammite: for her most chaste womb was reserved for him, and her mind was prepared by the working of the Holy Spirit. How, then, did Abishag not find him whom she sought upon the bed of her heart and received upon the bed of her flesh?

Consider, brothers, and, if you can, think and infer how deeply she felt concerning her most sweet son today, to what glory she came, and how perfectly the love and knowledge of his divinity absorbed her, so that before this time she says that she had not found him, though she is known to have borne him from her womb. We have spoken of her first seeking. Again she sought him after his Passion and death. This seeking was plainly full of pain and anguish. Then was fulfilled in her what Saint Simeon had prophesied: “A sword shall pierce your own soul also” (Luke II): the sword of pain, the sword [Col. 0314C] of sorrow, the sword of compassion. What torrents of tears then burst from her most chaste eyes when she saw her son hanging thus upon the cross, given gall to drink, mocked by the ungodly! With what grief did she hear, “Woman, behold your son” (John XIX), namely, that she should receive the disciple in place of her son! Then indeed the sword of sorrow pierced her soul, reaching almost to the division of her soul and body (Heb. IV).

Then undoubtedly she sought him whom her soul now loves; she sought him with affection and desire, so that she did not escape what the Apostle lamented: “The flesh lusts against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Gal. V). For from fleshly affection I do not doubt that she then wished her son to be freed from that death, the Jews’ mockery to be refuted, or, if she could, that she herself might undergo death. Then too it was night, because overwhelming adversity darkened all her joy; overwhelming sorrow had almost hidden the power of reason in his death. Therefore she then sought but did not find, because that fleshly will of hers was not fulfilled, by which she wished that her son should not suffer; rather, her spiritual will was fulfilled, by which she wished eternal salvation to be accomplished through the death of her son.

Third, she began to seek him after his ascension. She sought, I believe, in two ways. For what she had bodily seen of him still lived in her memory; she pondered his delightful manner of life, gracious speech, pleasing appearance, and most sweet affection of compassion. And because she still lived in the body, she often sought his [Col. 0315A] bodily presence as well. At other times, raising herself to higher things and reflecting in her mind upon that heavenly life, she used to disdain all earthly things, sigh after heavenly things with all her affection, and, though present on earth only in body, dwell in heart where she thought her son reigned above all things. Then the absence of her son was night to her; so too was the enclosure of her body, by whose bond she was then held, so that she could not wholly cling to her son’s embraces. By these nights, therefore—first before his coming, then in his Passion, and afterward when his ascension had been accomplished—she sought him whom her soul loves. “I sought,” she says, “and did not find”; and she added: “I will rise and go about the city; through the lanes and streets I will seek him whom my soul loves” (Song III).

[Col. 0315B] Here I understand the city to be the heavenly Jerusalem, whose streets, according to the Prophet, are paved with pure gold and through whose lanes *Alleluia* is sung. But what does she mean when she says, “I will rise and go about the city”? If I dared, I would say that the most blessed Mother of God, Mary, first left the flesh and afterward rose in that flesh to eternal life. But although I do not dare affirm this, because I have no means by which I could convince anyone who opposed it, I nevertheless dare to offer it as an opinion. Yet I do dare to affirm without doubt that on this present day the blessed Virgin, whether in the body or outside the body—I do not know; God knows—ascended into heaven and went about that entire heavenly city in the quickness of her mind. On this day she indeed entered that heavenly court, found the white robes of virgins, the rose-colored crowns of martyrs, the thrones of apostles, and her son reigning in all of them.

Why, then, does she still say: “I sought him and did not find him”? Recall, brothers, what I said a little earlier. For also in that first seeking, when she sought him, she found him on this day so perfectly and so blessedly that she rightly confesses that she had not found him before. So here as well: rising beyond all the heights of the saints, she attained such knowledge of the Divinity that she now first glories in having found him. Therefore she says: “The watchmen who guard the city found me” (ibid.). The watchmen are the angels who guard the city of God, namely the holy Church, and protect it from the devil’s assaults and snares. And certainly, brothers, it is certain that the whole host of angels came today to meet the most blessed Mary. They found her in the world and carried her out of the world. But though she saw the angels’ brightness, glory, and blessedness, this did not suffice her; rather, she desired more to see him alone whom she loved above all things. Therefore she says: “Have you seen him whom my soul loves?” And she adds: “When I had passed a little beyond them, I found him whom my soul loves.”

O blessed soul, which passed beyond not only patriarchs and prophets, apostles, martyrs, confessors, and virgins, but also angels, thrones and dominions, cherubim and seraphim, and every host of heaven, and thus came to her most sweet one. [Col. 0316A] Then she perfectly found him whom her soul now perfectly loves. She found him and held him. “I held him,” she says, “and I will not let him go.” She held him and holds him, and will never let him go. She holds him in the embraces of perfect charity and will never be able to lose him, because she will never be able to love less.

Let us therefore, brothers, raise our hearts to this our Lady, our advocate. Let us consider how great a hope we can place in her. For as she is more excellent than every creature, so she is more merciful and gracious. Let us therefore pray to her confidently: she is able to help us through her excellence and willing through mercy, so that she may intercede with her Son for us; that, as he deigned to be born of her for us, through her he may deign to have mercy upon us—he who lives and reigns as God with the Father [Col. 0316B] and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XIX. ON THE NATIVITY OF BLESSED MARY
“Come to me, all you who desire me, and be filled from my offspring; for my spirit is sweeter than honey, and my inheritance sweeter than honey and the honeycomb; my remembrance endures through generations of ages” (Sirach 24).

These words which we have just spoken are written in a certain book in the person of Wisdom. For Wisdom calls us and says: “Come to me.” You know, brothers, that our Lord Jesus Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God. Therefore these are the words of Christ, who calls us to himself and says: “Come to me.” [Col. 0316C] Look, brothers. He stands as though upon a high mountain, sees us placed in the valley, and says: “Come across.” Either a wall stands between us and him, or a sea, or something of that sort which we must cross in order to come to him. And I think that both are between us and him: both sea and wall; and, further, a cloud. Thus a certain saint says to the Lord: “You have set a cloud in the way, so that prayer may not pass through” (Lam. 3). We must cross all these things if we wish to come to Jesus: that is, the wall, the sea, and the cloud. But we must know the differences among these things, and afterwards the manner of crossing them. For we cannot cross the sea except by wood; the wall except by iron; the cloud except by light.

Let us know, then, brothers, that this sea which [Col. 0316D] lies between us and God is the present age, of which the Psalmist says: “This sea, great and broad of hands” [i.e. broad in extent] (Ps. 103 [104]). Unless we cross this sea, we shall in no way be able to come to him who says: “Come to me, all.” Some are drowned in this sea; others cross it. Those are drowned who are without a ship in this sea, or who leave the ship, or who are driven out by some storm. This ship, without which no one can cross this age, is the profession of Christ’s cross. Without this wood no one can cross the sea. Yet some have a better and stronger ship than others.

Marriage contracted in the faith of Jesus Christ is, as it were, a ship. But this ship is weak and leaky, and it takes much sea-water into its bilge; unless it is continually bailed out, it quickly sinks. For in this way of life there are [Col. 0317A] many worldly occupations; and very often there occur, if not sins that bring condemnation, at least many other sins. Unless these are bailed out by alms and great works of mercy, they sink this ship, so that it cannot reach the harbor. Yet this manner of life is, in this life, a profession of Christ’s cross; it is a ship, and by this ship a person can cross over to Christ. But whoever, after professing marriage, falls into adultery or other condemnable sins, has left the ship; therefore that person is drowned and cannot cross this sea, unless perhaps he returns again to his ship through repentance.

There is another ship: the renunciation of this world. Whoever has left the age and committed himself to some holy community, in order to be under another’s rule and authority, has [Col. 0317B] entered the ship so as to cross the age. But whoever, after entering a religious community, leaves it again and returns to the world has left the ship and will be drowned in the sea unless he returns to the ship again. The storm that throws a person out of this ship is temptation. Therefore I exhort you, dearest brothers, who have chosen this order for yourselves as a most strong and excellent ship, to hold fast within it; nor let yourselves be drawn out of this ship by any flattery or force.

For your adversary the devil circles around this ship: sometimes he flatters in order to draw you out, and sometimes he frightens you. He flatters when he sets before you the delights of the age and worldly glory; when he promises you a long life and displays to you the greatness of God’s mercy, and [Col. 0317C] other such things. He frightens you when he sets before you the harshness of this order, speaking, as it were, within your mind and saying: “How will you be able always to endure these things? You have a long time to live, and will always be in this misery, always struggling against your flesh, against your thoughts, never free from fear. And after thirty years, by one sin, you can lose all these labors.” These are his fabrications and lies. Let us not listen to them. Let us hold ourselves in this ship; let us cling to the cross of Jesus, so that we may come to him who calls us and says: “Come to me.”

There is still a wall between us and God. This is the wall which we have built out of diverse vices and sins, and many stones, of which the prophet says: [Col. 0317D] “Your sins separate between you and God” (Isa. 59). We cannot demolish and destroy this wall except by iron, and sharp iron. This iron is repentance. Therefore, whoever wishes his sins to be scattered—which without doubt are like a wall between us and God—must devote himself to works of repentance. By the iron of abstinence, let him destroy lust; by the iron of poverty, avarice; by the iron of silence, quarrels; by contempt for honor and dignity, as by the sharpest iron, envy; by the mortification of his own will, the wantonness of the mind. By each exercise, which is as it were a very sharp tool, let him break and crush each vice, like the hardest stones, and steadfastly cross over to him [Col. 0318A] who says: “Come to me.”

But a cloud still hinders us. The cloud is ignorance, by which we are often blinded, so that in many matters we do not know what we ought to do. Let us keep our eyes upon that lamp of which the Prophet says: “Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths” (Ps. 118 [119]). The word of God, Holy Scripture, is itself the light and lamp upon which we must look without ceasing, lest the cloud of ignorance hinder us: namely, so that we may perform these exercises which must be done only according to the rule of Holy Scripture and the teaching of those who minister the word of God to us. Therefore, brothers, since you are in the ship by which you can cross this great and broad sea—that is, the present age; since you have the best and sharpest instruments, by which you can destroy [Col. 0318B] that wall which separates you from God; since you have a lamp by which you can penetrate the cloud of ignorance: do not stand still, but cross over to him who calls you and says: “Come to me.”

But who says this? Who are those whom he calls? Hear: “Come to me, all who desire me.” Clearly, only those who desire him can cross over to him. Therefore those who desire gold, silver, the riches of this world, or honors cannot cross over to Christ. Therefore, brothers, desire Christ, and thus cross over to Christ. But what is it to cross over to Christ? There are three crossings to Christ: one in this life, another after death, and a third on the day of judgment after the resurrection. In this life [Col. 0318C] we must cross over to Christ, that is, to imitate him; after this life, to rest with him; on the day of judgment, to reign with him.

The most blessed Mary heard this voice, heard it and followed it. She perfectly crossed this sea of which we have spoken, this wall, and this cloud. Therefore she came perfectly to Wisdom itself, which cries and says: “Come to me, all who desire me.” Therefore these words are read especially on her feast. She desired Christ, and therefore crossed over to Christ. She desired him perfectly: from infancy, for love of him, she despised the world, cut off the desires of the flesh, and accounted all the world’s glory as nothing. Nor should you wonder that I said she desired [Col. 0318D] Christ from infancy, although Christ had not yet been born, since the Apostle says of Moses: “Esteeming the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures of Egypt” (Heb. 11). Moses lived long before Christ’s birth, yet in view of Christ’s sufferings he chose to undergo suffering rather than reign in Egypt.

So the most blessed Mary, because she knew that Christ was to be born, began to imitate his way of life, although his way of life had not yet appeared on earth; just as Moses already imitated his suffering, though his passion had not yet occurred. Thus blessed Mary so perfectly crossed over to Christ in heart that he also crossed over to her and remained in her even bodily. This was signified by the fact that Mary, the sister of Aaron, went before the children of Israel [Col. 0319A] when they crossed the Red Sea, and went before them with a timbrel (Exod. 15). For without doubt the most blessed Mary—the true Mary, of whom that Mary bore the type—goes before all who have crossed this sea, that is, the present age. She goes before them in dignity, holiness, purity, and also in mortification of the flesh—that is, with the timbrel. She also went before them in this: that she was the first of all humankind to escape the curse of the first parents. Therefore she deserved to hear from the angel: “Blessed among women” (Luke 1); that is, while all women are under the curse, you alone among them deserve this wondrous blessing.

Therefore, dearest brothers, let us imitate, as far as we can, our most blessed Lady; [Col. 0319B] let us desire Wisdom; let us cross over to Wisdom, who cries and says: “Come to me, all who desire me, and be filled from my offspring.”

What are the offspring of Wisdom? This may be understood in two ways: namely, as the offspring through which Wisdom itself is generated in us, or the offspring which Wisdom itself generates in us. Today the Gospel read: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ” (Matt. 1). And, as the Evangelist says later: “From Abraham to David, fourteen generations” (ibid.), and so forth, down to Christ. These, therefore, are the generations of Christ—and, if of Christ, certainly of Wisdom. But these are the generations through which Wisdom itself is generated in us according to [Col. 0319C] the flesh. Perhaps through these generations Wisdom is still spiritually born in us.

Therefore, if we may understand it thus: “Be filled from my offspring”—that is, let us have spiritually within ourselves Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Judah, and the other holy fathers according to whom the generations of Wisdom—that is, of Christ—are recounted; for without doubt Wisdom is born from these. Therefore, if you wish Christ to be born in you, possess and fill yourself with the offspring of Wisdom, that is, of Christ. How? Have within yourself Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and others such as those in whom Christ’s generations are described. Abraham was perfect in faith; Isaac was the son of promise; Jacob saw the Lord face to face. Therefore have perfect faith within yourselves, and you will have [Col. 0319D] Abraham spiritually. Hope for the promises to come; despise present pleasures, and you will have Isaac. Hasten, as much as you can, toward the vision of God, and you will have Jacob.

Likewise, if you are fervent in spirit, you will have Abraham; if rejoicing in hope, Isaac; if patient in tribulation, Jacob. For Abraham so burned in spirit that he wished to offer his only son to God. Isaac is interpreted “laughter,” and therefore signifies the joy which we ought to have in hope. Jacob was patient in labor, as he himself said to Laban: “By day and by night I was burned by heat and frost, and thus for twenty years I served you” (Gen. 31). Thus, if we have spiritually within ourselves all these fathers of whom the Gospel speaks today, then what Wisdom says will come to pass: “Be filled from my offspring.” [Col. 0320A]

But if you wish here to understand those offspring which Wisdom itself generates in us, consider that Wisdom is the mother and teacher of all virtues. For, as it is written of her: “She teaches sobriety, prudence, justice, and virtue” (Wis. 8). These are Wisdom’s first offspring: namely, the four principal virtues, which even pagan philosophers could recognize under reason’s instruction: temperance, here called sobriety; prudence; justice; and fortitude, here called virtue.

Other offspring are born from these, and yet others from these, with all of which Wisdom wishes us to be filled, when it says: “Be filled from my offspring.” Through temperance we are chaste; through prudence we choose good things [Col. 0320B] and reject evil things; through justice we love God and neighbor; through fortitude we persevere in all these things. Therefore cross over to Wisdom and be filled from her offspring. “For my spirit,” she says, “is sweeter than honey, and my inheritance sweeter than honey and the honeycomb.”

Nothing tastes sweeter than honey to the palate of the flesh; nothing sweeter than the Spirit of God to the palate of the heart. Yet he has set down two things here, his spirit and his inheritance; he seems to grant something greater to his inheritance than to his spirit: “For my spirit is sweeter than honey.” But what is sweeter than God’s Spirit, since God’s Spirit is God? What is more excellent, sweeter, or more delightful than God? But here we must understand the Holy Spirit according to [Col. 0320C] the way in which we now receive him within ourselves, as the Apostle says: “God, who accomplishes us for this very thing, has given us the pledge of the Spirit” (2 Cor. 5). These are the spiritual visitations and consolations by which, meanwhile, we are delighted as by a certain pledge, until we reach the perfect inheritance. This inheritance is in the kingdom of heaven; and fittingly this spiritual sweetness, by which we are refreshed in the present, is compared to honey.

The bee, whose product is honey, is a most chaste creature; for bees are not generated through carnal intercourse. Therefore the bee signifies a chaste and sober mind, such as Wisdom gladly inhabits. This chaste soul, then, like a bee, flies through the field of the Scriptures in diligent meditation. There, from the sayings and examples [Col. 0320D] of the saints, it gathers certain spiritual flowers. From these there arises in its heart a wondrous delight and a great sweetness of heavenly pleasantness; and it thus experiences that the Spirit of the Lord is sweeter than honey. “And my inheritance,” it says, “is sweeter than honey and the honeycomb.” The comparison is fitting. Do not those little cells which you are accustomed to see in a honeycomb show you a certain likeness of that inheritance of which the Lord says: “In my Father’s house are many dwelling places” (John 14)? Therefore he added honey with the honeycomb, because in those eternal dwelling places there is everlasting and ineffable sweetness.

See: although the crossing to Wisdom may seem laborious, its fruit is nevertheless great. Labor ought not to frighten you more than fruit delights you. It is indeed a great labor to cross the waves and storms [Col. 0321A] of this age, to tread underfoot all delights and pleasures, and to despise the rest and ease of the flesh.
