But this is the crossing by which one reaches Wisdom, whose spirit is sweeter than honey and whose inheritance is sweeter than honey and the honeycomb.

It may seem easy and pleasant to love worldly honors, follow one’s own will, and lead one’s life amid pleasures and delights; but the fruit is bitter. The Apostle distinguishes between these fruits, saying: “For the wages of sin is death, but the grace of God is eternal life” (Rom. 6). Eternal death is the bitter fruit; eternal life the sweet fruit. Sin leads there; here, not our merits but God’s grace leads. Why? Because we must attribute wholly to God’s grace everything by which we cross over to Wisdom; it grants us the strength by which [Col. 0321B] we can cross.

“My remembrance endures through generations of ages.” If you had remembrance of gold, silver, and riches, how far could that remembrance extend? At most, a hundred years. For who lives longer in these times? If you think of Christ, if you think of Wisdom, this remembrance can extend through generations of ages—that is, into eternity. For Wisdom will always be, and you can always be with Wisdom, because, as it is written, “Wisdom is immortal” (Wis. 4). So long as someone lives, he may perhaps be rich; thus the remembrance of riches may last for that long. But if anyone fixes his remembrance on lust and the pleasures of the flesh, how quickly they end, how briefly they last! In one moment all that delight passes away.

What of the delights [Col. 0321C] of the belly? When a rich man is filled with ten or twelve dishes, does not all pleasure in costly foods depart? Yet, to speak briefly, no remembrance of temporal things can extend beyond the time a person lives, because no one can think that he will possess temporal things any longer than he lives this life. But if he thinks of the kingdom of heaven, the glory of angels, and the blessedness which consists in the vision of God, incorruption, and immortality, this remembrance can extend through generations of ages—that is, into eternity—because these things will remain forever. Therefore he says: “My remembrance endures through generations of ages.”

Therefore, brothers, to bring our sermon at last [Col. 0321D] to an end, let us cross beyond these earthly and passing things, so that we may attain Wisdom and be filled from her offspring—that is, from those virtues by which she is generated within us. Let us experience, as far as we can, that her spirit is sweet and her inheritance sweeter than honey and the honeycomb. Let us remove, as far as we can, our remembrance from the world itself and transfer our heart to eternal things, so that, through the intercession for us of our most blessed Lady Saint Mary, whose feast we celebrate today, we may one day be able to attain those things which are eternal, through the granting of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XX. ON THE SAME SOLEMNITY, II

[Col. 0322A]

Wondrous is the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ. He is our judge, and he knows that we are wretched and cannot, by ourselves, have a good case in his judgment. He is merciful and wishes to have mercy on us, but he cannot judge except justly. How, then, has he provided for us? He teaches us to live well, but we live contrariwise. Through baptism he first forgave us all sins, and afterwards we fell. We have often promised amendment, and nevertheless we always sin. He gives us opportunity for repentance, and we neglect it. Yet beyond all this he spares us; and because we are unworthy, not such persons as he ought to hear, he sets before us his friends, so that we may ask them, [Col. 0322B] approach him through them, and be reconciled to him.

You know that people of this age customarily do this. When their lord is angry with them, they seek out his intimates, sometimes even his bride: so that, if perhaps they are not guilty, the lord may more readily hear their cause when it is stated by one whom he greatly loves; and, if they are guilty, may forgive them through that person’s prayer. We read of a certain holy king who rejoiced when someone pleaded for a person whom he was obliged by the laws to punish, so that he might have a just ground for forgiving him. Without doubt that king imitated our Lord, who, in order that he may also justly forgive us, wishes his intimates to pray for us.

Now let each person consider himself; let him see what [Col. 0322C] his case is like before the Lord. How have we lived before his sight? Certainly we are human beings; he is God. We are servants; he is Lord. We are creatures; he is Creator. We have not worshiped our God as we should; we have not obeyed our Lord as we should; we have not loved our Creator as we should. Therefore, brothers, if we consider ourselves rightly, we shall not be able to answer him one thing out of a thousand, as Scripture says (Job 9). What, then, shall we do? We can hide nothing from him. For, as the Apostle says: “All things are naked and laid open before his eyes” (Heb. 4). Let us offer him our prayers. Let us say to him: “Do not enter into judgment with your servants” (Ps. 142 [143]).

Still, it is too little to offer our prayers alone. Let us seek the help of her whose prayers he will in no way wish [Col. 0322D] to despise.

Let us therefore approach his bride; let us approach his mother; let us approach his most excellent handmaid. All this is blessed Mary. Therefore let us celebrate the Nativity of blessed Mary with joy, so that she may intercede for us with our Lord. If we have done anything good by God’s grace, if she presents it to her Son, he will not reject it. Concerning the evil we have done, she will undoubtedly obtain forgiveness. Therefore it is necessary for us to conduct ourselves before her in such a way that she will wish to undertake our cause. But what shall we do for her? What gifts shall we offer her? Would that at least we could render to her what we owe her as a debt! We owe her honor; we owe her [Col. 0323A] service; we owe her love; we owe her praise.

We owe her honor because she is the mother of our Lord. Whoever does not honor the mother undoubtedly dishonors the son. Again Scripture says: “Honor your father and mother” (Exod. 20). What then shall we say, brothers? Is she not our mother? Certainly, brothers, she is truly our mother. For through her we are born; through her we are nourished; through her we grow. Through her we are born, not for the world but for God; through her we are nourished, not with the milk of the flesh, but with that of which the Apostle says: “I gave you milk to drink, not solid food” (1 Cor. 3). Through her we grow, not in bodily size but in the strength of the soul. Let us now see what this birth is like, what that milk is, and what this growth is.

[Col. 0323B] We all were, as you believe and know, in death, in oldness, in darkness, in misery: in death, because we had lost the Lord; in oldness, because we were in corruption; in darkness, because we had lost the light of wisdom; and thus we had altogether perished. But through blessed Mary we have been born much better than through Eve, because Christ was born from her. In place of oldness we have recovered newness; in place of corruption, incorruption; in place of darkness, light. She is our mother: the mother of our life, the mother of our incorruption, the mother of our light.

The Apostle says of our Lord: “Who became for us wisdom from God, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption” [Col. 0323C] (1 Cor. 1). Therefore she who is the mother of Christ is the mother of our wisdom, the mother of our righteousness, the mother of our sanctification, and the mother of our redemption. Thus she is more our mother than the mother of our flesh. Therefore from her comes our better birth, because from her come our birth, our holiness, our wisdom, our righteousness, our sanctification, and our redemption. Therefore let us celebrate her Nativity with joy, since from her we have such a good birth.

Let us now see what milk we have received from her. The Word of God, the Son of God, the Wisdom of God, is bread and solid food. Therefore only those who were strong—that is, the angels—ate of him. We who were little could not taste this food because it was solid; we who were on earth could not [Col. 0323D] ascend to this bread, because it was in heaven. What, then, happened? This bread came into the womb of the Blessed Virgin and there became milk—such milk as we can suck. Consider now the Son of God in the Virgin’s lap, in the Virgin’s arms, at the Virgin’s breasts: all this is milk; suck it. This is the milk which our good mother supplied to us.

Now consider her chastity, her charity, and her humility; and by her example grow in purity, grow in charity, grow in humility, and thus follow your mother. See what sort of mother she is. Therefore we owe her honor. For the Lord commanded this, as we have said: “Honor your father and your mother.” We also owe her service, because she is our Lady. [Col. 0324A] For the bride of our Lord is our Lady; the bride of our King is our Queen. Therefore let us serve her. For the Apostle commands: “Servants, be subject with all fear to your masters” (1 Pet. 2). And if the person who does not serve these earthly masters acts against the Lord’s command, then without doubt those who do not serve this spiritual Lady are blameworthy. But how ought we to serve her?

Brothers, no service pleases her as much as this: that we humble ourselves to her Son with all love and affection. For every praise and every service which we render to her Son, she counts as rendered to herself. Let no one say: “Although I do this or that against the Lord, I care little; I will serve Saint Mary and be safe.” It is not so. As soon as a person [Col. 0324B] offends the Son, he undoubtedly also offends the mother. But when we wish to be reconciled to our Lord after our sins, then it is necessary to seek her and entrust our cause to her.

Likewise, we owe her love. For she is our flesh and our sister. Do not think what I say presumptuous. The Son of God, because he is Son of Man, is our brother; yet he is human through his mother alone, whereas she is so through both father and mother. See now how greatly we may claim kinship with her, since she is our sister. Let us love her, because she certainly loves us. We ought certainly to love this sister, whose holiness, kindness, and purity benefited not only herself but all of us. Again, we owe her [Col. 0324C] praise.

For Scripture says: “Praise the Lord in his saints” (Ps. 150). If our Lord is to be praised in those saints through whom he performs mighty works and miracles, how much more is he to be praised in her, in whom he made himself—he who is, beyond all wonders, wondrous! If those are praiseworthy who resolve to preserve chastity, how should she be praised who, without example, chose to preserve virginity and nevertheless, together with virginity, obtained fruitfulness! If those are praiseworthy through whom God raises the dead, how should she be praised through whose holiness he raised the whole world from everlasting death! Therefore, brothers, let us praise her and celebrate her Nativity with joy, that she may intercede for us with the Lord our God.

But if we praise with our voice, let us not reproach her [Col. 0324D] by our conduct. Therefore let us praise her not falsely but truly. He praises falsely who does not wish, as far as he can, to imitate what he praises. He truly praises the humility of Saint Mary who, as far as he can, strives to be humble. He truly praises her chastity who detests and despises every impurity and lust. He truly praises her charity who, with all intention and effort, presses toward being able to love God and neighbor perfectly.

Therefore, brothers, if we wish to praise her worthily, we ought especially to pursue these three things: good thoughts, holy speech, and upright works. Whoever has these things as far as he can, and strives to possess them perfectly, imitates Saint Mary. For the Holy Spirit commends these three things in her, saying through Solomon: “Your lips are a dripping honeycomb. Honey and milk are under your tongue, and the fragrance of your garments is like the fragrance of incense” (Song 4).

[Col. 0325A] By “lips” we should understand words, because we speak through the lips. A honeycomb is wax containing honey. A dripping honeycomb has such an abundance of honey within that it even begins to flow outward. Therefore the words of blessed Mary are rightly compared to a flowing honeycomb, because all her words were sweet, full not of carnal sweetness but of spiritual sweetness. Yet many have honey in their mouths but not a dripping honeycomb, because many speak sweet words which do not come from an abundance of inward sweetness. Such persons are in one respect like the bee, which has sweetness and a sting. On the one hand they have honey [Col. 0325B] because they speak sweetly, flatter everyone, and follow everyone’s wishes; but this is only outward. In their private dealings, or perhaps in their hearts, they sting with detractions and judgments those whom they have outwardly smeared with honey. They do not have a dripping honeycomb, because this sweetness of speech does not arise, as we have said, from an abundance of inward sweetness.

Blessed Mary was not so. “Your lips,” it says, “are a dripping honeycomb”: that is, your sweet words come from an abundance of inward sweetness. And, that we may know the source of this sweetness of speech, it immediately adds: “Honey and milk are under your tongue.” Whoever wishes to have holy sweetness in speech, such as pleases God, must have two things in his thoughts and heart: holiness toward himself and compassion toward his neighbors. [Col. 0325C] Whoever has these two things in his heart, whoever preserves his thoughts in these two things, will have speech full of spiritual sweetness. As honey is made from various flowers, so all holiness consists in many virtues. Therefore holiness can be understood by honey. Milk, because it is a sign of motherly love, nourishes little children, and makes the mother bend down toward her child, signifies compassion. Nothing makes a person speak piously, kindly, and sweetly with another more than compassion. But compassion without holiness is indulgence.

See therefore what is said: “Your lips, bride, are a dripping honeycomb; honey and milk are under your tongue.” It is as if he said: Your words are full of spiritual sweetness because they come [Col. 0325D] from inward holiness and compassion. Those things which have not yet reached the tongue are under the tongue. Therefore it says, “under your tongue,” as though saying, “in your thoughts.”

It follows: “And the fragrance of your garments is like the fragrance of incense.” By garments we should understand our good works, because through our good works our sins, as it were our shamefulness, are covered. They are also our adornments before God. In incense we can consider two things: its pleasant fragrance and its divine sacrifice. Therefore the garments of Saint Mary are compared to incense because they pleased God and gave human beings the fragrance of good repute. There are many whose garments have a pleasant fragrance but not the fragrance of incense. For there are many from whom an appearance of religion proceeds, [Col. 0326A] whose works seem holy to human beings, but who do not have the fragrance of incense because their works are not laid upon God’s sacrifice.

Therefore, dearest brothers, let us imitate the most blessed Mary as far as we can. Let holy meditation and compassionate mutual concern be in us, like honey and milk. Let our lips be like a dripping honeycomb, so that all our words may proceed from the sweetness of charity. If we rebuke, let it be done with charity; if we are rebuked by another, let us receive it with charity, so that, according to the Apostle, all that we do may be done in charity (1 Cor. 16). Through our works let us sacrifice to God with a good conscience; from them let us spread a good fragrance, so that others may take an example. Thus let us have not carnal joy—not in feasts, not in jokes, not [Col. 0326B] in the splendors of this world—but, with every spiritual joy, celebrate today the Nativity of blessed Mary, so that she may intercede for us with our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXI. ON THE NATIVITY OF BLESSED MARY, III
You know, dearest brethren, that today we celebrate the Nativity of our Lady Saint Mary; and therefore it is fitting that we rejoice in the Lord and recall to mind how great a joy came to us through her birth, because in her birth all our joy began to appear. And therefore it is fitting that we stir ourselves up [Col. 0326C] on this feast to praise our Lord. But since during this night you have been roused by chants, readings, psalms, and the other things suitable to the feast, so that nothing may be lacking to you, we too wish, as far as we can, to rouse you by our sermon. I hope, however, that even if our sermon does not increase that most ardent affection of your devotion, it will at least not diminish it. And, as it seems to me, nothing ought more to stir us to love and praise of our Lord, and to spiritual joy, than our recalling to you what our Lord began today to show us.

For today he began to display to us that wondrous mercy, that wondrous loving-kindness [Col. 0326D] which so many years before he had promised to Abraham—namely, that in his seed all nations should be blessed (Gen. 22). For today was born that seed from which arose Christ our God, the sun of righteousness; in him, without doubt, not one nation but all nations have been blessed, because the faith and blessing of Christ extend through all nations. That seed, brethren, is blessed Mary, who was born today from Abraham’s seed; she received such a wondrous blessing from the Lord that she took away the curse of the world.

For, as the Gospel read today relates, it is most certain that she is of Abraham’s seed. For there we read: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham” (Matt. 1). From this we know that our Lord, who had no father on earth, could not rightly be called the son of Abraham and the son of David unless his mother were of the same seed. Again, so that we might be certain that he is the one of whom God spoke to Abraham, the evangelist Matthew wished to recount to us the whole lineage of our Lord, from Abraham down to blessed Mary, from whom Christ our God, the sun of righteousness, arose.

We must further consider that the evangelist did not aim merely to show us simply those fathers from whom Christ was born, so that we might know his bodily lineage; rather, he also intended that we should derive spiritual fruit from his bodily lineage. For if the evangelist intended nothing else, why did he make those three divisions—that is, place fourteen generations, [Col. 0327A] or fourteen names, in each division? Thus he says: “From Abraham to David, fourteen generations; from David to the Babylonian deportation, fourteen generations; from the Babylonian deportation to Christ, fourteen generations” (ibid.). And because he did not wish to exceed this number, but to preserve these divisions, he omitted to count certain fathers and sons belonging to this lineage, and passed from a father to his great-grandson.

Therefore through those fathers and sons by whom Christ descended to us, we ought to understand something spiritual and to observe certain steps by which we must ascend to him. Let us therefore see how he recounts this lineage.

He begins with Abraham and, descending, comes [Col. 0327C] to our Lord. It seems that by this descent, through which our Lord came down to us, he wished to show us a certain ascent by which we must rise to him. For he descended in order that we might ascend. He became poor for our sake in order to make us rich. The evangelist begins this descent with Abraham. Now Abraham is interpreted “exalted father,” and by him may be signified he who is truly the exalted Father—namely, God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. From there, that is, from the bosom of the exalted Father, our Lord descended in order to come to us. He came to us by becoming a human being among us. And because he is human, he is surely the son of Mary. Therefore at the end of this descent [Col. 0327D] the evangelist says: “Jacob begot Joseph, the husband of Mary, of whom Jesus was born, who is called Christ” (ibid.).

Therefore, dearest brethren, if we wish to ascend to that place from which he descended to us—that is, to the exalted Father—let us begin our ascent here, with the son of Mary, that is, with Christ’s humanity, and so let us ascend to his divinity. For he is the way, as he himself says: “I am the way” (John 14). Without this way no one can reach the exalted Father. Therefore he says: “No one comes to the Father except through me” (ibid.). For no one can begin any good unless he begins with Christ. He is the foundation of all good things, as the Apostle says: “No other foundation can anyone lay besides that which has been laid, which is Jesus Christ” [Col. 0328A] (1 Cor. 3).

But because we are in the depths, while he to whom we must ascend is very high, we cannot arrive there except by certain steps. These spiritual steps by which we must ascend can, as we have said, be observed in those fathers through whom our Lord descended to us, so that we might rise to him. Therefore, just as he descended from Abraham—that is, from God the Father—to us through those fathers according to the flesh, so let us ascend through those fathers, understood spiritually, to God the Father himself. First let us see what the three divisions made by the evangelist signify.

I think that by these three divisions we should understand three states in which all are found who wish [Col. 0328B] to ascend by these steps to the place from which Christ descended to us. The first state is our conversion; the second, our purification; the third, our expectation. In this way each person ought to advance. First, a person is converted to the Lord from the vanity of this world; afterward he is cleansed from the vices contracted through evil habit. And after he has been cleansed of vices, as far as human frailty allows, then he ought with great longing to await his release: when he is to leave this body, come to Christ, and safely receive his reward.

But if a person wishes to ascend to this highest step, he must first be perfect in the first state, then in the second, and thus ascend to the third. Therefore anyone who is converted to the Lord must not be converted timidly or lukewarmly. He is converted timidly and lukewarmly to the Lord who, when he leaves the world, does not wish to abandon all that is his completely; but, contrary to the Lord’s command, is anxious about tomorrow, reserves something for himself from his possessions, begins to build some new dwelling, fears that he may be unable to endure the strictness of being under another’s authority, and begins to live independently, care for himself, and be a master before he is a disciple.

He too is converted lukewarmly to God who, although he leaves all that he possesses and places himself under another’s authority, chooses some place and settles there where he may have as many pleasures, or even more, than he had in the world. [Col. 0328D] And he too is converted lukewarmly to God who, in whatever house he may be, so far as he can always seeks ease and pleasures of the flesh, and cares for nothing except somehow to remain in the house to which he has come.

Again, there must be a certain perfection in our purification: it must not suffice us merely to abandon those abominations that we committed in the world while the eye of our heart is nevertheless stained by anger, envy, detraction, grumbling, and hidden filth. Again, there must be a certain perfection in our expectation: namely, perseverance unto the end and continually fervent desire. We may understand these perfections through the three groups of fourteen.

But why did he put this number—fourteen—in each division? This number [Col. 0329A] signifies perfection. For ten and four signify the Law and the Gospel, in which all perfection lies. Ten signifies the perfection of the Law, because of the Ten Commandments that were in the Law. Four signifies the perfection of the Gospel, because of the four books of the evangelists. The evangelist therefore set down this number, which signifies perfection, because in every state a person ought to be perfect; for our conversion must indeed be perfect. If we are not perfect in this state, we cannot in any way attain that other state. Unless we are willing to turn completely to the Lord from this world, we shall by no means be able to be cleansed of our vices. And unless we have been perfectly cleansed of our vices, we cannot safely await the heavenly reward.

But because a person cannot immediately attain either the first perfection, which is in conversion, or from there the others, he must ascend as though by certain steps until he arrives at the place from which our Lord descended to us. Therefore now, brethren, let us ascend and begin from Christ so that we may arrive at Christ. Let us begin from Christ insofar as he is human, and let us arrive at Christ where he is one with the exalted Father. And if through those fathers mentioned by the Gospel we wish to understand those spiritual steps by which we must ascend, we must first begin with Joseph and thus ascend as far as the Babylonian deportation. For [Col. 0329C] these are the steps belonging to the first state:

Joseph is interpreted “increase.” We must know that the Lord created the rational creature to share in that blessedness, so that nothing but God alone could suffice it for blessedness. This is the whole perfection of the rational creature and all its good: to cleave to him. Therefore, in withdrawing from him, it tends toward nothingness. In this way all human loss consisted in withdrawing from God. Accordingly, when a person turns to God, then his increase begins. Therefore, if we wish to ascend to him, the first thing is that we turn to him, and so our increase begins—a meaning we may understand through Joseph, whose name is interpreted “increase.”

Our Lord Jesus Christ, though he was in the form of God, did not consider equality with God a thing to be seized, [Col. 0329D] but emptied himself (Phil. 2) and descended even to our weakness. But because “what is weak in God is stronger than men” (1 Cor. 1), where he came down to our deficiency, there our increase began. Yet because we fell from that great brightness into these shadows, from that great rest which the first human being had in paradise into this great and wide sea, where the winds of temptations and the waves of persecutions abound, and into this night “in which all the beasts of the forest pass by” (Ps. 103),

there are also in this sea “creeping things without number” (Ps. 39), that is, evil spirits, who are always intent on deceiving us. Amid all these evils and dangers we must ascend to that place from which we fell; we must ascend in this night and ascend from the sea. We need some light to illuminate us, by which we may climb the steps themselves. Therefore today a certain star has risen for us: namely, our Lady Saint Mary, whose name is interpreted “star of the sea”—without doubt the star of this sea, that is, of this world. Therefore we must lift our eyes to this star that has appeared today on earth, so that she may lead us, illuminate us, show us these steps so that we may know them, console us lest we fail as we climb, and help us to be able to ascend.

Therefore, beautifully, in this ladder of which we speak, where we must [Col. 0330B] begin to ascend, Mary is placed, as the evangelist says: “Jacob begot Joseph, the husband of Mary” (Matt. 1), so that she may appear to us at once in our very first conversion, receive us into her protection, illuminate us with her light, and accompany us on this laborious way. Therefore, with her illuminating and instructing us in all things, let us who have begun to turn to God bring that conversion itself to perfection. Let us begin with Joseph, where our increase begins; let us advance and ascend until we pass through the Babylonian deportation, so that we who through vices and sins were captives under Nebuchadnezzar’s power in Babylon—that is, in confusion—may be freed by the grace of Christ to whom we have turned.

And thus, when by a perfect turning to God we have returned from Babylon, let us pass to the second state. Beginning to cleanse ourselves, let us ascend from step to step until we come to Solomon, whose name is interpreted “peaceful,” so that, cleansed of evil passions, we may have within ourselves a certain peace and tranquillity. Thus may we enter the third state, which begins with David, whose name is interpreted “desirable,” so that we too may desire and burn to see the desirable countenance of our Creator; and in that desire may come to Father Abraham, that is, to God the exalted one, and see him in Zion.

But because it would take a long time if we wished to run through all these names and seek these steps in each one, [Col. 0330D] let us instead see to what perfection we must arrive in each of these three states. First let us see that the foundation has been laid: namely, faith in Christ. “For without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. 11). Then let us carefully consider that we must always keep before our eyes this star that appeared today on earth, lest we fail because of the darkness of this night in which we are; and thus let us begin to ascend in the first state, so that our conversion may be perfect.

This state begins with Joseph. Joseph, as we have said, is interpreted “increase.” What this increase signifies, the Lord says in the Gospel: “Who among you, wishing to build a tower, does not first sit down and consider whether he has the resources to complete it?” (Luke 14). This tower is the perfection to which we must ascend. Therefore whoever wishes to build this tower spiritually must increase the resources by which he can finish it, so that he may be in this first step, that is, increase. But what is this expenditure? We should hesitate to say, unless the Lord himself, having first said that one must calculate the cost for this spiritual building, immediately at the end of this Gospel passage showed what sort of expenditure he meant, saying: “Thus whoever does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple” (ibid.).

A wondrous thing. People of this world, if they wish to build something great, not only preserve what they have but also gather and acquire much. But one who wishes to make a spiritual building must not only refrain from seeking what he does not have, but must even leave what he does have. Therefore what seems loss to them is our increase. For the more these bodily riches are diminished for Christ’s sake, the more spiritual riches are increased. Therefore for us, who desire to ascend and build a spiritual tower, Joseph—that is, increase—is first set before us, so that we may cast away earthly riches and spiritual riches may thus increase for us.

We must know that temporal riches and worldly preoccupations are like bonds by which the devil holds people fast, so that they cannot freely climb God’s ladder. Therefore a certain rich man, when he heard the Lord say, “Go, sell all that you have, and give to the poor; and come, follow [Col. 0331C] me” (Matt. 19), went away sorrowful. Why he went away sorrowful the evangelist shows us when he says: “For he had many possessions” (ibid.). The devil held him bound by worldly preoccupations as though by certain fetters. Therefore he was sorrowful. He saw what he had to do, but because he was bound by these fetters, he could not free himself without great sorrow.

Whoever, then, casts away the riches of this world for fear and love of God can easily ascend God’s ladder and overthrow the devil. For in no way can a person more readily overthrow the devil than by cutting off, through fear of God as by a sharp razor, the bonds by which the devil holds him bound. But since, when a person begins to turn from sins to God, excessive fear sometimes seeks [Col. 0331D] to lead him into despair, he should ascend higher, look to him who is truly merciful, place all his hope in him, and love him above all things; for he grants all sins without any doubt to all who turn to him.

Solomon says in Proverbs: “My son, when you come to the service of God, stand in righteousness and fear, and prepare your soul for temptation” (Ecclus. 2). For the devil does not care to tempt a person whom he has in his power. He who obeys his own desires in everything and satisfies the desires of his flesh—the devil does not care to approach him. But if he begins to cast aside those very desires and struggle against the things desired by his flesh, then the devil grieves and attacks [Col. 0332A] him in a sharper contest.

Let one attacked by the devil not fail, but ascend higher, despise the devil and all his devices, and say: “My God is my helper, and I will hope in him” (Ps. 17). “For if God is for us, who is against us?” (Rom. 8). The devil sets before a person’s eyes the riches of the world that he has cast aside and wishes to make him return to his vomit. But let him say with all confidence: “My God is my helper, and I will hope in him.” And let him consider that if earthly and transitory things are pleasant, then without any doubt he is more pleasant who made not only these earthly things but also every beautiful gift, heavenly and earthly alike. Let him despise all things for love of him and say: “My God, my riches, my honor, my treasure, and all [Col. 0332B] my good things.”

At this step all riches are now perfectly despised, because when a person considers the beauty of his Creator, whatever he left in the world seems little to him. But once riches have been trodden underfoot, since they cannot prevent his turning to God, carnal affections begin to attack: those concerning father and mother, brothers and friends. This place is very dangerous. For when a person wishes to leave the world and turn to God, everyone opposes him, holds him back, cries out: “Are you leaving us? Who will support your father in his old age? Who will console your widowed and forsaken mother? Who will help your brothers, sisters, and little ones, all of whom look to you?” Even if these things are not said outwardly, carnal affection itself or the devil says them in the heart.

From another side family members, friends, and companions, with whom he had lived very sweetly, come forward and say: “Are you leaving us thus? Shall we thus be separated?” But whoever climbs this spiritual ladder and wishes to sing the Song of Ascents should say: “Lord, deliver my soul from wicked lips and from a deceitful tongue” (Ps. 119); and again: “The wicked tell me of delights, but they are not according to your law, O Lord” (Ps. 118).

These affections, indeed, are like clouds that darken the soul and strive to hide every spiritual delight. But here above all we must think of this our star, which shines for us in this night, in this darkness. We must consider the ray that arose from this star, who in some manner [Col. 0332D] was obscured for our sake, in order to free us from these shadows. Let us set him against all carnal affections and regard him as father, brother, mother, and friend: father, because he instructs us; mother, because he consoles us and nourishes us with the milk of his sweetness; brother, because he assumed flesh from our flesh; friend, because he poured out his blood for us.

This is the straight way. But here thieves must be guarded against, for they hide themselves and often strike the unwary. Here the lion is accustomed to lie hidden in ambush—that one who prowls about, seeking whom he may devour (1 Pet. 5). Whomever he cannot wound with his own sword, he is accustomed to attack with the very weapons of the person whom he tempts. His missiles are the vices by which he openly attacks us. Our weapons are the virtues by which we resist him. Therefore, when [Col. 0333A] he cannot destroy us through manifest vices, which are his missiles, he seeks to kill us with our own weapons. For he strives to persuade our mind that we should glory in ourselves, as though by our own strength we had left riches and by our own strength had despised every affection.

Against this plague we must ascend, so that each person, when he has advanced, may remember that he has been helped by the Lord and has not attained, nor can attain, any good through his own power; and may glory not in himself but in the Lord. For it is he who works in us both the willing and the ability, according to his good will. Hence the Apostle says: “For what do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Cor. 4).

Therefore whoever wishes to be perfectly converted to the Lord should ascend [Col. 0333B] from step to step until he comes to the Babylonian deportation. Just as in the descent we understand the deportation made from Jerusalem to Babylon, so in the ascent we must understand the deportation which we must make from Babylon toward Jerusalem. This is the conversion of our perfection: that we leave Babylon. Babylon is interpreted “confusion.” As long as someone has his heart in the riches of this world, in pleasures, in carnal love for parents and friends, or in his own will, he is certainly in Babylon—that is, in confusion. For where these things are in the heart, there is without doubt great confusion and little peace. Therefore, for our conversion to be perfect, let us cast away all these things and migrate entirely from Babylon.

And let us not only migrate, but become masters of Babylon. For, my brethren, it is a great thing to be a master of Babylon. Consider, I ask you, this great mystery. All the children of Israel who were in Jerusalem were led captive into Babylon; yet among the captives themselves a division was made. Some served the Babylonians themselves, while others became masters in Babylon itself and ruled the Babylonians. For Daniel, Hananiah, Azariah, and Mishael were appointed rulers over all the satraps of the king of Babylon, though all were captives. “These things,” as the Apostle says, “happened as a figure of us” (1 Cor. 10).

For all of us, my brethren—all without exception—are held captive in Babylon, that is, in confusion. For who can declare himself free of this captivity when Paul says: “I see another law in my members warring against the law of my mind and leading me captive in the law of sin” [Col. 0333D] (Rom. 7)? Behold that wretched captivity. All groan who do not rejoice in the manner of madmen. The Babylonians by whom we are held captive are the desires themselves. Yet it is good, my brethren, to rule the Babylonians themselves. It is indeed miserable to live among them, but most miserable to serve them. Yet many serve and few rule.

Those, indeed, serve the Babylonians in Babylon who, in this miserable captivity of which we have spoken, obey the desires themselves, the impulses of the flesh themselves, and offer their members to sin as weapons of unrighteousness. Those rule who restrain those desires, who govern their members well, so that sin may not reign in their mortal body (Rom. 6), and who are masters of their confusion, not its slaves.

Because no one is sufficient to accomplish this by his own powers, let us cry with the Apostle: “Who will deliver us from this body of death?” (Rom. 7). Let my cry thus always be directed to God, our eyes always toward God, and so let us enter another state. For although we have perfectly done these things and cast aside riches, pleasures, every carnal affection, and our own will, our vices still assail us: anger, impatience, pride, lust, and other such things. Therefore let us enter the other state and begin to cleanse ourselves of our vices through labors, vigils, fasts, [Col. 0334B] prayers, compunction, reading, and meditation.

But because nothing is so effective for our purification as continual prayer to God, Jeconiah, whose name is interpreted “the Lord’s preparation,” is placed at the beginning of this division, so that we may know and commit to memory that we are not sufficient to prepare or cleanse ourselves. Rather, our turning to God by renouncing this world, and our being cleansed as we advance, must all be the preparation of the Lord, who prepares us so that, when every temptation has ended, we may be made worthy of the vision of God himself.

We must indeed know that, as long as any earthly desire has settled in our heart, we shall by no means be able to hunger for that true and delightful good. But whoever does not hunger here for righteousness—I do not know whether he can ever be filled there. Yet although we have abandoned the world, submitted ourselves to another’s will, resisted our former vices, and, presuming nothing of ourselves, persisted in prayer, certain desires still rush upon us from the very weakness that has not yet been perfectly healed. They darken the eye of the heart and do not permit us to behold the purity of the true light, for which we ought to long.

Therefore we must act and strive with every effort that this desire may diminish, this weakness be healed, and charity increase, so that the one true, sole, sweet, and truly delightful good may be loved more fervently, desired more attentively, and tasted more sweetly. Here an immense labor indeed arises, [Col. 0334D] but we must not despair; for we hope not in ourselves but in the Lord. Let us hope for salvation from the Lord, so that weakness may not overwhelm us, desire may not conquer us, and charity may be nourished. Therefore let us pray to him continually that he himself may prepare and cleanse us, and make us vessels for honor rather than dishonor.

Let us not cease from this work, but ascend rather from step to step until we find—or rather, until we ourselves become—Solomon, who is the final step in the second division. Solomon is interpreted “peaceful.” Therefore we must continue to cleanse ourselves of vices until we have peace within us, and the vices are at rest, unable to raise their head against us or ever wage war upon us. This is the perfection of the second state: that God cleanse us from our vices, [Col. 0335A] so that we may begin even in this world to taste certain firstfruits of that peace which we shall have in our resurrection, when we shall say: “Where is your victory, O death? Where is your sting, O death?” (1 Cor. 15).

But if we have been perfect in this state, what remains except that we desire Christ’s presence, sigh for that blessed vision, so that our tears may be our bread day and night (Ps. 41), and say with every affection of the heart: “When shall I come and appear before the face of God?” (ibid.). This state begins with David, that is, with holy desire; David is interpreted “desirable.” And who is more desirable than he of whom the prophet says: “The desired one of all nations shall come” (Hag. 2)? Truly desired, and to be desired.

But for this desire to be perfect, it must not end [Col. 0335B] until we come to Abraham, that is, to the exalted Father, so that we may see the God of gods in Zion (Ps. 83). This is the perfection to which we must ascend; this is the reward we await: namely, the vision of God, that is, of the exalted Father. O what a reward! How great! How good! The righteous will see him; the wicked will see him—but the wicked in one way and the righteous in another. “They shall see him whom they pierced” (John 19). And again: “Let the wicked be taken away, lest he see the glory of God” (Isa. 26).

The righteous will see him, but as he is, as John says: “Now we are children of God, but what we shall be has not yet appeared. Yet we know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3). God’s being is never to be unlike himself. Therefore we shall see him as he is, [Col. 0335C] because we shall contemplate him in the very substance of his divinity—something granted to none at all of the elect in this life, not even to Moses, who was accustomed to contemplate him in angelic form. For the Lord said to him: “You cannot see my face; for no human being shall see my face and live” (Exod. 33). Yet, because of the merit of his great holiness, he said to him: “I will show you every good thing” (ibid.).

Then we shall see him, “beautiful in form above the children of men” (Ps. 44), into whom angels desire to look (1 Pet. 1). For, as someone has said, so far as it is permitted to know, God is a spiritual substance of such inestimable beauty and such ineffable sweetness that angels, who surpass the sun sevenfold in their own beauty, desire continually and insatiably [Col. 0335D] to gaze upon him. Then we shall see him whose spirit is sweeter than honey, whose inheritance is beyond honey and the honeycomb; we shall embrace him with spiritual arms and kiss him with a certain wondrous sweetness.

Then we shall see and perceive how good and sweet it will be, in that blessed life, to enjoy the sight of our Creator, share in the fellowship of angels, and be endowed with eternal immortality. Then we shall see him who descended from the bosom of the Father into his mother’s womb, so that we, beginning, as we have said, from his humanity, which he assumed from his mother, may reach his divinity, which he always possesses with the Father. All this our good began with this feast, on which his blessed Mother was born—he who by his grace brings us to so great a height.

And [Col. 0336A] therefore at the beginning of this ascent Jesus himself is placed, and Mary is placed, so that under that mercy, under the mercy of his most gracious mother, no one may despair and no one hesitate to ascend. Rather, placing all hope and all delight in them, let him ascend securely, let him ascend fearlessly. For one who can be helped by such aids can never fail. Let us therefore raise our gaze to Christ himself, beseeching him through the merits of his most sweet mother that he may make us willing, help us as we ascend, and receive us when we come: he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXII. ON THE FEAST OF ALL SAINTS

[Col. 0336B] My brethren, if we are not sufficient to speak of one of God’s saints and express his glory, how shall we be sufficient to make a discourse concerning all his saints? Therefore this is more necessary: that we so conduct ourselves as to be able to attain their glory. What, then, must we do? How shall we be able to arrive at that exaltation? Therefore, brethren, let us hear wholesome counsel. For whom should we trust more than one who has already attained that excellence? He surely knows the way by which he himself ascended. Let us therefore hear one of Jesus’ great friends saying: “Humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you” (1 Pet. 5).

You know how today throughout the whole world everyone praises God’s saints: angels, archangels, apostles, martyrs, confessors, [Col. 0336C] and virgins. Hence there are chants today in the holy Church; hence hymns, lights, and the other things suited to the feast. Chant signifies that perpetual jubilation in which the saints are because of the ineffable joy they have in God. Hymns signify that inexpressible praise by which they always praise God. Hence the psalmist says: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord; for ever and ever they shall praise you” (Ps. 83). Lights signify that perpetual light in which the saints of God dwell. Hence in this night you sang: “Around you, O Lord, is a light that shall never fail.”

Now, brethren, consider, if you can, how greatly exalted in heaven are those who can thus be exalted and honored on earth. Certainly, brethren, if we could behold at once all the glory of the world, all the praise of the world, and all the joy of the world, in comparison with that joy it would be nothing but utter misery. Therefore, brethren, you ought to know that we observe these feasts with lights, chants, and other such things only for two reasons. These things do not benefit God’s saints; they do not delight in this earthly singing, nor do they glory in these earthly and trivial lights. Their praise is Christ; their light is he who enlightens every person coming into this world (John 1).

First, we do it so that by these renewals we may stir ourselves to greater devotion. Secondly, because of the signification mentioned above; and therefore we should do only so much as suffices for these two purposes. For those do not celebrate these feasts well or reasonably, as it seems to me, who with a certain excess and superfluity seek these outward glories and beauties, so that, while the outward person is occupied with so many chants, ornaments, lights, and other such beauties, he can scarcely think of anything except those things that he sees with his eyes, hears with his ears, or perceives through the other senses of the flesh.

We, brethren, who do not see these things, yet know that they are performed by many, should ponder and delight in that beauty which is true, in which the saints are without corruption; in those spiritual adornments which the saints possess in righteousness and holiness; in those hymns and praises by which they praise God without weariness; in that light which they behold [Col. 0337B] in the face of God. And let us celebrate our feasts in such a way that our mind is not turned back toward these earthly and perishing delights, but is rather stirred toward those spiritual and eternal things; and so let us contemplate their glory and exaltation. And that we may be able to attain their exaltation, let us hear the Apostle’s counsel, who says: “Humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God.” The Apostle knew very well the reason why we have been cast down, why we lost that exaltation in which we were created, why we were driven into this misery. What is that reason, brethren, except pride? Therefore, against that pride he teaches humility. “Humble yourselves,” he says. But because he knew that not all who humble themselves do so wisely, he added, “under the mighty [Col. 0337C] hand of God.”

Some humble themselves under the glorious hand of God; others under the strong hand of God; others under the generous hand of God; others under the mighty hand of God. There are good angels and evil angels; there are also good people and evil people. As the Apostle says: “At the name of our Lord Jesus Christ every knee should bend, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Phil. II). See, then, that all are humbled before our Lord and all are subjected to him—both good and evil alike—because none can resist his will, and all serve his will, willingly or unwillingly. Therefore the Apostle beneficially admonishes us to humble ourselves to him; that is, to subject ourselves to him by our own will, because then we shall have merit. For if we do not wish of our own will [Col. 0337D] to be subject to him, we shall be subjected unwillingly and shall incur eternal punishment.

Now let us see who those are who humble themselves under the glorious hand of God. They are those who expect from God’s hand nothing other than his glory, in which they themselves are blessed without end, each according to the rank in which he was created. But the evil angels are those who humble themselves under the strong hand of God, because God’s strength presses them and makes them, whether they will or not, serve his will. Hence it is said in the Psalm: “This dragon, which thou hast made for thy sport” (Ps. CIII). Does not our Lord mock him wisely when everything he did for the destruction of the elect, the Lord turns back to their advancement, and whatever he does to diminish Christ’s glory, that very thing increases Christ’s glory? And I think, my brethren, that [Col. 0338A] he himself considers himself mocked today. Today he contemplates the glory of the apostles, martyrs, and all God’s saints, and sees that through his malice their glory has been increased. For why is their glory so great, except because, as the Apostle says, “They endured mockings and scourgings, moreover bonds and imprisonment; they were stoned, sawn asunder, tempted, and died by the sword for Christ” (Heb. XI)? And all these things were inflicted on them through the devil’s malice. For he worked in the hearts of the unbelieving and ungodly who so tortured them. And behold, all those torments were turned for them into glory and a crown.

So too, my brethren, although we do not suffer the bodily torments which they suffered, the devil is nevertheless mocked through us. For he tempts and torments; but [Col. 0338B] because the strength of God’s hand restrains him so that he cannot tempt us beyond what we can bear, all these temptations contribute to our glory and to his disgrace. Likewise evil people humble themselves under God’s strong hand, because the Lord does not permit them to exercise their cruelty except as far as he sees fit.

Others humble themselves under God’s generous hand—though not all in the same way. Some, seeing that he is the one “who gives food to all flesh” (Ps. CXXXV), firmly believing that all riches and honours are in his hand and that he gives them to whom he wills, begin to serve him either in order to gain such earthly things or not to lose them. Others, better than these, considering his generous hand—he “makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil, and [Col. 0338C] rains upon the just and the unjust” (Matt. V), and also abundantly bestows these temporal things indiscriminately upon good and evil—conjecture how wonderful and ineffable are the things which he keeps for his good alone; and, out of desire for that blessedness “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man” (I Cor. II), they serve him and humble themselves.

Again, there are others who humble themselves under the mighty hand of God. They are those who, considering his power by which he humbles the proud and exalts the humble, by which he condemns whom he wills, are humbled with salutary, compunctive fear. To this humility the Lord invites us, saying: “Do not fear those who kill the body and have nothing further that they can do; but fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna” [Col. 0338D] (Matt. X). This is the first cause of our humility: fear of the Lord. But there is a more perfect degree, when one considers not that power by which he condemns the ungodly, but that by which he powerfully defends his own in this life and brings them into the kingdom of heaven on the day of judgment. To this degree the Apostle invites us, saying: “Humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God,” not out of fear of punishment, but “that he may exalt you in the time of visitation” (I Pet. V).

The time of visitation is the day of judgment. First he visited the world by mercy; afterward he will visit it by judgment. He visited us mercifully when he shed his blood for us; he will visit us in judgment when he renders to each according to his works (Matt. XVI).

There are also innumerable other visitations by which [Col. 0339A] the Lord visits here not only the elect but also the reprobate. He visits us in prosperity; he visits us in adversity. He visits us when we are tempted; he visits us when we are comforted. He visits us through hidden inspiration; he visits us through outward preaching. He visits us through the Scriptures; he visits us through the sacraments. All these things result in salvation for the good, in destruction for the evil. But if we wish to be exalted in all these visitations, let us humble ourselves under the mighty hand of the Lord.

And what are these feasts which we celebrate except certain visitations of his? Yet in these visitations some are exalted and others cast down. Behold, today we celebrate the feast of All Saints, and we alone do not celebrate it. For what Christian is there who does not celebrate this [Col. 0339B] feast today? But many do so amid luxury, revelry, drunkenness, impurity, and contaminations of that kind. These are not exalted in this visitation; rather, they are cast down. But whoever, in the present feast, considers within himself the saints of our Lord, the glory of angels, the teaching of apostles, the patience of martyrs, the steadfastness of confessors, and the chastity of virgins—and now desires the glory to which they attained, now burns to follow the path by which they went before; and thus is pierced with compunction, grieves, laments his past negligences and sins, resolves to serve God more fervently so as to attain the glory of angels, to endure every adversity more patiently so as to reach the crown of martyrs, [Col. 0339C] and henceforth to guard his heart and flesh more purely so as to enjoy the fellowship of virgins—that person is exalted in this time of visitation.

But who are they who do these things? Not the proud, not the distinguished, not the contentious, not the murmurers. But who? Certainly those who humble themselves under the mighty hand of God: those who always set the fear of God before their eyes, always consider divine power, and always keep the uncertainty of death before their eyes. Therefore, brethren, let us humble ourselves under God’s mighty hand, that he may exalt us in the time of visitation. May he exalt us in these visitations through good works and holy desires, so that, when he comes in that great visitation, when he requires of all what they have done in this life in order to render to each according to his works, he may then [Col. 0339D] exalt us perfectly, as we hear that delightful voice: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. XV). This will be our true exaltation, when we enjoy in heaven the fellowship of those whose feast we celebrate on earth today. May our Lord Jesus Christ grant this to us through their merits—he who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXIII. ON ALL SAINTS II

Blessed be our emperor, who does not cease to visit his poor household. Sometimes, dearest brethren, he visits us through one of his servants; sometimes through several; sometimes through his most dear [Col. 0340A] mother; sometimes—what is greater—through himself. For what are these feasts of saints, which we celebrate so frequently, except certain visitations through which our Lord visits and strengthens us?

Since it was fitting that we should always remain mindful of the benefits which he bestowed upon us through his bodily presence, and since he knew that our memory is corrupted by forgetfulness, our understanding by error, and our zeal by desire, he piously provided that his very benefits should not only be recounted to us through the Scriptures, but also represented to us through certain spiritual acts. Therefore, when he gave his disciples the sacrament of his body and blood, he said to them: “Do this in remembrance of me” (Matt. XXVI).

[Col. 0340B] For this reason, brethren, these feasts were established in God’s Church: that by representing now his birth, now his passion, now his resurrection, now his ascension, that wondrous mercy, wondrous sweetness, and wondrous love which he showed toward us in all these things may always remain fresh in our memory. Our faith also ought greatly to profit from this, when with our ears we see what Christ suffered for us, what he gives us even in this life, and what he promises us after this life. He suffered death for us; in the present life he gives us remission of sins; after this life he promises us eternal blessedness.

This deliverance of ours, dearest brethren, [Col. 0340C] this hope of ours, this blessedness of ours, we ought to recall when we celebrate his feast. But why do we celebrate the feasts of his faithful servants, except in order that we may contemplate more attentively the glory which God’s mercy has bestowed on them, and through this contemplation desire and love it more ardently? Likewise, by hearing of their lives, passions, and labours through which they came to so great a glory, we ought to conceive great consolation and great hope; and the more we see ourselves amid the labours and distresses of this life, the more confidently we may hope for that glory and happiness to which they have gone before us.

Beloved, let no one deceive you; let no thought [Col. 0340D] mislead you, nor any blandishment of the enemy. Certainly true is the Scripture which says: “Through many tribulations we must enter into the kingdom of God” (Acts XIV). My brethren, even if an angel tells you otherwise, let him be anathema. We frequently celebrate the feasts of apostles and martyrs, sometimes also of confessors, sometimes of virgins. Who among all these did not pass through the pains and tribulations of this life?

Behold, today our king himself, our emperor himself, visits us with all his army. Let us consider, as far as we can, all his battle-lines: how beautiful they are, how well ordered. Let us desire their fellowship, but let us not first shrink from their labour. The struggle is indeed severe, but the crown ought to delight us. Nor do we lack help [Col. 0341A] in this struggle. Around us are angels and archangels, of whom the Apostle says: “Are they not all ministering spirits, sent for ministry on behalf of those who shall receive the inheritance of salvation?” (Heb. I).

Let us therefore behold our emperor himself in the foremost rank; let us hear how he exhorts his soldiers. “In this,” he says, “world you shall have tribulation” (John XVI). Brethren, truth cannot lie. Therefore hear what he promised. There are two ages, the present and the future. Our Lord foretold to us how we are to fare in each. “In this world,” he says, “you shall have tribulation” (Matt. XIII). Again, he himself said what his own will be like in the other: “The righteous shall shine like the sun in the kingdom of my Father” (Matt. XXII). And again: “They shall be like the angels of God in heaven” (ibid.).

Therefore, [Col. 0341B] brethren, although perhaps that rich man of whom the Gospel speaks, who was tormented in hell and saw Lazarus in Abraham’s bosom, had done many evil things, and although perhaps the poor Lazarus had had many good things in himself, Abraham named no other cause for the rich man’s condemnation except that he had received good things in his life; nor any other cause for Lazarus’s salvation except that he had likewise received evil things in his life. For thus he says: “Remember, son, that you received good things in your life; and Lazarus likewise evil things” (Luke XVI). Therefore, brethren, as much as each person sees himself in the tribulations of this life for Christ, let him know with certainty that his glory grows by that much in the other life; and as much as he sees himself amid good things and delights in this life, by that much let him fear lest his glory be diminished in the other life.

[Col. 0341C] Therefore, brethren, we ought to keep these two matters in our memory: what we ought to be like in heaven with the Lord; and we must always perceive something of these two lives. Labour belongs to this life; rest to that life. Temptation belongs to this life; security to that. Poverty belongs to this life; riches to that. Mourning belongs to this life; consolation to that. Hunger and thirst belong to this life; fullness to that. This, my brethren, is what the Lord says in the Gospel: “Blessed are the poor, for yours is the kingdom of God. Blessed are you who weep, for you shall laugh. Blessed are you who hunger now, for you shall be filled” (Luke VI). And again: “Woe to you rich, who have your consolation. Woe to you who laugh now, for you shall mourn and weep” (ibid.).

But now observe [Col. 0341D] what I said: we must keep these two matters in memory—that is, what we ought to be like here and what we shall be like there. For if we attend only to those things which belong to this life, we shall be unable to endure. Who can always remain amid tribulations, miseries, and temptations without any consolation, without danger of murmuring and despair? Who is there, brethren, in this life who does not feel these miseries, unless he is altogether without feeling? Because of these miseries all seek to have some consolation. Worldly people, those who love this world, seek consolation in riches, honours, many curiosities, desires of the flesh, and pleasures. Such people are miserable when [Col. 0342A] they are sad, but much more miserable when they are thus consoled.

But you, “a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for possession” (I Pet. II), ought not to have the sorrow which they have, nor the consolation which they have. Consider this whole household of our emperor, which he displays to us today; and see in it these two things: the sorrow they had and the joy they received. This is that household of Christ, the bride of Christ, which says in the Song of Songs: “I am black, but beautiful” (Song I). Behold, brethren, those two things of which we have spoken. Blackness belongs to this life; beauty to that life in which, God granting, we shall be after this one. Whatever the saints had from this life was black, yet with this blackness they had great beauty.

[Col. 0342B] That tribulation, distress, and temptation which they endured in the world was, as it were, a certain blackness. Of them the Apostle says: “They went about in sheepskins and goatskins, needy, afflicted, oppressed—of whom the world was not worthy” (Heb. XI). They also had a certain beauty in faith, chastity, purity, and love.

Let us first consider the commanders of our army; let us hear what one of them says about them. “See your calling, brethren,” he says: “not many wise according to the flesh, not many noble; but God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise, and the weak things of the world, the contemptible things, and the things which are not” (I Cor. I). And again he says: “We have become as the refuse of this world, the offscouring [*peripsema*] of all” (I Cor. IV). This is the blackness of which we spoke. But where was their beauty? Hear: “This is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” (II Cor. I). Their beauty was within, not without.

What of the holy martyrs? Did not this appear in them when they were handed over to prisons, when they were led in chains before people, when they were stoned, scourged, and tortured with every insult and torment? Their voice is in the Psalm: “Have mercy on us, O Lord, have mercy on us; for we are exceedingly filled with contempt. For our soul is exceedingly filled with the reproach of the prosperous and the contempt of the proud” (Ps. CXXII). But all this blackness which was outside did not diminish [Col. 0342D] but increased the beauty which was within.

What of the other saints who were not in these persecutions, such as confessors, many holy virgins, holy monks, and hermits? Did they not have this blackness? Yet the Apostle says generally of all: “All who wish to live piously in Christ suffer persecution” (II Tim. V). That person lives piously who can truly say: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I do not burn?” (I Cor. XI). It is a great persecution, brethren, as we often experience, to know the weaknesses, pains, and burdens of many people. It is a great persecution to care for all, to grieve for all, to be sad when someone is sad, to fear when someone is tempted. For there is [Col. 0343A] another intolerable persecution which sometimes happens to us, when one of those whom we nourish, guard, and love as our own very entrails is overcome by the devil—to such an extent that he even departs from us, or lives so perversely and ruinously that we must expel him from among us.

Brethren, if you who are brethren feel grief and great sorrow when such things happen, how much sorrow do you think we have, who are brothers, fathers, and guardians, and have undertaken to render an account for such people? Certainly, brethren, you ought to have great compassion on us and to gladden us by your good conduct, since amid so many other matters we have sorrow. Yet blessed is the person who suffers this blackness for Christ. [Col. 0343B] This blackness does not make him ugly, but beautiful. For it comes not from the flame of desire but from the fire of love. Such a soul may say, “The sun has darkened me” (Song I): namely, the sun of love, which shines and burns in its heart and causes it, the more it loves, to suffer pain and sorrow more frequently for those whom it loves.

There is another kind of blackness which you often experience. It is precisely that which none of the saints was ever able to avoid. This blackness, brethren, is temptation, whether from the enemy, the flesh, or this world. Paul himself had this blackness, as he says: “There was given to me a thorn for my flesh, an angel of Satan to buffet me” (II Cor. XII). And concerning [Col. 0343C] temptation of the flesh he says: “I see another law in my members, resisting the law of my mind and leading me captive into the law of sin” (Rom. VII). The whole fellowship of God’s saints has experienced this blackness, so that it can say: “I am black, but beautiful” (Song I). Every holy soul, while it lives in this flesh, can say this as well. For what saint is free from temptation, when Job says: “Human life upon earth is temptation” (Job VII)?

“I am black, but beautiful.” Can not the soul of each one of us say this: “I am black, but beautiful”? Beautiful without doubt is the soul which despises the world, yet still black because it often turns the world over in its heart and thinks upon it. Beautiful is the soul which loves God as much as it can, [Col. 0343D] yet still black because it often feels within itself a love for carnal things. Beautiful is the soul which, as far as it can, does what it knows benefits others, out of love; yet it is still black because it often feels anger, impatience, and other things within itself which assail love. Finally, beautiful is the soul which consents to no vice, yet still black because it feels the vices themselves.

And what wonder, brethren, if saints pass through that blackness, when the Lord himself chose to live in this world with a certain blackness? He himself, brethren, could say: “I am black, but beautiful.” Therefore his bride—the whole fellowship of saints, or each holy soul—has no shame in confessing of herself: “I am black, [Col. 0344A] but beautiful.” But hear how: “Like the tents of Kedar, like the skins of Solomon” (Song I). This is what I said: our Lord himself chose to show a certain blackness in himself, but beneath that blackness he possessed great beauty.

Do you wish to hear both, his blackness and his beauty? Isaiah says of his blackness: “We saw him, and he had neither appearance nor comeliness, despised and the last of men” (Isa. LIII). David says of his beauty: “Beautiful in form beyond the sons of men” (Ps. XLIV). Yet he suffered temptations, as the Apostle says: “Tempted in all things after our likeness, without sin” (Heb. IV). Therefore all his saints followed his footsteps and example, so that every holy soul may say: “I am black [Col. 0344B] but beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem; like the tents of Kedar, like the skins of Solomon” (Song I).

Who is this Kedar, and who is this Solomon? I think that our Lord Jesus himself is Kedar in one respect and Solomon in another. For Kedar is interpreted “darkness,” Solomon “peaceful.” In order to see how these two names suit our Lord Jesus Christ, attend to what he himself says in the Gospel: “I came into this world for judgment, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John IX). Many were blinded by his presence and many enlightened. For, as Simeon says, he was set “for the fall and resurrection of many in Israel” [Col. 0344C] (Luke II).

To those who would not believe in him, but were blinded by their own malice in his presence, he was Kedar. Did not those who said, “Is this not the carpenter’s son?” take him for Kedar? They saw him poor, not seeking but rather fleeing worldly glory, hungry and thirsty; and therefore they despised him. They thought he was Kedar—that is, dark and lacking the light of divinity—like other human beings. But whence came this to them? Why did they take offense at him? Certainly because of his tent, that is, his flesh, in which divinity dwells as though in a tent. In this tent our Lord was blacker: he suffered hunger, thirst, and reproaches; at last they spat upon him, struck him with their fists, scourged him, and so crucified [Col. 0344D] him. But all this blackness was in the tent, that is, in the flesh; it was outside, not within. For within, he was “beautiful in form beyond the sons of men”; within, he was one “whom angels desire to look upon.” Therefore, brethren, all that blackness was more ours than his. We bear sinful flesh; he bore not sinful flesh, but the likeness of sinful flesh.

Let that Jacob come to mind who, in order to obtain the blessing, hid his own likeness within and assumed another’s likeness without. You have often heard this history, brethren. Rebecca clothed her son in goatskins after the likeness of hairy Esau (Gen. XXVII). For what did hairy Esau signify except the children of those who were cast out of paradise in garments of skin? [Col. 0345A] All Adam’s children are hairy and black because of sins and iniquities. The Son of God did not have this hair. For how could he have sin who was one with the Father, perfect and omnipotent God? Nor did he have in that divinity of his any likeness of sin or corruption.

Brethren, unless he assumed the likeness of our skin, the likeness of our hair, we could never be freed from our hairs. Therefore he deigned to put on the likeness of sinful flesh, so that outwardly he might show weakness and a certain blackness, while inwardly preserving that wondrous and ineffable beauty. Set before your heart, as though you saw Jacob covered with goatskins: could he not truly say, “I am black, but beautiful”? [Col. 0345B] Black because of the tents of Kedar, because of the black skin of goats; but beautiful within because of his own likeness.

So consider that true Jacob, our Lord Jesus Christ: black because of the likeness of sinful flesh; beautiful because he had no sin. Yet through this blackness he obtained a blessing for us, not for himself, since he had no need of it, but for us, who needed blessing because we were accursed. For without doubt we were signified, and blessed in signification, in that blessing by which Isaac blessed his son. Hear what he said: “Behold, the smell of my son is like the smell of a full field, which the Lord has blessed” (ibid.).

This is the field, brethren, which we ought especially to consider today. [Col. 0345C] This field is full of every fragrance, every sweetness, every beauty. For, as you sang a little earlier: “Its flowers lack neither roses nor lilies.” Here are the most sweet fruits of the apostles; here the roses of martyrs; here the lilies of virgins; here each saint, like fruitful trees in the Lord’s field. Would that we too, brethren, might belong to that full field which the Lord has blessed! To this field the Lord has granted, from the dew of heaven and the fatness of earth, an abundance of wheat, wine, and oil.

The dew of heaven is spiritual grace, which this field is accustomed to receive in compunction, meditations, psalms, and readings. What is the fatness of earth? Our earth is our flesh. Blessed is one who can receive fatness [Col. 0345D] from this earth. This fatness, brethren, is good works, which indeed we do only through our body. Those who know how to cultivate this earth well, wisely, and discreetly experience that vigils, labours, and fasts are a kind of wonderful fatness.

From these two things, therefore—from the dew of heaven and the fatness of earth, that is, to speak more plainly, from bodily and spiritual exercise—this field, namely the whole fellowship of saints, possesses an abundance of wine, wheat, and oil: wheat of wisdom, wine of contemplation, oil of love. So Paul, an excellent tree of this field, laboured with his hands night and day, which pertains to the fatness of earth; and prayed without ceasing, which pertains to the dew of heaven. Through [Col. 0346A] these he acquired this wheat, wine, and oil. For he spoke wisdom among the perfect, distributing his wheat to them. He was caught up in contemplation as far as the third heaven, and was made drunk with that wine which is accustomed to gladden the human heart. Therefore he says: “Whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God; whether we are sober, it is for you” (II Cor. V). When he calls himself sober, because he adapted himself to the measure of the weak, he undoubtedly intended to call that ecstasy of mind, which he said was for God alone, a certain spiritual drunkenness. There is no need to commend Paul’s love.

You see, brethren, what a blessing the Lord acquired for this full field: full, without doubt, of every virtue and every perfection. Nor is this surprising, since in this field are all the saints from the foundation of the world, and each has his own place, beauty, and virtue. [Col. 0346B] In this field he obtained this blessing for you by becoming black, by our Jacob’s clothing himself in skins of flesh. Those very skins are the tents of Kedar—that is, his flesh, that is, his humanity. Following his example, all the saints wished to be black in this life so that afterward they might be beautiful like the skins of Solomon.

What are these skins of Solomon? They were certain skins in which was the sanctuary possessed by that ancient people of the Jews: namely, that ark of which you have often heard, the altar of incense, and other things of this kind. Blessed Paul the Apostle openly shows what these signify: “Jesus did not enter into holy places made by hands, copies of the true ones, but into heaven itself” (Heb. IX). Therefore the skins of Solomon are the heavens. For in these skins he is not Kedar but Solomon. In these skins he displays his beauty, sweetness, and light; and he appears to all not dark but peaceful, because he is the peace and tranquillity of the angels, who are heavens in which God dwells.

[Col. 0346C] You now see what this beauty is, and what kind of beauty is that of which the holy Church—that is, the fellowship of saints—glories. The beauty of Solomon’s skins is the beauty of the heavens, the beauty of angels. It is the beauty which the Lord promises, saying: “They shall be like the angels of God” [Col. 0346D] (Matt. XXII). Blessed is the person who can say: “I am black, but beautiful; like the tents of Kedar, like the skins of Solomon” (Song I).

These two things, dearest brethren, ought to accompany one another in this life: the blackness of the tent and the beauty of the skins. But in this life that beauty can be only in the soul; after the day of judgment it will be in both soul and body. Where, brethren, shall we find in this life an imitation of the angels, the beauty of those who are in eternal blessedness with the Lord?
