Where shall we find those who imitate the burning love of God possessed by that order of angels which, because of the exceeding love by which they love God, are called Seraphim? Where shall we find those who imitate the knowledge of those who, because of the wondrous knowledge which [Col. 0347A] they possess, are called Cherubim, that is, “fullness of knowledge”? And, since it would take long to enumerate all those nine orders of angels, where shall we find those who imitate the chastity, purity, unity, and love which angels possess?

Blessed is the soul which can truly say and glory: “I am beautiful, like the skins of Solomon.” But see, brethren, from what you ought especially to take consolation and greatly rejoice. I think that I understand here one soul which can truly say both: “I am black, but beautiful; like the tents of Kedar, like the skins of Solomon.”

First, consider what this soul is. Each one of you, before coming here, had one soul [Col. 0347B], which belonged only to himself. You were converted to God; and behold, the Holy Spirit—that heavenly fire which our Lord sent upon the earth and desires to burn—kindled your hearts, kindled your souls (Luke 12), and from all your hearts made one heart and one soul. This is the soul that can truly say, “I am dark as the tents of Kedar, beautiful as the skins of Solomon.” It has a certain darkness, like the tents of Kedar, because it imitates Christ’s sufferings in labours, vigils, fasts, and the mortification of the flesh. It also has a certain darkness from its own tent, because of the temptations it suffers and the desires of the flesh not yet wholly extinguished; [Col. 0347C] yet it is beautiful as the skins of Solomon. For what virtue do the angels possess that this soul does not possess, although it does not possess them as perfectly as the angels do? The angels have chastity; and it is she who reigns in this holy congregation. The angels have charity, which can without doubt be found in great perfection in this holy fellowship. They have perfect humility, by which they humble themselves beneath God’s hand; they have obedience, by which they fulfil his commands and carry his messages to us. They have among themselves such unity and harmony that, although some are lower and others higher, through unity and harmony whatever belongs to each belongs to all, and whatever belongs to all belongs to each. [Col. 0347D] All this exists in this fellowship, though, because of the tents of Kedar, not so perfectly.

Therefore, brothers, those who may be weak and less capable, and cannot do as much as others can, should neither be saddened nor despair. Let each take care only that through sloth or negligence he does not knowingly withhold anything of what he is able to do. For let him fear what the prophet says: “Cursed is the man who does the work of the Lord negligently” (Jer. 48). For he who knowingly and without discernment withdraws himself from what he is able to do commits a fraud, because his virtue and strength belong not only to himself but to the whole congregation. Again, those who can do more should not exalt themselves above the others, because the grace they received [Col. 0348A] was received not merely for themselves, but also for those who can do less. If, then, true unity and charity are among you, without doubt whatever one does will belong to all, and whatever all do will belong to each; so that the soul of each one of you may say, “I am beautiful as the skins of Solomon.” He alone cannot say this who withdraws from this fellowship, or divides himself by discord, envy, or some grave sin. We might still speak of this darkness and this beauty; but the hour of day is passing, and we must praise the Lord not only in this manner, but also in another, and proclaim him wonderful in his saints. May our Lord Jesus Christ himself deign to bring us into their fellowship—he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXIV. ON THE FEAST OF ALL SAINTS, III

Our Lord Jesus Christ took care to provide not only bodily but also spiritual feasts upon the mountain, showing clearly that with every affection and every desire we ought to raise our hearts to that mountain of which Isaiah says: “In the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared on the summit of the mountains” (Isa. 2). This is that rich mountain from which heavenly abundance never ceases to flow to us. This is the curdled mountain from which spiritual milk is accustomed to distil for us. This is that lofty land of which Moses sang: “He set him upon [Col. 0348C] a high land, that he might eat the fruits of the fields, suck honey from the rock, and oil from the hardest stone” (Deut. 32).

Beautifully, therefore, the Evangelist says: “Jesus, seeing the crowds, went up the mountain” (Matt. 5), that is, to show himself as the mountain and to commend the excellence of his commandments. “Come, therefore, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord, and to the house of the God of Jacob, and he will teach us his ways.” For opening his mouth, he taught them, saying: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (ibid.). These are royal feasts, which were not to be set before crowds; and therefore Jesus, seeing the crowds, went up the mountain.

These are the crowds that rebuked the blind man of Jericho, crying out after Jesus, and told him to be silent. [Col. 0348D] These crowds hindered little Zacchaeus when he wished to see Jesus (Luke 19). But because he lacked the ability to climb the mountain, he found a sycamore tree, suitably fitted to his small stature. For high mountains are for stags, the rock a refuge for hedgehogs. Therefore, whoever desires to see Jesus, if he is great, should climb the mountain in order to see him glorified; if little, he should climb the sycamore in order to see him crucified. The sycamore is called the foolish fig, and by it the cross of Christ is most plainly prefigured. Hence the Apostle says: “We preach Jesus crucified: a stumbling-block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles” (1 Cor. 1). Whoever, then, wishes to see Jesus, if he is a beginner, should climb the sycamore, that he may embrace him dying for his sake; if he is perfect, he should climb the mountain, that [Col. 0349A] he may hear him uttering the Father’s secrets. Let him rise, I say, from the crowd, that he may hear the peace unknown to the crowd. For this crowd presses upon Jesus, as the disciples said: “The crowds press upon you.” The Lord had healed by his touch a woman suffering from an issue of blood, and said, “Who touched me?” And the disciples said, “The crowds press upon you, and you say, ‘Who touched me?’” (Luke 8). But the Lord did not say, “Who presses upon me?” but, “Who touched me?” It is one thing to touch Jesus, another to press upon him. Love touches; the crowd presses.

And we also, brothers, if at some time we touch Jesus with the hand of holy desire; if even for a moment we cling to him with spiritual glue—then the most importunate crowds of worldly thoughts rise up and press upon him, lest [Col. 0349B] he become sweet to our heart, or, what is most grievous, exclude him altogether. Jesus, seeing the crowds of carnal thoughts, goes up the mountain: that is, he leaves the troubled heart and rises into the mind that cleaves to heavenly things. There, as though seated in his own place, he reveals the hidden mysteries of his secrets.

“Jesus, seeing the crowds, went up the mountain. And when he had sat down, his disciples came to him.” To some Jesus walks, to some he stands, to some he sits. For when Adam sinned and turned from the straight path, the Lord was walking in the breeze after midday. To Moses he stood when he said, “But you, stand here with me” (Deut. 5). But to Isaiah he sat; for Isaiah saw the Lord sitting upon a high and exalted throne. [Col. 0349C] He sat when, by his hidden judgment, he revealed to Isaiah the blinding of the Jews and the enlightenment of the Gentiles. He also sat with the disciples on the mountain when he instructed them to enlighten those same Gentiles.

“When he had sat down, his disciples came to him.” Those who belong to the crowd do not go up to Jesus, because they are often troubled; rather, the disciples go up, those who pursue peace. And the Lord himself plainly teaches his disciples: “By this,” he says, “all will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 13). Come then, brothers: by this judgment let each see whether he is a disciple of Jesus. Let him not inquire into his wisdom, his understanding, the distribution of his abilities, or the wasting of his body. “Though I speak,” says the Apostle, “with the tongues of men and [Col. 0349D] angels, but have not charity, I am nothing” (1 Cor. 13). Let him not, I say, inquire into these outward things, but examine the love of his own heart. For whoever loves God also loves his brother—provided that he loves as Jesus himself commands: “This is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you” (John 15).

Therefore let the disciples go up the mountain; and let them not merely go up, but go up in contemplation, go up in love. “When he had sat down, his disciples came to him; and opening his mouth, he taught them” (Matt. 5). O wonderful condescension! “God, who spoke to the fathers long ago in many portions and in many ways through the prophets, has in these last days spoken to us in his Son,” who, opening his mouth, taught. “His mouth,” [Col. 0350A] it says. For in speaking to the ancient fathers, he sometimes opened the mouths of prophets; sometimes he employed the tongues of angels; sometimes he added the services of the elements. But to speak to us, “opening his mouth, he taught,” saying: “Blessed are the poor in spirit.”

See, my brothers, what an antidote this is against the venom of the ancient serpent, by which he infected the whole human race: “You shall be,” he said, “as gods” (Gen. 3). This is the golden cup intoxicating the whole earth: it displays the beauty of blessedness, but secretly offers the bitter draught of misery—“You shall be as gods.” The vessel is beautiful, but poison lies hidden within. Come, wretched Adam, made wretched by hearing, “You shall be as gods”; become blessed by hearing, “Blessed are the poor in spirit.”

There is poverty of the flesh, and there is poverty of spirit. Poverty of the flesh is the possession of no resources; poverty of spirit is a willing abasement of mind and body for God’s sake. Hence one poor in spirit glories, saying: “I chose to be lowly in the house of my God rather than dwell in the tents of sinners” (Ps. 83). Blessed, therefore, are the poor in spirit, whom the spirit of the fear of the Lord fills, and who from fear nourish love. This is the first day of our creation and re-creation, on which, by the Lord’s command, light rises for us: that is, humility from the knowledge of ourselves. [Col. 0350B] For it is humility that divides day from night, darkness from light, righteousness from iniquity, the elect from the reprobate, those to be condemned from those to be saved. This day indeed begins from evening, that is, from consideration of our weakness, and moves toward the morning of our restoration. And just as pride is the beginning of every sin, so every righteousness begins from humility; it is the first ascent to the kingdom of heaven. “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” But now the soul, knowing itself through humility, begins to know God through devotion.

Therefore, at the Lord’s command, let there be made for it the firmament called heaven: namely, that of which the prophet says, “Stretching out the heaven like a skin” (Ps. 103), signifying Holy Scripture. Let it raise its eyes to this firmament; here let it learn God. Jesus reproaches the Jews, saying: “You err, not knowing the Scriptures nor the power of God” (Matt. 22). [Col. 0350D] But Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God. Whoever, therefore, does not wish to be ignorant of Christ, the power of God, should strive to understand the Scriptures. Let him be meek, so that he may be slow to speak and quick to hear (Jas. 1): meek, that he may learn humbly; meek, that he may not resist importunately.

For in this virtue, as on the second day of our restoration, the firmament of the Scriptures appears especially to us, dividing the upper and lower waters—that is, angelic and human knowledge. The latter is below, the former above. This day likewise begins for us from evening, that is, from a sight of our ignorance, and moves toward morning, that is, the illumination of divine grace. And it is a step toward the promised land of the living, the land of everlasting dwelling. “Blessed are the meek, for they [Col. 0351A] shall possess the earth” (Matt. 5).

Now a person who knows himself and has begun in some measure to awaken to the knowledge of God needs knowledge—not knowledge that puffs up through pride, but that builds up through charity. For he must know how great are the miseries of this life; how great a fear is needed lest he fall into temptation; how great a fear lest he become proud in prosperity. Thus his tears may become his bread by day and night, and he may love mourning more than laughter. So, in this third beatitude, as on the third day, at the Lord’s command, let the waters under heaven—that is, fluid and earthly thoughts—be gathered into one place, and let dry land appear; receiving the rain of tears, it may bring forth green grass bearing seed, and the fruit-bearing tree making fruit. For the land of our heart, watered by tears, brings forth the fruit of good thoughts, transforming the old life into a certain greenness, so that from the new person a new fruit may appear to arise. This day likewise begins from evening, that is, mourning, and moves toward the morning of divine contemplation. “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (ibid.).

Thus, as a person advances and enters God’s service, he needs the spirit of strength, that he may stand firmly and prepare his soul not for rest but for temptation: that he may overcome prosperity firmly, endure adversity firmly, hunger and thirst for righteousness alone, and despise all things in its contemplation. In order to accomplish this, already in this fourth beatitude, as on the fourth day, the Lord shows us the greater light [Col. 0351C] to rule the day: namely, the example of our Saviour, to illuminate the day—that is, the time of prosperity—lest it be wrapped in the darkness of pride; and the lesser light and stars to rule the night: namely, the example of ecclesiastical patience and the endurance of the saints, lest the night—that is, the evening of adversity—be wholly without light. This day likewise has an evening, namely temptation and hunger for blessedness and righteousness; but it advances toward morning, that is, prosperity and eternal satisfaction. “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied” (ibid.).

Now he has learned to have mercy upon his own soul, pleasing God. Let him learn to have mercy upon his neighbour also. For no one is so righteous that he does not need mercy; and this is the one and only counsel: whoever wishes mercy for himself should also show mercy to another.

Therefore, at the Lord’s command, let the waters bring forth creeping things with living souls: that is, from good thoughts, good works—not dead but living. Let him break his bread for the hungry, bring the needy and wandering into his house, clothe him when he sees him naked, and not despise his own flesh (Ezek. 18); and thus let him be flooded, as it were, with the fifth light, the fifth beatitude. [Col. 0351D] It indeed has an evening, namely consideration of one’s own need, in which he learns to have mercy on others as he would wish mercy for himself; but it tends toward morning, namely reward from God’s mercy. “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (ibid.).

But he who has now turned away from evil and learned to do good is plainly worthy to rise to understanding. For those who strive to do good surely deserve to understand God. This understanding cleanses the eye of the heart, so that one who understands God through a mirror and in an enigma may then see him openly (1 Cor. 13). In this sixth beatitude, as on the sixth day, man is created in God’s image, so that he who through ignorance had been compared to beasts may through understanding be conformed to God (Ps. 48). This day also has an evening: the mirror and enigma, because he cannot see openly; but through purity of heart it tends toward that morning of which the Psalmist says: “In the morning I shall stand before you and see” (Ps. 5). “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5). Thus this intelligible world [Col. 0352B] and all its adornment are complete. What, then, remains except the Sabbath? After these works of six days, which are performed not without labour, one comes to rest and peace of mind; servile fear is shut out, and the love of children succeeds it. For from a servant one becomes a son of God, so that he may rest in God and God in him. “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (ibid.).

This, dearly beloved, is the way by which we must return to our homeland and attain the fellowship of those whose feasts we celebrate today. They ascended before us by this laborious way; no persecutions and no adversities could tear them away from it. For they had heard the consolation that the Lord consequently added in this [Col. 0352C] sermon: “Blessed,” he says, “are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake” (ibid.); and, “Blessed are you when men hate you, reproach you, and cast out your name as evil because of me” (Luke 6).

Let, therefore, brothers most dearly beloved, the true praise of all the saints be in our mouth, lest we praise with our mouth and condemn by our deeds. For we truly praise them if we strive to imitate them. Whatever we willingly do, we prove that we love; and although we are silent in speech, we praise by deed. Let us hasten, dearly beloved, to enjoy their most sweet fellowship and with them contemplate him who is “beautiful in form above the children of men” (Ps. 44). Let nothing hinder our course: neither sloth, nor faintheartedness, nor an undiscerning excess of labour. Against sloth, let us set before ourselves the examples of the saints; against the undiscerning excess of labour, let us trust that God’s grace alone will save us. Against faintheartedness, [Col. 0352D] let us look to the Lord’s help and the unceasing prayer of all the saints on our behalf. Why, indeed, should we be fainthearted when we fight with so many helping hands? For more are with us than against us. Let this only be our part: to ask our Lord that, through the merits of all his saints, he may both help us as we fight here and crown us with them in eternal blessedness—Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns as God with God the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXV. ON BLESSED MARY

> **[Note: Col. 0353D]** In the Clairvaux manuscript this sermon is the second on All Saints; but it is evident, especially [Col. 0354D] from its conclusion, that it concerns the Virgin and was delivered on her Assumption.

[Col. 0353A]

King Solomon—or rather, the Holy Spirit through Solomon—has described for us a certain strong, wise woman, an excellent worker, as I suppose in comparison with that foolish and weak woman in Paradise, who was deceived by the devil because of her foolishness and was therefore driven into this exile as her punishment. “Who shall find a strong woman?” (Prov. 31). This is she whose strength the Lord threatened to the serpent: “I will put enmities between you and the woman, between your seed and her seed. She shall crush your head” (Gen. 3). This is the wife of the new Adam, built for him from his own side while he slept upon the cross: his wife, his bride, [Col. 0353B] namely his holy Church—strong enough to conquer the world, wise enough to conquer the devil, and such an excellent worker as to gain heaven.

“Who shall find a strong woman?” Unless it is he who, leaving the ninety-nine sheep in the wilderness, went to seek the one that had strayed (Luke 15). But since this prophecy’s applicability to holy Church has often been treated by many, and especially since a moral exposition is normally both more useful and more pleasing, let us, who are debtors both to the wise and to the simple, discuss as we can how this prophecy applies to the perfect soul. It is altogether fitting that the perfection which belongs spiritually to the mother should be assigned also to the daughter, so that, beholding the mother’s perfection, the daughter may wish to imitate it.

Therefore, in my judgment, prophetic discourse paints for us, under the figure of a woman, a kind of pattern of the best life, and describes in mystical speech that toward which every advancing soul ought to strive. For Solomon, considering after that first universal sin how prone the human soul is to evil, how unstable in sinning, how weak against the devil, raised his mind’s gaze to evangelical grace; and marvelling at how much it accomplishes in the human soul, he said: “Who shall find a strong woman?” Since she was so weak in Paradise, who can find her strong in this place of misery? Brothers, strong is the soul that has left the world, tramples the desires of the flesh, and despises the glory of the world. [Col. 0353D] “Who,” he says, “shall find such a one?” Not Moses, not Joshua son of Nun, not David, not Solomon himself, but he who said: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have, give to the poor, and come, follow me” (Matt. 19). He finds such a soul so strong because he himself first taught this strength. This strength shone especially in the most blessed Mary, Mother of God, who, without another’s example, despised the world’s allurements, shrank from the defilement of the flesh, and, what no other woman had done before her, chose the modesty and purity of virginity. He found this strong woman who had provided her beforehand to be his mother before the world’s foundation.

[Col. 0354A]

Brothers, imitate this strength; emulate this purity. But it has already been accomplished—thanks be to God. For how great is your strength, you who have despised the world, undertaken this poor and arduous manner of life, and completely severed from yourselves the affection of fathers, mothers, brothers, and friends. Solomon, seeing this strength in the Spirit, marvelled. And because it could be accomplished not by any human power but by God’s grace alone, he cries out: “Who shall find a strong woman?” Not because there is none, but because no one except God alone can find her.

This strength appears in you; but something still seems to be sought. You have done great things and acted bravely; but for what price, with what intention, and toward what end? What reward have you hoped to be given for this strength? Certain foolish men, called wise by the world—for “the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God”—certain fools, then, Socrates and Diogenes, despised riches and in large measure cut off the world’s pleasures. What, then, distinguishes you from them? I see a strong woman, that is, a strong soul, in Paul, who was stoned, beaten with rods, and afflicted by hunger, thirst, and cold (2 Cor. 11). How many robbers endure such things bravely! What, then, is the difference? Certainly it lies in the cause: that is, the intention and the reward they expect.

Let us then hear the reward of this strong woman: “Her price is from afar and from the uttermost boundaries” (Prov. 31). Great is the strength of philosophers; great is the strength of robbers; but their reward is small. Why small? Because the former expect the world’s glory, popular favour, and the admiration of the multitude. The latter hope for a coin, a garment, a horse, or something else of this world. Their reward is worthless because it is near at hand. But the reward [Col. 0354C] of this woman is from afar, from the uttermost boundaries. If you think of gold, it is not far away; if silver, that too is not far away; if the world’s honours or temporal dignities, they are not far away either, because they are temporal. This woman’s reward is far away—wholly far away—because it is neither seen by eyes, perceived by ears, tasted by the palate, smelled by the nostrils, nor handled by the hands. What reward is this? “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man” (1 Cor. 2). This is far away: as far as heaven from earth, death from life, misery from blessedness, light from blindness. This woman is in darkness, but her reward is light; she is in death, but her reward is life; she is in misery, but her reward is blessedness; she is on earth, but her reward is heaven. Finally, she is human, but her reward is God. Therefore, “her price is from afar and from the uttermost boundaries.”

But why “from the uttermost boundaries”? There are two ends, one of the good and one of the evil. But each has earlier and final ends. Each person’s end is when he dies. Yet the wicked man dies in one way and the righteous in another, because “the death of sinners is most evil” (Ps. 33), while “precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Ps. 115). These are the earlier ends. Although the holy soul departing from the body obtains no small share of blessedness, still its reward is from afar and from the final boundaries. What are the final boundaries? When indeed all shall rise, though not all shall be changed (1 Cor. 15); when all troubles have ended and, now established also in the incorruption of the flesh, the strong woman shall hear from the Lord: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25), while the wicked, on the contrary, hear: “Depart from me, accursed, into eternal fire” (ibid.).

[Col. 0355A]

From these boundaries this woman expects her reward. For this reward she now sells herself as a servant, and, looking to it, sweats, labours, goes wherever she is commanded, and willingly endures whatever is imposed. Set this reward before your eyes, brothers; in view of this reward endure labours, vigils, and other hardships. If men undergo such bitter labours to obtain a coin, what ought you to do, for whom heaven is set forth? Thus, to speak briefly: Solomon, beholding a soul perfectly despising the world and hoping for nothing but things to come, says: “Who shall find a strong woman? Her price is from afar and from the uttermost boundaries.” And he adds: “The heart of her husband trusts in her, and he shall not need spoils.”

There is no need to explain to your charity who the husband of this strong woman is. He is the one of whom the Apostle says: “I have espoused you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (2 Cor. 11). Therefore, “the heart of her husband trusts in her.” The comparison is drawn from human affairs. [Col. 0355C] A husband who knows that his wife is chaste, sober, modest, and well-behaved knows, whether he is absent or present, that she will not admit adulterers, listen to seducers, or look upon deceivers. For she fears chastely and loves perfectly: she loves her husband not for what is his, but for himself; she fears not being beaten, but being even slightly abandoned. Such is the soul described here. If the soul is such—chaste, sober, loving perfectly, and fearing chastely—her husband’s heart trusts in her. He is securely absent, securely present, and securely entrusts his goods to her: not to squander them with adulterers or share them with fornicators.

But how does this spiritual husband come or depart, when he is everywhere and absent nowhere, since he is always, wholly, and everywhere present? Yet when we are worn down by adversities, he seems to depart; when we are comforted by prosperity, he seems to return. When he visits our mind with his grace, he seems present; when that grace is withdrawn, he seems far away. Blessed is the mind with which God, as it were securely, does all these things. Truly, the heart of her husband trusts in her. Blessed is the mind that is neither broken by adversity nor dissolved by prosperity, that neither complains in adversity nor grows proud in prosperity: surely the heart of her husband trusts in her. Blessed is the mind that does not despair when grace is withdrawn and does not exalt itself above others when grace is present: truly, the heart of her husband trusts in her.

Brothers, I do not want you to be unwary in this matter. For many, when they suffer no temptations, are not worn down by adversities, and are afflicted by no troubles, rejoice, dance for joy, and exalt themselves above others as though they had gained this by their own merits. But if all these things turn the other way, they grow sad, dejected, complain, and despair. Of such a soul it cannot be said: “The heart of her husband trusts in her.” Come, brother, whoever you are, who yesterday wept, prayed, and felt great sweetness from God: know that your husband was present. What then did you promise your husband? “I shall never be moved” (Ps. 29). Today matters have been reversed. Meditation is distasteful, prayer is dreadful, reading has become worthless; moreover lust attacks, the flesh is inflamed, and the mind is driven as if by furies. Your husband is absent. Now let us see whether it ought to be said of you: “The heart of her husband trusts in [Col. 0356B] her.” He is absent: you, be faithful. Why, as though despairing of your husband’s return, do you look toward adulterers—that is, unclean spirits—suggesting immoderate sadness or foolish joy in vain and superfluous things? Because you no longer feel your husband’s sweetness, will you throw yourself down into the worst sweetness of the flesh? Of such a soul it cannot be said: “The heart of her husband trusts in her.”

Brothers, I wish to instruct you a little against this most grievous temptation. If it happens that God’s grace visits you, fills you with a certain heavenly sweetness, and waters you with a flood of tears, watch yourselves carefully: let pride not creep in; let no negligence mingle with your other practices; do not become more lax in abstinence or more lukewarm in obedience; and [Col. 0356C] above all, do not judge inferior to yourselves one whom you do not perceive to be endowed with a like grace. For by such negligences grace is accustomed to be withdrawn, and a certain baseness and lukewarmness arise.

But if grace has been withdrawn and you remember having chosen any of these things, do not complain against God at all; rather, humbly accuse yourselves and gird yourselves manfully to repair what has been torn apart. But if you are conscious of no slackness, do not be irrationally saddened at grace’s withdrawal; instead, comfort yourselves with sure hope, as though you were about to receive the same grace again. For the Lord trains you to have humility in prosperity and patience in adversity.

Again, a husband who has a wife in whom he trusts securely entrusts his goods to her, whether to distribute or preserve. A good wife steals nothing for herself and shares none of it with adulterers and seducers. Let every soul now consider how faithfully it preserves its husband’s goods. If it has knowledge, wisdom, or understanding in the Scriptures, it received all these from its husband, not only to preserve but also to distribute. If it has grace in labours, vigils, or psalmody, it has received these also for distribution. If it has grace in compunction, prayer, spiritual affection, or contemplation, it has received these not for distribution but for preservation. Let every soul now see whether it is faithful to its husband and whether it should be said: “The heart of her husband trusts in her.”

First, it is necessary that in all these things it not grow proud or reckon to itself what belongs to its husband. Next, it must take care not to hide enviously what it has received to distribute, [Col. 0357A] nor distribute it arrogantly. Finally, it must not shamefully squander what it has received only to preserve. To put it more plainly: a soul that does not grow proud because of the grace bestowed upon it usurps none of her husband’s substance for herself. If it does not enviously hide what can benefit others, but humbly speaks for the praise of its husband and faithfully dispenses its husband’s goods; if it does not vainly boast of hidden grace received—for example, compunction, devotion, prayer, or contemplation—it prudently preserves its husband’s goods. Therefore, of such a soul it may be said: “The heart of her husband trusts in her.”

Observe briefly how this perfection shone in the most blessed Mary. Her humble answer to the angel testifies how little she was proud of grace bestowed upon her: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord” (Luke 1). Her humble visitation teaches how little she preferred herself to others: carrying God in her womb, she nevertheless went forth to greet even a handmaid. The Gospel narrative shows how reverently she preserved her husband’s goods, saying: “But Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart” (Luke 2). How faithfully she did not remain silent in speech is proclaimed by that honeyed hymn: “My soul magnifies the Lord” (ibid.). Deservedly, the heart of her husband trusts in her.

“And he shall not need spoils,” it says. What is that soul, adorned with so many ornaments, that it does not need another’s spoils? It is not one of the foolish virgins, who had reserved no oil for themselves and had to beg it from others. Spoils are called those ornaments or garments which are accustomed to be stripped away. There are many who possess no holiness within themselves yet, miserably envying others, cover their vices—like naked shamefulness—by detracting from others, imagining that they are well covered if they can take away from others the garments of good reputation. There are also others who, having nothing good in their own conscience, commend their reputation by performing some outward good work so as to appear religious before men. Therefore, on the day of judgment, because they are empty and naked within, they will need others’ commendation, as though they needed another’s spoils. Hence the cry of the foolish virgins: “Give us some of your oil, because our lamps are going out” (Matt. 25). Then this wise woman will have no need of spoils, because adorned with the glory of her own conscience she will securely go to meet her bridegroom. It may also be understood simply: “He shall not need spoils,” [Col. 0357D] because she abounded in the ornaments of virtues. It follows:

He will render to her—that is, to her husband—good and not evil, all the days of her life (Prov. 31). That this is how it should be understood is made clear by another translation, which reads: “She will work good, and not evil, for her husband.” If the husband of this woman is rightly understood to be Christ, then whatever good any soul performs in his service is rendered back rather than given. If pure humility, sweet charity, true obedience, or perfect patience is offered to him, from where does it come except from him? If there is fervour in labours, purity in vigils, restraint in food, humble silence, whence are these except from him, from whom comes every good gift and every perfect donation? (Jas. 1.) Therefore [Col. 0358A] the holy soul, because it first received these good things from God, rightly renders them back. “She will render to him good and not evil.” A great commendation, brethren. For many do otherwise. They receive good things and return evil. They receive riches, and thereby are all the more dissolved in lust; honours, and thereby wretches swell with pride; knowledge, and thereby exalt themselves above others. They receive bodily beauty, and the more beautiful they are, the more, because they misuse it, disgraceful they become. Why should I mention that they receive from God this common light, air, and bread, and misuse all these things to his injury? It cannot be said of such people: “She will render to him good and not evil.”

Brethren, it is indeed a great, great perfection to misuse none of God’s gifts. For what shall I say of spiritual gifts? [Col. 0358B] If we advance in the knowledge of God, if we penetrate the veins of the Scriptures somewhat more subtly, if we abound in tears, if we become weighty in speech and mature in conduct, and if from all these things we become proud, it will not be said of us: “She will render to him good and not evil.” Often, when the Lord visits us so that we may feel something of his sweetness, if, once that sweetness has been withdrawn, some temptation happens to assail us, and if we then, as though forgetful of that sweetness, are cast down, certainly we do not return good for good, but evil for good. Therefore, brethren, the soul which misuses none of God’s gifts is not undeservedly held worthy of this praise: “She will render good and not evil.” And because the reward is not promised to those who begin, but given to those who persevere, the prophetic utterance adds: [Col. 0358C] “All the days of her life.” Above it had said that she would not need spoils, because she would abound in her own ornaments. It therefore explains whence these ornaments came to her, adding: “She sought wool and flax, and worked according to the counsel of her hands” (ibid.). Rightly she will not need spoils. For she did not grow sluggish in idleness, nor was she rendered languid by sleep. “She sought wool and flax, and worked according to the counsel of her hands.” She knows that one who is idle will be filled with poverty. Therefore, ready for labour and untiring in work, she sought wool and flax. Why, except to weave garments, repel cold, and cover nakedness? Our garments are the works of righteousness themselves, by which our nakedness is covered and the cold of eternal condemnation avoided. For every soul without good works [Col. 0358D] stands naked before God’s eyes and grows altogether cold toward God’s charity. But there are garments of haircloth; there are woollen and linen garments; there are purple garments too. A haircloth garment pricks, but a woollen one drives away cold. Linen possesses no slight softness; purple is of great honour. Therefore, to refer these things to spiritual realities, as it seems to me, the haircloth garment belongs to penitents, the woollen to those raising themselves toward good works, the linen to those making progress, and the purple to the perfect. A soul still defiled by vices must be pierced by the great bitterness of repentance, so that the contagion of its iniquities may be covered by this harshness. This woman does not concern herself with that garment, since she has already passed beyond that stage of penitents. Scripture makes mention below of the purple garment [Col. 0359A]; but it sets wool and flax first. For it is not enough that someone should repent of past evils unless he girds himself manfully for good works. “She sought wool and flax, and worked.” Let us see, if you please, the difference between the woollen and linen garment, and from it carve out, if we can, some spiritual meaning.

A woollen garment is rougher, a linen one softer; yet the woollen garment drives away cold, while linen is not sufficient against the injury of winter. Therefore, one clothed only in wool suffers some roughness; one clothed only in linen has little warmth. It is better, then, to be clothed in both, so that wool may exclude the cold and linen temper the roughness. We have said that the garments of this woman—that is, of every ecclesial soul—are good works. Nor without reason. [Col. 0359B] By these she is clothed, by these adorned; by these, if through fellowship with the flesh she suffers something shameful, she is concealed from God’s sight. A soul lacking these garments will appear naked on the day of judgment, and there will be nothing by which its shame may be hidden. Therefore it will surely be cast into eternal fire. But all our good works consist in two things: the active life and the contemplative life. The active life is like a woollen garment; the contemplative life like a linen one. The former is rougher, the latter gentler; the former outward, the latter inward. The active life can indeed suffice against the cold of condemnation and wipe away every shame of sins. Without it, not even the contemplative life—at least in this mortal condition—can bring anyone to perfection. [Col. 0359C] Let no one deceive himself, my brethren. They are altogether mistaken, brethren, mistaken; indeed, as I think, they are not mistaken but strive to mislead others—those who err and lead others into error, since they know neither what they say nor the things about which they affirm (1 Tim. 1). Being themselves idle and slothful, doing nothing but meddling, they cloak their very idleness and meddlesomeness beneath the veil of contemplation, and say: “What need is there to work? What profit is there in cutting a trunk with an axe or striking a stone with a hammer? Mary has chosen the better part” (Luke 10). Paul rebukes them when he writes openly to the Thessalonians: “We have heard that some walk disorderly, doing nothing, but meddling. We command them in the name of the Lord Jesus [Col. 0359D] Christ to eat their own bread in silence” (2 Thess. 3).

Let them therefore contend with Paul and say: “Why does he command us to work? Mary has chosen the better part.” And it is true, brethren: Mary chose the better part. Truth himself said so. On this feast of St Mary, there has been read the account of those two sisters, Mary and Martha. Nor is it without reason that it is read on her feast, except because in the Blessed Virgin herself both the active and contemplative life worked perfectly. Mary indeed chose the better part. But we must consider that in the same house Martha laboured and Mary was at leisure, because in the soul that receives Christ both lives operate, each at its own time, place, and order. Therefore this strong woman is not only [Col. 0360A] a worker in wool but also a worker in flax. For she sought wool and flax, and worked. What else but this twofold garment, woollen and linen? But since we have spoken of these garments, let us now consider wool and flax, from which they are woven. In my judgment—indeed, in the judgment of most blessed Augustine—by wool are understood bodily works, through which the active life is perfected; by flax, spiritual works, out of which the contemplative life is woven. By bodily works I mean vigils, labour, and fasts; by spiritual works, prayers, readings, meditations, and compunctions. Some wear themselves out in bodily exercises but do not at all rise to spiritual ones. Others flatter themselves with spiritual things alone, as though with a linen garment, and grow cold toward every spiritual fervour. They would not grow cold, [Col. 0360B] if they adhered to spiritual things fervently and continually. But since those spiritual exercises cannot be practised without some alternation with bodily ones, while they disdain the latter, they become altogether lukewarm in the former. Both, therefore, refuse to imitate the wisdom of this woman, who sought both wool and flax, and worked. But where did she seek them? How did she seek them? Certainly, the soul eager for salvation and intent upon perfection surveys the life, conduct, and teaching of the holy Fathers. In one she seeks diligence in work, in another zeal in watching; she investigates that man’s abstinence and scrutinizes another’s obedience; from one she learns, so to speak, certain veins of prayer, and from another she adopts for herself a form of meditation. Gathering these things into her bosom, she works according to the counsel of her hands. [Col. 0360C] What is this “counsel of the hands”? Clearly, a person is fed by his hands and defended by his hands; hands direct the other limbs, and hands are set against blows.

Let us therefore consider that body of which the Apostle says: “For we who are many are one body” (1 Cor. 10). All of us who are in this congregation are one body. Some perform the office of feet, others of hands, others of eyes. Therefore, brethren, it seems to me that by the name of hands prelates may be understood: those who feed the others by teaching and defend them by prayers; those who also arrange the others as limbs and set themselves against the blows of outward cares. Therefore, brethren, if you have sought wool and flax for yourselves—that is, bodily and spiritual exercises—[Col. 0360D] then work. Yet not according to your own counsel, but according to the counsel of your hands, so that all your works may depend upon the judgment of your prelates. I had thought, brethren, to bring together in one sermon all that is said here concerning this woman; but I see that my sermon has been long, and that I have scarcely expounded four verses. Perhaps this too belongs to this woman’s flax. For when flax is seen on the distaff, it is not known how long a thread may be made from it. Therefore let us reserve what follows for another sermon—or, if we cannot do this, for other sermons.

(From these final words it is clear that the author intended to deliver further sermons on the Blessed Virgin concerning Proverbs chapter 21; whether he delivered them is unknown.)

[Col. 0361]

SERMONS OF BLESSED AELRED, ABBOT OF RIEVAULX, ON THE BURDENS IN CHAPTERS 13 AND FOLLOWING OF THE PROPHET ISAIAH.

LETTER OF BLESSED AELRED TO G. (19), BISHOP OF LONDON.

(*Bibliotheca Patrum Cisterciensis*, vol. V, p. 229.)

To the beloved, loving, and holy Father G., Bishop of London, whom he embraces with the sweetness of every devotion, Brother AELRED, offering with all affection the service owed to the poor of Christ who are at Rievaulx.

Hearing, most blessed Father, that amid the countless occupations imposed upon you both by the authority of royal majesty and by the necessity of pastoral care, you nevertheless, as a cultivator of wisdom, a friend of tranquillity, and a student of spiritual knowledge, devote yourself to reading and console the annoyance of pressing cares amid the sweet delights of prayer by frequent meditation on the holy Scriptures, I have become so eager for you that I dare aspire not only to the acquaintance of your Serenity but even, to say something foolish, to friendship with you yourself. For, forgetful alike of your exalted rank and my lowliness, I rely upon the laws of love, for which nothing is low and nothing exalted; love which, making heaven equal to earth, joined the Lord of heaven to earthly members, so that the Word might become flesh and dwell among us (John 1); which brought down the Lord and raised up the human being, so that, as it were, in a certain middle place, mercy and misery might meet one another (Ps. 84); so that power might be united to weakness in such a way that the Word and the soul might be in one flesh, and God and man might be one person in these three. What heights, then, would love not bring down, or what depths would it not lift up, so as to make them one in itself—love which, with the property of the natures preserved and not confused, has so wonderfully mingled heaven with earth, the Lord with flesh, and spirit with dust, through the soul as mediator?

Moreover, I see in every creature, rational, irrational, or insentient, a certain trace of love, through which diverse things are joined, discordant things brought into harmony, and opposites united. For in other creatures an image of love appears; but in the rational mind its truth operates. To love is common to God, angels, and human beings. Love, therefore, disregarding whatever lies outside nature, joins nature to nature, so that those may be one heart and one soul (Acts 4) who have one faith, one hope, and one charity.

Therefore my mind, following love’s impulse, passes by in a certain spiritual motion all things that are yours but are not you, all things around you that are neither yours nor you; piercing even the mass of your body by its subtlety, it pours itself entirely into the bosom of your mind, mingling affection with affection, perception with perception, and spirit with spirit, so that through participation in your spirit my spirit may be renewed, by the light of your perception my own perception may borrow for itself the light of knowledge, and moreover my affection may be warmed by the sweetness of your affection. There I behold how good you are; there I embrace and perceive how wise you are; there I delight in and taste how lovable you are.

Hence, most loving Father, I judged that whatever study I possess in sacred letters should be submitted to the examination of your discernment: so that, where my understanding is sound, your authority may confirm me; where I hesitate, truth may shine upon me through your teaching; where I err, your holy severity may correct me.

Accordingly, having at one time briefly discussed before the assembly of brethren the prophetic burdens of Isaiah, touching each one summarily, I was asked by many to pursue these same matters at greater length. I yielded to the will of those whose advancement I ought to serve. Beginning, then, with the burdens of Babylon, and proceeding thence through the burden of Philistia to the hidden meanings of the Moabite burden, I committed thirty homilies to writing. But lest perhaps I should run, or had run, in vain, I laid down my pen until judgment upon what I had written should proceed from your countenance, and your eyes might examine the reasoning of all these matters; so that, by the decision of your discernment, everything written might be erased, corrected, or approved.

Although the reading of these things may seem unworthy of such great wisdom, the vehemence of love nevertheless dares to demand it; for love so embraces charity that it almost irreverently rushes upon majesty. Moreover, the memory of your humility and kindness together gives me courage: when I was once in London, you anticipated me with “blessings of sweetness” (Ps. 20), [Col. 0363] and by the very one by whom it would have been a great thing for me even to be noticed, I deserved—amazed and trembling at such condescension—to be greeted in a kind of embrace of charity.

Hence, most blessed Father, this presumption has arisen: I desire that the acquaintance with your Serenity then begun may be brought to completion, and I do not despair that my mind, then knocking at the door of your friendship, may be brought into its inner chamber. Although it is a great thing for a wise man to grant even a little time to leisure, may it not weary my lord, I ask, to lose so small an amount of time, in which you may prune away what is superfluous, supply what is lacking, or erase everything we have written.

Thus, after setting first the sermon which gave us the occasion for writing the rest, we have appended nineteen homilies on the burden of Babylon (Isa. 13), three on the burden of Philistia, and nine on the burden of Moab, ready, at your discretion, either to stop here or to proceed further.

SERMONS ON THE BURDENS.

[Col. 0363]

SERMON I. FOR THE ADVENT OF THE LORD—ON THE ELEVEN BURDENS.

[Col. 0363A]

“The time has come, dearest brethren,” etc. It is extant among the works of St Bernard in Mabillon’s edition; see *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXXIV, col. 817.

SERMON II. ON THE BURDEN OF BABYLON. On the words written: “The burden of Babylon, which Isaiah son of Amoz saw.”

God is the primordial and efficient cause of all things that have been, are, or shall be; he himself is the end of all things. For since he is, so to speak, being properly speaking, all things whatsoever have from him that by which they are, because they have their being only from Being. It is certain that a human being and an angel exist; but existence is one thing, and [Col. 0363B] to exist as a human being or an angel is another, since something can exist without being either human being or angel. Let whoever can think, then, not of the existence of a human being or of an angel, but, apart from angel and human being, of Being itself—which belongs not only to human beings and angels, but to all things that are. Therefore that very Being, which belongs not particularly to this or that thing but universally to all existing—or, more exactly, all being—things, is without doubt God.

And just as he is the being of all existing things, so he is the life of all living things and the wisdom of all wise things. The rational creature was created according to this form, receiving from him not only existence and life, but also wisdom and wise living. Severing and separating himself from this form, [Col. 0363C] wretched man was compared to senseless beasts (Ps. 48), and began to be foolish and to live foolishly. Yet he did not cease to exist and live, for he could return to his former form when re-formed by him who had formed him.

That form itself is wisdom; the way by which one returns to that form is instruction. All instruction by which we are led back from this deformity to the form consists of three things: faith, hope, and charity—so that we may know what must be believed, hoped for, and loved, and may thus believe, hope, and love. Therefore wisdom, passing into holy souls (Wis. 7), made friends of God and prophets, through whom it supplied us with sacred Scripture, as it were the fountain of all instruction. The Spirit who composed it [Col. 0363D] arranged it with such wisdom that it could contain innumerable meanings. Since he reveals some of these to one person and others to another, Scripture is always fresh, always delightful through a certain renewal, for exercising the intellect and dispelling weariness. [Col. 0364A] But so that human error or demonic suggestion may be distinguished by a sure test and by the revelation of the Holy Spirit, the rule of faith has been laid down, the promises of hope prescribed, and the commandments of charity promulgated. Thus, whenever a meaning occurs to the mind and is found not to accord with these, you may unhesitatingly ascribe it either to demonic deceit or to human error; but whatever is fittingly drawn from the sacred pages, instructs toward faith, raises toward hope, or kindles charity, you should not doubt both that it was placed in the sacred writings by the Holy Spirit and that it has been revealed to you by him.

But for those hindered by the darkness of worldly business [Col. 0364B] or entangled in the nets of necessary occupations, the things once spoken or written from the Scriptures suffice—and more than suffice—to restrain their wandering and shameful excursions. These matters are so unknown to them that they can always seem new.

But for you, beloved, who have renounced the works of this world, who, freed from every worldly care and anxiety, have entered into combat with unclean spirits and your own thoughts, there is another rule and another necessity in meditating on the Scriptures. For the same discourse and the repeated reading of the same passage which produce weariness in many must be renewed when they seem old and familiar, either by adding certain meanings or at least by changing the words. [Col. 0364C] Thus zeal for inquiry is stirred; useless and empty excursions of the heart are recalled to what is useful; and the mind, which had drawn back in disgust from familiar things, returns profitably to that from which it had been, as it were sensibly, diverted, through the renewed sweetness of reading or discourse.

Hence I take into my hands the book of Isaiah, intending with your charity to examine a certain small portion of it. Although it may be very familiar through the exposition of the saints, I nevertheless judge it very useful if we repeat what they have said, if not differently in substance, then at least differently in manner; or if, taking the seeds of reasoning from their words, we bring forward as God grants those points which they seem to have passed over as very small or evident. Thus one who does not dare aspire to their perfect meanings, [Col. 0364D] as to solid bread, may approach—even if he is a little dog—the crumbs that, aided by your prayers, we can gather beneath their table. [Col. 0365A]

Thus, dearest brethren, thus let us redeem the time, so as to mock time, because the days are evil (Eph. 5); and with saving words and holy meditations let us preserve our mouths from idle speech and our hearts from vain thoughts. This holy prophet is so profound in meaning, so clear in foretelling future things, and so delightful in moral instruction that now he seems as though carried up into heaven itself, searching out the secrets of divine counsels; now, swiftly lowered by wing to the lower regions of the firmament, revealing heavenly mysteries; now descending in gentle flight even to us, walking in the fields of morals; now as though received into paradise, and again returning to us and reporting ineffable words [Col. 0365B] which it is not permitted a human being to speak.

He reveals all these mysteries of Christ and the Church in an oracle so manifest that he seems not so much to have foretold future things as to have narrated past ones. Although these things are, by their own character, sufficiently pleasing and savoury, they are made more pleasing and sweeter by the wonderful charm of his eloquence. But, leaving the rest aside, it has pleased us to set forth for your edification concerning the eleven burdens about which the prophet discoursed at the prompting of the Holy Spirit whatever that Spirit himself may suggest.

I confess that I am in every respect a debtor to your advancement, indeed because of my office, but especially because of affection. Yet necessity also presses upon me. “Woe to me if I do not preach the Gospel” (1 Cor. 9), [Col. 0365C] especially since whatever progress I make in spiritual teaching or understanding the Scriptures, I do not doubt is given not so much to me as transmitted to you through me. It should not be ascribed to my merits, for I am a sinner; nor to scholarly disciplines, for, as you know, I am almost unlettered; nor even to my study or diligence, for I am rarely at leisure and often occupied. It is altogether God’s: entrusted to me and transmitted to you, so that whoever glories may glory in the Lord.

Be present, therefore, good Jesus, and pour the grace of your blessing upon the loaves we have brought forth. Let the poor eat and be satisfied, and say with the Prophet: “How sweet are your words to my palate, sweeter than honey to my mouth” (Ps. 118). Behold, I set my hand to the task; grant your help, for without you I can do nothing. [Col. 0365D] You who inspired holy Isaiah to write, inspire me, I pray, to understand what he wrote, for you have already inspired me to believe; “for unless we believe, we shall not understand” (Isa. 43).

What, then, do we think this burden signifies? There is a burden which presses and a burden which crushes. Weakness presses; iniquity crushes. Temptation presses; condemnation crushes. First, therefore, the burden of Babylon is set forth; then the burden of Philistia; then the burden of Moab; afterward the burden of Damascus; next follows the burden of Egypt, succeeded by the burden of the wilderness of the sea, then the burden of Dumah, the burden in Arabia, then the valley of vision, the burden of Tyre, and lastly the burden of the beasts of the south.

Thus holy Isaiah displays the humiliation of certain cities or nations—or rather, of those who are signified in these [Col. 0366A] cities or nations—and he does not pass over in silence the manner, causes, and material occasions of that humiliation. He also inserts discourse concerning the blessedness of those who are burdened by this humiliation unto salvation rather than destruction. Everywhere it is evident: “Power belongs to God, and mercy to you, O Lord, for you render to each according to his works” (Ps. 61), dividing day from night and light from darkness, so that darkness itself may appear denser by comparison with light, and light may shine more abundantly by contrast with darkness.

And who judges and distinguishes among these things except he who says: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5)? And again: “For judgment I came into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John 9).

Since, therefore, [Col. 0366B] through the coming of the Lord and Saviour this separation of good and evil has taken place, together with the humiliation of some and liberation of others, it is clear that the principal subject of the prophet throughout the whole body of the book is the coming of the Lord himself. Of him holy Simeon says: “Behold, this one is set for the fall and rising again of many in Israel, and for a sign that shall be contradicted” (Luke 2). What Isaiah calls a burden, Simeon himself calls a fall.

He describes these burdens so that it appears that God presses some but does not crush them; crushes some but does not press them; and both presses and crushes some. He presses those whom he afflicts; he crushes those whom he abandons. He afflicts some, therefore, but does not abandon them, as it is written: “God scourges every person whom he receives” (Heb. 12). [Col. 0366C] Hence the Psalmist says: “I will visit their iniquities with a rod and their sins with stripes; but I will not withdraw my mercy from him” (Ps. 88).

He abandons but does not afflict some, of whom the Prophet says: “They are not in the labour of men, nor are they scourged with men” (Ps. 72). And again: “I let them go according to the desires of their heart” (Ps. 80). And through another prophet: “I will not punish your daughters when they commit fornication, nor your wives when they commit adultery” (Hos. 4).

Moreover, he both afflicts and abandons some, of whom he himself says through the prophet: “I have crushed them, and they refused to receive correction” (Jer. 5). Indeed, how and by what means affliction or abandonment takes place will, God willing, become clear when we begin to treat the burdens themselves. A burden may be called that of Babylon, Philistia, or Moab according to the burden by which they press, or according to that by which they are pressed; and likewise with the rest. But now, if you please, let us examine the heading of the following account. [Col. 0366D]

“The burden of Babylon, which Isaiah son of Amoz saw” (Isa. 13). By the name Babylon, brethren, which is interpreted “confusion,” the world is signified, as is well known to your charity. For there all things are confused: there good people live with evil, the reprobate with the elect; wheat with chaff, oil with dregs, and wine with grapes; there, as regards temporal matters, the righteous fare like the wicked; there a human being has no advantage over beasts.

Often, too, we understand Babylon as only that city of the reprobate with its king, [Col. 0367A] to which none of the elect belongs and from which none of the reprobate is excluded. We divide the reprobate into three classes: one class still shares in both the fellowship and works of the elect; another is separated from those works or that fellowship; a third, having now put off the body, is consigned to eternal punishments. Therefore, all of them together, each of these classes individually, and each person within the individual classes, are rightly designated by the name Babylon.

It is also clear that the elect are divided into three orders. For some have not yet been called, such as Jews or pagans; others are called but not justified, such as sinful Christians; and others are justified but not yet glorified, such as saints still subject to the miseries of this life.

Therefore, even though predestination has separated from Babylon those elect [Col. 0367B] who have not yet been called, as long as they are blinded by Babylonian errors, they do not depart from Babylon’s name. But those whom calling together with predestination has joined to the elect are nevertheless marked by the disgrace of the Babylonian name when abominable works separate them.

Babylon, then, is called that whole body of human beings in which elect and reprobate alike are entangled in the same errors and vices. A perverse and hardened heart, confused by vices and passions, is also called Babylon. Babylon is likewise the society of reprobates for which eternal confusion is prepared.

The burden of Babylon is that by which that confused multitude is destroyed through the separation of many from it; [Col. 0367C] by which it is also incessantly afflicted with temporal evils; by which in individual hearts the structure of vices and most evil passions, like a city of confusion, is overthrown; and by which, further, after this life the reprobate alone will be burdened with eternal punishments.

This is the burden of Babylon which Isaiah son of Amoz saw. How did he see it? Come now, brethren: those who are now called prophets were formerly accustomed to be called seers because of a certain more excellent and more divine vision, so to speak. The pressure of time and the business that has now intervened do not permit us to discuss it here. Let this consideration, then, be reserved for another sermon.

Meanwhile pray that, following the meaning of the Spirit, we may describe these burdens in such a way that we may bear bravely those which press us, avoid those which crush us, and escape [Col. 0367D] those which condemn us, through the help of him who for our sake willed to be burdened with our burdens: Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, through all ages of ages. Amen.

SERMON III. On the manifold kinds of vision, and on that vision which makes a prophet.

You know, dearest brothers, that, intending to speak about burdens, I have undertaken a heavy burden myself. Therefore we must invoke that same Spirit, so that he who first laid upon us the burden of charity may make light every burden that can serve our advancement; so that he who gave the desire by the infusion of his light may also grant the fulfilment. Yesterday, as far as the title was concerned, we explained as best we could the burden of Babylon [Col. 0368A]. But since it is written, “The burden of Babylon, which Isaiah son of Amos saw,” we think it necessary to ask how this burden was seen by Isaiah—especially since there are several kinds of vision, and because, by reason of a certain excellence of vision, prophets were called “seers.”

For there is sensory vision, imaginary vision, phantastic vision, spiritual vision, rational vision, and intellectual vision. Sensory vision is that by which bodily things are perceived through bodily senses. Imaginary vision is that by which images of things perceived through the body are seen inwardly, or, from things that have been perceived, other things not sensed are fashioned. Phantastic vision, however, is that by which phantasms of bodily things are presented either to the eyes or to the mind [Col. 0368B]. Spiritual vision is that by which images of visible things, bearing some signification, are formed within the human spirit. Rational vision is that by which truths are distinguished from falsehoods, or virtues from vices. Intellectual vision, finally, is that by which—not merely truth from falsehood is distinguished—but truth itself is contemplated in truths themselves.

Thus sensory vision is in the body, embracing all bodily senses and their power and nature. For we say: “Look, see how white it is”; “Taste and see how sweet it is” (Ps. 33 [34]); “Hear and see how resonant it is”; “Smell and see how fragrant it is”; “Touch, see how soft it is.” Every experience through the fleshly senses is therefore called sensory vision. Such a vision can indeed be prophetic, but cannot make someone a prophet.

The vision of the bronze serpent which Moses raised in the wilderness, through which the children of Israel were healed from serpent bites (Num. 21), was prophetic; yet it did not make its beholders prophets. Sensory too was that vision in which holy Abraham saw three men coming down the road (Gen. 18). He himself did not doubt that it was prophetic, for he saw three and worshipped one. Yet Abraham was not a prophet by virtue of that sensory vision, though prophetic; rather, by virtue of another vision through which he perceived that this sensory vision was prophetic. Thus the one who interpreted the writing traced upon the wall of Babylon’s royal hall was more truly a prophet than the one who saw the hand and its fingers writing (Dan. 5).

We call imaginary that vision in which, within the mind, we see images of bodily things that we have perceived by sense [Col. 0368D], because the likenesses of these things are not introduced into us from elsewhere, but, having been brought in by the senses, are imagined inwardly just as we saw them outwardly; or else we fashion other images from them. For inwardly I imagine the likeness of a four-footed stag which I have seen with my eyes; and from it I fashion the image of a six-footed stag which I have never seen. This vision is never prophetic and never makes a prophet—unless perhaps it may be called prophetic for this reason: that sensory things, when they are prophetic, can be imagined in the mind.

Phantastic vision, however, is sometimes caused by the body, sometimes by the soul, and sometimes by a spirit of another nature: by the body, either through sleep or illness [Col. 0369A]. Through sleep, when our body sleeps, while the soul—which cannot sleep—being released from the senses by which it was occupied in looking upon actual bodies, naturally ranges meanwhile among bodily phantasies. Through illness, when the senses are disturbed by some bad bodily condition and sights resembling bodies are perceived; this is plainly frequent among the delirious.

Phantastic vision comes from the soul itself when, while awake, the soul repeatedly turns over certain things in thought, and then, while asleep, beholds them through certain phantasies. But this vision is formed by a spirit of another nature when a person is deceived through vain phantasms, either in the eyes of the flesh; or, in sleep or sickness, when phantasies of things are presented to the soul by evil spirits; or when, though the body is awake and healthy, the soul is snatched away from its own senses [Col. 0369B].

For we know with certainty that many people’s eyes have been so deceived that a human being seemed a beast to them; that they judged water to be flowing where there was no water; that they supposed fire was raging where there was no fire; and many things of this kind. That many dreams are fashioned by demons seems incredible to no one. And although many visions may be produced in delirious persons, or those afflicted by any other illness, by their very sickness, it may nevertheless happen that many things are cast before their souls by evil spirits. But whenever an evil spirit snatches a soul from the senses, as into a kind of ecstasy, it makes the person deceived by phantasms either demoniac, possessed, or a false prophet. We therefore wholly separate the vision we have called phantastic from the office of prophets [Col. 0369C].

The vision which we call spiritual because it is formed in the human spirit by the operation of another spirit occurs either in sleep or in ecstasy. In sleep, when images of bodily things are formed in the mind of a sleeper by good spirits. Although this vision is certainly prophetic, it nevertheless does not make a prophet. The vision in which the patriarch Joseph saw the sun, moon, and eleven stars worshipping him was prophetic (Gen. 37). Yet he was not a prophet by this vision if he did not understand its mystery.

Nor do we call Pharaoh a prophet because he is said in dreams to have perceived a presage of the coming abundance and subsequent famine; rather, Joseph was the prophet [Col. 0369D] (Gen. 41), to whom God, on the occasion of that dream, disclosed the secret of his purpose. Nor do I judge Nebuchadnezzar worthy of the name of prophet because that statue appeared to him in sleep; rather Daniel, to whom it was granted to know both the dream itself and the power of the dream (Dan. 2).

Moreover, when, with the body healthy and the senses not lulled by sleep, the soul is carried by some hidden spiritual operation into visions resembling bodily things, this is called ecstasy or rapture; by this vision hidden things are revealed and future things foreshown.

When intellectual vision—of which we shall speak later—is added to this, one who sees such things becomes a prophet: whether speaking mysteries, disclosing secrets, or foretelling things to come. In an ecstasy of mind Peter saw a vessel descending from heaven [Col. 0370A], containing every kind of creeping thing and animal; and it was said to him, “Slay and eat” (Acts 10). He understood that vision, or command, certainly not then, but when intellectual vision was subsequently added, when he said: “Truly I have discovered that God is no respecter of persons; but in every nation whoever fears him and works righteousness is acceptable to him” (ibid.).

Further, we read that the holy prophet Ezekiel, in the spirit and not in the flesh, beheld many mysteries of Christ and the Church under the figure of a city set upon a mountain (Ezek. 40); and that, carried in ecstasy to Jerusalem, he detected with prophetic sight the most abominable acts of the Jews (Ezek. 8). Whether anything is at times done by good spirits upon human senses so that the senses themselves are deceived—as surely the sense of those was deceived whose eyes were held so that they did not recognize Christ—I do not wish to decide rashly [Col. 0370B]. For I am uncertain whether the Syrians were struck with blindness by good or evil spirits, so that they did not recognize Elisha or Samaria (Luke 24; 4 Kings 6).

Rational vision is that by which, without any assistance from bodily senses, we apprehend truth or falsehood by certain reasoning; by which we discern between vices and virtues; by which we prove the true relations of numbers, weights, and measures. Thus we perceive with the mind that the number three cannot be divided into two equal parts, as we see nothing more certainly by the flesh [Col. 0370C].

Thus, by sensory vision we see bodily things; by imaginary vision we imagine bodily things; by phantastic vision we are deceived through bodily images; by spiritual vision the spirit is instructed through bodily likenesses; by rational vision the mind is exercised among invisible things; by intellectual vision the mind is led into truth itself.

For we call intellectual that vision by which the mind, transcending every body and all bodily images and likenesses, rests in the very light of truth; in which all things past, present, and future are truly and really present, nor are future things otherwise than past things. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “I have many things to say to you” (John 16). He had many things to say to them, not in many things nor through many things, but in one and through one, where many things are not many but one [Col. 0370D]. “But you cannot bear them now.” For, occupied with sensory vision by the sweetness of his presence and attending bodily to his bodily words, they were unable to rise to that intellectual vision which excludes all memory of bodily things, where Truth itself speaks. Therefore he says: “It is expedient for you that I go” (ibid.), so that this bodily vision and bodily conversation may be withdrawn.

I know that in a monastery of virgins, who under the venerable and most reverently named holy Father Gilbert daily send abundant fruits of chastity to heaven, there was—or perhaps still is—a holy virgin. Having expelled from her breast all love of the world, all fleshly affections, every concern for the body, and every outward anxiety, she began, in a certain fervour of mind, both to loathe earthly things and to desire heavenly ones [Col. 0371A].

It happened once, while she was applying herself to prayer with her customary love, that a wondrous sweetness came upon her and extinguished every movement of the soul, every excursion of thought, and even every spiritual affection she had concerning friends. Immediately her soul, as though bidding farewell to the burdens that are in the world, was carried above itself; received by an ineffable and incomprehensible light, it saw nothing other than that which is, and that which is the being of all things. Nor was that light bodily, nor any likeness of a body. It was neither extended nor spread abroad so as to appear everywhere; nor was it itself contained, yet it contained all things—by a wonderful and ineffable manner, as being contains whatever is, and truth whatever is true [Col. 0371B].

Filled with this light, she began no longer to know according to the flesh Christ himself, whom she had formerly known according to the flesh, because Christ Jesus, the spirit before her face, had led her into truth itself. When no small time had passed for her in this ecstasy, and the sisters knocked, she could scarcely return to the bodily senses which she had left.

When this happened to her more often, and after much entreaty she at last explained to the others the manner of her ecstasy, very many began to emulate the excellence of this vision. Accordingly, withdrawing themselves from every worldly care and anxiety, many obtained the same grace through tears and continual prayers; indeed, they were often filled with this light among the gatherings of the sisters even against their will [Col. 0371C].

There was there a virgin, a woman of great discernment, who, knowing that not every spirit is to be believed, thought that all this should be ascribed either to illness or to phantastic illusions; and, as far as she could, she dissuaded the sisters from the frequency of such vision. But when she asked the woman who was considered foremost among them why nothing of the kind had happened to her, the latter replied: “Because you do not place faith in us, nor do you love in others a virtue which you do not possess yourself. Ask God,” she said, “that, if this is from him, the same thing may happen to you.”

After they had prayed for several days and achieved nothing, she again asked the same woman why and whence this was so. She replied [Col. 0371D]: “You must renounce every affection of this world and of all mortals, and occupy yourself with the remembrance of God alone.” The other said: “Then shall I not pray for my friends or benefactors?” To her the first replied: “At the time when you wish to ascend to higher things by contemplation of mind, you must commend and entrust to God all whom you love, and, as though about to depart from the world, bid farewell altogether to every creature and sigh toward the sight of him whom you love.”

Still unbelieving, she begged that by the other’s prayers, if these things were from God, she might obtain the fulfilment of her wish. “Yet,” she said, “I do not wish my soul to be so lifted and carried away from the body that all memory of things, especially of my friends, is erased from my mind. It is enough for me to know whether these things are from God” [Col. 0372A].

Accordingly, on Good Friday, while she was wavering amid anxious thoughts, she was suddenly filled with the light of which we have spoken, and began in an ineffable manner to be borne upward in it and lifted to higher things.
