But unable, with her weaker sight, to endure that inaccessible light shining upon her, she asked as best she could to be recalled to contemplation of the Lord’s Passion. Then, when she had seen, as though in a swift glimpse, that which is borne from higher things to lower, she was transferred into that spiritual vision and saw in the spirit Jesus hanging upon the cross, fastened with nails, pierced with a lance, blood flowing through the five wounds, and looking upon her with the gentlest eye. Then, dissolved in tears and at last returned to herself, she gave credence to the sisters and judged herself less fit for this light [Col. 0372B].

Perhaps not uselessly having inserted these matters, let us understand that this vision alone, which we call intellectual, makes a prophet, as it is written of wisdom: “Passing into holy souls, she makes them friends of God and prophets” (Wis. 7). For whatever is seen by other visions is either ambiguous or strengthened more by faith than by knowledge. But what is seen in truth itself—in which whatever is to come has been made—is both evidently luminous and certain.

Therefore, whenever that intellectual vision operates in sensory or phantastic vision, there is unquestionably the gift of prophecy. By what vision, then, Isaiah son of Amos saw the burden of Babylon—by intellectual vision alone, or also by sensory or spiritual vision—who could easily say? For from the sequence of his book we may know that he foresaw many future things by both kinds of vision, while intellectual vision enlightened him [Col. 0372C].

For by sensory vision he framed an oracle when he rebuked King Hezekiah with prophetic authority because he had shown the treasures of his house to Babylonian envoys. “What did these men see in your house?” he asked. And the king: “There is not a thing,” he said, “that I did not show them.” Then the prophet: “Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, when all the things which your fathers have gathered will be carried away to Babylon” (Isa. 39). By spiritual vision, however, when he says: “I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne high and lifted up” (Isa. 6), and the rest that follows [Col. 0372D].

But by whichever of these visions he saw the burden of Babylon, it is certain that he saw it with the mind, not the flesh, through the revelation of him who says: “I have been represented in the hands of the prophets” (Hos. 12). But since this distinction of visions has detained us long enough, let us defer the beginning of this prophetic vision until tomorrow.

**SERMON IV. On the words written: “Raise the standard upon the dark mountain,” etc.**

“When the fullness of time came, God sent his Son, made of a woman, made under the law” (Gal. 4). What is this fullness of time? Surely that of which the Lord says in the Gospel: “Lift up your eyes and see the fields, for they are already white for harvest” (John 4) [Col. 0373A].

For a time is called empty and barren when, because seeds in the ground have been dried by the sun’s harshness or rotted by an excessive flood of rains, a famine consuming all things leaves the field empty for reapers; when ten acres of vineyard produce a single small jar, and thirty measures of seed produce three measures. But time is full when all things abound; when the soil repays its cultivators with manifold crop; when the reaper runs naked through the field; when the harvest-song is sung everywhere in the vineyards; when granaries are filled with grain and presses overflow with wine.

Let the Saviour’s parable of the wheat and tares now come to mind, and let us observe what he said the wheat and tares were. “The good seed,” he says, “are the children of the kingdom; the tares, the children of the evil one” (Matt. 13) [Col. 0373B]. By “children of the kingdom” he means those whom mercy predestined for life; by “children of the evil one,” those whom justice appointed beforehand for punishment.

Therefore, before the coming of our Lord, when the children of the evil one occupied nearly the whole face of the earth and the few children of God’s kingdom lay hidden among them, famine of the word of God had spread everywhere, and an empty and barren time had left spiritual workers nothing upon which to labour. But the fullness of time came when everywhere on earth there abounded those who were to be separated from Babylonian errors, justified when separated, and glorified when justified. Of them the Saviour says: “The harvest indeed is plentiful, but the labourers are few” (Matt. 9; Luke 10).

Accordingly, by the coming of our Lord, Babylon—the city of confusion, in which the elect were held captive with the reprobate amid vices and errors—was to be invaded and destroyed by their separation [Col. 0373C]. And this is the first burden of Babylon which Isaiah son of Amos saw. Describing the manner of this destruction in prophetic speech, he began thus: “Raise the standard upon the dark mountain; exalt the voice; lift up the hand; let the leaders enter the gates” (Isa. 13).

Who speaks? To whom does he speak? We should note, I think, that holy prophets predict future things sometimes by narration, sometimes by prayer, sometimes by blessing or as though cursing, sometimes by doing something, but most often as though commanding. By narration, as in: “In the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be established upon the top of the mountains” (Isa. 2) [Col. 0373D]. By prayer, as in: “Show us your mercy, and give us your salvation” (Ps. 84 [85]); or: “Would that you would rend the heavens and come down” (Isa. 64). Holy Moses likewise: “I beseech you, Lord, send whom you will send” (Exod. 4).

As though cursing, as when the prophet says: “Scatter them by your power, O Lord, my protector” (Ps. 58 [59]); and, “As wax melts before fire, so let sinners perish before God’s face” (Ps. 67 [68]). Elsewhere the prophet says: “Give them, O Lord.” “What will you give them?” “A womb without children and dry breasts” (Hos. 9). By blessing, as Isaac says to his son: “May God give you from the dew of heaven and from the fatness of the earth abundance of grain, wine, and oil” (Gen. 27). By doing something [Col. 0374A], as Jacob raised a stone and anointed it (Gen. 28); as Moses raised the bronze serpent in the wilderness (Num. 21); and as this same Isaiah went naked and barefoot (Isa. 10). As though commanding, as it is written later in this book: “Go, swift angels, to a nation scattered and torn apart” (Isa. 18).

Therefore, seeing that, when the Lord and Saviour came in the flesh, the city of confusion would be overthrown through the ministry of the apostles and the teaching of preachers, the prophet, either in his own person or in that of the Lord, commands or exhorts them to do what he saw that they would do: “Raise the standard upon the dark mountain” (Isa. 13).

By the dark mountain we fittingly understand Babylon itself—that is, the world—according to the condition in which Christ found it [Col. 0374B]. It could be called a mountain because of pride, and dark because of error. The Roman Empire then was like a mountain: towering over the whole world, it was as swollen with arrogance as it was darkened by manifold error, above all by ignorance of God. Had not the worship of idols, the vanity of philosophers, the superstition of temples, and unrestrained lust covered the world in a certain dreadful darkness?

“Raise the standard upon the dark mountain.” What standard? Hear the Gospel: “Behold, this one is set for the fall and rising again of many in Israel, and for a sign which shall be contradicted” (Luke 2). This is the standard of the cross, opposed by human pride, while Jews and Gentiles, together with kings and rulers, the wise and prudent of this age, fought against it; and it was raised above the dark mountain by little ones. For you, Lord Jesus, hid the mysteries of your cross from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones. These little ones are the humble: apostles and apostolic men, who are commanded to raise the standard upon the dark mountain, so that they may teach the whole world to be subject to the Lord’s cross [Col. 0374C].

What is placed above something either presses it, closes it, or rises above it. The two cherubim were placed upon the ark of the covenant so that they might project higher; a stone is placed over a well so that it may close it; a press is placed over the winepress so that it may press. Therefore the banner of the cross is raised above the dark mountain in order that, by its power, it may press down this world’s might; close to the proud the mysteries of our redemption; but among the gentle and humble rise above all worldly glory.

That it presses down, hear most blessed Paul: “Christ became obedient to the Father unto death, even death on a cross. Therefore God also exalted him and bestowed on him the name which is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of heavenly, earthly, and infernal beings” (Phil. 2) [Col. 0374D]. See how heaven, earth, and hell are subjected to the mystery of the cross, and how everywhere the strength of Babylon’s king is pressed down and his power made void.

“When a strong man armed guards his court, the things he possesses are in peace. But if one stronger than he comes upon him, he despoils his goods, takes away his arms, and distributes the spoils” (Luke 11) [Col. 0375A]. The strong armed man is the devil; the court, the world; his goods, the wise of the world; his weapons, kings and rulers; the spoils, the common people. Behold Babylon, its king, and its riches. Before the stronger one came, this king ruled in peace—that is, with no one opposing him. But when the stronger one arrived, a burden was laid upon him: a burden pressing him down, conquering him, despoiling him.

This burden of Babylon is Christ’s cross, which conquered the devil, invaded Babylon, plundered the Egyptians, and enriched the Hebrews. These are the Hebrews of whom it is said: “Raise the standard upon the dark mountain” (Isa. 13): so that, when the power of the cross has been preached to all nations, the spoils of Babylon or Egypt may be seized by him who “delivered us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of his Son of light.”

For he chose little ones—that is, the humble; Hebrews—that is, “those who cross over”; things contemptible in this world but superior to the world; the weak things of the world yet stronger than its strong; the foolish things of the world yet wiser than its wise [Col. 0375B]. “For God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong; and God chose the ignoble and contemptible things of the world, and things that are not, to destroy the things that are” (1 Cor. 1).

These are those who despise themselves through humility, as little children; who cross over all that belongs to this world, as Hebrews do. They raise the cross and trample underfoot riches and pleasures contrary to the cross, considering the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures of Egypt [Col. 0375C].

Hear also how the preaching of the cross, raised over the world, conceals the depth of divine power and wisdom. “We,” Paul says, “preach Christ crucified: to Jews indeed a stumbling block, but to Gentiles foolishness” (1 Cor. 1). Thus the wisdom of God’s cross was hidden, and the power of God was shut away by the scandal of the cross. But from whom? From Jews and Gentiles, indeed—but not all of them: rather, those of whom he elsewhere wrote: “The word of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing; but to those who are being saved—that is, to us—it is the power of God” (ibid.). “We preach Christ crucified: to Jews indeed a stumbling block, to Gentiles foolishness; but to those who are called, both Jews and Gentiles, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God.”

Paul himself teaches how the cross rises above all worldly riches and honours among such people, saying: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal. 6) [Col. 0375D].

But if anyone thinks that the dark mountain should be understood in a favourable sense, let him recall what the same Isaiah says: “Go up upon a high mountain, you who bring good tidings to Zion” (Isa. 40). Let him reflect that, as a person’s teaching is exalted, so too must that person’s life be exalted; that one whose tongue converses in heaven should not crawl upon the earth with his hands; and that one who rises above himself in speech should not lie beneath himself in lower things.

Indeed, evangelical teaching itself may fittingly be understood under the name “dark mountain”: like a most lofty mountain it rises above all worldly wisdom, and through the veil of mysteries hides from the eyes of unbelievers, and even of the weak, the higher matters in a certain darkness [Col. 0376A]. The Scripture of the Old Testament too can be called a dark mountain; elsewhere it is called a shady and dense mountain. It is lofty on account of the spirit, dark on account of the letter. For beneath the darkness of the letter lie veiled the secrets of heavenly mysteries, which are revealed by him through the Gospel, of whom it is written: “The voice of the Lord prepares the stags and will reveal the dense thickets” (Ps. 28 [29]). Hence the prophet says: “Dark water in the clouds of the air” (Ps. 17 [18]). Solomon too says: “The Lord said that he would dwell in a cloud” (3 Kings 8). Hence Moses could not approach the darkness in which God was.

The preachers by whom the burden of Babylon is proclaimed are commanded not to lie low in base things, but to set ascents in their hearts; and, preaching the things above, to think upon the things above. Thus set upon the mountain rather than cast down into the depths of valleys, let them do what follows: “Raise the standard; exalt the voice.”

Or, since the first heralds of truth were chosen from the remnant of Israel’s children, had been instructed in legal decrees and accustomed to literal sacraments, the Holy Spirit commands them to pass from law to Gospel, from letter to spirit, and to ascend from the valley of carnal observances to the mountain of spiritual precepts [Col. 0376B]. Or they are commanded to prove from ancient writings that what they preach as fulfilled in the Gospel had been foretold, as the Saviour says: “Search the Scriptures, for they are those which bear witness of me” (John 5); and to the apostles: “It is necessary that the things written concerning me in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms be fulfilled” (Luke 24).

This prophetic speech can be read in two ways: “Raise the standard upon the dark mountain,” either so that they raise the standard above the dark mountain, or so that they themselves, set upon the dark mountain, raise the standard. “Exalt the voice; lift up the hand” (Isa. 40). Elsewhere you have: “Exalt your voice in strength, you who bring good tidings to Jerusalem” (ibid.). This is that exaltation of the evangelical voice which holy David is read to have expressed: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words unto the ends of the earth” (Ps. 18 [19]) [Col. 0376C].

What holy David saw as future and proclaims as already accomplished, using the past tense, Isaiah—or rather, the Lord himself in Isaiah—commands to be done: “Exalt the voice.” For, since vessels of wrath polluted by Babylonian lust throughout the world were to be changed into vessels of mercy, the voice of evangelists rang out with such power that no one could excuse himself on the ground that he had not heard the word of faith. Thus the Apostle says: “Indeed, their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words unto the ends of the inhabited world” (Rom. 10).

Therefore, just as in the raising of the standard we say that the mystery of the Lord’s cross is prefigured, so in the exaltation of the voice the excellence and efficacy of apostolic preaching is prophesied, as Jesus says to his disciples: “Go into the whole world; preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark 16) [Col. 0376D].

There are still other passages concerning the exaltation of the voice; but because the pressing hour compels us, on account of certain other business, we shall, God willing, take up the beginning of tomorrow’s sermon from this consideration [Col. 0377A]. But you, passing from the sermon to reading and from reading to prayer, knock upon the gracious ears of Jesus with devout petitions, that he may open our eyes and we may contemplate the wonders of his law: he who lives and is glorified with the Father and the Holy Spirit. Amen.

**SERMON V. On the same chapter.**
My dearest brethren, you have not forgotten from what point, according to our promise yesterday, today’s sermon ought to proceed. As we said, preachers of the truth are commanded to raise their voice [Col. 0377B], so that everywhere on earth the salvation which the Lord has wrought in the midst of the earth may be heard as the apostles preach, and thus all the ends of the earth may remember and turn to the Lord (Ps. 21); and in the distant islands they may say, “Our Saviour will come.”

Moreover, wishing by careful consideration to distinguish between the heralds of the Old and of the New Testament, the holy prophet urges the latter to raise their voice. You know that to this Jewish people, carnal and knowing nothing but the earth, earthly happiness was promised: abundance of bread and wine, plenty of milk and honey, according to the words: “If you are willing and obey me, you shall eat the good things of the earth” (Isa. 1). And again: “If you walk in the commandments of the Lord, cleaving to him, the Lord will destroy all these nations before [Col. 0377C] your face. Every place upon which your foot shall tread shall be yours” (Deut. 1). And in the prophet Amos: “The ploughman shall overtake the reaper, and the treader of grapes him who sows seed” (Amos 9). And many things like these.

Therefore those who promised earthly things did not raise their voice: those who preached low things to a people lying low; those who set temporal rewards before persons loving temporal things. But the voice of those whom Christ appointed evangelists of the New Testament is raised: they teach that heavenly things are to be desired and earthly things despised; they promise their hearers no reward in the present life—indeed, here they promise labours and contests, but in the future crowns and rewards.

Paul clearly raised his voice when he said: “Seek the things that are above, where Christ sits at the right hand of God; set your minds on the things that are above, not on things upon the earth” (Col. 3). And again: “That which is at present the momentary and light burden of our tribulation works in us, beyond measure in sublimity, an eternal weight of glory” (2 Cor. 4).

The most holy evangelist John also raised his voice and, like a son of thunder, thundered terribly against Babylon: “Do not,” he says, “love the world, nor the things that are in the world” (1 John 2). And: “The world passes away, and its desire” (ibid.). John the Baptist likewise, the first preacher of evangelical grace, took the beginning of his preaching not from an earthly kingdom but a heavenly one, raising his voice and saying: “Repent, for [Col. 0378A] the kingdom of heaven is at hand” (Matt. 3).

Thus he raises his voice who preaches spiritual things, who speaks of divine things, who promises heavenly things. “Raise your voice; lift up your hand.” Hands are lifted in prayer; they are lifted in good works; they are lifted in the performance of miracles. For preachers ought first to pray for those to whom they preach, that they may hear; then that they may believe; and finally that they may persevere in that faith and in good works. They ought likewise not to act contrary to what they teach, so that mind, voice, and hand may agree in purpose, speech, and action.

By the lifting up of hands we may also, not inappropriately, understand the signs and wonders performed among the people through the hands of the apostles. These words foretold what we read was fulfilled in the Gospel when the Lord [Col. 0378B] commanded: “Go,” he says to the disciples, “preach, saying: ‘The kingdom of heaven is at hand’” (Matt. 10). This is what Isaiah said: “Raise your voice.” And he added: “Heal the sick, cleanse lepers, cast out demons” (ibid.). And hence the prophet says: “Lift up your hand.”

But it will not, I think, be unfitting if by the lifting of hands or the raising of the voice we understand a right intention prefigured. If that intention alone is perverse and declines to lower things, then words and deeds, however lofty they may seem, will be judged by God as lowly. For those who preached the Gospel not sincerely nor from God’s truth, but from an ulterior motive, are those of whom Paul says: “All seek their own things, not those of Jesus Christ” (Phil. 2); and: “Such persons do not serve the Lord Jesus Christ, but their own belly” [Col. 0378C] (Rom. 16). They neither raised their voice nor lifted their hands, because whatever sounded lofty in their words, whatever appeared exalted in miracles, a base and perverse intention surely cast it all down to the depths.

Hence the prophet says: “They bent down their sacrifices into the deep” (Hos. 5). For the preaching of truth, the affliction of the flesh, the refreshing of the poor, constant and attentive prayer—these are saving sacrifices. Yet those certainly bend these sacrifices down into the deep who, abandoning the intention of heavenly rewards, twist them toward these low advantages of the present. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Take heed that you do not perform your righteousness before men, so as to be seen by them” (Matt. 7), and so forth.

Therefore those who expend the office of preaching, [Col. 0378D] the gift of prophecy, the grace of miracles, works of righteousness, or the light of knowledge upon the vanity of human praise or the greed of shameful gain, neither raise their voice nor lift their hands; and they await not heavenly rewards but eternal punishments. That very many abuse even those loftier gifts—namely prophecy and miracles—is readily demonstrated by Balaam’s prophecy and Judas’s miracles. Above all, however, we have as proof that terrible sentence of the Saviour in the Gospel, where he says: “Many will come on that day, saying: ‘Have we not prophesied in your name, and in your name performed many signs?’ And then I shall confess to them: ‘I do not know you’” (ibid.).

Come then, dearest brethren: strive after the better gifts—humility, patience, [Col. 0379A] charity. These are certainly better because they are more useful. For to the humble, to the obedient, to those who love one another in charity, the Lord will not say on that day, “I do not know you”—though we know that he will say it to many who prophesy and perform miracles. Therefore let none of you, brethren, think himself less acceptable to God because he does not see himself made glorious by miracles. Rather, by those three things of which we have spoken, let him measure without hesitation how pleasing he is to the divine eyes. For “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (Jas. 4); “In your patience you shall possess your souls” (Luke 21); and “By this all will know that you are Christ’s disciples: if you have love for one another” (John 13).

Thus the holy apostles and apostolic men, whom Christ sent into the world to overthrow [Col. 0379B] the court of the strong man, raised their voice in four ways: by preaching the kingdom of God, promising heavenly goods, despising present things, and directing their intention toward future things. O how beautiful upon the mountains of virtues are the feet—that is, the affections—of those who proclaim peace to people of good will, who despise earthly things for the sake of heavenly goods! Beautiful indeed are feet to which not even dust clings, but which are washed by Christ himself—as water placed in a basin—or, at the Lord’s own command, shake that dust off upon those because of whom it is gathered.

For whatever dust of earthly affections preachers or prelates gather through the occasion of their office is either washed away by Christ’s working through that charity for whose sake it is gathered, according to the words: “Charity covers a multitude of sins” [Col. 0379C] (1 Pet. 4); or else it is shaken off upon those for whom they labour, if they are ungrateful or disobedient, so that it may be imputed wholly not to the preacher but rather to them.

Having carefully considered all these things, let us set forth the meaning of the text in a brief recapitulation. It is the voice of the prophet—or rather the voice of the Lord through the prophet—addressed to the apostles: “Upon a dark mountain raise a banner” (Isa. 13). It is as though he said: Against Babylon—that is, the world, which is a mountain because of its pride and dark because of error—raise the banner of faith and of the Lord’s Passion, so that the pride of the world may be conquered by the humility of the cross and the darkness of errors driven away by the light of faith. Nor should this be done in one place or one region only; rather, raise [Col. 0379D] your voice, so that your sound may go forth into all the earth and your words to the ends of the world.

And so that the teaching of truth may be heard more willingly, believed more easily, and received more devoutly, lift up your hand, confirming by miracles what you teach in words. All these things were fulfilled when the disciples went forth and preached everywhere, God working with them and confirming the word through accompanying signs (Mark 16).

It may also be read thus: You preachers of the word of God, ascend from the valley to the mountain, from the letter to the Spirit, from the carnal ceremonies of the Law to the heavenly sacraments of the Gospel; and thus, placed upon that dark mountain in which God is—that is, in the knowledge of the Scriptures—raise the banner and the voice. Or thus: You whom I command to preach lofty things, ascend in mind to lofty things, so that upon the mountain of contemplation [Col. 0380A] you may learn what you are to teach in the valley of this world. And, established in what is lofty—that is, in action and contemplation—raise the banner by preaching the mysteries of the cross; raise your voice by promising not earthly but heavenly things; lift pure hands in every place, praying for those to whom you preach or performing good works with a right intention. Thus may Babylon’s walls be pierced by the sting of the cross and its spoils be plundered, and may what is written in this same prophet come to pass: “They shall rejoice before you as those rejoice in harvest, as victors exult when they divide the captured spoil. And leaders shall enter the gates” (Isa. 9).

For in all that has been said, the gates of the city are opened and leaders enter them. One of these leaders glories in the opening of the gates themselves and says: “A great and evident door has been opened to me, and there are many adversaries” [Col. 0380B] (1 Cor. 16). Babylon’s gates are found shut against the leaders where, since all are barred by unbelief and wickedness, no access to their hearts lies open for the word of God; where the preacher’s voice is heard as though knocking at a door, but the doctrine of truth is not received. Such indeed were the Jews to whom Paul said: “It was necessary that the kingdom of God should first be proclaimed to you; but since you reject it and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13). They too shut the door against these leaders who, hearing Stephen preach the glory of the Lord Jesus, stopped their ears (Acts 7).

Indeed, the preachers themselves are called leaders of the word because they introduce God’s word into their hearers’ hearts. They [Col. 0380C] entered the gates of the city when, received by the Gentiles, they presided over the Churches formed from them under the title of rulers and leaders. The gates may also be understood as the sacraments of faith themselves. For faith must necessarily go before, and then an entrance is opened for understanding. The leaders may then be said to have entered when, received through their hearers’ faith as though into their hearts, they pour into them the light of a higher and more hidden teaching.

I also consider the firstfruits of believers worthy of the name “gates,” through whom the apostles obtained easier access for converting the rest and entered the city itself, armed with heavenly weapons. I believe this is why the Apostle said: “A great and evident door has been opened to me, [Col. 0380D] and there are many adversaries” (1 Cor. 10). For the multitude of believers was like a door: through them Paul was admitted into the city of confusion and found an opportunity to contend hand-to-hand against adversaries whose number was not small.

And in all these matters Babylon’s burden is understood, according to what we said above: that by Christ’s coming it was overthrown through the separation of many from it. But now we bring this sermon to an end, lest, in desiring to serve your advancement in this respect, we seem to hinder other exercises equally necessary for you. Let prayer, however, precede tomorrow’s sermon, so that we may revisit in a tropological exposition what has been said allegorically, and that, once the foundation of good works has been laid, a structure may be built upon it, to the praise and glory of our Lord [Col. 0381A] Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns for ages of ages.

## SERMON VI. On the same chapter, in its moral sense

You ought to remember, dearest brethren, that we told your charity that a soul corrupted by the worst passions and vices is aptly understood under the name Babylon. For Babylon, as you know, is interpreted “confusion.” And what is so confused as that soul which now pride lifts up, now anger devastates, now sorrow contracts, now lust defiles, now gluttony disgraces? Such a soul may indeed be called a dark mountain. For whoever are such, their eyes are covered by a kind of blind darkness, so that, unable to distinguish between the light of virtues and the darkness of vices [Col. 0381B], they flee the former and delightfully wallow in the latter.

The cross is the burden of this Babylon. Now raised throughout the world, it is a burden to those who perish, but to those who are saved it is a useful and welcome relief. For what, my brethren, is so burdensome to lovers of the world as the cross? In the cross is commended contempt for glory, which they seek; affliction of the flesh, which they vehemently flee; mortification of one’s own flesh, which they detest; nakedness and the stripping away of temporal possessions, which they abhor.

Yet we too, brethren, insofar as Babylon’s remnants occupy us, are burdened by the cross, as daily experience teaches us. For insofar as the sweetness of the flesh delights, so much does its affliction torment; and as honour is pleasing, so disgrace is burdensome; and as flattery lifts one up, so detraction casts one down [Col. 0381C]. If riches are desired, poverty causes distress; and if lust appears sweet, chastity is judged difficult. Hence many of Christ’s disciples, hearing the mystery of the cross, went back and no longer walked with him.

Let us therefore, my brethren, labour to drive from our hearts whatever remnant of the world is within us, and, if possible, to destroy every trace of Babylon, so that we may experience how much sweetness, security, and glory there are in the cross. For it gives rise to love, than which nothing is sweeter; to martyrdom, than which nothing is more secure; and to contempt for the world, than which nothing is more glorious.

“Upon a dark mountain raise [Col. 0381D] a banner.” I believe that this voice is addressed to the angels, whom the Lord has commanded to be guardians of our souls, so that they may impress upon the hearts of those whom the world still delights or tempts the remembrance of the cross, and may set against every vice which devastates or attacks the soul a corresponding virtue of the cross. These are ministering spirits, sent for our sake; they are present when we sing psalms, stand by when we pray, and attend us when we read and meditate. They oppose themselves to unclean spirits; against spirits urging the world’s enticements they set the example of the Lord’s Passion; against those seeking to inflame the mind with anger they offer the goodness of the Lord’s patience; when they instil arrogance or pride, they urge upon us the humility of humble Jesus for our imitation.

Therefore, dearest brethren, [Col. 0382A] stand in church with reverence and fear; give honour to God; and show gratitude to these blessed spirits, your friends, lest perhaps, offended by your frivolity or some resentment against one another, they depart, and thus free access to your hearts be afforded to wicked angels.

Blessed is the soul which, while singing psalms, is inflamed with longing for him of whom it sings; and, as its affection is stirred and tears arise, addresses those whom it feels present in spirit: “Daughters of Jerusalem, tell my beloved that I am sick with love” (Song 5). With what joyful countenance and cheerful voice those blessed spirits seem to answer: “Behold, he comes, leaping upon the mountains, skipping over the hills” (Song 2); and, turning toward him as he now approaches the soul, they say: “This is she, beautiful among the daughters of Jerusalem” [Col. 0382B] (ibid.).

Unhappy and wretched are those who, in the manner of thorns and brambles, prick such a soul by unruly gestures or voices. Not only are they themselves deprived of so great a sweetness and handed over to demons for mockery, but, having become ministers of Satan, they also expose others, so far as they are able, to his darts and persecutions. O what a pleasing spectacle persons of this kind offer to unclean spirits! They tear away their voice, tongue, mouth, finally their very heart, and the labour of the whole night, from the most holy hands of angels, who had already received all these things to carry into the heavenly temple and place upon the divine altars before God; and thus they sacrifice everything to demons and not to God, so that they deserve to hear: “Your new moons, [Col. 0382C] your Sabbaths, your sacrifices—my soul has hated them; they have become burdensome to me” (Isa. 1).

O you holy soul, friend of God, bride of Christ, dwelling-place of the Holy Spirit: endure such persons patiently, so that if they attack, they may not conquer; if they draw you, they may not drag you all the way; nor may they turn you aside from yourself so as to turn you toward themselves and make you like themselves and unlike the holy spirits who stand by you. Rather, may your bridegroom glory in you and say: “As a lily among thorns, so is my beloved among the daughters” (Song 2).

Therefore, dearest brethren, whoever of you are spiritual, when you see someone of this sort, do not be angry with him. Rather, pray to those blessed spirits who are your familiar friends and are with you, that they may raise a banner over this dark [Col. 0382D] mountain, so that, checked by remembrance of the Lord’s Passion and cross, they may be confounded and ashamed, and so return to the unity of heart and voice.

And it is added: “Raise your voice; lift up your hand.” Since we have entered upon a discussion of the sacred vigils, the raising of the voice properly belongs to psalmody and the lifting of hands to prayer. And, lest we wholly disregard the literal sense at this point, the raising of the voice may express that fervour which is very necessary in an assembly of brethren: through the sound of the mouth that inward fire may burst forth on every side, and thus they may raise and kindle one another, so that, becoming one flame out of many, they may kindle in an odour of sweetness those marrow-rich burnt offerings brought to the divine altars by the ministry of angels.

The lifting of hands likewise commends purity in prayer, as the Apostle says: “Lifting pure hands in every place, without anger or disputing” [Col. 0383A] (1 Tim. 2). He lifts pure hands in prayer whose conscience, exulting at the time of prayer, raises itself in a certain confidence through remembrance of good works and presents itself to the divine gaze. Such confidence must arise either from innocence or from repentance: that is, either because he has committed nothing requiring tears, or because he has worthily wept over what he has committed.

“But when,” you ask, “may I presume that I have repented worthily and sufficiently?” Never at all. Whence then comes this confidence? Come, dearest brethren, let us compare spiritual things with spiritual things. “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above” (Jas. 1). In whose power, I ask, is it to pray in this manner whenever he wishes? Is it really so? [Col. 0383B] Whenever we wish, do we dissolve into tears, burn with devotion, rise in confidence, catch fire with the flame of charity, or are lifted up in contemplation? You have experienced how none of these things is in your own power. Rather, God sends the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, “Abba, Father.” Therefore this Spirit distributes these affections in prayer, apportioning to each one as he wills. Indeed, he so pours saving groaning into the hearts of those at prayer that he himself is said to intercede for us with unutterable groanings (Rom. 8).

“Unutterable,” I say. For who could sufficiently recount the many ways in which the mind is affected in prayer? At one time shame awakens groaning for sins; at another, love does so because of punishments; at another, devotion because of affection; at another, love because of desire [Col. 0383C]. Yet when we reflect on our present weakness or misery, we are often pierced with compunction and groan from weariness of this life; we set before our eyes the punishments which we fear and the kingdom for which we hope; we remember God’s boundless benefits toward us—and still we are stirred by no feeling of sorrow, pierced by no movement of fear, raised toward no desire for heavenly blessedness.

Often, while having none of these matters before our eyes, we are suddenly carried into all of them; passing from affection to affection in some ineffable way, we are flooded with a shower of tears. What is this? Surely it is because “The Spirit breathes where he wills; you hear his voice, but do not know whence he comes or whither he goes” (John 3). [Col. 0383D] You know when he comes, because when he breathes he does not allow himself to go unrecognized; you know when he goes, because the lukewarmness succeeding the departing fervour does not allow you to fail to recognize when he has ceased to breathe. But you do not know whence he comes or whither he goes.

Whence does the Spirit come, or whither does he go, he who fills the world? For that utterance is not foreign to him: “I fill heaven and earth” (Jer. 23). And yet he comes, and you do not know whence he comes; he goes, and you do not know whither he goes. Certainly you do not know whence he comes: whether from the secret chamber of mercy, from the tribunal of justice, from the abyss of judgments, or from the treasuries of knowledge. For when he comes to awaken the sluggish, to pierce the sinner with compunction, or to console the afflicted, he is said to have come forth as though from the chamber of mercy. But when he comes to reward one who does good works with the sweetness of spiritual compunction, we say that he has descended to us from the seat of justice [Col. 0384A]. When, however, he now inspires a saving affection in the minds of persons for whom all things work together unto evil, who, ungrateful for benefits, are reserved for punishments, and for whom both good and evil alike are for torment, do not doubt that he has come from the abyss of judgments. But if he deigns to come for the purpose that a mind cleansed by such a visitation may be rendered brighter and more fit to search out the secrets of divine knowledge, believe that he has come forth as though from the treasuries of knowledge.

But you do not know whence he comes, since you do not know whether you are worthy of love or of hatred (Eccl. 9), and cannot know whether he bestows mercy, restores a reward, or exercises judgment. Nor do you know whither he goes: whether he remains nearby and will return shortly; or goes farther away and will return after much time [Col. 0384B]; or withdraws offended, never to return again. Thus he breathes when he wills, where he wills, and as he wills, distributing to each one what he wills and as he wills (1 Cor. 12).

Yet whenever he raises the praying mind into a certain confidence, erases all that had darkened the conscience, entirely drives from the heart fear for sins and anxiety, and in a wondrous and ineffable way makes a person certain at that very moment of his salvation, do not doubt that his hands have been lifted high. Since this happens through the aid of holy angels, the words “Lift up your hands” may be understood as addressed to them.

Furthermore, against the three kinds of sin by which we sin—namely, in thought, word, and deed—these three things are prophetically required of us: “Upon a dark [Col. 0384C] mountain raise a banner; raise your voice; lift up your hand.” Since our heart is lofty by nature and inscrutable in its depth, it may be called a dark mountain; we must always fortify it with remembrance of the cross, lest we sin in thought. We are commanded to raise our voice lest we sin in speech. This is indeed a necessary command, especially in this age, when almost everyone’s tongue is occupied the whole day with low or harmful things, and rare is the person who lifts his voice on high.

Come, dearest brethren: it is shameful to say how, when many assemble together, detractions resound from every side and judgments rage. To say nothing of the lovers of the world, whose entire speech concerns gain or shamefulness: what shall I say of those [Col. 0384D] who seem to have renounced secular works, almost all of whose discussions and conversations concern the belly—not, I will not say, its pleasure, but its burden? Now disturbed by anger, now cast down by sorrow, now inflamed by hatreds, now oppressed by murmuring, now unrestrained in quarrelling, their minds are always conformed to their inward parts and stomach; from these they derive either their joy or their pain. Such persons do not raise their voice, but shamefully cast it down.

The same is done by those who spend the whole day discussing other people’s affairs, who boast of their own works, who criticize others by detraction, who, passing over serious and useful matters, introduce vain and ludicrous subjects. Against all these things the prophetic utterance commands us to raise our voice, so that our speech may concern heavenly things, instilling fear of God [Col. 0385A], pouring in love, increasing knowledge, or ordering conduct. We are also commanded to lift our hands, so that we may store up treasure in heaven, where neither rust nor moth destroys (Matt. 6): that is, that we may send all our works on to heaven, not doing our righteousness before people in order to be seen by them.

“And leaders shall enter the gates.” All these things, brethren, which we have said about raising the banner, raising the voice, and lifting the hand, are, so to speak, certain gates through which virtues are brought into the soul like a heavenly army, so that they may utterly drive out the vices by which Babylon—that is, the city of confusion—had been afflicted, and thus it may be called the holy city, the faithful city. Let us understand the leaders of this army to be the principal virtues: prudence, temperance, [Col. 0385B] fortitude, and justice. If our thoughts are holy, our speech good, and our works pure, these leaders enter as though through gates and bring the whole soul under their dominion, filling it with virtues and preparing a dwelling-place for the Holy Spirit.

This discourse has detained us longer than we expected. Would that it has been as useful as it has been lengthy! Let us therefore await another time to examine or discuss the matters that follow, beseeching him “who has the key of David, who opens and no one shuts, shuts and no one opens” (Rev. 3), that he may deign to open what is closed in his Scriptures: Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON VII. On the words written: “I have commanded,” through: “Rejoicing in my glory.”

[Col. 0385C]

As your charity remembers, we have already completed five sermons on the burden of Babylon, in which we have discussed, as far as we were able, the dark mountain, the raising of the banner, the lifting up of the voice, and the elevation of the hands. Now, lest it seem uncertain to anyone that this utterance was prophetically addressed, as we have said, to the heralds of the New Testament, the Lord’s own words spoken through the prophet clearly declare this very thing. For he says: “I have commanded my sanctified ones, and I have called my mighty ones in my wrath, those exulting in my glory.” He had indeed given the command that all things which were commanded should be done, but he had not stated by whom they were to be done. Therefore, as though answering one who asks and says, “Lord, to whom do you entrust undertakings so great and exalted?” he replies: “I have commanded my sanctified ones,” and so forth.

By these words, it seems to me, three orders of preachers are expressed: he calls the first “sanctified,” the second “mighty in his wrath,” and the third “exulting in his glory.” Here too a threefold condition of the Church is indicated: first, election; second, persecution; third, peace. For sanctification may be referred to election, wrath to persecution, and glory to peace.

First, therefore, the apostles and disciples of Christ were chosen, and these he certainly calls sanctified. For them especially he poured out that prayer which, after his final discourse at supper, he addressed to the Father with wonderful and ineffable affection:

> “Father,” he says, “I do not ask that you take them out of the world, but that you preserve them from evil. Father, sanctify them in truth” (John 17).

And again:

> “For their sake I sanctify myself, that they too may be sanctified in truth” (ibid.).

These, then, were truly sanctified in truth: by the presence of his body, by the teaching of his most sweet mouth, by the recommendation of his most efficacious prayer, and finally by the fresh outpouring of his most holy blood. They deserved to be sanctified all the more abundantly because they were nearer to him.

[Col. 0385D] He fittingly says, “I have commanded,” that is, “I have enjoined,” my sanctified ones; so that you may understand that those are designated here who received from his own honeyed mouth the ministry of preaching and the office of apostleship. But because the Church, founded through the apostles, was to be exercised by persecutions and tested by temptations, “I have called,” he says, “my mighty ones in my wrath.”

The wrath of God is understood in many ways in the Scriptures. God is said to be angry sometimes when he afflicts, sometimes when he spares, sometimes when he resists human desires, and sometimes when he favors them. For he was said to be stirred against Job, whom he allowed to be afflicted, as he himself says to Satan:

> “You moved me against him for no reason” (Job 2).

But he spared in anger those of whom he says:

> “My jealousy shall depart from them, and I shall no longer be angry with them” (Ezek. 16).

He also, as if angry, dismissed some according to the desires of their hearts; and again, as if angry, he hedged the ways of many with thorns, so that they might not find the lovers whom they seek. Thus the very affliction by which he permits his own people to be afflicted is called his wrath.

[Col. 0386C] Therefore, although he allowed the Church to be wearied by persecutors not to the detriment of its virtue but for the increase of its reward, it is nevertheless not unfittingly called the wrath of God—not with reference to the providence of the one permitting it, but to the suffering of the one experiencing it and to the judgment of one who does not know what will result from it.

Yet this wrath may truly be referred to those who, on account of persecution, withdrew from the faith and did not return to it through repentance. In anger he allowed these to be afflicted, for whom temporal punishment became an occasion of eternal condemnation; because it would have been better not to know the way of truth than, after knowing it, to turn back.

This wrath of God may also be seen as having raged against the persecutors of the saints. As was said of Pharaoh, they were raised up for this very purpose [Col. 0386D] (Exod. 9): that God might show his power against them and make known his might (Ps. 105). He allowed them to be hardened, lest they believe; blinded, lest they see; stirred up, that they might kill believers. Hence it is written in this same Isaiah:

> “Blind the heart of this people, make their ears heavy, and close their eyes, lest perhaps they see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their heart, and be converted, and I heal them” (Isa. 6).

In this wrath of God—whether that in which the elect were punished so that they might be crowned; or the reprobate, so that they might be recognized; or that in which tyrants were permitted to rage, that they might be condemned more severely or more unhappily—in this wrath of God, I say, the holy martyrs were found mighty. Having endured fire, sword, and beasts, they boldly proclaimed:

> “Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or the sword?” (Rom. 8).

[Col. 0387A] By the patience of these men the battered walls of Babylon fell, leaving a broad entrance for the leaders. Thus, in a wonderful manner, by suffering the martyrs subject to Christ those rulers who had subjected the world to themselves by fighting.

Then the banner was truly raised, when the cross was placed in the crown of the king as an object of glory—though it had been an object of terror as punishment and of shame as reproach. Then the glory of Christ began to appear even to the world, when throughout the world temples were overthrown, idols trampled down, and martyrs crowned, while the holy preachers of Christ exulted in this glory. Of them he says: “I have called my mighty ones in my wrath, those exulting in my glory.”

Thus he commanded the sanctified; he called the mighty or the exulting. He gave commands, indeed, to the sanctified—those whom his presence made glad, whom the teaching of his own mouth instructed, and on whom, when ascending into heaven, he laid the office of preaching and the dispensation of the sacraments:

> “Go,” he says, “teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28).

[Col. 0387B] All the others, whether martyrs or teachers, he called while absent in body but present in divinity; those called he justified (Rom. 8), and those justified he sent forth to call and instruct others.

Although, at whatever time they lived, all heralds of truth could be called sanctified because of chastity, mighty because of charity, and exulting because of hope. For nothing is holier than perfect chastity, nothing stronger than charity, and nothing more joyful than hope in heavenly things. These things were sought by faith, tested in persecutions, and made firm by the shining forth of Christ’s glory. Faith, therefore, bestowed holiness; wrath tested love; the sight of glory confirmed hope.

But let us too, dearest brothers, be sanctified in his grace; let us be mighty in his wrath; let us exult in his glory. That chastity is denoted by the name “sanctification” is established by the usage of Scripture. For when the children of Israel are sometimes told, “Sanctify yourselves for tomorrow” (Josh. 7), and sometimes, “for the third day” (Exod. 19), they are forbidden sexual intercourse for specified times.

Hence, when David sought bread from the priest and heard that there was no ordinary bread there, but only the bread of the Presence, he answered the priest’s question whether the young men were clean, especially from women:

> “Indeed, if women are in question, we have abstained from them since yesterday and the day before, and the vessels of the young men are holy” (1 Sam. 21).

Therefore the Apostle says:

> “Let each one know how to possess his own vessel in sanctification and honor, and not in the passion of desire” (1 Thess. 4).

It must be understood, however, that there is bodily chastity, sensory chastity, and spiritual chastity. Bodily chastity consists in a person restraining his will from every unlawful defilement. Sensory chastity consists in keeping the senses of all the members from every unlawful pleasure. Spiritual chastity consists in driving away every impure affection and unclean thought from the eyes of one’s heart, casting them out before they touch the flesh.

Come then, beloved: for that carnal people, who savored only carnal things, [Col. 0388A] a certain temporal sanctification was prescribed, one which restrains from the lower members alone the lust that belongs only to the flesh. But for us not only is that enjoined: in addition, a more sacred law imposes the discipline of every sense, so that we may be cleansed “from every defilement of flesh and spirit” (2 Cor. 7), and so that sanctification may be perfected in us—not subjecting one member of our body to the laws of chastity, but continually bringing all the senses of the inner and outer person under its rightful rule.

Therefore, brothers, let us not allow time to pass in negligence. Let us carefully examine whether any impurity still remains in the eyes; whether the ears are polluted by empty or harmful speech; whether the hands are clean; whether the nostrils are purified; whether speech is holy; whether taste is more restrained; whether the face is free from frivolity, and the walk from vanity. Let us thus cut away all that is contrary to sanctification, so that a certain most sweet fragrance may proceed from each of our members and senses, and so that our burnt offering may become rich (Ps. 19).

Then, ascending to that spiritual chastity which surpasses the others, let us protect all the affections and movements of the heart not only from every impurity but, as far as possible, from every wandering impulse of wantonness. Thus, joining inward chastity to outward chastity, let us offer God one sacrifice from the union of both.

Happy, happy is the person who, whether eating or drinking or doing anything else, does all things to the glory of God (1 Cor. 10), sanctifying himself to Christ, so that, sanctified in the truth of the heavenly commandments, he may share in the hidden mysteries [Col. 0388C] and become one of those of whom he says: “I have commanded my sanctified ones.”

Strength follows, which is necessary amid temptations. For that perfection of sanctification cannot be maintained in this life so unbrokenly that its serenity is never interrupted by any temptations. Yet just as the Lord our God appears sweet, lovable, and delightful when all things are peaceful and calm, so, when he exposes us to temptations of the flesh, to the suggestions of demons, to the troubles of this world, or wears us down by persecutions, he seems in some manner harsh and angry.

Happy is the one who is strong in this wrath of his—now resisting, now fighting, now fleeing—so as not to be found weak or feeble, whether through consenting or through despair. Therefore, brothers, whoever is not found strong in this wrath of his will not be able to exult in his glory.

If, then, we pass through fire and water, so that neither fire burns nor water overwhelms us, whose glory is this? Is it ours, so that we should exult in it as our own? Far be it! How many, brothers, exult—exult when they are praised by people, seizing personal glory from God’s gifts and not exulting in God’s glory! Some seek what is their own, not what belongs to Jesus Christ; and they lose what is their own, while failing to receive what belongs to Jesus Christ (Phil. 2).

[Col. 0389A] Therefore that person exults in Christ’s glory who does not seek his own glory but Christ’s, understanding that we have nothing in which to glory, since nothing is ours.

Thus, in individual persons the city of confusion is overthrown if chastity drives out luxury, strength overcomes temptations, and humility excludes vanity. Furthermore, we have sanctification from faith and the sacraments of Christ; strength from the charity of Christ; and exultation in the hope of Christ’s promises. Let us therefore do as much as we can, that faith may sanctify us, charity strengthen us, and hope make us glad, in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom belong honor and glory for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON VIII. On the passage written: “The sound of a multitude,” as far as “coming from a distant land.”

In the prophetic words which we examined yesterday, the following words occur, which today we have undertaken to explain with your charity:

> “The sound of a multitude on the mountains, like that of a great people; the sound of the noise of kings and nations gathered together.”

First we must ask whose voice this is: the prophet’s or the Lord’s. Then, whether it is connected with what precedes by a continuation of the thought, or whether this voice is the beginning of another prophecy, separated from the former by a difference in meaning.

These words seem to me to be those of the prophet exulting and lifting himself into a kind of jubilation of mind because of what he had seen in the Spirit. It is clear that they fit what precedes in this way. For, after the long and harsh trials of persecution, he saw kings and rulers of the world converted to Christ; he saw the Church of Christ shining throughout the world and exulting in his glory; he saw a great multitude of saints who, during persecution, had hidden in caves and caverns, now running everywhere with marvelous eagerness, preaching the word of God with voice and countenance made free, and restraining the powerful remnants of Babylon by the terror of their authority. From the abundance of his heart he burst forth into a cry of exultation:

> “The sound of a multitude on the mountains!”

[Col. 0389C] This must be read with a kind of pause, as an expression of astonishment and exultation. Thus the prophet seemed to himself, in the Spirit, to hear the very voice of those preaching and exulting, teaching and correcting; and he said: “The sound of a multitude on the mountains.”

A mountain signifies eminence, because a city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden (Matt. 5), nor can the voice of one speaking on a mountain fail to be heard. Therefore, once the Church was reigning through emperors, it was no longer hidden in darkness or whispering in corners; the saints had been granted freedom to preach openly and to instruct by evangelical teaching whomever they wished.

He says, then: “The sound of a multitude on the mountains, like that of a great people.” For then the order of preachers was so great that it seemed comparable to a multitude. But if by “a great people” you wish to understand the multitude of believers, it will not be absurd. For once peace had been granted to the churches and the saints freedom to preach, they ascended in a voice of exultation and confession to the mountains—that is, to the teaching of the apostles and prophets—of whom the Psalmist says:

> “Let the mountains receive peace for the people” (Ps. 71).

And elsewhere:

> “Its foundations are in the holy mountains” (Ps. 86),

that is, the foundations of the Church. These are the mountains to which we lift our eyes, so that help may come to us from there: that is, that we may be enlightened by their wisdom and instructed by their example.

> “The sound of the noise of kings and nations gathered together.”

In the “noise” terror is indicated: by it kings who believed in Christ commanded, by imperial edict, that temples be destroyed, idols broken, and sacrilegious sacrifices abolished. Thus, hearing spiritually the voice of their noise—that is, of their terror—against Babylon, the prophet says: “The sound of the noise of kings.”

[Col. 0390A] But because inferiors were converted to the faith by the example of superiors, the poor by that of the rich, the weak by that of the strong, and the nations by that of emperors, he adds: “And nations gathered together.” Certainly there was not one place in which the nations gathered, so that all might have one voice and one will in the same judgment and desire. Yet they were gathered: called from East, West, North, and South, so that kings and nations, meeting in the one catholic and apostolic Church, might cry to the Lord from the ends of the earth, with one mind and one mouth praising and glorifying God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.

This thought seems repeated in the words that follow, when he says:

> “The Lord has commanded the army of war, those coming from a distant land” (Isa. 13).

By “army of war” he means kings and nations: the war for fighting against the city of confusion and its rulers—namely, the powers of the air—by which he stirred up the power of kings, the glory of the rich, the ingenuity of the wise, and finally the faith of the nations.

This is that army which comes from a distant land, in contrast to the army which had come, as it were, from nearby. For those were thought to be nearby who possessed the covenant, the giving of the law, worship, and promises; whose were the fathers, and from whom Christ came according to the flesh. Were not the nations far away—without law, without faith, without God in this world? Far away were those ruled by vices, from whom virtues were banished; those with no hope of heavenly things and no expectation of things to come.

Therefore he fittingly says: “Those coming from a distant land.” From a land, indeed: that is, from earthly and clay-bound works; from earthly affections and desires; from the desires and defilements of this world.

[Col. 0390D] In saying, “The Lord has commanded the army of war,” he commends the power of divine virtue and grace under the name of a command. For by an ineffable inward impulse he stirred the nations to hear, enlightened them to believe, urged them to come and recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of God.

The Church can indeed be understood by the kingdom of God. In it the Gentiles were admitted to the grace of the patriarchs; cut off from the wild olive tree of unbelief, they were grafted into the good olive tree; and, made partakers of its root and richness, they obtain by the merits of one and the same faith as Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob the blessedness promised to them.

But even today, dearest brothers, Christ brings some into spiritual warfare from nearby and some from far away, and “makes those of one manner dwell in a house” (Ps. 67). He clothes them with the armor of God, that they may be able “to stand against the snares of the devil” (Eph. 6). Hence the Psalmist says:

> “Let those now say who have been redeemed by the Lord, whom he redeemed from the hand of the enemy; he gathered them from the regions” (Ps. 106).

[Col. 0391A] There are nearby regions and distant regions, from which his saints and elect were gathered, “who set his covenant above sacrifices” (Ps. 49). The younger son had gone into a distant region and there squandered all that he had, living extravagantly (Luke 15).

But if God is understood as the father, how could one depart from him or return to him who is everywhere? What region is distant from him, outside whom there is nothing? Yet the distant region is dissimilarity, just as likeness is nearness.

Therefore, for him who has complete likeness with the Father, the Father is so near that, although he is not the Father, he is nevertheless that very thing which the Father is. Of this likeness it is said: “As the Father is, so is the Son.” This one can neither approach the Father nor depart from the Father. For he was not made in the image and likeness of the Father; rather, he himself is the image and likeness of the Father, begotten from his substance, not from another substance.

But that son who was not born but made—and made in his image and likeness—was made not so that he himself might be the image and likeness of God, but so that he might have impressed and expressed within himself the image and likeness of God. He can depart, because he can become dissimilar; and he can return, because he can become similar.

Two things, therefore, must be considered. In the Creator they are one, but in the creature they are two: namely, nature and virtue. Immortality and incorruption belong to nature; wisdom and love belong to virtue. In God these are one, because these things are nothing other in God than God himself.

[Col. 0391C] But humanity possessed immortality and incorruption according to the nature in which it was created. It possessed wisdom and love as something added to it. But since humanity was neither immortality itself, nor incorruption itself, nor wisdom itself, it could depart from these things, become dissimilar to God, and then return through grace and become similar again.

Virtue, therefore, and blessedness, the reward of virtue, are the region of likeness; vice and misery are the region of dissimilarity. Since a person was first made dissimilar through vice, so as deservedly to become dissimilar through misery, it is necessary first to become similar through virtue, in order eventually to become similar through blessedness.

The more vicious anyone is, the more dissimilar to God and therefore the more distant that person is. The more virtuous anyone is, the more similar to God and therefore the nearer that person is. As many virtues as there are, so many regions there are, all belonging to that region of likeness which contains them all. And as many vices as there are, so many regions there are, belonging to that region of dissimilarity in which all vices are found.

For individual vices and individual virtues have their respective regions in which they subsist, outside of which they can scarcely, or never, be found or possessed. Thus chastity is a virtue whose region may be called abstinence; also labor and vigils, but especially inward solitude. [Col. 0392A] Chastity dwells in this region; whether it can be found outside it, let each person’s conscience examine.

But fornication is a vice whose region is gluttony, sleepiness, idleness, and especially cohabitation with the undisciplined. So too charity, which is a virtue, has voluntary poverty as its region; and avarice, which is a vice, has the love of temporal things as its region. This is easy to observe with the other vices and virtues.

Indeed, near to chastity is the person who does not exceed the bounds of marriage; far removed is the person defiled by fornications, adulteries, or sexual violations. Likewise, near to charity is the person who uses what is his freely, without plundering what belongs to another—unlike the person far removed, who neither distributes his own goods mercifully nor refrains from taking those of others.

Having likewise carefully examined the other vices and virtues, consider how many have come from far away and how many from nearby to the warfare which you have sworn to undertake. Therefore, those have come from afar who have ascended from the dung heap of vices to the mountains of virtues, where the one voice of all is heard as they sing psalms together and desire one thing besides.

Hearing this voice in the Spirit, the prophet says:

> “The sound of a multitude on the mountains, like that of a great people; the sound of the noise of kings and nations gathered together.”

For in this spiritual army some are kings and some common people: kings are those who preside, common people those who obey; or kings are the perfect, common people the imperfect. Kings are a terror to the people, just as the perfect are to the imperfect and superiors to their subjects. Hence he says: “The sound of the noise of kings.”

[Col. 0392C] Therefore, brothers, let thanksgiving and the voice of praise resound in your mouths and hearts. You have not merely departed from vices but—something granted to few—from the very regions of vices. You have ascended onto the mountains of virtues, and through this likeness to God which you possess in virtues, you hasten toward that blessedness which is still lacking.

But we, leaving these things, should restore ourselves by prayer and silence for investigating and discussing what follows. May Christ himself reveal our eyes, that we may behold the wonders of his law—he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages.

## SERMON IX. On the passage written: “From the height of heaven,” as far as “It shall waste away and be crushed.”

Hitherto the prophet has set forth the burden of Babylon—insofar as it has been destroyed, through the coming of our Lord and the preaching of the saints, by the separation of many—in few words indeed, but with profound meanings. But now the prophetic discourse turns to those who either have not received the truth of the Gospel so as to be saved, or who have corrupted the truth of the faith which they received by wicked works.

“The Lord comes from the summit of heaven, and the vessels of His wrath, to destroy the whole earth.” He does not foretell the destruction of this earth which we tread underfoot; rather, by the name “earth” he wishes us to understand those who savour nothing but earth, who prefer earthly desires to divine promises, who [Col. 0393A] choose temporal things before eternal ones, who, despising the truth of the Gospel, are entangled in the vanities and errors of the world. The prophet’s preceding declaration plainly states that these are to be destroyed.

It should certainly be known that sinners are destroyed in two ways: either when, converted to the Lord through repentance, they cease to be what they were and begin to be what they were not, according to the saying: “Turn the wicked, and they shall not be” (Prov. XII); or when, falling from evils into worse evils, they are finally consigned to eternal punishments. No Christian doubts that the former destruction is wrought by the Lord Himself in His own people, “who has mercy on whom He will”; Scripture proves that the latter comes about by His judgment indeed, but through the agency of wicked spirits. For the devil put it into Judas’s heart, first to betray the [Col. 0393B] Lord, then to hang himself (Matt. XXVII); and “the Lord sent upon the Egyptians anger, indignation, and tribulation, a sending forth through evil angels” (Ps. LXXIX).

But why one is taken and another left (Luke XVII), why this man is converted to be healed while that one is handed over to demons to be hardened or punished—let us know that this belongs to the hidden judgments and deep counsels of God. Therefore he says: “The Lord from the summit of heaven, and the vessels of His wrath, to destroy the whole earth.” The summit of heaven, as it seems to me, is the supreme and blessed Trinity itself, from whom the unchangeable decree surely proceeds: that our Lord Jesus, the Son of Man, to whom God the Father gave authority to execute judgment, may destroy some through repentance and others through punishment.

It follows: “Wail, because [Col. 0393C] the day of the Lord is near.” Thus the prophet commands sinners to wail, foreseeing that they will wail either in punishment or in repentance. Wailing fittingly signifies intense grief expressed with cries: the punishments brought upon the miserable wrest it from them, or repentance draws it from the hearts of sinners.

For what do we think, my brothers? “Wail,” he says, “because the day of the Lord is near.” He calls the day of judgment the day of the Lord, in which the Lord, appearing in power and majesty, will render to each according to his works (Matt. XVI). This day, certainly, begins for each person when, departing from the body, he receives either the first fruits of future blessedness in rest, or the beginnings of damnation in his soul, which he will receive also in his body.

“This day shall come as devastation from the Lord.” From the Lord indeed. For truly, O Lord, “the number of our months is with you, and you have set our bounds which cannot be passed.” “It shall come as devastation from the Lord.” For what does that day not lay waste? “Naked I came forth from my mother’s womb; naked shall I return there” (Job I), says a certain holy man. Where then are riches, where pleasures, where heaps of gold and silver, where storehouses full of gold overflowing from one thing into another? (Ps. CXLIII). Where are silken garments and war-horses? Certainly all things are laid waste for the dying man: “When he dies, he shall take none of these things with him, nor shall his glory descend with him” (Ps. XLVIII). Whatever strength there is in the body, whatever is pleasurable in the flesh, whatever is delightful to the senses, [Col. 0394A] whatever is agreeable in human habits—that day utterly overwhelms and consumes it all.

Blessed is the mind from which the remembrance of this day never departs. Solomon bears witness how useful meditation upon death is when he says: “My son, always remember your last things, and you shall never sin” (Ecclus. VII). For whom would sin delight, if that hour is always before his eyes? Therefore wail, O sinner, in repentance, lest you be compelled to wail in punishment. Let the day of the Lord become bitter to you in memory against the pleasures of this age, lest it become excessively bitter in experience and you feel what follows: “Therefore all hands shall be weakened, and every human heart shall waste away and be broken” (Isa. XIII).

By hands, action is understood. Come then, brothers: as the Lord says, “We must work while it is day. Night comes, when no one [Col. 0394B] can work” (John IX). “Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord. From now on, says the Spirit, let them rest from their labours” (Rev. XIV). Death therefore is the night in which no one can work. For one will either rest in good works or be punished for evil ones.

On that day of the Lord, therefore, all hands shall be weakened: when some, “bound hand and foot,” are cast into outer darkness (Matt. VIII), while others, after the work of six days, are received by the Sabbath—that is, by rest—and admitted to inward delights. For “from now on, says the Spirit, let them rest from their labours.” Therefore, “Whatever your hand is able to do, do it earnestly; for there shall be neither work, nor reasoning, nor wisdom, nor knowledge in hell, whither you hasten” (Eccles. IX). For all hands shall be weakened.

And what do you say, you who trust in [Col. 0394C] your own strength and boast in the abundance of your riches? Let your charity consider. Some do almost nothing; others do evil; others do good badly; others do good well. That evil and slothful servant does almost nothing who buries in the ground the money entrusted to him (Matt. XXV), neither defrauding anything from what he received nor increasing it through gain. Like him are the slothful and lukewarm, to whom it seems a great thing merely to abstain from obvious crimes, while they expend no labour or diligence in acquiring virtues. Such persons, therefore, are as though without hands. What will they do when no one can work? Certainly their works do not follow them. Therefore they shall not rest. They have no works in which to rest: all hands [Col. 0394D] shall be weakened, so that they cannot work.

What then remains except that the useless servant too be cast into outer darkness? Yet just as those who work well send their good works before them to God, so that when death intervenes and their hands are weakened they may rest and glory in those works, so surely those who work wickedly send their evil works before them to hell, to be tormented in them forever. “Those who have been powerful in evil here shall suffer powerful torments” (Wis. VI); the cruel shall be cruelly tortured; those foul with lust shall be afflicted with sulphurous stenches; those whom greed inflames shall be burned in Tartarean flames; and those defiled by gluttony and drunkenness shall be consumed by everlasting worms.

Beware, O human being. Every time you sin, you send before you into [Col. 0395A] hell the materials of the punishments by which you will be tormented. You kindle for yourself the fire in which you will be tormented; you raise up the stench by which you will be afflicted; you bring to life the worms that will consume you; you prepare the darkness that will blind you. Then your hands shall be weakened: neither fit for work nor strong for resistance, but enfeebled for suffering. “All hands shall be weakened.” It is no longer the time for working.

“From now on, says the Spirit, let them rest from their labours.” Who are they? Certainly those of whom it adds: “For their works follow them.” Will your works follow you—those which you either sold or scattered to every wind? Whatever good works you gathered, you have puffed away in your own mind by the winds of vanity and pride, and yet you think your works will follow you? Therefore, when you have nowhere to find consolation, what remains except [Col. 0395B] that you too be tormented?

You also, dearest one, who even do good works well, I do not wish you to trust in your own strength or boast in the abundance of your riches (Ps. XLVIII), even spiritual riches; for then all hands shall be weakened. How, you ask? Because “all our righteousnesses are as the cloth of a menstruating woman” in His sight. For “no living person shall be justified in His sight” (Ps. CXLII). Therefore all must wail: the wicked, lest by persevering in evil they be condemned; the slothful and lukewarm, lest, being neither cold nor hot, they be vomited from God’s mouth (Rev. III); likewise the one who does good badly, lest he walk the road with two paths; and the one who does good well, lest he be rejected by God’s hidden judgment.

Thus the prophet says: “Wail, because the day of the Lord is near; [Col. 0395C] it shall come as devastation from the Lord”—so that, at the sight of approaching death, the good may fear and the wicked may mourn, and those who refuse to wail in punishment may learn to wail in repentance. Although this utterance appears to concern all persons, according to the order of the prophetic prediction it is specially directed in threat against those who either fell during persecutions or were defiled by diverse crimes in the time of peace. He both urges repentance upon them and threatens punishment; while they live, they are granted the opportunity both to be converted and to do good works—an opportunity which is certainly taken from everyone when death comes.

For then all hands shall be weakened, and every human heart shall waste away and be broken. Come then, brothers: an ulcerous discharge arises from decaying flesh, and does not cease to flow until the flesh has utterly rotted away. Such discharge contains both horror and stench. Let each person now look at his own heart; let him see with what foods he has fed it. Certainly the food of the soul is the word of God: food that does not decay, generate corruption, or bring corruption to one who eats it.
