A good work is food for the soul, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “My food is to do the will of Him who sent me” (John IV). Compunction also is wholesome food for the soul, as the Prophet says: “You will feed us with the bread of tears” (Ps. LXXIX); and again: “My tears have been my bread day and night” (Ps. XLI). Sweet devotion to God is likewise food for the soul, like the fat of wheat by which Jerusalem is satisfied, as the Psalmist says to it: “He satisfies you with the fat of wheat” (Ps. [Col. 0396A] CXLIX).

These foods provide life-giving nourishment to the hungry soul, transforming it into themselves and making it a participant in their eternity. There are other harmful foods that nourish decay and supply material for rottenness: namely, the husks of swine, for which people often hunger so greedily (Luke XV). The soul feeds on them so pleasurably that they produce disgust for heavenly nourishment and nausea even at manna, food surely fit for angels (Num. XI). These are the meats that rotted between the teeth of the sinful people, who, miserably buried in the graves of craving, were consumed by the very corruption they had created.

Thus fornications, adulteries, thefts, and other such things are the husks of swine—that is, the food of demons. Although they taste pleasant in human hearts, they are nevertheless material for ulcerous decay and rottenness. A person will surely perceive their stench either beneficially in repentance or painfully in conscience when death is near. For then every human heart shall waste away, as the foul discharge of impurities and the filth of vices flows out from every hidden place of conscience. From these are bred that worm which does not die and kindled that fire which is not quenched (Mark IX). These are the worms by which the heart is broken in punishment, if it has not here been broken in repentance.

“Every human heart,” he says, “shall waste away and be broken.” Every heart, plainly, of one living according to the human way, such as those to whom the Apostle says: “While jealousy and contention are among you, are you not human?” (1 Cor. III). In the earlier statement, [Col. 0396C] when he said, “all hands shall be weakened,” he did not add “of man,” because the works of both good and wicked persons cease when death comes; but only the heart and conscience of those who live according to the human way shall be broken.

Therefore, brothers, let this hour not depart from our memory, so that if it is now a cause of fear to us, it may then become a gate of salvation through Jesus Christ our Lord. Amen.

## SERMON X. On what is written: “Pangs and pains shall seize them” (Isa. XIII), etc.

Hezekiah, lamenting in the person of the Church these unhappy times into which our age has fallen, says: “Behold, in peace my bitterness is most bitter” [Col. 0396D] (Isa. XXXVIII). Truly, brothers, it is so. Persecution seemed bitter, but in persecution itself there was no small consolation for the good, when there was no room for hypocrisy and no time for idleness or laxity; when a certain happy necessity governed all ranks alike, subjects as well as prelates.

But when fear was removed, laxity arose, ambition increased, honours and riches were preferred to virtues, and vices were nourished by luxuries. Therefore the prophet Isaiah, after describing the apostolic preaching and the fortitude of the martyrs, saw that many, when persecution had ceased, fell more grievously in time of peace; he therefore instilled in them the most salutary fear of coming calamity, saying: “Wail, because the day of the Lord is near; it shall come as devastation from the Lord. Therefore all hands shall be weakened, and every [Col. 0397A] human heart shall waste away and be broken.”

As your charity knows, we discussed these words yesterday and, as the Lord granted, explained how they concern both those repenting and those dying. It follows: “Pangs and pains shall seize them” (Isa. XIII)—namely, those whose hands have been weakened and whose hearts have wasted away and been broken.

Come then, brothers: all shameful acts take their origin from the belly, while crimes are perpetrated through the other members. From gluttony, which consists in filling the belly, arise the incitements of lust, from which fornications and every kind of uncleanness are generated. Through the tongue, moreover, blasphemies are committed; through the hands, thefts, murders, and other such acts—while the eyes serve this purpose by searching, the ears by hearing, and the feet by moving about.

Therefore understand by “pangs” the anguish of mind which arises, as death approaches, from the remembrance of shameful acts; and by “pains” the anguish which recollected crimes will bring forth. For what sadness, my brothers, will there then be for the disgraceful, when they see that through the corruption of a most vile and brief pleasure they have earned eternal punishments? What anguish too will there then be for criminals, whose cruelty will be repaid with most cruel torments? What do you think, dearest ones? Will that hour impart no bitterness to those tasteless foods that you use? Happy are those for whom the belly’s pleasures do not prepare these pangs, whose members are circumcised here so that they may not feel these pains [Col. 0397C] then.

“Pangs and pains shall seize them.” Whenever the memory of pleasure experienced affects your mind, awakens desire, produces distaste for this vile food, and brings horror, you suffer spiritual pangs. By these pangs you escape those which many feel at death, and you will rejoice that the sentence uttered by the holy patriarch concerning the purple-clad rich man and poor Lazarus is addressed to you: “You received good things in your life, and Lazarus likewise evil things; but now he is comforted and you are tormented” (Luke XVI).

It follows: “They shall suffer pain like a woman in labour.” Come then, brothers: there is no pain like that of a woman in labour. There is bodily childbirth, spiritual childbirth, and penal childbirth. Certainly, “when a woman gives birth, she has sorrow because her hour has come” (John XVI). Pain is in her limbs, death is in her eyes, fear occupies her conscience; but she does not know what the outcome will be.

Spiritual childbirth occurs when the saints, through teaching and care, beget spiritual children; one of them says: “My little children, whom I am again bringing to birth” (Gal. IV). Nor is this childbirth without pain, for such a one must rejoice with those who rejoice and weep with those who weep (Rom. XII). There is also spiritual childbirth when a barren and unfruitful soul conceives through fear of the Lord and, converted to the Lord, brings forth the beginnings of good works. And what pain there is in this childbirth, when the flesh resists the spirit, habit resists the will, and the mind itself now wills, now fears, now is driven by delight in good, now is drawn back by desire for evil!

There is also harmful childbirth, when a person “conceives pain and brings forth [Col. 0398A] iniquity” (Ps. VII), when he conceives in the desire to acquire and brings forth in the deed. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Woe to those who are pregnant and nursing” (Matt. XXIV). Woe indeed to those who conceive thus and give birth thus. Though they now exult when they have done evil and delight in the worst things (Prov. II), when death is already approaching they shall suffer pain like a woman in labour.

For just as a woman who conceived with pleasure is afflicted with great pains when she gives birth, so surely the soul corrupted by pleasures and vices, when the recompense of that very corruption begins to appear as it dies, is crushed by sorrow and pains; and late repentance, returning to itself, begins to feel what is written: “Walk in the light of your fire and in the flame which you have kindled for yourselves” (Isa. XXX). This childbirth may certainly be called penal, when the dying person as though gives birth in punishment; and, having died, receives the punishment which he conceived while sinning, as though bringing forth a most unhappy offspring.

How much more happily does a person conceive repentance for sins through the fear of the Lord and bring forth conversion of conduct! Although this childbirth is not without pain, it produces joy in the tranquillity of conscience; for “when she has borne a child, she no longer remembers the anguish because of joy,” and “those who sow in tears shall reap in joy” (Ps. CXXV). Therefore all who either abandoned the faith unwillingly, overcome by torments in persecution, or who were cut off in the time of peace through corruption by vices, shall suffer pain like a woman in labour—either beneficially through repentance or unhappily in dying.

“Each one shall be astonished at his neighbour.” Let your charity consider, dearest brothers. “Neighbour” is said in many ways: by place, time, nature, kinship, likeness, love, and mercy. By place, as one is called another’s neighbour because he lives nearby. By time, as the one who immediately succeeds the one who is descending, with no one else intervening. By nature, as every human being is neighbour to every human being. Hence it is said: “You shall love your neighbour as yourself” (Matt. XXII). No Christian doubts that this was spoken concerning every human being. By kinship, as son to father, brother to brother, kinsman to kinsman. By likeness, as good to good and evil to evil: though separated in place and time, they are nevertheless considered neighbours through likeness. By love, people can be so near [Col. 0398D] or united to one another that “the multitude of believers had one heart and one soul in the Lord” (Acts IV). By mercy, as the Samaritan is proved by the Gospel’s testimony to have been neighbour to the man who fell among robbers because he showed mercy to him (Luke X).

Thus, to a man living justly, soberly, and piously, anyone living likewise is a neighbour; an angel is also neighbour, most graciously favouring one who lives thus; and God Himself is further neighbour, supplying to one who lives thus the grace to do good works. Likewise, to every utterly wicked person every utterly wicked person is neighbour, whether human or spirit. For the spirit of fornication is said to be neighbour to the sexually immoral, the spirit of pride to the proud; and each person earns the neighbourhood of the one whose likeness he assumes in vices and virtues.

[Col. 0399A] We must therefore believe that at the death of persons both good and evil beings are present: the good may be received by the good, the wicked tortured by the wicked. Therefore, “each one shall be astonished at his neighbour.” When the demon of fornication appears to an unclean person as he dies, he cannot fail to be astonished at what he sees. What seems alluring and pleasant when it is suggested is felt bitter when it reproaches; and the miserable person is astonished to find harsh and merciless the one whom he had often experienced as sweet.

It matters to us, therefore, brothers, to make such neighbours for ourselves that in that terrible hour they may be a consolation, not a horror, to us. Blessed is one who by purity of life and integrity of conduct has merited to have angelic spirits so close that, like friends and neighbours standing by as he departs, they rejoice over him as one well known to them.

In trustworthy histories we read that angels have often stood by those dying, and that saints whom they had honoured with special devotion during life were present in their final necessity. Conversely, we know that wicked spirits have appeared to those who, while living, had defiled themselves with vices and crimes at their suggestion: dreadful in countenance, with flaming eyes, armed with infernal instruments. Thus both the saints, departing from the body toward such splendour, are struck with wonder and astonishment, and the reprobate, facing such horror, are rendered stunned by an alienation of mind. Therefore, “each one shall be astonished at his neighbour.”

And it is added: “Their faces shall be burnt countenances.” I think this should be referred only to the reprobate. It is chiefly by face and countenance that one person is distinguished from another, and individuals are recognized from individuals by their distinctive appearance. Those guilty of certain crimes are customarily marked in the face by branding, so that, because the face cannot be hidden, the crime made public by the disfigurement of the face may likewise be unable to remain hidden.

The countenance of the soul, as it seems to me, is conscience, the witness of all actions, words, and thoughts. Whatever a person may be, he cannot hide his conscience from himself. For conscience is like a mirror of the soul, in which surely our defect or our progress is perceived and every condition of the inner person is known.

Come then, dearest brothers: let no one be secure. We sin easily, transgress easily, easily slip into idle and empty things, and, as though without feeling it, are drawn into forbidden acts, as it is written: “Ephraim has become like a cake baked under ashes, which is not turned. Strangers have consumed his strength, and he did not know it. Grey hairs too have been scattered upon him, and he did not know it” (Hos. VII). Yet our sins do not pass away into the wind, nor are they given over to oblivion; rather, whether we wish it or not, they are written in conscience itself.

The Apostle says that some have a conscience “seared” (1 Tim. IV), that is, burned by the flame of wickedness. This burning is often concealed from us while we live; but when we die, it cannot remain hidden either from us or from the spirits who will be present. Rightly therefore he says: “Their faces shall be burnt countenances.” For when the hands have been weakened and the heart broken, amid the pangs and pains [Col. 0400A] which sinners endure as death approaches, whatever has not been healed by the remedy of repentance or the ointment of contrition will break forth openly; and many things that now seem wholly sound will then undoubtedly appear scorched.

There are certainly splendid works—labour, vigils, fasts. If all these have been corrupted by a perverse intention, they bring no beauty to the conscience, which the flame, made an accuser by its own thoughts, burns. If anyone should maintain that this statement also applies to penitents, it can suitably be understood that amid the pains which every penitent bears in recollection, while he reviews with keen indignation all that he has committed, many things then appear to him burned by the fire of desire which previously seemed bright and sound.

Since, therefore, those who live ruinously within the Church, or who have fallen away from the Church or the faith, are to be judged under the name Babylon, the burden has been described by which those converted are to be pressed through repentance, or by which those persisting in evil are to be oppressed when dying. The prophet proceeds to describe in mystical language that miserable time when iniquity will so abound and charity grow cold that they will deserve to have sent to them that worker of error—the man of sin, the son of perdition—of whom it is written: “Want shall go before his face” (Job XLI). The prophet does not pass over this want in what follows.

First, however, the discourse is woven concerning the day of judgment, so that, through fear of it, the vices which will then abound most greatly may be more easily avoided, or the torments which that blasphemer will inflict may be endured more nobly. He therefore continues and says:

“Behold, the day of the Lord comes, cruel, and full of indignation, wrath, and fury.” Having first spoken aptly enough concerning the last day of each individual, prophetic speech turns to that day which, as regards the present life, is the one last day of all, so that those who do not fear that day may at least be terrified by this one.

Four manifest indications of that coming calamity are mentioned here: cruelty, indignation, wrath, and fury. Cruelty is when anger exceeds its measure; indignation is when some definite mark of baseness becomes known in the person who committed the injury; wrath commonly appears in voice or countenance; [Col. 0400D] fury in action.

That day, then, will be cruel, because in it the spectacle of the greatest cruelty will appear: when the elements shall be dissolved by the heat of fire, “and fire shall burn before the Lord, and a mighty tempest round about Him” (Ps. XLIX). It will be full of indignation, when divine majesty and human frailty are made known; and it will be manifest to all how so great frailty raged against so great power, so that none may fail to see how greatly the King of glory ought to be indignant that He endured such injury from most contemptible dust. It will also be full of wrath, when that terrible voice is heard: “Depart from me, you cursed, into eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. XXV). The fury of the Judge inflicting affliction will surely follow that sentence, when those going into eternal burning shall have no possibility of escape and no hope of deliverance.

“To make the earth a desolation, and to crush its sinners out of it.” It is certainly clear that the earth will then be made a desolation, whether by “earth” you understand the world or that earthly city, Babylon. For when some have been taken up to heaven and others assigned to infernal punishments, the earth will remain without an inhabitant—that is, the world without humanity—and that condemned city alone will remain without the fellowship of any good person. Then the sinners of earth shall be crushed out of it. The sinners of heaven are demons, who, as soon as iniquity was found in them, were cast down from heaven, and “no place was found for them any longer in it” (Rev. XX). But the sinners of earth are human beings, who sin daily and inhabit the earth until, on the last day, once sentence has been given, they are utterly crushed out of the earth and cast down to hell.

It follows:

“Because the stars of heaven shall not spread their light; the sun is darkened at its rising, and the moon shall not shine in its light.” For on the day of judgment, when Christ appears in glory, just as a very small lamp seems to give no light within the sun’s ray, so all the stars, overwhelmed by that splendour, will appear dark to those who behold them.

But I think that these things, which we have briefly expounded concerning the day of judgment, may be referred to the time of Antichrist, so that the prophet, instructed in the Spirit, may be understood to have woven his oracle: first concerning the preaching of the apostles; afterward concerning the persecution of the Church; then concerning the conversion of the nations and the tranquillity of peace; then concerning the repentance of the fallen and the terror of death; and finally concerning the time of Antichrist, the reward of the righteous, and the condemnation of the wicked.

But since the hour has now passed, let us reserve another time for examining these matters, so that when we assemble more freely in one place, we may open our mouths in praise and glory of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XI. On the words, “Behold, the day of the Lord comes,” through “I will visit evils upon the cities” (Isa. XIII).

“Behold, the day of the Lord is coming, cruel, full of indignation, wrath, and fury.” As your charity [Col. 0401D] remembers, we said that these words of the prophet, although suitably applied to the last day, may nevertheless be referred to the times of Antichrist, so that holy Isaiah may be understood not only to have foretold the various conditions of the Church, but also to have preserved the order in which they were to succeed one another.

First, then, indicating the preaching of the apostles, he says: “Raise a banner upon the darkened mountain,” etc. Next, foretelling the persecution by which the martyrs were to be crowned, he says: “I have commanded my sanctified ones,” and the remaining words that follow. From the place where he says, “The sound of a multitude upon the mountains,” he declares that peace was restored to the Church through the conversion of kings and nations. Then, describing either the destruction or conversion of those who, yielding to persecutions, fell away, or who in time of peace were defiled by fillets, he says: “From the summit of heaven the Lord, and the vessels of his wrath,” etc. Finally, striking them with the fear of death, he added: “Wail, because the day of the Lord is near,” etc.

Lastly, because he saw that, as iniquity increased, almost the whole human race would renounce truth, abandon charity, and become entangled in vices and errors, he composed a prophetic oracle concerning that time: that such a worker of error would be sent to them that they might believe falsehood, and that those who do not believe the Gospel of God might be judged. Therefore, as it seems to me, he not inappropriately calls that time “the day of the Lord,” when that impious one, like the sword of God’s wrath, shall come forth from the abyss of His judgments as from a sheath, for the punishment of evildoers and the praise of the good (1 Pet. 2).

This day is indeed called cruel [Col. 0402B], because there will then undoubtedly be such tribulation as has not been from the beginning of the nations until that time. It is also called full of indignation, because throughout the earth the arrogance of that proud man will rage against the saints, when he sees that the poor hold him who is rich in contempt, the humble despise him who is exalted, and the weak disdain him who is powerful; and that they refuse to obey his commands, indeed resist his decrees and oppose his orders. That time will also be full of wrath and fury: wrath is to be understood in threats, fury in tortures.

All these things will be permitted by God’s just judgment, “to make the earth a desolation and to crush its sinners from it.” By “earth” in this place is understood the Church of Christ, of which it is said [Col. 0402C]: “The earth is the Lord’s and its fullness” (Ps. 23); and concerning which it is also said to Moses: “The place where you stand is holy ground” (Exod. 2). In it, certainly, good people live together with bad, humble with proud, counterfeit with true Christians.

And just as formerly among the Jews every perversity took its beginning, as a cause of the coming desolation, from the scribes and Pharisees, who possessed the key of knowledge and delivered the decrees of the Law to the people; so now, as I say with grief, the beginnings and causes of future evils are sown beforehand by us—that is, by clerics and monks—who seem to be the lights of the world. Of these it is said: “For the stars of heaven shall not give their light; the sun is darkened at its rising, and the moon shall not shine with its light.”

These, as it seems to me, are signs of the coming calamity, concerning which the Lord says in the Gospel: “There shall be signs in sun and moon and stars” (Luke 21). If you ask what signs, hear the prophet Joel: “The sun shall be turned into darkness and the moon into blood, before the great and manifest day of the Lord comes” (Joel 2).

Come, brothers: God made two great lights: “the greater light to rule the day, and the lesser light to rule the night” (Gen. 1). In the firmament of the holy Church there are likewise two great lights, created by the Lord: priesthood and kingship, king and bishop, ruler and cleric. Day signifies spiritual things; night, secular things. Therefore priesthood is the greater light, to rule the day—that is, spiritual matters; kingship the lesser light, to rule the night—that is, secular matters.

It is consequently contrary to nature [Col. 0403A] if the sun rules the night, if the moon rules the day; if a ruler intrudes into the celebration of spiritual sacraments; if a priest darkens the serenity of his conscience with the shadows of secular business. “No one serving as a soldier of God entangles himself in secular affairs” (2 Tim. 2). King Uzziah, presumptuously entering the Holy of Holies in the manner of a priest, was struck with leprosy (2 Chron. 2); and the prophet Balaam, favoring the desire of an impious king against God’s will, was blinded by avarice in the eyes of prophetic light (Num. 22).

How well these two lights agreed; how splendidly they shone from this spiritual firmament; how excellently they distinguished between days and months and seasons and years! That is, king and priest each remained within his own rank, when the power of the former served only the peace and equity of his subjects, while the wisdom and teaching of the latter kept watch to drive away the darkness of minds and to pour in the light of truth.

Woe to us, who have fallen upon these unhappy times, in which the sun appears to have been turned into darkness. “Into what darkness?” you ask. I do not wish to say it, brothers; I do not wish to say it, lest I seem to set my mouth against heaven. Let them look to themselves. Let them recall those whose offices they discharge, whose chairs they have obtained, whose mitres they glory in wearing. Let them consider what rays of knowledge, what lights of virtues, what sparks of charity, what flashes of spiritual correction Gregory, Augustine, Ambrose, and Hilary sent forth in their own times. And, to come nearer to home [Col. 0403C], let our own people reflect how Cuthbert and Dunstan shone in their times. Did not all these make the priesthood, as though one greatest sun, radiate through the whole world with incorporeal light?

Let these men now see how brightly they shine in the faith of those predecessors, and whether they themselves shine as much, more, or a little less. Let them thus compare times with times, merits with merits, persons with persons; and, according to the testimony of their conscience, judge whether the sun has been turned into darkness. Happy were the times in which a bad man was found as rarely as a good man is found now.

But what shall we say of royal power, which we judged comparable to the moon that rules the night? It shone then with its own light when, in driving away the darkness of this night—that is, of iniquity and injustice—kings and princes were a consolation to the good and a terror to the evil; fathers of orphans and judges of widows (Ps. 67); defenders of churches and repellers of wrongs; superior in power but inferior in humility, desiring rather to be of service than to exercise rule. Such was Constantine; such was that excellent Theodosius; and many others.

But then the moon shall be turned into blood when the hands of rulers are full of blood: when, through exactions and taxes, they pour out the very entrails of the wretched; justify the impious for bribes; and take away justice from the righteous. Then they misuse the people as plunder—tyrants, not kings; presenting themselves as destroyers of the poor, not their counselors; confusing and mingling what is just and unjust, lawful and unlawful [Col. 0404A]; following not right and equity but their own pleasure and appetite.

“And the stars,” he says, “shall fall from heaven.” By the stars—which are not said to rule the night, though they too illuminate it—I think those are to be understood who, having renounced the world, dwell in thought and desire in those heavenly mansions themselves. They were truly lights of the world when, surpassing the whole world in life, conduct, love, and contemplation, they despised all earthly and temporal things, accounting riches and honors as dung; chaste in body, most pure in mind, unmoved under insults inflicted upon them; subject to their superiors in humility and obedience; content with the smallest food; slow to anger, ready to give, ashamed to receive; never seeking what was their own but what belonged to Jesus Christ (1 Cor. 13).

What shall I say, dearest brothers? What shall I say? What are we? Where are we? Are we in heaven? Are we where Antony, Macarius, and Hilarion once were? Have we not rather fallen from heaven to earth, we who savor almost nothing but earth—loving earth, thinking of earth, speaking of earth; contentious, complaining, biting and devouring one another, envying one another and slandering each other?

What market is without monks? What fair? What council? I pass over many who are so swallowed up by earth that neither earth nor sea suffices for their greed; that they shrink from nothing they may desire; that, like Pharaoh’s tax-gatherers, they harass and torture the wretches over whom they rule [Col. 0404C]; that they extort money more cruelly than any secular persons; that, fattened, grown sleek, and swollen with the blood of the poor, they proceed even to the selling and buying of sacred things.

The holy prophet too, having said beforehand concerning the time of Antichrist, “Behold, the day of the Lord shall come, cruel,” and the rest, immediately adds the reason why they will deserve either to be deceived or oppressed by him: “For the stars of heaven shall not give their light.” What light, I ask, will darkened men spread abroad—men changed from stars into coals, plunging down from heaven into a dungheap?

“The sun is darkened at its rising.” Come, brothers: many shine at the beginning of their priesthood; their life is upright, their intention right, their election sound. Yet afterward they are darkened by a change of character. But as the time of Antichrist approaches, avarice and ambition will so rule human minds that even the very beginnings of promotion, as it were the rising of the sun, will be full of darkness. A most wicked life will indeed precede them, and a perverse intention and a shameful entry will follow. Therefore the sun shall be darkened at its rising, and the moon shall not shine with its light; because, as we have said before, the sun shall be turned into darkness and the moon into blood, so that the great and manifest day of the Lord may follow.

It follows:

“And I will visit evils upon the cities.” By “cities” I think we should understand communities which live in different places, under different rules and customs, yet in one Catholic faith. For just as many citizens gather in the same city under one law, so those who unite under one order into one fellowship make, as it were, one city [Col. 0405A]. Around that time there will be such corruption in communities of this sort that they will seem united not to worship God but only to fulfill their own desires and lusts. Of them the blessed Apostle says: “In the last days perilous times shall come; and men shall be lovers of themselves, covetous, proud, lovers of pleasures more than of God, having indeed a form of godliness but denying its power” (2 Tim. 3).

Many such persons exist today: in dress, in psalm-singing, and in tonsure they display an appearance of godliness, but they do not possess its power, which consists in charity, chastity, humility, and contempt for pleasures. Upon cities of this sort the Lord will therefore visit evils, exacting vengeance from sinners and denouncing their shamefulness, so that either, worn down by persecutions, they may be corrected; or, breaking forth from their crimes into unbelief, they may be crushed with Babylon in eternal punishments by God’s manifest judgment [Col. 0405B].

I see that you are eager to hear more, but spare a speaker now wearied by the preceding sermon. Pray that we may be found fit to investigate what follows, through Jesus Christ, to whom are honor and glory. Amen.

## SERMON XII. On the words written: “I will visit evils upon the cities” (Isa. 13), etc.

I confess, dearest brothers, that what has happened to me is otherwise than I had expected. For it seemed to me that the mysteries and sacraments of these burdens, of which we are speaking, could be completed in a few sermons; whereas now the Lord begins, as it were anew, to open before us the very greatest abyss of mysteries, saying through the prophet: “And I will visit evils upon the cities, and upon the wicked their iniquities. And I will make the pride of unbelievers cease, and I will humble the arrogance of the strong.”

But since these matters are sufficiently clear if we review what we have already said in other sermons, let us pass through them in a brief summary. In the time of Antichrist, then, the Lord will visit evils upon the cities, dispersing the communities of those who maintain an appearance of godliness in hypocrisy. He will visit their iniquity upon the wicked, punishing those who are openly found such, whether by tortures or errors. He will also make the pride of unbelievers cease, humbling the powerful of this world whom the Christian faith wounds; and He will humble the arrogance of the strong, suppressing by temptations and persecutions those who glory in their virtues.

For there are some who, because of their religious dress and their association in common life, appear publicly to be good, though in secret they are utterly wicked; these we understand to be signified by the name of cities. There are others who are not ashamed to seem openly wicked in the sight of men; these we think are called unjust and impious by the prophet. There are many also who are strangers to the Christian faith and proudly mock faith itself; these we judge should be called unbelievers. There are yet others, not only faithful but also devoted to virtues [Col. 0406A], who nevertheless trust in their own virtue and glory in themselves rather than in the Lord; these we not unjustly call arrogant. The heavenly oracle declares that all of them are either to be utterly crushed on the day of judgment or destroyed in the time of Antichrist.

It follows:

“A man shall be more precious than gold, and a human being than pure refined gold.” *Vir*, “man,” derives its name from *virtus*, “virtue.” Thus the prophet, commending the scarcity of virtues, says: “A man shall be more precious than gold.” All rare things are precious, while goods freely available are despised. Since in that time a person devoted to virtue will be rare; rare too one who does manly—that is, courageous—deeds; rare one who prefers bitter death to the allurements of this life; rare one who would rather be despised by the world and tortured by executioners for Christ than enjoy the pleasures of this world: truly a man will be more precious than gold—that is, rarer—and a human being, namely one who lives according to reason rather than according to sense like a beast, than pure refined gold.

Gold, or pure refined gold, may also fittingly signify the perfect persons who belonged to the early Church, whom we know were tested and examined like gold in a furnace (Wis. 3), and most fittingly placed in that golden garment in which the queen stood at Christ’s right hand (Ps. 44). But whoever in that final persecution is found a true man—yielding neither to tortures, nor agreeing to promises, nor believing signs and wonders—will assuredly shine among the other saints with a special prerogative, just as gold excels the other metals in price and beauty [Col. 0406C].

Certainly, when he says, “a human being than pure refined gold,” it is a repetition: what he first called “man” he later calls “human being,” and what he first called “gold” he later calls “pure refined gold.” He added: “For this reason I will trouble heaven, and the earth shall be moved from its place.”

The heaven of that time is called the Church, or the perfect persons within the Church; these, indeed, he says will be troubled then, seeing the wicked and unjust fight against the saints with a threefold weapon: promises, to entice them; miracles, to deceive them; tortures, to break them. Who, I ask, can be so perfect as not to be troubled in so great a temptation, when pseudo-apostles and pseudo-prophets shall arise and give signs and wonders, so that, if possible, even the elect may be led into error? “And the earth shall be moved from its place” (Luke 16).

What earth? Perhaps that portion of the Church which, because it clings in affection to earth, is called earth. Its place is now either faith or the Church itself. Departing from it through shrinking from tortures, marveling at prodigies, yielding to flatteries, it will be moved—either by abandoning faith itself, withdrawing from the Church, or hiding somewhere until iniquity passes by. For many, deceived by false signs, will forsake the faith; many, overcome by punishments, will depart from the Church and withdraw to hidden places. All these, in comparison with those called heaven because they boldly face every danger, are not inappropriately called earth.

But because the teachers will be so few, and those who remain will suffer such adversity, that they will be unable to gather the scattered, raise the fallen, correct the delinquent, or console the fainthearted, it immediately follows: “And it shall be like a fleeing doe, and like a sheep; and there shall be none to gather it.” He speaks of the earth, which shall be like a fleeing doe and like a sheep. The doe is a timid animal; the sheep is simple. The earth, therefore, shall be moved from its place: terrified by fear of persecution, it will flee from the fellowship of the perfect; or deceived by miracles because of its own simplicity.

He says, then: “And it shall be like a fleeing doe and like a sheep.” For just as a doe, alarmed and afraid, flees barking dogs and pursuing hunters, so many who then cannot fight the battles of the Lord with courageous hearts will avoid pressing dangers, either by yielding ground or agreeing with persecutors [Col. 0407B]. And just as sheep, when beasts rush into the flock and the shepherds are driven away or struck down, flee scattered in every direction, so the simple members of the Church, their teachers expelled or killed, will wander astray through byways, since there is no one to put forth a hand, gather the scattered, or bring back those who wander.

It follows:

“Each one shall turn to his own people, and each shall flee to his own land.” Come, brothers: there are two peoples, two nations, and two kingdoms—those of good and evil persons, wise and foolish, elect and reprobate. In this present time, when all things are mixed and confused, one cannot discern to which nation and people anyone belongs. Many are good only in appearance but utterly wicked in the hidden places of conscience; many praise the faith in words, because they dare do nothing else, though they oppose it by their corrupt conduct.

But when the time of winnowing comes, each one shall turn to his own people: chaff to chaff, grain to grain, good person to good person, utterly wicked person to utterly wicked person. Then each shall turn to his own people. There is, as it were, one people of those who shall sit and judge with the Lord; another of angels obedient to the Lord; another of sheep to be rewarded by the Lord; another of goats who shall hear from the Lord: “Depart from me, accursed ones” (Matt. 25).

“And each shall flee to his own land.” If anyone insists on examining this more subtly, let us comply and say that there is a land of the living, a land of the dying, a land of saints, and a land of the impious. The land of the living [Col. 0407D] is paradise; the land of the dying is the world; the land of saints is the Church; the land of the impious is Babylon. “I believe,” says the prophet, “that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. 26). For in paradise no one dies, where life is eternal.

But this world, in which nothing is stable and nothing eternal, where human life itself is the shadow of death, is most fittingly called the land of the dying. The Church of Christ, however, is the land of saints, of which Scripture says: “Let mercy be shown to the impious, and he will not learn to do justice; in the land of saints he has acted wickedly” (Isa. 26). The Church is rightly called the land of saints, since outside it in this life there is no saint, no righteousness, no sanctification.

The flesh of the saints may also be called the land of saints, of which it is said: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth” [Col. 0408A] (Matt. 5). Similarly, that city of confusion may be called the land of the impious; nevertheless, their flesh is also their land. For where will those flee who flee from the land of saints, except to the land of the impious, which is the city Babylon, the city of confusion? There are different doctrines and different errors there, some pursuing the pleasure of the flesh, others worldly honors, others riches and delights as the highest good.

Thus the land of the luxurious is the pleasure of the flesh; of the ambitious, the desire for possessions; of those who are wandering and unstable, their own will. Those therefore who abandon the Church and shrink from the tribulations it will then suffer will make their way to the city of perdition, each fleeing to his own land—that is, each using his own flesh according to his own pleasure.

It follows:

[Col. 0408B] “Everyone who is found shall be killed, and everyone who comes upon them shall fall by the sword.” Come, my brothers: not only will the unlearned crowd become entangled in those errors, but even many to whom the care of governing churches has been entrusted will join hands with that most impious one. And, as though you were asking by whom these things would be done, the Lord adds in Isaiah: “Behold, I will raise up against them the Medes, who do not seek silver nor desire gold; but they will kill children with arrows, will not pity nursing wombs, and their eye will not spare children.”

By the Medes I think hostile spirits, or the heralds of Antichrist, are designated. It is clear that deceiving powers do not seek this world’s riches, nor desire heaps of precious metals, since they keep watch only to deceive and kill souls. The contempt for gold and silver may also signify the hypocrisy of Antichrist’s disciples. Skilled at every sort of pretense and concealment, they will count gold as mud and silver as a most worthless straw, applying themselves solely to killing children with arrows.

For they possess the arrows of dialectical words and the subtleties of arguments, by which they turn every child—that is, the simple, who lack “the sharp arrows of the mighty with desolating coals” (Ps. 119)—away from the right faith. “And they will not pity nursing infants,” he says. The nursing infants are believers born in the womb of Mother Church, who still need milk rather than solid food. Neither false teachers nor demons pity their tenderness; rather, drawing them away from the milk of maternal charity, they give them the poison of errors to drink and kill them [Col. 0408D].

Certainly, their being said to be raised up by the Lord is proved to be the just permission of God, according to His most rigorous judgment, as it is written: “I will give them kings in my fury” (Hos. 13). Thus the Medes aptly take their name from a certain Medai, which is interpreted “from the mighty,” or “strong,” or “measure,” because by the mighty or strong God, in righteous judgment, the utterly wicked are appointed against powers; so that, as He repays good persons through good angels according to good works, He may also repay evil persons through evil agents according to their works.

Accordingly, a fixed measure is prescribed for the impious, which they are not permitted to exceed, whether in testing the good or punishing the evil [Col. 0409A]. Or the Medes are interpreted “measure” because the measure of punishment is extended according to the measure of guilt.

Certainly, the interpretation of all these statements concerning the raising up of the Medes may be taken in a favorable sense. Since I may not rightly deprive your eagerness of this, the very words of the prophet must be revisited and briefly explained. But this will more fittingly be reserved for the beginning of another sermon, so that meanwhile the things already said may be impressed more firmly upon your minds by diligent meditation, and you may be prepared, through an interval of silence, to fear the divine judgments, through our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.

## SERMON XIII. On the same chapter, explained in a moral sense.

Our Lord and Savior, ascending into heaven and bringing the mode of his bodily presence to an end, promised us a spiritual presence—not a temporal one, but an eternal one—saying: “Behold, I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28). Let no one therefore suppose that, in the time of Antichrist, the Lord will withdraw his presence from his own, to whom at that time he will grant such great strength that they will not only despise every contrivance of his cunning and mock his torments, but will even go boldly forth to meet the beast, armed with faith; and many whom he has led astray by terrors and enticements they will draw back from all wickedness and restore to Catholic truth.

He therefore says: “Behold, I shall stir up the Medes against them,” and so forth. The Medes may be called the perfect teachers of that time: made mighty by mighty Christ, strong by the Strong One, they will not cease to distribute to their fellow servants—labouring under a temptation hitherto unknown—the measure of wheat, that is, spiritual teaching. Raised up by the Lord against the Babylonians, that is, pseudo-Christians and false prophets, they will despise every abundance of temporal goods offered to them, represented by the price of gold or silver. Their chief care and concern will be to heal the wounds of souls and to prepare for the Lord a perfect people.

Come, brothers: that we may return to ourselves, three things must be observed in every good work: the virtue of discernment, purity of intention, and the foundation of humility. Discernment concerns the manner of action; intention, its cause; humility, its fruit. “If you offer rightly,” says the Lord, “but do not divide rightly, you have sinned” (Gen. 4, according to the Septuagint). He offers rightly who does good, but does not divide rightly if he exceeds measure in doing it. Yet if you are already doing good, and doing it well, examine for what cause, with what intention, toward what end.

But if a right and well-measured work is preceded by right intention, beware lest that twisting serpent raise its head: I mean pride, which must be guarded against everywhere and in everything, but especially in good works. For what profit is there if the ground has been excellently cultivated, the seed wisely sown, watered with suitable rains, the stalk has grown high, a fruitful ear has appeared, and, ripening in the fitting tempering of the sun, has already begun to invite the eager reaper—and then suddenly a storm, as though snatching everything from his hands, overwhelms it? So indeed, if you labour, fast, keep vigil, and devote yourself to works of mercy, pride alone nullifies the fruit of them all; self-exaltation alone consumes it.

Therefore nothing is more to be feared than that, because of pride, we should be forsaken by the Lord, and that there should come upon us the day of the Lord, cruel and full of indignation, wrath, and fury. Let each understand as he wishes; I judge that nothing crueller can happen to anyone than that, abandoned by the Lord, he should be left according to the desires of his own heart and go in his own devices (Ps. 80). This cruelty surely proceeds from God’s indignation, which awakens especially against those who glory in themselves because of good works, hating and detesting ingratitude above other vices.

O detestable pride, mother of ingratitude, moth of virtues, parent of vices! You provoke the Judge’s cruelty against wretched mortals; you stir up indignation, sharpen wrath, kindle fury. Therefore that day on which, in recompense for pride, a person is abandoned by God is indeed a cruel day, full of indignation and fury: “To make the earth a desolation,” he says. For when God forsakes the proud heart, it will surely be reduced to desolation, like rejected ground near to a curse—though it had previously seemed good and fertile ground—bringing forth the thorns and briars of sins and lying open only to the beasts of vices. “And to crush sinners out of it.”

Let your charity consider this, dearest brothers. When true humility reigns in our breast, we are always stirred to remember our sins and are always prompted to examine, even with precision, the good things we do. But when pride devours all that belongs to humility, the thoughts by which we used to be pierced through remembrance of our offences are driven out of the secret place of our heart. This is for sinners to be crushed out of the earth: that the remembrance of debts is obliterated when self-exaltation enters in.

Understand by the moon faith; by the sun, charity; by the stars, the other virtues. If all these are wrapped in the darkness of pride, they will produce no light, no grace, nothing pleasing to God, nothing profitable; rather, they will overwhelm the whole substance of the soul with the horror of impiety and unbelief. Therefore the Lord must visit such hearts—as cities hostile to him, shut in by the wall of obstinacy and fortified with towers of self-exaltation—with the evils which they do, “taking vengeance upon all their devices” [Col. 0410D] (Ps. 98), and “visiting their iniquities with a rod, and their sins with scourges” (Ps. 88).

For the proud are called unbelieving and impious, raging not so much against man as against God himself. See what a pestilential evil this is: it began with an injury to divinity; it made a devil out of an angel; it expelled man from paradise—while the one desired equality with the divine power, the other equality in knowledge. Thus, “whoever thinks himself to be something when he is nothing deceives himself” (Gal. 6). And “whoever thinks that he knows anything does not yet understand how he ought to know” (1 Cor. 8).

Would that the Lord might visit all such persons with the rod of his correction, causing the pride of unbelievers to cease and humbling the arrogance of the mighty [Col. 0411A]. It is advantageous for the proud, as a certain saint says, to fall into some manifest sin, that they may be humbled and that what is written may come about: “You will take away their spirit, and they shall fail and return to their dust” (Ps. 103). The spirit of a person, indeed, is properly the spirit of pride. When it is removed, he returns to his dust—that is, to the knowledge of his own frailty—so that the Spirit of God may be sent to him, who rests only upon one who is humble, quiet, and trembling at his words. Thus he may be refreshed and renewed, grow into a perfect man, and become a person wholly obedient to reason. And so what is written here may be fulfilled: “A man shall be more precious than gold, and a human being than pure gold.”

For this to happen, heaven—that is, the spirit—must be shaken by fear of God; and earth—that is, the body—must be moved from its place [Col. 0411B], renouncing its worst habit and its desires. Come, my brothers: as you have often experienced, even when the spirit is disturbed it is difficult to depart from the place of bad habit; difficult to unlearn a practice; difficult to lay aside a skin clinging to bones and flesh. Yet let humility be present in it from fear, and dread from humility; and it will be “like a fleeing doe and like a sheep.”

For every soul, my brothers, that desires to depart from the place of its worst habit, two things are necessary: namely, that, like a doe before pursuers, it flee in fear and trembling the material occasions of sin; and that, as a sheep—the model of simplicity—neither grows angry at the shearer nor resists the slaughterer, so it submit simply to one correcting it and patiently endure one rebuking it. Thus, when the city of pride has been destroyed and the stones of vices from which it was built scattered, and the soul has been founded upon true humility, no one will thereafter gather them together and raise up the ruins of the city.

“Then each shall return to his own people, and each shall flee to his own land.” Although all wicked spirits are instigators of all loves and vices, one is especially called the spirit of fornication because of its more shameful attachment to the filth of lusts; another, because it delights more in the exaltation of the human mind, the spirit of pride; another, because it more frequently suggests avarice, the spirit of avarice. When these have been expelled from the heart of the penitent through God’s grace, each will return to his own people: the spirit of fornication to the unclean, and so with the rest. And each will flee to his own land, seeking whatever rest it can among those who, favouring their suggestion, set their minds on earthly things.

Unhappy is the soul which, after one demon has been driven out, makes a place in itself for any other demon and receives its proper enemy, by whose sword of wickedness it is sure to be struck. Who is so depraved that there is not found in him some virtue, or at least a resemblance of virtue? But when the ancient enemy is received into the heart, he removes even the appearance of holiness, so that “the last state of that man becomes worse than the first” (Luke 11). Even if some useful thought should arise in him, it is easily extinguished by the one who occupies the whole place, so that it cannot reach the fruit of salvation.

Therefore “their infants are dashed in pieces before their eyes”: good thoughts, indeed [Col. 0412A], but still tender, are crushed when a certain hardness of heart comes upon them. “Their houses are plundered,” because whatever good is in the conscience is despoiled by malignant spirits. Even their “wives”—that is, the affections by which, as in lawful marriage, they had been used to beget the children of good works—are stained by foul loves and filthy thoughts.

Good Jesus, when will you look upon me, to restore my soul from this malice and my only one from these lions? Would that, Lord, you might stir up the Medes against us—that is, good angels—that they may “take hold of weapons and shield” (Ps. 34), strong from the Strong One and mighty from the Mighty One; that they may dispose all these temptations for us in measure (Wis. 11), not allowing us to be tempted above what we can bear (1 Cor. 10), but with the temptation may make a way out, so that we may endure it (1 Cor. 10).

But know this, brothers: these Medes despise those who are puffed up by worldly wisdom, and look down upon those who glory in vain eloquence. For they do not seek silver or desire gold. Rather, they gladly visit and willingly stand by them, and willingly set themselves against those who fight against them—those “who slay little children with arrows, have no pity on nursing wombs, and whose eye does not spare children.” But let us reserve this for tomorrow. May the Lord Jesus be with us, so that, searching the Scriptures, we may find in them him who was likened through the prophets and proclaimed by the voices of the apostles; who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XIV. On the words written: “And Babylon said” (Isa. 13), etc.

We said, when at the beginning we treated of “burdens,” that the burden of Babylon or of the Philistines can be understood in two ways: both according to their being oppressed and according to their oppressing. Having therefore described the burden of Babylon according to the manner in which, in the time of Antichrist, the city of the devil will oppress the city of God—that is, the Church—the prophet turns his discourse to Babylon’s own destruction.

“And Babylon,” he says, “that glorious kingdom, renowned for the pride of the Chaldeans, shall be as when the Lord overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah.” We have often already said that Babylon signifies the world; but in this passage it signifies that world which is always known to be unclean: the world which lies in the evil one; the world for which he who conquers the world does not pray; the world from which are chosen those who conquer the world (1 John 5). “I do not pray for the world,” he says, “but for those whom you have given me out of the world” (John 17).

O unclean world, why are you proud? Now you are indeed glorious in kingdoms; now you are renowned in the pride of demons or of most wicked rulers. For “Chaldeans” are interpreted as, so to speak, demons. Come, brothers: how glorious Babylon—that city of confusion, that city of the reprobate—will seem to itself when, in the time of Antichrist, power to rage throughout all the kingdoms of the earth is granted to it [Col. 0413A]! And how renowned in the pride and loftiness of earthly rulers who favour it, who, like demons, will seek not so much the destruction of bodies as the ruin of souls.

But why do you glory, O Babylon? Hear, I ask, the prophet: “That glorious Babylon in kingdoms, renowned for the pride of the Chaldeans, shall be as when the Lord overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah.” Of that region of Sodom and Gomorrah it was said that it was like the paradise of the Lord before it was overthrown by the Lord. They were so overthrown that no trace of their former beauty remains in them. Instead, even now a certain dreadful image of death, through sulphur and bitumen of intolerable stench, presents an image of the punishments of hell; fruits full of smoke and a lake receiving nothing living bear witness to the detestable horror of Sodomite crime [Col. 0413B]. There all things are against nature, where it is first read that the law of nature collapsed.

Rightly did that foul and detestable sin against nature leave foul and horrible traces, so that people may perceive to what punishments in hell those are subjected whom smoke blinds, stench corrupts, and the filth of uncleanness, like bitumen, binds in eternal chains; whom devouring flame consumes without consuming. This is the end of your delights, O Babylon, you who scatter the sweetness of your poison among miserable mortals in matters from which the eye turns away in horror, the mind in shame, and speech in obscenity.

Every creature preserves the natural order of its own nature, the union of different sexes producing offspring for each kind; man alone, in contempt of God, in insult to himself, and in injury to all things, exposes his own nature to such perversity that he does not shrink from perverting everything established by God, approved by reason, and confirmed by use. Woe to you, city of confusion, which today corrupt so many with the contagion of this crime that a Sodomite and Gomorrhean overthrow is justly prepared for you by the just Requiter. You shall be seen like them in punishment because you made yourself like them in guilt.

You therefore too shall be overthrown like Sodom and Gomorrah, so that there may remain to you no remembrance of your glory, riches, power, and unclean pleasures—except for punishment. Instead of sweet fragrance you shall have stench; worms instead of adornment; fire instead of lust; eternal punishment instead of brief pleasure [Col. 0413D].

“It shall not be inhabited unto the end, nor founded from generation to generation.” Let heretics be silent who falsely claim that Babylon will be visited in hell after many ages, since eternal destruction is prophesied for it. Prophetic authority proves that it can neither thereafter be inhabited nor afterward founded. “The Arab shall not pitch his tents there, nor shall shepherds rest there.”

“I will sing to you, O Lord, of mercy and judgment” (Ps. 100). Now is certainly the time for mercy; the time for judgment will follow. Now is the time for turning to the Lord; the time for recompense will follow. The Arab pitches his tents in Babylon; “Arab” is interpreted “western” or “of the evening,” and signifies Christ, who hires us in the morning and rewards us in the evening (Matt. 20). For he does not first—that is, in the morning—set forth good wine, and then at evening, when people have become drunk, that which is worse (John 2). Rather, he always gives first in the morning what is harsh, reserving what is sweet and pleasant for the evening.

“In this world,” he says, “you shall have tribulation” (John 16); and, “The world shall rejoice, but you shall be sorrowful” (ibid.). This is morning—that is, first. What follows? “Your sorrow shall be turned into joy” (ibid.). When? Certainly in the evening. Therefore, “Woe to you, O land whose rulers eat in the morning” (Eccl. 10), because through the temporal delights which they now misuse they lose those delights which will be rendered in the evening, that is, at the end of this temporal day.

He is called western because he looks not so much to a person’s rising as to his setting, attending always not to the beginning of the work but to its end [Col. 0414B]. Here the Arab has his tents: that is, the saints who are pilgrims in this world and, like a tent, are moved here and there by the Spirit of God. They have no enduring city in this Babylon, where they are now placed as tents, but seek the future city that is in heaven (Heb. 13). They are placed there in order to storm Babylon and cry with the prophet: “Flee from the midst of Babylon, and let each save his own soul” (Jer. 51). There too shepherds now rest, glorying in the faith and good works of converts.

Therefore now is the time to flee from the midst of Babylon; now the time to migrate to heavenly tents; now also the time to submit to the teaching and laws of shepherds. But when the city has been overthrown in the final overthrow of wrath and the saints transferred to heavenly kingdoms, “the Arab shall not pitch his tents there, nor shall shepherds rest there,” because medicine is applied in vain where no remedy can be hoped for.

“But beasts shall rest there, and their houses shall be filled with dragons,” and so forth. If we wish to refer these words to Babylon’s final destruction, when it will be cast into the lake of sulphur with the false prophets, as is written in the Apocalypse (Rev. 19), the literal force must be applied to show how, in Babylon already condemned, beasts—whether vices or malignant spirits—can rest, unless perhaps demons are said to rest in the damned because, when they have ceased from tempting either good or evil persons, they will rest in the punishments of those whom they have now enticed to consent to their will [Col. 0414D].

But if each person’s house is his own conscience, then its house will be filled with dragons when the vices which now seem pleasant and sweet in human conscience will bear the appearance of a dragon, whose face they will dread and whose flame they will not endure. These beasts are said to have a terrible aspect and such fiery natures that they seem to emit flames from themselves. Thus the vices and sins which now delight will appear horrible to the condemned and will supply the fuel of eternal fire.

Moreover, each individual crime in which people are here delightfully entangled will torture the conscience of the wretched with particular recollection. Thus ostriches are said to dwell there, shaggy creatures to dance there, owls to answer one another there, and Sirens to be in shrines of pleasure [Col. 0415A]. By ostriches, therefore, understand the pretence of hypocrites; by shaggy creatures, incentives to lust; by owls, the whispering of detractors or murmurers; by Sirens, the deceits of flatterers.

For the ostrich has feathers, yet is not raised from the ground by them: on the one hand the body’s weight, on the other the scantiness of its feathers, afford the appearance of flight but deny its actuality. The nature of this bird therefore expresses the vice of the pretender, who outwardly displays signs of virtues while inwardly he is weighed down by vices; who speaks great things but does little, sounds forth heavenly matters but thinks earthly ones; who shines in knowledge and overflows in intention, raises his wings on high as though about to fly to the stars, yet his mind, bound by its desires, presses his whole body down to the depths.

But the shaggy creature, called an *incubus*, is an impudent and hairy animal, ever burning for intercourse. It signifies the incentives of lust by which Esau, bristling with the hairs of vices, was stirred after the enticements of gluttony—for which he sold his birthright (Gen. 25)—and defiled himself by unlawful union with foreign women. Offending alike the eyes of his father and mother, he lost the blessing due to the firstborn.

Let your charity consider this. First, devoted to hunting, he preferred outward things to inward, vain matters to serious ones, restlessness to peace. Then, not restraining gluttony, he lost his birthright. Afterwards, to the offence of both parents, he lost chastity. Finally, he deserved to be excluded from his father’s blessing. Would that we did not know that such things are still done by many today: scorning the spiritual sweetness felt only within, and curiously pursuing external consolations and wandering excursions, they first subject themselves to the slavery of the belly; for its delights they deprive themselves of the glory of their birthright—that is, of the merits of renunciation—and thus, burned by the fire of lust, do not attain the Father’s blessing, awaited in the fruit of virtues [Col. 0415C].

Owls are said to be of the size of ravens, with extended necks and speckled markings; with their beaks plunged in marshes, they make a sound of dreadful voice or screeching. I ask: what is more spotted than detractors? Detractors have this characteristic: they always mix a few small praises with the condemnations by which they strive to defame others, and so render every speech of their detraction mottled with contrary judgments.

Flatterers are aptly compared with Sirens: with a pleasing but deadly sound they delight the listener’s ear; unless one passes by with one’s ear prudently closed, they will lead one onto the rocks of pride or into the Charybdis of presumption. For “the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and the wicked person is blessed” (Ps. 10). Unhappy is the person who trusts such people and, abandoning the testimony of his own conscience, exposes himself to be deceived by another’s judgment. Wretched are those to whom the Lord reproaches through the prophet, saying: “The prophets prophesied falsehood, the priests clapped their hands, and my people loved such things” (Jer. 5).

It follows: “The time for it is near to come, and its days shall not be prolonged” (Isa. 14) [Col. 0416A]. Everything that seems long to us is exceedingly brief to God, because a thousand years before his eyes are like yesterday when it has passed (Ps. 87). And certainly everything that passes is brief; brief is all that is someday enclosed by an end. The Holy Spirit therefore wishes us to fix our eyes upon eternity and not judge fleeting time to be of any length.

“The time for it is near to come,” he says. The time for what? Certainly for that of which he had said before: “Behold, the day of the Lord comes, cruel,” and so forth. The day of the Lord, therefore, is the Lord’s time, in which the good will be tested, the false exposed, the perfect crowned, and the reprobate punished. When will this be? What is the cause of this delay? It is delayed, indeed, until the fullness of the Gentiles enters in, and so all Israel may be saved (Rom. 11).

Thus, before these things begin to take place, “the Lord will have mercy and will again choose from Israel.” Come, brothers: that grave sentence still stands over Jacob which this same prophet says, in the earlier part of his book, was spoken by the Lord himself: “Blind the heart of this people, make their ears heavy, and close their eyes, lest perhaps they see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their heart, and turn, and I heal them” (Isa. 6).

A day will come when the veil shall be removed from them, so that they too, with unveiled face, may behold the glory of my Lord Jesus Christ; when it has been announced to Jacob: “Joseph your son lives and rules over all the land of Egypt” (Gen. 45) [Col. 0416C]. Then, awakening as it were from the heavy sleep of unbelief, he will say: “I will go and see him before I die” (ibid.). For the Lord will have mercy on Jacob, to whom he now seems hostile in the faith of the Gentiles, calling “not my people,” “my people”; “not beloved,” “beloved”; and “not having obtained mercy,” “having obtained mercy” (Rom. 9).

For the Lord will have mercy on Jacob and will again choose from Israel. “Again,” he says, “he will choose from Israel.” First he chose apostles, disciples, and a multitude of believers from Israel, that the primitive Church might be founded; at the end of the age he will choose more, by whom the final times of the age may be adorned. By the name of election we now understand all Jews whom that time will assist toward salvation. If you seek a distinction between Jacob and Israel, and between mercy and election, understand Jacob to mean the weaker, upon whom he has mercy lest they perish; Israel, the more perfect, from whom he chooses persons to teach and govern others.

It follows:

“And he shall make them rest upon their own ground.” What is this ground? Is it that promised land which was once theirs, from which they were uprooted and scattered throughout the earth? But we also, beloved, when Babylon has been destroyed in us, when we have become Jacob—Babylon, I say, being love of the world, where indeed are the spiritual beasts of which the Prophet says: “Do not hand over to beasts the souls confessing you” (Ps. 73); where dragons, that is, unclean spirits, have their place; where pretence reigns, lust disturbs, detraction tears apart, and flattery dissolves—when all these things belonging to worldly love have been destroyed, the Lord will have mercy on us.

For Jacob is interpreted “wrestler.” What is this wrestling? “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Gal. 5). What wrestling? “Our wrestling is not against flesh and blood, but against the rulers of the world” (Eph. 6). What wrestling? “The kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matt. 11). What wrestling? “Do not wonder if the world hates you, because it hated me first” (John 15).

Therefore we wrestle with the flesh, wrestle with the demon, wrestle with the world, and wrestle with God. The first belongs to beginners; the second, to those making progress; the third, to those who are tested; the fourth, to those being perfected. The first is laborious, the second dangerous, the third wearisome, the fourth fruitful. I ask: what is as laborious as having conflict within oneself and against oneself? Within is a fire which we must both nourish and beware of. For if it is not nourished, nature is overwhelmed; if it is not guarded against, chastity is endangered. Hence fear, grief, tears: they do not know the limits of necessity, dread the business of pleasure, do not dare to deny nature its due, yet wish to impose the bridle of sobriety upon gluttony. When they think they are providing for necessity, they are furnishing fuel to pleasure; and when they withdraw what they suppose necessary, they sustain loss in other goods which they love no less.

But the struggle against spiritual wickedness is exceedingly dangerous, since they have a thousand arts for harming, having practised such work for thousands of years. Among all the snares of demons, that is nevertheless the more dangerous by which they transform themselves into angels of light, covering vices with a likeness of virtues and administering poison to the wretched in a golden cup [Col. 0417C]. Then the wrestling is not against flesh and blood, when, after the flesh has been overcome, the wicked cunning of demons deceives us, persuading us to vices through virtues, or to pride on account of virtues.

Moreover, this world wrestles against us with two arms: prosperity and adversity. On the side of prosperity are abundance of temporal possessions; peace in abundance; security in peace. Likewise, the praises of men, the friendship of the rich, the goodwill and trust of companions, and the favour and grace of subjects. Some also think bodily health and soundness of limbs should be added among prosperities. Come, brothers: who can easily say how heavily the world presses us with this arm, how it wrestles against us, and how often it casts down the wretched and unwary? How rare is the person who, amid prosperity, does not relax his mind at least a little from its accustomed seriousness; who is not somewhat more lax in abundance, somewhat more cheerful in human praise, somewhat happier in the goodwill of rulers, more dissipated in the favour of friends, more insolent in the favour of subjects, and harsher in bodily strength! Whoever therefore wishes to be spiritual Jacob should know that he must exercise himself in continual wrestling against these things amid prosperity.

But the other arm of the world, which we called adversity, is more troublesome but less dangerous [Col. 0418A]. It includes lack of possessions, detractions, reproaches, persecution by the rich, hatred of rulers, betrayal by friends, rebellion of subjects, and bodily sickness. What is our struggle, brothers, against all these things? Who is there who, in adversities, is perhaps not found more faint-hearted; who is not moved by reproaches or saddened by detractions; who is not more angry in persecutions and more impatient against a treacherous friend? Blessed is the soul found superior in all things: temperate in prosperity and steadfast in adversity. Blessed also is the one who, although unable to conquer these things, nevertheless strives excellently in wrestling not to be conquered by them.

For the Lord will have mercy on Jacob—that is, the wrestler—so that, if he has not gained complete victory in this life, he may deserve, when the contest is ended, to receive an everlasting crown in heaven. Certainly, one who has been victorious in these struggles should begin to wrestle with God, passing from Syrian Mesopotamia to Mount Bethel (Gen. 28), from lower things to higher, from human things to divine, from bodily things to spiritual.

Stretch upward, therefore, O soul, your two arms—prayer and meditation. Carry them into the very secret places of heaven, where Christ sits at God’s right hand (Col. 3). Be urgent in season and out of season (2 Tim. 4), that you may behold his face; that he may descend to you, or draw you to himself; that you may taste how sweet he is and experience how gentle and merciful he is (Ps. 24). Thus, if in your prayer or meditation the fire of heavenly desires has blazed up; if incentives of love flame; if, burning and panting, you are moved by certain heavenly affections; if now you feel the one whom you love to be present as though grasped, now grieve and sigh because he has slipped from your hands and is absent—this is spiritual wrestling, giving you the name Israel, that you may be deemed worthy not only of mercy but also of election.

For the Lord will have mercy on Jacob and will again choose from Israel: because the one who struggles in his groaning against vices and washes his bed with tears is worthy to receive mercy; but the one who, having overcome vices, shines in the perfection of virtues will be transferred, like grain cleansed and chosen, into the heavenly granaries. “And he shall make them rest upon their own ground” [Col. 0418D].

A great blessedness is promised. Our ground is our flesh. Many are beneath it, many are in it, but few are above it. Beneath it are those ruled by the flesh’s desire. In it are those always doing and thinking the things of the flesh. Above it are those who discipline it with labours, vigils, and fasts, lest it itself become insolent. The first is carnal, the second natural, the third spiritual.

Paul forbids us the dominion of the flesh when he says: “Let not sin reign in your mortal body, that you obey its desires” (Rom. 6). What is it to obey the desires of the flesh except to be beneath the flesh? He also wishes us not to be in the flesh, when he says: “Make no provision for the flesh in its desires” (Rom. 13). Hear too the person above the flesh, courageously pressing down its desires: “I chastise my body and reduce it to slavery” (1 Cor. 9).

Yet so long as there is something against which one fights, there is labour, not rest. But if, with vices extinguished and passions overcome, one is so above the flesh that there is no longer anything in it to press one down, then one will indeed rest upon one’s own ground. This is the blessedness promised to the meek, as the Lord says: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth” (Matt. 5).

But because, having laboured long in speaking, we have reached that place of Scripture in which rest is commended, it is fitting that we rest a little in the harbour of silence, repairing together both mind and voice. Thus we may be found more fit to search out the mysteries of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XV. On the passage written: “The stranger shall be separated,” as far as “Worms shall be your covering” (Isa. 14).

[Col. 0419B]

Saint Isaiah, illuminated by the Holy Spirit, describes the conversion of the Jews, which we believe will occur in the last days:

“The Lord,” he says, “will have mercy on Jacob and will choose Israel, and will make them rest upon their own soil.” And he added: “The stranger will be joined to them and will cling to the house of Jacob.” By “the stranger” understand the people of the nations, who, seeing the calling of the Jews and the oracles of the prophets fulfilled, will hasten to join them in embracing the same faith. Or certainly the faithful people itself, whom the Jews had hitherto regarded with horror as strangers, will be joined to them in love, [Col. 0419C] when those two things which had been divided in the hand of the prophet Ezekiel shall become one (Ezek. 37); and, according to another prophet, Judah and Israel shall make for themselves one head and shall ascend from the earth (Hos. 1).

Thus the people of the nations will cling to the people of the Jews—that is, to the house of Jacob—so that they may have one God, one faith, one baptism (Eph. 4). “And peoples will take hold of them”: that is, Christians will take hold of the Jews in charity, in concern, in affection. “And they will bring them into their place,” that is, into the Church; for the place of Christians is the Church, prefigured by that place of which the Lord said to Moses: “Remove the sandal from your feet, for the place where you stand is holy ground” (Exod. [Col. 0419D] 3).

Of this land the prophet continued: “And the house of Israel shall possess them upon the land of the Lord as male and female servants.” For when the Jews have been received into the Church—which is indeed the Lord’s land—there will be such rejoicing among the peoples and such remarkable devotion toward them that those whom they now have as persecutors and masters they will then have, in charity, as male and female servants, according to the Apostle’s saying: “Through charity serve one another”; and, “They shall take captive those who had taken them captive” (Gal. 5).

As it seems to me, the prophetic utterance describes that mutual love by which Jews and nations will take one another captive and, as it were, embrace one another with the arms of love.
