Of this captivity Paul says: “Make room for us”; or, “They shall take captive those who had taken them captive” (2 Cor. 7). For just as believers from among the nations draw the Israelite people [Col. 0420A] into the bosom of the Church by the net of holy preaching, so, when they themselves have been converted to the Lord, they will subject many from among the nations to Christian laws by word and example alike. Hence it follows:

“And they shall subject their oppressors.” The oppressors of the Jews are unclean spirits, who compel those entangled in various errors toward curses and vices of many kinds. Armed with the sign of the cross, they will assuredly subject these spirits at the end of the age, when power has been given them to tread upon serpents and scorpions and all the power of the enemy (Luke 10).

“And it shall be, in that day, when God has given you rest from your labor, from your confusion, and from your hard servitude in which you formerly served, you shall take up this parable against the king of Babylon and say: ‘How has the oppressor ceased?’” and so forth.

The prophet has described the condition of the Church down to the times of Antichrist; he has described also the persecution of Antichrist itself, the overthrow of spiritual Babylon, and the conversion of the Jews. Now his mystical utterance turns to the overthrow of Antichrist himself—or certainly of the devil in Antichrist or together with Antichrist—and to the rest and rejoicing of the saints. Having foretold hardships concerning them as though in the third person, he addresses them directly in announcing prosperity: “And it shall be, when God has given you rest.” By this rest may be understood that peace which the Church may perhaps enjoy, Antichrist having been destroyed, until the day of judgment; or certainly that final rest in which, the last enemy death having been destroyed, there will be no one to attack or terrify.

Three kinds of misery are noted here, to which [Col. 0420C] the human race will be subjected and from which it will not easily be delivered before that time: labor, confusion, and servitude. Labor properly belongs to the body, confusion to the mind, and servitude to both. For in the time of Antichrist the Church will suffer labor, subdued by various torments; it will be put to shame by exposure to insults; it will be oppressed by servitude, afflicted with tributes. But when, he says, you have rested from all these things after that son of perdition has been destroyed, “you shall take up this parable against the king of Babylon and say: ‘How has the oppressor ceased? Has the tribute rested?’”

The elect will surely marvel that this importunate oppressor has perished so suddenly and has been erased from the earth—he who, both personally and through his agents, harassed the world, devastating everything with exactions and torments and drawing all things into agreement with his crime.

“The Lord has broken the staff of the wicked, the rod of rulers, striking the peoples in indignation with an incurable wound.” This wound is eternal death, by which many will be struck when Antichrist strikes—that is, persecutes—them. This wound is indeed incurable, because in hell there is no redemption: there is neither a place for repentance, by which sins may be cleansed, nor the remedy of confession, by which they may be healed, nor acceptable satisfaction, by which they may be restored.

“Subduing the nations in fury,” he says, “and persecuting cruelly. The whole earth has rested and become still; it rejoiced and exulted.” While Antichrist reigns, there is labor everywhere, lamentation everywhere, pain everywhere. When he has been cast down by divine power, all things will seem to rest, all things to be silent, all things to rejoice, because “there shall no longer be mourning, nor crying, nor any pain, because the former things have passed away” (Rev. 21). [Col. 0421A]

“The fir trees also rejoiced over you, and the cedars of Lebanon.” By fir trees understand those exalted in wisdom; by cedars, those eminent in power. Sacred history relates that these woods were employed by Solomon, most wise of men, for the building and adornment of the Temple (3 Kings 5). And as that Temple prefigured the Church, so by firs and cedars—which surpass other trees both in height and in fragrance—understand those eminent persons in the Church who become known to many by the fragrance of their good reputation. At that time they will be held to be the more exalted insofar as they have been found stronger in the time of persecution.

The prophet adds their voice as they rejoice and glory: “Since you fell asleep, no one has come up to cut us down.” This sleep signifies death. For once Antichrist is dead, there will be no one to cut down cedars or fir trees. “No one has come up.” Ascending expresses pride, power, or cunning, so that you may understand that after him none will rise in such pride, be exalted in such power, or be so shrewd in cunning as to be able, in the paradise of God—that is, the Church—to cut down from the foundation of faith any persons who are perfect like cedars and firs: whether raging through pride, oppressing through power, or deceiving through cunning. Therefore it is rightly said: “Since you fell asleep, no one has come up to cut us down.”

It follows:

“Hell beneath was troubled at your coming; it stirred up giants for you. All the princes of the earth rose [Col. 0421C] from their thrones, all the princes of the nations.” By the princes of the earth or the nations I understand opposing powers: each of these will then sit, as princes upon thrones, in persons who savor earthly things or in nations deceived by Antichrist. The mightiest of them all, as king of the rest, will claim for himself the body and soul of Antichrist as a throne surpassing all others.

When these princes see that the enterprise of their king, which he was carrying out through that instrument of his, has been rendered void by Christ’s power, terrified, they will be driven from their thrones—that is, from those over whom they presided—and, wondering at his ruin, will answer as it were and say: “You too have been wounded as we have; you have become like us. Your pride has been dragged down to hell.” The meaning is: the higher you raised yourself, the more deeply you fell.

“Your corpse has fallen.” The corpse of the prince of darkness may fittingly be understood as Antichrist himself, whom he will animate before all others by his malice and to whose utterly evil will he will furnish, as it were, the life-giving breath of effective wickedness. His corpse will fall when the Lord Jesus kills him by the breath of His mouth and destroys him by the brightness of His coming (2 Thess. 2).

“Beneath you moth and decay shall be spread, and worms shall be your covering.” The eternal punishment which will occupy the whole substance either of the devil or of Antichrist is described plainly enough. From below the moth will consume, from above the worms will gnaw, and decay within will consume. The moth stands for sensual pleasure, worms for cruelty, [Col. 0422A] decay for lust. Or: moth for unlawful speech, decay for unlawful thought, worms for unlawful action. Or again: the moth, which consumes secretly and almost imperceptibly, is the devil’s suggestion; decay, which produces horror and stench, is unclean delight; worms, which openly corrupt, are consent. From all these, moreover, arises the material of punishments, whether inwardly in the conscience or outwardly in punishment.

We have run briefly through this exposition, our minds hurrying, of course, to other matters. Remember, beloved, that it is written of the Lord Jesus, when He was about to withdraw His presence from His disciples: “While eating with them, He commanded them not to depart from Jerusalem” (Acts 1). Jerusalem signifies “peace.” Therefore we commend peace to you; we command peace to you. May Christ Himself, [Col. 0422B] who is our peace, making both one (Eph. 2), preserve you in the unity of the Spirit and in the bond of peace (Eph. 4). I commend you to His protection and consolation beneath the wings of the Holy Spirit, that He may restore you to me and me to you in peace and safety. May He grant this, who lives and reigns as God through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XVI. On the same chapter, expounded morally

Behold, I am here, my most beloved children, my joy and my crown in the Lord. This day is for me a day of exultation and gladness, for I have longed to see it, and the Lord has heard the desire of the poor man! (Ps. 10). O love, how sweetly you burn those who are absent! How delightfully [Col. 0422C] you nourish those who are present! Yet you do not satisfy the hungry until you establish Jerusalem in peace and satisfy her with the fat of wheat (Ps. 147).

This is the peace whose firstfruits refresh you meanwhile: “Taste and see how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity” (Ps. 132). This is the peace which, by a certain foretaste of charity, nourishes you on the way, until you are satisfied by its fullness in the homeland. Come then, sweetest brothers: all that I live, all that I know, I offer to your advancement; I devote it to your benefit. Make use of me as you wish, and spare not my labor wherever it can serve your progress.

Let us return, then, if it pleases you—or rather, because it does please you—to the work we interrupted; and let us search out the heavenly treasures which holy Isaiah stored under the covering of parables, as the Holy Spirit pours upon us the light of truth.

For, describing the parable which the people delivered from the tyranny of the king of Babylon will take up, he says: “And it shall be in that day, when God has given you rest from your labor, from your confusion, and from your hard servitude in which you formerly served: you shall take up this parable against the king of Babylon.” Let us therefore understand the parable as a parable, not supposing that it was spoken against Nebuchadnezzar, prince of that earthly Babylon, but rather against him who is from the north, the prince of confusion.

But because in that last sermon which we delivered to you on these matters we passed over them in an allegorical interpretation, let us now pursue the same things morally. Therefore, if any one of us, once placed in the confusion of vices and oppressed by the yoke of iniquity, now rejoices that he rests from [Col. 0423A] labor, has no shame concerning what has passed, and has cast off the yoke of most evil servitude, let him take up this parable against the king of Babylon.

Labor is in vices; rest in virtue; confusion in lust; security in chastity; servitude in covetousness; freedom in charity. There is labor in vices, labor for vices, and labor against vices. Labor in vices occurs when the ancient enemy imposes many toils in order that evil desires may be fulfilled. Labor for vices occurs when a person is afflicted unwillingly for the evils he has committed, or willingly wears himself down by the labor of penance. Labor against vices occurs when one converted to God is wearied by various temptations.

There is likewise confusion in vices, confusion for vices, and confusion against vices. Confusion in vices occurs when a man, scattered by utterly evil passions, is not governed by reason but is agitated in disorder by the tumult of vices. Confusion for vices occurs when someone, detected and convicted of a crime, is put to shame; or when, repenting and confessing what he has committed, he is cleansed by salutary shame. But confusion against vices occurs when a man converted to God resists a temptation he suffers by recalling the shame he has experienced.

The Lord cries in the Gospel: “Come to me, you who labor and are burdened” (Matt. 11). Elsewhere you have it written of certain people: “They labored in order to act wickedly” (Jer. 9). What labor do robbers and thieves undergo, whether to overpower a traveler by violence or to plunder a householder after breaking into his house? What labor do adulterers or fornicators undergo to obtain embraces they wickedly desire? Yet the miser who longs for another’s fields or treasures also has no small labor—if not of body, at least of heart. Confusion follows this labor, because, just as beauty consists in order among virtues, so tumult and confusion belong to sins.

“For everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin” (John 8). O hard servitude! It often compels even a resisting mind into vices, when the force of evil habit drives it toward a vice it already detests, so that, in a strange manner, it wills sin even as it weeps. Once a person has been freed from all these things, he will take up this parable against the king of Babylon and say: “How has the oppressor ceased? Has the tribute rested?”

Hear our Lord Jesus saying to Peter in the Gospel: “From whom do the kings of the nations receive tribute—from their own sons or from strangers?” And Peter: “From strangers.” To him the Lord says: “Therefore the sons are free” (Matt. 17). There are, then, three collectors demanding tribute: Caesar, the devil, and God. Caesar, as an importunate collector, extorts the image impressed upon the coin, which he has imposed upon man as a sign of his dominion. The devil, a harsh and cruel collector, demands payment in daily shamefulness: the likeness of himself which he has engraved upon the consenting soul through the disposition of vices and with the stylus of vicious habit. God reasonably requires from His creature the image of Himself which He impressed upon the nature of the rational soul.

For man was created in the image and likeness of God (Gen. 1); as long as he had not subjected himself to another’s power, he was not compelled to pay what it was evident that he did not owe. [Col. 0424A] But as a certain likeness of God shines in virtues, so the likeness of the devil is recognized in vices. A person remains free from that likeness as long as he gives no consent to the tempter. Consent, indeed, in some manner sketches the likeness of the devil upon the soul itself with a light, so to speak, stroke. But when, by consent, one breaks out into action, the wretched person already impresses upon himself the devil’s full image by the desire to sin.

Thus, when the devil gains power over a person through sin and oppresses him with the yoke of evil habit, he, as an intolerable collector, exacts from him the daily tribute of sin. But just as Pharaoh, afflicting the Israelite people with mud and brick, is recorded to have had many collectors under him (Exod. 5), so that prince of darkness assigns to each of his followers an individual instigator to exact this tribute. They impose labors upon them, harass the unwary with suggestions, and compel those crushed under the harsh servitude of sin to toil at filthy works.

But, whatever soul you are whom God’s mercy has delivered from this misery, He grants you rest from your labor, your agitation, and your hard servitude in which you formerly served. You surely marvel that continence, which had seemed impossible to you, is so easy; you marvel that the yoke of ingrained habit has vanished, though innate despair had withdrawn every effort even to lay it down. Take up, then, the parable against the king of Babylon. Rejoice with trembling; cry out in astonishment: “How has the oppressor ceased? Has the tribute rested?”

The spirit of fornication had pressed daily, demanding the tribute of some shameful and unclean act; and there was no ability to repel it, no strength to resist. How, then, has the oppressor ceased? Has the tribute rested? The spirit of anger, rising within me, repeatedly compelled me to utter words of fury. At one time the spirit of gluttony stirred desire for forbidden or unlawful foods; at another, demanding from me the bitter coin of daily grumbling and detraction, it made me unmanageable toward my teachers and impatient with my companions. [Col. 0424C]

The spirit of acedia, overthrowing every condition of my tranquility and suggesting horror of solitude and hatred of quiet, compelled me to pay it disordered wanderings and vain or dangerous signs. The spirit of pride, invading the very inner seat of my heart, at one time made me impatient of subjection, at another desirous of rule; at one time compelled me, despising others, to “walk in great matters and in things too wonderful for me” (Ps. 130); at another persuaded me to prefer myself to better people and to envy the progress of all.

How, then, has the oppressor ceased? Has the tribute rested? Was it by my own strength? Was it by my own sword? Far from it! How, then? Surely “the Lord has broken the staff of the wicked, the rod of rulers.” “The Lord who destroys wars: the Lord is His name.” Glory to You, Lord Jesus, who do not permit us to be tempted beyond what we are able to bear (1 Cor. 10). You did not put a sword in the enemy’s hand, but a staff or a rod. For a sword destroys; a rod or staff afflicts.

Thus Your voice says to Satan concerning blessed Job: “Behold, all that he possesses is in your hand; only do not stretch out your hand against him” (Job 1). Then, when You had given him power over Job’s body: “Nevertheless,” You say, “preserve his soul” (Job 2). A rod was given; a staff was given; but the sword was refused. The rod was given when he was permitted to take away temporal goods. A staff was also given when he was permitted to rage against Job’s body itself. The sword was refused when he was forbidden to destroy the soul.

Therefore he strikes with the rod when he touches external things; he strikes with the staff when he afflicts the body itself; he strikes with the sword when he drives the soul from the body. By this threefold temptation the devil has long raged against the martyrs; and at the end of the age Antichrist will rage against the faithful through the devil. Against us, who stand between the two times, since the sword has been taken from him, he contends with rod and staff. Therefore, when we are struck by loss of temporal goods, it is the rod; when by illness or some other affliction of the flesh, it is the staff. The rod also strikes when he entices by pleasure; the staff, when he draws toward consent; the sword, when he compels toward action.

When we have been delivered from all these things, this utterance will apply to us: “The Lord has broken the staff of the wicked, the rod of rulers.” The wicked are demons, who, neither from love of justice nor from the desire to correct, but from malice alone, do not cease to inflict wounds upon mortals over whom they are permitted to rule by the just judgment of God—either for a time, that they may be purified, or eternally, that they may be punished. Of their malice the text fittingly adds: [Col. 0425C] “Striking the peoples in indignation with an incurable wound.” This incurable wound pertains to the reprobate who, murmuring under the stroke of staff or rod, may be afflicted but cannot be healed.

And it adds: “Subduing nations in fury and persecuting cruelly.” By many temptations the wicked spirit subjects nations to himself, persecuting them cruelly not out of love for justice but in fury—not as Christ mercifully does, who strikes in order to heal, kills in order to give life, and leads down to hell in order to bring back (Job 13).

“The whole earth has rested and become still; it rejoiced and exulted.” In the earth of our heart and in the earth of our flesh, when we are wearied by different temptations, what tumult there is, what clamor of vices, followed by the army of innumerable sins! O what happiness when the whole earth rests and is silent: when in our flesh the incitements of lust, the stings of pleasures, the thorns of unclean passions, the swelling of pride, the onset of anger, and the whisper of suspicion or indignation are at rest!

But when the clamor of vices has rested and become silent, the delight and exultation of virtues follow. “It rejoiced,” he says, “and exulted.” O what joy, what exultation, when all things in a person’s conscience are glad, all things peaceful; when Satan has been crushed beneath the feet, every stain of vices has been erased by expulsion, and the soul glories in virtues alone! Hence it follows:

“The fir trees also rejoiced, and the cedars of Lebanon.” By firs and cedars, lofty and fragrant trees, understand the virtues, whose summit touches heaven and whose fragrance of good reputation fills the world. Then conscience truly rejoices in virtues when they are lofty in their heavenly intention and fragrant in the integrity of their reputation. This is what the Apostle says: “Providing things good, not only before God but also before men” (Rom. 12).

When, therefore, the firs and cedars have rejoiced—that is, when virtues succeeding vices have filled the mind with saving gladness—they say: “Since you fell asleep, no one has come up to cut us down.” This voice is directed to the king of Babylon, namely the prince of darkness. You have fallen asleep, O Satan; you have not perished. No security, my brothers, no security. The enemy sleeps; he has not perished. One who sleeps is easily awakened. There is peace, there is rest, because while he sleeps no one comes up to cut down the virtues.

Nevertheless, brothers, this is the voice of the perfect, who no longer struggle against the flesh, which often cuts down virtues through the concupiscence native to it, but against spiritual wickednesses (Eph. 6). While these are asleep—that is, while temptations cease—the perfect rest, having in themselves no material for battle arising from themselves. Yet you must certainly know, my brothers, that this peace can be neither continuous nor perfect until the last enemy is destroyed—death, that is, the devil, author of death. Then the company of saints will taunt him not as one sleeping but as one, as it were, dying: “Where, O death,” he says, “is your victory?” (1 Cor. 15). [Col. 0426C]

Isaiah says the same thing in different words: “How,” he says, “has the oppressor ceased? Has the tribute rested? Hell beneath was troubled; at your coming it stirred up giants for you” (Isa. 14). When the devil has been overcome by the saints, hell—that is, the company of unclean spirits—comes forward in disturbance, stirring up for him giants, that is, any stronger members of his companions. Returning with them to the house from which he had been cast out, if there is an opportunity to enter again, he will make the last state of that man worse than the former (Luke 11).

This alternation of temptation and peace is carried on with us until all the princes of the earth—that is, the princes of those who pursue earthly things—and also all the princes of the nations, namely the princes of the kingdom of the Persians or Greeks, as you have in Daniel (Dan. 12), or certainly the princes of the nations, that is, of vices, are driven from their seats and mourn the death of their prince. His corpse—that is, the whole company of the reprobate—will with him be given over to eternal punishments: the moth will consume it, decay will corrupt it, worms will gnaw it.

Do not be surprised if today I have detained you longer than usual, because, avid for you after a long hunger, I could not easily be satisfied by your presence. Do not suppose that I am satisfied even now: I stop speaking because I am weary, not because I am satisfied. “I shall be satisfied when the glory of Christ appears” (Ps. 16), in whom I now embrace you delightfully and in whom I hope to be with you happily, to whom be honor and glory through the ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XVII. On what is written: “How have you fallen from heaven, Lucifer, who rose in the morning?” (Isa. 14)

[Col. 0427A]

After the sacred solemnities of the Lord’s Nativity, returning to investigate the mysteries of the prophetic vision, most beloved brothers, we do not abandon spiritual delights, but exchange them; indeed, we do not even exchange them, since we recognize in prophetic words that those things which we recall as fulfilled during these holy days were foretold.

Everywhere we are fed and given drink by the one Word of God, who for this reason “was made flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1): that He might be heard by carnal people, whom He instructs by words, confirms by miracles, draws by examples, and finally redeems by the shedding of His own blood. Therefore, just as we find foretold in the prophets His nativity, passion, [Col. 0427B] resurrection, and ascension into heaven, together with the faith of the nations and the kingdom of the holy Church—all of which we rejoice to see fulfilled—so surely no Christian should deny that the tyranny of Antichrist, the Church’s final persecution, the destruction of that lost one, the future judgment of God, and the destruction of the devil with all his members, which the same Scriptures recount as future, are to be fulfilled.

Thus, having described the persecution of Antichrist down to his death, in which the power and dominion of Satan himself are also cast down, the prophetic speech arrives at the one against whom it still inveighs under the figure of the king of Babylon, saying: “How have you fallen from heaven, Lucifer, who rose in the morning?” These words, spoken in the figure of the king of Babylon, are understood as spoken, as it were, against the devil.

According to most blessed Augustine, however, these words are spoken not so much concerning the person of the devil as concerning his members; and the mystical discourse describes not so much that first fall of the devil, of which the Lord says, “I saw Satan falling like lightning from heaven” (Luke 10), as the apostasy of his members who depart from the Church. Since Antichrist is said to be the worst of all his members, and since in his time there will be the greatest multitude of apostates, the prophecy accordingly shows here the ruin of Antichrist and his followers.

Yet because the wicked constitute one body, let us not doubt that all who have fallen from the Church without returning to it share in this ruin. In all of them the head of that body—the devil, of course—is put to shame. To him the reproachful utterance of the prophet is directed: “How have you fallen from heaven, Lucifer, who rose in the morning?”

Lucifer may be called Antichrist because of the splendor of temporal glory, the pretence of holiness, a certain singular brilliance—as is supposed—of exceptional wisdom, or the display of deceitful miracles. By all these things his rising, that is, the beginnings of his manifestation, will shine forth. His being said to rise in the morning indicates the beginning of his manifestation. Or the morning signifies the present life, which declines into old age as into evening and is extinguished when death comes upon it as night.

Thus Solomon says of those who, in the present life, despising future things, enjoy whatever pleasures they can: “Woe to the land whose princes eat in the morning” (Eccl. 10). Antichrist’s glory will therefore be temporal, not eternal; brief, not lasting; not stable, but falling away. Therefore he says: “How have you fallen from heaven, Lucifer, who rose in the morning?”

Understand “heaven” here as the Temple, of which the Apostle says, speaking of Antichrist: “He opposes and exalts himself above everything that is called God or is worshipped, so that he sits in the temple of God, showing himself as though he were God” (2 Thess. 2). These words show that he will possess power in the Church of God, which perhaps he will first enter under the appearance of ruling it, while in reality intending to attack it.

Accordingly, some not unreasonably think that he will obtain within the Church some seat bearing an exalted title or a form of royal dignity, and thus gradually, supported both by lying signs and wonders and by the favor of kings and princes, will advance to such power, glory, and reputation that he will easily persuade Jews and nations that he is Christ and falsely claim that he is the Son of God, “showing himself as though he were God.”

The words of the Apostle, “He opposes and exalts himself above everything that is called God,” are followed prophetically by holy Isaiah with the very thoughts of exaltation by which he will aspire to that eminence: “You said in your heart: ‘I will ascend into heaven,’” and so forth. This is the heaven from which Isaiah had reproachfully said that he fell: “How have you fallen from heaven, Lucifer, who rose in the morning? You have fallen to earth, you who wounded the nations.”

No one who hears the Apostle saying, “His coming is according to the power of Satan, in every deception, in lying signs and wonders, for those who are perishing” (2 Thess. 2), can doubt that Antichrist will wound the nations with a grievous wound and a cruel blow. “You have fallen,” he says, “to earth.” For, cast down by the breath of God’s mouth, he will possess hell instead of heaven; and his body too, given to the earth, will decay in corruption.

The Seventy translators rendered not “you who wounded the nations” but “you who sent to all nations,” signifying that messengers of Antichrist are to be sent to all nations and will rage everywhere against Christ’s Church.

“You said in your heart: ‘I will ascend into heaven.’” These may be understood as the words of the devil speaking in Antichrist and desiring through him to subject to himself the entire city of Christ. Therefore Antichrist, inspired by the devil’s spirit, seeing that he has received from the prince of darkness power in worldly wisdom and in signs and wonders, will seek the rule of that which is regarded as having no higher place in this world: namely, the Church.

Having received, according to the Apocalypse (Rev. 13) or Daniel (Dan. 7), from the beast—that is, from the kingdom of that time, resplendent in power everywhere through ten kings as though ten horns—he will devise wickedness upon his bed, saying: “I will ascend into heaven,” that is, “I will gain dominion in the Church; above the stars of God”—those, namely, who shine like stars through the brightness of wisdom or the splendor of religious life—“I will exalt my throne,” subjecting them to my decrees and judgments.

And he added: [Col. 0429A] “I will sit upon the mountain of the covenant, on the sides of the north.” The mountain of the covenant may be called that earthly Jerusalem, in the temple of whose city some believe Antichrist will reign. Of it the Psalmist says: “Mount Zion, the sides of the north, is the city of the great King” (Ps. 47).

All these things are better understood of Christ’s Church, which is indeed a mountain, and Zion is the mountain of the covenant; its sides the north—that is, the cold multitude of the reprobate or persecutors—will always love.

“I will ascend above the height of the clouds.” The clouds are the preachers of the Gospel, of whom the Lord says through this same Isaiah: “I will command my clouds not to rain rain upon that vineyard” (Isa. 5). And elsewhere: “Who are these that fly like clouds?” (Isa. 60). The devil glories that through Antichrist he will ascend over such clouds, so that, being superior, he may rule over those beneath him and draw them into agreement with his will—enticing those who are willing, deceiving the unwary, compelling the unwilling, and punishing those who resist. It follows:

“I shall be like the Most High.” This is what Paul says: “showing himself as though he were God” (2 Thess. 2). Beware of pride, dearest brothers, beware. For how many, alas, as I say with grief, if perhaps they see that they have advanced in the light of wisdom, benefited others by word and example, and thus deserved to be called by the name of Lucifer—so that at morning, that is, at the beginning of their conversion, they are regarded as brighter than their companions in the same manner of life—first swell with a hidden intention; they despise their superiors [Col. 0429C] and accuse them of simplicity and ignorance. Then, because they are occupied with temporal matters, they mock and disparage them; they look upon everyone as beneath themselves, always keeping before their eyes whatever they find blameworthy in others; and when they find nothing, they invent it. Recalling what they themselves do before the eyes of men in a praiseworthy manner, they inwardly feed upon their own vanity.

Then whoever is such a person, judging all others unworthy of authority, says: “I will ascend into heaven.” O Lucifer, who rose in the morning, you devise iniquity upon your bed. What do you say? “Who is this man, or that man, that he should preside over us? A man unlearned and without letters, a man who gives himself up and entangles himself all day in earthly things; a man neither distinguished in eloquence nor practiced in the Scriptures, neither discerning in action [Col. 0429D] nor skilled in spiritual art.” Saying these things in his heart, like Absalom he prepares parricide. “Who,” he says, “will appoint me judge over this people?” (2 Sam. 15). “I shall ascend into heaven, worthy to preside over spiritual—that is, heavenly—persons, since my conversation is always in heaven” (Phil. 3). “Why this waste?” (Matt. 26). A waste, I say, of such wisdom, such virtue, and such eloquence, which would be of such benefit; but because I sit among inferiors, they cannot be of use. “Therefore, above the stars of God, I, brighter than the rest after the manner of Lucifer, shall exalt my throne; sitting on the mountain of the testament, I shall acquire likeness to God by benefiting others.”

For since Sacred Scripture is called the testament, the mountain of the testament may not unfittingly be called charity, which, surpassing all virtues, contains within itself the whole Law and the Prophets. Nothing, therefore, is more arrogant or ambitious than one who promises himself precedence in charity, whispering everywhere in corners against his superior, especially accusing him of harshness and inhumanity. He describes, and as it were paints before the brothers’ eyes, what kind of abbot he ought to be: how moderate, how devout, how loving toward his subjects, how compassionate toward their labors, how accommodating to their weaknesses. Then he confirms by the authority of Scripture that the refectory ought to be arranged in this way, and provisions made for the infirmary with such mercy, that his hearers answer in their hearts: “Oh, if this man were abbot—how wise, how eloquent, how merciful, how humane!” And he, noticing these things, says: “Who is like me [Col. 0430B] among the clouds of heaven? Who is so learned in the Scriptures as I? Who is so suited to preaching? Therefore I shall ascend above the height of the clouds, so that I may display my wisdom as surpassing all preachers, lest that which may appear for the advancement of many should remain hidden any longer. Thus the likeness of God restored in me shall shine forth”—that likeness which consists especially in wisdom and charity.

Such a man, when he has at some time gained his desired object and been promoted to the authority which he coveted, either by his own contrivance or by the faction of others, stripped of God’s grace, slips from pretended virtues into manifest vices. Thus, hated by all, he is cast out, so as to deserve to hear: “How have you fallen from heaven, O Lucifer, who rose in the morning? You have fallen to earth, you who boasted of [Col. 0430C] heavenly conduct,” so that it may appear that you did not offer healing to those below you but rather inflicted upon them the wounds of sins.

Since it is certain that all such persons belong to the body of that wicked head, the prophetic utterance does not keep silent concerning the punishment they deserve. But because we have prolonged this discourse at length, let us reserve what follows for treatment at another time, with the help of Him who lives and reigns through all ages of ages.

## SERMON XVIII. On the same chapter, expounded morally

Yesterday, brothers, according to the poverty of our understanding, we treated of the fall which the devil suffers, or will suffer, in his body. But because many think that these prophetic words were spoken concerning the person of the devil himself and his first fall—[Col. 0430D] the fall in which, made a devil from an angel and evening from Lucifer, he fell from his heavenly dwelling—I do not think that anything we can contribute on this point should be withheld from you.

Under the name of the king of Babylon, the prophet had described the devil, whether in himself or in his members, as hell: “Your pride has been dragged down to hell; your corpse has fallen. The moth shall be spread beneath you, and rot and worms shall be your covering” (Isa. 14). Then, turning his eyes back to the former glory in which he had once been glorious among heavenly beings, and marveling at so great and wretched a change, he says: “How have you fallen, O Lucifer, who rose in the morning?” He is thought to have been called Lucifer because, just as that morning star surpasses the other stars in the clearness of its light, so [Col. 0431A] that archangel is thought to have been brighter than all the angels. To him the prophet Ezekiel says: “Every precious stone was your covering” (Ezek. 28). He then adds the names of nine stones, in order, according to some, to show that he was adorned with the nine orders of angels—brighter than the rest in wisdom and surpassing the rest in beauty.

But that he is described as rising in the morning, I take to mean what we understand from the book of Job, where it is written concerning the devil: “He is the beginning of the ways of God” (Job 40). Morning, which is the beginning of the day, signifies the beginning of every creature. Thus he is said to have risen in the morning, or to be the beginning of God’s ways, because, just as his nature was more worthy than that of the rest, so in creation he preceded them all.

Thus far we have proceeded freely in our exposition. But concerning what follows, [Col. 0431B] what shall I say? “You who said in your heart: I shall ascend into heaven; above the stars of God I shall exalt my throne.” We must first ask what this heaven is, what these stars of God are, who this mountain of the testament is, what the sides of the north are, and what this likeness of God is. For since he is believed to have been in heaven before his fall—for otherwise he could not have fallen from heaven—to what heaven did he desire to ascend? And if angels are to be understood by the stars, how, when he is proclaimed more excellent than they, does he desire to exalt his throne above them? These matters are obscure: they should be touched upon by us rather than expounded. Therefore let us proceed by conjecture, not by assertion.

First, then, we must see that every creature was created mutable. But if the rational mind, which surpasses all creatures, had not been made mutable, [Col. 0431C] it would have had no need of its Creator’s help; for it could neither advance to something better nor fall away to something worse. Yet it was necessary that its mutability should become known to it, so that experience itself might teach it that, without the help of its Maker, it could neither remain in the good in which it had been created nor ascend to anything higher. Thus it might understand what is written: “But for me, it is good to cling to God” (Ps. 72), so that every mouth might be stopped and every creature might become subject to God.

Therefore, that the mutability of their nature might be shown to angel and human being alike, it was necessary that each should be tempted; that, having been tempted, each should be tested; and that, having been tested, each should be confirmed. Thus grace might be commended in those who conquered, while justice might appear in those who sinned by their own iniquity. For it pertained to the glory of the rational creature that, before it attained the fullness of blessedness to be bestowed upon it by its Creator’s beneficence, [Col. 0431D] some merit should precede through the grace of its Lord Himself, so that blessedness itself might be both gift and reward.

Holy Scripture plainly declares the temptation of man. A tree beautiful to the sight, delightful in appearance, and pleasant for food was set before him, and he was told not to touch it (Gen. 3). This was the material of his temptation, so that, if he conquered, it might become a cause of more abundant glory for him. Perhaps, therefore, just as that beautiful tree was set before the human being, another object was set before the angel, in which he too might be tempted, so that in the temptation itself both the mutability of nature might be proved and freedom of choice commended: grace might grant reward in some, and justice impose punishment in others.

Just as he saw that holy society in which God was to reign called heaven, so he arrogantly calls his own heaven those persons in whom he already desired to rule. Or rather, he strives to ascend into that holy society itself, as into God’s own heaven, which he saw was to be attacked by the reprobate; and he himself intended to attack it more fiercely in them and through them. “Above the stars of God I shall exalt my throne.” By his throne he means all the lofty reprobate persons of this world, in whom the devil especially reigns; [Col. 0432A] they are given power in this world even over the stars of God—that is, over the saints—to tempt, oppress, persecute, and punish them.

Recall, my brothers, how small, despised, and contemptible the number of the saints was when all the glory of the world—kings, princes, and above all the Roman emperors—despising God and despised by God, sacrificed to idols and grievously oppressed in hard slavery the few worshippers of God who were in Judea. Beholding in spirit their exalted position and power, as well as the scarcity and lowliness of the saints; seeing and approving every lofty thing, while despising what was lowly; longing for the dominion of the former and the oppression of the latter, he says: “Above the stars of God I shall exalt my throne.”

And as though someone said to him, “What then will you do with the Jews, who are called the mountain of the testament and resist your decrees?” he immediately replies with an impious thought: “I shall sit upon the mountain of the testament; [Col. 0432C] and, if not in all of it, at least upon the sides—that is, in the northern parts—among those who, in the northern cold of vices, prepare a seat for me in their hearts.” There are the exalted persons Annas and Caiaphas, namely the scribes and Pharisees, whom I shall employ to accomplish my will.

Then, seeing the Lord send His clouds throughout the world wherever they might resist him, trusting in his own strength and presuming upon the multitude of his tricks (Ps. 51), he says: “I shall ascend above the height of the clouds,” that is, the preachers, oppressing or deceiving them; “and I shall be like the Most High,” so that, just as God has His angels, prophets, and apostles through whom He provides for, governs, and draws His own to Himself, so I also have my angels—that is, the fugitive spirits—and my prophets and apostles, whom we call false prophets and false apostles, [Col. 0432D] so that they may draw my own to me and subject them wholly to my will.

For he foretells these things, as though a true prophet, as future events; but, deceived by pride, he promises himself such dominion in vain imagination. Therefore, although it is true that he said this—that he would ascend into heaven, place his throne above the stars of heaven, and so forth—yet, if it cannot be soundly understood that this occurred, we must understand that, desiring dominion over those whom he had seen in the Creator abandoned by their Creator, he was not foretelling future events but uttering boastful words. For certainly the proud one could not remain in heaven; though he would indeed have done so for a while, had he been allowed, after conceiving his ambition, sufficient delay of time to think such things.

But let us set aside the opinion of some who say that he, together with those who fell, was placed in the lower regions—that is, in the firmament—and aspired to that lofty heaven in which God dwells with those who did not fall. That interpretation of blessed Gregory on Ezekiel’s words would be shaken: “You were the seal of likeness, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty; you were in the paradise of God. Every precious stone was your covering” (Ezek. 28). But if his exposition is judged probable, we must understand that the one who first fell held primacy among the other angels, and that in him, according to Gregory, the likeness of God was more expressly impressed, especially since he is called full of wisdom and perfect in beauty. [Col. 0433B]

Let us add also that the same Father, commenting on these very words before us, called the mountain of the testament the people of the Jews; and that blessed Jerome, expounding this prophecy, interpreted the stars of heaven as those who shine in the Church, and the mountain of the testament as the Church. How, then, could he, placed before his fall in such great beauty, have desired to reign over those who shine in the Church or to sit in the Church itself, unless he had previously seen all these things there where they were, even before they were made?

“Yet you shall be dragged down into hell, into the depth of the pit.” A fitting recompense: that he who, lifted up, wished to ascend to heaven should be dragged unwillingly into hell; not merely to some part of hell, but, because he sought the highest things, should descend to the lowest depths of hell. This is what is meant by “into the depth of the pit.” This may also be understood of his members—namely, Antichrist and his other accomplices—of whom it may be said that after the glory and impious dominion of this world they are to be dragged down into hell, where eternal fire is prepared for the devil and his angels.

“Those who see you shall bow down toward you and gaze upon you.” Truly, brothers, whoever sees with the eyes of the heart and carefully considers from what perfection and glory the devil and his angels fell, and from what holiness the proud daily fall into the abyss of disgrace, will surely bow down, be humbled, and set before his eyes both their former glory and their present misery. This is what he says: “Those who see you [Col. 0433D] shall bow down toward you,” in humility, “and gaze upon you,” in continual remembrance.

Indeed, when he says, “they shall bow down toward you,” he looks especially to those who, after works of light and good beginnings of conduct, fall from the company of the saints as though from heaven and turn to works of darkness. The good bow down toward such people with a certain compassion, mourning the destruction of those whose holiness they had approved.

There follows the voice of those who mock him and marvel at such misery after such great blessedness: “Is this not the man who troubled the earth?” If it please your charity, let us put these matters off until tomorrow, lest this burden weigh us down too much. Since it is somewhat burdensome for you to understand, let us ask the Lord that He may not burden us in such a way that we feel it—He who lives and reigns as God through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XIX. On what is written: “Is this not the man who troubled the earth?” etc. (Isa. 14)

The prophetic words spoken figuratively against the prince of Babylon we first applied, according to the order of prophecy, to Antichrist and the body of the devil himself. Then we discussed how they could suit the head himself, and so showed that the holy prophet described the ruin of each. Maintaining the same order in what follows, let us say that Antichrist is called “a man,” not on account of virtue but of power.

“Is this not the man who troubled the earth?” Yet the prophet could also have called him “man” by way of reproach, as people say of any cowardly person, “What a man!” Antichrist will certainly trouble the earth and shake kingdoms when, according to the Apocalypse, the people dwelling on earth will marvel after the beast, and kings and kingdoms, shaken by a certain terror, will fear his power.

By kingdoms, however, understand the rule of those kings whose heart is in the hand of God, concerning whom the Lord says: “By me kings reign” (Prov. 12), and whose conversation is in heaven (Phil. 3). These are then the holy and perfect persons, who can indeed be shaken but cannot be overthrown. Concerning this shaking the Lord says in the Gospel: “False prophets and false apostles shall arise, and shall give many signs, so that, if possible, even the elect may be led into error” (Matt. 24). [Col. 0434C]

It follows:

“Who made the world a desert and destroyed its cities.” By “world” he means the Church, of which it is written: “For he established the world, which shall not be moved” (Ps. 95). Antichrist will in a certain sense make this world a desert when many desert it because of him. That wicked man will also destroy the assemblies of the saints and scatter the congregations of the faithful, either subjecting them to his decrees or persecuting them by tortures and proscriptions. “And he did not open the prison to its captives,” that is, to the captives of the world.

The captives of the world are those who, enclosed within the Church in the darkness of ignorance, are bound by the chains of evil habit. Of them the prophet says: “The cords of sinners have encircled me” (Ps. 118). That pestilent man will not open the prison for these captives, whom he will not draw out of error by teaching but will envelop more tightly in the darkness of his own iniquity and unbelief.

But if you wish to understand the devil by “man,” this will not be absurd, since he is called a human being in the Psalms, in the Gospel, and in many other places of Holy Scripture, according to the saying: “An enemy, a man, has done this” (Matt. 13), and: “Arise, O Lord; let not man prevail” (Ps. 9). Even now he does not cease to trouble the earth and shake kingdoms. The earth may be called the lovers of the world and seekers of worldly glory, whom he troubles now by anger, now by envy, now by wars and seditions.

And whoever among us, brothers, savors of the earth and loves anything earthly will not be free from this disturbance; rather, we shall certainly bite and devour one another and envy one another. But if we raise our heart from earthly things to heavenly things, we shall hear not, “You are earth and shall go into earth” (Gen. 3), but, “You are heaven and shall go into heaven.” Our kingdoms—that is, the virtues through which we have already begun to reign with Christ—may indeed be shaken, but they shall not be overthrown. So was shaken the kingdom of the man whose feet were almost moved and whose steps had nearly slipped (Ps. 72). Joseph was shaken when he left his garment with the adulteress, but he was not overthrown; he preferred prison to fornication and chains to adultery (Gen. 39). We too are shaken when we are tempted, but are not overthrown if we do not consent. [Col. 0435B]

“Who made the world a desert.” In this place we may understand by the name “world” those who are so in the world as to be, as it were, themselves a world: always laboring in a circuit and never reaching an end. Of such persons the prophet says: “The wicked walk in a circuit” (Ps. 11), that is, in the world. Such people are not merely troubled or shaken; they are so overthrown that no trace of virtue remains in them, so that, as a desert is given over to beasts, so they, deprived of virtues, are given over to vices.

Note these three kinds of human beings: the first is troubled, the second shaken, the third overthrown. The first, because they are earth, are troubled by the agitation of contrary passions. The second, because they are kings, are attacked by spiritual wickednesses. The third, because they possess no steadfastness in themselves but are “carried about with every wind of doctrine” (Eph. 4), are worn down by unclean spirits.

The cities of this world are their assemblies “of blood” (Ps. 15), which display an appearance of holiness while denying its force and power. The prince of darkness destroys such cities, overthrowing all their fortifications—that is, the instruments of virtues—together with the virtues themselves. “And he did not open the prison to its captives.” Those held bound in such cities by the cords of sins will be cast down by the king of confusion into the prison of despair, who closes to them the door of confession. Hence the prophet says: “Let not the storm of water overwhelm me,” that is, let not the force of temptation cast me down; “nor let the deep swallow me,” namely, evil habit; “nor let the pit close its mouth over me” (Ps. 68), shutting with the bars of despair the door of confession. [Col. 0435D]

Then, describing the end of this temptation, he adds the burden by which that one will in the last days be oppressed in punishments, together with those whom he himself oppressed by sins:

“All the kings of the nations have slept in glory, each in his own house; but you have been cast out of your tomb like a useless branch, defiled and wrapped up with those slain by the sword.”

Hear this, kings of the earth, who, shaken by Satan, were unable to be overthrown. Here is fear; here labor; here groaning. Here, continually stationed on the field of battle, “take up the armor of God, that you may be able to stand against the snares of the devil” (Eph. 6). For there is a reward for your labor. “What reward?” you ask. “All the kings of the earth shall sleep in glory.”

Truly glorious is that sleep in which kings rest after victory, because “precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Ps. 115), and is no less glorious for that reason. How gloriously did that great king—I mean Paul—fall asleep! Crowned with so many victories, he joyfully received the sleep of death, holding a foremost place among those of whom it is written in the Apocalypse: “Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord. From henceforth, says the Spirit, let them rest from their labors” (Rev. 14).

“All kings shall sleep in glory.” It is a great thing, brothers, to sleep in glory. Some sleep in dishonor; others in mercy; others in glory. In dishonor are those who persevere in sins; in mercy, those who repent; in glory, martyrs and the innocent. They sleep in dishonor who die in their crimes; in mercy, those who, cleansed from their crimes by confession and tears of repentance, fall asleep; in glory, those whom the merits of many virtues render glorious and whom angelic hands convey to heavenly things.

The rich man slept in dishonor and was buried in hell; Lazarus in mercy, who was brought into Abraham’s bosom; Abraham himself in glory, who could be a consolation not only to himself but also to Lazarus (Luke 16). Judas slept in dishonor, hanging himself with a noose (Matt. 26); the paralytic in mercy, whose sins the Lord forgave; Peter in glory, who glorified Christ by his death. [Col. 0436C]

“For each in his own house.” These are those eternal dwellings in which the perfect receive the imperfect—namely, those who make friends for themselves from the mammon of iniquity by giving temporal things so as to attain eternal ones (Luke 16). These are the most blessed dwellings in the Father’s house: differing abodes corresponding to the variety of virtues. Although all the perfect sleep in glory and all arrive at the kingdom of heaven, “one is the glory of the sun, another the glory of the moon, and another the glory of the stars; and star differs from star in glory” (1 Cor. 15). Therefore all kings sleep in glory, yet each in his own house.

Moreover, iniquity is a dishonorable sleep; weakness is a pitiable sleep; charity is a glorious sleep. To the one sleeping dishonorably Paul says: “Awake, you who sleep, and arise from the dead” (Eph. 5). Of those sleeping in weakness or sloth, the divine word says: “How long will you sleep, O sluggard?” (Prov. 6). But of the bride sleeping among the breasts, who glories in the embraces of the bridegroom, it says: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me” (Song 2). Between the bridegroom’s breasts, in the bridegroom’s bosom, upon the bridegroom’s breast, she rests sweetly. This most blessed sleep is confirmed by the bridegroom’s voice, saying: “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, do not awaken the beloved until she herself wills it” (ibid.).

I ask: when will she will it? When will she wish to lack these embraces, to be torn away from these breasts, and to be separated from that bosom or breast? Surely when charity itself, which has lulled her into this heavenly sleep, wishes to awaken her, standing at the door and knocking: “Open to me, my sister, my bride” (Song 5). Then hearing that her beloved’s head is full of dew and his locks with drops of the night, she awakens, rises, opens the door, and leaves the delights by which she had been cherished. Urged by charity, she goes out to instruct his locks—that is, those who cling to him by faith and have contracted some northern cold from the night of ignorance.

Hence blessed Paul desired to be anathema from Christ for his brethren, setting the salvation of many above his own delights, however great. Come then, brothers: all kings of the nations, whether those who preside over peoples in the Church or those who govern their own thoughts, perceptions, and motions—whether irascible or concupiscible—as though they were diverse nations, by saving discipline, sleep in glory: either receiving the crown of life in death or, withdrawn from bodily things, resting in contemplation. [Col. 0437B]

Since kings sleep thus, what shall become of him by whom they were shaken? What shall become of him? “But you,” he says, “have been cast out of your tomb like a useless branch.” The tombs of Antichrist himself and of all the reprobate are their bodies, in which their souls are corrupted by the rottenness of vices and defiled by the filth of every impurity. They are cast out from these tombs when their souls are taken from their bodies and thrown into outer darkness. They are cast out like a useless branch, to which nothing is owed but fire.

It follows:

“Like a rotten corpse, you shall have no fellowship, not even with them in burial.” This is the burial of the rich man clothed in purple, of whom the Gospel says: “The rich man also died and was buried in hell” (Luke 16). Although this burial belongs to all the reprobate, they will not all be tormented in it equally. Rather, as is written of the tares, “Bind them in bundles to burn” (Matt. 13), so that those who were alike in guilt here may likewise become equal in punishment. But Antichrist, or his prince the devil, just as no one surpasses him in wickedness, so has no one with whom he shares fellowship in burial. He is compared to a rotten corpse in order to signify his degradation, stench, and shame.

Then, adding the reason for which he will suffer such things, he says: “For you have destroyed your own land; you have slain your own people.” By the land of Antichrist he means his flesh, which he will destroy by passions of vices, or hand over to spiritual beasts to be destroyed. By his people likewise understand those who commit themselves to his rule.

It follows:

“The seed of the wicked shall not be called for ever.” This is that calling of which the Apostle says: “We know that all things work together for good to those who love God, to those who are called saints according to his purpose” (Rom. 3 [sc. 8]). By this calling the seed of the ungodly shall never be called—that seed which the enemy, a man, sowed over the wheat of the good householder. Explaining this parable, Christ Himself says: “The good seed are the children of the kingdom, and the tares are the children of the wicked one. Prepare your children for slaughter because of the iniquity of their fathers” (Matt. 13).

To whom does He speak? To the evil seed, namely the multitude of the ungodly, who were not created by Antichrist or the devil but, scattered throughout the world as though sown, are themselves evil and beget evil offspring for themselves by doctrine and example. Addressing them, the prophet says: “Prepare your children for slaughter because of the iniquity of their fathers.” It is as though he said: Just as you, begotten by ungodly persons, are destined for eternal punishments, so you surely prepare for the same slaughter—that is, damnation—the children whom you have begotten for yourselves in your errors.

“They shall not rise, nor inherit the earth, nor fill the face of the world with cities.” I think these words should be referred to the reprobate, who, prepared for destruction by evil teachers, shall rise no more. Rotting in the dung of their flesh, they will be unable to attain possession of that land of which the psalmist says: “May my portion, O Lord, be in the land of the living” (Ps. 1); and of which the Lord says in the Gospel: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth” (Matt. 5).

“Nor shall they fill the face of the world with cities”—that is, they shall not fill the face of the cities which are in the world. Above we said that the world signifies the Church, whose cities are the gatherings of the faithful living in one fellowship. Their face is the very appearance of holiness, which shines before people in clothing, countenance, food, and other such matters. Therefore, when the prince of darkness has been buried in hell with his whole body, the children of the wicked, begotten from most wicked fathers and already prepared for slaughter—that is, for final damnation—will neither rise through repentance nor henceforth aspire to that appearance of holiness which they displayed only to human eyes.

I thought that I ought to finish with this discourse; but because the hour has already passed, let us reserve the little that remains for the joy of the following day, praying that we may be so freed in this life from the works of Babylon that we may not hereafter be burdened with eternal punishments together with her, through Jesus our Savior, who lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XX. On what is written: “And I shall rise up against them” (Isa. 16).

[Col. 0438D]

On the words written: “How you have fallen from heaven, Lucifer, you who rose in the morning!” Although what has been said may seem sufficient to you, another interpretation has occurred to me, shorter to expound and easier to understand. Before proceeding to other matters, it is worthwhile to set it forth, so that each may choose what he wishes; for such is the nature of the human mind that it always judges truer the opinion which it finds better suited to its own capacity.

Let us therefore take the beginning of this exposition from the words of the most blessed Paul, who, weaving a saving oracle concerning the law of sin and death, says: “Death reigned from Adam until Moses, even over those who had not sinned in the likeness of Adam’s transgression” [Col. 0439A] (Rom. V). Therefore the ruler of death—that is, the devil—exercised dominion in humankind before the law of Moses, reigning, namely, without opposition; but when the law entered and sin resisted the divine commandments, he exercised tyranny. “For where there was no law, neither was there transgression.” “Therefore the law entered in, that the offence might abound” (ibid.).

From Adam, then, until the grace of Christ, sin held dominion; and through sin, the ruler of sin claimed a right for himself not only over the reprobate, but also over the elect—not yet called, not yet justified, not yet redeemed by Christ’s blood. The prophet may fittingly call these “heaven,” if he knows the power of predestination, in which things that will be are made. Thus the prophet, seeing [Col. 0439B] that the devil’s kingdom, in the morning—that is, at the very beginning of the world’s rising—had occupied almost the whole world, had defiled kings, princes, and every class of humankind, save very few, with idolatry, and had invaded even the elect and predestined; and marvelling that so great a power had been overthrown by Christ’s strength, says: “How have you fallen from heaven, Lucifer, you who rose in the morning!”

He is called Lucifer because he seemed to bring the light of knowledge when he said: “Taste, and you shall be like gods, knowing good and evil” (Gen. III). He fell from heaven and crashed to earth when, cast out from the elect and shut up, as it were, in a prison among the reprobate alone, he ate earth after the manner of a serpent.

“You who said in your heart: I will ascend into heaven.” When the devil saw, with Christ’s coming now at hand, that the entire human race subject to him savoured of nothing but earth, but that a very few Jews, cleaving to God by faith and works, meditated upon heavenly things, puffed up with pride he trusted that he could rule even them: “I will ascend,” he said, [Col. 0439C] “into heaven.” Hence we read also in blessed Job: “He shall swallow up the river and shall not marvel; and he shall be confident that Jordan may flow into his mouth” (Job XL).

“I will exalt my throne above the stars of God,” that is, above the saints who are in Judaea. “I will sit upon the mount of the covenant, on the sides of the north,” so that, just as sacrifice is offered in all the temples of the world, so also in the Temple of Jerusalem, concerning which it is written, “The sides of the north, the city of the great King” (Ps. XLVII), my majesty may be worshipped as divine. “I will ascend above the height of the clouds,” that is, I will surpass the excellence and renown of all [Col. 0439D] the prophets. “I will be like the Most High,” so that, when Judaea has been made subject to me, the whole earth may be mine just as the whole heaven is God’s.

This is why, when tempting the Lord, he presumed to claim lordship over the whole world, saying: “All these things I will give you, if, falling down, you worship me” (Matt. IV). Scripture rightly says: “Before ruin the heart is exalted” (Prov. XVI). For at the very time when he promised himself greater things, he lost even those which he possessed. Hence it is said: “Nevertheless you shall be brought down to hell, into the depth of the pit.” Of this fall the Lord says in the Gospel: “Now is the judgment of the world; now shall the prince of this world be cast out” (John XII).

Those who see you thus raised up will bow in humility and look upon you—that is, they will recognize that, although they had formerly considered you [Col. 0440A] strong and great, you are weak in comparison with Christ. “Is this the man who troubled the earth, who shook kingdoms,” causing nation to rise against nation and kingdom against kingdom (Matt. XXIV); “who made the world a desert for God’s worshippers, who destroyed so many cities, shut up so many captives?” No one who reads histories is unaware that all these things were done at his prompting before the Lord’s coming.

“And I will rise up against them”—namely, the most evil children begotten by most evil fathers—“and I will destroy the name of Babylon, and its remnant, and its shoot, and its offspring, says the Lord.” The name of Babylon is worldly glory; Babylon’s remnant is love of the world; Babylon’s shoot is the inclination to sin; Babylon’s offspring is knowledge of sin and consent to it. For people desire nothing more than a great [Col. 0440B] name, which Babylonians acquire for themselves by riches, foolish prowess, or worldly learning. When they cannot acquire these, or when they lose what they have acquired, certain remnants of all these things remain in their hearts: namely, love of the world itself, from whose wicked shoot proceeds a most evil inclination. Its offspring are wicked thoughts, like the little children of the daughter of Babylon, concerning whom the Psalmist says: “O miserable daughter of Babylon, blessed is he who shall seize and dash your little ones against the rock!” (Ps. CXXXVI).

All these things will be destroyed by the Lord at the end of the age, when there will be no glory of the Babylonian name, no delight in its love, no inclination to sin; when, according also to the Psalmist, “all their thoughts shall perish” [Col. 0440C] (Ps. CXLV). It follows:

“And I will make her a possession for the hedgehog, and pools of waters,” so that its conscience may always be pricked by the thorn of sin, and that it may be blinded by lust and pleasure which, like a muddy pool, give off smoke and stench. “And I will sweep her with a sweeping broom, says the Lord of hosts.” Just as a house is cleansed and emptied with brooms, so I shall destroy all Babylon’s glory, riches, and pleasures, sweeping it away and crushing it by torments and pains.

But we too, dearest brothers, from whom the devil has been cast out by the Lord’s coming, should prepare the children of evil seed for slaughter, so that the Lord’s sword, devouring flesh, may kill every carnal inclination and unlawful pleasure, and even perverse thoughts begotten, as it were, from a most evil [Col. 0440D] seed of carnal desire; so that they may neither rise again nor fill the face of the world with cities.

Understand the cities of the world to be the meditations held in our memory. Memory is indeed compared to the world, because everything which can exist bodily in the world can be comprehended imaginatively by memory. The face of the world, or of the cities, is the intention of our meditations, according to which all things done or thought by us are judged by Him from whom nothing is hidden.

Be present, therefore, Lord Jesus, and rise with merciful severity against the children of Babylon, so that in my soul Babylon’s name may perish and, when every confusion has been destroyed, it may be designated by the name Jerusalem. “And I will make them,” he says, “a possession for the hedgehog and pools of waters.” Let my heart, Lord, become a hedgehog full of thorns, [Col. 0441A] so that the memory of each of my sins may prick me as with separate thorns; and, just as vices possessed my whole soul, so may saving compunction occupy it wholly. Thus, made filthy by remembrance of its lusts like muddy pools, may it deserve to bring forth the fruits of repentance.

It follows: “And I will sweep her with a sweeping broom.” The sweeping broom is contrition of heart, by which Babylon is swept and crushed in our soul and all its filth is driven out. For “the Lord is near to those who are contrite of heart,” because “a contrite and humbled heart God does not despise” (Ps. L). God’s scourge may also be called a sweeping broom, with which He “visits our iniquities with a rod, and our sins with stripes” (Ps. LXXXVIII), so that, crushing vices, He may introduce virtues and may not withdraw from us His mercy [Col. 0441B].

Then it is made a possession for the hedgehog and pools of waters. These are the two vices into which the class of hypocrites most often falls by God’s judgment: avarice and lust. For according to the Saviour’s saying, riches and the cares of the age are compared to thorns. When a soul has been purified by love of these things, it is armed, like a hedgehog, with its own thorns, trusting in its own strength and boasting in the abundance of its riches (Ps. LI). But barren and muddy pools, in which animals delighting in mire creep about, are compared to the impurities of lust: filthy and muddy places indeed, in which unclean spirits revel, whose prince more willingly sleeps under the shade, in the green growth of reed and rush, which grow especially [Col. 0441C] in pools and damp places. Such a soul is swept, not in order that it may be cleansed, but that it may be crushed. It follows:

“The Lord of hosts has sworn, saying: Surely as I have thought, so shall it be; and as I have planned in my mind, so shall it come to pass.” Everything which the holy prophet sets forth concerning the burden of Babylon he confirms by the authority of the Lord who swears, so that no one may doubt that those things will come to pass which God Himself is known to have foretold under oath. That the Lord is said to swear—He whom, even when not swearing, no one doubts ought to be believed—is the greatest indication of truth and certainty.

“Surely as I have thought, so shall it be; and as I have planned in my mind, so shall it come to pass.” He speaks to human beings in a human fashion, because if He spoke in a divine fashion, He would not be understood by human beings. Yet this word, “I think,” is not always used in doubtful matters, as when the Lord in anger very often says to His servant: “Do you think that I am your Lord?” (Gen. XVII). Therefore, when He says that He thinks or deliberates in His mind, no doubt, anxiety, or distraction of mind is to be imagined in God’s nature; rather, His eternal and unchangeable ordinance is to be believed to be intimated in words by which it could be understood by us.

Such estimation or deliberation is used so that, just as people attain the best result in things they do not do rashly, but with a certain hesitation and consideration, so God, by no impulse of mind and no accidental event, but by His eternal counsel, “reaches mightily from end to end, and orders all things sweetly” (Wis. VIII). Therefore, as He has ordained, as He has thought, as He has willed, as He has planned, [Col. 0442A] so it shall come to pass. What shall come to pass? “That I will crush the Assyrian in my land, and tread him under foot upon my mountains.”

By the Assyrian understand all that multitude of proud spirits. They are crushed in the Lord’s land: by “land” understand the little ones and the carnal, whom the Apostle feeds with milk because they are less fitted to receive solid food: “For I judged,” he says, “that I knew nothing among you except the Lord Jesus, and Him crucified” (I Cor. III). By the mountains, however, understand the apostles and the perfect, to whom the Lord gave power to tread upon serpents and scorpions and every power of the enemy (Luke X). From them even the most grievous yoke of the devil himself was removed when “the yoke decayed because of the oil,” and He who was anointed with the oil of gladness above His fellows [Col. 0442B] (Ps. XLIV), having bound that strong man, “led captivity captive” (Eph. IV), and by His strength removed the burden which weighed upon their shoulders. “And his yoke shall be removed from them, and his burden shall be taken from their shoulders.”

There is a yoke or burden of iniquity which a person, at the devil’s persuasion, has laid upon his own neck. There is likewise a yoke or burden of evil habit, under which a person places himself by living badly. There is also a yoke or burden of misery, under which divine justice has cast down the sinful person.

The yoke or burden of sin was indeed heavy, which until the Lord’s Passion so weighed upon mortals that it could be removed by no one’s righteousness or power. It plunged into hell not only all the reprobate but also all the elect, though a great chasm was fixed between them: the latter being established, if not in glory, yet in rest; the former unhappily assigned to places of punishment. But through Christ’s Passion, when the devil was crushed and trodden under foot, this yoke and burden was removed, so that from then on every righteous and perfect person could ascend even to heaven in free flight.

Nevertheless, dearest brothers, we are still weighed down by the Assyrian’s yoke or burden, since we feel another law in our members resisting the law of our mind [Col. 0442C] (Rom. VII) and leading us captive in the law of sin which is in our members. This yoke, brothers, is heavy; this burden is heavy and intolerable. “Who shall deliver us from this body of death?” (ibid.)

What shall I say of the burden of habit, which whoever has heedlessly laid upon his own shoulders cannot put off without grievous pain and excessive labour? There is also “a heavy yoke upon the children of Adam from the day of their coming forth until the day of their return into the womb of the mother of all.” Poverty burdens us, illness burdens us, drowsiness presses us, sloth casts us down. I pass over persecutions, proscriptions, terrors and fears, temptations, murmurings, slanders, curses, false judgments, with all of which the world is full, as blessed Job says: “Man born of woman, living for a short time, is filled with many miseries” (Job XIV). It is plain that all these, together with death itself—the heaviest and final one of all—are contained under one yoke or burden of misery.

This is Babylon’s burden, by which not only Babylon itself is weighed down but also the citizens of Jerusalem [Col. 0443A] are burdened while dwelling there as pilgrims. Happy is the person who, though weighed down by these things, is not crushed by them. Certainly the day will come when the Assyrian shall be utterly crushed in the land and trodden under foot upon the mountains—not in any land whatever, nor upon any mountains whatever, but as the Lord says: “As I have thought, so shall it come to pass: I will crush the Assyrian in my land, and tread him under foot upon my mountains.”

Come then, brothers: Satan was crushed by the Lord’s Passion; he was trodden under foot by apostolic preaching. Did he not appear crushed and trodden under foot when he could not even have power over the swine by himself? Yet, brothers, he has not been utterly crushed or trodden under foot, since the power to tempt still remains to him, and in Antichrist he will also be given power to rage and persecute. But then he shall be fully crushed and trodden under foot [Col. 0443B] when “the last enemy, death, shall be destroyed” (I Cor. XV); when in the Lord’s land—that is, our flesh, already glorified by the eternal resurrection—no trace of diabolical power shall remain; nor shall there be any access for temptation to the Lord’s mountains—that is, to our spirits, raised up in the height of divine contemplation.

He shall then, I say, be utterly crushed, when all power of tempting or persecuting has been taken from him and he is thrust down into the abyss to be tortured in everlasting fires. Then surely the most grievous yoke of misery and the most weighty burden, which we bear in many ways in this life, shall be removed from our necks or shoulders, when all mortality and all weakness have been swallowed up by the power of the resurrection [Col. 0443C] and we burst forth in this voice of exultation: “Where, O death, is your victory? Where, O death, is your sting?” (ibid.)

This is indeed the burden, the end of the burden: by it the city of confusion—that is, Babylon—together with its prince the devil, shall be plunged into hell, loaded with eternal punishments; while the city of peace—that is, Jerusalem—with its prince Christ, having either wisely avoided, courageously endured, or powerfully escaped Babylon’s burden by which it was weighed down, shall be carried to heaven to be crowned. It avoided it, indeed, lest it be crushed by Babylon’s vices; it endured it when hard pressed by Babylon’s persecutions; it escaped it when, departing from the body, it was received into rest.

But lest anyone suppose that the prophet composed so divine an oracle concerning some one region, the Lord Himself, excluding every ambiguity, added [Col. 0443D]:

“This is the counsel which I have planned concerning the whole earth; and this is the hand stretched out over all nations.” What could be clearer? He shows that the matters spoken in this burden concern the whole world and all nations. Since these are divided into elect and reprobate, I judge that the counsel belongs to the former and the outstretched hand to the latter.
