Deep indeed and lofty is the counsel by which the elect, living with the reprobate in the same community, are weighed down by the same burden of miseries and are wonderfully assisted so as not to be crushed; by which, though often burdened with the same sins and crimes, they are separated from them by conversion and a better way of life; by which, whether they are burdened by vices, pains, or temptations, all things work together for their good [Col. 0444A] (Rom. VIII).

But how outstretched is the Lord’s hand over the reprobate, accepting none of their good deeds and washing away none of their evils; how outstretched the hand by which all things work together for their harm: they are burdened even by punishments, so that they may be corrupted by pleasures; they grow proud in virtues, so that they may gain no reward from them; they are not humbled in sins, so that they may deserve pardon. If they abandon evil, they return to it again; if they begin good, they do not persevere. Finally, the reprobate are condemned eternally, while the elect are crowned in the joys of eternal life.

After the Lord’s words confirming what has been said, the prophet himself adds in his own person: “For the Lord of hosts has decreed, and who shall be able to weaken it?” I understand this to have been said of the elect: no one can weaken the decree of the divine counsel concerning their salvation. “For if God is for us, who is against us?” (ibid.) Hear also how firm and eternal is the decree which none dares oppose, which none can or ought to change: “The firm foundation of God stands, having this seal: The Lord knows those who are his” [Col. 0444B] (I Tim. II).

But the words which follow, “And his hand is stretched out; who shall turn it back?” I think should be referred to the reprobate, as we said above. For just as mercy concerning the salvation of the elect is sure and steadfast, so justice concerning the condemnation of the reprobate is surely steadfast and unchangeable.

But now, at the end of this burden, let us make an end of this sermon, beseeching the Lord and our God that we may avoid the burden which lies in vices; that we may courageously endure the burden which lies in temptations [Col. 0444C] and miseries; and that we may deserve to escape that burden which shall be in eternal punishment, through our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be honour and dominion through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXI. On the beginning of the burden of the Philistines

Having expounded the burden of Babylon, we have undertaken to expound the burden of the Philistines, relying far more upon your prayers than upon our own strength. The prophet, therefore, understanding by the name Babylon the world in general, divided into elect and reprobate, described in mystical discourse the burden by which it was either weighed down or crushed, the Lord Himself bearing witness when He says: “This is the counsel which I have planned concerning the whole earth, and this is the hand stretched out over all nations” (Isa. XIV).

Now passing from genus [Col. 0444D] to species, he describes separately the several burdens of the individual nations, so that he may more fully set forth in detail what he had prophesied of the whole in a few words. First, he reveals the counsel of divine judgment against the Philistines, whose name is interpreted as “those falling by drink.” By them, I think, Jews are signified: drunk, as it were, on the letter of the law as on old wine, they fell away from grace. For, “ignorant of God’s righteousness and seeking to establish their own, they were not subject to God’s righteousness.” Those who thought themselves justified in the law fell from grace.

This is that old wine which failed at the wedding (John II), because our Lord Jesus Christ, coming forth from the Virgin’s womb “as a bridegroom from his chamber” (Ps. XVIII), brought the legal sacraments, as it were old wine, to an end, and served the new wine of the Gospel to all called to the wedding of the great king’s son [Col. 0445A]. The Jews, therefore, clinging to the letter of the law and ignorant of the Lawgiver, cried out as though drunk and intoxicated: “We have a law, and according to the law he ought to die.” O ruin! O fall! “We have no king but Caesar” (John XIX). To fall away from Christ and cleave to Caesar is a great fall.

And appropriately enough, intending to deal with the destruction of very many nations, he begins with the Jews: they were the first of all to receive Christ and the first to fall away from faith in Him. Thus he begins:

“In the year in which King Ahaz died, this burden came to pass.” Ahaz, a most wicked and proud king, a despiser of the divine law and worshipper of idols, signifies the devil. His life may be understood as his reign [Col. 0445B], which he gained over the human race because of the fault of the first transgression. When, then, did King Ahaz die? Certainly when that was fulfilled which the Lord says through the prophet: “I will be your death, O death!” (Hos. XIII). For He stripped principalities and powers on the cross, triumphing openly over them in Himself.

Therefore, brothers, as long as the devil held power over all nations, the Jewish people rejoiced in its prosperity, having Temple, altar, ephod, teraphim, priests, and sacrifices. But in the year—that is, at the time—when King Ahaz died, namely when the devil’s empire was destroyed, that people began to be weighed down by a heavy burden of miseries. Thus misfortune followed misfortune, until, cut off from the land of the living, they were wholly destroyed even from the land of the dying, which had been granted them as an inheritance.

“Do not rejoice, all Philistia, because the rod of him that struck you is broken.” Remember, brothers, that counsel which that people is recorded to have formed against the Lord, in which Caiaphas the high priest decreed that one man should die lest the whole nation perish. “For if,” they said, “we let him go on thus, all will believe in him; and the Romans will come and take away both our place and nation” (John XI). “They trembled with fear where there was no fear” (Ps. XIII).

The holy patriarch Joseph saw in a dream that he would be worshipped by his brothers. To prevent this, he was sold into Egypt [Col. 0445C] (Gen. XXXVII); yet this very action brought it to pass. Thus they maintain that Christ must be put to death lest, if peoples believe in Him, the Romans take from them both place and nation. Yet it was because He was slain that the whole world believed in Him; and nevertheless the Romans came and took away both their nation and their place.

They seemed, however, to have been freed from this fear when Jesus had been placed on the cross and given up to death, and they rejoiced that they had extinguished His name and power. Let us recall what the sacred history tells concerning the Philistines and Samson, in which the Philistines plainly represent the Jews, and Samson the Lord Saviour. Sent to the lost sheep of the house of Israel, he desired the embraces of the harlot Delilah, that is, the Church from among the Gentiles. The sacred Gospels relate how many injuries this Samson suffered from the Philistines; with what bonds he was attacked; and with what threats he was assailed [Col. 0446A] (Judg. XV).

The scribes and Pharisees watch his mouth; they raise questions and demand rulings in cases of various kinds, that there might be grounds on which to accuse him, hand him over to a judge, and consign him to death by a sentence. They come with questions as though with bonds; and having broken these bonds, he went out free as often as they attacked him. “Is it lawful,” they ask, “to pay tribute to Caesar or not?” (Matt. XXII). “They prepared a snare for his feet, but fell into it themselves” (Ps. LVI). He says: “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Matt. XXII).

Likewise concerning the adulterous woman: “Moses commanded that women such as this should be stoned. What do you say?” (John VIII). He broke the bonds in such a way that the adulteress was freed while they were struck by their own judgment and stoned by the accusation of their own conscience.

At last Samson, weakened by love of the harlot, falls asleep; stripped of his hair, he is also stripped of strength, handed over to the Philistines’ power, and exposed to mockery and suffering. So too my Samson, loving the harlot who lay prostrate beneath every leafy tree and upon every wooded hill, defiled by as many adulteries, as it were, as the idols she worshipped, laid aside his hair, concealed his strength, and accepted bonds. When the disciples had fled, he ascended, as though bald, the place of Calvary; handed over to the Jews’ will, he was mocked as he hung upon the cross.

But the prophet, seeing in the Spirit that they were filled with mad delight, shaking their heads before the cross, reproaching him with his miracles, and urging him to come down, restrains this foolish rejoicing, saying: “Do not rejoice, all Philistia [Col. 0446C], because the rod of him that struck you is broken.” As though freed by his blows, they insult him hanging on the cross, moving their heads with delight and saying: “If he is the Son of God, let him come down from the cross” (Matt. XXVII).

O Philistia! O drunken one! O drink-sodden one! O mad one! You fall, collapse, and are cast down. The rod—that is, the power—of him who struck you appears to you broken. You insult Samson when he is captive, his hair shorn and his eyes torn out. Do not rejoice, all Philistia. Samson will die and his power will appear broken; but his death shall mean your desolation, the crushing of your children, the diminution of your glory, the ruin of the Temple, the removal of the priesthood, and the scattering of the whole people. Therefore do not rejoice, all Philistia, because the rod of him that struck you is broken.

The words “all Philistia” express the greatness of the joy with which they exulted in Christ’s death. Do not rejoice; do not be glad; do not exult; do not insult. Divine justice will not leave so great a crime unavenged. Since they did not receive the mark of truth so as to be saved, God will send them an agent of error, that they may believe the lie. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “I came in the name of my Father, and you did not receive me; another will come in his own name, and him you will receive” [Col. 0446D] (John V). He is the agent of error, to be received by the Jews at the end of the age, by God’s just judgment, so that those who despised Christ may have Antichrist.

Therefore it is added: “From the root of the serpent shall come forth a basilisk, and its seed devouring the flying creature.” When the holy patriarch Jacob blessed his sons, and Dan came to be blessed among the others, he said of him: “Let Dan be a serpent in the way, a horned serpent in the path” (Gen. XLIX). Therefore, just as “a rod came forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower rose from his root”—that is, Christ—so also from the root of Dan, who was called a serpent, shall come forth a basilisk—that is, Antichrist.

The basilisk, also called the *regulus*, is said to be the king of serpents, killing people by its breath and gaze. This serpent is compared to Antichrist, who shall be full of its power and malice and is king of serpents, that is, prince of demons. Whose breath is wickedness and who is enlightened in knowledge (illuminatus scientia; wording uncertain), he shall kill many, turning them from the faith of truth. Consider those whom he deceives by cunning to have been struck by his gaze; and know those whom his malice compels to have been slain by his breath.

“And its seed,” he says, “devouring the flying creature.” He uses the singular for the plural. Just as the good seed is the word of God, so certainly the worst seed is the word of Antichrist. Therefore his word, his preaching, his teaching, like his seed, shall devour the Jews—not all of them, but those puffed up by pride, who can neither ascend to heaven nor are willing to descend to earth through humility, but, like birds suspended in this empty space between heaven and earth, deserve the company of those who, cast out of heaven, have received their place in this dark air [Col. 0447B].

For from the root of the serpent—that is, from the devil’s prompting—there came forth a basilisk: pride, hatred, and indignation against the Romans, whose emperor at that time, the utterly wicked Nero, is not undeservedly compared to a poisonous basilisk. His seed—that is, the intention which he conceived from the serpent’s breath—sent Vespasian into Judaea; and Vespasian, together with his son Titus, devoured all the power, pride, and glory of the Jews.

“And the firstborn of the poor shall be fed.” The prophetic speech reproaches the unhappy people for the hatred which they exercised not only against Christ but also against his disciples. As long as their power endured, Jewish persecution of Christ’s disciples did not cease: some were killed by them, some stoned, some driven from their homes, some worn out with scourges. The prophet therefore, seeing in the Spirit that after all these things the Jews were afflicted with many evils, while Christ’s disciples after their persecution—and indeed amid that very persecution—were cheerful in the confidence of a good conscience, says: “And the firstborn of the poor shall be fed.”

The poor are those of [Col. 0447D] whom the Lord says in the Gospel: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. VI). These are the poor who, renouncing the world and all its riches, bidding farewell even to father and mother, brothers and sisters, fields and possessions, follow naked Christ naked. The firstborn of all these were the holy apostles and Christ’s disciples, who first heard this teaching from his mouth and said with secure conscience: “Behold, we have left all things and followed you. What then shall we have?” (Matt. XIX).

Peter truly rested confidently in Christ when, ordered by the priests not to speak in Jesus’ name, he replied: “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts V). How great also was Paul’s confidence when, standing before the judge, he argued so powerfully concerning Christ and His commandments that Festus, unable to endure the thunder of his words, said: “Paul, you are mad; much learning drives you to madness” [Col. 0448A] (Acts XXVI).

This rest certainly signifies that tranquillity of mind by which they did not grow angry even at their persecutors; by which they were moved by no hatred against those who hated them; by which they learned to pray for their enemies, to do good to those who did evil to them, and to labour for the life of those who thirsted for their death. Thus Stephen intercedes for those stoning him (Acts VII); Peter does not withhold the word of salvation from those scourging him; and Paul has great sorrow and continual pain of heart for those who had once stoned him and scourged him five times [Col. 0448B].

But while they acted confidently and rested in the sweetness of charity, what happened to the Philistines who had mocked our Samson? Hear what follows:

“And I will cause your root to perish by famine, and I will kill your remnant.” Its root perished by famine when, after the Temple had been burned, the city likewise fell and all that nobility perished by famine or sword. High priests and priests may be called the root of the nation, since, just as life-giving sap flows from the root and is spread through the whole body and branches of a tree, so remedies of salvation were provided for the rest of the people through the teaching of the law administered by priests. But because they rejected Christ’s word and judged themselves unworthy of God’s kingdom, when they themselves perished by famine, [Col. 0448C] their remnant—that is, the rest of the multitude—having abandoned the life which is Christ, was punished by eternal death.

Though these things have been said as a prediction of future events, they must be repeated in a moral sense, so that the faith which the truth of prophecy confirms may be adorned by conduct, commended by life, and crowned by its end. This burden of the Philistines must not be understood only in the sense in which Philistia is weighed down or crushed, but also in the sense in which it weighs down or crushes.

Let us therefore, dearest brothers, beware of being crushed by the Philistines; for we cannot prevent ourselves from being weighed down. Let us be like Samson the Nazarite—that is, consecrated to the Lord—and, as the hair of our head grows, let us become holy. Let not our hair, in which our greatest strength lies, be betrayed to the harlot; [Col. 0448D] then we shall be able neither to be bound by chains, terrified by swords, shut up in prison, nor overcome by a multitude. And if perhaps the Philistines exult, and if at some time we appear captive and destined to be enslaved to their chains, they shall hear from the prophet: “Do not rejoice, all Philistia, because the rod of him that struck you is broken.”

But because these matters must be treated more fully and clearly, let us restore our strength by silence and our understanding by prayer; and tomorrow let us assemble to investigate these mysteries, for the praise and glory of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be honour and glory for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXII. On the same chapter expounded morally
The burden concerning the Philistines, which after the burden concerning Babylon we have undertaken to discuss with your charity, the prophet comprises indeed in few words, though in their depth of meaning he has supplied material for much discussion. Therefore, brethren, descending from allegorical mountains to the plains of moral interpretation, let us return to the beginning of the burden itself; and let us say that by the Philistines the proud also are understood, who trust in their own strength and glory in the multitude of spiritual graces (Ps. XLVIII). These are they who, having gone out from Sodom with Lot (Gen. X) and climbed the mountain of virtues, are made drunk by the two sisters, pride and vainglory; and thus, sensibly enticed into shameful things, they slip even into the worst abominations, so that they may rightly be called Philistines—that is, those who fall through drink.

Let your charity see, brethren, [Col. 0449B] that although, by nature, as individual vices are expelled virtues take their place, this pride, being nearer to virtues than to vices, grows more fiercely powerful against a person the more he has advanced. This beast has many forms; it can scarcely be guarded against, and in this life it can by no means be extinguished. Its own death, indeed, is the material of its life, and it rises more robustly from the very point at which it is thought most certainly to have been extinguished.

Do you understand what I am saying? So long as vices live in you, whose inciter is Ahaz, and your struggle with flesh and blood is grievous, and frequent wounds are inflicted on you, even though you fight most valiantly, that beast does not dare raise its head; it does not dare enter into a deadly contest against one who stands timid and fearful in battle array. But if, Ahaz being dead, the incitements of lust have become quiet, [Col. 0449C] immediately the twisting serpent raises its poisonous head and, puffing up the soul with the suggestion of its venom, first makes it empty of virtues; then, producing decay under the very fear of vices, it casts down into the vices from which it boasted of having escaped.

Therefore the prophetic utterance addresses those who stand, as it were, upon the summit of virtues and have already begun to glory, not in the Lord, but in themselves: “Do not rejoice, Philistia,” it says, “you who now are becoming drunk on the cup of pride, who now begin to fall from higher things to lower: do not rejoice, because the rod of him who struck you has been broken.” This Ahaz is our striker, to whom the Lord often gives a rod in his hand, that he may strike and scourge us, afflicting us with temptations and shaking us with suggestions. This [Col. 0449D] rod is broken when the power of tempting is removed.

Nevertheless, do not rejoice, O Philistia, as though you had already escaped; do not boast as though you had extinguished by your own strength that poisonous serpent. Beware, therefore, of the serpent’s root. “For from the root of the serpent shall come forth a basilisk”: from pride, contempt of God. The basilisk is the king of serpents, and contempt of God is more powerful than all vices; these are judged more damnable when they arise not from ignorance or weakness, but rather from contempt. Contempt is born from pride, because unless the human mind has first swelled with pride, it does not break out into injury against its Creator. “And its offspring devours the bird.” For contempt is despair, which excludes confession, mocks repentance, [Col. 0450A] and renounces satisfaction. “The wicked man, when he comes into the depth of evils, despises” (Prov. XVIII): blasphemous against God, unjust toward his neighbour, raging more ruinously against himself. Since he despairs of pardon, he heaps vice upon vice and supplies increasingly powerful fuel to despair itself.

By the bird—an animal furnished with wings and seeking the heights in swift flight—hope is signified. By hope we prefer heavenly things to earthly, eternal things to temporal, divine things to human; through it we have already been saved, and reign with Christ in heavenly places. Despair, then, devours this bird when its wings, by which one flies to heavenly things, have been torn off and the soul turns down toward what is lowest, so that, despising future things, it embraces earthly things and desires nothing further, because it hopes for nothing [Col. 0450B] beyond them.

But this also which is said—“Do not rejoice, all Philistia”—is very fittingly addressed to those who receive divine scourges with insufficient gratitude: lavish in prosperity, complaining in adversity; raised up by favour and disturbed by persecution. Come then, brethren: as the Apostle says, “What son is there whom his father does not correct? For he scourges every son whom he receives” (Heb. XII). Thus he too may be called a striker, who “strikes and heals, puts to death and makes alive, brings down to hell and brings back” (1 Sam. II). He indeed sends forth from Zion “the rod of his strength” (Ps. CIX), that he may visit our iniquities with a rod and our sins with blows (Ps. LXXXVIII).

It is a great sign, brethren, of divine mercy when he does not [Col. 0450C] spare us in the present; when he does not show pity; when he hedges our ways with thorns and closes them with a wall, so that, seeking death, we may not find it (Hos. II); when he sprinkles every sweetness for which we long with manifold bitterness, lest we cling to it. What are you, Philistine, falling through drink? The Lord has filled and made you drunk with bitterness; he has given you to drink from the cup of his wrath, and his arrows are fixed in you (Ps. XXXVII), whose indignation drinks up your spirit. Certainly, if you grow angry, murmur, are indignant, and push away the physician’s hand, you are a Philistine falling through drink, incurring ruin from that from which you might have hoped for restoration.

Woe to you if he turns his zeal away from you, so that he is angry with you no more; as he says through the prophet to some: “I will not visit your daughters when they have committed fornication, nor your wives when they have committed adultery” (Hos. IV). Unhappy, therefore, are those of whom he complains in the Psalms: “My people did not listen to my law, and Israel did not heed me” (Ps. LXXX). They did not listen to him who taught them; they did not endure him who corrected them: rebellious and unbelieving on the one hand, murmuring on the other; ungrateful in both respects. With what punishment, then, will they be chastised? What torments will be inflicted upon them for these things? Hear what follows: “And I let them go according to the desires of their heart” (ibid.).

Let your charity understand, my brethren. Many are corrected by the Lord for their sins: they are afflicted by poverty, worn down by persecutions, weakened in their limbs, tortured by various kinds of torment. But if they admit no correction, [Col. 0451A] and, just as they were excessive in prosperity, are found blasphemous in adversity, he suspends the rod and puts the sword into its sheath, handing them over to the desires of their own heart, “that they may go after their own inventions” (Ps. LXXX). “Then they rejoice when they have done evil” (Prov. II). To such, therefore, the prophet speaks, saying: “Do not rejoice, all Philistia, because the rod of him who struck you has been broken.” Do not rejoice that he who trained you has ceased from striking; his rod kept out the serpent’s head, drove away the basilisk’s venom, and dried up its most evil offspring.

“For from the root of the serpent shall come forth a basilisk”: from a corrupted will, namely, an unclean delight. Its offspring are evil works, which overwhelm and devour all that formerly had taste in our soul and, like a winged bird, sought higher things in desire and affection. But what shall the poor—that is, the humble—do, when the Philistines, that is, the proud, are weighed down by such a burden? It follows:

“And the firstborn of the poor shall feed, and the poor shall rest in confidence.” These are the poor to whom the Lord says: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for yours is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V). This poverty is judged according to disposition, not according to outward condition; for one abundant in riches and exalted in a kingdom says: “But I am needy and poor” (Ps. LXIX).

There are certain virtues in which we begin, certain ones in which we advance, and certain ones in which we are perfected. First of all is faith, which hope strengthens and charity rewards. But that faith is a virtue which works through love, since without hope [Col. 0451C] of reward no one works well. These are the firstborn of the poor—that is, of the humble—who glory not in themselves but in the Lord.

There is in this life a certain experience which proves faith, strengthens hope, and nourishes charity: namely, that anointing of the Spirit which teaches us concerning all things; which pours into us certain firstfruits of future blessedness, illuminating and at the same time inflaming our heart, so that it may see and love, taste and understand, when the Spirit himself bears witness to our spirit that we are children of God (Rom. VIII). Therefore, if these virtues are fed and nourished in this way, we advance more easily in the remaining virtues, which are introduced by them: when fear adheres to faith, patience to hope, and chastity to charity. Then fear [Col. 0451D] gives birth to prudence, patience to fortitude, chastity to temperance, and charity to justice. Finally, through these one ascends to wisdom as by streams to a fountain: faith passes into hope, hope into possession, charity into fullness.

Then indeed will take place what follows: “And the poor shall rest in confidence.” For when all humble persons—who do not know how to glory in their own merits, and whom the prophet calls poor—have reached the summit of virtues, they shall rest confidently. Hope of pride does not enter into them; and therefore they can neither be moved by the hand of the sinner nor dashed down by an approaching storm. “There”—that is, in pride—“have fallen those who work iniquity; they have been cast out and could not stand” (Ps. XXXV). There are the Philistines falling through drink, into whom the serpent inserts [Col. 0452A] its root; from it a basilisk is produced, whose offspring devours the bird. Of them the prophet continues:

“And I will cause your root to perish by famine, and I will kill your remnant.” Once the root has been killed, why should not the branches likewise die, so that when what is first perishes, all that remains may also be destroyed? Faith is the root; the other virtues are the remnant. Thus, where faith is corrupted, all virtues alike vanish, because “everything that is not from faith is sin” (Rom. XIV). What then? Does no remedy, no hope remain for the Philistines? It does, if they do what follows: “Howl, O gate; cry out, O city.” But because these words have not yet been expounded allegorically, let us for the present defer this moral exposition.

Yet, since the burden concerning the Philistines can be understood not only in respect of that by which it is oppressed, but also in respect of that which it oppresses, let us say that the Philistines are unclean spirits who, drunk with pride, fell from that heavenly dwelling. These wear us down by their suggestions, press us with temptations, and burden us with sorrows. Against them we have a struggle; by them we are sometimes wounded and struck, and in turn we strike and wound them. “Put on, therefore, brethren, the armour of God, that you may be able to stand against the snares of the devil” (Eph. VI). Guard your greatest strength, which, as in Samson, seven locks preserve for you. The Philistines press upon you and cast ropes over you while you sleep; but unless the seven locks have first been shorn, they accomplish nothing.

Of these ropes the Prophet says: “The cords of sinners have surrounded me” (Ps. CXVIII). But because God brought about what follows, “And I have not forgotten your law” (Ps. CIX), he confidently proclaims in another psalm: “You have broken my bonds” (Ps. CXV). There are three ropes by which the Philistines attack us: the desire of the flesh and of the eyes, and the pride of life. See to it, O Samson, that you do not sleep; see to it that you are not dissolved by idleness; see to it that you are not seduced by the allurements of the harlot, namely vainglory. Idleness is the enemy of the soul, for everyone who is idle lives in desires.

Let those hear this who seek occasions for wandering about, to whom the common work of the hands is a burden, who, while the brethren are engaged in necessary work, give themselves to idleness and tales. These are those whom [Col. 0452D] we often see bound in the ropes of the Philistines: now driven by the goads of the flesh, now unhappily entangled in foolish occupations, now driven as though by certain furies and exposed, through wandering about, to much detraction. The Philistines draw them by the rope of carnal desire toward lust, by the rope of desire of the eyes toward vanity, and by the rope of pride toward superstition.

Locks grow from the head, thoughts from the heart. Therefore your strength is preserved in seven thoughts, two concerning the past, two concerning the future, and three concerning the present. To the past belong remembrance of creation and redemption; to the future, dread of damnation and contemplation of eternal reward; to the present, consideration of our weakness and of divine goodness, together with remembrance of that consolation [Col. 0453A] which we often experience. If, sunk in deadly sleep, you betray these thoughts to the harlot—that is, hand them over to vainglory to be cut off—you will be handed over, weak and powerless as it were, to wicked spirits, the Philistines, to be mocked.

Yet while they exult, it may be said to them: “Do not rejoice, all Philistia, because Samson’s rod has been broken”; for his locks can grow again. Through them he may avoid both the serpent’s root and the basilisk’s offspring, if only, like a poor man set in a place of pasture (Ps. XXII), he can avoid hunger for the word of God and rest confidently in hope of divine mercy. For by God’s grace it will happen that the serpent’s root, when the material of sin has been withdrawn from it, will perish as though from hunger, having nothing on which to live; and thus the other vices which had sprouted from that most evil root will wither as the root dies.

But now let us at last put an end to this discourse, beseeching God’s mercy that we may deserve inwardly to be fed by that Word which has no end, which is Christ, to whom be honour and glory for ever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XXIII. From the words “Howl, O gate” to the end of the burden concerning the Philistines (Isa. XIV)

By the Philistines, whose name is interpreted as “those who fall through drink or a cup,” we have said, according to the type of things to come, that the Jews are signified. Because of their killing of the Lord and Saviour, they were crushed and oppressed by the Romans, scattered abroad and dispersed, because God rejected them (Ps. LII). [Col. 0453C] Hence the prophet says: “And I will cause your root to perish by famine, and I will kill your remnant.” Still describing their calamity, he adds: “Howl, O gate; cry out, O city; all Philistia has been laid low.”

This is that desolation of the city and nation which the holy Ezekiel also describes, when the Lord says to him: “And you, son of man, take for yourself a sharp sword, and draw it over your head and beard. And take scales for weighing, and divide them. Burn a third part in fire; cut down a third part with the sword; scatter the remaining third part to every wind; and unsheathe the sword after them” (Ezek. V). All these things require no exposition, but consideration.

Yet the prophet does not keep silent concerning the cause for which that people suffered. “For smoke shall come from the north, and there is none who shall escape its troop.” Smoke comes with a troop because many abominations followed ignorance: hatreds, curses, blasphemies. In these that wretched people daily grows in punishments, so that there is none among the reprobate who escapes the troop of that smoke. “What do you see,” says the Lord to Jeremiah, “what do you see?” And he answers: “A boiling pot, and its face is from the face of the north” (Jer. I).

You know who he is to whom the northern quarter was pleasing: namely, the cold hearts of mortals, alien from God’s warmth. He who sits upon them often kindles through them the pot of temptation, from which smoke goes forth, blinding the eyes of many and separating them from the light of truth. He says how Philistia has been laid low; and likewise on what grounds anyone may securely hope for pardon, if worthy repentance has gone before.

Paul, laid low in unbelief and raised up in faith—a persecutor in unbelief and a teacher in faith—says: “I obtained mercy because I did it ignorantly in unbelief” (1 Tim. I). Ignorance itself was like smoke; proceeding indeed from the north, it had wrapped his mind in the darkness of error. He therefore obtains pardon more readily, because he persecuted the Church of God out of zeal, blinded by the smoke of ignorance, not driven by malice.

You too, therefore, do not despair of pardon. For even if perhaps the smoke of ignorance has not touched you, the smoke of another’s suggestion has touched you; the smoke of carnal desire has touched you. He who knows our formation (Ps. CII) has mercy all the more quickly because we carry within ourselves that which is more easily darkened by the smoke [Col. 0454B] of that boiling pot. Philistia—that is, every proud soul—is certainly laid low because smoke proceeding from the north, that is, from diabolical temptation, whether of ignorance or of desire, either ensnares it when it is unwary or entices it when it is weak.

But do you howl with contrition of heart; cry out in confession, so that what is written in this same prophet may happen: “Take a harp; go around the city, harlot consigned to oblivion” (Isa. XXIII). Sing well; repeat the song often, so that remembrance of you may remain before the mercy of the Redeemer. For he knows that there is no one who escapes the troop of this most evil smoke. Who is there whose flesh or mind that northern enemy does not at some time kindle like a boiling pot, and from whom he does not raise smoke with the fiery darts of desire?

What, then, shall be answered to the messengers of the nations? If you please, understand by the messengers of the nations the angels of opposing power. They harass those worn by diverse temptations and set before them the arduous way of virtue; they reproach them with the frailty and corruptibility of the flesh, so that, cast down by a kind of despair, they may flee the way of salvation. I speak from experience. At the beginning of our conversion, amid severe temptations of flesh and spirit, when at one time the spirit of fornication burned us, at another anger inflamed us, at another gluttony stirred us with its desires, endurance in all these things seemed impossible—especially as there was set before us the slippery condition of youth, the manifold cunning of the tempter, and the easy fall arising from weakness.

What answer, then, shall be made to spirits suggesting such things? What is our hope, what our refuge? [Col. 0454D] (Ps. XC). “Because the Lord has founded Zion.” Brethren, “the firm foundation of God stands, having this seal: the Lord knows those who are his” (2 Tim. II). O Zion, O soul, who, as though placed upon a watchtower, awaits the coming of your Lord, do not fear; do not be disturbed. For if winds rush in and floods flow, you may be wearied, but you cannot be overthrown, since you are founded upon the rock (Matt. VII). For the Lord has founded Zion, who “will not allow us to be tempted beyond what we are able,” but “will make with the temptation a way out, that we may be able to endure it” (1 Cor. X).

This is the consolation of the wretched in this life; this is strength in temptations; this is security in tribulation; this is steadfastness in adversity. Certainly the Lord has founded Zion—the soul exalted by contemplation of God—establishing it upon the foundation of true humility. It is placed all the more securely and firmly inasmuch as, tested by frequent temptations, it can neither be deceived when unwary, nor enticed when already proved, nor overcome when trained. Thus the Lord has founded Zion; and in her shall her poor—that is, the humble—hope. By adding knowledge, they add sorrow, so that they may one day glory in that blessedness of which the Lord says in the Gospel: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. V): in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom, with God the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, be honour and glory for ever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XXIV. On the beginning of the burden concerning Moab

The burden concerning the Philistines having been explained, [Col. 0455B] the prophetic discourse arms itself against Moab. I see that I must first explain to you the meaning of this name. As you well know, dearest brethren, holy Lot, after departing from Sodom, when his wife, looking back, had been changed into a statue of salt, went up the mountain with only his two daughters; and after dwelling in an unclean city, became a new inhabitant of a cave. There each daughter stole intercourse with her drunken father; the elder conceived Moab and the other Ammon, sons born of incest (Gen. XIX).

Moab is interpreted “from the father,” or “fatherly water.” The father, unaware, begot him by his daughter, not from the affection of love which lawfully joins those who unite in a certain sweetness of spirit, but from that discharge which is accustomed to flow, like water and without the savour of love, from one asleep or drunk. What shall I say, dearest brethren? Will you consider me blasphemous if I say that in these events holy Lot bore an image of the Lord and Saviour?

Remember, I ask you, that Judah in intercourse with Tamar, whom he believed to be a harlot (Gen. XXXVIII), and David in his unlawful embrace of Bathsheba (2 Sam. XI), according to the holy Fathers represented a figure of the Lord Jesus. Here likewise do not wonder at Jesus the great priest, as he was shown in Zechariah (Zech. III), in filthy garments. As you know, Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God (1 Cor. I). From God’s wisdom there are begotten two kinds of knowledge, as it were two daughters: practical and theoretical knowledge. When, therefore, the wisdom of God brought these daughters into the cave—that is, into the dark hearts of the Gentiles—they conceived, not from the father’s voluntary seed, which is charity, but from their own curiosity and vanity, as though from incest, a certain knowledge of divine and human matters: from a good father indeed, but not lawfully.

For Paul bears witness that even the wise of this world, through God’s revelation, learned many things concerning human and divine matters. He says: “What is known of God is manifest among them, for God revealed it to them” (Rom. I). It follows:

“Because Ar has been laid waste by night, Moab is silent” (Isa. XV). Recall, I ask you, that God was betrayed by night and mocked by night, and that, as night was drawing on, he is known to have been taken down from the cross. In this night Ar was laid waste; Ar is interpreted “adversary,” of whom the most blessed Peter says: “Be sober and watchful, because your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking whom he may devour” (1 Pet. V). This is that adversarial city, namely, the court of that strong man armed, who, overcome by one stronger coming upon him, both lost his spoils and cast away his weapons.

Yet Ar, the city, may also be understood as the multitude of human beings, which was opposed to God and worshipped wood and stones. It was in a sense laid waste by night, because, astonished by the passion and patience of the saints, very many desolated the adversarial city by withdrawing from it. Then surely Moab—that is, the wisdom of this world—was silent, having no power in its voice either to establish its own teaching or to invalidate Christ’s teaching.

It follows: “Because the wall has been laid waste by night, Moab is silent.” The wall of the adversarial city—that is, of hell—was idolatry, which we see laid waste throughout the whole world by the power of the Lord’s passion. Moreover, the wall of opposing doctrine was dialectic, or the subtlety of disputation. Christian simplicity, placed in night—that is, in persecutions—overthrew it and destroyed all its arguments by the sincerity of faith. Then surely Moab—that is, the understanding of this world—was silent when the Lord thundered over many waters, stopped the mouth of those speaking iniquity (Ps. LXII), and brought to nothing every form of knowledge exalting itself against the knowledge of God.

Therefore what follows took place: “The house and Dibon went up to the high places to mourn.” House is not only the name for walls with roof and foundation, but also for the household within the house, which according to good or bad habits is called a good or bad house. Therefore understand by the house of Moab the heart of the wise of this world, in which no small household of perceptions, thoughts, and affections is active. Dibon, moreover, which is interpreted “their flowing,” signifies the diversity and wantonness of those perceptions, thoughts, or even opinions.

It may also be understood thus: when Christ’s teaching shone forth, the house of Moab—that is, the household of philosophers, namely their disciples—and the city Dibon—that is, the multitude of teachers who had been accustomed joyfully to take part in the worship of idols—went up to those idols with mourning and demanded from demons answers and assistance against the Gospel. Yet because many of the wise men of this world were converted to Christ and renounced their errors, while many persisted in their innate malice, this burden touches both groups in these words, teaching that the former are weighed down by repentance and the latter by distress of heart.

For many philosophers, both disciples and teachers, like a house and a city, left the valley of error and climbed to the heights of virtue, confessing their sins with mourning and tears and humbly repenting of their former errors and blasphemies. And the prophet added: “Moab shall howl over Nebo and over Medeba.” Nebo is interpreted “sitting”; Medeba, “from a woodland.” Sitting pertains to teachers, according to the saying: “The scribes and Pharisees sat upon Moses’ chair” (Matt. XXIII). By the woodland, where there are barren and unfruitful trees and a dwelling-place not for people but for beasts, the uncultivated hearts of Gentiles are represented—[Col. 0457A] those who, adhering to teachers of error, defended their doctrines by the authority of the multitude.

Moab’s howling is therefore described over those teachers and peoples, whom it could not see withdrawing from its fellowship and converting to the Catholic faith without severe grief, signified by howling. Therefore it adds: “On all its heads is baldness.” Understand by the heads of Moab the most renowned teachers of the various schools: Socrates, Plato, Diogenes, and others of that kind. These indeed are the heads of Moab, the leaders of secular learning. Which of them is there whose hair was not shorn through Christ’s grace, when disciples who had been accustomed to cling to them as their heads departed from their school and joined themselves to the grace of our Saviour?

Surely we now see the philosophers bald, their wisdom being surpassed by the teaching of fishermen, and no one professing or following their school. Therefore the prophet fittingly adds: “Every beard shall be shaved.” So long as a man is beardless, he is judged a boy; but when bearded, he receives the name of a man. Philosophers were, as it were, bearded when peoples were governed by their wisdom and teaching. But when Christ’s Gospel resounded everywhere and refuted their errors, and they were believed by all to be foolish and senseless, they appeared like persons disfigured and dishonoured by shaven beards, reduced as it were to childish folly.

Let us now consider what follows:

“In its crossroads they are girded with sackcloth; and upon its roofs and in its streets every howl descends into weeping.” Three things are set forth here: crossroads, roofs, streets. In the crossroads are represented philosophers’ byways; on the roofs, pride; in the streets, a ruined life. They had byways in the deception of sophisms, pride from human esteem, and a ruined life from corruption of flesh and mind. Many of them, converted to the Lord, were punished in all the things in which they had sinned.

For their tricks and deceptions, represented by the crossroads, they are described as clothed in sackcloth as a sign of repentance; for their pride, through which, with swelling cheeks, they had been accustomed to pronounce opinions concerning divine and human matters as though positioned upon a roof, they are shown to utter the howl of confession and contrition; and for that broad road upon which they journeyed toward death, humbled [Col. 0457D] and washed in their own tears, they are declared to have returned to the narrow and confined way that leads to life (Matt. VII).

Thus he says: “In its crossroads”—without doubt, those of Moab—“they are girded with sackcloth,” because, recalling the byways and deceptions by which they had mocked human simplicity, girded with sackcloth, that is, afflicted by the harshness of repentance, they took care to appease by worthy satisfaction him against whom they had sinned. “And upon its roofs and in its streets every howl descends into weeping.”

The Lord says in the Gospel: “What you have heard in the ear, preach upon the roofs” (Matt. XX). For a certain height and manifestation are indicated by the roof. By streets, likewise, which signify breadth, understand the broad way of destruction, upon which they themselves walked and furnished others examples of walking. But those who had ascended upon roofs through self-exaltation came down humbled through compunction; and those who had publicly proclaimed their errors as though in streets gave forth, in the hearing of all, the howl of a pitiable voice. It follows:

“Heshbon shall cry out, and Elealeh; their voice has been heard as far as Jahaz.” Heshbon is interpreted “thoughts,” Elealeh “ascent,” Jahaz “deed” or “command.” When the philosophers saw many thousands of people daily flocking to the faith and sacraments of Christ, they were disturbed; nor can it easily be said how great was then the turmoil in their thoughts—how they wondered, now grew indignant, now, lifted up in pride, resisted. All this is expressed through the cry of [Col. 0458B] Heshbon and Elealeh, that is, of thought and exaltation. Nor did this cry and murmuring cease until they proceeded from speech to action, either by openly persecuting or by obeying the faith and the divine commands. Therefore their voice was heard as far as Jahaz.

These matters, brothers, ought to have been expounded morally; but fear and trembling came upon me, and darkness covered me (Ps. 54); moreover, zeal for the house of God consumed me (Ps. 68). Indignation presses, grief drives me on, tears burst forth—yet anger restrains them, rivalry absorbs them. “My zeal has made me pine away” (Ps. 118), and now my speech longs to rage; but rather it bids me mourn for my mother, the Roman Church, which, stretching both hands toward heaven, seems to cry in a pitiable voice:

[Col. 0458C] stretching toward heaven, she seems to cry in a pitiable voice: “The sons of my mother have fought against me” (Song 1).

For although that dove of Christ is one—Christ’s beautiful one, Christ’s perfect one—to whom belong one God, one faith, one baptism (Eph. 4), nevertheless, because of diverse peoples and nations, many Churches are spoken of, united in one, subject to one, obedient to one. This is the holy Roman Church, whose sons, as you have heard, have fought against her. For some “were estranged from the womb; they went astray from the belly; they spoke falsehood” (Ps. 57). Moreover, “they have spoken iniquity on high” (Ps. 72). For at Pavia the kings of the earth stood by, and the princes assembled together against the Lord and against Alexander, His Christ [Col. 0458D] (Ps. 2). There many dogs surrounded him; an assembly of evildoers besieged him (Ps. 21). There false witnesses rose against him (Ps. 26): John and Guy; but iniquity lied to itself (ibid.).

Wretched and miserable men, who, descending from Jerusalem to Jericho, fell among robbers (Luke 10)! This is that utterly criminal Octavian, who, like a robber lying hidden in ambush for a long time, judged the papacy to be plunder and the Church to be spoils. Wretched man, who climbed into his father’s bed and defiled his couch. This is that most arrogant Haman, who prepared a cross for Mordecai, who compelled the king to pronounce a sentence of death upon Israel (Esth. 7). O when will the king awaken? When will he rise from his kingdom? When will he spend sleeplessly this dark night covered with the gloom of death [Col. 0459A]? When will he hear in his Annals how many good things our Mordecai has done for him? When will he perceive that, in his own presence, that most wicked man strives to oppress the queen herself?

This is the queen—not the wife of King Artaxerxes, but of Christ—of whom the Prophet says: “The Queen stood at your right hand” (Ps. 44). This is she who today, in her infirm members and in those less knowledgeable in the law, cries and says: “Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you pasture, where you lie down at noon” (Song 1). Rightly she answers with terror and reproach: “If you do not know yourself, go forth” (ibid.). How many today, brothers, not knowing the Scriptures or the power of God, have gone forth from the Church; separating themselves from Christ’s vicar, they follow the forerunner of Antichrist.

Brothers, [Col. 0459B] let no one deceive you with empty words (Eph. 5). Let no one say to you, “Behold, here is Christ,” or, “Behold, there” (Matt. 24), since Christ is always in Peter’s faith—a faith which the Holy Roman Church received in a special manner from Peter and keeps in the Rock, which is Christ. Let us therefore consider where this Church began, by whom it began, and whither it proceeded.

“The Lord said, This Gospel must be preached throughout the whole world, beginning from Jerusalem” (Luke 24). Therefore its beginnings were in Jerusalem. It was she who then, small and as if nursing, when the days of Pentecost were fulfilled, was in one place, and whom the Holy Spirit, visiting in tongues of fire (Acts 2), enlightened with wisdom and inflamed with love. From that time the voices of all nations became common in the Church’s mouth; and what was afterward accomplished in the conversion of all nations was anticipated in the union of all languages.

Peter was the first prince of this Church, to whom it was said: “Upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matt. 16); and again: “Feed my sheep” (John 21); and: “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven” (Matt. 16), etc. This is the Church which the holy Apostle calls that “of the firstborn”; the fullness of whose power, in its prince, first migrating from East to West by the authority of the Holy Spirit, took its seat in the Roman Church.

No sound-minded person doubts that the Roman Church is to be called, not its walls and stones, but the clergy first ordained at Rome by most blessed Peter [Col. 0459D]. Thus, as Clement succeeded Peter, Anacletus Clement, and Evaristus Anacletus, so indeed one after another of that clergy whom Peter ordained and established occupied the place and dignity. Thus “sons have been born to us in place of fathers” (Ps. 44). At length, when Constantine granted it and the Church also received temporal dominion, they were by human law established as “princes over all the earth” (ibid.).

From this point, because of the particular pre-eminence of that Church, its bishops, priests, and deacons were called cardinals, deriving the honour of this name from those of whom it is written: “For the pillars of the earth are the Lord’s, and He set the world upon them” (1 Sam. 2). For as the supreme pontiff obtains Peter’s primacy through legitimate and, so to speak, hereditary succession, so the authority of the other apostles is plainly transferred to the cardinals [Col. 0460A].

This is the Roman Church: whoever does not communicate with it is a heretic. It belongs to her to take thought for all, judge all, and provide for all; to her, in Peter, this saying is addressed: “And you, once converted, strengthen your brethren” (Luke 22). Whatever she decrees, I receive; I approve what she approves, and I condemn what she condemns. It belongs to her to choose for us the shepherd and bishop of our souls (1 Pet. 2). For what fleshly generation was in the Old Testament in the appointment of a high priest, regular election is in the New: a kind of spiritual generation. For, as it were, he who elects begets, and he who is elected is begotten.

Thus, brothers, what it was for Aaron to beget sons, it was for Christ to choose apostles. Among Aaron’s other sons Eleazar is preferred; among the other apostles Peter is set before them. And Peter, having spiritually begotten many, preferred Clement above the rest; and when Clement himself also had an abundance of sons, Anacletus alone succeeded him when he died, through the election of that very curia, as by a certain spiritual generation. Therefore, just as those whom the Church herself chose were always Peter’s lawful successors, so also those whom they themselves chose in each age as their assistants were the true successors of the other apostles.

Thus, from blessed Sylvester and his cardinals down to Adrian of our own time and his cardinals, we have no uncertainty concerning the legitimate succession. Behold: after Adrian, the lawful successor of Peter, died, the legitimate succession of the other apostles stands in the cardinals. Consider now Roland and Octavian placed in their midst—let us meanwhile call them thus—as if they were in the womb of their mother, the Roman Church, now in labour. I ask you, my brothers, is not this birth like Rebekah’s labour? Behold unhappy Esau, red and hairy: how he twists the very maternal entrails, and with raging hands attacks that simple Jacob whom the whole harmonious concert of the inner parts embraces with all its force! For you heard how that unhappy man, filled with a demon, tore the mantle from the neck of that most holy man [Col. 0460D]. And when he did not yield to him as he wished, he came forth from the womb to his mother’s utmost sorrow, and by the hairs of his greed and ambition struck supreme horror into those who saw him.

Two followed him, who likewise “were estranged from the womb, went astray from the belly” (Ps. 57), while all the rest chose Alexander, adhered to Alexander, and followed Alexander. Behold now John and Guy on one side, with Octavian among them; behold the rest of the curia on the other side, and Alexander among them. I ask: of whom is this voice spoken: “They went out from us, but they were not of us”? Surely either the Roman curia is in those three, or in all these others; or else it has perished from the earth, and that prayer of the Saviour was uttered in vain, of which He says: “But I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail” [Col. 0461A] (Luke 22)—which is madness to suppose. For who would be so senseless as to imagine that, after so many cardinal bishops, priests, and deacons were excluded, the force of the Roman curia remained seated in those two?

Thus now, brothers, I shall speak of these men as though they were still established within the Church of blessed Peter, where they had held the election, and as though they had merely separated from one another. Certainly the Roman Church has not perished; certainly no reason or human understanding admits that, with the rest rejected, it remained in those three. It follows, therefore, that it retained the force of apostolic dignity in that multitude which elected Alexander. Far be it from us to say that five cardinal bishops and fifteen or more cardinal priests or deacons went out from those three, rather than those three from these men—whose reputation was more celebrated, life holier, judgment deeper, number greater, and authority more exalted.

Since, therefore, it is evident that the Roman Church is the one that elected Alexander, and since it is certain that those men went out from it, whoever afterward adhered to them—whether Ymarus himself or another—joined himself not to Christians but to heretics; not to Catholics but to schismatics; not to the Church but to the synagogue of Satan, becoming himself a heretic and a schismatic. Let enemies say whatever they wish and lie as much as they wish: where the Roman Church is seen with the eyes, proved by reason, and confirmed by authority, there is my heart, there is my mind, there is my affection. From her faith—which, because Christ prays, will not fail [Col. 0461C]; from her unity—which the perversity of schismatics, while Christ preserves it, will not divide; from her subjection—whose prince will open heaven to me—neither death nor life nor any other creature, with God’s grace helping me, shall separate me (Rom. 8).

Let this suffice, brothers, as a warning to you, because of the wicked lips and deceitful tongues with which this country burns; so that, after our strength has been somewhat restored through silence, we may return to the delights of God’s word, to whom be honour and glory for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXV. A moral exposition of the same chapter

As your charity remembers, yesterday we expounded, as we could, the opening portions of the burden of Moab according to the prophecy [Col. 0461D]. But we postponed until today the moral exposition which an intervening fear prevented us then from pursuing. First, then, according to the laws of tropology, let us inquire who this Moab is, so that we may more clearly investigate how he either bears a burden or is burdened.

Moab is interpreted “from the father,” signifying, to be sure, something that proceeds from a father into a son; or those themselves who live according to what they have naturally derived from their father. Holy Scripture, indeed, calls someone “father” in many ways: by nature, by creation, by adoption, by imitation, by age, and by dignity.

By nature: when one man is called the father of another man who has been carnally begotten by him, as Abraham is Isaac’s father, Isaac Jacob’s father, and Jacob is called the father of the twelve patriarchs. Or indeed when any one ancestor is called the father of all born from his stock. Hence the Lord says to the Jews: “Do not glory that you have Abraham as your father.”

By creation: as God is declared the Father of every creature, from whom, indeed, every fatherhood in heaven and on earth takes its name.

By adoption: as all the elect are called sons of God, the Apostle saying: “You have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry: Abba—Father” (Rom. 8). For all who glory in this adoption steadfastly cry to God: “Our Father, who are in heaven” (Matt. 6).

[Col. 0462B] By imitation: as Christ Himself calls the faithless Jews sons of the devil: “You,” He says, “are from your father the devil” (John 8). That this was said by reason of imitation is made clear by the sentence which follows, for He says: “You wish to do the works of your father” (ibid.). Hence also, by imitating Abraham’s faith, those whom the Lord raised from stones are called sons of Abraham.

By age: as Paul says to Timothy, “Do not rebuke an older man, but exhort him as a father” (1 Tim. 5).

By dignity: as Naaman’s servants, when he was angry with Elisha because he seemed to heal the leprosy from which he suffered not by sight, prayer, and touch but by a command, nevertheless say to him as he departs indignantly: “Father, if the prophet had told you some great thing, you certainly ought to have done it; how much more, when he said to you: ‘Wash, and you shall be clean’?” (2 Kings 5).

Therefore, to the Father of all, who created us, we owe what we are; to the Father who adopted us as sons, we owe whatever goodness we have; and to the father who begot us in the flesh we owe our mortality, corruptibility, and subjection to various passions. From our fleshly father—that is, from corruptible nature—we possess impulses of lust, fears of desire, assaults of anger, the languor of sadness, disordered fear, and the swelling of pride. Opposed to that people is the one which the good Father, who adopted rather than begot us, graciously instils in us: love, joy, peace, patience, humility, chastity, and the rest. That people, then, is mystically called Moab; this one Israel.

Against this Moab war is undertaken for us. It is also fittingly interpreted “paternal water,” because these corruptions are implanted in us from the flow of paternal seed. May the Lord Jesus be with us and impose such a burden upon this Moab that, though it cannot be wholly destroyed in us, it may nevertheless be so suppressed that it cannot reign in us. Let us therefore hear this burden of Moab: “Because Ar has been devastated by night, Moab has fallen silent. Because the wall has been devastated by night, Moab has fallen silent.”

Night, as you know, signifies tribulation. Ar is interpreted “adversary,” and it was a city of the Moabites. That people of natural passions builds a city in our soul when original sins break out into actual sins: while we yield our members as weapons of iniquity to sin [Col. 0463A], and turn what we first suffered as punishment for sin into a willing practice and use of sin. As many sins as we embrace, so many most wicked citizens we receive into this city. This city is opposed to the other city, which is founded upon virtues and is therefore shown to be contrary to this one, which consists of vices.

The wall of the Moabite city is obstinacy, which excludes the humility of repentance and stops up the voice of confession. Come, brothers: when all things happen prosperously for us, when happy times smile upon us, when abundance of every possession produces luxury, this Moab rises more fiercely and afflicts more vehemently. It inflames the flesh, dissolves the mind, suggests every harmful and pleasurable thing. There arises in the soul a certain cry of vices, crying one to another and saying: “Lay it bare, lay it bare, even to its foundation” (Ps. 136).

Accordingly, the most gracious Saviour acts as the best physician and first cuts away the cause of diseases. When joyful things are withdrawn somewhat, and harsh and sorrowful things follow, pleasures too disappear. Thus a person compelled to return into himself finds there nothing bright, nothing serene, nothing pleasing, nothing delightful; but all things dark, all obscure, all filled with the horror of night and darkness. In this night Ar is devastated, when delights become worthless and pleasures perish: luxurious banquets and unlawful drinking no longer entice. The wall also is devastated—that is, the obstinacy of the mind—and all its strongholds, namely excuses for sins, are destroyed.

[Col. 0463C] Dearest brothers, those are mistaken who, remaining frequently or continually in gluttony and drunkenness, idleness and dissipation, or in the company of women or parasites, flatter themselves that they are chaste. I have learned by experience, dearest ones—and I believe you have also—that our Moab, struck as though by certain hammers through frequent fasts, continual vigils, and unceasing labours, raises its head even when crushed; and after a long period of silence, with revived cries it presses the unwary and overwhelms the unprepared.

Therefore, brothers, whenever gluttony creates a distaste for humbler food, whenever drowsiness or bodily heat instils a horror of vigils, think, I ask you, of the incentives of lust and the foulness of uncleanness; and, conversely, of the sweetness of chastity, purity of affections, and tranquillity of the members. Then all that had previously been thought burdensome will be found very easy.

Happy is the soul to whom Moab has been silent in this way, as at Nebo and Medeba, of which the text continues: “Over Nebo and Medeba Moab shall howl.” Nebo is interpreted “resting,” Medeba “from a forest.” This resting signifies security, the mother of negligence and the producer of carelessness. Some, I say it with grief, who after many crimes have professed this penitential life surrender themselves so completely to idleness and sloth, and so despise the necessary exercises of the order, as though they were “a nation that has done righteousness and has not forsaken the law of its God.” Others, dishonoured by daily passions and continually receiving the missiles of their enemies, nevertheless sit secure and laugh [Col. 0464A], as though the enemy had already fallen or every inward battle had ceased.

These too are said to be “from a forest,” which is Medeba, because they are unfruitful, wandering, and unstable; in them dwell those spiritual beasts of which the Prophet says: “Do not hand over to beasts the souls that confess you” (Ps. 73). For such people Moab does not fall silent; rather, with frequent howling it suggests vices, introduces unclean affections, and urges every evil thing. By Moab’s howling is meant the violent temptation of natural passions. And it is added:

“In all his heads is baldness; every beard shall be shaved.” The heads of Moab, it seems to me, are fittingly called the three natural faculties in a human being: the irascible, the concupiscible, and the rational [Col. 0464B]. From their corruption, I think, proceed the incentives of all natural passions. Hair is an ornament of the head; a beard is the sign of manly strength.

Thus the movement of anger is, as it were, adorned when a person is moved against his own vices, according to the saying: “Be angry, and do not sin” (Ps. 4). It is also adorned when it is wisely taken up as zeal for God against despisers of the law, according to the saying: “My zeal has made me pine away, because my enemies have forgotten your words” (Ps. 118). Indeed, it is adorned when this zeal is often rewarded by the Lord in many ways. For Phinehas, because of the merit of this anger of which we speak—by which he pierced fornicators with a spear—earned an everlasting priesthood (Num. 25); and Jehu son of Nimshi, because of the zeal with which he burned against the house of Ahab, by God’s favour transmitted Israel’s kingdom to his descendants down to the fourth generation (2 Kings 9).

Likewise the foulness of the concupiscible movement is concealed by a kind of adornment when one uses it only to beget children, or when, in taking food or drink, it is admitted only for the body’s necessary support. Hence a certain saint did not hesitate to compare Abraham’s marriage with blessed John’s virginity, considering the obedience by which, in the very marital act, Abraham obeyed the divine will, and also the honourableness of his intention in begetting children. Thus that concupiscible movement, without which the marital debt is not rendered, was covered, as it were, by a certain splendid veil.

[Col. 0464D] The rational faculty also is adorned in this way, if we do not use reason contrary to reason. For thefts, robberies, adulteries, and the other vices are perpetrated against reason’s laws; yet they are not practised without the operation of reason. A robber cannot, without the keenness of reason, select a place suitable for ambush or a time convenient for the business. Likewise an adulterer, borrowing cunning from reason’s force, looks for the night, the bedchamber, and the husband’s absence. Therefore those who misuse reason in vices deform the rational faculty itself. But he who always exercises it in virtues and saving knowledge adorns it with a most beautiful ornament.

Therefore it is rightly said of Moab, in whom all things are corrupt: “In all his heads is baldness,” because those faculties from whose corruption all vices proceed, and which the wise use well, appear ugly, deformed, stripped, and made bald of every virtue in those over whom natural impulses rule [Col. 0465A]. It is also rightly added: “Every beard shall be shaved.” For whoever yields himself to the passions themselves and gives himself over to the slavery of vices is recognized as stripped of every virtue, beardless, and as if effeminately dissolved.

Let your charity consider this, brothers. It is much easier to avoid vices before a fall than, once one has yielded them one’s hand, to withdraw oneself from their power. But if anyone has become entangled in the bond of habit, he is found weak and unarmed in all things, and, as it were, womanish. It follows:

“In his crossroads they have girded themselves with sackcloth; upon his roofs and in his streets every howling descends into weeping” [Col. 0465B].

Of the Moabites, some are at crossroads, others in streets, others on roofs. A person at a crossroads can turn this way or that, lest he be seen by everyone. A street lies open to everyone’s eyes, and nothing in it can be hidden. In the land of Jerusalem, it is customary for house roofs not to be raised high but spread flat; those wishing to announce or preach something to the people climb onto the roofs.

Therefore those who sin secretly are Moab in the crossroads; those who openly defile themselves with crimes are in the streets; those who not only sin but excuse and proclaim their sins are on the roofs. Thus, for one who sins secretly, simple contrition of heart and body is sufficient, fittingly signified by sackcloth. But one who openly commits every shameful deed needs howling, so that the genuineness of his conversion may not be hidden when the greatness of his crimes was not hidden. And one who, swollen with pride like Sodom, proclaims his sin must descend into weeping, so that, as in sinning he had climbed the mountain of exaltation, so humbled he may descend into the valley of lamentation.

Further, because a crossroads is called the place where three roads meet, the crossroads may signify the threefold mode of sinning: thought, speech, and deed. The threefold power of the soul through which every sin occurs—memory, will, and reason—may likewise fittingly be called a crossroads. Therefore, one who yields to threefold concupiscence, who sins in thought, word, and deed; whose memory thought defiles, whose will pleasure stains, and whose reason consent to sin weakens—such a person miserably dwells at the crossroads of Moab [Col. 0465D].

Sackcloth is a sign of mourning. This is the mourning of which the Lord says in the Gospel: “Woe to you who laugh now, for you shall mourn and weep” (Luke 6). Therefore, because those at Moab’s crossroads rejoice when they do evil and exult in most wicked things (Prov. 2), they shall be girded with sackcloth—that is, they shall waste away in miserable mourning.

By the roofs, if you please, understand the power and eminence of this world; by the streets, in which games and spectacles are displayed, freedom to sin. To those, therefore, who glory in this world’s elevation, or who, restrained by no bridle of discipline, plunge headlong into vices, holy Isaiah foretells descent and weeping: namely, that in return for the power by which they exalt themselves above others, as though standing upon roofs, and sin without anyone restraining them, as though standing in streets, they may know that they shall descend with howling to hell and be cast into outer darkness, where there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth (Matt. 8).

How they reached this misery the prophetic speech teaches: “Heshbon,” it says, “and Elealeh shall cry out; their voice has been heard as far as Jahaz.” We have given two meanings for the things set forth above: the first according to the repentance of converts, the second according to the everlasting punishment of the wicked. Let us retain the same order in this interpretation. Heshbon is interpreted “thoughts,” Elealeh “ascent.” Therefore, if you ask how, clothed in the sackcloth of repentance and grief, uttering the howl of confession, and descending to tears of contrition, they came from the crossroads to simplicity of life, from the roofs of pride to humility [Col. 0466B], from the streets of self-will to the narrowness of holy necessity—if, I say, you ask by what way they have proceeded thus far, the divine speech tells you: “Heshbon and Elealeh cried out.”

Perverse thoughts do not cease to weary the wretched soul with diverse temptations until the will is enticed to action; this is to have carried the cry of its voice as far as Jahaz. Therefore our thoughts must be discerned, dearest brothers, so that, if they suggest perverse things, we may immediately pass by with the ear stopped; but if useful or honourable things, we may pursue into action what they suggest. In either case, however, let the burden be recognized: for whether we voluntarily punish what we have committed, resist perverse things, or consent to everything best, we shall not escape without a burden that either weighs upon or oppresses us.

But because by our own strength we can neither avoid evil nor practise good, let us pray to God that He Himself may grant us both the strength to resist and the ability to act, through His beloved Son, our Lord, who lives and reigns with Him and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXVI. On what is written: “Upon this the liberated Moabites shall howl” (Isa. 15), etc.

Still, brothers, the burden of Moab is being handled in our hands, in which certain mystical meanings are expressed in the names of cities and places [Col. 0466D]. We have said that by Moab are prophetically figured secular wisdom, or certainly the wise men of this world themselves, who resist evangelical teaching. Of them it is said: “Heshbon and Elealeh shall cry out; their voice has been heard as far as Jahaz.” It follows: “Upon this the liberated Moabites shall howl; his soul shall howl for itself.”

There was a great cry in the thoughts of the wise when, on the one hand, they were refuted by the truth plainly revealed through the Gospel, while, on the other, swollen with pride, they opposed divine wisdom. From that point this conflict came to an end, when some, wishing to please men, “were put to shame because God despised them” (Ps. 52); while others, humbling themselves under the mighty hand of God (1 Pet. 5), became, in proportion as they had been slower to believe and subtler in inquiry, more ready in that very faith and doctrine [Col. 0467A].

These are the liberated Moabites: either because they freed themselves from the nets of deceptive wisdom, or because they proceeded readily along the evangelical way. They howled over what they had previously done, not only with the sound of their voices but also with the inward affection of their hearts. In the words, “Upon this the liberated Moabites shall howl,” outward confession is expressed; in what follows, “His soul shall howl for itself,” inward contrition is expressed.

It happened that those who, renouncing Moabite wisdom, followed the folly of the cross became more capable of divine knowledge in proportion as they had been more acute in human learning. Hence the prophet adds in the person of the Lord: “My heart shall cry out to Moab.” The heart of God is called the hidden meaning of sacred Scripture, because in it His will and the hidden mysteries of His counsels are revealed. Therefore God’s heart cries out to Moab when the mind of one who passes from worldly philosophy to God is more abundantly illumined by the light of spiritual knowledge: “Its bars shall reach as far as Zoar, a three-year-old heifer.”

Understand Moab’s bars as dialectical arguments, which in converted wise men began to benefit the Church they had harmed. For Moab’s bars reached as far as Zoar when the subtle arguments of philosophers benefited the Church. The Church, in the condition in which she then stood, is rightly called Zoar, that is, “small,” concerning which it is said in the Song: “Our sister is small and has no breasts. What shall we do for our sister, because she is small?” (Song 8).

She was indeed very small when she had not yet gone beyond the boundaries of the Jews and lay hidden, small and despised, even among them. She was small, I say, not in merit but in number. Hence fruitful Peninnah—that is, the Synagogue—insults barren Hannah, that is, the Church, until “the barren woman bore many, and she who had many sons became weak” (1 Sam. 1–2).

Zoar, that is, the Church, is aptly called a three-year-old heifer (*vitula conternans*), that is, one entering her third year: the first year being before the Law, the second under the Law, the third under grace. Or the first year may be understood as under the patriarchs, the second under the prophets, and the third under the apostles. This species of animal abounds in milk and has a very great attachment to its offspring. Unless tricked by artifice, it neither admits a strange offspring to its teats nor customarily lets down milk unless its own is present. These features fittingly apply to mother Church [Col. 0467D], who abounds in the milk of love and sweeter doctrine, and judges those whom she herself does not regenerate through the washing of sweet water to be strangers, unworthy of the most sacred mysteries. She may also be called three-year-old because, strong in faith, hope, and love, she advances to perfect maturity, to the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ.
