Therefore, when Moab’s bars have reached as far as Zoar—that is, when the wise men of this world have brought every support and argument of their wisdom to the Church—then occurs what the prophet immediately adds: “For by the ascent of Luhith he shall go up weeping, and on the way of Horonaim they shall raise the cry of contrition.”

Luhith is interpreted “cheeks.” In the cheeks, indeed, the condition of the inner person is often perceived [Col. 0468A]. Fear covers them with pallor, shame with redness, grief with horror, joy with brightness, love with sweetness. There are two things by which we judge the state of a human mind: deed and speech. For “out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks” (Matt. 12), and everyone acts according to what he loves.

Therefore Moab goes weeping up the ascent of Luhith when any wise man entering the Church, pierced with compunction for past sins, ascends by word and deed together to the heights of virtues. “And on the way,” it says, “of Horonaim he shall raise the cry of contrition.” This is that narrow way which leads to life (Matt. 7), namely the eye of the needle through which a camel, a humped animal, cannot pass (Matt. 19). It is aptly called the opening of sorrow, because whoever gives himself to this narrow opening will consider nothing sweeter than grieving. He grieves for unlawful things he has committed; he grieves for adversities which he feels in the present; he grieves for future evils which he fears; he grieves for future goods which he desires.

Therefore, while set upon this way of Horonaim, the wise men of the world raise the cry of contrition, knowing that “a contrite and humbled heart God does not despise” (Ps. 50).

“For the waters of Nimrim shall be deserted.” Nimrim is interpreted “leopard,” or “transgressors.” In leopards there is variety, and in variety impiety is understood. Therefore understand the waters of Nimrim as secular philosophy, in which there is such variety of sects and opinions that what one school asserts another destroys [Col. 0468C]; what this one approves, that one disapproves; and what one judges best, another judges worst. Yet in all of them one impiety reigns: they exchange God’s truth for a lie and serve the creature rather than the Creator.

But in those converted to the Lord, the waters of Nimrim are deserted, because those instructed in evangelical doctrine regard what were formerly gains as losses for Christ. “For the grass has withered, the sprout has failed, all greenness has perished.” The irrational herd feeds upon grass; if it should happen to wither, it does not even care to touch it. Thus, by the name of grass is expressed that learning of the philosophers by which they used to address and teach the uneducated populace. But “the grass withered and the flower fell” (1 Pet. 1), because [Col. 0468D] the Lord breathed upon it. For while God’s Spirit blows everywhere and breathes heavenly teaching into mortal hearts, all that learning has withered so thoroughly that it does not even delight rustic simplicity. As the grass withered, every greenness perished, because the verdure of glory which they possessed through popular esteem immediately faded. It follows:

According to the magnitude of their work, so also their visitation. “Visitation” may be understood both in relation to punishment and to advancement. “I will visit evils upon them,” he says, “and I will make my arrows complete in them” (Hos. 4). And elsewhere: “I will not visit your daughters when they have committed fornication” (ibid.). But God has visited us in his salvation; and “the Dayspring from on high, visiting us, has enlightened those who sat in darkness and the shadow of death” (Luke 1). Here understand what is more pleasing. [Col. 0469A] If it means punishment, understand that they were so visited according to the magnitude of their wicked work that they received a fitting recompense for their sins, either through inward contrition or through outward affliction. But if it means advancement, observe that, as great and exalted as they seemed to themselves in their own eyes, so humble were they made when the Spirit visited them. Or indeed they were so visited that, according to the measure with which they had measured—renouncing worldly glory for Christ’s name—the abundance of Christ’s grace was measured out to them. Thus visited, they shall be led to the torrent of willows.

This kind of tree is said to have such a nature that its seed, when drunk, takes away the power of generation. Hence it not unfittingly signifies the virtue of chastity; or those who, for love of purity, despising the propagation of children, delight to dwell in spiritual [Col. 0469B] torrents. Therefore Moab—that is, every wise man converted to the Lord—goes from strength to strength (Ps. 83), from knowledge of himself to repentance, from repentance to humility, from humility to chastity.

Willows may also be understood as barren and unfruitful people, who, dwelling amid the pleasures of this age as though amid torrents, are rendered devoid of every spiritual fruit. After their conversion, orators and philosophers were led to govern and instruct such persons, either by the teachers of the Church to whom they had attached themselves, or by the Holy Spirit, so that they might teach the faith which they had attacked and uphold the doctrine which they had formerly detested.

The torrents of willows may also signify tribulations and sufferings, [Col. 0469C] which they too endured together with ruined men, imitating him who “drank from the torrent in the way, and therefore lifted up his head” (Ps. 119).

Then the prophet shows how all these things came about: “For,” he says, “the cry has gone round the border of Moab.” This is the cry of apostolic preaching: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matt. 4). It could leave none of this world’s wise men untouched, when “their sound went out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the inhabited world” (Ps. 18).

It is added: “His howling reaches as far as Gallim, and his cry as far as the Well of Elim.” Gallim is interpreted as “heaps of sand.” Therefore the howling of Moab, in those who with foolish devotion mourned the repentant persons who had turned away [Col. 0469D] from their error, reaches as far as heaps of sand, in which there is nothing firm or stable, since they are easily scattered by every wind. And its cry, in those who have themselves been converted, reaches as far as the Well of Elim, which is interpreted as “rams”; because both the hardening of the former deserved dispersal, and the repentance of the latter deserved consolation from the well of rams—that is, from the teaching of the apostles.

He says, therefore: “His howling reaches as far as Gallim, and his cry as far as the Well of Elim,” so that he may teach that the same race of men are pierced with compunction in some by barren howling, in others by health-giving crying. For Holy Scripture has this custom: when speaking of one people, it now pronounces good things, now evil things, concerning that same people. Thus the Apostle, writing to the Romans concerning the Jews, says: “According to [Col. 0470A] the Gospel, indeed, they are enemies for your sake; but according to election, most beloved for the fathers’ sake” (Rom. 11). He called the same persons enemies and most beloved because within that people some were found to be enemies, persecuting Christ, while others were most beloved, faithfully clinging to Christ.

You will often find this rule of speech in Isaiah; unless you observe it carefully, everything will seem confused and contradictory to you. Thus, although under the one name or nation of Moab he understands the wise men of this world as prefigured—among whom some were found reprobate, others elect—he treats each group so subtly that, without changing the name, he seems to utter contrary judgments about different individuals as though about one.

Therefore, since Moab made no progress among the reprobate, howling and crying against sound doctrine, but, like heaps of sand, [Col. 0470B] was either gathered together or scattered by the wind of vanity, it is fittingly said of Moab: “His howling reaches as far as Gallim, and his cry as far as the Well of Elim.” It follows:

“For the waters of Dibon are filled with blood.” Dibon is interpreted as “flowing,” signifying those who, professing themselves wise, became foolish and sank into every vain and shameful thing. Their waters—that is, their teaching—are filled with blood: namely, that blood from which the Prophet asks to be delivered when he says, “Deliver me from blood-guiltiness, O God” (Ps. 50); and of which Isaiah himself says: “Their hands are full of blood” (Isa. 1).

Come, brothers: as many philosophers as they enrolled in their sect, so many did they strike down with the sword of impiety. “For their feet are swift to shed blood,” because they dealt deceitfully with their tongues; “the poison [Col. 0470C] of asps is under their lips” (Ps. 13). Thus we should rejoice. Let no one wonder that very many philosophers preferred the Well of Elim to the heaps of sand—that is, apostolic teaching to worldly wisdom—because the waters of Dibon are filled with blood. For perverse teaching does not give life to the souls of those whom it deceives, but kills them; nor does it cleanse them from defilement, but stains them with the blood of sin.

And the prophet added: “For I will place additions upon Dibon: a lion upon those who have fled from Moab, and upon the remnant of the land.” Now he plainly separates what is precious from what is vile. “Upon those,” he says, “who have fled from Moab, [I will place] a lion”—that is, for their benefit and advancement, I will place additions upon Dibon. For I will add blows to their blows, [Col. 0470D] pains to their pains, anxieties to their anxieties, fears to their fears; for here also they will rot away in their flowing state, which is the meaning of Dibon, and at last, to be tortured by everlasting punishments, they will descend to hell. And this will benefit those who have fled from Moab and, in fleeing, have escaped the lion who goes about seeking whom he may devour (1 Pet. 5).

And this will benefit not only those who have fled from the lion of Moab, but also the remnant of the land—those, that is, who have fled the lion, namely the devil, abandoning every earthly vice and pursuing virtues. They will benefit from the punishment of those who, persevering among the lost Moabites, will receive additional punishments for the flux of temporal things.

It may also be read thus: “I will place additions upon Dibon.” And, as though you asked which Dibon he meant, he adds in explanation: “Upon those [Col. 0471A] who have fled from Moab.” Since Dibon is also interpreted as “sufficient sorrow,” it signifies those who, in the manner described above, weeping and mourning, fled from Moab, abandoning the fellowship of unbelievers and cleaving to the Christian people. Upon their distress, which they had in repentance, the Lord placed additions of persecutions; for “to them it has been given not only to believe in Christ, but also to suffer for Christ” (Phil. 1).

For in explaining what additions he was to place, he says, “a lion,” expressing the persecution which that roaring one stirred up against the faithful—not only against those converted from worldly wisdom, but also, as we said above, against the remnant of the land. But if “the remnant of the land” is the correct reading, then as Gentiles are understood in Moab, so understand [Col. 0471B] Jews in the remnant of the land, concerning whom the Apostle says: “A remnant has been saved according to the election of grace” (Rom. 11). For this persecution by the lion troubled both Gentiles and Jews who received faith in Christ.

Come, brothers: because of the abundance of proper names, we have briefly and continuously, as best we could, unfolded this most obscure passage of the prophet, so that it might be understood more easily, slip less easily from memory, and the moral exposition which ought to follow might be heard more pleasantly. I wish to defer that exposition until tomorrow, lest I seem to burden you when you are either filled with food or wearied by work. Yet strengthened by your prayers, whatever the Spirit who reveals mysteries may suggest, tomorrow we shall set forth for your edification, to the praise and glory [Col. 0471C] of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the same Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXVII. On the Same Chapter Morally Expounded

Be present now, most beloved brothers, and listen attentively and pray in mind, so that we may be able to expound tropologically, for the edification of conduct, those things which yesterday we surveyed according to the prophetic exposition. For they are exceedingly deep and veiled by the covering of proper names; therefore both hearer and expositor need no little attentiveness.

Your charity well remembers in what way we said that Moab, which is interpreted “from the father,” [Col. 0471D] according to the moral sense figures those vices which pass from father to son through carnal generation, such as incitements to lust, goads of anger, and the like. Yet even those who, abandoning these very vices, have entered into spiritual conflict against them may in one respect be called Moab so long as they are troubled by temptations of this sort.

Among these, some who are less unencumbered are overcome; in them is fulfilled what he says: “Heshbon shall cry, and Elealeh,” and the rest. Others, because they contend unencumbered, “cry to the Lord when they are troubled” (Ps. 119), and “he delivers them from their necessities” (Ps. 106); concerning them he adds: “Therefore the unencumbered of Moab shall howl; his soul shall howl to itself.”

It seems necessary first to say who the unencumbered of Moab are. Here there comes to mind the memorable deed of our patriarch [Col. 0472A] Abraham, when, having mustered three hundred and eighteen trained household servants, he attacked, pursued, and overthrew the enemy, and powerfully recovered all the spoil which they had carried away from Sodom (Gen. 14). You know that Gideon likewise routed the army of the Midianites in nearly the same number, terrified by the light of the lamps and the sound of trumpets (Judg. 7). I would likewise call these men unencumbered, since, with no less prudence than courage, he excluded all those whom any impediment had rendered unfit for war.

For those whom fear had made cowardly, and love slack; those whom greed had weakened, or pleasure had swallowed up—the most discerning leader, instructed by the divine oracle, ordered to depart from the battle. Then some, lying prostrate, drink the waters with their whole mouths; others, bending down only a little, attend to necessity and leave excess aside. [Col. 0472B] You see, then, that not only vices but all superfluities are an impediment to those making progress and a burden to those fighting.

Therefore many who, enticed by natural impulses, have fallen into shameful things resolve, amid the very riches and delights in which they sinned, and amid worldly occupations, both to repent for the past, to restrain themselves in the future, and to undertake a certain conversion of conduct; but they do not persist even for a short time. For they are not the unencumbered of Moab. For Heshbon—that is, wicked thought—and Elealeh—that is, exaltation of mind—cry out in them until their voice is heard as far as Jahaz, and a most evil deed follows the most evil thought.

Therefore, wishing to render his soldiers unencumbered for this spiritual war, our leader says: “Whoever does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14). And again: “Whoever does not hate father, or mother, and wife, and children, and even his own life, cannot be my disciple” (ibid.). Thus those are called the unencumbered of Moab who, in order to resist more securely the Moabite vices into which they had fallen, free themselves from all the affairs and riches of this world, from all attachments and their own wills, and naked follow the naked Christ.

When they feel themselves assailed by natural impulses, suggestions of demons, or indeed their own thoughts, they send up to the Lord a vehement howling of heart and a pitiable wail of voice, with tears and sighs, saying with the Prophet: “I am afflicted and exceedingly humbled; I roared from the groaning of my heart” (Ps. 37). This is what Isaiah says: “Therefore the unencumbered of Moab shall howl.” But the following words, “His soul shall howl to itself,” express hidden contrition of heart, which rejects the eyes of men and seeks the divine gaze. It follows:

“My heart shall howl to Moab.” Thanks be to you, good Jesus: truly, “your mercies are over all your works.” If there within, where God sees, a human heart turns to God and is contrite, then immediately God’s heart turns toward it. By God’s heart is expressed his affection of mercy and compassion.

“My heart shall cry to Moab.” Moab howls in repentance; Christ cries in mercy. Moab howls in fear; Christ cries in compassion. Moab howls in confession; Christ cries in forgiveness. Moab sees a violent wind coming, fears, and howls; Christ, stretching out his hand and crying out, rebukes the wavering and trembling man: “O you of little faith, why did you doubt?” (Matt. 14).

Thus the cry answers the howling, affection answers affection; mercy answers the wretched man, the physician the sick man, compassion the laboring and suffering person. Truly, Lord, “according to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, your consolations have gladdened my soul” (Ps. 23). You cry, Lord; you cry inwardly in my soul when you raise one in despair into hope; when, with wondrous mercy and sweetness, you comfort one who fears and trembles; when you pour the dew of saving refreshment upon a mind already inclining toward bodily [Col. 0473B] heats; when you settle with a certain inward tranquillity a mind troubled against anger, hatred, and the like. Thus, as often as my soul howls to itself in these things and for these things, so often the heart of my God cries out by compassionating me.

Thus, my Jesus, when you were about to raise Lazarus, you cried out with a loud voice (John 11), expressing by a great cry the great affection of your mercy. O Lord, how long will the distress of these passions and temptations rage against me? How long will Moab, whom at the very beginning of conversion I thought I had escaped, renew its revived wars against me? Hear what follows: “Its bars shall reach as far as Zoar, a three-year-old heifer.”

Zoar is interpreted “small,” signifying humility, which makes the rich poor, the great small, and the proud humble. It is fittingly called a heifer, since this kind of animal abounds in milk; for “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (Jas. 4). It is called a three-year-old heifer—that is, one in its third year—because this age in cattle is found both suitable for the yoke and capable of bearing offspring. The three stages by which humility is recognized as advancing may also be expressed through the three-year-old heifer; humility consists in a threefold contempt.

The first stage is that a person despises himself, subjecting himself to one greater according to God. Then he adds that he despises no one and judges no one inferior to himself; and so he is subject to every creature for God’s sake. [Col. 0473D] Afterwards he endures being despised by all, either willingly or at least patiently, and sighs to God alone.

Humility consists in these three things. Whoever has advanced to it by God’s mercy will find everything so calm and peaceful that there will be nothing in the flesh resisting the spirit, nor anything in the spirit opposing God’s will. Therefore be certain, most beloved brothers, that whenever the lust of the flesh does not press toward vices, either hidden pride is rebuked or manifest pride is put to shame; or, lest it raise its accursed head because of consciousness of any virtue, it is brought low by the prick of a preceding vice. Therefore whoever desire to be freed from the dominion of carnal passions should devote the greatest diligence and labor to acquiring or preserving humility. [Col. 0474A] In its perfection lies the entire perfection both of chastity and tranquillity.

For the bars of Moab—that is, the strength of carnal passions—reach as far as Zoar, the three-year-old heifer; because where humility has become perfect, all that force and heat grows cold. But that we may know that we can ascend to this perfection, let us hear what the prophet adds: “For by the ascent of Luhith he shall ascend weeping, and in the way of Horonaim they shall raise a cry of contrition.”

Luhith is interpreted “cheeks,” Horonaim “the opening of sorrow.” Does not Scripture say, “Do not the tears of a widow run down upon her cheek, and does not the Lord God delight in them?” (Ecclus. 35). Tears indeed run down the cheeks, but their force and the cause for which they are poured out ascend secretly to heaven.

Therefore when a person recalls his former years in the bitterness of his soul, he is often dissolved into tears; and, washing his bed every night and watering his couch with tears, he says with the Prophet: “Streams of waters ran down from my eyes, because they did not keep your law” (Ps. 118). Thus he ascends weeping through Luhith—that is, through the tears of his cheeks—until, arriving at the opening of sorrow, namely Horonaim, he softens the cry of contrition.

Come, brothers: we must not pass over superficially what he says, “in the way of Horonaim.” For there is a way leading to Horonaim, that is, the opening of sorrow. What kind of opening is this? Who has seen it? Who has known it? Who has experienced it? Saving sorrow has its door, its window, and its opening. Through a door, entry into any house is frequent; through a window, sight is open; an opening admits nothing bodily, is passable only for light and air, gives the eye freedom to look out, but removes the capacity for close examination.

Therefore understand faith through the door, hope through the window, vision through the opening. Through faith we investigate God’s secrets; through hope we smell them; through vision we touch them. Faith teaches all things; hope promises things to come; vision presents what was promised.

There are three kinds of sorrow: the first is of fear, the second of consolation, the third of desire and delight. Since faith without works is dead and is not faith, a person then passes again to faith when, pierced by saving sorrow, he passes from a most evil life to amendment of conduct. First a person grieves in order to deserve to obtain remission [Col. 0474D] of sins; then he grieves in order to be comforted in hope of the divine promise; and thus he keeps the voice of contrition on this way, so that there may be opened to the grieving person an opening through which, as in a mirror, vision itself may appear.

O sorrow, sweet and desirable! Through you the dead are raised, the sick healed, the blind enlightened, and heaven’s gate opened. Not so is the sorrow of hypocrites, of which the prophet says: “For the waters of Nimrim shall be forsaken.” Nimrim is interpreted “leopard.” The leopard is a spotted and variegated animal, corresponding to the life and conduct of hypocrites: outwardly white, inwardly dark; chastity shines in them, while lust stinks; outwardly they glory in humility, inwardly they feed upon vanity; greed is in their mind, cheapness of dress in their clothing; truth in their words, impurity in their life.

“Streams of waters run down from their eyes”; but those waters shall be forsaken when he comes who “will bring to light the hidden things of darkness and will reveal the counsels of hearts” (1 Cor. 4), showing that barren and fruitless tears, wrung out merely for human eyes, are deprived of all grace and reward.

“For the grass has dried up, the shoot has failed, all greenness has perished.” The grass is, as it were, the beginning of good conduct; the shoot, the fruit of good work; the greenness, the purity of good intention. But in hypocrites the grass dries up when the beginning of good conduct is corrupted by vanity; the shoot fails when they do not persevere in praiseworthy work; all greenness perishes when purity of intention is abandoned as greed smiles upon them. [Col. 0475B] It follows:

“According to the magnitude of their work, so also their visitation.” This visitation must be understood in a good sense: namely, because by his holy presence, gladdening the hearts of the saints, he grants to each, in just equity, a share of himself according as each deserves. Therefore, according to the magnitude of their work, so also their visitation.

“He shall lead them to the torrent of willows”: namely, those Moabites who pass from vices to virtues and eagerly seek a place in which to exercise those virtues. Therefore they shall be led to the torrents of willows. The torrents of willows are the various orders of those who renounce the world. They are called torrents either because of the flood of tears or because of the violence of temptations.

Such was the torrent from which Elijah drank, when ravens brought him bread and meat in the morning, and bread and meat in the evening [Col. 0475C] (3 Kings 17). The torrent is called Cherith, which is interpreted “bald.” Since hair is superfluous to the body, those who renounce superfluities, content with the use of necessities, are bald. These are the unencumbered of Moab, one of whom was Elisha, whom boys mocked: “Go up, baldhead; go up, baldhead” (4 Kings 2).

These drink from the torrent on the way until “the rushing of the river makes glad the city of God” (Ps. 45), and the Most High consecrates his dwelling. For a torrent does not flow continuously; it flows when perhaps the south wind blows and melts the ice, or when abundant rain descends and fills the valleys with water.

Such, in the present life, is this visitation by which God pours over us the saving water of wisdom: now, as the Spirit blows, melting our hardness with sweet compunction; now watering every humble person with spiritual knowledge as though with heavenly waters. In torrents of this kind willows grow: namely, those who, despising the carnal propagation of children, have cut themselves off for the kingdom of heaven, possessing in God’s house “a name better than sons and daughters.”

This is that most welcome virtue of chastity and purity, to which, after bodily hardships, countless temptations of lust, frequent burnings of the flesh, and dangerous suggestions of the most unclean demon, the holy soul deserves to arrive through the ascent of Luhith and the way of Horonaim, with the Holy Spirit teaching and angels accompanying.

“For the cry has gone round the border of Moab.” This is the cry of which he said above: “My heart shall cry to Moab.” This cry goes round the border of Moab because the voice of God speaking within us examines the boundaries of vices and instills horror of them into us. How often, brothers, have I heard this cry with the ear of my heart, when the tumult of vices resounded all around, and he himself came against each one; and while they rehearsed their pleasures, he restrained their cry with his own cry, setting before them the limit—that is, the end—of such pleasure, exposing its foulness, and proposing to the captive mind the sweetness of spiritual delights!

But now let us hear the end of each cry: “His howling reaches as far as Gallim, and his cry as far as the Well of Elim.” If you please, let each thing be assigned to its counterpart, so that we may understand the howling of Moab—that is, of vices—of which he said above: “Moab shall howl over Nebo [Col. 0476B] and over Medeba”; while the cry is that of which he had said earlier: “My heart shall cry to Moab.” But that howling reaches the heaps of sand, which Gallim means; and this cry reaches Elim, which means “the well of rams.”

Wandering and unstable thoughts are like sand; gathered into one by this howling, as by a blowing wind, they make heaps of vices. But the well of rams is the depth of the Scriptures, administered through the rams—that is, through the prophets and apostles. When the Lord cries to us in our hearts, their secrets are unlocked.

Therefore, brothers, as much as outward persecution or inward disturbance grieves us, so much does divine consolation gladden us from the sacred writings. “For whatever things were written were written for our instruction, that through patience and the consolation of the Scriptures we might have hope” (Rom. 15). I tell you, brothers, no adversity can occur, nothing so sad or bitter can arise, which, as soon as the sacred page receives us, does not either quickly vanish or become easier to endure.

This is the field into which St. Isaac, as the day was already declining, went to meditate; there Rebecca met him and softened by her sweetness the pain which had befallen him (Gen. 24). How often, my good Jesus, does day turn toward evening! How often, after some slight consolation, like daylight, does unbearable sorrow succeed like the darkness of night! Everything turns to disgust; everything I see becomes burdensome. If anyone speaks, I scarcely hear; if anyone knocks, I scarcely feel. My heart grows hard like a stone, my tongue clings fast, the moisture of my eyes dries up. What then? I certainly go out to meditate in the field; I turn over the sacred book and impress my meditations on wax. Then Rebecca suddenly meets me—your grace, good Jesus—and with her light scatters the darkness, drives away disgust, and breaks hardness. Immediately tears follow sighs, and heavenly joy accompanies the tears.

Unhappy are those who, when any sad things disturb them, do not enter this field so as to rejoice. You know, brothers, that when something sad happens to lovers of the world, they seek consolations either in vain or harmful things. Thus the prophet fittingly adds concerning such persons: “For the waters of Dibon are filled with blood.”

The waters of Dibon, which means “their flowing,” signify the tears [Col. 0477A] of those who, because of the flux of temporal things, either laugh if they possess them or weep if they lose them. Therefore the waters of Dibon are filled with blood. For just as those who laugh over temporal things laugh to their own harm, so too those who weep over temporal things weep to their own harm. Such tears bring no cleansing; rather, they further defile them with the blood of sin.

Therefore it follows: “I will place additions upon Dibon.” For the Lord adds pains to their pains, so that they pass from tears to tears, enter the land by three ways, and are crushed with a double crushing. For wretched is the lot of those who, born of woman, live a short time: here they are filled with many miseries, and after this life they will be handed over to everlasting punishments (Job 14).

Happy, by contrast, are those who are consoled in the labors of this world by the visitation and light of God’s word, and who, passing out of the world, enjoy eternal joys. Therefore he will also place additions upon those who have fled from Moab, the lion: those who, fleeing vices, have at the same time escaped their very instigator. And he will place additions upon the remnant of the land also.

Here three kinds of persons are indicated: one, those who have wholly given themselves to vices and the world; another, those who renounce the world and take up Christ’s yoke; a third, those who abstain from crimes while remaining in the world, yet apply themselves to earthly works. The first are figured by Dibon, the second by those who fled from Moab, the third by the rest—or remnant—of the land. Upon all these the Lord will place additions. [Col. 0477C]

For upon the reprobate he will repay temporal pains in this life for their sins, and after this life eternal torments of soul and body. The Gospel history shows what doubled additions he gives to those who renounce this world, when the Lord says: “Everyone who has left father or mother, and the rest, for my sake, shall receive a hundredfold and shall possess eternal life” (Matt. 19).

Moreover, those who, avoiding lead, iron, and tin, build upon the foundation of Catholic faith wood, hay, and straw, will receive double from the Lord’s hand for all their sins. For these, being crushed by many afflictions and at last received into the fires, will suffer loss; yet they themselves will be saved, though only as through fire. The name Moab suits them all: the first are swallowed up by Moabite vices; in the others Moabite vices are either utterly destroyed or gloriously restrained. For the remaining group are never defiled by those vices, but are always wearied by them. Everywhere the burden of Moab is discerned: in some it is pressed down, in some it presses down, in some it crushes.

But now let us bring this sermon to an end, beseeching the mercy of our God that, cleansed from Moabite vices, he may render us acceptable to his will. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

## SERMON XXVIII. On the Words: “Send Forth the Lamb, O Lord” (Isa. 16), etc.

“God shall come from the south, and the Holy One from the shadowed [Col. 0478A] and thick mountain” (Hab. 3). Behold, most beloved brothers, our Lord Jesus suddenly emerges manifest from the densely thick forest of allegorical words, in whose shady density he has hitherto lain hidden, as the prophet says: “Send forth the Lamb, O Lord, the ruler of the earth, from the rock of the desert to the mountain of the daughter of Zion.”

Truly “my beloved stands behind our wall, looking through the windows, gazing through the lattice.” Who does not know that the Lord Jesus must be sought in the Scriptures, when he hears him himself saying in the Gospel, “Search the Scriptures” (John 5), and the rest? Yet between us and him there stands, as it were, a wall: the obscurity of Scripture itself, the riddles of its words, and the figures of its histories. But those spiritual craftsmen who built this wall for us adorned it with windows [Col. 0478B] and lattices, through which that Beloved often offers himself to be clothed by his lovers, so that no one may doubt that he is everywhere in the things which lie hidden, since the things which are open so plainly display him.

Therefore he says: “Send forth the Lamb, O Lord, the ruler of the earth.” We said at the beginning that prophets sometimes spoke by narrating, sometimes by commanding, and sometimes also by praying. Therefore, seeing in the Spirit that even the wise men of the world must be subjected to the power of the cross; that believers must be saved through the foolishness of preaching; and nonetheless that “the wisdom of the wise” must be destroyed and “the prudence of the prudent” rejected (1 Cor. 1), together with the other things set forth earlier in this burden, the prophet burns with desire, complains of delay, and now longs for Christ to be present, to fulfill the promises and make present what was foretold. Turning to the Father, he urgently demands the coming of his Son with burning affection: “Send forth,” he says, “the Lamb, O Lord, the ruler of the earth, from the rock of the desert to the mountain of the daughter of Zion.”

This is the Lamb who speaks through Jeremiah, saying: “And I was like an innocent lamb that is carried to the sacrifice” (Jer. 11). Of him Isaiah himself also says: “Like a sheep he shall be led to slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer he shall be silent” (Isa. 53). When the holy Baptist recognized him through the Holy Spirit’s revelation, he said: “Behold the Lamb of God” (John 1). And David sang of him: “He shall rule from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth” (Ps. 71).

“From the rock of the desert to the mountain of the daughter of Zion” [Col. 0478D] (Ps. 71). By the rock of the desert, I think, he means that cave, naturally formed in rocky desert places or cut out by human art, which received Lot when he fled from Sodom (Gen. 19). He says with great wonder that the Lamb will come forth from this rock of the desert, because Moab was begotten in it, and Christ was born from Moab’s race.

But he is sent from the rock of the desert to the mountain of the daughter of Zion because, born of the Virgin at Bethlehem, he visited Jerusalem by his presence—Jerusalem in which Mount Zion exists literally, or “mountain” means the excellence and glory of the daughter of Zion, that is, of the Synagogue, understood in the nobility of the Temple.

Allegorically, the rock of the desert is called the Synagogue, which, led out of Egypt and made a dweller in the wilderness for forty years, drank from the spiritual rock that followed them. [Col. 0479A] It is called the rock of the desert because, while many perished in unbelief during the exile of so long a time, it preserved firmness of faith among the more perfect. From it came the apostles, who transferred by their preaching to the peoples of the Gentiles that Lamb who took away the sins of the world, that he might rule the whole world. Thus the Church was born from the Synagogue as a daughter of Zion, whose mountain is the height of faith, the sublimity of hope, and the surpassing way of charity.

Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Christ had to suffer and rise from the dead on the third day, and repentance and remission of sins were to be preached in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem” (Luke 24).

Or indeed the Lamb, ruler of the earth, was then sent from the rock of the desert to the mountain of the daughter of Zion when Christ passed from the shadow of the Law to the truth of the Gospel; when, from the rock of the desert from which the children of Israel drank the sacrament of our redemption, he transferred them to the truth of his most sacred body and blood; when, removing the veil of the letter, he opened the mystery of spiritual understanding to the heralds of the New Testament.

“And it shall be”—what?—when the Lamb, ruler of the earth, has been sent from the rock of the desert to the mountain of the daughter of Zion: “As a fleeing bird, and as chicks flying from the nest, so shall the daughters of Moab be at the crossing of Arnon.” Understand by the daughters of Moab carnal and weak souls deceived by Moabite errors. Arnon is interpreted “their illumination.”

“My fugitives shall dwell with you, O Moab.” In this passage understand by Moab the wise men, whom we said above [Col. 0479C] were more prudent in divine things in proportion as they had been more perceptive in that worldly wisdom. This is the Moab whose bars reached as far as Zoar, the three-year-old heifer.

Such were the most blessed martyr Cyprian, Ambrose, Augustine, and Jerome, who transferred all that they had drawn from secular learning to the strengthening and advancement of the Church. Such men fought heretics more effectively; such men protected all the weak from the assaults of false apostles by their teaching. Under their care, as under maternal wings, they lay hidden more safely, lest they be deceived and snatched away by demons.

Christ addresses this Moab—that is, such wise men of this world—saying: “My fugitives of Moab shall dwell with you [Col. 0479D]; be a hiding-place for them from the face of the devastators.” He calls his fugitives those whom, once deceived and led away by the devil, he had again received by the victor’s right after defeating the enemy. The devil, grieving that they had been torn from him, stirred up heretics, set philosophers in motion, and sowed false doctrines, so that by deceiving the simple he might console himself for the injury of his loss through their destruction. But until iniquity passed away and truth was made manifest, the imperfect depended upon the faith of the perfect; and these wisely afforded the simple a saving refuge of teaching and providential care from the face of such devastators.

He therefore says: “My fugitives of Moab shall dwell with you; be a hiding-place for them from the face of the devastators.” And lest this seem difficult to one considering the devil’s power and cunning, he immediately adds [Col. 0480A]: “For the dust has been brought to an end; the wretch has been consumed.” The devil’s doctrine is compared to dust; it in some sense comes to an end when, with the Gospel shining forth, the world receives saving teaching. The prophet aptly calls the devil a wretch: future condemnation in eternal fire has been prepared for him; empty anxiety now presses his wicked heart; always labouring and accomplishing nothing, always thirsting for the souls of the elect yet unable ever to bring any one of them permanently under his power, he is judged all the more wretched because a heavenly and immortal spirit overcomes him, though he is overcome by earthly and mortal persons. Truly wretched is he who is oppressed by angels, mocked by all, despised by the perfect, and conquered by the weak.

He therefore says: “The dust has been brought to an end; the wretch has been consumed” [Col. 0480B]. Hence it is also added: “He who trampled the earth has failed.”

Let us give thanks, dearest brethren, to that Lamb who, sent from the rock of the wilderness to the mountain of the daughter of Zion, rescued the earth—trampled from the beginning, that is, by the devil—from his tyranny; indeed, he cast beneath the feet of the earth which he had trampled the very one who had trampled it, giving it power “to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and all the power of the enemy” (Luke 10). Hence the Apostle speaks to believers: “God will shortly crush Satan beneath your feet” (Rom. 16).

For the holy fellowship of all the saints is called “earth”: truly fertile and fruitful earth, yielding fruit now thirtyfold, now sixtyfold, and sometimes a hundredfold (Matt. 13 [Col. 0480C]). Until the Saviour’s coming the ancient enemy trampled this earth beneath the feet of his malice, exercising even over the elect, because of the guilt of the first transgression, a right of unjust condemnation. This continued until, exceeding the written bond on which he relied, he laid impious hands upon him who was bound by no pledge of sin, consigning to death him in whom no ground for death could be found. Thus, not undeservedly, as a transgressor of the written bond and compact—because he usurped what was not due—this exceedingly greedy and unjust collector lost even what was due to him, justice pronouncing the sentence. Therefore he who trampled the earth failed.

For God, blotting out the written bond which stood against us and fastening it to his cross, “stripped the principalities and powers, triumphing over them openly in himself” [Col. 0480D] (Col. 2). Thus, after defeating the enemy, he “led captivity captive, receiving gifts among men” (Eph. 4). “Therefore God exalted him and gave him the name which is above every name” (Phil. 2), and so forth.

From that time the prophet’s further words began to be fulfilled: “A throne shall be prepared in mercy; and upon it one shall sit in truth, in the tabernacle of David, judging and seeking judgment, and swiftly rendering what is just.” — “I will sing to you of mercy and judgment, O Lord” (Ps. 100). Let us, brethren, approach with confidence the throne of mercy, which he has prepared inwardly in the tabernacle of David—that is, in the Church—for now is the time for mercy, and the time for judgment will surely follow. But since these matters must be treated more fully when the very things said today [Col. 0481A] begin to be explained at greater length, according to our measure, in their moral sense, let us now bring this sermon also to an end. Tomorrow, God willing, taking up this same chapter again, we shall set forth what he himself suggests, to the praise and proclamation of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom belong honour and dominion through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXIX. On the same chapter, expounded morally

Plain prophecy concerning the Lord ought neither to be wrapped in allegorical coverings nor weakened by tropological figures, since nothing nourishes faith or builds character more than reading that the things we see plainly fulfilled were foretold by the holy prophets so long before [Col. 0481B]. For what is plainer than that we hear in the Gospel the Lamb whom we read in the prophet was to come pointed out by the blessed Baptist? The former says, “Send forth the Lamb, O Lord, ruler of the earth” (Isa. 16); the latter cries, “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world!” (John 1).

Elsewhere the same Baptist says of him: “He who has the bride is the Bridegroom” (John 3). What bride is this? Surely she whom the Father addresses in the psalm, saying: “Hear, daughter, and see; incline your ear, and forget your people and your father’s house” (Ps. 44). She, therefore, who now has God as her Father first had the devil as her father; she said to a stone, “You are my father,” and to a piece of wood, “You begot me” (Jer. 2). This is the Church gathered from the Gentiles, which, first Moab [Col. 0481C]—that is, begotten by the devil as father—passed into the adoption of the children of God. Her daughters of Zion are all Christian souls: by nature themselves daughters of Moab, by grace daughters of God.

But since, in the moral sense, we have said that Moab signifies the natural corruption which we contract from our father, we fittingly call daughters of Moab those souls which are either entangled in carnal vices or wearied by their suggestions and desires. Of them, then, it is said: “Like a fleeing bird and nestlings flying from the nest, so shall the daughters of Moab be at the crossing of Arnon.” Arnon is interpreted “their illumination.” Therefore, in order that the daughters of Moab may be united in saving marriage to that Lamb who was sent forth from the rock of the wilderness and took away the sins of the world, they must ascend from lower things to higher, leave errors and the darkness of ignorance behind, and be flooded with saving light; and let them say with the prophet: “The light of your countenance, O Lord, has been marked upon us” (Ps. 4).

In ascending thus they are compared to a fleeing bird and nestlings flying from the nest, “because a net is cast in vain before the eyes of winged creatures.” This is the flight which the prophet Jeremiah urges upon us: “Flee from the midst of Babylon” (Jer. 51). But there are diverse kinds of birds; and just as their natures differ, so souls assume their multitude according to their differing moral dispositions or natural character. Hence a certain holy soul, impatient of the darkness it suffered, after first saying, “Fear and trembling came upon me, and darkness covered me” (Ps. 54), pondering flight, says: “Who will give me wings like a dove, that I may fly and be at rest?” (ibid.) The same person is now compared to a pelican, now to a night-raven, now to a sparrow, now to an eagle.

Let your charity take heed. It often happens that someone living among a crowd, surrounded on every side by the vices of sinners, conceives an affection for virtues and desires their realization. He strives to ascend, but is weighed down by habit; his spirit is raised by newness, but dragged down by the proximity of sin. He delights in the serenity of virtues, but enticed by the example of evil people, he is as though unwillingly compelled to repeat what he detests. Hence there is sorrow if he yields, fear if he resists, trembling lest he perish among these things, and desire to flee. Darkness fills the conscience, sadness the heart, distress the thoughts. Thus, speaking in the bitterness of his soul [Col. 0482B], he says: “Who will give me wings like a dove, that I may fly and be at rest?” And he adds: “Behold, I fled far away” (ibid.).

That former daughter of Moab received what she had lost; flying like a bird, fleeing public life, and avoiding the occasions of sin, she chooses the secluded places of solitude. There, mortifying her members which are upon the earth, she becomes like the pelican of the wilderness. The pelican is said to be pale in colour; when it has hatched its young, it kills them with its beak, and then restores them to life by pitiable lamentation and the shedding of its own blood. Blessed is the soul which, borrowing the wings of the dove, has flown to the hidden places of solitude. There, mortifying her members which are upon the earth, she kills her former works as though they were her own young; then she gives them life in a new life through grief and toil, as by the shedding of blood, through unutterable groanings and saving compunction [Col. 0482C].

Then, borrowing heavenly food from the Scriptures, she becomes a spiritual night-raven: alike in night and day—that is, in adversity and prosperity, in joy and sorrow, in temptations and consolations—rejoicing and flying, advancing from virtue to virtue, until, made a mystical sparrow and waking from the darkness of this misery into that inaccessible light, she passes “to the place of the wonderful tabernacle, even to the house of God, with the voice of rejoicing and confession, the sound of one feasting” (Ps. 41).

Thus the soul entangled in Moabite vices, proceeding from darkness to light, as though to the crossing of Arnon, is compared to a fleeing bird and to nestlings flying from the nest. By “flight” is here meant the conversion belonging to those who renounce the world; by “flying,” the contemplation belonging to the perfect. For young birds, sitting in the nest, grow feathers; they are fed together by mother and father. When their feathers have grown and the plumage clings more firmly to their wings, they prefer the open air to the nest; seeking food by their own industry, now they pursue the heights of heaven in flight, now, lowering their wings, they descend to lower places.

There is a nest of desire, and there is also a nest of discipline. There are birds which attempt to fly but cannot; while they seem to strive to exert their wings, they are immediately weighed down by the burden of the flesh and slip into the depths. Such were the quails, which were suspended only one cubit above the ground, but soon cast down like stones to earth, satisfying the Israelites’ greedy desire with the food they craved (Num. 11 [Col. 0483A]). These are the vices of the flesh and bodily pleasure, which raise the soul to a certain empty joy; but, desire being satisfied, they plunge conscience into the depths. These are nourished in the nest of desire, but in no way attain heavenly flight.

There are other birds whose nest’s sweetness delights them so greatly that they are scarcely even summoned by their parents’ bites. Such are sluggish and inert souls, so dissolved by a kind of unhappy repose that, even when rebuked, they undertake no works of virtue. Not so the dove; not so the pelican; not so the night-raven; not so the sparrow. Not so the soul which has entered the nest of discipline, so that there, under a spiritual father and nourished by grace as mother with wholesome food [Col. 0483B], it may grow feathers and, raised on the wings of innocence and simplicity, ascend from the darkness of vices to the splendour of virtues, from public life to solitude, through solitude to knowledge, through knowledge to wisdom.

Moreover, our thoughts are compared to birds, which are carried and flit here and there with remarkable swiftness, pursuing now high things, now low, now clean, now every sort of filthy thing. For there are birds occupied around corpses and rotting flesh which prefer mire to heaven. Such are thoughts that pursue filth, love lusts, and prefer the pleasures of stinking flesh to the soul’s delights. Spending the entire day in uncleanness, they fly from shameful things to shameful things; ranging through various images of desires and crimes [Col. 0483C], they feed themselves on the most ruinous and polluted feasts of vices. Miserably reared in the nest of desire, they receive, under an unhappy omen, not wings by which they may be carried to the heights, but wings by which they may be pressed down to the depths.

There are other birds so wandering and unstable that they are almost always in motion, flitting through the windy air, now hanging suspended, living only from the empty air itself. Thoughts dreaming empty things, aspiring to honours and the glory of this world, and feeding themselves as though on wind with such imaginings and self-exaltation, are compared to these birds. Unhappy is the person who prepares a nest for these birds in his breast, so that, even if he seems willing, he cannot cling to Christ’s footsteps; the Lord reproves him and says: “Foxes have dens and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (Matt. 8 [Col. 0483D]).

More blessed than all these is the person who nourishes his thoughts in the nest of wisdom, so that, like a flying eagle, borne on the wings of contemplation into heaven itself, the empyrean, he may open unblinking eyes to behold at close range the splendour of the sun itself. Therefore the daughters of Moab—that is, the thoughts of the heart, which, drawn by that natural corruption toward vices, had committed adultery with many lovers—when they strive to pass from carnal love to spiritual love, as from darkness to light, are compared to a fleeing bird and nestlings flying from the nest. For they must first flee both vices and the very occasions of vices; and then [Col. 0484A], growing feathers in the nest of discipline and afterward of wisdom, they must pass from lower things to higher, from human to divine, from earthly to heavenly.

Now because the divine word saw that many converted from Moabite vanity and pleasure would advance not only in regular discipline but also to perfection in divine contemplation, for the salvation of many, it addresses them: “Enter into counsel; take counsel; make your shadow as night at noon.” As though it said: O Moab, now converted into Israel—you who until now have laid aside former vices and errors in the nest of discipline, and in the nest of wisdom have lain hidden among virtues and the delights of the Scriptures, as in the secret place of my countenance—rise, go forth, hasten about, so that you who until now have heard may henceforth say, “Come.”

But because you are as yet less practiced in these outward matters, “enter into counsel”: that is, learn the virtue of discernment; and thus “take counsel,” gathering many, namely, unto salvation and for the advancement of many. You, who with Elijah delight in angelic converse beneath the shade of the juniper tree (3 Kings 19), where all your works are performed as though at night, “bring forth your righteousness as light, and your judgment as noon” (Ps. 36), so that your light may shine before men; that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven (Matt. 5).

Come, my brethren, consider carefully by what stages one must ascend to pastoral care, so that you may more readily avoid the plague of the human race—the desire to rule—and may more safely choose, as the saying goes, to stand in the low place rather than endanger yourselves on the height. First, do not envy evildoers who, though fornicators, adulterers, effeminate men, and men who lie with males, shamelessly and irreverently ascend their father’s bed and defile his couch. They turn Christ’s bridal chamber into a brothel and so trample his blood that, laying aside shame, they squander its price not merely on vain and harmful things, but—even more horrid to say—as payment for disgrace. Do not envy such men, even though they prosper in their ways, “for they shall quickly wither like grass and soon fall like the green herbs” (Ps. 36 [Col. 0484C]). For if he commands the useless servant to be cast into outer darkness, what will he do with the unworthy, shameless, pestilential man who disgracefully thrusts himself into the chair?

[Col. 0484D] But leaving these aside, observe the path which the prophetic word describes for us. First, a person fleeing the world and avoiding every vice must make himself a stranger to worldly affairs. Then he must submit himself in all obedience to a superior, and whatever sins he recalls having committed he must cleanse and punish through hunger and thirst, vigils and labours, poverty and nakedness. Thus, when the best habit succeeds the worst, he may obtain wings of virtue in the nest of discipline; for one can never rule well who has not first learned to obey.

Thus cleansed of vices and adorned with virtues, he must pass to the investigation of the Scriptures, so that, as he has been formed for life, he may also be enlightened for knowledge. When he has learned from Scripture to refer all that lives and understands to love of God [Col. 0485A] and neighbour, borne up on the two wings of knowledge and charity, he ascends the mountain of contemplation. There he learns, according to the pattern of the heavenly tabernacle, to shape the structure of this earthly tabernacle, and hears with Moses: “See that you make all things according to the pattern shown you on the mountain” (Exod. 25).

Therefore the first stage is conversion; the second, purification; the third, virtue; the fourth, knowledge; the fifth, contemplation; the sixth, charity. These are perhaps the six steps on Solomon’s throne, as Solomon says: “King Solomon made himself a throne” (3 Kings 10), and the rest. And, to give the wise occasion to become wiser, Solomon’s throne is plainly called the priestly chair. Whoever tries to ascend to it without these steps ascends not so much to sit as to fall [Col. 0485B].

Whether the twelve little lions of that great Lion from the tribe of Judah may most suitably be fitted to the twelve sons of whom he says, “Can the sons of the Bridegroom fast while the Bridegroom is with them?” (Mark 2); whether gold is suited to wisdom, roundness to eternity, the rear portion to the end, and the two hands to the twofold work of charity—I leave this for your meditations to examine. It follows:

“Hide the fugitives, and do not betray the wanderers. My fugitives of Moab shall dwell with you; be a hiding-place for them from the face of the devastator.” The divine word addresses Moab, thus converted, thus changed, thus cleansed of vices, thus adorned with virtues, thus promoted to the height, commanding it to do what it foresaw, grace accompanying, that it would do. For just as it was necessary that he himself, while fleeing, should be hidden by others, so it is fitting that he, now in turn, should hide other fugitives. And as he himself, while still wandering, was not betrayed by those who received him, so he is rightly commanded not to expose to persecutors the wanderers whom he has received.

Those fleeing fornication, therefore, according to the Apostle (1 Cor. 5), must be hidden; and care must be taken lest those who are still wandering and unstable in heart, and prone to vices, be easily betrayed to evil teachers or inciters of vice. Come, my brethren: some newly arriving from the world are unlearned and simple, some learned and subtle; some are bound by the most evil habit of vice; some are of such a nature that they are scarcely moved to lust [Col. 0485D]; others are tempted by a slight occasion; some are irascible from their natural constitution, others naturally gentle.

It is therefore necessary carefully to consider and investigate the disposition and nature of each person fleeing the world: what may harm one person more, what another; by what spirit each is tempted, by what inclination he is driven. Thus provision must be made that, whether a person is assailed by vices or demons, by his own nature, corruption, inclination, or habit, or by the companionship, suggestion, or example of another person, a suitable refuge may be provided for each.

Some must be hidden from every external occupation; others from the familiarity and cohabitation of certain people. Some are usefully hidden from anger and indignation beneath the shadow of silence [Col. 0486A]; others are healthfully protected from natural incentives beneath the poverty of their diet; others are hidden from the wandering of the heart and instability of spirit beneath the shadow of labours and vigils; others are defended from the snares of unclean spirits by psalms and prayers, meditation, prayer, and reading.

He therefore says: “Hide the fugitives, and do not betray the wanderers. My fugitives shall dwell with you, Moab; be a hiding-place for them from the face of the devastators.” The devastator is the spirit of fornication; the demon of pride is a devastator. Therefore Moab provides a saving refuge for those fleeing such devastators when every prelate, once Moab but afterward Israel, sets particular exercises of virtues against the particular vices by which those subject to him are attacked.

As for what follows—“The dust has been brought to an end; the wretch has been consumed,” and so forth—it was expounded in the sermon which we had with you before this one, concerning the prince of vices himself. But in the moral exposition nothing else occurs to be said, unless perhaps we wish to understand by “dust” the sins which we contract through negligence, wandering of heart, or outward occupation; by “the wretch,” those into which we fall through the law of this corruptible flesh which makes us wretched; and by “he who tramples the earth,” the shameful deeds or crimes which so tread down and utterly crush the whole person—that is, unfruitful earth—that, like a threshing-floor after threshing, they render it barren and empty of every spiritual moisture and the sweetness of crops [Col. 0486C].

Therefore, when this dust has been brought to an end through humble conduct; when the natural but almost intolerable ardour of this flesh has been consumed by vigils, fasts, and labours; and when shameful deeds or crimes committed have failed through worthy contrition of heart, confession of mouth, and satisfaction in deed—then indeed, for those thus fleeing and hidden, Christ’s throne shall be prepared in mercy. On it he sits in the tabernacle of David—that is, in the Church which still journeys on earth—in which “mercy and truth have met one another; righteousness and peace have kissed.” There also he judges and seeks judgment: judging those who do not judge themselves, and seeking from us our own judgment, lest we be compelled to undergo his; for he will swiftly render what is just, repaying each according to his works—he who lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXX. On the words, “We have heard of the pride of Moab,” through, “I have taken away the voice of those who sing” (Isa. 16)

Thus far Saint Isaiah has woven his prophetic oracle concerning those who, renouncing Moabite wisdom and vanity, preferred Christ’s easy yoke and light burden to philosophical pride. He now directs a prophetic sentence against those who, blinded by their own pride, persisted in the darkness of their error.

He says, therefore: “We have heard of the pride of Moab: he is exceedingly proud.” What is more proud than those philosophers who, unable to rise, as it were, to heaven to the things believed concerning Christ’s divinity, and disdaining as something base and earthly the things asserted concerning his humanity, hung in this windy air between heaven and earth, companions of demons? What is more proud than those who, professing themselves wise, despised true wisdom—haughty, puffed up, irreligious in expression, superstitious in worship? “His pride, his arrogance, and his indignation are more than his strength.”

He sets forth three things: pride, arrogance, and indignation. Pride is marked in the heart, arrogance in speech, indignation in action. Pride produces arrogance; arrogance, indignation. From pride came contempt for Christ; from arrogance, blasphemy against Christ; from indignation, disputation against Christ. Since these philosophers accomplished nothing [Col. 0487B], they gnashed and wasted away with their teeth, grieving and murmuring among themselves. This is what follows: “Therefore Moab shall howl to Moab; all of it shall howl.” We have discussed this howling more fully at the passage where it is written: “For this Moab, being unburdened, shall howl; its soul shall howl to itself.” All Moab howls against all Moab: the worst against the good, the hostile against the converted, the proud against the humble.

Moreover, by this howling may be signified the pain which, we do not doubt, they will suffer eternally. Hence the prophet addresses holy preachers, saying: “Speak of its wounds to those who rejoice over the walls of baked brick.” O my preachers, speak of Moab’s wounds, if perhaps they may see and understand, be converted, and I may heal them. Speak especially to those who rejoice over the walls of baked brick.

The sons of Adam, once descending from the East into the plain of Shinar, began a tower whose height might reach even to heaven, so that it might ward off the danger if another flood should perhaps again overwhelm them. They had bricks for stones and bitumen for mortar (Gen. 11). Pharaoh too compelled the sons of Israel, whom he oppressed with harsh slavery, to build cities with brick walls (Exod. 1). But Solomon built the temple from precious stones, squared and fitted to one another in such a way that, when they were inserted into the walls, neither the sound of a hammer striking nor an axe cutting was heard in the temple (3 Kings 6).

[Col. 0487D] Now turn your eyes back, beloved, to those living stones, which the builders of our Solomon—namely, the teachers and pastors of the Church—both hammer with rebukes, cut with blows, level with teaching, conform to one another in conduct and faith, and square with virtues in this court of that heavenly Jerusalem, so that, carried from lower things to higher, they may be inserted into the sacred walls of that temple of which holy David sang: “Your temple is holy, wonderful in righteousness” (Ps. 46). These builders take great delight in the progress of those whom they look forward to inserting into heaven.

But their teachers [or: disciples; Latin text uncertain] depart from the true East into the plain of Shinar (Gen. 2), which is interpreted “their stench.” As though on the broad way leading to death, on which they stink with luxury, they raise a tower of pride. They seek bricks, compacted from soft mud and hardened in fire, having indeed the appearance of stones but ignorant of their strength. Such are the muddy hearts of carnal people, hardened by the habit of sinning and obstinacy of mind, repelling the sharp arrows with which Christ’s soldiers are armed to overthrow Moabite cities. With bricks of this sort Pharaoh builds cities and compels the sons of Israel, whom he has reduced to slavery, to toil in mud and straw (Exod. 3). With such bricks too the wise of this world and defenders of perverse doctrines have raised a wall against Christ’s Church, creating disciples for themselves who may defend error more stubbornly and repel objections more subtly.

Thus those who erect it rejoice over the wall of baked brick. It is best that holy preachers speak of the ruin and wounds of that wall, so that those endangered by excessive security may be corrected by fear. The prophet therefore says: “Speak of its wounds to those who rejoice over the walls of baked brick, for the suburbs of Heshbon shall be deserted, and the vineyard of Sibmah.” Heshbon is interpreted “thoughts.” The vineyard is suitably called Sibmah, which is interpreted “lifting up height,” expressing that puffing-up knowledge of which the Apostle says: “Knowledge puffs up” (1 Cor. 8).

It follows: “They wandered in the wilderness.” I think this is said of the shoots of the vineyard: that is, the disciples of errors. Seeing secular wisdom everywhere abandoned, they ranged in thought and mind through the various schools of philosophers, as though wandering through every byway, not knowing which they should flee, which they should embrace, which they should defend [Col. 0488C]. But the lords of the Gentiles, as is shown subsequently, crossed the sea, because, going across not only to the wise of this world but also to all nations, signified by the name of the sea, they subjected them to Christ’s yoke and to Gospel teaching.

For they “went down to the sea in ships and worked in many waters” (Ps. 101): that is, performing miracles among the peoples of the Gentiles, they saw the works of the Lord—namely, what a change was wrought by the right hand of the Most High in the conversion of the Gentiles, and his wonders in the deep: in the dark hearts of human beings, where, while they planted and watered outwardly, Christ’s grace gave the increase inwardly [Col. 0488D].

Come, dearest brethren: how many saints, seeing that such subtlety of intellect and such keenness of perception in human affairs would be lost, were moved by pity, dissolved in compassion, and, affected by mercy, shed how many tears for them! But who can doubt that the Holy Spirit worked this feeling in them? This is what he himself continues through Saint Isaiah, saying: “For this I will weep with the weeping of Jazer for the vineyard of Sibmah.” — “We do not know,” says Paul, “what we should pray for as we ought; but the Spirit himself intercedes for us with unutterable groanings” (Rom. 8).

The Holy Spirit, therefore, is said to weep for Jazer—that is, the power and strength [Col. 0489A] of secular learning—and for the vineyard of Sibmah, namely the multitude of those who stray, because he makes the saints groan and weep out of desire for their salvation or pain over their perdition; although the prophet himself could have said this either in his own person or in that of the saints. Hence it follows: “I will make you drunk with my tear, Heshbon and Elealeh.” He said “tear,” meaning “tears,” using the singular for the plural, as in the Psalm: “He spoke, and the locust came, and the caterpillar” (Ps. 104).

Thus those are made drunk by the lamentation, weeping, and tears of the saints who, converted from error and vices through their grief and prayers, and through a certain saving alienation of mind, forget the things behind and stretch forward to those before them. They cease to be what they were and begin to be what they were not. This spiritual drunkenness occurs in thoughts, by which the mind, with a certain fervour of spirit, ascends from lower things to higher, from vices to virtues. For Heshbon means “thoughts,” while Elealeh means “ascent”; by thoughts we ascend and descend.

We descend by recollection into imagination, by imagination into pleasure, by pleasure into consent, by consent into act. When the mind has subjected itself to this through a vicious habit, it staggers and is shaken like a drunkard, and all its uprightness is devoured. But if the Spirit first sanctifies your thoughts, and by his holy inspiration the mind, as by a kind of spiritual infusion of seed, conceives the fear of God, it will then ascend to piety; from piety [Col. 0489C] to knowledge; from knowledge to fortitude; thence to counsel; and thus to understanding, so that at last, arriving at wisdom, it may be made drunk by the abundance of the house of the Lord God and drink from the torrent of his delight.

He reveals whence this drunkenness arose when he adds: “For upon your vintage and upon your harvest the voice of those who tread has rushed.” Vintage and harvest signify the same thing. You have the Lord speaking to his disciples in the Gospel: “The harvest indeed is plentiful, but the labourers are few. Therefore ask the Lord of the harvest to send labourers into his harvest” (Luke 10). The voice of these labourers rushed upon Moab’s vintage and harvest because apostolic and evangelical preaching gathered many disciples from among the followers of secular wisdom.

These are the spiritual grapes, which the holy apostles gathered from the field or vineyard of the Lord of the Gentiles, to be pressed out in the winepress of suffering or threshed like grain on the threshing-floor of persecution and stripped of the chaff of their bodies [Col. 0489D]. They are called “those who tread” because of that special power of treading of which the Lord says in the Gospel: “Behold, I have given you power to tread upon serpents and scorpions” (Luke 10). Hence the prophet says also to every saint: “You shall walk upon the asp and basilisk; you shall trample the lion and dragon” (Ps. 90). It follows:

And joy and exultation shall be taken away from Carmel. Carmel is a mountain, and its name is interpreted “circumcision.” Now there is a carnal circumcision, a sensuous circumcision, and a spiritual circumcision. Carnal circumcision belongs to the Jews [Col. 0490A], sensuous circumcision to philosophers or heretics, spiritual circumcision to Christians. In the Jews one member was cleansed; the philosopher gloried in purity of all the senses; the Christian is cleansed from every defilement of the flesh. Therefore the circumcision of philosophers is compared to a mountain because of the elevation of their minds: their remarkable abstinence or conspicuous continence served worldly vanity. For they did everything in order to be seen by men. They enjoyed a twofold pleasure in that continence of theirs: inwardly, being pleased with themselves, they gloried in themselves and not in the Lord; outwardly, hunting for human praise, they delighted in people’s esteem. But when Christ’s disciples preached, joy and exultation were taken away from Carmel, because all [Col. 0490B] their superstition began to be held in contempt. Thus outward joy, having nothing on which to rest, vanished; and inward exultation, deprived of its desired fruit, languished.

“And in the vineyards he shall neither exult nor shout for joy.” The same statement is repeated, except that it is made explicit that this exultation or jubilant cry of theirs sounded especially in the vineyards. For, surrounded by a multitude of disciples, they discoursed grandly upon contempt for the world, the disgracefulness of pleasure, and chastisement of the body; and while disputing they swelled most vainly, delighting both in inward jubilation and in outward applause when their hearers marvelled at and praised what was said. All this was taken away when the trumpet of the Gospel sounded. Therefore he says of Moab: “In the vineyards he shall neither exult nor shout for joy.” And he added: “And he who was accustomed to tread shall not tread wine [Col. 0490C] in the winepress.”

For those men of Moab who toiled in the winepresses of their own wisdom so that the wine of unbelief might be pressed out by their hearers—of which it is written, “Their wine is the gall of dragons and the incurable venom of asps” (Deut. XXXII)—no longer work in that vineyard. The master of the household has now entrusted it, rescued from the worst cultivators, to the best husbandmen, so that they may render him its fruit in its seasons. “He has taken away the voice of those treading.” He continues the metaphor. Harvesters, treaders of grapes, and reapers, when an abundance of grain or grapes smiles upon them, ordinarily leap about and sing with great cheerfulness, expressing inward joy by voice, clapping, dancing, and varied movements of their limbs. But when a vineyard has been cut down or plundered by enemies, battered by hail, or burned by lightning, or when a field has been devastated, a reaper or vintager is seldom seen; and scarcely finding anything to gather, he proceeds with head bowed, mournful and weeping, his face grimy. Thus the teachers of errors, who, having gathered disciples from every side, gloried in their multitude as in a barren vineyard, babbling with puffed cheeks and manifold vanity, demanded from them belief in their sayings, pressing wine of unbelief from unripe grapes. But when the apostles and their successors preached God’s Gospel, and they had now either no hearer or scarcely one, they mourned in grief and fell silent in shame.

Let us give thanks, brothers, to the Lord our God, who made foolish [Col. 0491A] the wisdom of this world and, through the simplicity of fishermen, nullified the prudence and loftiness of philosophers, so that whoever glories may glory in the Lord—to whom be honour and glory throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXXI. On the same chapter, expounded morally.

Come, brothers: what we discussed allegorically yesterday, we shall today take up again for moral exposition. He had spoken of those who, converted from vices to Christ, advance to a perfect man, and of the great consolation they customarily afford to others converted from like vanity: “My fugitives shall dwell with thee, Moab; be thou a hiding-place for them from the face of the devastator” (Isa. XVI). And behold, seeing that very many, because of grace bestowed upon them, grow proud—ignorant of God’s righteousness, glorying in themselves [Col. 0491B] and not in the Lord, and arrogantly vaunting their own virtues—he elegantly mocks and reproves their presumption: “We have heard,” he says, “of the pride of Moab: he is exceedingly proud.”

Would that we, brothers, may not be found such people—daily bursting into the words of Elihu, and destroying by boasting whatever virtue they seem to have acquired! They promise great things, propose every kind of strong undertaking, walk in things great and wonderful beyond themselves, and with puffed-up speech declare that nothing in works is burdensome to them, nothing in Scripture obscure, nothing in practice difficult. Of them the prophet adds: “The pride of Moab and his arrogance and his indignation are greater than his strength.” Very fittingly. No strength in holy works follows the arrogant man’s words; neither his inwardly swelling presumptuous spirit, nor his outwardly self-praising grandiloquent tongue, nor the pride whereby, indignant with the rest as inferiors, he claims to have soared above all, is matched by his deeds.

“Therefore Moab shall howl to Moab.” Behold, you have Moab and Moab: the Moab to whom it is said, “My fugitives shall dwell with thee”; and the Moab of whom it is said, “We have heard of the pride of Moab.” The first is humble; the second proud. The first presumes upon himself; the second attributes all that he is to God. The first scatters his works on the wind of vanity; the second stores all his good things in the treasury of his own conscience. The first does all things to be seen by men; the second, to please the gaze of God alone. The first Moab therefore howls to the second when, plunged through the vice of pride into every shameful act, he confesses to him [Col. 0491D] his error in sorrow. The second howls to the first when, lamenting his fall, he summons him by groans and admonitions to repentance. Thus all howl: good and bad, humble and proud, converted and turned away.

Therefore, brothers, the conduct of a person whose intention is unknown is not immediately to be praised; for “if thine eye be evil, thy whole body shall be dark” (Matt. VI). Accordingly, the holy prophet restrains the joy of those who indiscriminately praise arrogant people, believing true everything which those people boast about themselves; he commands those who judge these matters more soundly to announce to them how great are the evils that await the arrogant. “Speak,” he says, “of his wounds to those [Col. 0492A] who rejoice over walls of baked brick.”
