By a wall of baked brick he means the condition of the inner man in the proud and arrogant: it does not receive a stable foundation, being built of squared stones—that is, true virtues—but, hardened by the fire of desire, from the mud of fetid intention and false, simulated virtues, it displays the appearance of godliness but knows not its power. Gold is mud; silver is mud; the fulfilment of any pleasure is mud; a man’s estimation of another man is mud. Therefore every thought occupied with such things is muddy, and every intention tending toward them is muddy. Yet from all these things the arrogant person shapes thoughts in his heart; he heaps up images of honours, pleasures, and riches. Once his will and intention are given over to these, he does all his works to be seen by men; and he so bakes and hardens, in the fire of his desires, the very likenesses of virtues through which he strives to attain what he seeks, that what seems hard and harsh because of the consideration of this most evil end appears to him easy.

Such people are more eager than others for vigils, readier for manual work, more severe in countenance than all, more solemn in speech, more fervent in fasts. They are indignant with the weak, disparage the simple, and speak things so great and strong that those less practised in such matters consider them holier than everyone else. These are those who rejoice over walls of baked brick, to whom the wounds of Moab must be announced. But let us now hear the wounds themselves: “The suburbs of Heshbon shall be deserted, the vineyard of Sibmah.” Heshbon signifies [Col. 0492C] “thoughts”; Sibmah, “lifting up height.” These are the thoughts from which that muddy wall is constructed, wherein images of innumerable desires are heaped together.

The intention itself formed from these thoughts is, as it were, a city; its suburbs are the virtues and works done according to that intention. In every proud person these, deserted by God’s assistance and protection, will lose even the appearance of goodness by which they seemed veiled. For often, when a proud person is frustrated in his hope and lacks the outcome of the desire he pursued, unable any longer to restrain himself, he bursts into open wickedness. He undergoes what the Lord threatens such a soul through another prophet: “Behold, I will uncover thee, and thy shame shall appear” (Ezek. XVI). Therefore the suburbs of Heshbon shall be deserted, and the vineyard of Sibmah deserted.

In the holy Scriptures we read of different kinds of wine. There is the wine of love, by which holy Noah, drunk in the figure of the Lord Saviour, concealed the strong things and exposed the weak: while asleep he is mocked; when awake, he avenges the injury inflicted upon him (Gen. IX). There is the wine of exultation, by which Lot was made drunk, so that, escaping the fires of Sodom, he was defiled by a secret fire (Gen. XIX). There is besides the wine of saving wisdom, by which Joseph’s brothers are drunk at midday, wine pressed from the vineyard of the Scriptures and making glad the whole city of God. There is also wine of bitterness, of which Jeremiah says: “My enemy has made me drunk with bitterness” (Lam. III). Moreover, Scripture does not pass over wine of lust in silence, Moses saying: “Their vine is of the vine of Sodom,” and so forth (Deut. XXXII). The Psalmist also mentions wine of compunction: “Thou hast shown thy people hard things; thou hast given us wine of compunction to drink” (Ps. LIX). Finally, there is the wine of evangelical and apostolic teaching—truly new wine—which, descending from the heavenly storehouse into the hearts of the apostles, throughout the whole world produces virgins and makes the hearts of believers drunk with the desire for perfection.

Therefore any proud or arrogant person, approaching the vineyard of the Scriptures and transplanting shoots of various sayings from it, sets them in the field of his heart. Cultivating them with many meditations, he creates for himself a vineyard of a certain puffed-up knowledge. From it, pressing wine for himself, he seeks someone before whom he may pour out his spirit [Col. 0493B] and display his wisdom. Thus this vineyard is not undeservedly called the vineyard of Sibmah—that is, “lifting up height.” For whatever lofty thing such a man savours, his spirit does not rest until it is brought into public; so that, by a certain manner of speaking, he seems to proclaim it by his inflated bearing and the gestures of his eyes: “Behold, my belly is like wine without a vent, which bursts new wineskins” (Job XXXII).

But this vineyard is deserted when the proud man, deprived of the fruit he hoped for from his knowledge, both grows weary of works and neglects study; and so all his learning withers. It follows: “The lords of the nations have cut down its shoots.” We read that “princes of nations” are hostile powers, as in Daniel, “the prince of the kingdom of the Persians” and “the prince of the kingdom of the Greeks.” Just as those wicked spirits are written to be the lords and princes of those nations, perhaps because of certain vices with which they especially delight to stain them by their suggestions (Dan. X), so perhaps other spirits, too, glory that they are lords and princes of other nations before those nations have received faith in the Lord Saviour—for example, of Greeks, Gauls, and Germans.

The princes or lords of such nations have cut down the shoots of the vineyard of Sibmah—that is, the branches from which clusters grow—when a wicked spirit cuts away from the proud person’s mind, with the sickle of suggestions and unclean thoughts, the meditations through which the arrogant person customarily presses the wine of teaching from the vineyard of knowledge of the Scriptures. But because, when evil desires or thoughts succeed good ones, even faith sometimes is disturbed—and the strength of all virtues consists in faith—it is fittingly added: “They reached as far as Jazer.” For Jazer is interpreted “their strength.” When a wicked spirit has taken possession of a soul and made it captive, it first excludes all virtues; and then, introducing vices, strives also to shake its faith. It follows:

“They wandered in the wilderness,” where there had been a city and suburbs, where there had been a vineyard, where there had been Jazer; where now was a wilderness—that is, a place empty of every virtue, dried up of all moisture of love. And just as one passing through a wilderness wanders freely here and there, with neither vineyards, nor crops, nor houses, nor walls obstructing him, [Col. 0494A] so wandering spirits safely traverse, as though it were a deserted place with no resistance, a soul in which the spiritual vineyard has been cut down and faith disturbed through the expulsion of virtues; and they hurl it, drunken and straying, into every error.

Therefore it is rightly said of the princes or lords of the nations, who cut down the vineyard’s shoots and reached as far as Jazer: “They wandered in the wilderness.” And it is added: “Its offshoots were left behind.” Continuing the vineyard metaphor, he says not only that it has been reduced to desolation, but that its offshoots also—those which could otherwise be moved and transplanted—have been abandoned. “They crossed the sea.” The sea signifies the bitterness of repentance.

It happens that after someone who had the appearance of holiness falls into the abyss of shamefulness, he initially grieves, weeps, is terrified, judges and condemns himself; he rises against himself, swears and resolves to keep the judgments of God’s righteousness, determines and solemnly declares that he will never repeat such deeds. Then, when either enticed by desire, forestalled by error, or overpowered by the force of diabolical temptation, he gives strength to pleasure by repeating the wickedness, his good disposition diminishes and the fire of wickedness grows through added fuel, until, conquered by habit, he falls into the abyss of despair. Thus he rushes headlong to death, so that he can be recalled from the shamefulness of his crimes neither by compunction through fear, nor by confusion through shame, nor by any bitterness of mind. It is rightly said of such a person’s desires and thoughts: “They crossed the sea.”

And the prophet added: “Therefore I shall weep for the vineyard of Sibmah with the weeping of Jazer” [Col. 0494C]. This is the voice of Christ speaking in Isaiah. He is the one who, seeing the city Jerusalem, wept over it, saying: “For if thou hadst known … that days shall come upon thee, and they shall hem thee in on every side and cast thee to the ground,” and so forth (Luke XIX). Prophet and evangelist agree. Christ sees a city powerful in honours, abounding in riches, luxuriating in pleasures, lifted up in pride and dissolved in joy. Foreseeing its future calamity, he weeps over it while it laughs and laments it while it exults, though it knows not what is to come upon it.

Likewise the prophet sees a soul lifted up by its virtues within itself; foreseeing how great a fall is afterward to come through them, he weeps in compassion, both in his own person and in that of other saints, to whom these things are often revealed by God’s Spirit. And having first enumerated the wounds of vices that were to be inflicted upon them, he says: “Therefore I shall weep for the vineyard of Sibmah with the weeping of Jazer.” The prophet weeps for two things: Jazer and the vineyard of Sibmah. He weeps for Jazer—that is, for the great strength by which the soul had formerly resisted the world, itself, and the devil, and appeared pre-eminent above others in human judgment—because it perished through the single vice of pride. He also weeps for the vineyard of Sibmah, that is, for teaching which could have benefited many if it had been kept beneath the shelter of humility, but which, cut down by the hoe of self-display and reduced to desolation, has withered.

It follows:

“I shall make thee drunk with my tears, Heshbon and Eleale,” he says. Violent grief multiplies tears and leaves nothing that ought to be lamented unlamented. “I shall make thee [Col. 0495A] drunk with my tears, Heshbon and Eleale,” he says. This grieving, weeping, lamenting person makes drunk. It sometimes happens that many who, through the sickness of pride, have fallen into unlawful deeds, if they see holy people detesting their crimes and, moved by compassion, mourning their ruin with tender concern, return to themselves and repent of the past. Intoxicated by the wine of compunction, they embrace bitterness instead of pleasure, labour instead of rest, and tears instead of laughter.

But he who knew the treasures of compassion and mercy hidden broadly in Christ’s breast pursued, drunk with love, even into the secret places of the wilderness, the thief who had been a disciple, the robber who had been a Christian, the most destructive murderer after the Church’s secret mysteries; and, having made him drunk with repentance, restored him to Christ’s members, from which he had been cut off. Therefore the prophet addresses Heshbon and Eleale—that is, the thought and exaltation of any perverse person—so that, as he himself was made drunk with love because of their destruction, that person likewise may be made drunk with compunction.

He then adds, pursuing the cause of his grief: “For over thy vintage the voice of those treading has fallen.” At the time of harvest and vintage the fruits of a year’s labour are received. The treaders are called wicked spirits: at the time when a soul, deceived by vanity and doing all things in pride and hypocrisy, believes itself to receive the fruit of its works, they come upon it with a cry. The wine which, because of the likeness of virtues, holy angels thought should be borne by it to the heavenly kingdoms, they wring from it to feed their own cruelty. “And joy and exultation,” he says, “shall be taken away from Carmel.”

Carmel signifies circumcision, and circumcision continence. Those who feed on human esteem especially tend to exult in chastity preserved; but at the time of harvest and vintage, when they see that through the perversity of their intention all these things deservedly lack virtue, grief and sadness succeed exultation and joy. Hence it follows: “And in the vineyards he shall neither exult nor shout for joy.” Who? Moab, certainly, who was accustomed both to exult inwardly and to shout outwardly in the vineyards of knowledge discussed sufficiently above. And the prophet adds: “He who was accustomed to tread shall not tread wine in the winepress; I have taken away the voice of those treading.” Here [Col. 0495D] “those treading,” who used to press wine from the grapes of this vineyard, signifies those who had been accustomed to borrow something from the knowledge of arrogant persons and who delighted, along with their teachers, to glory in it and sing, as it were, a sweet rowing-song.

Therefore, with such masters perishing, the prophet threatens that all their joys are condemned to eternal silence. We have run briefly through these matters, brothers, in order that what we unfolded yesterday in one sermon under an allegorical or prophetic plain sense might, when morally explained in one sermon, be made more intelligible. Let us now restore our understanding by silence, and tomorrow let us consider and discuss the small remainder concerning the burden of Moab, to the praise and glory of our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXXII. On the text, “My belly shall sound like a harp unto Moab” (Isa. XVI), to the end of the burden of Moab.

Brothers, we have proceeded in the burden of Moab as far as the harp, to which holy Isaiah—or Christ speaking in him—thought his belly comparable: “Therefore my belly shall sound unto Moab like a harp.” The beginning of this sermon must be connected with the end of that sermon which we delivered with you the day before yesterday on the prophecy of things to come. There we said that, when Christ’s Gospel shone forth, all joy was taken away from the wise men of the world, prophetically represented by Moab, because of the conversion of many. [Col. 0496B] “And now,” he says, “therefore my belly shall sound unto Moab like a harp.”

This is the voice of the prophet, or of Christ speaking in the prophet. “Therefore,” he says, “because of what I have said concerning Moab—its conversion, its humiliation, or its condemnation—therefore my belly shall sound unto Moab like a harp.” Christ’s belly may be called the holy Church, for within the belly the inward organs are contained. There is the heart, supplying vital motion to the whole body; there is the liver, nourishing the body’s heat and distributing life-giving blood through all the members; and there are the remaining entrails, each assigned its respective service for the body’s nourishment. So in the Church the Lord appointed some apostles, others prophets, and others pastors and teachers, “for the work of ministry, for the building up of the body of Christ” (I Cor. XII).

Likewise, although a harp has many strings and each has its own sound, yet all are arranged according to fixed proportions and numerical relations, so that all join in a single harmony and one most beautiful sound is made from all. Thus, although in Christ’s Church there are different ranks and orders, and moreover different gifts of virtues, all are founded in one love, through which, in discourse, they compose one most beautiful sound from many virtues.

By God’s belly, too, holy Scripture can be understood, in which his secrets are contained like inward organs in a belly. There diverse sayings and diverse precepts, agreeing in one rule of faith, emit a kind of sweetest melody to the hearts and ears of believers alike. Therefore he says: “Therefore my belly shall sound unto Moab like a harp.” Over all these things which have been said against Moab—that is, against the wise men of the world—the holy Church has given forth a most beautiful and harmonious sound of preaching: now teaching, now admonishing, now rebuking, now soothing, now overthrowing, by most powerful arguments, all the arguments of the dialectical art—that is, the supports of the philosophical school—as though they were a wall of baked brick. For when he says, “And my inward parts unto the wall of baked brick,” he repeats the same sense.

But since above we explained that Moab is spoken of in two ways, according to the conversion of some and the turning away of others, he seems to have explained which Moab he meant: namely, that Moab which was hardened like a wall at the voice of preachers. “Therefore,” he says, “my inward parts shall sound unto the wall of baked brick.”

Moreover, every saint has a spiritual belly, as Jeremiah says: “My belly, my belly, I am pained; the senses of my heart are troubled” (Jer. IV). As the things enclosed in the prison of the belly are hidden from all eyes and knowledge, so no one knows what is done in a man except the conscience of the man himself which is in him. Blessed is the soul in which all things are arranged and ordered as the strings of a harp, where virtues agree with virtues and outward things correspond to inward. Virtues are, as it were, spiritual strings, stretched between two timbers—namely, the upper and lower—which prefigure the mystery of the cross.

The first string of all is temperance, through which a man mortifies his members which are upon the earth and fastens all things to Christ. This string is fixed in the depth of the cross, so that, beginning from fear, it gives forth the grave sound of confession and compunction. Justice, the second string, touches the upper part of the cross, so that by rendering to each his due it bursts into the most piercing voice of love. And the string of prudence, standing across the transverse timber of the cross between the other two, tempers with the sweet sound of discernment the subtlety of the one and the gravity of the other. Further, the fourth string, called fortitude, embraces the length of the cross, providing the other strings with the power to endure and emitting the pleasing sound of patience. But each of these is attended on either side by many strings of virtues; and amid the diversity of many strings, according to fixed proportions of spiritual numbers, they compose one harmony.

Moab, therefore, which is interpreted “from the father,” as we have often said, signifies, according to the laws of tropology, the natural corruption implanted in our members, or those who live according to it. Therefore the prophet’s belly sounds to Moab like a harp when some perfect person commends the harmony of virtues to anyone given to vice, and the discord of vices, setting frugality against luxury, patience against anger, chastity against lust, and love against greed. Further, when any one of us sees wicked Moab lifting up its head within him and shaking all the members by the law of natural corruption, let him strike the harp, blunt its goads by meditation upon or imitation of the Lord’s Passion, and overthrow with the power of the cross the brick wall of vices, hardened into the use of habit. To such a person this saying is suitably applied: “My belly shall sound to Moab like a harp, and my inward parts to the wall of baked brick.”

This is David’s harp, whose most holy sound drives away demons, calms anger, and extinguishes lust. Blessed, blessed is the one who dedicates all his inward parts, like the entrails of a belly, to the cross, and thunders against the desires of the flesh, saying with the prophet: “Bless the Lord, O my soul, and all my inward parts, his holy name!” (Ps. CII). It follows:

“And it shall be, when it appears that Moab has laboured in [Col. 0498A] his high places.” Moab certainly then appeared to have laboured in vain when, defeated by ecclesiastical men wise in this age, it appeared wholly empty and void, with some converted, thus fulfilling what is written: “Where is the wise man? Where is the scribe? Where is the inquirer of this age? Has not God made foolish the wisdom of this world?” (I Cor. I). And before this he said: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and I will reject the prudence of the prudent.” “In his high places” is very aptly said. For philosophers always glory that they speak and do lofty and perfect things. This vanity indeed imposed no small labour upon them, since they strove with all their strength against evangelical and apostolic teaching. But what is the end of this labour? “And it shall be,” he says, “when Moab appears to have laboured in his high places”—that is, when the wise of the world saw that they had toiled fruitlessly against the Church and that the excellence of their doctrines had fallen before the simplicity of faith—they turned to prayers and tears, because they expected aid from the demons whom they regarded as gods and whose shrines they worshipped.

Therefore he says: “He shall enter into his holy places to entreat; and he shall not prevail.” For when their arguments fail and all knowledge exalting itself against the knowledge of God has been destroyed, they attempt, by entreaties, magical deceptions, and accursed mysteries of demons, to resist the Holy Spirit and shake God’s purpose. But that cautiously contrived prudence of theirs achieves nothing, because “their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words unto the ends of the world” (Ps. XVIII).

Likewise, those who have given themselves to Moabite corruption, after spending much labour and much time in satisfying pleasures, discover at the end of all things how vainly they laboured in doing wickedness. But when the foolish virgins, who in their high places—that is, in pride and greatness of heart—carried lamps without oil, received no help from the sellers of oil after all had gone out, they then, as though returning to holy places, offer prayers, saying, “Lord, Lord, open to us” (Matt. XXV). But how nothing was gained by that entreaty is declared by the dreadful answer: “Amen, I say to you, I do not know you” (ibid.).

Then the prophet, bringing the burden to its end, says: “This is the word which the Lord spoke from that time concerning Moab.” The divine discourse calls a “word” all that it had declared about Moab or to Moab. The ending corresponds to the beginning; for it began thus: “The burden of Moab.” “From that time,” therefore—that is, from the time when he began to speak of Moab—he spoke all these things. The prophet shows that what he had said was firm and true, and that he had not, like Montanus in his madness, spoken in an erring spirit without knowing what he said, but, filled with God’s Spirit, had uttered prophecies he understood.

With this statement suitably inserted, he declares in mystical discourse the times at which the things he had prophesied concerning the burden of Moab were to be fulfilled: “And now the Lord has spoken, saying: Within three years, as the years of a hired labourer, the glory of Moab shall be taken away from a great people.”

The prophetic discourse describes three periods of the Church: calling, testing, and consolation. It was called by the preaching of the apostles, tested by the persecution of martyrs, and consoled by the conversion of rulers. In these three periods, as in three years, the glory of Moab was taken away from every great people. For during the time of calling the philosophers still seemed glorious, when their most perverse doctrine had scarcely been attacked by Catholic men. But in the time when the patience of the saints was tested by many temptations, their glory seemed so much greater as Christ’s faith seemed more manifest. But when the kings of the age, having received the saving faith, exalted Christ’s Church more highly, their glory was taken away from above all the great people—namely, that people deceived by their error.

These are called the years of a hired labourer because, just as a hired labourer awaits the year’s end and, desiring his wage, thinks all the time long, so the wise men of this world, during these three periods as through three years, expected from day to day that Catholic doctrine would be destroyed. Hence, deceived by the oracles of unclean spirits, they presumptuously established a fixed number of years beyond which, they falsely claimed, Christ’s faith could not endure. It follows: “And there shall be left in it a small and scanty cluster, by no means many.” When the vintage is finished, just as a cluster is rarely found in the vineyard, so, after many have been cut off from that worldly wisdom by the Church’s sickle, scarcely anyone who professes it is found in these times.

[Col. 0499C] But, to return to ourselves, dearest brothers, let us consider that Moab which has been grafted into us: namely, the corruption which we contracted from our father, and the devil, its author and instigator. In each person there is a great multitude of thoughts, affections, and pleasures; and Moab boasts of ruling over them as long as the mind, enticed by his suggestions, consents. But within three years, like the years of a hired labourer, Moab’s glory over all the great multitude shall be taken away. For we have, as it were, three years, three stages of progress: conversion, purification, and contemplation. The first is in sorrow, the second in fear, the third in love.

The beginning of our conversion, then, is like the beginning of the first year: the will is changed; then evil habit is overcome, [Col. 0499D] evil is abandoned, and good is desired. And this is the first year, in which Moab still boasts not a little: for at his suggestion the will often grows lukewarm, habit prevails, evil introduced against one’s resolution creeps in, and the mind finds itself unable to accomplish the good that it desires. His glory is indeed diminished when a person, perfectly converted to the Lord, enters upon single combat with vices, and, entering the second year, strives as far as possible that Moabite corruption, like an old ingrained habit, may diminish, [Col. 0500A] and that the new and unfamiliar may increase.

Moab has some glory even in this year, since, although he cannot overcome one who fights, he must nevertheless sometimes wound even one who resists exceedingly well. In this year the mind, purified by spiritual exercises, passes on to heavenly contemplation and to continual meditation upon the Scriptures. Then virtue begins to grow sweet to it and vice contemptible; and from a certain infusion of love it tastes how sweet the Lord is. Then Moab’s glory over all the great multitude shall be removed, when whatever unclean love has remained in our affections and thoughts is emptied out by the experience of a new sweetness. Yet there remains, like a small and scanty cluster, that law in our members which resists the law of our mind.

[Col. 0500B] For as in a ravaged vineyard a cluster is found only rarely, so, when the multitude of vices has been weakened, there must remain that unavoidable impulse which infants themselves often endure and old men cannot escape. Moreover, these years are called those of a hired labourer because, just as a hireling sighs for his wages, so every person desiring conversion, while he endures the impossibility of continence, burns with a wondrous longing, awaiting the very possibility of chastity as the fruit of his labour. And, solicitous for his purification, so long as he is assailed by vices, he eagerly longs in a remarkable way to be released from temptations, and awaits that repose as a most abundant reward. Finally, even disdaining natural corruption itself, he ardently desires, with a burning heart, to be sprinkled on every side with the dew of chastity [Col. 0500C] and enriched with the sweetness of every virtue.

Hypocrites, too, may be signified by Moab: Moabite corruption pollutes them inwardly, while a certain feigned decency exalts them outwardly. Their years are the years of a hired labourer, because they do everything in order to be seen by men; and they shall hear from the Lord: “They have received their reward” (Matt. 6). But when the three years have passed—the first of which is in this life, the second after death, and the third after the resurrection—then all their glory shall certainly be removed, when, their oil failing and not obtained from those who sell it, they hear from the bridegroom: “Amen, I say to you, I do not know you” (Matt. 25).

Therefore, brothers, having arranged as best I can these matters concerning the three burdens of Babylon, the Philistines, and Moab, I lay aside my pen, wishing to submit what has been said or written to the judgment of him whom I have chosen as judge and corrector of my words: I mean holy G., bishop of London. According to his decision I intend either to delete these very things, or to stop here, or to proceed further. Meanwhile we shall meditate upon something useful and pleasant for your edification and that of others. May he grant this to us who lives and is glorified through all ages of ages. Amen.

[Note: [Col. 0499] Observe, reader, that Father Gibbon, who formerly published these sermons *On the Burdens*, obtained two copies. One, belonging to the Church of Cambrai, contained in many places certain material lacking in the other copy, which belonged to the Cistercian monastery of Clairmarais. Father Gibbon followed the Cambrai copy in his edition; but in this edition I have preferred to follow that of Clairmarais, because the Fusniacense copy, from which I transcribed the same sermons some years ago, agrees with it in every respect. For the agreement of manuscripts belonging to the Order indicates clearly enough that those additions taken from the Cambrai copy are not Aelred’s, or at least that they later crept into the text from the margin, where they had been written.]

[SPECULUM CHARITATIS — THE MIRROR OF CHARITY.]

[Col. 0501]

THE MIRROR OF CHARITY OF BLESSED AELRED, ABBOT OF RIEVAULX.

(*Bibliotheca Patrum Cisterciensium*, V, 293.)

LETTER OF GERVASE, ABBOT OF PARK, TO AELRED, COMMANDING THE PUBLICATION OF THE FOLLOWING BOOKS.

Humility is indeed a very great virtue in the saints, but only if it is true and discerning. Humility must not be grounded in any measure of falsehood, nor preserved through the sacrilege of disobedience. I requested your brotherhood—indeed, I commanded you; indeed, under attestation of the divine name, I adjured you—to write a few things for me, including a response to the complaints of certain persons who are striving from looser observance toward stricter discipline. I do not condemn or blame an excuse; but I do indeed accuse obstinacy. It might have been humility to make an excuse; but is it humility not to obey? Is it humility not to comply? On the contrary: “to resist is as the sin of divination,” and to refuse compliance is like the crime of idolatry.

But you cry out that womanish shoulders must be withdrawn from a heavy burden, and that it is safer not to undertake an offered work than, once one has taken it up, to collapse beneath the load. Let what I command, then, be heavy; let it be difficult; let it be impossible. Even so, you have no excuse. I persist in my judgment; I repeat the command. What will you do? Will not he to whose words you have sworn say: “Let the younger brother know that this is expedient for him, and, trusting in God’s help, let him obey” (St Benedict, *Rule*, ch. 68)?

Certainly, you have done as much as you ought, if not more than you ought; you have gone as far as you were allowed. You have set forth the grounds of your inability, saying that you are not much of a grammarian—indeed, almost unlettered; that you came from kitchens, not schools, to the hermitage, where, living as a rustic and countryman among rocks and mountains, you toil daily with axe and hammer for your bread; where silence is learned more than speech; where, beneath the garb of poor fishermen, the buskin of orators is not admitted.

I receive your excuse most gladly, because I feel that it increases rather than extinguishes the spark of my desire. For what you produce should taste all the sweeter to me if you have learned it, not in the school of any grammarian, but in the school of the Holy Spirit; if perhaps you possess the treasure for this reason in an earthen vessel, so that the surpassing greatness may be God’s power and not your own. How pleasant, too, that by a kind of presage of things to come you were transferred from the kitchen to the hermitage—perhaps because, for a time, the distribution of bodily food was entrusted to you in a royal house, so that someday, in the house of our King, you might compare spiritual things with spiritual, and refresh the hungry with the food of God’s word.

Nor do I dread the mountain heights, the roughness of rocks, or the hollows of valleys, since in these days the mountains drip sweetness and the hills flow with milk and honey; the valleys abound in grain; honey is sucked from the rock and oil from the hardest stone; and among rocks and mountains are the pastures of Christ’s sheep. Therefore I judge that with that hammer of yours you have struck out from those rocks something that you would not have drawn forth by native keenness from the chests of masters; and that at times, in the heat of noon beneath the shade of trees, you have experienced something such as you would never have learned in schools.

Therefore give glory not to yourself, not to yourself, but to his name: he not only rescued you in your despair from the pit of misery and the mire of filth, from the brothel-house of death and the mud of shame; but, mindful of his wonderful works, the merciful and compassionate Lord, in order more abundantly to raise up the hope of sinners, gave sight to the blind, instructed the unlearned, and taught the inexperienced. Since everyone who knows you knows that what is demanded of you is not your own, why are you ashamed? Why do you tremble? Why do you conceal it? Why, at the commanding voice of him who gave it, do you refuse to dispense what he gave?

Or do you fear the charge of presumption, or the envy of certain persons? As though anyone had ever written anything useful without envy; or as though you could be accused of presumption when, as a monk, you obey your abbot. Therefore I command you, in the name of Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God, not to delay setting down in writing what has become known to you through long meditation: concerning the excellence of charity, its fruit, and its order. Thus, in your work itself, as in a kind of mirror, we may recognize what charity is; how great is the sweetness found in possessing it; how great the oppression felt in covetousness, which is contrary to it; how the affliction of the outward person does not diminish charity’s sweetness, as some suppose, but rather increases it; and finally, what discernment must be observed in its exercise.

But, so that your modesty may be spared, let this very letter be placed at the head of the work. Thus, whatever displeases a reader in the *Mirror of Charity*—for this is the name we give the book—may be imputed not to you, who obeyed, but to me, who compelled one unwilling. Farewell in Christ, beloved brother.

PREFACE OF BLESSED AELRED.

The true and discerning humility of the saints is truly a virtue; but my humility, and that of people like me, is a deficiency of virtue—of the kind concerning which the Prophet says: “Look upon my humiliation, and deliver me” (Ps. 118). For he did not ask to be delivered from some virtue, nor did he exalt himself because of humility; rather, he implored aid for his lowliness.

Lest I should seem to conceal my miserable humility—would that it were as true humility, so also discerning virtue—under some importunate disobedience, I obey, as is fitting, though unworthily, the request, command, and adjuration of such condescension: at least so far as concerns me. I therefore undertake a work impossible, inexcusable, and deserving of accusation: impossible because of my own smallness of spirit; inexcusable because of your command; liable to accusation upon anyone’s inspection.

For who could fittingly endure someone who, at the very outset, with a certain apostolic authority, proposes to write about charity, “the more excellent way”—someone not merely unpractised in writing, or, as you have chosen to call him, unlettered, but tongue-tied as well, and not yet able fittingly to lick the milk? Or how should one who possesses only a portion of things—or indeed none at all—speak of charity’s eminence while himself unformed; of its order while barren; draw out its sweetness while insipid and without taste; or raise himself against covetousness while conquered by it? Finally, how charity is increased by the mortification of the flesh, and its exercise governed by discernment—who am I to explain these things? I who, contrary to what you think—though I say this with your permission—came from the kitchens to the hermitage and changed my place, not my occupation?

But you will say: “You ought not to make excuses.” I know it, my lord, I know. But because I am not permitted to excuse myself, I am pleased to accuse myself, so that an unfavourably disposed reader may not be compelled to proceed further when, on the very threshold, he sees why he may rightly take offence.

Yet how great a confidence for writing is supplied by the fact that you have unhesitatingly exposed your most holy affection of charity to troubles that may justly be inflicted upon me! And so, having scarcely any hope of completing it, I have put together, as I could, this *Mirror* concerning the charity you commanded, with that hammer of ours to which you alluded. In this I found the surest truth: when hope and all else have failed, charity always remains. He bestowed grace, though he did not grant skill.

Indeed, in this mirror of charity, charity will not reveal her countenance to anyone except one who remains in love; just as each person’s face is reflected in any mirror only when he stands in the light. As for my purpose in undertaking the present work: some things I had meditated privately with myself; other things I had dictated, scattered in epistolary form, as though with myself—indeed, more truly with myself, since I had shared them in one mind with my most reverend prior Hugh, who was more with me than I myself was with myself. Drawing material from these for my present purpose, and inserting the same things where they seemed suitable, I divided the whole into three sections.

Although I mention each subject in its own place, my intention is especially this: in the first part, to commend charity’s excellence, both from its dignity and from the condemnation of the covetousness opposed to it; in the second, to respond to the unsuitable complaints of certain persons; and in the third, to show how charity ought to be exercised. Therefore, if anything suited to my purpose has emerged in this labour, it is due to the giver of glory and to your prayer; but if anything is otherwise, let it be attributed to me, who possess neither skill nor practice.

But lest the great length of this work alarm you amid your occupations, first run through the chapters set below, and by looking at them discern what should be read and what may be passed over.

THE MIRROR OF CHARITY.

[Col. 0505]

BOOK ONE. Demonstrating the excellence of charity.

CHAPTER I. That nothing is more fitting than that the Creator should be loved by his creature.

[Col. 0505A]

You have stretched out your heaven, Lord, like a skin, placing stars in it to shine for us in this night, through which the beasts of the forest pass, the young lions roaring to seize prey and seek their food from you. You also cover its upper regions with waters, by which, through certain most secret sluices, you pour rain upon the earth of our heart, so that it may be multiplied from the fruit of its grain, wine, and oil, and so that we may not seek our bread with fruitless labour; but, seeking, may find; finding, may be fed and taste that you are sweet, O Lord.

My soul—my dry, barren, unfruitful soul—thirsts to be sprinkled with these most sweet drops, [Col. 0505B] so that that heavenly bread which feeds angels and which a little child sucks may appear to it; so that every delight may taste sweet to my inward palate; and so that I may no longer sigh for the pots of flesh which I left in Egypt, where, at Pharaoh’s demand, even when the straw had been taken away, I rendered bricks of mud.

Therefore let your voice sound in my ears, good Jesus, so that my heart may learn how to love you, my mind may love you, and the very inward parts of my soul may love you. Let the innermost marrow of my heart embrace you, my one and only true good, my sweet and delightful joy. But what is love, my God? It is, unless I am mistaken, a wonderful delight of the soul: sweeter as it is chaster; more pleasant as it is more sincere; more joyful as it is more expansive. It is the palate of the heart to which you are sweet, because you are sweet; the eye by which you are seen, because you are good; [Col. 0505C] and it is a place capable of containing you, though you are most high. For whoever loves you contains you, and contains as much as he loves, because you yourself are love, because you are charity.

This is that abundance of your house with which your beloved shall be made drunk, failing from themselves so that they may pass into you. And how, Lord, except by loving you? Yet this is done with one’s whole self. Let some small portion, I pray, Lord, of this great sweetness of yours descend into my soul, so that the breads of its bitterness may grow sweet to it. By the experience of a small foretaste, let it taste what it should desire, what it should long for, what it should sigh after in this pilgrimage. Let it taste beforehand by hungering; let it drink by thirsting. For those who eat you shall still hunger, and those who drink you shall still thirst; but they shall be satisfied when your glory appears, when that great multitude of your sweetness is revealed which you have hidden for those who fear you, [Col. 0506A] and which you reveal only to those who love you.

Meanwhile, Lord, I shall seek you, and I shall seek you by loving; for whoever advances in loving you surely seeks you, Lord; and whoever loves you perfectly has already found you, Lord. And what is more just than that your creature should love you, who has received from you this very power to love you? Irrational and insensible things cannot love you; that is not their mode. They too possess their mode, their form, and their order—not so that they are or can become blessed by loving you, but so that, beautiful, good, and well ordered through you, they may contribute to the glory of those who can be blessed because they can love you.

CHAPTER II. On nature, form, and use, which are bestowed in common upon all creatures.

[Col. 0506B]

For our God, whose being is supreme and unchangeable, whose being is always the same, as David says: “You are always the same” (Ps. 101), has distributed these three things in common to all his creatures: nature, form, and use. Nature, by which they are good; form, by which they are beautiful; use, by which, well ordered, they contribute to some purpose. For he who made them to exist also made them to be good, beautiful, and well ordered.

Since they are from him who is supremely and unchangeably existent, all things exist. Since he from whom they are is supremely and unchangeably beautiful, all things are beautiful. From him who is supremely and unchangeably good, all things are good. From him who is supremely and unchangeably wise, all things are well [Col. 0506C] ordered. Thus they are good by nature; beautiful by form; well ordered toward the beauty of the universe itself. “God,” it says, “saw all things that he had made, and they were very good” (Gen. 1).

Therefore, insofar as they exist, they are good; insofar as each part fits its whole, they are beautiful; insofar as, within the universe itself, every thing possesses its fitting place, time, and mode, they are most excellently ordered. Each thing has the place suitable to it in which it exists: for example, the angel has heaven, irrational creatures the ground, and man—being intermediate—the intermediate paradise. Likewise, each has its time: when or for how long it exists. Thus, in the beauty of the universe itself, one kind begins altogether at once but never ends, as angelic nature; another kind does not all begin together, but, once begun, never itself ceases, as human beings; another neither begins all at once nor remains forever, as irrational creatures.

[Col. 0507A] And lest we appear to have been silent concerning the mode in which each creature subsists, and the fitting mode allotted to all things: what is more fitting for a rational creature than blessedness, if it is just? What better befits it than misery, if it is unjust? Finally, what mode is more appropriate for irrational and insensible creatures than that, since they themselves can be neither blessed nor miserable, they should serve the salvation of the former and increase the unhappiness of the latter?

A certain wise man speaks with complete truth: “Water, fire, and iron; milk, bread, and honey; a cluster of grapes, oil, and clothing: all these things shall turn to good for the holy, and likewise to evil for the impious and sinners” (Ecclus. 39). Let no one complain that he now shares a place with beasts, when “being set in honour, he did not understand”; and therefore “he was compared to beasts and made like them”—and not merely in place. For who could easily say how great a likeness to irrational beasts has grown up when, in the rational mind, if not the image, at least the divine likeness has been destroyed? But of this elsewhere.

For the present, the Creator’s wisdom must be observed and praised: though he is not the creator or instigator of evils, he is nevertheless their most wise disposer. Why, then, should my Lord, who is at once most sweet and almighty, not permit evil to exist, when it could not in the slightest degree overthrow his eternal purpose? Indeed, in this way his omnipotence appears more manifest, [Col. 0507C] his wisdom more wonderful, and his mercy sweeter: he makes good from evils by his power; wisely orders what is disordered; and mercifully gives blessedness to the miserable.

CHAPTER III. That man was made in the image of his Creator and is capable of blessedness.

To man, then, in the very creation of the universe, God gave not only existence, nor merely, as to other creatures, a good existence; not only to be beautiful or ordered, but in addition to be blessed. Yet just as no creature exists of itself, nor is beautiful or good of itself, but is so from him who supremely exists and is supremely good and beautiful—and is therefore the goodness of all good things, the beauty of all beautiful things, and the cause of all things that exist—so no creature is blessed of itself, but by him who is supremely blessed and is consequently the blessedness of all blessed beings.

[Col. 0507D] Only the rational creature is capable of this blessedness. Made in the image of its Creator, it is fit to cleave to him whose image it is. This alone is the good of a rational creature, as holy David says: “But for me, it is good to cleave to God” (Ps. 72). This cleaving is plainly not of the flesh but of the mind. In it the author of natures implanted three things through which it attains divine eternity, shares in wisdom, and tastes sweetness. These three, I say, are memory, knowledge, and love or will. Memory is capable of eternity; knowledge, of wisdom; [Col. 0508A] love, of sweetness. In these three, man was made in the image of the Trinity: he held God in memory without forgetfulness, knew him by knowledge without error, and embraced him in love without coveting any other thing. Hence he was blessed.

CHAPTER IV. That through love, in which the taste of blessedness was more fully present, man departed from God; and, becoming miserable, corrupted God’s image in himself without wholly destroying it.

Although blessedness is fulfilled in these three, or by these three, its taste properly belongs to the third. For though it is most miserable to delight in the worst things, where there is no delight there is no blessedness. Moreover, where there is no love, there is no delight. And the greater the love of the supreme good itself, the greater the delight, and the greater the blessedness. Let memory acquire much and knowledge comprehend profound things: still there is no delight unless the will is turned toward what has been acquired or known.

But our first parent, endowed with free choice and assisted by God’s grace, could indeed delight perpetually in God himself, loving him in memory and knowledge, and could remain perpetually blessed. He could also turn his love toward something lesser; and thus, withdrawing from God’s love, grow cold and deliver himself over to misery. For just as the rational creature has no blessedness other than cleaving to God, so its misery is to depart from God.

[Col. 0508C] But “being set in honour, he did not understand.” What did he fail to understand? Perhaps what one who entered God’s sanctuary and understood not only the present but also the final things understood: “For behold,” he says, “those who remove themselves from you shall perish; you have destroyed all who commit fornication away from you” (Ps. 72). He did not understand that those who commit fornication away from God through pride fall into folly; and that one who usurps God’s likeness by robbery rightly puts on the likeness of beasts.

Therefore, using free choice wrongly, he turned his love away from that unchangeable good and, blinded by his own covetousness, turned it toward what was lesser. Thus, departing from the true good and failing toward that which was not good in itself, where he sought advancement he found loss; and by loving himself perversely he lost both himself [Col. 0508D] and God. Thus it was done with the utmost justice: he who desired, against God, God’s likeness, became through covetousness more unlike him whom he had wished through curiosity to resemble.

God’s image in man was therefore corrupted, but not wholly effaced. Accordingly, he retains memory, but liable to forgetfulness; knowledge, but subject to error; and love, but inclined toward covetousness. In this trinity there yet remains in the rational soul, though miserable, an imprint of the blessed Trinity itself, belonging to the remaining substance of the soul: the soul remembers itself, knows itself, and loves itself; it loves, knows, and remembers its own memory; it remembers, knows, and loves its own knowledge; likewise it loves, remembers, and knows its own love. In its substance it displays unity, and in these three names [Col. 0509A] which we have touched upon, trinity.

Hence the Psalmist says: “Nevertheless, man passes by in an image, yet he is troubled in vain” (Ps. 38). In these words holy David briefly but quite explicitly indicates both that the human soul does not lack the image by nature and that it suffers corruption by sin. For forgetfulness corrupts memory; error darkens knowledge; covetousness constricts love.

CHAPTER V. That after the Saviour’s coming God’s image is renewed in man; and that the perfection of its renewal is to be hoped for not here but in the life to come.

Now, through the Mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, the bond by which human nature was held liable has been loosed; the written indictment, by whose surety the dreadful pride of the ancient enemy held us bound, has been erased; the principalities and powers to which divine justice had consigned us have been stripped; and God the Father has at last been reconciled by that unique sacrifice on the cross. Accordingly, memory is restored through the teaching of sacred Scripture, understanding through the sacrament of faith, and love through the daily increase of charity.

[Col. 0509B] The reformation of the image is perfect when forgetfulness does not interrupt memory, no error darkens knowledge, and no covetousness interrupts love. But where and when will this be? Let this peace, this tranquillity, this blessed happiness be hoped for in our homeland, where there is no place for forgetfulness among those living in eternity; no stealthy invasion of error among those enjoying truth; no impulse of covetousness among those absorbed in divine charity.

O eternal and true charity! O true and dear eternity! O eternal, true, and dear Trinity! Here is rest; here is peace; here is happy tranquillity; here is tranquil happiness; here is happy and tranquil joy.

What are you doing, human soul? What are you doing? Why are you snatched in different directions? Yet one thing is necessary. Why seek many things? Whatever you desire in many things is in the One. If you seek pre-eminence, knowledge, delight, or abundance: all is here, perfectly here, and nowhere but here. Is there true pre-eminence in this lake of misery and mire of filth? Is there perfect knowledge in this region of the shadow of death? Is there true delight in this place of horror and vast solitude, or true abundance amid so many miseries?

[Col. 0509D] What worldly pre-eminence is not cast down by fear? How great is the knowledge of a person who cannot even comprehend himself? Finally, if you delight in the flesh, so do horse and mule, which have no understanding. If in glory or riches: “when you die, you shall take none of all things, nor shall your glory descend with you.” Therefore true pre-eminence is there where nothing higher can be sought; true knowledge, where nothing is unknown; true delight, which is not diminished by weariness; true abundance, which is never exhausted.

Woe to us, because we have departed from you, Lord! Alas for me, because my sojourning has been prolonged! (Ps. 109.) “When shall I come and appear before your face?” (Ps. 41.) “Who will give me wings like a dove? I will fly away and be at rest” (Ps. 54.) Meanwhile, Lord Jesus, [Col. 0510A] let my soul, I pray, grow feathers in the nest of your discipline; let it rest in the clefts of the rock, in the hollow of the wall. Meanwhile let it embrace you crucified; let it take a draught of your most sweet blood. Let this sweet meditation meanwhile occupy my memory, lest forgetfulness utterly darken it. Let me meanwhile judge that I know nothing except the Lord, and him crucified, lest vain error lead my knowledge away from faith’s firmness. Let this wondrous love of yours claim my whole love for itself, lest worldly covetousness swallow it up.

What then? Shall I desire this for myself alone? May that prophetic word be fulfilled, Lord, I pray; may it be fulfilled: “All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord” (Ps. 21). “They shall remember,” he says. Thus he understood God’s memory to be hidden, not entirely buried, in the rational mind, so that you may perceive not so much something new implanted as that ancient thing restored. For unless human reason naturally possessed at least some small spark of God’s memory, I think there would be no basis upon which even the fool could say in his heart: “There is no God” (Ps. 13).

CHAPTER VI. A disputation against the fool who said in his heart: “There is no God” (Ps. 13).

Tell me, whoever you are, so foolish as to have said in your heart, “There is no God”: do you consider anyone wise? Perhaps yourself. Let it be so. But are you wise in such a way that you cannot become foolish? Or, if foolish, so completely that you cannot become wise? [Col. 0510C] If you deny either of these alternatives, I shall say that you are not merely foolish but rather not alive.

Therefore, if you become foolish, do you think that wisdom perishes? But you can become wise. From where, I ask, except from wisdom? Therefore wisdom will exist even while you are foolish. “It will exist,” you say, “but in a wise human being.” But what human being cannot become foolish? Therefore, if all human beings should become foolish, wisdom would nevertheless exist; otherwise they could not become wise again. “But it exists in angels,” you say. Yet the great multitude of foolish angels shows that they too, at least by nature, can become foolish; their nature is equal to that of the rest, though their grace is unequal.

No creature, therefore, is wise of itself. Whence, then, except from wisdom? And where does the fool find it so that he may become wise again? If he finds it, wisdom surely exists, to be found by the fool so that he may become wise. Otherwise, how is that found which does not exist, unless it first begins to exist? “No,” you say, “I do not find it in that way; rather, by meditating and practising, I make myself wise.” Therefore you make your own wisdom? “Why should I not make it?” I had presented you as a fool, and behold, you have become so wise that you are even sufficient to make wisdom. Is it a small thing to be wise enough to make a wise person?

Yet if anyone were to say that a fool can make a wise person, who hearing it would not laugh? Whence, then, does the fool receive wisdom? Perhaps from some wise person. And whence is that person wise? Did he make himself wise? But before making himself wise, what was he except foolish? The absurdity already stated will therefore follow: a fool made a wise person. If you say that an angel can make a person wise: [Col. 0511A] whence is the angel wise? If he too made himself wise, the same absurdity nevertheless follows.

It remains, then, that wisdom, which makes others wise, is not made. Wisdom itself cannot become foolish, because wisdom cannot be folly, just as death cannot be life—although the death of Christ is our life; just as light cannot be darkness—although we were once darkness, but are now light in the Lord. For John was not the light, but bore witness to the light. “For there was the true light, which enlightens every human being coming into this world” (John 1). That is wisdom, which passes into holy souls so that they too may be wise.

Is this too little for you, O fool? I ask again: do you know that you exist? “Who,” you say, “does not know this?” Certainly not even an Academic skeptic. Have you always existed? Whence, then, did you receive existence? Did you make yourself? But how could one who was nothing make so great a thing? Whence, then, do you have being? From another human being? And whence did that person have it? From an angel, perhaps? And whence did the angel have it?

[Col. 0511B] It remains, therefore, that there is an uncreated essence from which all other things receive being, just as there is an uncreated wisdom from which all other things receive wisdom. Let all these ways of being wise and of existing be silent for you; let Wisdom itself and Being itself speak to your heart. Then you will no longer say in your heart, “There is no God,” seeing plainly that you could not even exist in order to say in your heart, “There is no God,” unless God existed.

Again I ask whether you wish to exist and to be wise. I suppose you do not deny it. Join together these three: to be, to know, to will. Return, then, transgressor, to your heart. Consider how great is the unity and equality in these three. And when you find that these three are in you but are not from you, think upon the eternal will. Do not say in your heart, “There is no God”; rather, remembering, turn to the Lord your God with every end of the earth.

CHAPTER VII. That man departed from God through the affection of his mind.

“Your knowledge has become wonderful beyond me, O Lord; it has grown strong, and I cannot attain to it” (Ps. 138 [139]). Meanwhile I will embrace you, Lord Jesus: the little one embracing the little one, the weak the weak, man the man—indeed, I will say more, the poor man. For you too, Lord, are poor, seated upon an ass and upon the colt, the foal of an ass [Col. 0511D] (Matt. 21). Thus, then, will I embrace you, Lord. For all my greatness is only that which is little in you; all my strength, that which is weak in you; all my wisdom, that which is foolish in you. I will run, Lord, after the fragrance of these ointments (Song 1). Do you wonder that I call “ointments” those things which heal the sick, strengthen the feeble, and gladden the sorrowful? Therefore I will follow you, Lord Jesus, stirred by the fragrance of these ointments and refreshed by their sprinkling. I will follow you, Lord, even if not upon the mountains of spices, where your bride found you (Song 8), or in the garden, Lord, where your flesh was sown (John 18). There indeed you leap; here you sleep. Here, Lord, here you sleep: here you lie down; here you keep a certain sweet Sabbath. Let my flesh be buried with you, Lord, so that the life I now live [Col. 0512A] in the flesh I may not live in myself, but in you, who gave yourself for me. Let the myrrh of chastity be joined to you, Lord, so that sin may no longer reign in my mortal body, and I may not become like a beast rotting in its own dung. But whence did you come into the garden? Whence, unless from the cross? Would that I too, Lord, might take up your cross and follow you. But how shall I follow you? “How,” you ask, “did you depart from me?” I think, Lord, not by a step of the feet, but by an affection of the mind. For unwilling to preserve the substance of my soul for you, I took it for myself; and wishing to possess myself without you, I lost even myself. I myself became burdensome to myself; I became for myself a place of misery and darkness, a place of terror and a land of want. Therefore I will arise and go to my Father [Col. 0512B] and say to him: “Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you” (Luke 15).

## CHAPTER VIII. That by the affection of charity a human being is reformed into the image of God.

It is clear, unless I am mistaken, that just as human pride, departing from the highest good not by a step of the feet but by an affection of the mind, and growing old within itself, corrupted the image of God in itself; so human humility, approaching God by an affection of the mind, is renewed into the image of God, who created him. Hence the Apostle says: “Be renewed in the spirit of your mind; and put on the new man, who has been created according to God” (Eph. 4). But how will this renewal occur except through the new [Col. 0512C] commandment of charity, of which the Savior says: “I give you a new commandment” (John 13)? Accordingly, if the mind perfectly puts on this charity, it will assuredly reform those two things which, we said, had been equally corrupted: namely, memory and knowledge. For this reason the summary of this one commandment is most beneficially prescribed to us: in it consist both the putting off of the old man, the renewal of the mind, and the reformation of the divine image.

For our love, infected with the poison of covetousness and miserably entangled in the tenacious birdlime of pleasure, was always borne downward—namely, from vice to vice—by its own weight. But as charity flows down from above and dissolves its innate torpor by its warmth, it raises itself toward higher things; and thus, putting off oldness and putting on newness, it receives the silvered wings of the dove, by which [Col. 0512D] it may fly to that sublime and pure good from which it also derives its origin. Blessed Paul declared this more openly to the Athenians. For after speaking subtly at length concerning God, and proving most forcefully from the books of the philosophers also that God is one, “in whom we live and move and are,” he says among other things: “For we too are his offspring” (Acts 17). And he added: “Therefore, since we are the offspring of God.”

Let no one suppose that the Apostle called us the offspring of God so as to establish that we are of the same natural substance or essence as God. Otherwise we could neither be changeable nor corruptible, nor could we ever be miserable, just as neither can his only-begotten Son, who was born from his substance and is shown in all things equal to the Father himself. Rather, he affirms—or, better, does not deny—that we are God’s offspring because the rational soul, created in his image [Col. 0513A], is known to be capable of sharing in his wisdom and blessedness. Thus charity raises our soul to that for which it was made; covetousness presses it down toward that into which it voluntarily sank.

## CHAPTER IX. That our love is divided against itself by the contrary impulse of charity and covetousness.

But since that part of our soul which is capable of charity and likewise of covetousness is more commonly called love, it is this love which, through the new infusion of charity and the remnants of old covetousness, is found to be divided against itself by a kind of contrary desire. Of this the Apostle says: “I do not do what I will” (Rom. 7). And again: “The flesh desires [Col. 0513B] against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh. These oppose one another, so that you do not do whatever things you wish” (Gal. 5).

It must certainly be understood that by the names “spirit” and “flesh” the Apostle has by no means described two contrary natures in one person, as the impure Manichaeans dream. Rather, by the designation “spirit” he expresses the newness of the mind arising from the infusion of charity—for “the charity of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5)—while by the term “flesh” he indicates the miserable slavery of the soul arising from the remnants of oldness. Between our old, ingrained condition and our new, newly introduced condition, he asserts that an unceasing conflict arises in one and the same mind.

## CHAPTER X. That free choice occupies a middle place in the soul, yet is not equally sufficient for good and evil.

[Col. 0513C]

Between these two—namely, the concupiscence which the Apostle calls that of the flesh (Gal. 5), not because every evil concupiscence comes from flesh, since demons, who have no flesh, are by no means without it, but because it is from man rather than from God, and that man is called “flesh” in the Scriptures is beyond doubt—between this concupiscence, which is most fittingly called covetousness, and that of the spirit which we may rightly call charity, which indeed is the Spirit not of ourselves but of God—for “the charity of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit [Col. 0513D] who has been given to us” (Rom. 5)—between these two, I say, that which in a human being is called free choice occupies, as it were, a middle place, so that toward whichever of them the soul turns, it does so by free choice.

Yet let no one be so foolish as to dare attribute to a human being an equal ability for good and for evil from free choice, since we are not sufficient to think anything from ourselves as though from ourselves; since it is God who works in us both willing and accomplishing, according to his good will; and since, finally, it belongs neither to one who wills nor to one who runs, but to God who shows mercy. What then? Is free choice thereby denied to be present in a human being? Far from it. For free choice is that power or nature of the soul—or whatever more fitting term may be used—that element of the human person by which one consents to anything not without the judgment of reason: not the consent to this or that thing, whether good or evil, but that by which consent is given.

For just as sight is one thing and seeing another—for sight is one of the five bodily senses, while seeing is the act of that sense itself—so we say that consent itself is one thing, and that by which one consents another. Consent, indeed, is a certain action of the soul; free choice is a certain power and nature of the soul by which it consents, having an innate judgment by which it chooses to what it will consent. But because consent is effected by the will and judgment by reason, these two—will and reason—constitute free choice. Reason presents, as it were, things good or evil, just or unjust, and things which are indifferent; the will consents, and it consents to whatever it does consent only by willing. [Col. 0514B] But where there is will, there is also a certain freedom.

Thus, as we have said, free choice appears to consist of these two: the freedom of the will and the judgment of reason. You see, then, how free choice is not prejudiced, from whatever source a good will arises in a person, since in either a good or an evil will one does not lose willing and therefore does not lose freedom, nor reason, and consequently not judgment. For what? Because it is God who works willing in us, have we therefore lost willing? Or because it is from God that we use reason rightly, do we therefore not use reason? Or because whatever good we accomplish is from God, do we therefore accomplish no good? Or because we are not sufficient to think anything from ourselves, since our sufficiency [Col. 0514C] is from God, is there therefore no sufficiency? Although what we do is from God’s grace, we nevertheless act; nor do we act without will or without reason; and therefore we do not act without free choice.

## CHAPTER XI. That grace does not take away free choice.

For those who lack will and reason and consequently free choice—such as cattle—God works nothing of this sort in them; and therefore they too perform nothing of this sort. But whatever good God works through us or concerning us without our will belongs to God alone and not to us as well; whereas whatever he works with our will belongs both to him and to us. For “if I do this willingly,” says the Apostle, “I receive a reward; but if unwillingly, a stewardship has been entrusted to me” (1 Cor. 9). Therefore, in order that the work which he performs in us or through us may also be ours, he inclines the will so that we consent; and thus, from his grace, the reward becomes ours. For “if I do this willingly, I receive a reward”; but in order that I may be willing in a good work, it is God who works the willing.

Then, stirring this very will to ask, seek, and knock, he gives grace for grace: namely, the accomplishing in return for the good will. Finally, since eternal life is the reward of good works, in giving it he crowns his own gifts, which he has willed to be our merits. See this whole matter in Paul: “I was,” he says, “a blasphemer and persecutor and insolent man” (1 Tim. 1). Here was will, but evil; merits, but most evil. “But I obtained mercy, that I might be faithful” (1 Tim. 1). Behold a good will; but see whence it came. It did not arise because anything good preceded in me, but because his mercy went before me. For “I obtained mercy, that I might be faithful.”

Indeed, as blessed Augustine says, someone may go unwillingly to church, hear the word of God, and receive Christ’s sacrament; no one can believe except willingly. Hear also concerning the work: “I labored more abundantly than all of them” (1 Cor. 15). Do you possess this, Paul, which you did not receive? On the contrary, I received it. And indeed, “I labored more abundantly than all of them—yet not I” (ibid.). How can both be true: “I,” and “not I”? “Not I,” because not from myself; not by my own powers; not by my own wisdom; not, finally, by my own merits, but by the grace of God (ibid.). What then? Does it take away your free choice, destroy your will, and eliminate the judgment of reason? Far from it! I said, “Not I,” because “the grace of God [was] with me.” In what way with me? By acting so that I consent to work, and thus cooperate myself—and cooperate willingly—lest, if it works concerning me or through me against my will, I should not be the one able to say: “I have fought the good fight; I have finished the course; I have kept the faith” (1 Tim. 4).

Therefore free choice is not sufficient for any good; but in it, or with it, or through it, God accomplishes many good things. In it, when by hidden inspiration he raises it toward some good; with it, when he joins free choice itself to himself through consent; through it, when, with God working, one person profits through another. “A crown of righteousness,” he says, “has been laid up for me” (ibid.). What crown but eternal life? “There has been laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord will render to me on that day” (2 Tim. 4). “He will render,” he says. Therefore, because it is rendered, eternal life is a reward. It is certainly a reward because a good work preceded it: “I have fought the good fight.” But whence came that work? “Yet not I, but the grace of God with me.” Thus our merits are God’s grace. On account of those merits he gives eternal life: grace for grace. Finally, “he will render to each according to his works.” Yet only those works are granted the heavenly reward which were first bestowed by his gift.

For hear from him himself that eternal life is grace: “For the wages of sin is death, but the grace of God is eternal life” (Rom. 6). Eternal life, I say, is grace, and a twofold grace: grace, because it is given for grace; grace, because glory outweighs merits. “For the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory which shall be revealed in us” (Rom. 8).

## CHAPTER XII. That free choice is not taken away either from the saved or the condemned, and that grace works only in free choice.

But in that glory shall we be without a will by which we consent to so great a good, or without reason by which we judge this good to be ours? Therefore neither shall we be without free choice—not by which we shall be able to do any evil, but by which we shall be found capable of that good. For cattle are capable neither of condemnation nor of salvation, precisely because they are devoid of reason and will.

For infants, although grace is not greater in them, it is more evident—in whom there are no merits even by gift—although because of the weakness arising from the punishment of sin they live and die without free choice, nevertheless, once stripped of this bodily covering by which they are hindered, must by no means be believed to share in eternal blessedness or deserved condemnation without a rational will. In all of these who are saved, grace becomes more evident, since they lack free choice to which merits can be attributed. Yet grace seems more abundant to me in the case in which both merits and rewards are given.

Therefore no one should glory, since nothing is ours. “For who distinguishes you,” O man? Free choice? Certainly—but from beasts, not from the unjust. For the unjust too possess free choice, without which they could not be unjust. Except only for original sin, which constrains everyone, even unwillingly, on another ground, no one can be just except willingly, and no one can be unjust except willingly; consequently, neither can one be so without free choice. But grace alone raises the will to righteousness; the will itself casts itself down into unrighteousness.

Moreover, wherever there is will, there is freedom. For wherever a thing exists by will, it is not compelled to exist by necessity. Therefore the will has, as it were, a freedom innate to it, because it cannot suffer any necessity. Do you wish to hear of a certain freedom even in unrighteousness? Hear the Apostle: “For when you were slaves of sin, you were free from righteousness” (Rom. 6). Do you see that freedom is not lacking to the will even in slavery to sin?

But does the judgment of reason, by which it distinguishes what it wills from what it does not will, lack in the freedom of an unrighteous will? Does it lack the judgment by which it judges advantageous, good, or pleasant even what it wickedly wills? For if either of these were absent, it could perhaps desire pleasant things only, but could not dissent from them by a kind of rational judgment—which is the function of free choice. That a human being can use reason even for evil is proved by that prophetic saying: “They are wise to do evil” (Jer. 4).

For even in the punishments of hell, free choice is not lacking, by which they voluntarily—and thus freely—dissent from the evils which they suffer; nor is the judgment of reason lacking, by which they accuse and judge themselves because they suffer such things by their own merits. The reasoning is clear, unless I am mistaken: neither does grace destroy free choice, nor does free choice diminish grace. For how could grace take away free choice when grace works only in free choice? This grace of which we speak does not work in brute animals or insensible things, but only in those capable of hearing command and prohibition: “Do this and do that; do not do this and do not do that.” Such words are undoubtedly spoken only to those who possess free choice, by which they can will this or that. But so that they may will the good, God’s grace works—not destroying free choice so that they will nothing, but inclining it so that they will the good. Therefore, whenever you do something good, do not suppose that you do it by your own powers; yet do not estrange it from your own will, since [Col. 0517A] a work ought not to be called good unless it is also voluntary.

## CHAPTER XIII. The reason why free choice is not equally sufficient for good and evil.

But someone will say: “I now agree, and it has indeed been sufficiently proved that the grace of God can so work all things in all persons as to prejudice the freedom of choice in no respect. But who knows whether it is so? What reason is there that, while free choice needs no assistance for evil, it is not sufficient for itself for good?”

Who is there for whom it is not enough that Catholic faith consents to this assertion, that the daily experience of everyone who advances well confirms it, that prophetic and apostolic testimonies further affirm it, and—greater than all these—that saying of that truthful mouth: “Without me you can do nothing” [Col. 0517B] (John 15)? Moreover, when eyes have been purified by this faith, reason cannot be lacking: understanding will be present, and the light of truth will pour itself in. Therefore let the one who can see, see; let the one who cannot see, believe. Let the one who sees rejoice, but humbly; let the one who does not see believe, but perseveringly, because “unless you believe, you shall not understand” (Isa. 7).

Let him see, I say, that since every creature has been made from nothing and made mutable, by a certain natural impulse of its mutability it always tends toward that from which it was made—that is, toward nothing. And indeed it is very easy to see that everything naturally mutable needs something immutable lest it change. For no mutable thing possesses immutability in itself; otherwise it would not even be mutable, much less could it bestow it upon another. But if a creature, unsupported by the aid of any protector, changes, who does not easily see that it is changed by a certain necessary impulse still more naturally, so to speak, and more plainly toward that from which it was made? Therefore, so that it may not sink to lower things through its mutability, may restrain its mutability in that which it is, and may rise toward higher things under happier auspices, it always needs the grace of him by whose power it was created.

## CHAPTER XIV. The difference between the grace which the first human beings had in Paradise and that which the predestined have in the world; and why an evil will is justly imputed to a human being, although the power of free choice is insufficient to obtain a good will.
