Thus in heaven for the angel, and in Paradise for the human being, although no weakness constrained them and no iniquity ruled over them, nevertheless, because each had a mutable nature, this grace was necessary for both. Certainly, had it not been bestowed, each could have sinned with excuse. But since, through creating grace, a good will had been bestowed upon them, and through assisting grace the ability to persevere in it if they themselves willed: no excuse remains based on mutable nature. For divine goodness would not have failed to sustain and advance that nature, if their own iniquity had not abandoned it.

Whether such grace is sometimes still bestowed upon the reprobate, so that a good will is inspired in them and grace added by which, if they themselves will, the ability to persevere is not lacking, I do not dare rashly to pronounce. But upon the elect, because misery presses upon them more greatly than upon the first human beings in Paradise, a greater grace is bestowed; and the greater the weakness which attacks them, the more abundant is the ability granted to resist. For to those first persons, as has been said, we know that it was granted to be able to persevere if they willed; to these, moreover, it is granted that they may persevere.

“But,” you say, “what fault is it in a human being if he does not possess a good will, which he can neither acquire by his own powers nor retain by his own powers once acquired?” Yet when he was created with a good will, through whose fault was he made worse? Why should that very incapacity not most justly be imputed to him—an incapacity which the Creator did not impose upon him, but to which he voluntarily subjected himself? And even if it perhaps seems unfair that he should be blamed because he does not now have a good will, which indeed he cannot have unless he receives it: is it unjust that he be charged with having lost what he received? Is it unjust that the evils be imputed to him which he committed with no one compelling him?

## CHAPTER XV. That even the condemnation of little children is most just.

To this, you say, reason most justly condemns those who are capable of reason and lack neither the judgment by which to choose nor the will by which to consent. But what reason assigns little children to condemnation, whom neither creation made evil nor their own will made unjust? What then? Do you judge it unjust for fire to consume a useless and fruitless tree? Consider, I beg you, the whole human race as a dry tree, a fruitless tree, corrupted in its very root because it was infected with the venom of the ancient serpent: most justly consigned to flames, destined for fire, adjudged to condemnation.

What then? Do you show yourself ungrateful, O useless tree, because certain little branches, cut from your dead root, are rescued from the fire in order that, grafted into a fruitful stock, they may be restored to their former beauty? Behold that green tree, the tree of life, whose leaves do not fall and whose every work prospers. In his own most sweet side, which for this reason he willed to be opened on the cross, it made room for branches distinguished from that condemned root by his mercy alone, so that, grafted and planted together with him and made one with him, they might revive and flourish—not by their own power, which is none, but by participation in his Spirit. Receiving that voluntary rain which God sets apart for his inheritance, warmed also by the sun of divine charity, and taking up anew the sap of heavenly grace, they may bear spiritual fruit to be stored in the heavenly granaries.

“But I,” says that useless branch, “was left behind.” Certainly you were left. Why do you complain? “Is your eye evil because I am good?” I gave much indeed to many, though I owed it to no one; and do you therefore become evil and envious, make this an objection, and frame an accusation from this? “But,” you say, “when equal condemnation holds both little children equally entangled, why is one chosen and the other rejected?” Hear why: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (Rom. 9). You cry that this is unjust. “Does the thing formed say to him who formed it, ‘Why have you made me thus?’ Or does not the potter have power from the same lump of clay to make one vessel for honor, another for dishonor?” (ibid.).

If, then, a human being assigns to honor whichever vessels he wishes among those he makes, and exposes whichever he wishes to dishonor, and no one complains that it is unjust: do you accuse God if, from vessels all exposed indeed to most just dishonor, he takes whichever he wishes, leaves whichever he wishes, restores whichever he wishes to their former honor, and inflicts deserved condemnation upon whichever he wishes? If, I say, in distinguishing the vessels which the potter forms from the same clay his will itself is justice, how much more, in distinguishing, ordering, taking, separating, saving, and condemning all things which the Almighty created from nothing, must his will itself be supreme justice? Therefore “he has mercy on whom he wills,” gives mercy to whomever pleases him, hardens whom he wills by most justly abandoning them, softens whom he wills by most mercifully showing mercy; and he does whatever he wills, yet does nothing unjust, since between just and unjust his will alone makes the distinction. That will is nothing other than equity itself; nor does his will depend on another law of justice, but the law of justice depends upon his will.

We have said these things lest the condemnation of little children appear unjust. Therefore, O human being, “do not think lofty thoughts, but fear.” For if God does not spare branches with which your condition is equal and your merit alike, perhaps he will not spare you either. See, therefore, the severity and goodness of God: severity indeed in those who are abandoned, but goodness toward you, if you remain in goodness. Otherwise you too will be abandoned.

Moreover, so that you may not be abandoned but rather be distinguished from those abandoned, do not presume upon yourself; do not despair of God’s goodness; do not be negligent in working; do not be sluggish in praying with the Prophet, who says: “Judge my cause against an unholy nation” (Ps. 42 [43]). But so that you may persevere in this goodness, do not flatter yourself concerning your own powers; rather, place your confidence in him to whom the Prophet likewise cries: “You, O Lord, will preserve us and guard us from this generation forever” (Ps. 11 [12]). That is, from the generation concerning which he immediately added: “The wicked walk in a circle” (ibid.). These are those who, like Samson with the hair of virtues cut off and the lights of knowledge and reason gouged out, are assigned to the mill, so that, abandoning the short way of charity, they may keep to the circuit of covetousness.

## CHAPTER XVI. That charity lacks nothing of perfection.

[Col. 0519D]

What of you, O my soul? Have you become sufficiently entangled in this circuit? “The head of their circuit: the labor of their lips shall cover them” (Ps. 139 [140]). What, I ask, is the profit of this labor? Is it anything other than the husks of swine? Not even from these is there satisfaction; or, if there is satisfaction, what kind is it? O how sweeter, more pleasant, and finally more welcome is the hunger of charity than the satisfaction of covetousness! But as to blessedness, there is no comparison at all. For the more anyone is fattened by covetousness, the emptier he is of truth, and therefore the more miserable.

Therefore, O my soul, hearing the reproach of many dwelling in [Col. 0520A] the circuit, become like a discarded vessel, so that, ceasing from yourself and passing wholly into God, you may not know yourself to live or die for yourself, but may live and die for him who died and rose again for you. O who will grant me to be made drunk with this saving cup, flooded with this stupefaction of mind, put to sleep with this most sweet lethargy? So that, loving the Lord my God with all my heart, all my soul, and all my strength, I may never seek what is mine but what belongs to Jesus Christ; and loving my neighbor as myself, may seek not what is useful for me but what is useful for another.

O word that completes and shortens in equity! Word of charity, word of love, word of affection, word of all perfection! A completing word, to which nothing can be lacking; a shortening word, on which the whole Law and the Prophets depend. O Jew, what need have you of so many things? Here is circumcision; here is Sabbath; here are saving sacrifices; here is fragrant offering; here is incense of every sweetness. Hold fast to charity, and none of these will be lacking; neglect charity, and none of these will profit you.

## CHAPTER XVII. On spiritual circumcision, which is contained in charity.

This is plainly not the carnal cutting away of a single member, but rather the true and perfect circumcision of the inner and outer human being: it cuts away pleasure, extinguishes lust, restrains gluttony, checks anger, thoroughly uproots envy, and assaults pride, the mother of every vice. It tempers the gnawing stings of sorrow by a kind of spiritual sweetness, and meets the languor of clinging sloth. Piercing the plague of avarice with the most welcome sword of liberality, it frees and preserves the soul from the vice of idolatry.

What, I ask, is more perfect than this circumcision, by which the limbs of vices are cut away, the body of sin is destroyed, the hairy clothing of the first-formed human beings is laid aside, and every stain and foulness of ancient oldness is cast off? For a mind filled with the sweetness of charity is not constricted by fear, defiled by lust, torn apart by anger, or puffed up by pride; it is not blown about by the empty smoke of vainglory [Col. 0520D], agitated by rage, disemboweled by the goad of ambition, tightened by avarice, cast down by sorrow, or wasted away by envy. For charity “does not envy; does not act perversely; is not puffed up; is not ambitious; does not seek its own; is not provoked; thinks no evil; does not rejoice over iniquity” (1 Cor. 13).

You see that this spiritual circumcision destroys every vice. It also purifies every bodily sense with a kind of divine knife: cutting off the wantonness of the eyes, rooting out the itching of the ears, driving away the excessive refinements of taste, removing the impertinence of the tongue, excluding seductive perfumes from the nostrils, and eradicating the ruinous softness of touch.

## CHAPTER XVIII. That the true and spiritual Sabbath is in charity.

[Col. 0521A]

Let the Jew now consider what kind of Sabbath this is—if indeed a lowly little man, groaning beneath the burden of sins, bound in the nets of passions, who has certainly tasted little or nothing of this sweetness, can say anything about it. O if even a slight rest were granted me from Pharaoh’s taskmasters, so that it were permitted for my soul to repose for even half an hour in the silence of this Sabbath! Surely, sleeping in peace in the selfsame place, I would be silent and rest in my sleep with kings and counselors, who build solitudes for themselves and fill their houses with silver.

But whence comes so great a hope to one so wretched? I will seek, I will seek that Sabbath; perhaps, Lord, you will hear the desire of the poor and, once brought forth from the pit of misery and the mire of filth, grant me to learn by the experience of some little drop how great is the abundance of your sweetness, which you have hidden for those who fear you (Ps. 30 [31]), because you reveal it only to those who love you. For those who love you rest in you; and there are true rest, true tranquillity, true peace, the true Sabbath of the mind.

But whence, O Jew, comes Sabbath to you? “Because,” you say, “God rested on the seventh day from all his works” (Gen. 1). What then? Did he not rest during the preceding six? “Indeed,” you say, “God made heaven and earth in six days; on the seventh he rested.” Therefore you are commanded to be at leisure—to be at leisure, I say, not to dance. O if you knew how to be at leisure and to see that Jesus himself is God, then, once the darkness of unbelief had immediately been removed, with unveiled face you would see in charity the perfect Sabbath-rest; nor would you any longer greatly desire the carnal feasts of your carnal Sabbath. Having entered “the place of the wonderful tabernacle, even to the house of God,” amid the voice of exultation and confession, the sound of one feasting, you would break forth joyfully into that song: “We shall exult and rejoice in you, remembering your breasts more than wine” (Song 1). And, taking up also that saying of Habakkuk to increase your joy: “But I will rejoice in the Lord, and exult in God my Jesus” (Hab. 3).

## CHAPTER XIX. How greatly the seventh day is preferred to the others, and that God’s charity is commended in it.

[Col. 0521D]

But now let us briefly consider the prerogative of the seventh day. Great indeed was that day on which, when the darkness had been scattered, light shone forth at God’s command; and great too that on which the divine voice divided the waters below from those above by the interposed firmament. Nonetheless precious was that day on which, when the waters had been gathered together in one place by God’s word, the dry land was clothed with grasses, made lovely with trees, adorned with flowers, and made fruitful with fruits. Nor was that day inferior on which the heaven was embellished with lights, by which are ordered the succession of days, the changes of seasons, the course of the year, and the ranks of the signs. How eminent, likewise, was that day on which the water, bringing forth kinds of diverse living creatures, submerged one part in its whirlpools and sent another through the air! [Col. 0522A] Nor is the sixth day devoid of wonder, on which quadrupeds and creeping things are brought forth from the earth, and on which at last man, formed from clay, is animated by the divine breath. Yet none of these days seems comparable to the seventh, on which there is indeed no creation of nature, but the rest of God himself and the perfection of all creatures are commended. For thus you have it: “And God completed on the seventh day his work which he had made, and rested from all the work which he had accomplished” (Gen. II). Great is this day, great the rest, great the Sabbath. O, if you understood!

Unless I am mistaken, this day is not measured out by the course of this visible sun; it does not begin with its rising or end with its setting. In short, it has neither morning nor evening. Now concerning the first day—if indeed it ought to be called the first, for Scripture does not call it “first” [Col. 0522B], but “one.” “But how,” you ask, “is the following day called second if this one is not first?” Consider whether perhaps it is called “one day” on the second day, and likewise on the third; so that, with “one day” repeated six times, the number six may be commended to us. But whatever may be the case with this obscurity, it says: “And evening and morning came to be, one day” (Gen. I). And below: “And evening and morning came to be, the second day” (ibid.). The same applies to the rest.

I think that by these words the mutability of all creatures is marked: their decline and advancement, beginning and end. Of the seventh day nothing of the kind is said. Neither evening nor morning is ascribed to it; neither end nor beginning. Therefore the day of God’s rest is not temporal but eternal. A little earlier you had imagined God as labouring in time and, as though fatigued, resting in time [Col. 0522C]. That was not to think of God, but to fashion an idol. You must beware lest, while you have no idol in the Temple at Jerusalem, you have one in your heart.

He created nothing by labouring at it, for “he spoke, and it was done.” Nor did he, wearied, rest only for one particular day, for the day of his rest is eternal. Therefore his rest is his eternity. You had supposed him like yourself and had therefore imagined that he created something because he needed it—something in whose sight he might delight, or in whose enjoyment he might rest. Accordingly, his rest is not described as being in any creature, so that you may know that he needs none, but is sufficient to himself in all things; and that he created nothing to relieve any want of his own, but to satisfy his most abundant [Col. 0522D] charity.

Moreover, he created so that all things might exist; he sustains all things that remain so that they may remain; he himself brings all things to their appointed ends. Nor does he do this from any necessity, but solely by his most sweet will. For he reaches mightily from end to end, by his most present and omnipotent majesty; but he orders all things gently, always at rest and reposing in his most tranquil charity. His rest itself is immutable and eternal; his tranquillity eternal and immutable; his Sabbath eternal and immutable. This alone is the cause why he creates things to be created, governs things to be governed, administers things to be administered, moves things to be moved, advances things to be advanced, and perfects things to be perfected.

Therefore, most fittingly, where his rest is commemorated, there the perfection of all things is shown. For his charity [Col. 0523A] is his will; it is also his goodness; nor is this whole reality anything other than his being. For to rest always in his most sweet charity, his most tranquil will, and his most abundant goodness is, for him, to be always. Therefore, just as in the days succeeding one another and, as it were, varying their turns by morning and evening—the days in which all created things are narrated—the mutability of creation is indicated; so in this day, a day to which nothing comes, from which nothing passes away, and to which nothing succeeds, which is constrained by no beginning and bounded by no end, his very eternity is rightly commended. In it his rest is most aptly described, lest he be thought to have created anything as needy or labouring. But why is the number six used there, and the number seven here? From this too receive such instruction as we are able to give.

## CHAPTER XX. Why the number six is commended in God’s work, and the number seven in his rest.

[Col. 0523B]

The number six certainly seems to contain the highest perfection. For it consists of all its own parts and does not exceed them. Its parts are one, two, and three. For if you ask what part of six one is, the answer is a sixth; what part two is, one may answer a third; what part three is, the answer is a half. Now within six there is no other number of which one could answer what part of it that number is. Therefore all the parts of six are one, two, and three. Add these together and you will find neither more nor less than six. This number, then, was observed in the creation of the world, so that you may judge that in the totality of creation there is nothing superfluous and nothing imperfect.

[Col. 0523C] But the number seven is dedicated in God’s rest. We have said that God’s rest is his charity. Nor without reason. “The Father,” he says, “loves the Son, and shows him all things which he himself does” (John V). And again: “As I have kept the commandments of my Father and remain in his love” (John XV). And the Father himself says: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. III). This mutual love of Father and Son—the sweetest love, the welcome embrace, the most blessed charity, in which the Father rests in the Son and the Son reposes in the Father—this indeed, this is the untroubled rest of both, their sincere peace, eternal tranquillity, incomparable goodness, indivisible charity. This is the one reality of both, indeed that in which both are [Col. 0523D] one: the sweet, delightful, joyful, holy Spirit, as we call him. He is believed for this reason to have properly taken this name for himself, because it is acknowledged to be common to both.

For although both Father and Son are Spirit, and both are holy, yet he who belongs to both—namely, the charity and consubstantial unity of both—is properly called the Holy Spirit. Although he is one, and one with the Father and the Son, nevertheless, because of the sevenfold grace believed to flow from the fullness of that fountain, he is designated in the Scriptures by the number seven. Thus, in the one stone, according to Zechariah, seven eyes are seen (Zech. III); and according to the Apocalypse, there are seven spirits before the throne of God (Rev. V). You see, then, how great is the excellence of charity, in which the [Col. 0524A] Creator and Ruler of all things keeps a certain everlasting and ineffable Sabbath.

## CHAPTER XXI. That in all creatures a certain trace of divine charity appears; and that therefore all things tend, as it were, toward the Sabbath—that is, toward rest.

Moreover, if you contemplate more closely every creature, from the first to the last, from the highest to the lowest, from the highest angel to the smallest worm, you will surely discern the divine goodness—which we call nothing other than his charity—not by a local infusion, a spatial diffusion, or a moving progression, but by the stable and incomprehensible simplicity of his substantial presence, abiding in itself, containing all things, embracing all things, [Col. 0524B] penetrating all things, joining lower things to higher, and binding opposites together in a certain harmonious peace: cold with hot, dry with moist, smooth with rough, hard with soft. Thus in the whole creation nothing can be hostile, nothing contrary; nothing unfitting, nothing disturbing, nothing that may mar the beauty of the universe itself. Rather, in the tranquillity of that order which he has appointed for the universe itself, all things rest as it were in a certain most peaceful peace.

Hence whatever, swelling outward, oversteps the order of divine goodness is immediately received into the order of his unconquered power, so that, although it is restless and disordered in itself, it not only does no harm to the tranquillity of the universe but even greatly benefits it, [Col. 0524C] since by comparison with it those things which are beautiful are judged more beautiful, and those that are good better. Therefore each thing tends toward its own order and seeks its own place; outside its order it is restless, but once ordered it rests.

For if you throw a stone into the air, does it not immediately, as though suffering violence, lay itself down by its own weight upon solid ground, there to have rest only when it neither swerves to either side nor slips downward through the lack of resistance from some solid body? But if you pour oil over other liquids, it immediately, unable to endure its lower position, rises to the surface and never ceases striving until, standing above the others, it obtains the rest of its proper order. What of vegetables and shrubs? Do they not, the more fruitfully and abundantly they bear, seek—as it were—one a firmer soil, another a [Col. 0524D] softer, another a richer, another clayey, another sandy soil? Once they have been placed or transplanted, planted or replanted, according to the order of their nature, they testify by the very fact of their growth that they seek nothing further.

Finally, if you carefully observe each individual body, you will undoubtedly see that each consists of its own parts; that its parts are bound to one another as by a bond of unity; that it preserves the order of its nature and rests in it as in a certain peace. Thus, if you wish to transfer any thing from the condition in which it is, the peace of its parts is in some manner disturbed, until, having been brought into the condition you wish, it rests again in a renewed tranquillity. [Col. 0525A] And what effort do irrational animals make to preserve their safety, avoid destruction, and seek the satisfaction of bodily appetites? Once this is attained, having nothing further to desire, they rest. For lacking reason and knowledge, they cannot even desire what exceeds bodily sensation.

## CHAPTER XXII. That a rational creature rests only upon attaining blessedness, and why, although it desires blessedness, it nevertheless abandons, in remarkable wretchedness, the path by which it might obtain it.

But for you, O rational soul, this prerogative is reserved above other living beings: that, rising beyond bodily senses, you may strive toward higher things. Nor will you ever satisfy your desire until, in fortunate inquiry, you attain that which is highest, that which is best, than which nothing is higher and nothing more excellent. [Col. 0525B] Wherever below this you stop, however lofty, however great, however pleasant it may be judged, you will unquestionably remain wretched. Wretched because needy; needy because something remains for you to seek, something remains for you to long after; and finally, blessedness itself remains, toward whose pursuit some natural force impels the rational soul.

Therefore, since every person’s conscience testifies that all people desire to be happy, and since this desire can in no way be abolished, it is clear that the rational creature obtains the rest desired by all only in the attainment of blessedness. Accordingly, the blind perversity of wretched man is greatly to be lamented: although he earnestly desires blessedness, he not only fails to do what will obtain the thing desired, but with a more eager inclination commits those acts by which he piles up his own wretchedness all the more.

[Col. 0525C] In my opinion, he would never do this unless, on the one hand, a false image of happiness deceived him and, on the other, the likeness of true misery frightened him. For who does not see that poverty, mourning, hunger, and thirst are no small portion of misery? Yet by these very things true misery is often averted and eternal blessedness sought. For Jesus says: “Blessed are the poor, because yours is the kingdom of heaven. Blessed are you who mourn, because you shall be comforted. Blessed are you who hunger now, because you shall be satisfied” (Matt. VI). Poverty, therefore, is rewarded with eternal riches; mourning is changed into eternal joy; eternal satisfaction is reserved for the hungry. For that riches, joy, and satisfaction are not lacking to blessedness, [Col. 0525D] no one can doubt.

But because a certain appearance of pleasure deceives every reprobate person in whatever inclination of his own will, and false delight dissolves him in the fulfilment of desires, the wretched man does not know how great is the consolation of the elect amid afflictions, nor their rejoicing in hope. He shudders at the image of unhappiness that appears openly, but beneath the colour of happiness he accepts true unhappiness: preferring false pleasure, which does not escape true pain, to that misery to which true blessedness succeeds.

It is as if a sick man intensely desired health but, because of immediate discomfort, recoiled from surgery, shrank from cautery, and, enticed by a certain present sweetness, sought soothing applications of oil—although his disease were such that it [Col. 0526A] grows hotter through this very gentleness and cannot diminish without the pain of cautery or surgery. So the wretched person, whether deceived because he thinks that what is not happiness is happiness, or enticed by a present sweetness that is false, both gives himself over to misery and does not lose the desire for blessedness. Thus, labouring in an unhappy circuit, he never rests.

Indeed, since for the rational soul God alone is superior, the angel is its equal, and all other things are judged inferior, what could be nearer to madness than, forsaking what is superior, to hunt for rest in those things over which it itself is made superior?

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the prerogative of the rational creature; and that the rest it naturally desires is to be sought neither in bodily health nor in the riches of this world.

[Col. 0526B] O marvellous creature, inferior only to your Creator, to what do you cast yourself down? Do you love the world? Yet you are yourself superior to the world. Do you marvel at the sun? Yet you are yourself brighter than the sun. Do you philosophize about the revolving arrangement of this heaven? Yet you are higher than heaven. Do you search out the hidden causes of creatures? Yet no cause is more hidden than you. Do you doubt this, although you judge all these things, while none of them judges you? But if you wish to judge them, do not love them. Nor should you love judging them itself. Love him who set you over all these things, not beneath them. He set you over them, not so that you might become happier from them, but that there might be that over which you are superior—subjecting all things to you as an increase of honour, while reserving himself for you as the fruit of blessedness.

Why then do you pursue fleeting beauties, when your own beauty neither withers with old age, nor is made foul by [Col. 0526C] poverty, nor grows pale with illness, nor even perishes in death itself? Seek what you seek, but do not seek it there. You seek a state in which nothing is lacking to your will, and in which you may thus rest. Seek this, then. “Where?” you ask. Do not seek it in bodily health. If health is loved in such a way that this rest is sought in it, observe, if it is absent, with how much labour it is acquired and how often a grievous illness is expelled by a painful remedy. And if it is present, with how much care must it be preserved; how many diseases, how many fevers, how many plagues, how many deaths, in short, lie in wait for it.

What then? Is it in riches? But what labour is involved in acquiring them, what anxiety in preserving them, what fear lest they be lost, what pain if they slip away? You have increased your money, and nevertheless increased your fear. You fear a powerful person lest he take it away; a thief lest he diminish it; a servant lest he lose it. Then who can say how often what a certain wise man says happens as well: “Riches kept for the harm of their owner” (Eccl. V)? Therefore the poor man rests more easily. “For the traveller empty-handed and naked,” as someone says, “does not fear the ambushes of a robber.” The poor man sleeps secure from nocturnal thieves even if he does not fortify his doors. Hence also that poetic line:

> The empty-handed traveller will sing before the robber.

But a certain wise man, elegantly ridiculing the biting cares of the rich, says: “The abundance of the rich does not allow him to sleep” (ibid.). Although this often happens literally—when some rich man, filled to nausea, tries to settle himself to sleep under the burden of an overloaded stomach, only to be awakened by frequent [Col. 0527A] belching—yet the saying ought rather to be understood of that sleep of which the bride boasts in the Song of Songs: “I sleep, and my heart watches” (Cant. V); and of which the Psalmist says: “In peace, in the selfsame place, I shall sleep and rest” (Ps. IV).

This is the sleep in which, when bodily senses are lulled and temporal cares are driven from the inner chambers of the heart, the holy soul rests in God’s sweetness, tasting and seeing how sweet the Lord is (Ps. XXXIII); and how blessed is everyone who hopes in him (Ps. XXXIII). Far be it, then, that you should suppose that any rich person is lulled to sleep by this sleep: one who always thirsts for gain and, the more he has amassed, desires with an ever more insatiable greed what he does not possess. [Col. 0527B] Hence Solomon says: “The miser will not be satisfied with money, and whoever loves riches will gain no fruit from them” (Eccl. V). He also incurs that prophetic curse: “Woe to him who gathers what is not his own.” And immediately the same prophet mocks his heap of metals: “Why does he heap up against himself thick clay?” (Hab. II).

## CHAPTER XXIV. The difference between elect and reprobate rich persons.

It should certainly be noted that Solomon does not say, “He who has riches,” but rather, “He who loves riches will gain no fruit from them” (Eccl. V). For all the elect, even if they happen to possess riches, do not love them and therefore do not seek rest in them. Instead, hearing the Apostle’s command to the rich not to be proud or to hope in the uncertainty of riches [Col. 0527C] (I Tim. VI), but to give readily, share with others, and lay up for themselves a good foundation in order to obtain the true life, they receive no small fruit from their riches. For they will surely hear from the Lord: “Come, blessed of my Father; for I was hungry, and you gave me food,” etc. (Matt. XXV).

Such people do not labour to acquire riches, fearing that saying of the Apostle: “Those who wish to become rich fall into the snare of the devil” (I Tim. VI). Empty anxiety does not torment them in preserving their possessions, for they frequently rehearse the promise of the Lord, who both forbids anxiety and promises necessities: “Do not be anxious, saying, ‘What shall we eat?’ or ‘What shall we drink?’” And a little later: “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things shall be added to you” (Matt. VI). Finally, they do not murmur at the loss of these things; indeed, they receive joyfully the plundering of their goods, considering that they possess a better and abiding substance (Heb. X).

[Col. 0527D] But for the perverse, the contrary results. They suppose that an abundance of the most worthless worldly things can satisfy the desire of the rational soul, for which God alone suffices. Yet, because no amount of possessions can benefit them, they do not free themselves even slightly from their wretched cares, nor do they ever lay aside their labour. And yet, what is more miserable, they swell with empty blindness at the acquisition of such things. Such is their condition in the present; but what is their end? Let us rather hear their final words, which sacred Scripture does not conceal. “They shall say among themselves, repenting and groaning in anguish of spirit”; and it adds their words [Col. 0528A], including these:

> “We have grown weary in the way of iniquity and destruction, and have walked difficult paths; but the way of the Lord we have not known. What has pride profited us, and what has the boasting of riches brought us? All things have passed away like a shadow, like a messenger running ahead, and like a ship passing through the surging waters, of which, after it has passed, no trace can be found. So we, having been born, immediately ceased to be; and indeed we could show no sign of virtue, but were consumed in our wickedness.”

Such things said in hell those who sinned: “For the hope of the wicked is like down carried away by the wind, like foam scattered by a storm, like smoke dispersed by the wind, and like the memory of a guest passing through for one [Col. 0528B] day” (Wis. V). Therefore this rest and this Sabbath must be sought elsewhere.

## CHAPTER XXV. That rest is not to be sought in worldly friendship.

“But to love and be loved,” you say, “what is more peaceful?” Certainly, if this is in God and for God, I do not disapprove; indeed, I greatly approve. But if it is according to the flesh or the world, observe how many envies, suspicions, and burning torments of a jealous mind exclude peace of mind. Even if none of these occurs, death—which all must undergo—will break this union: bringing grief to the survivor and punishment to the departing person. Moreover, even in this life we know that grave enmities have arisen between the closest friends. But we shall discuss elsewhere the love that exists among the good.

## CHAPTER XXVI. That rest is found neither in bodily pleasure nor in worldly power.

We are compelled, as though to insert a certain blemish into this discourse, to speak of carnal pleasure. It would indeed be better to be silent about it, if we did not see many people, as though stripped of humanity, so clothed in a bestial likeness that they judge the whole fruit of their lives to be placed in the pleasure of the belly and the things beneath the belly. Therefore, lest anyone suppose that the rest of the mind is to be sought in such things, we must say a few words on this subject.

For what is more perverse than to place the good of the rational mind in the gluttony of the belly and to subject that which excels in a human being [Col. 0528D] to some most worthless part of his flesh—especially when he sees that in these things he can differ in no way from the most foolish beasts? Hunger brings torment, and satiety produces disgust. For if a person satisfies pleasure, he must necessarily exceed the bounds of necessity; but if he exceeds the measure of nature, it is impossible to avoid bodily pain.

Moreover, to delight in the filth of lusts and to wallow, like some most unclean creature, in the mire of one’s own shame—just as nothing is more disgraceful, more foul, more shameful, or more deserving of condemnation, so surely nothing is more restless or so wholly devoid of every rest and tranquillity. What need be said of its foulness, when this foulest plague both contaminates the flesh and effeminates the mind, burying and overthrowing alike whatever is honourable, becoming, and finally [Col. 0529A] manly in the soul?

And while other vices commonly cloak themselves with certain coverings of virtues and thus not only do not blush before human eyes but even swell with pride before them, this vice alone bears on its very face such a horror of itself that, precisely at the moment when it grips and claims the flesh for itself, it violently shuns the eyes. Indeed, even though those members were honourably placed in the human body by the wisest Creator, it has brought upon them such shame through its obscenity that the man who preferred seeing them to reverently covering them was punished with his father’s eternal curse; whereas those to whom their nakedness brought the mark of shame were rewarded with the grace of perpetual blessing.

[Col. 0529B] Nor is it surprising, now that the cross of Jesus—that conqueror of effeminacy—triumphs and shines everywhere, that the filth of this passion has been exposed and laid bare. In that demon-worshipping people, by contrast, where the most cunning conspiracy of demons had made the crimes of false gods objects of sacred cult, dances were performed in theatres in supposed reverence for them; yet not even under the foulest Jupiter did any foul person ever shed the mark of shame. For even among the worshippers of adulterous gods adultery was punished, and chastity was greatly praised.

What, then, should those do who worship the Son of the Virgin, the author of virginity? They must surely beware lest what the prophet said of some come upon them: “The beasts rotted in their dung” (Joel I). [Col. 0529C] By these words he quite aptly expressed the end and limit of this most filthy passion: declaring that the person swallowed by the Charybdis of lust is corrupted by the pollution of his flesh, as though by an outpouring of his own dung. Thus you should regard him not merely as extinguished or swallowed up, but should perceive him as rotting and stinking like a buried corpse, with the pus of most unclean itching flowing forth.

Therefore the mind in which this evil spirit has taken its seat must necessarily be driven by certain furies, assailed by the fiery goads of lust, and, drunk and wandering toward every shameful act with the bridle of all decency loosed, be impelled onward. Once the fire of one passion has been quenched, it is nevertheless kindled again in another and more violent heat. It is therefore utterly absurd to hunt for the rest of the rational mind in such pleasure, particularly since we never read that divine justice inflicts a greater punishment in this present life than when someone is given over to be defiled by his own desires. [Col. 0529D] Scripture says: “My people did not hear my voice, and Israel did not heed me; and I abandoned them according to the desires of their heart” (Ps. LXXX). And the Apostle says more plainly concerning those who exchanged the glory of God for idols: “For this reason God gave them up to the desires of their hearts, unto impurity, so that they dishonour their bodies among themselves” (Rom. I). Not that God compelled them to such disgrace as an instigator of evils, but that, having most justly been abandoned by him, they could not avoid these crimes.

I suppress in silence much that comes to my mind against this most filthy plague, out of regard, surely, for your most chaste eyes, my most dearly beloved and longed-for friend, to whom I have dedicated this present little work. [Col. 0530A] For I seem almost to see your modest face suffused, at what has been written, with the mark of honourable shame, and commanding me to be silent by the sweetest motion of your eyes. For I know that most chaste breast, so filled with the sweetness of charity and so full of the flowers of sweet-smelling chastity, breathes so heavenly and divine a fragrance that even to hear the stench of this pollution is burdensome.

Therefore, passing on to other matters, let us consult concerning the pleasure of the ears, eyes, and other senses, and concerning dominion and power, that richest, most powerful, most luxurious, yet wisest king—Solomon, that is; indeed, let Wisdom itself be heard most attentively in him. [Col. 0530B] First, speaking either in his own person or that of another, he declares: “I said in my heart: I will go and abound in delights and enjoy good things” (Eccl. II). And below: “I built houses; I planted vineyards; I made gardens and orchards; and I planted them with trees of every kind.” Adding many such things, he continued: “I possessed male and female servants, and a very great household. I amassed for myself silver and gold, the wealth of kings and provinces.” And after adding the pleasure of the ears—“I provided for myself male singers and female singers”—he shortly afterwards says: “Whatever my eyes desired, I did not deny them; nor did I forbid my heart to enjoy every pleasure and to delight itself in the things I had prepared.”

What, I ask, could be more luxurious? What sweeter? What more pleasant according to this life? But hear that nothing could be more vain. “When I turned,” he says, “to all my works and to the labours in which I had sweated in vain, I saw vanity and affliction of spirit in all things, and that nothing endures under the sun” [Col. 0530C]. Therefore he had first laid down the general judgment: “I saw all things that are done under the sun, and behold, all is vanity and affliction of spirit” (ibid.).

Let us add also this saying of our Saviour: “Everyone who commits sin is the slave of sin” (John VIII). Let these three things, then, be joined together: vanity, slavery, and affliction of spirit. Where, then, is rest? Where is Sabbath? Especially when the Law says: “You shall do no servile work on it” (Lev. XXIII). Certainly, everyone who commits sin is the slave of sin. Where then is there sure freedom from this servile work? Where is the contagion of this slavery guarded against? Where does true and [Col. 0530D] perfect Sabbath observance take place? Finally, “There is no righteous person upon earth who does not sin” (Eccl. VII). And holy David says: “I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother conceived me” (Ps. L).

## CHAPTER XXVII. That charity is the sweet yoke beneath which true rest, as it were the true Sabbath, is found.

Let us therefore hear him who says: “If the Son sets you free, then you shall be truly free” (John VIII). Let us hear him, I say, calling, crying aloud, and inviting the weary to rest and to Sabbath: “Come to me, all you who labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. XI). Behold refreshment, as it were preparation for Sabbath. Now let us hear of Sabbath itself: “Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me [Col. 0531A], for I am meek and humble of heart, and you shall find rest for your souls.” Behold rest, behold tranquillity, behold Sabbath: “You shall find rest for your souls. For my yoke is sweet and my burden light” (Matt. XI).

Truly this yoke is sweet and this burden light; therefore you shall find rest for your souls. This yoke does not press down but unites; this burden has wings, not weight. This yoke is charity; this burden is brotherly love. Here one rests; here one keeps Sabbath; here one is free from servile works. For charity “does not act improperly” and “does not think evil” (I Cor. XIII); and love of neighbour “does no evil.” You see, Jew, where Sabbath is. In it, although some sinful lapse may occur—not from charity, indeed, but from some weakness—nevertheless, because “charity covers a multitude of sins” (I Pet. IV), the Sabbath observance is not lost.

And fittingly this freedom from servile work is dedicated on the seventh day, because “the charity of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. V). We have already said above that the Holy Spirit is signified by the number seven.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. An example from himself and his conversion.

Behold, sweet Lord, I have ranged through the world and the things that are in the world; for whatever is in the world, as that knower of your mysteries says, is either the desire of the flesh, or the desire of the eyes, or the pride of life. I sought in these things rest for my unhappy soul; but everywhere there was toil and groaning, pain and affliction of spirit. [Col. 0531C] You cried out, Lord; you cried out, you called, you terrified, you broke through my deafness; you struck, you chastised, you overcame my hardness; you made yourself sweet, you gave savor, you exposed my bitterness. I heard—but alas, late—the voice crying: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened” (Matt. XI). And I said: “You will stretch out your right hand to the work of your hands” (Job XIV). For I lay defiled and enwrapped, bound and captive, entangled in the birdlime of clinging iniquity, crushed beneath the mass of inveterate habit.

Thus I turned my attention upon myself: who I was, where I was, what I was like. I shuddered, Lord, and was appalled at my own likeness; the foul image of my unhappy soul terrified me. I displeased myself because you pleased me. I wished to flee from myself and flee to you, but I was held fast within myself. I was held fast, as someone has said [Note: [Col. 0531D] AUGUSTINE, *Confessions*, VIII, ch. 11], by “trifles of trifles and vanity of vanities,” my old friends; the chain of my most evil habit bound me, the love of my own kin fettered me, the bonds of social favor tightened around me, and above all the knot of a certain friendship, sweeter to me than all the sweetnesses of that former life.

These things had savor, these things pleased; but you more. For, considering each of them, I saw that bitter things were mingled with sweet, sad with joyful, adversity with prosperity. The pleasant union of friendship pleased me, but offense was always feared, and a future separation was certainly to come at some time. I considered the beginnings of those pleasures, observed their course, and looked ahead to their end. I saw that neither their beginnings could lack reproach, nor their [Col. 0532A] middle course offense, nor their end condemnation. The dread of death terrified me, because certain punishment awaited such a soul after death.

And people, observing certain outward circumstances but not knowing what was taking place within me, said: “How well things go for him! How well things go for him!” They did not know that it went ill with me precisely where alone it could seem to go well. For my wound was deep within—tormenting, terrifying, and corrupting all my inward parts by an intolerable stench. And unless you had quickly laid your hand upon me, unable to endure myself, I might perhaps have applied the worst remedy, that of despair.

Therefore I began to conjecture, as far as I could in my inexperience—indeed, as far as you granted—how great is the delight in loving you, how great the tranquillity together with that delight, how great the security together with that tranquillity. [Col. 0532B] The choice of one who loves you does not go astray, because nothing is better than you; hope is not deceived, because nothing is loved more fruitfully; excess of measure is not feared, because in loving you no limit is prescribed; death, destroyer of worldly friendship, is not dreaded, because life does not die. In loving you offense is not feared, because there is none unless love itself is abandoned; no suspicion intervenes, because you judge by the testimony of conscience itself. Here is delight, because fear is excluded; here tranquillity, because anger is restrained; here security, because the world is despised.

Meanwhile you began gradually to taste sweet to my palate, though it was not yet sound; and I said, “Oh, if I were healed!” I was snatched toward you, but again fell back into myself. And, as though I were in shackles, those things which I experienced delightfully through the flesh held me by a certain force of habit; yet the things that the mind surmised through reason pleased me more. And I often said, even in the hearing of others: “Where now, I ask, are all our delights, all our pleasures, all our enjoyments, which we have enjoyed down to this present hour? At this very instant, what do we feel from them? Whatever was pleasant has passed away. Of all these things only this remains: what pricks the conscience, what instills fear of death, what consigns us to eternal condemnation. Let that one possession of Christ’s servants—that they do not fear death—be compared, I beg you, with all our riches, all our pleasures, all our honors.”

I became vile in my own eyes at these words, often, and at times I wept amid the most bitter [Col. 0532D] contention of soul. Everything I saw became worthless to me, yet the habit of fleshly pleasure oppressed me. But you, who hear the groans of prisoners and release the children of the slain, tore apart my bonds; and you, who offer your paradise to prostitutes and tax collectors, converted me, the first of all sinners, to yourself. And behold, I breathe beneath your yoke and rest beneath your burden, because your yoke is sweet and your burden is light.

## CHAPTER XXIX. How greatly those err who complain of the harshness of the Lord’s yoke, when whatever toil is felt comes from the remnants of desire, and whatever rest from the infusion of love.

[Col. 0533A] They err, Lord, they err; they are deceived who, ignorant of themselves and not attending to what is done within them, complain of the harshness of this yoke and the weight of its burden. “What then,” you say, “do you, who seem to have placed your neck beneath this yoke and your shoulders under this burden, never labor?” On the contrary, very often. For today also I have labored somewhat.

When a word slipped from me a little too incautiously, one of my dearest friends took it so badly that he even revealed his offense by his expression, and raised me from my prostration at his feet somewhat slowly. Nor has my spirit yet wholly sweated out that grief: Lord, you know—not because I was raised slowly, but because he was offended and I had been overtaken by an incautious speech. And perhaps, because of the special familiarity by which I am accustomed to speak to him more openly, speech here slipped more readily from me, according to the common saying: “A familiar master makes a foolish servant.”

And now, Lord, examiner of my weakness, physician of my soul, sole hope of my salvation: against you alone I have sinned, even in what I sinned against him. For it is not a sin because I offended him, but because you forbade me to offend. [Col. 0533B] Against you, Lord, against you alone sins whoever sins; because when sin is committed, either what you command is not done, or what you forbid is done. Murder, Lord, is a sin because you said, “You shall not kill” (Exod. XX). Therefore, when at times you said, “Kill,” not only was it not a sin to kill, but it was a very great crime, at your command, to refuse to kill.

Your law likewise condemns deceit; and yet when, at your command, the Hebrews plundered Egypt by borrowing vessels and garments (Exod. XV), because they obeyed you, they certainly did not sin. You nevertheless say, “You shall not commit fornication”; and therefore to commit fornication is a most monstrous crime. Yet, at your command, your prophet did not hesitate to take a prostitute as his wife, so that he might beget children of fornication (Hos. I)—which he certainly would not have done had he joined her to himself in the bond of marriage. Although it is doubtful whether this happened literally.

“Against you alone I have sinned” (Ps. L). Scripture does not readily present this as said by a human being, “I have sinned against you,” although it is said, “I have sinned in you.” I do not know what great matter is indicated by the phrase “against you.” What then is “Against you alone I have sinned,” except: “My sin is to be assessed by your judgment, judged by your judgment, punished by your judgment”? “Against you alone I have sinned.” Why does the Jew prepare a stone? “Against you alone I have sinned.” “Let him who is without sin among you,” he says, “first cast a stone at her” (John VIII). Therefore I have sinned against him alone to whom judgment concerning sin belongs; whose judgment establishes that this is sin.

You therefore, Lord, forgive what I have sinned, because against you alone I have sinned. Yet because I sinned also against him, I will still cast myself at his feet; but do you inspire him also to forgive me for offending him—although, as you know, I did not then intend or wish to offend him.

But to return to what preceded: [Col. 0534A] is this labor of mine derived from the Lord’s yoke, or rather from my own sickness? I certainly perceive that whatever tranquillity, peace, or delight I possess, this sweetest yoke produces it all for me; while whatever labor, weariness, or indeed heaviness I experience proceeds from the remnants of worldly desire. For beneath that yoke which the prince of Babylon—that is, of confusion—placed upon my most unhappy neck, my strength was weakened and my bones crushed. And although captivity has in some measure been loosed, some weakness remains from the ancient oppression. From this, the serenity of sweetness now somewhat experienced is often disturbed, until he who forgives all my iniquities also heals all [Col. 0534B] my infirmities, and, redeeming my life from destruction, crowns me with mercy and compassion (Ps. CII): when this corruptible shall have put on incorruption and this mortal shall have put on immortality, and the saying written is fulfilled: “Death has been swallowed up in victory” (I Cor. XV). Meanwhile, from the sweetness of this yoke comes no small consolation, and against implanted weakness some struggle.

## CHAPTER XXX. Those who complain of the weight of the Lord’s burden are rather crushed beneath the burden of the world.

Accordingly, those who complain of the harshness of this yoke have perhaps either not wholly cast off the exceedingly heavy yoke of worldly desire, [Col. 0534C] or have resumed it, after casting it off, with greater disgrace. Outwardly they display the Lord’s yoke, but inwardly place their shoulders beneath the load of secular business. They impute to the weight of the Lord’s burden the labors and pains to which they devote themselves. Thus, despising the Lord’s commandments, which, as John says, are not burdensome (I John V), and, like dogs, returning to their own vomit, under the garb of abstainers they indulge the belly; beneath the tunic of penitents they pant for worldly glory and honors; beneath the sacred dress of the continent they are stained by the filth of the flesh. Wearing lambs’ wool while bearing a wolfish spirit and burning with insatiable avarice, they join house to house and field to field; they spare not widows, take no pity on orphans, claim for themselves the property of the poor. For these things they incline toward lawsuits and disputes, stand ready for judgments, are consumed by continual cares, are inflamed by hatreds, and are scattered by anxious thoughts; because not the Lord’s yoke but the world’s is harsh, and the world’s burden is heavy. Yet the Lord’s yoke is sweet, and the Lord’s burden light.

## CHAPTER XXXI. How great is perfection in love, and how it differs from the other virtues.

What is sweeter, what more glorious, than, through contempt for the world, to see oneself higher than the world; standing on the height of a good conscience, to have the whole world beneath one’s feet; to see nothing one desires, no one one fears, no one one envies; to count as one’s own nothing that another can take away, and as evil nothing that another can inflict? While directing the mind’s gaze toward that incorruptible, undefiled, and unfading inheritance reserved in heaven, [Col. 0535A] what is sweeter than to despise, with a certain nobility of mind, secular riches as corruptible, fleshly enticements as defiled, and all worldly pomp as fading, and to exult in that prophetic saying: “All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass. The grass has withered and the flower has fallen, but the word of the Lord remains forever” (Isa. XL)?

What, I ask, is sweeter or more tranquil than not to be agitated by the turbulent motions of the flesh, not to be burned by the fires of fleshly incentives, not to be moved by any enticing sight, but to have the flesh, growing cool with the dew of chastity, subjected to the spirit—not now a temptress toward fleshly pleasures, but a most obedient helper toward spiritual exercises? What, finally, is so close to divine tranquillity as not to be disturbed by injuries inflicted, not to be frightened by any punishment or persecution, to maintain one steadfastness of mind in prosperity and adversity alike, to regard enemy and friend with the same eye, and to be conformed to the likeness of him who causes his sun to rise upon the good and the evil, and rains upon the just and unjust? (Matt. V).

All these things together are in love, and nowhere but in love are all of them together. Accordingly, in it are true tranquillity and true sweetness, because it itself is the Lord’s yoke; if, at the Lord’s invitation, we take it up, we shall find rest [Col. 0535C] for our souls, because the Lord’s yoke is sweet and his burden is light (Matt. XI). For love is patient and kind; it does not envy, does not act perversely, is not puffed up, is not ambitious (I Cor. XIII), and so forth.

The other virtues are for us either like a vehicle for the weary, provisions for a traveler, a lamp for those in darkness, or weapons for those who fight. But love, though it must be in all things if the other virtues are to exist, is more especially itself both rest to the weary, lodging for the traveler, full light to one who arrives, and a perfect crown to the victor. What is faith except our vehicle by which we are carried to our homeland? What is hope except our provision by which we are sustained amid the miseries of this life? What are those four virtues—temperance, prudence, fortitude, justice—except our weapons by which we fight?

But when, through love—which is perfected only in the vision of God—death shall have been more fully swallowed up for those in whom love is begun here by faith, faith will no longer exist, because what is seen and loved need not be believed; nor will hope exist, because for one embracing God in the arms of love, nothing remains to be hoped for. Temperance fights against desires, prudence against errors, fortitude against adversities, justice against inequalities. But in love there is perfect chastity, and therefore no desire against which temperance fights; in love perfect knowledge, and therefore no error against which prudence fights; in love true blessedness, and therefore no adversity [Col. 0536A] that fortitude conquers; in love all things are at peace, and therefore no inequality against which justice must keep watch.

Nor is faith a virtue unless it works through love; nor hope unless what is hoped for is loved. Indeed, if you observe more subtly, what is temperance but love which no pleasure seduces? What is prudence but love which no error deceives? What is fortitude but love bravely enduring adversities? What is justice but love, by a certain equitable moderation, setting in order the inequalities of this life? Thus love is begun in faith, exercised in the other virtues, and perfected in itself.

## CHAPTER XXXII. How the works of the six days correspond to the other virtues, while the rest of the seventh day is assigned to love.

[Col. 0536B] Let faith therefore be for us like the first day, by which we faithful are separated from unbelievers as light from darkness. Let hope be the second, through which, dwelling in heavenly things and hoping, for the merits of faith, only for things above the heavens, we are distinguished, by God’s advancing aid, from those who savor earthly things and demand from God only earthly things, who dissolve and drift like waters beneath heaven’s firmament.

Let temperance dawn for us like the third day, in which, mortifying our members that are upon earth and restraining fleshly desires, like most bitter waters, within necessary boundaries, the dry and waterless ground of our heart may appear, thirsting for the Lord its God. Let prudence, then, break forth like the light of the fourth day, by which we distinguish things to be done from things not to be done, as day from night. With its help, let the light of wisdom shine forth like the splendor of the sun; let the light of spiritual knowledge—which increases in some of us and decreases in others—appear like the glory of the moon; and through it let the devout mind look up to the examples of the fathers who went before as to clusters of stars. By it let the mind distinguish between days and years, months and hours: let it discern, by fair examination, what differs between those before the Law and those under the Law; between these and those under grace; what is suitable for each; which commands, times, customs, and sacraments belong to each.

Let fortitude be for us like the fifth day, by which we endure the storms [Col. 0536D] of this great and wide sea, that is, this present age; and, made spiritual fishes through God’s working, preserve our life amid waves and tempests. Raising the desires and affections of our mind like winged birds toward heavenly things, and setting our minds on things above, let us, with God’s blessing, render manifold fruits of good works.

Let justice appoint the sixth day for us, by which, reclothed in the divine likeness, we may rule with noble authority over the most savage beasts of vices, earthly desires as creeping things, and bodily motions as beasts of burden; acting so that the body may be subject to the mind and the mind to God, and so, as justice directs, what is due may be given to each. Here again there is blessing—not to beasts of burden, not to creeping things, but to human beings.

We are plainly warned by this history, though the events occurred literally, to receive spiritual fruits: for we read that God’s blessing came upon the fishes of the sea and the birds of heaven; yet we do not see divine generosity bestowed upon the beasts, beasts of burden, or creeping things of the earth, although they too increase and multiply—a gift which God is seen to have granted to birds also by the aforementioned blessing. For thus it is written: “God blessed them, saying: ‘Increase and multiply, and fill the waters of the sea; and let birds multiply upon the earth’” (Gen. I). Nothing of this is said to the beasts and beasts of burden.

Doubtless blessing, multiplication, and succession through spiritual generation are due to virtues and holy affections, which we believe should be compared to fishes and birds. But as beasts and beasts of burden are subjected, by God’s blessing, to the human being created in God’s image and likeness, so spiritual beasts—of which the Psalmist says, “Do not hand over to the beasts the soul that confesses you” (Ps. LXXIII)—are subjected by God’s command to one restored, through the merits of justice, to that image and likeness; and to such beasts no succession is due.

The seventh day remains: that is, the Sabbath, in which all these works are brought to completion, true rest is received, and a limit and end are assigned to our labor. It is love, the completion of all virtues, the sweet refreshment of holy souls, the honorable ordering of conduct. It is the root from which every good work is perfected. It is the seventh day by which divine grace refreshes us; it is the seventh month in which, after the flood of temptations, the ark of the heart rests sweetly. [Col. 0537C] Temperance serves it; prudence keeps watch; fortitude fights for it; justice ministers to it.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. In this life the other virtues serve love; after this life they must be transformed into the fullness of love.

For since it belongs to temperance to restrain and blunt alluring motions of flesh or soul, lest the mind, enticed by the sweetness of harmful pleasure, prefer it to the sweetness of true love; since the ever-watchful concern of prudence distinguishes what should and should not be loved, lest desire, cloaked in the color of love, forestall the unwary heart; and since the strength of fortitude opposes itself to the adversities of this world for no other reason than that, when events turn out less than one wishes, or hardships of every kind rush in together, the oppressed soul may in no way depart from the law of love—it is clearly evident that these three should be counted as virtues only if their use is directed in every respect toward attaining or preserving love.

Otherwise temperance is not judged a virtue: even if it conceals or restrains the itch of the flesh, yet if the mind, under the name of chastity, turns itself to the greed of shameful gain, it does not restrain that so destructive wantonness of the inner person. Nor should that prudence be judged a virtue by which someone, skilled in deception, distinguishes not between things to be loved and not loved, but between temporal profits and losses, and strives, with love wholly absent, to secure some advantage for himself at the ruin of others.

[Col. 0538A] Far be it that Catiline’s fortitude should be numbered among the virtues. For although he was able to endure every adversity in an astonishing manner, nevertheless, seeking from that fortitude only the reward of worldly power, or at least of his own pleasure, he deprived himself of the reward due to virtue. Accordingly, however self-controlled a man eager for popular glory may appear, however prudent and clever in the judgment of the crowd some wealthy person may be thought; although some philosopher, hardened even in monstrous insensibility, may be moved by no adversity: our philosophers judged that whatever does not spring from the root of love must be excluded from the fruits of virtue; and they perceived with subtle discernment that whatever is not directed by a straight line of construction toward that one cubit must be measured outside the building of the spiritual ark.

True temperance, therefore, acts so that the rational mind, enticed by no pleasure, may not exceed the norm of love; true prudence, so that it may not be deceived; true fortitude, so that it may not be overwhelmed. But when perfect love has transferred its followers into the kingdom of its tranquillity—when every allurement of the flesh has been consumed together with the mortality of the flesh itself, every darkness of error driven away by contemplation of the divine light, and the troubles of this world succeeded by secure certainty—then, laying aside, so to speak, the arms it uses in this time of war, love itself will refresh the victors solely by its own sweetness.

Then the other virtues will so pour themselves into the fullness of love that, in that blessed state, temperance, prudence, and fortitude will be regarded as nothing other than love: love so chaste that no enticements tempt it; [Col. 0538C] so luminous that no errors obscure it; so strong that it is assailed by no adversities at all. Promising us the condition of this tranquillity in mystical speech, the Lord says: “I will take away evil beasts from the land, and I will cause you to sleep in safety” (Lev. XXVI). For when the most savage beasts of passions have been removed from our land—that is, from the flesh which we bear—he will cause us to be lulled into heavenly sleep, when, absorbed in the immense sea of that divine brightness and ineffably lifted outside ourselves, we shall be perfectly still and see that the Lord himself is God, celebrating that everlasting Sabbath of love which Saint Isaiah the prophet describes: “And it shall be month from month, and Sabbath from Sabbath” (Isa. LXVI).

That is, from this Sabbath, in which, tasting certain beginnings of love, we rest from busy actions as far as the evil of the day permits, we shall be led into that perfect Sabbath, where, no trouble interrupting and no misery of the flesh impeding, we shall love the Lord our God with all our soul, all our strength, and all our powers, and our neighbors as ourselves (Deut. VI).

Justice, moreover, by which to each person what is his own is given, according to the Apostle’s saying, “Render to all their dues: tribute to whom tribute is due; fear to whom fear; honor to whom honor” (Rom. XIII), I would call a certain incentive to brotherly love. Its beginning indeed is to harm no one; its advance is to present oneself to all without complaint. For one greatly wins others’ minds by the sweetness of goodwill who, by the peacefulness of his conduct, offends no one: obeying elders, accommodating equals, yielding to juniors; showing fear and reverence to superiors, honor and goodwill to equals, and humble compassion to inferiors.

This virtue also moves those who observe it toward the good of love in monetary matters. In accordance with the Apostle’s command quoted above, it does not defer a debt until an importunate creditor demands it, but rather, with a certain cheerfulness, anticipates the claimant. If, therefore, this virtue embraces only the dispensation of temporal things, I do not hesitate to remove it from the tranquillity of that most blessed state, [Col. 0539B] where, in supreme repose, some are struck by the irrevocable sentence of condemnation, while others receive the reward of eternal blessedness, as the one who dispenses rewards or punishments gives to each according to merits; so that, when eternity exists on both sides, there can be no variation of temporal things.

But if you consider more deeply the rules of justice itself, no one gives to each person what is his better or more perfectly than one who loves things worthy of love, and loves them as much as they ought to be loved: namely, God above himself, his neighbor as himself; God only for God’s own sake, and himself and his neighbor only for God’s sake. You see, unless I am mistaken, that the perfection of justice depends upon the perfection of love, so that justice appears to be nothing other than ordered love; and in proportion as anyone advances in it, so also does that person rest.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. At the intervention of a friend’s death, consideration of the threefold desire is postponed, and this first book concludes with his epitaph.

[Col. 0539C]

Accordingly, those three things which the holy Apostle describes as being in the world seem to require consideration: the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life (I John II), lest perhaps whatever we endure as less pleasant beneath the Lord’s yoke may proceed from the poisonous root of these passions. But grief forbids further progress, and the recent death of my Simon violently impels me rather to the task of weeping.

Hence perhaps that fear by night which agitated my mind; hence that terror of dreams which robbed me of necessary rest: because my dearest one was soon to be snatched away from the earth. Nor is it surprising if my mind, through a certain disturbance of itself, foresaw the departure of one whose life it enjoyed so delightfully. Behold, now the fear which I feared has come upon me, and what I dreaded has happened. Why do I dissemble? Why am I silent? Perhaps this tribulation remains upon me for that very reason. Let what is concealed in my heart come forth before my eyes, come forth upon my tongue, so that perhaps, by drops of tears and little streams of words, the grieving heart may sweat out the sorrow conceived in its deepest recesses.

“Have pity on me, have pity on me, you who are my friends, because the hand of the Lord has touched me” (Job XIX). You marvel that I weep; rather, marvel that I live. For who would not marvel that Aelred lives without Simon, unless he knows how sweet it was to live together, how sweet it would have been to return together to our homeland? Bear patiently, therefore, my tears, my groaning, the roaring of my breast.

And you, my beloved, although you have been admitted to the joy of your Lord, feast delightfully at the table of that supreme householder, and happily grow drunk with that new fruit of the vine in the kingdom of the Father together with your Jesus, nevertheless allow me to offer you my tears, to unburden my affection to you, to pour out to you, if it may be, my whole soul. Do not forbid these tears, which the sweet memory of you, my dearest brother, draws forth. Let not this groaning burden you: it is aroused not by despair but by affection. Do not restrain these tears, which tenderness elicits, not a failure of faith.

And surely, if you remember whither you have come, what you have escaped, and where [Col. 0540B] you have left that familiar companion of yours, you will see how just my grief is, how much my wound deserves tears. Allow me, therefore, to bewail my wound a little—my wound. For your death is not to be mourned, since a life so praiseworthy, so lovable, so pleasing to all preceded it; a life commended by that astonishing conversion of yours, that praiseworthy manner of life, that blessed perseverance.

Truly astonishing was your conversion! Who would not be amazed, who would not marvel, that a tender and delicate boy, noble in birth and conspicuous in appearance, took up such a way, and took it up thus? You departed, my sweet brother, knowingly ignorant and wisely untaught. Like that first patriarch, departing from your land, your kindred, and your father’s house (Gen. XII), you went where you did not know and came where you knew not. But he who led you knew: he who had kindled your still tender heart with the flame of his love; and you ran after the fragrance of his ointments.

He went before you, beautiful in form beyond the children of men, anointed with the oil of gladness beyond his companions (Ps. XLIV), anointed with the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety (Isa. XI); and you ran after the fragrance of these ointments (Song I). The humble spiritual one went before you through rough and mountainous paths, scattering his way with the spices of myrrh and frankincense and every powder of the perfumer; and you ran after the fragrance of these ointments.

The boy Jesus went before his boy, showing him the manger of his poverty, the resting-place of his humility, the chamber of his love, filled with the flowers of his grace, rich with the honey of his sweetness, and sprinkled with the balm of his consolation; and you ran after the fragrance of these ointments. [Col. 0540D] I know not what great and ineffable thing that mind had already tasted, when it judged that hay should be provided as food for its little body, failing from hunger like a wearied beast of burden.

The devout boy fled from the face of his father, but more truly toward the face of his Father. He wished indeed to forget his people and his father’s house, so that the King, the King’s Son, might desire his beauty, and they might be two in one spirit; so that he whose Father is his by nature might become his father by grace.

O wondrous devotion; O wondrous forgetfulness of self! It was too little for this emulator of the venerable patriarch Joseph, having left behind the little cloak by which he was held fast to the Egyptian woman (Gen. XXXIX), to escape naked from the hands of the woman embracing him. He was also a vigorous practitioner of evangelical perfection: he did not think about tomorrow. For, undertaking a journey sufficiently laborious without provisions, when his limbs were already on the point of failing from hunger, he said: “I have heard that Christ’s servants feed on herbs. Why should we not do likewise?” Turning a little aside from the road, he began to pluck them.

“O,” he said, “how sweet!” O good boy, what had savor for you? What, I ask, was that herb—faith? That hay—love? It truly had savor; but Jesus was in the heart, and therefore hay in the mouth. Whence, I ask, whence came such things to a boy? They are yours, Lord Jesus, who give and receive, bestow and demand. For who gives you anything that is not yours? And if anyone should wish to give what he has not received from you, you do not deem it worthy of acceptance.”

This boy therefore received, Lord Jesus; he received from you and gave back; he received and offered. He received and offered this devotion of mind, this fervor of faith, this ardor of love.

All things, therefore, are yours, Lord: you who consecrated the beginnings of his conversion by these miracles; who afterward accepted the pleasing sacrifice of his devout life; who have now mercifully conveyed that most acceptable holocaust into your exalted temple. There, in Abraham’s bosom, rests my Simon, my sweetest friend, yet your poor man, Lord Jesus. There he rests, transferred from death to [Col. 0541C] life, from labor to rest, from misery to blessedness.

Behold, having begun to grieve, I have found cause to rejoice. I have found it indeed—but in you, my beloved brother, not in myself. “Do not weep over me,” he says, “but weep over yourselves” (Luke XXIII). For you, my beloved brother, I rejoice with you; but for myself I grieve. You should rejoice; I should be wept for, I should be mourned—I who can live without Simon. Yet it is strange if I should be said to live when such a portion of my life has been taken from me, such sweet consolation in my pilgrimage, such unique relief of my misery. It is as though my entrails were torn out, as though my unhappy soul were rent apart. And am I called living? O wretched, lamentable life—life without Simon!

The patriarch Jacob wept for his son (Gen. XXXVII); Joseph wept for his father (Gen. L); holy David wept for his dearest Jonathan (II Kings I). This one Simon was all these things to me: a son in age, a father in holiness, a friend in love. Weep then, unhappy man, for your dearest father; weep for your most loving son; weep for your sweetest friend. Let the floodgates of your wretched head burst open; let your eyes pour forth tears by day and night. Weep, I say, not because he has been taken up, but because you have been left behind.

My father, my brother, my son—who will grant me that I may die with you? For I would not wish to die in your place. That would not have been to provide for you, but rather for myself.
