Holy David indeed said this concerning his parricidal son: “Absalom, my son, my son Absalom, who will grant that I may die for you?” (II Kings XVIII). Did he say this concerning Jonathan, his friend? Did Joseph say it [Col. 0542A] concerning his father? It must be said of a parricide; it ought to be said of a sinner, because “the death of sinners is most evil.” It was dutiful to wish to die for the ungodly person, so that someone might remain who could repent, someone who could weep, someone upon whom God might have mercy, lest he perish eternally. But those transferred to rest were not to be called back any longer into this misery; they were not to be subjected again to so many fears and pains.

Finally, Rachel weeping for her children refused to be comforted (Jer. 31). What did she mourn? Affection. Yet that affection would have been comforted if her son had been recalled from the dead, if the mother had once more enjoyed the sight of him. Rachel did not will this. Why? Because, if he were recalled from the dead, he would be cast down from blessedness into misery. She did not wish her son to be recalled, but herself to be taken up to her son in rest [Col. 0542B]. Affection sought her children, lest they be recalled; reason opposed affection; but divine providence deferred the mother’s assumption. Therefore Rachel, weeping for her children, refused to be comforted.

My case is similar. I grieve for my most beloved one, my one-hearted companion, snatched away from me; I rejoice because he has been received into the eternal tabernacles. Affection seeks his sweet presence, by which it was delightfully nourished; but reason does not consent that the soul dear to me, released from the flesh, should again be subjected to the miseries of flesh. My soul longs to enjoy with it, its own portion, the embraces of Christ; but my weakness opposes it, my sinfulness opposes it, and divine providence also opposes it. Certainly, he who was ready entered with the bridegroom into the wedding feast; for me, wretched man that I am, the door is still shut [Col. 0542C] (Matt. 25). Would, Lord Jesus, would that it might at last be opened! Yet I hope in your mercy, Lord, that it will one day be opened. I have sent ahead my firstfruits; I have sent ahead my treasure; I have sent ahead no small part of myself. Let what remains of me follow you. Where my treasure is, there let my heart be also. Here, Lord, I will follow his paths, so that in you I may enjoy his companionship.

And indeed I could do so, Lord, though with a slow step, while his devout way of life stood before my eyes: when the humility I beheld in him checked my pride; when the tranquillity I considered in him restrained my restlessness; when my frivolity was held tight by the bridle of his remarkable gravity. I remember that often, when my eyes wandered here and there [Col. 0542D], one glance from him would so cover me with shame that, suddenly withdrawn within myself, I would restrain all that frivolity by the hand of seriousness; gathering myself to myself, I would begin to occupy myself with something useful. The authority of our order forbade us to speak together, but his look spoke to me, his bearing spoke to me, his very silence spoke to me: a modest look, a measured gait, gravity in speech, silence without bitterness.

Finally, in this last year of his life, as though not unaware of his coming summons, with what tranquillity, what peace, what watchfulness he passed his life! He seemed, as though forgetful of everything outward—even of me—and shut within certain narrow bounds of his own mind [Col. 0543A], to portray more vividly that man whom the holy prophet Jeremiah describes: “It is good for a man when he has borne the yoke from his youth; he shall sit alone and be silent, because he shall lift himself above himself” (Lam. 3).

He took up the yoke of your discipline, Lord Jesus, in the bloom of youth, choosing that narrow way which leads to life: to eat his bread in the sweat of his brow and to submit his will to another’s judgment. He also bore the heavy yoke of illness from youth itself, with which, as I believe, you chastised him in fatherly love for eight years without interruption, even to his last days. And therefore, finding almost nothing outwardly in which he might take delight, he shut himself up in the inward solitude of his mind, sitting alone and silent, yet not torpid in idleness [Col. 0543B]. For he wrote or read, or devoted himself more secretly to meditation upon the Scriptures, being one whose mind was alert. Even his prior scarcely spoke to him, except concerning necessities. He walked like a deaf man who does not hear, and like a mute man who does not open his mouth, becoming like one who does not hear and has no rebukes in his mouth.

Yet if anyone, upon an opportunity arising, addressed him in any manner, such sweetness at once breathed from his speech, such cheerfulness without any levity appeared in his face, that both his manner of speaking and his humility in listening showed how free his silence had been from bitterness and how full of sweetness. Behold what I have lost; behold what has been taken from me. Where have you gone, O exemplar of my life, the ordering of my conduct? Where have you gone, where have you withdrawn? What shall I do [Col. 0543C]? Where shall I turn? Whom shall I now set before myself to follow? How were you torn from my embraces, removed from my sight, taken away from my eyes?

I embraced you, beloved brother—not with flesh, but with heart. I kissed you, not with contact of the mouth, but with the affection of the mind. I loved you, who from the very beginning of my conversion received me into friendship; who showed yourself more intimate to me than to others; who joined me to Hugh in the very depths of your soul. For your love toward us both was so great, your affection so alike, your devotion so one, that, as I think I gathered from your words, your affection preferred neither of us to the other, although sound reason judged his holiness altogether to be preferred to mine. Why then did you pass on while I was absent [Col. 0543D]? Why, when you had regarded one person present as two, did you not wish him present when you departed? Did you judge that both of us, namely you and I, ought to be spared—lest your departure should afflict my eyes, and my grief should even slightly sadden your happy and peaceful passing? Or perhaps, as I more readily believe, divine mercy provided for you alone: that it might transfer that tranquil and peaceful soul, with all tranquillity, from the miseries of this life to the homeland you desired, and loosen the bond of its bodily dwelling with such ease, almost without your knowing it, that not even a slight fear of death might trouble the soul beloved to it.

Finally, the man who sat beside your bed detected in you no sign of approaching death. Indeed, a more cheerful face and easier speech increased hope of your recovery [Col. 0544A]. But when, gently inclining your head, you yielded up your spirit, he thought that you had fallen asleep, not died. Thus provision was made for you, my beloved brother—for you who passed over in such tranquillity, and who, by your peaceful death, showed most plainly that you had been received by the ministers of peace.

Nor is this surprising. You did not dread that hour, but rather desired it; for on the day before you left us, when the prior of our monastery visited you, you said that you wished for no further reprieve of life. What then have you achieved, O bitter death? What have you achieved? You have indeed invaded the tent in which he lived as a stranger, but you have broken the bond by which he was held. You have overthrown the dwelling which he temporarily enjoyed, but you have removed the burden under which he was oppressed.

“For we know,” says the Apostle, “that if our earthly house of this dwelling should be dissolved, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in heaven” (2 Cor. 5). Therefore that soul, a friend to virtues, desirous of rest, devoted to wisdom, victorious over nature, having cast off the covering of this flesh, flies with freer wings, so to speak, toward that high and pure Good; and it is received into the long-desired embraces of Christ. “But,” you say, “the flesh, committed to the earth, is dissolved into ashes.” Certainly. But why do you exult? It has died in order to be made alive; it is dissolved in order to be restored more perfectly. It was sown in corruption, but it shall rise in incorruption. It was sown in dishonour, but it shall rise in glory. Finally, a natural body was sown; a spiritual body shall rise [Col. 0544C]. “Where, O death, is your victory? Where, O death, is your sting?” (1 Cor. 15).

Certainly, where you seem to have done something to him, there you are proved to have benefited him. You have poured out all your venom upon me; in seeking him, you inflicted cruel wounds on me. I, I bore all that bitterness and anguish—I from whom the guide of my journey, the master of my way of life, has been taken. But what is this, O my soul, that you gazed so long upon that sweet funeral without tears? What is this, that you dismissed that body beloved to you without kisses? I grieved, wretched man, and roared aloud; from the depths of my breast I drew long sighs; yet I did not weep. And I saw so clearly that I ought to grieve, that I did not even believe myself to be grieving, even while I grieved intensely [Col. 0544D]. Thus I realized afterward. For such stupor had seized my mind that, even when his limbs had already been stripped for washing, I did not believe that he had passed away. I marvelled that he whom I had bound to myself with the close bonds of sweetest love had suddenly slipped from my hands; I marvelled that that soul, which was one with mine, could be stripped of the body without my embraces.

But now that stupor has yielded to affection, to grief, to compassion. What are you doing now, O eyes? Do not, I beg you, hold back; do not dissemble. At the funeral of my beloved, offer whatever you have, whatever you can. Why am I ashamed? Do I alone weep? See how many tears, how many groans, how many sighs are everywhere! Are these tears blameworthy? Yet your tears excuse us, Lord Jesus—the tears which you shed at the death of your friend [Col. 0545A] (John 11), expressing indeed our affection but revealing your love. Lord, you took upon yourself the feelings of our weakness, but when you willed; therefore you were also able not to weep. O how sweet are your tears, how gentle! How greatly they refresh my anxious mind; how greatly they console it! “See,” they say, “how he loved him” (ibid.). And see how my Simon was loved by all, embraced by all, cherished by all.

But perhaps some who consider themselves strong now judge my tears, thinking my love excessively carnal. Let them interpret them as they wish; but you, Lord, see them, regard them. Others see what is done outwardly; they do not heed what I suffer inwardly. Your eyes are there, Lord. Certainly this your servant possessed nothing in my eyes that might hinder him from passing into your embraces [Col. 0545B]. But no human being knows what takes place in a person except the human spirit within that person. Your eye, Lord, penetrates even to the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow; and it discerns the thoughts and intentions of the heart. And, as a certain praiseworthy servant said: “Woe even to the praiseworthy life of human beings, if it be examined apart from mercy.”

Behold, Lord, the source of my fear; behold, the source of my tears. Attend to them, O most compassionate, most sweet, most merciful one. Receive them, O my one hope, my one and only refuge, the end of my desire, my God, my mercy. Receive them, Lord, as a sacrifice which I offer to you for my most beloved friend; and if any stains have remained upon him, either forgive them or impute them to me [Col. 0545C]. Let me, let me be struck; let me be scourged; let me pay the whole penalty. Only, I beg you, do not hide your blessed face from him; do not withdraw your sweetness from him; do not delay your merciful consolation to him.

Let him experience, my Lord, the sweetness of your mercy, which he so vehemently desired, in which he so confidently trusted, which he commended with such affection, and which tasted so delightfully to him on that night when the others had withdrawn to rest, leaving one brother to keep watch with him, and he burst forth joyfully in this cry [Col. 0546A]: “Mercy, mercy, mercy!” As they say, he tried to sing the whole verse: “I will sing to you, Lord, of mercy and judgment” (Ps. 100). But, as I suppose, carried back by the sweetness of that first word, he lingered more familiarly in repeating it; then, turning to the man who sat beside his bed, he repeated the same saying again and again. And seeing him become almost stupefied, as though indignant at such insensibility—that he was not filled with a like sweetness, did not enjoy a like savour—he began as though to awaken the sleeping man with his hand, and repeated more emphatically and more urgently: “Mercy, mercy.”

What is this that I behold, my Lord? I seem indeed almost to see [Col. 0546B] that mind, melted in some ineffable joy at the draught of this verse, as it saw its sins swallowed up in the boundless sea of divine compassion, leaving nothing to weigh it down, nothing even slightly to darken its conscience. I delight to behold that soul, washed in the fountain of divine mercy, its burden of sins laid aside, striving upward by the natural impulse itself, as though with certain most light motions, and eagerly desiring at any moment to be stripped of the remains of the flesh, meditating only upon the mercy of God on which it wholly rests.

Come then, return now, O soul, to your rest, for the Lord has dealt bountifully with you; pass to the place of the wonderful tabernacle, even to the house of God, amid the voice of exultation and confession, the sound of one feasting. I will follow you with my tears [Col. 0546C]; I will follow you with whatever prayers I can offer; I will follow you with my affection; I will follow you with the very sacrifice of our unique Mediator. And you, father Abraham, again and again stretch out your hands to receive this poor man of Jesus, another Lazarus, as it were (Luke 16); open your bosom, spread out your lap, and receive him mercifully as he returns from the miseries of this life; cherish and console him. Grant also to me, wretched as I am, his poor lover, a place of rest someday with him in your bosom. Amen.

## BOOK TWO

In which the author answers the complaints of certain persons.

[Col. 0545]

## CHAPTER ONE

What he proposed for consideration in the first book; and that those who are plainly vicious must be excluded from this consideration.

[Col. 0545D]

In the preceding part of this little work, while discussing the perfection of charity, we showed as best we could that the sum of all virtues consists in it. For no virtue should be called such if this root has not produced it; nor should any work be considered perfect if this end has not completed it. In charity are shown to consist both the fulfilment of the Law and evangelical perfection, since in it are spiritual circumcision of the inward and outward person, the true sabbath-rest of the mind, the reality of sacrifices, and the whole fullness of the commandments [Col. 0546D]. Concerning circumcision we touched briefly above; and we showed that the sabbath of the mind is, and can be, nowhere but in charity. For this is that easy yoke and light burden to which the mercy of the Saviour invites us: “And you shall find rest for your souls” (Matt. 11).

But because many of us who appear to have placed our necks beneath this yoke are proved to labour in many ways [Col. 0547A], we have endeavoured to show that the yoke of captivity produces this labour. Therefore we proposed for consideration those three things in which the Evangelist John seems to have comprised every kind of covetous desire: the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life (1 John 2). But the death of our most beloved interrupted the work; and, giving ourselves for some time to tears and mourning, we reserved this consideration for another beginning.

Therefore, to take our beginning from Paul’s words, we say that covetousness is the root of all evils (1 Tim. 6), just as charity, conversely, is the root of all virtues. Accordingly, as long as this poisonous root remains lodged in the very depths of the soul, though certain little branches be cut off from the surface, others must sprout again from renewed growth, until the root itself is uprooted utterly and leaves no further source from which the most destructive offspring of vices may arise [Col. 0547B].

There are, moreover, certain persons entangled in more manifest and, so to speak, gross vices, who display the mark of their disgrace immediately on their countenance. I judge these should be removed from the present consideration, since it has been sufficiently demonstrated above that their minds are wholly devoid of rest. But let us who appear to have subjected the shoulders of our minds to the evangelical yoke—which the Saviour’s declaration pronounces most sweet—and to the Lord’s burden—which the same authority likewise proves most light (Matt. 11)—yet are proved to labour: let us, I say, professed followers of Christ’s cross, take up the key of God’s word, unlock the barriers of our hearts [Col. 0547C], penetrate to the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, discern the thoughts and intentions of the heart, and, seeing without flattering caress what lies more secretly hidden in the recesses of the soul, strive rather to pluck up the very roots of our diseases.

## CHAPTER II

That outward labour is shaped by the character of the inward state, and is sometimes diminished by it.

This labour is of the heart, not of the flesh; just as the rest of which we speak belongs to the heart, not to the flesh. Yet outward labour is shaped by the inward condition, and no labour should be called outward if there is none inward. For example, consider hunters, bird-catchers, or any followers of such vanities [Col. 0547D]. If you observe the outward motions of their bodies, what is more laborious? If you consider the state of their minds, what is more delightful? The same point is very easy to demonstrate even in praiseworthy cases.

How great was the outward labour of the apostles when they were handed over to prison, bound in chains, and most severely beaten with whips! Yet they went away rejoicing from the presence of the council because they had been counted worthy to suffer dishonour for the name of Jesus (Acts 5). At that time many sacrilegious persons endured a similar punishment; but because their consciences differed, those persons were miserable in both respects, labouring inwardly and outwardly, whereas the apostles rejoiced in outward punishments because of inward rest. Nor is it surprising, since outward labour is often diminished by inward labour, and the most intense heat of the body is tempered by the ardours of the soul.

What hardship do adulterers suffer? What punishment do thieves suffer [Col. 0548A]? The former, that they may enjoy unlawfully desired embraces; the latter, that they may enjoy another’s spoils. But the one, burning inwardly with the fire of lust, does not know what he suffers outwardly; the more secret flame of avarice causes the other not to feel the evident pains of his body. Of such people the prophet says: “They have laboured in order to act wickedly” (Jer. 9).

When these things have been carefully examined, it is plainly evident that outward sufferings of the body do not produce inward labour; rather, the root residing in the inner depths shapes, according to its own nature, whatever is cut away outwardly. For why is it that, when two sit at the same table and the same foods are set before them, one rejoices and the other complains? Why is it that, when the same wounds are received, one is cast down by the sickness of sorrow while the other is flooded with remarkable joy? Two men are struck at once by the misfortune of bereavement or poverty, and yet one blasphemes while the other gives thanks. The same sight is presented to the eyes of both: one is shamefully stirred, the other enjoys his customary peace. When an opportunity is offered to seek some honour, one is inflamed with such a passion for ruling that, in hope of obtaining high office, he shrinks from no crime; another is so free from this passion that he either does not consent, or scarcely consents, to accept even the offered insignia of dignities [Col. 0548B].

## CHAPTER III

That charity moderates all occurrences by its tranquillity, whereas covetousness corrupts all things by its perversity.

Is it not also evident that the same thing happens to bodies: according to the condition of their health, what happens outwardly is experienced either as distressing or as agreeable? Food which aggravates one person’s illness benefits another’s health; and the sun, which takes light from a bleary eye, shines more pleasantly upon a sound one. Therefore, just as in bodies, according to the measure of their inward nature, things applied outwardly are found either healthful or harmful, so, from the signs mentioned above, it is easy to see that one person’s rest and another’s labour depend upon the inward quality of the mind.

For a mind possessed by the most sweet and tranquil yoke of the Lord—that is, perfect charity—will transform every occurrence into the condition of its own tranquillity [Col. 0548D]. It will not permit itself to be disturbed by any changes of circumstances, but compels the very alterations of things to serve its own advancement. But if a mind is enslaved to the most grievous yoke of covetousness, then, so long as there is no cause of disturbance, relaxed ease falsely imitates the sweetness of the Lord’s yoke. But when a cause for any indignation arises, immediately, from the recesses of the heart as from most hidden caves, a savage beast bursts forth and tears and bloodies the wretched soul with the most cruel bites of its passions, allowing it no time for peace or rest.

Therefore let the yoke be corrupted by the presence of oil—the yoke, that is, of covetousness, by the presence of charity—and at once one experiences how light, how sweet, how pleasant, how heaven-lifting and earth-delivering the burden of Christ is, as a certain man says [Col. 0549A]. Therefore, if we wish to experience the sweetness of this rest, let us diligently seek out the causes and roots of our labour: not tepidly, as though with a blunted blade, cutting off only outward matters, but penetrating with more ardent desire to the very sources of our diseases.

## CHAPTER IV

That every inward labour arises from the threefold lust.

I think that, if we investigate more subtly, we shall most clearly recognize that whatever labour arises in us is derived, as from certain poisonous fountains, either from the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, or the pride of life. If, then, harsh food still distresses me, fleshly lust imposes labour upon me [Col. 0549B]. I do not labour because I have accepted Christ’s yoke, but because I have not wholly cast off the yoke of covetousness.

What if, inflamed by desire for more sumptuous food, I am disturbed by a more ordinary dish? Or if it is prepared in less than the customary quantity, or too late, or carelessly, and I am consumed by the plague of grumbling? What produces these anxieties in me: the passion of covetousness or the sweetness of charity? What if a monk demands from his superior a number of dishes proportionate to the number of nocturnal lessons, and, according to the splendour of some feast, seeks more luxurious fare and exotic flavours? What if, when something of this sort is lacking for any reason, he bursts into quarrels and disputes and, unable to bear the heat of a most evil passion, disturbs the peace of the brethren by importunate shouting and secret whispering [Col. 0549C]? Has not worldly lust brought upon him the yoke of this wretched slavery and the constriction of most degrading labour? James rightly rebukes such people: “Whence are wars and contentions among you? Are they not from your desires, which wage war in your members?” (Jas. 4).

## CHAPTER V

On the opinion of those who say that outward labours are contrary to charity and inward sweetness.

“But,” you say, “to waste the body by continual vigils; to afflict the flesh by daily labours; to weaken the strength of the limbs by the meanest foods—not only entails considerable labour, but is so contrary to the charity that you strive so earnestly to commend that, by emptying all sweetness from the mind, it renders it barren of every spiritual delight” [Col. 0549D].

This is the laughable opinion of certain persons who locate spiritual sweetness somehow in the pleasure of the flesh, maintaining that bodily affliction is contrary to the spirit and that the sufferings of the outward person diminish the holiness of the inward. “For,” they say, “since flesh and spirit are joined by their natural affection, they must communicate their sufferings to one another; and thus it is impossible for the cheerfulness of one not to be disturbed by the oppression of the other, so that a spirit cast down by a certain anxious sorrow cannot possibly breathe within that spiritual joy.”

These things seem to be investigated—or proved—with acuteness. What a shameful thing! Spiritual grace is sought according to the rules of Hippocrates [Col. 0550A]. Thus indeed, thus do those err who rely on physical arguments rather than apostolic precepts. This certainly is wisdom not descending from above, which is first indeed chaste and then peaceable; but it is altogether earthly, animal, devilish. This is the wisdom of the flesh, which, while teaching the sweetness of the flesh, strives to empty the cross of Christ. Yet, as regards the flesh, there is in that cross nothing sweet, nothing soft, nothing tender, nothing at all luxurious.

But the cross is not emptied by this teaching. Rather, it overturns this delicate doctrine: the sacred nails driven into Christ’s limbs overthrow it; the spear, with its healing point driven into his sweet entrails, defeats it. I entirely think the contrary, and boldly declare that bodily affliction—provided a sound intention comes first and discretion is maintained, a discretion which must be learned not from one’s own conjecture but from the examples of the elders, lest perhaps laxity and dissipation disguise themselves under the colour of discretion—I say that bodily affliction is not contrary to the spirit, nor does it diminish divine consolation; rather, I hold that it provokes it. Indeed, I judge that in this life these two always correspond: outward tribulation and inward consolation [Col. 0550B].

“What then?” you say. “Should I believe your opinion rather than my own experience? And what if another testifies that he has experienced something quite different? Which of you should I chiefly believe? You maintain that, after undertaking a stricter mode of life, spiritual grace was diminished in you; another finds that the more he afflicts himself, the greater is the grace of divine sweetness he experiences. To whose judgment, then, should belief be given? Or shall we here also think that divine grace must be subjected to physical reasoning? Far from it, far from it! Certainly he has mercy on whom he wills. Perhaps, then, he bestows the sweetness of his consolation upon one abounding in riches and delights, while withholding it by strict judgment from his little poor one, who dies daily for him.”

Far be it from us to think this of him who is most sweet, most gentle, most loving, most compassionate. But if I say it, you may doubt; if Christ says it, it is heretical not to believe.

## CHAPTER VI

The opinion stated above is refuted by apostolic and prophetic authority.

Let then that most valiant athlete, most faithful witness, eminent disputant, in whom Christ speaks, who dies daily for Christ, who endures every tribulation, who has conflicts without and fears within, who chastises his body and reduces it to slavery, who does not eat his bread for nothing but works in weariness night and day, whose hands supply necessities both for himself and for those with him; who finally toils under the standards of Jesus as a most strenuous soldier amid labour and hardship, many vigils, hunger and thirst, cold and nakedness—let him, I say, decide this question and show whether such great tribulation and remarkable exhaustion have deprived him of spiritual consolation [Col. 0550D].

Perhaps a head dried of all natural moisture by so many vigils and labours could produce no tears, and a heart weakened by so many pressures drew in no spiritual sweetness. But I see him writing to certain persons “with much tribulation and anguish of heart, through many tears”; I see him mourning for certain people who had sinned before and had not repented; I see him rejoicing with those who rejoice and weeping with those who weep; I hear him groaning because he does not wish to be unclothed but to be clothed over. What shall I say of his spiritual sweetness, when at its most sweet taste he considers even what had seemed gains to him as dung? Was he not drawn by wondrous sweetness to long for Christ’s very embraces, saying, “I desire to depart and to be with Christ, for it is much better” (Phil. 1) [Col. 0551A]? Was he not intoxicated with such wonderful love of Christ that he utterly renounced all glory, except, he says, in “the cross of my Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal. 6)? Was he not aroused by the fervour of excessive charity to pronounce anathema upon those who do not love the Lord Jesus: “If anyone does not love our Lord Jesus Christ, let him be anathema. Maranatha!” (1 Cor. 16).

Yet let him himself say whether he was left without consolation in his tribulation, and make known what we ought to hope for in our own tribulation. Thus let him pierce with the apostolic sword-point the serpent’s head that hisses this noxious venom into human minds. For these are the serpent’s ways: it crawls upon its belly, eats earth, sleeps under shade in damp hiding-places, and pursues the business of belly and lust under the appearance of holiness. For it thinks that it can more easily frighten the simple away from apostolic poverty and evangelical purity if they suppose that a greater grace of divine sweetness will be present in a more relaxed life [Col. 0551C]. They will believe it holier to present faces wet with tears amid banquets and wines, royal dishes and elaborate feasts, idle conversations and nightly drinking bouts, than to show pale faces and dry eyes amid labour and hardship, many vigils, hunger and thirst, cold and nakedness, the mortification of one’s own will, daily toil, contempt for the world, and disdain for the flesh.

Let Paul then say whether that compassionate Comforter leaves his own without consolation in present tribulation, and by his authority forestall the heresy of Jovinian as it sprouts anew. Yet this heresy appears more pernicious than Jovinian’s; for while his equates feasting with abstinence, this one gives feasting precedence. Therefore let those who place the greater consolation of divine sweetness in fleshly pleasure rather than tribulation hear Paul saying: “Blessed be God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all consolation, who consoles us in all our tribulation” (2 Cor. 1) [Col. 0551D].

Whether, then, we are worn down by fasts, afflicted by vigils, or exhausted by labours, blessed be God, who consoles us in all our tribulation. If we are crushed with stones, bound in chains, beaten with rods, or endure the confines of prison, blessed be God, who consoles us in all our tribulation. Let the world rage, let the world be cruel, let it persecute with hatred, assail with curses, plunder possessions, stain reputation: blessed be God, who consoles us in all our tribulation. “So that,” he says, “we may also console those who are in every affliction” (ibid.) [Col. 0552A]. Here he promises his consolation not to those who live amid riches and pleasures, but to those who are in every affliction. And leaving nothing unresolved in the question, he added: “For as the sufferings of Christ abound in us, so through Christ our consolation also abounds.”

What could be clearer? This is exactly what we said shortly before: these two correspond, namely, outward sufferings and inward consolations. Who, then, is so dull or presumptuous as, in opposition to the most evident truth and apostolic authority, relying on physical arguments, shamelessly and vainly to maintain that sharing Christ’s sufferings is contrary to the spirit and diminishes the grace of spiritual sweetness?

To share Christ’s sufferings is to submit to regular discipline, mortify the flesh through abstinence, vigils, and labours, submit one’s own will to another’s judgment, prefer nothing to obedience, and—in order to embrace much in few words—to carry out our profession, made according to the Rule of blessed Benedict. This is, as our same lawgiver testifies, to participate in Christ’s sufferings. For he says:

> “And thus, persevering in the monastery until the end, may we share in Christ’s sufferings through patience, so that we may deserve to be companions of his kingdom.”
>
> [Note: [Col. 0551D] St Benedict, Prologue to the Rule.]

The Apostle says the same: “Knowing,” he says, “that as you are partners in the sufferings, so shall you also be in the consolation” (2 Cor. 1) [Col. 0552C]. How necessary the affliction of the outward person is, we are most plainly taught by the same Apostle’s declaration: “Although our outward person is decaying, yet the inward is renewed. For the present, momentary, and light burden of our tribulation works in us beyond all measure an eternal weight of glory on high” (2 Cor. 4).

Finally, Solomon declares in mystical words upon whom divine consolation is to be poured, saying: “Give strong drink to those who are sorrowful, and wine to those who are bitter in soul. Let them drink and forget their want, and remember their sorrow no more” (Prov. 31). By these words he plainly promises that wine which gladdens the human heart not to those dissolved in idleness, nor to those spending their days in laughter and tales [Col. 0552D], but to those bitter in soul. And he declares that the strong drink made from new and old fruits, which the bride keeps among the bridegroom’s delights, is to be granted not to those feasting and drinking, but to those sorrowing because of this life’s afflictions and labouring under need and grief. “Let them drink,” he says, “and forget their want,” affirming that the magnitude of their labour is lessened by divine consolation.

The Psalmist most plainly agrees with this judgment: “According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, your consolations have gladdened my soul” (Ps. 93) [Col. 0553A]. Therefore let no one dread that arduous way which leads to life; let no one, in timid unhappiness, return to the more relaxed way he has once rejected. Rather, as our lawgiver says, let him endure without growing weary or departing, knowing that according to the multitude of labours which he bears for Christ, consolations will gladden his soul.

## CHAPTER VII

The question why some are moved to compunction by greater sweetness in a more relaxed life than in a stricter one.

But what is it, you ask, that when I lived somewhat more laxly—using richer food, relaxing a little over drink, allowing myself rather more sleep, neither wearing down my body with labour or such rough clothing, nor being restrained by so much silence—I was so deeply compunct, [Col. 0553B] so moved, so melted by a certain sweetness of mind; whereas now, in this strictness, I go about so dry and parched that I cannot even force tears from my eyes?

And I ask you what judgment you think should be made of one who, when swallowed up in an immense whirlpool of vices, gave himself over to every kind of filth and impurity, shuddered at no disgrace whatever, and yet in such a life was more often compunct, more often wept; and this not merely through fear of punishment and remembrance of his sins—which perhaps no one would find surprising—but even, dissolved by a wondrous affection into the sweetness of love for Jesus, seemed to embrace him himself with a kind of kiss of the mind. What then? Is that man’s life to be emulated, those morals to be followed, the flesh to be surrendered to allurements, the members [Col. 0553C] subjected to lust, so that we may enjoy similar sweetness? Who, most madly deranged, would say so? Nor do I state these things as doubtful; rather, as Jesus himself knows, I declare them true and certain.

I myself know a brother who, after spending the whole day mixed with worldly men and women, occupied with tales and drinking, returns to the monastery in the evening and breaks out into tears and sighs so that by his importunate groans he compels the ears even of many people; yet he does not for that reason restrain himself in the least from such allurements. Is regular strictness, then, to be abandoned in hope of this compunction, and similar filth to be pursued? Whose hearing does not recoil from this?

## CHAPTER VIII. That there is a threefold cause of spiritual visitations.

Let us therefore know that such visitation does not [Col. 0553D] always show holiness; for it often summons it forth and often preserves it. So far as presently occurs to me, there is a threefold cause of this visitation. It sometimes takes place for awakening, sometimes for consolation, and most often also for reward: for awakening those who sleep, for consoling those who labour, and as a reward for those who sigh after heavenly things. The first rouses the sluggish, the second restores the weary, the third receives those ascending. This first compunction summons to holiness; the second preserves holiness; the third rewards it. The first terrifies the contemptuous or draws the fearful; the second cherishes and advances the striving person; the third embraces the one who comes. The first is like a goad correcting one who has strayed, the second like a staff supporting the weak, the third like a bed [Col. 0554A] receiving one at rest.

Accordingly, just as divine mercy commonly summons those living tepidly or ruinously to salvation by word, by example, sometimes by rebuke, and sometimes even by the scourge, so also by a hidden compunction—aroused by fear or produced by love—it invites them to a better way of life. Yet the purpose of this visitation is twofold: it is given to the elect for progress, and to the reprobate for judgment.

## CHAPTER IX. That the first kind of compunction, like certain other graces, comes to the reprobate for judgment and to the elect for progress.

Nor should it surprise us that this grace is commonly shared by reprobate and elect alike, since we know that even more excellent charisms—the word of knowledge, prophecy, kinds [Col. 0554B] of tongues, and the grace of miracles—have been bestowed even on the reprobate. For Saul was among the prophets, and Judas among the apostles. “Many,” he says, “will say to me on that day: ‘Did we not cast out demons in your name and perform many signs in your name?’ And then I will confess to them that I never knew you” (Matt. 7).

That we may see the same concerning the grace of compunction: Balaam, being compunct, said, “Let my soul die the death of the righteous, and let my last end be like theirs” (Num. 23). Lamenting also his own perversity, he says: “Balaam son of Beor has spoken; he who hears the words of God has spoken, he who falls and has opened eyes” (ibid.). Yet he profited nothing from this compunction, he who taught Balak to place a stumbling-block before the children of Israel, to commit fornication and drink, [Col. 0554C] and to eat things sacrificed to idols.

How often the children of Israel in the wilderness, rebuked by Moses, wept before the Lord; yet that compunction profited them nothing, because they again gave themselves up to their former desires (Num. 11 and elsewhere). And when, having been brought into the promised land, the angel spoke to them at the place of weeping, they raised their voices and wept; nevertheless after this they went on doing evil before the Lord (Judg. 2). What of Judas? Did he not, compunct, say: “I have sinned in betraying innocent blood” (Matt. 26)?

But that such compunction profits nothing for those who repeat their perversity is testified by that wise man who says: “He who is washed by the dead, and touches the dead again—what does his washing profit him?” (Ecclus. 34). One is washed by the dead when, compunct, he laments a life devoid of all warmth [Col. 0554D] of zeal, or at least foul and buried in vices. But such washing will profit nothing unless correction follows. The elect, however, for whom all things work together for good, are aroused by such compunction not for judgment but for progress. Stirred by this heavenly visitation, they do not grow more secure in a laxer life; rather, the greater the sweetness of divine love which they enjoy, the more ardently they equip themselves for the stronger exercises of virtue.

## CHAPTER X. On the twofold purpose of the second visitation, and how from it one passes to the third, which is more excellent than the rest.

Those who, having shaken off their lukewarmness, immediately undertake sweats and struggles [Col. 0555A] for Christ, are received by that more excellent kind of compunction which heals the sick, strengthens the feeble, and relieves the despairing. It is consolation for those who groan, rest for those who labour, protection for those tempted, provision for travellers on the road.

Those deprive themselves of this consolation who, recoiling as soon as the first exertions come, either fall back into their former lethargy or seek cheap consolations in frequent talk, visits from friends, or indeed freedom to do their own will. Despising the filth of such consolations, the holy Prophet says: “My soul refused to be consoled” (Ps. 76). What then? Were you left without every consolation? Far from it: “I remembered God and was delighted” (ibid.).

The purpose of this visitation too is twofold. It comes sometimes to those under temptation so that they may not fall, and sometimes to those about to be tempted so that they may bear it more lightly. The former are refreshed; the latter are armed. Let no one measure his holiness by that first kind of visitation, which manifestly happens at times even to the reprobate; nor yet by this second kind, which, although more excellent, prepares holiness rather than displays it. In the former, holiness is as it were brought to birth; here it is nourished. Indeed, one accustomed in this second state to frequent compunction, fed with frequent sips of divine sweetness, is advanced by a higher step to that more sublime visitation, which no longer strengthens and confirms the weak but rewards, with more abundant grace, one who is like a perfected victor.

## CHAPTER XI. What God works in each of these visitations.

[Col. 0555C]

In the first state, then, the soul is awakened; in the second it is purified; in the third it enjoys the tranquillity of the Sabbath. In the first state mercy works; in the second loving-kindness; in the third justice. Mercy seeks what is lost; loving-kindness restores what has been found; justice rewards that which is now perfect. Mercy raises the fallen; loving-kindness helps the combatant; justice crowns the victor.

And truly, what greater proof of divine compassion can there be than that this sweetness, this delight, this wonderful serenity—in which nothing defiled finds entry—should bestow the grace of its visitation upon a soul still defiled? It not only shakes it with terror but, breaking through all the inner barriers of the mind locked by the bolts [Col. 0555D] of vices, impresses upon lips still foul a kind of kiss of its own sweetness, and by its ineffable sweetness caresses one who turns away, draws one who hesitates, and encourages one who despairs.

O sweet Lord, what shall I render to you for all that you have rendered to me? O how sweet is your Spirit in all things! Truly, Lord, your mercy is great over me: you sent forth your hand from on high, rescuing and delivering me from many waters and from the hand of alien sons; you rescued my soul from the lower hell, where I licked a drop of your sweetness and heard your voice as though from afar. “What are you doing, unworthy and filthy one? Why do you roll about in this filth and take delight in these shameful things? Behold what sweetness, what pleasantness, [Col. 0556A] what delight is with me! Do you despair because of the enormity of your crimes? But shall I, who pursue one fleeing, reject one who comes? Shall I, who embrace and draw you when you turn your face away from me, repel you as you flee beneath the wings of my mercy?”

And your voice, Lord, is your inspiration. For whence comes so great a hope to the despairing soul, unless you, Lord, grant it—you who in wonderful ways heal our infirmities and give form to our deformity? But what is to be said of that second state, in which divine loving-kindness works so wonderfully in a human being that he profits from temptation and grows stronger still from weakness? Although every soul naturally shrinks from labours, temptations, and pains, it is encouraged by such consolations in its temptations that it not only endures assaults but in some sense even provokes and seeks those that delay [Col. 0556B] their coming.

That holy man had advanced to this state who said: “Test me, Lord, and try me” (Ps. 25); and again: “Test me, Lord, and know my heart” (Ps. 138). In this state the mind, accustomed to innumerable incentives of heavenly affections, gradually advances to that most sublime and very rarely experienced kind of visitation, where it begins to taste certain first-fruits of its future reward. Passing “to the place of the wonderful tabernacle, even to the house of God,” and pouring out its soul upon itself, it becomes intoxicated with the nectar of heavenly secrets; and, contemplating with utterly pure sight the place of its future rest, it cries out with the Prophet: “This is my rest for ever and ever; here will I dwell, because I have chosen it” (Ps. 131).

Therefore, just as in that state [Col. 0556C] where no merits have preceded, mercy alone works, so in this state, where God crowns his gifts—which nevertheless he has willed to be our merits—justice works together with mercy.

## CHAPTER XII. That fear belongs especially to the first visitation, consolation to the second, and love to the third.

Moreover, I think it should be noted that although, in that first visitation, God sometimes mingles the sweetness of delight with fear, and in the second commonly employs the goad of fear together with sweetness, the former properly belongs to fear and the latter to the sweetness of consolation; for in the third perfect charity casts fear out. “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom”; [Col. 0556D] but the love of the Lord is the consummation of wisdom. In fear is beginning; in love, perfection. Here is labour; there is reward. One ascends from this to that; yet one reaches it only through this.

For a drop of wondrous sweetness, descending from the balm of that fertile mountain, that curdled mountain, pours itself out as it were in a most gentle flow upon the mind which fear commonly afflicts, pain presses, despair casts down, sorrow swallows, and sloth gnaws away. At the radiance of that divine light all the mist of irrational sensations is dissolved; at its most sweet taste all bitterness is driven away; the heart is enlarged, the mind is enriched, and the ability to ascend is wonderfully prepared. Thus lukewarmness is excluded by fear, and fear is moderated by the taste of divine sweetness. Fear rouses the mind lest it grow sluggish in low things; affection nourishes it lest it fail through labour. By this alternation it is trained until the whole mind, absorbed in that ineffable charity, no longer grows rich from love but, ardently desiring the most longed-for embraces of him who is fairer in form than the children of men, begins to wish to be dissolved and to be with Christ, saying daily with the Prophet: “Alas for me, for my sojourn has been prolonged” (Ps. 119).

Thus the Lawgiver will give blessing, administering to beginners the wine of compunction together with its fear; to those making progress, milk from the breasts of its consolation; and when they have been weaned from milk, they shall feast from the entrance into its glory. Therefore the first visitation reproves iniquity; the second sustains weakness; but the third [Col. 0557B] displays holiness. Let no one therefore glory in the first, in which the wicked or the lukewarm person is convicted; nor in the second, in which the weak person is tested; but in the third, let whoever glories glory in the Lord.

## CHAPTER XIII. What the fruit is in each, and why some are deprived of the consolation of the second visitation.

The fruit of the first visitation is true conversion to God; the fruit of the second is the mortification of one’s own will and of all passions; the fruit of the third is perfect blessedness. Finally, once the fruit of the first compunction has been received, in the excellence of perfect consolation, those things that have, so to speak, completed their task cease; immediately there follows the testing of temptations and [Col. 0557C] labours, so that the sweet devotion toward God may fittingly succeed.

For the affection of this sweetness is not easily granted without labour or temptation preceding, accompanying, or at least immediately following it. It is granted not for the merit of one’s life, but to sustain weakness or lighten temptation. Thus those who recoil at once from their first temptations and labours and, like certain disciples of the Lord, take offence and recoil from communion in the Lord’s body and blood—that is, imitation of his passion—saying, “This saying is hard; who can hear it?” (John 6), and thus look back, being less fit for the kingdom of God; or who receive those most abject earthly and human consolations—such persons, I say, exclude themselves from the sweetness [Col. 0557D] of this consolation. Miserable everywhere, they neither ascend to that sublime kind of visitation nor undertake exercises of virtue without such consolation; yet, because conscience resists, they do not dare return to their former life.

They might perhaps justly complain that divine consolation had abandoned them if, completely renouncing their former ways, wholly mortifying their own will, they did not prefer the cheap and abject consolations of the world to God’s consolation. But now, when they have entered upon the way of a stricter resolve, they immediately begin, I know not how, to dream of the insignia of dignities and arrogate freedom to themselves in a most vain presumption. The wretches do not wait until they are told, “Friend, go up higher” (Luke 14); rather, as much as they can, they rudely thrust [Col. 0558A] themselves toward and seek higher places. In the language of the Gospel, they desire the first seats in synagogues, the first places at dinners, the first greetings in the marketplace, and to be called Rabbi by men (Matt. 23)—wishing, plainly, to be teachers who have not spent even a single day learning to be disciples.

Since they themselves are conscious of such absurdities, I wonder with what face and with what irreverence they suppose that divine sweetness should be granted them, and that a soul prostituted to earthly affections should be cherished in the most sweet and pure embraces of Jesus. If any drop of heavenly sweetness should flow to them, it should certainly be understood to come not as a merit of holiness or a solace for labour, but rather as an awakening for persons still weak. Yet after receiving knowledge of the truth [Col. 0558B] and taking up the path of perfect purity, this kind of grace is bestowed scarcely, if ever, upon those who sin deliberately or lie sluggish in inertia.

This must, however, be said: it is one thing merely to be assailed by those earthly affections; another for them very rarely to fall upon someone; another to yield and consent to them, or wholly give oneself over to them; and another, if some such occupations are imposed, to undertake them unwillingly.

## CHAPTER XIV. Certain divine testimonies are set forth by which each person may measure his own state.

Accordingly, if you wish to see more clearly the causes and grounds of your visitation, first examine with discerning scrutiny the state to which you have advanced and the quality of your life and conduct. Investigate them carefully, with conscience as witness, not according to your own guesswork but according to the rules of Scripture, the lines of heavenly commands, and the standard of your profession.

For the Lord says: “Take heed lest your hearts be weighed down by gluttony and drunkenness and the cares of this life” (Luke 21). And again: “Everyone who is angry with his brother shall be liable to judgment; whoever says, ‘Raca,’ shall be liable to the council; and whoever says, ‘Fool,’ shall be liable to the hell of fire” (Matt. 5). And elsewhere: “Whoever wishes to be greater among you, let him be servant of all” (Matt. 20). Again: “Whatever good things you wish people to do to you, do also to them” (Matt. 7). And: “For every idle word that people speak, they shall render account on the day of judgment” (Matt. 12).

The apostle Paul also says: [Col. 0558D] “Not in revelry and drunkenness, not in beds and indecencies, not in strife and jealousy; but put on our Lord Jesus, and make no provision for the flesh in its desires” (Rom. 13). And he himself says: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular business” (2 Tim. 2). And to the Galatians: “If you bite and devour one another, see that you are not consumed by one another” (Gal. 5). And to the Thessalonians: “We ask you, brothers, to abound more and more, and to endeavour to be quiet, to attend to your own business, to work with your hands, to walk honourably toward those outside, and to desire nothing from anyone” (1 Thess. 4). In the second Epistle to the same: “If anyone is unwilling to work, neither let him eat” (2 Thess. 3).

James also says: “My brothers, do not hold the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ with respect of persons” (Jas. 4 [as cited]). Again: “If you have zeal of souls and contentions in your hearts, do not glory; for where zeal and contention are, there are instability and every evil work” (ibid.). And shortly afterward: “Whoever wishes to be a friend of this world shall be constituted an enemy of God” (ibid.). The same writer continues: “Do not speak evil of one another, my brothers” (ibid.).

Let us come to the prince of the apostles: “I beseech you,” he says, “as strangers and pilgrims, abstain from fleshly desires” (1 Pet. 2). And in the same Epistle: “Putting away all malice, all deceit, hypocrisies, envies, and all slanders” (ibid.). And below: “If anyone speaks, let him speak as the words of God” (1 Pet. 4). A little later, to pastors: [Col. 0559B] “Feed the flock among you, not for shameful gain, nor lording it over the clergy,” he says. Likewise, young people, be subject to the elders. And all of you, clothe yourselves with humility toward one another” (1 Pet. 5). The same writer says in his second Epistle: “Escaping the corruption of the lust that is in the world” (2 Pet. 1); and again: “Be sober and watch” (2 Pet. 5 [as cited]).

Now we must come to that disciple whom Jesus loved: “He who says that he knows God and does not keep his commandments is a liar” (1 John 2). And: “Do not,” he says, “love the world, nor the things which are in the world” (ibid.). And below: “Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John 3). Jude the apostle also says: “Woe to those who have gone in the way of Cain, have poured themselves out in the error [Col. 0559C] of Balaam for reward, and have perished in the rebellion of Korah. These are stains at their feasts, feasting together” (Jude 11). And a little later: “These are murmurers, complainers, walking according to their own desires” (ibid., v. 16). And below: “Hating even the garment stained by the flesh” (ibid., v. 23).

Set before yourself, then, these and similar testimonies of evangelical and apostolic teaching as a kind of spiritual mirror. Look more carefully upon the face of your soul. If you still find yourself floating amid banquets, repeatedly heated by wine, entangled in secular affairs, stretched out by worldly cares, and bent upon fleshly desires; if you occupy the day with quarrels and tales, tear the flesh of your brother with the unclean bites of slander; if, given over to idle indolence, [Col. 0559D] disturbed as it were by every kind of spur, you flit here and there in restless mobility; if you procure the pleasures of your belly not by your own labour but by the blood and sweat of the poor; if, finally, you are frequently stained by anger, impatience, envy, and disobedience; if you attend more diligently to the care of your belly than to that of your mind, continually overstep the bounds of your profession—then, if in all these things you go about sleek and fat, do not, I beg you, glory much in your little tears. Perhaps, to say something ourselves in accordance with the physicians, they flow more readily when veins are swollen with wine and the moisture of the head is increased by the varied vapours of foods and flavours.

Or if you are compunct in this condition by fear of God or by affection, do not abuse so great a grace of God so shamelessly as to roll more securely in your filth; [Col. 0560A] and do not compel God—who by this sign appears not yet wholly to have cast you off from the warmth of his inward compassion—to vomit you out because of your lukewarmness, so that your latter end becomes worse than your former. Daily experience teaches us that this happens to many.

## CHAPTER XV. By what means one passes to spiritual consolations.

But if, awakened by such stings of affection, you have cast away the filthy pots of Egypt and preferred the poverty of Jesus to all the riches of the world; if you have exchanged royal dishes for the food of coarse bread and the cheapest vegetables; if you have set submission and lowliness in place of honours; if, stripped of worldly cares and affairs, you have chosen to seek your livelihood not amid the curses of peasants but by your own [Col. 0560B] labour and that shared with your brothers; if in place of talkativeness you have taken up silence, and in place of frequent quarrels the affection of brotherly love; if you have already begun to render the vows your lips uttered—if, I say, by these and similar signs you find that you have departed from Egypt and, like a true Israelite, crossed the waves of this great and wide sea, namely this world—then, if heavenly sweetness does not immediately pour forth manna for you, do not murmur against God; do not test God and say, “Is God among us or not?” For carrying out his commands is the clearest indication of his presence, he himself saying: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my commandments; and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John 14).

Do not, I say, murmur and fall into that blasphemy of saying: “It is vain to serve God; and what profit is it that we have kept his commandments?” (Mal. 3). Or that saying of the Psalmist: “Therefore in vain have I justified my heart and washed my hands among the innocent; and I have been scourged all day, and my chastisement has come in the morning,” seeing that sinners and those who prosper in the world have obtained riches (Ps. 72)—and, what is greatest, spiritual riches. If more abundant riches bring a more abundant grace, why are we “put to death all day, reckoned as sheep for slaughter”? Is it not better to eat and drink and enjoy good things in this life and in the next? Is it not the act of a foolish person to seek with great [Col. 0560D] bodily torment what can easily be obtained without labour?

But where then is what Paul says: “Through many tribulations we must enter into the kingdom of God” (Acts 14)? And to the Thessalonians: “Let no one,” he says, “be disturbed by these tribulations, for you yourselves know that we are appointed for this” (1 Thess. 3). Yet you wonder that heavenly sweetness does not immediately receive you.

And still, the children of Israel, who in Egypt had been repeatedly awakened by the glory of divine miracles and had eaten the sacred flesh of that mystical lamb, did not immediately deserve the consolation of angelic food after their passage through the Red Sea. Rather, they were first brought to the waters of Marah, and there tested; then, passing by the twelve springs to the hidden places of a more remote wilderness, they were wonderfully fed with heavenly bread (Exod. 15).

[Col. 0561A]

You too, therefore, having left Egypt, if you have passed dry-footed through the swelling waves of this age, must first be led to the waters of Marah—that is, bitter waters—so that the bitterness of bodily labours may frighten you and you may experience the Gospel saying that “narrow is the way which leads to life” (Matt. 7). There you will be tested by the Lord, if perhaps you may deserve to pass into the company of those to whom he says: “You are those who have remained with me in my temptations” (Luke 22).

Then you will pass by a higher stage to the twelve springs, namely the streams of apostolic teaching, so that, accustomed to continual meditation on the Scriptures, you may in a sense become outside the world. Borrowing from the divine utterances—indeed, silver tried in fire—the wings of a silvered dove, you will fly like a most chaste turtledove into the spiritual desert. There, [Col. 0561B] if the loving-kindness of the Creator pours out for you any drop of spiritual refreshment, know that it does not rest with your choice when you gather, how much you gather, or how long you keep what you have gathered. For if on the Sabbath you go out to seek some heavenly food, it cannot even be found. On the other days, however, a fixed quantity—the *gomor*, that is, the measure of divine judgment—will be prescribed for you.

Moreover, if you try to store something for the next day so that you may feed upon heavenly food without daily labour, your expectation will breed worms for you. But when you have tasted spiritual sweetness, do not immediately dissolve into idleness; for Amalek will soon rise against you from the spiritual side, to be overcome not by weapons but by prayers. Thus, as certain consolations succeed each other by divine loving-kindness, and many labours arise from your own desires, after innumerable struggles you will ascend, rewarded, to that ineffable kind of visitation. Burning afresh with the ardour of charity at the entrance of God’s glory, [Col. 0561C] you will be happily satisfied as though by the fruit of the promised land; and when the fire of divine love has utterly consumed the yoke of concupiscence, you will rest in the pallor of gold, the brightness of wisdom, and the sweetness of divine contemplation. You will experience fully that the Lord’s yoke is sweet and his burden light (Matt. 11).

## CHAPTER XVI. That no one should abandon a purpose of stricter life even if he does not experience that sweet affection.

But suppose that none of this sweetness flows, that no pleasantness of tears soothes you. You must not on that account return to your former state. Rather, the fruits of each way of life must be compared and weighed in the scales of conscience with an even balance, lest lesser things perhaps outweigh greater ones in your estimation, or worse things be compared with better; lest the more certain be prejudiced by the doubtful, or the fewer by the more numerous.

For if you can do no otherwise, it is surely better for you, with one limb weakened or, if necessary, amputated, to go sound and strong in the rest, than, with all your limbs withered, to depend too insistently on the health of a single limb.

## CHAPTER XVII. The questions of a certain novice, together with his own answers.

[Col. 0562A]

Not long ago a certain brother, renouncing the world, came to our monastery. The most reverend abbot entrusted him to my insignificance to be instructed in regular discipline. At one time he began, wondering, to ask what cause I thought there was for his having been so often compunct while still living in secular dress and conduct, dissolved into an affection of divine love, and enjoying such sweetness of spirit as, he said, he was now unable not merely to retain for longer but even rarely to taste.

Then I said: “Do you think that former manner of life of yours was holier and more acceptable to God?”

“By no means,” he replied, [Col. 0562B] “would I say that—especially because I now do many things such that, if I had done any one of them then, I should not merely have been regarded as holy but, so to speak, as worthy of adoration by everyone.”

“I ask you,” I said, “to what extent did you experience that apostolic saying: ‘Through many tribulations we must enter into the kingdom of God’ (Acts 14), and that saying of blessed Job: ‘If I were righteous, I would not lift up my head, filled with affliction and misery’ (Job 10)?”

“I remember,” he replied, “feeling none of those things; but for the most part I perceived myself to love Christ more distinctly and sweetly.”

“And did you then suffer as much for Christ as you suffer now?”

“Not for one hour,” he said, “as much as I endure here without ceasing. For, to say nothing of the rest, I would in no way have allowed myself for even one day to be pressed by such silence, or restrained by any means from idle and vain words. Indeed, after those tears which I mentioned, I at once returned to laughter and tales, and according to the impulse of my mind was carried here and there in restless motion. Possessing the freedom of my own will, I delighted in the company of my parents, smiled at the conversations of companions, attended prepared banquets, did not shrink from drinking parties, took morning sleep at my pleasure, and stuffed myself with food and drink even beyond the limits of necessity. I say nothing of the stings of anger by which I was sometimes driven, quarrels, disputes, and desires for worldly things, to which I devoted myself as much as I could.”

“But now,” I said, “what are your morals, your life, your deeds?”

And he, smiling, said: [Col. 0562D] “It is easy to say, for they do not permit themselves to be unknown. Food is indeed scantier, clothing rougher; drink comes from the fountain, sleep for the most part on a book. In short, a poorly soft mat is spread beneath tired limbs; whenever sleep has become sweeter, we are compelled to rise at the ringing of the bell. I pass over the fact that we eat our bread in the sweat of our face, and that we speak only with three men, and this very rarely, and scarcely even of necessary matters.

“Is not that apostolic command most plainly fulfilled in us: ‘Mortify your members which are upon the earth’ (Col. 3)? And that saying of the Psalmist: ‘I have become as a beast before you’ (Ps. 72)? Truly we have become like beasts: wherever we are led, we go without contradiction; whatever [Col. 0563A] is imposed upon us, we bear without resistance. There is no place for one’s own will, no time for idleness or dissipation.

“I do not think certain things should be passed over which delight no less than these others fatigue. Nowhere are there quarrels; nowhere contention; nowhere the complaining lament of peasants under cruel oppression; nowhere the pitiable cry of injured poor persons; no lawsuits, no secular courts. Everywhere there is peace, everywhere tranquillity, and a wonderful freedom from worldly tumults. Among the brothers there is such unity and concord that each thing seems to belong to all and everything to each one. And what delights me wonderfully is that there is no respect of persons, no consideration of birth. Necessity alone produces distinction; infirmity alone inequality. What is worked for in common [Col. 0563B] is distributed from all to each, not as carnal affection or private love may dictate, but according as each has need.

“How wonderful also that, among, I think, three hundred men, the will of one man is law: whatever has once fallen from his mouth is observed by all with such care as if all had sworn an oath to it or had heard it from the mouth of God himself. And, to encompass much in a few words, I find nothing at all of perfection in evangelical and apostolic commands, nothing in the writings of the holy Fathers, nothing in the sayings of ancient monks, that does not accord with this order and this profession.”

Then I said: “You are a novice, and so I attribute this not to boasting but rather to fervour. Yet I want you to be cautious, lest you think that there is any profession at all in this life that has no hypocrites. If perhaps you see someone exceeding the standard either in speech or action, do not be troubled as though something new had occurred outside your expectation. Yet do you think all these things which you enumerate so fervently are comparable to those tears of yours?”

“Far be it,” he replied, “for that outpouring of tears never gave me a secure conscience, never stripped me of the fear of death. But now I care little; indeed, I greatly desire that my Creator should take me away after a short while. Although this may perhaps be faint-heartedness, as you are accustomed to reproach me—that is, that I would prefer to be released from these labours—I could by no means desire it without a sure hope in divine mercy. Therefore [Col. 0563D] I greatly wonder why I loved God with greater love when I enjoyed less security.”

“I ask you,” I said, “if you had two servants, one of whom not only obeyed your commands most faithfully but endured certain labours on your account, while the other daily transgressed your commands and consented to endure nothing adverse for you—if both said, ‘I love my master,’ which would you choose to believe?”

“Who,” he says, “would not see that this man ought to be most richly rewarded, while that one ought to be reproved not merely for transgression but also for excessive shamelessness?”—“Thus,” I said, “you ought to judge yourself between these two states of yours.”—“But,” he says, “if I am not to trust my own experience, what reasoning can persuade me?”—“If,” I said, “[Col. 0564A] someone were to ask you which is better, one who loves God more or one who loves him less, would you not, without any hesitation, pronounce better the one whom you knew to love more?”—“It would be madness,” he says, “to hesitate even on that point.”—“I ask you now,” I said, “to put aside whatever still flatters you, as a novice, with worldly sweetness, whatever allures you by remembered pleasure. Do not attend to what the flesh suggests, but to what reason dictates; and answer me according to the rules of truth and the testimony of your conscience: whether you would prefer now to be in that former state rather than in the state in which you now are.”—“Absolutely,” he says, “if I do not wish to deceive myself or make my own mouth to me ‘the oil of the sinner,’ to make my head fat, I must [Col. 0564B] confess that, if I preferred that state, it would plainly be not for Christ’s sake but for the world’s; not from a desire for greater perfection but from distaste for present labor, or at least from an appetite for greater pleasure.”—“Now then,” I said, “being, as it were, conscious of your own fervor, I do not hesitate to affirm that you do not wish to be now in that state.”—“You are not mistaken,” he says. “But if,” I said, “you loved God more in that state, you were certainly better then. If better then, why are you safer now? Do you choose to be safer rather than better? And if someone should say that the man who strives more earnestly to fulfill the Lord’s commandments is better than one who strives less, I think you would not deny it.”—“I am hemmed in on every side,” he says, “and, as though driven from rock to rock by the force of reason, I am dashed about and find no [Col. 0564C] escape. For that I then loved God more, and more often drew breath, as it were, into his love through certain sweet tears, I ought not to doubt, as a matter I have experienced. Yet I do not dare deny that one is better who has been more fervent in God’s love. Moreover, the entire authority of Holy Scripture resists my preferring that former life to this way of life; reason opposes it; our very conscience protests. Thus I judge it utterly mad to doubt which is better: the one whose conduct agrees more with the authority of Scripture. But since there is no slight conflict in these matters, I must consider in what respect doubt is less dangerous: concerning the truth of Scripture, concerning the most evident reason, or rather concerning the inference from my own experience.”—“But against Scripture,” I said, “no [Col. 0564D] Catholic may stand; against evident reason, no peaceable person. Yet in one’s estimation of oneself, to whom does deception not readily creep in? Experience is deceptive; and, as it is written, ‘Not every spirit is to be believed,’ and ‘at times Satan transforms himself into an angel of light’ (2 Cor. 11).”—“Nevertheless,” he says, “although perhaps I loved God more then, yet now I obey his will more, strive more to fulfill his commandments, and afflict myself more for his name. Hence my mind is safer, my conscience more cheerful, and my soul, conscious of so many labors, more ready even to undergo death in hope of rewards.”—“You assert two things,” I said, “that are greatly opposed to each other: namely, that you loved God more and obeyed his will less. The saying of the Savior himself overturns [Col. 0565A] this opinion of yours: ‘If anyone loves me, he will keep my commandments’ (John 14). And again: ‘He who has my commandments and keeps them, he is the one who loves me’ (ibid.). And again: ‘He who does not love me does not keep my words’ (ibid.). Hence that disciple whom Jesus loved, whose resting-place for his head was that sacred breast: ‘This is the love of God: that we keep his commandments’ (1 John 5). Therefore, as a certain holy man says: ‘Whoever violates God’s commandments in wicked speech, deed, or even thought vainly believes that he loves God.’ Hence also blessed Gregory: ‘The love of God is never idle: if it exists, it does great things; if it disdains to act, it is not love. Therefore the proof of love is the performance [Col. 0565B] of a work’ (Homily 30).”

“What then?” he says. “Must that most sweet feeling be thought empty, and those tears judged deceptive?”—“Not at all,” I said. “Indeed, they bear very great fruit, if only you understand it. Know first, then, that the love of God is by no means to be assessed according to that momentary and, so to speak, hourly feeling. This is clear from contrary examples. For when, in tragedies or empty poems, someone is represented as injured or oppressed, whose lovable beauty, marvelous courage, and pleasing disposition are praised: if someone, while hearing these things sung or seeing them recited, is moved by some feeling even to tears, [Col. 0565C] is it not utterly absurd to infer from this most empty pity the character of his love, and to assert that he loves that fabulous person—whoever he may be—because of whose rescue, even if all these things were truly taking place before his eyes, he would not allow even a small portion of his property to be spent? It is a similar folly—indeed, a far greater madness—if someone who is self-indulgent or lukewarm, stirred by some inward feelings through God’s hidden dispensation, pronounces upon his love, so that he is believed from this to love God more than one who has subjected himself so completely to divine service that he detests with every horror whatever he knows to be contrary to God’s will, and embraces with all fervor whatever labor is imposed upon him for God’s name.”

[Col. 0565D] At these words he was suffused with a certain shame; lowering his head and fixing his eyes on the ground, he said: “Most true, most true. For I remember that even in fables commonly invented about some Arthur or other, I have sometimes been moved to the shedding of tears. Thus I am not a little ashamed of my own emptiness: if I can perhaps wring from myself some tear at things that are piously read, sung, or publicly spoken concerning the Lord, I immediately congratulate myself so greatly on my holiness, as though some great and extraordinary miracle had happened to me. And indeed it is the judgment of a most empty mind to be puffed up with vain glory over such feelings, even if they happen in connection with piety—feelings by which it used to be stirred in fables and lies. But since you said shortly before that there is no small [Col. 0566A] fruit in these feelings, I ask you to continue what you had begun.”—“Most gladly,” I said. “For knowledge of the truth is not to be denied you, a truth for which, as you yourself judge, no indulgence is to be shown even to yourself. For many people, if they happen to hear something argued against sloth, devise certain sophistical little arguments by which to resist the truth, even while conscience protests; and, turning their heart toward words of wickedness, they love excuses for sins. It is certainly better to confess to the Lord and say, ‘Have mercy on me, for I am weak’ (Ps. 6), than to say, ‘I am rich and wealthy and need nothing,’ while one is wretched, pitiable, blind, poor, and naked (Rev. 3).” But let us come to the matter at hand.

## CHAPTER XVIII. In what the love of God ought to be believed to consist.

[Col. 0566B]

“Therefore, as we have said, God’s love is not to be assessed according to these momentary feelings—which no spiritual person is ignorant are by no means subject to our will—but rather according to the enduring quality of the will itself. For to join one’s own will to God’s will, so that whatever the divine will prescribes the human will consents to it, and so that there is no other reason why one wills this or that except because one knows that God wills it: this, certainly, is to love God. For the will itself is nothing other than love; nor can good and bad wills be called anything other than good or bad loves. Indeed, the very [Col. 0566C] will of God is his love, which is nothing other than his Holy Spirit, through whom love is poured out in our hearts. This outpouring of love is the union of the divine and human wills. It occurs when the Holy Spirit—who is surely God’s will and love, and is God—enters and pours himself into the human will; raising it from lower things to higher, he transforms it wholly into his own likeness and quality, so that, adhering to him by the indissoluble glue of unity, it becomes one spirit with him. The Apostle expresses this more plainly: ‘He who is joined to the Lord becomes one spirit’ (1 Cor. 6). This will, to be sure, must be judged according to two things: endurance and action—namely, whether it patiently bears what God has brought upon it or permitted to be brought upon it, [Col. 0566D] and fervently fulfills what he has commanded.
