Otherwise, as blessed Gregory says (Homily 20), let no one believe whatever the mind answers itself concerning God’s love apart from works. For this is the judgment of him who does not lie: ‘He who has my commandments and keeps them, he is the one who loves me’ (John 14). Therefore, however God’s judgments—which are a great deep—may distribute these unfamiliar feelings and inward visitations; for whatever causes they may sometimes, so to speak, suddenly be poured into people who neither seek nor knock, and withheld from others who labor with every effort to acquire them: whoever’s will agrees with God’s will, patiently bears what God has brought upon him, and fervently performs what he has commanded, must without any hesitation be said to love God. [Col. 0567A] Otherwise, if our love is to be measured by these feelings, so that we are said to love God or any human being only when we experience such a feeling, we must be said to love not continuously but only at exceedingly rare intervals.

“It should also be said that, if a righteous person should at some time will, for example, someone’s salvation, while God does not will it, nevertheless that person’s will does not disagree with God’s will, since God’s will itself works in him that he wills this; for God wills all people to be saved (1 Tim. 2), because he causes this to be desired by his own people. Furthermore, this love has its beginning, its progress, and its perfection. To discuss all these matters more fully perhaps belongs neither to the present occasion [Col. 0567B] nor to our capacity. Accordingly, to feel those affections is not, as you suppose, to love God; it is rather to perceive, by a sweet attraction, a drop of that sweetness offered—indeed poured—into the mind, as though present to the inner palate. For it is one thing for a person hungry for honeyed sweetness to labor with all his strength to acquire it; another, if it should be poured upon the lips of someone who neither seeks nor loves it, so that he cannot escape the sensation of its sweetness. The former does not taste it, yet loves it; the latter does not love it, yet tastes it. Thus, to speak more simply so that you may understand more easily: one who strives as much as he can to possess God—namely, by obeying his commandments and living soberly, [Col. 0567C] justly, and piously according to apostolic and evangelical precepts—must nevertheless be said to love God, even if he tastes none of this sweetness. He himself testifies to this when he says: ‘He who keeps my commandments is the one who loves me’ (John 14). But one who experiences this feeling every day and nonetheless sets his own desires before the divine will must be believed not to love God, but only to be unable not to sense the spiritual taste introduced into his mind by divine dispensation.”

## CHAPTER XIX. The fruit of various forms of compunction is explained to the inquiring novice.

“This experience of sweetness is a great stimulus to good works for those who are negligent; a necessary consolation for those who toil in good works; and a sweet and secure refreshment for those standing at the summit of perfection. Therefore that wonderfully merciful One works our salvation in marvelous and ineffable ways: he himself is wisdom, enlightening; he himself is justice, terrifying; he himself is the sweetness of delight, drawing us. It is as if you wished to kindle in someone ignorant of honey a desire for it, but saw him delighted by other flavors, though less wholesome; and neither by speech nor by any praise of honey could you inflame him with a desire for it. Taking a small drop of that liquid, you would instill it into his throat. Having tasted it, he would burn so with desire for it that he would not shrink from undertaking even immense labors to acquire it. Yet whenever you saw him, exhausted by the enormity of the labor, growing lukewarm in the fervor he had begun, you would soothe him with a similar drop of sweetness. [Col. 0568A] Thus the clemency of our most merciful Savior, by a taste of inward sweetness, draws to salvation those immersed in carnal enticements whom neither the light of reason nor the fear of the future judgment can restrain from the prevailing sweetness of evil flattery; until, gradually attracted by their own pleasure, in accordance with the saying:

> Each is drawn by his own delight.  
> (Virgil, *Eclogues* 2.65.)

he places upon them the yoke of his service. But because one approaching the service of God hears Scripture saying, ‘Stand firm and prepare your soul for temptation’ (Ecclus. 2), it is necessary that, whenever the labor of temptation overwhelms him, some spiritual savor should flow in upon one already wavering and almost despairing. Refreshed by its sprinkling, he may undertake the struggle against vices with a fiercer ardor [Col. 0568B] of mind, endure it courageously, and more easily overcome or avoid it.

“Examine yourself more carefully. After that experience of sweetest feeling, did you not return to frivolous and empty things, and then, when you returned again to yourself, become ashamed and inflamed, as it were, with a salutary hatred against yourself? From this you began to contemplate undertaking a stricter life and placing such necessity upon yourself that, even if your will consented to such things, you would nonetheless have no power to return to them.”—“Entirely so,” he says.—“You see, then,” I said, “that your fervent conversion and this exceedingly strict manner of life are, as it were, the fruit of those tears. For this purpose they were given; this they gradually accomplished—or rather, through them God accomplished it. What wonder, then, [Col. 0568C] if they ceased when their task, so to speak, had been completed? You must now undertake labors for Christ, exercise the virtue of patience, chastise the insolence of the flesh by frequent vigils and fasts, bear temptations, and withdraw your mind from every earthly concern. Above all, your own will must be mortified by the virtue of obedience. But whenever your spirit is exhausted beyond measure in these things, you must hasten with the devout concern of prayer to the maternal breasts of Jesus; drawing from their abundance the milk of wondrous consolation, you may say with the Apostle: ‘Blessed be God, who comforts us in all tribulation’ (2 Cor. 1); and: ‘As the sufferings of Christ abound in us, so through Christ our consolation also abounds’ (ibid.). Thus that pious feeling which had first awakened [Col. 0568D] one who was sluggish lest he perish will comfort one who labors lest he fail, until, after countless victories, like a soldier now discharged from service, with the temptations by which you are now wearied as a novice wholly put to sleep, you rest in the sweetness of virtues. Admitted by the grace of divine mercy also to that most exalted kind of consolation which is known to be, as it were, the reward of the righteous, you will say with the Prophet: ‘How great is the abundance of your sweetness, O Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you!’” (Ps. 30).

Then he, with tears rising, said: “What you say pleases me—indeed, pleases me greatly—because I infer not only by reason’s instruction that these things are so, but see them in myself more clearly than light. For I have experienced that first kind of visitation exactly as you state; and, through your instruction, I perceive that the second [Col. 0569A] is now beginning to take place in me. But I trust that I shall one day attain that sublime and ineffable kind.”

## CHAPTER XX. The novice is shown to have loved God less precisely by that from which he proved to himself that he had loved him more; and it is shown to whom the shedding of tears is beneficial.

“See then,” I said, “how the matter has turned out contrary to your opinion.”—“How?” he says.—“Lest perhaps,” I said, “you be convicted of having loved God less by the very thing from which you believed that you loved him more.”—“To some extent,” he says, “this reasoning is dawning upon me also; nevertheless I should like to understand it more fully through your argument.”—“Is it not true,” I said, “that the more negligent or weaker in mind anyone is, the more imperfect he is shown to be in the love of God?”—“It cannot [Col. 0569B] be denied,” he says.—“But, as you say that you see yourself more clearly, that first feeling reproved you while you were straying; this second sustains you while you are weak.”—“Entirely so,” he says.—“They therefore prove,” I said, “that you loved more imperfectly.”

Then he sighed and said: “Oh, how miserably deceived they are, how they betray their own salvation, who, entangled in innumerable and damnable vices, if they experience even a little of this feeling of which you speak, not only promise themselves pardon for the past, but in some way return to the same things more securely. Such people make no progress through spiritual encouragement; but, judging themselves holier on this account, they roll about more shamelessly in their filth or negligence. Perhaps the Apostle speaks of such people when he says: ‘God gave them a spirit of compunction, eyes that they should not see, and ears that they should not hear’ [Col. 0569C] (Rom. 2). Does not this kind of compunction blind the eyes and stop the ears—of those only who suppose that the monstrous filth of their vices can be washed away without fruits of repentance by these few tears?”—“The shedding of tears,” I said, “is indeed a sacrifice most pleasing and acceptable to God, a sufficient whole burnt offering for all sins committed—if it belongs to those who repent and confess, yet do not repeat the things for which they repent; who flee to the merciful heart of Jesus with a spirit of humility and a contrite mind, and strive according to their ability to produce worthy fruits of repentance. Therefore you, and everyone concerned for his salvation, must labor so that this mortification of the flesh, this diligence in vigils and labors, this cheapness of clothing, this austerity of food, this gravity of silence—this, I say, [Col. 0569D] whole inner and outer person, as it were a most acceptable burnt offering—may be made rich with the fatness, so to speak, of tears and the sweetness of most devout feelings; so that, when the fire of love has been received in the ark of the heart, it may give forth a sweet fragrance, and thus, according to the Prophet, ‘May your burnt offering be fat’ (Ps. 19). But if you cannot have both, it is better to live without tears in apostolic poverty and evangelical purity than, with daily tears, to oppose the divine commandments every day. For even if they raise the dead, cast out demons, and give sight to the blind, nevertheless [Col. 0570A] all who are workers of iniquity will hear from the Lord: ‘Depart from me’ (Matt. 7:3).”

## CHAPTER XXI. From the foregoing insertions one may observe what love and what covetousness accomplish in one who is making progress.

Thus far we have perhaps inserted these matters not without usefulness. If all of them are considered attentively, carefully, and finally humbly, it will, I think, be very easy to see how any convert is raised upward by a fresh infusion of love, by eager effort, and by certain very slight movements of the mind; yet, with covetousness pressing downward and always driving toward the depths by its natural weight everything to which it clings, he labors somewhat even in that very effort. The more deeply the pernicious shrub [Col. 0570B] has fixed its roots in the recesses of the soul, the greater the difficulty of uprooting them and therefore the less ease in ascent. But just as a lazy, idle man unskilled in farming slowly clears and cleans his field even when it is only partly overgrown with thistles and thorns, while one who is diligent, attentive, and practiced in that craft more quickly uproots a dense growth of brambles even if it has occupied the whole surface of the field, making it rich and fruitful from barren and unproductive: so surely one who renounces the world, if he is slow, lukewarm, and insufficiently attentive to his purification, will advance more slowly to serenity of conscience and freedom of love, even though he was less polluted in the world. But [Col. 0570C] if he is fervent in spirit, diligent and attentive, grounded in the virtue of discernment, and, taking up the tools of spiritual exercises, powerfully uproots the offspring of vices from the field of his heart, he will more quickly breathe the air of a purer conscience; and, having shaken off the yoke of covetousness and laid down the burden of passions, he will find that the Lord’s yoke is sweet and his burden light.

## CHAPTER XXII. How great is the delight in contempt and victory over pleasures.

And by experience he will prove that it is not merely without labor but indeed supremely delightful to be filled with the sweetness of chastity, although it is burdensome to restrain by the bridle of temperance the natural impulses and impure desires that arise from the concupiscence [Col. 0570D] of the flesh. Likewise, after the desire of gluttony has been overcome, it is not only delightful but also glorious to see oneself not as the slave of one’s belly but as its master, dancing in that wondrous exultation:

> But I have learned to be content in whatever circumstances I am. I know how to be brought low, and I know also how to abound. Everywhere and in all things I have been instructed both to hunger and to be filled, both to abound and to suffer need.  
> (Phil. 4)

And if the love of the flesh has been perfectly put to sleep, or at least absorbed by the fire of divine love, there will be no labor in outward things; for the mind cannot be disturbed by its affliction if it cannot be dissolved by its love. Although some people disgracefully abuse the allurements of odors, those of whom we are now speaking suffer little or nothing either in desiring or losing them; therefore I refrain from saying more on this point. But the pleasure of eyes and ears brings no little labor upon very many—a labor [Col. 0571A] that is by no means rightly ascribed to the Savior’s yoke, since perverse habit rather produces it entirely. Because they feel it burdensome to cut off this habit, they prefer to complain of the harshness of the Lord’s yoke, whose gentleness they have not experienced. Yet, since that yoke consists in contempt for pleasures, it certainly grants no less freedom to those who despise them than those vain, frivolous, and harmful pleasures produce sweetness.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the vain pleasure of the ears.

But since we have plainly judged the wicked to be excluded from this consideration, let our discussion now concern those who cover up the business of pleasure under the appearance of religion, who appropriate to the use of their vanity things which the ancient Fathers beneficially practiced as types of things to come. Therefore, I ask: now that types and figures have ceased, why are there so many organs and cymbals in the Church? What purpose, I ask, does that dreadful blast of bellows serve, expressing rather the crash of thunder than the sweetness of a voice? What is the point of that tightening and breaking of the voice? One singer sounds in accompaniment, another against it; another divides and cuts up certain intermediate notes. Now the voice is drawn tight, now broken, now struck, now expanded in a more diffuse sound. Sometimes, shameful to say, it is forced into equine neighing; sometimes, its masculine strength laid aside, it is sharpened into the thinness of a woman’s voice; sometimes it is twisted and retwisted in some artificial winding. [Col. 0571C] At times you may see a man with open mouth, as though suffocated, breathe out rather than sing; and, through a ridiculous interruption of voice, as though threaten silence. Now he imitates the struggles of the dying, or of those undergoing ecstasy. Meanwhile the whole body is agitated with certain theatrical gestures; lips are twisted, shoulders roll and play; and a flexing of fingers answers each individual note. And this ridiculous dissipation is called religion; and where such things are performed more frequently, there God is said to be served more honorably.

Meanwhile the crowd, trembling and astonished, marvels at the sound of the bellows, the clatter of cymbals, and the harmony of pipes; but it watches the lascivious gestures of the singers and the courtesan-like alternations and breaking of their voices [Col. 0571D] not without loud laughter and mirth. You would think that they had assembled not in an oratory but in a theatre, not to pray but to watch. That dreadful majesty in whose presence they stand is not feared; nor is reverence shown to that mystical manger at which they minister, where Christ is mystically wrapped in swaddling clothes, where his most sacred blood is poured forth in the chalice, where heaven is opened, angels stand present, earthly things are joined to heavenly, and human beings are associated with angels. Thus what the holy Fathers instituted in order that the weak might be stirred to feelings of piety is adopted for unlawful pleasure. Sound ought not to be preferred to meaning; rather, sound together with meaning should generally be admitted as an incentive to greater feeling. Therefore sound must be such—so measured, so grave—that it does not [Col. 0572A] carry off the whole mind into delight in itself, but leaves the greater part to the meaning.

For most blessed Augustine says (*Confessions*, Book 10, ch. 33): “The soul is moved to a feeling of piety when it hears divine song; but if the desire of hearing seeks sound more than meaning, it is disapproved.” And elsewhere: “When,” he says, “songs please me more than the words, I confess that I have sinned culpably, and would prefer not to hear singers.” Therefore, when someone, rejecting that ridiculous and damnable vanity, turns himself to the ancient moderation of the Fathers, if the honorable gravity produces an immense distaste in ears itching for the memory of theatrical trifles, and so he scorns and judges all the holiness of the Fathers to be mere rusticity—preferring to the manner of singing which the Holy Spirit established through his most holy instruments, namely Augustine, Ambrose, and especially Gregory, [Col. 0572B] what are called Iberian ditties or the utterly empty trifles of certain schoolmen—if he is tortured and grieved by this, and anxiously longs for the things he had vomited forth: I ask, what is the source of this labor—the yoke of love or the burden of worldly concupiscence?

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the concupiscence of the eyes situated in curiosity, which afflicts converts to a more perfect way.

But now a few things must be said about the concupiscence of the eyes, which the holy Fathers considered should be called curiosity; for they judge it to pertain not only to the outward but also to the inward person. Curiosity of the outward person, then, includes every superfluous beauty beloved by the eyes in varied forms, bright and pleasing colors, diverse works of craftsmanship, clothes, shoes, vessels, paintings, sculptures, and various images which exceed necessary and moderate use. Lovers of the world seek all these for the enticement of their eyes: following outward things that are made, they abandon within themselves him by whom they were made, and destroy what they were made to be. Hence also, in monastic cloisters, cranes and hares, little does and stags, magpies and ravens: not instruments of Antony and Macarius, but feminine amusements. These things in no way provide for monastic poverty, but feed curious eyes. If anyone, therefore, preferring the poverty of Jesus to these enticements of the eyes, confines himself within the bounds of necessity, and in place of that superfluous spaciousness and needless height of buildings seeks the cells of certain poor brothers, then perhaps enters an oratory built of rough stone, where nothing painted, nothing sculpted, nothing precious meets his eye; where there are no marble floors spread with carpets, no walls clothed in purple displaying stories of the nations, battles of kings, or perhaps sequences from Scripture; no astonishing blaze of candles, no glitter of shining metal in various utensils—if, when none of these things meets his gaze, all that he sees begins to seem sordid to him, and he complains that he has been cast out of a kind of paradise and plunged into a prison-like squalor: [Col. 0573A] from where comes this distress of mind, from where all this labor? I ask: if he had learned from the Lord Jesus to be meek and humble in heart, and to contemplate, according to the Apostle, “not the things that are seen but the things that are unseen; for the things seen are temporal, but the things unseen are eternal” (2 Cor. 4); if he had tasted even a little of that inward glory concerning which it is written, “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within” (Ps. 44); and that saying of the Apostle, “Let each person test his own work, and then he will have glory in himself and not in another” (Gal. 6)—and if not in another person, how much less in mute and insensible metal? If, I say, with the inner neck subjected to the yoke of divine love, that sweet Jesus had been sweetly savored there within, would he, I ask, have desired these outward little glories very much?

Now a few things must be said concerning inward curiosity, which chiefly consists in three things: the desire for harmful or empty knowledge; the investigation of another’s life, not in order to imitate it but to envy it if it is good, or to mock it if bad, or merely from curiosity in order to know whether it is bad or good; and finally, a certain inquisitive restlessness to know worldly matters or events. From all these things no small labor arises in captive minds, either when they are indulged without restraint or when they are forbidden to those who gladly indulge them. Thus many people who devote their mind to empty philosophy, who are accustomed to study the *Eclogues* together with the Gospels, read Horace together with the prophets and Cicero together with Paul, to play with verse and weave love poems in ornate meters, or challenge one another with invectives—when they withdraw to a place where all these things are condemned by the strictness of the rule as seedbeds of vanity, beginnings of quarrels, or incentives to lust, they begin to be sad and angry. And, having nowhere to pour out the seeds of the vanity they have conceived, they seem to burst forth into those words of Elihu: [Col. 0573C] “Behold, my belly is like wine without a vent; it bursts new wineskins” (Job 32). It is easy to judge, then, whence this labor arises.

Hence also, when, having devoted the whole day to empty spectacles or attending to rumors, we have in some way gone out from ourselves, on returning to ourselves again we bring in images of vanities. Carrying a heart full of phantoms even to our place of rest, we pass sleepless nights over the most foolish emptiness; with most foolish presumption we portray before our eyes battles of kings and victories of commanders, and arrange all the affairs of kingdoms in idle mental wanderings even during our psalmody or prayers. There is yet another, most pernicious kind of curiosity, by which only those who are conscious of great virtues in themselves are tempted: namely, the testing of one’s own holiness by the performance of miracles. This is to test God. The Mosaic law forbids this kind of curiosity thus: “You shall not test the Lord your God” (Deut. 6). Hence also the Apostle: “Let us not test Christ, as some of them [Col. 0574A] tested him and perished by serpents” (1 Cor. 10). If anyone consents to this most pernicious vice, then, from excessive distress of mind when he does not obtain his wish, he will incur either the snares of despair or the sacrilege of blasphemy.

## CHAPTER XXV. On the pride of life, and first on vanity.

There remains the third branch of the harmful root, which the holy Apostle called the pride of life. Since it has many kinds, two concern the present question. The first instills a love of empty praise; the second introduces a desire to rule. Who could easily say how much labor and distress of mind arise from these? Whenever I am disturbed at being corrected or insulted [Col. 0574B], confused by any slander or criticism, or—what is more lamentable—consumed by the plague of sadness, if I wish to investigate the causes of this labor more closely, I find the root of vanity lurking deep in the recesses of the soul. By it the mind, presuming great things about itself, deludedly depicts itself as such that it ought not merely not to be corrected or rebuked, but moreover to be praised and honored by everyone. Or when, with the mind infected by the poison of this wicked plague, someone has imagined himself holy and admirable in others’ estimation, as soon as he sees others dissent from his vanity, deprived of his glory and joy—which he had placed in the false opinion of others—he must necessarily be gnawed by the stings of sadness. From this most pernicious disease there are also sought the first seats, [Col. 0574C] first greetings, first voice in councils, and first places at an assembly. All these things disturb as much when denied or taken away as they delight when offered or acquired.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the desire to rule.

If the lust for dominion has corrupted the mind, only one who has experienced the tyranny of this most wretched passion and has at last, by God’s help, been freed from its mastery can know how much labor it imposes upon it. For as soon as the deranged mind has conceived this harmful poison, it prostrates itself in degraded servility before the person from whom it hopes to secure the fulfillment of its desire; and, before that person is preferred to others, it itself becomes the most abject servant of all whom it sees may be able either to harm or to help it. [Col. 0574D] Hence, through fear of them, comes suppression of the truth; through desire for their favor, shameful flattery. Thus all freedom of speech is taken from it, so that it is compelled to praise what conscience sees ought to be rebuked, and to rebuke what that same conscience declares ought to be approved.

Finally, if it sees someone who enjoys the familiar favor of the person on whom it relies drawing nearer, the captive mind is immediately pierced by darts of suspicion. Fearing that this other person may attain more quickly the honors which it itself courts, it is afflicted by the anguish of fear. Thus it is scourged with the iron rods of envy, so that neither food benefits it nor sleep brings it rest. Then it turns to detractions and whisperings; whatever it observes in that person that deserves rebuke, it exposes and publishes; whatever it cannot rebuke openly, it stains through malicious interpretation. [Col. 0575A]

But if, with all its hope frustrated, another is advanced, what crosses, what torments then afflict that soul! It is confounded, crushed, disturbed, scattered; unable to endure its inward heat, it is either shaken out of the community by the battering blows of so many passions, or, if human shame binds it to remain within the community, it is wholly turned to the opposite course. Unable to bear the flame of ambition once conceived, it gasps, burns, and is tortured, so that bitterness appears in its silence and indignation in its words; and, like an earthen vessel under the force of a hidden furnace, it cracks wretchedly through the movements of the outward person—speaking with biting harshness, looking fiercely, and replying to every objection with swollen arrogance.

Then it openly resists, contradicts, and reviles those whom it had previously flattered shamefully; secretly it gnaws at them with malicious detraction, while publicly it rebukes them without any reverence or decency. [Col. 0575B] Then, maliciously inquisitive about every word of its elders, it lays snares for each syllable and investigates their acts; surveying, as it were, all their movements and goings with shameless eyes, it recounts everything, judges everyone, and interprets all things according to the rancor of its own malice.

And if, as human frailty is prone to do, an elder should be overtaken by some lapse, then, having found an opportunity to avenge what it considers its own injury, that person raises his eyebrows, wrinkles his brow, and opens his lips in importunate cries. Yet, in order to deceive observers into thinking that he is moved by zeal for God, he sometimes squeezes out a few drops of tears, produces deceitful sighs, and complains loudly that charity is being abandoned; he groans that purity is violated and justice trampled underfoot. [Col. 0575C] If one did not know better, one would say that he was moved by that spirit in which the prophet Jeremiah once burned: “The word of the Lord,” he says, “became like a burning fire in my bones; and I failed, unable to bear it” (Jer. 20).

Thus, proclaiming that the fire of zeal for God consumes his inward being, he falsely claims that he rises for justice, contends for order, and has even incurred hatreds for charity’s sake. Why say more? At length he proves so rebellious and stubborn that extreme necessity compels his expulsion, or at least requires that he be appeased by some concession of liberty to follow his own will.

From this has arisen a remarkable abuse. When the state of religious life was formerly governed in great purity, as the rule of truth requires, those who were humbler, quieter in obedience, readier for reproaches, more fervent in every good work, and especially those who did not seek honors—such persons were not merely promoted, but compelled either to govern others or to undertake certain offices. Now, on the contrary, because the insolence of some is feared, rebellion guarded against, or wickedness dreaded—because they are querulous, irascible, fickle, and slothful, unable to remain on their own feet in the house, now outside, now within—because, in short, they are feared, they are promoted. [Col. 0576B] And what ought to have been for them a cause of abasement and humility becomes fuel for pride.

But let this suffice concerning this threefold desire. In all these matters, whoever carefully considers the countenance of his own soul as though in a mirror will discover, unless I am mistaken, not only what deformity it possesses, but will also recognize in the light of truth the hidden causes of that very deformity. Thus he will accuse not the harshness of the Lord’s yoke—for there is none—but his own perversity.

Therefore, once these roots of the passions, as the causes of all our labor, have been utterly torn out, and the yoke of charity laid upon the shoulders of our mind, we shall learn from the Lord Jesus, because he is meek and humble of heart, and we shall find rest for our souls: keeping Sabbath, not with the Jews in a carnal Sabbath, but eternally and spiritually in the sweetness of charity.

## BOOK THREE

*In which it is shown how charity is to be exercised.*

[Col. 0575]

## CHAPTER I. The law concerning the distinctions among Sabbaths is set forth.

[Col. 0575D]

In the Old Testament we read of certain distinctions among Sabbaths (Lev. 23), and to their consideration we dedicate the beginning of this book. For in the Law you have three periods consecrated to Sabbath rest: namely, the seventh day, the seventh year, and, after seven times seven, the fiftieth year. Thus the first is the Sabbath of days, the second of years, and the third is rightly called the Sabbath of Sabbaths.

For it consists of seven sabbatical years, with one added, so that the number seven may be enclosed in unity—a number which proceeds from unity and is completed in unity. Every good work likewise begins from faith in the one God and is advanced by the sevenfold gift of the Holy Spirit, in order that one may come to him who is truly one, where all that we are may become one with him. And since in unity there is no division, let there be there no dispersal of the mind among diverse things. Rather, let there be one in the One, with the One, through the One, concerning the One: thinking one thing, knowing one thing; and, because always one, always at rest, and thus keeping an everlasting Sabbath.

Meanwhile, you have the Sabbath of days, the Sabbath of years, and, in a certain foretaste, the Sabbath of Sabbaths. Who is so enlightened by the Spirit of God that he may speak of these distinctions among Sabbaths not by borrowing another’s words through the aid of memory, but as one who feels them at work within himself—speaking not only from memory but from inward judgment? Be present, good Jesus; be present to this little poor man of yours, begging not the crumbs of the rich man clothed in purple, but, like a little dog, the crumbs that fall from the table of my masters, your children. [Col. 0577A]

For that great son of yours—and because he is your son, my Lord—the holy Moses, having surely been admitted to your table, feasted on your bread at Solomon’s banquet. And I know, my sweet Lord, for you have said: “It is not good to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs” (Matt. 15). But since the little dogs eat from the crumbs which fall from their masters’ table, break this bread for your little dog, that he may gather the crumbs, though he is not sufficient even for a crust.

## CHAPTER II. That the distinction of these Sabbaths must be sought in threefold love; and what unity there is within the distinction of threefold love.

[Col. 0577B]

Let us therefore hear him who breaks the bread: “You shall love the Lord your God,” he says, “with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind; and your neighbor as yourself. On these two commandments hang all the Law and the Prophets” (Matt. 22).

If, then, we believe—or rather, because we believe the truth—we must seek in these two commandments the distinctions among the Sabbaths, for they too are from the Law. If you examine these two commandments carefully, you find three objects of love: yourself, your neighbor, and God. For where it says, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself,” it is evident that you ought also to love yourself. Yet this is not a command, because it is implanted by nature. For, as the Apostle testifies, “No one has ever hated his own flesh” (Eph. 5). And if not his flesh, then certainly much less his mind, which every person, even unknowingly, loves more than the flesh. For there is no one who would not prefer to live weak in body rather than mad in mind.

Therefore, let a person’s love of self be the first Sabbath; love of neighbor the second; and love of God the Sabbath of Sabbaths. As we said above, the spiritual Sabbath is rest of the soul, peace of heart, tranquility of mind. This Sabbath is sometimes felt in love of oneself; at times it is drawn from the sweetness of brotherly love; but in love of God it is fulfilled without any ambiguity.

Yet care must be taken that a person love himself as he ought, his neighbor as himself, and God above himself; for he loves neither himself nor his neighbor except for God’s sake. But, God willing, we shall later note how this love is to be extended toward one’s neighbor. For the present, we must consider that, although a clear distinction exists in this threefold love, there is nevertheless in it a remarkable interweaving: each love is found in all the others, and all are found in each; none is possessed without all the others, and if one wavers, all depart. [Col. 0577C]

For one does not love oneself if one does not love either one’s neighbor or God; nor does one love one’s neighbor as oneself if one does not love oneself. Moreover, one is shown not to love God if one does not love one’s neighbor. “For one who does not love the brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see?” (1 John 4).

Thus, in a certain sense, love of neighbor precedes love of God, and love of self precedes love of neighbor: it precedes in order, I say, not in dignity. It precedes, however, that perfect love of which it is said: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind” (Matt. 22). For some portion of this love, even if not its fullness, must necessarily precede both love of self and love of neighbor; without it each of those loves is dead, and therefore nonexistent.

It seems to me that love of God is, as it were, the soul of the other loves: in itself it lives most fully, and by its presence imparts vital being to the others, while by its absence it brings death. Thus love of God begins in a person when the person loves himself; it is conceived, as it were, in a more capacious bosom when he loves his neighbor, so that this divine fire, growing somewhat warm, may at last wonderfully absorb the other little sparks into its own fullness, drawing the whole affection of the soul toward that sublime and ineffable good. There neither the person himself nor the neighbor is loved except insofar as each, ceasing to rest in himself, is wholly transferred into God. [Col. 0578B]

Meanwhile, these three loves are conceived from one another, nourished by one another, and kindled by one another; moreover, they are all perfected together. Yet it happens in a wonderful and ineffable manner that, although all three loves are possessed together—for it cannot be otherwise—they are not always felt equally. At one time that rest and delight are felt in the purity of one’s own conscience; at another they are received from the sweetness of brotherly love; and at another they are more fully attained in the contemplation of God.

For just as a king who possesses various storehouses of spices enters now this one, now that one, and is now suffused with the scent of this spice, now of that; so the mind, retaining within the bounds of its conscience certain chambers filled with spiritual riches, walks now through this, now through that, and finds the substance of its delight differently supplied according to the variety of its riches. [Col. 0578C]

## CHAPTER III. How the spiritual Sabbath is experienced in love of oneself.

When a person withdraws from this outward tumult into the inner chamber of his mind, and, having shut the door against the crowds of clamoring vanities, surveys his inward treasures, [Col. 0578D] and finds nothing disturbed, nothing disordered, nothing that bites the conscience, nothing that barks against him; but all things pleasant, all harmonious, all peaceful, all tranquil; and when, like a most well-ordered household, the entire throng of thoughts, words, and works smiles upon the soul itself as the master of the house—then a wonderful security suddenly arises. From security comes a wonderful delight; and from delight a kind of jubilation, breaking out all the more devoutly into God’s praises because it sees more clearly that whatever good it recognizes in itself is his gift.

This is the pleasant solemnity of the seventh day, which must be preceded by six days—that is, by the completion of works—so that we may first toil in good works and only then rest in the tranquility of conscience. For purity of conscience is born from good works, and love of oneself is judged according to that purity. Just as one who practices or loves wickedness does not love but hates his own soul, so certainly one who loves and practices righteousness does not hate but loves his own soul.

This is the pleasant solemnity of that first Sabbath, in which the servile works of the world are not performed, in which no fire of shameful desire is kindled and no burdens of passions are carried. [Col. 0579A]

## CHAPTER IV. What Sabbath is derived from brotherly love, and how the six years preceding the seventh are fitted to charity.

[Col. 0579B]

But if, from that more secret chamber in which he celebrated this first Sabbath, a person passes to that lodging-place of his heart where he is accustomed to rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep, be weak with the weak, and burn with those who are scandalized; and if there he feels his soul united with the souls of all his brothers by the glue of charity—stirred by no stings of envy, inflamed by no heats of indignation, worn down by no darts of suspicion, consumed by no bites of devouring grief—and so draws them all into a most tranquil bosom of his mind, where he embraces and cherishes all with a sweet affection and makes with them one heart and one soul, then, at the sweetest taste of this sweetness, every tumult of desires falls silent and the noise of vices grows still. There is then within an entire freedom from all harmful things, and a grateful, pleasant rest in the sweetness of brotherly love. [Col. 0579C]

That brotherly charity permits no vice whatsoever to remain in the rest of this Sabbath is testified by the Apostle Paul, the continual celebrant of this very Sabbath. For he says: “You shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal; you shall not bear false witness; and if there is any other commandment, it is summed up in this word: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself’” (Rom. 13).

Suffused with the rest and sweetness of this Sabbath, the prophet David burst forth in the tone of a rejoicing festival, saying: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity” (Ps. 132). Truly good; truly pleasant. Good indeed, because nothing is more beneficial; pleasant, because nothing is sweeter.

And just as only one day is devoted to that first Sabbath, because it is singular, consisting in the tranquility of each person’s own conscience, so a whole year is rightly consecrated to this one. For as a year is made from many days, so one heart and one soul are forged by the fire of charity from many souls. If you wish to draw some mystical meaning from those six years which precede this spiritual Sabbath, know that there are six classes of people in whose love the mind must be exercised. Just as a year contains many days, so in each of these classes many people are joined to us by the bond of love. [Col. 0579D]

First, our love proceeds by natural order to those of our own blood. Since the possession of this love is implanted in nature itself, not to possess it is exceedingly inhuman. Hence the Apostle says: “If anyone does not provide for his own, and especially for members of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever” (1 Tim. 5).

Nor should anyone think this apostolic saying contrary to the Lord’s words: “Whoever comes to me and does not hate father and mother, and even his own soul, cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14). But we shall consider these matters later.

Therefore, because there are some who are more savage than beasts and do not care even for their own household, one who loves his own people as he ought has already advanced somewhat toward this spiritual Sabbath. Since this love proceeds from nature itself, it is established in the first place among the commandments that concern love of neighbor, as God declares: “Honor your father and mother” (Exod. 20). [Col. 0580B]

From there our love proceeds to those joined to us by the covenant of spiritual friendship or by mutual duties of service, and in some sense expands into a wider bosom. Yet this love does not surpass the righteousness of the Pharisees, to whom it was said: “You shall love your friend and hate your enemy” (Matt. 5).

Certainly, though each of these loves earns little reward when observed—for natural law impels us to the first, and bestowed grace urges us to the second—yet neglecting them brings an increase of condemnation. Concerning them the Lord says in the Gospel: “If you love those who love you, what reward will you have? Do not even the Gentiles do this? And if you greet only your brothers, what more do you do?” (ibid.).

Therefore, that our love may reach toward something greater, let it embrace also those who are subjected with us to the same yoke of religious profession. This love assuredly will not be deprived of reward, because God is the reason why it is shown. In this state the mind, clinging to the garments of Jesus, receives for itself some share of the anointing which descends from the head, flows also upon the beard of the true Aaron, and reaches even to the hem of the garment. Strengthened for a while by the richness of that anointing, it first receives in a more spacious embrace of love all those whom that very anointing reaches, granting them a share in the name of Jesus, so that, as anointed persons from the Anointed One—that is, Christians from Christ—they may be called Christians. [Col. 0580C]

Two classes of people still remain. If they too are bound to our hearts by the bonds of love, nothing at all will prevent us from enjoying the rest of that true Sabbath. For we must grieve over the ignorance of those outside—namely, Gentiles and Jews, heretics and schismatics—have compassion on their weakness, mourn their wickedness, and bestow upon them, with devout affection, the consolation of our prayers, so that they too may be found with us in Christ Jesus our Lord.

From there one must pass to that in which the summit of brotherly charity consists, in which a person becomes a son of God, and in which the likeness of divine goodness is more fully restored. As the Savior says in the Gospel: “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute and slander you, that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5). [Col. 0581A]

What then remains but the seventh year, in which we are not permitted to exact debts and in which the slave is granted freedom? For the person who knows how to look even upon enemies with an unclouded eye is the one who can truthfully say: “Forgive us, as we also forgive” (Matt. 6). “For everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin” (John 8). Each person is bound to this lamentable slavery until, by forgiving and loving, he is forgiven and loved, and becomes from a slave not merely free but also a friend.

Truly it is a time of peace, a time of rest, a time of tranquility, a time of glory and rejoicing. For what trouble, disturbance, sorrow, or anxiety can interrupt the joy of one who advances by fuller grace from that first Sabbath, in which he is nourished by the fruits of his labors, to this state of divine likeness? Embracing every class of humanity with one affection of mind, he is moved by no one’s injury; but, like a most indulgent father toward a son most dear to him who suffers from frenzy, so is he disposed toward his enemies, that the more they injure him, the more deeply, in charity’s affection, he has compassion on those causing him trouble. [Col. 0581B]

Possessed of this virtue, then, he must especially be said to celebrate this Sabbath when, entering his heart, he directs his mind toward the sweetness of brotherly love and, melted toward those dear to him into a most sweet affection, tastes how good and pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity (Ps. 132). [Col. 0581C]

## CHAPTER V. How both these loves are preserved by love of God.

But because, as we said above, each of these loves—by which we either care for our own salvation or are united to our neighbors in pure affection—must be animated by some portion of divine love, it should be known that God’s love moves and advances us toward this twofold love, in accordance with the saying, “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1).

For in this twofold love innocence is acquired, and it is clear that innocence consists in two things. Innocent is the one who harms neither himself nor another. A person harms himself when he corrupts himself by the stain of some vice or shamefulness. [Col. 0581D] Since pleasure and delight of the flesh especially impel a person toward this corruption, anyone easily rejects or avoids it if, clothed in devout affection for the flesh of our Savior, he delights to contemplate with spiritual eyes the Lord of majesty bent down to the narrow confines of a manger, longing for virgin breasts, clasped in a mother’s embraces, and kissed by the blessed lips of the trembling old man, holy Simeon.

One who delights to imagine before the gaze of his mind how gentle he was in appearance, how sweet in speech, how compassionate toward sinners, how condescending toward the weak and miserable—how, in wonderful kindness, he did not shrink from either the touch of a prostitute or a meal with tax collectors (Luke 7), how he took up the case of one adulteress lest she be stoned (Matt. 9), and conversed with another, so that an adulteress might in some fashion become an evangelist (John 8; John 4)—who is there for whom, at this sweet sight, every pleasure of foul flesh does not become loathsome?

From it certain sweet tears readily arise, by which every heat of desires is extinguished; the flesh grows cool, the greed of the throat is moderated, and every tickling of vanities is quieted. [Col. 0582A]

Moreover, nothing so encourages us toward love of enemies—in which the perfection of brotherly charity consists—as grateful consideration of that wondrous patience by which he who was “fairer in form than the children of men” (Ps. 44) offered his lovely face to be spat upon by the wicked; by which he subjected those eyes, at whose nod all things are governed, to the covering of the unrighteous; by which he exposed his sides to scourges; by which he submitted his head, dreadful to principalities and powers, to the harshness of thorns; by which he gave himself over to reproaches and insults; and by which at last he patiently endured the cross, nails, lance, gall, and vinegar—gentle, meek, tranquil in all things.

Finally, “he was led as a sheep to slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer was silent and did not open his mouth” (Isa. 53). Consider, O human pride, O proud impatience, what he endured, who endured it, and how he endured it! I ask that these things be pondered, not written. Who, at this wondrous sight, does not immediately have his anger cool? Who, hearing that wondrous voice, full of sweetness, full of charity, full of unchanging tranquility—“Father, forgive them” (Luke 23)—does not immediately embrace his enemies with his whole affection? [Col. 0582B]

“Father,” he says, “forgive them.” What gentleness, what charity could be added to this prayer? Yet he added something: it was too little merely to pray; he wished also to excuse them. “Father,” he says, “forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.” They are indeed great sinners, but they have little understanding; therefore, Father, forgive them. They crucify him, yet they do not know whom they crucify; for “if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2). Therefore, Father, forgive them. They think him a transgressor of the Law; they think him one who presumptuously claims divinity; they think him a deceiver of the people. “I hid my face from them”; they did not recognize my majesty. Therefore, Father, forgive them, because they do not know what they are doing.

Therefore, that a person may love himself, let him not corrupt himself through any delight of the flesh. And that he may not yield to fleshly desire, let him extend all his affection toward the sweetness of the Lord’s flesh. Moreover, that he may rest more perfectly and sweetly in the delight of brotherly charity, let him embrace even his enemies in the arms of true love. But lest this divine fire grow cold amid injuries, let him always behold with the eyes of his mind the tranquil patience of his beloved Lord and Savior. [Col. 0582D]

## CHAPTER VI. How perfect Sabbath is found in love of God, and how the fiftieth year is compared to this love.

But when the mind has been purified by this twofold love, it longs all the more devoutly, because more securely, for the blessed embraces of the Godhead itself. Kindled by excessive desire, it passes beyond the veil of flesh; entering that sanctuary where Christ Jesus becomes a spirit before its face, it is wholly absorbed by that ineffable light and unfamiliar sweetness. Having become silent from all bodily, sensible, and mutable things, it fixes its penetrating gaze upon that which is, and thus always is, and is itself: upon that One. It is at leisure and sees that the Lord himself is God; and in the sweet embraces of that charity, it undoubtedly keeps the Sabbath of Sabbaths. [Col. 0583A]

This is the jubilee year, in which a person returns to his own possession—namely, his Creator himself—so that he may be possessed and possess, be had and have, be held and hold. This is the possession that had been alienated for the cheap price of sin, when human love flowed away from him by whom it was made and clung to the thing that was made.

The number fifty is rightly dedicated to this Sabbath, in which servile fear is cast out, not only the desire of the flesh but even its memory is put to sleep, and the Spirit is received. “Before,” he says—that is, before Pentecost—“the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus was not yet glorified” (John 7). Not that he had not been given at all, but not in such fullness or perfection. He is certainly given in the first Sabbath and also in the second, but in the Sabbath of Sabbaths his fullness is poured forth.

For in that twofold Sabbath Jesus is seen as small, not great; humble, not exalted; suffering injury, not glorified. Therefore the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus was not yet glorified. But because charity is poured into our hearts only through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us (Rom. 5), the number seven is observed there, while the growth of charity is recognized through multiplication of that same sevenfold number. For the seventh day is, as it were, the beginning of charity; the seventh year, its advance; and the fiftieth year, which follows seven times seven, its fullness. [Col. 0583C]

In each there is rest; in each, freedom from occupation; in each, a certain spiritual Sabbath-keeping. In the first, rest lies in purity of conscience; then, in the sweetest union of many minds; finally, in contemplation of God himself. In the first Sabbath one is free from sin; in the second, from desire; in the third, from every kind of discord whatsoever. In the first the mind tastes how sweet Jesus is in his humanity; in the second it sees how perfect he is in charity; in the third, how sublime he is in deity. In the first it gathers itself into itself; in the second it extends itself beyond itself; in the third it is carried above itself. [Col. 0583D]

## CHAPTER VII. What love, charity, and desire are.

The place and occasion require us to pursue somewhat more fully what we deferred above: namely, how charity ought to be exercised. To make this clearer, I see that we must explain more precisely what charity is. It is indeed evident that charity is love, although it is no less evident that not every love is charity. Therefore, a more subtle inquiry is necessary, so that it may first become clear to the observer what love is, and, once the genus is known, the species may not remain hidden from the inquirer.

Ordinary usage shows that “love” is said in two ways. Love is called a certain power or nature of the rational soul, by which the capacity either to love something or not to love is naturally present in it. Love is also called a certain act of the rational soul itself, exercising that power when it uses it either in matters where it ought or matters where it ought not; this act is usually called love with an addition, for example, love of wisdom or love of money. Such love must certainly be either good or bad.

But that power or nature of the soul by which this love, whether good or bad, is exercised is a good thing belonging to the soul, and it can never fail to be good in either good or evil. [Col. 0584B] For it belongs to the nature of the substance itself, which is from the highest Good, who made each thing good, and all things very good. Yet a human being, endowed with free choice, uses this, as he does the other goods of his nature, either well, with the help of grace, or badly, when abandoned by justice.

Therefore, since, as someone has said, neither good nor bad character is made except by good or bad loves: good use of the aforementioned good makes a person good, because it produces good love; but misuse, because it produces bad love, makes a person bad. Why then should we hesitate to call the right use of love itself charity, and its misuse desire (*cupiditas*)?

## CHAPTER VIII. How the right or perverse use of love consists in choice, movement, and fruition.

[Col. 0584C]

Let us now distinguish somewhat more subtly between its right and perverse use. Its use, it seems to me, consists in three things: choice, movement, and fruition. Choice belongs to reason; movement lies in desire and action; fruition lies in the end.

For just as a rational creature is created capable of blessedness, so it is always desirous of blessedness itself; but it is by no means sufficient to attain blessedness by itself. Instructed accordingly by its own unhappiness that it is not sufficient for blessedness, it sees that, in order to obtain the blessedness it desires, it must enjoy some thing other than itself. Therefore, according to the measure of his faith and understanding, or according to the deception of error, or according to sensory experience, each person first locates blessedness in the enjoyment of some one thing, or indeed of any number of things. [Col. 0584D]

Then, whatever it may be whose enjoyment he imagines can make him blessed, he chooses for his enjoyment without any hesitation. Love makes this choice; for the rational soul makes it through that power or nature which we above called love. Love always has reason as its companion—not because it always loves rationally, but because reason sharply distinguishes what it chooses from what it rejects. It belongs to reason to distinguish Creator from creature, temporal things from eternal, bitter from sweet, harsh from pleasant; but it belongs to love to choose for enjoyment whatever it wills.

Moreover, choice itself is called love and is an act of the soul. But although the love by which it chooses is always good, this choice—also nevertheless called love—must be good or bad; and therefore love may be good or bad. For if the mind, enticed by experience of some pleasure or deceived by any error, chooses for enjoyment things which ought not to be enjoyed, it surely loves unhappily. By “enjoyment” we mean using something with delight and joy.

The hidden movement of love itself immediately follows, or even accompanies, that choice: in some manner it arouses and moves the mind toward desire for the thing which it has judged ought to be chosen. This movement likewise is an act of the mind; it is from love and is called love. If it is directed toward what it ought, and as it ought, it is good love; but if toward what it ought not, or otherwise than it ought, it is bad love. [Col. 0585B]

But if a person desires the thing he has chosen for enjoyment and, through appropriate actions, attains it as he wishes, he then rests in its use with joy and delight. We call this use, to name it in a single word, fruition. Therefore charity or desire seems to consist in these three: in the mind’s choice, movement, and fruition. Choice is the beginning of good or bad love; movement is love’s course; fruition is love’s end.

If, then, the mind chooses for enjoyment what it ought, moves toward it as it ought, and enjoys it as is fitting, such a wholesome choice and useful fruition are rightly judged worthy of the name charity. In this choice charity begins; by movement it expands; but in fruition it is perfected. But if the mind chooses foolishly, moves improperly, and makes shameful misuse, it may readily be seen that desire is brought to completion by these, as by steps. These are the two fountains, the origins of goods and evils: for “desire is the root of all evils” (1 Tim. 6), and charity is the root of all goods. [Col. 0585C]

## CHAPTER IX. What we ought to choose for enjoyment.

Since, then, we have distinguished between good and evil love, it remains for us now to show—as he in whose hand are both we and our words may inspire us—what the mind ought to choose for enjoyment, and how it ought to be moved toward that which it has chosen [Col. 0585D]. Thus we shall recognize both what is to be loved and how it ought to be loved. Yet this must be said: we are not said to love everything that we choose for our use, but only that which we choose for enjoyment. For the mind that, plunged into the dung-heap of the flesh, strives to aspire to nothing subtle that surpasses the grossness of sense, chooses for itself, as the intended end of its aim, either deceitful riches, useless honors, bodily pleasures, the favors of the world, some one of these, or all of them together, falsely imagining happiness in the attainment of such things.

Yet not all strive toward the enjoyment of these things by the same path. One chooses commerce, another military service, another the practice of some art; another makes for his intended end by plunder and robbery [Col. 0586A]. Of all these things a person is to be called a lover only of that for the enjoyment of which his whole intention hastens; he uses the rest as certain aids by which he may more easily attain the possession of the thing desired. But so long as the perverse mind does not obtain its wishes, it paints an image of happiness in their enjoyment; or, after attaining its desire, when it finds itself laboring under its usual neediness, or indeed recoiling with a kind of disgust from the things which it has abused, it is inflamed with the appetite for some other thing—not in order to be satisfied, but to be shamefully deceived again by the same folly of vanity. This is the circuit of the wicked, concerning whose miserable neediness enough and more than enough has been discussed in the first part of this work.

But he whose mind is sounder, whose eye is purer, whose life is more refined, investigating the matter with loftier understanding, sees clearly, since it is manifest that no one can suffice for his own blessedness, that what is of lower and more abject nature can cast a human being down through love of itself, not raise him higher; and can entangle him more deeply in miseries than confer the consolation of true happiness. Hence, beginning to measure himself and to assess the privilege of his nature, he sees plainly how worthily, magnificently, and justly the divine law commands humankind: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve” (Deut. 6; Matt. 4). It would by no means have said this if there were any nature higher to which human nature owed that singular service [Col. 0586C], or from which it could expect the reward of blessedness.

Therefore he himself is to be chosen by us above all things, that we may enjoy him; and this is the beginning of love. He himself is to be desired above all things; and this is, as it were, the course and advance of love itself. In the attainment of him, because there will be perfect love of the perfect good, there will also be perfect blessedness. Rightly, therefore, the divine law gave the first and greatest commandment concerning the love of God: “You shall love,” it says, “the Lord your God” (ibid.).

But because, when we have attained that beatifying good, each person will enjoy it according to his capacity, while all together will have greater capacity than any individual: that blessedness itself will undoubtedly be fuller if what any person of lesser capacity cannot possess in himself begins to be possessed by him in another. But another’s good will not be one’s own unless one loves that very good in the other. And this will be equally impossible unless one loves the other himself. Accordingly divine authority most fittingly established the second commandment: “You shall love your neighbor” (Matt. 5). But since our supreme good will be God—in himself, in us, and in another—he is commanded to be loved wholly: “You shall love the Lord your God with your whole heart, with your whole soul, and with all your strength.” And since our neighbor’s good will bring us as much joy as our own, it is rightly said: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.”

It is clear, therefore, that two things are to be chosen by us for enjoyment: God and neighbor [Col. 0587A], though in different ways. For God is to be enjoyed in himself and for his own sake; our neighbor is to be enjoyed in God—or rather, God is to be enjoyed in him. For although the word *to enjoy* (*frui*) is customarily taken in a stricter sense, so that we are said to enjoy no thing but God alone, Paul nevertheless, speaking to a human being, says: “Yes, brother, let me enjoy you in the Lord” (Philem. 20). Therefore, when reason has discerned that these two are to be chosen, as we have said, and the assent of the mind has chosen them, despising all other things in comparison with their contemplation, love of God and neighbor has surely begun; for love itself is turned toward that toward which it ought to be turned.

## CHAPTER X. That our love is moved toward action and desire, and that it is moved toward these two sometimes by feeling, sometimes by reason.

[Col. 0587B]

Let what has been said concerning choice suffice, so that we may now proceed to what must be said concerning the movement of love itself. Its movement is toward two things: inwardly toward desire, or outwardly toward action. It moves toward desire when the mind stretches itself by an inward motion and appetite toward that which it has judged is to be enjoyed. It moves toward action when some hidden force of love itself compels the mind to do something outwardly as well.

Accordingly, I think we must inquire what those things are by which, as by incentives, love itself is stirred and moved toward these two ends, and which in some fashion regulate and prescribe its course. Then we must inquire more subtly what it ought to follow, how far it ought to follow it, what it ought to reject, what to admit, what to diminish [Col. 0587C], and what to increase, so that its movement may be fitting.

There are, it seems to me, two things by which the mind is in some manner moved and stirred toward the two ends mentioned above: feeling (*affectus*) and reason. For our love is sometimes inflamed toward outward action or inward appetite by feeling alone, and sometimes by reason alone. Therefore we shall attempt to discuss each of these as much as seems necessary. This, however, must be said: since reason has taught above that two things, namely God and neighbor, are to be chosen for enjoyment, all else being set aside, we must next consider how our love ought to be moved toward these two.

Let us therefore see which of all the motions by which our love is variously altered ought especially to be followed [Col. 0587D]. But first let us carry through our discussion of the twofold origin of its movement, which we have begun.

## CHAPTER XI. What feeling is, how many kinds of feeling there are, and how spiritual feeling is understood in several senses.

Feeling, then, is a certain spontaneous and sweet inclination of the mind itself toward someone. Feeling is either spiritual, rational, irrational, dutiful, natural, or carnal.

Spiritual feeling can be understood in two ways. The mind is stirred by spiritual feeling when, through the hidden and seemingly sudden visitation of the Holy Spirit, the stricken mind is melted into the sweetness of divine love or the pleasantness of brotherly charity [Col. 0588A]. I recall that above I showed, as clearly as I could, the manner and causes of this visitation. Opposed to this feeling is that which is produced by the devil’s injection. By it those are known to have been enticed to every shameful act concerning whom the prophet says: “The spirit of fornication deceived them” (Hos. 4).

For by a double torment the most unclean enemy assails the chastity of the saints: now inflaming the flesh with an intolerable fire, now dissolving the mind by the feeling of ruinous sweetness. Unless I am mistaken, Amnon, David’s son, dissolved by the feeling of harmful sweetness through the injection of that most cunning enemy, burned with illicit embraces of his own sister; and, defiling the house of so great a father with incest, he provoked his brother’s sword against himself [Col. 0588B] (2 Kings [2 Samuel] 13), and sowed beforehand certain occasions and causes of the future parricide by which unhappy Absalom, coveting the kingdom, assailed his father (2 Kings [2 Samuel] 15). Let no one, indeed, shrink from our calling this feeling spiritual because it is produced by spiritual vices; nor let him object to the name, since the reality itself is evident.

## CHAPTER XII. On rational and irrational feeling.

Rational feeling is that which arises from consideration of another’s virtue: namely, when the virtue or holiness of someone, examined by our own eyes, made known by report, or discovered through reading, suffuses our mind with a certain sweetness of delight. This is the feeling that, when we hear of the triumphant passion of the martyrs [Col. 0588C], pierces us with sweetest devotion and portrays before our eyes, in delightful meditation, the memorable deeds of those who went before.

Hence that utterance by which the admirable athlete of Jesus—I mean Paul—commends his courageous deeds commonly draws tears, the signs of conceived rejoicing, from his hearers’ eyes, and suddenly constrains the mind with an infused devotion as it eagerly hastens to embrace him. For who, hearing of those “dangers from rivers, dangers from robbers, dangers from my own people, dangers from the Gentiles” (2 Cor. 11), and, further, that voice of strength, “In all things and everywhere I have learned both to be full and to hunger, to abound and to suffer want; I can do all things in him who strengthens me” (Phil. 4)—who, I say, hearing or reading these things, is not moved by wonderful feeling toward such a man?

This feeling consecrated the first beginnings of most holy love between David and Jonathan, and bound the bond of companionable grace in a covenant of most welcome charity, not even to be dissolved by paternal authority [Col. 0588D]. For when he saw that unchanging steadfastness of heart by which an unarmed boy had overthrown an armored giant, what would have been a seedbed of envy in another became an increase of virtue in that excellent young man; for the friend of virtue was stirred to feeling for the virtuous youth. Scripture says: “The soul of Jonathan was bound to the soul of David, because Jonathan loved him as his own soul” (1 Kings [1 Samuel] 18).

The one who is wonderfully merciful, mercifully transforming this feeling into himself, looked upon the young man who had disclosed his virtues to him and, as the Evangelist says, loved him (Mark 10) [Col. 0589A].

Opposed to this feeling is irrational feeling, which is moved by a certain inclination of the mind toward someone because some vice of his has been discovered. Many have inclined their minds toward certain persons because of the emptiest philosophy or the most foolish audacity in military affairs. And, what is more lamentable, many draw and incline toward themselves the feelings of others because they are prodigal, because they are lustful, because they betray and persecute chastity; because they are admirers and supporters of the basest people; because they are the most frivolous, though most attentive, spectators of empty spectacles.

## CHAPTER XIII. On dutiful feeling.

We call dutiful that feeling which is produced by the benefit of gifts or services [Col. 0589B]. When holy Moses was fleeing Pharaoh’s snares, he gained for himself the memorable feeling of the priest of Midian through an act of service. For when, though a foreigner, he had most steadfastly protected the priest’s virgin daughters from the violence of shepherds, the man, admiring the young man’s kindness, sought not only to make him his friend but also his son-in-law (Exod. 2).

Likewise Barzillai the Gileadite, who had received King David as he fled before Absalom with most dutiful devotion, stirred in him a feeling ready to bestow gifts (2 Kings [2 Samuel] 17). David clung so steadfastly to this man of exceptional constancy that, as he was about to die, he immediately charged his son Solomon among his hereditary instructions to repay such generosity [Col. 0589C] (2 Kings [1 Kings] 2).

## CHAPTER XIV. On natural feeling.

There is, further, a natural feeling in everyone toward his own flesh, in a mother toward her son, and in a person toward a member of his own household and lineage. “No one ever hated his own flesh” (Eph. 5); and: “Can a mother forget her infant, so as not to have compassion on the son of her womb?” (Isa. 49); and: “Whoever does not provide for his own, especially those of his household, has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever” (1 Tim. 5).

The first of these did not escape even the holiest men. Moved by that feeling by which no one hates his own flesh, they are said, anxious concerning burial, to have bound their descendants by solemn charges that, when dead, they should be laid not in a foreign place but in the tombs of their fathers (Gen. 47) [Col. 0589D].

The wisest Solomon, when two women who were prostitutes disputed before him concerning the surviving child—for one mother had overlaid the other child—thought it should be tested. Finally, when a sword was brought and royal majesty had decreed the division of the child, natural feeling betrayed the mother; she yielded to feeling though she had not yielded to wickedness. She who had struggled lest the mother be deprived in vain of her own pledge began to struggle that it might be handed over to another. “I beg you,” she said, “give her the living child, and let it not be killed.” On the other hand, she who had hardened herself without pity toward another’s womb said: “Let it be neither mine nor yours, but divided” (3 Kings [1 Kings] 3).

The third kind likewise outweighed even fratricidal injury in the breast of most holy Joseph. When he branded his fratricidal brothers with the imputed crime of espionage in stern administration, he saw them grievously distressed and tormented by their late, though ample, repentance for betraying their brother; yielding to feeling, as Scripture says, “he turned away for a little while and wept” (Gen. 42) [Col. 0590A].

The savagery of his parricidal son did not erase this feeling from the affectionate heart of the patriarch David. When Absalom sought him to kill him, David sent men to oppose his madness; forgetting the injury and remembering nature, he feigned not to recognize his persecutor in order that he might show himself a father: “Preserve for me,” he said, “the young man Absalom” (1 Kings [2 Samuel] 18).

The Savior himself, transferring this feeling into himself by wonderful compassion, saw the city that was his mother-city according to the flesh, from which he had fathers according to the flesh; moved by natural affection, he mourned its coming destruction with an outpouring of tears. His imitator Paul, pierced, as I think, by natural feeling, wished at one time to be anathema from Christ for his brothers according to the flesh (Rom. 9) [Col. 0590B].

## CHAPTER XV. On the twofold carnal feeling.

Carnal feeling has a twofold origin. Often it is not a person’s virtue or vice, but some outward bearing of the external person, that inclines the mind of one who looks upon him. Indeed, a more graceful form, sweeter speech, a mature gait, and an attractive appearance easily provoke and strike feeling, even in one ignorant of what sort of person the man himself is.

This grace shone so brightly in Moses while he was still a child that, against Pharaoh’s tyrannical command, by which he had destined the male Hebrews for death, he was preserved by his parents for three months, as the Apostle says, “because they saw that the child was beautiful” (Heb. 11; Exod. 2) [Col. 0590C]. When he was exposed to danger, the beauty of his appearance also drew the compassion of Pharaoh’s daughter to him. Adopted by her as a son, he became great before all Pharaoh’s servants as well.

But whoever is pricked by a wrongly flattering sweetness, in whatever form, toward remembrance of harmful pleasure, no one of sound mind will doubt to be moved by carnal feeling. This feeling overtook David unguarded as he walked upon the roof of his house at the sight of Bathsheba (2 Kings [2 Samuel] 11); it dissolved him when overtaken and overwhelmed him when dissolved. And in the contrary direction, the same feeling that enervated him for the embrace of another man’s wife armed him for the cruel death of his own soldier [Col. 0590D]. This feeling swallowed up Solomon’s wisdom and cast him, dissolved by carnal lust, into the abyss of spiritual fornication through the most abominable worship of idols.

## CHAPTER XVI. What should be thought concerning these feelings.

These feelings present themselves to one engaged in reflection. I would call them certain origins or roots of loves, rather than loves themselves. For we do not judge it highly praiseworthy to be aroused or stirred by these feelings if they are good, nor ruinous if they are evil. For many abuse even the first, although it is the best, to their own destruction, as we taught in the preceding book; and by this last, which is judged more fearful than the others, even excellent men are sometimes tickled for the purpose of testing [Col. 0591A].

Accordingly, we judge it useful or harmful not to be moved by these feelings, but to be moved according to these feelings. For when these feelings move the mind, there is either a visitation or a temptation; when the mind is moved according to them, there is full consent of the will itself. Consent is either hidden or manifest: hidden when one is inwardly stirred by desire arising from consent; manifest when desire itself bursts outward into action.

Whether our love ought to be moved according to these feelings, and how far it ought to be moved, we shall investigate, if first we set forth a few things concerning reason, which we have called another cause of its movement.

## CHAPTER XVII. How the mind is moved by reason toward love of God and neighbor.

[Col. 0591B]

A mind which no feeling moves toward the love of God and neighbor is often moved by reason—indeed, all the more sacredly because more securely, and more purely because nothing can be more useful or purer than rational love. Therefore, in order to stir a lukewarm mind to desire its Creator, reason relies upon three arguments: our need, our advantage, and his worthiness.

Reason urges that God is to be loved because this is necessary for us, advantageous, and worthy. It is necessary that we may avoid condemnation; advantageous that we may gain glorification; worthy because he, having first loved us, justly requires repayment for his love [Col. 0591C]. God is to be desired by a human being as his own good, without whom he must always be miserable, and with whom he cannot but be most blessed; God, who has no need of our goods, was willing to be miserable for us.

Therefore, if the mind assents to this reasoning and rouses itself to desire for God—not from feeling, yet from the will—reason immediately carries forward its work, proving that one must zealously persist in fulfilling his commands if one wishes to attain the object of desire. Thus the desire born in the inward depths proceeds to action under the compulsion of reason.
