Since, however, among God’s commandments the greatest is found to be that a person should care for his neighbor as for himself [Col. 0591D], reason presses the mind to be moved to confer benefit upon its neighbor. Every neighbor is either a friend, one who is not a friend, or even an enemy. A friend is so because he benefits or has benefited us; one who is not an enemy, because he neither harms nor has harmed us; an enemy, because he harms or has harmed us. A friend is such by blood or grace; one who is not an enemy, by innocence; an enemy, by injury.

Therefore reason sets before a person three grounds for giving himself to a friend, two for doing so to one who is not an enemy, and one for doing so to an enemy. A benefit is owed to a friend by nature, by duty, and by command: by nature, because he is a human being or even a member of one’s household; by duty, because he is a friend; by command, because he is a neighbor. To one who is not an enemy it is owed by nature, because he is a human being, and by command, because he is a neighbor. To an enemy it is owed only by command [Col. 0592A], because it is the Lord’s command that an enemy be loved. Therefore, if the mind yields to these reasons and prepares itself to confer benefit not only upon a friend but even upon an enemy, it will not lose the merit of charity even if it feels no affection.

## CHAPTER XVIII. A distinction between the twofold love amid which the mind of one making progress wavers.

These two loves, then, must be distinguished: one from feeling, the other from reason. Between these two loves the mind of one making progress and desiring to possess ordered love often fears and wavers, because it thinks it loves less the person who ought to be loved more, or loves more the person who ought to be loved less.

For ordered love is this: that a person neither loves what ought not to be loved, nor fails to love anything that ought to be loved; yet does not love more than ought to be loved; does not love equally things that ought to be loved differently; and does not love differently things that ought to be loved equally [Col. 0592B].

Let us set before our eyes two people. One is gentle, gracious, calm, pleasant, fit for the company of all good people, inviting others into intimacy with himself, sweet in speech, and restrained in manner, though less perfect in certain virtues. The other, though more perfect in the highest virtue, is sadder in face, sterner in expression, and furrowed in brow with austere manners. He does good to all, gives what is asked of him, yet is not pleasant in company and does not invite everyone by his own kindness.

The mind is moved toward loving the former by a certain spontaneous feeling; reason and the ordered rule of charity urge it toward loving the latter [Col. 0592C]. Therefore, when a person feels his mind embracing the former with a certain sweetness and hardening toward the latter, devoid of every pleasantness, he is distressed, grieves, and fears that he has overstepped the rule of charity, thinking that he loves the former more than he ought and the latter not even as much as he ought.

## CHAPTER XIX. Why a kindly and pleasant person, though less perfect, is loved with greater and sweeter feeling than one who is austere and more perfect; this is shown by a twofold comparison, and it is shown how love for each is not dangerous.

[Col. 0592D]

I first wish to explore the hidden places of my own conscience, lest this feeling deceive me if I happen not to know its cause and origin. Since the person toward whom my mind is moved by a certain sweet inclination, although less perfect, is nevertheless not vicious but adorned with many virtues, why should this feeling not be thought to have its beginning in virtue, and therefore be not feared but rather embraced? But if I say that virtue is its origin or cause, why is the mind not directed by an easier, or at least similar, movement toward the other, whom I recognize as more virtuous?

Must this feeling, then, be judged carnal, because it is produced by a certain fittingness of the outward person? But if so, why do I not embrace another, equally adorned with outward manners, with the pleasantness of the same sweetness, since I nevertheless judge him vicious? For it has sometimes happened to me that someone’s outward bearing, so long as virtue was hoped for in him or vice was unknown, greatly inclined my mind toward him; but when his vice was revealed, it swallowed up all that feeling and brought no small horror upon my mind [Col. 0593A].

What then? Perhaps virtue and vice should be judged like food for the soul, useful or harmful; while the austerity or kindness of the outward person should be judged like vessels, rustic or elegant. Useful food is often taken in ugly vessels, while harmful food is not admitted even in precious ones. Yet it happens, indeed very often, that food of somewhat poorer quality is more pleasantly received because of the beauty of the vessel, while food of the greatest value is more foolishly rejected because of the ugliness of the vessel.

Thus it sometimes happens that a vicious person displeases even when his body is most adorned, while virtue greatly pleases even amid a certain harshness and austerity of the external person [Col. 0593B]. Nevertheless, it is plainly possible that one more willingly sees lesser virtue in a kindly and pleasant person, while greater virtue tastes less pleasant in one who is hard and austere.

But the comparison will, I think, be more elegant and also more exact if virtue is regarded as truth and vice as falsehood; excessive severity of manner as harsh and rustic speech; and the agreeable pleasantness of the outward person as polished and eloquent speech. Just as falsehood is not to be accepted in sweet speech, so truth is not to be despised in harsh and rustic speech. In the same way, vice should not please in a person outwardly adorned, nor should virtue displease in one however hard and austere.

Finally, if two persons begin to persuade us of something, one doing so bluntly, unattractively, coldly, the other keenly, elegantly, pleasantly, and forcefully, then, while it remains unknown which relies on truth and which overflows with falsehood, it is no wonder if the hearer delights more in the speech of the one who knows, by the aid of his speech, how to conciliate opponents, raise the indifferent, and make his hearer well-disposed, attentive, and teachable by his opening; or who can indicate, to those who do not know where his argument is tending or what they ought to expect, what it aims to say [Col. 0593C].

But if both are known to advance things equally true and equally great, health is received in the former’s words with a certain bitterness, while in the latter’s are received, more gladly and eagerly, both pleasant healthfulness and healthful pleasantness. For the more welcome pleasant sweetness is in a true assertion, the more readily healthfulness benefits.

But if both advance true things, and the less eloquent man endeavors to assert things more magnificent and profound, those things that are spoken pleasantly, although smaller, enter the ears more pleasantly. Yet no small force is needed to prevent the mind from becoming weary of hearing those precious things because of the ineptness of the speech in which they are uttered, from taking no pleasure in understanding them, and finally from being unwilling to believe them [Col. 0593D].

Likewise, if two people are set before us, one kindly, affable, pleasing to the eye, delightful in speech, pouring himself into the hearts of those who look upon him by a certain pleasantness of the outward person; the other hard, austere, and by excessive gravity seeming to instill fear in those who behold him: while the virtue or vice of both remains hidden, who can blame the inward sense if it receives the former more sweetly, and rejects the latter not by will or reason but by feeling?

But if it has found them equal in their other virtues, or even found the pleasanter one less perfect in some respects, it is neither surprising nor irrational if inward virtue, offered in outward pleasantness, tastes more delightfully—as truth does in beautiful speech—and it receives virtue amid excessive austerity of manners, as truth in harsh and rustic speech, with a certain anxiety or even compulsion of mind [Col. 0594A].

But just as there is one kind of eloquence appropriate to youth and another appropriate to old age, and as what is judged vigor and liveliness in younger age is judged frivolity in more mature age, so indeed in a young person there may be a more cheerful, ready, and prompt kindness toward service, more agile in action; while in an older person there may be a kindness that is honorable, grave, cheerful without all dissipation, free from levity and full of maturity. The former ought not to be accused of levity, nor the latter of austerity.

However, then, the feeling of this lover may vary: if he gives to the person whom his mind embraces affectionately neither himself nor anything else beyond what reason allows, and if he does not omit to give the other anything that reason shows ought to be given, he certainly does not exceed the rule of charity [Col. 0594B]. For since these feelings are by no means placed within our power, since we are sometimes moved by some feelings entirely against our will and cannot experience others even if we wish to, love is by no means from feeling when feeling moves the mind, but when the mind directs that movement in accordance with feeling. The same judgment must be made concerning the movement produced by reason.

## CHAPTER XX. That there are three loves: from feeling, from reason, and from both.

Therefore love is from feeling when the mind assents to feeling; it is from reason when the will joins itself to reason. A third love can also be composed from these two, namely when these three—reason, feeling, and will—come together as one [Col. 0594D]. The first is sweet but dangerous; the second harsh but fruitful; the third perfect by prerogative. Experienced sweetness entices toward the first; manifest reason compels toward the second; in the third it has savor.

This last differs from the first because, although in the first that which ought to be loved is sometimes loved, it is nevertheless loved more for the sweetness of feeling itself. But in the latter, a thing is loved not because it is sweet, but because it is worthy of love; and for that reason it is sweet.

## CHAPTER XXI. A recapitulation of what has been said, and how true love of God is recognized.

Therefore, from all that has been said, let us briefly gather wherein the whole force of love consists [Col. 0595A]. First, if the mind chooses something for enjoyment; then stretches itself toward it by a certain inward desire; finally, does that by which it can attain the object of its desire: this must undoubtedly be called love. The more fervently and earnestly each person does this, the more he loves. If he does it from feeling, he loves more sweetly and consequently acts more easily. But if one does by feeling all that another does by reason alone, the latter loves less sweetly indeed, but will not attain what he desires more slowly.

If, however, the choice itself is perverse, so that one chooses for enjoyment what ought not to be chosen, then the things which follow that choice are plainly perverse as well; and such love will be perverse, to be designated by the name of covetousness rather than charity. But, as we have taught above, whatever else the mind chooses for enjoyment, whether enticed or deceived—apart from God in himself and one’s neighbor in God—it oversteps the bounds of true love [Col. 0595B].

Moreover, the choice itself can be sound while both movements are perverse. Choice and the following movement of desire may be governed by reason, while the other movement, which is in action, corrupts the whole love. This will become clearer through examples.

If someone chooses God for enjoyment, this choice is sound. But if, in the very enjoyment, he desires something carnal, thinking that when he arrives at God he will, as Jewish tales relate, have the opportunity both to overflow with feasts and to lie immersed in pleasures, the integrity of his choice will avail him nothing when it is followed by so great a perversity of desire [Col. 0595C]. And even if he chooses God as the enjoyment of his happiness, and desires in God nothing but God, yet seeks to attain so great a good through improper actions—for example, by Jewish ceremonies, Gentile sacrifices, or some other superstition—he will wholly void the fruit of love.

Let the choice, therefore, be sound, the desire fitting, and the action rational; thus it will not exceed the bounds of charity. It matters, moreover, how affectionate, discerning, and strong one is in this love: affectionate, that one may love sweetly; discerning, that one may love prudently; strong, that one may love perseveringly. Affectionate, so that what one has chosen may have savor in desire; discerning, lest one exceed measure in action; strong, lest some temptation turn one away from it. Feeling is useful against perverse pleasures; discernment against deceptions [Col. 0595D]; strength against persecutions.

If anyone is known to be perfect in these three things, he loves not only felicitously but also sweetly. Yet if he cannot be affectionate, let him at least be discerning and strong; and if he does not advance toward present happiness, he will nevertheless advance no less toward future happiness.

## CHAPTER XXII. What consideration is required in love of one’s neighbor.

Let us consider these same matters in love of neighbor. If, then, we choose our neighbor for fellowship in that enjoyment which is in God, our choice is sound. But if shameful desire or disordered action follows this choice, the whole soundness of the choice is defiled.

In the love of God we do not provide for God himself; for God is ours and has no need of our goods. But in mutual love, because we need one another, we must necessarily provide for one another [Col. 0596A]. Therefore desire itself ought to extend to two things, and action likewise ought to be exercised in two ways. Desire ought to be directed toward this: that, as is fitting, we may mutually enjoy one another in God, and that we may mutually enjoy God in the other.

Since a human being consists both of body and soul, our action ought, insofar as ability provides, to look to both. The more fervent and prudent anyone is in these matters, the more perfect he is in charity; and the more affectionate he is, the sweeter charity itself is shown to be.

But just as, as we said, feeling sometimes moves us toward these things and reason sometimes does, so each endeavors to order, according to its own character, both modes of desire and action [Col. 0596B]. Accordingly careful consideration is needed, that we may see which feelings ought to be followed and how far they ought to be followed.

## CHAPTER XXIII. Which feelings are not to be admitted, and how far the spiritual feeling that is from God ought to be followed.

Thus the spiritual affection that comes from the devil, the irrational affection that is for vice, and the carnal affection that tends toward vice—these three affections are not merely not to be followed; they are not even to be admitted. Rather, so far as possible, they must be torn up by the roots from our hearts. But the spiritual affection that comes from God is not only to be admitted, but must also be stirred up and increased in every way. Our desire follows it most healthfully, so that, the more sweetly its excellence makes itself known to us, the more ardently we desire its desirable presence. [Col. 0596C]

Certainly our action too ought to be stirred by this affection, but ought not to be ordered according to it. It should be stirred, so that the will to act well—indeed, perfectly—may never grow lukewarm; but the action itself ought not to be ordered according to affection, lest it exceed the bounds of bodily capacity. For the body is a kind of instrument through which this action must be exercised; and since it is of clay-like constitution, subject to innumerable sufferings and unable to bear the force of a fervent spirit unless outward activity is tempered by some moderation, it will undoubtedly fail and collapse before the task is completed.

For affection has this characteristic: it often knows no measure, does not gauge human strength, swallows up bodily sufferings, and, rushing blindly upon the beloved, thinks only of what it desires and despises everything outside it. Undertaking what is burdensome, arduous, even impossible, as though it were light and effortless, it does not feel the most troublesome injuries of the outward person because of the delight of inward affection. Therefore, in order that the will may be warmed with continual fervour, and that one may endure patiently—indeed joyfully—the sufferings inflicted from without, this affection is to be borne as far as the impulse of desire itself. But when it advances to voluntary actions, it must be restrained by the moderation of reason, lest it exceed the bounds of bodily capacity.

Some, ignorant of this measure of life and inopportunely following the whole force of their affection, become weaker rather than holier. Thus, when affection grows lukewarm because of immoderate action, the will itself too, more immoderately oppressed, grows lukewarm. Concerning the moderation of action itself, which must be effected according to reason, we shall note in its proper place whatever the Spirit—the inspirer and arranger of good affections, but only the arranger of bad ones—may suggest as useful. For the present, let us continue the distinction of affections which we began. [Col. 0597A]

## CHAPTER XXIV. On rational affection, and how far it too should be followed

Rational affection, then, which arises from contemplating another’s virtue, is evidently more perfect than the other affections by which we are kindled to love of our neighbour. For love of virtue itself is no slight evidence of virtue. Accordingly, it is most useful to assent to this affection: both because emulation of the virtues themselves is more readily aroused by this affection, and because vices become loathsome through careful consideration of virtues.

Nor do I judge our desire, if directed according to this affection, either harmful or dangerous. Nothing hinders our desiring—and indeed much is gained by desiring—the presence of one by whose example we may be corrected, if we are evil; advanced, if we are good; or strengthened by mutual exchange, if we are equally perfect. The temporal presence of saints is indeed to be desired, but still more that eternal presence which will be with Christ in heaven. [Col. 0597B]

Although a similar affection stirs us toward the desire for either presence, we do not attain the two by similar action. For we seek the bodily presence of saints, if they are absent, by travelling across distances of land; but we seek their eternal presence by living holily, justly, and devoutly. If, therefore, the same affection incites us to each action, the latter action, so far as inward exercise is concerned, should follow its impulse without hesitation. For excess is not to be feared in inward holiness. But the outward exercise of virtues, of which it is said, “Do not be excessively righteous” (Eccles. VII), must be tempered by the moderation of reason.

Moreover, although the bodily presence of saints may rightly be desired, it is not always to be sought. Hence in this action reason must be consulted, not affection followed. How welcome was the bodily presence of Paul and Barnabas to the brethren at Antioch! They were instructed by their knowledge, strengthened by their example, and defended by their arguments against those who held differing opinions. Yet, hearing from the Holy Spirit, “Set apart for me Barnabas and Paul for the ministry to which I have called them” (Acts XIII), although affection resisted, they nevertheless laid hands upon them, prayed, and sent them away. [Col. 0597C]

Did not Paul approve Timothy’s affection from the abundance of his tears? Had so great a man yielded to it, Timothy would surely have clung to Paul’s footsteps irrationally. “I give thanks,” he says, “to my God, making remembrance of you, remembering your tears, that I may be filled with joy” (II Tim. I). [Col. 0597D]

## CHAPTER XXV. In what respect official affection must be guarded against, and in what respect admitted

[Col. 0598A]

Next comes official affection, more dangerous than the other affections that are to be admitted. It must indeed be admitted, but most carefully guarded against. For what is more worthy, more consonant with reason, than to return kindness to one who loves us, service to one who renders service, gratitude to one who offers gifts? Yet what must be guarded against more than this: that, softened by services or enticed by gifts, you may either cherish vices or favour a vicious person?

I am not speaking of those who love gifts and pursue recompense, who make justice saleable and favour not the person but the gifts; but of those who, moved by services or gifts, embrace no longer the gifts but the person himself with a certain inward affection. This affection, I say, must be admitted, but also guarded against: admitted, lest one be ungrateful for a service; guarded against, lest it be bestowed not so much on the person as on vice.

Therefore, although great discernment must be exercised in accepting gifts or services, this must be observed: when we are moved by some affection toward the person whose benefits we enjoy or by whose services we are assisted, the worthiness of that person must be examined more carefully. If perhaps that person has such merit, official affection may pass into rational affection, and the one whom we began to love because he was kind to us may begin to be loved because he is adorned with virtues. [Col. 0598B]

It sometimes happens that an excellent man, because of a certain outward austerity, as we said above, does not easily enter the observer’s heart through affection. But if, when an occasion presents itself, we find him generous toward us, the affection that this austerity had in some manner pressed down and buried is itself imperceptibly raised and awakened, so to speak. The virtue which had formerly pleased but not delighted now imparts and pours its sweetness into affection itself—as though into the palate of the heart, although applied to another purpose—and is thus wonderfully relished and enjoyed.

But if the person should be such that there is no virtue in him which can please, affection may be admitted only insofar as his correction can be desired. That simple affection which, though moved and moving by certain causes, nevertheless embraces a person without regard to any other cause, must in every respect be moderated. [Col. 0598C]

The return of services or gifts should likewise be rendered to each according to affection. So too the desire by which their presence is desired, and the action by which that presence is obtained, should follow reason, not affection. [Col. 0598D]

## CHAPTER XXVI. On natural affection; and what it is to love in God and to love for God’s sake

Let us now inquire more carefully what measure should be observed in natural affection. Just as it is impossible not to admit this affection, so it is the highest virtue not to follow it. “No one has ever hated himself”; and yet the Saviour says: “Whoever comes to me and does not hate his own life cannot be my disciple” (Luke XIV). Likewise he says: “Whoever comes to me and does not hate father and mother cannot be my disciple” (ibid.). Conversely, the Apostle says: “Whoever does not provide for his own, and especially for members of his household, has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever” (I Tim. V). [Col. 0599A]

What then? Are teacher and disciple, servant and Lord, Truth itself and the friend of truth to be thought to have held contrary opinions? Far from it. The two loves of which we spoke above must therefore be distinguished: one according to affection, the other according to reason. It is natural for a person to have affection toward himself and his own; but he ought not to have love according to affection, whereas he ought to have it according to reason.

Affection itself is shown when the Apostle says: “No one ever hated his own flesh” (Eph. V). But love according to affection is forbidden by the authority of the Saviour himself, who says: “Whoever comes to me and does not hate father and mother, and even his own life, cannot be my disciple” (Luke XIV). Love according to reason is commanded when the same Apostle says: “Whoever does not provide for his own, especially for members of his household, has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever” (I Tim. V). [Col. 0599B]

Love according to affection is condemned when the same Paul, foretelling future evils, says among other things: “People will be lovers of themselves” (II Tim. III). That he here means love according to affection is shown by what follows: “For people will be lovers of themselves, greedy, arrogant, lovers of pleasures more than lovers of God” (ibid.).

For this affection always suggests what is soft and sweet. It gladly embraces what is pleasant and tender, voluptuous and delicate; but it flees and avoids with every horror what is arduous, harsh, and contrary to the will. Therefore the carrying-out of this affection is perverse love: it strips a human being of humanity and clothes him in a beastly form, in some way covering over and concealing reason, honour, and finally utility itself. This love properly belongs to beasts; it is excused in children, for reason is not yet infused into them, while in the former it is asleep. [Col. 0599C]

Finally, the Saviour himself distinguishes these two loves quite briefly: “Whoever loves his life will lose it, and whoever hates his life in this world will find it for eternal life” (John XII). Therefore, as that holy man says (Augustine, *Tractate 51 on John*): “If you love badly, then you hate; if you hate well, then you love.” For one who loves according to affection surely hates, since “he who loves iniquity hates his own soul” (Ps. X). But one who hates according to affection loves according to reason.

For this reason he added, “in this world,” because “everything that is in the world is either the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, or the pride of life” (I John II). Thus whoever loves his own life according to affection loves it in this world, because he loves it in the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life—all of which affection suggests. [Col. 0599D]

This distinction also resolves what some ask: namely, what is the difference between love that is in God and that which is shown for God’s sake. Affection is not taken up for God’s sake, but arises in the soul itself either carnally or accidentally. Therefore, if all love according to this affection is shown toward one to whom the mind pours itself out with a certain spontaneous and sweet inclination, that person is loved neither in God nor for God’s sake, but rather for his own sake.

But if the one embraced by this affection is at the same time taken up into the love of God, then, although the love itself has the flavour of affection, its expression depends upon the moderation of reason. Such love is not first taken up for God’s sake, but is beneficially exercised in God. On the other hand, if we conduct ourselves as we ought toward one whom affection itself rejects and avoids, out of consideration for the divine command, and give whatever reason dictates according to that person’s need, that person is loved not for his own sake, but solely for God’s sake. [Col. 0600A]

Thus the friend who cannot help being loved should be loved in God; the enemy, who cannot be loved for his own sake, should be loved for God’s sake. The former is loved from affection, the latter from reason. This measure must therefore be observed in natural affection: it is indeed to be possessed and felt, but in all things and through all things moderated by reason.

Thus holy Joseph first showed his natural affection toward his brothers by tears (Gen. XLII). Had that holy man followed it while setting reason aside, his brothers would by no means have been cleansed from the crime of betrayal by salutary sorrow. Likewise, our Saviour, clothed in tender affection toward his own, mourned with wondrous compassion over the city that was about to fall (Luke XIX); nevertheless, by the rigor of justice he punished that city’s crimes with the penalty of utmost calamity. [Col. 0600B]

Would that rulers of the Church disciplined their own affection by this rule! Many of them, embracing those of their own blood far too carnally, not only restrain them by no severity from worldly vanity and pleasure, but even, by damnable presumption, supply from the very price of Christ’s blood the means by which they may satisfy their lusts. Alas! Such is the state of some of our bishops’ houses—and, more shamefully still, of monks in cowls—as though one were entering Sodom and Gomorrah. Certain long-haired, effeminate persons come forth, with buttocks half uncovered and dressed in the fashion of prostitutes—of such persons Scripture says: “They have put boys in a brothel” (Joel III). [Col. 0600C]

And for the lusts of such people your blood is employed, Lord Jesus; your cross is raised, your wounds are laid open, the price of your death is spent. That these men may possess running dogs, flying birds, and foaming horses, your sides are stripped in the poor; your scourges are mocked; your entrails are poured out. You see these things, my Jesus; you see them and remain silent. But will you always remain silent? “Indeed,” you say, “I shall cry out like a woman in labour” (Isa. XLII). But let us return to our subject. [Col. 0600D]

## CHAPTER XXVII. On carnal affection: that it is neither to be rejected altogether nor admitted without reserve

Thus carnal affection, produced by a certain adornment of the outward person, is not to be rejected altogether, nor admitted in such a way as to pour itself out without restraint. For that affection which leads to vices is near to it; and unless this one is more prudently guarded against, the other slips in almost without the sufferer’s awareness.

This affection is therefore healthfully admitted, provided that it is admitted in a manner that is restrained and moderated: namely, so that, if virtue shines in the person, it may be embraced more readily; but if vice does, his correction may be pursued more vigorously. Whatever we have said concerning official affection, we should judge applicable to this affection as well. Yet this affection is wisely rejected by those who are still assailed by carnal vices, since they very rarely experience it without the incitement of vice. [Col. 0601A]

## CHAPTER XXVIII. That not only the origin, but also the course and end, of affection must be examined; and that affection passes into affection, as examples show

Moreover, not only the origin of these affections must be examined, but their course and end must also be carefully considered. For one sometimes arises very subtly and ends in another, or is certainly transformed into another. It will suffice to demonstrate this from two or three cases.

A person is stirred by the reputation of some virgin, holy both in body and spirit, of sincere faith, outstanding discernment, humility grounded in the virtue of complete self-contempt, renowned for remarkable abstinence and highest obedience. In admiration of so many virtues, he reveres her with the strongest affection. We have called this affection rational. [Col. 0601B]

If he begins, then, to enjoy her familiarity, to honour her with service, to be refreshed by conversation, and frequently to send blessings (*eulogia*), letters, or perhaps small gifts, this rational affection almost imperceptibly passes into official affection. The woman whom he began to love because of the merit of her holiness begins to be frequented because of the favour of mutual generosity. Then, when this affection extends itself toward certain caresses, that carnal affection—the most pernicious of all—creeps in, as vice tempts.

I have known this to happen to men most chaste and continent, who detested all impurity with the utmost horror. While they saw certain women, still of tender age, attaining the highest virtues and advancing incredibly, through remarkable gravity of morals and holiness of life, into what may be called a spiritual old age, they honoured and embraced them with a most devout and sweet affection. [Col. 0601C]

But while they too readily granted them access to themselves and rested more sweetly in their sight and, as it were, embrace, a vicious affection subtly crept in and greatly troubled them. Men who would not merely refuse to look upon others conscious of that crime, but would reject them from the bosom of a nauseated mind with utmost horror—these very chaste and grave women, perhaps even serene in virginal beauty, whom even an unchaste person, because all hope was excluded, could look upon only chastely—could scarcely be frequented without some incitement of vice.

Why was this? Certainly because official affection is more readily transformed into carnal affection than an unchaste affection is embraced by a chaste heart, or a person of manifest chastity is desired by an unchaste person. Therefore, when our affection, even though rational or spiritual, extends toward an age or sex that gives cause for suspicion, it is most prudent to restrain it within the very recess of the mind and not allow it to flow out toward vain caresses and soft endearments—unless perhaps it occasionally proceeds with mature moderation precisely so that the virtue loved and praised may be practised more fervently. [Col. 0602A]

## CHAPTER XXIX. That different affections often struggle in the same mind, and which must be preferred to which

It remains to say of these affections that several sometimes fight within one mind and in some way struggle to overcome one another. When this happens, great discernment is necessary, so that one may recognize which is to be preferred to which, and so that the necessary virtue may prevent the higher affection from being expelled by the lower.

Thus Abraham, ordered to sacrifice his own son, did not harden himself against his own flesh so as to be devoid of natural affection. But when the natural affection by which he embraced his son and the spiritual affection by which he embraced God struggled in the holy man’s breast, he preferred the higher to the lower; indeed, for the sake of the higher he disregarded the lower.

Likewise the excellent young man Jonathan did not, to injure his father, reveal to David—bound to him by a sacred covenant—the plan by which his father had destined David for death. Rather, he preferred rational affection to natural affection by the lawful right of the former. Nor is it surprising that love for his friend effaced affection for his father in that most sacred heart; for the sake of that friend he despised with unchanging virtue what was thought to be an injury to himself. [Col. 0602B]

For when David was fleeing from Saul’s presence and that man of unconquered love met him in a more secluded place in order to reveal his father’s plans, they embraced and kissed, poured themselves out in mutual tears, and professed tender affection by tender weeping. Then Jonathan renewed their covenant, saying: “You indeed shall be king, and I shall be second after you” (I Reg. XX).

O man worthy of the highest praise! A man free from envy and empty of greed, who preferred his friend to the kingdom, who willed that what seemed to be his should belong to another. “I,” he says, “shall be second after you.” O heart of the highest humility! He was of royal stock, to whom an inheritance was hoped for by succession; whose hope of attaining the throne had been increased by birth, virtue, the favour of soldiers, popular approval, and even the wondrous fame of his triumph, in which, supported by only one companion, he attacked the armed ranks of an enemy host and won an unexpected victory for his people—yet he placed himself below a servant: “I,” he says, “shall be second after you.” [Col. 0602C]

This man, whose praises are still sung: “Jonathan’s arrow never turned back, and his sword did not return empty” (II Reg. I), as though forgetting himself in order to know his friend, says: “You shall be king, and I shall be second after you.” Who, I ask, would even think such a thing about his own brother from the same womb without monstrous envy? Who would, for a friend’s sake, bring all his hope into despair?

The sons of the patriarch Jacob (Gen. XXXVII), excessively jealous of their father’s favour, by which one brother was cherished more tenderly than the others, brought slavery upon their brother and deepest grief upon their father. That chief priest, together with his sister the prophetess, overtaken, if I am not mistaken, by envy, spoke against his exceedingly gentle brother and barely escaped divine punishment through Moses’ own prayer (Num. XII). The wisest Solomon destroyed his brother, his rival for the kingdom, upon whatever occasion he could obtain (III Reg. II). Jonathan alone, despising himself beneath his friend, and despising father, country, and kingdom, says: “You shall be king, and I shall be second after you.” [Col. 0602D]

Had he said, “I shall be king, and you shall be second after me,” he would have violated neither the law of friendship nor affection for his friend. “Both wept,” Scripture says, “but David more” (I Reg. XX). Doubtless that separation, more bitter than death, was impending: it would deprive those united hearts of one another’s sight; it would end their sweet conversation, their consolation that relieved every danger, and that disclosure of mutual secrets, dearer even than life itself. Therefore both wept.

Observe, I pray, a man of love most rightly ordered. Jonathan owed affection to his friend, but obedience to his father; favour to his friend, but protection to his father’s old age. Had he followed affection and clung to his friend, he would have injured the claims of filial love. But had he withdrawn his favour from his friend at his father’s warning—indeed command—he would have violated the law of the covenant he had made and of their most sacred friendship. Union pleased each from affection; separation pleased them from reason. By weeping, therefore, they paid what they owed to affection; but by separating, though compelled, they yielded to reason. Both wept because both loved. [Col. 0603A]

Why then did David weep more? Jonathan had in some manner foretold his own decline and his friend’s advancement: that he himself would be deprived of the kingdom and David raised to it. Therefore the law of friendship required that Jonathan should weep with compassion over his friend’s injury, while David, lest he seem to grieve at his friend’s success, should restrain his tears somewhat. Jonathan thus preferred rational affection to natural affection, but ordered his action according to reason.

David himself, when his faithful army had won victory over his parricidal son, yielded to natural affection and mourned his son’s death (II Reg. XIX). But rebuked by a soldier, he preferred official affection to natural affection; laying aside his grief, he came forth joyfully to greet the victorious people.

Our Saviour too, when from the natural affection by which “no one has ever hated his own flesh” (Eph. V) he had cried out, “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matt. XXVI), subjected it, by the right of reason, to the spiritual affection by which he always clung to the Father: “Nevertheless,” he said, “not as I will, but as you will” (ibid.). [Col. 0603C]

The rule to be observed among these affections, therefore, is this: the affection by which our mind is stirred toward God must be preferred to all others; then rational to official, official to natural, and natural to carnal.

## CHAPTER XXX. What usefulness is to be sought in affections

When what has been said about the distinction of affections has been carefully considered, it is clear, I think, what usefulness is to be sought in them: namely, that by these affections, as by certain goads of love, we may be stirred to desire the things that ought to be loved; that by the sweetness infused by these affections we may hold love itself more sweetly and therefore more diligently; and that we may practise the very actions by which we strive toward what we desire, the more delightfully the more affectionately, and the more fervently the more delightfully.

Although desire itself ought to stir affection, it should very rarely follow affection itself, as has been shown above. Similarly, it is most useful for affection to be stirred toward the exercises of good works, and to be sustained by affection in those works; but to order the works themselves according to affection is disorderly. It remains, then, that we say briefly, according to our ability, how these works themselves must be ordered according to reason. [Col. 0604A]

For desire itself is uniform according to reason: yet in that love which comes from affection it is felt, whereas in that which comes from reason it is reckoned in the will alone. [Col. 0604B]

## CHAPTER XXXI. By what actions we ought to strive toward God, and by what actions provide for ourselves and our neighbours

There are certain actions by which we spiritually strive toward that highest good which ought to be loved and desired supremely. There are others by which we provide either for our own necessity or at once for our neighbours’ necessity and salvation; yet these actions too are undoubtedly to be referred by providence to the same end.

The Apostle seems to have set forth the whole condition of the perfect life in a few words: “Let us live soberly, justly, and devoutly in this age” (Tit. II). Sobriety is a certain measure and temperance of human life, prudently avoiding both extremes and leading our course along the royal road between right and left. The wise people of this world call this virtue frugality; and the most eloquent of them all explains its excellence clearly enough: “Let everyone call it what he wishes; I consider frugality—that is, measure and temperance—to be the greatest virtue.” [Col. 0604C]

For since he toward whom we supremely strive is a certain measure, lacking nothing, burdened by nothing, with nothing superfluous and nothing deficient; and since, when we attain him, there will be nothing outward that we desire and nothing inward that we disdain, it is altogether necessary that we keep ourselves within a certain measure and limit: neither falling below what is necessary nor being carried above what is right by destructive presumption.

By “justice,” moreover, I think the Apostle here means that virtue by which, providing for our neighbours’ need or salvation and discerning in those very benefits what is fitting for each and who ought to be preferred to whom, we render to each what is just. To these two virtues, sobriety and justice, he most wisely adds devotion, lest philosophers or any persons alien to Christ’s faith should glory in them; for devotion consists in sincere faith and pure intention. Intention itself, however, appears to consist in the choice of love, concerning which we have already spoken.

Perhaps the reader will now demand that we explain more plainly the very measure of life which it seems dangerous—indeed ruinous—to exceed. Who does not see how arduous and difficult it is to treat this subject? For there are as many kinds of people as there are people, and scarcely even two are ever found to whom everything is equally fitting. What is enough for one is too little for another; what advances one causes another to fail; and what is necessary for one is evidently superfluous for another. Yet something seems to be required that is suitable for all, which everyone may apply to himself, and by the guidance of reason may judge whether he exceeds the necessary measure of life. [Col. 0605A]

## CHAPTER XXXII. Beginning to treat the measure of human life, he shows what sobriety must be observed in the natural order

[Col. 0605B]

There are, then, three orders of human conduct: the first natural, the second necessary, the third voluntary. The first is permitted, the second prescribed, the third offered. The first proceeds from freedom, the second from necessity, the third from will. Grace is due to the first, mercy to the second, glory to the third. Let us discuss each in turn, as clearly as we can, insofar as seems necessary.

The natural order is this: one who has committed nothing unlawful may, if he wishes, use lawful things, yet lawfully. Lawful things are, for example, eating meat, drinking wine, marital intercourse, and possessing riches. As the Apostle says: “All things are clean to the clean; and nothing is to be rejected which is received with thanksgiving” (Tit. I). For the Apostle himself judges as heretics those who forbid marriage and command abstinence from foods “which God created to be received with thanksgiving by believers” (I Tim. IV). [Col. 0605C]

Yet if the use of these things is to be lawful, measure must be observed, and time, place, and kind must be more carefully considered. The Saviour himself prescribes a certain measure to be kept by all and in no respect to be exceeded by anyone: “Take heed,” he says, “lest your hearts be weighed down by gluttony and drunkenness and the cares of this life” (Luke XXI). Concerning marital intercourse Paul says: “Let each one know how to possess his own vessel in sanctification and honour, not in the passion of desire” (I Thess. IV). Peter also describes the use of clothing: “Not in costly apparel,” he says (I Tim. II).

The measure to be observed in using lawful things, then, is this: in eating and drinking, one must restrain oneself short of gluttony and drunkenness; in retaining riches, remove anxious care; in the use of a spouse, avoid shameful passions; and in dress seek not expense but necessity. [Col. 0605D]

A fitting time must also be observed for every use. For example, in seasons when ecclesiastical tradition commands abstinence from food, fasting must not be broken without reasonable necessity; in times appointed for prayer, marital intercourse must not be exercised; on days which Christian authority has consecrated to salutary leisure for hearing the word of God, worldly concerns must not be pursued; and on days on which sacred religion has established that sorrow or penitence be displayed by a change of clothing, no one should make use of festive garments.

Likewise, place must be considered in every use that is necessary. Who would not judge it sacrilege to devote oneself in church to feasts, marital intercourse, or business? Writing to the Corinthians, the Apostle rebukes them for not observing the lawful time in eating and drinking: “When you come together, it is no longer to eat the Lord’s supper; for each one takes his own supper beforehand to eat” (I Cor. II). For they did not observe a fitting time, since before receiving the Eucharist they presumed to take ordinary food contrary to apostolic decrees. [Col. 0606A]

Reproaching the same persons for transgressing measure, he adds: “One is hungry, while another is drunk” (ibid.). Then, reproaching them for contempt of place, he says: “Do you not have houses in which to eat and drink, or do you despise the Church of God?” (ibid.).

Finally, the kind of things which it is lawful to use must be discerned more subtly—not because anything among God’s creatures is believed unclean without sacrilegious impiety, but because sacred authority compels us to abstain from things known to have been offered in sacrifices to demons, or proved to have been taken from others by theft or robbery, lest their use appear to be consent to impiety in the impious or the weak. Hence the Apostle says: “If anyone says, ‘This has been sacrificed to idols,’ do not eat” (I Cor. X). [Col. 0606B]

Likewise, when holy Tobias, blind in his eyes but sound in mind, noticed a bleating animal which his wife had brought home as payment for work, he feared that unlawful eating might bring injury to a neighbour and defilement to himself. “See to it,” he said, “that it is not stolen” (Tit. II).

Let these remarks suffice concerning the natural order. Though we have not noted everything which people lawfully use, the diligent inquirer will discover from these examples what measure must be kept in other matters. Let us now touch briefly on the necessary order. [Col. 0606C]

## CHAPTER XXXIII. The measure of satisfaction and purification in the necessary order is described

The necessary order is that one who has committed unlawful acts should restrain himself even from the use of lawful things. Two matters must be considered in this restraint: the measure of satisfaction and the necessity of purification.

The measure of satisfaction requires that the strictness of continence be extended in proportion to the measure of the fault, so that, in the words of the Baptist, we may “bear fruits worthy of repentance.” But since the nature of satisfaction belongs to pastoral care, and holy Fathers have written books and laid down determinate rulings on it, I forgo saying more.

Yet not only the measure of satisfaction must be preserved; the necessity of purification must also be investigated. We must refrain from lawful things not only for satisfaction, but must also undertake laborious works to drive out or lessen the passions that grow strong through vicious habit. [Col. 0606D]

For the exercises of the outward person are instruments of the inward person. By them vicious passions that infect the soul itself are more readily cut away, and the stains of the inward countenance are more fully washed, as it were, by a harsher cleansing preparation. Therefore one concerned for one’s purification must first attend to the passions by which one is attacked; then examine those by which one is most severely troubled; and finally, with shrewd circumspection, seek what instruments are most effective against which passions. Having considered these matters, one should apply what is suitable to each passion and, against that which attacks more strongly, persist with more fervent effort so that it may be overwhelmed.

Thus restraint of the belly easily checks the passion of lust; the affliction of vigils weakens a wandering and unstable heart; silence moderates anger; the assiduity of work chastens weariness of mind. Yet one must not devote one’s entire force to extinguishing a single passion so that bodily strength fails as an instrument for suppressing the others. Nor must one labour so excessively that no passion whatever is felt; rather, when one arises, it must be restrained according to the judgment of reason. [Col. 0607A]

Let it suffice to have touched briefly upon the manner of purification. But whoever desires fuller knowledge of the assaults of vices and their remedies should read the book of John Cassian which he entitled *On the Instruction of Renunciants*. In it he has arranged in lucid style their origins, the manner of their assault, and the remedy for their expulsion. [Col. 0607B]

## CHAPTER XXXIV. What the voluntary order is, and what measure must be observed in it
The voluntary order is next to be considered by us, concerning which the Psalmist says: “I will sacrifice willingly to thee” [Col. 0607C] (Ps. LIII). For it is a freewill whole-offering, an acceptable victim, a voluntary sacrifice, when someone, by the liberty of the spirit, strives from things permitted, through things commanded, toward those rewards of greater glory set before those who long for them. Inviting the more fervent to this summit of perfection, the Savior says: “If thou wilt be perfect, go, sell what thou hast, and give to the poor; and come, follow me” (Matt. XIX). And elsewhere: “There are eunuchs,” he says, “who have made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven. He who is able to receive it, let him receive it” (ibid.). Thus renunciation of the world, the resolve of chastity, and the profession of any more rigorous manner of life are reckoned among voluntary sacrifices.

For although, after renouncing the world, entrance into the kingdom of heaven is not open to one who looks back [Col. 0607D]; although, after a vow of chastity, every unlawful corruption of the flesh is forbidden; although, after resolving upon a stricter life, it is a fall to lapse into looser observance—yet far be it that this perfection of life, which a person undertook voluntarily and not under compulsion, should be counted among necessary and compulsory things rather than among voluntary ones. For even the necessity itself, which no one imposed upon an unwilling person, but to which he voluntarily subjected himself through desire for perfection, must be called voluntary, not compulsory.

Therefore, whoever has devoted himself to these lofty and exalted things should first carefully examine the rule of his vow or resolution—what it consists in and how great its obligations are; then he should weigh and discern, on the scales of experience, the powers of his inward and outward person. By inward powers I mean those by which, through daily practice, he fights against the warfare of temptations; by outward powers, those by which he bears the burdens of bodily labours with tireless patience. Although labour of both the inward and outward person is necessary for anyone advancing in any state, bodily exercises especially cleanse the soul itself from the filth of passions; while spiritual exercises, like certain heavenly spices, suffuse it with the sweet fragrance of spiritual perfumes [Col. 0608A].

Accordingly, since that sweetness of anointing does not suit a soul foul with the grime of vices, affliction of the outward person is more necessary for one still assailed by passions of the flesh. But when the passions themselves have been lulled or extinguished, one may moderately relax external observances, while practising spiritual exercises more earnestly and fervently. Yet not so as presumptuously to exceed the rule of one’s profession [Col. 0608B], or to overthrow and confuse the distinctions of times prescribed in the rule to which one has submitted oneself. Rather, preserving the appointed time for each task, one should practise those tasks more quietly or more fervently, as one knows to be beneficial.

## CHAPTER XXXV. A discussion against a certain letter concerning the rule and profession of monks

Although this may seem not altogether relevant to the subject, I nevertheless think it advisable that, in providing for ourselves who are called monks, we should examine more carefully the force of our own Rule. Since many things concerning spiritual matters and many concerning bodily matters are discussed there, we should investigate with greater care wherein chiefly lie the force of the Rule itself and the norm of our profession [Col. 0608C].

I read the letter of someone who replied as follows to a person asking about this question:

“I do not hesitate to say that the rule of the monastic condition is the virtue of the monastic order—indeed, the substance of the monastic profession: those things which, when all else is absent, make a monk, and without which the rest, I do not say do not make one, but do not even have savour. But what are these things? Those which we vowed, for whose stability and observance we called God and his saints to witness. And what are they? ‘Stability,’ he says, ‘in our monastery; conversion of our ways; and obedience according to the Rule of Saint Benedict.’

“And below: ‘I desire to turn again to monks the volume of Blessed Benedict, and, whatever I discover in it to belong to that which we have prescribed as the substance of our Rule—indeed, of the monastic profession—I shall embrace as necessary in mind, so that I may strive, with entire devotion, to fulfil the vows and promises which I have made, as the Lord grants me power. But the rest I shall attempt to carry out in practice, not as the body of our Rule, but as things assisting and nourishing that body.’”

We might perhaps have wondered what these “rest” were, had he not later made this clear himself: namely, not going out of the cloister; manual work; the quantity, multiplicity, or at least variety of food and drink; the arrangement of the bed; and the use of drawers except for those setting out on a journey. “For what,” he says, “if these belonged to the substance of the monastic profession, would it ever be permissible to dispense with anything in them, even for a moment, or to alter anything of them? Otherwise, once the substance is absent [Col. 0609A], I am no monk, if I have destroyed the substance of monkhood in myself.”

And at the end of his treatise: “Thus, beloved brother, since dispensation may be made in these things—as Blessed Benedict himself makes a dispensation concerning the eating of meat for those wholly infirm, and concerning the use of drawers at least for those setting out on a journey—thus, I say, because dispensation and alteration are possible in these things, they are not part of the substance of the profession.”

So he speaks. But whether what he said concerning the use of drawers and the use of meat should be called a dispensation or an institution of Blessed Benedict, let him consider for himself. Certainly, Benedict commanded that mercy be shown to the aged and to children, not by dispensation but by authority of the Rule: “The authority of the Rule,” he says, “shall make provision for them.” But let us return to the earlier points.

It is clear what he called the body of the Rule and the substance of the monastic profession: namely, stability of place, conversion of manners, and obedience according to the Rule of Saint Benedict [Col. 0609B]. But I wonder why, when speaking of matters which he asserts do not so much constitute the Rule as assist it, he was silent about reading. For since reading itself admits dispensation, it is clear that, according to him, it does not belong to the body of the Rule.

Therefore, if manual labour, the quantity of bread and drink, the number of dishes, the manner of clothing, the amount of vigils, the character of bedding, the strictness of silence, the length of reading, the chanting of psalms, the prolonging of fasting, the reception of guests, and any other matters of this kind are not held to be the body of the Rule or the substance of the monastic profession—precisely because many dispensations and alterations are found in them, so that in many monasteries nothing at all is practised in every respect as the Rule prescribes—where, I ask, shall I find in the Rule the body of the Rule and the substance of monastic profession? Is not the entire Rule composed of all these things—indeed, almost of these things alone?

“But,” you will say, “I call only those things which we profess the body of the Rule and the substance of monastic profession: we have prescribed those three things.” Therefore no dispensation can be made in changing one’s place. What then is the meaning of the fact that, after the Rule had already been made and promulgated, Father Benedict himself sent Maurus into Gaul? If I had read such a change prescribed in the Rule, I would indeed judge that it ought to be called not a dispensation but an institution of the Rule [Col. 0609D]. But now, since I find that it was not prescribed by the Rule but done after the Rule’s establishment, why should I not freely call it a dispensation? Especially since he assigns to dispensation the eating of meat, which the authority of the Rule permits to those who are wholly infirm.

Do we not daily see dispensations of this kind made by our abbots? How often are monks transferred, by dispensation of their abbots, not merely from monastery to monastery, but even from region to region? How then can stability of place, subject to so many dispensations, belong to the body of our Rule and the substance of monastic profession—which, on his account, admits no dispensation? Moreover, those who are often taken into the clerical state are released by ecclesiastical authority not merely from the stability of that place [Col. 0610A], but even from obedience to their own abbot. Does so great a change destroy the substance of monkhood? What dispensation, then, if made concerning stability of place, would destroy the monk?

Perhaps he will say: if a monk migrated from one monastery to another without his abbot’s consent, when no danger to his salvation compelled him. Is this a dispensation, rather than a transgression? But if it is not a transgression, I confidently say that not even such a change destroys the monk. Perhaps, then, he will abandon his argument and affirm that these three things are the substance of monastic profession, not because they admit no dispensation, but because they alone are professed by the monk. Meanwhile, let us grant even this very point.

Let stability of place, conversion of manners, and obedience according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, then, be the body of the Rule and the substance of monkhood [Col. 0610B]. I ask that we join hands for the moment and inquire more carefully what this stability of place, this conversion of manners, and this obedience are. Yet I should like to know whether he thinks that, as the last is “according to the Rule,” so also the two former are according to the Rule; or whether he thinks that the monk professes them simply, without qualification.

I would not think this question worth raising at all had I not learned that certain persons say they professed themselves in such a way that they promised obedience alone according to the Rule, while they maintain that they promised the other two, not according to the Rule, but without any qualification. Yet since the Rule of Blessed Augustine, to which canons submit themselves by their profession, is one thing, and that of Saint Benedict, to which monks submit themselves, another, I ask what distinction there is between their professions. For both profess stability of place, conversion of manners, and obedience [Col. 0610C]. But if the two former are promised without qualification, it appears that the Rule of Saint Benedict differs from other rules only in the profession of obedience.

Will obedience according to the Rule of Benedict, then, differ from obedience according to the Rule of Augustine? Blessed Benedict commends an obedience which he does not wish to be slow or lukewarm, sorrowful or murmuring, exhausted by injuries or adversities, or failing before death. Will obedience according to the Rule of Saint Augustine be different? Or will that obedience differ which a cleric owes to a bishop, a bishop to an archbishop, and an archbishop to the bishop of bishops [the pope; Col. 0610D]? Can that obedience be slow or lukewarm, sorrowful or murmuring, exhausted by injuries or adversities, or fail before death? In what, then, does the difference between these professions consist?

Perhaps obedience “according to the Rule” means being subject to the precepts of the Rule itself, to which professed followers of other rules are not bound. What, then, are those precepts?

If they are the things it teaches concerning charity, humility, patience, and the other virtues, what canon—not to say what Christian—is not bound by these precepts? Does Benedict commend one charity in his Rule and Augustine another in his? Or rather, do not both commend that charity which Christ commends in the Law and the Gospel [Col. 0611A]? The same question may be asked concerning the other virtues. For who, being of sound mind, when exhorting people to virtue, would say that these are his own precepts rather than Christ’s? What diversity of precepts, then, will there be in different rules?

Surely it is in eating thus, dressing thus, reading thus, chanting psalms thus, correcting and being corrected thus, and other such matters, which are found to differ in different rules. These are specially called Augustinian or Benedictine because they are not imposed upon all Christians by evangelical authority, but proposed; whereas to those who profess the respective rules they are no longer merely proposed, but also imposed. Or, if these are not the relevant matters, what are they? Certainly, whatever they set down in their rules concerning charity, humility, and the other virtues, they commend not as their own but as the Lord’s precepts [Col. 0611B]; and they invite not merely monks, but all Christians, to them—not as to their own precepts (for who would believe them?), but as to Christ’s.

Therefore, if obedience according to the Rule of Saint Benedict is obedience to the Rule’s own precepts, and the precepts of that Rule consist in the matters mentioned above, how does one preserve the substance of monastic profession—since the obedience which we profess is that substance—if one does not keep those matters? But perhaps he will say, as indeed must be said, that the first two also are professed according to the Rule; and he will affirm that the difference among rules does not consist in stability of place or obedience, which are imposed alike upon monks, clerics, canons, and bishops [Col. 0611C], but only in conversion of manners.

For does not one and the same necessity concerning stability of place bind everyone: namely, that no one should, by rash presumption, change his place without the consent of the person set over him? Moreover, if we profess conversion of manners not according to the Rule but simply and without qualification, so too do those who in the Church are called penitents, and those fleeing from the shipwreck of fornication into the harbour of marriage. For who among them does not profess conversion of manners?

It remains, then, to inquire what conversion of manners according to the Rule of Saint Benedict is. But if here we have recourse to virtues—if, for example, we say that the one hitherto proud is henceforth found humble, the one hitherto wrathful henceforth gentle—we surely say that this conversion of manners is imposed upon all Christians from the Gospel, not merely upon monks by the Rule of Saint Benedict [Col. 0611D]. Therefore, if some difference is to be found between the conversions of manners professed according to different rules, there is nowhere to turn except to those matters which alone are established differently in different rules, and of which enough has already been said. How, then, does one preserve one’s profession if one does not keep them?

But someone will say: “If, therefore, someone is proud, stubborn, and impatient, yet observes all the matters mentioned above, is he to be said to observe the Rule of Saint Benedict?” I confidently say that if a monk commits any of these things against God’s Rule, but corrects them according to the manner prescribed in the Rule, he will not be guilty of violating his profession [Col. 0612A].

But what if someone understands the Rule of Saint Benedict as a kind of instrument by which vices are more easily cut away and evangelical precepts more carefully fulfilled, and supposes that it can happen that someone, misusing this excellent instrument, neither cuts away his vices by it nor acquires virtues, and therefore possesses the Rule to his own destruction while failing to fulfil Christ’s precepts? Does not Blessed Benedict himself indicate this very thing?

“We are therefore about to establish,” he says, “a school for the service of the Lord, in which we hope to establish nothing harsh, nothing burdensome. But if anything somewhat stricter …” etc.

Here I first ask what is that strictness which he urges beginners not to fear [Col. 0612B]. Surely he affirms that his own institution lies in this strictness. If patience, humility, and the other virtues are meant, would he say that he was going to establish these as though they were something new? Certainly there is nowhere to turn except to those things which he himself newly established, and which neither Law nor prophet nor Christ himself commanded. Such strictness seems by no means slight to beginners when they consider the small and poor quantity of food and drink, the roughness of clothing, the affliction of fasts and vigils, the wearing burden of daily labour, and the other such things which are found instituted by him in the Rule itself.

But if anyone will not agree that the Rule consists in these things alone, let him at least grant—what only stubborn obstinacy denies—that our profession and the Rule consist in both: virtues, namely, and observances; and consequently let him not deny that both must necessarily be kept by us [Col. 0612C]. Although the founder of the Rule himself seems, in the words we have begun to consider, to prove something else: “But if,” he says, “anything somewhat stricter should be introduced, at the prompting of the reason of equity, for the safeguarding of charity and the correction of vices.”

I ask: why do we seek darkness in the light? Why a knot in a reed? Why do we grope at noon as though in night? In every institution, is not the institution itself one thing and the cause of the institution another? Does he not here most clearly distinguish between the institution and its cause? Does he not testify here that safeguarding charity and correcting vices are the cause of his institution [Col. 0612D]?

But behold another rising at one’s side: “Why do you throw the Rule at me?” he says. “Have charity, and do whatever you wish.” Then let us eat and drink, not because tomorrow we shall die (Wis. II), but because we are full of charity. Full of charity, I ask, or of vanity? “What then,” you say, “does one who has charity not fulfil the Rule?” How many holy canons, holy priests, holy bishops, and even holy married persons know that they possess charity, yet know that they have neither promised nor observe the Rule and profession of monks.

But if this is said of those who profess the Rule itself, it is true—provided what is said is understood. “Why, then,” you ask, “do you compel me, on the Rule’s authority, to those harsh things?” Rather, if you have charity, there is no need for you to be compelled to fulfil your vows, which your lips have uttered [Col. 0613A]. But if you despise to fulfil what you vowed, having made the written undertaking and called God and the saints as witnesses, you are surely proved not to possess charity. For how do you love him whom you mock? “Let him know,” he says, “that if he acts otherwise”—that is, otherwise than he promised—“he is to be condemned by God, whom he mocks.”

What then? Do we condemn dispensations made or being made by the Fathers within the Rule itself? On the contrary, from this we establish that they can reasonably be made: they concern human, not divine, precepts. For no human being is permitted either to alter anything in divine precepts or to lessen them. Care must indeed be taken that alteration or variation itself may be a dispensation and not a destruction. Since safeguarding charity and correcting vices are the cause of the institution, a dispensation will surely be reasonable if that dispensation advances this cause [Col. 0613B]. But if vices are nourished more by dispensation than by the institution, and charity is violated, then the dispensation, if perhaps not ruinous, is certainly proved dangerous.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. The manner to be observed in the voluntary order is likewise described

Therefore, whoever by a voluntary order aspires to the summit of perfection should first continually keep before his eyes, as the intended end toward which he directs his entire course, charity: by which we draw nearest to God, indeed by which we cleave to him and are conformed to him, and in which the fullness of all perfection consists [Col. 0613C]. Then, by the tireless eagerness of the spirit, he should strive along the way which the norm of his vow or profession prescribes for him toward its fullness.

Let abstinence serve this end; let vigils minister to it; let reading attend upon it; let daily labour toil for it. But if charity, for whose sake these practices were instituted, is found to be violated by any of them, then it becomes necessary for the one entrusted with dispensation to temper and arrange everything so that charity is not abandoned for their sake, but its fruit is sought in all things. Yet this must not result in omitting some instituted practices or confusing the fixed times assigned to particular exercises, unless extreme necessity compels it; otherwise there will be not dispensation but destruction [Col. 0613D]. Rather, particular exercises should be adjusted at particular times according to each person’s condition and state of mind.

This is what the saint himself says when laying down the rule concerning manual labour: “Let him,” he says, “temper and arrange everything so that souls may be saved, and that what the brothers do, they may do without murmuring.” [Note: [Col. 0613D] St Benedict, Rule, ch. 48.] And elsewhere: “Nevertheless, let all things be done in moderation, on account of the faint-hearted.” Did he say that this or that should be omitted on account of the faint-hearted? Rather: “Let such a craft be enjoined even upon the weak and delicate, so that they may neither be idle nor crushed by the violence of labour.” Therefore even the weak and delicate are to work, but their work should be tempered so that they are not crushed. Whom, I ask, does he exempt from labour when he compels even the weak and delicate to it [Col. 0614A]?

It is useful for everyone to observe this measure in the exercises themselves: one should so engage in one that one does not fail in the others; yet one should practise with greater fervour that in which one feels oneself making greater progress. I have at hand the words of a certain wise man on this matter, and I judge it more fitting to insert what is ready to hand than to compose new words expressing the same thought.

“Meditation,” he says, “first considers in moral conduct what is owed, whether by precept or vow; and it judges that those things must first be done which, when done, have merit, but when not done incur guilt. Therefore these must first be done, which cannot be omitted without sin. After these, if anything is added by voluntary exercise, it must be done in such a way that what is owed is not hindered [Col. 0614B]. Some desire what they ought not because they are unable to do what they ought; others, though able to do what they ought, bring voluntary hindrances upon themselves by desiring what they ought not.

“Again, two evils must especially be avoided in good action: affliction and distraction. By affliction the sweetness of the mind is made bitter; by distraction its tranquillity is scattered. Affliction occurs when a person is consumed by impatience over things which he is unable to do; distraction, when he is excessively occupied in doing things which he is able to do. Therefore, lest the soul be wrongly embittered, let it bear its own incapacity patiently; and lest it be wrongly overoccupied, let it not extend its capacity beyond its proper measure.”

## CHAPTER XXXVII. What a person owes to oneself and to one’s neighbour is shown, and whether one should prefer oneself to one’s neighbour or one’s neighbour to oneself is explained

[Col. 0614C]

These things have been said concerning the measure to be observed at the several stages: so that, striving toward him whom we see must be loved supremely, we both provide for the salvation of the soul and grant to the body what nature requires. But since divine authority teaches that our neighbour is to be loved by us equally with ourselves, it is first necessary that our understanding should not be ignorant of what order is suitable to each person; then we must labour with all our strength lest anyone in any order exceed the prescribed manner of living.

But since it is clear that some are set over others, some are subject, and some are equals, whenever the lawful measure is transgressed by any of them, the inferior ought indeed to make a representation to the superior [Col. 0614D]; an equal should correct an equal; and a superior should even compel an inferior, if necessary. Yet representation, correction, and compulsion themselves should be tempered according to the condition of each person: so that submission may be felt in representation, unity in correction, and compassion in compulsion.

One who rightly occupies an inferior order may be admonished to ascend to higher things, but may not be compelled. One who has voluntarily submitted himself to a superior must be treated in accordance with the manner of his profession; but he ought not to be compelled, without his considered consent, to stricter things. Let him indeed be solicitous for love of his neighbour, whom he must love as himself; yet let him not exceed the measure of love by which he ought to love himself. This happens when he neglects himself, whom he ought to love above himself [Col. 0615A].

For we must not listen to those who think the saying, “Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself” (Matt. XXII), should be understood so that one ought to love each individual as oneself, but two or more persons above oneself, and therefore ought to will one’s own destruction rather than that of others. For what exchange shall a person give for his soul? What does it profit him if he gains the whole world—even for its salvation—yet suffers loss to his own soul? (Matt. XVI.)

It must also be observed that whatever, beyond the measure just stated, is added to brotherly love is wholly subtracted from divine love. For since self-love is measured by the measure in which one loves God, one loves oneself less only when one loves God less. But one who loves oneself—whose destruction does he spare? How, then, will he love another as himself, who does not even love himself?

When the Apostle says, “I was wishing at one time to be anathema from Christ for my brethren according to the flesh” (Rom. IX), he disclosed his feeling in order to draw them to salvation by the example of his extraordinary charity; he did not state a considered judgment [Col. 0615B]. We have sufficiently shown above how differently feeling and reason may suggest things within one mind. Therefore, when the Apostle said, “I was wishing to be anathema from Christ for my brethren,” he spoke truly, because he expressed the feeling he experienced. If he had afterwards said, “I would rather the whole world perish than that I alone be separated from Christ,” he would likewise have spoken truly, because he would have disclosed reason’s judgment.

The Savior himself, too, out of the feeling by which no one ever hated his own flesh (Eph. V)—the flesh which he voluntarily took from us and for us—desired that the hour of suffering might pass from him (Matt. XXVI); but by the judgment of reason he himself brought it about that it should not pass. Scripture, moreover, wisely does not say, “Thou shalt love thy neighbour as much as thyself,” but “as thyself” (Matt. XXII). It therefore prescribed a manner of loving, not an amount.

One’s self-love must be exercised in such a way that one first provides for the salvation of one’s own soul, which is the better part of oneself; and then for the necessities of one’s body.
