If necessity ever requires one of these to be neglected, one should even suffer the body’s destruction, provided one does not suffer loss to the soul [Col. 0615D]. This is not to hate the body, but to prefer the soul to the body in love.

Let one therefore never depart from this self-love. Keeping it firmly and perseveringly, let one safely approach the task of providing for one’s neighbour. Let one take the measure of such provision from the rule by which one provides for oneself. Let one therefore do for one’s neighbour all one can, so that the neighbour may be safe in body and sound in mind. For if one neglects either, one surely does not love one’s neighbour, who consists of both.

But if one’s neighbour is such that he cannot attain the salvation of his soul without some loss, let one, with compassion and contrition of heart, permit his flesh to perish, so that his spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord. Yet no reason or precept compels anyone to purchase a brother’s soul’s salvation by the destruction of one’s own soul, or to avert the death of a brother’s body by the death of one’s own body [Col. 0616A]. For the command that we lay down our lives for the brethren (1 John III) concerns contempt for life, not injury to the soul. Thus one lays down one’s life not for destruction but rather for salvation. Therefore, to lay down one’s life in this way is surely to provide for one’s own soul.

Moreover, those who avert the temporal death of their temporal lords by their own temporal death—when they rightly do so—act not so much for the safety of another’s body as for that of their own soul. For their conscience tells them that faith must be kept with their lords, so that in such danger they judge their lords’ life preferable to their own. But those who do this not to keep faith but to win glory and avoid disgrace do it foolishly indeed; yet even they do it not for another body, but for the value of their own reputation [Col. 0616B].

It may perhaps be done laudably when, from love alone, a person exposes one’s own body for another’s body. But to suffer injury to one’s own soul for the salvation—not merely of one soul but even of the whole world—cannot be done without violating the order of true love. For injury to the soul is to depart from love of him who must be loved supremely. Who would say that this can ever be done laudably, or even without blame?

One departs from love of God when one either commits something deserving condemnation or omits something without which there is no salvation. There are, however, certain intermediate things: reading, meditation, bodily labour, fasting of the belly, the sweetness of prayer, and other such things. All these must, for a brother’s salvation, be dispensed with, varied, altered, and sometimes even omitted. Of these the Apostle says: “Let each seek not his own interests, but those of others” (Phil. II). And again: “Thus I please all persons in all things, not seeking what is useful to me, but what is useful to many, that they may be saved” (1 Cor. X) [Col. 0616C].

Finally, the Apostle’s words, “I was wishing to be anathema from Christ for my brethren” (Rom. IX), may also fittingly be understood in this sense: that he wished, for the salvation of his brethren, to be called away from that secret retirement of his prayers, where he rested sweetly in the embraces of Jesus; from that height of ineffable contemplation, by which he surveyed the secrets of heavenly mysteries with most pure eyes; and from that sweetness of most welcome compunction, which bathed that soul thirsting for heavenly things with the sweetest drops of spiritual affections. He does not hesitate to call such a summons separation from Christ—he who, according to his capacity, has leisure and tastes how sweet the Lord is (Ps. XLV), and how blessed is everyone who trusts in him.

But one who has chosen thus to be separated from Christ at the prompting of brotherly love, or consented when compelled by the authority of superiors, must take care lest this necessity overwhelm him and that sweetness perish. What we have said about reading or prayer must also be understood of bodily comforts, indeed of the body itself: whatever one sees must be disregarded, expended, or varied for one’s own salvation, one should recognize must likewise be done for the salvation of one’s neighbour [Col. 0617A].

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. Among neighbours themselves, who is to be preferred to whom is distinguished

Since, then, in treating of charity we have shown according to its law what a person owes to oneself and to one’s neighbour, and since such a multitude does not allow us to provide for the bodily necessities of everyone, it remains for considered reason to discern, among persons themselves, who is to be preferred to whom.

Let us consider the breadth of our heart as a kind of spiritual ark, constructed of incorruptible wood—that is, good habits and virtues. Setting within it chambers and three-storied compartments, that is, spiritual dwelling-places [Col. 0617B], let us assign individual places to individuals according to each person’s dignity or rank.

Let us shut in the lower places the beasts—that is, our enemies, raging with beastly habits and thirsting for our blood with murderous fury. To them let us offer the aid of prayer and, after others, the assistance of this common life. But since there are interior and exterior chambers, let exterior things suffice, among this class of people, for those who are outside; while the inner dwelling should not repel those who, even if only outwardly, share the common faith with us.

A place higher than these should be granted to creeping things and beasts of burden: those who, although they savour earthly things and defile themselves with the filth of the belly and the impurity of lust, debase themselves beneath human dignity, yet devise nothing inhuman, nothing cruel, nothing hostile against us [Col. 0617C]. To them let us give the remedy of prayer, the help of exhortation, the cautery of correction, and—before those lower down, but after those higher up—the supplement required by necessity. Among them, those nearer to us either by community of blood or by the kindness of human service should receive the inner places of this rank; the rest should not be excluded from the exterior places.

Now let us place human beings in the higher compartments: namely, those who, though not borne above human level by desire for perfection, nevertheless do not sink into beasts through savagery, into cattle through pleasure, or into creeping things through filth. Here too there are degrees: the nearer someone is to us by kinship, the more pleasing by friendship, or the more liberal in bestowing benefits [Col. 0617D], the more inward should be that person’s place in the dwelling of our heart.

But let a loftier place be given to birds: those who, borne above human beings on the spiritual wings of virtues, ought, insofar as they are nearer to God, to hold higher places in this spiritual ark. Among them, whoever is joined to us by the sweetest bond of spiritual friendship should be stored more sweetly in the more inward and secret places of our heart, bound more closely, and cherished more tenderly.

There is, moreover, a place higher than all others, in which Jesus alone—the maker and restorer of this spiritual ark—sits, beautiful without companion, ordering all lower things by his sweetness. May he be savoured in all things, fragrant in all things, radiant in all things, resplendent in all things; and may he draw the entire lower breadth [Col. 0618A] by the straightest line toward the one cubit of his love. He alone in all things, he alone before all things, both moves our affection and claims our love. He requires for himself a seat in the dwelling-place of our heart not only more worthy, but higher; not only higher, but more inward.

Let this principle therefore be observed in this distinction: while preserving a willingness to provide for all, when present need cannot suffice for everyone, let the higher rank be preferred to the lower; and within each rank, let provision rather be made for the more inward person.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. Who they are with whom we can enjoy fellowship in this life
One thing still remains, which the logic of our division now compels us to discuss. For we said that charity consists in this: that the mind chooses for enjoyment what it ought, is moved as it ought, and makes fitting use of it. [Col. 0618B] Concerning choice and motion, we have said enough for the present work. But if the choice is sound and the motion whole, can the use nevertheless be perverse? Yet in attaining the one whom it loves, both its motion can vary and its judgment can go astray. For someone may, even with a right intention and fitting motion, obtain the presence of the person whom he chose to enjoy; yet in that very enjoyment and in his intention he may change and vary his motion, and exceed the proper measure.

But since a little above we arranged our neighbours according to different ranks and different merits, we must certainly say whether we ought, or indeed are able, to enjoy all of them, or only some. There is a temporal enjoyment by which we may enjoy one another in this life, as Paul enjoyed Philemon (Phil. 20); [Col. 0618C] and there is an eternal enjoyment by which we shall enjoy one another in heaven, as the angels enjoy one another in the pure unity of their minds. Therefore, since to enjoy is to use with joy and delight, I think it plain that in the present life we cannot enjoy everyone, but only very few.

For, as it seems to me, we can indeed use some persons for testing, some for instruction, some for consolation, some for support. We use enemies for testing, teachers for instruction, elders for consolation, and those who provide necessities for the support of life; but we use, for the sweetness of life and the delight of the spirit, only those whom we embrace with a certain sweet affection, whatever class they may belong to. Thus [Col. 0618D] we can enjoy these even in the present life—that is, use them with joy and delight.

Accordingly, in this life charity, as regards choice and the motion expressed in action, can be shown by everyone to everyone; but as regards enjoyment, it can be shown to everyone by few, or perhaps by none. For few there are—if indeed there are any—by whom the whole human race is cherished not only with rational but also with affectionate love. Finally, even to God charity is shown by many both in choice and in motion, although they do not partake in this life of the fruit of love for him; it is reserved after this life in his most blessed vision.

For even those in whom some beginning of this sweetness is granted in the light of contemplation and the sweetness of compunction—if you look to the joys to come—cannot be said to enjoy even God, [Col. 0619A] but rather to use him. For it has sufficiently been shown above that to most people the sweetest taste of that sweetness is granted not so much as the fruit of love as for the support of weakness.

Moreover, it is no small consolation in this life to have someone whom you can unite to yourself by a certain intimate affection and the embrace of most sacred love; to have one in whom your spirit may rest and to whom your soul may pour itself out; to whose welcome conversation you may flee, as to consoling songs, amid every sorrow; to whose most welcome bosom of friendship you may safely draw near amid so many scandals of the world; to whose most loving breast you may, as though to yourself, entrust without hesitation the inmost contents of all your thoughts; by whose spiritual kisses, like medicinal fomentations, you may sweat out the languors of your turbulent cares; [Col. 0619B] who may weep with you in distress, rejoice with you in prosperity, and seek with you amid uncertainties; whom you may lead, in the bonds of charity, into that inner chamber of your mind, so that, though absent in body, he may nevertheless be present in spirit, where you may commune alone with one who is alone; and so that, when the noise of the world is stilled, in the sleep of peace, the embrace of charity, and the kiss of unity, with the sweetness of the Holy Spirit flowing between you, you may rest alone with one who is alone. Indeed, you may join and bind yourself to him, and mingle soul with soul, so that out of many there may become one.

We can therefore enjoy in the present life those whom we love not only by reason but also by affection; and among these especially those who are joined to us more intimately and closely than others by the most welcome bond of spiritual friendship. Lest this most sacred form of charity appear blameworthy to anyone, [Col. 0619C] Jesus himself, ours, condescending to us in all things, enduring and suffering with us in all things, and transforming us by the manifestation of his love, granted to one, not to all, a place to recline upon his sweetest breast as a special sign of love: so that a virginal head might be supported by the flowers of a virginal breast, and the fragrant secrets of the heavenly bridal chamber might instil the fragrance of spiritual ointments into virginal affections more abundantly the nearer they were. Hence, although all the disciples were cherished by their most compassionate teacher with the sweetness of the highest charity, to this one nevertheless, by the prerogative of a more familiar affection, he granted this title: “that disciple whom Jesus loved” (John 19).

## CHAPTER XL. How we ought mutually to enjoy one another.

[Col. 0619D]

Therefore, whoever finds it sweet to enjoy a friend must see that he enjoys him in the Lord, not in the world; not in the pleasure of the flesh, but also in the joy of the spirit. But you ask: what is it to enjoy in the Lord? The Apostle says of the Lord: “Who was made for us by God wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification” (1 Cor. 1). Therefore, since the Lord is wisdom, sanctification, and righteousness, to enjoy in the Lord is to enjoy in wisdom, to enjoy in sanctification, to enjoy in righteousness.

By wisdom worldly vanity is excluded; by sanctification the filth of the flesh is cut off; by righteousness every form of flattery and adulation is restrained. For then charity exists, if it is, as the Apostle says, “from a pure heart, and a good [Col. 0620A] conscience, and unfeigned faith” (1 Tim. 1). A pure heart receives wisdom; chastity makes the conscience serene; unfeigned faith adorns righteousness.

There are people who enjoy one another in empty and frivolous things, in the pomp of the age and the spectacles of the world, in the pursuit of vanity and the delight of falsehood. These do not enjoy one another in wisdom and consequently not in him who is the power of God and the wisdom of God. Others, if not worse, are certainly more sordid: people in whom almost nothing of the human remains, whom obscene foulness has transformed into beasts. They enjoy one another in luxurious banquets and unclean desires; and because they do not enjoy one another in sanctification, which consists in the sweetness of chastity, they certainly do not enjoy the Lord, who was made for us by God sanctification.

But those who enjoy one another flatteringly, caressing one another and agreeing with one another, while each avoids giving the other offence, incur mutual ruin; because they do not enjoy one another in the freedom [Col. 0620B] of righteousness, they do not enjoy one another in the Lord. Therefore, if mutual conversation delights you, let the conversation be about morals; let it be about the Scriptures. Let us now groan together over the miseries of this life; now rejoice together in the hope of good things to come; now be refreshed by the disclosure of one another’s secrets; now together long for that blessed vision of Jesus and the goods of heaven.

But if, as is sometimes useful, we relax a strained mind with certain lower and pleasant things, let even the relaxations be full of decency, empty of frivolity, though they lack edification. Let us enjoy one another in sanctification, so that each may know how to possess his own vessel, [Col. 0620C] that is, his own body, in sanctification and honour, not in the passion of desire. Let us enjoy one another in righteousness, so that in a spirit of freedom we may exhort one another and correct one another, knowing that “the wounds of a friend are better than the deceitful kisses of an enemy” (Prov. 27).

## CHAPTER XLI. Epilogue of the whole work, and the author’s apology for himself.

These, most beloved Father, are my meditations on charity. If in them its excellence, its fruit, and the fitting manner of showing it are displayed as a kind of image, let the book itself, as you have written, be called *The Mirror of Charity*. Yet I beg you not to bring that mirror before the public, [Col. 0620D] lest perhaps charity should not shine in it, but instead the image of its author should appear sordid.

But if you issue it, to my confusion as I fear, I entreat the reader by that sweet name of Jesus not to judge that I approached this work presumptuously. Paternal authority, fraternal charity, and my own necessity compelled me to it. For it is dangerous not to obey a superior; pleasant and delightful, when my dearest friend is absent, to converse in spirit on such matters; and I judged it necessary to bind the wandering and useless excursions of my luxuriant mind with the bonds of these meditations. If anyone by reading these things advances either in affection or in knowledge, let him repay my labours in this way: let him intercede for my innumerable sins with the just and merciful Judge.

[Col. 0621]

## COMPENDIUM OF *THE MIRROR OF CHARITY*

Observe, from the most reverend Angelus Manrique, volume II of the *Cistercian Annals*, under the year 1166, chapter 3, and from the Reverend Dom Carolus de Visch, prior of the monastery of Dunes, book *On the Writers of the Cistercian Order*, that the author first wrote this work; and that subsequently, on its occasion and at the urging of friends, he treated the same subject more fully and published the larger *Mirror of Charity*, divided into three books. In the same way, having written one Homily on the Burdens of Isaiah, he later, when asked and urged, published another thirty-one Homilies on the same matters.

## CHAPTER I. That the Creator should be loved by his creature.

[Col. 0621A]

Nothing is more fitting than that the Creator should be loved by his creature. Therefore reason, in order to stir a cooling soul toward desire for its Creator, rests upon three arguments: namely, our necessity or advantage, and his worthiness. Reason urges that God must be loved because this is necessary for us, beneficial for us, and worthy in itself: necessary, that we may avoid damnation; beneficial, that we may obtain glorification; worthy, because he first loved us and by the merit of that love rightly requires a return.

God must be desired by a human being as his own good, without whom he must always be miserable, and with whom he cannot fail always to be most blessed; [Col. 0621B] God, who, needing none of our goods, chose to be miserable for us. O Lord God, how great is the delight in loving you! How great the tranquillity in that delight! How great the security in that tranquillity! The love of one who loves you does not go astray, because nothing is better than you; hope is not disappointed, because nothing is loved more fruitfully; no excess need be feared, because no limit is prescribed to love. Death, which sunders worldly friendship, is feared.

In your love no offence is feared, for there is none unless love itself is abandoned; no suspicion intervenes, because you judge by the testimony of conscience itself. Here is delight, because fear is excluded; here tranquillity, by which anger is restrained; here security, by which the world is despised. Compare, I pray, with all riches, all the world’s pleasures, all honours, this one possession of Christ’s servants: that they do not fear death. [Col. 0621C] What, I ask, is delightful in the world, when its very delight pricks the conscience, instils fear of death, and consigns its lovers to eternal damnation?

## CHAPTER II. (*Mirror*, book I, chapter 10.) That charity lacks no perfection: “You shall love the Lord your God,” etc. (Matt. 22).

O word that completes and makes brief in equity! Word of charity, word of love, word of affection, word of all perfection! A completing word, to which nothing can be lacking; a shortening word, upon which the whole Law and the Prophets hang (ibid.). O Jew, what need have you of so many things? Here is circumcision; here the Sabbath; here saving sacrifices; here fragrant sacrifice; here incense of every sweetness. Hold fast to charity, [Col. 0622A] and none of these will be lacking. Neglect charity, and none of them will avail.

Here indeed is not the carnal cutting off of one member, but the true and perfect circumcision of the whole outward and inward person: cutting away pleasure, extinguishing lust, checking gluttony, restraining anger, utterly overturning envy, and conquering pride, the mother of every vice. This tempers the ravenous stings of sorrow with a certain spiritual sweetness and meets the languor of lingering sloth. Piercing the plague of avarice with the most welcome blade of generosity, it frees and preserves the soul from the vice of idolatry.

What, I ask, is more perfect than this circumcision? By it the members of vices are cut away, the body of sin is destroyed, the hairy covering of the first-created humans is laid aside, and all the decay and foulness of ancient corruption is cast down. [Col. 0622B] For the mind filled with the sweetness of charity is not constricted by fear, defiled by lust, torn by anger, lifted up by pride, fanned by the empty smoke of vainglory, agitated by frenzy, disembowelled by the spur of ambition, contracted by avarice, cast down by sorrow, or wasted away by envy. For charity “does not envy, does not act perversely, is not puffed up, is not ambitious, does not seek its own, is not provoked, thinks no evil, does not rejoice at iniquity” (1 Cor. 13).

You see that this spiritual circumcision destroys every vice. It purifies every bodily sense with a kind of divine knife: cutting away the wantonness of the eyes, rooting out the itching of the ears, driving off the excessive sweetnesses of taste, stripping away the impudence of the tongue, excluding from the nostrils seductive scents, and rooting out the harmful softness of touch.

## CHAPTER III. (*Mirror*, book I, chapter 10.) That our love is divided against itself by the contrary impulses of charity and cupidity.

The Apostle says: “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh; for these are opposed to one another, so that you do not do the things you wish” (Gal. 5). Since the only portion of our soul capable of charity or cupidity is that which is more commonly called love, it is love itself which, from the new infusion of charity and the remnants of old cupidity, is found to be divided against itself as by a contrary impulse.

Hence we must understand that by the names of spirit and flesh the Apostle did not describe in one human being contrary natures, as the impure Manichees imagine; [Col. 0623A] rather, by “spirit” he expresses the newness of the mind resulting from the infusion of charity, while by “flesh” he indicates the wretched bondage of the soul arising from the remnants of its old state. Between our ingrained oldness and our unaccustomed newness, he declares that a continual conflict arises within one mind.

This desire, therefore, which the Apostle calls that of the flesh (ibid.), is not so called because every evil desire comes from flesh—for demons, who lack flesh, are not without it—but this evil desire is most appropriately called cupidity. It is called the desire of the flesh because it is not from God but from humankind, which Scripture unquestionably calls “flesh.” The desire of the spirit, however, is not without reason called charity, which is poured out [Col. 0623B] in our hearts through the Holy Spirit (Rom. 5).

## CHAPTER IV. (*Mirror*, book I, chapters 21 and 22.) That a rational creature rests only in attaining blessedness, and why, though it desires blessedness, it nevertheless with astonishing unhappiness flees the path by which it may obtain it.

Even for irrational animals it is a great labour to preserve safety, avoid destruction, and seek satisfaction for bodily appetites; once they have attained this and have nothing further to desire, they rest. For, lacking reason and knowledge, they cannot even desire what exceeds bodily sensation.

But for you, O rational soul, this prerogative is reserved above other living creatures: withdrawing yourself from bodily sensations, [Col. 0623C] you press onward to higher things, and you never satisfy your appetite until, in blessed inquiry, you reach that which is highest, that which is best, that above which there is nothing, than which there is nothing more excellent. Wherever below this you stop, however lofty, great, or pleasant it may be judged, you will undoubtedly remain miserable. Miserable because needy; needy because something remains for you to seek, something remains for which you must yearn: blessedness itself remains, and a certain natural power impels the rational soul to desire it.

Yet deeply lamentable is the blind perversity of miserable man: although he vehemently desires blessedness, he not only does not do the things by which he may attain what he desires, but with a more eager inclination commits the things by which he heaps misery still more upon himself. It is as if someone sick intensely desired health, but because of immediate discomfort avoided surgery and recoiled from cautery, and, enticed by a present sweetness, sought soothing applications of oil—although his disease were of such a kind that it becomes more inflamed by this indulgence and cannot be relieved without the pain of cautery or surgery.

Thus miserable man, deceived either because he thinks to be happiness what is not happiness, or because he is enticed by a present sweetness that is false, both consigns himself to misery and does not lose the desire for blessedness. Therefore, labouring in an unhappy circuit, he never rests. For since God alone is above the rational soul, the angel its equal, and all else is judged inferior, what is closer to madness than, abandoning the higher, to seek rest [Col. 0624A] in things which it itself surpasses?

In my judgment it would never do this unless, on the one hand, a false image of happiness deceived it and, on the other, a likeness of true misery frightened it. For poverty, hunger, thirst, and such things are judged misery; yet by them true misery is often avoided and eternal blessedness sought. “Blessed are the poor,” Jesus says, “for yours is the kingdom of heaven. Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted. Blessed are you who now hunger, for you shall be satisfied” (Matt. 5; Luke 6). Poverty is therefore rewarded with eternal riches; mourning is transformed into eternal joy; eternal satisfaction is reserved for the hungry. For no one can doubt that all these things—riches, joy, satisfaction—are not absent from blessedness.

[Col. 0624B] Yet because a certain appearance of delight deceives every reprobate person in whatever inclination of his own will he may have, and false pleasure dissolves him in the fulfilment of his desires, the wretched man, ignorant how great is the consolation of the elect even under pressure and their rejoicing in hope, recoils indeed from the image of unhappiness apparent on the surface. But beneath the colouring of happiness he embraces true unhappiness and false delight, which does not escape true pain, preferring it to that misery which is succeeded by true blessedness.

## CHAPTER V. (*Mirror*, book I, chapters 23 and 26.) That the rest naturally desired by the rational creature must be sought neither in bodily health, nor pleasure, nor riches.

[Col. 0624C] O wonderful creature, inferior only to the Creator, to what do you cast yourself down? Do you love the world? Yet you are higher than the world itself. Do you admire the sun? Yet you yourself are more radiant than the sun. Do you philosophize about the motion of this revolving heaven? Yet you are more exalted than heaven. Do you search out the hidden causes of creatures? Yet no nature is more hidden than you. Do you doubt, when you judge all these things, while none of them judges you? But if you wish to judge, do not love them. Nor should you love even the act of judging them. Love him who set you above all these things, not beneath them. He set you above them, not so that through them you might be happier, but so that there might be something over which you were higher: subjecting all things to you as an increase of honour, while reserving himself for you as the fruit of blessedness.

Why then do you pursue fleeting beauties, when your own beauty neither withers in old age, is soiled by poverty, pales in sickness, [Col. 0624D] nor even perishes in death itself? You seek to lack nothing that you will, and thus to rest; seek this, then. “Where?” you ask. Do not seek it in bodily health, in the pleasure of the flesh, in power, or in riches. For what is more perverse than to place the good of a rational mind in the gluttony of the belly, and to subject what is pre-eminent in a human being to some most worthless part of his own flesh—especially when he sees that in these things he is unable to differ at all from the stupidest beasts?

For hunger produces torment and satiety disgust. Even if one satisfies pleasure, one must exceed the bounds of necessity; but if one exceeds the measure of nature, it is impossible to avoid bodily pain. Moreover, to delight in the filth of lusts and, like an utterly filthy sow, to wallow in the mire of shameful conduct—just as nothing is more shameful, foul, deserving of blushes, or worthy of disgrace, so assuredly nothing is more restless, nothing so devoid of every peace and tranquillity.

For what need be said of its foulness, [Col. 0625A] when this most sordid pestilence both contaminates the flesh and feminizes the mind, and at once overwhelms and overturns whatever is honourable, beautiful, or finally manly in the soul? Although other vices commonly cloak themselves in certain coverings of virtues, and consequently not only do not blush before human eyes but even swell with pride under their gaze, this vice alone bears such horror on its very face that at the very hour when it grips the flesh and claims it for itself, it strongly avoids the eyes.

What, then, must those do who worship the Son of a Virgin and the author of virginity? They must certainly beware lest what the prophet says of some should happen to anyone: “The beasts have rotted in their own dung” (Joel 1). By these words he aptly expresses the end and measure of this most filthy passion: he declares that the person whom the Charybdis of lust has swallowed up is corrupted by the filth of his flesh—indeed, by the discharge of his own excrement—so that you should consider him not merely extinguished or swallowed, but, like a buried corpse, should perceive him putrefying and stinking as the pus of most unclean itching flows forth.

It is therefore necessary that the mind in which this wicked spirit has taken its seat should be driven by certain furies; assaulted by the fiery goads of lust, drunken and wandering toward every shameful act, and impelled solely by the bridle of all decency; and that, once the blaze of a conceived passion has been extinguished, it should nevertheless be kindled by another heat still more violent.

## CHAPTER VI. (*Mirror*, book I, chapter 27.) On the sweet yoke of charity.

“Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart; and you shall find rest for your souls. For my yoke is sweet, and my burden light” (Matt. 11). This yoke is fraternal love. This yoke does not press down but unites; this burden has wings, not weight. Those who complain of its harshness have certainly not yet cast off the yoke of cupidity by the roots. Perhaps under the habit of religion they serve their bellies; under the tunic of penitents, [Col. 0625D] they pant after worldly glory and honour; beneath sheepskin they bear a wolfish heart and burn with insatiable avarice. Hence they are disembowelled by continual cares, inflamed by hatreds, and scattered by anxious thoughts, because the yoke of the world is harsh and the burden of the world is heavy. But the Lord’s yoke is sweet, and the Lord’s burden light.

## CHAPTER VII. (*Mirror*, book I, chapter 31.) How great is the perfection found in charity.

For what is sweeter or more glorious than, through contempt for the world, to see oneself higher than the world and standing upon the summit of a good conscience, with the whole world beneath one’s feet: to see nothing to desire, no one to fear, no one to envy; to possess as one’s own nothing that another can take away, and to regard as evil nothing [Col. 0626A] that another can inflict? And while directing the gaze of the mind toward that inheritance incorruptible, undefiled, and unfading, reserved in heaven, what is sweeter or more glorious than to despise, by a certain nobility of mind, worldly riches as corruptible, fleshly enticements as defiled, and every pomp of the world as fading, and to exult in that prophetic saying: “All flesh is grass, and all its glory is as the flower of grass. The grass has withered and the flower has fallen, but the word of the Lord remains for ever” (Isa. 40)?

What, I ask, is sweeter or more tranquil than not to be agitated by the turbulent motions of the flesh, not to be scorched by the burning incentives of carnal desire, not to be moved by any seductive sight; but to have the flesh, cooled by the dew of chastity, subject to the spirit, no longer an enticer toward fleshly pleasures but a most obedient helper in spiritual exercises? [Col. 0626B] What is nearer to divine tranquillity than not to be moved by insults, to be frightened by no punishment or persecution, to preserve one constancy of mind in prosperity and adversity alike, to look upon enemy and friend with the same eye, and to conform oneself to the likeness of him “who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil, and sends rain upon the just and the unjust” (Matt. 5)?

All these things are together in charity, and nowhere but in charity are all together. Therefore in it are true tranquillity and true sweetness, because it is the Lord’s yoke. If we take it up at the Lord’s invitation, we shall find rest for our souls, because the Lord’s yoke is sweet and his burden light.

The other virtues are for us either like a vehicle for the weary, provisions for a traveller, a lamp for those in darkness, or weapons for combatants. But charity—which must indeed exist in all the other virtues—is in a special sense itself rest for the weary, a lodging-place for the traveller, full light for one who has arrived, and a perfect crown for the traveller. [Col. 0626C] For what is faith but our vehicle, by which we are carried to our homeland? What is hope but our provision, by which we are sustained amid the miseries of this life? What are those four virtues—temperance, prudence, fortitude, and justice—but our weapons with which we fight?

But when the mind has been more fully absorbed in charity—which is perfected only in the vision of God, for those in whom it is begun here by faith—there will be no faith, because one who is seen and loved need not be believed in; nor will there be hope, because for one embracing God in the arms of charity nothing remains to be hoped for. Temperance fights against lusts, prudence against errors, fortitude against adversities, justice against inequalities. But in charity there is perfect chastity, and therefore no lust against which temperance must fight; in charity perfect knowledge, and therefore no error against which prudence must fight; in charity true blessedness, and therefore no adversity which fortitude must overcome; in charity all things are at peace, and therefore no inequality against which justice must keep watch.

Thus true temperance, true prudence, and true fortitude presently act so that the rational mind, neither enticed, deceived, nor overcome, may not exceed the rule of charity. [Col. 0627A] Moreover, if you consider more carefully, what is temperance but love which no pleasure entices? What is prudence but love which no error deceives? What is fortitude but love courageously enduring adversity? What is justice but love regulating by a certain equitable measure the inequalities of this life? Charity, then, is begun in faith, exercised in the other virtues, and perfected in itself.

But when perfect charity has brought its followers into the kingdom of its tranquillity, when every enticement of the flesh has been consumed together with the flesh’s mortality, every darkness of error scattered by the contemplation of divine light, and the sure security that succeeds the troubles of this world has arrived, then, having laid aside, so to speak, the weapons used in this time of war, charity itself will refresh the conquerors by its sweetness alone. For then all the other virtues will pour themselves into the fullness of charity, so that in that blessedness temperance, prudence, and fortitude will be thought to be nothing other than charity: so chaste that it is tempted by no enticements, so bright that it is clouded by no errors, so strong that it is assailed by no adversities whatsoever.

## CHAPTER VIII. (*Mirror*, book I, chapter 32.) That the works of the six days are suited to the other virtues, but the rest of the seventh day is assigned to charity.

Faith, then, is like the first day for us, in which we faithful are separated from unbelievers, as light from darkness. Let hope be the second, through which, dwelling in heavenly things and hoping beyond the heavens alone for the rewards of faith, we are, by God’s advancing grace, distinguished from those who set their minds on earthly things and ask from God only earthly things, who melt and drift about beneath the firmament of heaven like waters.

Let temperance shine upon us like the third day, in which, as we put to death our members that are upon the earth and restrain fleshly desires like most bitter waters within necessary bounds, the dry and waterless ground of our heart may appear, thirsting for the Lord its God. Let the light of prudence now break forth like that of the fourth day, by which we distinguish between things to be done and things not to be done, as between day and night. With its help, the light of wisdom may shine like the splendour of the sun; the light of spiritual knowledge, which increases in some of us and declines in others, may appear like the beauty of the moon; and the devout mind may look up to the examples of preceding fathers as to spheres of stars. [Col. 0627D] By it the mind may also distinguish days and years, months and hours: namely, what difference there is between those before the Law and those under the Law; between these and those under grace; what is suitable for each; and, by fair examination, what precepts, times, customs, and sacraments are to be distinguished.

Let fortitude be like the fifth day for us, by which we may endure the storms of this great and wide sea, that is, of this age; and, made spiritual fish by God’s working, may preserve our life amid waves and tempests. Let us raise the desires and affections of our minds, like winged birds, to heavenly things; setting our minds on things above, may we, with God’s blessing, yield abundant fruits of good works.

Finally, let justice assign to us the sixth day, [Col. 0628A] by which, reclothed in the divine likeness, we may rule with noble authority over the savage beasts of vices and earthly desires, as over creeping things, and over the motions of the body, as over beasts of burden. Let us act so that the body is subject to the mind and the mind to God, and thus, as justice ordains, that to each may be rendered what is its own.

The seventh day remains: that is, the Sabbath, on which all these works are completed, true rest is received, and a limit and end are set to our labour. It is charity, the consummation of all virtues, the sweet refreshment of holy souls, the honourable ordering of character. It is the root from which all good works arise as good, and in which all good works are perfected. It is the seventh day in which divine grace refreshes us; it is the seventh month [Col. 0628B] in which, after the flood of temptations, the ark of the heart rests sweetly. Temperance serves it, prudence keeps watch for it, fortitude fights for it, and justice ministers to it.

## CHAPTER IX. (*Mirror*, book III, chapter 1.) On the distinction of the three Sabbaths.

We read in the Old Testament of certain distinctions among Sabbaths. In the Law you have three periods consecrated by Sabbath rest: namely, the seventh day, the seventh year, and, after seven times seven, the fiftieth year. Thus the first is the Sabbath of days, the second of years, and the third is not improperly called the Sabbath of Sabbaths. For it consists of seven Sabbaths of years, with one added, so that the number seven may be enclosed in unity—a number which proceeds from unity and is perfected in unity.

For every good work begins from faith in the one God and is advanced by the sevenfold gift of the Holy Spirit, so that one may come to him who is truly one, where all that we are may become one with him. Meanwhile, we have the Sabbath of days, the Sabbath of years, and, in a certain foretaste, the Sabbath of Sabbaths.

## CHAPTER X. (*Mirror*, book III, chapter 2.) That the distinction of these Sabbaths must be sought in threefold love.

In the Law it is thus written: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind; and your neighbour as yourself. On these two commandments hang the whole Law and the prophets” (Matt. 22). We must therefore seek in these two commandments the distinctions of the Sabbaths, for they too come from the Law. Now, if you examine these two commandments carefully, you find that three things are to be loved: namely yourself, your neighbour, and God. For where it is said, “You shall love your neighbour as yourself,” it is clear that you ought to love yourself also. Yet this is not a commandment, because it is implanted by nature. For, as the Apostle testifies, “No one ever hated his own flesh” (Eph. 5); and if not his flesh, much less his mind, which everyone, even unknowingly, loves more than the flesh. For there is no one who would not rather live weak in body than unsound in mind.

Let love of oneself, then, be for a person the first Sabbath; love of one’s neighbour the second; and love of God the Sabbath of Sabbaths. The Sabbath, as we said above, is spiritual rest: repose of soul, peace of heart, tranquillity of mind. This Sabbath is sometimes experienced in the love of oneself; sometimes it is drawn from the sweetness of brotherly love; and in divine love it is brought to completion without any ambiguity. This, indeed, must be provided for: that a person love himself as he ought, his neighbour as himself, and God above himself; for he loves neither himself nor his neighbour except for God’s sake. Moreover, the person who does not love his neighbour is proved not to love God. For “he who does not love the brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see?” (1 John 4).

Thus, in a certain sense, love of neighbour precedes love of God; and love of oneself precedes love of neighbour. It precedes, I say, in order, not in dignity. It precedes—but that perfect love of which it is said: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind.” For surely some portion of this love, though not its fullness, must necessarily precede both the love of oneself and the love of one’s neighbour; without it, both are dead and therefore are nothing.

For it seems to me that the love of God is, as it were, the soul of the other loves: it lives most fully in itself, communicates its life-giving essence to the others, and, when absent, brings death. Thus, when a person loves himself, the love of God is begun in him; when he loves his neighbour, it is conceived, as it were, in a more capacious bosom. There the divine fire, gradually gathering strength, finally absorbs the other loves—like so many little sparks—into its own fullness in a wonderful way, drawing the whole love of the soul toward that sublime and ineffable Good, where neither the person himself nor his neighbour is loved except insofar as each, failing to remain in himself, is wholly transferred into God.

Meanwhile, these three loves are conceived from one another, nourished by one another, and kindled by one another; yet all are perfected together. It happens in a wonderful and ineffable manner that, although all three loves are possessed together—for it cannot be otherwise—they are not always felt equally. At one time that rest and delight are felt in the purity of one’s own conscience; at another, they are derived from the sweetness of brotherly love; at another, they are more fully attained in the contemplation of God. For just as a king who possesses various storehouses of spices enters now one, now another, and is suffused now with the fragrance of one kind, now of another, so the mind, retaining within the bounds of its conscience certain storehouses filled with spiritual delights, ranges now through this, now through that, and according to the diversity of its riches varies the substance of its joy.

## CHAPTER XI  
*(Book III of the Mirror, chapter 3.) How the spiritual Sabbath is experienced in love of oneself.*

When a person has withdrawn from outward tumult into the inner chamber of the mind, and nothing troubled, nothing disordered, nothing that gnaws at him, nothing that barks against him occurs; but all things are pleasant, harmonious, peaceful, tranquil; and, as in some most orderly and peaceable household, the whole throng of thoughts, words, and deeds smiles upon the soul itself as upon the master of the house—then there suddenly arises a wonderful security, from security a wonderful joy, and from joy a kind of jubilation, breaking forth all the more devoutly into the praises of God as it more keenly perceives that whatever good it recognizes in itself is God’s gift.

This is the delightful solemnity of the seventh day. It must be preceded by the perfection of six days—that is, of works—so that we may first toil in good works and only then rest in tranquillity of conscience. For purity of conscience arises from good works, and love of oneself is judged according to that purity. For just as one who works or loves iniquity does not love but hates his own soul [Col. 0630B] (Ps. 10), so surely one who loves and works righteousness does not hate but loves his own soul. This is the delightful solemnity of that first Sabbath: in it the servile works of the world are not performed; in it neither is the fire of shameful desire kindled nor are the burdens of passions carried.

## CHAPTER XII  
*(Book III of the Mirror, chapter 4.) What kind of Sabbath is obtained from brotherly love, and how the six years preceding the seventh are fitted to charity.*

But if, from this more secret chamber in which he celebrated this first Sabbath, he transfers himself to that lodging-place of his breast where he is accustomed to “rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep” (Rom. 12), to be weak with the weak, to burn with those who are scandalized; and if there he feels his soul united with the souls of all his brothers by the glue of charity—agitated by no stings of envy, inflamed by no heats of indignation, worn down by no darts of suspicion, consumed by no bites of devouring grief—and thus draws all into a certain most tranquil bosom of his mind, where he embraces and cherishes all with a sweet affection and makes with them one heart and one soul, then, at once, at the most sweet taste of this sweetness, all the tumult of desires falls silent and the noise of vices comes to rest. There is then, inwardly, a release from all harmful things and a welcome, delightful repose in the sweetness of brotherly love.

In the rest and sweetness of this Sabbath, the prophet David burst forth in the sound of rejoicing solemnity, saying: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity!” (Ps. 132). Truly good, truly pleasant: good indeed, because nothing is more useful; pleasant, because nothing is sweeter.

But if you wish to draw forth something mystical from those six years which precede this spiritual Sabbath, know that there are six classes of persons in whose love the soul must be exercised. First, therefore, our love is directed, in the natural order, toward those of our own blood. Since such love is implanted in nature itself, it is exceedingly inhuman if it is absent. Hence the Apostle: “If anyone does not provide for his own, and especially for those of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever” (1 Tim. 5).

Because this love proceeds from nature itself, it is established first among the commandments that concern love of neighbour, as God himself declares: “Honour your father and your mother” (Exod. 20). From this, our love advances toward those joined to us by a special bond of friendship or by reciprocal duty, and is, as it were, expanded into a wider embrace. Certainly both these loves, though their observance earns little reward—for natural law impels us to the one and grace bestowed upon us summons us to the other—nonetheless bring an increase of condemnation when neglected. Of these the Lord says in the Gospel: “If you love those who love you, what reward will you have? Do not even the heathen do this? And if you greet only your brothers, what more do you do?” (Matt. 5).

Therefore, that our love may tend toward something greater, it should embrace also those who are subjected with us to the same yoke of profession. This love indeed will not be deprived of reward, because God is the reason why it is shown. There still remain two classes of persons: those who are outside—namely Gentiles and Jews, heretics and schismatics. We must grieve for their ignorance, sympathize with their weakness, lament their wickedness, and impart to them, with pious affection, the consolation of our prayer, so that they too may be found with us in Christ Jesus our Lord.

From there one must proceed to that in which the summit of brotherly charity consists, in which a person becomes a son of God, in which the likeness of divine goodness is more fully restored. As the Saviour says in the Gospel: “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute and slander you, that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven” (ibid.). What then remains except the seventh year, in which we are not permitted to demand repayment from debtors, and in which a slave is granted freedom? For the one who knows how to look even upon enemies with a single eye is the one who can truly say: “Forgive us, as we also forgive” (Matt. 6). “Everyone who commits sin,” he says, “is a slave of sin” (John 5); and each person is bound to that lamentable slavery until, forgiving and loving, he is forgiven and loved, and from being a slave becomes not only free but also a friend.

## CHAPTER XIII  
*(Book III of the Mirror, chapter 6.) How the perfect Sabbath is found in love of God, and how the fiftieth year is compared to this love.*

But the mind, purified by this twofold love, hastens all the more devoutly, because more securely, toward the blessed embraces of the Godhead itself. Inflamed by excessive desire, it passes beyond the veil of the flesh and is wholly absorbed by that ineffable light and unfamiliar sweetness. When it has become silent with regard to all bodily things, all sensible things, and all changeable things, it fixes one penetrating gaze upon that which is, and thus always is, and is directed toward itself; resting and seeing that the Lord himself is God, it keeps Sabbath without doubt in the Sabbath of Sabbaths among those sweet embraces of charity.

This is the year of jubilee, in which one returns to one’s own possession—namely, to one’s own Creator—so that one may be possessed and possess, be possessed and have, be held and hold. This is that possession which had been alienated for the cheap price of sin, when human love flowed away from him by whom it was made and clung to a thing that was made.

The number fifty is not without reason dedicated to this Sabbath. In it servile fear is driven out; not only the desire of the flesh, but even its remembrance, is put to sleep; and the fullness of the Spirit is conceived. “Before,” he says—that is, before Pentecost—“the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus was not yet glorified” (John 7): not that he had not been given at all, but not with such fullness or such perfection. He is indeed given in the first Sabbath and in the second; but in the Sabbath of Sabbaths his fullness is poured out.

But because charity is poured out in hearts (Rom. 5) only through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us, the number seven is everywhere retained; yet the progress of charity itself is discerned in the multiplication of that number seven. For the seventh day is, as it were, the beginning of charity; the seventh year, its advancement; and the fiftieth year, which comes after seven times seven, its fullness. In each there is rest; in each, release from work; in each, a certain spiritual Sabbath-keeping. First, there is rest in purity of conscience; then, in the sweetest union of many minds; finally, in the contemplation of God himself. In the first Sabbath one is free from sin; in the second, from covetousness; in the third, from every distraction whatsoever. In the first the mind is gathered into itself; in the second it is extended outside itself; in the third it is carried above itself. In the first it tastes how sweet Jesus is in his humanity; in the second it sees how perfect he is in charity; in the third, how exalted he is in divinity.

## CHAPTER XIV  
*(Book III of the Mirror, chapter 5.) How both kinds of love, namely of oneself and of one’s neighbour, are preserved by love of God.*

Since, as we said above, both forms of love—by which we either care for ourselves or are united with our neighbours—must be enlivened by some share of divine love, it must be understood that the love of God moves and advances us toward this twofold love, according to the saying: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1).

For innocence, which consists in two things, is acquired in this twofold love. Innocent is the person who harms neither himself nor another. But one harms himself who corrupts himself with the stain of some vice or shameful act. Since pleasure and bodily delight especially urge one toward this corruption, anyone readily rejects or avoids it if, clothed with a devout affection toward the flesh of our Saviour, he rejoices to behold with spiritual eyes the Lord of majesty stooping down to the narrowness of a manger, longing for virginal breasts, held in maternal embraces, kissed by the blessed lips of the trembling old man, holy Simeon (Luke 2). Whoever finds it sweet to picture to the gaze of his mind how gentle he was in appearance, how sweet in speech, how compassionate toward sinners, how condescending toward the lowly and miserable—who is there for whom, at such a sweet spectacle, every delight of foul flesh does not become disgusting?

From this certain sweet tears readily arise, by which every heat of desires is quenched: the flesh cools, the voracity of the belly is moderated, and every tickling of vanities is subdued. Moreover, toward the love of enemies—in which the perfection of brotherly charity consists—nothing so strongly encourages us as grateful consideration of that wondrous patience by which he, “fairer in form than the sons of men” (Ps. 44), offered his lovely face to be spat upon by the ungodly; by which he subjected to the covering of wicked men those eyes by whose command all things are governed; by which he exposed his sides to scourges; by which he submitted his head, terrible to principalities and powers, to the harshness of thorns; by which he surrendered himself to insults and outrages; by which he patiently endured the cross, nails, spear, gall, and vinegar—gentle, mild, and tranquil in all things.

Finally, “he was led as a sheep to the slaughter, and as a lamb before its shearer was silent, and he opened not his mouth” (Isa. 53). Consider, O human pride, O proud impatience, who endured, why he endured, and how he endured. I beg you: let these things be thought upon, not written down. Who is there whose anger does not at once cool at this wonderful sight? Who, hearing that wonderful voice, full of sweetness, charity, and tranquillity—“Father, forgive them”—does not immediately embrace his enemies with all his affection?

“Father,” he says, “forgive them.” What could be added to this prayer in gentleness or charity? Yet he added something. It was too little to pray; he wished also to excuse them: “Father,” he says, “forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23). They think him a transgressor of the Law; they think him a presumptuous claimant to divinity; they think him a seducer of the people. “I hid my face from them; they did not acknowledge my majesty.” Therefore, Father, forgive them, because they do not know what they are doing.

Therefore, that a person may love himself, he must not corrupt himself with any delight of the flesh; and, so that he may not succumb to fleshly desire, he must direct all his affection to the sweetness of the Lord’s flesh. Moreover, that he may rest more perfectly and sweetly in the delight of brotherly charity, he should embrace even enemies in the arms of true love. But lest this divine fire grow cool under the breath of injuries, let him always behold with the eyes of his mind the tranquil patience of his Lord and Saviour.

## CHAPTER XV  
*In what things we should believe the love of God to consist.*

God says in the Gospel: “He who has my commandments and keeps them, he is the one who loves me” (John 14). The love of God is not to be assessed according to momentary feelings, but rather according to the enduring disposition of the human will itself. To join one’s own will to God’s will, so that whatever the divine will prescribes the human will may consent to it; so that there may be no other reason for willing this or that except because one knows that God wills it—this indeed is to love God. For will itself is nothing other than love; and good or evil wills are nothing other than good or evil loves.

This will must certainly be judged according to two things: namely endurance and action—whether it patiently bears those things which God has brought upon it or has permitted to be brought upon it, and fervently fulfils those things which he has commanded. Otherwise, as blessed Gregory says (*Homilies on the Gospels*, Homily 30), let no one believe whatever the mind may say to itself about the love of God without works.

Therefore, whoever’s will agrees with God’s will, patiently bears what God has brought upon him, fervently carries out what God has commanded, and, as far as he can, strives to possess God by obeying his commandments, “living soberly, righteously, and godly” (Titus 2)—such a person must without any hesitation be said to love God. For this is the judgment of him who does not lie: “He who has my commandments and keeps them, he is the one who loves me.”

This love has its beginning, its progress, and its perfection. It matters, indeed, how affectionate, discerning, and strong a person is in this love: affectionate, that he may love sweetly; discerning, that he may love prudently; strong, that he may love perseveringly. Affectionate, so that what he has chosen may be sweet in desire; discerning, lest he exceed due measure in action; strong, lest any temptation turn him away from it. Affection is useful against perverse pleasures, discernment against deceptions, strength against persecutions. If anyone is known to be perfect in these three, he loves not only happily but also sweetly. But if he cannot be affectionate, let him nevertheless be discerning and strong; and, if not toward present sweetness, he will nevertheless advance no less toward future blessedness.

## CHAPTER XVI  
*(Book III of the Mirror, chapters 8 and 9.) In what right or perverse love consists.*

This love consists in three things: choice, movement, and fruition. Choice comes from reason; movement lies in desire and action; fruition lies in the end. Love always has reason as its companion, not because it always loves rationally, but because by its keen discernment it distinguishes what it chooses from what it rejects. It belongs to reason to distinguish between Creator and creature, temporal and eternal things, bitter and sweet things, harsh and pleasant things; but it belongs to love to choose for enjoyment what it wills.

For if the mind, enticed by the experience of any pleasure or deceived by any error whatever, chooses for enjoyment things that ought not in the least to be enjoyed, it surely loves unhappily. By *enjoyment* (*frui*) we mean using something with delight and joy. Immediately after, or even alongside, this choice follows the hidden movement of love itself, which in some fashion awakens and moves the mind toward desire for that thing which it considered ought to be chosen. But if it desires the thing it has chosen for enjoyment and obtains it as it wishes, it immediately rests with joy and delight in the use of it; and this use we call fruition.

Thus charity or cupidity appears to consist in these three things: namely in the choice of the mind, in movement, and in fruition. Choice is the beginning of love, whether good or evil; movement is the course of love itself; fruition is love’s end. If, therefore, the mind chooses for enjoyment what it ought, moves toward it as it ought, and enjoys it as is fitting, then such a wholesome choice, such a fitting movement, and such a beneficial fruition are rightly judged worthy of the name charity. Charity begins in this choice, extends itself in movement, and is perfected in fruition. But if the soul chooses foolishly, moves through desire improperly, and makes shameful use of what it has chosen, it is easy to see that cupidity is brought to completion by these, as it were, stages.

These are the two sources, the origins of good and evil; for “cupidity is the root of all evils” (1 Tim. 6), and charity the root of all goods. This, however, must be said: we should not be said to love everything that we choose for our use, but only that which we choose for enjoyment. Therefore God must be chosen before all things, so that we may enjoy him; this is the beginning of love. He must be desired before all things; this is, as it were, the course and advancement of love itself. In attaining him, because the love of the perfect Good will be perfect, blessedness too will be perfect.

Thus two things must be chosen by us for love: God and neighbour, though not in the same manner. God is to be loved so that we may enjoy him in himself and for his own sake; our neighbour, so that we may enjoy him in God—indeed, so that we may enjoy God in him as well. For although this word *enjoy* (*frui*) is usually taken more strictly, so that one says that nothing but God alone is to be enjoyed, Paul, speaking to a human being, nevertheless says: “Yes, brother, let me enjoy you in the Lord” (Philem. 20).

When reason has seen that these two things are to be chosen, and when, despising all other things through contemplation of them, the consent of the mind has chosen them, then love of God and neighbour has certainly begun, because love itself has been turned toward what it ought to pursue.

## CHAPTER XVII  
*(Book III of the Mirror, chapter 10.) That our love moves toward action and desire, and that it is moved toward these two sometimes by affection, sometimes by reason.*

The movement of love is toward two things: inwardly, toward desire; or outwardly, toward action. It moves toward desire when the mind stretches itself by an inward movement and appetite toward that which it has judged ought to be enjoyed. It moves toward action when a certain hidden force of love itself compels the mind to do outwardly what it loves.

Accordingly, I think we must investigate what things, as it were by incentives, arouse and move love itself toward these two ends; and what, in some manner, orders and prescribes its course. Then we must inquire more carefully what it ought to follow, or how far it ought to follow; what it should reject, what admit, what diminish, and what increase, so that this movement itself may be fitting.

There are, as it seems to me, two things by which the soul is moved and aroused toward those two things that we have set forth: affection and reason. Sometimes our love is inflamed outwardly toward action or secretly toward desire by affection alone; sometimes by reason alone. Therefore, that we may see which of all the movements by which our love is variously altered is especially to be followed, let us first speak briefly of the twofold origin of its movement, namely affection and reason.

## CHAPTER XVIII  
*(Book III of the Mirror, chapter 11.) What affection is, and how many kinds of affection there are; and how spiritual affection is understood in two ways.*

Affection, then, is a certain spontaneous and sweet inclination of the soul itself toward someone. Affection is either spiritual, rational, irrational, dutiful, natural, or carnal.

Spiritual affection may be understood in two ways. For the soul is aroused by a spiritual affection when, through a hidden and, as it were, sudden visitation of the Holy Spirit, the mind, pierced with compunction, melts into the sweetness of divine love or the sweetness of brotherly charity. Again, an affection generated by the instigation of the devil may be called spiritual. By this affection Amnon, David’s son, burned for the embraces of his own sister. By this affection also those are known to have been enticed to shameful things, of whom the prophet says: “A spirit of fornication deceived them” (Hos. 4). For with a twofold torment the most unclean enemy pursues the chastity of the saints: now setting the flesh aflame with an intolerable fire, now dissolving the mind by the affection of destructive sweetness.

## CHAPTER XIX  
*(Book III of the Mirror, chapter 12.) On rational and irrational affection.*

Rational affection is that which arises from consideration of another’s virtue: namely, when some person’s virtue or holiness, investigated by our own eyes, made known by public report, or learned through trustworthy reading, suffuses our mind with a certain sweet delight. This is the affection which pierces us with sweetest devotion when we hear of the triumphant suffering of martyrs, and which paints before our eyes, in delightful meditation, the memorable deeds of those who have gone before.

Contrary to this affection is irrational affection, by which anyone is moved toward another through a certain inclination of the mind when that person’s vice has become known. For many, whether through the emptiest philosophy, the most foolish boldness in military affairs, or any wickedness whatever, entice and draw toward themselves the affection of others.

## CHAPTER XX  
*(Book III of the Mirror, chapter 13.) On dutiful affection.*

We call dutiful affection that which is produced by the benefit of gifts or services. For many have won to themselves the hearts of others either by the advantage of gifts bestowed or by the rendering of services.

## CHAPTER XXI  
*(Book III of the Mirror, chapter 14.) On natural affection.*

Natural affection belongs to everyone toward his own flesh, to a mother toward her son, and to a person toward members of his own household and blood. For “No one ever hated his own flesh” (Eph. 5); “Can a mother forget her infant?” (Isa. 49); and “He who does not provide for those of his own household has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever” (1 Tim. 5).

## CHAPTER XXII  
*(Book III of the Mirror, chapter 15.) On carnal affection, understood in two ways.*

Carnal affection is twofold. For often it is not virtue or vice, but some quality of the outward person, that inclines toward itself the mind of the observer. A more elegant appearance, sweeter speech, a dignified gait, or a graceful countenance easily draws out and captivates affection, even in one who does not know what sort of person the other is. This grace shone so greatly in Moses as a child that, contrary to Pharaoh’s command, he was kept by his parents for three months, as the Apostle says (Heb. 11; Exod. 2), because they saw that the infant was beautiful. When he was likewise exposed to danger, the beauty of his appearance attracted the compassion even of Pharaoh’s daughter; adopted by her as a son, he became great before all Pharaoh’s servants.

But whoever is wickedly enticed toward harmful pleasure by an alluring sweetness in any appearance, no person of sound judgment will doubt that he is moved by carnal affection. This carnal affection found David, walking on the roof of his house, unguarded before the sight of Bathsheba; having found him unguarded, it dissolved him; having dissolved him, it overwhelmed him (2 Kings 11). This affection swallowed up Solomon’s wisdom (3 Kings 11), and, having dissolved him in carnal lust, cast him down into the abyss of spiritual fornication, the most abominable worship of idols.

## CHAPTER XXIII  
*(Book III of the Mirror, chapter 16.) What should be thought concerning these affections.*

These affections occur to one in reflection. I would call them certain origins or roots of love, not love itself. For we do not consider it especially praiseworthy to be aroused or stirred by these affections if they are good, nor fatal if they are evil. For even excellent men are sometimes tickled by carnal affection—the most fearsome of all the others—for the merit of their testing. Therefore, we judge it useful or harmful not to be moved by these affections, but to be formed by them.

For when these affections move the soul, there is visitation in the case of good affections, or temptation in that of evil ones. When the soul is disposed according to these affections, there is full consent of the will itself. Consent is either hidden or manifest: hidden, when it is agitated inwardly by the consent of desire; manifest, when desire itself breaks outwardly into action. But whether our love ought to be moved according to these affections, or how far it ought to be moved, we shall try to investigate—if first we have said a few things about reason, which we called another cause of love.

## CHAPTER XXIV  
*(Book III of the Mirror, chapters 17 and 18.) How the mind is moved by reason toward love of God and neighbour.*

For a mind which no affection moves toward love of God and neighbour is often moved by reason—indeed, all the more sacredly because more securely; more securely because more purely; and more purely because nothing can be more useful or more pure than rational love.

Reason therefore first persuades the rational creature to love the Creator, without whom it must necessarily always be miserable and with whom it cannot fail to be always most blessed. If the mind consents to this reasoning and arouses itself to desire God, reason immediately carries forward its work, proving that one must earnestly persevere in fulfilling God’s commandments if one wishes to attain the object of desire. Thus desire, innate in the inmost parts, proceeds to action under reason’s compulsion.

Since among God’s commandments the greatest is found to be that one’s neighbour should be loved (Matt. 22), reason urges that the soul should move itself to confer benefit upon its neighbour. Every neighbour is either a friend, not an enemy, or an enemy. A friend is such because he does good or has done good; one who is not an enemy, because he does no harm and has done none; an enemy, because he does harm or has done harm. A friend may be so by blood or by grace; one who is not an enemy, by innocence; an enemy, by injury.

Therefore, reason sets before a person three considerations for giving himself to a friend, two for giving himself to one who is not an enemy, and one for giving himself to an enemy. A friend is owed kindness by nature, by duty, and by commandment: by nature, because he is a human being, or even a member of one’s household; by duty, because he is a friend; by commandment, because he is a neighbour. One who is not an enemy is owed kindness by nature, because he is human, and by commandment, because he is a neighbour. An enemy is owed it only by commandment, because it is the Lord’s command that an enemy be loved (Matt. 5).

If, yielding to these reasons, the soul prepares itself to confer benefit not only on a friend but also on an enemy, it will not lose its merit, even if it does not feel the affection of charity. Thus these two loves must be distinguished: one proceeding from affection, the other from reason. This distinction also resolves the question asked by some: namely, what is the difference between love which is in God and that which is shown for God’s sake.

For affection is not assumed for God’s sake, but arises in the soul either naturally or accidentally. Therefore, if all love according to that affection is shown to the person toward whom the mind pours itself out in a spontaneous and sweet inclination, that person is loved neither in God nor for God’s sake, but rather for his own sake. But if the person embraced by this affection is at the same time taken up into the love of God, and the love itself has sweetness from affection while its expression depends upon the moderation of reason, then this person’s love is not first assumed for God’s sake, but is healthfully exercised in God.

But if, toward one whom this affection rejects and avoids, we offer ourselves as we ought through consideration of the divine commandment, and grant, according to his need, whatever reason dictates, he is loved not for his own sake but only for God’s sake. Therefore, let the friend, who cannot but be loved, be loved in God; let the enemy, who cannot be loved for his own sake, be loved for God’s sake: the former from affection, the latter from reason.

## CHAPTER XXV  
*(Book III of the Mirror, chapter 19.) That affections are not placed within our power.*

Something further must be said concerning these affections: they are by no means placed within our power, since we are sometimes moved by certain of them wholly against our will and cannot experience certain others even if we wish to do so. Therefore love proceeds from affection not when affection has moved the mind, but when the mind has directed that movement in accordance with affection. The same judgment must be made concerning the movement generated by reason.

## CHAPTER XXVI  
*(Book III of the Mirror, chapter 20.) That there are three loves: from affection, from reason, and from both.*

Love from affection exists when the soul consents to affection; love from reason, when the will joins itself to reason. A third love may be formed from these two, when reason, affection, and will come together as one. The first is sweet but dangerous; the second hard but fruitful; the third perfect through the prerogative of both. Sense entices toward the first through sweetness; manifest reason compels toward the second; in the third, reason itself becomes sweet.

This last differs from the first because, although in the first that which ought to be loved is sometimes loved, it is loved more for the sweetness of the affection itself. In the latter, however, it is loved not because it is sweet, but because it is worthy of love and therefore sweet.

## CHAPTER XXVII  
*(Book III of the Mirror, chapter 21.) What it is to love.*

Let us therefore briefly gather from all that has been said wherein the whole force of love consists. First, if the mind chooses something for enjoyment; then stretches itself toward it by a certain inward desire; and finally does that by which it is able to attain what it desires—then it must without doubt be said to love. The more fervently and persistently anyone accomplishes this, the more he loves.

If he does this from affection, he loves more sweetly and therefore acts more easily. But if one person does by affection what another does wholly by reason alone, the latter loves with less sweetness, but will not attain what he desires more slowly.

## CHAPTER XXVIII  
*(Book III of the Mirror, chapter 22.) What discernment must be observed in love of one’s neighbour.*
[Col. 0639D] If, therefore, we choose our neighbour for fellowship in that enjoyment which is in God, this choice is sound. But if a shameful desire or disordered action follows this choice, the whole soundness of the choice is stained. Moreover, if the choice itself is perverse—so that it chooses for enjoyment what ought not to be chosen—then those things which follow upon that choice will plainly also be perverse; and such love will be perverse, deserving the name of cupidity rather than charity. But whatever else the mind, whether enticed or deceived, chooses to enjoy—apart from God in himself, and one’s neighbour in God—goes beyond the bounds of true love. Let the choice, therefore, be sound, the desire fitting, and the action rational; and thus it will not exceed the limit of charity. Indeed, desire itself ought to extend in two directions, and action likewise ought to be exercised in a twofold manner. For desire ought to be directed to this: that, as is fitting, we may mutually enjoy one another in God; [Col. 0640A] and that we may mutually enjoy God in himself. Since a human being consists of body and soul, our action, so far as ability permits, ought certainly to provide for both. In these matters, the more fervent and prudent a person is, the more perfect he is in charity; and the more affectionate he is, the sweeter charity itself is shown to be. But just as, as we have said, affection sometimes moves us toward these things, and reason sometimes does, so it strives to order both modes of desire and action according to their proper character. Therefore careful consideration is needed, that we may see which affections are to be followed, and how far they are to be followed.

## CHAPTER XXIX. (Book III of the *Mirror*, chapter 23.) Which affections are not to be admitted, and which are to be followed.

[Col. 0640B] Thus, the spiritual affection that comes from the devil; the irrational affection that arises from vice; and the carnal affection that leads to vice—these three affections are not merely not to be followed, but not even admitted; indeed, so far as possible, they must be uprooted from our hearts. But the spiritual affection that comes from God is not only to be admitted, but stirred up and increased in every possible way.

This affection has the special quality that it generally knows no measure, does not calculate human strength, absorbs bodily feelings, and, rushing blindly upon the beloved with a certain force, meditates only upon what it desires and despises everything outside it.
