It undertakes even what is burdensome, arduous, and even impossible, as though it were light and effortless work; and, because of the delight of inward love, does not feel the most grievous injuries of the outward person. [Col. 0640C] Therefore, in order that the will may grow warm with unceasing fervour, and that one may bear patiently—indeed, joyfully—the sufferings inflicted from without, this impetus of affection must be endured as far as the movement of desire itself. But when it proceeds to voluntary actions, it must be restrained by the governance of reason, lest it exceed the limits of bodily possibility.

For excess in inward holiness is not to be feared; but the outward practice of virtues, concerning which it is said, “Do not be excessively righteous” (Eccles. VII), must be moderated by reason. In action, reason must always be consulted; affection must not be followed.

## CHAPTER XXX. (Book III of the *Mirror*, chapter 24.) How far rational affection is to be followed.

[Col. 0640D]

Rational affection, then, which arises from contemplation of another’s virtue, is evidently more perfect than the other affections by which we are inflamed toward love of our neighbour. For love of virtue itself is no small indication of virtue. Accordingly, it is most beneficial to consent to this affection: both for the emulation of the virtues themselves, which is more readily aroused by such affection, and because vices become loathsome through diligent consideration of virtues.

Nor do I judge our desire harmful or injurious if it is guided by this affection. For it does no harm—indeed, it is very advantageous—to desire the presence of someone by whose example we may be corrected if we are bad, advanced if we are good, or, if equally [Col. 0641A] perfect, strengthened by mutual interchange. The temporal presence of saints is indeed to be desired; but still more that eternal presence which shall be with Christ in heaven. We strive toward it not by traversing earthly distances, but by living soberly, righteously, and devoutly (Tit. II).

## CHAPTER XXXI. (Book III of the *Mirror*, chapter 25.) In what respect dutiful affection must be guarded against, and in what respect it must be admitted.

Next comes dutiful affection, more dangerous than the other affections that may be admitted. It should indeed be admitted, but guarded against most carefully: admitted, lest you prove ungrateful for a service; guarded against, lest it be bestowed not so much upon the person as upon vice. For what must be guarded against more than this: that, softened by services or enticed by gifts, you should either foster vices or favour a vicious person?

Therefore, [Col. 0641B] although great discernment must be exercised in receiving gifts or services, one must take care to examine the dignity of the person more diligently; so that, if perhaps that person deserves it, the dutiful affection itself may pass into rational affection, and the person whom we began to love because he was agreeable to us may begin to be loved because he is adorned with virtues. The return of services or gifts must likewise be rendered according to reason, not according to affection. And let the desire by which the beloved’s presence is desired, or the action by which that presence is obtained, follow reason rather than affection. The affection itself which spontaneously embraces a person without regard to another cause must also be moderated in every respect.

## CHAPTER XXXII. (Book III of the *Mirror*, chapter 26.) What measure must be observed in natural affection.

[Col. 0641C]

Let us now inquire more carefully what measure must be observed in natural affection. Just as it is impossible not to admit this affection, so not to follow it is the height of virtue. For this affection always suggests what is soft and pleasant: it gladly embraces what is agreeable, tender, pleasurable, and delicate; but it flees and avoids with every horror what is arduous, harsh, or contrary to the will. Therefore, yielding to this affection is perverse love.

This love is forbidden by the authority of the Saviour when he says: “He who loves his life shall lose it; and he who hates his life in this world shall keep it unto eternal life” (John XII). Accordingly, [Col. 0641D] as that holy man says: “If you love badly, then you hate; if you hate rightly, then you love” (St Augustine, *Tractates on John*, tract. 51). One who loves his life according to affection surely hates it, because “he who loves iniquity hates his own soul” (Ps. X). But one who hates it according to affection loves it according to reason.

For this reason he added, “in this world,” because all that is in the world is either the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, or the pride of life (John XII). Therefore, one who loves his life in this world according to affection loves it because he loves the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life—all of which affection suggests. The two kinds of love of which we spoke above must therefore be distinguished: one according to affection, the other according to reason.

It is natural [Col. 0642A] that a person should have affection for himself and his own; but he ought not to have love according to affection, while he ought to have love according to reason. Affection itself is indicated when the Apostle says: “No one ever hated his own flesh” (Eph. V). But love according to affection is forbidden by the Saviour’s own words: “Whoever comes to me and does not hate father and mother, and even his own life, cannot be my disciple” (Luke XIV). Love according to reason is commanded when the same Apostle says: “Whoever does not provide for his own, and especially for members of his household, has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever” (I Tim. V). Love according to affection is reproved when the same Paul, foretelling future evils, says among other things: “People will be lovers of themselves, covetous, proud, lovers of pleasures [Col. 0642B] rather than lovers of God” (II Tim. III). Let this, then, be the measure observed in natural affection: that it be possessed and felt, but in all things and through all things moderated by the governance of reason.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. (Book III of the *Mirror*, chapters 27 and 28.) On carnal affection: that it is neither to be rejected altogether nor fully admitted.

Carnal affection, produced by a certain beauty of the outward person, is neither to be rejected altogether nor admitted so freely as to pour itself out without restraint. For that affection which leads to vices is near to it; and unless this one is more prudently guarded against, the other slips in almost without one’s noticing its birth.

This affection, therefore, is beneficially admitted only if it is admitted in a restrained and temperate fashion: namely, so that if virtue shines in the person, one may embrace it more readily; but if vice does, one may labour vigorously for its correction. For just as falsehood must not be admitted in pleasant speech, and truth must not be despised in harsh and rustic speech, so likewise vice must not please in a person adorned outwardly, nor virtue displease in one who is harsh and austere. Whatever we have said concerning dutiful affection should also, in our judgment, be understood concerning carnal affection.

Yet this affection is wisely rejected by those who are still assailed by carnal vices, since they very rarely experience it without the stimulation of vice. Therefore, when our affection—even though rational or spiritual—has shown itself in relation to a suspicious age or sex, [Col. 0642D] it is most prudent to restrain it within the inward recess of the mind and not allow it to flow forth into vain caresses and soft endearments—unless perhaps it sometimes advances purposefully and temperately in order that the virtue loved and praised may be practised more fervently.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. (Book III of the *Mirror*, chapter 29.) That diverse affections often contend within a single mind.

We must also speak of these affections, since several sometimes fight within one mind and, as it were, strive to overcome one another. When this happens, great discernment is needed in order to recognize which ought to be preferred to which, and virtue is necessary lest the higher be driven out by the lower.

Thus Abraham, when commanded to sacrifice his own son, did not harden himself against his own flesh and blood as one devoid of natural affection. Rather, when natural affection, by which he embraced his son, and spiritual affection, by which he embraced God, struggled in the holy man’s heart, [Col. 0643A] he preferred the higher to the lower; indeed, for the higher’s sake he disregarded the lower.

The Apostle himself, when he said, “I was once wishing to be accursed from Christ for my brothers according to the flesh” (Rom. IX), disclosed the affection he felt, in order by setting forth his extraordinary charity to draw them to salvation; he did not state his considered judgment. Yet he spoke truthfully, because he expressed what he felt by affection. If he had afterwards said, “I would prefer the whole world to perish than that I alone should be separated from Christ,” he would likewise have spoken truthfully, because he would have disclosed the judgment of reason.

Our Saviour also, when from natural affection—according to which no one ever hated his own flesh (Eph. V)—he cried out, “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matt. XXVI), subjected it to the law of reason through the spiritual affection by which he always clung to the Father: “Nevertheless,” he said, “not as I will.” Thus from the affection which he voluntarily assumed from us and for us, he wished the hour of suffering to pass; but by the counsel of reason he himself brought it about that it should not pass. Therefore, this order must be maintained among these affections: that the affection by which our mind is stirred toward God be preferred to all the rest; then rational affection to dutiful affection, dutiful affection to natural affection, and natural affection to carnal affection.

## CHAPTER XXXV. (Book III of the *Mirror*, chapter 30.) On the usefulness of these affections.

[Col. 0643C] Having carefully considered what has been said about the distinction of affections, it is clear, I think, what usefulness is to be sought in them. Their purpose is that we may be stirred by these affections, as by certain spurs of love, toward desiring what ought to be loved; that, through the sweetness infused by these affections, we may hold love itself more sweetly and therefore more diligently; and that we may perform more delightfully the acts by which we strive toward what we desire, the more affectionately we perform them—and the more delightfully, the more fervently.

Yet although desire itself should be aroused according to affection, it should very rarely follow affection itself. Likewise, it is most useful to be stirred by affection toward the practice of good works, and to be sustained by affection in those works; but to order the works themselves according to affection is contrary to order. For desire itself is uniform according to reason; this is felt only in the love that arises from affection, whereas in that which arises from reason it is reckoned in the will alone.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. (Book III of the *Mirror*, chapter 39.) On the use of love.

It is clear from what has preceded that charity consists in this: that the mind choose for enjoyment what it ought, be moved as is fitting, and use it appropriately. We have sufficiently discussed choice and motion for the present; let us say something further about use. If choice is sound and motion whole, can use nevertheless be perverse? Yet in obtaining the one whom a person loves, both the motion may change and the estimation prove mistaken. For even with a right intention [Col. 0644A] and fitting motion, someone may obtain the presence of the person chosen for enjoyment, and yet in that enjoyment change both intention and movement and exceed the proper measure.

But because neighbours stand at diverse degrees and have diverse merits, we must ask whether we ought, or even can, enjoy all persons or at least some of them. There is a temporal enjoyment by which we may enjoy one another in this life, just as Paul enjoyed Philemon (Philem. 20); and there is an eternal enjoyment by which we shall enjoy one another in heaven, as angels enjoy one another through the pure unity of their minds.

Therefore, since to enjoy is to use with joy and delight, I think it clear that at present we cannot enjoy everyone, but only very few. For, as it seems to me, we can indeed use some people for testing, some for instruction, some for consolation, and some for support: enemies for testing, teachers for instruction, elders for consolation, and those who provide necessities for the sustenance of life. But we may enjoy, for life’s sweetness and the spirit’s delight, only those whom we embrace with a sweet affection, whatever class among these they may belong to. [Col. 0644B] We may therefore enjoy these even in the present, that is, use them with joy and delight.

Accordingly, in this life charity can be shown by everyone toward everyone insofar as choice and the movement expressed in action are concerned; but insofar as enjoyment is concerned, it can be shown toward everyone by few—or perhaps by no one. For few, if any, cherish the whole human race not merely with rational but also with affectionate love. Indeed, charity is shown to God by many both in choice and in movement, though the enjoyment of that love is not granted to them in this life but reserved after this life in his most blessed vision.

Even those in whom some beginning of this enjoyment of love is found in the light of contemplation or sweetness of compunction, if you look to the joys to come, should not be said to enjoy God himself but rather to use him. For it is sufficiently evident that the sweetest taste of that sweetness is granted to many not so much as the enjoyment of love as for the support of weakness.

But it is no slight consolation in this life to have someone with whom you can be united by an inward affection and the embrace of most sacred love; [Col. 0644D] to have someone in whom your spirit may rest, to whom your mind may pour itself out; to whose welcome conversations, like certain consoling songs, you may flee amid all sorrows; to whose most welcome bosom of friendship you may safely approach amid so many scandals of the age; to whose most loving heart, as if to your own self, you may entrust without hesitation the inmost contents of all your thoughts; with whose spiritual kisses, like medicinal fomentations, you may sweat out the languors of your turbulent cares; who may weep with you in anxieties, rejoice with you in prosperity, and seek with you amid uncertainties; whom you may introduce into the inner chamber of your mind, so that, although absent in body, that person may nevertheless be present in spirit; where, alone with one alone, you may converse all the more sweetly because more secretly; alone with one alone confer; and, with the sweetness of the Holy Spirit flowing between you, alone with one alone rest. Indeed, you may join and attach yourself to that person, and mingle mind with mind, so that from many [Col. 0645A] one may be made.

We can enjoy in the present those whom we love not only from reason but also from affection, especially among them those who are joined to us more intimately and closely than others by the most welcome bond of spiritual friendship. Lest this most sacred taste of charity seem blameworthy to anyone, Jesus himself, condescending to us in all things, granted to one—not to all—the resting-place of his most sweet breast as a sign of special love, so that a virgin head might be supported by the blossoms of a virgin breast, and that the fragrant mysteries of the heavenly bridal chamber, the fragrance of spiritual ointments, might be instilled into virgin affections more abundantly the nearer they were. Hence, although all the disciples were cherished by the most loving Master with the sweetness of highest charity, to this one was granted, by the prerogative of more familiar affection, the name by which he was called “that disciple whom Jesus loved” (John XIII). [Col. 0645B]

## CHAPTER XXXVII. (Book III of the *Mirror*, chapter 40.) How we ought mutually to enjoy one another.

Whoever finds it sweet to enjoy a friend, then, should see to it that he enjoys the friend in the Lord—not in the world, nor in fleshly pleasure, but in spiritual delight. But you ask what it is to enjoy in the Lord. The Apostle Paul says of the Lord: “Who was made to us by God wisdom and righteousness and sanctification” (I Cor. I). Therefore, since the Lord is wisdom, sanctification, and righteousness, to enjoy in the Lord is to enjoy in wisdom, to enjoy in sanctification, and to enjoy in righteousness.

By wisdom, worldly vanity is excluded; by sanctification, the filth of the flesh is cut away; by righteousness, every sort of flattery and adulation is restrained. For charity exists only if it is, as the Apostle says, “from a pure heart, and a good conscience, and unfeigned faith” (I Tim. I). Wisdom receives a pure heart; chastity makes the conscience serene; unfeigned faith adorns righteousness.

There are people who enjoy one another in frivolities and amusements, in the pomp of the age and spectacles of the world, in devotion to vanity and delight in falsehood. Such people do not enjoy one another in wisdom, and therefore not in him who is the power of God and the wisdom of God. Others have scarcely anything human left in them, being transformed into beasts by foul depravity; [Col. 0645D] they enjoy one another in luxurious banquets and unclean desires. Since they do not enjoy one another in sanctification, which consists in the sweetness of chastity, they certainly do not enjoy the Lord, who was made to us by God sanctification.

But those who enjoy one another flatteringly—mutually stroking and mutually agreeing with one another—while each avoids offending the other, incur mutual ruin, because they do not enjoy one another in the freedom of righteousness; they do not enjoy one another in the Lord. Let us therefore mutually enjoy one another in sanctification, so that each may know how to possess his own vessel, that is, his own body, in sanctification and honour, not in the passion of desire. Let us enjoy one another in righteousness, so that in a spirit of freedom we may mutually exhort and mutually correct one another, knowing that “the wounds of a friend are better [Col. 0646A] than the deceitful kisses of an enemy.”

Therefore, if mutual exchange of words delights us, let our conversation concern conduct; let it concern the Scriptures. Now let us groan together over the miseries of this life; now rejoice together in hope of future blessings; now be refreshed through disclosure of mutual secrets; now together long for that blessed vision of Jesus and the goods of heaven. But if, as is sometimes useful, we relax a strained mind with certain lower and pleasant things, let those relaxations themselves be full of honesty and empty of frivolity; and, if they lack excessive seriousness, let them nevertheless not lack edification.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. (Book III of the *Mirror*, chapter 31.) By what actions we ought to strive toward God and provide for our neighbours.

It remains for us to say briefly, according to our ability, how our actions ought to be ordered according to reason—those by which we either strive especially [Col. 0646B] toward God, or provide at once for our own needs and for the needs and salvation of our neighbours. The Apostle seems to have set forth the whole condition of the perfect life in a few words: “Let us live soberly, righteously, and devoutly in this age” (Tit. II).

Sobriety is a certain measure and moderation of human life, prudently avoiding either excess and guiding our course along the royal way between right and left. For the one toward whom we strive supremely is a supreme measure, lacking nothing, having nothing superfluous, and deficient in nothing. When we have reached him, there will be nothing outside us for which we may long, nor anything below that we may disdain. [Col. 0646C] It is therefore necessary that we keep ourselves within a certain measure and limit: neither falling below what is necessary nor being borne beyond what is fitting by destructive presumption.

Here I understand the Apostle to call justice that by which, when we provide for the needs or salvation of our neighbours and discern in those very benefits what suits each person and who ought to be preferred to whom, we render to each what is just. But lest philosophers or any persons estranged from faith in Christ should glory in these two virtues of sobriety and justice, he most wisely adds devotion, which consists in sincere faith and pure intention. That intention itself, moreover, seems to consist in the choice of love which has already been discussed.

Perhaps the reader will demand that we prescribe a rule of life for every individual. Who does not see how arduous and difficult this is to treat, since there are as many kinds of people as there are people, and not even two can be found for whom everything is equally fitting? For what is enough for one is too little for another; what benefits this person is lacking to that one; and what is necessary for one is plainly superfluous for another. Yet something should be said that suits everyone, which each person can apply to himself and by strict reasoning may judge whether he exceeds the proper measure of life.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. (Book III of the *Mirror*, chapter 32.) On the three orders of human conduct, and first on the natural order.

Thus three orders of human conduct present themselves: [Col. 0647A] the first natural, the second necessary, the third voluntary. The first is permitted; the second is commanded; the third is offered. The first proceeds from liberty, the second from necessity, the third from will. Grace is due to the first, mercy to the second, glory to the third.

The natural order is this: one who has committed nothing unlawful may, if he wishes, make use of lawful things, provided he does so lawfully. Lawful things include, for example, eating meat, drinking wine, marital intercourse, and possessing wealth. The Saviour himself prescribes a certain measure to be observed by all, not to be exceeded on any terms, saying: “Take heed lest your hearts be weighed down with gluttony and drunkenness and the cares of this life” (Luke XXI). Therefore, in the use of food and drink, this measure must be observed: in receiving them, each person must restrain himself below the point of gluttony and drunkenness. [Col. 0647B] A diligent inquirer will discover for himself what measure must be maintained in using the other things that people use lawfully. Let us now touch briefly upon the necessary order.

## CHAPTER XL. (Book III of the *Mirror*, chapter 33.) On the necessary order.

The necessary order is that one who has committed unlawful acts should restrain himself from the use of lawful things. In that restraint two matters must be considered: the measure of satisfaction and the necessity of purification. The measure of satisfaction requires that the rigour of continence be extended in proportion to the measure of the fault, so that, according to the Baptist’s words, we may “produce fruits worthy of repentance” (Matt. III).

But not only the measure of satisfaction must be observed; the need for purification must also be investigated. One must abstain from lawful things not merely for satisfaction, but must also persist in laborious works in order to expel or lessen the passions that grow strong through vicious habit. For exercises of the outward person are instruments for the inward person, by which both the vicious passions that infect the soul are more easily cut away and the stains of the inward countenance are more fully washed away, as if by a harsher cleansing preparation. Therefore, one concerned for his own purification must first attend to the passions by which he is attacked; then consider which ones most afflict him; and finally [Col. 0647D] carefully seek which instruments most effectively oppose which passions. Having considered these, let him apply an appropriate instrument to each passion, and oppose with more fervent insistence the passion that attacks more strongly, so that it may itself be overwhelmed by the resistance.

Thus restriction of the stomach readily represses the passion of lust; the affliction of vigils strengthens the wandering and unstable heart; silence moderates anger; diligent work chastises weariness of mind. Yet one must not devote all one’s energy to extinguishing a single passion in such a way that bodily means are lacking for repressing the rest; nor must one labour so excessively that no passion is felt at all. Rather, when a passion arises, it should be restrained according to the judgment of reason.

## CHAPTER XLI. (Book III of the *Mirror*, chapter 33.) On the voluntary order and the measure to be observed in it.

[Col. 0648A]

Next follows the voluntary order, which we must now examine. Of it the Psalmist says: “I will sacrifice to you willingly” (Ps. LIII). For it is a freely offered holocaust, an acceptable victim, a voluntary sacrifice, when one ascends in the freedom of the spirit from what is permitted, through what is commanded, to those things set before those who long for the rewards of greater glory.

Inviting the more fervent to this summit of perfection, the Saviour says: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell what you have and give to the poor; then come, follow me” (Matt. XIX). And elsewhere: “There are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven. Let one who is able to receive this, receive it” (ibid.). [Col. 0648B] Thus renunciation of the world, a resolution of chastity, and the profession of any stricter form of life are counted among voluntary sacrifices. Far be it from us to count this perfection of life, which a person undertook voluntarily and not under compulsion, among necessary and compulsory things rather than among voluntary things. Even the necessity which no one imposed on an unwilling person, but to which he voluntarily subjected himself from desire for perfection, ought to be called voluntary, not compulsory.

Whoever, then, has devoted himself to these lofty and sublime things should first examine carefully the rule of his vow or purpose—what it consists of and how extensive it is. Then he should weigh and discern, on the scale of experience, the strengths of the inward person: the inward strengths by which he combats the wars of temptations in daily exercise; [Col. 0648C] and the outward strengths by which he endures the burdens of bodily labours with untiring patience.

Although labour of both the inward and outward person is necessary for anyone advancing in any state, the affliction of the outward person is more necessary for one still assailed by passions of the flesh. But when those passions have been lulled or extinguished, one may moderate outward observances somewhat, while practising spiritual matters more diligently and fervently. Yet not in such a way as presumptuously to exceed the rule of one’s profession, or to destroy or confuse the distinctions of times prescribed in the rule to which one has submitted. Rather, while preserving the time appointed for each work, one should practise those works more gently or more fervently, as one knows to be beneficial. [Col. 0648D]

## CHAPTER XLII. The measure in these very exercises is likewise described.

It is beneficial for anyone to maintain this measure in the exercises themselves: to conduct himself in one matter in such a way that he does not fail in the others, but to practise with greater fervour that in which he feels himself making greater progress. I have at hand the words of a certain wise man on this matter:

> “Meditation concerning conduct first considers the duties that are owed, whether by command or by vow, and judges that those things should be done first which, if done, have merit, but if left undone produce guilt. Therefore those things must first be done which cannot be omitted without fault. After these, if anything is voluntarily added, it should be done in such a way that the duty is not hindered.”

Some people will what they ought not because they cannot do what they ought; others, though they can do what they ought, bring voluntary hindrances upon themselves by willing what they ought not. Likewise, two evils especially must be avoided in good action: distress and over-occupation. By distress, sweetness of mind is made bitter; by over-occupation, tranquillity is scattered. Distress occurs when one is consumed through impatience over things one cannot do. Over-occupation occurs when, in doing what one can do, one is agitated through intemperance. Therefore, lest the mind be bitterly embittered, let it bear its own inability patiently; and lest it be wrongly over-occupied, let it not extend its ability beyond its measure.

## CHAPTER XLIII. (Book III of the *Mirror*, chapter 37.) What a person owes to his neighbour.

[Col. 0649B]

These things have been said concerning the measure to be observed in each rank, so that in striving toward him who must be loved supremely, we may provide both for the soul’s salvation and for the body what nature is due. But since divine authority teaches that our neighbour must be loved by us equally with ourselves, first it is necessary that we not be ignorant which order suits each person; then we must labour with utmost diligence to ensure that no one exceeds, in whatever order, the prescribed rule of life.

But since it is evident that some are set over others, some are subject, and some are equals, whenever anyone among these transgresses the lawful measure, an inferior ought to advise a superior, an equal to correct an equal, and a superior, if necessary, even to compel an inferior. [Col. 0649C] Yet correction or compulsion itself must be moderated according to each individual’s condition, so that submission may be evident in advice, love in correction, and compassion in compulsion. One who lives lawfully in a lower order may be admonished in order to ascend to higher things, but may not be compelled. One who has voluntarily submitted himself to a higher order ought to be treated according to the rule of his profession; but he ought not to be compelled, without consulting his will, to undertake stricter observances.

## CHAPTER XLIV. (Book III of the *Mirror*, chapter 27.) How love ought to be shown to oneself and to one’s neighbour.

Scripture says: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Matt. 22). Wisely it does not say, “You shall love your neighbor as much as yourself,” but “as yourself.” [Col. 0649D] It therefore prescribes the manner of loving, not its quantity. One should show love to oneself in such a way as first to provide for the salvation of one’s own soul, which is the better part of oneself, and then for the necessities of one’s body. If at any time necessity demands that one of these be disregarded, one should even suffer bodily death, provided one does not endure loss to the soul. This is not to hate the body, but to prefer the soul to the body in love. Therefore let one never depart from this love of oneself, and let one approach the care of one’s neighbor without anxiety.

Let one do for one’s neighbor all that one can, so that the neighbor may be sound in body and healthy in mind. For if one neglects either of these, one certainly does not love one’s neighbor, who consists of both. By no reasoning or commandment is anyone compelled to purchase the salvation of a brother’s soul by the destruction of his own soul, or to prevent the death of a brother’s body by the death of his own body. For when we are commanded to lay down our souls for our brothers (1 John 3), this concerns contempt for life, not injury to the soul. Thus the soul is laid down not for destruction, but rather for salvation. Hence to lay down one’s soul in this manner is certainly to provide for that soul itself.

It may perhaps also laudably occur that, out of love alone, someone exposes his own body for another’s body. But that one should suffer injury to one’s own soul—not merely for the salvation of one soul, but even for that of the whole world—cannot occur while the true order of love is preserved. “What exchange shall a man give for his soul?” What does it profit him if he gains the whole world, [Col. 0650A] even for its salvation, but suffers loss of his own soul? (Matt. 16). For the soul’s loss consists in departing from the love of him who is to be loved above all. One departs from God’s love either by committing something deserving condemnation or by omitting something without which there is no salvation. Whatever, apart from the preceding principle, is added to brotherly love is wholly subtracted from divine love. For since self-love is measured according to the manner in which one loves God, one loves oneself less only when one loves God less.

Moreover, who that loves himself does not spare himself from destruction? How then will one love another as oneself who does not even love oneself? For when the Apostle says, “I wished at one time to be accursed from Christ for my brethren” [Col. 0650B] (Rom. 11), he disclosed an affection, not a considered judgment. Yet above we have sufficiently shown how differently affection and reason may suggest things within one mind. Therefore, when the Apostle said this, he indeed spoke truly, because he expressed the feeling he experienced. If he had afterward said, “I would rather that the whole world perish than that I alone be separated from Christ,” he would no less have spoken truly, because he would have disclosed reason’s judgment.

Yet what he says, “I wished to be accursed from Christ for my brethren,” may also be understood appropriately in this way: that he wished, for his brothers’ salvation, to be summoned from that secret place of his prayers, in which he rested sweetly in Jesus’ embraces; from that ineffable height of contemplation in which he surveyed the hidden mysteries of heaven [Col. 0650C] with most pure eyes; from that sweetness of most welcome compunction, by which it drenched with the sweetest drops of spiritual affections the soul thirsting for those heavenly things; and be summoned to the world’s tumult. He does not hesitate to call that summons a separation from Christ, who, according to his measure, tastes and sees that the Lord is sweet, and that blessed is everyone who hopes in him (Ps. 33). Moreover, one who chose thus to be separated from Christ when prompted by brotherly love, or consented when compelled by the authority of superiors, must take care lest this necessity overwhelm him and that sweetness perish.

## Chapter XLV. On matters in which dispensation may be made

[Col. 0651A]

There are certain intermediate things—reading, meditation, bodily work, fasting of the stomach, the sweetness of prayer, and the like—which must all, for a brother’s salvation, be dispensed, varied, altered, and sometimes even omitted. Of these the Apostle says: “Let no one seek his own interests, but those of others” (Phil. 2). And again: “As I please all men in all things, not seeking what is useful to me, but what is useful to the many, that they may be saved” (1 Cor. 10).

What we have said about reading or prayer must also be understood concerning bodily comforts—indeed, concerning the body itself: whatever someone sees must be despised, expended, or altered for his own salvation, he should recognize that the same must be done for his neighbor’s salvation. Yet one must take care that this alteration or variation be a dispensation, not an utter destruction. Since, as blessed Benedict himself indicates, the purpose of the institution is the safeguarding of charity and the correction of vices, that dispensation will surely be reasonable which advances this purpose. But if vices are fostered more by dispensation than by the observance itself, charity is violated; such dispensation is certainly proved dangerous.

## Chapter XLVI. On the manner of dispensation

Therefore one who by a voluntary rule aspires to the summit of perfection should first unceasingly behold charity—as the appointed end toward which to direct his course: charity by which we draw nearest to God, indeed by which we cleave to and are conformed to God, and in which the fullness of all perfection consists. [Col. 0651B] Then, with the tireless eagerness of a ready spirit, let him press toward its fullness by the path prescribed to him by the rule of his vow or profession.

Let abstinence therefore serve this end; let vigils minister to it; let reading be vigilant for it; let daily labour sweat for it. If through any of these charity, for whose sake they were instituted, is found to be violated, then the person entrusted with dispensation is under the necessity of tempering and ordering everything in such a way that charity is not abandoned for their sake, but its fruit is sought in all things. Yet this should not be done so that any instituted observance is omitted, or that fixed times assigned to particular exercises are confused, unless extreme necessity compels it. Otherwise it will not be dispensation but destruction. Rather, at fixed times, fixed exercises should be moderated according to each person’s condition and state of mind.

This is what the saint himself says when laying down a rule concerning manual work: “Let him so temper and order all things that souls may be saved, and that the brothers may do what they do without murmuring” (St Benedict, *Rule*). And elsewhere: “Yet let all things be done in moderation, because of the weak.” Did he say that this or that should be omitted because of the weak? On the contrary: “Let such a craft be assigned even to the sick and delicate, that they may neither be idle nor oppressed by the violence of labour.” Therefore the sick and delicate too should work, but their work should be so moderated that they are not oppressed. I ask: whom does he excuse from work, when he compels even the sick and delicate to it?

## Chapter XLVII. On the best rule for those in the cloister

[Col. 0652A]

“I became as a beast of burden before you” (Ps. 72). Truly we have become like beasts of burden, going wherever we are led without objection and bearing whatever is imposed without reply. There is no place for one’s own will, no time for idleness or laxity. Food is indeed scantier, clothing rougher, drink from the spring, sleep commonly upon a book.

How remarkable also is this: among innumerable persons, one person’s will is law. Thus whatever has once fallen from his mouth is observed by all with such care as if they had all conspired to it, or had heard it from God’s own mouth. And, wonderfully pleasing, there is no respect of persons and no consideration of birth. Necessity alone produces difference; infirmity alone produces inequality. For what is earned in common is distributed to individuals, not as carnal inclination or private affection may dictate, but according to each person’s need.

## Chapter XLVIII. *(Mirror*, book II, chapter 1.) Why some labour under Christ’s yoke

The Lord invites us to rest, saying: “Come to me, all you who labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you,” and so forth (Matt. 2). Certainly charity is that sweet yoke and light burden to which the Saviour’s mercy invites us; “and you shall find,” he says, “rest for your souls” (ibid.).

But because very many of us who seem to have placed our necks beneath this yoke are shown to labour greatly, let us endeavour to show that the yoke of covetous desire produces this labour. For “covetousness is the root of all evils” (1 Tim. 6), just as charity, conversely, is the root of all virtues. Accordingly, so long as this poisonous root remains lodged in the deepest parts of the soul, although its little branches are cut off on the surface, new shoots must necessarily spring up again, until the root itself is utterly uprooted and nothing remains from which the most destructive offspring of vices may arise.

## Chapter XLIX. *(Mirror*, book II, chapter 2.) That outward labour is shaped by the condition of the inward person

Certainly this labour of which we complain is not of the flesh but of the heart; just as the rest of which we speak here belongs to the heart, not the flesh. Yet outward labour is shaped by the condition of the inward person; indeed, no outward labour should be called labour if there is none inwardly. [Col. 0652C]

For example, consider hunters, bird-catchers, or any followers of such vanities. If you observe the outward movements of their bodies, what could be more laborious? If you observe the condition of their minds, what could be more delightful? The same is very easily seen in commendable matters. How great was the apostles’ outward labour when they were thrust into prison, bound in chains, and most fiercely beaten with scourges! Yet they went rejoicing from the presence of the council because they had been deemed worthy to suffer reproach for Jesus’ name (Acts 5).

At that time many sacrilegious persons suffered a similar punishment; but because their consciences differed, those persons were miserable in both respects, labouring inwardly and outwardly, whereas these rejoiced in outward punishments through inward rest. Having carefully considered these matters, it is therefore clear that bodily sufferings from without do not produce inward labour. Rather, the root dwelling in the inner depths shapes whatever happens externally according to its own nature.

For why is it that, when two sit at the same table and the same foods are placed before them, one rejoices while the other complains? Why is it that, when they receive the same wounds, one is cast down by the sickness of sorrow while another is suffused with wonderful joy? Two are struck at once by the misfortune of bereavement or poverty, and yet one blasphemes while the other gives thanks. The same sight is offered to both their eyes, and one is shamefully aroused while the other enjoys his customary peace. When an opportunity for some honour is presented, one is inflamed by the desire to rule, while the other despises it.

## Chapter L. *(Mirror*, book II, chapter 3.) That charity tempers every occurrence by its own tranquillity, while covetousness corrupts everything by its perversity

[Col. 0653B]

Is it not manifest that the same thing occurs in bodies: according to the quality of health or illness, things that happen from without are experienced either as painful or pleasant? For food that worsens one person’s sickness benefits another’s health; and the sun that takes light from a bleary eye shines more delightfully upon a healthy one. Therefore, just as bodily things applied from without are found either wholesome or harmful according to the inward condition, so it is plain that one person’s rest and another’s labour depend upon the inward condition of the mind.

For the mind possessed by the most sweet and tranquil yoke of the Lord—that is, perfect charity—transforms every occurrence into the state of its own tranquillity. It does not allow itself to be disturbed by any agitations of things, but compels those agitations themselves to serve its progress. [Col. 0653C] But if the mind has been subjected to the most grievous yoke of covetous desire, then so long as no occasion of disturbance arises, a relaxed repose falsely imitates the sweetness of the Lord’s yoke. Yet when a cause of any indignation appears, immediately a savage beast bursts forth from the recesses of the heart, as from the deepest caverns, tearing and bloodying the wretched soul with the harshest bites of passions, granting it no time of peace or rest.

Let the yoke therefore rot away before the oil—the yoke, that is, of covetous desire before the presence of charity—and immediately one will experience how light, sweet, delightful, heaven-lifting, and earth-delivering is Christ’s burden. Therefore, if we wish to experience the sweetness of this rest, let us diligently investigate the causes and roots of our labour—not with lukewarm feeling, as with a blunted blade cutting away only what is outward, but penetrating with a more vehement desire to the very origins of our diseases.

## Chapter LI. *(Mirror*, book II, chapter 4.) That all labour arises from a threefold concupiscence

I think, however, that if we investigate more closely, we shall clearly recognize that whatever labour arises for us is derived as from certain poisonous springs—from the concupiscence of the flesh, the concupiscence of the eyes, or the pride of life (1 John 2). If harsher food still saddens me, the concupiscence of the flesh imposes labour upon me. I do not labour because I have taken on Christ’s yoke, but because I have not wholly cast off the yoke of covetous desire. [Col. 0654A] And if, inflamed by desire for richer food, I am upset by a humbler serving; or if it is prepared less than customary, too late, or carelessly, and I am consumed by the plague of murmuring—what produces these distresses for me: the passion of covetous desire, or the sweetness of charity?

## Chapter LII. *(Mirror*, book II, chapter 24.) On the concupiscence of the eyes

The holy Fathers call the concupiscence of the eyes “curiosity,” and they judge it to concern not only the outward but also the inward person. Outward curiosity includes every superfluous abundance that the eyes love: varied forms, bright and pleasing colours, diverse workmanship, garments, shoes, vessels, paintings, sculptures, and various artificial objects exceeding necessary and moderate use. Lovers of the world seek all these for the eye’s enticement, pursuing outwardly what they do inwardly: abandoning him by whom they were made and destroying what they were made to be.

Hence also, in the cloisters of certain monks, there are cranes and hares, little deer and stags, magpies and ravens—not Antonian or Macarian implements, but feminine amusements. These things do not at all serve monastic poverty, but feed curious eyes.

## Chapter LIII. On inward curiosity

[Col. 0654B]

Inward curiosity consists in three things: the appetite for harmful or empty knowledge; inquiry into another person’s life, not in order to imitate it, but to envy it if it is vain, to mock it if it is evil, or merely out of curiosity, simply in order to know whether it is good or bad; and finally, a certain curious knowledge of secular affairs or actions. From all these things no slight labour of captivity arises in minds.

Hence it also happens that, when we have given the whole day to empty spectacles or attentive listening to rumours, and have in some manner gone out from ourselves, on returning again to ourselves we bring in images of vanities. Carrying a heart full of images into our place of quiet, we pass sleepless nights and arrange various affairs in idle mental wanderings during the psalmody itself or our prayers. [Col. 0654C]

There is yet another, most evil kind of curiosity, by which only those conscious of great virtues in themselves are tempted: namely, testing one’s own holiness by displaying miracles. This is to tempt God. Hence: “You shall not tempt the Lord your God” (Deut. 6).

## Chapter LIV. *(Mirror*, book II, chapter 5.) On the opinion of certain people who say that outward labours are contrary to charity and inward sweetness

“But to waste the body by continual vigils, afflict the flesh by daily labours, and weaken the vigour of the limbs by the meanest foods is not only a considerable labour; it is also plainly contrary to the charity which you strive so earnestly to commend, [Col. 0655A] so that, by exhausting all sweetness of mind, it leaves the mind barren of every spiritual sweetness.”

This is the laughable opinion of certain people who place spiritual sweetness, as it were, in the pleasure of the flesh. They maintain that bodily affliction is contrary to the spirit and that the sufferings of the outward person diminish the holiness of the inner. “For,” they say, “since flesh and spirit are joined to one another by their natural affection, they must communicate their sufferings to one another. Thus it is impossible for the oppression of one not to disturb the gladness of the other, so that the spirit, cast down by a certain anxiety of sorrow, is wholly unable to breathe into that spiritual joy.”

These claims seem to be either subtly investigated or proved. Shameful mouth! Spiritual grace is sought according to the rules of Hippocrates. Thus, indeed, thus do those err who rely more upon medical arguments than upon apostolic precepts. These are the notions of him who crawls upon his belly, eats earth, sleeps beneath the shade in damp places, and pursues the business of the belly and lust under a show of holiness. [Col. 0655B] For he thinks simple people may more readily be frightened away from apostolic poverty and evangelical purity if they suppose that a more relaxed life will bring them a greater grace of divine sweetness in the future.

Clearly this is a wisdom not descending from above, but wholly earthly, animal, devilish (Jas. 3). This is the prudence of speech, the wisdom of the flesh, which, while teaching fleshly pleasure, strives to empty the cross of Christ. Yet as regards the flesh there is certainly nothing sweet, soft, tender, or in any way luxurious in that cross. But the cross is not emptied. Rather, it overturns this delicate teaching—this teaching which the nails driven into the sacred limbs assail, which that lance, impressed with saving sharpness into the sweet entrails, conquers.

I, on the contrary, think—and boldly declare—that bodily affliction, if a sound intention comes first and discretion is preserved (though discretion must be learned not from one’s own conjecture but from the examples of one’s elders, lest laxity and dissipation perhaps cloak themselves under the pallor of “discretion”)—that bodily affliction, I say, is not contrary to the spirit but necessary to it. Nor does it diminish divine consolation; rather, I hold that it calls it forth. Thus I judge that in this life at least these two things are always matched: outward tribulation and inward consolation. [Col. 0655C]

What? Perhaps God imparts the sweetness of his consolation to one abounding in riches and luxuries, while withholding it, under a strict reckoning, from his poor little one who daily dies for him? Far be it from us to think or believe this of him who is most sweet, most gentle, and most compassionate! If I say it, perhaps one may doubt; but if Christ says it, not to believe is heretical. “What then,” you ask, “should I believe your opinion rather than my own experience?” But what if someone else testifies that he has experienced something altogether different? Certainly, the more he is afflicted, the greater the grace of divine sweetness that he experiences. Clearly, God has mercy on whom he wills.

## Chapter LV. The preceding opinion refuted by apostolic and prophetic authority

[Col. 0656A]

Let that most valiant athlete, most faithful witness, and outstanding disputant come forward—he in whom Christ speaks; who dies daily for Christ; who suffers every tribulation; who has conflicts without and fears within; who chastises his body and brings it into servitude (1 Cor. 2); who does not eat his bread without payment, but works in toil night and day; whose hands provide necessities both for himself and for those with him; who finally sweats as the keenest soldier under Jesus’ banner in labour and hardship, in many vigils, hunger and thirst, cold and nakedness. Let him, I say, decide this question and show whether such great tribulation and such wonderful exhaustion have taken spiritual consolation away from him.

Let Paul therefore say whether that pious comforter leaves his own without consolation in their present tribulation, and whether he forestalls by his authority the heresy of Jovinian now sprouting again. This heresy, however, seems more pernicious than Jovinian’s; for whereas that one equated feasting with abstinence, this one gives feasting preference. Therefore let those who place the greater consolation of divine sweetness in fleshly pleasure rather than in tribulation hear Paul saying: “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all consolation, who comforts us in all our tribulation” (2 Cor. 1). [Col. 0656B]

Whether we are weakened by fasts, afflicted by vigils, or worn down by labours: blessed be God, who comforts us in all our tribulation. Though we are overwhelmed by stones, bound in chains, beaten with rods, or endure the confinement of prison: blessed be God, who comforts us in all our tribulation. Let the devil rage, the world become savage, pursue us with hatred, attack us with curses, plunder our possessions, or stain our reputation: blessed be God, who comforts us in all our tribulation, “that we ourselves,” he says, “may be able to comfort those who are in every affliction” (ibid.).

Here he promises his consolation not to those living in riches and luxuries, but to those who are in every affliction. And, leaving no question unresolved, he adds: “For as the sufferings of Christ abound in us, so through Christ our consolation also abounds” (ibid.). What could be clearer? This is precisely what we said a little before: that these two things are matched—outward sufferings and inward consolations.

Finally Solomon declares in mystical words to whom divine consolation is to be poured out: “Give strong drink to those who mourn, and wine to those who are bitter in soul. Let them drink and forget their poverty, and remember their sorrow no more” (Prov. 31). Openly, in these words, he promises that wine which gladdens the human heart (Ps. 103) not to those relaxed in idleness, not to those spending the day in loud laughter and tales, but to those bitter in soul. And he declares that the strong drink made from new and old fruits, which the bride keeps among the bridegroom’s delights, is to be given [Col. 0656C] not to those feasting and drinking, but to those sorrowing because of the distresses of this life and labouring under poverty and grief.

“Let them drink,” he says, “and forget their poverty”: that is, he says that the magnitude of their labour is diminished by divine consolation. The Psalmist most plainly agrees with this saying: “According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, your consolations have made my soul glad” (Ps. 93). O consolation that heals the weak, strengthens the frail, and relieves the despairing! It is consolation for those who groan, rest for those who labour, protection for the tempted, and provision for travellers.

Those deprive themselves of this consolation who, recoiling at the first drops of sweat, either fall back into their former torpor or seek certain paltry consolations in frequent conversation, visits from friends, or indeed the freedom of their own will. Despising such filth of consolations, the holy Prophet says: “My soul refused to be comforted” (Ps. 76). What then? Were you left without all consolation? Far from it: “I remembered God and was delighted” (ibid.).

Therefore let no one dread that arduous way which leads to life. Let no one, with fearful unhappiness, seek again the relaxation once rejected. Rather, as our lawgiver says (St Benedict, *Rule*), let him endure without growing weary or departing, knowing that according to the multitude of labours which he endures for Christ, Christ’s consolations will make his soul glad. But having tasted spiritual sweetness, do not immediately dissolve into ease; for the spiritual Amalek will quickly rise at your side, to be overcome not by arms but by prayers. [Col. 0657A] For whenever the soul is exhausted beyond measure in temptations, it must hasten with the attentive devotion of prayer to the motherly breasts of Jesus. Drawing from their abundance the milk of wonderful consolation, you may say with the Apostle: “Blessed be God, who comforts us in all our tribulation” (2 Cor. 1); and, “As the sufferings of Christ abound in us, so through Christ our consolation also abounds” (ibid.).

## Chapter LVI. How charity and covetousness operate in one who is making progress

Perhaps we have not uselessly set forth these matters thus far. If they are considered attentively, diligently, and finally humbly, it will, I think, be very easy to see that anyone newly converted is raised by a fresh infusion of charity, by eager effort, and by certain very light movements of the mind toward higher things. Yet, pressed downward by covetous desire, and always driven toward the depths by the natural weight of everything to which it clings, that person labours somewhat in the very effort. [Col. 0657B] And the higher that pernicious shrub has driven its roots into the recesses of the soul, the greater is the difficulty in uprooting them and, correspondingly, the less ease in ascending.

But just as a lazy, idle, and agriculturally unskilled man slowly clears and cleanses his field, even though it is overgrown with thistles and thorns only in a small part; while an energetic, attentive, and skilled cultivator more swiftly roots out the density of briars, even if it has occupied the whole surface of the field, and makes it rich and fertile from barren and unproductive—so also, when someone renounces the world, if he is sluggish and insufficiently concerned for his purification, though he was less defiled in the world, he will progress more slowly toward a serene conscience and the freedom of charity. But if he is fervent in spirit, diligent and attentive, and grounded in the virtue of discretion, and if, taking up the instruments of spiritual exercises, he powerfully uproots the shoots of vices from the field of his heart, he will more quickly breathe the air of a purer conscience. Having shaken off the yoke of covetous desire and laid aside the burden of passions, he will discover that the Lord’s yoke is sweet and his burden light (Matt. 11).

## Chapter LVIII. How great is the delight in contempt for pleasures and in victory

Thus, through experience, he will prove that to be suffused with the sweetness of chastity is not merely without labour, but a supreme delight, although it is burdensome to restrain by the bridle of temperance the natural impulses and unclean desires that arise from the concupiscence of the flesh. [Col. 0658A] Likewise, when the craving of gluttony has been overcome, it is not only pleasant but also glorious to see oneself not as the slave of one’s belly but as its master, exulting in that wonderful joy: “But I have learned to be content in whatever circumstances I am. I know how to be humbled, and I know also how to abound; everywhere and in all things I have been instructed both to hunger and to be satisfied, both to abound and to suffer want” (Phil. 4).

And if love of the flesh has been perfectly lulled to sleep, or indeed absorbed by the fire of divine love, there will be no outward labour, because the mind whose love cannot be dissolved cannot be disturbed by affliction. Therefore the sweetness of the Lord’s yoke and the lightness of his burden consist in contempt for pleasures. Let no one therefore suppose that delight is greater in vices than in virtues.

[Col. 0659]

# The Book of Blessed Aelred, Abbot of Rievaulx, on Spiritual Friendship

A compendium of this little work is found among the works of Saint Augustine, volume IV, accompanied by Erasmus’s censure of the author, whom he did not know, for having supposedly sought to appear to be Augustine—an absurd opinion. Erasmus himself elsewhere often passes judgment on similar books by other authors that had crept into the works of the Fathers. For what advantage could our Aelred, or other learned and pious men, have hoped to gain from this? A person may attribute another’s writings to himself in order to win a name for himself; heretics too have sometimes falsely ascribed to the Fathers books filled with errors. But this was foreign to pious Catholics, who abhor fabrication and falsehood.

It was therefore through the error of those who published the Fathers’ works that writings belonging to others were mixed with theirs. This little work *On Friendship* commonly bears, in manuscripts, the name of Aelred, Abbot of Rievaulx. Indeed, it is a dialogue whose speakers are Aelred himself and Ivo, one of his monks. It is arranged in three books and is four times longer than it is in Augustine; and, since the version found in Augustine is mutilated, it is unsurprising that it appears less pleasing.

The little flowers of expression criticized by Erasmus—such as *ita quod* in place of *pro invicem*, and the like—do not disfigure the work so much that it could not have come to be believed, as Erasmus himself admits, to be Augustine’s. The Fathers often disregarded their own eloquence and willingly employed the phrases of our version of Scripture, though these were less elegant.

## Prologue

[Col. 0659A]

While I was still a boy at school, and greatly delighted in the affection of my companions, amid the habits and vices to which that age is accustomed to be exposed, my whole mind gave itself and devoted itself to affection and love. Nothing seemed to me sweeter, more pleasant, or more useful than to be loved and to love. Thus, tossed among diverse loves and friendships, my mind was swept hither and thither; and, ignorant of the law of true friendship, it was often deceived by friendship’s likeness.

At length there came into my hands the book which Tully wrote on friendship. It at once seemed useful to me in the seriousness of its thoughts and sweet in the charm of its eloquence. Although I did not consider myself suited to that kind of friendship, I nevertheless rejoiced that I had found a certain pattern of friendship to which I might learn to recall the wanderings of my loves and affections.

But when it pleased my good Lord to correct one who had gone astray, raise one who had been cast down, and cleanse a leper by his healing touch, I abandoned hope in the world and entered a monastery. At once I applied myself to the reading of the sacred writings, though previously my bleary eye, accustomed to carnal darkness, had not sufficed even for their surface. [Col. 0659B] Therefore, as sacred Scripture became sweet and that small store of learning which the world had imparted to me became worthless by comparison, the things I had read about friendship in the aforementioned little book came to mind. I was already astonished that they no longer tasted as they once had.

For then nothing that had not been sweetened with the honey of the most sweet Jesus, nothing that had not been seasoned with the salt of the holy Scriptures, wholly drew my affection to itself. Turning these same matters over repeatedly, I asked whether perhaps they could be supported by scriptural authority. But when I had read many things concerning friendship in the writings of the saints, wishing to love spiritually yet unable to do so, I resolved to write on spiritual friendship and to prescribe for myself rules of chaste and holy love.

Accordingly, we have divided this little work into three books. In the first, we set forth what friendship is and commend its origin or cause; in the second, we present its fruit and excellence; in the third, we explain, as best we can, how and among whom it may be preserved unbroken to the end. If anyone gains profit from reading this, let him give thanks to God and intercede at Christ’s mercy for my sins. But if anyone judges what we have written superfluous or useless, let him spare my unhappiness, which compelled me to restrain the flow of my thoughts by the occupation of this meditation.

## Book I. On the origin of friendship

[Col. 0661]

[Col. 0661A] **AELRED.** Here are you and I, and I hope that Christ is a third among us. There is no one now to make a disturbance; no one to interrupt our friendly conversation; no voice or tumult intrudes upon this welcome solitude. Come then, dearest friend: open your breast and pour into friendly ears whatever pleases you. Let us not receive ungratefully this place, time, and leisure. For a little while ago, as I sat among the gathering of brothers, while all around us were making noise, one asking questions and another disputing—this one raising questions from the Scriptures, that one concerning conduct, another about vices, another about virtues—you alone were silent. Then, raising your head, you were preparing to bring something forward; but as though the voice were caught in your very throat, you lowered your head again and were silent. Then, withdrawing a little way from us and returning, you wore a sorrowful expression. From all this I was given to understand only that, while you wished to utter the conception of your mind, you both dreaded the crowd and desired privacy.

**IVO.** Indeed it is so; and I rejoice greatly to understand that you have care for your boy, whose mind and purpose of mind none other than the spirit of charity has disclosed to you. And would that your graciousness might grant me this: whenever you visit your sons [Note: [Col. 0661] Ivo appears to have been a monk not of Rievaulx, but of another monastery subject to Rievaulx.] who are here, may I at least once, when the others have withdrawn, be allowed to have you to myself and express without disturbance the agitations of my heart.

AELRED. I will indeed, and gladly. For I am greatly pleased that I do not see you inclined toward these vain and idle matters, but [Col. 0661C] always ready to speak of something useful and necessary for your progress. Speak, then, freely, and share all your cares and thoughts with a friend, so that you may either learn something or teach; give and receive; pour forth and draw in.

IVO. I am ready, indeed—not to teach or to give, but to receive; to draw in, not to pour forth—as my age prescribes, my inexperience compels, and my profession urges. But lest I foolishly spend on these things time needed for other matters, I wish you to teach me something about spiritual friendship: namely, what it is; what benefit it brings; what its beginning is; what its end; whether it can exist among all persons, and, if not among all, among whom; also how it can be kept unbroken and brought to a holy conclusion without any distress of disagreement.

[Col. 0661D] AELRED. I wonder why you think these questions should be asked of me, when it is abundantly clear that the most ancient and excellent teachers have treated all these matters—especially since you spent your youth in studies of this kind and read Tully Cicero’s book [Col. 0662A] *On Friendship*, in which he discussed most fully, in an agreeable style, everything that seems to concern it, and set forth, as it were, certain laws and precepts for it.

IVO. The book is not altogether unknown to me, since I once took great delight in it. But ever since some sweetness began to flow out to me from the honeycombs of the holy Scriptures, and the honey-sweet name of Christ claimed my affection for itself, whatever I read or hear discussed, however subtly and eloquently, without the salt of heavenly writings and the savor of that most sweet name, can be neither savory nor luminous to me. Therefore I should like those very matters which have been stated—if indeed they accord with reason—or else other matters which the usefulness of this discussion requires, to be proved to me by the authority of the Scriptures [Col. 0662B]; and I should like to be taught more fully how the friendship which ought to exist between us is begun in Christ, preserved according to Christ, and directed toward Christ as its end and benefit. For it is plain that Tully did not know the power of true friendship, since he utterly failed to know Christ, its beginning and end.

AELRED. I am overcome, I confess, so that, as one ignorant of myself and not measuring my own strength, I shall not exactly teach you these things but rather discuss them with you. For you yourself have opened the way for us both and, at the very threshold of our inquiry, kindled that most splendid light which will not allow us to wander by side-paths, but will lead us by a sure road to the certain end of the question proposed [Col. 0662C]. For what loftier, truer, or more useful thing can be said about friendship than that it ought to be begun in Christ, carried forward according to Christ, and brought to completion by Christ? Come now: declare what you think ought first to be asked concerning friendship.

IVO. I think we must first discuss what friendship is, lest we seem to paint in empty space if we do not know what that is about which the sequence and course of our discussion ought to proceed.

AELRED. Is not Tully’s saying enough for you? “Friendship is agreement in things human and divine, with goodwill and affection.”

IVO. If that definition satisfies you, I consider myself satisfied.

AELRED. Therefore, wherever people have the same judgment and the same will regarding [Col. 0662D] human and divine things, together with goodwill and affection, we shall confess that they have attained the perfection of friendship.

IVO. Why not? Yet I do not see what that pagan meant by the terms “affection” or “goodwill.”

[Col. 0663A] AELRED. Perhaps by “affection” he expressed the disposition of the mind, and by “goodwill” the effect produced in action. For agreement itself in human and divine matters ought to be dear to the minds of both—that is, pleasing and precious; and the performance of deeds in outward matters should likewise be well-disposed and agreeable.

IVO. I admit that this definition pleases me well enough, except that I think it applies equally to pagans, Jews, and even wicked Christians. Yet I confess that I am persuaded that true friendship cannot exist among those who are without Christ.

AELRED. In what follows it will become sufficiently clear to us whether the definition lacks anything or contains anything superfluous, so that it may either be rejected by us or admitted as sufficient and admitting nothing beyond itself. [Col. 0663B] Yet from the definition itself, though perhaps it may seem to you less than perfect, you will at least be able to understand what friendship is.

IVO. I beg you, do not find me burdensome if this does not suffice for me unless you unfold the meaning of the word itself.

AELRED. I will comply with your wish, provided you spare my ignorance and do not compel me to teach what I do not know. A friend, it seems to me, is called so from love (*amor*), and friendship from friend. Love is an affection of the rational soul through which it seeks and desires something for enjoyment; through which it enjoys that object with a certain inward sweetness, embraces it, and preserves what it has attained. We have explained this affection and motion as lucidly and carefully as we could in our *Mirror*, which you know well enough.

[Col. 0663C] Moreover, a friend is called, as it were, the guardian of love—or, as some have preferred, the guardian of the soul itself—because my friend ought to be the guardian of mutual love or of my very soul: preserving all its secrets in faithful silence; tending and bearing, to the limit of his power, whatever fault he sees in it; rejoicing with it when it rejoices, grieving with it when it grieves, and feeling that everything belonging to his friend is his own. Friendship itself, therefore, is the virtue by which souls are joined by the bond of such love and sweetness and are made one out of many. Hence even the philosophers of this world placed friendship not among transient and perishable things, but among the virtues themselves, which are eternal; and Solomon seems to agree with them in Proverbs: [Col. 0663D] “A friend loves at all times” (Prov. 17), plainly declaring that friendship is eternal if it is true. But if it has ceased to exist, it was not true even when it seemed to exist.

IVO. What then are we to make of the serious enmities which we read arose between the closest friends?

AELRED. We shall discuss that more fully in its proper place, God willing. For the present, I want you to believe this: a man was never a friend if he could harm one whom he had once received into friendship; nor has he tasted the delights of true friendship if, when injured, he ceased to love one whom he had once loved. For a friend loves at all times: though reproved, though injured, though handed over to flames, though afflicted on the cross, a friend loves at all times. And, as our [Col. 0664A] Jerome says: “A friendship that can cease was never true.”

IVO. Since true friendship possesses such great perfection, it is no wonder that antiquity commended so few as true friends. For, as Tully says, fame celebrates scarcely three or four pairs of friends in all the ages gone by. If in our own—that is, Christian—times friends are equally rare, then, it seems to me, I labor in vain in the pursuit of this virtue. Terrified already by its wondrous loftiness, I almost despair of attaining it.

AELRED. As someone has said, the very attempt at great things is great. Thus it belongs to a virtuous mind always to contemplate lofty and difficult things: either that it may attain what it desires, or that it may understand and know more clearly what is to be desired, since one should be considered to have made no small progress [Col. 0664B] if, through the knowledge of virtue, one has learned how far one is from virtue. Yet no Christian ought to despair of acquiring any virtue, for the divine voice resounds daily from the Gospel: “Ask, and you shall receive,” and so forth (Matt. 7).

Nor is it surprising that among pagans the followers of true virtue were few, since they did not know the Lord, the giver of virtues, of whom it is written: “The Lord of hosts, he is the King of glory” (Ps. 23). In faith in him I shall offer you, not three or four, but a thousand pairs of friends who were prepared to die for one another—precisely what the pagans call or invent as a great marvel concerning Pylades and Orestes. Did not those of whom it is written possess the virtue of true friendship according to Tully’s definition? “The multitude of believers [Col. 0664C] had one heart and one soul, and no one said that anything was his own, but all things were common to them” (Acts 5). How could there fail to be among them the fullest agreement in divine and human matters, with affection and goodwill, when they had one heart and one soul? How many martyrs laid down their lives for their brethren! How many spared neither expense nor labor nor the torments of their own bodies!

I believe you have often read, not without tears, of that girl from Antioch who was rescued from brothels by the very beautiful stratagem of a certain soldier, and who afterward shared martyrdom with the very man whom she had found to be the guardian of her chastity in the brothel. I could offer you many examples of this, were I not prevented by their length [Col. 0664D] and commanded to silence by their very abundance. For Christ Jesus proclaimed, spoke, and they were multiplied beyond number. “No one,” he says, “has greater love than this: that one lay down one’s life for one’s friends” (John 15).

IVO. Shall we then judge that there is no difference between friendship and affection?

AELRED. On the contrary, there is a very great difference. Divine authority has ordained that far more persons be received into the bosom of affection than into the embraces of friendship. For by the law of affection we are compelled to receive not only friends but enemies as well into the shelter of love. But we call friends only those to whom we do not fear to entrust our heart and everything in it, and who in return are bound to us by the same law and security of faith.

[Col. 0665A] IVO. How many people living secularly, agreeing with one another in every vice, are joined by a compact of like disposition and find the bond even of such friendship more welcome and sweet than all the world’s delights! Do not find it troublesome, amid so many friendships, to separate from their, so to speak, fellowship that friendship which we believe should be called spiritual in distinction from the others. It is, in a sense, wrapped up and obscured among them; and they meet and obstruct those who seek and desire it. Make it clearer to us, and therefore more desirable, by comparison with them; thus stir and inflame us more strongly toward attaining it.

AELRED. Those among whom there is agreement in vices falsely take to themselves the noble name of friendship. For one who does not love is not a friend; and one who loves wickedness does not love a human being. “Whoever loves iniquity does not love but hates his own soul” (Ps. 10); and one who does not love his own soul certainly cannot love another’s. Hence it follows that such people boast falsely in the name of friendship; they are deceived by its likeness but not upheld by its truth.

Yet, since such great and such deep sweetness is experienced in that kind of friendship which lust defiles, greed fouls, or luxury makes incestuous, it is pleasant to conjecture how much sweetness belongs to that friendship which is safer the more honorable it is; more delightful the chaster it is; and happier the freer it is. Let us nevertheless allow even friendships [Col. 0665C] which are not true to be called friendships because of a certain likeness felt in the affections, provided they are distinguished from that which is spiritual and therefore true by definite judgments. Let one friendship, then, be called carnal; another worldly; another spiritual. Agreement in vices creates carnal friendship; hope of gain inflames worldly friendship; likeness of life, morals, and pursuits binds spiritual friendship among the good.

But the beginning of carnal friendship proceeds from an inclination which, like a prostitute, spreads her legs to every passerby, following its own ears and eyes as they range wantonly through various things. Through their entrances, images of beautiful bodies or pleasurable things are carried all the way into the mind. To enjoy these as one pleases is thought to be happiness; but to enjoy them without a companion is judged [Col. 0665D] less pleasant. Then, by motion, gesture, words, and services, one mind is captured by another and one is inflamed by the other, and they are fused into one; so that, having entered a wretched compact, one commits and suffers every crime and every sacrilege for the other. They think that nothing is sweeter than this friendship and judge nothing more just, supposing that friendship’s laws command them “to will the same things and not to will the same things.”

This friendship, therefore, is neither undertaken by deliberation, approved by judgment, nor ruled by reason. It is swept in diverse directions according to the impetus of inclination, observing no measure, pursuing no honorable object, considering neither advantages nor disadvantages, but proceeding in all things rashly, indiscriminately, frivolously, and without restraint. Therefore, either as though driven by certain furies, it is consumed by itself, or dissolved with the same levity with which it was contracted.

But worldly friendship, born of desire for possessions or temporal goods, is always full of fraud and deceit.
