Nothing in it is certain, constant, or secure, because it always changes with fortune and follows the purse. Hence it is written: “There is a friend for a season, and he will not remain in the day of tribulation” (Ecclus. 6). Remove hope of profit and he will immediately cease to be a friend. A certain verse elegantly mocks this friendship:

> He is not a friend of the person but of prosperity:  
> Whom sweet fortune holds, bitter fortune drives away.

Yet the beginning of this defective friendship sometimes advances some people toward a certain share in true friendship: namely, those who first enter into a compact in hope of common profit and, while keeping faith with one another in unrighteous mammon, come, at least in human affairs, to the greatest and most agreeable harmony [Col. 0666B]. Nevertheless, no friendship can truly be called friendship if it is undertaken and preserved for the sake of temporal advantage.

Spiritual friendship, which we call true, is desired not with a view to any worldly usefulness, nor from any externally arising cause, but from the dignity of its own nature and the feeling of the human heart, so that its fruit and reward are nothing other than itself. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “I have appointed you that you may go and bear fruit” (John 15), that is, that you may love one another. For in true friendship itself one goes forward in progress, and one receives fruit by tasting the sweetness of that perfection.

Spiritual friendship, then, is born among the good from likeness of life, morals, [Col. 0666C] and pursuits; it is agreement in human and divine things, with goodwill and affection. This definition seems to me fully sufficient for expressing friendship, provided that, in our customary sense, it is called “affection,” so that every vice is excluded from friendship; while “goodwill” expresses the very feeling of loving, which is moved inwardly with a certain sweetness. Where such friendship exists, there certainly is willing and not willing the same things—so much the sweeter as it is more sincere, so much the more pleasant as it is more sacred—where those who so love can desire nothing unbecoming and reject nothing advantageous. Prudence guides this friendship, justice rules it, fortitude guards it, and temperance moderates it; [Col. 0666D] we shall discuss these in their place.

But now, if you think enough has been said about what you considered the first question, namely what friendship is, say so.

IVO. What has been said is entirely sufficient, and nothing further occurs to me to ask. But before we go on to other matters, I wish to know how friendship first arose among mortals: whether it entered human use by nature, by chance, by some necessity, or indeed by a command or law imposed upon humankind; and whether practice made it commendable.

AELRED. Friendship’s inclination, it seems to me, was first impressed upon human minds by nature itself; experience afterward increased it; and finally the authority of law ordered it. For God, supremely powerful and supremely good, is a good sufficient unto himself, since he himself is his own good, joy, glory, and blessedness. There is nothing outside him that he needs—not man, not angel, not heaven, not earth, nor anything contained in them. To him every creature cries: “You are my God, because you have no need of my goods” (Ps. 15). Nor is he sufficient merely to himself; he is also the sufficiency of all things, giving existence to some, sensation to others, and knowledge besides to others: the cause of all that exists, the life of all that feels, the wisdom of all that understands.

[Col. 0667A] He, then, the highest Nature, established all natures, ordered all things in their places, and apportioned all things distinctly in their times. He willed—for so his eternal reason prescribed—that peace should compose all his creatures and fellowship unite them, so that all things might receive from him, who is supremely and purely one, some trace of unity. Hence he left no kind of thing solitary, but joined many together in a certain fellowship.

For, to begin with insensible things: what soil or what river produces a single stone of one kind? Or what forest brings forth a single tree of one kind? Thus even among insensible things a kind of love of fellowship shines forth, since none of them is alone, but each is both created and persists in a certain company of its own kind. But among sentient beings, who could easily describe how great an image of friendship, fellowship, and love shines out? Certainly, although in every other respect they are found to be irrational, in this regard they imitate the human mind so closely that they are thought almost to act by reason. Thus they follow one another, play together, express and reveal their feeling together through movements and cries, and enjoy mutual fellowship so eagerly and pleasantly that they seem concerned with nothing more than the things belonging to friendship.

[Col. 0667C] Divine wisdom likewise arranged matters among the angels so that not one, but many, should be created. Among them agreeable fellowship and the sweetest love produce the same will and the same affection, lest, when one appeared superior and another inferior, room should be opened for envy—unless the affection of friendship resisted it. Thus multitude excludes solitude, and the communion of affection increases delight among many.

Finally, when God had created man, in order to commend more deeply the good of fellowship, he said: “It is not good for man to be alone; let us make [Col. 0667D] him a helper like himself” (Gen. 2). Nor indeed did divine power form this helper from something merely similar, or even from the same material; rather, to provide a more explicit incentive to affection and friendship, he produced woman from the very substance of the male. The second human being is beautifully taken from the side of the first, so that nature might teach that all are equal, as though side by side, and that there should be no superior or inferior in human affairs—something proper to friendship.

Thus nature impressed upon human minds, from the beginning, the inclination to friendship and affection; and an inward sense of loving soon increased it with a certain taste of sweetness. But after the fall of the first human being, when affection grew cold and desire entered in, causing private interests to be preferred to the common good, greed and envy corrupted the splendor of friendship and affection, bringing contentions, rivalries, hatreds, and suspicions into the corrupted habits of humankind.

[Col. 0668A] Then all good people distinguished between affection and friendship, observing that love must be bestowed even on enemies and the perverse, whereas no community of wills or counsels can exist between the good and the wicked. Friendship, therefore, which at first, like affection, was maintained among all and by all, remained by natural law among a few good people. Seeing that many violated the sacred rights of faith and fellowship, they bound themselves with a tighter bond of love and friendship, resting amid the evils which they saw and suffered in the graciousness of mutual affection.

Yet reason, which could not be extinguished in those whose impiety had obliterated every sense of virtue, left them the very inclination toward friendship and fellowship. Thus neither wealth delights the miser without companions, nor glory the ambitious, nor pleasure the lustful. Accordingly, even among the worst people certain detestable compacts of fellowship were made. Since they were veiled under the most beautiful name of friendship, they had to be distinguished from true friendship by law and precepts, lest, while pursuing the latter, one should heedlessly fall into the former because of some likeness between them.

Thus friendship was instituted by nature, strengthened by use, and ordered by the authority of law. It is therefore clear that friendship is natural, like virtue, wisdom, and the other things which, as natural goods, ought to be desired and preserved for their own sake. Whoever possesses them uses them well; no one at all misuses them.

[Col. 0668C] IVO. But surely many misuse wisdom: those who wish through it to please people, who become proud in themselves because wisdom has been granted them, or indeed those who hold it for sale and think piety a means of gain?

AELRED. Our Augustine will answer you here. His words are these: “Whoever pleases himself pleases a foolish man, because he is certainly foolish who pleases himself.” But one who is foolish is not wise; and one who is not wise is not wise precisely because he does not possess wisdom. How, then, does someone misuse wisdom if he does not possess wisdom? In the same way, proud chastity is not a virtue, because pride itself, which is a vice, makes that which was thought to be a virtue conform to itself; therefore it is no longer a virtue, but a vice.

IVO. But, with your leave, what you say does not seem fitting to me: you have joined wisdom to friendship, though there is no comparison between them.

AELRED. Lesser things are often joined with greater things, goods with better goods, and inferior things with stronger things. Though they are not equal, they are nevertheless joined, especially among virtues; for although they differ from one another by degrees, they are yet akin through a certain likeness. Widowhood is near to virginity, and marital chastity to widowhood. Although there is a great difference between these virtues, still there is some agreement in their being virtues. Marital purity is not therefore not a virtue because widowed continence excels it; and although holy virginity is preferred to them, it does not obliterate [Col. 0669A] their grace.

Indeed, if you carefully consider what has been said concerning friendship, you will find it so near or so bound up with wisdom that I might almost say friendship is nothing other than wisdom.

IVO. I confess I am astonished, and I do not think this can easily be persuaded to me.

AELRED. Have you forgotten Scripture’s saying: “A friend loves at all times” (Prov. 17)? And, as you remember, our Jerome also says: “A friendship that can cease was never true.” It has also been shown abundantly that friendship cannot even subsist without affection. Since, then, eternity flourishes in friendship, truth shines in it, and affection is sweet in it, consider whether you ought to deny the name of wisdom to these three.

IVO. What is this? Shall I say of friendship what John, the friend of Jesus, says of affection: “God is friendship”?

[Col. 0670A] AELRED. This is certainly an unusual expression and has no authority from Scripture. Yet I do not hesitate to attribute to friendship what follows concerning affection, because: “Whoever remains in friendship remains in God, and God in him” (1 John 4). When we begin to discuss its fruit or benefit, we shall see this more clearly. But now, if, given the modest capacity of our little intellect, we have said enough about what friendship is, let us reserve for another time the remaining matters which you proposed for clarification.

IVO. Though this delay is very troublesome to my eagerness, I am compelled to it not only by supper-time, from which I am not permitted to be absent, but also by the rather pressing expectation of the many to whom you are indebted.

## BOOK II. On the Fruit of Friendship and Its Excellence

[Col. 0669]

[Col. 0669B] AELRED. Now, brother, come nearer. Tell me what was the reason that a little while ago, when I was comparing those carnal things with other carnal things, you sat alone somewhat apart from us; and now you turned your eyes this way and that, now rubbed your forehead with your hand, now touched your hair with your fingers, and now, showing anger in your very face, complained through frequent changes of expression that something had come upon you against your wish.

WALTER. It is exactly so. For who could patiently endure that certain agents of your Pharaoh, whoever they may be, should have access to you all day, while we, to whom you are especially indebted, can scarcely have a conversation with you?

AELRED. We must also accommodate those whose favors we desire or whose ill will we fear. But now that they have at last been excluded, solitude is more welcome to me in proportion as the disturbance that preceded it was more troublesome. Hunger is the best seasoning of food; neither honey nor any flavor makes wine as savory as intense thirst makes water. Therefore perhaps this conversation of ours will be like a kind of spiritual food or drink to you, all the more delightful because a more burning heat preceded it. Come now; do not delay to bring forth what you were preparing to unfold a little while ago from your anxious heart.

[Col. 0669C] WALTER. I will indeed. For if I should complain about the hour which those people have left us—an exceedingly brief one—I would seem to make it shorter. Tell me, then, I ask you, whether it has escaped your memory or whether you still remember what was once agreed between you and your Ivo concerning spiritual friendship; what questions he proposed to you; how far you proceeded in explaining them; and what you committed to writing concerning them.

AELRED. The remembrance—indeed, the continual embrace and affection—of my dearest friend is always so fresh to me that, though he has paid sufficiently to the condition of humanity by being taken from it, he never seems to have died in my mind. There he is always with me; there his devout face shines before me; there his sweet eyes smile upon me; there his pleasant words taste so sweetly to me that I seem either to have passed with him to better things or that he still lives with me in these lower regions.

[Col. 0670B] You know that many years have passed since the little document on which I had written down his questions concerning spiritual friendship and my answers slipped from our possession.

WALTER. These things are not unknown to me. But, to tell the truth, all my eagerness and impatience arises from this: I have heard from certain people that the document itself was found three days ago and delivered to you. Show it, I beg you, to your boy. My spirit does not rest until, having examined everything and observed what is lacking to that discussion, I bring before the judgment of your fatherhood the questions which either my own mind or some hidden inspiration suggests should be asked—whether they are to be rejected, admitted, or explained.

AELRED. I will comply with your wish, but I want you to read what is written alone and not bring it out in public, lest I perhaps judge that some things must be cut out, some added, and very many corrected.

[Col. 0670C] WALTER. Here I am, with my ears hanging on your words, all the more eagerly because what I read about friendship tasted sweeter. Since I have read a magnificent discussion of what friendship is, I should like you to show me what benefit it produces for those who cultivate it. For when something is as great as this, and you seem to have proved it by convincing arguments, it is then desired more intensely when its end and fruit are known.

AELRED. I do not presume that I can explain this in a manner worthy of so great a matter. For among human things nothing holier is desired, nothing more useful sought, nothing more difficult found, nothing sweeter experienced, nothing more fruitfully possessed. Friendship bears fruit for present and future life. By its sweetness it displays all virtues and by its strength pierces vices; it moderates adversity and orders prosperity. Thus, without a friend, almost nothing can be pleasant among mortals; and a human being is likened to a beast if he has no one to rejoice with him in prosperity, grieve with him in sorrow, [Col. 0671A] receive the outpouring of a distress conceived in his mind, or share something unusually lofty or luminous that has come to him. “Woe to one who is alone, for when he falls, he has no one to raise him up” (Eccl. 4). He is altogether alone who is without a friend.

But what happiness, security, and delight it is to have someone with whom you dare speak as with yourself; someone to whom you do not fear to confess if you have sinned; someone to whom you are not ashamed to reveal any progress you have made in spiritual matters; someone to whom you entrust all the secrets of your heart and commend your counsels. What, then, is more delightful than so to unite another’s mind with one’s own and make one out of two, that no boasting is feared, no suspicion dreaded; that neither is pained when corrected by the other, nor does either criticize or accuse the other’s praise as flattery?

“A friend,” says the Wise Man, “is a medicine of life” (Ecclus. 6). This is excellently said. For in every temporal matter there is no remedy stronger or more effective for our wounds than to have someone who meets every misfortune with compassion and every advantage with congratulation, so that, joining their shoulders, they bear one another’s burdens—except that each person bears an injury done to himself more lightly than one done to a friend.

[Col. 0671C] Friendship therefore makes prosperity more splendid, and, by dividing and sharing adversity, makes it lighter. A friend is thus life’s best medicine. The philosophers too held this view: we make use of water, sun, and fire in fewer places than of a friend. In every action, every pursuit, in certainties and doubts, in every event and every circumstance, in private and public, in every deliberation, at home and abroad, friendship is welcome everywhere; a friend is necessary; kindness proves useful.

Therefore, Tully says, friends are present to one another even when absent; the needy are rich; the weak are strong; and, harder still to say, the dead live. Friendship, then, is glory for the rich, a homeland for exiles, wealth for the poor, medicine for the sick, life for the dead, favor for the healthy, strength for the weak, and reward for the strong. Such honor, remembrance, praise, and longing attend friends that both their life is judged praiseworthy and their death precious.

And what surpasses all these things: friendship is a certain step near the perfection that consists in the love and knowledge of God, so that from being a friend of a human being, one becomes a friend of God, according to the Savior’s saying in the Gospel: “I shall no longer call you servants, but my friends” (John 15).

[Col. 0671D] WALTER. I confess that your discourse has moved me so deeply, so wholly set every desire of my soul aflame with longing for friendship, that I do not think I am living while I lack this great good and its manifold fruit. But I desire that final point—the one which wholly seized me and almost tore me away from earthly things—to be explained more fully: namely, that friendship is held to be the best step toward perfection.

And very opportunely our Gratian has now entered, whom I should rightly call a foster-child of friendship itself. His whole concern is to be loved and to love, lest, excessively eager for friendship and deceived by its resemblance, he receive a false friendship for a true one, a feigned friendship for a solid one, or a carnal friendship for a spiritual one.

[Col. 0672A] GRATIAN. I thank your kindness, brother, because at last you grant entrance to the spiritual banquet to one who was not invited but has rather shamelessly intruded himself. If you seriously, and not in jest, thought me worthy to be called a foster-child of friendship, I ought to have been summoned at the beginning of the conversation, and I would not have revealed my eagerness by laying aside modesty. But you, Father, continue where you began, and add something to the table for my sake; so that, if I cannot be filled like this man—who, after devouring I know not how many courses, has now disdainfully invited me, as it were, to his leftovers—I may at least be somewhat refreshed.

[Col. 0672B]

AELREDUS. Do not be concerned, my son, for there still remains so much to be said about the good of friendship that, if any wise man were to pursue the matter, you would think that we had said nothing. But attend briefly to the manner in which friendship is a certain step toward the love and knowledge of God. For in friendship there is nothing dishonourable, nothing feigned, nothing pretended; whatever is there is holy, voluntary, and true. And this too is characteristic of charity. Yet friendship shines with a special prerogative in this: among those joined together by the bond of friendship, all things are pleasant, all secure, all sweet, all delightful. [Col. 0672C] Therefore, from the perfection of charity we love many persons who are a burden and a grief to us; although we assist them honourably—not falsely or hypocritically, but truly and willingly—we nevertheless do not admit them to the secrets of our friendship. Thus in friendship are united honourableness and sweetness, truth and delight, tenderness and willingness, affection and action. All these begin in Christ, are advanced through Christ, and are perfected in Christ. Therefore the ascent does not seem excessively difficult or unnatural: from Christ, inspiring the love by which we love a friend, to Christ, offering himself to us as the friend whom we may love; so that sweetness succeeds sweetness, tenderness tenderness, affection affection.

[Col. 0672D] Thus a friend, cleaving to his friend in the Spirit of Christ, becomes with him one heart and one soul; and so, ascending through the steps of love to Christ’s friendship, he becomes one spirit with him in one kiss. Longing for this kiss, a certain holy soul says: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” (Song of Songs 1). Let us consider the character of this bodily kiss, so that we may pass from bodily things to spiritual, from human things to divine. Human life is sustained by two kinds of nourishment, food and air. Without food one can indeed survive for some time, but without air not even for one hour. Therefore, in order to live, we draw air in through the mouth and send it out again. What is emitted or received is itself called spiritus, “breath” or “spirit.” Accordingly, in a kiss two breaths meet, mingle, [Col. 0673A] and unite; and from them arises a certain sweetness of mind which moves and touches the affection of those who kiss.

There is, then, a bodily kiss, a spiritual kiss, and an intellectual kiss. The bodily kiss is made by the contact of lips; the spiritual kiss by the union of souls; the intellectual kiss through God’s Spirit, by the infusion of graces. The bodily kiss, therefore, should be offered or received only for definite and honourable reasons: for example, as a sign of reconciliation, when persons who were previously enemies become friends with one another; as a sign of peace, as when those about to communicate in church show their inward peace by an outward kiss; as a sign of love, as is permitted between bridegroom and bride, or as friends offer and receive it after a long absence; [Col. 0673B] or as a sign of catholic unity, as when a guest is welcomed.

But just as many misuse water, fire, iron, food, and air—things naturally good—as instruments of their cruelty or pleasure, so the perverse and shameful seek somehow to season their own depravity even with this good, which natural law established to signify the things we have mentioned. They defile the kiss with such foulness that to kiss in this manner is nothing other than to commit adultery. Every honourable person understands how detestable, abominable, avoidable, and abhorrent this is.

The spiritual kiss, however, properly belongs to friends who are held under one law of friendship. It is not produced by the touch of mouths but by the affection of minds; not by the joining of lips but by the mingling of spirits, while the Spirit of God makes all things chaste and, through participation in himself, imparts a heavenly savour. [Col. 0673C] I would call this kiss Christ’s kiss—though he offers it not with his own mouth, but with another’s—by inspiring in those who love him that most sacred affection, so that they seem to be one soul in different bodies and say with the Prophet: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together as one” (Psalm 132 [133]).

A mind accustomed to this kiss, and not doubting that all this sweetness comes from Christ, as though reflecting within itself and saying, “Oh, if he himself had drawn near,” longs for that intellectual kiss and cries with the greatest desire: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” [Col. 0673D] (Song of Songs 1). Thus, when earthly affections have been softened and all thoughts and desires belonging to the world have been lulled to sleep, it may delight in Christ’s kiss alone and rest in his embrace, rejoicing and saying: “His left hand is beneath my head, and his right hand shall embrace me” (Song of Songs 2).

GRATIAN. This friendship, as I see, is not commonplace, nor the kind we have been accustomed to imagine. I do not know what Walter has thought up to now; but I believed friendship to be nothing other than such an identity of wills between two persons that neither wills anything which the other does not will; and that such agreement should exist between them in good and evil alike that neither spirit, property, honour, nor anything belonging to one should be denied to the other for enjoyment at will and abuse.

WALTER. [Col. 0674A] I remember learning something altogether different in the earlier dialogue, where the definition of friendship itself was set forth and explained. It rightly stirred me to look more deeply into its fruit. Having been sufficiently instructed about it, we ask that a fixed limit be prescribed for us, indicating how far friendship ought to proceed, since different people hold different views. There are some who think that one must support a friend against faith, against honour, against the common or private good. Some judge that faith alone is to be exempted, while the rest need not be guarded. Others think that for a friend wealth should be despised, honours rejected, the enmity of powerful persons incurred, and even exile not avoided; that one should expose oneself, where one does not harm one’s country or injure another against right and law, even to shameful and disgraceful acts.

[Col. 0674B] There are also those who set this limit in friendship: that each person should become toward his friend as he is toward himself. Some think that to return a corresponding benefit or service to a friend in every case is enough to satisfy friendship. This discussion has convinced me sufficiently that none of these people should be believed. Therefore I ask you to establish for me some fixed limit in friendship, especially for the sake of this Gratian, lest, in accordance with his name, he should wish to be so pleasing that he carelessly becomes vicious.

GRATIAN. I do not take this concern of yours on my behalf ungratefully—unless my thirst for hearing were holding me back, I might perhaps even now repay you in kind. But let us listen together to what he would rather answer to your inquiries.

[Col. 0674C] AELREDUS. Christ himself has prescribed the fixed limit of friendship: “No one has greater love than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends” (John 15). See how far love between friends ought to extend: namely, that they should be willing to die for one another. Is this enough for you?

GRATIAN. Since friendship cannot be greater, why should it not be enough?

WALTER. But what if utterly wicked people or pagans love one another in a shared purpose of crimes and disgraceful acts so that they are willing to die for one another? Shall we admit that they have ascended to the height of friendship?

AELREDUS. Far from it, since friendship cannot exist among the utterly wicked!

GRATIAN. Tell us, please, [Col. 0674D] among whom it can either arise or be preserved.

AELREDUS. I say briefly: it can arise among the good, advance among the better, and be brought to completion among the perfect. For as long as evil delights anyone through deliberate choice, as long as pleasure is more agreeable to him than purity, rashness than moderation, flattery than correction, how can he lawfully even aspire to friendship, whose origin proceeds from the esteem of virtue? It is difficult, indeed impossible, for you even to taste its beginnings if you do not know the source from which it can arise. For that is a foul alliance of love, unworthy of the name of friendship, in which something shameful is demanded from a friend. Whoever has not yet either lulled or subdued his vices must do such a thing, since he is enticed or driven toward whatever is unlawful. Therefore the opinion of those [Col. 0675A] who think one should act for a friend against faith and honour is detestable. There is no excuse for sin if you have sinned for a friend’s sake.

Adam, the first-created man, would more salutarily have rebuked his wife’s presumption than, by yielding to her, have seized what was forbidden (Genesis 3). The servants of King Saul also preserved faithfulness to their lord far better when, contrary to his command, they withheld their hands from bloodshed than did Doeg the Edomite, who, serving the king’s cruelty, slaughtered the priests of the Lord with sacrilegious hands (1 Samuel 22). Likewise Jonadab, Amnon’s friend (2 Samuel 13), would more laudably have forbidden his friend’s incest than offered counsel by which he might gain the object of his desire. Nor does friendship excuse Absalom’s friends (2 Samuel 16), who, assenting to treason, took up arms against their country.

And, to come to our own times, Otto, cardinal of the Roman Church, certainly did far better in withdrawing from his most intimate friend Guy than John did in adhering to his Octavian in such a schism. You see, therefore, that friendship cannot stand except among the good.

GRATIAN. What, then, have we to do with friendship, since we are not good?

AELREDUS. I do not cut “good” so closely to the quick as do some, who will have no one considered good unless nothing is lacking to him for perfection. We call a person good who, according to the measure of our mortality, “lives soberly, righteously, and godly in this world” (Titus 2), and who neither wishes to ask anything dishonourable from anyone nor, when asked, to grant it. We do not doubt that friendship can arise among such persons and be perfected by such persons. [Col. 0675C] For those who, excepting faith, danger to their country, or injury to another contrary to right and justice, expose themselves to their friends’ desires, I would call not so much foolish as insane: sparing others, they do not think themselves worthy of being spared; providing for others’ honour, they disastrously betray their own.

WALTER. I almost fall in with the opinion of those who say that friendship ought to be avoided, as something full of anxiety and cares, not free from fear and liable to many griefs. Since it is more than enough for each person to care for himself, they call it imprudent to bind oneself to others in such a manner that one must become entangled in many cares and afflicted with troubles. They further judge that nothing is more difficult than for friendship to continue until the final day of life, and that it is exceedingly shameful for a friendship once begun to turn into its opposite. Therefore they think it safer to love someone in such a way that one may hate him whenever one wishes; to loosen friendship’s reins so that one may tighten or relax them whenever one wishes.

GRATIAN. Then we have laboured in vain—you in speaking and we in listening—if we are so readily to be restrained from desiring friendship, whose fruit you have commended to us as so holy, so useful, so acceptable to God, so near to perfection, and so manifold. Let that view belong to the person who is pleased to love today in order to hate tomorrow; to be a friend to everyone so as to be faithful to no one; to praise today and blame tomorrow; to flatter today and bite tomorrow; to be ready today for kisses and tomorrow for reproaches; [Col. 0676A] whose love is bought at a cheap price and departs at the slightest offence.

WALTER. I thought doves lacked gall. Yet explain how the opinion of those people, which so displeases Gratian, may be refuted.

AELREDUS. Cicero speaks finely on this point: “They seem to remove the sun from the world who remove friendship from life, than which we have nothing better from God, nothing more pleasant.” What kind of wisdom is it to detest friendship in order to avoid anxiety, to be free from cares, to rid oneself of fear? As though any virtue could be acquired or preserved without concern! Does prudence fight against errors within you, temperance against lusts, justice against wickedness, or courage against cowardice, without your great vigilance? Who, I ask, especially among the young, can preserve chastity or restrain a wanton inclination without great pain or fear?

Paul was foolish, then, for refusing to live without care and concern for others; rather, because of charity, which he regarded as the greatest virtue, he became weak with the weak and burned with those who were scandalized. He also had great sorrow and continual grief in his heart for his brethren according to the flesh. Therefore charity ought to have been abandoned by him, lest amid so many fears and griefs he should now be again in labour with those whom he had begotten (Galatians 4), now cherish them as a nurse (1 Thessalonians 2), now rebuke them as a teacher (Colossians 1), now fear lest their minds should be corrupted from the faith (2 Corinthians 11), [Col. 0676C] now summon them to repentance with much grief and many tears (2 Corinthians 2), now mourn those who had not repented.

You see how they endeavour to remove virtues from the world who do not fear to remove from its midst concern, their companion. Was Hushai the Archite foolish to preserve with such faithfulness his friendship with David (2 Samuel 16), that he preferred concern to security and would rather share his friend’s griefs than dissolve himself in the joys and honours of a parricide? I would call not so much human beings as beasts those who say that one should live in such a way as to be no consolation to anyone, and no burden or grief to anyone; who conceive no delight from another’s good, inflict no bitterness upon others by their own perversity, and care to love no one and to be loved by no one. Far be it from me to grant that anyone loves who considers friendship a source of gain—[Col. 0676D] professing themselves friends only with their lips when the hope of some temporal advantage smiles upon them, or when they try to make a friend the instrument of some shamefulness.

WALTER. Since, then, it is certain that many are deceived by the resemblance of friendship, explain, please, what kinds of friendships we ought to avoid and which we ought to seek, cultivate, and preserve.

AELREDUS. Since it has been said that friendship cannot endure except among the good, you can readily understand that no friendship unworthy of good people should be embraced.

GRATIAN. But perhaps we are in the dark concerning what is fitting or unfitting in making this distinction.

AELREDUS. I shall comply with you and briefly note the friendships which occur to me as needing avoidance. There is a childish friendship, created by wandering and wanton affection, [Col. 0677A] spreading its legs to every passer-by: without reason, weight, measure, or consideration of any advantage or disadvantage. For a time it strongly moves, binds, and sweetly attracts. But affection moved without reason is a beastly impulse, inclined toward every unlawful thing—indeed, unable to distinguish lawful from unlawful. Although affection commonly precedes friendship, it must never be followed unless reason guides it, honour restrains it, and justice governs it.

Therefore this friendship, which we call childish because affection rules more in children, must altogether be avoided by those delighted by the sweetness of spiritual friendship. It is faithless, unstable, and always mingled with impure loves. We call it not so much friendship as friendship’s poison, [Col. 0677B] because in it the lawful measure of love can never be kept—the measure which is from soul to soul. Instead, a kind of smoke rising from the lust of the flesh clouds and corrupts its honourable vein, neglects the spirit, and draws it toward fleshly desires.

For this reason, the beginnings of spiritual friendship should first have purity of intention, the governance of reason, and the bridle of temperance. Then the most delightful affection, when it comes, will assuredly be felt to be sweet in such a way that it never ceases to be ordered.

There is also the friendship brought about by similarity in the habits of the very wicked; I pass over it, since, as we said above, it is not considered worthy even of the name of friendship. There is, moreover, the friendship kindled by consideration of some advantage, [Col. 0677C] which many think ought for this reason to be sought, cultivated, and preserved. But if we admit this, how many people altogether worthy of love shall we exclude—people who have nothing and possess nothing, from whom no temporal benefit can be obtained or hoped for?

If, however, you count among benefits counsel in uncertainties, consolation in adversities, and other things of that sort: these indeed are to be expected from a friend, but they should follow friendship, not precede it. For he has not yet learned what friendship is who wishes its reward to be something other than itself. Friendship will plainly be a reward to those who cultivate it when, wholly transferred into God, it buries in his contemplation those whom it has united. For although faithful friendship among good persons produces many great benefits, [Col. 0677D] we do not doubt that these arise from friendship, rather than friendship from them.

We do not believe that the friendship between Barzillai the Gileadite and David (2 Samuel 19 [20]) was established among such great men from the benefits by which Barzillai welcomed, sustained, and endowed the king as he fled from his parricidal son; rather, we do not doubt that such favour proceeded from friendship itself. For no one who reflects can deny that the king first needed that man. Yet it is plainly evident that Barzillai, a man of great wealth, hoped for no reward from the king in return, because when the king readily offered him all the delights and riches of the city, he consented to accept nothing, wishing to be content with his own possessions.

So also that venerable covenant between David and Jonathan, consecrated not by hope of future benefit but by the contemplation of virtue, we know brought much advantage to both: by the diligence of the one, the other’s life was preserved; by the favour of the other, the first’s posterity was not destroyed. [Col. 0678A] Therefore, since friendship among the good always comes first and usefulness follows, it is not so much advantage gained through a friend as love for the friend himself that delights.

Whether, then, we have said enough concerning the fruit of friendship; whether we have also clearly stated the definite persons among whom it can arise, endure, and be perfected; whether, further, we have manifestly exposed the flatteries that are falsely veiled under the name of friendship; and whether we have likewise shown the fixed limits to which love between friends ought to extend—judge for yourselves.

GRATIAN. I do not sufficiently remember that final point being explained.

AELREDUS. You remember, I believe, that I refuted the opinion of those who set friendship’s limits in agreement in disgraceful acts and crimes; likewise that of those who think one must go as far as exile, and, provided no one else is harmed, into whatever shamefulness; and no less that of those who measure the degree of friendship according to the scale of hoped-for advantage. For I did not consider two of the views proposed by Walter worthy even of mention. What could be more absurd than that friendship should extend only so far as one repays a friend in offices or services, when all things ought to be common to those who ought, surely, to be one heart and one soul? And how shameful is that other view: that one should feel toward a friend no differently than toward oneself, when each person ought to think humbly of himself and highly of his friend. [Col. 0678C]

Having rejected these false limits of friendship, we thought that its limit should be drawn from the Lord’s words, who ordained that death itself is not to be avoided for friends. But lest persons of any shameful kind, if they were willing to die for one another, should be thought to have attained the height of friendship, we said among what persons friendship can arise and be perfected. Then we held that those who think friendship ought to be avoided because of the many anxieties and cares it produces should be charged with foolishness. Finally, we explained as briefly as possible what friendships all good persons must avoid.

From all this, therefore, the certain and true limit of spiritual friendship is evident: nothing is to be denied to a friend, and nothing is to be refused for a friend, which is less than the precious life of the body itself, which divine authority ordained should be laid down for a friend. [Col. 0678D] Therefore, since the life of the soul is far more excellent than that of the body, we judge that one thing must absolutely be denied to a friend: that which brings death to the soul, namely sin, which separates God from the soul and the soul from life. But this is not the time to unfold what measure must be observed and what caution employed in things to be supplied to a friend or endured for a friend.

GRATIAN. I confess that our Walter has contributed not a little. Provoked by his question, you have comprehended in a short summary the whole of what has been discussed, almost painting it before our eyes in our memory. Come now, I pray, explain to us what measure must be observed and what caution employed in the very services of friends.

[Col. 0679A] AELREDUS. These matters, and certain others concerning friendship, remain to be said; but the hour has already passed, and those who have just arrived, as you see, compel us by their importunity to another business.

WALTER. I certainly withdraw unwillingly, but tomorrow, when time offers itself, I shall surely return. Let Gratian take care to be present early in the morning, so that neither he may accuse us of negligence nor we him of tardiness.

BOOK THREE. How, and among whom, friendship may be kept unbroken.

[Col. 0679]

[Col. 0679B] AELREDUS. Where from, and where to?

GRATIAN. The reason for my arrival is not unknown to you.

AELREDUS. Is Walter present?

GRATIAN. Let him see to it himself; certainly today he cannot accuse us of tardiness.

AELREDUS. Do you wish us to continue the matters proposed?

GRATIAN. I trust him; for I consider his presence necessary to me: his understanding is keener for comprehension, his tongue more trained for questioning, and his memory more tenacious for retaining.

AELREDUS. Did you hear, Walter? Gratian is more your friend than you thought.

WALTER. How could he fail to be my friend, who is everyone’s friend? But since we are both here, let us not be ungrateful for this leisure, remembering your promise.

AELREDUS. The source and origin of friendship is love. Love can exist without friendship, but friendship never without love. Love proceeds from nature, from duty, from reason alone, from affection alone, or sometimes from both together. From nature, as a mother loves her son. From duty, when certain people are joined by a special affection on account of what has been given and received. From reason alone, as we love enemies not by a spontaneous inclination of mind but from the necessity of a command. From affection alone, when someone inclines his affection toward certain persons solely because of bodily things—for example, beauty, strength, or eloquence. From reason together with affection, when one whom reason advises us to love on account of the worth of virtue impresses himself upon another’s mind by sweetness of character and the charm of a praiseworthy life; and so reason joins with affection, so that love is chaste from reason and sweet from affection. [Col. 0679D] Which of these seems to you more suitable for friendship?

WALTER. Certainly the last, which both contemplation of virtue forms and sweetness of character adorns. But I desire to know whether all whom we love in this way are to be admitted to friendship’s sweet secret.

AELREDUS. First, a firm foundation of spiritual love itself must be laid, upon which its beginnings are to be placed. Thus, when someone ascends by a straight line to its higher things, he should use the greatest caution lest he neglect or exceed the foundation. That foundation is the love of God. To it must be referred everything suggested by love or affection, everything urged either secretly by some spirit or openly by any friend. [Col. 0680B] You must carefully examine whether whatever is affirmed accords with the foundation; and whatever is found to exceed it, you should not hesitate to recall to its form and correct wholly according to its character.

Nevertheless, not all whom we love are to be received into friendship, because not all are found fit for it. Since a friend is the companion of your soul, to whose spirit you join and attach your own, mingling it so that you wish two to become one; a person to whom you entrust yourself as to another self, from whom you conceal nothing and fear nothing: first, surely, one must choose someone thought suitable for these things; then test him; and only then admit him. Friendship must be stable and bear a certain likeness to eternity, always persevering in affection. [Col. 0680C] Therefore we must not change friends in a childish fashion through some wandering inclination.

Since no one is more detestable than one who has violated friendship, and nothing torments the soul more than either abandonment by a friend or attack by one, a friend must be chosen with the utmost care and tested with the greatest caution. Once admitted, he must be tolerated, treated, and followed in such a way that, as long as he has not irrevocably departed from the foundation already laid down, he is yours and you are his, in bodily as well as spiritual matters; and there is no division of souls, affections, wills, or judgments. You see, therefore, four stages by which one ascends to the perfection of friendship: the first is choice, the second testing, the third admission, [Col. 0680D] and the fourth a complete agreement in divine and human things, joined with a certain charity and goodwill.

WALTER. I remember that in your first discussion with Ivo you established this definition sufficiently; but since you discussed many kinds of friendships, I wish to know whether it embraces them all.

AELREDUS. Since true friendship cannot exist except among the good, who can neither will nor do anything against faith or good morals, this definition plainly embraces not just any friendship, but friendship itself as it is true.

GRATIAN. Why, then, should not that definition which delighted me greatly before our discussion the day before yesterday be equally approved: “to will the same things and not to will the same things”?

AELREDUS. Certainly, among people whose habits have been corrected, life well ordered, and affections regulated, I do not think even that formulation should be rejected.

WALTER. [Col. 0681A] Gratian should take care that these conditions come first both in himself and in the one whom he loves; then let him will and not will the same things with him, neither consenting for himself nor granting at another’s request anything unjust, dishonourable, or unbecoming. But we await your instruction concerning what should be thought about the four points you set forth.

AELREDUS. Let us treat first of choice itself. There are certain vices with which, if anyone is entangled, he will not long keep friendship’s laws or rights. Persons of this kind should not easily be chosen for friendship; but if their life and character otherwise please us, every effort must be made to heal them so that they may be fit for friendship: namely, the irascible, the unstable, the suspicious, and the talkative. For it is difficult that one frequently agitated by the fury of anger should not sometime rise up against a friend, as is written in Ecclesiasticus: “There is a friend who will expose hatred, quarrel, and insults” (Ecclesiasticus 6 [not 16]). Therefore Scripture says: “Do not be a friend to an angry man, nor walk with a furious man, lest you take a snare for your soul” (Proverbs 22). And Solomon says: “Anger rests in the bosom of a fool” (Ecclesiastes 7). [Col. 0681B] Who would not think it impossible to keep friendship long with a fool?

WALTER. Yet we have seen you, unless we are mistaken, cultivate friendship with the deepest loyalty with a very irascible man. We have heard that you were never offended by him until the end of his life, although he often offended you.

AELREDUS. Some people are irascible from a natural mixture of temperaments, but are so careful to restrain and moderate this passion that they never fall into the five things by which, according to Scripture, friendship is dissolved and corrupted—although they sometimes offend a friend by an inconsiderate word or action, or by zeal that lacks sufficient discretion. If we happen to receive such people into friendship, they must be borne patiently; and, since we are assured of their affection, if there is any excess in word or deed, it must be forgiven to a friend, or else he should gently and cheerfully be reminded of the matter in which he has exceeded.

GRATIAN. The man of yours whom, as it seems to many, you approve as your friend above all of us, said and did something a few days ago, as we thought, after being overcome by anger—something that he could not possibly have been unaware would displease you. Yet we neither believe nor see that anything of your former favour toward him has been diminished. [Col. 0681D] We were not a little astonished that, although among ourselves you are unwilling to pass over even the smallest matter which he wishes, he was unable to endure some small thing for your sake.

WALTER. He is much bolder than I am. I too know these things, but knowing your feeling toward him, I did not dare to speak to you about them.

AELREDUS. That man is certainly most dear to me. Once received by me into friendship, he can never cease to be loved by me. Therefore, if in this matter I was perhaps stronger than he, and where the will of each of us did not agree in one, it was easier for me to break my own will than for him to break his; where no dishonour intervened, faith was not injured, and virtue was not diminished, I had to yield to my friend: both to endure what seemed to be his excess [Col. 0682A] and, where his peace was endangered, to prefer his will to my own.

WALTER. But since the former has now passed into the realm of fate, and the latter, although we did not see it, has made satisfaction to you, I should like you to explain to us those five things by which friendship is so injured that it is dissolved, so that we may be able to avoid those who are in no way to be chosen as friends.

AELREDUS. Listen—not to me, but to Scripture speaking: “He who reviles a friend dissolves friendship. Even if a friend has drawn a sword, do not despair: for there is a return to friendship. If he has opened a sorrowful mouth, do not be afraid” (Ecclus. 22).

See what it says. If perhaps a friend, overcome by anger, has drawn a sword, or uttered a grievous word; if, as though no longer loving you, he has withdrawn himself from you for a time; if he has at some point preferred his own judgment to yours [Col. 0682B], or disagreed with you in some opinion or dispute—do not judge friendship to be dissolved on these grounds. “There is,” it says, “reconciliation with a friend, except in the case of reviling, reproach, pride, disclosure of a secret, and a treacherous blow. In all these cases a friend will flee.”

Let us therefore consider these five matters more carefully, lest we bind ourselves in the bonds of friendship to those whom either the frenzy of anger or some other passion is accustomed to drive into these vices. Reviling injures one’s reputation and extinguishes charity. For such is human malice that whatever is hurled by a friend at a friend under the prompting of anger is proclaimed true, as though uttered by one privy to his secrets, even if it is not believed. Many indeed delight as much in others’ disparagement as in their own praises [Col. 0682C].

What is more wicked than reproach, which even by a false accusation covers an innocent person’s face with pitiable blushes? And what is less tolerable than pride? It excludes the one remedy by which a broken friendship might have been restored—humility and confession—making a person bold in inflicting injury and swollen with indignation at correction.

The disclosure of secrets: nothing is more shameful, nothing more detestable; it leaves nothing of love or sweetness between friends, but fills everything with the bitterness of resentment and sprinkles all things with the gall of hatred and sorrow. Hence it is written: “He who reveals a friend’s secrets loses trust” (Ecclus. 24). And shortly afterwards: “To reveal a friend’s secrets is the despair of an unhappy soul” (ibid.). For what is more unhappy than one who loses trust and languishes in despair?

The last thing by which friendship is dissolved is a treacherous blow, which is nothing other than secret detraction. Certainly a treacherous blow: the deadly bite of serpent and asp. “If a serpent bites in silence,” says Solomon, “he who secretly detracts is no better” (Eccles. 10). Therefore, whenever you find someone habitually given to these vices, beware of him; and until he is healed, do not choose him for friendship.

Let us renounce revilings, for God avenges them. Shimei, assailing holy David with revilings as he fled before Absalom (3 Kings 2), is decreed to be put to death, by the authority of the Holy Spirit, among the hereditary charges which the dying father entrusted to his son. Let us likewise beware reproach. Unhappy Nabal the Carmelite, who reproached David with his servitude and flight, deserved to be struck down and killed by the Lord (1 Kings 25) [Col. 0683A].

Should it happen that in some matter we transgress the law of friendship, let us avoid pride and recover the favour of our friend by the service of humility. When King David mercifully offered to the son of King Nahash of the Ammonites the friendship which Nahash had shown him (2 Kings 10), Hanun, proud and ungrateful toward a friend, added insult to contempt. For this cause both he himself and his people and cities were consumed by sword and fire.

Above all, let us regard the revealing of friends’ secrets as sacrilege, by which trust is lost and the despair of a captive soul is brought in. Thus the utterly impious Ahithophel (2 Kings 17), agreeing with the parricide, after he had betrayed to him the father’s counsel, saw that his own counsel, given against it, had not been carried into effect; and he received a traitor’s fitting end by hanging himself with a noose [Col. 0683B].

Finally, let us regard detraction against a friend as the poison of friendship—a poison which covered Miriam’s brow with leprosy (Num. 12) and, after she had been cast outside the camp for six days, deprived her of communion with the people.

In this choosing one must beware not only of those excessively prone to anger, but also of the unstable and suspicious. For since security is a great fruit of friendship, by which you trust and entrust yourself to a friend, how can there be any security in the love of someone who is carried about by every wind and acquiesces in every counsel? His affection is like soft clay: all day long, according to the will of the one impressing it, it receives and takes on diverse and contrary images [Col. 0683C].

Moreover, what better suits friendship than a certain mutual peace and tranquility of heart, of which the suspicious person is always deprived? He never rests. For curiosity always accompanies suspicion, continually sharpening its goads and providing it with materials for unrest and disturbance. If he sees his friend speaking privately with someone, he will think it betrayal. If his friend shows kindness or pleasantness to another, he will proclaim that he himself is loved less. If his friend corrects him, he will interpret it as hatred. If his friend thinks him worthy of praise, he will complain that he is being mocked.

Nor do I think a talkative person should be chosen, for “a man of the tongue shall not be justified.” “Do you see,” says the wise man, “a man hasty in speaking? A fool has more hope than he” (Prov. 29) [Col. 0683D]. Therefore you should choose as a friend one whom the frenzy of anger does not disturb, instability does not divide, suspicion does not wear down, and talkativeness does not loosen from due seriousness. It is especially useful to choose one whose character accords with your own and whose disposition harmonizes with yours. For, as blessed Ambrose says, friendship cannot exist between dissimilar characters; and therefore the grace of both must agree.

GALTERUS. Where, then, will such a person be found—one who is neither irascible nor unstable nor suspicious? For whoever is talkative cannot remain hidden.

AELREDUS. Although it may not be easy to find someone who is not moved by these passions, there are certainly many found superior to all of them: people who restrain anger by patience, check frivolity by preserving seriousness [Col. 0684A], and repel suspicions by contemplating love. I would say that those especially should be taken into friendship as being more seasoned, who, overcoming vices by virtue, are possessed all the more securely because they have grown accustomed to resisting even vices when they assail them more forcefully.

GRATIANUS. Please do not be angry if I speak. That friend of yours, whom we mentioned a little while ago, whom we do not doubt has been received by you into friendship—I wish to know whether he seems to you irascible.

AELREDUS. He is indeed; but not in friendship.

GRATIANUS. What, I ask you, is it not to be irascible in friendship?

AELREDUS. You do not doubt that friendship has been formed between us.

GRATIANUS. Certainly not.

AELREDUS. When have you heard anger, quarrels, disagreements [Col. 0684B], jealousies, or disputes arise between us?

GRATIANUS. Never; but we attribute that not to his character but to your patience.

AELREDUS. You are mistaken. No person’s patience will in any way restrain anger which affection does not restrain, since patience rather provokes the irascible person into fury, as he wishes to give himself at least some slight consolation if someone in a quarrel proves his equal. Yet the man of whom we are now speaking preserves the laws of friendship toward me in such a way that, when he is stirred up and even already breaking out into words, I restrain him by a gesture alone; and he never brings into public what displeases him, but always waits for privacy in which to vent what he has conceived in his mind. If nature rather than friendship imposed this upon him, I would judge him neither so virtuous nor so worthy of praise [Col. 0684C]. But if, as often happens, my judgment sometimes differs from his, we defer to one another in such a way that sometimes he prefers my will to his own, and more often I prefer his to mine.

GALTERUS. Gratianus has been sufficiently answered. But I should like you to explain to me: if someone has rather incautiously fallen into friendship with those whom you said should earlier be avoided, or if any of those whom you said should be chosen fall into these very vices, or perhaps into others worse still, what faith ought to be kept toward them and what favour shown?

AELREDUS. These things should, if possible, be guarded against in the very act of choosing, or even of testing, lest we love too quickly, especially those wholly unworthy. Those are worthy of friendship in whom there is, in themselves, a reason why they should be loved [Col. 0684D]. Yet in those judged tested and worthy, vices often break out—both against their friends themselves and against outsiders, though the resulting disgrace falls back upon their friends. Every care should be applied to heal such friends.

But if that proves impossible, I do not think friendship ought to be broken or dissolved; rather, as someone has elegantly said, it ought gradually to be unstitched—unless, perhaps, some intolerable injury has flared up, such that it is neither right nor honourable for separation or severance not to take place at once. For if a friend plots something against father or country that needs immediate and swift correction, friendship is not injured if the traitorous enemy is exposed.

There are other vices for which we judge friendship not to be broken, as we have said, but gradually dissolved; yet in such a manner [Col. 0685A] that it does not burst forth into enmity, from which quarrels, curses, and insults arise. For it is very shameful to wage such a war with one with whom you have lived intimately.

For even if you are assailed by all these things from one whom you had received into friendship—for some people behave in this way: after they have lived so as no longer to deserve love, should any misfortune befall them, they cast the blame back upon a friend; they say friendship has been injured, and hold suspect every counsel their friend has given. When their fault has come publicly to light, they call themselves betrayed, and, having nothing further they can do, heap hatred and curses upon their friend, slandering him in corners, whispering in darkness, falsely exalting themselves, and accusing others in the same way.

If, therefore, after friendship has been relinquished, you are assailed by all these things, so long as they are tolerable, they must be endured. This honour must be rendered to old friendship: let the fault lie with the one who acts, not with the one who suffers injury. Friendship is indeed eternal; hence: “At every time he who is a friend loves” (Prov. 17). If the one whom you love injures you, still love him. If he becomes such that friendship must be withdrawn from him, love nevertheless must never be withdrawn. As far as you can, provide for his welfare; protect his reputation; and never betray the secrets of his friendship, though he himself has betrayed yours [Col. 0685B].

GALTERUS. What, I ask, are those vices for which you say friendship should gradually be dissolved?

AELREDUS. Those five which we described a little before; but especially the revelation of secrets and the hidden bites of detractions. We add a sixth to these [Col. 0685C]: if he harms those whom you are equally bound to love and, even after correction, does not cease to furnish occasion of ruin and scandal to those whose welfare it concerns you to protect—especially where the disgrace of his vices touches you. For love must not outweigh religion, faith, charity toward fellow citizens, or the welfare of the people.

King Ahasuerus hanged upon the gallows the exceedingly proud Haman, whom he had held as his friend above all others (Ezek. 7), preferring to the friendship which Haman had injured by deceitful counsels the safety of the multitude and the love of his wife. Jael, wife of Heber the Kenite, although there was peace between Sisera and the house of Heber, preferred the welfare of the people to this friendship and put Sisera to sleep with a nail and hammer (Judg. 4). Holy David the prophet, though by the right of friendship he ought to have spared the kindred of Jonathan (2 Kings 21), nevertheless heard from the Lord that, because of Saul and his bloody house, since he had slain the Gibeonites, the people had continually suffered famine for three years; he gave seven men of Saul’s kindred to the Gibeonites to be punished [Col. 0685D].

But I do not want you to be ignorant of this: among the perfect, whom true and spiritual friendship has joined after they have been wisely chosen and cautiously tested, dissension cannot arise. For when friendship has made two into one, just as what is one cannot be divided, so friendship cannot be separated from itself. It is clear, therefore, that this friendship which suffers division was never true in that part in which it is injured.

Yet friendship and virtue are shown more worthy in this: that what it was does not cease to be in the one who is injured—loving one by whom he is not loved; honouring one by whom he is despised; blessing one by whom he is cursed; doing good to one who devises what is harmful to him [Col. 0686A].

GALTERUS. How, then, is friendship dissolved, if such things must be shown to the excluded person by the one who dissolves it?

AELREDUS. Four things seem to pertain especially to friendship: love and affection, security and delight. To love pertains the bestowal of benefits with goodwill. To affection pertains a certain inward delight proceeding from the heart. To security pertains the disclosure, without fear or suspicion, of all counsels and secrets. To delight pertains a sweet and friendly exchange concerning all that happens, whether joyful or sorrowful; all that is thought, whether harmful or useful; and all that is taught or learned [Col. 0686B].

Do you see in what respects friendship must be dissolved with those who deserve it? Certainly that inward delight which one continually drew from the friend’s breast is withdrawn; the security by which one revealed one’s hidden matters to him perishes; the delight which friendly conversation produced is set aside. That intimacy, therefore, in which such things consist must be denied him; but love must not be withdrawn. And this should be done with a certain moderation and reverence, so that, unless the aversion is excessive, certain traces of the former friendship may always appear to remain.

GRATIANUS. These things which you say certainly please me.

AELREDUS. Now tell me whether what we have said about choice is enough.

GALTERUS. I would like the sum of what has been said to be given us in a brief epilogue.

AELREDUS. I shall comply with your wish. We have said that love is the beginning of friendship—not love of just any sort, but that which proceeds jointly from reason and affection. It is chaste by reason and sweet by affection. Next, we said that the foundation of friendship must be laid in the love of God, to which all the matters proposed must be referred, and it must be examined whether they accord with it or depart from it.

Then we judged that four stages in friendship, by which one reaches its summit, must be observed: first a friend is to be chosen, then tested, then at last admitted, and thereafter treated as is fitting. In discussing choice [Col. 0686C], we excluded the irascible, unstable, suspicious, and talkative—not all such persons, however, but only those who cannot or will not order and moderate these passions. For many are touched by these disturbances in such a way that not only is their perfection harmed in no respect, but their virtue is even increased more praiseworthily by their moderation.

For those who, as though unbridled, are always driven headlong by these passions inevitably slip and fall into those vices by which friendship, according to the testimony of Scripture, is both injured and dissolved: namely revilings, reproach, revelation of secrets, pride, and a treacherous blow. Yet if you suffer all these things from someone whom you have once received into friendship, we do not say that friendship should immediately be broken, but gradually dissolved. Such reverence for the old friendship should be preserved [Col. 0687A] that, though you remove him from your secrets, you never withdraw love from him, withdraw aid, or deny counsel.

And should his madness even burst out into blasphemies and curses, you must nevertheless show regard for the bond and for charity, so that the fault lies with the one who inflicted the injury, not with the one who endured it. But if he is found harmful to father, country, fellow citizens, subjects, or friends, the bond of intimacy must immediately be broken, and love for one person must not be preferred to the destruction of a multitude.

To prevent these things from occurring, care must be taken in the very choice, namely that the person chosen is not driven to such deeds by frenzy, drawn by levity, rushed headlong by talkativeness, or led away by suspicion; above all, that he does not differ too greatly from your own character or disagree with your disposition [Col. 0687B]. But because we are speaking of true friendship, which can exist only among the good, we make no mention of those about whom there can be no doubt that they are not to be chosen—shameful persons, the avaricious, the ambitious, and criminals. If we have said enough to you about choosing, let us next proceed to testing.

GALTERUS. This is timely; for my eye is always upon the door, lest someone perhaps burst in, either to put an end to our pleasures, mix in some bitterness, or bring in something empty.

GRATIANUS. The cellarer is present; if he is permitted to enter, you will have no opportunity to proceed further. But see: I shall watch the door; you, Father, continue where you began.

AELREDUS. Four qualities must be tested in a friend: faithfulness, intention, discernment, and patience [Col. 0687C]. Faithfulness, so that you may safely entrust yourself to him. Intention, so that you expect nothing from friendship except God and its natural good. Discernment, so that you do not fail to know what should be given to a friend, what should be requested from him, over what matters one should grieve for him, in what one should rejoice with him, for what one should correct him, and the proper measure, time, and place. Patience, so that when corrected he does not take offense, does not despise or hate the one correcting him, and does not shrink from enduring any adversity for his friend.

Nothing in friendship is more excellent than faithfulness, which seems to be its nurse and guardian. It shows itself equal in every adversity and prosperity, in joyful and sorrowful circumstances, in pleasant and bitter ones, looking with the same eye upon the lowly and exalted, poor and rich, strong and weak, healthy and sick. A faithful friend properly sees nothing in his friend that is outside the friend’s soul [Col. 0687D]: embracing virtue in its proper seat, he thinks little of all other things as though placed outside the person, neither valuing them greatly when present nor seeking them when absent.

Faithfulness itself lies concealed in prosperity but stands out in adversity. “A friend is tested in need.” Many are friends of the rich; but whether they are true friends is tested by intervening adversity. Solomon says: “At every time he who is a friend loves, and a brother is proved in distress” (Prov. 17). Rebuking the unfaithful man, he says: “A rotten tooth and a weary foot is one who trusts in an unfaithful person in the day of distress” (Prov. 25).

GRATIANUS. If no adversity ever interrupts our prosperity, how will a friend’s faithfulness be tested?

AELREDUS. There are many other means by which a friend’s faithfulness is tested, though especially in misfortunes [Col. 0688A]. For, as we said above, nothing harms friendship more than betrayal of counsels. The Gospel saying is: “He who is faithful in a little thing will also be faithful in much” (Luke 16). Therefore, to friends whom we still think need testing, not all our secrets, nor our deepest ones, should be entrusted; but first external or minor matters, about which it is not of great concern whether they are concealed or disclosed—yet with as much caution as if disclosure would cause very great harm and concealment would bring benefit.

If he is found faithful in these matters, do not hesitate to test him in greater ones. And if perhaps some adverse report has spread about you, if someone maliciously attacks your reputation, and he is induced by no suggestion to believe it, stirred by no suspicion, disturbed by no doubt, then you should have no further hesitation concerning his faithfulness, but rather no small exultation in it as certain and steadfast [Col. 0688B].

GRATIANUS. I now remember that overseas friend of yours, of whom you have often spoken to us, whom you judged your truest and most faithful friend for this reason: that, when false reports about you were brought to him, he not only gave them no credence but was not troubled by any hesitation. You did not think this could be assumed even of your very close old friend, the sacristan of Clairvaux. But since faithfulness has been sufficiently discussed, proceed to explain the remaining qualities.

AELREDUS. We said also that intention must be tested. This is most necessary, for there are very many who know no good in human affairs except what is temporally profitable [Col. 0688C]. They love friends as they love their oxen, from which they hope to gain some benefit. Such people plainly lack genuine and spiritual friendship, which is to be sought for God’s sake and for its own sake; nor do they see in themselves the natural model, in which its force, character, and greatness are easily perceived.

The Lord and our Savior himself prescribed for us the form of true friendship: “You shall love your neighbour as yourself,” he says (Matt. 22). Here is the mirror. You love yourself—indeed, if you love God, and if you are such as we have described a person to be who should be chosen for friendship. Do you think, I ask, that any reward for this love of yourself is to be demanded from yourself? Certainly not; rather, each person is dear to himself for his own sake. Unless, then, you transfer this same affection to another, he cannot be dear to you equally with yourself [Col. 0688D]. For then the one whom you love will be another self, if you have poured your love into him.

For, as Saint Ambrose says, friendship is not a tax-paying arrangement, but is full of beauty and full of grace. It is a virtue, not a profit, because it is acquired not by money but by grace; not by competitive bidding of prices, but by rivalry in goodwill. Therefore the intention of the person you have chosen must be tested carefully, lest he wish to join himself to you in friendship according to the hope of some advantage, judging friendship a hired service rather than a free gift.

Friendships of the poor are generally more trustworthy than those of the rich, since poverty removes hope of profit in such a manner that it does not diminish but rather increases friendship’s charity. The rich, therefore, receive flattering services; toward a poor person no one is a pretender. Whatever is offered to a poor person is genuine, because his friendship is free from envy [Col. 0689A]. We say this so that in friends we may test character rather than appraise wealth.

Thus intention is tested. If you see that he is more desirous of your possessions than of you, always angling for something that your resources may confer upon him—honour, glory, riches, liberty—then, if a worthier person is preferred to him in all these things, or if what he desires is simply not in your power, you will easily perceive with what intention he has attached himself to you.

Let us now consider discernment. Some people, perversely enough—not to say shamelessly—want to have as a friend someone such as they themselves cannot be. These are they who bear even their friends’ slight transgressions impatiently, correct them harshly, and, lacking discernment, neglect great matters while rising up against every trifling thing. They throw everything into confusion, observing neither the place where, nor the time when, nor the persons before whom a matter ought to be made public or concealed [Col. 0689B].

Accordingly, the discernment of the person you choose must be tested, lest by joining some careless or imprudent person to yourself in friendship you procure daily disputes and quarrels for yourself. It is quite easy to see that this virtue is necessary in friendship: whoever lacks it will be borne along like a ship without a rudder, driven by the force of the wind in a movement always unstable and irrational.

Likewise, there will be no lack of occasions by which the patience of the person whom you desire as a friend may be tested, since it is necessary to correct the one whom you love. Sometimes this must be done more harshly, as if deliberately, so that his endurance may thereby be tested or exercised [Col. 0689C].

Yet this should be observed: although in the person you are testing there may be found things that offend the mind—whether an incautious disclosure of some secret, greed for some temporal benefit, an insufficiently discreet correction, or some transgression of due gentleness—you should not immediately recoil from your intended love or choice, so long as any hope of his correction shines forth.

And let no one find it burdensome to be diligent in choosing or testing friends. The fruit of this labour is a medicine of life and the firmest foundation of immortality. For, although very many are sufficiently skilled in multiplying treasures, in raising, selecting, and purchasing oxen and asses, sheep and goats [Col. 0689D], and although sure indications for knowing all such things are not lacking, it is madness not to devote the same effort to acquiring or testing friends, and not to learn certain marks by which those whom we choose as friends may be proved fit for friendship.

One must certainly beware a certain impulse of love which runs ahead of judgment and removes the possibility of testing. It is therefore the part of a prudent person to wait, restrain this impulse, set a limit to goodwill, and proceed gradually into affection, until, once the other has been tested, he gives and entrusts his whole self to his friend.

GALTERUS. I confess that I am still moved by the opinion of those who think it safer to live without friends of this kind.

AELREDUS. That is surprising, since no life at all is pleasant without friends.

GALTERUS. Why, I ask you?

[Col. 0690A] AELREDUS. Let us suppose that the entire human race has been removed from the world and that you alone remain alive. Behold before you all the pleasures and riches of the world: gold, silver, precious stones, walled cities, turreted strongholds, spacious buildings, sculptures, paintings. Further, imagine yourself restored to your original state, having all things subject to you: “all sheep and oxen, and besides the beasts of the field, the birds of heaven and the fish of the sea, which pass through the paths of the sea” (Ps. 8). Tell me now: could all these things be pleasant to you without a companion?

GALTERUS. Not at all.

AELREDUS. What if you had one person whose language you did not know, whose habits you did not understand, and whose love and disposition toward you were hidden from you?

GALTERUS. Unless I could by some signs bring it about that he became a friend, I would prefer to have no one rather than such a person [Col. 0690B].
