AELREDUS. But if there were someone present whom you loved as yourself and by whom you did not doubt you were likewise loved, would not everything that formerly seemed bitter become sweet and pleasant?

GALTERUS. Entirely so.

AELREDUS. And would you not judge yourself happier in proportion as you had more such persons?

GALTERUS. Most truly.

AELREDUS. This is that wonderful and great happiness for which we wait: God himself working and spreading between himself and his creature, among the ranks and orders which he has distinguished, and among each individual whom he has chosen, such friendship and charity [Col. 0690C] that each loves another as himself; and thus each rejoices in another’s happiness as in his own. So the blessedness of each becomes the blessedness of all, and the totality of all blessednesses becomes the blessedness of each.

There is no concealment of thoughts there, no dissimulation of affections. This is true and eternal friendship, begun here and perfected there; here belonging to few, where few are good; there belonging to all, where all are good. Here testing is necessary, where wise and foolish are mingled; there those whom that angelic and, in a sense, divine perfection makes blessed have no need of testing.

Let us therefore acquire friends according to this likeness, loving them no differently from ourselves; let all things be bare to us with them, and let us disclose to them all our secret matters; let them be firm, stable, and constant in all things [Col. 0690D]. Do you think there is any mortal who does not wish to be loved?

GALTERUS. I do not think so.

AELREDUS. If you saw someone living among many people, suspecting all of them, fearing all as though they plotted against his life, loving no one, and thinking himself loved by no one, would you not judge him most miserable?

GALTERUS. Certainly most miserable.

AELREDUS. Then you will not deny that the happiest person is one who rests in the affections of those among whom he lives, loving all and loved by all, whom neither suspicion separates from this sweetest tranquility nor fear disturbs.

GALTERUS. Very well and most truly.

AELREDUS. But if it is perhaps difficult at present to find this among all people, since it is reserved for us in the future [Col. 0691A], then the more such people we have in abundance, the happier we shall judge ourselves.

The day before yesterday, as I was walking around the enclosure of the monastery, while the most loving company of brothers sat together, and as though amid the delights of paradise I admired the leaves, flowers, and fruits of the individual trees, I found no one in that multitude whom I did not love and by whom I did not trust that I was loved. I was so filled with joy that it surpassed all the delights of this world. For I felt my spirit poured out into all of them, and the affection of all passing over into me, so that I said with the Prophet: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity!” (Ps. 132).

GRATIANUS. We are not to suppose that you have taken into friendship all those whom you love in this way and by whom you are so loved?

[Col. 0691B] AELREDUS. We embrace very many with all affection, yet do not admit them to the secrets of friendship, which consist especially in the disclosure of all our secrets and counsels. Thus the Lord says in the Gospel: “I shall no longer call you servants, but my friends”; and, adding the reason why they deserved the name of friends, he says: “Because I have made known to you all things which I heard from my Father” (John 15). Elsewhere: “You are my friends if you do what I command you” (ibid.).

On these words, as Saint Ambrose says (*On Duties*, book 3, ch. 21): “He gave the form of friendship which we should follow: that we should do a friend’s will; that we should open our secrets to a friend, whatever we have in our heart; and that we should not be ignorant of his hidden matters [Col. 0691C]. Let us show him our breast, and let him open his to us. For a friend conceals nothing. If he is true, he pours out his soul, just as the Lord Jesus poured out the mysteries of the Father.”

So Ambrose. How many people, then, do we love, to whom it is less safe to disclose our mind in this way and pour out our inmost feelings—people whose age, understanding, or discernment is insufficient to bear such matters!

GALTERUS. This friendship is lofty and perfect, so that I do not dare aspire to it. For Gratianus and me, that friendship is enough which your Augustine describes (*Meditations*, book 4, ch. 8): namely, to talk together and laugh together, to render mutual and kindly services, to read together, discuss together, play together, and behave honorably together; sometimes to disagree without hatred, as a person does with himself, and by that very rare disagreement to season the many agreements; to teach one another something or learn from one another; to miss absent friends with sorrow [Col. 0691D], and receive those who arrive with joy. By these and similar signs, proceeding from the heart of those who love and are loved in return—through mouth, tongue, eyes, and a thousand most pleasing movements—their souls are, as by kindling, fused together and made one out of many. This is what we believe should be loved in friends: so that our conscience seems guilty to itself if we do not love one who loves us in return, or do not return the love of one who loves us.

AELRED. This is the friendship of carnal persons, especially of the young—such as he himself and the friend of whom he was then speaking had once been. Yet, apart from trifling and falsehood, if no indecency has intervened, it should be tolerated in hope of fuller grace, as certain beginnings of a holier friendship. As religion increases, spiritual pursuits become alike, maturity of age comes, and spiritual perceptions are enlightened, they ascend with a purer affection to higher things, as though from close at hand. Thus, as we have said, from human friendship one passes more easily to friendship with God himself, because of a certain likeness. But now it is time to consider henceforth how friendship ought to be cultivated.

Faith, then, is the foundation of steadfastness and constancy in friendship; for nothing faithless is stable. Friends ought to be straightforward, open, harmonious, and moved by the same things toward one another: all these qualities pertain to faithfulness. [Col. 0692A–B] For a complex and crooked disposition cannot be faithful; nor can those who are not moved by the same things and do not agree in the same things be stable either in friendship or in faith. Above all, suspicion must be avoided, for it is the poison of friendship. Let us never think ill of a friend, nor believe or agree with one who speaks ill of him.

Let pleasantness be added in conversation, cheerfulness in the countenance, sweetness in manners, and serenity even in the glance of the eyes—no slight seasoning in friendship. Sadness indeed, and a more severe expression, possess a certain honourable gravity; but friendship ought sometimes to be more relaxed, freer, and sweeter, more inclined to courtesy and ease, though without frivolity and dissipation. [Col. 0692B–C]

Furthermore, it belongs to friendship that the superior should make himself equal to the inferior. For those of lower rank, order, dignity, or learning are often admitted into friendship by persons of greater distinction. Such persons ought to despise and account as nothing and empty all things external to nature, and always to attend to the beauty of friendship: friendship is not adorned with silks or gems, enlarged by possessions, made rich by luxuries, abounding in wealth, exalted by honours, or puffed up by dignities. Returning thus to the principle of origin, they should carefully consider the equality which nature has given, rather than the external trappings which mortal greed has bestowed. [Col. 0692C–D]

Therefore, in friendship—which is the best gift alike of nature and of grace—the lofty person should come down, the lowly rise; the rich should need, the poor become rich. Thus each should share his condition with the other, so that equality may result. Hence it is written: “He who had much did not have too much, and he who had little did not have too little” (2 Cor. 8). Never, then, prefer yourself to your friend. If perhaps you are found superior in the matters we have mentioned, do not hesitate all the more to submit yourself to your friend, to inspire confidence, to raise up one who is ashamed, and to show him so much the more honour as his condition or poverty prescribes that less honour should be shown him.

Jonathan, the most excellent of young men, paid no attention to royal lineage or to the prospect of a kingdom. He made a covenant with David and, making a servant equal with his lord in friendship, preferred him to himself—though David had been driven out by Jonathan’s father, was hiding in the wilderness, had been sentenced to death, and marked for slaughter. He humbled himself and exalted David: “You,” he said, “will be king, and I shall be second after you” (1 Sam. 20). [Col. 0692D–0693A]

O most splendid mirror of true friendship! A marvelous thing! The king raged against a servant and, as against a rival for the kingdom, stirred up the whole land; he accused the priests of treachery and slaughtered them on suspicion alone. He scoured woods, searched valleys, and besieged mountains and rocks with armed force. All pledged themselves as avengers of royal indignation. Jonathan alone—he alone who might most justly have been jealous—thought that his father must be resisted, his friend honoured, counsel given in so great an adversity; and, preferring friendship to a kingdom, he said: “You will be king, and I shall be second after you.”

See how the father stirred envy in the young man against his friend, assailing him with insults and frightening him with threats, reminding him that he would be stripped of the kingdom and deprived of honour. For when Saul had pronounced sentence of death upon David, Jonathan did not fail his friend: “Why should David die? What has he sinned? What has he done? He put his life in his own hand and struck the Philistine, and you rejoiced. Why then should he die?” (ibid.). [Col. 0693A–B]

At these words the king was driven to madness and tried to pin Jonathan to the wall with a spear. He added insults to threats: “Son,” he said, “of a woman who takes a man of her own accord, I know that you love him to your shame and to the shame of your disgraceful mother.” Then he vomited out all the venom with which the young man’s heart might be sprinkled, adding the spur of ambition, the fuel of envy, the incentive of jealousy and bitterness: “So long as the son of Jesse lives, your kingdom shall not be secure” [Col. 0693B–C].

Who would not be moved by these words? Whose love, favour, or friendship would they not corrupt, weaken, or obliterate? But that most loving young man, preserving the laws of friendship, was strong against threats and patient under insults; for friendship’s sake he despised a kingdom, forgot glory, and remembered grace: “You will be king,” he said, “and I shall be second after you.”

Cicero says that some have been found who considered it base to prefer money to friendship; but that it is impossible to find those who would not prefer honours, magistracies, commands, powers, wealth, and possessions to friendship—so that, when these things are offered on one side and the claims of friendship on the other, they would not choose those many things. For human nature is too weak to despise power. “For where,” he asks, “will you find a man who prefers his friend’s honour to his own?” [Col. 0693C–D] Behold, Jonathan was found: conqueror of nature, despiser of glory and power, preferring his friend’s honour to his own, saying, “You will be king, and I shall be second after you.”

This is true, perfect, stable, and eternal friendship: envy does not corrupt it, suspicion does not diminish it, ambition does not dissolve it. Thus tested, it did not yield; thus battered, it did not fall. Beaten by so many insults, it is seen to remain inflexible; attacked by so many injuries, it remained unmoved. “Go, and do likewise” (Luke 10).

But if you judge it hard, or even impossible, to prefer before yourself one whom you love, at least do not neglect to make him your equal, if you wish to be a friend. For friendship is not rightly cultivated by those who do not preserve equality. “Yield to your friend as to an equal,” says Ambrose (*On Duties*, book III, chapter 21); “do not be ashamed to precede your friend in service.” Friendship knows no pride. For a faithful friend is medicine of life, through the grace of immortality. [Col. 0693D–0694A]

Let us now consider how friendship ought to be cultivated in acts of kindness, and let us draw something here from other hands. “Let this law,” says someone, “be established in friendship: that we ask honourable things from friends and do honourable things for friends, and that we do not wait to be asked. Let hesitation always be absent! If money is to be lost for a friend, it should much more be contributed for a friend’s advantage or need.” But not everyone can do everything. One abounds in money; another in lands and possessions; one has greater influence in counsel; another excels more in honours. Consider prudently what sort of person you ought to show yourself to your friend in these matters.

Scripture has said enough concerning money: “Lose money,” it says, “for a friend” (Ecclus. 26). But since “the eyes of the wise are in his head,” and if we are members and Christ is the head, let us do what the Prophet says: “My eyes are always toward the Lord” (Ps. 24), so that we may receive from him the pattern for living. Of him it is written: “If anyone lacks wisdom, let him ask the Lord, who gives generously to all and does not reproach them” (James 1). [Col. 0694A–B]

So give to your friend that you do not reproach him, do not expect repayment, do not knit your brow, turn away your face, or cast down your eyes. Rather, with a serene face, cheerful expression, and pleasant speech, interrupt the words of one asking; meet him with goodwill, so that you seem to grant unasked what is requested. A noble spirit judges nothing more shameful than asking. Therefore, since you and your friend ought to have one heart and one soul, it is unjust if your money is not one also.

Let this law, then, be kept among friends in this respect: that they expend themselves and their possessions for one another, so that the giver retains cheerfulness and the receiver does not lose confidence. When Boaz observed the poverty of Ruth the Moabite, gleaning ears after his harvesters, he spoke to her, consoled her, invited her to the servants’ meal, and, generously sparing her modesty, ordered the harvesters deliberately to leave ears for her to gather without shame. [Col. 0694C] So too we ought to investigate our friends’ needs more carefully, anticipate with benefits the person who is about to ask, and observe such a measure in giving that the recipient seems rather to confer a favour than the giver.

GALTER. What then shall be the benefit of spiritual friendship in this respect for us, to whom neither receiving nor giving anything is permitted?

AELRED. “Men,” says the wise man [Note: Plato, Col. 0693D], “would live a most blessed life if these two words were removed from their midst: ‘mine’ and ‘thine.’” Holy poverty gives great strength to spiritual friendship, and it is holy precisely because it is voluntary. Since greed is fatal to friendship, friendship once gained is preserved all the more easily as the mind is found more cleansed of that pestilence. [Col. 0695A]

Yet there are other benefits in spiritual love by which friends can support and help one another. First, they should be concerned for each other; each should blush for the other, rejoice for the other, mourn the other’s fall as his own, and count the other’s progress as his own. In every way he can, one should raise up the faint-hearted, support the weak, console the sad, and bear with the angry. Further, he should reverence his friend’s eyes so greatly that he dares neither do anything dishonourable nor say anything unbecoming. For whatever fault he himself commits so rebounds upon his friend that he not only blushes and grieves within himself, but the person who sees or hears it reproaches the friend as though he himself had sinned. Certainly, therefore, though not sparing himself, he thinks that he should spare his friend. [Col. 0695A–B]

Modesty is thus the best companion of friendship; and whoever removes modesty from friendship takes away its greatest ornament. How often has a glance from my friend restrained or extinguished the flame of anger conceived within me and already bursting into public! How often has his sterner look repressed an indecent word which had reached my very throat! How often, when I had carelessly given myself over to laughter or fallen into idle talk, did I recover the gravity due to me at his arrival!

Moreover, whatever must be urged is more readily received and more securely retained when it comes from a friend, whose authority in persuasion ought to be great, since neither his faithfulness is doubtful nor his flattery suspect. Therefore let friend urge upon friend what is honourable, confidently, openly, and freely. Friends must not only be warned but, when necessary, rebuked. For although truth is unpleasant to some, because hatred arises from it—as the saying has it, “Compliance produces friends; truth, hatred”—yet compliance is far more harmful when, indulging sins, it lets a friend rush headlong. [Col. 0695B–C]

A friend is especially blameworthy, and especially to be rebuked for this reason, if he rejects truth and is driven into sin by compliance and flattery. Not that we ought not to serve friends sweetly and often speak kindly to them; but moderation must be observed in everything, so that admonition lacks bitterness and rebuke lacks insult. In acts of service and kindness there should be a certain sweet and honourable affability; but flattery, the helper of vices, must be driven far away. It is worthy neither of a friend nor even of a free person. The salvation of one whose ears are closed to truth, so that he cannot hear truth from a friend, must be despaired of.

Accordingly, as Ambrose says, if you discover some fault in a friend, correct him privately; if he does not listen, correct him publicly. Corrections are good, and often better than silent friendship. Even if your friend thinks himself injured, still correct him. Even if the bitterness of correction wounds his mind, still correct him. For the wounds of a friend are more bearable than the kisses of flatterers. Therefore correct a friend who is in error. [Col. 0695D]

Above all, anger and bitterness of mind must be avoided in correction, lest one seem less to wish to correct a friend than to satisfy one’s own indignation. I have seen some, when correcting friends, disguise conceived bitterness and boiling rage now under the name of zeal, now under that of frankness. Following impulse rather than reason, they never benefited their friends by such correction, but indeed harmed them greatly. Among friends there can be no excuse for this vice. A friend ought to suffer with his friend, to accommodate himself, to regard the other’s fault as his own, and to rebuke humbly and compassionately. [Col. 0696A]

Let a sadder expression rebuke him, a quieter voice; let tears interrupt the words, so that he may not only see but feel that the correction proceeds from love, not resentment. If he rejects the first correction, he may receive the second. Meanwhile, pray; weep; wear a sad face while preserving a compassionate affection. The character of his mind must also be examined. There are some whom gentle words benefit and to whom they submit more willingly. Others make little of them and are more easily corrected by word or by rod. Therefore let a friend adapt and fit himself to his friend in a way suited to that friend’s character; and he who ought to help in outward adversity should hasten still more to meet what is adverse to the spirit. [Col. 0696A–B]

Just as it properly belongs to friendship to admonish and to be admonished—the one to act freely but not harshly, the other to receive patiently and not defiantly—so we must hold that in friendships no pest is greater than flattery and obsequious assent. These belong to frivolous and deceitful people, who say everything according to another’s wish and nothing according to truth. Therefore let there be no hesitation among friends, no pretence—for pretence is especially opposed to friendship. A person owes truth to a friend; without it the name of friendship can have no force.

“Let the righteous man correct me in mercy and rebuke me,” says holy David, “but let not the oil of the sinner fatten my head” (Ps. 140). A pretender and schemer provokes the anger of God. Hence the Lord says through the prophet: “My people, those who call you blessed deceive you and ruin the way of your steps” (Isa. 3). For, as Solomon says, “A pretender with his mouth deceives his friend” (Prov. 11). [Col. 0696B–C]

Therefore friendship must be cultivated in such a way that, if for definite reasons dissimulation may sometimes seem permissible, pretence never is.

GALTER. How, I ask, is dissimulation necessary? It always seems to me to be a vice.

AELRED. You are mistaken, my son; for God too is said to dissimulate the sins of offenders, not willing the death of the sinner but that he should be converted and live.

GALTER. Distinguish, I ask you, between pretence and dissimulation.

AELRED. Pretence, in my view, is a kind of deceitful agreement contrary to the judgment of reason. Terence expressed it quite elegantly in the character of Gnatho: “Does someone deny it? I deny it. Does he affirm it? I affirm it. Finally, I have commanded that everyone agree with me in everything.” Perhaps that pagan borrowed this from our treasures, expressing the thought of our prophet in his own words. For it is clear that the prophet uttered this also in the person of a perverse people: “See empty things for us; speak pleasing things to us” (Isa. 30). And elsewhere: “The prophets prophesied falsehood, the priests applauded with their hands, and my people loved such things” (Jer. 5). [Col. 0696D–0697A]

This vice must be detested everywhere and avoided always and everywhere. Dissimulation, on the other hand, is a prudent postponement either of punishment or correction, without inward agreement, according to place, time, and person. If, for example, a friend established among the people commits a fault, he should not immediately be rebuked publicly. Rather, the matter should be passed over according to the circumstances; indeed, insofar as truth permits, what he has done should be excused, and a familiar private occasion awaited for the due correction.

Likewise, when a person’s mind is occupied with many concerns and is less fit for what must be said, or when other causes have arisen and his feelings are somewhat more agitated and disturbed, dissimulation is necessary until the inward tumult has been calmed and he can bear correction with a more tranquil ear. When King David, overcome by desire, had joined murder to adultery, the prophet Nathan, intending to rebuke him (2 Sam. 12), deferred to royal majesty. He did not immediately and while the mind of so great a person was disturbed thrust the crime upon him; rather, by suitable dissimulation first, he wisely drew from the king himself a judgment against himself. [Col. 0697A–B]

GALTER. This distinction pleases me greatly. But I should like to know whether, if a friend is more powerful and can promote whomsoever he wishes to honours or any dignities, he ought in such advancement to prefer those whom he loves and by whom he is loved above others, and, among them, prefer those whom he loves more?

AELRED. It is worth investigating how friendship ought to be cultivated in this respect too. Some think that they are not loved because they cannot be promoted; and they complain that they are despised if they are not burdened with responsibilities and offices. We have therefore known no small quarrels to arise among those considered friends, so that estrangement followed indignation, and curses followed estrangement. [Col. 0697C]

Accordingly, in dignities and offices, especially ecclesiastical ones, great caution must be exercised. Attention should be paid not to what you are able to grant, but to what the recipient can bear. Many ought to be loved who nevertheless ought not to be promoted; and we embrace many commendably and sweetly whom we would involve in responsibilities and business only at grave peril to ourselves and the greatest danger to them. Therefore reason must always be followed in these matters, not affection. This honour or burden must be imposed, not upon those whom we have as closer friends, but upon those whom we judge better fitted to bear it. Yet where equality of virtue is found, I do not greatly disapprove if affection has some part for a while. [Col. 0697C–D]

Let no one, then, call himself despised because he has not been promoted. The Lord Jesus preferred Peter to John in this matter, yet did not withdraw his affection from John because he gave primacy to Peter. To Peter he entrusted his Church; to John, his sweetest mother (John 21). To Peter he gave the keys of his kingdom; to John he opened the secrets of his breast. Peter, therefore, was higher; John, safer. Peter, though set in authority, when Jesus said, “One of you will betray me” (John 13), feared and trembled with the others. John, made bolder by sharing his bosom, at Peter’s prompting asked who it was. Peter was thus assigned to action; John was reserved for affection, because, he says, “Thus I will that he remain until I come” (John 21). [Col. 0697D–0698A]

For he gave us an example, that we too might act thus. Let us give a friend everything that belongs to love, favour, sweetness, and charity. Let us impose empty honours and burdens upon those whom reason has designated, knowing that no one truly loves a friend for whom the friend himself is not enough unless he adds these worthless and contemptible things. We must take great care, however, that a more tender affection does not hinder greater benefits—when, because we embrace certain people with greater charity and a great hope of richer fruit shines forth, we are unwilling either to send them away or to burden them.

This is ordered friendship: reason governs affection, and we consider not so much what their sweetness asks as what the advantage of many requires. [Col. 0698A–B]

I now recall two friends who, though removed from the present world, live for me and will always live. The first I had acquired at the beginning of my conversion, through a certain similarity of character and equality of pursuits, while I was still a young man. The other, chosen by me almost from the time of his childhood and tested in many ways and on many occasions, I admitted into the highest friendship when age was already changing my hair.

The first, when I was still burdened by no pastoral care and distracted by no concern for temporal things, I had chosen as companion and partner in the delights of the cloister and the spiritual sweetnesses into which I was then being initiated. I asked nothing and gave nothing except affection and a certain sweet judgment of that affection, as charity dictated. The other, now a young man, I called into a share of my responsibilities and had as a helper in these labours of mine. [Col. 0698B–C]

Looking back and distinguishing the two friendships by memory, I see that the former rested more on affection, the latter on reason—although the former did not lack reason, nor was the latter without affection. For the first was taken from me at the very beginnings of our friendship; he could be chosen, as we have prescribed, but not tested. The other, granted to me from boyhood until middle age and loved by me, climbed with me through every degree of friendship as far as the imperfection of such things allowed.

At first the contemplation of his virtues inclined my affection toward him. Long ago I brought him from the southern regions into this northern solitude; I was the first to instruct him in monastic discipline. From that time he conquered the body, endured labour and hunger, became an example to very many, an object of admiration to many, and to me a source of glory and delight. [Col. 0698C–D]

Even then I thought that he should be nurtured in the beginnings of friendship, since I saw him burdensome to no one and pleasing to all. He came in and went out at the command of the elders: humble, gentle, grave in manners, sparing of speech, knowing neither indignation, grumbling, resentment, nor detraction. He walked “as though deaf, not hearing, and like a mute not opening his mouth.” He became like a beast of burden (Ps. 37), following the bridle of obedience and bearing tirelessly in mind and body the yoke of monastic discipline.

Once, while still a boy, he entered the infirmary and was reproved by my holy father and predecessor because he had so quickly yielded himself, though a boy, to rest and idleness. He was so ashamed that, on leaving, he immediately submitted himself with such fervour to bodily exercises that for many years, even when oppressed by serious illness, he relaxed nothing of his accustomed strictness. [Col. 0699A]

These things bound him to my inmost heart in wonderful ways and so entered my mind that I made him, from an inferior, a companion; from a companion, a friend; from a friend, a most intimate friend. Seeing him advance into a certain gray maturity of virtue and grace, I laid upon him, at the brothers’ advice, the burden of the sub-priorate. He accepted it unwillingly, indeed, but modestly, because he had devoted himself to obedience.

Yet he spoke with me privately that he might be released, pleading his age, his inexperience, and the friendship in which we had already begun to be joined—lest perhaps on this occasion he should either love less or be loved less. Since he gained nothing by these arguments, he began, in a free voice, humbly and modestly to set forth whatever he feared for us both, whatever he found displeasing in me. As he later confessed, he hoped that I would be offended by this apparent presumption and so be more easily inclined to grant his request. [Col. 0699A–B]

But this freedom of his mind and speech increased the fullness of our friendship, because I wished to have him as no ordinary friend. When he saw that I received gratefully what he had said, answered each point humbly, and had given him sufficient satisfaction on everything, he found that he had received not merely no offence but, beyond this, a richer fruit. He began himself to love me more closely than usual, to loosen the reins of affection, and to pour his whole self into my heart.

Thus his freedom was proved to me, and my patience to him. I too repaid my friend in kind. On an occasion I thought him to be rebuked somewhat sharply, sparing him not even certain words that might seem insults; yet I found him neither impatient with my frankness nor ungrateful. Then I began to reveal to him the secrets of my counsels, and he was found faithful. [Col. 0699B–C]

Thus love grew between us, affection warmed, charity was strengthened, until we came to have one heart and one soul, to will and not will the same things. This love was free from fear, knew no offence, lacked suspicion, and abhorred flattery. Nothing was pretended between us, nothing coloured; nothing was dishonourably soft, nothing unbecomingly harsh; there was no circumlocution, no hidden corner, but everything was naked and open. I regarded his heart in some manner as my own, and mine as his; and he likewise.

Thus, as we walked in a straight line of friendship, no one’s rebuke produced indignation, no one’s agreement produced fault. Proving himself my friend in all things, he watched over my peace and, insofar as he could, my quiet. He exposed himself to dangers and met scandals as they arose. [Col. 0699C–D]

At times, because he was already becoming weak, I wished to offer him some temporal consolation; but he forbade it. He said that care must be taken lest our love be measured according to such consolation of the flesh, lest it be ascribed more to my carnal affection than to his need, and thus my authority be diminished. He was therefore as my hand, as my eye, the staff of my old age. He was the resting-place of my spirit, the sweet comfort of my sorrows. The bosom of his love received me when I was weary from labour; his counsel renewed me when I was plunged in sadness or grief. He calmed me when disturbed and softened me when angry. Whatever less joyful thing arose, I referred to him, so that what I could not bear alone I might more easily endure with shoulders joined. [Col. 0700A]

What then? Was it not a certain share of blessedness to love thus and be loved thus; to help thus and be helped thus; and, from the sweetness of brotherly charity, to fly upward more deeply into that more sublime brightness of divine love—now ascending on the ladder of charity to Christ’s own embrace, now descending to love of neighbour to rest there sweetly?

In this friendship of ours, which we have introduced by way of example, if you see anything to imitate, turn it to your own advancement. But, that we may at last close this conversation as the sun is setting: you do not doubt that friendship proceeds from love. But how can one who does not love himself love another? And a person ought to order love of neighbour according to the likeness of the love by which he is dear to himself; yet he does not love himself if he either demands from himself or commands himself anything shameful or dishonourable. [Col. 0700B–C]

Therefore, the first requirement is that each person make himself chaste, granting himself nothing unbecoming and withholding from himself nothing useful. Loving himself in this way, let him love his neighbour by the same rule. But because this love gathers many people together, let him choose from among them one whom he may admit by a familiar law into the secrets of friendship, upon whom he may pour out his affection abundantly—laying bare his heart even to an inspection of its inward parts and marrow, of the thoughts and intentions of the heart.

Let that person be chosen not by the wantonness of affection but by the discernment of reason, through similarity of character and contemplation of virtues. Then let him devote himself to his friend so that all levity is absent and pleasantness is present, and so that the ordered offices and services of goodwill and charity are not lacking. [Col. 0700C–D]

Thereafter let his faithfulness be tested, his integrity tested, his patience tested. Let a sharing of counsels be added gradually, the regular practice of similar pursuits, and a certain conformity of countenance. Friends ought to be so conformed to one another that, as soon as either sees the other, even the likeness of one’s expression is reflected in the other—whether one is cast down by sadness or bright with joy.

When he has thus been chosen and tested, and you are certain that he wishes nothing unbecoming either to ask from a friend or to offer when asked; when it is established that he considers friendship a virtue, not a gain; that he flees flattery and detests obsequious assent; and when he is found free with discretion, patient under correction, firm and steadfast in love—then that spiritual sweetness is felt: namely, “How good and pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity” (Ps. 132). [Col. 0701A]

How useful then is it to grieve for one another and labour for one another, when each finds it sweet to disregard himself for the other, to prefer the other’s will to his own, to meet the other’s need rather than his own, and to oppose and expose himself to adversities! How sweet, meanwhile, they find it to confer with one another, disclose their pursuits mutually, examine everything together, and agree in one judgment concerning all things!

Prayer for one another is added: in remembrance of a friend it is sent to God so much more effectively as it is more affectionate, with tears flowing—tears which fear shakes out, affection draws forth, or grief brings forth. Thus, praying to Christ for his friend and desiring to be heard by Christ for his friend, he fixes his attention diligently and longingly upon the friend. Suddenly and imperceptibly, affection sometimes passes into affection; and, as though touching from close at hand the sweetness of Christ himself, he begins to taste how sweet he is and to feel how delightful he is. [Col. 0701B–0702A]

Thus, ascending from that holy love by which he embraces his friend to that by which he embraces Christ, he will joyfully gather with full mouth the spiritual fruit of friendship, awaiting the fullness of all things in the future. Then fear will be removed, by which we now fear and are anxious for one another; every adversity which we must now endure for one another will be driven away; and the sting of death, together with death itself, will be destroyed. Wearied as we are often by its wounds, we must necessarily grieve for one another. But, having gained security in the eternity of that supreme good, we shall rejoice, when this friendship—to which here we admit only a few—will be poured out into all and returned by all into God, when God shall be all in all (1 Cor. 15). [Col. 0702A–B]

[Col. 0701]

**TREATISE OF BLESSED AELRED, ABBOT OF RIEVAULX, ON JESUS AS A BOY OF TWELVE YEARS.**

(It is extant among the works of St Bernard in the Mabillon edition. See *Patrologia*, vol. 184, col. 849.)

[Col. 0701]

**RULE, OR INSTRUCTION, OF BLESSED AELRED, ABBOT OF RIEVAULX, FOR RECLUSES.**

(It is extant in the appendix to volume I of the works of St Augustine, under the title *Book on the Eremitic Life Addressed to a Sister*. See *Patrologia*, vol. 32, col. 451.)

**PART TWO OF THE WORKS OF BLESSED AELRED, ABBOT OF RIEVAULX: HISTORICAL WRITINGS**

[Col. 0701]

**ON THE BATTLE OF THE STANDARD, IN THE TIME OF KING STEPHEN.**

(Twisden and Selden, *Ten Writers of English Affairs*, London, 1652, folio, vol. I, p. 337.)

Here begins the account by the venerable man Ethelred, abbot of Rievaulx, concerning the battle between the king of Scotland and the barons of England at the Standard, near Northallerton.

[Col. 0701C] In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1138, while King Stephen was occupied in the southern regions, the king of the Scots assembled an innumerable army, summoning not only those subject to his rule but also no small multitude from the islanders and the Orcadians. Advancing with the greatest pride and ferocity, he proposed either to bring all northern England under his dominion or to lay it waste by slaughter and fire.

His arrival did not escape the Trans-Humbrian nobles. At the exhortation and urging of Archbishop T. and Walter Espec, of whom we shall speak later, they assembled together and resolved to resist his undertaking. They therefore gathered an army small in number but exceptionally strong in arms and force. Setting up in a very broad plain near Northallerton the royal standard commonly called the Standard, they resolved there to meet the enemy. [Col. 0702C–0703A]

Archbishop Thurstan likewise issued an episcopal command throughout his whole diocese: from every parish, priests carrying the cross, banners, and relics of the saints at their head were to hasten to the nobles with all who could go to war, in order to defend the Church of Christ against the barbarians.

The foremost leaders in the southern army were William, count of Aumale, then a very brave young man and much experienced in arms. He had with him many knights both of the Pontii and of the Morini, outstanding no less in military skill than in courage. Walter of Ghent also, now near death through extreme old age, was a gentle and devout man. He too brought a very strong force of Flemings and Normans, and greatly encouraged the rest of the multitude by the wisdom and weight of his words. [Col. 0703A–B]

Ilbert de Lacy likewise, neither sluggish nor accompanied by few men, hastened to the field. Exiled in King Henry’s time, he stood the more secure in this necessity in proportion as he had become accustomed to labours and hardships. Robert de Brus too, although he had loved the king of Scotland greatly, did not fail his own people in this emergency. With his excellent young son Adam, he brought so strong a force that they adorned the whole host greatly not only by their strength but also at once by their distinction and youth.

So great a zeal for resisting the Scots seized everyone that they even caused Roger de Mowbray, still a boy, to be present with the army—yet most wisely placed among the others in a manner suitable to such an age. With him all the military force of his lands assembled with such devotion that the youth of their lord seemed to bring no disadvantage at all to the army; indeed, that force appeared inferior to none of the others in wisdom, courage, or number. [Col. 0703C–D]

Walter Espec also was present: an old man, full of days, keen in intellect, prudent in counsel, moderate in peace, provident in war, preserving friendship toward his companions and unfailing loyalty toward kings. He was of great stature, all his limbs of such size that they did not exceed proportion and suited so lofty a height. His hair was black, his beard long, his brow open and untroubled, his eyes large and penetrating, his face very broad yet well formed, his voice like a trumpet; and he framed the eloquence natural to him with a certain majesty of tone. Moreover, he was noble by birth, but nobler by Christian piety. [Col. 0704A] For, although he lacked children as heirs, and yet did not lack vigorous nephews, he nevertheless made Christ heir to the best of his possessions. In a most pleasant place called Bircham he founded a monastery of regular clerics, adorning it with many gifts and enriching it with estates; moreover, converting his palaces, his chambers, and his cellars into dwellings for Christ’s servants.

He also brought the Cistercian Order into these parts, an order whose very reputation England had scarcely heard of, with the favour of the glorious King Henry; he received brothers from the most noble monastery of Clairvaux through the hand of Bernard, the abbot beloved by God. Arriving in England in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1132, they obtained a place in a very deep valley on the bank of the River Rye, from which [Col. 0704B] the monastery itself received the name Rievaulx. By the renown of their religious life they stirred many to emulate the highest pursuits; and thus, soon multiplied beyond number, they founded very many monasteries in both kingdoms, namely England and Scotland.

For the aforesaid Walter, not yet satisfied by such great benefactions, founded through these same brothers a most famous monastery in the territory of Warden. In the same year as their arrival in England, certain monks of the church of Blessed Mary at York, zealously desiring Cistercian purity and poverty, and relying on the help of the venerable Archbishop Thurstan, abandoned riches and luxuries contrary to monastic purity and, in the greatest poverty and with marvellous fervour, on the sixth day before the Kalends of January [27 December], established Fountains Abbey. [Col. 0704C] Then, more fully joining the order of the aforesaid brothers, they too founded many noble monasteries throughout the island of Britain. The brothers of Waverley also, who had hitherto lain hidden as though in a corner, learning that they belonged to the same order, increased the number of Cistercian monasteries. Thus some, begotten by the Rievaulx monks themselves, and others, moved by their example, made the island more illustrious through many monasteries. Hence Rievaulx Abbey deservedly excels all the other houses of that order in England in fame and religious observance.

Who can doubt that all these good things should be ascribed to that most energetic man, who brought from afar the seed of such great fruits and found a place in which it might be sown? Therefore, since he was revered by the whole [Col. 0704D] army as a father, both because of his age and because of his wisdom, he mounted the engine which they had constructed around the royal standard. Towering above all the people from the shoulder upward, he raised spirits cast down by a kind of fear, and more fiercely inflamed those already ready, with this speech:

“It is not useless, most valiant men, for young men to listen to an old man. I mean myself: through the changing course of many times, changes of kings, and the varied outcomes of wars, I have learned both to review the past, to assess the present, and to draw conjectures about the present from the past and about the future from the present. Certainly, if all who hear me were wise and understanding, and foresaw what is to come upon us today, I would rather remain silent and rest in sleep, [Col. 0705A] or play dice, or contend at chess; or, if such things were less fitting to my age, I would devote myself to reading histories, or, as is my custom, lend a more attentive ear to one recounting the deeds of the ancients.

“But now I see most men certain of battle, yet wavering in spirit concerning victory, and grievously afraid lest our small numbers be swallowed up by the immense multitude of the Scots. Yet victory does not depend on numbers: it is either won by strength, or obtained from the Almighty through just prayers and an honourable cause. As for me, considering by what reasoning, for what cause, under what necessity, and who are fighting today against whom, I stand fearless—no less assured of victory than I am certain of battle.

“For why should we despair of victory, when victory has been granted by the Most High to our race as though in fief? Did not our forefathers [Col. 0705B] invade the greater part of Gaul with a few soldiers, and with that people erase even the name of Gaul from it? How often has the army of the Franks been routed by them? How often have the men of Maine, Anjou, and Aquitaine—few against many—carried off victory? Certainly our fathers and we quickly subdued this island, which Julius, once most victorious, could scarcely at last obtain only after many years and much slaughter of his own men; we quickly subjected it to our laws and bound it to render us obedience.

“We have seen—seen with our own eyes—the King of France turning his back upon us with his whole army; the foremost nobles of his kingdom captured by us; some ransomed, others bound in chains, others condemned to prison. Who subdued Apulia, Sicily, and Calabria except our Norman? [Col. 0705C] Did not both emperors turn their backs upon the Normans on the same day and almost at the same hour, one fighting against the father, the other against the son? Who, then, would not laugh rather than fear because the contemptible Scot comes to fight against such men with his buttocks half naked?

“These are indeed the men who formerly thought we ought not to be resisted but yielded to, when William, conqueror of England, penetrated Lothian, Clydesdale, and Scotland as far as Abernethy; there that warlike Malcolm became ours by surrender. And now they challenge their conquerors, their lords, to battle. They expose naked hide to our lances, our swords, and our missiles, using calfskin as a shield, animated more by an irrational contempt for death than by strength.

[Col. 0705D]

“Why then does the excessive length of those spears which we see from afar frighten us? Their wood is brittle; their iron is blunt. While it strikes, it is destroyed; when it is struck, it breaks; it scarcely suffices for one blow. Catch it at least with a staff, and the Scot will stand unarmed. Or are we terrified by their multitude? Yet the greater the number of those to be conquered, the greater the glory of the conquerors. I pass over what I think of their number, lest I seem to diminish anything from our future glory.

“Or do we distrust our cause? Yet we undertake no unjust war for our king, who did not seize a kingdom owed to him, as his enemies slanderously claim, but accepted one offered to him: he whom the people sought, whom the clergy elected, whom the bishop anointed, and whom apostolic authority confirmed in the kingdom. But even setting the king aside for the moment, no one will surely deny [Col. 0706A] that our taking up arms for our country is just; that, fighting for our wives, our children, and our churches, we are repelling the imminent danger.

“For necessity presses. Recall what they did in the regions beyond the Tyne, and expect nothing gentler if the Scots prevail. I pass over slaughter, plundering, and arson, acts which enemies in some fashion commit according to human custom. I shall speak of deeds such as neither fables report nor histories narrate as done by the most cruel tyrants. I shall speak—if horror does not utterly deprive me of speech, or if the hearer does not flee away.

“They spared no age, no rank, no sex at all. Noble boys and girls alike were led into captivity. Chaste marriages were violated with unbelievable lust. Little children were tossed into the air and caught upon the points of spears, furnishing a delightful spectacle to the men of Galloway. [Col. 0706B] A pregnant woman was cut through the middle; the tender foetus was drawn from her womb and dashed against a rock by an impious hand. Wearied by slaughtering the innocent, they cut up flesh for eating with the unwashed knives by which they had spilled the entrails of the wretched; mixing human blood with water, they quenched their thirst with a cruel drink, saying that they were most fortunate to have been preserved by fortune until the time when they could drink the blood of the French.

“Several little children were found by chance in the same house. A man of Galloway stood there and, seizing them one after another by both feet, dashed their heads against the doorpost. When he had gathered them into one heap, he said with a laugh to his companion: ‘Look how many Frenchmen I have killed by myself today.’

“I shudder to say how they entered the temple of God, how they polluted His sanctuary, how they trampled underfoot the sacraments of Christian salvation. [Col. 0706C] What are you doing, most valiant men? You are not fighting against men but against beasts in whom there is no humanity, no pity: whom heaven abhors, whom earth detests, whom the seas curse, whom the very lights of the world hate; whom the earth has not swallowed, heaven has not struck with lightning, and the seas have not drowned for no other reason than that they might be preserved for your victories and perish by your hands.

“Consecrate your hands in the blood of sinners. Happy are those whose hands Christ has today chosen to avenge His injuries. Hasten, and bury this accursed race of men beneath the earth; entomb them in hell, lest, should they live longer, the sun conceal its light, heaven deny rain, and crops wither in a certain dryness. Consider [Col. 0706D] the absent king, and how much glory will accrue to you when you bring back triumph over the king without the king. Yours will be the court; yours the kingdom; through your counsels all things will be governed—you through whom today a kingdom will be secured for the king, peace for the kingdom, and glory for peace. The king will confess that today he has been crowned anew by your hands.

“Therefore let us engage confidently: our cause is more just, our hand stronger; necessity presses us, glory summons us, divine help stands ready for us, and the entire heavenly court will fight with us. Michael will be present with the angels to avenge His own injury, for they have defiled His church with human blood and polluted His altar by placing a human head upon it. Peter with the apostles will fight for you, whose basilicas they have turned now into a stable, now into a brothel. The holy martyrs will lead [Col. 0707A] your ranks, for they have burned their shrines and filled their altars with slaughter. Though holy virgins may hesitate to take part in battle, they will nevertheless fight for us in prayer. I say more: Christ himself will take up weapons and shield and rise to help us.

“They come against us in pride; we advance in humility. They belch forth the stolen flesh which they have devoured; we, after sacred fasts, are fed with the flesh and blood of Christ. Players, male dancers, and female dancers precede them; the cross of Christ and the relics of the saints precede us. But why do I delay? Certainly we must either conquer or die. For who would wish to survive a Scottish victory, to see his wife subjected to Scottish lust and his little children pierced by spears?”

[Col. 0707B]

Having said this, he turned to the Count of Albemarle and, giving him his right hand, said: “I pledge my faith that today I shall either conquer the Scots or be killed by the Scots.” All the nobles bound themselves by a similar vow. And, so that all hope of flight might be utterly removed, they moved all the horses farther away and resolved to fight on foot, desiring either to die or conquer.

Meanwhile the king, having assembled the earls and the foremost nobles of his realm, began to deliberate with them on the plan of battle. Most agreed that all the armed knights and archers present should advance before the entire army, so that armed men might attack armed men, knights engage knights, and arrows meet arrows. The men of Galloway objected, saying that it was their right [Col. 0707C] to form the first battle line, make the first charge against the enemy, and animate the rest of the army by their valour. Others said it was dangerous for unarmed men to meet armed men in the first assault, because, if the first wedge failed to withstand the force of battle and gave way in flight, even the hearts of the brave would easily lose courage. The men of Galloway nevertheless persisted, demanding that their right be granted.

“For why,” they said, “O king, are you afraid, and why do you excessively dread those iron tunics which you see from afar? We assuredly have iron sides, bronze breasts, and minds empty of fear; our feet have never known flight, nor have our backs ever felt a wound. What did armour profit the French at Clitheroe? Did not these men, unarmed as they call them, force them to throw away their coats of mail, disregard their helmets, and abandon their shields? Let your prudence, O king, therefore consider [Col. 0707D] what sort of confidence can be placed in things which, in need, are more a burden than a comfort. At Clitheroe we carried off victory over mailed men; today we too shall cast down these men with our spears, though they use courage as a shield.”

When this had been said, and the king seemed inclined to follow the counsel of the knights, Máel Ísu, Earl of Strathearn, greatly angered, said: “What is this, O king, that you entrust yourself more to the will of the French, when none of them with his weapons shall today go before me, unarmed as I am, in battle?” Alan de Percy, the illegitimate son of the great Alan, a most vigorous knight and thoroughly tested in military affairs, took these words badly and, turning to the earl, said: “You have spoken a great word, one which today you will not be able to make good at the cost of your life.”

[Col. 0708A]

Then the king restrained both sides, lest a disturbance suddenly arise from this quarrel, and yielded to the will of the men of Galloway. He formed the second battle line from the king’s son, the knights and archers with him, and the Cumbrians and men of Teviotdale joined to them, with great skill. The young man was beautiful in face and handsome in appearance; so humble that he seemed inferior to all, so authoritative that he was feared by all; so sweet, lovable, and approachable that he was loved by all. So chaste in body, so restrained in speech, so honourable in all conduct, so constant in church, so devoted to prayer, so benevolent toward the poor, so stern against evildoers, and so humble before priests and monks, that in the king he seemed to display a monk, and in the monk a king.

[Col. 0708B]

Moreover, his valour was such that no one in that army was his equal, whether attacking enemies or magnanimously enduring their attacks: stronger than the rest in pursuit, fiercer in repelling, slower to flee. Eustace, son of John, one of the great nobles of England, joined him and took part in his battle line: a man once most intimate with King Henry, of the highest prudence and great counsel in secular affairs. He had left the King of England because the king had caused him, against ancestral custom, to be seized in court and compelled to surrender the castles which King Henry had entrusted to him. Offended for this reason, and wishing to avenge the wrong done to him, he had gone over to the king’s enemies. The men of Lothian, with the islanders and the men of Lorn, formed the third wedge. [Col. 0708C] The king retained in his own battle line the Scots and the men of Moray, and also assigned some English and French knights to guard his person. Thus the northern army was arranged.

Since the southerners were few, they were most wisely massed into one wedge. The bravest knights, placed in the first rank, interspersed spearmen and archers among themselves, so that, protected by military armour, they might rush against the enemy more fiercely because more securely, or receive their assaults. But the nobles of more mature age were posted around the royal standard, so as to support the rest; some were placed higher than others upon the engine itself. Shield was joined to shield and side pressed against side; banners were unfurled, [Col. 0708D] lances raised; coats of mail shone white in the brightness of the sun. Priests, clothed in white sacred vestments and bearing crosses and relics of saints, went around the army and, both by speech and by prayer, most worthily strengthened the people.

Then Robert de Brus, a man advanced in age and of great wealth, grave in manner and sparing in speech, who spoke with a certain dignity and weight, though by right subject to the King of England, had nevertheless adhered from youth to the King of Scots and advanced into his closest familiarity. Therefore, like a veteran soldier and a man thoroughly acquainted with such affairs, foreseeing by natural shrewdness the danger threatening the king, he obtained leave from his companions out of regard for their ancient friendship and approached the king, intending either to dissuade him from war or lawfully to withdraw from him according to ancestral custom. [Col. 0709A] For he was bound to him not only by friendship but also by the obligation of fealty. When he saw the king at close quarters, he said:

“I am here, O king, your faithful man, now to offer you counsel honourable for you, useful for your kingdom, and beneficial in future for your children. It is not the part of a wise man, O king, to look only to the beginnings of things and not to their outcomes and ends, and, for present concerns alone, to abolish memory of the past and foresight of the future. Against whom do you raise arms today and lead this innumerable army? Certainly against the English and Normans. O king, are these not the men whose counsel you have always found useful, whose help ready, and whose service welcome? From what source, I ask you, my lord, have you found such faith in the Scots that you so confidently deprive yourself and yours of English [Col. 0709B] counsel, revoke Norman assistance, as though Scots alone were sufficient for you even against Scots?

“This confidence in the men of Wales is new to you—you who today attack with arms those through whom hitherto you ruled, beloved by the Scots and feared by the men of Galloway. Do you think, then, O king, that that heavenly Majesty will behold with impartial eyes your striving to destroy those through whom your kingdom and your security in the kingdom are maintained for you and yours? With what forces and aids did your brother Duncan overthrow the army of Donald and recover the kingdom which that tyrant had seized? Who restored your brother Edgar—indeed, more than your brother—to his kingdom, except our army? You yourself, O king, when you demanded from your brother Alexander the portion of the kingdom which this same brother had bequeathed to you at his death, obtained without bloodshed through our terror whatever [Col. 0709C] you wished.

“Recall last year, when you sought English help against Malcolm, heir to his father’s hatred and persecution: how gladly, eagerly, promptly ready to assist, and ready to face danger Walter Espec and many other English nobles met you at Carlisle; how many ships they prepared, what arms they brought, with what fighting men they strengthened you, how they terrified all your enemies until they captured Malcolm himself after he had been betrayed, bound him after capture, and handed him over in bonds. Thus our terror bound his limbs indeed, but even more the hearts of the Scots; and, frustrating every hope of advancement, it took away their boldness to rebel.

“Whatever hatred and enmity the Scots bear against us, then, is on account of you and yours: for you we have fought against them so often; we deprived them of hope of rebellion and subjected them in every respect to you and your will. Let the Scots therefore laugh that you procure vengeance for them against us, when they have nothing else to avenge upon us except that we loved you and yours, kept faith with you and yours, protected your own person with our arms, and preserved the kingdom for you. [Col. 0709D]

“Spare yourself, therefore, O king; spare your kingdom; and, above all, spare your son, most splendid among youths. Today you strip him of counsel and all supports, exposing him to the Scots’ treachery and setting him before their rage. Take care also lest you be entangled in the sins of impious men, at whose hands are required the slaughter of little children, the lamentation of pregnant women, injury to priests, and contempt even for the Godhead itself. [Col. 0710A] Against them the blood cries from the earth not of one Abel but of innumerable innocents.

“You saw, O king, the abominations which these men committed—the most dreadful abominations. You saw them, I say; you saw, shuddered, wept, beat your breast, and cried out that this had been done against your command, against your will, against your decree. Show now that you spoke truly, by recalling them from like wickedness; so that, when they have returned, they may be punished without you if they commit such deeds without you.

“And these things would suffice if no one opposed your undertaking or if victory were certain. But now an army not to be despised stands against you: though smaller in number than yours, it is stronger in arms and strength. You do not know, O king, how dangerous desperation is, when death is certain, but the choice of the manner of death still remains. Certainly, if you conquer, we shall die. [Col. 0710B] We shall die, I say; our little children will die; our priests will be slaughtered at the altars; our wives will be defiled by shameful lust. We have therefore chosen either to conquer or to die gloriously, though we have no doubt whatever concerning victory.

“From this comes my grief; from this my tears: that I shall see my sweetest lord, my most beloved friend, my ancient companion—in whose friendship I have grown old, whose generosity I have experienced in the lavish bestowal of varied gifts and also of estates and many possessions—after the youthful games in which we trained together, after the business of arms in which we have always stood together amid many dangers, after splendid banquets which the same kingdom supplied to us both, after the pleasures which the hunting of birds and beasts afforded to us both, [Col. 0710C] either die perilously or flee dishonourably.”

When he had said this, tears and sobs cut off the speaker’s words. The king too, moved by natural affection, dissolved into tears and was on the very point of making an agreement. But William, the king’s nephew, a man of great spirit and the chief instigator of the war, came up, furiously accused Robert himself of treachery, and turned the king from his decision. Robert, without delay, dissolved according to ancestral custom the bond of fealty by which he had until then been bound to the king, and returned to his own men, not without grief.

Immediately their station was broken up, lances were raised, and the northern army advanced. The shrill sound of the trumpet followed, the blast of horns, the crash of lances striking [Col. 0710D] against one another. The earth trembled, the sky roared, and echo made the neighbouring mountains and hills resound. Meanwhile Ralph, Bishop of Orkney, whom Archbishop Thurstan had sent there, stood in a higher place. Having enjoined upon the people the necessity of fighting for the remission of sins, they beat their breasts, lifted their hands, and prayed for divine assistance. When absolution had been pronounced over them, the bishop added the blessing in a solemn voice, and all responded aloud: “Amen, amen.”

Then the wedge of the men of Galloway, according to its custom uttering three howls in a dreadful voice, charged the southerners so violently that it compelled the foremost spearmen to abandon their position. But, driven back again by the force of the knights, they recovered courage and strength against the enemy. When the brittleness of the Scottish spears had been frustrated by the solidity of iron and wood, [Col. 0711A] they drew their swords and tried to fight at close quarters. But southern “flies,” pouring from the caverns of quivers and flocking like a dense rain, rushing most importunately against the breasts, faces, and even eyes of those opposing them, greatly checked their effort.

You might see a man of Galloway, like a hedgehog enclosed with spines, surrounded on every side with arrows, yet nevertheless brandishing his sword; in a certain blind frenzy he rushed forward, now striking an enemy, now beating empty air with futile blows. Already those in the rear, struck by fear, were beginning to break into flight, when the illustrious young son of the king came up with his battle line and hurled himself with leonine ferocity against the opposing wing. Having scattered that portion of the southern mass like a spider’s web, [Col. 0711B] he advanced by cutting down all who opposed him beyond the royal standard. Thinking that the rest of the army would follow in order to deprive the enemy of the protection of flight, he attacked the guard-post of the horses, scattered it, and forced its men to retreat as far as two stadia.

The unarmed populace was terrified and gave way before this remarkable attack. But by the contrivance of a certain clever man, who raised aloft the head of one slain and cried out that the king had been killed, they were recalled and rushed upon those before them more violently than usual. Then the men of Galloway, no longer able to endure the rain of arrows and the swords of the knights, took flight, after two of their leaders, Wlgric and Donald, had first been killed. The wedge of the men of Lothian, however, scarcely awaiting the first attack, immediately dissolved.

Then the king leapt from his horse, and the nobles who were with him [Col. 0711C] advanced against the enemy. But the Scots, alarmed by the flight of the others, fell away from every part of the royal battle line and began to flee, so that soon, when the rest had fallen away, few remained around the king. The English army advanced against them, resolved certainly either to kill or capture the king himself with all his men, had not the knights, although the king utterly rejected flight, forcibly lifted him onto a horse and compelled him to retreat.

[Col. 0712A]

Then those who had fled, seeing the royal banner—easily recognized because it was fashioned in the likeness of a dragon—return, and knowing that the king had not fallen but was returning, went back to him and formed a terrible wedge against the pursuers. Meanwhile that ornament of young men, glory of knights, delight of old men, the king’s son, looking back, saw that he had been left with a few men amid the enemy. Turning to one of his companions and smiling, he said:

“We have done what we could, and certainly, so far as lay in us, we have won. Now counsel is no less necessary than valour. There is no greater indication of a steadfast spirit than not to be broken in adverse fortune, and, when you cannot overcome an enemy by strength, to overcome him by counsel. Let us therefore cast away the standards by which we are distinguished from the rest and mingle among the enemy themselves, as though pursuing together with them, until we have passed them all and, yielding to necessity, can come as quickly as possible to my father’s battle line, which I see remaining in strength at a distance.”

Having said this, [Col. 0712B] he spurred his swift-stepping horse and cut through the middle of the enemy, until he had passed those in front; then he slowed the horse to a gentler pace. To show how calm and provident was the spirit he displayed in adversity: while the other knights cast away their burdens of armour wherever they could, this excellent young man, patient of hardship, bore his until, arriving at a poor man’s hut, he summoned the poor man, removed his breastplate, and, throwing it at the man’s feet, said: “Take, man, what is a burden to me; let it provide for your need.”

But the king had already gone far onward, advancing in ordered and terrible array, so that by capturing some of the pursuers he greatly frightened the rest who pressed on. Thus he reached Carlisle; there, secure concerning himself but fearful for his son, he did nothing but wait for two days. At length, on the third [Col. 0712C] day, he received the long-desired son safe and unharmed.

The English nobles, pursuing for a long time, killed countless Scots and men of Galloway, and captured many soldiers. On each side, however, individual knights fell. All the English commanders returned safe and sound and, gathered around Walter Espec, whom they revered in the place of a leader and father, gave immense thanks to almighty God for their unexpected victory.

[Col. 0711]

## Genealogy of the Kings of England

(TwisdEN, as cited above, p. 347.)

## Here Begins the Letter of Aelred, Abbot of Rievaulx, to the Illustrious Duke H., Subsequently King of England

[Col. 0711D]

To the most illustrious Henry, Duke of the Normans and Aquitanians and Count of the Angevins, Brother A., servant of the servants of Christ who are at Rievaulx: greetings and prayers.

Virtue is so much according to nature, and vice contrary to nature, that even the vicious person praises and approves virtue; while vice, if one follows the judgment of human reason, not even the vicious person excuses. [Col. 0712D] For vice itself, as though blushing for itself because of its innate ugliness, always seeks hiding places and desires secrecy. Virtue, on the contrary, conscious of its own beauty and honourableness, rejoices and exults at every gaze, fleeing public notice and shrinking from human testimony only through humility.

Since love of virtues and hatred of vices are naturally present in the rational soul, whoever devotes himself to good conduct and virtue easily draws [Col. 0713A] to himself and inclines the affection of all. Hence it is, most illustrious man, that the fame of your virtue has impressed you upon the minds of many who have not seen you with their eyes: you are the admiration of all and no less their delight. In such an age, such wisdom; amid such pleasures, such self-restraint; amid such great affairs, such foresight; in such high station, such severity; and in such severity, such kindness.

For who would not marvel that a young man contending for a kingdom abstains from plundering, spares slaughter, guards against fires, imposes no burden on the poor, and preserves peace and reverence for churches and priests? Thus you are deservedly proclaimed by all as the glory of the Angevins, protector of the Normans, hope of the English, and ornament of the Aquitanians. Only this [Col. 0713B] remains: that you acknowledge Jesus Christ as the giver of these gifts and desire Him as their preserver.

For my part, considering the stock from which you derive your origin, I give thanks to the Lord my God that such a son, like a new splendour, has shone upon us from such ancestors. Although the virtues of all your predecessors have met in you, I rejoice especially that in you the spirit of David, that most Christian king, has found rest. I judge that divine providence arranged that the belt of his most pure hands girded you with the military belt, so that through them Christ’s grace might pour into you the strength of his chastity, humility, and piety. Yet because I am grieved by his recent death, I have briefly set down his life and character, as love, fear, hope, and grief now variously move my feelings. [Col. 0713C] Not as history, but as lamentation, receiving you with the intimate love of my heart as heir to his piety, I have taken care to send you this lamentation itself. When you read in it his praiseworthy life and precious death, imitate the former that you may deserve to attain the latter. For every praise is sung at the end; reward is not promised to those who begin, but is given to those who persevere. May almighty God preserve and increase His grace in you, most excellent and illustrious lord.

## Concerning David, Holy King of the Scots

The religious and pious King David has departed from the world. Although he has found a place worthy of such a soul, his death nevertheless commands us to mourn. For who would not [Col. 0713D] grieve that a man so necessary to the world has been taken from human affairs, unless he begrudges peace and advancement to human affairs? Who could readily say what benefit to human life this gentle king, just king, chaste king, humble king conferred? Gentleness made him beloved, justice formidable, chastity self-controlled, humility accessible to all. If these things are judged most worthy of praise in any private individual, how much more in a king, to whom power grants licence for whatever he wishes, whose vices inferiors readily favour—inclined to imitate and quick to flatter—when impunity gives boldness and lust sharpens and inflames sensuality?

We know that he did not seek kingship but shrank from it, and that he accepted it rather because of another’s necessity than, overcome by the lust of ruling, greedily seized it. Accordingly, he so recoiled from those acts of homage which, according to ancestral custom, are rendered by the Scottish people at the new accession of kings that he could scarcely be compelled by the bishops to receive them.

Once raised to the kingship, he displayed nothing proud in conduct, nothing cruel in speech, nothing dishonourable in deeds. Therefore all the barbarity of that people, immediately softened, subjected itself to the king with such goodwill and humility that, forgetting its natural savagery, it bowed its neck beneath the laws which royal gentleness prescribed and gladly received the peace it had previously not known. [Col. 0714A] Thus he deservedly seemed beloved by God and men: beloved by God indeed, for from the very beginnings of his reign he diligently performed the things of God, [Col. 0714B] building churches and founding monasteries, which he enlarged with estates and heaped with honours.

Since throughout the whole kingdom of the Scots he found only three or four bishops, while the other churches, without a shepherd, were tossed about to the detriment both of morals and of temporal goods, at his death he left nine—both in ancient sees which he restored and in new ones which he himself established. He left not a few and not small monasteries, full of brethren, of the Cluniac, Cistercian, Tironian, Arrouaisian, Premonstratensian, and Beauvais orders. Among them he had been as though one of themselves: praising what was good and, if anything less worthy of praise emerged, passing it over in modest silence; subordinate to all, solicitous for all, giving much and demanding nothing.

O sweet soul, where have you gone? Where have you withdrawn? Where are those eyes full of piety and grace, by which you were accustomed both to rejoice with those who rejoiced and to weep with those who wept (Romans 12)?

I saw with my own eyes that, when he was once prepared to go hunting and, with his foot in the stirrup, was about to mount his horse, at the voice of a poor man asking to be heard, he drew back his foot; leaving the horse, he returned to the hall and, not intending to return to his purpose that day, kindly and patiently heard the case for which he had been appealed to. Moreover, he was accustomed, sitting at the door of the royal hall, diligently to hear the causes of poor people and old women, who on appointed days were summoned from every region whence they came, [Col. 0714D] and often to satisfy each one, with much labour. For they often disputed with him, and he with them: he would not, contrary to justice, show partiality toward a poor person, while they would not accept the reason he set before them. Finally, if priest or soldier, monk, rich man or poor man, citizen or traveller, merchant or peasant had business with him, he discussed with every one, suitably and humbly, their concerns and duties, so that each individual thought that he alone was the object of the king’s care; and thus he dismissed them all pleased and edified.

Stricken by the illness through which he was to be released from the flesh, on Wednesday—that is, the thirteenth day before the Kalends of June [20 May]—when he understood that the dissolution of his body was imminent, he summoned his household and without hesitation explained to them what he himself perceived concerning his condition. [Col. 0715A] But they, in the ordinary human fashion, comforted the sick man, altogether promising him life and health. Yet when, on Friday, the disease grew worse and the force of the illness deprived him alike of the ability to stand and to walk, he summoned clerics and religious men and asked that the sacrament of the Lord’s Body be given to him. As they were preparing to carry out what he had ordered, he forbade them, saying that he would receive the most holy mysteries before the most holy altar.

Accordingly, borne into the chapel by the hands of clerics and soldiers, after the solemnities of Mass he asked that the venerable cross called “the Black” be brought forth for him to adore.

That cross is the length of a palm, fashioned of the purest gold with marvellous workmanship, [Col. 0715B] and opens and closes in the manner of a reliquary case. Within it is seen a portion of the Lord’s Cross—as has often been proved by the testimony of many miracles—bearing an image of our Saviour, very finely carved in ivory and wonderfully adorned with gold divisions. The devout Queen Margaret, mother of this king, descended from the royal stock of the English and Hungarians, brought it into Scotland and handed it down to her sons as an hereditary gift.
