When the king had most devoutly adored this cross, no less awe-inspiring than beloved by all the Scottish people, having first confessed his sins with many tears, he fortified his departure by receiving the heavenly mysteries.

Then, carried back to his chamber, when the priests came to complete the sacraments of holy anointing, [Col. 0715C] he rose as best he could and cast himself from the bed onto the ground. He received that saving rite with such devotion that he restrained, both by gesture and by word, the clerics when they chanted the psalms somewhat too hastily; he himself attended to every word and himself responded to every prayer. When all had thus been duly performed, he awaited his final day in the greatest peace of body and mind, earnestly beseeching his people to make his death known to everyone immediately after he had died. “For,” he said, “the sooner my death is known, the sooner divine mercy will grant me some consolation through the good offices of my friends.” In this devotion the day closed for him, and he continued through the following night in great tranquillity.

[Col. 0715D] On the Sunday preceding Christ’s Ascension—that is, at the dawning of the Kalends of June [1 June]—when this sun, rising, drove away the darkness of night with the rays of its light, he himself passed from the darkness of the body to the joys of the true Light. He did so with such tranquillity that he seemed not to have died but to have fallen asleep; with such devotion that he was found to have raised both hands together above his breast toward heaven.

Come to his aid, saints of God; meet him, angels of the Lord; receive the soul worthy of your fellowship; place it in Abraham’s bosom with Lazarus, whom he did not despise but cherished; with the holy apostles and martyrs, whose memorial churches he diligently built and honoured; with Christ’s priests and confessors, whom he venerated in their successors [Col. 0716A] and basilicas; with the holy virgins, whose chastity he imitated; with the despisers of the world, whom he had made friends for himself by the mammon of iniquity, to whom he subjected himself in Christ’s name with all humility. May that Mother of Mercy be present to him, whose power is acknowledged to exceed that of all others, and whose compassion therefore may prove all the more effectual for him!

And I, though a sinner and unworthy, yet mindful of your benefits, sweetest lord and friend—those which you bestowed upon me from the beginning of my life; mindful of the favour with which at this last you received me; mindful of the kindness by which you granted all my petitions; mindful of the generosity you displayed; mindful of the embraces and kisses in which, not without tears and to the amazement of all present, you dismissed me—I pour out and [Col. 0716B] shed my tears for you; I pour forth my affection and my whole spirit. This sacrifice I offer to my God for you. This return I make for your benefits. And because this is too little, there my mind will remember you from the depths of its very marrow, where the Son is daily offered to the Father for the salvation of all.

## On the genealogy of the kings of England and of King David of Scotland

Since we have recorded a few matters concerning the excellent character of the devout King David, I have judged it fitting briefly and truthfully to append the genealogy which is also yours, most illustrious Duke Henry. Thus, when you see how great was the uprightness of your forebears, what virtue supported them, and what piety shone in them, you may recognise [Col. 0716C] also how natural it is for you to abound in riches, flourish in virtues, be distinguished by victories, and—what surpasses all these things—to shine in Christian religion and the prerogative of justice. For one of the greatest incentives to attaining the best character is to know that one has inherited nobility of blood from the very best; since a noble mind is always ashamed to be found degenerate in a glorious lineage, and it is contrary to the nature of things for evil fruits to spring from a good root.

Therefore, so far as I have been able to discover in the most truthful and ancient histories or chronicles, beginning with you yourself, most renowned of men, and ascending through your most glorious mother and most illustrious grandmother, I shall briefly show you the line of your kindred as far as Adam himself, the father of all mortals. [Col. 0716D] Thereafter, omitting the most ancient persons whose histories antiquity itself has destroyed, we shall return through the more eminent kings of England, touching summarily upon their more exalted deeds. Thus, when you see that their great glory has perished through death and age, and that for the merits of their lives they have won the heavenly reward which cannot perish, you may learn always to prefer justice to riches and worldly glory, so that after temporal life you may attain eternal life. Amen.

You, then, excellent man, are the son of the most glorious Empress Matilda. Her mother was the most Christian and most excellent queen of the English, Matilda, daughter of the most holy woman, Margaret, queen of the Scots, who preferred the holiness of her character to the splendour [Col. 0717A] of her name. Her father was Edward, son of the unconquered King Edmund; his father was Æthelred; his father Edgar the Peaceful; his father Edmund; his father Edward the Elder; his father the noble Alfred, who was the son of King Æthelwulf, who was the son of King Egbert; his father was Alcmund; his father Eafa; his father Eoppa; his father Ingild, whose brother was the most famous King Ine; their father was Cenred, son of Ceolwald, son of Cutha, son of Cuthwine, son of Ceawlin, son of Cwichelm, son of Creoda, son of Cerdic, son of Elesa, son of Eda, son of Gewis. This man was the head of his people, from whom that whole people also received its name.

His father was Wig; his father Frewine; his father Freodgar; his father Brand; his father [Col. 0717B] Bealdag; his father Woden. Woden was the son of Fredewald, son of Freolof, son of Frederewlf, son of Fingondwlf, son of Geta, son of Gearwa, son of Beu, son of Celdwa, son of Heremod, son of Itermod, son of Hathra, son of Wala, son of Beadwig, son of Shem; Shem’s father was Noah; Noah’s father Lamech; Lamech’s father Methuselah; Methuselah’s father Enoch, son of Mahalaleel, son of Cainan, son of Enos, son of Seth, son of Adam, father of all.

Seth was born in place of Abel, whom Cain killed (Gen. 4). As Christ’s Passion was prefigured in Abel, so Christ’s Resurrection is prefigured in Seth. For *Seth* is a Hebrew name and in the Latin language means “resurrection.” [Col. 0717C] From this Seth, therefore, the generation is traced as far as Enoch, who was taken alive by the Lord and, together with Saint Elijah, awaits the coming of Antichrist. From there one comes to Noah, who alone with his sons and their wives deserved to be saved when the world perished; his firstborn, Shem, deserved to be blessed by his father. The Jews say that he was priest of the Most High God and was afterwards called Melchizedek, who offered bread and wine as a figure of our priesthood. Hence Christ is told in the Psalms: “You are a priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. 109 [Vulgate CIX]).

From this Shem, then, the genealogy is traced to Woden, who possessed such authority among his people that they dedicated to his name the fourth weekday, which pagan Romans called the day of Mercury. The English [Col. 0717D] observe this custom to the present day, for they call that day *Wodensdei*, that is, “Woden’s day.”

Further, the line of your kindred extends from Woden to Geat, who also was considered to possess such wisdom and virtue that pagans worshipped him as a god. From there the line proceeds to the most Christian kings of England, Ingild and Ine. Although Ine was among the most powerful kings of England, he abandoned his kingdom, set out for Rome as a pilgrim, and, having happily lived there as a pilgrim, at last ascended still more happily to the heavenly dwelling. From Ingild, however, the line of your kindred extends to Egbert, whose excellence was such that he subjected to his power all England south of the Humber, which had previously lain divided under several kings, [Col. 0718A] and was therefore called the first monarch of all England.

## On King Æthelwulf

His son was Æthelwulf, certainly the most splendid head of his future race and the most precious root from which most holy fruits were to arise. In his earthly kingdom he continually contemplated the heavenly, so that it was manifestly evident that he was not overcome by desire but prompted by charity: as king, he provided for the needs of others, rather than satisfying his own will by ruling. For he was a father of orphans and judge of widows, defender of churches and promoter of monasteries. He devoted himself so earnestly to almsgiving that he tithed his whole land for Christ and distributed the tenth part through churches and monasteries.

At length he went to Rome with great retinue, [Col. 0718B] spent a full year there, frequented the holy places, devoted himself to vigils and prayers, and gave many alms to the poor. He also bestowed numerous gifts, in royal generosity, upon the churches of the most blessed Peter and Paul and upon the supreme pontiff himself. Thus, returning to England enriched by the rewards of many virtues, after two years he wisely divided the kingdom among his sons. Throughout all his territories he apportioned resources for feeding and clothing the poor; he mercifully scattered his treasures and gave them to the poor (Ps. 111 [Vulgate CXI]). Of these he assigned no small portion to the churches of the apostles at Rome and to the bishop of the supreme see. Thus, in a good old age, he was gathered to his fathers—certainly not losing his kingdom but exchanging it, abandoning the temporal kingdom and [Col. 0718C] attaining the eternal.

## On the most pious King Alfred

His son was Alfred, the glory of the English, the jewel of kings, and model of virtues. He was younger in age than all his brothers, but older in virtue; therefore his father loved him more than all his brothers, because of the likeness of his character and a certain privilege of spiritual grace which shone marvellously in him even while he was a boy. Accordingly, while he was still very young, his father sent him to Rome with many soldiers and very great gifts, that he might be commended to the prayers of the most holy apostles and blessed by the supreme pontiff. The venerable high priest Leo, then head of the Roman Church, beheld [Col. 0718D] the boy’s face and bearing; and, perceiving in him by the signs of his sparkling virtues the presence of the divine majesty, he anticipated the time and age of his reign by the sacrament of royal anointing. As Samuel of old did with the boy David, so the most holy bishop most devoutly consecrated him king.

Later, when he returned to Rome with his father, he merited to be his father’s partner and helper in every good work. From almost his infancy he delighted in reading and learning, was assiduous in attending churches, most frequent in prayers, obedient to his parents, humble and devoted to his companions. In his boyhood he pondered those things which a devout old man might fulfil. Finally, he always carried in his bosom a small book containing the portion of the Psalter in which he most delighted, [Col. 0719A] so that what that heart inwardly pondered might pass forth from the breast of his outward man.

After the death of his brothers, with whom he had reigned for a time, the whole kingdom passed to him by hereditary right. Raised above all, he became the servant of all, so that he could say with the Prophet: “Though exalted, I have been humbled, and I have not been confounded” (Ps. 88 [Vulgate LXXXVII]). He showed himself so lovable to the good, terrible to the wicked, reverent toward ministers of churches, pleasant to friends and companions, gentle and generous to the poor, that he seemed suited to the character and nature of all people, useful and necessary to all. And—what is now rarely found on earth—he considered it the highest dignity of a king to possess no authority in Christ’s churches.

“The dignity,” he said, [Col. 0719B] “of one who rules consists in recognising that, in Christ’s kingdom, which is the Church, he is not a king but a citizen; in not domineering over priests by laws, but humbly submitting to the laws of Christ which the priests have promulgated.”

Furthermore, he imitated the example of the most pious Emperor Constantine. Although he had presided over city and world, after his conversion to Christ’s faith he showed priests such reverence that, when bishops once brought him written complaints against one another on sheets of parchment, he folded them up in his lap and ordered them to be consumed by fire, saying: “It is not for me to judge concerning priests.” Calling the bishops together, he said: “Most holy fathers, do not contend in litigation, especially before us, whose errors it is yours to judge. But if any question arises among you, let it be dealt with modestly in the Church, lest anything unworthy of your holiness be conveyed to the knowledge of those outside. Indeed, if I saw one of your order sinning with a woman, I would cover them with my own cloak, lest an occasion for the impious to disparage your religion be given.”

Blessed Alfred, following the example of this and other holy kings, provoked against himself the envy of the prince of this world. For, as Satan once sought [Col. 0719C] permission to test holy Job (Job 1), so he sought it for Alfred: “Does Alfred worship God for nothing?” And the Lord said to him: “Behold, all that he possesses is in your hand; only do not stretch out your hand against him.”

[Col. 0719D] Therefore Satan went out from the presence of the Lord and sent against him most wicked enemies, namely the Danes and Frisians, alien to Christ’s faith. Coming into England with a great fleet, they consumed the greater part of the kingdom with plundering and fires. Although the most valiant king had often repelled them, they were at last permitted to prevail and occupy the province so completely that the most Christian king, providing for his safety by flight, was stripped of his kingdom and hid with a very few of his household in woods and marshes, sustaining his own life and theirs by catching fish.

In all these things Alfred did not sin with his lips, nor did he speak anything foolish against God. He grieved not so much because he had lost the kingdom as he rejoiced because he had found a suitable time and place to devote himself to God. [Col. 0720A] But Christ’s soldier had to be tested further. One day, while his companions were occupied in catching fish, he sat in a little hut meditating on God’s law and consoling the wrong of his exile with Davidic hymns. There came a man in pilgrim’s dress, of venerable countenance, humbly asking alms.

The king, cheerful of face and joyful in spirit, raised both hands toward heaven and said: “Thanks be to God, who has visited his poor man in a poor man; who, though he gives generously to all and does not reproach them, nevertheless deigns both to demand what he has given and to restore with interest what he has demanded. But what was God’s servant to do? He had nothing except one loaf and a little wine in a flask.” He therefore called his attendant: “Come here, boy,” he said, “what shall we do? [Col. 0720B] Christ is here, who formerly visited royal treasures in his poor. He does not disdain the scantiness of this little loaf and our very small drink. Break it, then—quickly break this bread for the hungry man, and divide the wine. Let Christ receive half of all our food; let half be reserved for me and my little household.”

The poor man gave thanks for the king’s generosity and, leaving no footprint impressed in the marshes, either departed or vanished. The king found the loaf whole in the little room and the former quantity of wine in the flask, and was filled with amazement. Then, behold, those who had gone fishing returned with such a multitude of fish that the greatness of the later miracle increased that of the earlier.

On the following night, after he had prolonged his vigil with psalms, prayers, and salutary [Col. 0720C] meditation, he at last gave way to sleep and saw a man standing nearby with a most radiant face, dark hair, shining eyes, and the insignia of a bishop’s office; upon his breast he bore a book resplendent with gold and gems. After giving him holy admonitions concerning love of God, observance of justice, mercy to the poor, and reverence toward priests, he added again: “Christ, looking down from on high upon your patience, my Alfred, has set an end to your labours and sufferings. Therefore, when morning comes, sail to the nearest shore and sound your own horn three times. Strong helpers from among your best friends will come to you. By their counsel, gather the remaining army and attack [Col. 0720D] the enemy; you shall without doubt be made illustrious by victory.” Thus spoke the Saint.

The king, gazing at him with trembling eyes, said: “Who are you, most blessed one, who have come as bearer of such good news to this exile?” And the saint replied: “I am called Cuthbert, once bishop of Lindisfarne, and I have care for you and your people. Yesterday, when I was testing the purpose and devotion of your heart, you divided mercifully the bread and wine—indeed your entire sustenance—with me when I visited your little dwelling. Know, then, that you and your sons, under my patronage, will obtain the monarchy of all England, provided that you walk in the ways of the Lord. But remember me when prosperity comes to you.” Having said this, the light vanished together with the speaker.

In the morning, when the king perceived in the arrival of his friends, and in the arrival of the rest of the army that followed them, [Col. 0721A] the fulfilment of the night’s promise, after embraces, kisses, and tears shed upon one another, he stood in their midst and encouraged his army with this speech:

“Thanks be to my God, fellow-soldiers, who has not removed my prayer or his mercy from me. For he strikes and heals; he kills and gives life; he makes poor and makes rich; he humbles and raises up; he is the Lord making peace and creating evil, the Lord doing all these things. Until now God has scourged us repeatedly for our sins, but he has not delivered us to death. He has again looked upon the prayer of the humble and has not despised their petition. Behold: through his mercy the remnant of the English shall be saved. Who can doubt it? Who summoned us from so many hiding places, gathered us from so many regions, and compelled us, casting off fear amid the raging forces of the pagans, to come to this meeting—some singly, some with companions?

“Recognise, therefore, that our enemies are troubled and shaken; trembling has seized them. For they have prevailed over us not by their own strength or the might of their own hands, but because the right hand of God and the rod of his wrath, raging not so much against us as against our sins, [Col. 0721B] has used the cruelty of pagans for purification, not destruction. Behold, once more the eyes of the Lord are upon us and his ears open to our prayers. Therefore act manfully and let your hearts be strengthened, for according to the multitude of our sorrows which we have endured hitherto, his consolations shall gladden our souls.

“Consider who we are, against whom we fight, for what reason, and indeed under what necessity. Christians fight against pagans; the devout against the impious; the contrite in heart and humble in spirit contend against the proud. And on what ground? They have indeed destroyed churches, undermined altars, and spared neither age nor rank nor, in short, sex. Moreover, we seek not what belongs to others but reclaim what is ours. They have torn our property from us; they possess our property; they squander our property in luxury; they spend our property upon sacrifices to their idols.

“Indeed, if you ask the necessity for fighting, hear it briefly: that the nations may no longer insult the Christian name with irreverence; that they may not prefer idols to the true God; that they may not ascribe to the power of the demons they worship the victories which, because our sins demanded it, they have so often won over us. Finally, [Col. 0721C] that our wives may not be carried off, our sons enslaved, our virgins violated, and that the impious and perverse may not reduce the entire nobility of the English to a degrading servitude. Since, therefore, we have received double punishment from the Lord’s hand for all our sins, now tested, now tried, now purified, let us engage confidently. For our faith is surer and our cause more just; Christ invites us, piety urges us, necessity compels us; Christ is with us, angels favour us, saints stand ready for us, and divine oracles resound for us from heaven.”

When he had said this, he unfolded to all who heard the oracle of the night vision. On hearing it, the people cried out: “The Lord will give strength and power to his people; blessed be God.” Immediately they seized [Col. 0722A] their arms and rushed upon the enemy. And soon, as wax melts before fire, so the pagans perished before God. They were struck down, put to flight, scattered. Leaving behind their most celebrated standard—which, because in demonic prompting they had disfigured it with the likeness of a raven, they called *Raven*—all who could escape the hands of their pursuers sought refuge in forest hiding places.

From that day onward Alfred prospered in all things, because the Lord was with him and directed all his works, until, after the enemies had been driven out or subdued, the land rested after the Lord and after Alfred his servant. Yet in the days of peace he did not grow sluggish in idleness or waste time on empty spectacles and aimless excursions, but laboured at reading, writing, and translating the sacred texts into the English tongue. His proverbs, containing abundant edification as well as elegance and delight, still survive. He both wrote and promulgated most Christian laws, in which his faith and devotion toward God, his concern for his subjects, mercy toward the poor, and justice toward all are evident to every reader.

He laboured tirelessly to restore churches which an impious hand had destroyed and to repair, enrich, and adorn monasteries. Among these, he founded two very noble monasteries at great expense: one for monks at the place called Edelingeheie, the other for women in the city called Scettebprig. He enriched them with many possessions and adorned them with many gifts. Moreover, he took the greatest care that the poor should not be oppressed by sheriffs and officials or burdened with unlawful exactions. Hence [Col. 0722C] his name became famous throughout the world, even in the great city of Rome; for he often sent many gifts and very lavish alms to the churches of the apostles and to the supreme pontiff himself. The supreme pontiff, gladly embracing such devotion and moved by his pious prayers, freed the school of the Saxons from every tribute and toll. He also sent the king numerous gifts, including a piece of the Lord’s Cross. On hearing of his fame, the patriarch of Jerusalem likewise honoured the king with precious presents.

Concerning the annual revenue paid to him, he ordained a most just distribution: one third was assigned to the pay of warriors; one third went to the wages and maintenance of workers; [Col. 0722D] and one third was reserved for royal gifts, which he was accustomed to distribute most generously to all arrivals, rich and poor alike. The liberty and possessions of the church of Durham still show how he remembered Cuthbert the pilgrim. Thus King Alfred, having reigned twenty-nine years and six months, passed from the earthly kingdom to the heavenly, leaving his son Edward heir to his kingdom and his character.

## On King Edward the Elder

In learning Edward was inferior to his father; in holiness not greatly inferior, but in power superior. He extended the borders of his kingdom far more widely than his father, founded new towns, and renewed ruined ones. The utterly impious people of the Danes, whom [Col. 0723A] his father had not expelled, rebelled against him; after crushing them in many battles, he either wholly drove them away or reduced them to miserable servitude, and restored the face of the island to the likeness of its ancient beauty.

The king’s sister Æthelflæd also added greatly to its splendour. Though a woman in sex, she surpassed a man in spirit and courage. Apart from those founded by the king, she built the towns of Brunesburch, Bruge, Scorgate, Thamewrthe, Swaford, Edebirath, Werewicum, Ciresbirith, Warebirich, Runconere, and Liecestre. She fought against the Welsh and conquered them; she stormed and captured Derby. She shone with such courage that many called her king.

King Edward, therefore, gentle and devout, beloved and approachable to all, inspired such universal affection that the Scots, Cumbrians, Welsh, [Col. 0723B] Northumbrians, and the remaining Danes chose him with complete devotion not so much as lord and king as father. Thereafter he governed his subjects with such moderation and judged with such justice between neighbour and neighbour that he seemed not merely unwilling, but unable, to act against truth. Thus he is said to have told certain persons in anger: “I tell you, if I could, I would have repaid you in kind.” What could not a king do to subjects, a lord to slaves, a powerful man to the weak, a commander to soldiers? Yet whatever equity did not dictate, whatever was opposed to truth, whatever justice did not permit, whatever did not befit royal gentleness, he considered impossible for himself.

He founded the New Minster at Winchester, while his mother, the most holy woman Ælswith, built a monastery of virgins in the same city. King Edward lived in the kingdom for twenty-four years and begot sons and daughters: by the most noble woman Ecgwynn, his firstborn son Æthelstan; by Queen Eadgifu, Edwin, Edmund, Eadred, and four daughters. The first, Eadburh, was chosen and consecrated as God’s bride. The second was taken in marriage by Otto, emperor of the Romans. The third was designated to be taken in marriage by Charles, king of the Franks. The king of the Northumbrians received the fourth in marriage.

Some relate that the king once laughed, contrary to his custom, while the solemnities of Mass were being celebrated and he was in an ecstasy of mind. Those present marvelled and, [Col. 0723D] at a fitting time, asked the cause. The king said:

“The Danes and Northmen agreed to come to England for plunder. A great multitude of ships was gathered in a harbour; arms were brought in, and provisions necessary for the voyage were assembled. The time for sailing had now arrived: sails were to be entrusted to the winds and ships to the sails. But behold, a certain man came out from a house near the harbour carrying a cup full of mead and invited the chieftains to drink. They laughed, but he persisted. At last, calling down upon them a shameful name if they would not drink even once, he lured them all away from the ship. As cup followed cup and the habit of drinking inflamed their appetite, drunkenness broke into talkativeness, talkativeness burst into quarrelling, and the quarrel provoked and armed the Danes for fighting.

“A tumult arose among the revellers. In a kind of blind madness, each rushed upon his companion, not knowing whom to spare and ignorant whom he struck. Therefore, amid mutual slaughter, while some were struck down and others wounded, some preserved their lives by flight, some boarded the ships and crossed the seas; thus all were scattered and abandoned their intended plan and purpose. This is the cause of my laughter: ‘The Lord has made laughter for me, and whoever hears will laugh with me.’ Yet I hope in my God that in my time foreigners will not oppress England.”

See, I pray you, with what great light from God the royal mind was illuminated: he sensed distant things, disregarded what was present, and foresaw what was to come.

## On King Æthelstan

King Edward slept with his fathers, [Col. 0724B] and his son Æthelstan reigned in his place. He walked in the ways of his fathers and did not turn aside to right or left, maintaining the same faith in God, graciousness toward subjects, devotion toward churches, mercy toward the poor, and reverence toward God’s priests. Against him the remnants of the Danes, according to their custom, raised their impious heads; but they were crushed beneath his feet and reduced to dust. The Northumbrians and Scots rebelled against him and broke the treaty they had made with him.

The king assembled a very great army and advanced by land and sea to attack the impious. When he came into the province of Lindsey, he encountered a considerable crowd of poor and middling people. Asking where they had come from, they answered: from Beverley, where they had arrived to visit the relics of Saint John in hope of obtaining healing. The king asked whether any had obtained the desired effect of his prayer. One replied: “I, who was born blind, received sight at the body of the most holy man.” Another said: “I, lame from my mother’s womb, walk sound, as you see, through Saint John’s prayers.”

Hearing these and similar things, the most Christian king said: “This John is great; and in this great undertaking I think it beneficial to win the favour of so great a man and implore his aid. Since, therefore, it is not right for us to pass by without visiting such a patron of our kingdom, let our army proceed by the royal road; I, with a few companions, shall take care to visit his tomb, of whose mercy [Col. 0724D] I hear such things, and invoke it.”

Then the most illustrious king came to the saint’s tomb. After holding night vigils in the custom of his ancestors and pouring out prayers with a suppliant heart, when he had drenched the pavement with most devout tears, he drew a little knife from its sheath and laid it upon the holy altar: “Behold, most blessed John,” he said, “the pledge of my promise: when, with your aid, I return prosperously after subduing my enemies, I shall redeem it at a fitting price, and as long as I live I shall be grateful and devoted to you.”

The king then returned to his army and immediately invaded the enemy’s territories with power. The time for battle had now come, when, on the preceding night, the king was overcome by sleep and saw Saint John standing beside him and exhorting him to engage confidently: “Gratefully accepting your devotion [Col. 0725A] which you showed at my tomb, I have prayed to my God for you, and he has heard my voice. Therefore observe and hear my voice: walk in the ways of your fathers, and I shall be an enemy to your enemies and afflict those who afflict you; and God’s grace shall protect you.” Having said this, he vanished.

When morning came, the king rushed upon the enemy and, having gained the victory, compelled the king of Scotland to surrender. After he had explored the situation of that land for no short time, he took the king’s son as a hostage and returned to York. From there he proceeded to Beverley and redeemed his knife by granting many possessions and very great liberty. After he had then lived sixteen years as king, he died, and his brother Edmund reigned in his place.

## On the noble King Edmund

[Col. 0725B]

He was in every respect an imitator of his father Edward: a simple and upright man, fearing God (Job 1), and remaining in his innocence until the end of his life. When he was raised to the kingship, he was zealous for the faith of Christ; and, taking it grievously that the remnants of the pagans and the worship of idols should defile the beauty of his realm, he wrested from their hands the five most noble cities—Lincoln, Leicester, Stamford, Nottingham, and Derby—which they had inhabited until then, and, having wiped away all unbelief, illuminated them with the light of Christian faith. When he had cleansed the kingdom of foreigners and brought it wholly under his authority, he took especial care of monasteries and churches; by the counsel of the most holy Dunstan, he established what needed establishing and corrected what needed correction. [Col. 0725C] He entrusted Glastonbury to blessed Dunstan to be founded as a dwelling-place for monks, and, with Saint Dunstan’s assistance, arranged many other good things. Thus, while England flourished in great peace and glory under so great a father rather than king, it suddenly withered in grief and fear at his untimely death, which he suffered through a wicked treachery after reigning five years and seven months.

### Concerning King Eadred

His brother Eadred succeeded him in the kingdom and walked in his brother’s ways, obeying blessed Dunstan’s counsels in all things and governing his subjects by most just laws. For he was of such excellence that he easily overcame the Northumbrians and Scots when they rebelled against him, [Col. 0725D] and restored them to their former submission without much trouble. A precious death brought his praiseworthy life to its close. For when blessed Dunstan was summoned to the sick king, on the journey itself he heard the voices of angels in heaven saying: “King Eadred has now fallen asleep in the Lord.”

### Concerning King Eadwig

After him Eadwig, son of King Edmund, received the kingdom of the English. He did not walk in the ways of his fathers; rather, in that holy lineage a new Herod arose, who indulged in adulterous embraces with a certain Herodias-like woman—most impious against God, against the laws, and against the very laws of nature—and followed most wicked counsels. [Col. 0726A] Nor was the spirit of John lacking in the holy man Dunstan: he rebuked the adulterous king and scourged the adulteress with fitting denunciations. Incited by a Jezebel-like spirit, she plotted the destruction of our Elijah; and she would have obtained her desire had not the saint, forewarned by the Spirit, preferred exile from his country. The king, deceived by this most wicked woman’s counsels and ruling neither justly nor wisely, was stripped of the greater part of his kingdom, which was immediately transferred to his brother Edgar. At length, remorseful, he renounced the adulteress and followed sounder counsels. For the Lord remembered his fathers, the kings—namely, most Christian men—and, lest anyone of that sacred stock should perish, found an occasion by which he might be saved. For when, at his death, he was being dragged away by unclean spirits [Col. 0726B] to punishment, one of the demons announced his death to Dunstan, as though the saint would rejoice in the misfortune of his persecutor. Dunstan immediately dissolved into tears and, prostrate, long supplicated and wept before merciful Jesus for him, until he was freed from the demons and obtained the pardon for which the saint had prayed.

### Concerning King Edgar the Peaceful

When King Eadwig had died, his brother Edgar succeeded. He was the son of Edmund, a most noble king, who was the son of Edward the Elder, a most Christian prince, who was the son of Alfred, a most victorious leader. This Edgar, happier than all his predecessors, inferior to none in holiness, surpassing all in sweetness of character, [Col. 0726C] shone like the morning star amid a cloud and like the full moon in his days. He was no less memorable to the English than Cyrus to the Persians, Charles to the Franks, or Romulus to the Romans. For he ordered the kingdom of the English with a kind of heavenly peace and joined peoples of many languages in the covenant of one law. Hence he shared a name with Solomon, so that he was called, by the common voice of all, “the Peaceful,” *Pacificus*, which is the interpretation of “Solomon.” Nor is this surprising. At the very time of his birth blessed Dunstan heard angels singing: “Peace to the Church of the English in the time of this child who is now born.” Therefore, as dawn drives away the darkness of the departed night with the rays of its brightness, so, by the accession of this most holy king, the night of unbelief was banished throughout England, and the shadows of wrath and [Col. 0726D] discord were driven away.

For he displayed such signs of inward sweetness in speech, expression, and manners that, with God’s aid, the whole island yielded to him without bloodshed; and Scotland, Cumbria, and Wales gladly hastened to submit themselves to him. During his reign the sun seemed brighter, the sea calmer, the earth more fruitful, and the appearance of the whole kingdom more beautiful in richer splendour. In his days neither tortures nor crosses nor exile nor proscription were feared as much as even a slight offence against a good prince. Since, then, everyone throughout England converged in one spirit of affection toward him, the king devoted care and labour to building and adorning churches and to founding and enriching monasteries. In short, throughout the kingdom of the English he caused forty monasteries to be built, [Col. 0727A] assigning some to monks and others to virgins. He completed Glastonbury, which his father had founded. With great zeal he founded and carefully endowed Abbendon, Peterborough, Thorney, Ramsey, and Wilton, a monastery of virgins.

In winter and spring he used to travel throughout his kingdom, province by province, carefully examining judicial proceedings, customs, and the conduct of officials and princes; investigating closely how the rights of the laws and the ordinances he had decreed were being observed; and diligently guarding against the oppression of the poor by the powerful through wrongful judgments. He had prepared three thousand six hundred very sturdy ships. On the return of summer, he customarily sailed around every province of the whole island with them in great display, to strike fear into foreigners and exercise his own people. [Col. 0727B] Meanwhile he continually conferred with bishops and most learned men concerning the law of God and the sacred Scriptures; and what he could learn himself, he strove to teach his subjects not only by word but also by example. When, through a most prudent inquiry, he had carefully learned the lives and conduct of bishops, clerics, and monks, he summoned to himself the fathers of churches and monasteries and addressed them as follows.

### Address of King Edgar to the Clergy

“Since the Lord has magnified his mercy toward us, it is fitting, most reverend Fathers, that we answer his countless benefits with worthy works. For we do not possess [Col. 0727C] the land by our own sword, nor has our own arm saved us, but his right hand and his holy arm, because he has taken pleasure in us. It is therefore right that, since he has placed all things beneath our feet, we should also subject our souls to him; and that we should labour diligently to make those whom he has subjected to us subject to his laws.

“It is indeed my concern to treat laypeople according to the rule of equity; to render just judgment between a man and his neighbour; to punish sacrilegious persons; to restrain rebels; to rescue the needy from the hand of those stronger than they; and to deliver the poor and destitute from those who plunder them. But it is also my duty to provide necessities for the ministers of the churches, the communities of monks, and the choirs of virgins, and to provide for their peace and quiet. The examination of the conduct of all these belongs to you: whether they live chastely; whether they conduct themselves honourably toward outsiders; whether they are diligent in divine offices; whether they are assiduous in teaching the people; whether they are temperate in food; moderate in dress; and discerning in judgments.

“With your leave, reverend Fathers, if you had attended to these matters by diligent scrutiny, such horrendous and abominable reports about clerics would not have reached our ears. I pass over the fact that their crowns are not properly exposed, nor their tonsure fitting; that wantonness in dress, insolence in bearing, and obscenity in speech proclaim the madness of the inner person. Moreover, how great is their negligence in divine offices, when they scarcely deign to be present at the sacred vigils, and when they seem to gather for the sacred solemnities of Mass more for play than for psalmody. I shall say it—yes, I shall say what the good mourn and the wicked laugh at; I shall say in sorrow, [Col. 0728A] if it can indeed be said, how they abandon themselves to feasting and drunkenness, to beds and shameful acts, so that the houses of clerics are now thought to be brothels of prostitutes and meeting-places of actors. There are dice-games there, dances and songs there, vigils prolonged with clamour and horror until the middle of the night.

“Thus—thus are squandered the patrimonies of kings, the alms of the poor, indeed, what is more: the price of that precious blood! Was it for this that our fathers exhausted their treasures? For this that the royal treasury, deprived of many revenues, was swollen? For this that royal generosity bestowed lands and possessions on the churches of Christ: that prostitutes might be adorned for the pleasures of clerics, luxurious banquets prepared, dogs and birds and such amusements procured? This is what soldiers cry out, [Col. 0728B] the common people murmur, mimes sing and dance; and do you neglect it, spare them, and pretend not to see?

“Where is the sword of Levi and the zeal of Simeon, who cut down even the circumcised Shechemites because they had violated Jacob’s daughter by fornication—those Shechemites bearing the figure of those who defile Christ’s Church by corrupt acts? Where is the spirit of Moses, who did not spare even members of his own household when they worshipped the head of the calf? Where is the dagger of Phinehas the priest, who, piercing the fornicator together with the Midianite woman, appeased God’s anger by this holy zeal? Where is the spirit of Peter, by whose power avarice is destroyed and Simonian heresy condemned?

“Be zealous, O priests; be zealous for the ways of the Lord and the justice of our God. It is time to act against those who have destroyed God’s law. I hold Constantine’s sword; [Col. 0728C] you hold Peter’s sword in your hands. Let us join our right hands; let us join sword to sword, so that lepers may be cast outside the camp, the sanctuary of the Lord cleansed, and the sons of Levi minister in the temple—those who said to father and mother, ‘I do not know you,’ and to their brothers, ‘I do not recognize you’ (Deut. 33).

“Act diligently, I beseech you, lest we repent of what we have done and what we have given, should we see it consumed with unpunished freedom not in God’s service but in the luxury of the worst men. Let the relics of the saints move you, for they insult them; let the venerable altars move you, before which they rage. Let the wondrous devotion of our predecessors move you, whose alms the madness of clerics misuses. My great-grandfather, as you know, tithed his entire land to churches and monasteries. My ancestor Alfred of holy memory [Col. 0728D] thought that, in enriching the Church, neither his treasures nor patrimony nor expenditures nor revenues should be spared. How much my grandfather Edward the Elder bestowed upon churches is not unknown to your fatherhood. You ought to remember with what gifts my father and his brother heaped up Christ’s altars.

“O Dunstan, father of fathers! Behold, I beseech you, my father’s eyes shining upon you from that bright region of heaven; hear with some pity his plaintive voice resounding in your ears. You, Father Dunstan, gave me sound counsel concerning the building of monasteries and churches; you stood by me as helper and fellow-worker in all things. I chose you as shepherd and bishop of my soul, and guardian of my conduct. When have I not obeyed you? What treasures have I ever preferred to your counsels? What possessions did I not despise at your command? If you thought something should be given to the poor, it was ready. If you judged that something should be bestowed on churches, I did not delay. If you complained that monks or clerics lacked anything, I supplied it. You said that almsgiving was eternal, and that none was more fruitful than that bestowed on monasteries or churches, by which God’s servants are supported and what remains is distributed to the poor.

“O splendid almsgiving! O worthy price of the soul! O healing remedy for our sins—that it should stink, from the bosom of a Sibyl, in the pelt of a foreign mouse; that it should adorn her ears, decorate her little fingers, bind a consecrated body in fine linen and purple! Is this the fruit of my almsgiving? Is this the result of my desire and your promise? What answer will you give to this complaint of my father?” [Col. 0729B]

“I know, I know. When you saw a thief, you did not run with him, nor did you cast your lot with adulterers. You rebuked, entreated, and reproved. Your words were despised: we must proceed to blows. You have here with you the venerable Father Æthelwold, bishop of Winchester; you have the most reverend Oswald, bishop of Worcester. I entrust this business to you: by episcopal censure and royal authority let those living disgracefully be expelled from the churches, and those living according to rule be introduced.”

Knowing that the good hand of the blessed rulers was with them, they expelled from the churches of Winchester, Worcester, and many others those who lived dishonourably, introducing religious men who illuminated the whole island with a new kind of splendour. O how truly blessed then was [Col. 0729C] the Church of the English, adorned by the chastity of innumerable monks and virgins, and gladdened by the devotion of the people, the restraint of soldiers, the fairness of judges, and the fruitfulness of the land! In his days the most blessed king rejoiced that the order of all things had found its proper nature: men rendered their due service to God, the earth to man, the heaven to the earth, through justice, produce, and temperate weather.

That we may know how greatly God rewarded him, even in this life, for his good works: when kings, counts, and nobles of many provinces had once assembled for his greatest festival, one day he ordered ships made ready, desiring to visit the church of Blessed John the Baptist for the sake of prayer. [Col. 0729D] Having assigned many ships to the counts and satraps, he himself entered one ship with eight kings subject to him. The eight kings took their places at as many oars, while he sat in the stern and performed the office of helmsman. It cannot be told with how much glory and what wealth that festival was celebrated, when the very elements seemed to serve at his nod—him whom they saw obeying the commands of his Creator with the greatest devotion. But alas: nothing on earth is eternal, nothing among transient things stable, nothing among mortals immortal. For when King Edgar was transferred to the heavenly kingdoms, his son Edward succeeded in the earthly kingdom. Unjustly slain by wicked men, he obtained, by God’s gift, both the name and merit of a saint, alike because of the holiness of his life and [Col. 0730A] the bitterness of his death.

### Concerning King Æthelred

His brother Æthelred, namely the son of Edgar and the queen, succeeded him in the kingdom, and was anointed and consecrated by Saint Dunstan and the other bishops of the English. Blessed Dunstan is said to have given him this prophecy:

“Because the English conspired against the blood of their most holy king and brother, blood and sword shall not fail among them, until a people of an unknown language comes upon them and reduces them to destruction and final slavery. Yet at the last the Lord will visit them.”

Accordingly, during the reign of the aforesaid king, the Danes arrived and devastated a great part of the land with fire and sword. Then the king sent envoys into Normandy and sought and received as his wife Emma, daughter of Duke Richard, though he had already had a son, Edmund, by the daughter of the most noble Count Thorold. [Col. 0730B] By Emma he subsequently had two sons, Edward and Alfred, of whom we shall speak later. Then, stronger than usual, the king ordered all the Danes throughout England to be killed on one day and at one and the same hour, letters having been sent out. When the overseas Danes heard this, they turned to fury. Under their leader Swein, they entered England with an innumerable army, spread and scattered through the provinces, sparing neither rank, sex, nor age, and not withholding sacrilegious hands even from the sacred places and sanctuaries of churches and monasteries.

Although the most vigorous king had often resisted them, he was at last defeated through the treachery of his own people; he sent the queen with her little children to Normandy, and afterward, stripped of his kingdom, followed them himself. But Swein the Dane, either overtaken by sudden death or struck by Saint Edmund with an invisible punishment, received in hell the wages of his cruelty. Æthelred, recalled by the English, was raised again to the royal diadem and once more rose in mighty strength against the Danes. [Col. 0730C] Against him Cnut, son of Swein and king of the Danes, did not cease to exercise his father’s hatred. Æthelred, after reigning most laboriously yet most bravely for thirty-seven years, died in London, leaving his son Edmund heir to his struggle and his kingdom.

### Concerning King Edmund, Surnamed Ironside

Whatever I might say of his wondrous courage would be too little. Hence, because of the invincible strength of his body, he received the name *Prensyde*, that is, “Ironside.” His arrow never turned backward, and his sword did not return empty. Against enemies he had the fierceness of a lion; toward his own people, the simplicity of a dove. None was stronger than he, yet none gentler; none more daring, yet none more prudent; none more secure in adversity, yet none more restrained in prosperity.

Moreover, the Danes and those English who had defected from the king chose Cnut as their king. But the most vigorous King Edmund, ranging over the land with his army like a roaring lion, recovered in surrender, without opposition, many regions which Cnut had occupied. Yet how often he fought him, how often [Col. 0731A] he put his army to flight, how often with a few men—indeed, almost alone—he overthrew the mighty force summoned from overseas; how often, finally, he would have exterminated that wicked people and reduced them to nothing, had certain traitors to their country not obstructed him—this is too much to include in the present work. Not only my own powers, I say, but even those of Virgil or Homer would fail beneath such material.

For whenever the two kings very often met in battle with great armies, either Edmund always won or neither did. Sometimes, indeed, contending on the field of March from morning until evening, Cnut excelling in numbers and Edmund in strength, when blinding darkness fell they withdrew on both sides without victory, their countless men slain, intending to return the next day to the same contest and the same outcome. [Col. 0731B] At length both armies grew weary. They saw that Edmund’s strength increased every day, while Cnut’s numbers increased from overseas; and Cnut, fearing this very thing, cunningly contrived a plan. The nobles of both sides compelled them to hold a conference. Among them one man, older than the rest, stood up and asked for silence.

“I desire,” he said, “O men of courage, to offer counsel for these dangers of ours. I am indeed less than you in wisdom, but, as these wrinkles and white hairs bear witness, I surpass you in age. Perhaps use has taught what natural ability did not possess, and experience has supplied what learning denied. Certainly we have seen and learned much; moreover, our fathers have told us much. Not without reason, therefore, do we demand a hearing, so that from things certain and plain we may give a judgment not open to doubt.

“A dangerous business is at hand. We endure evils, see worse things, and dread the worst. Every day we fight and do not conquer; yet neither are we conquered—indeed, we are conquered and no one conquers. [Col. 0731C] For how are we not conquered, wounded, overwhelmed, exhausted, deprived of strength, and stripped of arms as we are? We neither flee, because there is no one to pursue us, nor attack, because strength fails on both sides. How long will there be no end to these marvels? When shall there be rest from this labour, calm after this storm, safety after this fear? Edmund is certainly invincible because of his marvellous valour; Cnut too is invincible because fortune favours him. We are worn down; we are slaughtered; we are scattered; we lose our dear pledges; we expose our sweet relations to death.

“But what fruit, what end, what reward, what profit is there in this labour—what, I ask, except that, when soldiers on both sides have been slain, the leaders, compelled by necessity, will make terms, or else fight alone without soldiers? Why not now? Certainly, while we live, while we breathe, while an army remains, that would be more useful, more honourable, and safer. I ask: what is this arrogance—rather, this violence—rather, this madness? England, once subject to many kings, both flourished in glory and abounded in wealth. O ambition, always blind, which, desiring everything, loses everything! Why, I ask, should what was once enough for five kings not suffice for two? If they have such a passion for rule that Edmund scorns an equal and Cnut a superior, let those who alone desire to rule fight alone; let those who alone desire to be crowned contend [Col. 0732A] alone for the crown. Let the leaders themselves enter the hazard of single combat, so that one of them may at least be defeated in this way; lest, if the armies fight too often, all men may be killed and there be no soldiers over whom they may rule, none to defend the kingdom against foreigners.”

While he was still preparing to say more, the whole people, as it were in the midst of his very utterance, stopped him short, shouting: “Let them either fight themselves or make peace.” The kings approved the judgment of the nobles when it was brought to them. Therefore, both assembled with their armies on the bank of the River Severn: Edmund with his men took position on the western bank and Cnut with his on the eastern. In the middle of that river lies an island called Holinghege. The kings were ferried to it, protected by most splendid armour, and entered into single combat while both peoples looked on. [Col. 0732B]

But when the force of their spears—driven with great power and received by the opposing shields of very brave men—was spent, they drew their swords and attacked each other at close quarters. They fought fiercely while valour aided Edmund and fortune Cnut. Swords rang about their helmeted heads; sparks flew from the clash of metal. But when that most strong breast of Edmund grew hot with anger from the very motion of combat, as usually happens, he became stronger as his blood heated. He raised his right hand, brandished his sword, and repeated blows upon his opponent’s head with such violence that to the spectators he seemed not so much to strike as to hurl lightning. For at every blow fire appeared to burst forth between sword and helmet, seeming not only to be visible but even to burn.

Cnut, perceiving that his strength was failing with shorter breath, thought to approach the young man about peace. But, being shrewd, he feared that if the young man learned of his weakness, he would not even listen to the proposal of peace. So he gathered all his breath within himself, strained with every effort whatever strength he possessed, and with marvellous courage rushed at Edmund in one assault. Then he immediately drew back a little and asked the young man to pause briefly and listen to what he wished to say. [Col. 0732C]

Edmund, gentle in spirit as he was, lowered the bottom of his shield to the ground, leaned quietly upon its upper part, held his sword upward in his right hand, and attended to the speaker’s words. Then Cnut said:

“Until now I have desired your kingdom; now, bravest of men, I desire you yourself still more, since I see that you are to be preferred, I say not to the kingdom of the English, but surely to the whole world. Denmark has yielded to me; Norway has submitted to me; the king of the Swedes has given me his hand. Yet your wonderful courage has already more than once frustrated the assault of my enterprises, which I believed no mortal could withstand. Therefore, although fortune has promised that I shall be victorious everywhere, your remarkable excellence has so drawn me into friendship that beyond measure I desire you as a friend and wish you as partner in the kingdom. Would that you too desired me: that I might reign with you in England and you with me in Denmark! Certainly, if your courage is joined to my fortune, Norway will be afraid, Sweden will tremble, and Gaul itself, accustomed to war, will quake.”

Why say more? Edmund assented, and Cnut agreed to the division of the kingdom. He yielded to words who had not yielded [Col. 0733A] to swords, and he was bent by speech who could not be bent by arms. Having laid aside their weapons, they rushed into one another’s embrace, while both armies rejoiced and the clergy also resounded in a loud voice with “We praise thee, O God.” Then, as a sign of their covenant, they exchanged garments and arms. Returning to their own men, they laid down the terms of friendship and peace; and thus each returned joyfully to his own side.

After these events, a certain traitor of the Danish party, wishing to make himself pleasing to Cnut, plotted against King Edmund. Finding no suitable place in which to kill the king, he devised a most wicked and shameful kind of ambush. He hid himself beneath the privy, and, when the king was naked and attending to natural needs, struck him among the buttocks; then the most wicked and shameful murderer fled, leaving the weapon behind. [Col. 0733B] Standing before King Cnut, he said: “Hail, sole king.” When Cnut asked why he had greeted him with such a salutation, he reported the matter.

The king replied: “Because you thought to oblige me by such a service, I shall raise your head above all the nobles of England.” He ordered the man’s head cut off and hung upon the highest gate of London. Thus the most vigorous King Edmund died and was buried at Glastonbury with his grandfather Edgar. Cnut then wished to deprive not only Edmund’s brothers, who were exiles in Normandy, but also his young sons Edmund and Edward, entirely of hope of the kingdom. He summoned the greatest nobles of the realm and asked what agreement he and Edmund had made in dividing the kingdom: whom King Edmund had designated as his heir; whom he had appointed guardian for his still infant sons; and what he had commanded concerning his brothers Alfred and Edward. [Col. 0733C]

But they preferred falsehood to truth in order to please the king. Forgetting justice, forgetting natural affection, wicked witnesses rose against the innocent, and iniquity lied against itself. Thus, traitors to their own blood, they said that King Edmund had entrusted to Cnut the care of the kingdom and of his sons, whereas he had designated his brothers as heirs and appointed them guardians of his little sons. Since, therefore, in flattering the king, they lied to their own destruction, their sword entered into their own hearts, and their bow was broken by Cnut, whom they had preferred—an alien—to their natural lords. For once he had obtained the monarchy of the island through their support, he exterminated all those who had first joined in that counsel, and expelled from the kingdom or killed every survivor of royal stock whom he found. [Col. 0733D]

But, ashamed to kill Edmund’s little sons openly, he sent them to the king of the Swedes to be put to death. The king of the Swedes, however, pitying the distress of the noble children, sent them to the king of the Hungarians to be brought up. He received them kindly, cherished them more kindly, and most kindly adopted them as his sons. He gave his own daughter in marriage to Edmund, and joined Edward in marriage to the daughter of his brother, Emperor Henry. But shortly afterward Edmund passed from temporal things to eternal; Edward enjoyed safety and prosperity.

### Concerning Saint Edward, King, Confessor, and Virgin

[Col. 0734A]

Meanwhile, after Cnut and the sons who reigned after him had died, Edward, Edmund’s brother and the son of Æthelred, who, as we have said, was exiled in Normandy, was summoned to the kingdom of the English. For his brother Alfred had perished in England by a cruel death through the treachery, as is thought, of Godwin. Edward therefore came to England and was received by all the clergy and people with the greatest rejoicing. At Winchester, on holy Easter Day, he was anointed and consecrated king by the archbishops of Canterbury and York and almost all the bishops of the kingdom. He walked in the ways of his father Edgar: a gentle and devout man, protecting his realm more by peace than by arms; one who conquered anger, despised avarice, and knew nothing of pride. [Col. 0734B]

When he had obtained peace both from his own people and from foreigners, and had proved pleasing and beloved to neighbouring kings and princes, he sent envoys to the Roman emperor, asking him graciously to send his nephew—that is, the son of his brother Edmund Ironside—to be heir of the kingdom rightly owed to him. The emperor graciously received the king’s envoys and kept them for no short time with the highest honour. At last, ships having been prepared and all that seemed necessary for those about to sail supplied, he sent Edward to England, as the king requested, with his wife Agatha, daughter of the emperor’s brother, and their children Edgar Ætheling, Margaret, and Christina, with great splendour and riches. Coming to England under favourable passage, he gladdened both king [Col. 0734C] and people by his arrival. But after a few days he departed from life, changing joy into mourning and laughter into tears.

Not long afterward the king himself, having with the greatest splendour dedicated the noble monastery which he had founded in the western part of London in honour of Blessed Peter, ended his praiseworthy life by a happy death on the vigil of Epiphany, after completing twenty-three years, six months, and twenty-seven days in the kingdom. He filled the whole island with tears and sorrow. When so great a man had been buried, as befitted him, in the aforesaid monastery, some endeavoured to make Edgar Ætheling, to whom the kingdom was due by hereditary right, king. But because the boy seemed insufficiently suited to so great an honour, Earl Harold, of a race of traitors—whose mind was more cunning, purse fuller, and soldiery more abundant—obtained the kingdom under an evil omen. [Col. 0734D]

### How King William Succeeded Harold

William, duke of the Normans, heard that no one of the royal line but Harold had seized the kingdom of his kinsman King Edward. The kingdom was more justly due to William both by the right of blood relationship and by an earlier agreement between Edward and himself, as well as by Harold’s own sworn pledge. Therefore, gathering an innumerable army from overseas, he came into England and, by God’s judgment, deprived Harold himself at once of kingdom and life.

Edgar Ætheling, seeing English affairs disturbed on every side, boarded a ship with his mother and sisters and attempted to return to the land of his birth. But a storm arose at sea [Col. 0735A] and compelled him to make land in Scotland. By this occasion Margaret was given in marriage to King Malcolm. A book published concerning her adequately recounts her praiseworthy life and precious death; her sister Christina was blessed as Christ’s bride.

What manner of heart this King Malcolm possessed will be made clear to readers by one deed of his which I learned from the account of the noble King David. Once someone reported to him that one of his chief nobles had conferred with the king’s enemies about killing him. The king ordered the informer to keep silent, and himself also remained silent, waiting for the arrival of the traitor, who had perhaps then gone away. When the man came to court with great retinue, intending to plot against the king, the king ordered all the huntsmen to attend early in the morning with their dogs. The dawn had already driven away the night [Col. 0735B] when the king summoned all the nobles and knights to himself, hastened out to hunt, and came to a broad plain encircled like a crown by a very dense forest. In its middle a small hill seemed to rise. Painted in beautiful variety with flowers of different colours, it offered a pleasant resting-place every day to knights wearied by the hunt.

When the king had taken his place on it above the others, he assigned each noble with his dogs a separate station according to the rule of hunting which the common people call “the sad [hunt],” so that the beast, surrounded on every side, might find death wherever it chose an exit. He himself kept the traitor with him and withdrew from the others, alone with the one man. Removed from every person’s sight, the king halted, looked at him, and said: “Look: [Col. 0735C] you and I are alone together, protected by like armour and mounted on like horses. There is no one to see, no one to hear, no one to bring aid to either of us. Therefore, if you are able, if you dare, if you have courage, carry out what you proposed; pay my enemies what you promised them. If you think that I ought to be killed, when could it be better, safer, freer, or finally more manly?

“Have you prepared poison? But everyone knows that is a woman’s device. Or do you lie in wait by a bed? Adulteresses can do that as well. Or have you hidden a weapon so that you may strike secretly? That is the part of assassins, not a soldier; no one doubts it. Do instead what is fitting for a soldier, what is fitting for a man: engage alone with one man, so that at least your treachery may lack shame, though it could not lack disloyalty.”

The man scarcely endured this speech; immediately, as though struck by a heavy thunderbolt, he fell from his horse and, throwing down his weapons, ran with tears and trembling to the king’s feet. [Col. 0735D] The king said to him: “Do not be afraid; you will suffer no harm from me.” The man thereafter promised, under oath and with hostages named, that he would prove faithful and friendly to the king. At a suitable time they returned to their companions, telling no one what they had done or said.

But let us return to our subject. Queen Margaret bore six sons and two daughters. Three of them—Edgar, Alexander, and David, the glory of his race—were kings. Edgar was a gentle and lovable man, in every respect like his kinsman King Edward. He exercised nothing tyrannical, harsh, or greedy toward his people, but governed his subjects with the greatest charity and goodwill. [Col. 0736A] Alexander, moreover, was sufficiently humble and agreeable to clerics and monks, but exceedingly formidable to his other subjects: a man of great spirit, stretching himself in all things beyond his strength. He was learned and most zealous in ordering churches, seeking out relics of saints, making and arranging priestly vestments and sacred books, and he was generous beyond his means to all visitors. Toward the poor, however, he was so devout that he seemed to delight in nothing more than receiving, washing, feeding, and clothing them.

What we are to think of King David has been set forth, however briefly, in the foregoing account. Their sister Matilda married Henry, the most glorious king of the English. Whoever wishes to write of her wondrous glory and strength of spirit, [Col. 0736B] of her constancy and devotion in the divine offices and sacred vigils, and of her humility amid such great power, will reveal to our own age another Esther. We have omitted to do this both because of the greatness of the subject and because our knowledge of these matters is still too slight. Yet I shall relate one deed of hers, which I heard from the lips of King David—often to be named and never to be forgotten—by which, I think, it will sufficiently shine forth what she was like toward Christ’s poor.

“When I was serving as a young man at the royal court,” he said, “one night, while I was doing I know not what in my lodging with my companions, I was summoned by the queen herself and went to her chamber. And behold, the house was full of lepers, and the queen stood in their midst. Having laid aside her cloak and girded herself with a linen cloth, she put [Col. 0736C] water in a basin and began to wash and dry their feet; when they had been dried, she clasped them with both hands and kissed them most devoutly. I said to her: ‘What are you doing, my lady? Certainly, if the king knew of this, he would never deign to kiss with his lips your mouth, defiled by the corruption of lepers’ feet.’ Then she smiled and said: ‘Who does not know that the feet of the eternal King are to be preferred to the lips of a mortal king? I called you, dearest brother, precisely so that you might learn from my example to do such things. Take up the basin, therefore, and do what you see me doing.’ At these words I was greatly alarmed and replied that I could by no means do it. For I did not yet know the Lord, nor had his Spirit been revealed to me. She persisted in what she had begun; but I, to my shame, laughed and returned to my companions.” [Col. 0736D]

The sister of this most blessed woman, named Mary, was given in marriage to Eustace, Count of Boulogne. From this most excellent and most Christian queen was born Matilda, who was married first to the Roman Emperor and afterwards to Geoffrey, the most noble Count of Anjou. From Mary, moreover, was born Matilda, who was given in marriage to the then Count of Boulogne and now King of the English, Stephen. King David, meanwhile, at King Henry’s arrangement, took as wife Matilda, daughter of Count Waltheof and Judith, who was niece of King William the First. By her he had a son, Henry: a gentle and pious man, of sweet spirit and a heart of milk, altogether worthy to have been born of such a father. I lived with him from the cradle itself and grew from boyhood alongside him; as a youth I knew his adolescence. When the flowers of youth were opening in him, I left him—just as I had left his father, whom I loved above all mortals—now resplendent with the bloom of old age, in body indeed in order that I might serve Christ, but never in mind or affection.

These are the surviving remnants of this holy lineage. From the Empress Matilda come you, most illustrious man, whom we now rejoice to have as Duke of the Normans and Aquitanians, Count of the Angevins, and heir of England; and also your brothers Geoffrey and William, of whom we hope good things and for whom we likewise wish good things. From Queen Matilda and the pious King Stephen comes William, Count of Warenne and Boulogne. From Henry come Malcolm, William, and David, heir to his ancestral name. May God have mercy on their childhood; and may you also have mercy, you whom divine goodness has established as the most noble head of your whole race. [Col. 0738A] May your gaze upon them be kindly, your affection sweet, and your action effective in whatever service they need from you. For they were left to you as orphans by their grandfather, who loved you above all men; you will be a helper to the fatherless, since you possess greater strength of age, a stronger hand, and more practised judgment. At the end of this book I beseech my God that, by the gift of his mercy, your character may be such, your deeds so holy, your life so chaste, your mind so free from desire, so devoid of pride, so unacquainted with cruelty, so humble and gracious toward the poor, and so devoted to the worship of God, that we may have something worthy of everlasting remembrance to transmit concerning you to posterity through the service of letters. May almighty God preserve and increase his grace in you, most excellent and most illustrious lord.

[Col. 0737] Here ends the book of A., Abbot of Rievaulx, of blessed memory, composed on the lineage of King Henry.

[Col. 0737]

# THE LIFE OF ST EDWARD, KING AND CONFESSOR, BY BLESSED AELRED

(Tw[ysden], cited above, p. 369.)

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0737B] We have learned that many writers of old made it their concern to describe the deeds and life of illustrious men who flourished in their own times, and by their writings to perpetuate the memory of those whose blessedness they believed to be everlasting. They also judged that it would be of great benefit to posterity not to be ignorant of those whom they ought to imitate. For nothing more provokes and inflames the human mind to emulate perfection than to read or hear the virtues of any perfected persons, learn their manner of life, and consider their glory. No one should think impossible for himself what he has learned another to have done; nor can he doubt the reward if he lives well, when he has read that another attained it.

Thus, from the time when the world received the saving faith, our Lord and Saviour willed that, among many weak persons, some should be perfect, [Col. 0737C] so that through their example others might be drawn to faith or stirred to the best conduct. And so, down to these unhappy times, in which vices increase and virtues grow rare, such sons have always been born in place of fathers: through their teaching the unlearned might be instructed, by their authority supported, and by their example formed.

But above all cities and kingdoms of the earth, England glories in the holiness of her kings. Some of these, crowned with martyrdom, passed from an earthly to a heavenly kingdom; others, preferring exile from their native land, chose to die abroad for Christ; some laid aside the diadem and submitted themselves to monastic discipline; others, reigning in justice and holiness, preferred to benefit their subjects rather than to rule them. Among them the glorious King Edward shone forth as an eminent star: like the morning star amid the clouds, and like the full moon in his days.

At the command of the venerable Father Laurence, Abbot of Westminster, I have committed to writing, as best I could, the life of this man, remarkable for miracles. I have thought it right to send it to you, most glorious King Henry, that you may know how great is his merit before God—he with whom Edward reigns in heaven—whom in your time, with your royal authority supporting the act, holy Mother Church judged should be exalted more highly [Col. 0738C] on earth. For the great justice of so great a king is to be imitated; it is delightful to marvel at such continence amid so much wealth and luxury. To derive the origin of his flesh from Edward’s holy line is a special glory of our Henry. We believe that he promised you to us for the consolation of all England; we have learned that, when he was already near his end, he designated you by a prophetic parable. In you, as in a cornerstone, we rejoice that the two walls of the English and Norman peoples have met. [Col. 0739A] But of these things elsewhere.

Now, most illustrious king, who have received the kingdom of so great a father by a double right, and who have inherited from both his father and mother both the kingdom and noble blood: commend yourself often to Edward’s prayers, commit yourself diligently to his protection, and strive also to imitate his holiness, so that you may obtain eternal blessedness with him. Amen.

## PREFACE TO LAURENCE, ABBOT OF WESTMINSTER

[Col. 0739]

[Col. 0739B] To the beloved and loving, and to be embraced with the inmost affections, the venerable Father and Lord, Lord LAURENCE, Abbot of Westminster: Brother AELRED, unprofitable servant of the brothers at Rievaulx, sends the love owed in Christ.

“I have become foolish; you compelled me.” For who am I, what sort of man am I, what learning have I, what eloquence, that you should wish the holy King Edward—a man to be admired in every age—to be brought before the public by my writing, commended by my words, celebrated by my little discourse? Why commit to my judgment a subject under which Cicero’s eloquence would fail, to be not so much illuminated as obscured? To what should I judge this to be attributed—faith or affection? Why not to both? Judging neither to be despised, [Col. 0739C] I joined my faith to your faith and my affection to your affection. Thus, desire on the one side and boldness on the other having arisen, I examined the codex which your dignity gave me to translate.

And behold, I find a man above men: a man who in his days pleased God and was found righteous; who, having conceived the saving seed, was not content with the thirtyfold or sixtyfold yield, but, aspiring to perfection, rose to the hundredfold fruit of virginity. Therefore, entrusting myself wholly to his faith, dedicating myself wholly to his service, trusting in his help and prayers, I did what I could—not merely because the command of your holy fatherhood pressed me, but because devotion awakened by observing both his humility and his simplicity drew me on. That prophetic wine which makes virgins flourish I have, as best I could, poured from an old vessel into a new one: not indeed so refined, but no less useful to the simple.

Without departing from the sense of that codex, I have added, not uselessly as it seems to me, a few matters which I either drew from most truthful chronicles or learned from the reliable and true report of the ancients. I also thought that letters concerning the privilege of the king and the Roman pontiff, together with the exposition of the final difficulty, should be inserted in such a way that they may suitably [Col. 0740C] be read in their proper order, yet may be omitted without interrupting the sense. As the reward of my labour, I ask the prayers and Eucharistic offerings for my sins of you and of your holy community, who under your command serve in the service of so great a king, so that, through the aid of this most precious confessor, eternal life may be granted to me though it is not owed to my merits.

## THE LIFE BEGINS

[Col. 0739]

### On his noble birth and holiness

[Col. 0739D] As we are about to commit to writing the life of the glorious and God-beloved King Edward, let us take our beginning from the words of the most blessed Peter, chief of the apostles. Marvelling at the calling of the centurion, he said: “In truth I have found that God is not one who shows partiality; but in every nation, whoever fears God and works righteousness is acceptable to him” (Acts 10). In every nation, therefore, and in every rank, the Lord knows those who are his. He has mercy on whom he wills and grants mercy to whom he pleases, reaching mightily from end to end and ordering all things sweetly (Wisdom 8).

For neither poverty of itself confers holiness nor riches take it away; obscurity does not make one perfect, nor splendour reprobate; freedom does not shut paradise, nor slavery open it.
