Abraham, first of the patriarchs, is recorded as both rich and perfect; in the abundance of every possession his admirable faith and imitable obedience are proclaimed. Joseph, made lord of Egypt by the king, offered to the whole world an example of chastity. The loss of his wealth proved what holy Job was amid riches; bodily illness, his wife’s temptation, and his friends’ reproaches made him more illustrious through conspicuous patience. King David, than whom none was richer but none holier, none higher but none humbler, is both buried amid innumerable treasures and reckoned more beloved than others among the friends of God.

Therefore let no one wonder if our Edward is called both king and saint: we see him poor amid riches, sober amid pleasures, humble in purple, and a despiser of the world beneath a golden crown. In all these things he appears not so much to have been born lofty as to have possessed the whole example of holiness in the most holy and excellent kings from whom he drew the substance of his flesh. For he was sixth by descent from the most renowned and most Christian King Alfred, whom holy Pope Leo himself consecrated and anointed king in the city of Rome; [Col. 0741A] and tenth in succession among those who reigned from Alfred’s line. He obtained the fruit of both numbers: stoutly bearing the burden of the day and heat, he had the sixfold number in the perfection of his work, and at evening deserved, through the generosity of the heavenly householder, the tenfold reward.

After Alfred, now sons succeeding fathers and now brothers ruling after brothers, all happiness and holiness alike seem at last to have been poured into King Edgar, who surpassed all others in holiness, honour, and glory. Angels are reported to have sung at his birth and promised peace to England in his time. Accordingly, both because of the heavenly oracle and because of its fulfilment, he shared Solomon’s name: the peaceful condition of his kingdom in both fact and name. His son, the most valiant King Æthelred, took as wife Emma, daughter of Richard, the most noble Duke of the Normans, so that from the doubled holiness of both lineages a holier offspring might be produced. What manner of men were the illustrious dukes of Normandy—Richard and Robert, the brother and nephew of this most glorious queen—their praiseworthy lives and likewise precious deaths make clear. Born of this stock, our Edward ennobled his noble blood through wisdom and life. But now we must carefully consider what were the beginnings of his holiness, what its progress, and what its end, and set them forth in writing for the edification of many.

### How, before he was yet born, he was chosen king

When the glorious King Æthelred had fathered a son, Edmund, surnamed Ironside, by the daughter of Thored, a most distinguished earl, and had also fathered Alfred by Queen Emma, blessed Edward, enclosed within his mother’s womb, was preferred to both, through the working of him who accomplishes all things according to the counsel of his will, who rules in the kingdom of men and gives it to whom he wills.

There was a great assembly before the king of bishops and nobles, and a great concourse of people and common folk. Since grim indications of the coming disaster had already appeared, they deliberated concerning the state of the kingdom. Then, wishing to designate a successor, the king sought the opinion of each man and of all together. The matter hung in doubt as varying views were expressed. Some judged that Edmund should be preferred to the rest because of the unconquerable strength of his body; others thought it safer to advance Alfred because of the prowess of the Norman blood. But he who knew all things to come, foreseeing the very brief life of the former and the premature death of the latter, turned the wishes of all toward the child not yet born. He was still enclosed in the womb and was chosen king; unborn, he was preferred to those already born; the man whom the earth had not yet received was designated lord of the earth. The king gave his consent to the election; the nobles joyfully gave their oath. By an unheard-of miracle, those who did not know whether he would be born swore fealty to him. [Col. 0742A]

These are your works, Christ Jesus, you who work all things in all, who by these signs revealed as ruler of your people the one chosen and beloved by you before the foundation of the world: although elected through them, he was elected not by them, but rather by you. For who does not see that it was neither useful nor fitting to the time, neither consonant with reason nor bearable to human understanding, that, with legitimate and grown sons passed over and the enemy sword threatening, a little child not yet born should be elected king—one whom in such need enemies would neither fear nor citizens respect? But almighty God poured the spirit of prophecy into both the voice and will of the people, tempering their present evils with the hope of future consolation, so that all might know that he would be king for the consolation of the whole realm: a king whom no one could doubt had been chosen by God himself, though the people did not know what they were doing.

### How he lived in exile with his mother in Normandy

The blessed child having been born, he was washed in the water of holy baptism and anointed with sacred chrism, more fully incorporated into Christ. Having become a dwelling-place of the Holy Spirit, he was reared in its discipline. Shortly thereafter barbarians invaded England and devastated the greater part of the island with slaughter and fire. The queen crossed over into Normandy with her sons, so that the king, freed from the heavy burden of anxiety, might all the more boldly either drive back or meet the enemy, being secure about both his wife and sons and fearing no harm to them through anyone’s treachery. [Col. 0742C]

The boy Edward grew and was strengthened; the Lord was with him and directed all his works. A child, he lived in his ancestral house among children, yet was free from those vices into which either that age or that race of men commonly becomes entangled. Though little, he displayed something of an old man in his honourable and mature manners: chaste in body, sparing in speech, simple in action, pure in affection. Thus, with wonderful kindness and gracious services, he won the affection of all his contemporaries. Even at that age he found it sweet to attend church frequently, to devote himself more often to prayer, to be present at the sacred solemnities of the Mass, to devote effort to visiting monasteries, and to form friendships with the monks whom he knew to be holier. Two of them, whom he embraced with more familiar affection, are said to have appeared to him when he was near death, as we shall relate below. [Col. 0742D]

### What was revealed at Glastonbury to a certain bishop concerning him and his kingdom

Meanwhile the hostile sword raged in England; everything was filled with slaughter and plunder; everywhere was mourning, everywhere lamentation, everywhere desolation. Churches were burned and monasteries devastated; and, to use the words of the prophet: “They poured out the blood of the saints around Jerusalem, and there was none to bury them” (Psalm 78). Priests, driven from their residences, hid wherever in monasteries or deserted places they found any peace and quiet, lamenting the common misery.

Among them, the venerable Brihtwald, Bishop of Winchester, entered the monastery of Glastonbury grieving and sorrowful, [Col. 0743A] and occupied himself with prayers and psalms. Once, while he was pouring forth prayers and tears for the liberation of the kingdom and people, he broke out as it were into these words: “And you, Lord—how long? How long will you turn away your face and forget our poverty and our tribulation? They have slain your saints, overthrown your altars, and there is none to redeem or save” (Romans 11). “I know, Lord, I know that all you have done to us you have done in true judgment; but will God cast off for ever, and will he no longer be favourable? Will there be, Lord my God, will there be an end to these wonders? Or will your sword rage against us for ever and strike us unto utter destruction?”

At last, exhausted amid prayers and tears, he was overtaken by a sweet sleep. In a dream he saw a heavenly choir with light, and the most blessed Peter stationed in a place of greater eminence, displaying a bearing worthy of such majesty. Before him there appeared a man of distinguished countenance, comely in form and clothed in royal insignia. When the apostle had consecrated and anointed him king with his own hands, he added counsels of salvation, especially commending a celibate life, and disclosed how many years he would reign. Astonished by the novelty of so great a miracle, the bishop asked the saint to reveal to him the mystery of this vision; moreover, concerning the state of the kingdom and the approaching end of the danger, he demanded an apostolic oracle.

Then the saint, gazing with serene countenance upon the one who looked upon him, said: “O bishop, the kingdom is the Lord’s, and he shall rule among the children of men. [Col. 0743C] He transfers kingdoms and changes empires, and because of the people’s sins makes a hypocrite reign. Your people have sinned against the Lord, and he delivered them into the hands of the nations, and those who hated them ruled over them. But God will not forget to have mercy, nor will he restrain his mercies in his wrath. For when you have slept with your fathers and been buried in a good old age, the Lord will visit his people and accomplish the redemption of his people” (Luke 1). “For he will choose for himself a man after his own heart, who will do all his wills; and, aided by me, when he has obtained the kingdom of the English, he will put an end to the Danish fury. He will be acceptable to God and pleasing to men, beloved by citizens, dreadful to enemies, and beneficial to the Church. [Col. 0743D] When he has completed in justice and peace the prescribed term of his reign, he will bring his praiseworthy life to its close with a holy end.”

The event’s outcome proved that all these things were fulfilled in blessed Edward. On waking, the bishop turned again to prayers and tears. Although he himself would not see the happiness of his people, he was made certain of the end of their evils and rejoiced greatly, giving thanks to God. Thus made more tranquil in spirit, he preached repentance to the people, steadfastly promising that God’s mercy would not fail them.

### On the beginning of his reign, and on his brother and nephews

The storm’s force still stood fast and its waves rose high; to external evils civil discord was added, [Col. 0744A] so that no one knew whom to trust or to whom to entrust the secrets of his mind. The island was full of traitors: nowhere was loyalty safe, nowhere affection without suspicion, nowhere speech without pretence. At length civil treachery and hostile cunning advanced so far that, when the king had died, a great part of the island, rejecting the rightful heirs, submitted to Cnut, who had seized the kingdom. After the killing of the invincible King Edmund, heir alike of his father’s honour and struggle, they even sent his sons, still in their cradles, to the barbarians to be killed.

Thereafter, when everything had turned out as Cnut wished, he feared that the rightful heir, supported one day by Norman power, might reclaim the kingdom due to him by right. Therefore, in order to bind the duke’s favour more closely to himself, he married Emma, widow of the dead king. After some time had passed, Alfred, Edward’s brother, crossed to England to meet his mother and was killed with unheard-of cruelty by enemies and countrymen. Edward was then deprived of all human help. He lived as an exile from his homeland, but not from justice; from his kingdom, but not from faith; from honour, but not from virtue. He feared the snares of the wicked, which he had often experienced, and greatly dreaded being betrayed by his own people or purchased for death by his enemies.

Having found a saving counsel, he prostrated himself before God as was his custom, lamenting his solitude in these words: “Behold, Lord, there is no help in me, and my close companions have withdrawn from me. My friends and neighbours have drawn near and stood against me. My father departed this life after many labours; the cruelty of persecutors swallowed up my brothers; my nephews were driven into exile; my mother, given in marriage to our rival, made an enemy my stepfather. [Col. 0744C] Thus I have been left alone, and they seek my life. But I am left poor to you, Lord; you will be a helper to the fatherless. You once preserved Edwin, a most noble man of our people, when he had been exposed to death, in a wonderful manner, both for life and for the kingdom. You made that glory of England, holy King Oswald—king though an exile—stronger than all enemies through the sign of the cross. If, therefore, you are with me, guard me, and restore me to my father’s kingdom, you shall always be God to me, and the apostle St Peter my patron. I promise, with your consent, your guidance, and your companionship, to visit his most holy relics in the city where he rests with his fellow apostle.”

He had spoken, and thereafter the blessed man was stronger in faith and more cheerful in hope. He waited, indeed waited, for the Lord, and was not disappointed in his expectation. For when Cnut was removed from human affairs and his sons carried off by premature death, the English, freed from the Danish yoke as though from Egyptian slavery, chose as king blessed Edward, to whom the whole island had sworn fealty while he was not yet born. Received in England with the highest honour and the greatest rejoicing of all, he was anointed and consecrated king by the Archbishops of Canterbury and York and nearly all the bishops of England.

What glory then belonged to the English, what common joy, [Col. 0745A] when their former happiness was seen to have returned, and the people recovered in Edward the peace they had mourned as almost beyond hope; the nobles recovered glory, and the Church liberty. Then the sun was raised and the moon stood in its order: when Edward was crowned with glory and honour, priests shone with wisdom and holiness, monasteries flourished in every kind of religious observance, the clergy stood in its proper office, and the people in its proper rank. The earth itself appeared more fertile, the air healthier, the sun brighter, and the sea calmer, because while a peaceful king reigned for a long time, all things were united in one bond of peace: nothing pestilential was in the air, nothing stormy in the sea, nothing barren upon the earth, nothing disordered among the clergy, nothing tumultuous among the people.

The fame of so great prosperity, as soon as he assumed power, was carried into all the neighbouring kingdoms. Kings and princes were overwhelmed with astonishment at so great a change of affairs, and rejoiced to make an alliance, establish friendship, and arrange peace with so great a king. The Roman Emperor, whose kinswoman had married the king’s nephew, the son of Edmund Ironside—one of the two whom Cnut had condemned to exile—rejoicing in the king’s great prosperity, sent envoys and bound Edward to himself by a closer friendship and treaty. The King of France, his neighbour by blood, became still nearer through the mediation of peace. Thus we know that what Holy Scripture records of Solomon applied to blessed Edward: “All the kings of the earth desired to see his face and to hear his wisdom” (2 Chronicles 9). Denmark alone, still breathing slaughter and thirsting for it, threatened the destruction of the English; but the following account will show the end of so great an undertaking. [Col. 0745C]

### On his venerable manner of life and character

In all this the blessed man was not raised up into human glory. Rather, recognizing more deeply God’s goodness toward him, he diligently meditated the saying of the Wise Man: “Have they made you ruler? Do not exalt yourself, but be among them as one of them” (Ecclesiasticus 32). Setting before himself this pattern of life, he showed himself equal to those of his household, humble to priests, gracious to the people, compassionate to the wretched, and generous to the needy. Wonderful was his devotion toward the worship of God, and wonderful his care in building and restoring churches and monasteries. [Col. 0745D]

With him there was no partiality, but he judged the poor in justice and rebuked with equity on behalf of the meek of the earth. Though he was a king exalted on his throne and adorned with gold and purple, he was yet the father of orphans and judge of widows. The wealth of the whole world seemed his public treasury, the common storehouse of the poor. For the king regarded all that he possessed as belonging not to himself but to all: if asked, he gave; if something was taken, he was silent. He was a modest recipient and a cheerful giver, never forgetting what he received, but immediately forgetting what he had given.

The holiness of his inner spirit shone even in his body: a certain singular sweetness appeared in his face, dignity in his bearing, simplicity in his disposition. His speech, composed with a certain dignity and cheerfulness and always seasoned with the sweet name of Christ and of his blessed mother, was now frightening, now gentle, now instructive, now consoling. No one ever saw him puffed up with pride, unrestrained in anger, or dishonoured by gluttony. Owing to his innate simplicity and sincerity toward all, he might perhaps sometimes be deceived and unknowingly go beyond what was proper; but he could neither be driven by anger nor enticed by desire into knowingly doing wrong. There is no need to praise his chastity, for it remained dear to him in exile, his companion in adversity, and his inseparable attendant in prosperity. Moreover, he despised money beyond the ordinary human measure: he did not seem sadder at its loss or more cheerful at its acquisition. Let us give one example of so great a virtue, through which his wonderful simplicity, tranquillity of heart, and unconquerable gentleness will appear. [Col. 0746B] It became known throughout the whole world in a widely circulated English tale: some marvelled at the king’s simplicity, others praised his holiness.

### How a thief stole his treasures while he watched

Once the king lay upon his bed to rest, but some thought, as often happens, kept sleep away. The custodian came to the chest in which the royal money was kept and, as seemed appropriate to him at the time, either removed or put away something. Then, forgetting to close the coffer, he went out to do some other task. A poor boy, said to have been employed at the tables gathering up dishes, noticed this. Going to the chest, he placed in his bosom a sizeable handful of coins and, leaving, hid them where he judged it safe for the moment. He returned and, while the king watched the deed, repeated it. When he had attempted it a third time, the king, seeing, as I think, in the Spirit that the guardian of the treasure was now about to arrive, and wishing to avert danger from the thief, said: “You are acting rashly, boy. If you trust me, take what you have and run. For, by the Mother of the Lord, if Hugelin comes”—for that was the name of the royal chamberlain—“he will not leave you even one coin.” The boy fled, neither betrayed nor driven away by the king.

The thief had scarcely set foot outside when the attendant returned, found the royal treasures plundered, and was astonished. Pallor seized his face and trembling his body; cries and sighs disclosed the anguish of his heart and rage of his mind. The king rose and, as though unaware of what had happened, asked the reason for this disturbance. When he had learned it from the chamberlain, he said: “Be silent. Perhaps the one who took it needed it more than we do; let him keep it. What remains is enough for us.” [Col. 0746D]

I ask: what is more perfect than this king, what simpler in outlook? What mind gentler than his, who saw his goods stolen and was silent, and furthermore advised the thief for his safety? Let each interpret it as he wishes. For my part, I consider that his enlightening of the blind, his healing of the lame, and his deliverance of many from grievous illness are to be placed after this simplicity and patience of his. Having inserted these matters, I think not without usefulness, let us return to the order of our narrative.

### On his chaste marriage, and the virginity of himself and the queen

[Col. 0747A]

With King Edward’s rule confirmed, and all things settled in the highest peace and prosperity, the nobles, anxious about the succession, approached the king concerning the taking of a wife. The king was troubled, fearing for his treasure, which, stored in an earthen vessel, might easily be melted by heat. But what was he to do? If he resisted too stubbornly, he feared that the sweet secret of his purpose would be revealed; if he assented to those urging him, he dreaded shipwreck of chastity. At last, judging it safer to yield to their timely and untimely insistence, he commended his chastity to the Lord in words such as these:

> “Good Jesus, once in thy mercy thou didst preserve three boys unharmed amid the Chaldaean flames (Dan. III). Through thee Joseph, leaving his cloak to the wicked harlot, escaped with the title of chastity (Gen. XXXIX). By thy power the admirable constancy of Susanna triumphed over the unchaste elders (Dan. XIII). The singular chastity of holy Judith, who amid the royal feasts and barren cups of Holofernes could neither be harmed nor tempted, armed a woman’s hand with steel for the destruction of that wicked head and freed the city from siege (Judith XIII). And surpassing all these: thou didst will that my sweetest lady, thy mother, the world’s only hope, should be both wife and virgin; nor did the sacrament of marriage break the seal of chastity. Behold, I, thy servant and the son of thy handmaid—however much thy lover, and the lover of thy only mother—do not presumptuously aspire to equality with such majesty as thine; yet, fearing, I sigh after some likeness to so great a thing. Therefore aid me, O my Lord, Son of the Virgin my Lady; and thou, my Lady, Virgin and Mother of my Lord: that I may receive the sacrament of marriage in such a manner as not to incur danger to chastity.”

The king therefore consented to the nobles’ wish, and they sought a virgin suited to the embraces of so great a king both by nobility of blood and by uprightness of character. Among the powerful men of England, the most powerful of all was Earl Godwin: a man of great wealth, but of singular cunning, a betrayer of kings and kingdom. Skilled in deception and accustomed to disguise every kind of intention, he could easily incline the people’s consent toward any faction whatsoever. Yet, as a thorn bears a rose, Godwin begot Edith, who indeed received from him the material of her flesh, but from God’s Spirit instruction in holiness. Christ had prepared her for his beloved Edward, inspiring her from infancy with love of chastity, hatred of vices, and affection for virtue.

Even in her girlish years she displayed the gravity of old age; avoiding public life, she frequented the privacy of her chamber. There, neither idly relaxed nor oppressively wearied, she was accustomed to read or to work with her hands: to adorn garments with remarkable skill, to weave gold into silk, and to represent all manner of things in pictures. By such work and meditation she avoided wantonness and shunned the conversation of young men. Moreover, she was beautiful in face, but far more beautiful in moral excellence.

Godwin, wishing to bind more closely to himself the king’s affection—which he greatly feared on account of the murder of the king’s brother and no few acts of treachery—worked through his friends and the king’s confidential officers to have his daughter deemed worthy of royal marriage. Those also who clung to their lord with more devoted affection, greatly fearing the earl’s treachery, which they had often experienced, judged this very arrangement most necessary for the king. Thus, although not with the same intention, all agreed in one opinion.

From the wealth of both parties a wedding feast was prepared; the bishops completed the sacrament; the girl was blessed as wife and crowned as queen. When they had come together, king and queen made an agreement to preserve chastity, and they judged that no witness other than God ought to be admitted to this pledge. She became a wife in mind, not in flesh; he a husband in name, not in deed. Between them continued marital affection without conjugal intercourse, and the embrace of chaste love without the deflowering of virginity. He loved, yet was not corrupted; she was loved, yet was not touched. Like some new Abishag, she warmed the king with love, not inflamed him with lust; she soothed him by service, but did not weaken him through desires.

And lest anyone withhold belief from this virtue of the king, let him know that in those times this was so widely reported and believed throughout all England that most people, certain of the fact, disputed about the intention. For some, understanding nothing but flesh and blood, charged the king’s simplicity with this: that, compelled, he had joined himself to the family of traitors, and that, lest he produce traitors, he abstained from the marital act. But if the love with which they embraced one another is considered, such an opinion is easily dismissed. I thought this worth inserting so that it may be known that at that time no one doubted the king’s continence, when they debated its cause in this manner.

Certainly, the purity of his mind bears witness to the king’s chastity: cleansed of every dreg of assailing vice, it was able to contemplate things far off as though present, and to know future things as though placed before its eyes, as the following chapter shows.

## How he saw in the spirit the King of Denmark drowned by divine judgment

The anniversary day was at hand on which the Spirit of the Lord filled the world in order to renew the face of the earth (Ps. CIII [104]); when the divine fire, descending upon the purified minds of the disciples (Acts II), both illuminated them unto knowledge, melted them unto grace, and hardened them unto punishment. On that day the blessed king stood devoutly at the divine praises. Outwardly he was distinguished by sceptre, splendid in dress, crowned with royal diadem; inwardly he regarded whatever honour was in these things as dung, while he bore what was sacramental for conscience’ sake.

All the nobility of England was present, surrounded by the varied splendour of gold-wrought dress, honouring as best they could both the sacred solemnity of the day and the royal majesty. Therefore, amid the sacred solemnities of the Masses celebrated in the church of St Peter, gathering his whole self within himself and putting all temporal things after spiritual ones, he fixed his mind upon the sacrifice offered for the salvation of all, humbly praying for grace for himself, peace for the people, and pardon for everyone.

And behold, at the hour when spiritual food was given to those present, the king suddenly became more cheerful in countenance and more alert in eye, and broke into a slight laugh, while retaining royal gravity. Those present marvelled, and not without cause: they knew that this had happened to him contrary to his custom. When all that appeared to pertain to the worship of so great a day had been completed, those who had noticed it asked him to explain the reason for his laughter.

As he was of remarkable simplicity, he simply confessed all to those who asked simply:

> “The Danes, with their king, have agreed to repeat their old crime and to disturb the peace which favourable divinity has granted us. For when the Lord chastened us severely, they, ignorant of God’s justice and exalting their own strength, said: ‘Our hand is high, and not the Lord has done all these things’ (Deut. XXXII). Since God, angry with our fathers, delivered us into the power of the Danes, they attributed this to their own strength and readily thought that the same could now be done, not knowing that he who strikes also heals; he who kills also makes alive; and he who brings down to hell also brings back (1 Sam. II).
>
> “Therefore the Danish king, having assembled his army, ordered ships to be made ready today, with the winds blowing as desired. Provisions are brought together; weapons are carried aboard; sailors prepare the rigging; soldiers are placed in assigned stations. The ships were already to be entrusted to their sails and the sails to the winds, when, at the very hour in which my face was made serene, the wicked king, through excessive pride, as though unable to contain himself, spread apart both feet and legs [the reading *sinouse* is uncertain]. Extending one foot too carelessly, he slipped from the prow; immediately the abyss enclosed him and the sea covered his head. Thus he opened a pit for us and dug it, and fell into the hole he had made (Ecclus. XXVII). The Lord struck the head from the house of the wicked and cursed his sceptres (Hab. III), and his whole army, who were coming as a whirlwind to scatter us. As, when the head is cut off, all the limbs wither, so, when their wicked leader is drowned, the army is scattered.
>
> “But I hope in the Lord my God and in his sweetest mother that during my lifetime none of their attempts will have effect. These are the things which, through Christ’s revelation, I have known and seen; and I laughed and rejoiced. For the Lord has made laughter for me, and whoever hears will laugh with me.”

The time and hour were recorded. Messengers were sent to Denmark; they inquired carefully into everything and found that all had happened in precisely the same hour in which it had been revealed from heaven to the most blessed king. As report of so great a miracle spread, fear fell upon all who heard the account. Knowing that God himself fought for Edward, both the Danes and the other peoples concluded a treaty with him through the exchange of messengers and gifts.

## He addresses the nobles of the kingdom concerning the fulfilment of his vow, and envoys are sent to Rome

As prosperity followed prosperity, the blessed king by no means forgot his promise; nor, in days of good fortune, was he unmindful of adversity. Reflecting again and again on the great things that the Lord had done for him—who had enriched the needy, exalted the humble, and crowned the obscure—he prepared to pay the vows uttered by his lips. He readied funds, set apart gifts, and, summoning the chief men of the whole realm, addressed them as follows concerning both the state of the kingdom and his own pilgrimage:

> “Blessed be God, who has magnified his mercy in dealing with us; who visited our iniquities with a rod (Ps. LXXXVIII [89]) and our sins with stripes, yet did not remove his loving-kindness from us. Behold how he has put down the mighty and exalted the lowly; how he has filled the hungry with good things and sent the rich away empty (Luke I). ‘By me kings reign,’ he himself says, ‘and princes decree just things’ (Prov. VIII).
>
> “We have not forgotten how, when barbarians burst into our inheritance, we became a reproach to our neighbours, a mockery and derision to those around us (Ps. LXXVIII [79]). Some were killed, others put to flight, others crushed beneath the yoke of shameful servitude; they left almost no honour, almost no glory, to our line. At last, when my father had died, my brothers had been murdered, and my nephews driven into exile, while fortune favoured our enemies in all things, it seemed that no hope remained for me.
>
> “But I, believing beyond hope in hope and entrusting myself wholly to the Lord’s mercy, vowed a pilgrimage to the thresholds of the holy apostles, and thereafter committed myself to divine protection and governance. He looked upon my prayer and did not despise my petition (Ps. CI [102]); he removed my reproach (Ecclus. XLVII), restored me to my father’s kingdom, and moreover heaped riches upon me, increased my glory, and made me illustrious with heavenly gifts. Without bloodshed he subdued rebels, overthrew enemies, and ordered all our affairs in a kind of beloved peace.
>
> “Far be it, far be it, that we should prove ungrateful for benefits so many and so great. Rather, having been delivered from the hand of our enemies, let us serve him in justice and truth. Let us do what the Prophet says: ‘Make vows and pay them to the Lord your God’ (Ps. LXXV [76]). Determine with me, then, how the kingdom of the English may stand while I am on pilgrimage: by what law, what peace, what judge all things shall be ordered; who is to be set over which region; who shall care for fortresses, who for cities, who for private and who for public affairs.
>
> “Yet God shall be the one guardian and protector of all; and he himself will preserve the peace he has given, travelling with me and remaining with you. May he guard you and bring me back.”

At these words all that multitude trembled and disclosed its inward sorrow through tears and sighs. They now feared the Danish hand which they had escaped through his merits; they now feared that the whole country would be destroyed. Speech burst forth among the people: behold, shouting; behold, tumult; and, as though fires already raged, the island appeared full of tears. One might see the poor now stretch their hands to heaven, now again fall to the earth, and, as though they would die of hunger if the king departed, think only of burial and the grave.

Then all together cried out to the king, urging that they were not to be abandoned, not to be exposed to the sword, that their homeland was not to be betrayed to enemies, that the pledge of peace which by God’s gift they had received was not to be dismissed, and that so many dangers were not to be incurred for one supposed good. The bishops commanded, the nobles begged, the people compelled: if he did not judge this journey to be abandoned, he should at least judge it to be postponed.

Feeling himself pressed by so many tears, cries, and prayers, he long wavered between compassion and desire. For he judged it dangerous to neglect his vow, yet inhuman not to yield to the prayers and weeping of so many. At last, desiring to know what was more fitting before God, he considered it wiser for the time being not to abandon the pilgrimage but to postpone it, until, after consulting the counsel and will of apostolic authority, he might by its judgment either redeem or fulfil the vow.

When this was heard, such joy came upon rich and poor alike that they thought their Edward restored to them again, recalled once more from exile. Each person, according to rank, office, and means, acted so that the king might not grow weary of the delay: some promised prayers, others alms, and some even their own pilgrimage on his behalf.

Envoys were immediately chosen to be sent to the Apostolic See: Ælred, Archbishop of York; Hermann, Bishop of Winchester; moreover two abbots of proven religious life; together with several others, both clerics and laymen. Meanwhile the necessary preparations were made; receiving their commission from the king, they set out for Rome. It must be believed that God’s providence arranged that the royal representatives found there assembled a very great synod, over which Pope Leo of blessed memory presided and in which ecclesiastical business was being discussed.

That illustrious company of holy men rejoiced at their arrival and welcomed the presence of such great fathers as though comfort had been sent them from heaven, judging it a great gift of God that men such as these had come from the ends of the earth at such a time to such an assembly. Therefore, at the command of the most blessed father, the envoys came forward to state the cause for which they had come, while the fathers seated there offered the most devout silence.

They set forth the king’s desire, the kingdom’s danger, the loss of peace, the cry of the poor, and the tears of orphans. They further declared that the scar of the not-yet-healed wound inflicted upon the English by Danish fury would, if the king departed, be feared to become more painful. When the envoys fell silent, thanksgiving and a voice of praise sounded from every mouth. The king’s devotion toward God and the people’s devotion toward their king were proclaimed. They marvelled that the gentleness of David, the prudence of Joseph, and the riches of Solomon had come together in such a ruler.

At last, the supreme pontiff dictating the judgment, all together decreed that, for the peace of the kingdom, the benefit of the Church, the need of the poor, and the tranquillity of monasteries, the king should solemnly be absolved from the bond of this vow by the authority of God, of blessed Peter, and of the present most holy synod; and that the funds prepared for the journey should be distributed to the poor. In compensation for the vow, a monastery was to be built with royal resources in honour of St Peter, or some monastery destroyed by barbarians was to be repaired.

Thereupon the envoys, having offered the gifts which the holy king had sent to the churches of the saints, received the pontiff’s blessing and returned joyfully to their homeland with apostolic letters. Having crossed to the island, they delivered the letter before the council which royal authority had convened for this very purpose.

## PAPAL RESCRIPT

**LEO, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son EDWARD, king of the English: greeting and apostolic blessing.**

Since we have learned that your intention is praiseworthy and pleasing to God, we give thanks to him through whom kings reign and princes decree just things (Prov. VIII). But since the Lord is near in every place to all who call upon him in truth, and the holy apostles, united with their head, are one spirit and hear pious prayers alike; and since it is evident that the English realm would be endangered by your departure, you who restrain its seditious motions with the bridle of your justice: by the authority of God, the holy apostles, and the holy synod, we absolve you from the sin of that vow for which you fear God’s displeasure, and from all your negligences and iniquities. We exercise, namely, that power which the Lord granted us in blessed Peter, saying: “Whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven” (Matt. XVI).

Thereupon we command you, under the name of holy obedience and penance, to distribute to the poor the funds which you had prepared for this journey, and either to build a new monastery of monks in honour of St Peter, prince of the apostles, or to enlarge and restore an old one; and from your revenues to establish sufficient provisions for the brethren, so that, while they praise God there continually, glory may be increased for the saints and pardon for you.

By apostolic authority we command that whatever you have bestowed, whatever has been bestowed, or whatever shall be bestowed upon that place shall remain valid; that it shall always be a habitation of monks; and that it shall be subject to no lay person except the king. Whatever privileges relating to God’s honour you may wish to establish there, we grant and confirm by most firm authority; and we condemn their violators with eternal curse.

## On the vision which appeared to a certain recluse concerning the king himself

A heavenly oracle concurred with the king’s marriage agreement and the pontiff’s letters. While the envoys were not far away, the prince of the apostles appeared to a certain holy man, who knew nothing of what they had done at Rome, and declared it to him. This man was beloved of God and men. Shut up for many years in an underground cave, he was already near the reward of his merits.

The most blessed Peter stood beside him in a vision of the night; and, having dispelled fear by the gentleness of his voice and countenance, he said:

> “King Edward, concerned about the vow by which he bound himself while still in exile, and also about the peace of his kingdom by the counsel of his people, and likewise about the need and prayer of the poor, judged that the Roman Church ought to be consulted about all these matters. Therefore let him know that by my authority he has been released from this obligation, and that from the supreme pontiff he has received a saving command concerning the construction of a monastery in honour of my name.
>
> “Let him therefore place unwavering faith in the apostolic letters, obey the commands, and accept the counsels. For this word proceeded from me: from me whom he once chose as his patron, me as his companion and bestower of grace. In the western part of London there is a place belonging to me, chosen by me and beloved by me, which I once consecrated with my own hands, ennobled by my presence, and further made illustrious by divine miracles. The place is called Thorney. Once, because of the sins of the people, it was given into the power of barbarians; from rich it became most poor, from lofty lowly, from noble contemptible.
>
> “At my command let the king undertake to restore it as a dwelling-place for monks: to raise it up with buildings and enlarge it with possessions. There shall be there nothing other than the house of God and the gate of heaven (Gen. XXVIII). There a ladder is to be raised, by which angels descending and ascending (ibid.) may bear human prayers and vows to God and bring back grace. To those who ascend from there I shall open the gate of paradise, so that, in the office entrusted to me by my Lord and Saviour, I may loose those who are bound, receive those who have been loosed, and open to the justified the gate of the heavenly homeland which sin had closed against them.
>
> “But you, committing to letters all that you have heard and learned from me, send someone to carry it to the king, so that, God’s gift being doubled, he may be more secure concerning his absolution, more devout in carrying out the command, and more disposed toward love and service of me.”

When these words had been spoken, the light disappeared with the speaker. The man delayed no longer, but quickly committed to a sheet and to writing, through a notary, what he had seen and heard. Giving the letter to a messenger, he sent it, as he had been commanded, to the court, which was then many thousands of paces distant.

Therefore, on that same day, in the same place and in the same council where the envoys returning from Rome reported the apostolic command, the letter of the man of God, presented to the king, was likewise brought forward. After St Pope Leo’s rescript had been read, the written words of the blessed old man were next recited. God was blessed outwardly by voice and inwardly by joy in his gifts, and praised in all his works. All marvelled at the king’s holiness, embraced the apostles’ glory, were strengthened in faith, raised in hope from earthly things to heavenly ones, and more sincerely inflamed with love of God.

There could be no doubt of the oracle’s truth, since that man, secluded from human intercourse in the district of Worcester, could not have known what had been done at Rome, what commands had been received, or when the envoys had returned, unless God had revealed it. Then the king, joyful and eager, as had been decreed for him, “scattered abroad and gave to the poor” (Ps. CXI [112]) the money he had provided for the support of his pilgrimage, and, turning his mind to the work enjoined upon him, poured out treasures.

Moreover, with royal liberality he remitted that most burdensome tribute which in his father’s time had first been paid to the Danish fleet and later paid annually into the royal treasury; and he released England forever from this intolerable burden. Therefore the words written are fittingly applied to this holy king: “Blessed is the man who is found without blemish, and who has not gone after gold, nor hoped in treasures of money” (Ecclus. XXXI). He was indeed found without blemish through the privilege of chastity. He did not go after gold, which he rather scattered abroad; nor did he hope in treasures, which he did not so much diminish as consume in God’s work.

Who is this man, that we may praise him? For he did wonderful things in his life: restoring sight to the blind and walking to the lame, driving away fevers, healing paralytics, and curing diverse human illnesses. We consider some of these worthy to be inserted in this work.

## On the cripple whom the holy king healed by carrying him

While the peaceful king was once staying in the royal city, in the palace beside the basilica of St Peter, there came a miserable man, Irish by race, called Gillemichel in the language of that people, deprived of the use of both feet. For sinews contracted at the knee had twisted his legs backwards toward the rear of his body, fastening them to his buttocks; the joints of his feet, buried in flesh, had distorted his body from the loins downward. With hands stretched to the ground and little benches placed beneath them, he crawled; made burdensome even to himself, he dragged himself after himself, presenting a pitiable sight to observers and drawing the compassion of many.

The poverty of his household added to the sum of his wretchedness, so that hunger’s injury and the harshness of the weather had at once wasted and emaciated that half-consumed body. Having thus crept into the court, he presented himself to the king’s chamberlain:

> “Hugelin,” he said, “will you not look upon me? Will you not pity me? Will so great a calamity in one man not move you?”

And the chamberlain said: “What do you want me to do?”

The poor man replied:

> “Six times I have visited the thresholds of the holy apostles in the city where they rest, crawling as wretchedly as you now see, yet I have not so far obtained health. But the most blessed Peter has not denied it to me; he has postponed it, wishing to have Edward as his partner in this miracle, knowing him to be devoted to himself in all things. Now, as I am about to set out for the city a seventh time, I received from the holy apostle himself the command to approach the king and convey the apostolic command: that he should carry me upon his sacred back to his church beside the palace. If he does this, I shall receive through his merits complete health of my limbs.”

When this was reported to the king, he gave thanks to God and promised that he would obey the apostle and not fail the needy man, but would render him the service commanded. The sick man was immediately summoned and came. The king, like that spiritual “strong ass, crouching between the boundaries,” put his shoulders under the burden. “Hear this, all nations; give ear, all who inhabit the earth” (Ps. XLVIII [49]). Gather for a spectacle such as no circus ever offered and no theatre invented.

A poor man, full of filth, hangs from the shoulder of so great a ruler; with foul hands and scaly arms he embraces that royal breast and neck. O necklace more splendid than every jewel! O collar more precious than every gold, more radiant than every electrum! Meanwhile, some of those standing by laughed; some joked that the king had been deceived by the poor man; others interpreted the righteous man’s simplicity and gentleness as foolishness. Behold a new David, dancing and applauded; behold a new Michal, contempt and laughter. Yet those of sounder mind judged him happier beneath such a burden than beneath a golden crown. For thou, Christ Jesus, wast carried in the poor man—thou who once wast clothed in the poor man whom Martin clothed. But then thou didst disclose this by an oracle, now by a miracle.

When, therefore, burdened with that noble burden, the king had gone a little way, suddenly the sinews that long-standing sickness had contracted were stretched out; the channels of blood which the rigidity of the veins had closed were opened; the bones were moistened; the withered flesh grew warm. The joints emerged from the flesh; the feet were released from the buttocks. The man stretched out his legs, his knee now supple; and, as pus and blood flowed out, the royal garment was adorned rather than defiled.

Then all cried that it was enough: the sick man had been healed, and the burden, because of the filth of his sores, must now be put down. But he, remembering the command he had received, passed by the song of the sirens with stopped ears. Entering the church, he fulfilled before the holy altar the offering which he had brought to God and St Peter. Godric, sacristan of that church, a man of great religion, took the poor man from the holy king’s shoulders; after his limbs had been washed and his sores treated, he soon dismissed him sound and whole.

The man stood upon his feet; when his ankles and soles had been strengthened, he was presented to the king. Receiving travelling provisions from him, he set out for Rome, blessing God, to give thanks to St Peter the apostle and proclaim everywhere the merits of the holy king. In testimony of so great a miracle, the benches upon which that wretched man had been accustomed to support himself while crawling were hung in the church, offering a pleasing spectacle to observers and displaying the king’s holiness to visitors.

This miracle surely gave the holy king the strongest incentive at once to love and revere the merits of St Peter, and kindled and drew forth his desire to complete the work he had begun in Peter’s name. Yet, among all places in England consecrated to St Peter, he chose this one especially for restoration, because he had learned that it was dearer to Peter than all the rest, not only from the oracle of the heavenly vision, as we have said above, but also from the testimony of a most ancient miracle. Though this may seem outside our subject, we believe it should be inserted in this work in order to show the king’s careful judgment in this choice.

## On the church of Westminster which St Peter dedicated

At the time when King Æthelberht, who ruled in Kent, had received the sacraments of faith through the preaching of blessed Augustine, his nephew Sebert, who ruled the East Saxons, also received the faith through the preaching of the same bishop. In London, regarded as the metropolis of his kingdom, Sebert, who ruled the East Angles, built within the walls a church in honour of the most blessed Paul and wished it to be exalted as an episcopal see. St Mellitus, whom blessed Pope Gregory had sent with several others to assist Augustine, was the first to preside over it in both merit and episcopal honour.

But wishing to prove himself acceptable to each apostle, the king founded a notable monastery in honour of St Peter in the western part of the same city, outside the walls, adorning it with many gifts and enriching it with possessions. The time came when the church was to be dedicated. All things appropriate to the place, the occasion, and the monastery’s dignity had been prepared; the bishop was spending that night in tents and awaiting the following day.

The people had great expectation. Still inexperienced in the faith, they rejoiced to attend these solemnities not only from devotion but also from wonder. That same night, St Peter the apostle appeared in pilgrim’s dress to a fisherman on the farther bank of the River Thames, which flows beneath that monastery. He asked for and obtained passage across from him in return for promised payment.

Having left the little boat, the apostle entered the church in the fisherman’s sight. And behold: heavenly light suddenly flashed forth; illuminating everything with marvellous splendour, it turned night into day. With the apostle came a multitude of citizens of heaven, going out and entering; and, as choirs singing hymns went before, heavenly melody resounded. Everything was full of light, everything filled with sweetness. The pleasure of angelic voices delighted the ears; the fragrance of indescribable perfume flooded the nostrils; heavenly light illumined the eyes. Earthly things seemed mingled with heavenly, human things joined with divine; and, as on Jacob’s ladder, angels descending and ascending (Gen. XXVIII) were seen in those sacred rites.

What more need be said? When all the solemnities belonging to the dedication of the church had been completed, the excellent fisher of men returned to the fisherman of fish. Finding him terrified by the radiance of the divine light and almost bereft of his senses, he restored the man to himself and his mind to reason by gentle consolation. The two fishermen entered the boat together; and in conversation the apostle addressed the man in the same words in which his Master had once addressed him:

> “Do you have nothing to eat?”

The fisherman replied:

> “Stupefied both by the flooding of unaccustomed light and by waiting for you, I have caught nothing; but I have confidently awaited the payment you promised me.”

To this the apostle said:

> “Now put out the nets for a catch” (Luke V).

The fisherman obeyed the command, and immediately a very great multitude of fish filled the net. When they had been drawn to shore, the apostle said:

> “Take to Bishop Mellitus from me the fish that surpasses the others in size and value. As payment for the passage, take the rest for yourself. I am Peter who speaks with you. With my fellow citizens I have dedicated the basilica built in my name; by my authority I have anticipated the episcopal blessing with my own consecration. Therefore tell the bishop what you have seen and heard, and signs impressed on the walls will bear witness to your words. Let him therefore refrain from the dedication; let him complete what we have omitted, namely the most holy mysteries of the Lord’s body and blood. Instructing the people by his word and confirming them by his blessing, let him make known to all that I shall visit this place often, that here I shall be present at the voices and prayers of the faithful, and that I shall open the gate of heaven to those who live soberly, justly, and devoutly in this place” (Titus II).

With these words the keeper of the heavenly keys disappeared. Dawn had now put an end to the darkness of night, when the fisherman, carrying the fish, met blessed Mellitus as he was setting out to celebrate the mysteries of the forthcoming dedication. When he had handed the fish over to the bishop, he recounted all that the apostle had commanded him.

The bishop marvelled. Opening the doors of the sacred basilica, he saw the pavement marked with inscriptions in both alphabets; the wall anointed in twelve places with consecrating oil; the remains of as many candles adhering to twelve crosses; and everything still wet, as though from a recent sprinkling. No further doubt could remain in anyone’s mind concerning the fisherman’s assertion, since heavenly signs testified to his account.

The bishop reported these things to the people, and immediately the united voice of all struck heaven as they praised and blessed God, who, to confirm the faith of all, had made the commonwealth of heaven and earth one in the dedication of this most holy temple. The whole succession of that fisherman’s family gave credence to the miracle: just as they had received the practice from their father, they never failed to offer tithes to St Peter and to those serving him from all the profit which that trade thereafter brought them. Yet one man, having once dared to commit fraud, immediately lacked the benefit of his trade until he confessed his guilt, restored what he had taken, and promised amendment.

## On envoys again sent to the lord pope by the holy king himself
Having learned these things from the account and writings of the ancients, blessed Edward’s heart burned within him; and in his meditation a fire was kindled to raise the aforesaid monastery still higher in buildings and ornaments, as also in dignities and possessions. In order that these might endure firm, whole, and unimpaired in future times, he believed that everything should be confirmed by apostolic authority. Moreover, amid the frequent miracles by which he was daily made illustrious, amid the joys of peace which he enjoyed, standing upon the most solid rock of humility, [Col. 0757D] he was always fearful, always suspicious of his own frailty. Truly blessed is the man who always fears the Lord and greatly delights in his commandments (Ps. 111). Therefore glory and riches are in his house, and his righteousness endures for ever (ibid.). Now released by apostolic authority from his vow, yet still anxious concerning it, he prepared once more to send envoys to the thresholds of the apostles, once more to consult the apostolic majesty, and once more to ask that this very thing, or some other matter, be imposed upon him as recompense for his vow.

Other matters also had arisen in the English Church concerning which that See ought especially to be consulted, of which it was specifically said: “The gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Matt. 16). Accordingly the holy king, taking thought for all things, wishing that all should be done according to the rule of Catholic truth, [Col. 0758A] and desiring also to benefit all men, so that he himself might be made more secure concerning his own affairs and apostolic teaching might be offered to others for their salvation, sent with Ealdred, Archbishop of York, two men elected to episcopal office: namely, Giso to the church of Wells, and Walter to that of Hereford. In the presence of the archbishop with whom they had come, they received from the lord pope the gift of consecration; and, in a council which had perhaps assembled in the Lateran Palace at that time by God’s prompting, as we believe, they took their seats with honour among the other fathers. Then, at a suitable time, when they had produced the king’s letter, they added the other matters entrusted to them.

The unanimous and reasonable judgment of the supreme pontiff and of the whole sacred assembly favoured the desires of the royal saintliness. Having received [Col. 0758B] the holy father’s letter, and suffering no adversity whatsoever throughout their journey, they returned with the greatest rejoicing to king and country.

## LETTER OF THE KING ADDRESSED TO POPE NICHOLAS

To NICHOLAS, supreme Father of the universal Church, EDWARD, by the grace of God King of the English, due submission and obedience.

We glorify God because he has care for his chosen Church, when, in the place of a good predecessor, he has appointed you an excellent successor. Therefore we judge it right to sharpen and test all our good actions upon you as upon a solid rock, and to possess your knowledge and fellowship in what is good, so that you may renew and enlarge for us those gifts and privileges which we obtained from your predecessor; namely, that you may ratify what he imposed upon us under the name of obedience and penance on account of the vow which I had vowed, to go to Rome and, for the remission of all my sins, to construct a monastery of monks in honour of the Apostle Peter; and that you may confirm, renew, and enlarge the privileges of its possessions and the dignity of that same place, and decree that they stand unchangeable for ever.

I too, according to my measure, enlarge and confirm the donations and customary payments of money which Saint Peter possesses in England; and I send you the money thus collected together with royal gifts, that you may pray for me and for the peace of my kingdom, and establish a continual and solemn commemoration of the whole English people before the bodies of the holy apostles.

## PRIVILEGE OF LORD POPE NICHOLAS

[Col. 0758D]

NICHOLAS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the most glorious, most devout, and most worthy of every honour, and also our special son, EDWARD, King of the English: all-embracing visitation, honey-sweet salvation, and apostolic benediction.

We render thanks to Almighty God, who has adorned and endowed your most prudent excellence in every respect toward blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and has caused you to have affection for us and to agree in all things with apostolic judgments. We therefore send letters to your nobility, and through them grant you the fellowship of the holy apostles and our own fellowship, praying for the mercy of him who alone is Lord of all and King [Col. 0759A] above all things, that he may make you a participant in all such good works as are before God among ours; that he may establish us as brothers and companions in love ever more fully at all times; and that in his kingdom he may assign you no smaller share of our service than we desire to come to ourselves.

We shall also henceforth undoubtedly pray for you without ceasing, that God himself may subject to you the enemies and foes who desire to rise against you; that he may establish you upon your ancestral throne and in your own inheritance; and that blessed Peter may be your guardian and helper in every tribulation. For it is evident that the kings of the English, on account of the reverence and devotion which they showed to blessed Peter the apostle, flourished in glory and honour and obtained famous triumphs through his patronage. By the merits of this blessed apostle may Almighty God grant fulfilment to your desire and will, establish for you the sovereignty of your paternal kingdom, grant it increase, and, after the course of this present life, lead you to the everlasting dominion of enduring glory.

We therefore renew, confirm, and enlarge your privileges; namely, that you may be absolved, by the authority of him who, although I am unworthy, willed me to preside over his holy Church, from that vow which you feared, and from all your other sins and iniquities. Moreover, concerning that place which you have undertaken to build and improve under the name of holy penance: since, as is reported, it received its first consecration in ancient times from blessed Peter the apostle, whose unworthy vicars we are, and since it has from ancient times been a royal [Col. 0759C] seat, we grant, permit, and most firmly confirm, by the authority of God, of the holy apostles, of this holy Roman See, and of ourselves, that henceforth and for ever it shall be a place of royal foundation and consecration, a repository for royal insignia, and the perpetual dwelling-place of monks.

These monks shall be subject to no person whatsoever except the king; they shall have authority, according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, to elect suitable abbots through their successors; nor shall any outsider be introduced by force, except one whom the unanimous community has chosen to preside. We also absolve that place from every service and episcopal lordship, so that no bishop shall enter there to ordain or command anything, except by the consent and request of the abbot and monks. Let that same place also possess a free precinct—that is, an enclosure and cemetery for the dead around it—without episcopal or anyone else’s claim or exaction. And everything that, through our authority, can accrue to the liberty and exaltation of that place, pertaining to the honour of God, we grant with most ready and cheerful will.

We strengthen by divine and our own authority, and decree to be valid and stable, the possessions which ancient kings, or any other persons, you also and your barons, have bestowed upon that same place, and the charters which have been made concerning them. We condemn with Judas the traitor, under an eternal curse, those who violate, invade, diminish, disperse, or sell them, so that they may have no share in the blessed resurrection; but let them know that they will be judged by blessed Peter the apostle [Col. 0760A] when he sits with his fellow apostles judging the twelve tribes of Israel.

To you and to your descendants who are kings we entrust the advocacy and protection of that same place and of all the churches of all England, so that, in our stead and with the counsel of bishops and abbots, you may establish everywhere what is just. Know that thereby you will receive a worthy reward from him whose kingdom and dominion shall neither cease nor diminish for ever.

When, therefore, the letters of the apostolic majesty had been read, the most blessed king rejoiced with joy and was freed from all the anxiety which he had contracted through the obligation of his vow. Entrusting all the affairs of the kingdom to dukes and nobles, he devoted his whole self to divine service. And the more he withdrew himself from bodily things, the more brightly [Col. 0760B] he gave himself to spiritual contemplations. Hence he frequently deserved to be refreshed by revelations of heavenly secrets and by the sweetness of spiritual visions, as what follows will show.

## How He Saw Jesus Christ upon the Altar in the Sacrament with a Certain Earl

In the monastery of blessed Peter the apostle, which he had undertaken to build and enlarge, the most Christian king was present before the altar consecrated in honour of the divine Trinity for the most sacred mysteries of our redemption. Present also, with all reverence and sweetness of spirit, was Earl Leofric, whose memory is in blessing, together with his wife Godgifu, who magnificently fulfilled by her actions the interpretation of her name. For it means “good gift”: either because Christ had given her to his Church as a good gift for its benefit, or because she herself continually offered to God a most acceptable gift of faith and devotion.

Thus the most holy earl, with such a companion at his side, always intent upon God’s work, became founder of many monasteries; and living soberly, righteously, and devoutly in all things (Tit. 2), he made Christ heir of his possessions and treasures. He stood there somewhat apart at the king’s side, altogether worthy to be aware and witness of so great and such a miracle. The heavenly mystery was being performed at the altar; the divine sacraments were handled in the priest’s hands. And behold, he who is fairer in form than the sons of men (Ps. 45), Christ Jesus, standing upon the altar, [Col. 0760D] visibly appeared to the bodily eyes of both; and, stretching his sacred right hand over the king, he traced upon him, in blessing, the sign of the holy cross.

The king, bowing his head, adored the presence of the divine majesty; and, humbling his body, showed reverence to so great a blessing. But the earl, unaware of what was taking place in the king’s mind and wishing the king to share in so great a vision, began to wish to proceed toward him. The king, however, understanding what the earl was turning over in his mind, said: “Stay, Leofric, stay: what you see, I also see.” Then, turning to prayers and tears, they were intoxicated with the abundance of God’s house and drank from the torrent of his delight (Ps. 36).

After the end of the office they spoke together concerning the heavenly vision; and, filled with heavenly food, “day uttered speech unto day” [Ps. 19:2]. As their conversation was frequently interrupted by sighs, the king said: “Now, my Leofric, I adjure you by the majesty of him whom we have seen that, so long as we live, this account shall not be made public, lest either pride, because of popular favour, assail us to our destruction, or the jealousy of unbelievers disparage the truth of what has been said.” In this he followed the example of his Lord, who, having been transfigured before the disciples, said to them as they came down from the mountain: “Tell the vision to no one until the Son of Man has risen from the dead” (Matt. 17).

But the earl, departing from court, instructed, as is believed, by divine inspiration, so observed his lord’s command that the sublimity of so great a miracle should not be hidden from posterity. Coming therefore to Worcester monastery, he revealed the matter in confession to a certain religious man, whom he bound by the same adjuration by which the king had bound him; and he asked him to commit the secret of so great a vision to writing and to place it in such a spot that it might be concealed from those then living yet not perish from the knowledge of those to come. The holy man assented to the petitioner’s desire, committed the account of the vision to a little written slip, and placed it with holy relics in a shrine. Much time had already passed since the holy king’s death when, by divine prompting as we believe, and through no human action, the shrine was found open. As the brethren carefully examined the holy relics, they found and unfolded the written slip; unwilling that so great a treasure should remain concealed, they read all its contents publicly to the people. Thus what the king wished to be hidden was disclosed by God’s providence, so that the king’s humility might be proved and, nevertheless, the faith of believers confirmed by the revelation of the miracle.

## Of Swellings and Worms Expelled from a Certain Woman by the Royal Touch

From this point miracles became more frequent, signs were multiplied, and the hand of the Almighty was stretched forth to declare more highly the king’s merits. A certain young woman, given in marriage, suffered from a double affliction. Disease had disfigured her face, and barrenness had deprived her of her husband’s love. For beneath her jaws there had grown, as it were, glandular swellings, which, disfiguring her whole face with a hideous tumour, changed the blood into pus through the decay of fluids beneath the skin. Worms born from this emitted a most foul odour. Thus the disease inspired horror in her husband, while barrenness diminished his affection. The unhappy [Col. 0761D] woman lived hated by her husband and burdensome to her parents. Few friends approached her because of the stench, and her husband seldom looked upon her because of horror. Hence pain, tears, and sighs by day and night, since barrenness brought her reproach and infirmity contempt. Poverty prevented recourse to physicians’ skill.

What was the wretched woman to do? Since human help was lacking, she prayed for the divine aid which alone remained, as though breaking forth into the words of that equally unhappy woman: “I beseech thee, Lord, either free me from this bond of reproach, or take me away from the earth” (Tob. 3). At last she was commanded in a dream to go to the palace and hope for a remedy from the king’s hands; if she were washed, touched, or signed by them, she would recover health through his merits.

When the woman awoke, forgetting at once her sex and social condition, she rushed into the court, presented herself before the king’s eyes, related the oracle, and begged for help. Overcome by compassion as was his custom, he neither avoided the filth nor recoiled from the stench. Water was brought; with his own hands he washed the parts of her body which the disease had disfigured, felt the swollen places with his fingers, and impressed the sign of the holy cross. What more need be said? The skin suddenly burst; worms poured out with the pus; the tumour subsided; every pain departed. Those present marvelled at such holiness beneath purple, such power residing in sceptre-bearing hands. For a few days the woman remained at court, performing necessary services for the royal attendants, until a scar had formed over the wounds and she returned unharmed to her home. But, that nothing might be lacking either to the king’s glory or to the poor woman’s favour, unexpected fruitfulness was bestowed on the barren woman; enriched with the longed-for fruit of her womb, she readily regained her husband’s affection.

## Of a Blind Man Healed by the Washing of His Hands

Under the teaching of most blessed Paul, we have learned that the gifts of grace are diverse and that not all have received all things. “To one,” he says, “is given by the Spirit the word of wisdom; to another the word of knowledge by the same Spirit; to another faith; to another gifts of healings” (1 Cor. 12). Although the most Christian king possessed this gift of healing especially fully through God’s Spirit, he shone with a particular grace in enlightening the blind, because, as is believed, of the purity of the inward person: since singular purity had clarified the sight of his heart, he himself drove away in others [Col. 0762C] the outward darkness of their eyes.

A certain blind man, well known among the people, had long lamented the loss of light. It pleased the Saviour, by one and the same miracle, both to disclose the king’s power and to relieve the poor man’s calamity. The wretched man was therefore taught by an oracle that he would gain his lost light through the king’s merits if he used water with which the king himself had washed his face. Led by the hand, he came to the palace and told the chamberlains of the vision. When they reported it to the most devout prince, he was astonished and greatly indignant. He declared that the man had been deceived by fantasies; that a sinner should expect nothing of the kind; that this was apostolic power; and that dreams were not to be believed.

They replied that dreams were not wholly to be discredited, since Joseph and Daniel learned future things in nocturnal visions, and Christ’s foster-father learned, through an angel appearing in a dream, that he must flee with the child and later return. They added that God, to whom all things are subject, can, whenever he wills, bring aid to the wretched, to whom he wills, and through whom he wills; that it is not for man to resist divine commands, nor to deny anyone the remedy which God himself has provided.

Thus, while the king’s mind fluctuated for a short time between humility and compassion—unless humility had yielded to the petitioners’ insistence, compassion would not have fulfilled its part—the hour arrived at which the king, intending to proceed to church for the solemn vigil of All Saints, was, as usual, to wash his hands. Water was received in a basin. While the king was attending the sacred solemnities of Mass, the blind man was summoned by the attendants; they poured the water upon the circles of his eyes, washed his face, and prayed that divine power might be present through the merits of the holy king.

A wondrous thing: as though a new Siloam had flowed from the king’s hands, his eyelids opened; he received the light, looked around at everything in astonishment at the unfamiliar brilliance of the sun, and rejoiced that the world had, as it were, been restored to him anew. The greatness of his joy brought forth tears, while thanksgiving and a voice of praise resounded from the mouths of those standing by. The man entered the oratory to give thanks to God and stood with the others at divine worship. He was seen but not recognized. Some said, “It is he”; others, “No, but he resembles him”; while he himself affirmed that he was the man he had been. One looked at another, one spoke to another, while they whispered among themselves; the Mass ended, and the king, leaving the oratory, was received by the attendants who came to meet him.

Hearing of the miracle, he turned his steps back to the church and called the man to him. “Do you truly see, man?” he asked. He replied: “Truly, my lord king.” “And what do you see me doing?” He replied: “You stretch out to me your beloved hand, my lord.” “And now what?” The poor man answered: “You separate your forefinger from the middle finger, as though threatening my eyes.” “Now answer me a third time,” he said, “and declare what I am doing.” The man replied: “You are grasping your beard, king.” Then the saint burst into tears and prostrated himself before the holy altar, giving thanks and ascribing everything to God and nothing to himself. He proclaimed those words of David: “Not unto us, O Lord, not unto us, but unto thy name give glory” (Ps. 113).

## Of Another Blind Man Similarly Enlightened through the Blessed Man

What had happened in such a place, at such a time, and through such a person could not remain hidden; and the man whose sight had been restored lived for a long time at court, sustained by royal alms. Everywhere it was reported that a man had lost the darkness of his eyes through water with which the king had washed his hands. England rejoiced that it had a prophet presiding over it rather than merely a king: one who healed diseases and foretold things to come, who judged the earth in righteousness and peoples in equity (Ps. 67).

There was a citizen of the city of Lincoln whose sight had been taken away by accident or illness, and whose life’s sweetness had been swallowed up. Hence arose sorrow. Already his third year in darkness [Col. 0763D] had passed when the report of so great a power raised him in hope of recovering health. As though returning to himself, he said: “What is this? Why do I delay? A prophet is in England, and I am blind. I sit in darkness and walk in darkness, while near me shines the light of a new holiness and apostolic power is conspicuous in our king.”

Meanwhile the man fell asleep; and behold, in a nocturnal vision a swift remedy was promised him, if he too obtained the same medicine by which, he had learned, the blind man had been cured. The man hesitated no longer, came to court, and asked for—and obtained from the chamberlains—the gift he desired. His face was washed in the healing water, and immediately the desired light succeeded long-lasting darkness. The man gave thanks and thereafter returned to his homeland as a witness to the king’s holiness, carrying to his people the greatest joy together with his health.

## Of a Certain Blind Man Likewise Cured by the Royal Touch

It happened once that a royal palace was being built in a place named Bruheham. A considerable band of country people was sent by the overseers of the works to cut timber. After their labour, filled with food, and while the sun burned fiercely in the noon heat, they scattered here and there into the shade and gave their bodies rest. A little later, while the rest gladly returned to the work assigned them, a young man named Wulfwin rose from sleep and, opening his eyes, saw nothing. The wretched man twisted his head this way and that, rubbed his brow with his hand, and wiped his eyes with his fingers, but did not wipe away [Col. 0764B] the darkness. At last he understood that he had been deprived of sight; immediately breaking into cries and tears, he called his companions and told them what had happened. They gave such comfort as they could for his misfortune and, leading him by the hand, brought him back to his home.

He sat in darkness and the shadow of death for nineteen years; and behold, the time had come for mercy upon him. One day, as he lamented his misfortune piteously, a matron of honourable life and grave character came to comfort him. Having asked about his condition, as many are accustomed to do, and having heard his reply according to the state of mind he then had, she said: “I have been sent to you as bearer of good news: if you follow it without any doubt, the darkness will at once be driven away and your lost light restored.”

The man began to leap for joy and, promising things beyond his strength, deserved to receive such an answer from the woman: “You must, my friend, go barefoot and without linen garments around eighty churches, humbly ask the assistance of the saints, and then, with unfeigned faith, certain hope, and a cheerful spirit, hasten to the palace.
