You will receive from the royal hands your former health.” Without delay, having sought a guide, he visited the churches as he had been commanded. Then, full of faith, he entered the court and sought someone who would announce him to the prince.

All, weary of the multitude of petitioners, disregarded the poor man’s cry; indeed, they rebuked him and ordered him to be silent. But, an outstanding imitator of the blind man of the Gospel, he cried out all the more. At last the attendants, overcome by the persistence of his knocking, reported his case to the king. Already accustomed to such works, he said: “Let him come. For who am I, that I should be distressed rather than rejoice, if divine mercy has granted through my hands, unworthy though they are, the promised benefit to a poor man?”

The sightless man was summoned and came. The king dipped his fingers in water and anointed his face, impressing the sign of the cross upon the dark circles of his eyes. Immediately the Saviour’s grace was present, and abundant blood flowed from both eyes between the king’s hands; it cleared the pupils and reduced the swelling of the eyelids. Thus the man was restored to light; looking upon the king standing beside him, he said: “I see you, my lord king, and your face is like the face of an angel standing before me.” The king gave thanks to God and ordered the man to be keeper of the royal palace beside the church of blessed Peter the apostle for as long as he lived. He lived [Col. 0765A] until the time of William the Great, an experienced witness of Edward’s power.

## Of Three Blind Men and One One-Eyed Man Enlightened through the Blessed Man

These things indeed are wonderful, but more wonderful things follow. Four men were found before the palace doors, enjoying the comfort of a single eye. For one one-eyed man led the three who were wholly deprived of sight—clearly faithful in a little, that he might deserve to receive much. A certain courtier felt compassion for men suffering the same great calamity. Having seen so great a power issue from the royal hands, he furtively took, in pious theft and full faith, a portion of the water by which sight had been restored to the blind man, believing that it would also work in many persons because he had seen it work so plainly and effectively in one.

The faithful man went out to the wretches, urged them to trust in the Lord and believe that health would be restored to them through the merits of the holy king. Then he applied the washing, washed the poor men’s darkened faces, signed them with his thumb, and prayed that God might deign to regard not his own merits but those of blessed Edward. Immediately the Lord’s hand was present; their eyelids opened, and he poured into them the light they had desired. Night was changed into day for them, and their darkened faces were flooded with the sun’s brightness. Thus seven lamps shining from the foreheads of four men made our Edward more illustrious through all ages.

For the present, let it suffice to have written these things about the blind whose sight he restored, so that in this last miracle, in which we made mention of seven lamps, we may show that the holy king was filled with the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit: to him the spirit of the fear of the Lord, driving away the darkness of pride, opened the eye of humility; after cleansing the blindness of unbelief, the spirit of piety poured into him the light of faith; the spirit of knowledge, having scattered the darkness of falsehood, illuminated him with the light of truth; the spirit of fortitude made him stronger than every enemy, bodily as well as spiritual; having driven away the darkness of ignorance, through the spirit of counsel he received the light of discernment; the spirit of understanding transferred him from earthly to heavenly things, from bodily to spiritual things, from the night of this world to contemplation of heavenly lights; and the spirit of wisdom endowed him with the grace of prophetic light and knowledge of divine counsels. [Col. 0765D] Rightly, therefore, did he flood men’s outward eyes with sevenfold light after driving away blindness, since he deserved inwardly to be illumined by the light of the seven eyes seen in the heavenly field.

## What the King Prophesied Concerning the Two Sons of Earl Godwin

But let us now, God granting us the ability, set down some things revealed to him concerning future events or heavenly secrets. The blessed king was once sitting at table, and at his side was Earl Godwin, father of the queen, of whom we have spoken above. His two sons, still boys, Harold and Tostig, were playing before them. When one of them, more bitterly than the pleasure of play demanded, rose against the other, they turned play into a fight. Behold, Harold [Col. 0766A] attacked his brother more violently, caught both hands in his hair, and, unless he had been rescued quickly, would, being stronger, have suffocated him as he lay prostrate.

Then the king turned to the earl and said: “Do you see nothing else in this, Godwin, than a simple boys’ game or fight?” He replied: “Nothing else, my lord king.” The king said: “My mind tells me something very different, and through this conflict reveals to me what shall happen to these boys. When their boyish years have passed and each has come to manhood, jealousy will burn in each breast against the other. At first they will seem, by private stratagem and intrigue, merely to be playing; but in the end the stronger will outlaw the weaker and overthrow him when he rebels, and the calamity of the second, following soon after the death of the first, will expiate it.”

All these things are proved to have been fulfilled, with all England as witness. For Tostig, driven away by Harold, came into England shortly afterward, after Harold had succeeded Edward in the kingdom, to fight against his brother with King Harold of Norway, surnamed Harfager, accompanying him, and with a great fleet and a large army. Harold led his battle-line against them and proved victorious. Tostig was struck down in the battle; the king of Norway, taking to flight, escaped in a single ship with a few men. In the same year Harold himself was deprived of the kingdom of the English and either died miserably or, as some think, escaped, preserved only for repentance.

## Of the Miserable Death of Earl Godwin

But since we have again touched upon Godwin, I think it should be inserted how the avenging wrath of divine judgment consumed him with the wages of his treacheries, and how, before the people’s eyes, he paid the very punishment he deserved for the detestable crime he had committed against the king and his brother. For, abusing the king’s simplicity, he did many things in the kingdom contrary to right and justice in pursuit of power, and often attempted to bend the king’s mind to agreement with his own wickedness. At last his cunning advanced so far that he drove from the country, through fraud, deceit, and intrigue, almost all the king’s kinsmen and friends whom he had either brought from Normandy or summoned—bishops as well as clerics and laymen of other ranks—believing that everything would [succeed] according to his wishes if, stripped of indispensable friends, [Col. 0766D] the king used only his counsels.

But Edward, overlooking everything for the sake of place, time, and religion, devoted himself to divine service, declaring that God’s justice would avenge the duke’s great malice, and sometimes not concealing this very thing from Godwin himself. One day, celebrated among the people, the king sat at the royal table with Godwin present. During the meal, one of the servants struck one foot too violently against some obstacle and nearly fell; yet the other foot, advancing with a firm step, restored him to his position without harm. As many discussed this occurrence together and rejoiced that foot had come to the aid of foot, the earl remarked jokingly: “Thus does brother help brother, and one come to the aid of another in need.”

The king said to the duke: “My brother would have done this for me, if Godwin had permitted it.” At these words Godwin was terrified; with an exceedingly sorrowful expression he said: “I know, king, I know that your mind still accuses me concerning the death of your brother, and that you still judge those not to be disbelieved who call me traitor either to him or to you. But may God, who knows all secrets, judge me; and may he cause this morsel which I hold in my hand to pass through my throat and keep me unharmed, just as I am neither guilty of treachery against you nor conscious of participation in your brother’s death.”

He had spoken; putting the morsel into his mouth, he thrust it down to the middle of his throat. He tried to draw it farther in but could not; he tried to expel it, but it stuck more firmly. Immediately the passages through which breath was carried were closed, his eyes rolled, and his arms stiffened. The king looked upon him as he died miserably, and, perceiving divine vengeance to have come upon him, addressed those standing by: “Take out this dog,” he said. His sons rushed forward and, drawing him out from beneath the table, carried him into the bedchamber, where shortly afterward he met the end due to a traitor.

## What the Lord Spiritually Revealed to Him Concerning the Seven Sleepers
I cannot sufficiently wonder what the reason was that, at the very time when he appeared more splendid in royal dress, more severe surrounded by the retinue of magnates, and more lavish, in the judgement of onlookers, amid richer banquets, he deserved a more abundant grace of spiritual revelations [Col. 0767C]. Yet surely man sees the face, but God sees the heart. He bore a sword, indeed, but for his office; he used royal things, but sacramentally; he went attended by many soldiers, but from necessity; he sat exalted at a banquet, but by custom. Happy the man who used all these things so as not to misuse them, yielding his body to earthly matters and mingling his spirit with heavenly things.

Thus it happened that, on the day of the Lord’s resurrection, clad in the imperial robe, with a sceptre adorning his right hand and a crown his head, already filled with the flesh of the heavenly Lamb, he approached the royal table, to be refreshed more by spiritual than by bodily food. For, fearing, I suppose, lest a more plentiful table, more festive attire, or more splendid pomp might bend even slightly toward itself a mind fixed upon heaven [Col. 0767D], he gathered himself more closely than usual into himself; and, setting God before his eyes, he counted all these earthly things as dung. Suddenly his face became more serene than usual, and inward joy loosened his lips into laughter; then, resuming his customary gravity, he wore a more sombre expression. Those standing and sitting by wondered; and although, from what had happened, they did not doubt that some secret thing had been divinely revealed to the king, no one dared ask what had occurred.

When at last the feast was ended and the tables removed, the most blessed king entered his chamber to put off his royal ornaments. Earl Harold followed him, and, having summoned one bishop and one abbot, they together approached the king on this subject. Then he said: “Blessed is the man whose hope is the name of the Lord, and who has not looked toward vanities and false madnesses” (Ps. 39 [Vulgate]). For in proportion as anyone withdraws himself from vain things, he will cling more closely to true things. “Behold, amid abundant cups, rich dishes, and the splendour of shining metal, I remembered the Lord my God and poured out my soul within me” (Ps. 41 [Vulgate]). With the bosom of my mind opened wide, my inward eye, flooded with a special light, extended its rays with marvellous swiftness as far as the city of Ephesus; and, advancing as far as Mount Celion, it beheld with the clearest distinctness the features of the faces, the size of the limbs, and the quality of the garments of the holy Seven Sleepers resting in the cave [Col. 0768A]. While I saw these things with a radiant heart, signifying inward joy by laughter, suddenly—while I looked on—they turned by divine power from their right side, upon which they had rested for many years, to their left; by this change of their sides they marked a dreadful omen for mortals [Col. 0768B]. For thereafter, as it is written in the Gospel: ‘Nation shall rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom; and there shall be pestilences, and famines, and great earthquakes in divers places’ (Matt. 24). During these seventy years—for so long shall they rest on their left side—the Lord will visit the iniquity of his people, delivering them into the hands of the nations, that those who hate them may rule over them (Ps. 105 [Vulgate]). Enemies of Christ’s name will rise against Christians; servants will rebel against masters; kings will plot against kings [Col. 0768C], and princes against princes; and in every land the avenging sword will rage over the injury done to Christ.”

All who heard this utterance were astonished; and since, being situated outside the world [i.e. remote from it], they had heard nothing of the Seven Sleepers, they asked who and whence they were. The king set forth their life, names, martyrdom, and manner of sleeping. On hearing this, they resolved, in order to furnish posterity with proof and to investigate the truth of the account, that the duke should send a soldier, the bishop a cleric, and the abbot a monk, with the king’s letter, to the emperor of Constantinople. When they reached the imperial city, they were honourably received by the emperor. When the letter had been read, his spirit exulted with joy, and he rejoiced greatly that the treasures of Greece had been divinely revealed to the English [Col. 0768D].

They were sent to Ephesus; and, by the emperor’s command, the bishop, with clergy and people, went before the envoys. Having brought them with spices into the cave, he showed them the bodies, faces, and garments of the saints, and the saints themselves resting on their left side. And behold, great fear came upon them when they saw in the martyrs in Greece every sign which the holy king in England had learned through the teaching of God’s Spirit. Therefore, after prayers had been made and gifts offered, they returned home with the greatest prosperity, while the Greeks rejoiced in the things which they had heard and seen, as had been said to them; for the messengers brought to both the king and people of the English an unheard-of miracle and a sure proof of the faith.

The oracle did not deceive the king, for after he had been transferred to the heavenly kingdom all the kingdoms of the earth were shaken [Col. 0769A]. Syria was subjected to pagans; monasteries were destroyed; churches were razed from their foundations; all things were full of funerals through the death of the rulers of Greeks, Romans, Franks, and English; and the remaining kingdoms were disturbed. It is therefore clear that the most holy king was endowed with a fuller grace of the prophetic spirit: to him, at one and the same time, past things were laid open, present things did not remain hidden, and future things were likewise revealed.

## Concerning the ring which the holy king gave to blessed John the Evangelist, and how he received it back

Meanwhile the holy king, now burdened with age, was preparing for the rewards of his service. Day by day his affection for God and God’s mother increased, as did his devotion toward God’s saints. Among these he venerated most blessed Peter as his special patron [Col. 0769B], while he embraced with marvellous sweetness of mind that disciple whom Jesus loved because of the singular privilege of his chastity. He considered both equal before God: Christ had granted to one the primacy of the whole Church, while to the other he had bestowed more abundantly the sweetness of his love. What the latter lacked in primacy, affection supplied; what the former possessed less of in affection, the dignity conferred upon him compensated. Hence they are fittingly called together by Christ; together they were on the mountain with Christ; together they were sent to the large furnished upper room that the Passover might be prepared for Christ; together they ran to the tomb that Christ’s resurrection might be proved; together they went up to the temple at the ninth hour of prayer that the lame man might be healed.

And what was sweeter to this apostle [Col. 0769C], who was made drunk with wisdom from Jesus’ breast and bosom, and was given to drink of the milk of his love? As blessed Edward thoughtfully considered these and similar things with loving admiration, after the prince of the apostles he loved this friend of Jesus more closely, gladly devoted himself to his service, spoke often of his excellence, and often meditated upon his virginity.

It happened that a church built in honour of this apostle was consecrated to God under his name. The blessed king presided at the dedication and, joyful in honour of the Evangelist, attended the divine offices. As he followed the procession surrounded by many soldiers, a man in a pilgrim’s dress suddenly cried out to the king, asking that something in alms be given him for the love of Saint John. The king immediately put his hand into his purse, but he had already spent all that it contained upon a similar work [Col. 0769D]. The pilgrim persisted and multiplied his entreaties. The king called his treasurer, but, hindered by the crowd, he was not at hand. The saint was distressed in mind and did not know what to do. At length, remembering the ring encircling his finger, he quickly drew it off and gave it to the pilgrim. The latter gave thanks for such generosity, and either departed or disappeared.

Later two men set out for Jerusalem to worship at the Saviour’s tomb. One day, having turned aside from the public road, they followed every byway. Behold, as the sun declined, day closed and the air was darkened by shadows; the men could not think what to do or where to turn. As they stood still and discussed what had happened [Col. 0770A], a troop of youths dressed in white passed before their eyes, two candles going before and cutting through the darkness of night with wondrous light. Behind those who went before followed, with two men at his side, an old man venerable in his snowy hair; marvellous sweetness of face and native gravity alike gave him grace and increased his comeliness. Looking at the youths, he paused a little. “Ho there!” he said. “Men, who are you, and whence are you? What is your country, who is your king, what is your law, and what is the cause of your pilgrimage?”

They answered him: “England is our native land, King Edward our king. Subject to Christian laws, we purpose to visit the most holy places of the Lord’s Passion and Resurrection. But today, having by chance strayed from our companions, we confess to your venerable person that we do not know where we are, who will receive us as guests, or who will show us the hospitality due.” Then the old man, cheerful in countenance and pleasant of face, looked upon those looking at him and said: “Follow me, and the Lord will provide you with everything necessary” [Col. 0770B]. Giving thanks, they accompanied the old man and entered a most noble city. Received as guests, a table was prepared; and, richly refreshed, they gave their limbs to rest.

When morning came, the old man accompanied them as they departed; and, when they had gone beyond the city, he addressed them in these words: “Brother men, do not doubt that you will return home with the greatest prosperity, for God of our salvation will make your journey prosperous. And for love of your king I will keep my eyes fixed upon you throughout every road that you travel. For I am John, apostle and evangelist, that disciple whom Jesus loved. On account of his merit of chastity I embrace your king with the highest love. I ask you to greet him on my behalf; and, lest he withhold belief from the oracle, return to him this ring which he gave me at the dedication of my church, when I appeared in a pilgrim’s dress [Col. 0770C]. Announce to him that the day of his death is at hand, and that within six months I shall come to visit him, so that he may follow with me the Lamb whithersoever he goes (Rev. 14)—he in whom integrity of mind, purity of flesh, and beauty of character are united.” He spoke, and immediately the men found themselves in the place which they themselves had chosen.

Returning to their country with the greatest joy, they presented the ring to the king and explained the oracle; apart from the others they discussed the king’s end [Col. 0770D]. At once, at the name of John, the king burst into tears; and after he had inquired more carefully about all that they had seen and heard, he sent the messengers back to their homes with thanksgiving.

## Concerning the king’s illness and the dedication of his monastery of Westminster

Thus instructed by such an oracle, blessed Edward knew his death long beforehand; accordingly, when later he was about to depart for his homeland, he diligently sent before him suitable messengers—namely prayers and tears. He also distributed his treasures with a liberal hand, making for himself friends from the mammon of iniquity who might receive him into everlasting dwellings. But he wished the already-built basilica of Blessed Peter to be dedicated before his death [Col. 0771A], judging it a fair completion of his works if he should see, while alive, finished by pontifical blessing the church which he had undertaken to renew for the remission of his sins and in fulfilment of his vow.

The festival day was approaching, more joyful than the rest, on which our Saviour Jesus, clothed in the robe of mortality, came forth from the virginal womb like a bridegroom from his chamber. On it all the nobility of the English ought to assemble at the king’s court and attend the king, as was their custom, adorning him with sceptres and crown. Considering, therefore, how the consecration itself might be celebrated more solemnly, he decreed that, after the royal festival had been observed, this celebration should be completed on the feast-day of the Holy Innocents [Col. 0771B].

But on the very night of the Lord’s Nativity he was seized by a fever, and the imminent joy was immediately changed into pain and the festival into weeping. Nevertheless he concealed it, forestalled, I suppose, by a twofold consolation. For he felt that his passage to things above was imminent, and the sacred solemnity of the most sweet Nativity of the most sweet Jesus greatly rejoiced his mind. For three days, therefore, victorious over nature and triumphing over the sickness itself, he wore the royal insignia and sat at the solemn feast among bishops and magnates with all the cheerfulness he could command.

On the third day, sensing that the time of his calling had come, he ordered that, when all things had been prepared, the church should be consecrated on the next day. He too prepared gifts, brought forth varied ornaments, set apart diverse kinds of vessels, and assigned properties [Col. 0771C], by all of which that most holy oratory might be endowed, adorned, and enriched. Thus the joyful feast of the Holy Innocents dawned, and, as bishops and all the magnates of the kingdom gathered together, the sacred solemnity of the dedication began. The king supported the ceremony as far as his health allowed; but the queen, arranging everything, providing everything, anxious over everything and attentive to everything, fulfilled the part of both.

When all things required for so great a solemnity had been completed, as though the king said, “It is finished” (John 19), he bowed his head upon the bed and thereafter began to be exhausted by severe pain. Then came the grief and lamentation of all, one voice of mourners. Many foresaw in his death the desolation of the country [Col. 0771D], the destruction of the people, the ruin of the whole English nobility, the end of liberty, and the collapse of honour.

## Concerning the vision which he saw at the end

Courtiers stood around; the queen lay prostrate before the bed and warmed his chilling limbs in her own lap. And behold, whether dissolved in sleep, or overcome in the manner of illness, or—as is credible—carried away in an ecstasy of mental rapture, for almost two days he lay apparently lifeless. At last, as if waking from deep sleep, he opened his eyes and sat up; raising his hands to heaven, he said: “Almighty God, in whose power all things are placed, who knowest all things before they come to pass, transferring kingdoms and changing empires, and rendering the iniquities of fathers upon sons (Exod. 34): if the things revealed to me have proceeded from the light of truth [Col. 0772A], grant to my voice a voice of power, and put into my mouth speech that is right and clear-sounding, that I may declare thy wonders, and that those who hear me may learn to fear thee and, in a spirit of humility and a contrite heart, appease thy face, so that thou mayest repent of the evil which thou hast purposed to do to this people.”

A wondrous thing! He had scarcely ended his prayer when strength came to his body and power to his voice; grace loosed the tongue which illness had bound. Those present marvelled how he who shortly before, oppressed by sickness, could scarcely be heard by them, suddenly raised his voice, while his speech recovered its former strength and a clearer sound. Then the holy man, taking up a parable, related the following vision in most lucid words:

“When, as a young man, I lived in exile in Normandy [Col. 0772B], the friendship of good men was always pleasing to me, and whoever seemed better in the sacred sheepfolds of the monastic life was more intimate to me than others. Among them, two men had bound me to themselves by a special affection: the honesty of their conduct, holiness of their life, sweetness of their manners, and affability of their speech. I visited them more often; their words were sweet to my throat, above honey and the honeycomb to my mouth. Thus I lived, and in such things was the life of my spirit. I saw these men, translated to heaven many years ago, standing beside me a little before in a dream and, by God’s command, telling me what would happen to my people after my death. They say that the wickedness of the English is full, and iniquity brought to completion provokes wrath and hastens vengeance.

“The priests have broken the Lord’s covenant; with polluted breast and defiled hands they handle holy things [Col. 0772C]. They are not shepherds but hirelings, exposing the sheep to wolves rather than protecting them; they seek milk and wool, not the sheep, so that death, having cast them down into hell, may feed on both shepherds and sheep. The rulers of the land too are faithless, companions of thieves, plunderers of their country; they neither fear God nor honour the law; truth is a burden to them, justice an object of contempt, cruelty a delight. Thus neither do superiors preserve justice nor subjects discipline. And behold, the Lord has brandished his sword, bent his bow, and made it ready. Hereafter he will show wrath and indignation to this people, and moreover assaults through evil angels; handed over for one year and one day, they are to be punished together by fire and sword. These were their words.

“But I, grieving and sighing because of the calamity threatened to my people, said: ‘You who know the heavenly secrets, if they turn and do penance, will not God forgive them and leave a blessing behind him? Surely repentance suspended the sentence uttered by God against the Ninevites, and even the due vengeance impending over the most impious Ahab [Col. 0772D]. I shall therefore urge my people to repent of past deeds and beware of future ones; and perhaps God will then have mercy, so that he will not bring this great evil upon them, but he who prepared to punish those turned against him may, in his customary goodness, receive the converted back into grace.’

“‘By no means,’ they said, ‘for the heart of this people is hardened, their eyes blinded, and their ears made heavy, so that they neither hear one who rebukes, nor understand one who admonishes, nor are frightened by threats, nor drawn by benefits’ [Col. 0773A].

“As these words of theirs increased my anxiety still further, I said: ‘Will God then be angry for ever and no longer add that he may be favourable? When will joyful things succeed so many sad ones? Or what consolation will temper so many adversities? What remedy is to be hoped for amid these evils, so that, as affliction terrifies and makes us sorrowful on that side, so on this side the promise of divine mercy may offer at least some comfort?’ To this the saints proposed to me the following riddle. Let any green tree be cut from its trunk and separated from its own root by the space of three jugera; when, without any human hand compelling it and without any necessity pressing it, it has returned to its trunk and received itself again into its old root, and, having recovered its sap, has blossomed again and borne fruit [Col. 0773B], then comfort in this tribulation and a remedy for the adversity which we have foretold may be hoped for. When they had said this, they returned to heaven, and I was restored to you.”

The queen sat beside him as he related the vision; so did Robert, keeper of the sacred palace; Earl Harold, the queen’s brother; and Stigand also, who “went up to his father’s bed and defiled his couch,” having seized the see of Canterbury while Archbishop Robert was still alive. For this he was suspended by the supreme pontiff and shortly afterwards burst, and all his entrails were poured out. At the voice of the narrator he hardened himself; he was neither frightened by the oracle nor gave credit to the prophet, but muttering rather that the king, worn out by old age, was delirious, chose to laugh rather than mourn. But the others [Col. 0773C], whose minds were sounder, wept abundantly and sighed, for they knew well that priests and rulers did nothing other than what he had said. They recalled that these very things had often been reported to the supreme pontiff, and that he himself had very often rebuked their madness both through envoys and by letters; they remembered too that the king and queen had applied diligence to cure these evils, but had accomplished nothing.

At last they learned by experience that the holy king had not prophesied these things from his own spirit, when King Harold, who had seized the kingdom contrary to the oath which he had sworn to Duke William, was defeated by William in battle and put an end to English liberty and a beginning to servitude. Hence some say that the king set forth the preceding comparison as an impossibility, especially those who mourned that the whole English nobility had so perished [Col. 0773D] that scarcely a king, bishop, abbot, or any prince of that people could be seen in England.

## Explanation of the riddle proposed by the king

For my part, upon considering that the most holy man Dunstan foretold this calamity and nevertheless promised consolation, I hold another view. Accordingly, the matter may not inappropriately be explained thus. This tree signifies the kingdom of the English: beautiful in glory, fruitful in wealth and delights, lofty through the excellence of royal dignity. The root from which all this honour sprang was the royal stock, which is said to have descended in a direct line of succession from Alfred—who is said to have been the first Englishman anointed and consecrated king by the supreme pontiff—to Saint Edward. The tree was cut from the trunk [Col. 0774A] when the kingdom was divided from the royal race and transferred to another stock. The separation lasted for the space of three jugera, because during the reigns of three kings there was no union of the new with the old royal stock: Harold succeeded Edward, William succeeded Harold, and William the younger succeeded his father William.

The tree came to its root when the glorious King Henry, into whom all the splendour of the kingdom had passed, married as his wife Edward’s great-niece Matilda—not compelled by any necessity or pressed by any hope of gain, but from affection of love implanted in him—thus joining the stock of the Norman and English kings and, through the work of marriage, making one from two. The tree indeed blossomed when the Empress Matilda proceeded from both stocks [Col. 0774B]. But it bore fruit when from her our Henry arose like the morning star and, like a cornerstone, joined both peoples together. England now certainly has a king of English descent; from the same people it has bishops and abbots, and also princes and very good soldiers, begotten from the union of both stocks, who are an honour to some and a consolation to others. If this explanation displeases anyone, let him either explain it otherwise himself or await another time for its fulfilment, lest prophet be found contrary to prophet; and let it not be believed that Saint Edward denied what we know Saint Dunstan promised. With these perhaps not inappropriately inserted, let us return to the order of the narrative.

## Concerning the death and funeral of the holy king

[Col. 0774C]

Knowing, therefore, that his hour had drawn near for passing from this world to Christ, the king ordered his people to restrain their tears and not to interrupt by an idle sorrow the joy which hope brought forth. As though addressing those present in these words, he said: “If you loved me, you would surely rejoice because I go to the Father, to receive the joys promised to believers—not through my merits, but through the grace of the Lord Saviour, who has mercy on whom he will and bestows mercy on whom he pleases. But follow your friend with prayers, and resist with psalms and alms those who beset my way to the things above; for although the faith of the Crucified could not be overcome by them, scarcely anyone is so perfect that they do not try either to hinder or to terrify him [Col. 0774D].”

He then commended the queen to her brother and the magnates, highly praising her service and proclaiming her chastity: in public she conducted herself as his wife, but in private as his sister or daughter. He further ordered that everything which royal generosity had bestowed upon her in the name of dowry should always remain secure and unimpaired to her. He earnestly commended to the natives those who had followed him from Normandy, whether they preferred to return home with favour or remain with honour. He asked to be buried in the church of Blessed Peter the apostle which he himself had built from the foundations, and that his death should immediately be made known to all, lest, if knowledge of his death were delayed, the assistance of prayers too should be delayed [Col. 0775A].

When all things had been arranged as they ought, the saint ordered the priests and ministers of the church to be present and immediately fortified his departure by receiving the Lord’s body and blood. Seeing the queen among the others weeping more profusely and sighing more frequently, he said: “Do not weep, my daughter; for I shall not die, but live; and, departing from the land of the dying, I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living.” At last he wholly commended himself to God and, in the faith of Christ, under Christ’s sacraments, in hope of Christ’s promises, an old man full of days passed from the world. Leaving pure flesh, his pure spirit was joined to the Author of spirits, to live for ever; the citizens of heaven meet him, the heavenly key-bearer opens heaven to him, and John, the disciple whom Jesus loved, the faithful fulfiller of his promise, comes to meet him, with whom, a virgin himself, he shall follow the Lamb whithersoever he goes (Rev. 14) [Col. 0775B].

He died in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1066, having reigned twenty-three years, six months, and twenty-seven days, in the fourth indiction, on the day before the Nones of January [5 January]. With him all the prosperity of the English alike collapsed; liberty perished, every vigour died. It cannot be told how great a fear immediately seized all, how sorrow occupied them, or how a certain dark horror filled the whole island. His kinsmen and friends stood by the sacred remains [Col. 0776A] of the king when suddenly the lifeless corpse displayed a sign of future blessedness: its face, suffused with a heavenly blush, drew toward itself the eyes of all present. All marvelled; yet the glory of the stripped body increased their wonder, for, shining with snowy whiteness, it so gleamed that even unbelievers could not fail to perceive the splendour of his virginity.

Meanwhile the royal funeral rites were prepared; the body was wrapped in precious linen and the finest coverings; Christ’s poor were relieved by abundant alms. Bishops were present, a numerous company of priests and clerics assembled, the dukes of the realm gathered with earls and magnates, companies of monks hastened together, and an innumerable multitude of both sexes from villages and cities flocked to the king’s funeral [Col. 0776B]. Here psalms resounded; there tears and groans broke forth; everywhere joy was mingled with sorrow, since all saw in the king cause for joy and felt in themselves cause for grief. They bore to the church that temple of chastity and dwelling-place of virtue; the saving sacrifice was offered for him. Thus he was honourably buried in the place he himself had appointed, to be granted blessed resurrection on the last day through Jesus Christ our Lord, to whom be honour and glory for ages of ages. Amen.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 0775]

## Concerning a cripple healed at his tomb

[Col. 0775C]

After he had been removed from human affairs, the world could not fail to know how powerful blessed Edward was in divine things. The virtue of his virginal body could neither be buried by earth, shut in by stone, nor buried with his body; for the power hidden in his limbs broke forth in miracles, since by restoring sight to the blind, walking to the lame, and health to the sick, it demonstrated by sure signs that the death of Edward was precious in the sight of the Lord.

Among the poor whom the saint had supported in his lifetime was a certain Ralph, a Norman by birth. His sinews were contracted at the knee, and his feet were also twisted backward so as to be concealed; he was deprived not only of natural walking but, because pain prevented it, could not even creep upon his knees, as is the custom of such disabled persons [Col. 0775D]. Necessity, mistress of invention, devised a new kind of relief. He procured a hollow vessel in the shape of a basin; placing his buttocks and joined limbs within it and binding it tightly to himself, he supported the front with his hands and dragged the rear along, as though sailing over the ground.

When the king had been transferred to the higher world and the wretched man’s customary support failed, he began to bear still more painfully the disability of his limbs. Remembering the man of God who had supported him while alive, whose marvellous holiness could not be unknown even to him, he mounted his little vessel full of faith and came to the holy king’s tomb before the eighth day after his burial [Col. 0776C]. There, addressing the king as though alive, he said: “Are you not he who, still surrounded by corruptible flesh, healed the weak and sick by heavenly power? And I, my lord, bore the loss of my limbs more lightly while you lived, because for that reason food, drink, comforts, and necessary clothes were supplied to me in the greatest abundance. But now, as want adds misery to infirmity, either do not conceal from me what I should do, where I should turn, whose majesty I should entreat, whose mercy I should seek; or yourself apply your customary healing hand, that, since I am not permitted to aspire to the spiritual delights which you now enjoy, you may by your powerful might restore to me limbs by which I may obtain bodily ones.”

He had spoken, and behold, immediately the king’s holiness shone forth, grace blossomed, and the invoked compassion gleamed [Col. 0776D]. A certain hidden power suddenly stretched out the sinews and restored the legs and feet to their natural condition; blood flowed as the joints were torn from the flesh, and gradually, as their moisture returned, the bones formerly dry received their former strength. Those present rejoiced that the same power which they had seen shine in him alive had shone in him dead; thereafter they strove to visit more often and honour more devotedly the sacred relics of King Edward, knowing that they did not lack apostolic grace for healing the sick and expelling diseases. The man, then, recovering his strength, stood upon his feet, giving thanks to God and Saint Edward [Col. 0777A], who, after the first grace by which he had supported his disabled body, now added a second by removing the disability itself.

## Concerning six blind men and a seventh one-eyed man enlightened at his tomb

We have said that blessed Edward possessed a special power for giving sight to the blind while he lived; the following chapter will show that this grace was not taken from him by the intervention of death. While the thirtieth-day office for the king was still being celebrated after his death, six blind men, following one one-eyed man, hurried to the royal tomb. It was a marvellous sight: one was led by another, while the one man with eyes went before and guided seven men. Placed before the shrine of the sacred body by him whose direction governed the steps of all [Col. 0777B], they tearfully set forth their misery, beg for aid, and seek the help of the most blessed king against the weariness of their long darkness.

Nor did they think it difficult for one established in the region of light, which no night interrupts, to obtain earthly light for mortal bodies from the Lord of light; nor did they judge him, mingled with the choirs of angels, to be of less merit than he had been when enclosed in corruptible limbs. As they persisted in prayer, divine mercy did not fail them: it made the merits of its saint more widely known and did not deny the wretched men their desired comfort. For suddenly he who had been the others’ guide received, as the reward of his charity, light doubled; looking upon his companions, he saw that they too shone with the infusion of a new light [Col. 0777C]. They looked at one another, each asking the other whether he saw. All were amazed and, as though beside themselves, did not know that what was happening was real; for they thought they were seeing a vision. At last, returning to themselves and experiencing the great abundance of divine goodness, they burst into a cry of exultation and praise. Many ran up, marvelled for joy, and praised God in his Saint Edward. Those who had received the saving gift returned home, giving thanks to God, proclaiming the merits of the most blessed king, and proving his power by visible evidence.

## Concerning King Harold’s victory through the merits of the blessed king
Meanwhile Harold, son of Godwin, irreverently usurped for himself a kingdom which, by the faith of his oath, he ought to have preserved for William, kinsman of King Edward—though it was due to him neither by right nor by nature. By violating the compact and breaking faith, he hastened the evil which, according to the oracle of the holy king, the Lord had prepared for the English. Yet, that with his strength reduced he might more easily be conquered by the enemies whom he had unjustly provoked, God raised up against him from the north enemies: Harald, surnamed Harfau, king of the Norwegians, and his own brother Tostig, whom he himself had expelled from England and who, in King Edward’s time, had lived an exile in Flanders. These men, hurrying with a great fleet up the Humber towards York, met the army of the Northumbrians in battle; gaining the victory, they inflicted a great slaughter upon those who resisted.

When this was reported to Harold, he gathered a large army from every part of England. One night, the blessed Edward appeared in a dream to a religious abbot named Alsi, who presided over the monastery of Ramsey. The prudent man was awestruck at his majesty; but Edward gently comforted him, saying:

> “Go and tell Harold to attack confidently those men who are invading the borders of this kingdom against right and law. For I shall be the leader and protector of his army, since I cannot fail the justice of this people; through me, on this occasion, he shall gain triumph over the enemy. And lest he withhold belief from your words, disclose to him the secret of his heart, so that, when you have told him what he had been turning over in his mind with no one privy to it, he may ascribe this not to your invention but to my promise. On the preceding night, when he was tormented with pain, although the impending illness pressed him severely, he nevertheless kept silent, thinking to himself that, if he made his sickness public, he would become an object both of contempt to his own men and of mockery to his enemies. Such were his thoughts. But now, since health has succeeded sickness and he has recovered from that affliction, let him, trusting in my aid, undertake a just war against the barbarians and rescue his fellow-countrymen from imminent danger.”

The venerable man rose from sleep, went to Harold, and explained the oracle. So that hesitation might not steal in, he revealed the secret which the saint had ordered him to disclose, to Harold’s great astonishment. Then Harold, made bolder by the heavenly promise, advanced with a strong hand as far as the province of York. At the place then called Steinfordebrigge, but now, from the event itself, also called the Bridge of Battle, he encountered the enemies. Battle was joined, and both leaders were struck down: namely, the king of the Norwegians and Tostig, the English king’s own brother; and almost their whole army was destroyed. Thus no one can doubt that, in Harold’s one victory, there was fulfilled both what the saint had long before foretold concerning the two brothers when they were still boys, and what he had promised in the recent vision.

## How a blind man saw blessed Edward come forth from the tomb, and thus received his sight

Moreover, in the monastery of the blessed apostle Peter there was a young man of no mean birth, handsome in appearance but deprived of the use of both lights—that is, both eyes. Those then in charge of the monastery, pitying his misfortune, ordered him to ring the bells by which the brothers were summoned to their various duties, and to mark the other hours appointed for the stated solemn observances by the sound of bells.

The man therefore performed the office entrusted to him wisely. He frequented the church, persisted often in prayer, and diligently prayed that the merits of the blessed king might aid him. One day in summer, while the brothers rested at the midday hour and he too lay down in the oratory to give his limbs rest, he saw in a dream the blessed Edward come out of the tomb and look upon him. Then the saint reproved the man for sleeping, and ordered him, by ringing, to end his sleep and awaken the brothers for the ninth-hour service, which had already almost passed. Having given him these instructions, the saint appeared to him as the king himself, crowned and proceeding to the altar. As the young man gazed intently upon him, fixing his eyes upon the splendor of that flashing light, the blessed vision vanished.

The young man awoke, suddenly opened his eyes, drew in the light, and felt that his former health had been restored. He disclosed the vision to the brothers, and confirmed his words by the testimony of the miracle. All marvelled and blessed God in his works, who granted blessed Edward a better life after death, and caused his dead bones, from their resting-place, to flourish in wondrous works.

## On the unjust deposition of blessed Wulfstan, and his just restoration through the blessed king

“The Lord takes pleasure in those who fear him, and in those who hope in his mercy.” The simple justice of the blessed bishop Wulfstan and the mighty magnificence of the holy King Edward made this clear in the following miracle.

When King William had subdued the whole island and had either driven rebellious men from it, reduced them to chains, or oppressed them with servitude, he began also to deal with ecclesiastical affairs together with his own advisers. He therefore caused a synod to be assembled, in the presence of legates of the Apostolic See: Hermenfrid, bishop of Sion, and the cardinal priests John and Peter. By them Stigand—who, as we said above, had trodden underfoot the sanctuary of God with defiled feet—was stripped of all glory and honor, and condemned by the king to perpetual imprisonment.

He was succeeded in the see of Canterbury by Abbot Lanfranc, a man supremely learned in every respect, highly skilled in all the liberal arts and alike in divine and secular letters. Lanfranc, therefore, as though appointed by God “to pluck up and to break down and to destroy, and to build and to plant,” endeavored, supported by the authority of his legation, to restore the English Church to a new form. He promptly began to correct what needed correction, establish what needed establishment, and prescribe a more honorable manner of life for clerics and monks.

Before him the man of God Wulfstan was accused of simplicity and lack of learning; and, as though an uneducated and illiterate man, was decreed to be deposed, with the king consenting—or even himself directing this. Accordingly, at the synod which Lanfranc held at Westminster in the king’s presence, amid the other matters under discussion, he ordered the venerable man to surrender his staff and ring.

But the man of God, unchanged in face or spirit, rose and, holding the pastoral staff in his hand, said:

> “Truly, lord archbishop, I know well that I am neither worthy of this honor nor fit for this burden nor equal to this labor. I knew this when the clergy chose me, when the bishops compelled me, when my lord King Edward invited me to this office. By the authority of the Apostolic See, he alone placed this burden upon my shoulders and ordered that I be invested in the episcopal rank by this staff. And now you demand the pastoral staff which you did not give; you take away an office which you did not confer. I, indeed, knowing my insufficiency and yielding to the sentence of you and this holy synod, will resign the staff—but not to you: rather, to him by whose authority I received it.”

Having said this, he went with his attendants to the stone enclosing the remains of the most glorious king. Standing before the tomb, he said:

> “You know, my lord Edward, how unwillingly I accepted this burden: how often I evaded it; how often, when I was sought, I kept myself absent. I confess that I became foolish, but you compelled me. For although there were the election of the brethren, the petition of the people, the will of the bishops, and the favor of the nobles, yet above them all your authority prevailed; your will pressed me more strongly. And behold: a new king, a new law, a new pontiff establish new rules and promulgate new judgments. They accuse you of error, because you commanded; me of presumption, because I consented. Then indeed you could have been mistaken as a man; but can you now, united to God? Therefore I resign the staff not to those who demand what they did not give, who, being human, can deceive and be deceived, but to you who gave it—who, now brought into Truth itself, have escaped the darkness of error and ignorance. To you, I say, I resign the staff; to you I leave the care of those whom you entrusted to me; confidently I commit them to you, whose merits I do not fail to know.”

Having said this, he raised his hand a little and thrust the staff into the stone covering the holy body:

> “Receive it, my lord king,” he said, “and give it to whomever you please.”

Then he descended from the altar, removed his pontifical vestments, and sat again among the monks, himself a simple monk. All who saw marvelled at the staff sunk into the stone, standing as though supported by roots and inclining neither to the right nor to the left. Some tried to pull it out, but it remained immovable.

A murmur and whispering arose among the crowd. People came running from every side; seeing the mighty works of God, they were amazed and stood transfixed. Now they advanced a little, now they halted; now they stretched out a hand, now they withdrew it; now, lying on the ground, they examined how the iron adhered to the stone; now, standing upright, they pressed one another together to see. The matter was reported to the synod.

But Lanfranc did not believe the report. He summoned to him Gumulph, bishop of Rochester, a venerable and religious man, and ordered him to go to the tomb and bring forth into the midst the staff which the saint had laid down. The lesser bishop obeyed the superior prelate; but the power of the virgin body, though dead, proved stronger than the hand of the living bishop. That hand tried to pull out the staff; but the former, though lower in rank yet superior in power, caused it to adhere immovably to the stone, as though held by a marvelous force from beneath.

Then Bishop Lanfranc, astonished by the novelty of the miracle and wishing the king to share in so great a wonder, sent men to summon him to the synod. When the king came with his nobles, Lanfranc rose. Together they hastened to the king’s tomb; after prayer, the pontiff laid on his hand and tried to draw out the staff, but, the power of the holy king resisting, his effort lacked the desired result. The king cried out; the pontiff wept; both proclaimed glory to God and praises to Edward, whose judgment in the advancement of blessed Wulfstan was shown by sure signs not to have erred.

Then Lanfranc approached the saint and said:

> “Truly the Lord is just and loves righteous deeds; his face beholds equity. Truly he walks with the simple, and his converse is with the simple. Your righteous simplicity, brother, was mocked by us; but he has brought forth your justice as the light and your judgment as the noonday. Lamentable is the darkness in which, wrapped about, we call evil good and good evil. Our judgment erred—erred concerning you, brother; and God raised up his spirit in his king, to annul our sentence and reveal to all your simplicity, pleasing to God. Therefore, by the authority which we exercise—or rather by the divine judgment by which we stand convicted—we again entrust and impose upon you the charge of which we too rashly deprived you. We know by experience that a little belonging to the just man is better than the many riches of sinners. Indeed, a little learning with faith, which works in simplicity with love, is better than the riches of secular wisdom and knowledge, which many misuse either for the vanity of human praise or for the greed of shameful gain. Come therefore, my brother; come to your lord—indeed, to ours as well. For we believe that his holy right hand, which denied the staff to us, will readily restore it to you when you extend your hand.”

Hearing this, the holy bishop, following his own simplicity, obeyed the command. Approaching the altar, he said:

> “Behold me, my lord Edward—behold me, who committed myself to your judgment, who submitted myself to your sentence, to whom I resigned the staff which you had granted. What now pleases you? What do you will? What do you determine? You have surely preserved your dignity, cleared my innocence, and manifested your magnificence. If then your former judgment concerning me still stands, restore the staff; but if it has changed, declare to whom it is to be given.”

As he said this, he tried with a light touch to draw out the staff. It followed his hand and sprang free as though it had been set in soft mud. The king and archbishop came running together, prostrated themselves, asked pardon, and commended themselves to the holy man’s prayers. But he, who had learned from the Lord Jesus Christ to be meek and humble of heart, likewise prostrated himself before them and begged to be blessed by so great a pontiff. Who could easily tell what tears, what sighs, and what humble contention there then was among the holy bishops concerning the blessing itself?

At last, blessing one another and holding each other’s hands, they returned to the synod, while all rejoiced, many wept for joy, and all together proclaimed God wonderful in his saints. The king, stirred to love for his kinsman and predecessor, adorned the most holy tomb with a shrine fashioned of both silver and gold, as may still be seen, with remarkable care.

## On his first translation and the incorruption of his body

While Saint Edward thus flourished in these and similar miracles, there was frequent discussion among the brethren concerning his sanctity. Day by day their affection for so great a patron increased, and this affection urged them more strongly to inspect his holy relics. There was also among them a friendly, recurring dispute. Some affirmed that the king’s virginal flesh remained untouched by corruption, whole and undefiled in the sacred dwelling-place of his body. Others, fearing such presumption, urged silence, lest, if this hope were disappointed, the glory of so great a confessor might readily be diminished.

“For,” they said, “although the bodies of apostles, martyrs, and innumerable saints have been reduced to ashes, if nature does this same thing in Edward, he ought neither to be less loved by us nor judged less acceptable to God.” As this debate took place before the venerable Gilbert, surnamed Crispin, abbot of that monastery, he decided that the body of so great a patron must by all means be examined, and that reliable signs must determine what should be thought about these matters.

He therefore appointed a day on which the holy man’s relics would be brought forth, to satisfy the faith of the former party and the affection of the latter. He invited reputable and religious persons to this heavenly spectacle, among whom Cumulfus, bishop of Rochester—whom we mentioned above—held a special preeminence both in favor and distinction.

Accordingly, in the thirty-sixth year after Edward had departed from human affairs, those invited for this purpose approached the holy man’s tomb. When the stone enclosing the sarcophagus was removed, such a fragrance filled every nostril that the church itself was filled, and they thought perfumes were flowing out within the tomb. First they saw that the pall which had wrapped the most sacred limbs retained its former beauty and soundness. Encouraged by hope of greater glory, they removed the pall and examined the other ornaments and garments; they found everything whole and intact.

They drew out the arms, bent the fingers, examined the joints, and found everything sound, flexible, and exceptionally firm in its old vigor. Finally, they examined both the integrity and color of the flesh, which, purer than glass and whiter than snow, displayed beforehand the glory of the future resurrection. But, while all alike feared to touch his desired face, the aforementioned bishop of Rochester, emboldened by the testimony of conscience or of love, laid his hand upon the cloth covering the most holy head. Tearing it from the lower part, he drew out the blessed snowy-white beard and, full of faith, felt it adhere firmly to the chin as though Edward were alive.

Delighted by the miracle and inflamed with desire, he tried to pull out and keep for himself one hair; but it adhered more firmly, and his wish did not attain its effect. Gilbert noticed this and gently rebuked the bishop:

> “Father, desist. Do not seek to disturb the rest of so great a king, nor diminish in any respect the integrity which Christ has preserved until now.”

The bishop replied:

> “You speak very well, Abbot. Yet do not attribute this attempt of mine to presumption but to devotion. If opportunity had been granted me, I would have valued even a small portion of his relics above the riches of Croesus. But since the royal spirit disdains to have anything taken from it, let him keep all things for himself and await, in his integrity, the day of blessed resurrection.”

They therefore retained the pall in which his most holy limbs had been wrapped, placed upon him another equally precious one, and carefully laid that most sweet body, duly tended, back in its chamber. Through his merits many benefits are bestowed there; of these, for the praise of our Lord Jesus Christ, we believe that a few out of many should be set down below.

## On the girl healed at his tomb

The most holy prophet Elisha, mocked by more than forty boys, avenged the injury by his curse and gave them all over to beasts for punishment. Blessed Paul condemned the most impious magician Elymas, who blasphemed the apostles, to sudden blindness. Christ therefore declares that an injury inflicted upon his saints falls back upon himself: “He who hears you hears me, and he who despises you despises me” (Luke 10).

The Lord Jesus showed this in his Edward, punishing those who disparaged his sanctity with great severity and rewarding those who served him by granting benefits. In the city there was a noble matron named Matilda, highly skilled in the art of purple-dyeing. She was accustomed to adorn the garments of kings and wealthy persons with gold, make them brilliant with gems, and vary them with pictures and flowers in embroidered work.

A certain most noble and wealthy woman had entrusted to her a work of no small value. This woman, married to the earl of Gloucester, was accounted little inferior to the queen; and, among all the countesses of England, she sought to surpass the rest as much in the magnificence of her garments as in wealth. She pressed Matilda daily to complete everything not only artistically but quickly.

Meanwhile came the illustrious feast of the blessed King and martyr Edward, uncle of our own prince Edward, who, killed without guilt by wicked men, is believed to have been crowned by the martyrdom of innocence. The wise woman was troubled in mind: she thought that delaying the work would bring upon her the anger of a most haughty lady, but she feared that violating so holy a festival by working would give occasion for divine vengeance. Looking at a young girl who assisted her in the work, she said:

> “What do you decide between the necessity of this labor and the feast of the holy King Edward? For I judge idleness costly, but work on so great a festival dangerous.”

The girl smiled and replied:

> “Is this the Edward whom this rustic crowd at Westminster venerates as a king? What have I to do with him? Let others take leisure and either mourn the dead with their songs or honor him; but I shall not, for his sake any more than for that of any rustic, abandon the work already begun, if you order it otherwise.”

Her mistress was horrified. Her heart grew hot, and the fire seething in her meditation burst forth in rebuke and indignation, as though she would lash with harshest words a blasphemer forestalled by a diabolic spirit. The maid laughed; mocking her mistress’s simplicity, she piled blasphemy upon blasphemy. Suddenly, while many stood by, she was seized with paralysis. Her blaspheming mouth was twisted back as far as her right ear, depriving her of the use of the tongue which she had abused. Her lips foamed, her teeth ground and dried up, and her whole body was contorted by a pitiable twisting of the limbs.

When the mistress saw that this had happened to the girl by God’s just judgment, sorrow succeeded indignation and mourning anger. She wept, as did all her household; and she who had rebuked the blasphemer pitied her as she endured so many and so intolerable torments. The matter became known throughout the city. Many came running, either to console the mistress or to behold the maid in wonder.

As she asked what ought to be done, a person of sufficiently venerable appearance stood by and urged that they put the unfortunate woman on a boat and carry her to the most holy body of him whom she had blasphemed. Through his merits, he said, she would receive a remedy, since for his injury she had felt so dreadful a punishment laid upon her. He spoke, and it was done.

The unhappy woman was brought to the tomb of the holy king. A candle of the length of her body was lit, while her mistress persisted in vigils and prayers. There was much mourning and lamentation around her, for her pain seemed incurable and her wound most grievous. The mercy of Edward was everyone’s one and only hope: Edward, who had learned from the Lord Jesus to return good for evil and love for hatred.

Thus she was tormented throughout the night, while the others wept and prayed. The brothers of the monastery also prayed for her, and their superior offered solemn litanies over her with great devotion. Before the most merciful king there strove: prayer and sickness; the wrongdoing of the sinful maid and the faith of her compassionate mistress; the greatness of the crime and the multitude of her pains. At last, through the merits of the blessed king, that mercy by which Jesus is accustomed to be overcome prevailed. It soon met Truth in the sick woman and tempered by its gentleness the sentence that Truth had decreed.

So, having continued in pain through the night and into the day, at the hour when the sacred feast of that day was concluded with evening praises, suddenly, amid the voices of psalm-singers and the groans of those praying, her health was restored. She looked upon those standing by, marvelled at those who wept, and, her speech restored, asked where she was, what she had suffered, where she had been brought, and what had caused so great a pain. For the mouth which the illness had contracted returned to its natural position, and she was granted both her former appearance and health.

When she heard all that had occurred, she burst into tears. Mouth, tongue, mind, and senses proclaimed confession, while frequent sighs revealed inward contrition. Then those present sang to the Lord of mercy and judgment: he “strikes and heals, kills and makes alive, brings down to hell and brings back” (1 Samuel 2). Giving thanks to God and to his most blessed servant Edward, she returned safely home with her mistress. Thereafter, whenever she heard the glorious king’s name, she was so seized with fear that pallor struck her face and trembling seized all her limbs.

## On a brother freed from quartan fever through the holy king

Moreover, in the monastery where Edward’s holy relics are kept, there was a brother named Osbert. His most upright life was adorned by learning, made illustrious by eloquence, and raised yet higher by philosophy, both secular and ecclesiastical. Once, about the middle of July, he was seized by quartan fever. For six months he was so afflicted that nature seemed on the very point of yielding to disease. His flesh was wasted, his blood exhausted, and his bones emptied of their marrow; he looked more like an image than a man.

The feast of the Lord’s Nativity, to be embraced by all mortals, was at hand. The man was afflicted with a double distress: he was tortured by the force of the fevers, and it seemed more bitter to him than the fevers themselves that he could not take part in those festive joys. Faith therefore brought force to bear upon nature, and devotion triumphed over illness; contrary to everyone’s expectation, they compelled the man of God to attend the most sacred vigils.

About cockcrow, when, as the Church customarily does on that day, Mass was celebrated and the Gospel was read in which the evangelist Saint Luke recounts the virgin birth, the shepherds’ watch, and the angelic vigil, Osbert considered with the greatest devotion the humility of the child born for us and the tenderness of mother and virgin. Dissolving wholly into tears, he was wonderfully suffused both with inward joy and with an outward sweetness that refreshed his wasted limbs.

He sang psalms in spirit and in understanding; he prayed in spirit and in understanding. Between mother and son, between bosom and manger, devout thought ranged together with speech. He believed the affliction he had long endured to be extinguished. Yet the merciful Jesus, wishing to reveal the merits of his Edward, had suspended it but had not extinguished it.

For two days, because of the man’s devotion, the fevers were confined by a certain divine power. On the third day they attacked his wretched body more severely than usual, pouring themselves into his limbs, nerves, joints, and even his deepest organs; by pains and torments they tore apart everything within and without him. In these tortures, as each succeeding day seemed crueler than the preceding one, there came the desired day on which the most glorious prince Edward, after temporal glory, deserved eternal glory through Christ’s reward.

At the hour when the saving sacrifice was offered in memory of so great a king, the sick man came to the holy tomb and, prostrate upon the ground as though about to breathe his last, gave way to grief. My God, what sighs then shook that miserable body; what groans; what sobs! What words did pain dictate to him, faith suggest, and hope compose! Now he challenged the saint as though reasoning with him; now he addressed him in supplication:

> “And you, Lord—how long? How long will you forget me utterly? How long will you turn your face from me? Where, I ask, are your mighty works which our fathers have told us of—the works which you performed in their days? Is it thus that you, who have learned always to pity and spare others, close the bowels of compassion to those who serve you, who are assigned to your praises, who are devoted to your service? Is it thus that you expose to consumption by fevers the body which royal generosity has hitherto sustained? Would that it were consumed quickly; but alas, alas! I am devoured and not consumed; I am tortured and do not die. Life is pain and does not end; death is desired and is not granted. But what am I doing, as though contending with you in judgment, when I ask for mercy and do not presume upon judgment? Therefore I beg you, good king, most loving prince, sweet patron: may the great pain of your little servant move your most merciful heart. With the eye by which you are accustomed to see things far off, look more carefully upon what is happening in these my pitiable inward parts, and how intolerably I pass from extreme cold to extreme heat. O dreadful trembling! O unspeakable burning! Attend, sweetest lord; attend and see whether there is any sorrow like mine (Lamentations 1). If you judge me unworthy of health, at least end my pain by death.”

Amid these words sobs and tears burst forth, and thereafter the matter was conducted not with words but with feelings. Then, after the solemnities of the Mass had been completed, he rose from prayer; and behold, all pain had gone away, and as though bathed in a new refreshment all his limbs had regained their former strength. He even began to think of food; his nausea was at once banished, and appetite was stirred toward a desire for eating. What more need be said? Restored to perfect health, he thereafter devoted himself all the more earnestly to the service and praises of the holy confessor, in proportion as he had experienced the saint’s power in himself.

## On a knight healed of the same illness

This man was a scribe learned in the kingdom of heaven, and when often commanded to preach to the people, he brought forth from his treasury things new and old. It happened after he had recovered health by such a miracle that the circuit of the year again brought round the anniversary memorial of the most holy king’s death. No small crowd from the city had gathered, as it did every year, rejoicing to take part, for Edward’s glory, both in the vigils and in the solemnities of the Masses.

This brother, second after the abbot, put on the sacred vestments and went to the altar to celebrate Mass. After the reading of the holy Gospel, he turned toward the people and delivered to them a discourse on the king’s sanctity and power. The man of God preached Edward’s humility, praised his patience, and exalted his chastity. He demonstrated by sure proofs of miracles how great his merit was before God. Finally, setting forth before them the power which he had experienced in himself the year before, he moved all to compassion and many even to sighs and tears.

There was present a knight named Gerinus, a royal palace guard. He had been excessively afflicted for days and months by quartan fever and had spent much on physicians in vain. The disease, sparing neither him nor his resources, had drained his purse of money and his body of blood. His spirit was spent, and the grave alone seemed left to him. But when he heard that this man had been freed from a similar suffering through the merits of blessed Edward, hope followed the faith he had conceived and love inflamed his fearful heart.

Made more cheerful by all this, on the following night he kept vigil at the king’s tomb with candles lit. It was the vigil of the Lord’s Epiphany, a night solemnized by a threefold joy, on which are commemorated the faith of the Gentiles, the sacrament of baptism, and the beginning of Christ’s miracles. In the gathering of the brothers hymns resounded and readings rang out; Gerinus, wholly intent upon Edward, offered tears and multiplied prayers. Edward heard Gerinus; Christ heard Edward; and by one act he made the king sublime in glory and honor, and Gerinus, his fevers extinguished, whole.

## On the woman whom he healed while absent

The royal official whose son was ill judged the bodily presence of the Lord necessary for healing him at Capernaum; the Savior’s own saying judges him to have been of lesser faith. But we know that Christ himself preferred the faith of the centurion to Israelite religion especially because, when he had promised to come and drive the paralysis from the boy, the centurion, full of faith and mindful of Christ’s divine majesty, said: “Not at all, Lord; but only speak the word, and my child shall be healed” (Luke 7).

A religious woman in the monastery of Berching, emulating the likeness of this faith, made the merits of the blessed King Edward more illustrious through her faith. She too suffered from quartan fever, and now the second year passed in that illness had taken away hope of regaining health. One day, while the rest of early sleep refreshed her wasted limbs, she saw in a dream that she had set out with companions to visit her own country and parents. After they had gone a little way, someone asked her to turn aside to Westminster, so that, refreshed there with food and drink, they might more easily bear the labor of the journey.

She said:

> “How shall I turn aside to people whose faces I have never seen, whose names I do not know, and with none of whom I have ever had dealings of giving and receiving?”

He replied:

> “There is there the noble King Edward. If you visit his tomb with devotion and faith, he will easily obtain from the Lord his God for you such refreshment that your body will recover its former strength.”

The woman awoke and reflected upon the dream. She rose from her bed, supported her weak limbs with a staff, entered the oratory, and prostrated herself before the altar. Singing the Seven Psalms called Penitential with the utmost contrition of heart, she added the solemn Litanies. Then, addressing the holy king in devout prayers, she said:

> “Lord, I believe that, as has been promised me, healing awaits me at your holy tomb if I go there. But what need is there for this labor of mine—indeed, this danger of mine? It will be no small loss to my peace to procure a conveyance, provide travel money, and arrange companions for the journey; above all, on the outward and return journeys, to hear many things and see many things that may lift up the mind and take away its seriousness, and either to engage in trifles myself, to be idle, or to watch those doing such things. Why, then, is it necessary for me to seek the bodily presence of your sacred body, when you are present in spirit, and, for one who beholds the Creator, every creature is small? I know, indeed I know, that in that light which penetrates all things my misery is open to you; and since you share in that supreme power, if the will is present, the ability will not be lacking. Therefore speak the word, and your handmaid shall be healed.”

After uttering these and similar things in great anguish of heart, she returned, fearful and trembling, to her bed of pain; for it was the day on which the hour of that dreadful attack was expected. But it came on, so to speak, with slow step and inflicted little or no distress upon the sufferer. The woman, now more at peace, gave herself wholly to entreating the most blessed king. After the relief of two days’ rest, the expected attack of the quartan fever was feared.

When that terrifying hour came upon her, she entered the oratory again. After first reciting psalms, she repeated her tears and multiplied her prayers. What more need be said? She passed that day also without suffering. When, by the same remedy as before, she met the third attack of the illness, she was restored to perfect health and gave thanks to the holy King Edward for as long as she lived.

## On a monk healed of a threefold illness
I judge that it ought not to be passed over in silence what divine mercy, through the merits of the blessed king, bestowed upon one of the servants of Westminster, a religious and honorable man. This man was indeed held by a wonderful affection for blessed Edward, and the remembrance of that name was sweeter to him than honey, and the memory of his holiness sweeter than honey and the honeycomb; accordingly, in thanksgiving he chanted five psalms daily for his soul.

It happened, however, that he was afflicted by a threefold sickness, and no remedy but a [Col. 0788C] heavenly one was hoped for. For after bloodletting, blood had gathered and coagulated around a small wound, hardening into a very bad abscess; pain invading the neighboring parts had also deprived his arm of its strength; moreover his heart was tortured by shortness of breath, and his constricted chest emitted breath with great difficulty. An intolerable swelling had also seized his foot and had almost entirely taken away its use. The annually recurring solemn day was approaching on which the holy king passed to the heavenly realms; and he, suffering under so grave an affliction, awaited the joy desired by all with more than his usual sadness.

That same night, at the fitting time, while the throng of brethren eagerly assembled to ring the bells in honor of the king, he sat sorrowful, weighed down by illness, because he could offer no expression of joy [Col. 0788D] and could provide the brethren no assistance in so great a task. While they therefore pulled the bell-ropes with the utmost devotion, the holy man was in anguish and, no longer able to endure himself, said: “So then, my Edward, will you not help me, and will you deny strength to this desire of mine? Be present, I pray you; for I am rising and joining myself to the choirs of the brethren.”

He seized one of the ropes and, despising his illness, pulled with both hands with all his strength.
