At once the abscess burst, the congealed putrid blood flowed out, and, when the swelling subsided, all pain departed. Thus one of the three afflictions having been removed, he was anxious about the distress in his chest; but now, having experienced the power of the holy king, he began with greater confidence in faith and greater cheerfulness in hope to contemplate it.

It was his custom, when the brethren returned to their beds after the vigils, to remain in the church [Col. 0789A] and to devote himself privately before a certain altar to psalms and prayers. On that same night on which he had felt the divine presence aiding him in the cure of his arm, he devoutly approached the beloved retreat which he was accustomed to frequent. Prostrate before God and his holy confessor Edward, he gave thanks for the benefit received and pleaded for that which had not been received. It was not to presumption but to faith that he attributed his prayer that heavenly gifts might be bestowed upon him threefold. He persisted, wept, and prayed, joyful for his arm but sad for his chest. While he prayed, abundant sweat issuing from his body restored his breathing stronger than usual. Then his chest, sprinkled with a certain heavenly dew, recovered its customary health.

The distress of his foot still remained, preventing him from attending the assembly of his brethren [Col. 0789B]. Therefore, while he lay in the infirmary cell with a certain elderly man, one day near sunset they refreshed themselves with mutual conversation, and in their talk recalled in pleasant speech the power of the blessed king. Then he who had already been cured of two diseases said: “How great, dearest brother, is the abundance [Col. 0790A] of his power! I, a sinner, have experienced it in myself and dare to say that whatever he wishes, he will easily obtain from the Lord his God.”

As he explained to him the miracle wrought in himself, he extended his foot, deformed by an unbearable swelling, and said: “If he had healed this foot for me by removing the pain, there is nothing further that I should have thought necessary to ask of him.” Comforting themselves with these words, as the sun set they withdrew to their beds. But in the morning, when the man whose foot had hurt rose and put his hand to the pain as usual, he found nothing in his foot either swollen or painful, and realized that through blessed Edward he had been granted perfect health. He cried out joyfully and, revealing such a heavenly miracle to his companions, moved every heart to love more sweetly, praise more devoutly, and extol more expressly [Col. 0790B] the patron of such great merit, to the praise and glory of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom is honor for ages of ages. Amen.

Here ends the Life of Saint Edward, king and confessor, together with his miracles.

[Col. 0789]

## CONCERNING THE NUN OF WATTUN

(TWISDEN, ibid., p. 415.) Concerning a wonderful miracle, by Aelred, abbot of Rievaulx.

[Col. 0789C] To know and conceal the miracles of the Lord and the manifest signs of divine mercy is a share in sacrilege. For what can serve as consolation to those present, edification to posterity, and devotion to all, ought not to perish unknown to everyone. Yet we are often deterred by the foolishness of many people who, either wasting away through envy or languishing in unbelief, scarcely believe their own eyes concerning any person in matters that are good, while they are readily induced, by the slightest hearing, to believe evil things about anyone whatsoever.

For this reason I thought that this wonderful matter, unheard of in our age, ought especially to be disclosed to you, most loving father: your holy simplicity is accustomed to think well of all and to suspect nothing unfavorable of anyone without certain evidence. Let there be no hesitation concerning the truth of the words [Col. 0789D], since I myself have seen some of what must be told with my own eyes, and all the rest has been reported to me by persons whom neither maturity of age nor proven holiness could, on any grounds, permit to lie.

Among the monasteries of virgins which the venerable and God-beloved man, Father and priest Gilbert, built with wonderful zeal through different provinces of England, there is one situated in the province of York, in a place surrounded by waters and marshes and named from that fact. It is called Wattun, that is, “the wet settlement.” This place once, as the venerable priest Bede relates in his *History of the English*, flourished with a great company of holy women [Col. 0790C]; there too the blessed bishop John healed, by salutary touch and prayer, a girl almost despaired of because of an incautious bloodletting.

Since, then, through the diligence of the aforesaid father, ancient religious life is renewed in that same place, ancient miracles likewise are renewed. For Christ’s handmaids there, amid their daily manual work and their customary psalmody, devote themselves to spiritual services and attend heavenly contemplations, so that many of them, as if bidding farewell to the world and everything in it, are often caught up into certain inexpressible ecstasies and seem to take part in angelic choirs. They have frequent converse with good spirits, by whom they are now rebuked, now instructed, now forewarned about definite and necessary matters.

So great is the love among them, so great their concern for one another, that when one dies, the others never cease from prayers until some certainty has dawned for them either concerning her punishment or her glory. Thus it happens that the dead appear to the living not only in dreams, as is customary, but visibly to bodily eyes, and declare now the punishment, now the glory, which each has deserved.

It happened on one occasion that a woman held in the highest esteem by all passed from the body to heaven. She was loved by everyone, but was especially cherished by one woman. This woman persisted in prayers that divine mercy might not conceal from her the merit of the virgin [Col. 0791A]. When the yearly cycle had turned, the anniversary of her death came round. The girl multiplied her customary prayers. She burned with longing and was drenched with copious tears.

Meanwhile, the saving sacrifice was being prepared to be offered for the dead woman’s passing. The priests performed their appointed office. The virgin, turned toward Christ’s altar, awaited the fulfillment of her desire, when, behold, a ray of sunlight was cast down from above to below and settled before the altar step. She looked more attentively, and at once saw sitting in that very ray the virgin whom she had loved, shining with excessive splendor. She was astonished and froze; and while the spirit spoke, her fleshly tongue was silent. But because her body stood motionless with her senses somehow lulled, she asked by desire alone that the virgin might come nearer, so that she might see her more clearly [Col. 0791B].

Immediately the ray of sunlight rose from the place where it had stood, came closer, and standing before the virgin’s face, offered to the loving woman at close range for contemplation the face she had desired. Thus suffused with inexpressible joy, she awaited the end of the heavenly office. But when the Mass was concluded at the deacon’s proclamation, she returned to herself and the ray returned upward. Having introduced these matters apart from our subject, let us pass to the narrative which we have undertaken.

While Henry, of holy and pious memory, was bishop in the church of York, a certain girl, thought to be four years old, was received to be brought up in that monastery through the prayers of that same holy father. As soon as she passed beyond infancy, she put on girlish wantonness together with her girlish years. She had no love for religious life [Col. 0791C], no concern for discipline, no inclination toward the fear of God. Her eye was bold, her speech improper, her gait wanton. She walked clothed in the sacred veil but displayed in her conduct nothing worthy of such attire. She was rebuked in words but not corrected; she was pressed with blows but not reformed. She stole hours from the eyes of her teachers, either to indulge in idleness, abandon herself to disorderly gestures, devote herself to chatter, or persuade others toward something useless.

She was constrained by the discipline of the order and compelled against her will somehow to preserve the outward decency of the external person. Everything in her rested on fear; nothing on love. And when she had become marriageable, she preferred externals to inward things, idle repose to serious pursuits, and amusements to what was earnest [Col. 0791D].

It happened that brethren of the monastery, to whom the care of external affairs had been entrusted, entered the women’s monastery in order to perform some work. Observing this, she came closer and watched their work and faces with excessive curiosity. Among them was a young man more handsome in face and more polished in age than the others. The miserable girl cast her eyes upon him, and he fixed his upon her. They looked at one another with a more caressing eye; and soon the twisting serpent entered both breasts and hissed its deadly poison through all their vital parts. At first the affair was conducted by nods, but the nods were followed by signals. At length, silence having been broken, they began conversation about the sweetness of love. They inflamed one another and scattered on both sides the seeds of pleasure and the incitements of lust. He plotted fornication; she afterwards said that she had thought only of love [Col. 0792A].

Meanwhile their affections grew together. But, in order to speak with one another more freely or enjoy one another more fully, they agreed upon a place and time. Thus, casting away the weapons of light, they preferred a darker night. Those avoiding public notice find a more secret place pleasing. That utterly wicked robber gave the signal for his prey: at the sound of a stone which he promised to throw against either the wall or the roof of the building in which she was accustomed to sleep, she was to come out to him, fully assured of his arrival.

Where then, Father G., was your vigilance in guarding discipline? Where were all your so carefully devised contrivances for excluding the occasion of vices? Where then was that concern so prudent, so cautious, so clear-sighted, and that faithful watch around every door, window, and corner, that even evil spirits seemed to be denied entrance [Col. 0792B]? One girl mocked all your diligence, father, because unless the Lord guards the city, the watchman watches in vain (Ps. 126 [127]).

You did, blessed man, all that a human being could do, because that was fitting. But just as no one can correct one whom God has rejected, so no one can save one whom He has not saved. And you, wretched girl, what are you doing? What are you thinking? Why do you raise your ears so attentively toward the tiles? Where is fear, where is love, where is reverence for that holy congregation? Where is the sweet memory of the blessed bishop who entrusted you to this monastery? None of these calls you back from so great a crime. All of them erased, a shameful desire alone lived in your heart.

You rise, miserable woman; you go to the door. As you attempt to go out, divine power drives you back; you try again, but accomplish nothing. [Col. 0792C] You return and for a little while celebrate the customary vigils of the blessed Virgin with twelve lessons. What more ought Christ to have done for you that He did not do? O wonderful blindness of heart! Why do you again devise an escape? Behold, like Balaam, you are allowed to follow the desires of your heart, that you may walk in your own devices. You must be led into Babylon; perhaps there you will be healed. What more need be said? Alas! She goes out. Close your ears, virgins of Christ; cover your eyes. Christ’s virgin goes out, soon to return an adulteress. She goes out and, like a deceived dove without understanding, is immediately caught in a hawk’s claws. She is thrown down, her mouth is stopped so that she may not cry out, and, corrupted first in mind, she is corrupted in flesh.

The pleasure once experienced compelled her to repeat the crime. When this happened often [Col. 0792D], the sisters, wondering at the sound which they repeatedly heard, suspected deception. Above all, she came under suspicion, since her conduct had been suspect to everyone. The flight of the young man increased the suspicion. For when she revealed that she had conceived by the adulterer, he, fearing that he too might be exposed, left the monastery and set out for the secular world.

Then the wiser matrons confronted the girl. Unable to conceal the matter any longer, she confessed her transgression. Astonishment seized all who heard the report. At once zeal blazed in their bones; looking at one another and clapping their hands, they rushed upon her. Having torn the veil from her head, some thought she ought to be given to the flames, others flayed alive, others tied to a post and roasted over coals placed beneath her. The matrons restrained the ardor of the younger women [Col. 0793A]. Yet she was stripped, stretched out, and beaten with lashes without any pity.

A prison was prepared; she was bound and thrust into it. Two rings with their little chains were put upon each foot; two chains of no small weight were attached to them, one fastened by nails to a huge log, the other drawn through a hole and secured outside by a bar. She was kept on bread and water and daily filled with reproaches. Meanwhile her swelling womb brought her conception to term.

Oh, how great then was the grief of all! How great especially the laments of the holy virgins, who, fearing for their own honor, feared that one woman’s crime would be laid upon all; they felt as though they themselves had already been exposed to every eye for mockery, as though given over to everyone’s teeth to be gnawed. All wept, each wept; and inflamed by excessive grief, they again rushed upon their captive [Col. 0793B]. Unless the more mature women had spared the unborn child, they would scarcely ever have ceased from punishing her.

She bore all these evils patiently, declared herself worthy of greater torments, but said that she believed the rest would suffer no harm because of her unfaithfulness. They deliberated what ought to be done. If she were expelled, this would redound to the infamy of all, and a serious danger would threaten all their souls if the mother, deprived of assistance, should incur the danger of death together with her offspring. If they were kept, they declared that the birth could not be concealed.

Then one woman said: “The best course is that this harlot, pregnant with adulterous offspring, should be entrusted to that most wicked young man, and that she should be left to the care [Col. 0793C] of the man in whose wickedness she consented.” To this the unhappy woman replied: “If this can be a remedy for you, although I know it will be my ruin, behold: on that night, at that hour, in the place that knows our iniquity, the young man will meet me as he promised. It will then be in your judgment to hand me over to him. As the will is in heaven, so let it be done.”

At once they caught the words from her mouth. Already breathing vengeance against the young man, they sought from her the truth about everything. She confessed, affirming that what she had said was true. Then the master of the congregation, having summoned certain brethren, disclosed the matter. He ordered that on that night one man, his head covered with a veil, should sit in the appointed place, while others should remain secretly present to seize the visitor and, after striking him with staffs, hold him bound.

What he said was done. The young man, unaware of what was being done with his [Col. 0793D] mistress, arrived not only secular in mind but even in dress. Burning with lust, as soon as he saw the veil, like a horse and mule without understanding, he rushed upon the man whom he believed to be a woman. But those present administered to him a bitter remedy with clubs and extinguished the fever he had conceived.

The matter was reported to the virgins. At once certain women, having zeal for God though not according to knowledge, wishing to avenge the injury done to virginity, asked the brethren to hand the young man over to them for a short time, as though they were going to learn something secret from him. Received by them, he was thrown down and held. The cause of all the evils, the woman, was brought in as though for a spectacle. An instrument was put into her hands, and against her will she was compelled to cut off the man’s genitals with her own hands. Then one of the women standing by seized the severed parts and, as they were foul with blood, threw them into the face of the sinful woman [Col. 0794A].

You see with what zeal those emulators of chastity, persecutors of impurity, and lovers of Christ above all else burned. You see how, by mutilating him and pursuing her with reproaches and insults, they avenged the injury done to Christ. Behold Levi’s sword, Simeon’s jealousy: avengers of violated chastity, who think that not even the circumcised should be spared. Behold the zeal of Phinehas the priest, who won eternal priesthood by the slaughter of fornicators. Here too shines the wisdom of Solomon, who pronounced a sentence of death upon his own brother when he sought the virgin Abishag for concubinage.

I do not praise the deed, but the zeal; I do not approve the shedding of blood, but I extol the holy virgins’ great indignation against shamefulness [Col. 0794B]. What would they not endure, what would they not do to preserve chastity, when they could do so much to avenge it? But let us return to our subject. The mutilated man was handed back to the brethren; the woman, disgraced, was thrust back into prison.

Thus far, miserable woman, we have written the history of your misery. Henceforth let us pursue in writing how Christ’s most merciful loving-kindness was poured down upon you; for where sin abounded, grace abounded more exceedingly (Rom. 5). When vengeance had been exacted and zeal had cooled, the sacred virgins threw themselves at Christ’s feet. They wept and prayed that He might spare the place, provide for virginal honor, avert disgrace, and drive back danger. And they daily summoned divine clemency by prayers and tears [Col. 0794C].

The sinful woman, moreover, moved those compassionate bowels of Jesus by her sufferings, reproaches, and insults which she endured. O good Jesus, who most of all revealest thy omnipotence by sparing and showing mercy: if, when thou wast once present in the flesh, one miserable woman had been afflicted with such misery, what would that compassionate heart do, in which, as all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, so all the treasures of mercy, rested? Let the righteous hear and rejoice before God, and delight in gladness. Let sinners hear, that they may never despair of his goodness, who so exercises judgment that he does not abandon mercy.

You looked, good Jesus, you looked upon both the zeal and fear of so many of your handmaids and the affliction of your one sinful servant. [Col. 0794D] The child was now alive in her womb; milk flowed abundantly from her breasts. Indeed, her womb seemed so swollen that she was thought likely to bear twins. A leaden color surrounded her eyes, pallor invaded her face, and, though her breasts were emptied of fluid, after a little while they were filled again with their usual liquid. The prison scarcely contained her; what was necessary for childbirth was already prepared. They took every possible precaution that an infant’s crying should not reveal the birth.

And behold, in the silence of the deep night, when the miserable woman had given herself to sleep, she saw in dreams standing by her the bishop through whom, as we have said, she had been devoted in that same monastery to divine service. He was clad in a cloak, with a monastic habit beneath it. Looking sternly at her, he said: “Why is it that you curse me every day?” Terrified by great fear, she denied it. [Col. 0795A] Then the saint said: “It is true; why do you deny it?” Finding herself detected, she answered: “Truly, lord, because you entrusted me to this monastery, in which such great evils have befallen me.”

The bishop replied: “Rather blame yourself, because you have not yet disclosed your sins as you ought to your spiritual father. But see that you confess as soon as you can; and receive this command from me: chant these psalms daily to Christ.” At once, having written down for her the number and names of the psalms, he disappeared. Waking and becoming more composed, she committed the vision and the psalms to memory.

On the following night, when she was thought to be on the point of giving birth and the expectation of that bitter hour seemed near, though the very delivery was feared still more, the venerable bishop again appeared in a dream [Col. 0795B], bringing with him two women of beautiful appearance for the despairing woman. The bishop approached the miserable woman, placed her head back upon his knees, and covered her face with the cloak in which he was clothed, rebuking her and saying: “If you had been cleansed by true confession, you would plainly see what is being done. Now you will indeed feel the benefit, but you will not be able to know the manner and nature of the deed.”

A little later, rising, she saw the women, as it seemed to her, carrying an infant covered in white linen in their arms and departing after the bishop. When she awoke, she felt no weight in her womb. She touched her body with her hand and found it entirely empty.

In the morning the guards came. Looking at her, they saw that her womb had gone down, that her face had assumed a girlish—indeed, one might say virginal—beauty, that her eyes were bright, and that the leaden hue had gone [Col. 0795C]. At once, scarcely believing their own eyes, they said: “What is this? Have you added this too to your many crimes, that you should kill your own child?” Immediately they tore apart the narrow prison in which she sat chained. The tightness of the cell, the meanness of its furnishings, and the scantiness of its straw afforded no place in which anything could be hidden.

“And what,” they said, “miserable woman—have you given birth?” She answered that she did not know. “And where,” they asked, “is your child?” She replied: “I do not know.” Recounting the vision, she declared that she knew nothing further. Struck with terror at the novelty of the event, they did not believe her. They felt her womb; behold, such thinness had succeeded the swelling that you would have thought her belly clung to her back. They tested her breasts, but drew no fluid from them. Yet, not sparing her, they pressed harder, but extracted nothing. Their fingers ran over every limb; they examined all things, but found no sign of childbirth and no indication of conception.

Others were summoned, and others after them, and all found the same thing: everything sound, everything clean, everything beautiful. Nevertheless, they presumed to decide nothing and to judge nothing without the father’s authority. She was still held in bonds; iron still remained around her feet; the chains clanked.

She saw two ministers of divine mercy come to her [Col. 0796A]. One seized the chain by which she was most tightly bound and departed, accompanied by his companion. In the morning, the sisters noticed that the chain was missing, wondered, investigated the cause, heard the account, but believed little. They searched all her furnishings, but found nothing. A little later they found that one of the bonds had fallen from her feet. Finding it whole, and with the same firmness with which it had been fastened to her feet by smiths’ tools, they were greatly astonished. But why delay with many words? In the same manner she was freed from the rest; only one foot remained held by a single shackle.

Meanwhile the holy father arrived; when he had learned everything from evident signs and entirely trustworthy witnesses, being a man of remarkable humility, he thought my insignificance ought to be consulted about all these matters. Thus the servant of Christ came to our monastery, disclosed the miracle to me in secret, and asked that I would not deny my presence to Christ’s handmaids. I willingly agreed.

[Col. 0796B] When he had received both me and the companions of my journey with the utmost kindness and cordiality, we went to that inner chamber where she sat enclosed in her cell. Present were many virgins and widows, now advanced in age, endowed with wisdom and discernment, distinguished for holiness, and much exercised in regular discipline. After they had told us everything, I began to handle the shackle with my own hands and understood that neither others nor the woman herself could free it without God’s power.

Some, not yet freed from fear, asked us whether other bonds ought to be placed on her [Col. 0796C]. I forbade this, declaring it improper and a sign of unbelief. Rather, we must wait and hope that he who had freed her from the other bonds would also rescue her from this one by which she was still held. At the father’s command, moreover, many things worthy of eternal remembrance were reported to us, by which it was plainly made known that the Lord takes pleasure in those who fear him, even in those who hope in his mercy.

Therefore, commending ourselves to their holy prayers, consoling them as best we could with the word of the Lord, we returned to our monastery, praising and glorifying the Lord in all that we had heard and seen, and that the holy virgins had related to us. After a few days, [Col. 0796D] letters were brought to us from that venerable man, informing us that the shackle in which we had found her bound had fallen off, and asking my unworthiness what ought thereafter to be done. Among other things, I wrote back these few words: “What God has cleansed, do not call common; and her whom he himself has freed, do not bind.”

I thought it especially necessary to write these things to you, my dearest friend, who are far from these regions, both to remove an occasion for the envious and yet not to keep silence about Christ’s glory. Farewell.

[Col. 0795] Here ends a certain wonderful miracle, described by the venerable man Ethelred [Aelred], abbot of Rievaulx, concerning a certain nun of Wattun.

[Col. 0797]

## TO THE READER

Fabricius lists the *Life of Saint Margaret, Queen of Scotland*, among the works of Blessed Aelred: “Surius,” he says, “has it, though abridged, under 10 June; the *Acta Sanctorum* has it more fully on that day.” Yet the *Life of Saint Margaret* printed in the *Acta Sanctorum* acknowledges not Aelred but Theodoric, monk of Durham, as its author. Father Papebroch brings forward only certain fragments from Aelred’s book, reprinted above, *On the Genealogy of the Kings of the English*. Here are Papebroch’s own words:

“Laurentius Surius, who had been unaware of Margaret in the first edition of 1571, inserted in the second edition of 1579 a Life, received—I do not know through whom—under the name of an uncertain author, prefacing it with the statement that Saint Aelred, abbot, first composed it. John Bale, in listing the works of Saint Aelred, cent. 2, chap. 99, and John Pits after him, call him Ealred. In these works a *Life of Queen Margaret*, book 1, is noted; but both testify that they had not seen it, since they omit its opening words, which they add elsewhere. Among the ten writers later published and transmitted to us, however, the fourth is Ethelred; and among his other works there is a Letter to the illustrious Duke H.—that is, Henry, later king of the English—the grandson through his daughter Matilda of the saint. To this letter, written in 1144, the title *Genealogy of the Kings of the English* is given in the aforesaid volume.

“Since I find word for word the same things which are added to Theodoric’s account in Capgrave concerning Queen Matilda, as received from the mouth of David, the king’s youngest brother and an eyewitness, I strongly suspect that he wrote nothing about the saint except what appears in the aforesaid *Genealogy*. If, however, he wrote anything further, that too is earnestly desired.”

## HENRY, ARCHDEACON OF HUNTINGDON, A HALF-CENTURY LATER

[Col. 0797]

## NOTICE

(FABRICIUS, *Bibliotheca mediae et infimae Latinitatis*, vol. III, p. 222)

Henry, formerly a canon of Lincoln, was archdeacon of Huntingdon—Huntindonensis or Huntingtonensis. See Bale, II.82, and Pits, p. 211. At the request of Alexander, bishop of Lincoln, he wrote a *History of the English* in eight books, from the origin of the people, and especially from the arrival of the Angles and Saxons in Britain, down to the death of King Stephen, A.D. 1153. It appeared in H. Savile’s *Writers on English Affairs*, London, 1596, and at Frankfurt, from the Wechels’ press, 1601, folio, p. 296.

To these eight books Henry added a ninth, tenth, eleventh, and twelfth, which, for the most part still unpublished, H. Warthon noted as preserved in two very fine manuscript codices of the Lambeth Library, in his preface to vol. II of *Anglia Sacra*, p. XXIX. Of these, Book Nine treats of the saints of England and their miracles. Book Ten is entitled *On the High Points of Affairs*. In its preface, written in 1135, he discusses the end of the world.

The preface is followed by a letter to King Henry, likewise manuscript in the Cottonian Library, p. 76, on the succession of the Jewish, Assyrian, Persian, Macedonian, and Roman kings and emperors down to Emperor Conrad III, or to Henry’s own times. Then comes another letter to Warin the Breton, *On the Origin of the Kings of the Britons from Brutus to Cadwallader*, whom he had omitted in his *History* but afterwards found in Geoffrey Arthur’s book at Bec. D’Achery published this at the end of Guibert of Nogent, p. 736.

This is followed by a third letter to Walter, bishop of Winchester, written in 1145, *On Contempt for the World from Those Things Which We Have Seen Ourselves*; or, as another manuscript has it, *On the Image of the World*; another, *On Desire for the World*; or *On the Bishops and Illustrious Men of His Own Time*. The aforementioned Warthon printed it from both Lambeth codices in vol. II of *Anglia Sacra*, pp. 692–702, with variant readings of the other manuscript placed in the margin. D’Achery had earlier published it in his *Spicilegium*, vol. VIII, p. 178 (new edition, vol. III, p. 503).

Book Eleven contains satires and epigrams; Book Twelve contains sacred hymns, amorous games, and poems of various kinds. From this single historical work Bale, II.82, and Pits, chap. 204, p. 212, manufactured more than twenty books, often listing individual letters and poems repeatedly under several titles arbitrarily invented. It should be investigated whether the little work *On the Province of Britain*, which Cave noted as preserved in the public library at Cambridge, is a different work.

Henry himself, mentioning his poems to Walter, refers to those found in Book Eleven:

[Note: [Col. 0797] Vol. II, *Anglia Sacra*, p. 702.]

[Col. 0799]

Henry, bearing garlands for you, first brought epigrams,  
Then Venus’ battles, then “Buds” (*Germina*) [Note: [Col. 0799] Variant reading: *Gramina*—“Grasses.”].

Now, Walter, I bring you a funeral poem,  
Wholly another Henry than he who bore three garlands.

The verses in praise of Æthelflæd, Lady of the Mercians, and of Alfred are taken from Book Five of this Henry’s *History*, pp. 354 and 352 of the Wechel edition.

[Note: [Col. 0799] Vol. I, *Anglia Sacra*, pp. 207, 208.]

[Col. 0799]

# THE EIGHT BOOKS OF HISTORIES OF HENRY, ARCHDEACON OF HUNTINGDON

(Henry SAVILE, *The Principal Writers on English Affairs after Bede*, London, 1596, folio, p. 167.)

## PROLOGUE. TO ALEXANDER, BISHOP OF LINCOLN

Since I observe that in almost every pursuit of letters there is, while one lives, an inherent sweet alleviation of labor and supreme consolation in sorrow, I have thought that the splendor of histories should be embraced with the more delight and with the prerogative of greater brilliance. For nothing in life is more excellent than to trace out and travel excellently the paths of life. Where, moreover, do the magnificence of brave men, the wisdom of prudent men, the judgments of just men, and the moderation of self-controlled men shine more brilliantly than in the connected narrative of deeds performed? We have indeed heard what Flaccus, praising Homeric history, declared when he said:

> He who—what is honorable, what shameful, what useful, and what not,
He speaks more fully and better than Chrysippus and Crantor. (HOR. *Epistles*, book I, epistle 2, verses 3–4.) Crantor indeed and Chrysippus, philosophizing on moral instruction, laboured over many books. Homer, however, as though refining in a spectacle the prudence of Ulysses, the courage of Agamemnon, the moderation of Nestor, and the justice of Menelaus—and, conversely, the imprudence of Ajax, the weakness of Priam, the intemperance of Achilles, and the injustice of Paris—set forth by historical narrative what is honourable and useful and their opposites more clearly and delightfully than philosophers do. But why linger over foreign examples? See how sacred history teaches the principles of conduct, when it assigns justice to Abraham, courage to Moses, moderation to Jacob, prudence to Joseph; and conversely, when it displays the injustice of Ahab, the weakness of Uzziah, the intemperance of Manasseh, and the imprudence of Rehoboam. Above all, O good God, what a beacon of humility it is that holy Moses, placing with his brother the fragrance of incense to turn aside from his enemies the God who was protecting and avenging him, threw himself into the midst of terrible danger; that he shed tears for Miriam when she blasphemed against him, and continually toiled in prayer for those ill-disposed toward him! What a light of kindness it is that David, injured by Shimei’s [otherwise, Cushi’s] curses, insults, and blasphemies, and violently provoked by him, forbade that one man—though he was pursuing him and was weak—to be struck, though David himself was armed, attended, and most powerful against him; and later, when victorious and restored to his kingdom, did not allow vengeance to be taken upon him.

Thus also, in the deeds of all peoples and nations—which are surely God’s judgments—kindness, generosity, integrity, prudence, and things like these and their opposites not only kindle the spiritual to good and repel them from evil, but also urge secular persons toward good and fortify them amid evils. History presents things past to sight as though present, and judges things future by imagining them from things past. Beyond these, it has the splendid advantages of acquaintance with past events, since this especially distinguishes rational beings from [Col. 0801] brutes. For brutish men, like animals, do not know whence they are, do not know their race, do not know the disasters and deeds of their native land; indeed, they do not even wish to know. I judge such men more unfortunate, because what beasts possess by creation, they lack through their own emptiness; and what beasts could not do even if they wished, these men refuse to do though they can. But we must now pass on from those whose death and life deserve to be endowed with everlasting silence.

Considering these things, therefore, I have undertaken, at your command, Bishop Alexander—who appear to be the flower and summit of this kingdom and people—to narrate the deeds of this realm and the origins of our race. Following, as far as I could, the Ecclesiastical History of the Venerable Bede at your counsel, also extracting some matters from other authors, and compiling chronicles preserved in ancient libraries, I have represented the past down to things within our hearing and sight. In this work, when the attentive reader finds what is to be followed and what avoided, he will, through imitation and avoidance of these examples, God cooperating, be improved and will bring me the fruit I desire. For we have often returned to the very purity of morals by the straight path of history; but since we begin nothing without divine invocation, let us begin by invoking God.

Adonai, maker, shepherd, our support,

Beginning of things, their quickening and their end,

Breathe upon this work; guide it, and bring it to its end, we pray.

This work which you yourself, the Parent, have wrought in the fathers,

Great in judgment, raising kingdoms up and pressing them down,

By judgment now hidden, now openly displayed:

Delaying punishment for these while their crimes were being completed,

Weighing punishment for these once their crimes had been completed.

For whatever kings or peoples devise,

That they may do it—if they accomplish it—you cause it to be done,

Both making peace and hastening evil, as the prophet testifies;

You alone are, and remain as great as you have willed:

He from whom, through whom, and in whom alone all things are.

And you, father of your country, prince second to the king,

Bishop Alexander: if what we have written shines through your praise,

We pray that you may make fitting what is less fitting.

Here you see kings and peoples whom the dice of fate

Raised and crushed; but from these measure things to come.

Look, great Father, where the mighty have come to:

Look how worthless are the honour, brightness, and glory of the world.

## Book I

[Col. 0801A] Britain, therefore, is the most blessed of islands: fertile in crops and trees, rich in streams and woods, delightful for the hunting of birds and wild beasts, productive of birds of many and diverse kinds on land, sea, and rivers, and marvellous for the feeding of cattle and beasts of burden. Hence Solinus says: “Britain is so rich in pasture in certain places that, unless livestock are sometimes kept from the grazing grounds, abundance drives them into danger.” It abounds also in rivers very full of fish and in splendid, plentiful springs; and especially it overflows with salmon and eel. It is abundant too in seals; likewise herrings and oysters abound marvellously there, as do various kinds of shellfish. Among these are mussels, in which they often find an enclosed pearl, excellent in every colour: reddish, hyacinth-coloured, [Col. 0801B] purple, and leek-green, but especially white. Nor are there lacking snails from which a scarlet dye is made, whose very beautiful red can never be faded by any heat of the sun or harmed by any violence of rains; rather, the older it is, the more beautiful it is usually. Dolphins and whales too are often caught. Hence Juvenal, X.14:

> How much larger than dolphins is the British whale.

It also abounds in veins of metals: copper, iron, [Col. 0802A] tin, and lead, and likewise silver, though more rarely. Silver is brought from the nearest part of Germany by way of the Rhine in exchange for its remarkable abundance of fish and meat, most precious wool, milk, and countless herds, so that silver seems more plentiful there than in Germany; hence all its coinage is made from pure silver. It also produces a great quantity of excellent jet. This is black as a gem and inflammable; kindled by fire, it drives serpents away; warmed by rubbing, it holds fast things placed against it, just like amber. It also has springs of salt-water; there are hot springs too, and from them streams of hot baths, suited in distinct places to every age and sex according to each person’s condition. For water, as Saint Basil says, acquires a burning quality when it runs through [Col. 0802B] certain metals, becoming not merely hot but fiery.

This noblest of islands, formerly called Albion, later Britain, and now England, lies between north and west. It is 800 miles long and 200 broad, excluding only the more extended stretches of its various promontories, which make its circumference amount to 4,875 miles. To the [Col. 0803A] east it has Germany and Dacia; to the west, Ireland; to the south, Belgic Gaul. The nearest shore of this Gaul, for those crossing over, is opened by the city called the port of Rucupi [otherwise Rutubi], now corruptly called Reptacester by the English people; it is separated by sea from the shore of Gesoriacum among the Morini, the nearest crossing being fifty miles, or, as some have written, 450 stadia. Belgic Gaul was named from the Belvaci, formerly a most famous city of Gaul. This province now appears divided into two: namely, that called Ponthieu, and that called Normandy, where the Normans, a new but very powerful people, now dwell. To the north, where it lies open to the boundless Ocean, it has the nine Orkney Islands; of the last of these it was said:

[Col. 0803B]

> Let remotest Thule be subject to you.  
> (Virgil, *Georgics* I.30)

Though Britain has very many islands, it has three larger ones: one, the Orkneys, already mentioned; another, Man, or Eubonia, situated in the middle of the sea between Ireland and Britain; and a third, Wight [otherwise Guith], which is southern and faces the Normans and the Armoricans, now called Bretons. Thus the ancient proverb said when judges and kings were discussed: “He shall judge Britain with its three islands.”

It was once distinguished by twenty-eight most noble cities, besides innumerable castles, themselves equipped with very strong walls, towers, gates, and bars. [Col. 0803C] The names of the cities in British were these: Kair-Ebranc, that is, York; Kair-chent, that is, Canterbury; Kair-Gorangon, that is, Worcester; Kair-Lundene, that is, London; Kair-Legion [otherwise Lirion], that is, Leicester; Kair-Collon, that is, Colchester; Kair-Glou, that is, Gloucester; Kair-Cel, that is, Chichester; Kair-Bristou; Kair-Ceri, that is, Cirencester; Kair-Guent, that is, Winchester; Kair-Grant, that is, Grantchester, now called Cambridge [otherwise Grantebridge]; Kair-Lion, which we call Carlisle; Kair-Dauri, that is, Dorchester; Kair-Dorm, that is, Dormchester, which was situated in Huntingdonshire on the river called Nen and has been utterly destroyed; Kair-Loitchoit, that is, Lincoln; Kair-Merdin, which is still [Col. 0803D] so called; Kair-Guorcon; Kair-Cucerat; Kair-Guortigern; Kair-Urnac; Kair-Celemion; Kair-Meguaid; Kair-Licelid; Kair-Peris, that is, Porchester; Kair-Legion [otherwise Lerion], where there was an archbishopric in the time of the Britons, though now its walls scarcely appear, where the Usk [otherwise Osca] flows into the Severn; Kair-Draiton; Kair-Mercipit; Kair-Segent, which was upon the Thames not far from Reading and is called Silchester. These were the names of the cities in the time of the Romans and Britons.

From the beginning until the present, divine vengeance has inflicted five plagues upon Britain, a vengeance that not only visits the faithful but also judges unbelievers. The first came through the Romans, who conquered Britain but later withdrew. The second came through the Picts and Scots, who grievously harassed it with wars but did not possess it. The third came through the English, who conquered it and possess it. The fourth came through the Danes, who obtained it by war but afterwards perished. The fifth came through the Normans, who overcame it and at present rule the English.

When the Saxons subjugated this land, they established seven kings and gave their kingdoms names at will. The first kingdom was called Kent [otherwise Cent]; the second, Sussex, in which Chichester stands; the third, Wessex, whose capital was Wilton, now given to nuns, and in which are Winchester, Salisbury, and many other cities; the fourth kingdom, Essex, did not endure but was subjugated to the other kingdoms; the fifth was East Anglia, in which are the provinces [Col. 0804B] called Norfolk and Suffolk; the sixth, Mercia, in which is Lincoln and many others; the seventh, Northumbria, in which is York.

After the kings of Wessex prevailed over the rest and obtained the monarchy, they divided the land among themselves into thirty-five provinces. Although their locations and names are well known to their inhabitants, it will not be burdensome to set them down. For perhaps it will come to pass that, just as the aforesaid names of cities, once pleasing and exalted, are now turned into barbarism and ridicule, so too, with the course of time, things now most familiar will become unknown and incredible. Hence it is clear how wretchedly and vainly we inhabitants of provinces seek the fame of our name, since not even the names of the cities or provinces themselves can endure.

[Col. 0804C] The first province, therefore, is Kent [otherwise Cent], in which are the archbishopric of Canterbury and the bishopric of Rochester; the second is Sussex, in which is the bishopric of Chichester; the third, Surrey; the fourth, Hampshire, in which is the bishopric of Winchester; the fifth, Berkshire; the sixth, Wiltshire, in which is the bishopric of Salisbury; the seventh, Dorset; the eighth, Somerset, in which is the bishopric of Bath, or Akenchester; the ninth, Devonshire, in which is the bishopric of Exeter; the tenth, Cornwall [otherwise Cornugallia]; the eleventh, Essex; the twelfth, Middlesex, in which is the bishopric of London; the thirteenth, Suffolk; the fourteenth, Norfolk, in which is the bishopric of Norwich; the fifteenth, Cambridgeshire, in [Col. 0804D] which is the bishopric of Ely; the sixteenth, Lincolnshire, whose capital is Lincoln, and to which seven other provinces are subject: Leicester, Northampton, Huntingdon, Hertford [otherwise Herteford], Bedford, Buckingham, and Oxford. For the bishopric of Lincoln extends from the great river Humber to the Thames.

The twenty-fourth is Gloucestershire; the twenty-fifth is Worcestershire, in which is the bishopric of Worcester; the twenty-sixth, Herefordshire, in which is the bishopric of Hereford; the twenty-seventh, Shropshire; the twenty-eighth, Cheshire, in which is the bishopric of Chester; the twenty-ninth, Warwick; the thirtieth, Stafford. After the thirtieth, the first is Derby; the second, Nottingham; the third, Yorkshire, in which is the archbishopric of York; [Col. 0805A] the fourth is Northumberland, over which the bishop of Durham [otherwise Dunhelm] presides; the fifth, that region in which is the new bishopric of Carlisle. *Shire* in English is called *provincia* in Latin.

England, therefore, flourishes in our time, distinguished by seventeen bishoprics. There are far more towns than bishoprics, such as Gloucester, Leicester, Oxford, and many others lacking bishops; but in the western part of Britain called Wales, three bishoprics remain. One is at Saint David’s; another at Bangor [otherwise Paingor]; the third at Glamorgan. Yet these three are bishops of no cities because of the desolation of Wales, which alone remained to the conquered Britons. In our own time the bishop of Saint David’s received the pallium from the pope, [Col. 0805B] which had formerly been at Caerleon, though he immediately lost it.

The aforementioned cities shine, planted in pleasant places beside rivers, fertile and most beautiful. There are two rivers more famous than the rest, the Thames and the Severn, like Britain’s two arms, through which it exports and imports its own wealth and that of others. It is especially characteristic of Britain that its inhabitants, when setting out on pilgrimage, can be recognized among all peoples as more splendid in dress and expenditure by the very fact of whence they come. Though Britain abounds in so many things, it is fertile also in vineyards; yet it is rare for those who seek to purchase its riches to have something to bring in with them. Of its praise someone wrote thus:

> That island, blessed indeed with far-renowned splendour,  
> Surpasses all others in soil, milk, and honeycombs—  
> The island ruled by that God from whose foaming mouth  
> The Ocean flows.

And shortly afterwards:

> Let London, rich in ships, bear witness; Winchester in Bacchus’ gift,  
> Hereford in flocks, Worcester overflowing with grain;  
> Bath in its lake, Salisbury in wild beasts, Canterbury in fish;  
> York in woods, Exeter famed for metals.  
> Norwich in Danes, Chester in Irishmen,  
> Chichester in Gauls, Durham bordering on Norwegians.  
> Let Lincoln’s people, countless in beauty, bear witness;  
> Let Ely, lovely in situation, and Rochester in appearance bear witness.

Nor do I think it should be left unmentioned that Britain has a most agreeable climate and is therefore exceptionally healthy for its inhabitants. Since it lies between north and west, the heat it receives from the setting sun moderates [Col. 0805D] the cold it receives from the north. No person there has ever been seized by the sacred fire, but those brought there from Gaul are usually cured. And because it lies near the northern pole of the world, it has bright summer nights, so that observers often have to inquire in the middle of the night whether evening twilight still remains or morning twilight has already arrived; for the sun during the night, not far beneath the earth, returns eastward through the northern regions. Hence its summer days are extremely long, as its winter nights are in turn: namely, eighteen hours. Likewise, its summer nights and winter days are extremely short, namely only six equinoctial hours; whereas in Armenia, Macedonia, [Col. 0806A] Italy, and the other regions on the same parallel, the longest day or night comprises fifteen hours and the shortest nine.

There are four things in England that seem marvellous. The first is that wind comes out of caverns in the earth on the hill called the Peak, with such force that it repels garments thrown into it and hurls them far away after lifting them high. The second is at Stonehenge, where stones of marvellous size have been raised in the fashion of gateways, so that gateways seem set upon gateways; and no one can conceive by what art such great stones were lifted so high, or why they were erected there. The third is at Cheddar Hole [otherwise Chederhole or Chedrenhole], where there is a cavity under the earth. Though many have often entered it and travelled there across great stretches of ground and rivers, they have never been able to reach its end. [Col. 0806B] The fourth is that in certain places rain seems to rise from mountains and spread without delay across the plains.

Britain’s favour to its inhabitants was so great that they constructed within it, by royal authority, four roads raised from end to end, so that no one would dare attack an enemy upon them. The first runs from east to west and is called Icknield; the second runs from south to north and is called Ermine Street; the third runs crosswise from Canterbury to Chester, namely from the south-eastern wind to the north-west wind, and is called Watling Street; the fourth, greater than the rest, begins in Caithness and ends in Totnes, namely from the beginning of Cornwall to the end of Scotland. This road runs crosswise from the south-west wind [Col. 0806C] to the north-east wind, is called the Fosse, and goes by Lincoln.

These are England’s four principal roads, very broad indeed, but no less splendidly safeguarded by kings’ edicts and the venerable writings of laws. Britain uses five languages: those of the Britons, English, Scots, Picts, and Latin; Latin has been made common to all the rest through learning in the Scriptures. Yet the Picts now seem to have been destroyed, and their language so entirely extinguished that the fact that their mention occurs in ancient writings now appears fabulous. Who would not feel love for heavenly things and horror at earthly ones if he reflected that not only their kings, princes, and people perished, but that [Col. 0806D] their whole stock, language, and even memory together failed? And if this were not remarkable in other respects, it appears remarkable at least concerning a language—one which God established from the beginning among the other languages.

Thus far, concerning the situation and condition of Britain: though we have said little concerning many things, let what has been said suffice. Now we must say by whom and at what time it was first inhabited. What is not found in Bede, I have discovered in other authors. They wrote that the Britons’ origin sprang from Dardanus. Dardanus was the father of Troius; Troius the father of Priam and Anchises; Anchises the father of Aeneas; Aeneas the father of Ascanius; Ascanius the father of Silvius. Silvius, having taken a wife and she being pregnant, was told by a certain magician that the son with whom she was pregnant would kill [Col. 0807A] his father. The magician was therefore killed for that prophecy; the son was born and called Brutus. Much later, while he was playing with boys, he killed his father with an arrow-shot, not deliberately but by accident. For this reason, expelled from Italy, he came to Gaul; there, after founding the city of the Turones, called Tours, he occupied the Armorican region. Coming here from Armorica, he claimed for himself the southern parts of the great island and called it Britain after his own name.

Those authors say that, when Brutus ruled in Britain, Eli the priest judged Israel, and Posthumus, or Silvius, son of Aeneas, ruled among the Latins; Brutus was his grandson. After an interval of eighty years, it happened that the people of the Picts, having entered the Ocean from Scythia, were driven by winds beyond Britain’s bounds to Ireland; they entered its northern coasts and, having found there the people of the Scots, sought settlements for themselves also in those regions, but could not obtain them. The Scots therefore said: “This island could not contain us both; but we know that there is another island not far from ours toward the rising sun, which we often see from afar on brighter days. If you wish to go there, you can make it habitable for yourselves; or, should anyone resist you, use us as allies.” Thus the Picts sought Britain and began to dwell in the northern parts of the island, for the Britons occupied the southern parts. When the Picts, having no wives, asked the Scots for them, [Col. 0807C] the Scots agreed to give them only on the condition that, whenever the matter came into doubt, they should choose their king from the female rather than the male line of kings. This, it is established, has been observed among the Picts down to the present day.

These are the things transmitted from ancient writings about the arrival of the Britons in that part of the world called Britain, and about the arrival of the Picts upon the same island. Although it is an island, since it is of such vast extent its being an island is no less excellent, since the whole world is an island. But because the common saying goes, “Rain is mingled with wind, and laughter with sorrow,” Britain, by reason of its pre-eminent advantages, stirred envy and jealousy against itself from all the surrounding lands through its riches. Therefore it was often conquered and even more often attacked. As time went on, moreover, the Scots came from Ireland to Britain under the leader Reuda. In the territory of the Picts, either by friendship or by the sword, they claimed for themselves settlements which they still possess; from this leader they are called Dalreudini. For in their language *dal* means “part.”

We must therefore say a little about Ireland. Although this is not part of the plan, it is near at hand, and I shall add it in writing to the praise of almighty God.

Ireland, after Britain, is the best of all islands. Though it yields to Britain in wealth, it greatly surpasses it in the breadth of its territory and in the healthfulness and serenity of its air. Just as it is shorter toward the north, so it extends very far southward beyond Britain’s limits, reaching opposite the northern regions [Col. 0808A] of Spain, although a great expanse of sea lies between. Snow never, or rarely, remains there for more than three days. No one cuts hay in summer because of winter or builds stables for beasts of burden. No creeping thing is usually seen there, and no serpent can live; for serpents often brought there from Britain die as soon as, with the ship nearing land, they are touched by the scent of that air. Rather—*cum potius* (variant *quin potius*)—everything from the same island is effective against poison. We have in fact seen persons bitten by a serpent: scraped leaves of books that came from Ireland were given to them, the scrapings immersed in water and administered as a drink; and they immediately absorbed and calmed all the force of the spreading poison and all swelling of the distended body.

[Col. 0808B] By a marvellous gift, therefore, God enriched this island and placed in it a multitude of saints for its protection. Moreover, he enriched it with milk and honey, did not leave it without vineyards, and distinguished it by hunting of fish and birds, stags and roe-deer. This is properly the homeland of the Scots. If anyone wishes to know at what time it was first inhabited, I find nothing on this in the Venerable Bede, but I have found the following in a certain author. When the Egyptians were drowned in the Red Sea, those who survived expelled from among themselves a certain noble Scythian who lived with them, lest he seize dominion over them. Once expelled, he wandered long through Africa and came with his household to the altars of the Philistines. By the Salt Lake they came between Russicada [otherwise Rusicada] and [Col. 0808C] the mountains of Syria; they came by the river Malva, crossed Mauritania, sailed to the Pillars of Hercules and the Tyrrhenian Sea, reached Spain, and lived there many years. Their descendants multiplied greatly. Then, 1,002 years after Israel’s passage through the Red Sea, they came to Ireland.

The Britons, however, occupied Britain first. The Britons came to Britain in the third age of the world; the Scots came to Ireland in the fourth. Though these things are not altogether certain, this at least is certain: they came from Spain to Ireland, and a part of them subsequently left it and added a third people in Britain to the Britons and Picts. For the part that remained there still uses [Col. 0808D] the same language and is called Navarrese. There is a very great inlet of the sea which in ancient times separated the people of the Britons from the Picts. It breaks far into the land from the west, where there still stands today a most strongly fortified city of the Britons called Aldclud [otherwise Aldclid]. To the northern side of this inlet came the Scots whom we have mentioned, and they made for themselves a homeland there.

Julius Caesar was the first Roman to assail Britain in war, sixty years before the Incarnation of our Lord, in the 693rd year from the foundation of the city. Having held the consulship with Lucius Bibulus, and having rightfully overcome the Germans and Gauls in war—who were then separated only by the river Rhine—he came from there to the Morini, whence the crossing to Britain is shortest. [Col. 0809A] He therefore ordered eighty transport and swift vessels to be prepared and himself crossed over to Britain with the legions. Yet matters did not turn out as he hoped: when disembarking from the ships, he experienced from the Britons a battle fiercer than he could have believed possible. Seeing therefore that his men were fewer and the enemy more formidable than he had expected, he was compelled by force to re-enter the ships. Then caught by a storm, he lost a great part of his fleet, a great number of soldiers, and almost all his cavalry. Confounded and returned to Gaul, he burned more fiercely with resolve; while the legions wintered, he prepared six hundred ships of both types. In spring the man returned to Britain, as expected, with very great forces. As he disembarked, he marched with his army against the enemy. Meanwhile, the ships, fixed by their anchors, were seized by a storm, dashed together, and broken. Forty of them perished; the rest were repaired only after a long time and not without difficulty.

The great commander, therefore, having lost hope of escape, urged the soldiers’ spirits more strongly; and in the very course of his exhortation he engaged the enemy. On both sides they fought with one accord, strength and spirit stretched to their utmost: the Romans having no hope of escape, the Britons their usual assured hope of victory. Labienus, then, a military tribune, drove the first line more fiercely into the wedge of Dolobellus, who was the proconsul of the British king; cutting down, overthrowing, and pursuing those who yielded, the royal battle-line was driven in between Caesar’s forces and Labienus’ phalanxes. The king was called Belinus, brother of King Cassibellanus; he was son of King Lud, a most powerful king [Col. 0809C] who had occupied many islands of the sea by war. Labienus, surrounded with his whole battle-line, was cut down and suddenly sent to death. Julius, seeing that the day was unlucky and declaring that the Britons must be fought by skill rather than strength, allowed a retreat before he suffered greater losses. The Britons pursued the Romans, and after killing many were held back by the proximity of the woods.

For a third time Caesar encountered the Britons and exhorted his own men as follows:

> Most valiant comrades, whose courage neither the harshness of the sea nor the toil of lands could thwart, whose strength neither the boldness of the Gauls nor the courage of the Germans could endure: do not think that I exhort you in order to increase your valour by words. For what is highest and most perfect, proved so often amid so many dangers, can neither grow nor knows how to diminish: that valour, I say, which has always shone more brightly in the most severe circumstances, advancing with certain hope where others despair and fighting with confident cheerfulness. Why should I recall things known to you—indeed, to all peoples? How often, defeated, have we conquered our conquerors, and, compelled by anger, become stronger than those stronger than ourselves? Injured valour ought to grow angry. Therefore now, if there is any glory in the Roman name, show military discipline—perfectly learned by you, more perfectly practised, and most perfectly displayed in the final danger. I, certainly, have inevitably chosen one of two things: either to conquer today, which is blessed, or to die for my country, which is safer; flight alone belongs to the wretched. Therefore, if any of you has the same spirit, let him raise his unconquerable right hand, and let the enemies be astonished that we are revived by losses and strengthened by diminution.

Thus he spoke and raised his right hand. The whole army, raising its shout to the stars, growled with hands uplifted; and amid that very cry they engaged the enemy. Roman valour appeared, as they fought more cautiously through being more wisely ordered and persisted more obstinately. Therefore, while the Britons grew weary from striking and the Romans strove to protect themselves, after the battle had lasted long, Caesar’s men seemed fresh to the exhausted islanders. Then the Romans became victors, though not without great danger to their own men.

From there Caesar advanced to the river Thames [otherwise, Tamensis]. On its farther bank, under Cassibellanus’ command, an immense multitude of enemies had taken position. They had fortified the riverbank and almost the whole ford beneath the water with very sharp stakes. [Col. 0810B] The traces of these stakes are visible there to this day; and it appears to observers that each is as thick as a human thigh and, sheathed with lead, remains fixed immovably in the bed of the river. But the Romans discovered this and, avoiding them, attacked the barbarians. Unable to bear the legions’ assault, they hid themselves in woods, from which they grievously and often harassed the Romans with repeated attacks.

But the very strong city of Trinovantum, under the leader Androgeus, surrendered itself to Caesar, giving seventy hostages; likewise many other cities entered an alliance with the Romans. On their guidance Caesar finally captured, in a severe battle, Cassibellanus’ town, situated between two marshes, further defended by the cover [Col. 0810C] of woods, and abundantly supplied with every resource. After Caesar returned from the Britons to Gaul, he sent legions into Ireland [otherwise Hiberna]; being suddenly surrounded by the pressing demands of wars, he sent for the legions that remained in Britain and in Ireland [otherwise, “Ireland” or “the Irish”], so that they might go with him to Rome. On this Lucan says:

> The fair-haired Britons are released from their long station.

Having retaken unwilling Rome, he ordered the month Quintilis to be called July in his honour; for he was treacherously killed in the senate-house on the Ides of March. But since we must treat of Caesar and his successors, who ruled Britain down to the time of Martianus, the forty-fourth from Caesar, let it not be burdensome to touch briefly upon their praises, so that our Christian princes, if they are not ashamed to equal them in morals, may at least be ashamed to be found worse than they.

An authoritative praise of Caesar from Solinus: “As the bravest soldiers, Sergius and Sisinnius, surpassed other soldiers, so Caesar outshone all commanders—indeed, all men of every age. Under his command 1,192,000 enemies were killed. For he did not wish to record how many he had slain in civil wars. He fought fifty-two pitched battles, surpassing Marcus Marcellus alone, who had similarly fought thirty-nine times. Moreover, none wrote more swiftly, none read more quickly; he even dictated four letters at once. He was of such [Col. 0811A] goodness that those whom he had subdued by arms he conquered more by clemency.”

Augustus, succeeding Julius Caesar, held the monarchy of the whole world. He made a register of the entire world and took tribute from Britain as from the other kingdoms, as Virgil says (*Georgics* III.25):

> Britons raise purple embroidered curtains.

He did this in the forty-second year of his reign, when the true Light born for the world became known, through whom all kingdoms and islands of the world, oppressed by darkness, came to know that God is one and saw him who created them. When Augustus had reigned fifty-five and a half years, he followed the law of death.

Praise of Augustus from Eutropius: “Augustus, apart from the civil wars in which he was undefeated, subdued Armenia, Egypt, Galatia, Cantabria, Dalmatia, Pannonia, Aquitaine, Illyricum, Raetia, the Vindelici, the Thalassians, Pontus, and Cappadocia. He so defeated the Dacians and Germans that he settled 400,000 captives from them on the bank of the Rhine in Gaul. The Persians gave him hostages, as they had given none before, and restored the standards stripped from Crassus. He was gentle, agreeable, and of a courteous disposition; beautiful in his whole body, but especially in his eyes; merciful toward citizens and so great toward friends that he almost made them his equals. He declared war upon no people save for just causes, deeming it a very bad thing to hazard uncertain outcomes for the sake of triumph. He was so beloved by barbarians that some kings freely came to Rome to submit to him, while others founded cities in his honour, such as Juba and [Col. 0811C] Herod. Every day he read, wrote, and declaimed; he abstained greatly from food and wine; he did not avenge insults spoken against him; he granted pardon to those accused of plotting against him; he found Rome built of brick and left it of marble.”

Tiberius, Augustus’ stepson, ruled after him for twenty-three years, over Britain as well as over the other kingdoms of the whole world. Praise of Tiberius: Tiberius was prudent in war and fortunate. Thus under Augustus he earned the right to succeed him. He was most learned in letters, but more distinguished in eloquence, better in sudden replies or counsels than in premeditated ones. Yet he was accused of dissimulation, as though hostile to those whom he loved, while seeming well-disposed toward those whom he hated.

Gaius, surnamed Caligula, ruled over the world [Col. 0811D] for almost five years.

Claudius assumed the empire sixty-two years after the Incarnation of the Lord, in the seven hundred and ninety-eighth year from the founding of the City. In the fourth year of his reign he came to Britain and very swiftly received into submission, without any battle or bloodshed, certain rebels. He also added to the Roman Empire the Orkney Islands, situated in the Ocean beyond Britain, of which we have spoken before; and in the sixth month after setting out he returned to Rome, and gave both himself and his son the name Britannicus. Of him Juvenal says:

> And displaying thy belly, noble Britannicus.

In the same year a most severe famine occurred throughout Syria, which Luke in the Acts of the Apostles recalls as having been foretold by the prophet Agabus. In the time of Claudius, Peter, the chief of our faith, took up the see at Rome, which he held for twenty-five years, that is, until Nero’s final year. Vespasian was sent by that same Claudius into Germany and then into Britain; thirty-two times he fought with the enemy; he crushed two very powerful peoples; he took twenty towns by force of arms; and he brought under Roman rule the Isle of Wight, adjoining Britain. After reigning thirteen years and more than half a year, he entered upon the way of his fathers.

Praise of Claudius: Claudius conducted many affairs calmly and moderately, though some less cautiously. He enlarged the Roman Empire and was a man of war. Yet he showed such courtesy toward certain friends that he himself accompanied in triumph the nobleman Paulinus, who had performed many notable deeds in the British campaign, and, as Paulinus ascended the Capitol, walked at his left side.

Nero reigned thirteen years and more than half a year. Although vigorous in youth, when he became emperor he grew slack in military affairs; consequently, among other losses to the Roman Empire, Britain was almost lost. For under him two most renowned towns there were overthrown and destroyed. In the year in which he killed Peter and Paul, he himself perished shamefully.

Vespasian, who destroyed Jerusalem, reigned nearly ten years. He was the very man who had gone to Britain under Claudius and subjected the Isle of Wight to Roman dominion. It measures about thirty thousand paces from east to west and twelve from south to north; in its eastern parts it is about six miles, and in its western parts three miles, from Britain’s southern coast. This most distinguished man also set up a colossal statue, one hundred and seven feet high.

Authentic praise of Vespasian: At Rome he conducted himself with the greatest moderation in imperial office. He was somewhat too eager for money, yet never unjustly took it from anyone. Although he gathered it with every provision of careful diligence, he bestowed it with the greatest generosity, especially upon the needy; nor before him was any emperor’s liberality found to be greater or more just. He possessed a gentleness of the mildest kind, so that he did not readily punish those accused of treason against him beyond the penalty of exile. He conquered Judaea, Achaea, Lycia, Rhodes, Byzantium, Samos, Thrace, Cilicia, and Commagene. He was forgetful of offences and enmities; he bore insults from advocates and philosophers lightly; and he was lovable and agreeable to the senate, the people, and everyone.

Titus, his son, reigned two years and two months, a man wonderful in every kind of virtue, so that he was called “the love and delight of the human race.” He built the amphitheatre at Rome, and at its dedication killed five thousand wild beasts.

Highest praise of Titus: Titus was most eloquent, most warlike, and most moderate. He pleaded cases in Latin and composed poems and tragedies in Greek. While serving under his father in the siege of Jerusalem, he pierced its defenders with twelve arrows. At Rome he governed with such courtesy that he punished no one at all. He released men convicted of conspiracy against himself and retained them in the same friendship as before. His kindness and generosity were so great that, when he refused nothing to anyone and was reproved by his friends, he replied that no one ought to leave the emperor sorrowful. Because of this unprecedented favour he was beloved; and at his death public grief was so great that all mourned as though bereaved in their own households. Though he died far from Rome, when news of his death was announced about evening, the senate entered the curia by night and bestowed upon the dead such praises and thanks as it had never offered him while alive and present.

Domitian, Titus’s brother, reigned fifteen years and five months. He was the second after Nero to persecute Christians. Divine providence, having made him hated by all, compelled him through the senate to destroy himself.

Nerva held the empire of the world for one year and a little more.

Trajan reigned nineteen and a half years. He governed Britain and the other kingdoms with remarkable vigour. For he spread far and wide the Roman Empire, which after Augustus had been defended rather than enlarged. He is the man who, for the sake of justice, put out his own eye and his son’s eye, and whom Gregory recalled from hell. Understand, therefore, you who read, how great justice is: it could not leave even an unbeliever, so perfect a lover of itself, abandoned.

Praise of Trajan from Suetonius: Trajan, a man of unprecedented courtesy and courage, subdued Dacia and the regions about the Danube, as well as Armenia, which the Parthians had occupied. He gave a king to the Albanians, and received into allegiance the kings of the Iberians, Sauromatians, Bosporans, Arabs, Osrhoenians, and Colchians. He occupied the Cordueni and Marchamedi, and conquered Antemusium, a great region of Persia, together with Seleucia, Ctesiphon, Babylon, and the Messenians. He held these territories as far as the boundaries of India and came to the Red Sea; there he made three provinces—Armenia, Assyria, and Mesopotamia—with the peoples who border upon Madena. Later he reduced Arabia to the form of a province and established a fleet on the Red Sea, so that by it he might ravage the borders of India.

Yet he surpassed military glory by courtesy and moderation, presenting himself at Rome and through the provinces as the equal of all; frequently visiting friends merely to greet them, including those who were sick; reciprocally sharing unceremonious banquets with them when they held festival days; often riding in their carriages; injuring no senator; doing nothing unjust to increase the treasury; generous toward all; enriching everyone publicly and privately; advancing to honours even those whom he knew through only moderate acquaintance; building up the world; granting many immunities to cities; and doing nothing that was not peaceful and gentle. So much so that in all his lifetime only one senator was condemned—and even he by the senate, without Trajan’s knowledge. Therefore throughout the world he was considered next to God, and deserved every reverence both living and dead.

Among his other sayings, this excellent saying of his is reported. When his friends criticized him for being excessively gracious toward everyone, he answered that he wished to be such an emperor to private persons as, were he himself a private person, he would wish emperors to be to him. Alone among all men, he was buried within the city. His bones were placed in a golden urn in the forum which he built, beneath a column one hundred and forty feet high. Such honour was granted to his memory that down to our own age emperors are acclaimed in the senate in no other terms than: “May you be more fortunate than Augustus and better than Trajan.”

Hadrian governed the world for twenty-one years. He subdued the Jews when they rebelled a second time; he rebuilt Jerusalem and deprived the Jews of permission even to see it.

Praise of Hadrian: Hadrian was a middling emperor. He had peace throughout his reign and fought only once, through a governor. He travelled around the Roman world, built many things, was most eloquent in Latin speech, and highly learned in Greek.

Antoninus Pius held the monarchy of the world for twenty-three and a half years.

Praise of Antoninus Pius: An honourable man of outstanding merit, he is compared with Numa Pompilius, as Trajan is compared with Romulus. Harsh toward none and kind toward all, he was moderate in military affairs, seeking to defend provinces rather than enlarge them; he sought out the most equitable men to administer the commonwealth, honoured the good, and detested the wicked without any harshness. He was so revered by friendly kings that they brought their disputes before him and obeyed his judgment. Most generous toward friends, he nevertheless left the treasury wealthy. He was called Pius because of his clemency.

Marcus Antoninus Verus, together with his brother Aurelius Lucius Commodus, ruled nineteen years and two months. They were the first to administer the empire with equal authority, whereas until then there had been only individual Augusti. They then conducted war against the Parthians with remarkable courage and success. In their time, while Eleutherius presided over the Roman Church as pontiff, Lucius, king of the Britains, sent him a letter begging that, by Eleutherius’s command, he might become a Christian. He soon obtained the fulfilment of his pious petition; and the Britons preserved the faith they had received, inviolate and whole, in peaceful tranquillity until the time of the emperor Diocletian.

Praise of Antoninus Verus from Roman history: When his colleague Antoninus died of apoplexy, he remained beyond praise in imperial office. He never altered his expression either through joy or through sorrow. Devoted to Stoic philosophy, he was a supreme philosopher in character and learning, highly accomplished in Latin and Greek letters, fair to all, never arrogant, most ready in generosity, kind and moderate toward the provinces. He fought successfully against the Germans; he waged the Marcomannic war against the Quadi, Vandals, Sarmatians, Sucti, and all barbarian peoples, a war greater than any remembered in history, so that it is compared to the Punic wars. Thus this godlike man, victor in so great a conflict, celebrated a triumph with his son Commodus. When, with the treasury exhausted, he had sold royal furnishings, he later repaid their prices to those who wished to return them; those who did not wish to do so he left untroubled. He permitted men of higher rank to give banquets with the same display as his own and with similar servants. In presenting public games after victory he was so magnificent that he is said to have displayed one hundred lions at once.

Commodus, son of the aforesaid Commodus, ruled thirteen years. He waged war successfully against the Germans and, having removed the head of a colossal statue, ordered the head bearing his own likeness to be put upon it.

Aelius [or Celius] Pertinax ruled six months. He was killed in the palace through the crime of Julianus the jurist.

Severus Pertinax, after the murder of Julianus the jurist, reigned seventeen years. An African by birth, a Tripolitan from the town of Lepcis, fierce by nature and continually assailed by many wars, he governed the commonwealth most bravely indeed, but with the greatest labour.
