Victor in the civil wars that had confronted him most grievously, and having killed at Lugdunum Didius Albinus, who had made himself Caesar in Gaul, he crossed into Britain. There, after frequent great and severe battles, he judged that the recovered part of the island should be separated from the remaining unsubdued peoples, not, as some suppose, by a wall, but by a rampart.

For a wall is made of stones; but a rampart, by which camps are fortified to repel the enemy’s force, is made of turf. The turves, cut round, are raised from the earth and built up like a high wall above the ground, with a ditch before it, from which the turves were lifted; above this are fixed stakes of very strong timber. Accordingly Severus drew from sea to sea a great ditch and a very strong rampart, fortified besides with frequent towers. There at the town of York he died of illness. He left two sons, Bassianus and Geta. Geta, declared a public enemy, perished. Bassianus, having assumed the surname Antoninus, obtained the throne.

Praise of Severus from Eutropius: Severus waged many wars successfully. He conquered the Parthians, Arabs, and Azabeni; hence he was called Parthicus, Arabicus, and Azabenicus. Throughout the world he restored many things to Roman glory. Besides military fame, Severus was also distinguished in civil pursuits, learned in letters, and fully possessed of philosophical knowledge; he was called Divine.

Antoninus Caracalla, Severus’s son, held the kingdom of the world for seven years.

Macrinus, after reigning one year at Archelais, was killed with his son in a military mutiny.

Marcus Aurelius Antoninus held dominion over the world for four years. Aurelius Alexander ruled thirteen years. He was singularly devoted to his mother Mammaea and therefore beloved by all.

Praise of Alexander: Having undertaken war against the Persians, he most gloriously defeated King Xerxes. He maintained military discipline with the greatest severity and dismissed entire mutinous legions from service. He was very popular at Rome; he perished in a military mutiny in Gaul.

The elder Maximian ruled lands and islands for three years. He defeated the Germans in war.

Gordian ruled six years. Origen flourished, who wrote five thousand books, as Jerome relates. Gordian defeated the Persians.

Philip, together with his son Philip, ruled seven years. He was the first of all emperors to be a Christian; and after the third year of his reign the thousandth year from Rome’s foundation was completed. This most august year of all preceding years was celebrated with magnificent games by a Christian emperor.

Praise of the younger Philip: His disposition was so grave that no contrivance could move him to laughter; he reproved his father, when laughing loudly, merely by turning his face away. He always resisted vices and aspired to the difficult heights of virtue.

Decius ruled one year and three months. Having killed Philip father and son, he persecuted Christians from hatred of them.

Gallus, with his son Volusianus, ruled two years and four months.

Valerian, with his son Gallienus, ruled fifteen years. When he stirred up a persecution against Christians, he was immediately captured by the king of the Persians; there, blinded, he grew old in wretched servitude.

Claudius the Second ruled one year and nine months. He defeated the Goths, who had been ravaging Illyricum and Macedonia for fifteen years. For this reason a golden shield was granted to him in the senate-house and a golden statue in the Capitol.

Aurelian ruled five years and six months. While he was persecuting Christians, lightning struck before him, to the great terror of those around him; shortly afterwards he was killed by his soldiers.

Praise of Aurelian from *Deeds of Wonderful Men*: While Alexander had subdued the world in thirteen years and Caesar in fourteen, he pacified it in three years and three battles. He was the first Roman to assume a diadem and to use jewels and garments wholly embroidered with gold. He corrected lax military discipline and corrupt morals; but he was excessively fierce, proud, and cruel at all times.

Tacitus ruled six months, after whose murder in Pontus Florianus reigned three months and was likewise killed at Tarsus.

Probus ruled six years and four months. At last, having destroyed the enemy, he completely liberated Gaul, long occupied by barbarians.

Praise of Probus from authentic sources: Probus was an illustrious man—keen, energetic, and just. He almost equalled Aurelian in glory, but surpassed him in civil character. Having waged innumerable wars, when peace had been secured he said that soldiers would soon no longer be necessary.

Carus ruled two years. After overcoming the Persians, he perished beyond the River Tigris.

Diocletian, with Herculius Maximian, ruled twenty years. In their time a certain Carausius, though of very low birth, was ready in counsel and action. Stationed to guard the coasts of the Ocean, then harried by Franks and Saxons, he acted more to the ruin than to the advantage of the commonwealth [variant: “than to the commonwealth’s benefit”]. He restored none of the booty taken from pirates to its owners, but claimed it all for himself, thus arousing suspicion that by artful negligence he even allowed the enemy to raid the frontiers. Therefore, when Maximian ordered him killed, he assumed the purple and occupied Britain [variant: “the Britains”]. Having most valiantly asserted and held it for himself for seven years, he was at last killed through the treachery of his associate Allectus.

Afterwards Allectus held the island, taken from Carausius, for three years. Asclepiodotus, prefect of the praetorium, overthrew him and recovered Britain after ten years. Compelled by wars, the aforesaid emperors appointed Constantius to rule in the West and Galerius Maximinus in the East. At that time a most cruel persecution against Christians blazed up throughout the world.

In that persecution Saint Alban offered himself as a sacrifice to God. Fortunatus writes of him in his praise of virgins:

> Fruitful Britain brings forth noble Alban.

When Alban was a citizen at Verulamium, he gave lodging to a certain cleric fleeing from pagans; and meanwhile, through the hidden man, he was converted. When the pursuers sought the cleric, Alban offered himself for punishment in his place. As he was being tortured and led away for beheading, the river was dried up through the saint’s prayer, because so great a crowd could not cross by the bridge. When, among others, the executioner who was to strike him saw this, he threw himself at Alban’s knees, became a believer, and was martyred with him. A spring also attended his martyrdom and, after his martyrdom, returned to its natural state. The eyes of the man striking him fell to the ground together with the saint’s head.

He suffered near Verulamium, that is, Wirlamecester or Wadlingeceaster, where afterwards a church of wonderful workmanship and a most renowned abbey were built; there, even to this day, the sick are healed and miracles are performed. At that time Aaron and Julius, citizens of the city of the legions, also suffered, as did many others of both sexes through unheard-of dismemberment and diverse tortures, bearing witness to God Most High. This persecution was so frequent that within one month seventeen thousand martyrs are found to have suffered for Christ.

When, in the twentieth year of their reign, Diocletian at Nicomedia and Maximian at Milan laid aside the purple, the persecution began to be mitigated until the time of Arius.

Praise of Diocletian: Diocletian was crafty in manner, shrewd besides, and possessed of a highly subtle intellect; he wished to discharge his severity through others’ unpopularity. Yet he was a most diligent and industrious ruler, although, against Roman liberty, he commanded that he should be adored, whereas before him other emperors were merely greeted. He put gems into garments and footwear. He showed unprecedented courage in becoming, alone of all men, voluntarily a private citizen after so high a station. It therefore happened to him, as to no one else since mankind began, that after dying a private citizen he was nevertheless enrolled among the gods. Maximian, however, was an exceedingly cruel man and terrible in appearance.

Constantius, who under the aforesaid emperors had ruled Gaul, Britain, and Spain for fifteen years, ruled one year in the western regions after their abdication, while Maximinus ruled in the East. He founded Constantia [variant: “the city of Constantia”] in that part of Gaul now called Normandy, and took as wife Helena, the daughter of Coel, the British king of Colchester, whom we call saintly; by her he begot Constantine the Great. Constantius, a man of the highest greatness and courtesy, died at York in Britain.

Praise of Constantius: Constantius, a most excellent man, sought the wealth of provincials and private persons and did not greatly desire the revenues of the treasury, saying that public resources were better held by private persons than shut away within a single enclosure. He was modest in display and gentle in spirit. He was not only loved but also revered by the Gauls.

Constantine, flower of Britain, reigned thirty years and ten months. British by birth and homeland, no one like him had arisen from Britain before or after. He led an army from Britain and Gaul into Italy. For Maximian had established his son Maxentius as Augustus at Rome. As Constantine, still an unbeliever, marched against him, he saw an angel of God showing him the sign of the cross and exhorting him to believe. He immediately believed, and God drowned Maxentius in the river.

Constantine, therefore, having gained the empire, twice overcame Maximinus under the law of war and alone held the kingdom of the world. Cleansed, as writings relate, from the disease of leprosy through Saint Silvester in baptism, he built at Rome, where he was baptized, the basilica of John the Baptist called the Constantinian; likewise, a basilica for Peter and Paul in the temple of Apollo, enclosing the body of each in Cyprian bronze, five feet in thickness; likewise, a basilica in the Sessorian palace called Jerusalem, where he deposited wood from the Lord’s cross; likewise, a basilica of Saint Agnes, the holy mother, at the request of his daughter; likewise, a basilica for Blessed Lawrence on the Tiburtine Way in the Veranian field; likewise, on the Lavican Way, a basilica for the martyrs Peter and Marcellinus, and a mausoleum in which he placed his mother in a purple sarcophagus [sartophago; variant: sarcophago]; likewise, a basilica in the town of Ostia near the harbour of Rome; likewise, in the town of Alba, a basilica of Saint John the Baptist; likewise, a basilica in Naples.

When Constantine established the city bearing his own name in Thrace, he intended it to be the seat of the Roman Empire and capital of the entire East. Likewise, he restored the Bithynian city of Depranum, in honour of the martyr Lucian buried there, and called it Helenopolis after the name of his mother. He decreed that pagan temples should be closed without any slaughter of men.

Helena, a noble foster-child of Britain, is said to have enclosed London with a wall that still remains, and to have adorned Colchester with fortifications. Among many other works, she also restored Jerusalem and, having cleansed it of idols, adorned it with many basilicas.

Praise of Constantine from the sacred archives: In the first period of his reign he may be compared with the best emperors, in the last with middling ones. Countless virtues of mind and body shone in him: supreme in military glory, equal in good fortune and industry, devoted to civil arts and liberal studies, eager for the love of justice, and excellent toward friends. Yet the arrogance produced by success eventually altered him somewhat from that teachable disposition which had won him favour.

Constantius, together with his brothers Constantine and Constans, ruled twenty-four years and five months. The Arian heresy, supported by the protection of King Constantius, afflicted Catholics grievously and in various ways.

Julian the Apostate ruled two years and eight months. As an enemy of God, he was deservedly killed while fighting barbarians.

Praise of Julian from Paul: He was not unlike Marcus Antoninus, whom he also strove to imitate. He was excellently educated in the liberal disciplines, possessed a retentive and extensive memory, immense and ready eloquence, and was more akin to a philosopher. He was courteous toward all, eager for glory, and for that reason often excessive in spirit.

Jovinian, good and pious, ruled eight months; premature death spoiled his auspicious beginnings.

Valentinian, with his brother Valens, held imperial authority for eleven years.

Praise of Valentinian from Paul’s history: He was like Aurelian—handsome in appearance, ingenious in mind, serious in character, stern, forceful, hostile to vices, and especially hostile to avarice; skilled at painting most beautifully, devising new arms, and making likenesses in wax or clay; most polished in speech, prudent, and astute.

Valens, together with Gratian and Valentinian, sons of his aforesaid brother, reigned four years. Valens, baptized by Arians, persecuted Catholics. By a law commanding monks to serve as soldiers, he ordered those unwilling to do so to be beaten to death. The people of the Huns, long shut away in inaccessible mountains, suddenly stirred by a mad fury, burst forth against the Goths and drove them, scattered and distressed, from their ancient homes. The Goths fled across the Danube and were received by Valens without laying down their arms. Soon, however, through the avarice of the commander Maximus, they were compelled by hunger to rebel. Having defeated Valens’s army, they spread through Thrace, laying all things waste at once with slaughter, fire, and plunder.

Gratian, with his brother Valentinian, reigned six years from the three hundred and seventy-seventh year after the Incarnation of the Lord, although he had long already reigned with his uncle Valens. Seeing the commonwealth’s condition afflicted and almost ruined, he clothed Theodosius, a Spaniard, in the purple at Sirmium because the state needed restoration, and at once entrusted him with the empire of the East and Thrace. Theodosius accordingly defeated in many great battles those mighty Scythian peoples—that is, the Alans, Huns, and Goths.

Meanwhile Maximus, a native of Britain, a vigorous man indeed and worthy of praise had he not emerged as a tyrant in Britain against the faith of his oath, was there made emperor and crossed into Gaul. There, by a sudden attack, he killed Gratian Augustus, whom he had terrified, and expelled Gratian’s brother Valentinian Augustus from Italy; Valentinian fled to Theodosius in the East.

Praise of Gratian: Gratian was quite well educated in letters: he could compose verse, speak ornamentally, and explain controversies in the manner of rhetoricians. Day and night he did nothing but practise with javelins, believing it the greatest pleasure and a divine art to strike what he had aimed at. He was sparing in food, and master of sleep and desire.

After Gratian’s death Theodosius reigned eleven years with Valentinian, whom he restored to his kingdom after shutting up and killing the tyrant Maximus within the walls of Aquileia. The Britons whom Maximus had brought with him remained in Armorican Gaul down to the present day; hence they are called Armorican Britons. Britain, stripped of them, withered away.

Praise of Theodosius: Theodosius was an outstanding enlarger and defender of the commonwealth. In character and body he resembled Trajan, as the writings and portraits of the ancients show, and from him he also derived his lineage: the same towering stature, the same limbs, similar hair, though his eyes were not so large. I do not know whether he had such grace and bloom of countenance or such dignity in walking; but his mind was altogether similar, so much so that nothing can be said which does not seem transferable to this man from the books. Merciful and approachable, he believed that he differed from others only by his dress; he was respectful toward all men, though more lavishly toward the good. He loved simple minds, admired learned ones, provided they were harmless, and gave great gifts with a great spirit.

Yet he so detested the things with which Trajan was charged—namely drunkenness and the desire for triumph—that he did not initiate wars but found them already begun. By law he prohibited wanton attendants and female psalm-singers from being used at banquets. Moderately educated in letters, he was plainly shrewd and very diligent in learning the deeds of his ancestors. When he read of the arrogance of rulers, he abhorred it, especially in the treacherous and ungrateful. He could be angry at things unworthy of endurance, yet was quickly appeased; and, a virtue rare indeed, after his imperial power had increased with the years, he restored from his own resources to many persons weights of gold and silver taken away by tyrants. He treated his uncle as a father and nephews and relatives as sons. He gave elegant and cheerful, though not expensive, banquets; he mingled conversation appropriate to persons and ranks, speaking with pleasant gravity. He was an affectionate father and a harmonious husband. He maintained his health through restraint in eating and moderate walking. His gentleness among men and his devotion toward God were both supreme.

Arcadius, son of Theodosius, ruled with his brother Honorius thirteen years. The Goths attacked Italy, while Vandals and Alans attacked Gaul. Pelagius the Briton and Julian of Campania spread their heresy far and wide. Saint Augustine, as did the other orthodox Fathers, answered them with many thousands of Catholic arguments; yet they could not correct their madness. Worse still, their insanity, when rebuked, chose to increase through opposition rather than to be reformed by favouring truth. Hence Prosper the rhetorician says in verse:

> Against Augustine, it is said, there creeps a certain writer  
> Whom devouring envy has long consumed.  
> Either the Britons of the sea fear him for his fruit,  
> Or his heart swells with Campanian grass.

Honorius, with the younger Theodosius, son of his brother Arcadius, ruled fifteen years. In his time, while Alans, Suebi, and Vandals raged throughout all Gaul, Gratian, a municipal official, was made tyrant in Britain and killed. In his place Constantine was chosen from the lowest military rank, merely because of hope attached to his name and without any merit of courage. As soon as he seized imperial power, he crossed into Gaul. There he was repeatedly deceived by barbarians through unreliable treaties, to the great harm of the commonwealth.

Soon afterwards, at Honorius’s command, Count Constantius set out for Gaul with an army, shut Constantine up in the city of Arles, captured him, and killed him. Constantine’s son Constans, whom he had made Caesar from being a monk, was killed by his own count Gerontius at Vienne. It happened that Alaric, king of the Goths, invaded and captured Rome in the one thousand one hundred and sixty-fourth year from its foundation. Having burned part of it, he left the plundered city on the sixth day, nearly four hundred and seventy years after Julius Caesar had subjected Britain to himself.

The Romans lived within the rampart—which we have recalled that Severus made across the island—on the southern side, as the cities, bridges, lighthouses, and roads made there still testify today. They also possessed by right of dominion the more remote parts of Britain and even the islands beyond Britain.

Britain, therefore, stripped of its military forces and flourishing youth—which had chiefly been taken away by the tyrant Maximus, and afterwards its remnants by the recently mentioned Constantine—lay exposed as prey only to the most savage peoples, the Scots and Picts. These are separated from the Britons by two intervening inlets of the sea, one extending far inland from the eastern sea and the other from the western, though they cannot connect with one another (pertinere; variant: pertingere, “reach”). The eastern inlet has in its midst the city of Guidi; above the western—that is, on its right—lies the city of Aldclyhit, which in their language means “Rock of Clyhit”; it is beside a river of that name.

Because of the attacks of these peoples, the Britons sent envoys to Rome with letters begging for aid. A legion was immediately dispatched; it struck down a great multitude of the enemy and drove the rest from the borders. It then returned home in great triumph, instructing the Britons to build a wall above Severus’s rampart, so that where the protection of water was lacking, the defence of the rampart might be present. But the Britons built a wall of turf rather than stone and set up something of no use. The traces of that very broad and very high rampart are still visible today. It begins at a distance of nearly two thousand paces from the place called Peneltune and ends westward near the city of Adclyhit.

But when the former enemies saw that the Roman soldiers had departed, they immediately came in ships and attacked more fiercely. At the Britons’ entreaty, the Romans returned once more, drove the defeated enemy beyond the seas, and, joining with the Britons, placed a wall from sea to sea, not as before out of turf but out of stone. On the southern coast as well, because an enemy was feared from that direction, they set towers at intervals to watch the sea. Thus they bade farewell to their allies as men who would return no more, saying that they could no longer be wearied by such arduous expeditions.

When the Romans had returned home, the enemies attacked more fiercely and occupied the part of the island as far as the wall. Then they destroyed the wall and the adjoining towns; afterwards they ravaged the country far within the wall, so that the Britons themselves, through robbery and plundering, might moderate their famine, until the entire region was emptied of every support of food except the consolation of hunting.

Praise of Honorius: In character and religion Honorius was not greatly unlike his father Theodosius. In his time, although many foreign and civil wars arose, they came to rest with either no bloodshed or very little.

Theodosius II, called the Younger, lost control of Britain. He ruled the Romans for twenty-eight years. In the twenty-third year of his reign Aetius, an illustrious man, held the consulship with Symmachus. To him the remnant of the Britons sent a letter, whose opening ran, “To Aetius, consul for the third time.” In it they set forth their miseries thus: “The barbarians drive us to the sea; the sea drives us back to the barbarians. Between these arise two kinds of death: we are either slaughtered or drowned.” Yet by doing this they could obtain no assistance from him, since at that time he was occupied with very grievous wars against Bledda and Attila, kings of the Huns. Although in the preceding year Bledda, Attila’s own brother, had been killed through treachery, Attila himself remained so intolerable an enemy of the commonwealth that he was ravaging almost all Europe, its cities and fortresses being destroyed and overrun. Moreover, at the same time famine invaded Constantinople, and pestilence followed without delay; many portions of that city’s wall, together with fifty-six towers, fell. When many cities had likewise collapsed, famine and the pestilential stench of the air destroyed many thousands of people and beasts of burden. The aforementioned famine afflicted Britain also, as it did the other provinces.

Then the Britons, seeing that human help failed, invoked divine aid. The Lord Almighty had compassion on them and tested them, and put strength into their arms and sharpness into their swords. Therefore they sprang out from the mountains, hiding-places, and forests, and, rushing upon the Scots and Picts from every side, began unceasingly to strike them down and overthrow them. The enemies no longer recognized themselves in their blows, nor did they now trust in the protection of their weapons—arms which, of course, had become like garments for the Britons. Thus the hearts of the enemies melted; their strength dissolved, and in terror they fled. An innumerable slaughter was therefore made among them. The Scots returned to Ireland in disgrace. The Picts then first, and thereafter, remained quiet in the furthest part of the island. And the Lord gave victory to His people, and those who confounded them were confounded.

At this time, namely in the eighth year of Theodosius, Palladius was sent by Pope Celestine to the Scots, to become their first bishop.

[Col. 0822D] Theodosius also lost control of Gaul, Spain, and Africa. For the nations of the Vandals, Alans, and Goths had seized and destroyed everything by sword and fire. But the blessed Augustine, bishop of Hippo, lest he should see the ruin of his city, departed to the Lord in the third month of its siege, while the most cruel Geiseric was besieging it.

When the Britons had thus gained victory and been granted peace, the Lord sent them an ineffable abundance of crops, such as no past age remembered: so that, as triumph had relieved their former humiliations, so abundance might relieve the aforementioned famine. And God tested whether complete prosperity would make grateful those whom no adversity had made amend their ways. But then they surpassed all their former crimes, raging in luxury [Col. 0823A] and beginning, without regard for God, to indulge every plague of wickedness. At last cruelty, hatred, and the love of falsehood blazed up among them to such a degree that, if any one of them seemed gentler and in any measure nearer to truth, against him, as though he were the destroyer of Britain, all their hatred and weapons were hurled without restraint. Nor did secular men alone act thus, but the very flock of the Lord and its shepherds as well: through drunkenness, violence, litigation, strife, envy, and other crimes of this sort, they bent their necks beneath these things, having cast off the light yoke of Christ.

Therefore the Lord looked upon them, and, stirred to anger, crushed these men of corrupted mind with a bitter pestilence. In a short time it laid low so great a multitude that the living were not even sufficient to bury the dead. Yet neither the death of their own people nor fear of death could recall those who survived [Col. 0823B] from the death of the soul, by which they were cast down through sinning. Therefore, by a just and manifest [Col. 0824A] judgment, God determined to exterminate that nation, and immediately commanded the instruments of His wrath—the Scots and Picts. They came more angrily than usual to avenge their slaughter, and rushed upon the Britons like wolves upon lambs; they recognized themselves in their blows, and the Britons in their flight.

Accordingly, as was their custom, the Britons again resorted to hiding-places, forests, and wooded valleys. Afterwards they took counsel what should be done and where help ought to be sought, in order to avoid or repel such savage and frequent invasions by the northern peoples. It pleased them all, together with their king Vortigern, to summon the Saxon people from overseas regions as auxiliaries. It is clear that this was arranged by the will of the Lord, so that evil might come upon the wicked, as the event’s outcome [Col. 0824B] more plainly proved.

## BOOK II

[Col. 0823]

[Col. 0823B] In what precedes, forty-five emperors have been discussed, who ruled both Britain and the other parts of the world. If any of them attain glory in heaven, they have that alone, because here they now have none. For discourse about them has become worthless, and a prolonged telling of their deeds seems [Col. 0823C] bitter, generating weariness and loathing. Therefore let us consider, by comparison with those whose power and majesty scarcely found the whole world sufficient, how insignificant are our glory, our power, and our pride, for whose sake we labour, sweat, and go mad. But if we desire glory—speaking in human terms—I grant that we may desire it, but let it be true glory; if fame, let it be fame that does not vanish; if honour, let it be honour that does not wither. Not such as the aforesaid emperors possessed, whose entire glory is now nothing but worthless remnants of tales. We shall possess true glory, fame, and honour if we rest with gladness and joy upon Him who alone is true; if we place all our hope and trust [Col. 0823D] in God, not in the sons of men—as did the Britons, who, having cast aside God and the majesty of His fear, sought aid from pagans and received aid such as they deserved.

For the people of the Saxons or Angles, invited by the aforesaid king, arrived in Britain in three long ships in the year of grace 449, while Martian and Valentinian, whose reign lasted seven years, were ruling, in the twenty-fourth year after the Frankish kingdom had begun. Its first king was Pharamundus. The Saxons were assigned a place to remain in the eastern part of the island by order of that king, as if they were to fight for the country, though in reality they were to conquer it. They joined battle with the Picts and Scots, who had already come as far as Stamford, situated in the [Col. 0824B] southern part of Lincolnshire, forty miles distant from it. While the latter fought with javelins and spears, the former fought most fiercely with axes and long swords. The Picts could not bear so great a force, but sought safety in flight. The victorious Saxons won triumph and plunder.

When the news was brought to Saxony, along with word of the island’s fertility and the Britons’ indolence, a larger fleet immediately sent a stronger body of armed men there. Joined to the force sent ahead, it made an invincible army. Those who arrived received from the Britons a place of habitation among them, on the condition that they should fight against their enemies for the peace and safety of the country, while the Britons should provide the soldiers with their due pay.

They came from the three strongest peoples of Germany: the Saxons, Angles, and Jutes. From Jutish stock came the Kentish people and the Victuarii: this is the people that holds the island of Wight, and that which to this day is called the nation of the Jutes in the province of the West Saxons, situated opposite the island of Wight itself. [Col. 0824D] From the Saxons—that is, from the people [variant: region] now called the Old Saxons—came the East Saxons, South Saxons, and West Saxons. From the Angles (that is, from the country called Angulus, “the Angle,” which has remained deserted from that time to this day and is said to lie between the provinces of the Jutes and Saxons) sprang the East Angles, the Middle Angles, the Mercians, all the race of the Northumbrians—that is, the peoples dwelling north of the river Humber—and the remaining peoples of the Angles.

Their first leaders are said to have been two brothers, Hengist and Horsa. They were sons of Widgils, son of Wicta, son of Wecta, son of Woden, son of Frealof, son of Fredulf, son of Fin, son of Flocwald, son of Jeta, whom they called the son of a god—that is, of some idol. From the lineage of these forefathers [Col. 0825A] the royal houses of many provinces took their origin. Soon, therefore, as crowds of the peoples named above poured eagerly into the island, the population of the newcomers began to grow so greatly that they became a terror even to the native inhabitants who had summoned them. Some say that King Vortigern, fearing their strength, took Hengist’s pagan daughter as his wife. It is also said that, to complete his condemnation, he took his own daughter and begot a son by her; on this account he was excommunicated by St Germanus and the entire assembly of bishops.

King Vortigern’s son-in-law and his army, seeking an occasion for war by God’s will, demanded that provisions be supplied to them more abundantly. They threatened that, unless a more lavish supply of food were given, they would break the treaty and devastate all [Col. 0825B] parts of the island. Nor were they slow to carry their threats into effect. Having made a treaty with the Picts and assembled an innumerable army, they found nowhere anyone who dared stand against them.

The fire kindled by the hands of pagans exacted just vengeance for the sins of God’s people, not unlike the fire once kindled by the Chaldeans which consumed the walls—indeed, all the buildings—of Jerusalem. Thus here too, while the impious victor acted, or rather while the just Judge ordained it, the fire, devastating every neighbouring city and field, continued from the eastern sea to the western without anyone stopping it, and covered nearly the entire surface of the perishing island. Public and private buildings alike fell; priests were slaughtered everywhere among the altars; [Col. 0825C] bishops with their people were consumed alike by sword and flame, without any regard for rank; and there was no one to commit them, cruelly slain, to burial.

Accordingly, some who were seized in the mountains were slaughtered; others, worn out by hunger, came forth and surrendered themselves to the enemy, about to undergo perpetual slavery in return for relief in food—if only they were not immediately slaughtered. Others sorrowfully made for lands beyond the sea. Others, remaining in their homeland, lived in fear and poverty in mountains, forests, or steep rocks, their minds always apprehensive. King Vortigern, hated by all, lived in the western part of Britain among precipitous mountains and forests. It is said that, when the king refused to hear the preaching of St Germanus and fled from the saint who followed him, one night fire fell from heaven upon the fortress in which the king was. The king, destroyed both by the collapse and by the fire, was nowhere found.

But when the Saxons, after dispersing the natives, had sent their surplus forces home, the Britons, emerging from their hiding-places, began to recover strength and courage. They assembled a very great army and marched their standards into Kent against Hengist and Horsa. At that time they had as their leader Ambrosius Aurelianus, a modest man, who perhaps alone of the Roman race had survived that aforementioned storm, his parents—who bore the name and insignia of kings—having been killed in it. With him were Vortigern’s two sons, Gortimer and Catiger, as commanders. Ambrosius led the first battle-line, Gortimer the second, and Catiger [Col. 0826A] the third. Horsa and Hengist, though much fewer in number, nevertheless met them with the greatest boldness, and the two brothers directed two battle-lines against the enemy.

In the seventh year after the Saxons’ arrival in England, a battle was fought at Aylesford. At the outset Horsa struck Catigern’s line with such force that it was thrown down, scattered in a great cloud of dust, and the king’s son fell slain. But his brother Gortimer, a man truly valiant, attacked from the flank and broke Horsa’s line. Horsa himself, bravest of men, having been killed, the remnants of his troop fled to Hengist, who was fighting invincibly against Ambrosius’ wedge of troops. Thus the whole weight of battle fell upon Hengist. Hemmed in by Gortimer’s valour, after holding out for a long time he was defeated, not without great loss to the Britons, and fled—he who had never fled before.

Some wrote that Hengist fought against them three times later in the same year and could not withstand Gortimer’s valour and the number of the Britons; that he fled once to the island of Thanet and once to his ships, and sent home for replacements for those who had left.

In the following year, under the Emperor Leo, who reigned seventeen years, Gortimer, the flower of young men, died of illness. With him the Britons’ hope and victory were extinguished. Hengist and his son Æsc, having received aid from their homeland and relying on the young man’s death, prepared for war at Crayford. The Britons, however, set forth four very large divisions, fortified by four most valiant commanders, for battle. But when the Britons entered into the game of war, they bore badly the Saxons’ greater-than-usual numbers. For the newcomers, who had arrived as chosen men, horribly split the Britons’ bodies with axes and swords. Yet the Britons did not yield until they saw their four commanders overthrown and slain. Then, more terrified than can be believed, they fled from Kent as far as London, and afterwards never dared come into Kent [Col. 0826C] to fight. Thereafter Hengist and his son Æsc reigned in Kent. Thus the kingdom of Kent began in the eighth year after the Angles’ arrival.

About this time Germanus, bishop of Auxerre, a man renowned for holiness and miracles, and Lupus, bishop of the city of Troyes, came into Britain to destroy the Pelagian heresy. [Col. 0826D] Having defeated its adherents by argument before all the people, Germanus, to confirm his reasoning, healed the tribune’s daughter, who had been blind for ten years. Moreover, he saved from a fire raging all around and consuming the buildings joined to it the little dwelling in which he lay sick. Seeking the tomb of St Alban, he placed there relics of various martyrs, and took away a mass of dust still red with the martyr’s blood, intending to carry it with him. In that place he converted an innumerable crowd of people to the Lord on that same day.

Meanwhile the Saxons and Picts joined their forces in war against the Britons. The frightened Britons sought the help of St Germanus. Arriving, the saint declared himself commander of the battle. Therefore, in a valley enclosed among mountains, opposite the direction from which the enemy’s arrival was expected, he himself, as leader of the column, arranged the army. The fierce multitude of enemies was already at hand, and scouts saw them approaching. Then the saint, suddenly acting as standard-bearer, warned all to answer his voice with one shout. The priests cried out “Alleluia” three times, while the enemies, confident that they would come upon them unexpectedly, were unsuspecting; [Col. 0827A] all the people followed with one voice, and the echo, confined by the mountains and rebounding through the air, multiplied their loud cry.

The hostile force was struck down in terror. They trembled at the rocks surrounding them, and even at the very fabric of heaven above them. As the fugitives scarcely thought the swiftness of their feet sufficient, they fell everywhere, cast away their weapons, and rejoiced if only they had rescued their bare bodies from danger. Many, blinded by fear, were swallowed by the river they had crossed. The innocent army looked upon its vengeance and joyfully gathered the spoils of its heavenly victory. The bishops triumphed: the enemies were routed, and victory was won without blood by faith, not by strength.

The blessed bishops, having overcome the enemies of mind and body, returned to their own homes. But not long afterwards, when the Pelagian heresy again sprouted up, Germanus returned at the prayers of all Britain’s priests with Severus, bishop of Trier. Restoring the true faith, he healed before all men the son of the chief Elafius [variant: Elavi], whose sinews and knee were contracted. When all had been successfully accomplished, he went thence to Ravenna to petition for peace for the Armorican people. There he was received with the highest reverence by Valentinian [variant: Valentian] and departed [Col. 0827C] to Christ. Not long afterwards Valentinian was killed by the retainers of Aetius the patrician, whom he had killed. The Britons had once sent the letter to Aetius, as we have said; and with Aetius the western empire fell together.

When reinforcements had arrived, after some time King Hengist and his son Æsc assembled a most invincible army in the seventeenth year after their arrival in England. Against them all Britain, having gathered its forces, set twelve nobly ordered divisions at Wippedesflede. The battle was long and fierce, until Hengist struck down the twelve leaders of the divisions and, after casting down their standards and driving their companies into disorder, forced them into flight. He himself, however, lost many leaders of his own and of his people, [Col. 0827D] including a great chieftain called Wipped, from whose name he named the battle-site as stated above. Their victory, then, was grievous and hateful, so that afterwards for no small time neither Hengist dared enter British territory nor the Britons dared enter Kent.

Thus, while foreign wars ceased in Britain, civil wars did not cease. Amid the destruction of cities ruined by the enemy, the citizens who had escaped the enemy fought one another. Yet, while the memory of the suffering inflicted was still fresh, kings, priests, commoners, and nobles each somehow kept their proper order. But when a younger generation had grown up, having experienced only the tranquillity of the present time, all the restraints of truth and justice were shaken and overturned, so that I will not say a trace of them, but not even their memory, appeared anywhere save among a few—and very few. [Col. 0828A] Therefore God sent, over the succession of time, several most ferocious leaders from Germany to destroy the people hateful to God. First came the leader Ælle and his three sons, Cymen, Pleting, and Cissa.

Ælle, with his sons and a fleet most fully equipped with military forces, landed in Britain at Cymenesore. When the Saxons disembarked from the sea, the Britons raised a cry, and innumerable people came running from the surrounding places; battle began at once. The Saxons, very great in stature and strength, received them rashly; but the Britons came rashly. For, arriving scattered and at intervals, they were slain by men massed together; and as each came in bewilderment, he unexpectedly encountered ominous reports. Therefore the Britons were put to flight as far as the nearest wood, called Andredesleige. The Saxons occupied the seacoasts in Sussex, taking ever more territory for themselves, until the ninth year after their arrival. Then, when they were more boldly advancing farther into the region, the British kings and tyrants assembled at Mercredesburne and fought against Ælle and his sons. Victory was nearly uncertain: each army, badly injured and diminished, praying for the other’s defeat, returned home.

Ælle therefore sent to his compatriots [Col. 0828C] to request help. The year in which Ælle came into England was about the thirtieth from the Angles’ arrival, the forty-second [year after that arrival; the chronology is uncertain as printed].

King Hengist of Kent died in the fortieth year after his arrival in Britain. His son Æsc reigned in his place for thirty-four years, in the time of Emperor Zeno, whose reign was seventeen years. Æsc, by inherited valour, powerfully maintained his fatherland against the Britons and enlarged his kingdom at the expense of theirs.

The kingdom of Sussex begins, which Ælle held for a long time and most powerfully. Auxiliaries from his homeland had come to him in the third year after Hengist’s death, in the time of Anastasius, emperor of the Romans, who reigned twenty-seven years. Relying on immense forces, he besieged the strongly fortified city of Anderida. The Britons gathered like bees; by day they attacked the besiegers with ambushes, and by night with raids. There was neither day nor night in which grievous and fresh reports did not embitter the Saxons’ spirits. Yet they became more ardent and harassed the city with continual assaults. Whenever they attacked, however, the Britons pressed them from behind with archers and missiles fitted with thongs. The pagans therefore turned their steps and weapons away from the walls against the Britons. Then the Britons, superior in speed, ran to the forests; and, when the Saxons again moved toward the walls, they reappeared behind them. By this tactic the Saxons were wearied for a long time, and an innumerable slaughter of them took place, until they divided their army into two parts: while one part stormed the city, the other stood drawn up behind them against the raiding battle-lines of the Britons. [Col. 0829A]

Then at last the citizens, crushed by prolonged famine and unable any longer to bear the weight of their assailants, were all consumed by the sword, women and little children included, so that not one person escaped. Because the foreigners had suffered such losses there, they destroyed the city so completely that it was never rebuilt afterwards. Only the site, desolate, is shown to passers-by as that of a once most noble city.

In the forty-seventh year after the Angles’ arrival, Cerdic and his son Cynric came with five ships to Cerdicesford. On the same day a multitude from the region assembled and battle was fought against them. The Saxons stood motionless in close formation before their ships; the islanders boldly rushed against them and returned without pursuit, for the newcomers never left their position. [Col. 0829B] Thus they fought by rushing forward and returning until the darkness of night ended the contest. Finding the Saxons formidable, the Britons withdrew, and neither side gained victory. Yet Cerdic and his son, lodging in hostile territory, began increasingly to occupy the coastal districts, not without frequent wars.

In the seventh year after Cerdic’s arrival, Port and his two sons, Beda and Megla, came in two great ships to Portsmouth, and immediately a great outcry filled the entire province. The leader of the province and the whole multitude entered the battle; without order, as each arrived, they perished in the blink of an eye. For boldness drove the Britons [Col. 0829C] against the enemy, but the enemy’s strength turned their rashness to confusion. The leader and people having been killed or put to flight, Port—after whom Portsmouth is named—and his two sons gained the victory.

I shall write of the battle which Nazaleod, the greatest king of the Britons, fought against Cerdic and his son Cynric, in the sixtieth year after the Angles’ arrival. Nazaleod was a man of great name and great pride; the region was named Nazaleoi from him, and is now called Cerdicesford. Having assembled all the multitude of Britain, Cerdic and his son, in their utmost need, requested help from Æsc, king of Kent, from Ælle, the great king of the South Saxons, and from Port and his sons, who had recently arrived. They set two battle-lines in the field: Cerdic commanded one and his son Cynric [variant: Cenric] the other. Cerdic commanded the right wing, Cynric the left.

When battle began, King Nazaleod saw that the right wing was the stronger and rushed upon it with all his forces, so that the strongest part might first be overthrown. The standards were cast down and the line pierced; Cerdic turned to flight, and a very great slaughter of his line was made in a moment. But Cynric, seeing that the right wing led by his father had been destroyed, rushed into the rear of the pursuers. The battle became exceedingly fierce; King Nazaleod fell, his men turned to flight, and five thousand of them were slain. Swiftness was a protection to the rest. The Saxons therefore gained the advantage of victory, and peace was granted them [Col. 0830A] for not many years; strong and numerous helpers came to them.

In the sixth year after the aforesaid battle, Cerdic’s nephews Stuf and Wihtgar came with three ships to Cerdicesford. At first light the British commanders arranged their battle-lines against them most skilfully, according to the rules of war. Part of their force advanced in the hills and part in the valley, cautiously and deliberately. When the rising sun appeared, its rays struck their gilded shields; the hills shone from them, and the surrounding air gleamed more brightly. The Saxons were seized by great fear and moved toward battle. When the very powerful armies clashed, the Britons’ strength was scattered, because God had rejected them. A clear victory resulted, [Col. 0830B] and the aforesaid commanders gained no few territories. Through them Cerdic’s power became terrible and passed through the land with grievous force.

About this time Ælle, king of the South Saxons, died. He held under his dominion all the authorities of the English kingdom—namely kings, nobles, and tribunes. His son Cissa reigned after him, and then their descendants. But in the course of time they were greatly diminished, until they came under the authority of other kings.

The kingdom of Wessex begins in the seventy-first year after the Angles’ arrival, in the year 519 from the Incarnation of the Lord, during the time of Justin, called the Elder, who ruled eight years. In the course of time this kingdom subdued all the others to itself and acquired the monarchy of all [Col. 0830C] Britain. For that reason it is fitting to connect the dates of all other kingdoms with these kings, so that, as their power grew, the times of the kingdoms may be recognized through them.

Cerdic reigned seventeen years in Wessex. In that same year the strongest of the Britons made war against him at Cerdicesford. Their commanders stood courageously and fiercely on both sides until, as the day was already declining toward evening, the Saxons gained victory, and on that day a great slaughter was made among the inhabitants of Albion. It would have been far more dreadful had not the setting sun prevented it. Cerdic’s name was enlarged, and the fame of his and his son Cynric’s battles spread through the whole [Col. 0830D] land. From that day began the kingdom of the West Saxons, which endures to our own times, all other kingdoms having been claimed for itself.

In the ninth year of his reign Cerdic and his son Cynric again fought the Britons at Cerdicesford, and there was great slaughter on both sides. At that time many men came often from Germany and occupied East Anglia and Mercia, though these had not yet been brought under a single king. Many nobles eagerly seized territories, and hence innumerable wars arose; but because the nobles were many, they lack names.

Arthur, a warrior, in those times fought most invincibly against them as commander of the Britons’ soldiers and kings. He was battle-leader twelve times, and victor in battle twelve times [variant: “of battles”]. His first battle against them was beside the mouth of the river called Glenus [variant: Glemu]. His second, third, fourth, and fifth battles were upon another river, called in British *Dulgas* [variant: *Duglas*], which is in the region of Iniis. His sixth battle was on the river called Bassas. His seventh battle against them was in the forest of Celidon, called in British *Cattoit Celidon*. His eighth battle against the barbarians was near the fortress of Guinnion. In it Arthur himself carried upon his shoulders the image of Saint Mary, Mother of God and ever-virgin; and throughout that day, through the power of our Lord Jesus Christ and Saint Mary His mother, the Saxons were turned to flight, and many of them perished in a great slaughter.

His ninth [Col. 0831B] battle was in the city of Leogis, called in British *Kaerlion*. His tenth battle was on the bank of the river which we call Tracteheuroit. His eleventh was on the mountain called Brevoin, where he put them to flight, which we call Cathbregion [variant: Catheregio]. Arthur fought his twelfth and fiercest battle against the Saxons at Mount Badon. In it, by his assault, 440 men fell in one day, with no Briton joining him in assistance, the Lord alone strengthening him.

Gildas the historian recounts these battles and battle-sites. Yet all these places are unknown in our age. We think that this came about through God’s providence, to disdain popular applause, flattering praise, and fleeting fame. Meanwhile, many battles took place everywhere, in which now the Saxons, now the Britons were victorious. Yet the more Saxons were struck down, the more came to their assistance, invited from all the surrounding lands.

The kingdom of Essex—that is, of the East Saxons—begins. It was first held, as is thought, by Erchenwin, insofar as we may infer from ancient writings. He was son of Ossa, son of Biedcan, son of Sigewlf, son of Spoewe, son of Gesac, son of Andesc, son of Saxnat. After Erchenwin, his son Sledda reigned. Sledda married the daughter of Ermericus, king of Kent, that is, Æthelbert’s sister, and by her begot Sæberht [variant: Siberct], who was the first of the kings of Essex to be converted to the faith.

[Col. 0831D] Cerdic and his son Cynric, having assembled immense forces, fought at Wihtland. Having won the battle, they took the island and made an innumerable slaughter of enemies at Wihtgarabyrg in the thirteenth year of their reign. In the fourth year after this they gave the same island, which in Latin is called Vecta, to their two nephews Stuf and Wihtgar.

Cerdic, the first king of Wessex, died after reigning eighteen years, and his son Cynric reigned after him for twenty-six years, while Justinian ruled at Rome. He ruled thirty-eight years, in the time of Pope Vigilius.

In the fifth year of Cynric’s reign the sun was darkened from morning until the third hour, in the month of March. In the seventh year of his reign [Col. 0832A] the sun was darkened from the third hour almost to the ninth, so that the stars appeared. On the twelfth day before the Kalends of July, in the tenth year of his reign, Wihtgar died and was buried at Wihtgarabyrg, which is so called from him.

The kingdom of Northumbria begins in the thirteenth year of Cynric’s reign. After the English nobles had subdued that land to themselves through many great battles, they appointed as their king the most noble young man Ida. He was son of Eoppe [variant: Coppe], son of Æsc [variant: Ese], son of Inguim, son of Argenwit, son of Aloc, son of Beonoc, son of Brand, son of Bældæg, son of Woden, son of Fredelaf, son of Fredeulf, son of Fin, son of Godwlf, son of Heata. He reigned very strongly for twelve years, always armed and labouring. He built Bamburgh [Col. 0832B] and first surrounded it with a hedge, then with a wall. This kingdom began in the year of grace 547.

In the eighteenth year of his reign King Cynric fought against the Britons, who had come with a very great army as far as Salisbury. Having gathered auxiliaries from every side, he met them most invincibly; after overwhelming great forces, he scattered them in every direction and put them to flight.

In the twenty-second year of his reign Cynric and his son Ceawlin [variant: Cheuling] again fought the Britons. The battle was fought thus. The Britons, as though to avenge the disgrace of the battle which they had endured about five years before, assembled men equipped for war with arms and numbers and drew up battle-lines at Barbury. [Col. 0832C] Having set nine divisions, a number most suitable for battle—three in the front, three in the middle, and three at the rear—with commanders appropriately placed in the divisions, and with archers, throwers of missiles, and cavalry deployed according to Roman practice, the Saxons, massed all together in a single line, rushed at them with the greatest boldness. After standards had collided and been thrown down and spears broken, they fought with swords, until, as evening came on, the victory remained uncertain. Nor should this seem surprising, since those men were of great stature, strength, and courage, whereas armies in our own time, made up of men now small in stature, strength, and courage, immediately put one another to flight in the very first clash.

[Col. 0832D] Cynric died after reigning twenty-six years, and his son Ceawlin reigned in his stead for thirty years. Likewise in the same year Ida, king of Northumbria, died, and Ælle reigned after him for thirty years, although he was not Ida’s son but the son of Iffa, son of Usefrea, son of Witgils, son of Westrefalena, son of Sefugil, son of Seabald, son of Sigegeat, son of Wepdeg, son of Woden, son of Fredealaf.

In the sixth year of Ceaulin [otherwise Cheuling] reigning over Wessex, Æthelbert, the great king, began to reign over Kent, in the time of the emperor Justin. He was in fact the third among the kings of the English nation to rule over all their southern provinces, which are separated from the northern peoples by the river Humber and the borders adjoining it. For the first to hold such an overlordship was Ælla, king of the South Saxons; the second, Ceaulin, king of the West Saxons; the third, as we have said, Æthelbert, king of the Kentish people; the fourth, Rædwald, king of the East Angles, who, even while Æthelbert was alive, exercised leadership over his own people; the fifth, Edwin, king of the Northumbrian nation, who with greater power than all ruled over the peoples of Britain, both English and Britons, except only the Kentish people, and moreover subjected to English rule the British islands of Mevania, situated between Ireland and Britain; the sixth, Oswald, most holy king of Northumbria, held the kingdom within the same boundaries; the seventh, his brother Oswiu, for no small time held the kingdom within almost equal limits. He also subdued in large measure the peoples of the Picts and Scots, who occupy the northern regions of Britain, and made them tributary. The eighth was Egbert [otherwise Egbriht], king of Wessex, who ruled as far as the Humber; the ninth, his grandson Alfred, who brought all parts of the kingdom under his authority; the tenth, Edgar, the grandson of Alfred’s grandson, a strong and peaceful king, who had both the English and the Scots either under dominion or altogether at his own pleasure, as did his heirs after him down to this day. In the time of King Æthelbert the English were converted to the faith; this will therefore be treated carefully in what follows.

In the ninth year of Ceaulin [otherwise Cheuling]’s reign, he and his brother Cutha [otherwise Chuta], men of the greatest boldness, compelled by various causes, fought against Æthelbert, who had entered their kingdom with arrogant forces. Entering battle at Wibbandun, they struck down in war his two ealdormen, namely Oslaf and Cnebba, and an innumerable multitude with them, and drove King Æthelbert in flight as far as Kent. This was the first war which kings of the English waged against one another.

In the twelfth year of Ceaulin, his brother Cutha fought against the Britons at Bædanford, now called Bedford, and now the chief town of the surrounding district. He fought and won, and by force of arms took four fortified places: namely Lienberig [otherwise Lienbirig], Aylesbury, Benson, and Eynsham. But Cutha, the king’s great brother, died in that same year.

[Col. 0833D] The kingdom of East Anglia begins, comprising Norfolk and Suffolk. Uffa was the first to hold this kingdom; from him the kings of the East Angles are called Uffings. It was afterwards held by his son Titulus [otherwise Titilus], father of Rædwald, the most powerful king of East Anglia.

In the eighteenth year of his reign Ceaulin and his son Cutwine fought against the Britons. Their three kings, Commagil, Candidan, and Farinmagil, drew up dense and splendid battle-lines against them according to the laws of war at Deorham [otherwise Deorham]. The battle was fought with the utmost strength; but the Lord Almighty gave victory to their enemies and cast down His own people, who had offended Him vainly. On that day the three aforesaid Christian kings fell, and the rest turned to flight. The Saxons, made terrible to them in pursuing them, seized for themselves three most distinguished cities: Gloucester, Cirencester, and Bath.

In the twenty-fifth year of his reign Ceaulin and Cutwine fought the Britons at Fedhanlea [otherwise Fedhalnea]. The battle was destructive and dreadful on both sides. Cutwine, overwhelmed by a great host, was struck down and killed. Thus the English were defeated and put to flight; but King Ceaulin, having again restored his army when his men had renounced flight, at last won as victor in battle, pursued the Britons, and took many districts and countless spoils.

The kingdom of Mercia begins, which Crida, as we may infer from writings, was the first to possess. Now, therefore, all the kingdoms of the English have begun. Their periods and changes, according as we find them in the books of the ancients, we shall set forth as distinctly as we can, comparing them nevertheless with the chronology of the kings of Wessex.

In the thirtieth year of his reign Ceaulin died, and Ceolric reigned after him for five years. Likewise, in the same year Ælla, king of the Northumbrians, died, and Æthelric reigned after him for five years. In the third year after this, Britons and Saxons made war at Wednesbury. While the Britons advanced their battle-lines in ordered Roman fashion, and the Saxons rushed upon them boldly and in confusion, a very great battle took place; and God granted victory to the Britons. The Saxons, however, who had customarily been so much more excellent in battle, became correspondingly more sluggish in flight and were severely crushed.

After these times Crida, king of Mercia, died, and his son Wibba succeeded him. About this time also, after Æthelric, Æthelfrith—called “the Fierce”—reigned over Northumbria. In these times the Lombards occupied Italy; and not long afterward Gregory directed the city of God toward England.

While Ceolric reigned over Wessex, Æthelfrith over Northumbria, and Wibba over Mercia, King Æthelbert of Kent and the Kentish people were converted to the faith, as we shall show in the following book. After Wibba reigned Ceorl [otherwise Keorl], who was not his son but his kinsman.

[Col. 0834D] Ceolric, having reigned five years, came to the end of life. After him Ceolwulf reigned over Wessex for fourteen years, and throughout all the days of his reign he fought either against the English, or against the Scots, or against the Picts. Ceolwulf was son of Cutha; Cutha, son of Cynric; Cynric, son of Cerdic.

In the seventh year of King Ceolwulf, the first year of the emperor Phocas, who ruled at Rome for eight years, Æthelfrith, the fierce king of the Northumbrians, strong and more desirous of glory than all the kings of the English, devastated the nation of the Britons. No commander, no king, had made more of their lands, after exterminating or subjugating the inhabitants, either tributary to the English nation or habitable by it. To him that saying could fittingly be applied: “Benjamin is a ravening wolf: in the morning he shall devour the prey, and at evening he shall divide the spoil” (Gen. 49).

Therefore Ædan [otherwise Aedan], king of the Scots who inhabit Britain, moved by his successes, came against him with an immense and strong army, but was defeated and fled away with a few men. For at the celebrated place called Degsastan almost his entire army was slain. In this battle also Theodbald, brother of Æthelfrith, was killed with the whole army which he himself commanded. From that time onward no king of the Scots dared come against the English nation in battle (Bede, Book I, final chapter).

In the ninth year of King Ceolwulf, the aforesaid King Æthelfrith fought the Britons and was victorious at Caerleon. Of this war, the greatest of wars, an account must be given in the book on the conversion of the English which follows this one.

Ceolwulf, amid many wars waged against many peoples, omitted for brevity, fought a most important battle against the South Saxons. In it both armies were unspeakably shattered; yet a more dreadful disaster befell the South Saxons.

Ceolwulf, having reigned fourteen years, ceased to be a man. Cynegils then reigned after him over Wessex for thirty-one years, in the time of the emperor Heraclius, who ruled for twenty-six years.

Cynegils was son of Ceola [otherwise Ceolric], son of Cutha, son of Cynric, son of Cerdic. In the fourth year of his reign he took his brother [otherwise son] Cwichelm into partnership in the kingdom, and they went to war against the Britons at Beandun. Thus, the companies, wedges, and battle-lines having been arranged, while centurions, ealdormen, and leaders on either side presided over them according to established custom, battle began. When the lines met each other terribly and splendidly, with banners lowered, at the very first collision horror seized the Britons. Fearing the array of the great glittering axes and the long spears, they fled at the beginning, though late they gained possession [of the field; reading uncertain]. The Saxons, therefore, victorious without loss to themselves, counted the Britons slain, and two thousand and sixty-two were found dead.

When Cynegils had reigned six years, Æthelbert, king of Kent, died, and his son Eadbald succeeded him. In the following year King Æthelfrith of Northumbria and Rædwald, king of East Anglia, provoked one another and met with numerous armies. Battle was fought in the borders of Mercia, on the eastern side of the river called the Idle; hence the saying: “The river Idle was stained with the blood of Englishmen.”

King Æthelfrith the Fierce, scorning and wondering that anyone dared resist him, rushed upon the enemy with chosen soldiers accustomed to war, very boldly indeed, but without order, although Rædwald’s battle-lines were elegantly arranged and terrible in appearance. For bristling with helmets and spears, and adorned with innumerable banners, they advanced in three ranks, and greatly outnumbered their enemies. Yet the king of the Northumbrians, falling suddenly upon the massed wedges as though he had found prey, struck down with swords Rægenhere, the king’s son, together with his entire battle-line, and sent him before himself to hell. Rædwald, however, not terrified by so great a disaster but made more wrathful, stood invincibly with two battle-lines. Since the Northumbrians were impenetrable to them, Æthelfrith, breaking through the wedges, advanced far beyond his strength and far from his own men, and was struck down amid a great slaughter of the enemy. Thus, their king lost, his entire army fled.

Edwin succeeded him in the kingdom and later became a Christian. So great was the peace in Britain in King Edwin’s time, wherever his rule extended, that a woman with a newborn child could safely walk from sea to sea. Beside clear springs along the roads, the king had bronze cups hung upon posts for the refreshment of travellers; and no one, either from greatness of fear, dared touch them, or from love, wished to do so. Everywhere banners were carried before the king; and through the streets that kind of standard which the Romans call a *tufa* and the English call a *tuf* was customarily borne before him wherever he went.

When Cynegils had reigned sixteen years, he and Cwichelm, fighting against the aforesaid King Edwin—whom they had previously prepared to hand over to death by treachery—were justly slain [otherwise defeated], as will be said later. In the same year Penda the Valiant began to reign over Mercia, and he reigned for thirty years. Penda was son of Wibba, son of Crida, son of Cynewald, son of Cnibba [otherwise Cnida], son of Icel, son of Comer, son of Angelthean [otherwise Angeltheau], son of Offa, son of Wærmund, son of Witlac, son of Woden.

In the same year Sæberht, king of Essex, died, and his two sons succeeded to the kingdom. Not long afterward they fought against Cynegils and Cwichelm, boldly indeed, though with fewer men against more; but unsuccessfully. For each young man fell by the sword in battle, and from their whole army scarcely anyone could take flight, blocked by heaps of their own corpses and torrents of blood. Sigeberht, surnamed the Little, succeeded them; after him came Sigeberht, a holy man full of virtues, whom his own people killed by treachery.

In the third year after this Cynegils and Cwichelm fought against Penda at Cirencester, a great multitude having assembled on either side. Since each army, having renounced flight, stood fast invincibly, they were separated by the setting of the sun. But in the morning, seeing that both would be reduced to destruction if they engaged, they moderated their attacks on both sides and made peace.

When Cynegils had reigned twenty-three years, King Edwin was killed by Penda the Valiant; this event will be worthily and fully treated in the following book. In the following year the holy King Oswald gained the kingdom of Northumbria and reigned for nine years. In the year following that Cynegils was converted to the faith. In the next year Cwichelm, who reigned jointly with his brother Cynegils, was baptized and died in the same year.

In those same days Eorpwald [otherwise Carpwald], king of the East Angles and son of King Rædwald, was converted to the true faith. Soon after he was killed by Penda the Valiant, his brother and successor Sigeberht was converted through Bishop Felix, and with him the entire nation of the East Angles. In the fourth year after this Eadbald, king of Kent, died, having reigned twenty-three years. His son Erconberht [otherwise Erchenbriht] reigned after him for twenty-six years, in the time of the emperor Heraclonas [otherwise Eradonas], who ruled for two years.

Cynegils, having reigned thirty-one years, died in the time of the emperor Constantine, who had ruled for thirty-three [otherwise twenty-eight] years, namely the son of the earlier Constantine, who had reigned for half a year. Cynegils was succeeded by his son Cenwalh [otherwise Kenwalkius], who reigned over Wessex for thirty-one years, as his father had done. In the same year the holy King Oswald was killed, as will be stated in the following book, and his brother Oswi reigned after him for twenty-eight years.

In the fifth year of his reign Cenwalh was invaded by King Penda because he had dismissed Penda’s sister. But he could not resist him as his father had done; defeated in battle, he fled before him and was driven from his kingdom. After three years, however, when he had recovered his kingdom, Cenwalh gave to his kinsman and helper Ædred three thousand estates near Ashdown [otherwise Esesdune].

In these times Sigeberht, brother of Eorpwald, king of the East Angles, succeeded him as a servant of God. He clung so wholly to God that, committing the kingdom to his kinsman Ecgric [otherwise Egnice], he entered a monastery and received the tonsure. But after many years they compelled him to go out against King Penda; yet he bore nothing but a staff in his hand in battle. Thus he was killed together with King Ecgric and their whole army. Anna, son of Eni, of royal stock, a most excellent man and father of an excellent offspring, succeeded them.

When Cenwalh had reigned thirteen years, Penda the Valiant invaded Anna, the aforesaid king of the East Angles. To him that saying of Lucan might well be applied:

> Raging wholly toward arms, he rejoices  
> To have no paths except those made by bloodshed.

Thus he rose against the doomed army of King Anna; he rose and gnashed his teeth,

> As a wolf at the sheepfolds, lavish in unjust wrath,  
> Slaughters and devours the tender flock, not for their deserts;  
> His jaws drip with gore, his side flows everywhere with blood;  
> He stands fierce and does not depart until he has poured out all together.

Thus King Penda was borne upon his stunned neighbours. Therefore King Anna and his army were devoured by the mouth of the sword in a moment, so that scarcely anyone of them survived. Anna was succeeded by his brother Æthelhere. Soon after he was killed by King Penda, Æthelwald [otherwise Adelwold] succeeded to the kingdom. Having plundered that kingdom, Penda the Valiant turned his battle-lines and banners toward Northumbria.

When Cenwalh had reigned fourteen years, Penda, who killed others by the sword, was himself killed by the sword, according to the saying: “Whoever shall strike with the sword shall perish by the sword” (Matt. 26). He was struck down by King Oswiu at the river Winwæd. Hence it is said:

> At the river Winwæd was avenged the slaughter of Anna,  
> The slaughter of Kings Sigeberht and Ecgric,  
> The slaughter of Kings Oswald and Edwin.

His son Peada succeeded him. He was the first of the kings of Mercia to be baptized; with him, and through him, the people of the Mercian kingdom—also called Middle Anglia, that is, central England—were converted to the faith. But after he himself was killed a short time later, his brother Wulfhere reigned in his stead for twenty years, a man heir to his country’s valour. At that time also the king of Essex, that is, of the East Saxons, named Sigeberht, was baptized; he held the kingdom of that province after Sigeberht surnamed the Little.

In the seventeenth year of the reign of Cenwalh [otherwise Cenworth or Cenwalh], king of the West Saxons, he fought the Britons at Pen. Knowing that he had been defeated by Penda the Valiant and driven from his kingdom, and judging him less fit to bear the burden of battle, they gathered a great multitude and proudly entered the war. At the first collision the Britons somewhat drove back the English. But since the English feared flight more than death and persisted in striking back, the Britons were wearied, and their strength melted away like snow. They therefore turned their backs to their attackers and were driven from Pen as far as the Parrett; and on that day an incurable wound was inflicted upon the offspring of Brutus.

In the twentieth year of Cenwalh’s reign he fought differently against Wulfhere, king of Mercia and son of Penda. The Mercian king, using his native valour and good fortune, prevailed over his enemy in the chances of Mars. When the king of Wessex had been expelled from the field of Mars and chosen flight, Wulfhere crossed the enemy land with a great multitude, attacked and took the island of Wight beyond it. Through his efforts Æthelwealh [otherwise Edelwalkius], king of the South Saxons, was the first king there converted to the faith. Wulfhere gave him the island of Wight, received from the font, as a token of adoption; and, that he might convert the same island to the faith of Christ, he sent there the priest Eappa to preach. Yet the island could not then be converted.

In the third year after this the sun was darkened, on the third day of May; and this sign was followed by a most severe pestilence both in Britain and Ireland. In that year Erconberht, king of Kent, and Deusdedit, archbishop of Kent, died on one and the same day. Afterwards the son of the aforesaid king, Egbert, reigned over Kent for nine years. This King Egbert and King Oswi sent the priest Wighard [Bede: Wigard] to Rome to become archbishop; but he died there, and Pope Vitalian sent in his place the great Archbishop Theodore, of whose excellence an account will be given in its place.

In the twenty-ninth year of King Cenwalh, Oswi, the greatest king of Northumbria, died of illness. His son Ecgfrith reigned after him for fifteen years.

Cenwalh, having reigned thirty-one years, died. His wife Seaxburh reigned after him for one year. In the preceding year there was a very great battle of birds in England. That this may seem more credible, the same also happened in our own time in Normandy, under King Henry, who was the first of the kings of England so called. (This is specified because perhaps someone else in a future time will be called thus.) Birds fought openly near Rouen, so that thousands of birds were found killed and the foreign birds were seen to have fled. This, indeed, was a sign of the battle fought between Henry, lord of England and Normandy, and Louis, son of Philip, king of France. In that battle the strong King Henry proved victorious, and Louis, defeated, fled.

While Seaxburh reigned, Egbert, king of Kent, died, and Lothair succeeded to the kingdom. At that time Theodore also held a council at Thetford. Lothair, the son of the aforesaid king, reigned for twelve years.

Æscwine began to reign over Wessex, but his reign was brief, death cutting it short. In the second year of this king there was a most serious battle between him and Wulfhere, king of Mercia. The Mercian king, employing native and ancestral valour, was somewhat superior in battle; yet each army was terribly shattered, and many thousands on both sides were plunged into hell.

It is worthwhile to observe how worthless the deeds of men are, how worthless the glorious wars of kings and noble exploits. For, when the aforesaid kings had inflicted so great a calamity upon their people for the sake of display, pride, and empty glory, one of them, namely Wulfhere, perished of illness in the same year, while the other died in the next. After him Æthelred reigned over Mercia.

Æscwine, having reigned two years, was taken from life, and Cenwine reigned over Wessex for nine years. In that same year Æthelred, the new king of Mercia, rose against Lothair, king of Kent. But Lothair, fearing his native and ancestral valour, withdrew from his sight and did not come out to meet him. The Mercian king destroyed the city of Rochester, passed through the province of Kent, and carried away innumerable spoils.

In the third year of King Cenwine a comet appeared for three months and shone like the sun each morning (Bede, Book IV, ch.). In the following year Ecgfrith, king of Northumbria, and Æthelred, king of Mercia, fought a most severe battle near the Trent. There Ælfwine [Bede: Alwine], brother of King Ecgfrith, a young man much beloved by both provinces, was killed. For King Æthelred had married his sister, called Osthryth. Since the material of a fiercer war and a longer hostility between fierce kings and peoples seemed to have arisen, Theodore, the bishop beloved by God, aided by divine help, entirely extinguished by his saving exhortation the fire of so great a danger which had begun. Thus, once kings and peoples had been reconciled, no human life was demanded for the king’s slain brother, but only a due payment of money was given to the avenging king. The bonds of that peace endured for a long time thereafter between those kings and their kingdoms. In the same year Æthelthryth, who had been the wife of King Ecgfrith, but a perpetual virgin, died.

In the seventh year of his reign King Cenwine encountered the Britons and, victorious, drove them in ill resistance by violent slaughter and burning as far as the sea. About this time Theodore held a council at Hatfield.

When King Cenwine had died, Cædwalla came to the kingdom. He promptly caused the conquered island of Wight to be converted to the faith, to which he himself was later converted.

Thus all the kings of England had now become believers, and every region enjoyed the light and grace of Christ.

We have treated, as we think, in this book—which we call *On the Coming of the English*—the deeds of the English while still unbelieving, in a confused manner; and we have carried the account in order from the very invasion of Britain made by the Saxons, until the several kingdoms had been made illustrious by their kings and each king had been illuminated by the radiance of faith. Now, therefore, since this book, though brief in words, contains many deeds, events, and wars, it must be given an ending. For more careful writing is required in the following book: concerning the preachers—at whose exhortation, by what miracles, through what preaching, which kings, and in what order they converted to the faith of our Lord.
