These wars occurred in the time of fourteen emperors, over about 218 years: in the time of Marcian, who reigned seven years; of Leo, who reigned seventeen years; of Zeno, who likewise reigned seventeen years; of Anastasius, who reigned eighteen years; of Justin the Elder, who reigned eight years; of Justinian the Great, who reigned thirty-eight years; of Justin the Younger, who reigned eleven years; of Tiberius, who reigned seven years; of Maurice, who reigned twenty-one years; of Phocas, who reigned eight years; of Heraclius, who reigned twenty-six years; of Heraclonas, who reigned two years; of Constantine, who reigned half a year; and of Constantine his son, who reigned thirty-eight years.

Therefore, since the names of all the kings of England down to this point are scattered in confusion, if I briefly recapitulate them according to each kingdom, I shall, I think, prove not tedious but clearer and more pleasing to the reader.

The kings of Kent [otherwise Kentish kings] are these in order.

The first king, Hengist, won a kingdom for himself for eight years and afterwards reigned for thirty-two years. His son Oisc reigned gloriously for thirty-four years. Octa reigned obscurely for about twenty years. Eormenric likewise reigned for about twenty-five [otherwise ten] years. Æthelbert, son of Eormenric, the first Christian, reigned most splendidly for fifty [otherwise fifty-six] years. Eadbald, thirty-four. Erconberht, thirty-four. Egbert, nine. The ninth, Lothair, twelve.

The kings of Wessex are these in order. The first, Cerdic, in the seventy-first year from the coming of the English, reigned for seventeen years. Cynric, son of Cerdic, reigned twenty-six years. Ceuling [otherwise Cheuling], son of Cynric, reigned thirty years. Ceolric, son of Ceuling, reigned five years. Ceolwulf, son of Cutha, brother of Ceuling, reigned fourteen years. Cynegils, son of Ceola, son of Cutha, reigned thirty-one years and was the first to receive the faith. Cenwalh [otherwise Chenwalh], son of Cynegils, likewise reigned thirty-one years. Seaxburh [otherwise Sexburh], wife of Cenwalh, reigned one year. Æscwine, son of Cenwalh, reigned two years. Cenwine, kinsman of Æscwine, reigned nine years.

The kings of Essex are these in order: first Eschenwin [otherwise Erchewine]; Sledd; Sæberht [otherwise Seberth], the first to receive the faith; Sigeberht; Sibert; Swithelm; Sæbbi; Sigeheard.

The kings of Northumbria are these in order: first Ida; Ælla; Æthelfrith; Edwin, the first to receive the faith; Oswald; Oswi; Ecgfrith.

The kings of East Anglia are these in order: first Uffa; Titilus [otherwise Titulus]; Rædwald; Eorpwald, the first to receive the faith; Sigeberht; Egnicus; Anna; Æthelhere; Æthelwald; Aldwulf.

The kings of Mercia are these in order: first Crida; Wibba; Ceorl; Penda; Peada, the first to receive the faith; Wulfhere; Æthelred.

The kings of Sussex are these in order: first Ælle; Scisse.

The rest are concealed by the scarcity of writers or by obscure report, except King Æthelwald [Adelwold], who still rightly has a name, because he was the first to acknowledge the name of Christ. And these matters are concluded. See then, reader, and consider how many names have so quickly come to nothing. Attend, I pray, and strive, since nothing here endures, to acquire for yourself that kingdom and substance which shall not fail; that name and honour which shall not pass away; that memorial and glory which shall not grow old through any ages. To meditate beforehand on this is the height of wisdom; to acquire it, the height of shrewdness; to attain it, the height of blessedness.

## BOOK THREE

[Col. 0841D] In the year of grace 582, Maurice, the fifty-fourth emperor from Augustus, assumed the empire. In the fourteenth year of this ruler, the servant of God Gregory sent Augustine and several other monks with him to preach in England, about the one hundred and fiftieth year after the arrival of the English in Britain.

Obeying the pontiff’s commands, as they approached England they were struck, indeed, with very great fear. They considered returning home rather than approaching so savage a people, whose language they did not even know. Without delay they sent Augustine home—him whom Gregory had intended to ordain bishop over them if they were received by the English—that he might obtain from blessed Gregory, by humble supplication, that they should not undertake so dangerous, laborious, and uncertain a journey.

Gregory sent them a letter of encouragement, urging them to proceed with the work of the word in reliance upon divine help. The form of that letter is as follows:

> GREGORY, servant of the servants of God, to the servants of our Lord.
>
> Since it would have been better not to begin good things than, after they have been begun, to return in thought backward from them, you must, most beloved sons, with the utmost zeal complete the good work which, with the Lord’s help, you have begun. Let neither the toil of the journey nor the words of slanderous men deter you; but with all diligence and all fervour carry out, God being your author, what you have undertaken, knowing that great toil is followed by the greater glory of eternal recompense.
>
> In all things humbly obey Augustine your superior when he returns, whom we have appointed your abbot, knowing that whatever you fulfil at his admonition will profit your souls in every respect. May Almighty God protect you by His grace and grant that I may see in the eternal fatherland the fruit of your labour, so that, if I cannot labour with you, I may be found with you in the joy of recompense, because I desire, indeed, to labour. May God keep you safe, most beloved sons.
>
> Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of August, in the fourteenth year of the reign of our lord Maurice Tiberius, most pious Augustus, in the fourth indiction.

Strengthened, therefore, by the confirmation of the blessed Father, the preachers reached Britain. At that time Æthelberht was the most powerful king in Kent, and he had extended the boundaries of his dominion as far as the great river Humber, which divides the southern and northern peoples of the English.

On the eastern side of Kent lies the not insignificant island of Thanet, having, by the English customary reckoning, an extent of six hundred households. The river Wantsum separates it from the mainland. It is about three stadia wide and can be crossed in only two places, for both its mouths extend into the sea.

There the servant of God Augustine and his companions landed, men said to number nearly forty. Having sent interpreters, he informed the aforesaid king that they had come from Rome, bringing the best of messages: that, if he obeyed it, they promised him beyond all doubt eternal joys in heaven and an endless kingdom with the living and true God.

Hearing this, the king ordered them to remain on the island they had entered, and that necessities should be supplied to them, until he should see what he would do concerning them. For the report of the Christian religion had already reached him. He had also a Christian wife, a queen of the Frankish people named Bertha, whom he had received from her parents on the condition that she should have permission to preserve inviolate the rite of her faith and religion, together with Bishop Liudhard, whom they had given her as helper.

After a few days the king came to the island and, sitting in the open air, ordered Augustine and his companions to come there to confer with him. He had taken care, following an ancient augury, that they should not enter any house to him, lest by their arrival, if they possessed any magical art, they might deceive and overcome him. But they came endowed not with demonic but with divine power, carrying a silver cross as their standard and an image of the Lord and Saviour painted on boards. Singing litanies for their own eternal salvation and that of those for whom and to whom they had come, they entreated the Lord.

When, at the king’s command, they were seated and preached the word of life to him and to all his attendants present, he answered:

> “The words and promises which you bring are indeed beautiful; but because they are new and uncertain, I cannot give them assent, abandoning what I have observed for so long with the whole English nation. Yet because you have come here as strangers from far away and, as it seems to me that I have perceived, wished to communicate also to us what you believed true and best, we do not wish to trouble you. Rather, we shall take care to receive you with kindly hospitality and supply what is necessary for your sustenance. Nor do we forbid you to unite with the religion of your faith by preaching all whom you can.”

He therefore gave them a dwelling in the city of Canterbury, the capital of his entire realm. As he had promised, he supplied their temporal sustenance and did not withhold from them permission to preach. It is said that, as they approached the city in their customary manner with their cross and image of the great King, our Lord Jesus Christ, they sang this litany in harmonious voice:

> We beseech Thee, O Lord, in all Thy mercy, that Thy fury and Thy wrath may be removed from this city and from Thy holy house, because we have sinned. Alleluia.

Entering the city, and imitating the apostolic life of the primitive Church, by their heavenly conduct and the sweetness of their teaching they compelled many to faith and baptism. They baptized and celebrated Masses in the church of Saint Martin, built long ago by the Britons east of the city itself, where the aforesaid queen had customarily prayed.

When, among others, the king was delighted by the saints’ most pure life and by the showing of miracles, he was converted to the faith; and countless people began to join the Church of Christ. The king loved them more closely, but compelled no one to the faith. For he had learned from the authors of his salvation that the service of Christ ought to be voluntary, not compelled. Nor did he delay to confer a suitable site for their see and various possessions.

Then Augustine, the man of God, went to Arles and, in accordance with the pope’s command, was ordained archbishop by Ætherius, archbishop of that city. He returned to Britain and sent the priest Laurence to Rome. Through him he reported the events to the supreme pontiff and consulted him concerning nine questions of future action. He received the pope’s replies; because these are lengthy, let the reader seek and find them in the decretals or canons.

Pope Gregory also sent to Bishop Augustine, then from the city of Rome, many fellow workers and ministers of the word. Chief and foremost among them were Mellitus, Justus, Paulinus, and Rufinianus. Through them he also sent vessels and vestments, books and ornaments necessary for churches. He also sent a letter, of which this is the text:

> GREGORY, servant of the servants of God, to his most reverend and most holy brother AUGUSTINE, fellow bishop.

Since it is certain that ineffable [or: inestimable] rewards of the eternal kingdom are reserved for those who labour for almighty God, we must nevertheless confer upon them the benefits of offices, so that, through the prospect of recompense, they may labour more abundantly in the pursuit of spiritual work. And because the new Church of the English has been brought to the grace of almighty God, by the same Lord’s bounty and through your labour, we grant you the use of the pallium therein, but only for the celebration of the solemnities of Mass; so that in each place you may ordain twelve bishops subject to your jurisdiction, in such wise that the bishop of the city of London must always thereafter be consecrated by his own synod and receive the pallium of honour from this holy and apostolic see, which, by God’s appointment, I serve. [Col. 0845A] But to the city of York we wish you to send such a bishop as you judge fit to ordain, provided that, if that city with its neighbouring districts receives the word of God, he too may ordain twelve bishops and enjoy metropolitan honour.

For we intend, with the Lord’s favour, to bestow the pallium upon him also, if life accompanies him; yet we wish him to be subject to the direction of your brotherhood. After your death, however, he shall preside over the bishops whom he has ordained, without being in any way subject to the jurisdiction of the bishop of London. Between the bishops of the cities of London and York, let this distinction of honour henceforth obtain: he is to be accounted first who was ordained first. But by common counsel and united action, let them unanimously arrange whatever must be done for zeal for Christ; let them hold right opinions, and carry out what they have determined without disagreement among themselves. Your brotherhood, however, shall have subject to it in our Lord Jesus Christ not only the bishops whom you ordain, nor only those ordained through the bishop of York, but also all the priests of Britain; so that from the speech and holiness of your life they may receive a pattern both of right belief and of good living, and, fulfilling their office in faith and conduct, may attain, when the Lord wills, the heavenly kingdoms. May God keep you safe, most reverend brother.

Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of July, in the seventeenth year of the reign of our most pious lord Maurice Tiberius Augustus. [Col. 0845C]

When the aforesaid envoys were making for Britain, the apostolic pope sent letters after them, in which he plainly showed how solicitous he was for the salvation of our people, writing thus:

**Gregory, servant of the servants of God, to his most beloved son Mellitus, abbot.**

Since the departure of our community which is with you, we have been greatly anxious, because we have had no opportunity of hearing anything concerning the success of your journey. Therefore, when almighty God has brought you to our most reverend brother Augustine, the bishop, tell him what, after long reflection, I have decided concerning the cause of the English: namely, that the temples of idols among that people ought by no means to be destroyed; but the idols which are in them are to be destroyed. [Col. 0845D] Let holy water be made and sprinkled in those same temples; let altars be built and relics deposited. For if those temples are well built, they must be converted from the worship of demons to the service of the true God, so that, when the people themselves do not see their temples destroyed, they may put error away from their hearts and, knowing and worshipping the true God, may more readily resort to the places to which they have been accustomed.

And because they are accustomed to kill many oxen in sacrifice to demons, some solemnity should also be changed for them in this matter: on the day of dedication, or on the feast-days of the holy martyrs whose relics are placed there, let them make for themselves booths of tree branches around the same churches which have been converted from temples, and celebrate the solemnity with religious feasts. Let them no longer sacrifice animals to the devil, [Col. 0846A] but let them slaughter animals for their own eating to the praise of God, and give thanks to the Giver of all things for their fullness. And while some outward joys are retained for them, they may more easily consent to inward joys. For there can be no doubt that it is impossible to cut away everything at once from hard minds, because one who strives to ascend to a high place rises by steps or paces, not by leaps.

Thus indeed the Lord made himself known to the people of Israel in Egypt; yet he retained for them in his own worship the use of sacrifices which they had been accustomed to offer to the devil, commanding them to sacrifice animals in his sacrifice, so that, changing their hearts, they might abandon one thing in sacrifice and retain another. Thus, even though the animals themselves were those which they had been accustomed to sacrifice, yet when they sacrificed them to the true [Col. 0846B] God and not to idols, the sacrifices themselves would no longer be the same. You must therefore tell these things to your beloved brother aforesaid, so that he, being personally stationed there, may consider how he ought to arrange everything. May God keep you safe, most beloved son.

Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of July, in the nineteenth year of the reign of our most pious lord Maurice Tiberius Augustus; in the eighteenth year after the consulship of the same our lord, in the fourth indiction.

He also sent Augustine a letter concerning his miracles, lest he should be exalted by them, in these words:

“I know, dearest brother, that almighty God has willed to show miracles through your beloved self among the people whom he has chosen. Therefore it is necessary that you both rejoice with fear at this heavenly gift and fear while rejoicing: rejoice, that is, because the souls of the English are drawn through outward miracles to inward grace; but fear, lest amid the signs that are performed a weak mind raise itself up in presumption, and from the source by which it is outwardly lifted up to honour, it fall inwardly through vain glory. For we must remember that when the disciples returned joyfully from preaching and said to their heavenly Master, ‘Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name’ [Luke 10], they immediately heard: ‘Do not rejoice in this, but rather rejoice because your names are written in heaven’ [ibid.].”

For they had fixed their minds on a private and temporal joy when they rejoiced in miracles; but they are recalled from private to common joy, from temporal to eternal joy. To them it is said: “Rejoice in this, because your names are written in heaven.” For not all the elect work miracles, but their names are nevertheless recorded in heaven. The disciples of Truth ought not to have joy except in that good which they share with all, and in which their joy has no end.

It remains, therefore, dearest brother, that amid the things which you outwardly do through the Lord’s working, you should always examine yourself inwardly with discernment, and carefully understand both who you are and how great is the grace in that people for whose conversion you have received gifts even of performing signs. And if at any time you remember that you have sinned against our Creator either by [Col. 0847A] speech or by deeds, always call these things to mind, so that the remembrance of guilt may restrain the rising glory of the heart; and whatever you receive or have received in the performance of signs, count it not as granted to yourself, but as granted to those for whose salvation it has been bestowed upon you.

Pope Gregory also sent King Æthelberht a letter together with gifts of various kinds, in order that he might exalt with temporal gifts one whom he had marked with the gifts of heavenly grace.

**Gregory, bishop, to his most glorious and most excellent son Æthelberht, king of the English.**

For this reason almighty God brings good men to the governments of peoples: that through them he may bestow the gifts of his mercy upon all over whom they are set. We have learned that this has happened among the English people. [Col. 0847B] Your glory has therefore been placed over them, so that, through the good things granted to us, heavenly benefits might also be bestowed upon the people subject to you. And so, glorious son, carefully preserve in your mind the grace which you have received from God; hasten to spread the Christian faith among the peoples subject to you. Increase the zeal of your uprightness in their conversion; pursue the worship of idols; overthrow the buildings of temples; build up the character of your subjects through exhortation, intimidation, persuasion, correction, and the example of good works, with great purity of life. Thus you may find in heaven as your rewarder him whose name and knowledge you have spread upon earth.

For he will also render the name of your glory glorious to posterity, whose honour you seek and maintain among the nations. Thus once the most pious Emperor Constantine, recalling the Roman commonwealth from the perverse worship of idols, subjected it together with himself to almighty God and our Lord Jesus Christ, and turned himself with the peoples subject to him to God with his whole mind. [Col. 0847C] Hence it came about that this man surpassed the name of ancient rulers by his own praises, and exceeded his predecessors as greatly in renown as in good works.

Therefore now let your glory hasten to pour the knowledge of the one God—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—into the kings and peoples subject to it; so that you may surpass the ancient kings of your own people in praises and merits, and, in proportion as you cleanse even the sins of others among your subjects, may be made more secure concerning your own sins before the terrible judgment-seat of almighty God. Gladly hear, devoutly perform, and diligently retain in memory whatever our most reverend brother Augustine, the bishop—trained in the rule of the monastery, filled with knowledge of Holy Scripture, and endowed with good works by God’s authoring—admonishes you to do. For if you heed him in what he says on behalf of almighty God, that same almighty God will more swiftly hear him when he prays for you. But if—God forbid!—you set his words aside, how can almighty God hear on your behalf one whom you neglect to hear for God’s sake? Therefore bind yourselves to him with your whole mind in the ardour of faith, and aid his endeavour by the power divinity has granted you, so that he may make you sharers in his kingdom, whose faith you make easy to receive and preserve in your own kingdom.

Moreover, we wish your glory to know [Col. 0848A] that, as we learn from the words of almighty God in Holy Scripture, the end of the present world is now near, and the kingdom of the saints is to come, which can never be ended by any limit. As that end of the world approaches, many things are impending which have not existed before: changes in the air, terrors from heaven, storms contrary to the order of the seasons, wars, famines, pestilences, and earthquakes in various places. Yet not all these things will come in our days; after our days all will follow.

Therefore, if you learn that any of these things occurs in your land, do not let your mind be disturbed in any way, because these signs of the world’s end are sent beforehand so that we may be concerned for our souls and wary of the hour of death, and may be found prepared in good works for the coming judgment. I have now said these things briefly, glorious son, so that when the Christian faith has increased in your kingdom, our discourse also may grow more extensive among you; and we may be more eager to speak in proportion as the joys in our minds are multiplied by the complete conversion of your people.

I have sent small gifts, which will not be small to you when they are received by you with the blessing of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. May almighty God perfect in you the grace which he has begun, extend your life here through the course of many years, and after a long time receive you into the assembly of the heavenly country. May heavenly grace keep your excellence safe.

[Col. 0848C] Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of July, in the nineteenth year of the reign of our most pious lord Maurice Tiberius Augustus; in the eighteenth year after the consulship of the same lord, in the fourth indiction.

Augustine, however, consecrated in the royal city, as his own see and that of his successors, the church which Roman believers had formerly built, in honour of the Saviour. The king built and dedicated, east of the city, the church of Peter and Paul, in which the bodies of the archbishops and kings of Kent might be laid. Its first abbot was Peter the priest, who, having been sent as envoy to Gaul, was drowned in the inlet of the sea called Amfleot and given an undistinguished burial by the inhabitants of the place. But almighty God, to show what his merit had been, caused a heavenly light to appear every night above [Col. 0848D] his grave, until the neighbouring people, observing it and seeing that the man buried there had been holy, investigated where he came from and who he was, removed the body, and placed it in a church in the city of Boulogne with honour fitting for so great a man.

When six hundred years of grace had passed, the great pope Gregory departed to the true life, in the fifth year after this, in the second year of the Emperor Phocas. Roman by family and noble by birth, he cast aside wealth and chose the monastic life. Afterwards he was taken from the monastery and sent by Pope Felix to Constantinople as apocrisiarius [papal representative], where he began the *Moralia on Job*, which he later completed as pope. There also, in the emperor’s presence, he condemned the heresy of Eutychius [or: Euticius]. [Col. 0849A] He also composed the outstanding book called the *Pastoral Rule*, four books of *Dialogues*, and forty *Homilies*, and expounded the first and last portions of Ezekiel, although throughout his youth he was tormented by pains of the bowels and weakness of the stomach, and by slow but continuous fevers.

These things are said of his immortal genius, which not even so great bodily pain could restrain. For other pontiffs indeed devoted themselves to adorning churches, whereas he distributed everything among the poor, so that he could say with blessed Job:

> The ear that heard me called me blessed,  
> and the eye that saw me bore witness for me,  
> because I delivered the poor man crying out  
> and the orphan who had no helper.  
> The blessing of one perishing came upon me,  
> and I comforted the heart of the widow.  
> I put on righteousness, [Col. 0849B]  
> and I clothed myself with my judgment as with a garment and a diadem.  
> I was an eye to the blind and a foot to the lame;  
> I was a father to the poor,  
> and I investigated with utmost care a cause I did not know.  
> I broke the jaws of the wicked  
> and took the prey from his teeth.  
> (Job 19)

And a little later:

> If I denied what the poor desired,  
> or made the eyes of the widow wait;  
> if I ate my morsel alone  
> and the orphan did not eat from it—  
> for compassion grew with me from childhood  
> and came forth with me from my mother’s womb.  
> (Job 31)

Among other things, the blessed pope caused Masses to be celebrated over the bodies of the apostles Peter and Paul; and in the celebration of Mass itself he added three words of the highest perfection: “Order our days in your peace, command that we be delivered from eternal damnation, and command that we be numbered in the flock of your elect.” [Col. 0849C]

It is said, as Bede relates, that the aforesaid man of God, once going to the market in Rome, saw some young Englishmen very handsome in body, face, and hair. When he learned that they had come from Britain and were pagans, he sighed and said: “Alas, what sorrow that the author of darkness should possess men of such bright faces!” He then asked what the people’s name was, and received the answer that they were called Angli, “English.” He said: “Well indeed; for they have angelic faces, and such men ought to be fellow-heirs with angels in heaven.” “What is the name,” he asked, “of the province from which these men have been brought?” The answer was that the inhabitants of that province were called Deiri. He said: “Well indeed, Deiri—rescued *de ira*, ‘from wrath,’ [Col. 0849D] and called to Christ’s mercy.” “By what name is the king of that province called?” The reply was that he was named Ælle. Playing upon the name, he said: “Alleluia must be sung in those regions in praise of the Creator.”

He therefore approached the Roman pontiff—for he had not yet become pontiff himself—and asked for a mission to preach to them. When he could not obtain it, as soon as he himself was made pope, he accomplished through others the work he had long desired. He was buried in the church of the blessed apostle Peter, before the sanctuary, where there is an epitaph as follows:

> Earth, receive the body taken from your body,  
> which you will be able to restore when God gives life.  
> The spirit seeks the stars; the laws of death will harm nothing  
> for him to whom death itself is rather a pathway to another life.  
> The limbs of this supreme bishop are enclosed in this tomb,  
> [Col. 0850A] yet he lives everywhere in countless good works.  
> By teaching mercy he converted the English to Christ,  
> multiplying the seeds of faith among a new people.  
> Thus, made the Lord’s consul, rejoice, Gregory:  
> for now the triumphant laurel is yours.

Augustine also ordained Justus as bishop in Kent itself, in the city of Dorubrevis, which the English call Rochester after a certain prince named Rof. There King Æthelberht built a church of the apostle Andrew and endowed it with lands and possessions. It is twenty-four miles distant from Canterbury. Thus has been related how the king and people of Kent were converted to the faith of Christ.

The second part begins, showing how the king and people of the East Saxons received the word of God. Augustine therefore sent to them to preach a perfect and tested man, namely Mellitus. The East Saxons are divided from Kent by the Thames; their metropolis, London, is a market frequented by many peoples coming by land and sea. [Col. 0850B] At that time Sæberht, Æthelberht’s nephew, reigned there under him, Æthelberht ruling, as said above, over all peoples as far as the Humber. Therefore, after affairs had prospered and King Sæberht and the people had converted to the faith, King Æthelberht built in London a church of Paul as an episcopal see and endowed it with many estates; therein Mellitus was fittingly established as bishop.

With the assistance of King Æthelberht, Augustine, together with Bishop Mellitus and Justus, summoned to a conference bishops or teachers from the greatest and nearest province of the Britons, in a place which even to this day in the English tongue is called Augustine’s Oak—that is, Augustine’s tree—in the borderland of the Wiccii [variant: Picts] and the West Saxons. As he disputed with them concerning the celebration of Easter against the Scots and Picts, and they would not assent to the most compelling argument, he confirmed his assertion by healing, in public, a blind Englishman who had been brought forward by agreement to establish the case of one party or the other. When their bishops could not cure him, Augustine knelt before all and gave sight to the blind man, for the enlightenment of the whole people.

Then the Britons and Scots requested a postponement and sought the advice of a certain man who seemed to them prudent and religious, asking what ought to be done. [Col. 0850D] He told them: “If he is a servant of God, agree with him.” But they said: “How can we ascertain this?” Then he said: “If he is meek and humble of heart, he seems to be a servant of God.” They replied: “How can we know whether he is humble?” He told them: “If he rises for you, let him be judged humble; but if, although you are greater in number, he refuses to rise, then despise him as well.”

Accordingly, when they met, Augustine, seated in a chair according to Roman custom, did not rise for them; and they departed reproaching him and remaining at variance. Augustine foretold to them that, if they refused to receive peace with their brethren, they would receive war from their enemies; and that, if they would not preach the way of life to the English people, they would suffer the vengeance of death at their hands. By divine judgment, all came about exactly as he had foretold. For afterwards Æthelfrith, the fierce king of the English of whom we have spoken, gathered a great army and inflicted a vast slaughter upon the unbelieving people at the city of legions, called by the English Leeg-Cestre, but more correctly called by the Britons Kaerlegion. [Col. 0851A]

As he prepared for battle and saw their priests, who had assembled to pray to God for the soldiers fighting the battle, standing apart in a safer place, he asked who they were and for what purpose they had gathered there. Very many of them were from the monastery of Bangor [or: Brancor], in which the number of monks is said to have been so great that, when the monastery was divided into seven sections under their appointed heads, no section had fewer than three hundred men. All of them were accustomed to live by the labour of their own hands.

Many of these, having completed a three-day fast, joined others at the aforesaid battle line in order to pray. They had a defender named Brocmail, whose task was to protect them, while intent on prayer, from the swords of the barbarians. When King Æthelfrith understood the reason for their coming, he said: “Then if they cry to their god against us, they are surely fighting against us even though they do not bear arms, since they pursue us with hostile imprecations.” Therefore he ordered weapons to be turned first against them, and then destroyed the remaining forces of that accursed host, though not without great loss to his own army. It is said that about twelve hundred of those who had come to pray were killed in that battle, and only fifty escaped by flight. [Col. 0851C] At the first arrival of the enemy, Brocmail turned his back with his men and left those whom he ought to have defended, unarmed and exposed, to the striking swords.

Thus was fulfilled the prophecy of the holy bishop Augustine, although he had already long before been taken to the heavenly kingdoms: the faithless men felt the vengeance even of temporal destruction because they had rejected the counsels of eternal salvation offered to them.

The beloved of God, Augustine, died and was buried outside beside the church of Peter and Paul, because it was not yet completed or dedicated. But when it was dedicated, his successor Laurence fittingly transferred him into its northern portico, in which the bodies of all the archbishops down to Theodore were buried; for the portico could hold no more. The following epitaph was written on the tomb of the saint:

> Here rests the lord Augustine, first archbishop of Canterbury, formerly sent here by the blessed Gregory, pontiff of the city of Rome. Supported by God through the working of miracles, he brought King Æthelberht and his people from the worship of idols to Christ’s faith; and having completed the days of his office in peace, he died on the seventh day before the Kalends of June, while the same king reigned.

While still alive, Augustine had ordained Laurence archbishop, following the example of blessed Peter, who likewise ordained Clement, lest, after his own death, the still unformed condition of the Church should falter when deprived, even for an hour, of a shepherd. Laurence vigorously enlarged the faith that had been founded, caring not only for the new Church of the English but also for the ancient Britons and Scots, who erred in their observance of Easter. He also sent them a letter, whose opening is this:

**Laurence, Mellitus, and Justus, bishops, servants of the servants of God, to their dearest brethren, the bishops and abbots throughout all Scotland.**

Since the apostolic see, according to its custom throughout the whole world, sent us to preach to pagan peoples in these western regions, and it came about that we entered this island, before we knew them we honoured both Britons and Scots with great reverence for holiness, believing that they followed the custom of the universal Church. But upon becoming acquainted with the Britons, we judged the Scots to be better. Yet through Bishop Dagan and Abbot Columbanus we learned that the Scots differed in no respect from the Britons in their manner of life. For when Bishop Dagan came to us, he would take neither food with us nor even food in the same lodging in which we ate. [Col. 0852B]

Mellitus, bishop of London, went to Rome and attended the council of Pope Boniface, in which the life and repose of monks were discussed. This Boniface was the fourth pope after Pope Gregory. He obtained from Emperor Phocas the temple of the Pantheon, which he dedicated in honour of all the saints.

King Æthelberht died in the six hundred and sixteenth year of grace. He had reigned fifty-six years and was buried in the aforesaid church of Peter and Paul. This greatest and most distinguished man, among other good works, wrote judicial decrees for his people. But after Æthelberht’s death, his unbelieving son Eadbald took his father’s wife; and many therefore returned to their former vomit. The king himself, however, was punished by frequent madness of mind.

The king of the East Saxons died and left three pagan sons as heirs to his kingdom. Since they were idolaters, they mockingly said to the bishop during the solemnities of Mass: [Col. 0852C] “Why do you not also give us the bright bread which you gave our father and still give to the people?” He replied: “If you are willing to be washed in that saving font in which your father was washed, you can also be partakers of the holy bread of which he partook. But if you despise the washing of life, you can by no means receive the bread of life.” They said: “We do not wish to enter that font, for we know that we have no need of it; yet we want to be refreshed by that bread.”

Though he carefully and repeatedly warned them that no one could possibly share in the most holy offering without most holy purification, at last, moved by rage, they said: “If you will not agree with us in this very easy matter which we ask, you will no longer be able to remain in our province.” They expelled him and ordered him and his companions to leave their kingdom. Expelled from there, he came to Kent to confer with his fellow bishops Laurence and Justus about what should be done. By common counsel it was decided that it would be better for them all to return home and serve the Lord there with free minds than to remain fruitlessly among barbarians rebellious against the faith. [Col. 0853A]

Accordingly Mellitus and Justus departed first and withdrew to Gaul, intending to await there the outcome of events. But not long afterwards the kings who had expelled from themselves the herald of truth did not serve demonic cults with impunity. Going out to battle against the people of the Gewisse, they all fell together with their army. Nor, when its leaders had perished, could the populace trained in wickedness be corrected and recalled to the simplicity of faith and charity which is in Christ.

When Laurence too was about to follow Mellitus and Justus and leave Britain, he ordered a bed to be prepared for himself that night in the church of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, of which we have often spoken. Having there poured out many prayers and tears to the Lord for the state of the Church, he laid down his limbs to rest and fell asleep. The most blessed prince of the apostles appeared to him and, in the secret of night, severely chastising him for a long time with stripes, asked him with apostolic sternness why he was abandoning the flock entrusted to him, and to which shepherd he would leave, as he fled, Christ’s sheep set among wolves. [Col. 0853B]

“Have you forgotten my example,” he said, “I who, for the little ones whom he entrusted to me as a proof of his love, endured bonds, beatings, prisons, afflictions, and finally death itself—even death on a cross—from unbelievers and enemies of Christ, in order that I might be crowned with Christ?”

Warned by this, Laurence immediately revealed everything to the king. The king, terrified with exceeding fear, renounced his unlawful marriage and was baptized; and he sent to Gaul to recall Mellitus and Justus. The people of Rochester received Justus. The Londoners rejected Mellitus, preferring the service of idolatrous bishops. King Eadbald, however, did not possess power as great as his father’s, and could not restore the bishop against their will.

In the time of King Eadbald, Laurence died, and Mellitus, bishop of London, succeeded him. He and Justus, bishop of Rochester, governed the Church of the English with great labour. Mellitus suffered from gout, but was sound in the steps of his mind; noble in flesh, but nobler in mind. One work of his power was this: when flames were consuming the city, he ordered himself carried out to meet them and immediately, by prayer, destroyed the onrush of the flames. [Col. 0853D]

Justus, bishop of Rochester, succeeded Mellitus after he had been archbishop for five years. Pope Boniface, successor of Deusdedit, sent him the pallium with this letter:

**Boniface to his most beloved brother Justus.**

How devoutly and vigilantly your brotherhood has laboured for Christ’s Gospel has been shown not only by the tenor of the letter sent by you, but indeed by the success granted from above to your work. For almighty God has not abandoned either the sacrament of his name or the fruit of your labour, since he faithfully promised to the preachers of the Gospel: “Behold, I am with you always, even to the consummation of the age” [Matthew 28].

Having received the letter of our son King Eadbald, we have discovered with what instruction in sacred speech your brotherhood has brought his mind to the belief of true conduct [Col. 0854A] and undoubting faith. We therefore send the pallium to your brotherhood through the bearer of this letter; and we have granted you permission to use it in the celebration of the most holy mysteries. We also permit you, when necessity requires and the Lord’s mercy goes before you, to perform the ordinations of bishops, so that Christ’s Gospel may be spread by the proclamation of very many people among all nations not yet converted. May God keep you safe, most beloved brother.

The third part begins concerning the conversion of the Northumbrians, that is, those who dwell in the region north of the river Humber. Their king Edwin possessed such great power in his earthly empire that—what no Englishman before him had done—he held the whole extent of Britain, and every province inhabited by either English or Britons was under his rule. [Col. 0854B] He also subjected to the empire of the English the Mevanian Islands: the first, which lies to the south and is greater in area and more fortunate in the yield and abundance of its crops, contains the measure of nine hundred and sixty households; the second occupies the space of more than three hundred.

That king, while still pagan, had married Æthelburh, the Christian daughter of King Æthelberht, who was also called Tate. Paulinus came with her to preach there, having been ordained bishop for that purpose by Archbishop Justus. In the following year a certain assassin, named Eumer, was sent by Cwichelm, king of the West Saxons, to kill King Edwin. Pretending to be his lord’s envoy, he rushed upon the king with a poisoned double-edged dagger beside the river Dorvencion. Lilla, the king’s attendant, seeing this, threw himself before the blow and was pierced through; the king himself was slightly wounded by the same stroke; and, after another knight had been killed, the assassin was cut down by swords. [Col. 0854C]

That same night the queen gave birth to a daughter named Eanflæd [variant: Einflat]. As the king gave thanks for this to the gods, Paulinus said that by his prayers to God he had obtained that the queen should bear her without pain. Delighted by his words, the king promised to serve Christ if Christ granted him victory over Cwichelm; and, as a pledge that he would fulfil his promise, he ordered his daughter to be baptized. She was baptized with eleven members of his household.

When the king, after overcoming Cwichelm and either killing his enemies or receiving them into submission, returned victorious to his country, he did not immediately become a Christian. Rather, being a man of naturally keen intelligence, he often considered alone, and often with others, what he ought to do after hearing the reasoning of the faith.

Pope Boniface therefore sent him letters exhorting him to the faith. He also sent gifts, which he mentions at the end of the letter in these words: “Moreover, we have sent you the blessing of your protector, the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles: namely, one *comisia* [uncertain object] with gold ornamentation, and one Ancyrian mantle; and we ask that your glory receive them with the same kindly disposition with which you know they have been sent by us.”

He also sent Queen Æthelburh letters and gifts, of which he says at the end of the letter: “Moreover, we have sent you the blessing of your protector, the blessed Peter, [Col. 0855A] prince of the apostles: namely, a gilded ivory comb and a silver mirror; and we ask that your glory receive them with the same kindly disposition with which you know they have been sent by us.”

Paulinus then revealed to King Edwin the oracle formerly shown to him by the Holy Spirit, in this manner. When, pursued by Æthelfrith, who had reigned before him, he was living as an exile with King Rædwald, he learned from a certain friend that Rædwald, corrupted by gifts from King Æthelfrith, intended to kill him; and the friend promised to lead him out of that province if he wished. Edwin replied: “Where am I now to flee, having for so many years escaped the snares of my enemies throughout all the provinces of Britain? But if I must die, I would rather be killed here than be killed more ignobly elsewhere.” [Col. 0855B]

Having said this, he remained alone; and while he was consumed by anguish of mind and a hidden fire, in the unseasonable silence of the night he saw an unknown man saying to him: “Do not be afraid, for I know the cause of your sorrow. But what would you give to one who freed you from this danger and persuaded King Rædwald to love you?” When Edwin replied, “Everything I could,” the other added: “What if he also truly promised that, once your enemies had been destroyed, you would become a king more powerful than your predecessors?” Edwin giving the same answer as before, he added again: “What if he showed you a better way of life than any of your forefathers had possessed—would you obey him?” When Edwin most firmly promised this, the other continued, laying his hand upon Edwin’s head: “When this sign comes upon you, then remember this time and this conversation.” At these words he suddenly vanished, so that Edwin understood that he was not a man but a spirit.

And while the royal youth was still sitting there alone, the aforesaid friend came and said: “Rise in good spirits: the king’s heart has changed, and, on the counsel of the queen, he has determined to keep his pledged faith with you.” Why say more? Rædwald gathered an army and killed Æthelfrith, who came to meet him, on the borders of Mercia, on the eastern side of the river called the Idle. There Rædwald’s son, named Rægenhere, was also killed; and thus Edwin obtained the kingdom of the Northumbrians. When Paulinus told the king this oracle, he laid his hand upon his head and raised him up as he was about to fall at his feet.

The king, therefore, being ready for the faith, asked what his people thought, so that he might win them over. Coifi, the chief priest, said to him: “No one has served the gods more zealously than I, for the sake of earthly gain. Yet there are many who have received greater benefits; from this I have proved that the gods have no power.” Then another of the king’s nobles added:

“Such, it seems to me, O king, is the present life of men on earth in comparison with that time which is unknown to us. When you are sitting at supper with your commanders and attendants in wintertime, with a fire kindled in the middle and the hall made warm, while outside furious storms of wintry rain or snow rage everywhere, one sparrow may swiftly fly through the house. Entering by one door and immediately departing through another, during the moment when it is within it is untouched by the wintry storm; yet, when that very brief interval of calm has passed in an instant, it immediately returns from winter into winter and escapes your sight. Thus this life of men appears for a little while; but what follows it, or what preceded it, we know absolutely nothing. Therefore, if this new teaching has brought something more certain, it seems rightly to be followed.” [Col. 0855D–0856A]

When the rest said similar things, Coifi added that he wished himself to hear Paulinus speak concerning God. Having heard him, he exclaimed that he and the others had wholly erred, and they all together promised to receive the faith of Christ. Coifi the priest, having received from the king a stallion—for a priest of idols was permitted to ride only a mare—and having seized a sword and spear, which was likewise forbidden, before the eyes of all set fire to and destroyed the altars which he himself had consecrated. The place of those former idols is shown not far east of York, beyond the river Dorvencion, that is, the Derwent, and is today called Godmundham [otherwise Godmundingeham]. [Col. 0856B]

Accordingly King Edwin was baptized on the holy day of Easter, together with many others, in the church of St Peter, which he had built of wood as the episcopal seat of Paulinus. He immediately began a larger church of stone, which Oswald later completed. Also baptized were Osfrith and Eadfrith, sons of King Edwin, both born to him during his exile by Cwenburh, daughter of Cearl, king of the Mercians. At a later time his children born to Queen Æthelburh were baptized as well; two of these died while still wearing their baptismal white garments and were buried at York in the church.

So great, moreover, is said to have been the Northumbrian people’s trust in the words preached and their desire for the saving font, that when Paulinus on one occasion came with the king and queen to the royal estate called Adgefrin, he remained there with them for thirty-six days, wholly occupied in catechizing and baptizing. In the province of Bernicia he baptized in the river Glen, beside the place called Melmin; but in the province of Deira, in the river Swale [otherwise Swalna], which flows past the settlement of Cataract.

Paulinus also converted the province of Lindsey, situated on the southern bank of the river Humber. He first converted Blecca, the prefect of the city of Lincoln, together with his household; in that city he made a church of excellent workmanship and in it consecrated Honorius as archbishop. Though its roof has fallen, whether through long neglect or hostile violence, its walls are still seen standing. The city of Lincoln, then called Lindocolina, together with the adjoining province of Lindsey—which is enclosed on every side by rivers, marshes, or sea—belongs to the kingdom of Mercia. The city is splendid in position, and the province rich in many resources; whence a certain writer says:

> The city is set upon a hill, and the hill slopes southward.

The abbot of Partney related that he had seen an old man baptized by Paulinus, together with a great crowd, before King Edwin in the river Trent beside the city which was then called Fingecester [otherwise Tiowlfingacestre]. He said of the man’s appearance that he was tall, slightly bent, with black hair, a lean face, a very narrow hooked nose, and an aspect at once venerable and formidable. [Col. 0856D–0857A]

Pope Honorius, having heard these things, sent encouraging letters to King Edwin. I have thought it necessary to include the final part of them, which expressly treats of what was to be done concerning the archbishops of England, in these words:

> Being frequently occupied in reading the writings of your preacher, my lord Gregory of apostolic memory, keep before your eyes the zeal for teaching which he gladly exercised for the sake of your souls, so that his prayer may increase your kingdom and people, and present you blameless to Almighty God.  
>   
> As for the provisions which you hoped we would make for your priests: in return for the sincerity of your faith, which has been commendably made known to us in many reports through the bearers of this letter, we provide these things with a willing heart and without any delay. We have sent two pallia for the two metropolitans, namely, Honorius and Paulinus, so that, when either of them is summoned from this world to his Creator, the other may, by this authority of ours, appoint another bishop in his place. We have been moved to grant this both by affection for your charity and by the great distance of the provinces known to lie between us and you, so that in all things we may give our support to your devotion according to your wishes. May heavenly grace preserve your excellency in health. [Col. 0857A–C]

The fourth part begins, concerning the conversion of the East Angles. Their king Eorpwald, son of King Rædwald, at the urging of his close friend King Edwin, received the faith. His father Rædwald had long before received the faith in Kent, but to no effect; for on returning home, led astray by his wife and certain perverse persons, he kept an altar of Christ and an altar of a demon in the same shrine. Aldwulf, king of the same province, who lived in the age of the venerable Bede, testifies that it endured until his own day.

But Eorpwald, not long after he believed, was killed by a pagan man, Ricberht. He was succeeded by his brother Sigeberht, a most Christian man, who converted others with Bishop Felix, whom Bishop Honorius had sent there from Burgundy to preach. Felix held the episcopal see, aptly named after himself, in the city of Dommoc for seventeen years, and died there in peace. [Col. 0857C–D]

Meanwhile, after the death of Archbishop Justus, Paulinus consecrated Honorius, who had come to meet him, in the city of Lindocolina, now called Lincoln, in the church which he himself had built there, as was said above. Pope Honorius sent Archbishop Honorius the pallium and letters concerning the appointment and rank of the two archbishoprics, in this form:

> HONORIUS TO HIS MOST BELOVED BROTHER HONORIUS.  
>   
> Among the many good gifts which the mercy of our Redeemer deigns to bestow upon His servants, the generous bounty of His compassion also mercifully grants this: that, whenever through brotherly affection He sets before the eyes of one the unanimous love of another in contemplation, we continually render thanks to His majesty for them; and with humble prayers we beseech Him that He may strengthen your belovedness in lasting steadfastness, as you labour and bear fruit in the preaching of the Gospel and follow the holy rule of Gregory, your teacher and head, and that through you He may raise up greater growth for the increase of the Church. Thus may the acquisition of yourselves and of your predecessors, which has sprung up through the beginning made by Lord Gregory, extend yet further as it gains strength in faith and works, in the fear of God and charity; so that in the future the promises of the Lord’s word itself may look upon you, and that voice may summon you to the eternal feast: “Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will refresh you” (Matthew 11); and again: “Well done, good and faithful servant; because thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will set thee over many things; enter thou into the joy of thy Lord” (Matthew 25). [Col. 0858A–B]  
>   
> And we, dearest brethren, promising you these words of exhortation out of everlasting charity, do not cease to bestow also such provisions as we perceive may be appropriate for the privileges of your churches. In accordance both with your request and with that of our sons the kings, by this present decree, in the place of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, we grant you authority that, when God commands one of you to be summoned to Himself, the survivor shall appoint another bishop in the place of the deceased. For this purpose we have likewise sent pallia individually to your belovedness, for celebrating that appointment, so that by the authority of our decree you may carry out an appointment pleasing to God. The great distances of land and sea that lie between us and you compelled us to make this concession, so that no loss whatsoever may come upon your churches under any pretext or occasion, but rather that you may more fully advance the devotion of the people entrusted to you. May God keep you safe, dearest brother.

Given on the third day before the Ides of June, in the twenty-fourth year of the reign of our most pious lord Augustus Heraclius, the twenty-third year after his consulship, and the third year of his consulship; and in the third year of Heraclius, most fortunate Caesar, that is, his son; in the seventh indiction: that is, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 634. [Col. 0858C–D]

The same Pope Honorius also sent corrective letters to the nation of the Scots concerning the observance of Easter, lest they should suppose their small number wiser than all the Churches of Christ throughout the world. John also, who succeeded Severinus, successor of that Honorius, sent letters to correct the same error and the Pelagian heresy, which he had learned was reviving among them. This heresy maintained that a human being can exist without sin by his own will and not by the grace of God. For no man can be without sin except Jesus Christ, conceived and born without sin. All other human beings, even if free from actual sin, nevertheless contract original sin, according to the words: “For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother conceived me” (Psalm 50). [Col. 0858D–0859A]

But after seventeen years of his reign, Edwin was killed in a fierce battle on the field called Hatfield [otherwise Hethfield], by Cadwallon, king of the Britons, aided by Penda the Valiant, who from that time was king of the Mercians. His whole army was either slain or scattered. His warlike son Osfrith was also killed before him. Another son, Eadfrith, driven by necessity, fled to Penda; but later, during Oswald’s reign, he was treacherously put to death by him. Hatfield, it is said, smoked everywhere with the red blood of nobles. There a pitiable and unexpected slaughter of the bravest men took place.

King Cadwallon, indeed, a most powerful ruler, had brought with him an innumerable multitude; Penda the Valiant had brought the bravest warriors. Thus there was a great slaughter in the Church of Northumbria. Penda was a pagan; Cadwallon was fiercer than a pagan, sparing neither women nor little children and resolved to erase the English from Britain. Nor do the Britons associate with the English any more than with pagans, holding their faith in no esteem.

The head of King Edwin was brought to York and placed in the church of Peter, which he had begun and Oswald completed. Since the Northumbrians had no refuge but flight, Paulinus took with him Queen Æthelburh, whom he had formerly brought there, and returned by ship to Kent. There he was honourably received by Archbishop Honorius and King Eadbald, bringing with him also Edwin’s son and daughter. Their mother later sent them to Gaul to be reared by King Dagobert, who was her friend, because she feared Kings Eadbald and Oswald; and the children died there. He also brought with him Edwin’s precious vessels, a large golden cross, and a golden chalice, which are still in the church of Kent.

When Romanus, bishop of Rochester, was swallowed by the waves of the Italian sea while travelling as Honorius’s envoy to Rome, Paulinus held that bishopric until his death. At his death he left there the pallium which he had received from the pope. In his church at York he had left James the deacon, a holy man, who thereafter baptized and taught until peace had been restored in the province and the number of believers had increased. He began to be a teacher of ecclesiastical chant after the Roman custom; and he himself, old and full of days, followed the ways of the fathers according to the Scriptures. [Col. 0859B–D]

Osric, Edwin’s kinsman, succeeded King Edwin in the province of Deira. Eanfrith, son of King Æthelfrith, received the kingdom of Bernicia; for the Northumbrian people had from ancient times been divided into these two provinces. These young men were baptized while exiles among the Scots and Picts during King Edwin’s reign; but when they became kings, they turned to idols. King Cadwallon impiously but justly killed them. First, in the following summer, he suddenly burst forth with all his men and destroyed the unprepared Osric, while he rashly besieged him in a fortified town. Then, after a year, he killed Eanfrith, who came to him with twelve soldiers to seek peace.

That ill-fated year, because of both the kings’ apostasy and Cadwallon’s tyranny—by which he did not acquire lands as a conqueror but destroyed them as a pestilence—is reckoned among the following years of King Oswald. After the killing of his brother Eanfrith, Oswald came with a small army, raised with his own hands the sign of the holy cross, fixed it in a hollow with turf, and said: “Let us bend our knees and together beseech Almighty God, living and true, that in His mercy He may defend us from the fierce and proud enemy. For He knows that we undertake a just war for the salvation of our people.” This done, at dawn they joined battle with Cadwallon and those forces which he boasted that nothing could resist, and they fell at Denisesburne, that is, “Denis’s stream.” Hence it is said: “The slaughter of Cadwallon checked Denis’s course.” The place is held in great veneration, as will be related in the Book of Miracles. [Col. 0859D–0860B]

King Oswald, therefore, in order to increase the faith, sent to Scotland, where he had been an exile, and received Bishop Aidan, a very great man, although he did not celebrate Easter correctly, according to the custom of the northern Scots. The southern parts of the island of Ireland had long before accepted the correct Easter at the admonition of the pope. When the bishop came, the king gave him his episcopal seat on the island of Lindisfarne.

The faith thus began to spread, and it was often a beautiful sight that, while Aidan preached—he did not know the English language perfectly—the king himself acted as interpreter for his commanders and attendants. During the long period of his exile he had fully learned the language of the Scots. The faith therefore grew, and, as monks came from Scotland, it was zealously taught. For the bishop himself was a monk from the island called Hii, whose monastery held the chief place among the northern Scots and all the Picts. The island belongs legally to Britain, being separated from it by no great strait; but it was handed over to Scottish monks by the gift of the Picts who dwell in those regions of Britain, because they had received the faith from them. [Col. 0860B–C]

For in the year of grace 565, when Justin the Younger reigned after Justinian, Abbot Columba had come from Ireland to preach to the northern Picts—that is, those separated from the southern Picts by the high and dreadful ridges of mountains. The southern Picts had been converted earlier through Bishop Ninian, a Briton taught at Rome. His episcopal seat, named for St Martin, where Columba himself was buried, is now possessed by the English people. The place belongs to the province of Bernicia and is commonly called Ad Candidam Casam, “at the White House,” because Ninian built there a church of stone, in a manner unfamiliar to the Britons.

Columba came in the twentieth year of the reign of Bridei, son of Maelchon, the most powerful king of the Picts, and converted that people. He therefore received from them the aforesaid island, estimated by the English to contain five families’ holdings; his successors possess it to this day, and there he too was buried. There was also another famous monastery in Ireland, at Armagh, that is, “the field of oaks.” From both monasteries very many foundations spread through Ireland and England; among them all the monastery of Hii holds the primacy. By an unusual arrangement, the entire province, and even the bishops, are ordinarily subject to the abbot of that island, because Columba the preacher was not a bishop but a presbyter and monk. His successors, following his example, became very illustrious; yet they erred in their observance of Easter until the Englishman Egbert corrected them. Aidan, sent from there, held the Northumbrian bishopric. [Col. 0860D–0861B]

King Oswald, formed by Aidan’s instruction, advanced in mind and likewise in kingdom more than all his predecessors. He brought under his dominion all the peoples of Britain—namely Britons, English, Picts, and Scots—yet, despite such greatness, he was humble and kind to strangers and the poor.

The fifth part follows, concerning the conversion of the West Saxons, who were anciently called Gewisse; this was accomplished through Bishop Birinus. At the counsel of Pope Honorius, Birinus came, and was ordained bishop by Asterius, bishop of Genoa. Entering the thoroughly pagan people of the Gewisse, he baptized them and their king, Cynegils. It fittingly happened that holy King Oswald was present and received Cynegils from the baptismal font; Oswald was to take Cynegils’s daughter in marriage. Both kings gave Birinus the city of Dorchester as his episcopal seat, and there, after churches had been built, he was buried.

Many years later, while Hedda held the bishopric, Birinus was translated from there to the city of Venta, called Winchester, and placed in the church of Peter and Paul. After King Cynegils died, his son Cenwalh succeeded him. He rejected the faith, and not without punishment. Having repudiated the sister of Penda, king of the Mercians, whom he had married, and having taken another wife, he was defeated in war by Penda and deprived of his kingdom. During three years of exile with Anna, the faithful king of the East Angles, he acknowledged the faith again.

When Cenwalh had been restored to his kingdom, he appointed as bishop Ægilbert [otherwise Ailbert], a Gaul by nation, who had then come from Ireland for the sake of study. Later, however, the king, who knew only English and was entirely weary of the foreign language, introduced into the province a bishop who spoke his own language: Wine, himself consecrated in Gaul. Dividing the province into two dioceses, he gave him a seat at Venta. Ægilbert, offended because the king had done this without consulting him, returned to Gaul and held the bishopric of Paris until his death.

Afterward the same king also expelled Wine from his bishopric. Wine withdrew to Wulfhere, king of the Mercians, and bought from him, for a price, the see of the city of London, remaining its bishop until his death. Since the province was thus without a shepherd, and the king was often afflicted by enemies and disasters on that account, he sent to Paris for Ægilbert. Ægilbert, unwilling to abandon that bishopric, sent his nephew Leuthere. Consecrated bishop by Archbishop Theodore, he governed the bishopric of the Gewisse alone for a long time. [Col. 0861B–0862A]

At that time, after Eadbald, king of Kent, his son Eorcenberht ruled nobly for twenty-four years. He was the first in the whole kingdom to order idols destroyed and the Lenten fast observed, establishing penalties for transgressors. He married Seaxburh, the elder daughter of King Anna. King Anna sent his younger daughter Æthelburh and Sæthryth, the daughter of his wife, to the monastery at Bruges to serve the Lord; though both were foreigners, each became abbess at Bruges on account of her merits in virtue. At that time the nobles of England sent their daughters to be educated in the monasteries of Bruges, Calais, and Andelys.

Eorcenberht likewise sent his daughter Eorcongota, a holy and illustrious virgin of Christ, to Bruges. The inhabitants of that place recount to this day the works of her virtues and the signs of her miracles; we shall speak of her praise in the Book of Miracles. [Col. 0862A–B]

At the same time Oswald, after reigning nine years, not counting the aforesaid year attributed to the other kings, was killed by Penda the Valiant in a fierce battle at Maserfield [otherwise Maseuseld], in the thirty-eighth year of his age, on the fifth day of August. Hence it is said: “The field of Maserfield shone white with the bones of saints.” By the hidden judgment of God, pagans hateful to God slaughtered His beloved ones and gave them as food to the birds of heaven. Miracles take place at the site of that slaughter to this day.

The holy king was succeeded by his brother Oswi, who ruled twenty-eight years in the province of Bernicia. But in the province of Deira, Oswine, son of the aforesaid King Osric, reigned for seven years. When causes of conflict grew serious and the kings were about to fight at Wilfaresdune, that is, “Wilfar’s hill,” about ten miles westward from the settlement of Catterick, Oswine saw that he was inferior in strength. He dismissed his army and hid in the house of Count Hunwald, whom he considered his closest friend, with only one soldier, named Tondhere. But the same count betrayed him to Oswi, and Oswine was killed, together with that soldier, by Oswi’s official Æthelwin [otherwise Eilwin] at Gilling, in a death detestable to all. There a church was built for the souls of both kings: that is, the king slain and the king who ordered the killing. [Col. 0862B–D]

King Oswine was handsome in appearance, tall in stature, pleasant in speech, courteous in manners, and generous in hand; therefore he was loved by all and attended by nobles from every province. Among the deeds of Saint Aidan, whom Oswine dearly loved, we shall relate an account worthy of record concerning Oswine’s humility.

In the second year of King Oswi, Ithamar succeeded the great Paulinus as bishop in the church of Rochester. At that time, after Carpwald, successor of Rædwald, Sigeberht, his brother, a religious man, governed the kingdom of the East Angles. While in exile in Gaul because of Rædwald’s hostility, he had been baptized. When he became king, he established schools for boys, as he had seen done in Gaul, with the help of Bishop Felix. Saint Fursey, coming from Ireland, was honourably received by him. The king became so devoted to God that, after entrusting the kingdom to his kinsman Ecgric [otherwise Egric], he entered a monastery and received the tonsure. Many years later they compelled him to go out against King Penda. Yet in battle he had nothing in his hand but a staff. He was therefore killed with King Ecgric and their army. They were succeeded by Anna, son of Eni, of royal stock, a good man and father of good offspring; Penda afterward killed him too.

Thomas succeeded Felix as bishop of the East Angles, and Boniface succeeded Thomas. After Archbishop Honorius had consecrated all of these, he died. Deusdedit, the sixth archbishop of Kent, succeeded him, having been consecrated by Ithamar, bishop of Rochester. Damian succeeded Ithamar. [Col. 0862D–0863B]

The sixth part follows, concerning the conversion of the Middle Angles, that is, the Midland English, under Prince Peada, whom his father had placed over that people. King Oswi gave Peada, son of King Penda, his daughter on the condition that he should become a Christian. This was chiefly brought about by the persuasion of Alfred, son of King Oswi, who had married Peada’s sister Cyneburh, daughter of Penda.

Peada was baptized with his followers by Bishop Finan at the settlement called Ad Murum, “at the Wall.” Taking with him the priests Cedd and Adda [otherwise Abda], Betti, and Diuma, he returned home. Penda [otherwise Peada] did not forbid those of his own people—that is, the Mercians—who wished to believe; indeed, he despised believers who lived wickedly.

After two years the Mercians were converted in this manner. King Oswi, unable to endure King Penda’s intolerable invasions, offered him countless gifts. But Penda the Valiant, having determined to destroy Oswi’s people, scorned the gifts. Oswi, inflamed with extreme grief, said: “If the pagan does not know how to receive our gifts, let us offer them to God, who does know.” He therefore vowed to consecrate his daughter to God and to give twelve estates to monasteries; then, with few men, he attacked many.

It is reported that the pagans had an army thirty times greater; they brought thirty legions, equipped with most noble leaders, into battle. King Oswi, with his son Alfred, had a very small army, as I have said; yet, trusting in Christ as his leader, he met them. His other son, Ecgfrith, was at that time held hostage in the province of the Mercians by Queen Cynwise. Æthelwald, son of King Oswald, who should have aided Oswi’s side, was among the opposing force and was to serve as their commander in battle against his own country and uncle. Yet at the very moment of battle he withdrew from the fighting and waited in a safe place for the outcome of the contest.

When battle was joined, the thirty pagan leaders were routed and slain. Almighty God was with His own; He broke the strength of King Penda and took the accustomed vigour from the sinews of his arms, and caused his great heart to melt away. Thus he no longer knew himself in his blows, nor was he impenetrable to the enemies’ weapons. He was amazed that his enemies were such as he himself had been to enemies, while he himself had become such as they had been. He who had always shed another’s blood felt what he had done, as he now soaked the ground with his own blood and spattered it with his brain. Nearly all those who had come to his aid were killed. Among them was Æthelhere, brother of King Anna of the East Angles, who reigned after him; the very instigator of the war, he was slain, with his troops or auxiliaries destroyed.

Because the battle was fought near the river Winwæd, which, owing to flooding rains, had then overflowed its channel widely—indeed, all its banks—it happened that the water destroyed far more men fleeing than the sword did fighting. [Col. 0863B–0864A]

Ælfflæd, daughter of King Oswi, became a nun at Hertey [otherwise Herten], that is, “the Isle of the Stag.” Later, when a monastery had been built at Streaneshalh, she died there as abbess. There her father Oswi was buried, together with her mother Eanflæd and her maternal grandfather Edwin.

For three years after Penda’s death, Oswi ruled the Mercian people, the other southern provinces, and a great part of the Pictish people. He also gave Peada, son of Penda and his kinsman, the kingdom of the southern Mercians, who numbered five thousand family holdings, separated by the river Trent from the northern Mercians, who numbered seven thousand family holdings. But Peada was killed through the treachery of his wife. The Mercian people were therefore subject to King Oswi for three years; after their treacherous head had been cut off, they were converted through him to the grace of the Christian faith.

Diuma was then made bishop of the Middle Angles, the Mercians, and the Lindsey people; he died there. He was succeeded by Ceollach [otherwise Coellec], who returned to the Scots whence he had come. But after three years the Mercian leaders rebelled and raised Wulfhere, Penda’s son, as king. During his reign of seventeen years, the first bishop was Trumhere, the second Jaruman, the third Ceadda, the fourth Wilfrid. [Col. 0864A–C]

At that time also the East Saxons, who had formerly expelled Mellitus, were converted again. Their king was Sigeberht, who reigned after Sigeberht surnamed the Little and was a friend of King Oswi. Since he often visited Oswi and was preached to by him, he was baptized by Bishop Finan at the settlement at the Wall, which lies twelve miles from the eastern sea. Cedd, called from the Middle Angles, was made bishop over the East Saxons. He baptized chiefly in the city of Ythancæstir, on the bank of the river Panta, and at Tilaburh, on the bank of the Thames.

He forbade a certain count all communion because of an unlawful marriage. When the king despised this prohibition and ate with him, he fell at the feet of the bishop when he met him on his return. Angry at him as he lay there, the bishop touched him with a staff and foretold that he would die in that very house. It happened that the aforesaid count and his brother killed him in that house. They said that they had done it because he was excessively lenient toward enemies.

Swithhelm succeeded Sigeberht. He was baptized by Cedd himself in East Anglia, at Rendlesham, that is, “Rendle’s dwelling”; King Æthelwald of that people, brother of their King Anna, received him from the baptismal font. Æthelwald, son of King Oswald and king of the Deirans, granted the same Bishop Cedd a place at Lastingham for building a monastery. After it was built, Cedd often returned there from the East Saxons and died there during a time of plague. His brother Ceadda succeeded him in the bishopric. [Col. 0864C–0865A]

Meanwhile Bishop Finan built on the island of Lindisfarne a church entirely of hewn oak. After Archbishop Theodore dedicated it, Bishop Eadberht covered its walls and roof with lead. After Finan’s death, Colman succeeded him. He kept Easter incorrectly, as Aidan and Finan had done. Consequently the matter was debated before King Oswi and King Alfred, his son. On one side stood Colman and the aforesaid Bishop Cedd; on the other were Ægilbert, bishop of the West Saxons, who had come to his friend King Alfred, and James, deacon of Paulinus. The latter party rightly prevailed. Cedd thereafter kept the correct Easter. Colman, unwilling to change his party, returned to his homeland with part of the bones of Father Aidan. Tuda succeeded him in the Northumbrian bishopric. Eata, formerly its custodian and afterward bishop, became bishop of Lindisfarne.

These three Scottish bishops—Aidan, Finan, and Colman—were men of remarkable holiness and frugality. They did not receive the powerful men of the world, who came to them only for prayer. The king himself, with five or six attendants, either departed after praying or ate the brothers’ food. So free from greed were the priests of that time that they did not accept lands unless compelled to do so.

Not long afterward, on the third of May, at the tenth hour of the day, there was an eclipse of the sun. A grievous plague followed it, devastating Britain and Ireland with great slaughter. Bishop Tuda died in this plague and was buried at Wimale. [Col. 0865A–C]

Alfred, son of Oswi, now ruling a part of his father’s kingdom, sent the priest Wilfrid to the king of the Gauls to have him consecrated bishop. The aforesaid Ægilbert, then bishop of Paris, honourably consecrated him with many bishops in the settlement called Compiègne. King Oswi, imitating his son’s enterprise, sent the priest Ceadda—since the archbishop had already died—to Wine, bishop of the West Saxons, by whom he was consecrated bishop of the church of York.

Bishop Ceadda began to follow his teacher Aidan and the example of his brother Cedd: he travelled not on horseback but on foot, diligently attended to reading, pursued truth, was a friend of chastity and a servant of humility. Wilfrid too, having come to Britain already a bishop, contributed much to the Church of the English through his teaching. [Col. 0865C–D]

After Swithhelm, king of the East Saxons, when Sighere and Sebbi reigned, Sighere and his people returned to idols because of the aforesaid plague. But King Wulfhere sent Bishop Jaruman to them, and through him happily recalled them to the faith.
