At that time Pope Vitalian sent letters to the most noble English kings Oswi and Ecgbert, having been consulted concerning the state of the Church and Easter. Not long afterward he sent them Archbishop Theodore. [Col. 0865D–0866A]

Theodore, after Damian, ordained Putta bishop of Rochester; at the request also of King Wulfhere he transferred Ceadda from the monastery at Lastingham to the bishopric of Lichfield, where he shone by miracles, which will be recounted in their place. When King Oswi died of illness, and his son Ecgfrith was reigning in the third year, Theodore convened a council with the other bishops, whose decrees will be set down at the end of the books. After this, offended by a certain act of disobedience, Theodore deposed Winfrith, bishop of the Mercians, and ordained Sexwulf in his place. He also made Erconwald bishop in London, in the time of the aforesaid kings Sebbi and Sighere, whose miracles will be recounted in their place. At that time Æthelred, king of the Mercians, ravaged Kent and destroyed Rochester; Bishop Putta fled. Cwichelm succeeded him, but withdrew because of poverty. Then Gebmund succeeded. In the same year a comet appeared in the morning for three months.

King Ecgfrith of Northumbria expelled Wilfrid from his bishopric. In his place Bosa received the province of the Deirans and Eata that of the Bernicians: the latter at York, the former in the church of Hexham or Lindisfarne. At that time Eadhæd was also ordained bishop in the province of Lindsey, which King Ecgfrith had very recently acquired after defeating Wulfhere. And this province first received him as its own bishop, then Æthelwin [alternatively, Eadwine], third Eadgar, and fourth Cyneberht, whom it has at present, says Bede. Before Eadhæd it had Sexwulf as bishop, who was at the same time bishop of the Mercians and the Middle Angles; hence, when he was expelled from Lindsey, he remained in the governance of those provinces. Eadhæd, Bosa, and Eata were ordained at York by Theodore. After Wilfrid’s three years of absence, Theodore added two bishops to their number: Trumberht for the church of Hexham, Eata remaining at Lindisfarne; and Trumwine for the province of the Picts, then subject to the English. He placed Eadhæd, returned from Lindsey because King Æthelred had recovered that province, over the church of Ripon.

[Col. 0866D] The seventh part follows, concerning the conversion of the South Saxons by Bishop Wilfrid. Expelled from his bishopric, as was said above, he went to Rome and returned to Britain; and he converted to the faith the South Saxons, numbering seven thousand households. Their king Æthelwealh [alternatively, Æthelwalh] had been baptized a little earlier in the province of the Mercians at the persuasion of King Wulfhere, who also received him from the font. As a token of adoption Wulfhere gave him the Isle of Wight and the province of the Meonwara among the West Saxons. With the king’s consent—indeed, with his rejoicing—Wilfrid preached and first washed the commanders and soldiers, then the common people, in the sacred font. On that very day rain came upon the people, having ceased for three years; consequently a most severe famine had laid the populace low.

Indeed, they say that often forty or fifty people at once, wasted by hunger, went out to some precipice or seashore cliff; and, after pitifully binding their hands together, all fell together, either to perish in the fall or to be swallowed by the waves. But when baptism and rain came together, the land flourished anew; with the fields growing green, the year returned joyful and fruitful. Thus the heart and flesh of all rejoiced in the living God. The bishop also taught them to fish; for previously they knew how to fish only for eels. Having therefore gathered nets, he cast himself into the sea, and, when three hundred fish had quickly been caught, he gave one hundred to the poor, one hundred to those whose nets they were, and reserved one hundred for his own use. Seeing this, the people began more readily to hope for heavenly goods from the words of one through whose ministry they had received temporal goods.

[Col. 0867B] King Æthelwealh gave him an island of eighty-seven households, called Selsey, that is, “island of the seal.” It is surrounded on every side by the sea, except for a sling’s throw on the west: such a place is called by the Latins a peninsula, and by the Greeks χερσόνησος, “peninsula.” There Wilfrid founded a church and remained for five years, that is, until the death of King Ecgfrith; there he made two hundred and fifty of his male and female slaves Christians and free persons.

Meanwhile Cædwalla, a youth of royal stock among the Gewisse, while in exile killed King Æthelwealh. But he was soon expelled by the king’s commanders Berhthun and Andhun, who ruled before him. Yet when Cædwalla became king of the Gewisse, he killed the former and grievously harassed the province, both he and his successor. Therefore, throughout that whole time, being recalled home, Wilfrid’s community lacked its own bishop and was subject to the bishop of Winchester.

King Cædwalla subdued the Isle of Wight, still idolatrous, and in accordance with a vow gave a fourth part to Bishop Wilfrid, who happened then to be present after arriving from his own people. The island contains twelve hundred households; consequently the bishop was given a possession of three hundred households. The two sons of Arwald, king of the island, already bereft of their father and about to be killed, were permitted by Cædwalla to be baptized first by Abbot Redford—that is, “reed-ford.” Thus Wight, the last district of Britain, was converted.

[Col. 0868B] Therefore, after all the provinces of Britain had received the faith of Christ, Archbishop Theodore, in order to confirm the faith both of recent converts and of those long established, convened a council with the bishops of Britain to treat of the Catholic faith; and he committed its proceedings to synodal letters for perpetual remembrance. I have thought it fitting to set forth these letters at the beginning of the following book, which we shall carry down from the deeds of the faithful kings of the English to the coming and wars of the Danes. For all the parts of this book have been treated in accordance with their order and purpose.

# BOOK FOUR

[Col. 0867]

[Col. 0867C] In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Saviour. In the tenth year of the reign of our most pious lord Ecgfrith, king of the Humber-folk; in the fifth year of the reign of Centwine, king of the West Saxons; in the sixth year of the reign of Æthelred, king of the Mercians; in the seventeenth year of the reign of Aldwulf, king of the East Angles; in the seventh year of the reign of Hlothhere, king of the Kentish people; on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October, in the seventh indiction; Theodore, by God’s grace archbishop of the island of Britain and of the city of Canterbury, presiding, and the other venerable bishops of the island of Britain sitting with him; the most holy Gospels having been set before us, in the place called in the Saxon tongue Hatfield: deliberating together, we set forth the right and orthodox faith, as our Lord Jesus Christ incarnate handed it down to his disciples, who personally saw and heard his words; and as the Creed of the holy Fathers handed it down, and generally all the holy and universal synods, and the whole choir of approved teachers of the Catholic Church.

[Col. 0867D] Therefore, following them piously and orthodoxly in accordance with their divinely inspired teaching, we profess that we steadfastly believe and confess, according to the holy Fathers, properly and truly, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit: a Trinity consubstantial in unity, and unity in Trinity; that is, one God in three subsisting and consubstantial persons, of equal glory and honour. And after many similar matters pertaining to the confession of the right faith, the holy synod added this also in its letters:

“We receive the five holy and universal synods of blessed and God-pleasing Fathers: namely, those three hundred and eighteen assembled at Nicaea against the most impious Arius and his doctrines; the one hundred and fifty at Constantinople against the madness of Macedonius and Eudoxius and their doctrines; the first at Ephesus, of two hundred, against the most wicked Nestorius and his doctrines; at Chalcedon, of four hundred and thirty, against Eutyches and Nestorius and their doctrines; and again the fifth council assembled at Constantinople in the time of Justinian the Younger against Theodore, the letters of Theodoret and Ibas, and their doctrines against Cyril.”

And a little later:

“We have received the synod held in the city of Rome in the time of the most blessed Pope Martin, in the first indiction, in the ninth year of the reign of the most pious Constantine; and we glorify our Lord Jesus Christ as they glorified him, adding nothing and subtracting nothing. We anathematize in heart and mouth those whom they anathematized; and those whom they received, we receive, glorifying God the Father without beginning, and his only-begotten Son, begotten of the Father before the ages, and the Holy Spirit proceeding ineffably from the Father and the Son, as the holy apostles, prophets, and teachers whom we have mentioned above preached.”

[Col. 0869A] And all of us who set forth the Catholic faith together with Archbishop Theodore subscribed. John, chief singer of the church of St Peter at Rome and abbot of St Martin, was present at this synod. He had lately come from there by the command of Pope Agatho with the venerable Abbot Benedict. Benedict had built a monastery of St Peter by the mouth of the river Wear. Having gone to Rome to obtain confirmation of the privilege of that church by grant of King Ecgbert, he brought the aforesaid John back with him. Ceolfrith, under whom Bede lived, succeeded this Benedict as abbot. There John taught singing in the Roman manner and left there written copies of the decrees of the synod of Pope Martin, at which he himself had been present. But, returning to Rome to report on the nature of the faith of the English, he died on the journey and was buried at Tours.

Now that these matters have been treated, we must return to the thread of the history of the kings of the English, which we cut off at the end of the second book; this discussion must be joined to that narrative, so that the account may extend continuously.

Centwine [alternatively, Kentwine], king of the West Saxons, having died, Cædwalla succeeded him and by the aid of his brother Mul made the Isle of Wight his own by force. For his brother Mul was admirable and gracious, formidable in strength, and handsome in appearance; therefore he was beloved by all and most renowned for the distinction of his fame. The aforesaid brothers went into the province of Kent to exercise their strength and enlarge their reputation. They were not yet baptized, although their predecessors and all the people were Christian. Entering Kent, therefore, with no one resisting them, they plundered the whole province.

[Col. 0869D] For as Cædwalla was taking possession of his kingdom, Hlothhere, king of Kent, left his kingdom by dying. The energetic King Hlothhere had been wounded in a battle with the South Saxons, whom Eadric son of Ecgbert had assembled against him; and, while receiving treatment, he died from the severity of his wounds. After him that same Eadric ruled for one year and a half without the love or respect of the Kentish people.

At that time also Ecgfrith, king of Northumbria, died. In the preceding year he had sent the commander Berht with an army into Ireland; Berht miserably devastated a people innocent and always friendly to the English nation. The Irish, resisting to the extent of their power and invoking the aid of divine mercy, begged God by continual imprecations that vengeance might be sent from heaven. Although the revilers may not possess the kingdom of God, it was nevertheless believed that those who were cursed on account of their impiety would soon, with the Lord as avenger, pay the penalties for their guilt. Thus, in the following year, when the same king rashly led an army to ravage the province of the Picts—

[Col. 0870A] despite the strong warnings of his friends, and especially of Cuthbert of blessed memory, who had recently been ordained bishop (for in that same year he had made Rixid bishop of Lindisfarne)—he was led, while the enemy feigned flight, into the narrow passes of inaccessible mountains, and was slain with the greater part of the forces he had brought with him. It was granted to him that he should not hear his friends calling him back, because he had refused to hear Father Egbert, who urged him not to attack Ireland, which had done him no harm. From that time the hope and strength of the English began to ebb and decline: the Picts recovered their land, part of which the English had held; the Britons also regained some measure of freedom, which they retain to this day. The man of God Trumwine, abbot of Abercorn, situated indeed in the land of the English but near the strait which separates the lands of the English and the Picts, fled thence and died in the often-mentioned monastery of Streanæshalch.

Alfrith succeeded Ecgfrith in the kingdom, a man most learned in the Scriptures, said to have been his brother and a son of King Oswi. He nobly restored the ruined condition of the kingdom, although within narrower boundaries.

In the second year of his reign Cædwalla sent his very valiant brother Mul, and with him very valiant young men, to plunder Kent, at that brother’s request. For the glorious profit of the preceding year and the welcome reward of fame had enticed him. Going into Kent, he found no one to resist him; but, reducing the land to desolation by plunder and afflicting undeserving servants of Christ, he experienced the deserved force of their curses. For, leading effeminate enemies and foreseeing no danger corresponding to his strength, he rushed far from his own men with only twelve soldiers into a certain house to plunder it. There, surrounded by an unexpected multitude, though he did not cease killing enemies he could not prevail; and, since he could not be cut down by weapons, he was burned by fire in that very house with his twelve soldiers.

[Col. 0870D] Thus the flower of the young men perished and the youthful army vanished. From this it is apparent how worthless confidence in strength is beside the power of almighty God. Hearing this, Cædwalla entered Kent again; there, sated with marvellous slaughter and countless plunder, when he found nothing left to kill or plunder, he returned to his own land a great avenger and cruel victor.

After reigning for two years, King Cædwalla renounced himself and his kingdom and sought Rome for God’s sake and for the eternal kingdom, considering it a singular glory if he should be baptized and die there. Pope Sergius therefore baptized him and named him Peter after the apostle. According to his vow, the king died in his baptismal white garments within seven days, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of May, and was buried in the church of St Peter. The following epitaph was written over him:

> Rank, wealth, offspring, mighty kingdoms, triumphs,  
> Spoils, nobles, walls, forts, and homes—  
> All that ancestral valour, and that Cædwalla himself,  
> Had amassed, he left through love of almighty God,  
> That as a royal guest he might behold Peter and Peter’s see,  
> [Col. 0871A] And, blessed, drink the pure waters of his font;  
> And by radiant draught might partake of the splendid beam  
> From which life-giving brightness flows everywhere.  
> Rejoicingly receiving the rewards of renewed life,  
> He turned away the barbaric fury and even his own name;  
> Exulting in conversion, he was commanded by the bishop Sergius,  
> Himself a father, to be called Peter.  
> Whom the grace of Christ’s rebirthing font cleansed,  
> It immediately bore, clothed in white, to the citadel of heaven.  
> Wondrous is the king’s faith; greatest is Christ’s mercy,  
> Whose counsel no one can attain.  
> For, coming safely as a youth from Britain’s utmost world,  
> Through diverse peoples, straits, and roads,  
> He saw the city of Romulus and beheld  
> Peter’s venerable shrine, bearing mystical gifts.  
> White among Christ’s companionable sheep he shall go;  
> In body he holds the tomb, in mind the things above.  
> You would think he had exchanged rather the insignia of sceptres,  
> Seeing that he has earned the kingdom of Christ.

[Col. 0871B] Ine reigned after him over the West Saxons for thirty-seven years. Ine was son of Cenred, son of Ceolwald. Ceolwald was brother of Cynewald, and both were sons of Cuthwine, son of Ceawlin, son of Cynric, son of Cerdic. In the second year of this king, Archbishop Theodore died in the twenty-second year of his episcopate. In his place Brihtwald, abbot of Reculver, was elected and consecrated archbishop. Up to this time the archbishops had been Romans; from then they were English. Brihtwald himself ordained Tobias bishop of Rochester, a man abundantly instructed in Latin, Greek, and Saxon. At that time there were two kings in Kent, not so much by royal descent as by usurpation: namely, Nithred and Webhard.

[Col. 0871C] In Ine’s sixth regnal year, the legitimate king of Kent, Wihtred, strengthened in his kingdom by religion and diligence alike, freed his people from foreign usurpation. Wihtred was son of Ecgberht, son of Erconberht, son of Eadbald, son of Æthelberht. He held the kingdom of Kent nobly and peacefully for thirty-two years. In the same year King Ine led ordered and dreadful battle-lines into Kent, to avenge the burning of his kinsman Mul. King Wihtred met him, not with fierce arrogance but with peaceful entreaty; not with snarling threats, but with the sweetness of rhetorical honey. By this he persuaded the fierce king to lay down arms and accept a large sum of money from the Kentish people for the killing of the young man. Thus the dispute ended and peace, having been confirmed, revived. The king of Kent thereafter always reigned in peace.

In the third year after this, the Mercians, also called the South-Humbrians [alternatively, Subhimbri], committed a shameful crime: they inhumanly killed Queen Osthryth, wife of their king Æthelred and sister of King Ecgfrith.

In Ine’s eleventh regnal year, Berht [alternatively, Briht], the aforesaid commander of Ecgfrith, felt the curses of the Irish, whose churches he had destroyed, as his lord had also felt them. For just as King Ecgfrith, entering the land of the Picts, suffered slaughter there, so Berht, entering the same land to avenge his lord, was killed by the same people. About this time seven hundred years had elapsed from the Incarnation of the Lord.

Æthelred, son of Penda and king of Mercia, visited by the kindness of the Almighty, became a monk in the twenty-ninth year of his reign and was happily buried at Bardney. His kinsman Cenred, like him in virtue and blessedness, succeeded him. For after holding the kingdom nobly for five years, he left the sceptre of the kingdom far more nobly. Going to Rome and becoming a monk there during the pontificate of Constantine, he remained so until his last day. With him Offa, son of Sighere king of the East Saxons—who would have been king had he remained—went to Rome, led by equal devotion, and embraced monastic life.

[Col. 0872A] Therefore imitate, O kings, the most blessed zeal of these two kings, Æthelred and Cenred, whose name endures for ever. Abandoning crowns, wives, cities, kinsmen, and all things, they became an example to many thousands to do the same. O good God, what crowns, and how great, will you restore to them! With your own hand, as supreme pontiff, you will set them upon their necks in the day of exultation and gladness, when all the countless hosts of heaven and earth receive the aforesaid kings with triumph and desire to behold their faces; then they will bring forth not merely a hundredfold fruit, but rather a thousandfold—fragrant fruit, desirable fruit, fruit delightful to your own sight. O good God, who now, inflamed also by the fire of the Holy Spirit, may follow the examples of those kings, truly kings, so that the exultation of new fruit may still increase for them, and their followers, by their excellence, may offer you richer gifts with most devoted joy? Alas, poor us! We must leave discourse concerning the kings of heaven—oh, would that it might be fixed for ever in our wretched and most sluggish hearts! But we must return from heaven to earth.

[Col. 0872C] Ceolred succeeded the aforesaid kings in the Mercian kingdom. For eight years he governed it most splendidly as heir to his country’s and ancestors’ valour.

In the twentieth year of his reign Ine divided the bishopric of Wessex, which had formerly been one, into two. Daniel held the eastern part, Aldhelm the western. Forthhere succeeded Aldhelm. In the same year Bishop Wilfrid, of whom miracles will not be passed over in silence, died at Oundle in the forty-fifth year of his episcopate and was buried at Ripon. In the next year King Ine and his kinsman Nun fought against Geraint [alternatively, Gerente], king of Wales. At the beginning of that battle Commander Hægebald was killed; in the end Geraint and his men turned their backs on the English and, fleeing, left arms and spoils to their pursuers.

At that time also Commander Berfrith opposed the pride of the Picts, fighting between Heve and Cere; there, after a great multitude of Picts had been laid low, he became the avenger of King Ecgfrith and Commander Berht. The priest Acca succeeded Bishop Wilfrid. Four years earlier Alfrith, king of Northumbria, had died of illness at Driffield before completing the twentieth year of his reign. His son Osred succeeded him; a boy of eight years, he reigned for eleven years. King Osred was then killed in battle by the Wear. Cenred succeeded him, reigned two years, and died. After them Osric ruled there for eleven years. These four kings, indeed, reigned in Northumbria during the time of King Ine.

[Col. 0873A] In the twenty-sixth year of his reign Ine fought against Ceolred, king of Mercia and son of King Æthelred, at Monebirih. The fighting was so terrible on both sides that it is not known to whom the more dreadful slaughter befell. In the following year Ceolred, the same king of Mercia, departed this world and was buried at Lichfield. Æthelbald succeeded him in the Mercian kingdom, a strong and vehement man, and reigned victoriously for forty-one years.

In the same year the venerable Egbert converted the monks who were at Iona to the Catholic Easter and canonical tonsure. Having remained with those converted monks for thirteen years, now assured of the correction of the brethren, on Easter Day, after celebrating the solemnities of Mass, he rejoiced to see the Lord’s day: he saw it and was glad (John 8). At that time Nechtan, king of the Picts, had been converted to the correct Easter through instructional letters sent by Abbot Ceolfrith, who, after Benedict, of whom we spoke above, governed the monastery at the mouth of the river Wear and beside the river Tyne, in the place called Jarrow. He therefore wrote the king letters concerning Easter and tonsure, full of great authority. What he persuaded by letter, the king carried out throughout his whole kingdom by royal authority. About this time Cuthburh, sister of Cneburh, founded an abbey at Mineburn, which had been given to Ecgfrith of Northumbria but, during his lifetime, separated from him.

[Col. 0873C] In the thirty-sixth year of his reign Ine advanced his army into Surrey, fought the South Saxons mightily and victoriously, and killed in that battle Ealdbrith, whom he had earlier expelled from the fortress called Taunton. King Ine had built this fortress; but because the aforesaid young man Ealbriht, an enemy of the king, had entered it, Queen Æthelburh, Ine’s wife, captured it by force of arms, destroyed it after its capture, and compelled him to flee into Surrey. In the same year Wihtred, king of Kent, died after ruling almost thirty-four years, leaving three sons as heirs: Æthelberht, Eadberht, and Ælric. About this time Tobias, bishop of Rochester and disciple of Archbishop Theodore and Abbot Hadrian, died; Aldwulf succeeded him.

[Col. 0873D] Ine, a powerful and blessed king, leaving his kingdom to his kinsman Æthelheard, sought Rome; and while a pilgrim on earth he earned his reward in heaven. In the time of this king, so that the swiftness of the world’s mutability may hence be perceived, the emperors were: Justinian the Younger, who reigned ten years; Leo, who reigned three years; Tiberius, seven years; Justinian the Second, six years; Philippicus, one year and a half; Anastasius, three years; Theodosius, one year; Leo, nine years; and Constantine, in the third year of whose reign Ine departed for Rome. The popes in his time were Sergius, John, another John, Sisinnius, Constantine, and Gregory, in whose time King Ine, voluntarily victorious over desire, went into exile.

[Col. 0874A] The kings of the Franks in order during his time were King Childeric, King Theuderic, King Clovis, King Childebert, and King Dagobert. In the time of this king the following ascended to the palaces of heaven: Saint Heddi, bishop of Winchester; Saint Guthlac, hermit of Crowland; and Saint John, archbishop of York.

The neighbouring kings Cædwalla and Ine, great in strength—which they shared with beasts—but greater in holiness—which is the property of angels and of human beings, though few—acted nobly. Therefore all generations will call them blessed, as also the two neighbouring kings of Mercia, Æthelred and Cenred, did; leaving all false goods, they attained the true and highest good, which is God. Therefore, kings now on earth, imitate the aforesaid wise and blessed kings, not the mad and unhappy ones, whose distinction is shown in this account by their deeds and the end of their deeds. These four kings, therefore, are lights to all kings of the earth: that the good may have men to imitate, and the evil may have no ground for excuse. You also who are not kings, imitate the aforesaid kings, that you may become kings of heaven. For if, when they left greater things, you refuse to leave lesser ones, the aforesaid holy kings will be judges of your condemnation.

[Col. 0874B] In the first year of his reign Æthelheard, king of the West Saxons, fought against Oswald, a youth of royal stock attempting to obtain the same kingdom for himself. Oswald was son of Æthelbald [alternatively, Æthelbold], son of Cynebald, son of Cuthwine, son of Ceawlin, son of Cynric [alternatively, Cinric]. Although the youth, inferior in number to the royal troops, bore the burden of battle for a long time, when he could no longer do so he left the kingdom to the king by flight. The aforesaid king was therefore strengthened in his kingdom.

In the third year of King Æthelheard, two terrible comets appeared near the sun. One preceded the rising sun, the other followed the setting sun, as though portents of dreadful destruction for east and west alike; or rather, one anticipated the day’s rising and the other the night’s, signifying that evils threatened mortals at both times. They bore an appearance of fire toward the north, as though to set aflame the [uncertain: acelivem]. They appeared in January and remained for nearly two weeks. At that time a most grievous Saracen devastation was laying waste Gaul and Spain far and wide with miserable slaughter. Not long afterwards they themselves paid in the same province the penalties deserved by their faithlessness.

[Col. 0874D] In the same year Osric, king of Northumbria, departed this life, leaving the kingdom, which he had governed for eleven years, to Ceolwulf, brother of the man who had ruled before him in the time of King Cenred. King Ceolwulf held the kingdom for eight years. This is the king for whom Bede, holy and venerable man, a man of flourishing intellect and a philosopher of Christ, wrote the Ecclesiastical History of the English; and the blessed end of the king showed how much he had profited from the work sent to him.

When Æthelheard had reigned five years, Archbishop Brihtwald died after nearly thirty-eight years; and Tatwine, who had been a priest at Bredon in Mercia, became archbishop. He was consecrated by men of blessed memory: Ingwald, bishop of London; Daniel, bishop of Winchester; Aldwulf, bishop of Rochester; and Aldwine, bishop of Lichfield. After two years, the most mighty Æthelbald, king of Mercia, gathered a terrible army and besieged Somerton, his camps arranged in a ring. Since no one could bring aid to those enclosed or resist the besiegers, he took it into his own possession. King Æthelbald of Mercia, raised by the greatest valour above the kings of his own age, wished—and achieved—that all the provinces of England as far as the river Humber, with their kings, should be subject to him. In the same year the sun was darkened.

[Col. 0875B] In the eighth year of King Æthelheard, Archbishop Tatwine, a man distinguished by religion and prudence and nobly instructed in sacred letters, appeared no more among men. Ecgberht [alternatively, Egbricht], having received the pallium at Rome, ascended in his place. In the same year the venerable Bede, whose mind always dwelt in heaven, ascended to the palaces of heaven. By his royal virtue and by restraining others’ vices, and being in no respect inferior to kings themselves, he most deservedly should be placed among kings, as a king.

Bede, priest of the monastery at Wearmouth and Jarrow, educated and instructed by Abbot Benedict of that place and then by Ceolfrith, always studied the Scriptures. He left the world in the sixty-second year of his age, old in years and wisdom, and full of days not spent in vain, as appears from the number of his works. He wrote: from the beginning of Genesis to the birth of Isaac, three books; on the tabernacle, its vessels, and vestments, three books; on the first part of Samuel up to the death of Saul, four books; on the building of the Temple allegorically, two books; on the books of Kings, a book of thirty questions; on the Proverbs of Solomon, three books; on the Song of Songs, six; on Ezra and Nehemiah, three; on the song of Habakkuk, one; on the book of Tobit, one; also chapter-headings for readings from the Old Testament; on the Gospel of Mark, four books; on Luke, six; on the Apostle, he transcribed in order everything he found in Augustine’s shorter works; on the Acts of the Apostles, two books; on the seven Catholic Epistles, seven books; on the Apocalypse, three books.

[Col. 0875D] Likewise, chapter-headings for readings through the whole New Testament, except the Gospel; likewise, a book of letters to various persons; likewise, *On the Histories of the Saints*; likewise, *On the Life of Saint Cuthbert*, first in heroic verse and afterwards in plain prose; likewise, two books *On the Lives of the Abbots of His Monastery*; likewise, a martyrology; likewise, a book of hymns; likewise, *On Times*; likewise, *On the Art of Metre*; and the *Ecclesiastical History of the English* in five books, in which he devoutly prays that he may find among all readers the fruit of intercession.

Concerning the ecclesiastical condition in his own time, Bede himself says this:

“At present, the archbishop of Canterbury is Tatwine; the bishop of Rochester, Aldwulf; the bishop of London, Ingwald. Over the East Angles are Bishops Eadberht and Heaðolac; over Mercia is Bishop Aldwine; over the people who dwell west of the river Severn is Bishop Walhstod; in the province of the Hwicce is Bishop Wilfrid; in the province of Lindsey, Cyneberht. The Isle of Wight belongs to Daniel, bishop of Winchester; and the province of the South Saxons, now for several years without a bishop, acknowledges the same. Under King Ceolwulf are four bishops: Wilfrid of York, Æthelwold of Lindisfarne, Acca of Hexham, and Pecthelm at Candida Casa, which, newly established as a bishopric, has him as its first bishop. The king of Kent is Eadberht; the king of the West Saxons is Æthelheard [alternatively, Æthelred]; the king of the East Angles, Sælred; the king of Northumbria, Ceolwulf; the king of Mercia, Æthelbald, greatest of all. In about the two hundred and eighty-eighth year after the coming of the English, in the year seven hundred and thirty-four of the Lord’s Incarnation, in whose everlasting kingdom may the earth rejoice; and may many islands rejoice, Britain rejoicing with him in its faith (Psalm 96), and may they give thanks to the memory of his holiness (Psalm 29).”

[Col. 0876B] Up to this point, in composing this history, we have followed the authority of the venerable priest Bede, especially in all that has been said concerning ecclesiastical affairs; and in other matters also, so far as we have been able. Hence, whatever we have been able to find in the writings of the ancients, gathered by diligent investigation, we have endeavoured to commit to letters for the instruction of posterity. For, as the most learned Bede testifies in the prologue to his history of the English: “The true law of history is simply to make known to posterity in writing what is gathered from current report.”

In the tenth year of King Æthelheard, Nothelm, archbishop, received the pallium from the pope; and not long afterwards Bishop Forthhere and Queen Frigedida [alternatively, Fridegia], abandoning splendid possessions and the pleasures of luxury, set out for Rome. In those times many English people, noble and low-born, clerics and laypersons, men and women, were accustomed eagerly to do the same. At that time also Adilwald, bishop of Lindisfarne, ended his life; after him Chenewolf received the dignity of the episcopate. Nor did the venerable priest Acca, afterwards bishop of Hexham, long remain: he too was stripped of bodily things.

In the eleventh year of King Æthelard, Ceolwulf, most noble king of Northumbria, acted most nobly. For Ceolwulf was son of Cutha, son of Cudwine, son of Ledwold, son of Egwold, son of Aldelin, son of Ocche, son of King Ida. Therefore Ceolwulf, since he often conversed with Bede while Bede was alive, and often before and after Bede’s death set before his eyes the history written for him, began carefully to consider within himself the deeds and end of each king. He saw more clearly than daylight that earthly kingdoms and human affairs are acquired with toil, possessed with fear, and lost with grief. And because to some less discerning persons, or to those tender in age, when they see temporal things beautiful and delightful [Col. 0877A] and hear them proclaimed to be things that must be abandoned and despised, this appears frivolous and contrary to reason—because they have not yet learned how the riches of the world bite, how they come to nothing, and how at last they bear no fruit save late repentance—none of these things hindered the discerning and experienced king. For he had experienced in himself that a kingdom had been acquired by him with toil and held with fear; yet he was unwilling to lose it with grief. Thus, of his own will, not a slave but master of riches, he cast them aside as trivial, like a great man.

What especially inflamed him was that, while boys, women, the common crowd, and even the wealthier people rushed out to behold him and marvel at his blessedness, he himself was inwardly tortured by dreadful anxieties of death, treachery, and manifold [Col. 0877B] calamity, and was worn away in mind and body. While others judged him most blessed, he alone, who knew the secrets of his own heart, judged himself most miserable. Therefore, though he had reigned only a short time, that is, eight years, it seemed to him exceedingly long, and he was deeply troubled that for so great a period he had wasted his life upon vain cares and fragile disciplines. He strove, at least, to devote the remainder of his life not to erring folly but to wisdom and his own true benefit.

Taking an example from the aforesaid history of the blessed man, this truly brave man followed six very brave kings: namely, King Æthelred of Mercia and his successor Cenred; also King Cædwalla of the West Saxons and his successor Ine; likewise Sigeberht [al. Sibrect], king of the East Angles, who became a monk and whom Penda afterwards killed; and King Sebbi of the East Saxons, who became a monk, foresaw the joyful day of his death, and saw it with gladness. These men did not devour their substance with harlots; rather, going forth with sorrow, they sowed their seed, that they might come again with exultation, bringing their sheaves to God (Ps. 125). Thus Ceolwulf completed the week—the seven—of perfect kings; and, having assumed the monastic habit, a crown of precious stone was placed upon his head by the Lord (Ps. 20). He left the sceptres of the kingdom to his kinsman Egbert [al. Eadbert]. For Egbert was son of Ecca [al. Etata], son of Ledwold [al. Lethwold], and he reigned fifty-one years.

[Col. 0877D] In this exchange of kings, the proud Mercian King Æthelbald, a man of another spirit and therefore given to another kind of end, despising holiness and setting aside right for the sword, entered Northumbria; and, since there was none able to resist him, he seized plunder and carried away to his own people as much as he wished.

King Æthelard died in the fourteenth year of his reign, and his kinsman Cuthred reigned in his place over the West Saxons for sixteen years. But the proud King Æthelbald frequently afflicted him, now by seditions, now by wars. Changeable fortune, in its various turns, now raised one and now the other by the outcomes of Mars. At times they established peace between themselves; but after holding it for a short time, they again made war [al. rebelled]. In the same year Egbert [al. Eadbert] was consecrated archbishop in the time of Pope Zachary, and Dun bishop at Rochester.

In the fourth year of Cuthred’s reign, he and King Æthelbald of Mercia, then reconciled to one another, fought with united forces against an innumerable multitude of Britons gathered from every quarter. While the most valiant kings and their most distinguished armies, divided from each other, struck down the British ranks from either side in emulous rivalry, the Britons could not endure such a burden of warfare. Choosing flight, therefore, they turned their backs to their attackers and left their spoils to those pursuing them. The victorious kings returned to their own lands and were received with triumphal rejoicing. In the following year Wilfrid died, having been bishop at York for ten [al. thirty] years. In that same year a marvellous sign appeared in the sky: stars darted here and there through the air, a great portent to all who beheld it. In the year after this Daniel died, in the forty-third year since he had become bishop. In the year following those already mentioned, King Selred was deprived of life. The writings of the ancients say that he was killed in this year; but they do not say how, or by whom, he was killed.

In Cuthred’s ninth year his son Cyneric was killed—the glory of arms and conqueror of wild beasts; tender in age but fierce in arms, small in years but great in strength. Because he pressed on in his successes and sought the fortune [Col. 0878C] of Mars too eagerly, a slaughter inflicted by military sedition punished the excess of his spirit. In the same year Eadbert, king of Kent, died, having possessed the royal diadem for twenty-two years.

In the eleventh year of his reign Cuthred fought against Æthelhun, a most daring ealdorman. Raising rebellion against his lord, though far inferior to his lord in number of soldiers, he nevertheless stood long and most fiercely upon the field of Mars; and the ealdorman’s outstanding valour was worth thousands. When victory was already almost clapping its joyful wings for him, the wound at last fixed in his body, and perjury in his soul, compelled the king’s just cause to triumph.

In the thirteenth year of Cuthred, since he could no longer endure the proud exactions and insolence [Col. 0878D] of King Æthelbald, he met him at Nereford [al. Bereford] with bannered legions, setting every hope of life behind liberty. He brought with him the aforesaid ealdorman Æthelhun, now reconciled to him; relying upon his strength and counsel, he was able to enter upon the hazard of war. Æthelbald, king of kings, had brought with the Mercians the men of Kent, the East Saxons, the Angles, and numerous forces.

When the battle-lines had been drawn up and they approached in a direct advance, Æthelhun went ahead of the West Saxons, bearing the king’s standard, namely a golden dragon, and pierced the enemy standard-bearer. A shout arose; Cuthred’s side was greatly strengthened, and the lines immediately clashed. Thus the thunder of war—that is, the collision of weapons, the sound of blows, and the cries [Col. 0879A] of the falling—flamed up terribly; a battle immense and beyond estimation began, one that would subject either the Mercians or the West Saxons, whoever prevailed, for a long posterity.

You might have seen battle-lines bristling with coats of mail, sharp with helmets, shaggy with spears, painted with standards, gleaming with gold; then, in a short time, drenched in blood, empty of spears, scattered in collapse, spattered with brains, and dreadful to behold. Men on each side, fierce and exceedingly brave, gathered around the standards and, wielding swords and Amazonian axes, rushed their battle-lines mournfully against battle-lines. There was no thought of flight; each side had certain hope of victory. The swelling of pride urged the Mercians on; horror of servitude fired the West Saxons. Wherever the aforesaid ealdorman thrust himself into the ranks, a path of destruction lay open, while his most terrible axe, like lightning, split bodies and armour alike. But wherever the most valiant King Æthelbald charged, there was slaughter of the enemy, since to his invincible sword armour was as clothing and bones as flesh.

As though two fires set in different places consumed everything opposing them, it happened that king and ealdorman came face to face. Each, terrible to the other, ground his teeth; each brandished his right hand, gathered himself within his armour, and with every blow attacked armour of equal resistance. But God, who resists the proud, and from whom strength, courage, and greatness of soul proceed, set a limit to his favour toward King Æthelbald and took from the king’s spirit its customary confidence. Therefore, unable to recognize either his own courage [Col. 0879C] or strength, though his men still fought, terrified by almighty God he was the first to begin flight. From that day until his death God allowed him no prosperity. For four years later, fighting again at Secandune, he was killed, though not without a wondrous destruction of armies, while refusing to flee. Killed at Secandune, he was buried at Repandune. Thus that most powerful king, having reigned forty-one years, paid the penalties of unrestrained pride. From this time the kingdom of the West Saxons, greatly strengthened, did not cease to grow to its full stature.

In the fourteenth year of Cuthred’s reign he fought against the Britons, who, vainly resisting the victorious King Æthelbald as has been said, swiftly took flight and deservedly suffered a very great slaughter without loss to the enemy. In the following year King Cuthred, great and exalted, having obtained so many successes and victories, had his joy ended by the ruthlessness of death.

Sigeberht, kinsman of the aforesaid king, succeeded him, but held the kingdom for only a short time. For, puffed up and insolent through the fortunes of his predecessor, he was intolerable even to his own people. Since he mistreated them in every way and either corrupted the laws to serve his own advantage or evaded them for his own advantage, his most noble ealdorman Cumbra, at the prayer of the whole people, laid their complaints before the savage king. Because Cumbra had urged the king to govern his people more mildly, to lay aside inhumanity, and to appear pleasing to God and men, he at once ordered him to be killed by impious murder; and, more savage and intolerable toward the people, he increased his tyranny.

[Col. 0880A] At the beginning of the second year of King Sigeberht’s reign, because his pride and wickedness were incorrigible, the nobles and people of the whole kingdom assembled. By prudent deliberation and the unanimous agreement of all, he was expelled from the kingdom. Cynewulf, a distinguished young man sprung from the royal stock, was elected king. King Sigeberht, driven out by his own people and fearing no lesser fate by his deserts, fled and hid himself in the great wood called Andredeswald. There a certain swineherd of Ealdorman Cumbra, wickedly murdered as we have said, found the hidden king; recognizing him when found, he killed him as avenger of his lord.

Behold the manifest judgment of the Lord; behold how the justice of the Lord repays according to deserts not only in the world to come but also in this one. For, choosing wicked kings for the deserved crushing of their subjects, he allows one to rage for a long time, so that both a perverse people may be long afflicted and a more perverse king more sharply tormented for eternity—as with the aforesaid King Æthelbald of Mercia. But another he forestalls by swift destruction, lest his people, oppressed by excessive tyranny, be unable to breathe, and lest the unrestrained wickedness of the ruler incur, by due desert, the swiftest penalties of eternal vengeance—as with this Sigeberht of whom we are speaking. The more wicked he was, the more basely he was killed by a swineherd, passing from pain to pain.

[Col. 0880C] Therefore praise and glory to the Lord of eternal justice, now and always.

In the first year of King Cynewulf, Beornred succeeded King Æthelbald of Mercia in the kingdom, but only briefly. For Offa expelled him in the same year and reigned over Mercia for thirty-nine years. Offa was a most noble young man, son of Winferth, son of Eanwulf, son of Osmod, son of Epa, son of Wippa, son of Creoda, son of Cynewald, son of Cnebba, son of Icel, son of Eomer, son of Angeltheow, son of Offa, son of Wermund, son of Wihtlæg, son of Woden. Offa was a most vigorous king: he defeated the Kentish in battle, likewise the West Saxons in battle, and likewise the Northumbrians in battle. Offa was a religious man: he transferred the bones of Saint Alban to the monastery which he had built and enriched in many ways [Col. 0880D]; and he gave to the pontiff of the Roman city, the vicar of blessed Peter, a perpetual fixed revenue from every household of his kingdom.

In the third year of King Cynewulf, Eadbert, king of Northumbria, seeing the wretched lives and unhappy ends of the aforesaid kings Æthelbald and Sigeberht, but the praiseworthy life and glorious end of his predecessor Ceolwulf, chose the better part, which shall not be taken away from him. Leaving the kingdom, he received the tonsure of the head that would produce an eternal diadem, and put on dark garments which would confer heavenly brightness. He is the eighth of those kings who voluntarily gave up their kingdoms for Christ—or rather, to speak more truly, exchanged them for an eternal kingdom. The everlasting joy of the eight beatitudes delights them ineffably with manifold [Col. 0881A] delight; to imitate their valour is the part of the blessed (Matt. 5).

His son Osulf succeeded to the kingdom; but after reigning one year he was killed by wicked treachery from his own household. After him Mol Æthelwold reigned for six years. About this time Archbishop Cuthbert was taken from life.

When Cynewulf had reigned six years, King Æthelberht of Kent reached the bounds of life. In the same year Ceolwulf—then a monk, formerly a king—did not die here but departed from here to receive wonderful rewards. In the following year Mol, king of Northumbria, killed Oswine, the bravest of his ealdormen. Oswine had joined battle against his lord at Eadwinescliu [al. Edwinescliue]; having rejected the law of nations, he was killed by the law of God. In the following year Jambeth became Archbishop of York. Then too Fridwald, bishop of Chester, ceased to live; he had become bishop in the sixth year of Ceolwulf’s reign. At that time Witwine became bishop of Whithorn. Mol, after reigning six years, relinquished the kingdom of Northumbria; after him Alred reigned eight years. In the second year of his reign, Archbishop Egbert of York gave up his soul, having been archbishop thirty-six years, and Friderbert, bishop of Hexham, died, having been bishop thirty-four years. Adelbert succeeded Archbishop Eadbert; Alcmund succeeded Bishop Friderbert. In the fourth year of King Alred, Pippin king of the Franks, Stephen pope of the Romans, and Eadbert son of Eata [al. Ecca], a most famous [Col. 0881C] ealdorman of the English, died.

In the year of grace 769, the fifteenth year of King Cynewulf, “the right hand of the Most High began to change” (Ps. 76). For the Roman Empire, which had for so many years been most eminent in itself, became subject to Charles, great king of the Franks, after thirty years of his reign—which began in this year—and from that point passed to his successors down to this day.

In the twentieth year of King Cynewulf, King Offa fought with the Mercians against the Kentish at Oxford. After a dreadful slaughter on both sides, Offa shone forth illustrious through the fortunes of war. In the same year the Northumbrians expelled their king Alred from York in Easter week and chose as their king [Col. 0881D] Æthelred son of Mol, who reigned four years. In this year red signs were seen in the sky after sunset, and terrible serpents were seen in Sussex, to great amazement. In the second year after this, the Old Saxons, from whom the English people are descended, were converted to the faith. In that year Bishop Witwine of Whithorn died in the twenty-fourth year of his episcopate.

In the twenty-fourth year of Cynewulf’s reign, he fought against Offa near Benetune. Weakened by the chance of Mars, he withdrew from the place, and King Offa brought that fortress under his own control. In the same year Æthelbert was consecrated at York as bishop at Whithorn. In the following year Æthelbald and Herebert, ealdormen of the king of Northumbria, rebelling against their lord, killed Aldulf son of Bose, commander-in-chief of the royal army, in encounters of Mars at Kingsclive. Afterwards the ealdormen of King Cynewulf and Eggan killed the aforesaid ealdormen in a great battle at Hilathirnum. The aforesaid King Æthelred, having lost his ealdormen and hope alike, fled before them. They established Alfwold as king, and he reigned ten years. In the following year the princes and officials of Northumbria burned a certain ealdorman and their justiciar because he had proved harsher than was right. In the same year Archbishop Eadbert died at Chester, and Enbald succeeded him. In the same year Kinebold became bishop of Lindisfarne. In the same year the Old Saxons and Franks fought, and the Franks were victorious. In the next year King Alfwold of Northumbria sent to Rome for the pallium and gave it [Col. 0882B] to Archbishop Enbald. Then, upon the death of Alcmund, bishop of Hexham, Tilberht succeeded him. In that year Charles went to Rome. About this time a council was held at Acle.

Cynewulf, after reigning twenty-six years and victoriously waging many battles against the Britons, having subdued them on every side, at last determined to exile the young man Cyneard, brother of Sigeberht. Cyneard attacked the king at Weretune, where he had gone privately to visit a certain woman. When the king learned of it, he defended himself bravely in the doorway, until, seeing the young man, he sprang outside and wounded him. Then all Cyneard’s companions, fighting against the king, killed him. When the cry was heard, the king’s soldiers [Col. 0882C] who were in the town ran upon the young man. Rejecting the lands and money offered them by him, they all died fighting, except for one Welsh hostage, who was grievously wounded. In the morning the king’s soldiers who were nearby, at the courtyard where the king had been killed, besieged the young man and his followers. He said to them: “Your kinsman is with me, and I shall give you land and money according to your heart’s desire, if you do not fight against us. I offered the same to your companions, but they refused and perished.” But they answered that no money was dearer to them than their lord, and that they would avenge the blood of their lord and companions. Breaking in through the gate in a fierce battle, they killed the young man and the eighty-four who were with him. There remained only the young man’s little son, though wounded.

[Col. 0882D] Thus Cynewulf, in the thirty-first year of his reign, was buried at Winchester, and the young man at Axminster.

Brictric, who was also of the lineage of the often-mentioned King Cerdic, reigned after Cynewulf over the West Saxons for sixteen years. In his second year Pope Adrian sent legates into Britain to renew the faith preached by Augustine. Received honourably by kings and peoples, they built beautifully upon a firm foundation, with Christ’s mercy cooperating. They held a council at Cealtide, where Jænberht surrendered part of his diocese. There also Hygeberht was elected by King Offa. In the same year Egfert [al. Egferd] was consecrated king of the province of Kent. In the following year, which was [Col. 0883A] the year of grace 786, the sign of a cross appeared in garments—something that may seem marvellous to every age in telling and hearing. Was this done as a sign of the expedition to Jerusalem with crosses taken up, which occurred three hundred and nine years later in the time of William the Younger? Or was it instead done for the correction of nations, so that, corrected, they might endure the Danish scourge which closely followed? We define nothing rashly, but leave the Lord’s secrets to the Lord.

In the fourth year of Brictric’s reign he married Eadburh, daughter of Offa, king of the Mercians; strengthened thereby in his kingdom, he advanced into pride. In these days the Danes came with three ships to Britain for the purpose of preaching. When the king’s official of that province saw them, he went out against them too incautiously, intending to seize them and bring them to the royal stronghold. He did not know who those who had landed were, or why they had landed. But as soon as he joined them, he was killed. He was the first Englishman slain by the Danes, after whom many thousands upon thousands were killed by the same people; and these were the first ships which the Danes brought here. In the following year a council met in Northumbria at Wincenhale.

In the sixth year of King Brictric a synod assembled at Aclea [al. Adea], while Sigan killed King Alfwold of Northumbria by wicked treachery. At the place where the king, friend of the Lord, was killed, a heavenly light was often seen; and he was buried in the church at Hexham. After him Osred began to reign, but in the following year he was betrayed and expelled from the kingdom, and Æthelred son of Mol was restored to the kingdom. Four years after he had become king, Osred returned with gathered forces to drive Æthelred—the man through whom he had been expelled—from the kingdom; but he was captured and killed [the printed reading *inter eumdem* is uncertain], and buried at Tynemouth. How well, then, spoke the man who said:

> … O blind  
> > mind of humankind concerning the future!  
> > (Lucan, *Pharsalia* XI.14.)

For when the aforesaid young Osred became king, dancing and rejoicing, how little did he reckon that in the second year of his reign he would be deprived of the royal throne, and in the fourth of the light of life. Therefore, amid prosperity we should always be anxious, [Col. 0883D] knowing not how near adversity may be.

At that time Offa, king of Mercia, ordered Saint Æthelberht’s head cut off. Also Archbishop Lambrith lived no longer, and Abbot Æthelred was chosen archbishop. Archbishop Eubald of York consecrated Baldulf bishop at Whithorn.

In Brictric’s tenth year fiery dragons were seen flying through the air; two plagues followed this sign: first a very great famine, then a pagan people coming from Norway and Denmark. They first miserably destroyed the Northumbrian people and afterwards horribly destroyed Christ’s churches, with their inhabitants, in the province of Lindisfarne on the Ides of January. At the same time Ealdorman Sigga, who had shamefully betrayed [al. *prodierat*, “had gone forth”] the blessed King Alfwold, perished deservedly.

[Col. 0884A] In the eleventh year of King Brictric, the Northumbrians killed their king Æthelred. In the year in which King Osred had been killed, raised up in pride, he had dismissed his own wife and taken a new one, not knowing that he himself was to be slain after two years and that the brief joy of his reign would so swiftly be ended by the desolation of death. After him Ardulf took the kingdom of Northumbria. Archbishop Eubald, Bishop Æthelbert, Bishop Higebald, and Bishop Baldulf consecrated him king, and he was raised to the royal throne at York. Not long after, Archbishop Eubald died at York, and another Eubald succeeded him. In these days Pope Adrian and the great King Offa reached the bounds of life. Afterwards Egfert, Offa’s son, reigned over Mercia and died after one hundred and forty-one days; King Cenwulf succeeded him. In the same year Eadbrict, called by another name Pren, acquired the kingdom of Kent. The pagan people plundered Northumbria and despoiled the monastery of Egfert at Donemuth. But when the most noble and war-experienced English encountered them, their leaders were killed and they were defeated, fleeing to their ships. As they persisted in flight aboard the ships, some of them were broken by a storm and many men were shipwrecked. Some, however, were taken alive and beheaded beside the shore. Not long afterwards Cenwulf, king of Mercia, overran and plundered the province of Kent; he captured their king Pren, unequal to him in strength and therefore hiding by secret places and byways, and, victorious over the defeated man, led him away with him.

In the fourteenth year of King Brictric, the Romans cut out Pope Leo’s tongue, tore out his eyes, and drove him from his see. But he, as the writings report, through the Lord’s mercy was again able to see and speak, and became pope again. Three years later King Charles was made emperor and consecrated by Pope Leo; he condemned to death those who had dishonoured the pope, but afterwards, at the pope’s prayers, remitted their death and consigned them to exile. Three years later also King Brictric of the West Saxons died. At this time there was a great battle in Northumbria at Wellehare, in which Alric son of Heberht [al. Hereberht] and many others with him perished. The excessive length of the work necessarily prevents a full determination of the deeds, outcomes, and manner of every individual battle. For the English people were naturally harsh and proud, and therefore continually worn down by civil wars.

[Col. 0884D] Egbert, in the year of grace 800, the eighth in number among the most valiant kings whom we marked in Book II with the special prerogative of excellence, reigned thirty-seven years and six months over the West Saxons. In his youth his predecessor Brictric and Offa king of Mercia had driven him from this land; he therefore lived in exile for three years with the king of the Franks, nobly and illustriously. When the aforesaid king had died and Egbert returned and received the kingdom, on that same day Ealdmund [al. Adelmund], ealdorman, departed from Wicum and, coming to Kinemeresford, met Ealdorman Wicstan with the Wylas. They immediately fought together; both ealdormen were killed, and the Wylas prevailed. Four years after this Æthelred, archbishop of Kent, died, and Wulfred was consecrated in his place. Two years later King Cuthred of Kent was deprived of the breath of life; in the following year King Hardulf of Northumbria was expelled from his kingdom.

In the fourteenth year of Egbert’s reign he plundered through the kingdoms of the Britons from east to west, and there was none who even attempted to resist his violence. In the following year Charles, king of the Franks and Roman emperor, died. In the year after this Saint Leo, venerable pope, laid down his body, and Stephen succeeded him; Paschal succeeded Stephen. A short time later King Cenwulf of Mercia was delivered to death. Ceolwulf reigned after him in his place; but three years later he lost the kingdom, and Beornwulf seized it for himself.

In the twenty-fourth year of Egbert’s reign he engaged King Beornwulf of Mercia in battle at Ellendune. Hence it is said: “The stream of Ellendune reddened with blood; it stood still with slaughter; it decayed with stench.” There, after a very great destruction of the people on both sides, Egbert emerged a grim victor. Pressing his success and pursuing fortune, he then sent his son Æthelwulf, later king, Bishop Alcstan [al. Healestan], and Ealdorman Walard with a great army into Kent. They drove King Balred beyond the Thames. Thus King Egbert received into his lordship the peoples of Kent, Surrey, Sussex, and Essex, whom his kinsman Pren had previously unjustly lost.

[Col. 0885C] In the same year the king of the East Angles with his people received King Egbert as protector. Later in that same year the East Angles killed Beornwulf, king of Mercia; Ludecan succeeded him. In that year also a very great battle took place between the Britons and the people of Devonshire at Gavelford, where many thousands fell on both sides. In the following year Ludecan, king of Mercia, and five ealdormen with him were killed.

In the twenty-seventh year of Egbert’s reign he expelled Wiglaf, king of Mercia, who had succeeded King Ludecan, and acquired the kingdom for himself. Since he then held every kingdom south of the Humber, he led an army against the Northumbrians at Dore. They devoutly offered the great king peace and submission, and they parted peaceably. In the following year King Egbert, moved by mercy, allowed Wiglaf to hold the kingdom of Mercia under him. Egbert then led an army into North Wales and subjected it to himself by the protection of arms. In the following year, after the death of Wilfrid, archbishop of Kent, Celnod [al. Ceolnod] succeeded him.

In the thirty-third year of King Egbert, the Danes returned to England, thirty-eight years after they had been defeated and put to flight at Donemuth. They first plundered Sheppey. In the following year King Egbert fought with his army against those who had arrived in thirty-five very large ships, at Carrum; there the Danes prevailed by the hazard of war, [Col. 0886A] and two bishops, Hereferth and Wigferth, and two ealdormen, Dudda and Osmod, perished. In the following year a naval army of Danes came into West Wales; the Welsh united with the Danes and rose against King Egbert. But the king, enjoying better fortune, crushed the Danes and Welsh with crushing defeat and triumphantly routed the very brave men at Hengistendune [al. Hengistesdune]. In the following year King Egbert, monarch of Britain, yielded to fate. He made his sons heirs of the kingdoms held in his own hand: Æthelwulf over the West Saxons, Æthelstan over Kent, Sussex, and Essex. But since we have now reached the monarchy of England and the terrible scourge inflicted by the Danes, a separate book must be devoted to these new matters.

Yet, as was done in Book II, the matters related in this book must briefly be recapitulated; and the succession of each kingdom shall be set out in order, so that this abridgment may carefully make clear what has been confused amid the intermingling of so many kings. Thus, if I prove more pleasing to the reader, through the Lord’s grace I shall receive the desirable fruit of my labour.

This is the abridgment concerning the kings of Kent previously treated in this book.

Lothair reigned twelve years and was put to death in a battle against the South Saxons.

Eadric reigned a year and a half, being foreign to the royal lineage.

Nidred and Wibbehard, likewise foreigners, reigned [Col. 0886C] six years and were expelled.

Wihtred, born of royal stock, reigned thirty-four years in peace and made an agreement with King Ine.

Edbriht, son of Wihtred, held the kingdom with two brothers for twenty-two years.

Æthelberht possessed the royal sceptre for twelve years.

Egfert held the same kingdom for thirty-four years, so far as we can infer from the writings.

Edbrit Pren reigned three years, was captured, and was carried off by Cenwulf, king of Mercia.

Cuthred possessed the royal diadem for nine years.

Balred reigned eighteen years, and King Egbert of the West Saxons expelled him from the kingdom.

Egbert, king of the West Saxons, held the conquered kingdom [Col. 0886D] while he lived and, dying, left it to his son Æthelstan. Thus the royal lineage of Kent ceased, and the kingdom passed into foreign hands.

This is the abridgment concerning the kings of the West Saxons previously treated in this book.

Cædwalla, after reigning two years, acquired the Isle of Wight; he plundered Kent twice and, going to Rome, died in white baptismal garments, exchanging the insignia of royalty.

Ine reigned thirty-seven years. He defeated Geraint, king of the Welsh, in battle, subdued the South Saxons by war, and, seeking Rome, happily laid aside his kingdom.

Æthelard, kinsman of King Ine, ruled in peace for fourteen years the kingdom entrusted to him by Ine.

[Col. 0887A] Cuthred reigned sixteen years, and by the law of battle defeated the Britons twice and King Æthelbald.

The cruel Sigeberht [al. Sigebrict] reigned one year and a little more; justly expelled from the kingdom, he was afterwards killed.

Cynewulf reigned twenty-three years; Sigeberht [al. Sigeberch], brother of the king, put him to death.

Brictric reigned sixteen years. In his time Danish savagery first assailed Britain.

Egbert reigned thirty-seven years, plundered through Britain from east to west, and defeated in war Beornwulf, king of Mercia; Balred, king of Kent; King Wiglaf; and the Danes.

This is the abridgment concerning the kings of Northumbria indicated in this book.

[Col. 0887B] Alfrid, brother of King Egfrid, learned in the Scriptures and vigorous in war, reigned twenty years.

His son Osred reigned eleven years and was killed while fighting.

Cenred reigned two years and, having fallen ill, was overtaken by swift death.

Osric reigned eleven years and was deprived of the light of life.

Ceolwulf, brother of the aforesaid King Cenred, reigned eight years and became a monk. In his time the venerable priest Bede, philosopher of Christ, happily died.

Egbert [al. Adbricht], his kinsman, reigned twenty-one years and, becoming a monk, brought his fragile life to its end in glory.

[Col. 0887C] Osulf, his son, reigned one year and was betrayed and killed by his own household.

Mol Æthelwold reigned six years and was compelled to relinquish the kingdom.

Alred reigned eight years and was driven out and deposed by his people.

Æthelred [al. Aedelred], son of Mol, reigned three years and fled before his rebellious ealdormen.

Alfwold reigned ten years; Ealdorman Sigga killed him by treachery.

Osred, nephew of the aforesaid king, reigned one year [Col. 0888A] and was expelled from the kingdom by his own people, then killed after three years.

Æthelred, son of Mol, reigned again for four years and was killed by his ever-most-wicked people.

Ardulf reigned twelve years and was driven from his kingdom by his own people. Afterwards the Northumbrians, as appears, overwhelmed for a while by the madness of wickedness, were without a king and came to terms with King Egbert.

This is the abridgment of the kings of Mercia mentioned in this book.

Æthelred [al. Æthelred], son of Penda, reigned twenty-nine years and gloriously became a monk.

Cenred, his kinsman, reigned five years, sought Rome, and victoriously received the monastic life.

[Col. 0888B] Ceolred, son of King Æthelred, reigned eight years and fought vigorously against King Ine.

The proud Æthelbald [al. Adelbald] reigned forty-one years. He plundered Northumbria, defeated the Welsh people, and held authority over all the kings of England. But at last he was defeated by King Cuthred and afterwards killed.

Beornred held the kingdom one year, but the mighty Offa drove him out.

Offa reigned thirty-nine years. He weakened King Cynewulf of the West Saxons in war, as well as the Kentish and the Northumbrians.

Egferd, son of King Offa, did not live out one full year.

[Col. 0888C] Cenwulf reigned peacefully for twenty-six years and died an ordinary death.

Ceolwulf held the kingdom three years, but then fierce Beornwulf violently seized it from him.

Beornwulf reigned one year and, defeated in war by King Egbert, languished away.

Ludicen, king, was killed in the first year of his reign together with his five ealdormen.

Wilaf, defeated in battle by King Egbert, held the kingdom under him as a tributary. The kingdom of the East Angles had already been subjected in various ways to other kingdoms.

## Prologue to Book Five

[Col. 0887]

At the beginning of this history we said that Britain had been struck by five scourges. In the present book we shall treat of the fourth, inflicted by the Danes. This was indeed far more savage and far more cruel than the rest. For the Romans quickly subdued Britain and governed it magnificently under the law of rulers. The Picts and Scots repeatedly made incursions from the northern part of Britain; but they neither attacked it from every side nor, when disastrously repulsed, failed for a considerable time to desist from invasion. The Saxons, however, gradually gained possession of the land by war according to their strength; what they captured they held, what they held they built up, and what they built up they governed by laws. Likewise the Northmen, having swiftly and briefly subjected the land, granted the conquered life, liberty, and their ancient laws by right of kingship; of them something must be said later.

The Danes, however, continually and for a very long time rushed upon and assailed the land from every side, seeking not to possess it but to plunder it, desiring to destroy everything rather than to rule. If they were ever defeated, the victors gained nothing, since elsewhere a larger fleet and army would arise. And in a remarkable fashion, when the kings of the English marched eastward to fight them, before they approached the hostile companies a messenger would fly up saying: “King, where are you going? An innumerable fleet of heathens has occupied the shores on the southern side of England, and, ravaging cities and villages, gives all things to slaughter and fire.” That same day another would hasten up, saying: “King, where are you fleeing? A terrible army has landed on the western side of England. Unless you return speedily against them, thinking that you have fled, they will pursue you from behind with slaughter and flame.” The same day or the next another messenger would arrive, saying: “Where are you going, nobles? The Danes have landed in the northern regions; they have already burned your houses, carried away your possessions, caught your children tossed aloft on the points of their spears, violated some of your wives by force, and carried others away with them.”

Thus the king and people, struck by so many grievous reports, were shattered in hand and heart and wasted away. Therefore, even when they won, they had no joy, as is usual [Latin variants: assolent, “they are accustomed”; assolet, “it is accustomed”], nor any hope of safety. The reason why God’s justice blazed against them with such fury was this. In the first age of the English Church religion shone with the greatest brilliance, so that kings and queens, dukes and bishops sought either monastic life or exile, as we have shown before. But with the passing of time every virtue so withered among them that they allowed no people to equal them in treachery and wickedness. This is especially evident in the history of the kings of Northumbria. As their impiety is described in royal deeds, so men of every rank and office pursued deceit and treachery. Nothing but piety was disgraceful, and innocence was the worthiest cause of murder.

Therefore the Lord Almighty sent in, as though swarms of bees, the most cruel nations, sparing neither age nor sex: namely, Danes with Goths, Norwegians with Swedes, Vandals with Frisians. From the beginning of the reign of King Æthelwulf until the coming of William, king of the Northmen, they devastated this land for two hundred and thirty years. Not infrequently, too, as God’s avengers and goads, because of their proximity to Britain they cruelly invaded France according to its deserts. But now, these matters explained, we must return to the order of the history.

## Book Five

[Col. 0889]

[Col. 0889A] In the first year of his reign Æthelwulf, while he himself was resisting the aforesaid enemies in one part of his kingdom, sent Ealdorman Wulfheard with part of his army to fight the Danes, since a multitude of heathens was pouring in from every side. They had landed with thirty-three ships at Hamton, where, after a great slaughter of the enemy, he won a most brilliant victory. King Æthelwulf also sent Ealdorman Æthelhelm to fight another army at Port with the army of Wessex. After they had fought for a long time, the aforesaid ealdorman was killed, and the Danes were victorious.

In the following year Ealdorman Hereberht fought them at Merseware; the Danes prevailed, his men fled, and he was killed. The heathen army then moved through the eastern regions of England—Lindsey, [Col. 0889B] East Anglia, and Kent—and took the lives of countless people by the sword. In the year after this, advancing deeper into the country, the army laid low a great multitude around Canterbury, Rochester, and London.

In the fifth year of Æthelwulf’s reign, he fought with part of his army—for the armies had been divided—against a people of thirty-five ships at Carrum, and the Danes were victorious. Although the number of ships was small, the number who had boarded the very large vessels was great. In the year following this fifth year, Bishop Alestan [variant: Algstan], a venerable man, and Ealdorman Ernulf with the men of Somerset, and Ealdorman Osric with the men of Dorset, fought the Danes at Pedredesmuth. With God’s help they struck down many of them and gained the splendour of victory.

In the sixteenth year of Æthelwulf’s reign, [Col. 0890A] he and his son Æthelbald, having assembled all their forces, fought the greatest army, which had landed at Thamesmouth with two hundred and fifty ships. It had destroyed the famous cities, illustrious for many years, namely London and Canterbury, and had put to flight the defeated King Beorhtwulf of Mercia with his army; he never again flourished. Burred succeeded him in the kingdom of Mercia. Entering Surrey, the Danes met the royal battle-lines at Aclea. Thus a battle was joined between the greatest armies, so great and so severe that no one had ever heard of such a battle fought in England [Latin forms: Angliam; variant Anglia].

There one could see warriors on both sides falling like a crop, while streams of blood bore away the heads and limbs of the slain. But would it not be excessive and wearisome prolixity [Col. 0890B] to record every detail? God therefore granted the fortune of war to those who believed in Him, and unspeakable crushing to those who despised Him. King Æthelwulf thus emerged as a most illustrious victor.

In the same year Æthelstan, king of Kent, and Ealdorman Ealhere fought a naval battle against the Danes at Sandwich. After a great slaughter of the enemy, they captured nine of the Danish ships; the rest fled. An ealdorman named Ceorl likewise fought the heathens with the people of Devonshire, struck down many, and was victorious at Wienorne [variant: Wienbeorne]. This year was therefore fortunate for the English people. In this year the heathen army first spent the entire winter in this country [variant: “at Thanet”].

In the eighteenth year of his reign Æthelwulf powerfully aided King Burred in subduing the North Welsh to himself and gave him his daughter in marriage. [Col. 0891A] In the same year King Æthelwulf sent his son Alfred to Rome to Pope Leo, who later blessed him as king and received him in the place of a son. In this year Ealdorman Ealhere with the men of Kent, and Huda with the men of Surrey, fought the heathen army at Thanet. A great number on each side were killed and drowned, and both ealdormen died.

In the nineteenth year of his reign Æthelwulf, who had tithed all his land for the use of churches out of love for God and for his own redemption, afterwards went to Rome with great honour and stayed there one year. Returning thence, he took as wife the daughter of Charles the Bald, king of France, and brought her with him into this country. After he had kept her for two years, he was taken from men [Col. 0891B] and buried at Winchester. He had first been bishop at Winchester [Latin forms: Wincestre; variant Winceastre]; but upon the death of his father Egbert, compelled by necessity, he became king. Having taken a wife, he begot four sons, all of whom were kings after him. About this time the heathens spent the whole winter at Sheppey.

The most noble king left to his son Æthelbald the hereditary kingdom of Wessex; to his son Æthelbert he left the other kingdom of Kent, Essex, and Surrey. The two brothers, young men of excellent disposition, held their kingdoms most prosperously as long as each lived. King Æthelbald of Wessex, after holding his kingdom in peace for five years, was carried off by untimely death. [Col. 0891C] All England mourned the youth of King Æthelbald; great lamentation arose for him, and they buried him at Sherborne. Thereafter England perceived how much it had lost in him.

Æthelbert, brother of the aforesaid king, succeeded him as king over Wessex; he had earlier been king of Kent. In his days a naval army came, landed, and destroyed Winchester; and thus:

> An ancient city falls, long mistress through many years.  
> *(Virgil, Aeneid* II.363.)

Then Ealdorman Osric with the men of Hampshire and Ealdorman Æthelwulf with the men of Berkshire fought the same army. After putting them to flight with great destruction, our men were victorious.

In the fifth year of King Æthelbert, a heathen army came to Thanet. The men of Kent promised them money for a truce, but during the truce, unexpectedly breaking out one night, they plundered Kent from its eastern side. In the same year Æthelbert, having reigned five years over Wessex and ten over Kent, tasted death. His brother Æthelred received the insignia of the kingdom after him. In this year a very great heathen army came into the land of the English. Its leaders were Hinguar and Ubba, men most vigorous but most cruel. Wintering in East Anglia, they received a truce and horses from its people, and for the sake of rest spared their strength for a time.

[Col. 0892A] In the second year of King Æthelred, the aforesaid army led by Hinguar and Ubba came to York in Northumbria.
