Among the people of that country there was, in accordance with their customary treachery, much distress, because they had rejected their king Osberht and accepted another, a base man named Ælla. Thus, only belatedly united and having assembled an army, they came to York, where the heathen army was. Breaking down the wall, they rushed inside and fought with them. There both kings, Osberht and Ælla, were killed, along with an innumerable multitude of the Northumbrian people both within and outside the city. Those who remained made a truce with the heathens. In this year Bishop Ælfstan died and was buried at Sherborne, where he had been bishop for fifty years.

[Col. 0892B] In the third year of his reign King Æthelred went with his brother Alfred to Nottingham to assist King Burred of Mercia. For the aforesaid army had come to Nottingham and wintered there. When Hinguar saw that all the English forces had assembled and that his men were besieged and inferior in strength, he obtained a truce from the English by fox-like cunning and flattering words. Returning to York, he remained there cruelly for one year.

Saint Edmund ascended to the palaces of heaven in the year 870 of the Lord’s Incarnation, the fifth year of King Æthelred. The aforesaid army of King Hinguar came through Mercia to Thetford, remained there for the winter, and inflicted the greatest disaster upon the most miserable people. [Col. 0892C] King Edmund, choosing rather to suffer death than to behold the desolation of his people, was captured by them. His most holy body was pierced through on every side with the arrows of the impious, fastened to a stake; but God’s mercy showed many miracles concerning him.

In the sixth year of King Æthelred a new and immense army came into Wessex as an overflowing river, carrying all things along with it, as far as Reading. Because of its excessive multitude, it could not move all together, but advanced in separate troops and places. Its leaders were two kings, Basreg and Aldene [variants: Hamdene or Alfdene]. Accordingly, after three days, Ealdorman Æthelwulf met two Danish ealdormen, fought their army at Englefield, defeated it, and killed one named Sidrac.

Four days later King Æthelred and his brother, arriving at Reading with a great force, fought the army. Many fell on both sides, and the Danes were victorious. Four days later King Æthelred and his brother Alfred again fought the entire army at Ashdown, which was divided into two parts. On one side were the heathen kings Basreg and Aldene, against whom King Æthelred fought and killed King Basreg. On the other were the heathen ealdormen, against whom Alfred, the king’s brother, fought and killed five ealdormen: Sidroc the elder, Sidroc the younger, Osbern, Frena, and Harold. The army was put to flight, many thousands were killed, and the battle lasted until night.

Fourteen days later King Æthelred and [Col. 0893A] his brother Alfred fought the army at Basing, and the Danes won. Again, after two months, King Æthelred and his brother Alfred fought the army at Beredune. Many fell on both sides; the Danes, long put to flight, were victorious in the end. Bishop Edmund and many nobles of England were killed there. After this battle, a great army came in summer to Reading. In this year King Æthelred died after Easter and was buried at Wimborne Minster; he had reigned five years. Then his brother Alfred, son of Æthelwulf, ruled over Wessex. About one month later he fought with a small force against the army at Wintune, put it to flight for a long time, and afterwards the Danes prevailed.

In this year nine pitched battles [Col. 0893B] were fought against the army in the kingdom south of the Thames, besides the attacks which Alfred, his brother, and the king’s ealdormen often made. In this year one king and nine ealdormen were killed, and the nobles of Wessex made a truce with the heathen army.

In the first year of King Alfred [variants: Alwred or Alvred], the army came from Reading to London and remained there through the winter; the Mercians made a truce with it. In the second year King Halfdan led the same army to winter in Lindsey at Torksey [variant: Torcheseige]. In the third year they wintered at Repton. Then three other kings joined him—Guthrum, [Col. 0893C] Oscetel, and Anwed—and they became invincible. They drove King Burred, who had ruled Mercia for twenty-two years, across the sea. King Burred went to Rome and, dying there, was buried in the church of St Mary at the English School.

The Danes entrusted the kingdom of Mercia to a certain foolish king, Ceolwulf, to hold for their benefit. He swore and gave them hostages that he would restore the kingdom to them whenever they wished, and would himself be ready with all whom he could bring to their aid.

In the fourth year of King Alfred the army departed from Repton and was divided. King Aldene went with one part of the army into Northumbria and wintered near the Tyne. He seized the land and divided it among his men; [Col. 0893D] they cultivated it for two years and often raided the Picts. The aforesaid three Danish kings came with the larger part of the army to Cambridge and remained there one year. In this year King Alfred fought a naval battle against seven ships, captured one of them, and put the others to flight.

In the following year the army of the three kings came to Wareham in Wessex. King Alfred made a truce with it after receiving hostages from among their nobler men. They swore to him—something they had never done to anyone before—that they would quickly leave his kingdom. But in the following night the army departed secretly, and those who had horses went to Exeter. In this year Rollo came with his men to Normandy; in the following year the perjured army came from Wareham [Col. 0894A] to Exeter, while the naval army, rowing round, was overwhelmed by a storm. One hundred and twenty ships perished at Swanage. King Alfred followed the mounted army with a great force, but could not catch them before Exeter. Then the army gave him as many hostages as he wished and swore to keep peace, and kept it well. The army then went into Mercia, held part of the kingdom, and gave part to Ceolwulf.

In the seventh year of King Alfred, when the Danes already possessed the whole kingdom north of the Thames [variants: Tamisis or Tamasis], King Halfdan ruled in Northumbria, Halfdan’s brother was in East Anglia, and the aforesaid three kings with their King Ceolwulf were in Mercia, London, and Essex, while [Col. 0894B] nothing remained to King Alfred except the land beyond the Thames, the Danes thought it intolerable that even this should remain to him. The three kings therefore came to Chippenham in Wessex with a marvellous multitude newly arrived from Denmark. Covering the land like locusts, they seized it for themselves, since no one could resist them.

Part of the population fled overseas; part followed King Alfred, who hid in the woods with a few men; and part submitted to the enemy. But when King Alfred had neither land nor hope of obtaining it, the Lord looked upon the remnant of His people. Halfdan’s brother came with twenty-three ships into Devonshire in Wessex. King Alfred’s people killed him and eight hundred and forty men [Col. 0894C] of his army, and captured their banner, called the Raven. Strengthened by this success, King Alfred prepared a certain stronghold at Athelney; relying upon it, he often fought the army with the aid of the Somerseters, who were nearby.

In the seventh week after Easter he went to Egbrightstone, east of Selwood [variant: Sealwdic]. All the Somerseters, Wiltshire men, and those remaining from Hampshire came to meet him, rejoicing at his arrival. On the following day he went to Æglea, and from there the next day to Edington. There he fought the army and put it to flight, pursued it to its stronghold, and remained there fourteen days. Then the army gave the king hostages and swore that it would leave [Col. 0894D] his kingdom. It also promised that its king would be baptized; and this came to pass. Guthrum, the foremost of their kings, came to King Alfred and was baptized. Alfred became his godfather and, after keeping him with himself for twelve days, gave him many gifts as he departed.

In the eighth year of Alfred, the aforesaid army went from Chippenham to Cirencester and wintered there in peace. In the same year the Vikings [Latin forms: Wincigi; variant Wicingi] assembled a new army and remained at Fulham near the Thames. In this year the sun was darkened. In the following year the army of King Guthrum departed from Cirencester, went into East Anglia, took possession of that land, and divided it. In the same year the army that had been at Fulham crossed the sea and stayed [Col. 0895A] one year at Ghent. In the following year they fought the Franks and defeated them; in the third year they entered France by way of the Meuse.

At this time Alfred captured four Danish ships in a naval battle and killed those within them. In the fourth year the army came to Condé at Scat and remained there one year. In this year Pope Marinus sent King Alfred a piece of the Lord’s wood, that is, a relic of the Cross. Alfred sent his alms to Rome and also to India, to St Thomas, in accordance with the vow he had made when the hostile army wintered at London.

In the fourteenth year of King Alfred, part of the army which was in Gaul came to Rochester. Besieging the city, they began to construct another stronghold there. [Col. 0895B] When the king arrived, they fled to their ships and crossed the sea. King Alfred sent a naval force to Kent in East Anglia. When it reached Stourmouth, it met sixteen Viking ships and defeated them in battle. But when they returned with spoils and victory, they encountered a large Viking army and, fighting it, were defeated.

In the same year a boar killed Charles, king of France, son of Louis, son of Charles the Bald, whose daughter Juheta [variant: Juheth] King Æthelwulf had married. Pope Marinus also fell asleep. In the following year the Danish army came by way of the Seine to the bridge of Paris and wintered there. King Alfred besieged London, since the greater part of the Danes had followed the Gallic army. All the English at once submitted to him [Col. 0895C] and received him; the Danes fled. The king entrusted the city to Ealdorman Æthelred for keeping.

In the year following, the army departed from the bridge of Paris, went by the Seine to the Marne, and by the Marne to Chezy, and remained for two years there and at Jorna [variant: Jorata]. About this time, through the faction of Ernulf, five kings were made in France.

In the nineteenth year of King Alfred, Guthrum, the Danish king who had been King Alfred’s godson and ruled in East Anglia, was deprived of life. In this year the army came from the Seine to Scald, which lies between Britain and France. The Bretons fought them and drove them into a certain river, killing many. Here Plegmund was chosen archbishop by God and the whole people.

In the following year the army went east, and King Arnulf fought the army with Franks, Saxons, and Bavarians and repulsed it. Afterwards the great army returned to England with all its possessions, to the harbour of Limen with two hundred and fifty ships. This harbour lies in eastern Kent near the great wood of Andredsweald, which extends one hundred and twenty miles in length and thirty in breadth. After disembarking, they built a fortress at Appledore. Meanwhile Hasting came with eighty ships into the harbour of the Thames and built a fortress at Milton. Afterwards he swore to King Alfred that he would do him no harm in any respect. The king had therefore given many gifts to him, his wife, and his sons, one of whom [Col. 0896A] the king himself had held at baptism and the other the great ealdorman Æthelred.

But Hasting, always faithless, built a fortress at Benfleet. While he was raiding against the king, the king destroyed the aforesaid fortress and took there Hasting’s wife, sons, money, spoils, and ships. He returned the wife and sons to Hasting because he was their godfather.

A messenger came to King Alfred, saying: “A hundred ships have come from Northumbria and East Anglia and are besieging Exeter.” While the king marched there, the army at Appledore invaded Essex and built a fortress at Shoebury. Proceeding from there, they came as far as Buttington beside the Severn and built a fortress there. But, driven off in battle, they fled to their fortress in Essex. Those who had besieged Exeter, hearing of the king’s approach, fled to their ships and remained plundering at sea. A fourth army came in the same year from Northumbria as far as Chester, but was besieged there and suffered such hunger that they even ate their own horses.

In the twenty-third year of King Alfred, the Danes who were at Chester went round through North Wales and Northumbria to the island of Mersea in Essex. Afterwards, in winter, they dragged their ships across the Thames into the River Lea. The army that had besieged Exeter was caught plundering near Chichester, where it lost many of its men and some of its ships.

In the following year the army on the Lea built a fortress beside that river, twenty miles from London. [Col. 0896C] The Londoners came to that fortress and, fighting the Danes, killed four of their leaders; at the fitting time the Almighty Lord gave victory to His people. When the Danes had fled into the fortress, the king caused the waters of the Lea to be divided into three channels, so that they could not bring their ships back through it. Discovering this, the Danes abandoned their ships, went as far as Quatbridge near the Severn, built a fortress there, and wintered there, having entrusted their wives to East Anglia. The king pursued them with his army. The Londoners took some of the abandoned Danish ships to London and burned others.

Thus during these three aforesaid years—from the time when the Danes landed at the harbour [Col. 0896D] of Limen—they inflicted many evils upon the English, but they themselves endured far more. In the fourth year the army was divided: part went into Northumbria, part into East Anglia, and part crossed the sea to the Seine. Afterwards some Danish ships came near the shores of Wessex. By repeated incursions, often plundering and often fighting, they caused no slight destruction to the inhabitants of Wessex.

Of their many conflicts I shall relate one, because its outcome was unusual. King Alfred ordered long ships, namely of forty oars or more, to be prepared against the aforesaid Danish ships. Six Danish ships, while standing at a certain shore in Devonshire, were intercepted by nine royal ships. Seeing this, the Danes moved three ships against them; for three other Danish ships stood motionless on the shore because the sea had withdrawn. Six English ships thus fought three Danish ships. The remaining three English ships advanced against the three Danish ships standing on the shore.

The three Danish ships fought against six with desperate, uttermost daring, and for a long time maintained a most bitter struggle. Yet the greater number prevailed, and two Danish ships were captured; the third fled, though all those aboard the two captured ships had been killed except five. When this had been done, the English ships wished to return to their companions, which were on the opposite shore beside the Danish ships, [Col. 0897A] but they were left dry by the retreating sea. Seeing this, the Danes came out from three ships and fought the English force which was in three vessels.

One could see the men of the six ships watching the battle and unable to bring help, beating their breasts with their fists and tearing their hair with their nails. The English nevertheless acted bravely, and the Danes attacked most fiercely. Forty-two Englishmen and one hundred and twenty Danes fell. Yet the Danes killed Lucheman, commander of the royal force, who was pressing them hard. For this reason, as the English gradually gave way, the Danes seemed almost victorious. But behold: as the sea returned, the Danes made for the open water in their ships. Nine English ships pursued them afterwards, late and in vain.

A contrary wind then struck the victorious Danes and threw two of their ships ashore. Their men were captured and brought before the king; all were hanged at Winchester. Those in the third ship, severely wounded, landed in East Anglia. In the same year twenty ships with their crews perished off the southern coast.

When King Alfred had ruled for twenty-eight and a half years over all England except those parts subject to the Danes, he felt the sting of death. We have judged it fitting to speak in verse of his laborious rule and inextricable affliction.

> The nobility born in you gave you the honour of virtue,  
> Mighty Alfred in arms; and virtue gave you labour,  
> And labour an everlasting name. Joys were ever mingled  
> With sorrow for you, and hope was always mingled with fear.  
> If you had now won victory, you feared tomorrow’s battles;  
> If you had now been defeated, you prepared for tomorrow’s battles.  
> Your garments, stained by continual sweat, and your dry clothing  
> Dyed continually with blood, proved what a burden kingship is.  
>
> [Col. 0897D] Through the vast regions of the world there was no one  
> Who amid so many adversities was permitted even to breathe.  
> Yet, worn down by iron, you could neither lay aside the iron  
> Nor end the labours of life by the sword.  
> Now, after the pains of life and kingship have passed,  
> May Christ be his true rest and his everlasting sceptre.

Edward, son of King Alfred, held his father’s kingdom for twenty-four years. His younger brother Eadwold [variant: Æthelwold] took a wife and seized Wimborne without the consent either of the king or of the nobles of the kingdom. Therefore King Edward went with an army to Bath, near Wimborne. Eadwold, remaining in Wimborne with his men and closing the gates, declared that he would either remain there or die. Yet by night he departed and went to [Col. 0898A] the army in Northumbria. Delighting in the young man’s nobility, they made him king and ruler over their kings and ealdormen.

The king seized his wife, whom the aforesaid young man had married against the bishop’s prohibition, because she had been consecrated as a nun. In the same year Ealdorman Eadred of Devonshire [variant: Devon] had died one month before King Alfred’s death; he had fought many faithful and courageous battles with Alfred.

In the third year of King Edward, the king’s brother Æthelwold gathered his forces and led an immense fleet into Essex, and the East Saxons immediately submitted. In the following year he led a very great army into Mercia and ravaged it everywhere as far as Cricklade. Crossing the Thames there, he seized Inbrithenden [Col. 0898B] [variant: Inbrithenden] and everything in the surrounding region. When they had thus accomplished their deed, they returned home joyfully.

But King Edward assembled an army as quickly as he could, followed them, and ravaged all their land between the Dicum [variant: Ducum] and the Ouse as far as the marshes in Northumbria [variant: “the North”]. Afterwards, when he wished to withdraw, he ordered throughout his army that all should depart together. All withdrew except the men of Kent, who remained contrary to the king’s order. The king sent seven messengers after them.

Then the Danish army intercepted them there and fought them. Ealdorman Siulf, Ealdorman Sigbelm [variant: Sighelm], Æthelwald, the king’s thegn, Abbot Cenwulf, Sigeberht son of Siulf, Eadwold son of Acca, [Col. 0898C] and many others were killed, though only the wealthier are named. On the Danish side King Eoric was killed, as was the young Æthelwold whom they had chosen as king, and Beorhtsige son of Beorhtnoth the Ætheling, Hispohold, Occelhold [variant: Oscetelhold], and many others whom we could not name. A great many people fell on both sides; more were killed on the Danish side, although they won the victory. In this same year Ealhswith, wife of King Edward, died.

In the fifth year of King Edward, he made a truce with the East Angles and Northumbrians at Itingford. In the following year the king sent a very strong army from Wessex and Mercia, which took enormous booty, both men and animals, from the army in Northumbria. After killing many Danes, they remained five weeks in their land, plundering.

In the following year a Danish army came to plunder Mercia. The king had assembled one hundred ships and sent them against the army. When the army learned of them, it thought that it would receive assistance from them and could proceed more safely wherever it wished. But the king sent an army after them from Wessex and Mercia. It caught them from behind as they returned home and fought them. A mighty battle was joined. The Lord crushed the unbelievers with great crushing, and bloody death devoured many thousands of them. Their leaders fell in confusion and, consumed in the dust, were defiled. For [Col. 0899A] King Halfdan, King Eolwulf, Ealdorman Uthere, Ealdorman Scursa, Owlfhold, Benesinghold, Hanlafinger, Wtserhold, Offerhold, Offerdhlyte, Hahmundhold, Gudferdhold, and another Gudferd were killed.

The servants of the Lord, having gained so great a victory, rejoicing in the living God, blessed the Lord of Hosts in hymns and songs. In the following year, after the death of Ealdorman Eadred of Mercia, King Edward seized London, Oxford, and all the land belonging to the Mercian province.

In the ninth year of his reign King Edward built a fortress at Hereford, not immense but very beautiful, between the rivers Beneficia, Mimera, and Lea—rivers not deep but very clear. In the same year he built a borough at Witham in Essex, [Col. 0899B] and meanwhile remained at Dealdune. A great part of that people, formerly under Danish domination, submitted to him.

In the following year the Danish army came out from Hampton and Chester, broke the truce which the king had granted them, and made a great slaughter of the English at Hocheneretune and in the surrounding country of Drinefordshire. After they had returned home, another band immediately came out and went to Leighton. When the people of that country learned of them, they fought them, put them to flight, took from them all the booty they had captured, and also their horses.

In the eleventh year of King Edward, a great naval army came from the south, from Lidwic, with two earls, Uther [alternatively, Uhter] and Rahald. They sailed around [Col. 0899C] westward until they came to the shore of the Severn; there they plundered in North Wales wherever they could along the coasts, captured Bishop Camelegeac, and took him to their ships. King Edward redeemed him for forty pounds. Afterwards the army went out intending to plunder Yrcingafeld; then the men of Leicester and Hereford, together with men from the other neighbouring strongholds, met them, fought them, and put them to flight. They killed Earl Rahald and Geolcil, brother of Earl Uther, as well as a great part of the army; and they drove them into a certain fortress, besieging them there until they gave hostages and swore to withdraw from the king’s land. The king then caused the southern shore of the Severn to be guarded from Wales as far as the Avon, so that they dared not in any way make an incursion on that side. Yet twice they came out secretly: once from the eastern side of Weced, and another time near Pordacan. On each occasion few escaped who were not killed, except those able to swim to the ships. They then remained on the island of Stepen in great misery, so that food failed them and many died of hunger, because they could not procure provisions. Then they withdrew to Deomedum, and thence to Ireland. In the same year King Edward went with an army to Buckingham and remained there four weeks; before departing he had an earthwork made on both sides of the water. Earl Turchefel there submitted to the king, as did all the [Col. 0900A] earls and the better barons dependent upon Bedford, and many of those dependent upon Hampton.

In the twelfth year of King Edward, the writings of the ancients report that there was a battle at Holme between the men of Kent and the Danes; but do they not leave undetermined which side was victorious? In the second year after this, the moon was greatly darkened and was a great terror to those who saw it. In the third year a comet appeared; in the fourth, Leicester was rebuilt; in the fifth, the body of Saint Oswald was translated from Bardney into Mercia; in the sixth, English and Danes fought at Totanhale [alternatively, Totenhale]. Who could set down in writing the dreadful assaults of battle-lines, the fiery clashes, fearful din, savage attacks, wretched deaths, and [Col. 0900B] terrible cries? At last divine mercy adorned its own people with victory and disgraced the faithless Danes alike by slaughter and flight. In the same year Æthelflæd [alternatively, Adelfled], Lady of Mercia, who governed the kingdom of Mercia under her infirm father Æthelred, built the borough of Brunesburih.

In the eighteenth year of King Edward, Æthelred, lord of Mercia and father of Æthelflæd, died. He had long been infirm, and he gave his land to his daughter because he had no son. In the second year after this Æthelflæd, Lady of Mercia, built a borough at Scoriate and, in the same year, one at Bruge; in the third year she built the borough of Camemythe at the beginning of summer, and before August that at Stafford; in the fourth, Æthelflæd built [Col. 0900C] the borough of Edelbirh at the beginning of summer, and at the end of August that at Wirengewic; in the fifth, she built a borough at Cereburih after Christmas, one at Wardebirh in summer, and in the same year one at Rumcoven. In the sixth year she sent an army into Wales; having defeated the Welsh, she broke Brecanammere, where she captured the Welsh king’s wife with thirty-three men. In the seventh year Æthelflæd, Lady of Mercia, acquired Derby with the district dependent upon it. Since the multitude of enemies shut up inside Derby did not dare come out against her, she attacked the fortress most fiercely; and at the very entrance of the gate the greatest violence of battle flared up, where four most valiant leaders of Æthelflæd were slain. Nevertheless, her men broke the gate and [Col. 0900D] walls. In the eighth year Æthelflæd, Lady of Mercia, conquered Leicester, and the greater part of the army there submitted; the men of York had promised themselves to her, some of them having given their faith and others having sworn that they would aid her.

But after this agreement she died at Tamworth, twelve days before the feast of Saint John, in the eighth year from the time when she obtained the lordship of Mercia; and she was buried at Gloucester in the portico of Saint Peter. This lady is said to have been of such power that some called her not merely lady or queen but even king, in praise and wonder at her excellence. And, as it was thought and said, had she not been snatched away by the swiftness of fate, she would have surpassed all in strength of courage. Therefore, in memory of such great worth, we have been compelled to bid the Muse, bestower of lasting fame, say at least a few words:

> O mighty Ælfleda, O maiden, terror of men,  
> Victor over nature, worthy of a man’s name.  
> That you might become more splendid, nature made you a girl;  
> Your excellence made you bear a man’s name.  
> It is fitting that you alone should change the names of sex:  
> A mighty queen, and a king preparing trophies.  
> Not even Caesar’s triumphs have deserved so much;  
> Maiden warrior, more splendid than Caesar, farewell.

In the twenty-sixth year of his reign King Edward deprived of the lordship of all Mercia Ælfwynn, sister of Æthelflæd, who afterwards held that kingdom, caring more whether she acted usefully or uselessly than whether justly or unjustly. Afterwards he built a borough at Glademuthan. Not long after, he departed from the body at [Col. 0901B] Ferandune, and Ælfweard his son died soon after his father at Drineforde; they were buried at Winchester. Not much earlier, Sihtric, king of Northumbria, had killed his brother Nigellus; after that crime King Ragnall had conquered York.

Athelstan, son of Edward, was chosen king in Mercia and consecrated at Kingston. He lived only a short time in the kingdom, yet shone greatly by glorious deeds. Though challenged by the bravest men, he could never be conquered in war. In the course of the following year, provoked to war by Guthfrith, king of the Danes and father of the aforesaid King Ragnall, he repelled him in battle, pursued him when repelled, and destroyed him when put to flight. Not long afterwards, struck by adverse fortune, he lamentably lost his brother Edwin, a young man of great vigour [Col. 0901C] and good disposition, in the waves of the sea. But King Athelstan, after these events, intending to lead the treacherous Danish people and the faithless Scots to destruction, led a very numerous army by land and sea into Northumbria and Scotland. Since there was none who could begin resistance or persevere in it, he advanced throughout the lands and plundered as he pleased, returning with the triumphal laurel.

King Athelstan, in the year of grace 945, the fourth year of his reign, fought the greatest of battles at Bruneburh against Anlaf, king of Ireland, who had strengthened his forces with a people of Scots and Danes dwelling in England. English writers, speaking of the greatness of that battle in something like verse, and using foreign words and figures alike, deserve a faithful translation [Col. 0901D] so that, interpreting their language almost word for word, we may learn from the gravity of their words the gravity of the deeds and spirits of that people.

King Athelstan, glory of leaders, giver of noble torques, and his brother [alternatively, son] Edmund, splendid through a long succession of ancestry, struck in battle with the edge of the sword at Brunelburh; they shattered walls of shields; nobles fell, the household remnant of the dead Edward. For it had been inborn in them from the knees of their kindred to defend, in frequent wars against hostile nations, their country’s treasures, homes, wealth, and gifts.

The Irish people and the inhabitants of the ships fell doomed; the hills resounded; armed men sweated, from the time when the sun rose in the morning, gleaming brightly, gladdening [Col. 0902A] the depths—the lamp of God, the Creator’s torch—until that same noble leader hid himself in setting. There many men of Danish origin lay, pierced by missiles and speared beneath shields, and likewise Scots exhausted by battle. But all the people of Wessex, chosen before the day and then untiring, laid low the masses of the hated people. Noble men bent spears; Mercian men hurled sharp darts in the hard sport of hands. There was no safety for those who, with Anlaf, crossed the fields of the sea in the bosom of wood, seeking land in order to die in war.

Five young kings fell in the place of battle, struck by swords, and seven leaders of King Anlaf; Scots fell without number, and the pride of the Northmen perished. For they had brought with them no small number to the contest of war; but with a few the king, carried over the sea’s waves in a ship, groaned inwardly. [Col. 0902B] Likewise Froda, leader of the Northmen, and King Constantine, a leader with his companions, could not boast of the encounter of Mars, where the wreck of his kindred appeared, where his friends had fallen in the station of battle, overthrown in war, and where he left his dear son destroyed by wounds upon the field of battle.

Nor could the Dane Gude make a speech, though smooth in words and old in mind; nor could Anlaf himself, with his remnant, falsely claim what his men had achieved in the field of battle—amid the savagery of blows, the piercing of weapons, in the assembly of the valiant. Mothers and daughters-in-law lamented that their men had played the game of war with Edward’s sons, when the Northmen, in nailed ships, and Anlaf, broken, had returned beyond the deep water to their own lands with sorrowful mind. [Col. 0902C] Thereafter both brothers returned to Wessex, leaving behind the leavings of war, the flesh of men prepared as food. Thus the black raven with horned beak, the livid toad, the eagle with the kite, the dog, and the wolf of mixed colour were long refreshed by these delights.

No greater battle was fought in this land, nor had such slaughter preceded this, since Saxons and Angles came here across the broad sea to drive out the Britons: illustrious workers of war, they conquered the Welsh, put kings to flight, and received kingdoms. Having inserted these matters for refreshment, let us return to the history.

Athelstan, after reigning fourteen years, appeared no more among men. His son Eadmund succeeded him and reigned six [alternatively, nine] years and a half. In the fourth year of his reign William, son of Rollo, who had acquired from the king of France the land called Normandy, was killed through the treachery of the king of France. [Col. 0902D] From Rollo the Norman people derived their origin.

King Eadmund, leading an army into that part of Mercia which had long been subject to pagans, as far as the very broad river Humber, defeated the Danes by the fortune of war and victoriously captured five cities: Lincoln, Leicester, Stamford, Nottingham, and Derby. He utterly rooted out the Danes, who even then were called Northmen; and, once faithlessness had been removed from the aforesaid cities, by God’s grace he restored the brightness of the faith. At that time King Anlaf, of whom we have spoken, died. Afterwards King Eadmund received in baptism another Anlaf, king of the Danes, who yielded both to the king’s force and to preaching [Col. 0903A] in belief. A few days later he held Ragnall, king of York—of whom we have spoken, because he had conquered York—at the bishop’s hand.

When King Edmund returned to Wessex and had been received with honourable triumph, the aforesaid Danish kings, namely Anlaf son of Sihtric and Ragnall son of Guthfrith, broke the peace which they had made with him, plundering the part of the kingdom that had been taken from them. The most valiant King Eadmund therefore advanced with military forces into Northumbria, and having engaged in battle drove both kings from the kingdom; he was the first king of Wessex to hold Northumbria in his own dominion. In the following year, because he could not wholly tame the treacherous people of Cumberland, unused to laws, [Col. 0903B] he plundered and crushed all Cumberland and entrusted it to Malcolm, king of Scotland, on the condition that it should aid him by land and sea.

The unconquered King Edmund, after happily reigning six years and a half and enjoying prosperity in everything, being called the sole king in England, was stabbed by wicked treachery on the day of Saint Augustine, detested in every age. May Christ’s compassionate kindness pardon him, snatched away by an immeasurable death.

Edred, brother of King Eadmund and son of King Athelstan, succeeded his brother in the kingdom. In the same year he marched with a strong force of armed men against the Northumbrians, unwilling to bear the yoke of his lordship, and conquered them all for himself. He then directed his standards into Scotland. The Scots, struck with excessive terror, submitted to the king without [Col. 0903C] battle; both Northumbrians and Scots swore him the fidelity due to their lord—an oath which nevertheless did not long endure.

For when Edred had returned to the southern parts of his kingdom, Anlaf, who had fled from the kingdom of Northumbria, returned with a great fleet to Northumbria. He was joyfully received by his people and restored to the kingdom, which he held with strength for four years. But in the fourth year the Northumbrians, following their usual faithlessness, expelled their king Anlaf and received Hirc, son of Harald, as king; but he too held the kingdom only briefly.

In the seventh year of his reign King Edred was received again into the kingdom of Northumbria. For the people of that country, unable long to endure a lord, had in the third year of his reign as lightly cast off Hirc, son of Harald, as they had lightly received him; and they voluntarily summoned King Edred to themselves and restored him to the royal seat. [Col. 0903D]

The distinguished and unconquered King Edred, after at last reigning as sole king over all parts of England, put off human nature in the eighth year after he had been raised to the insignia of the diadem, when, as the text has it, “sufficient demands were being made.”

Edwy, son of King Edmund, reigned over all England after him. Edmund, son of the most excellent King Athelstan, son of the fortunate prince Edward, son of the laborious leader Alfred, son of the great father Æthelwulf, son of Egbert—who was the first greatly to raise the kingdom of Wessex on high and, through the diligence of his strength, extend it into a monarchy—[Col. 0904A] had two sons: Edwy, the elder, and Edgar, the younger. The order of succession allotted them the order of ruling according to the order of their birth. In the second year of his reign Archbishop Wlstan was deprived of the breath of life. The aforesaid King Edwy, however, held the royal dignity not without praise.

In the fifth year of King Edwy, when at the beginning his kingdom flourished most fittingly, untimely death cut short its prosperous and joyful beginnings.

Edgar the Peaceful, brother of the aforesaid king, reigned sixteen years. In his days this land was greatly improved, by the grace of God Almighty, which he most devoutly deserved to the extent of his power. As long as he lived, he reigned in peace. He greatly extended Christ’s faith in his kingdom and, by his example, most clearly made fruitful works of salvation. Beloved by God and men, he constantly endeavoured to keep the peoples of his land at peace; nor could any of his predecessors hold the kingdom in such peace and joy. He honoured the name of God and, frequently inquiring into God’s law, gladly learned it and joyfully taught it; eager in words and works, he invited his people to the practice of good works. Almighty power repaid its servant Edgar’s good deeds not only in the world to come but also in this present age, for he subjected to his will, with fear and affection, all petty kings, earls, and the people of the whole land, without battle or any disturbance of Mars. The king’s most renowned fame and name spread very widely through all lands, and foreigners came to see his glory and hear the teaching of his mouth. [Col. 0904C] Yet in this he sinned: he strengthened too much the pagans living under him in this country, and, loving foreigners brought here beyond measure, made them very strong. For nothing in human affairs is utterly perfect.

In the fifth year of Edgar the Peaceful, the venerable Æthelwold happily assumed the bishopric of Winchester. In the second year of his episcopate, he expelled certain canons dwelling in the Old Minster at Winchester, who observed their rule sluggishly and negligently, and installed monks. This church has in our own times been removed from its site, because it stood too close to the mother church, the bishop’s seat. Therefore, with the consent [Col. 0904D] of the bishop and abbot of the same monastery, it was founded outside the city walls. Æthelwold, that distinguished bishop, was a builder of hedges: he turned back the paths of wickedness and planted the roots of charity. He was indeed the sower of the best counsel; King Edgar, whose mountain he was, established new plantings and tender groves most pleasing to God. He built the abbey of Glastonbury; he ordered the abbey of Abingdon on the Thames; he established the abbey at Burgh near Stamford; and he fixed the abbey of Thorney, near the one at Burgh, amid the marshes, yet in a most pleasant place. By the counsel also of Bishop Æthelwold, Earl Ailwin of the same king established Ramsey Abbey on a most beautiful island within those same marshes.

The marsh of which we speak is [Col. 0905A] very broad and pleasing to behold, watered by many flowing rivers, adorned with many great and small lakes, and flourishing with many woods and islands. Within it are Ely church, Ramsey Abbey, Chatteris Abbey, Thorney Abbey, and Crowland Abbey; beside it are Burgh Abbey, Spalding Abbey, the church of Saint Ivo on the river Ouse in Huntingdonshire, the church of Saint Giles on the river Granta in Cambridgeshire, and the church of the Holy Trinity at Thetford.

In the eleventh year of his reign King Edgar ordered the island of Thanet to be plundered because its people had scorned royal rights—not as a raging enemy, but as a king punishing evil with evil.

In the thirteenth year of his reign King Edgar was consecrated [Col. 0905B] on the day of Pentecost at Bath. After Pentecost he led his army to Leicester, where six kings came against him. All were subject to his authority, and all gave their lord the fidelity due from them: they would serve him by land and sea at his command.

Edgar the Peaceful, a magnificent king, a second Solomon—in whose time no army of foreigners came into England, to whose authority the kings and princes of England were subject, and to whose power even the Scots bowed their necks—after reigning happily for sixteen years and two months, died happily. He could not die badly who had lived well, who had founded so many churches for God and established so many enduring good things in a short time. The more earnestly the foundations he planted do not cease to praise God, [Col. 0905C] the more the glory of the blessed king in heaven does not cease to increase. We have advanced the Muse to say a little in praise of his merits:

> Author of riches, avenger of crimes, giver of honours,  
> Sceptre-bearing Edgar seeks the kingdoms above.  
> This second Solomon, father of laws, a pathway of peace,  
> Was more renowned because his realm lacked wars.  
> He gave churches to God, monks to churches, fields to monks—  
> A fall to wickedness and a place to justice.  
> For he knew how to seek true kingship beyond false,  
> The boundless beyond the limited, the eternal beyond the brief.

Edward, son of King Edgar, called the saint, reigned after his father. At the beginning of his reign a comet appeared, a sign, namely, of the great famine that followed in the next year. Then a certain most wicked earl, named Ælfhere, with the consent and faction of some powerful men, destroyed many abbeys which King Edgar and Bishop Æthelwold had built. The Lord, moved to anger, then resolved to renew the former calamity.

In the fourth year of Saint King Edward, all the English nobles fell from a certain seat at Talne except Saint Dunstan, who resisted by grasping a beam. Some of them were severely injured and others died. This was a sign from God Most High that, through the treachery and killing of their king, they would fall from God’s love and be crushed in deserved destruction by diverse peoples.

[Col. 0906A] Saint Edward, after reigning five years, was killed through the treachery of his faithless people at twilight, at Corvelgate. Prolonging against the dead the hostility they had inflicted upon him while alive, they buried him without royal honour at Wareham, so that, as they had extinguished the king’s life, they might also extinguish his name. Here it became known that the depraved and inscrutable heart of man does not suffice against divine providence. Him whom the faithless had cast down upon earth, God gloriously received in heaven; and the Lord marked with eternal remembrance the man whose memory the traitors had sought to obscure. Thereupon the Lord, stirred again to anger and more incensed than usual, determined to inflict an inextricable evil upon that most wicked people. It is said that his stepmother—that is, the mother [Col. 0906B] of King Æthelred [alternatively, Ailred]—struck him with a knife while handing him a cup.

Æthelred [alternatively, Adelred], son of King Edgar and brother of Edward, was consecrated king at Kingston before the English leaders, under an ill omen, as Saint Dunstan had prophesied of him when he was a little child. For he urinated in the sacred font while being baptized. Therefore the man of God foretold that the destruction of the English would occur in his time. A short time after Æthelred began to reign, Earl Ælfhere, compelled by God’s will, transferred the body of Saint Edward from Wareham to Shaftesbury with due honour. In the third year of King Æthelred, seven Danish ships arrived, as though heralds of the devastation to come, and plundered Hampton. Afterwards Earl Ælfhere [Col. 0906C] departed this life, and Ælfric succeeded him; the king cruelly exiled Ælfric. At that time Saint Æthelwold, bishop, father of monks, and star of the English, attained the vision of the Lord for which he had always longed. Not long afterwards Saint Dunstan, archbishop, passed from the world’s darkness to the glory of heaven. When these two lights had been taken from the English people, England lacked the armour of its protection and lay exposed, desolate, to the foreordained vengeance of God. Ælgar succeeded Saint Dunstan, and Sigeric succeeded Ælgar after a year. King Æthelred had cruelly destroyed the bishopric of Rochester. The Lord, stirred again to anger, did not delay what he had prepared to do. Danes came from many parts [Col. 0906D] and covered England like clouds of heaven. On one side Wecheporte [alternatively, Wechport] was plundered. The Danes then advanced and met the English army; fighting, they killed Gada [alternatively, Goda], the English army’s leader, and brought that part of the army to destruction. On another side Wic was plundered. Earl Byrhtnoth, meeting them with great forces, fought, was defeated, and fell cut down by swords; his formations were destroyed.

In the thirteenth year of King Æthelred, the English first resolved, by the disastrous counsel of Archbishop Sigeric, to pay tribute to the Danes so that they might cease from plunder and killing; and they gave them ten thousand pounds. This evil has endured to [Col. 0907A] the present day and, unless God’s mercy intervenes, will endure for a long time. For we now pay our kings by custom what was paid to the Danes out of unspeakable terror. After this the king plotted treachery against the Danes. Earl Ælfric, whom the king had exiled but afterwards received back, caused an army to be made ready. Yet it is rightly said: “Whom you have once grievously injured, you will not readily believe faithful to you.” When the royal fleet came from London, commanded by Earls Ælfric and Thorold in order to intercept the Danes, all the Danes, forewarned, escaped. Then the greater Danish army came against the royal ships, fought a naval battle, killed many Londoners, triumphantly captured the fully armed ships, and captured Earl Ælfric [Col. 0907B] who was aboard them.

In the same year Saint Oswald, archbishop of York, passed to the glory of heaven, and Eadwulf received the see of York. Thereafter Bamburgh was broken and plundered; afterwards the army moved into the Humber and plundered on both sides, in Lindsey and Northumbria. But when the English had gathered military forces and drawn up battle-lines against them, before the actual clash Fræna, Godwine, and Fridegist—the leaders of the English army—began to flee. At that time Edwin had Ælfgar, son of Earl Ælfric, blinded; thus hatred and the infamy of his cruelty increased. Then, after the death of the elder Richard, his son Richard succeeded in Normandy. After these events Anlaf [Col. 0907C] and Sweyn attacked London with ninety-four ships on the Nativity of Saint Mary. Through the aid of that glorious Virgin the Christians were delivered from the pagans. For while attacking the city and preparing to destroy it with flames, they were repelled in immeasurable confusion. Their hope frustrated, they took horses in Essex, Kent, Sussex, and Hampshire, and proceeded more savagely than usual, filling everything with slaughter and fire. Therefore the king, sending messengers, promised them tribute and provisions; accepting these, they wintered peacefully at Hampton. King Æthelred then sent for King Anlaf; after hostages had been given, he honourably received him at Andover and, sponsoring him at the bishop’s confirmation, delighted him with many gifts. Anlaf accordingly promised the king that he would never again come into the land of the English without peace, and he kept his promise. In these times Archbishop Sigeric died, after whom Ælfric obtained the pallium.

In the nineteenth year of King Æthelred, the Danes went around Cornwall into the Severn, plundering in Devon and South Wales. Going out to Wecheport with iron and flame, they returned thence around Penwistrit [alternatively, Penwihtstrict] on the southern side; coming to Tamremuth, and then to Lideford, they committed everything to torches and flame and burned Ordulf’s monastery at Esingestoche. After this the enemy went to Frondmudham; leaving their ships, they ranged through Dorset with their customary devastation, none resisting. [Col. 0908A] Yet that year they sometimes spent two nights on the island of Wight and fed themselves from Hampshire and Sussex. Afterwards they came into the Thames and thence by the river Wedewei to Rochester. There the men of Kent assembled, formed battle-lines, and began the fight most fiercely. But the Danes, ever striving alone in the warfare of Mars, at last gained the field. King Æthelred then went with a very great army into Cumberland, where the Danes had their chief settlement; he defeated the Danes in a great battle and laid waste nearly all Cumberland by plundering. When this was done, a Danish army came to Erammuth and tried to storm the fortress there, but yielded before the courageous resistance. They then spread through the country in every direction with their customary leaders, Mars and Vulcan. The men of Somerset therefore assembled against them and fought at Penho. The Danes, always trained in war, gained the fortune of battle. But now this book, by the merits of the Danes’ greatness, must be granted its conclusion.

As is customary, the illuminating opening born from an ordered abridgement, having touched upon the chief points of this book, should be carefully set before the reader.

A few words must be said concerning the kingdom of Kent. When Egbert, king of Wessex, had driven out Baldred and held the kingdom of Kent under his own lordship, he left it at his death to his son Athelstan. When Athelstan died, that kingdom returned to his brother Æthelwulf, king of Wessex. Æthelwulf left it by hereditary right [Col. 0908C] to his son Æthelberht; and when another of his sons, Æthelbald, king of Wessex, died after five years, both kingdoms were made subject to Æthelberht and were never afterwards divided. Here, then, the kingdom of Kent wholly concludes.

Concerning the kingdom of Wessex, let this explanation be supplied:

Æthelwulf reigned nineteen years. Defeated by the Danes at Carrum, he defeated them disastrously at Aclea.

Æthelbald, son of the aforesaid king, reigned five years and was buried at Sherborne.

Æthelberht, his brother, reigned five years; his commanders and army defeated the Danes at Winchester.

Æthelred, their brother, reigned five years and a little more; he fought marvellously against the Danes at Reading with his brother. [Col. 0908D]

Alfred reigned twenty-eight years and a half. Nothing can briefly be said of him, because he did many and wonderful things.

Edward reigned twenty-three years. He fought against the Danes in Northumbria and at the crossing of the Werce; he gloriously defeated them and killed mighty kings. He also defeated the Danes at Cotenhale and conquered Werce.

Athelstan, son of Edward, reigned fourteen years; he fought the greatest battle at Bruneburh.

Edmund reigned six years and a half; he captured five cities from the Danes and, after conquering them, held Northumbria in his dominion.

Edred, Edmund’s brother, for nine years happily held all parts of England.

[Col. 0909A] Edwy, son of Edmund, held it for four years, with the same extent and power.

Edgar, son of Edmund, ruled for sixteen years peacefully and more gloriously than all others.

Edward, the saintly king, held the kingdom for five years and was happily killed.

Æthelred, his brother, reigned wretchedly, disturbed by the wrath of God; much remains for us to say about him.

The kingdom of Northumbria must also be touched upon briefly. In the time of King Æthelwulf, Osbricht ruled there. Having, as was their custom, cast him off, they made Ælla king. When both had been killed by the Danes, the Danes ruled in Northumbria for a long time: namely, King Halfdan, Guthfrith, [Col. 0909B] Nigellus, Sihtric, Ragnall, and Anlaf. The Danes ruled confusedly: now there was one king there, now two, now many petty kings. Afterwards it came into the lordship of King Edred of Wessex and his successors. Here, then, the kingdom of Northumbria wholly concludes.

A few words must be said concerning the kingdom of Werce. In the third year of his reign Britwulf, king of Werce, was driven out [Col. 0910A] by the Danes. Burhred too, after reigning twenty-two years, was driven from the kingdom. The Danes, therefore, having conquered that kingdom for themselves, first entrusted it to Ceolwulf to hold; afterwards they divided it among themselves in small portions. Thus part of the country and its nobles was at times under the laws of Wessex. King Edmund of Wessex subjected all Werce to his dominion. Here, then, the kingdom of Werce, wholly subjected to the dominion of Wessex, concludes.

The kingdom of East Anglia, which had long been subject to other kingdoms in various ways, as stated above, was now held in dominion by kings of Wessex or Kent, and now was given by them to one or several persons. Thus at times there was one king there, at other times many petty kings. Yet the last Englishman to reign there under the king of Wessex [Col. 0910B] was Saint Edmund. After he was killed, the Dane Guthrum reigned; afterwards the Danes divided the kingdom little by little, and it remained under them until it was for the most part made subject to King Edward. Here, then, the kingdom of East Anglia, coming under the lordship of Wessex, concludes; and now we reach the beginnings and cause of the coming of the Normans.

## Book Six

[Col. 0909]

[Col. 0909C] In the year one thousand from the Incarnation of the Lord, the aforesaid King Æthelred considered taking in marriage the daughter of Richard, earl of the Normans, for the protection of his kingdom. For Richard was very powerful and feared throughout the whole kingdom of the Franks. Æthelred saw himself and his own people greatly weakened, and he dreaded the coming disaster no little. It is clear that this occurred by God’s will, so that evil might come upon the wicked. For Almighty God had resolved to destroy the English people because their sins demanded it, just as he had humbled the Britons when their sins accused them. He prepared a double crushing for them and, as it were, laid military ambushes: on this side the raging persecution of the Danes, on that the growing connection with the Normans, so that [Col. 0909D] if they escaped the open thunderbolt of the Danes, they should not escape the unforeseen stratagem of the Normans joined with strength. This was made apparent in what followed, when, from this union of the king of the English with the daughter of the Norman duke, the Normans justly both laid claim to England according to the law of nations and acquired it.

A certain man of God also foretold to them that, because of the enormity of their crimes—not only because they constantly devoted themselves to slaughter and treachery, but because they were always given over to drunkenness and neglect of the house of God—an unexpected dominion would come upon them from France, which would depress their eminence forever and scatter their honour beyond all possibility of restoration. He further foretold that not only that people, [Col. 0910C] but also the Scots, whom they held most contemptible, would rule over them to their deserved confusion. He likewise foretold that an age so variable would be created that the variety hidden in human minds and evident in their actions would be signified by manifold variation in clothing and dress. Accordingly, once the king of the English had obtained the duke of Normandy’s consent to his request through envoys sent to him, at the appointed time English nobles were sent into Normandy to receive and bring back their lady; she was sent to England with a splendid and kingly retinue.

In the year 1002, Emma, the jewel of the Normans, came to England and received the crown and title of queen. Elated by this success into pride and carried forward into treachery, King Æthelred [Col. 0910D] caused all the Danes living peacefully in England to be massacred by a secret betrayal on one and the same day, namely on the feast of St Brice. In our youth we heard some very aged men speak of this crime: they said that the aforesaid king had sent secret letters to every city, by which the English, on the same day and at the same hour, either struck down all the unsuspecting Danes with swords or burned alive those suddenly seized. In the same year the aforesaid king exiled Leofric the ealdorman, because he had killed Effic, the king’s reeve.

In the year 1003 the Danes’ wrath blazed up—justly—like a fire which someone tries [Col. 0911A] to extinguish with blood [variant: *sangimine*]. Thus, swooping down like a multitude of locusts, some came to Exeter, utterly destroyed the whole city, and carried away all the spoil with them, leaving only ashes. They put to death Hugh the Norman, whom Queen Emma had already appointed there as reeve, to their ruin. The peoples of Hampshire and Wiltshire were therefore assembled to fight the army. But as they approached battle, their leader Ælfric pretended to be ill and forced himself to vomit; and thus he betrayed the English people whom he led. Since the common saying is true, “When the leader fails, the army becomes worthless,” the Danes, seeing their enemies’ collapse, pursued them as far as Wilton; having plundered and burned it, they came [Col. 0911B] to Salisbury, and thence returned to their ships with plunder and triumph.

In the fourth year, Sweyn, the mighty king of the Danes, to whom God had destined the kingdom of England, came with many ships to Norwich, plundered it, and burned it. When Usketel [variant: Wlfketel], ealdorman of that province, saw this, he made peace with the army, being unable to withstand its unexpected arrival. Yet, within the peace, after three weeks the army secretly went to Thetford and, having plundered it, burned it. Learning this, Ealdorman Ulfketel unexpectedly met the army as it returned to its ships in the morning with a small force. He resisted them fiercely and for a long time, but could not persist.

[Col. 0911C] In the fifth year the Danes returned to their own country. Yet lest the English should meanwhile be without affliction, so great a devastation of famine overwhelmed Britain that no living person could remember its like.

In the sixth year, when Sweyn [variant: Swein], a most daring man, returned with a great fleet to Sandwich—always attended by three companions, plunder, burning, and killing—all England groaned and was shaken like a reed-bed struck by a quivering west wind. The king assembled an army and held out against them throughout the whole autumn, but accomplished nothing; for they moved their fleet elsewhere and practised their usual game. At the beginning of winter they remained on the Isle of Wight; and, as was said through the prophet, “I will turn your feast-days into mourning” (1 Maccabees 1), at Christmastide [Col. 0911D] they ranged through Hampshire and Berkshire as far as Reading; then to Wallingford; then to Coleseige; then, near Elendune [variant: Etsesdune], to Chichelnestowe. Wherever they went, they cheerfully ate what had been prepared; and when departing, as payment for their entertainment, they gave their host slaughter in return for provisions and fire in return for lodging. When the Danes returned to the sea, the army of Wessex met and fought them. But what else did it accomplish except to enrich the Danes, already wealthy with spoils, by its defeat? Thus the people of Winchester saw the hostile army, proud and bold, passing beside the gates of the city and carrying with it food which it had procured more than fifty miles from the sea, and spoils which it had taken from those conquered in war. But King Æthelred, in sorrow and confusion, [Col. 0912A] was at his estate in Shropshire, often wounded by the stings of reports.

In the seventh year, the king and council of the English, uncertain what they should do and what they should leave undone, by common deliberation made a burdensome agreement with the army and gave it thirty thousand pounds for the observance of peace. In the same year, by God’s providence and for the ruin of the English, Eadric was made ealdorman over Mercia—a new traitor, but the greatest of traitors.

In the eighth year, which was the thirtieth year of the aforesaid king’s reign, the king ordered throughout England that one ship should be equipped from every three hundred and ten hides, and a coat of mail and helmet from every eight hides. A hide is called in English a quantity of land sufficient for the annual cultivation of one plough.

In the ninth year the king sent [Col. 0912B] his messengers to Richard, duke of the Normans, to seek counsel and assistance. The aforesaid ships were assembled at Sandwich, with men excellently armed; and never in Britain, in anyone’s time, had so great a number of ships existed. But God frustrated them. For the king had exiled Wlnod, a noble youth of Sussex. He began to plunder the seacoasts with twenty ships. Then Brictric, brother of Ealdorman Eadric, wishing to win renown for himself, took with him eighty of the aforesaid ships and promised the king that he would bring him the enemy alive or dead. But while he was on his way, a wind of extraordinary violence dashed all his ships disastrously upon the shore. Wlnod, coming upon them, immediately burned them. Harassed by adverse tidings, the remaining ships [Col. 0912C] returned to London. The army too was divided, and thus all the English labour came to nothing.

At harvest-time a new and innumerable Danish army came to Sandwich; and advancing thence to Canterbury, it would immediately have taken it, had not the citizens obtained peace by paying three thousand pounds. The Danes then came to Wight, and from there plundered Sussex, Hampshire, and Berkshire. King Æthelred, having gathered all the strength of the English, met the Danes as they returned and would have put an end to their savagery, had not Ealdorman Eadric, always a traitor, dissuaded the king from battle with invented rumours and false alarms. Afterwards the Danes returned and wintered on the Thames, frequently attacking London and frequently being repelled. After Christmas they went through the Chilterns [Col. 0912D] to Drineford. Having burned it, they returned; remaining in Kent, they repaired during Lent their ships which had been brought against them.

In the tenth year the Danes came to Ipswich on the day of the Lord’s Ascension and rose against Ealdorman Ulfketel; the East Angles immediately fled. But the men of Cambridgeshire resisted bravely; hence, while the English ruled, the fame of the province of Cambridge flourished splendidly. As the battle-lines clashed fiercely together and scorned the chance of death, Æthelstan, the king’s brother-in-law, was slain, as were Ealdorman Oswi, Eadwi the brother of Eofic, Ealdorman Wulfric, and the nobles with them. But when the English retained no memory of flight, Turcetil Mireneheved—that is, “Ant’s Head”—was the first to begin fleeing, and earned [Col. 0913A] everlasting disgrace. The victorious Danes for three months either plundered or burned the land of East Anglia, and also the marshes described in the preceding book, together with their churches. They also destroyed Thetford and burned Cambridge. Departing from there through the most delightful uplands of the pleasant place called Valesham [variant: Belesham], they put to death there every person they found, catching boys whom they tossed upon the points of their spears.

A certain man, worthy of remembrance, climbed the external steps of the tower of a church which still stands there, and, fortified both by his position and by his courage, alone defended himself against the entire army. The Danes then crossed Essex and came to the River Thames. Nor were they sluggish in advancing their columns from there into Drinefordshire [Col. 0913B] and Buckinghamshire; then, beside the Ouse, to Bedford; and so to Cemesford. The River Ouse runs through three fortresses that are the chief places of the provinces—Buckingham, Bedford, and Huntingdon. Huntingdon, that is, “the hunters’ hill,” situated on the other side of the river opposite Godmancester, once a famous city but now a village not without charm, surpasses the two aforesaid fortresses greatly: in the brilliance of its situation and its own beauty, in nearness to the aforesaid marshes, and in abundance of wild animals and fish. At the feast of St Andrew they turned aside to Northampton. Having burned it, they crossed to this side of the Thames, burned the whole land, and returned to their fleet for Christmas.

In the eleventh year, after the Danes had already plundered, north [Col. 0913C] of the Thames, East Anglia, Cambridgeshire, Drinefordshire, Buckinghamshire, Essex, Middlesex, Herefordshire, Bedfordshire, that part of Huntingdonshire which lies on this side of the river, and much of Hampshire; and south of the Thames, Kent, Surrey, Hastings, Sussex, Berkshire, Hampshire, and much of Wiltshire—they besieged and took by treachery Canterbury, the metropolis of England. For Almar, whose life Archbishop Ælfheah [variant: Ælfes] had saved, betrayed it. Having entered, they captured Archbishop Ælfheah, Bishop Godwine, Abbot Leofwine, Ælfword the king’s reeve, clergy with monks, and men with women; [Col. 0913D] and so, victorious, returned to their ships.

You might have seen the dreadful spectacle: the entire face of that ancient and most beautiful city reduced to ashes; citizens’ corpses lying thickly through the streets; earth and river blackened with blood; the weeping and wailing of boys and women being led into captivity; and the head of the English faith and fountain of learning shamefully dragged along in chains.

In the twelfth year, when Saturday came in Easter week, the Danes were angered against the archbishop because he forbade money to be paid for him. They were also drunk on wine which had come from the south. The archbishop was brought into their midst, and they threw at him bones and ox-heads. As he joyfully returned thanks from the depth of his heart to Almighty God, [Col. 0914A] he was struck on the head with an axe. Thus the man of God fell, sprinkling the earth with his holy blood; his blessed soul adorned the courts of heaven. In the morning Bishops Eadnod and Helhum received the body, bore it away with due honour, and buried it at the monastery of St Paul, where God displayed the merits of the holy martyr. Leofwing succeeded him as archbishop.

Then, far too late, the king made peace with the Danish army, giving them eight thousand pounds. Peace was never made at a suitable time, until the land lay exhausted by excessive affliction. Forty-five Danish ships submitted to the king, promising that they would defend England, while the king would provide them food and clothing.

In the thirteenth year Sweyn, king of the Danes, came up the Humber [Col. 0914B] as far as Gainsborough. Immediately Uhtred, ealdorman of Northumbria, and all that people submitted to him. The people of Lindsey as well, and the people of the Five Boroughs, and all those north of Watling Street gave him hostages. The king handed over hostages and ships to his son Cnut for safekeeping, and, proceeding to Oxford and Winchester, brought those peoples under his power. Returning thence toward London, he lost many people in the Thames because they did not take care to go to the bridge. But the citizens, because King Æthelred was among them, resisted him bravely. Sweyn therefore withdrew from there, went to Wallingford, and thence to Bath; and all Wessex submitted to him. Afterwards, when Sweyn had returned to his ships, the Londoners too submitted to him, because they feared he would bring them to destruction.

Seeing this, [Col. 0914C] King Æthelred sent Queen Emma to her brother Richard in Normandy, and afterwards his sons Edward and Ælfred. Sweyn was regarded as king by all the people, and ordered provisions and tribute to be given to his army throughout England. Turchil likewise ordered provisions to be supplied to his own army, which was at Greenwich. King Æthelred sought refuge in Wight; having remained there through Christmas, he crossed the sea as an exile to Richard, duke of Normandy.

In the fourteenth year Sweyn, now king of the English, perished by a sudden death at the beginning of his reign. His army chose his son Cnut as king. But the English sent messengers into Normandy to King Æthelred, informing him that if he were willing to treat them more humanely than had been his custom, they would receive no one more gladly as king. He sent ahead his son Edward, promising them all things worthy of king and people; then, arriving, he was received with joy by the entire English nation. Cnut, meanwhile, remained with his army at Gainsborough until Easter and made an agreement with the men of Lindsey. Hearing this, King Æthelred came upon them with a very large army, burned that province, and killed almost all its inhabitants. Cnut, deeply grieving that that people had been destroyed on his account, went by ship to Sandwich, and there, sending out (*emittens*; variant *admittens*, “admitting”) the noblest hostages who had been entrusted to his father, cut off their hands and noses. Besides this evil, the king ordered twenty-one thousand pounds to be paid to the army at Greenwich. [Col. 0915A] The Lord added to the customary evils an unusual evil: for the sea, rising higher than usual, submerged villages with innumerable people.

In the fifteenth year Ealdorman Eadric betrayed the distinguished nobles Siferth and Morcar: after summoning them into his chamber, he had them killed. Edmund, son of King Æthelred, seized their land and married Sigeferth’s wife. Cnut returned from Denmark to Sandwich, and, coming into Wessex at Frothemutham, plundered Dorset, Somerset, and Wiltshire. King Æthelred lay ill at Chosam. Then Edmund, the king’s son, and Ealdorman Eadric assembled an army against Cnut; but when they had come together, the ealdorman wished to betray the young man. Therefore they separated, and battle was abandoned. Thus Wessex submitted to Cnut, king [Col. 0915B] of the Danes.

In the sixteenth year Ealdorman Eadric submitted to King Cnut with forty ships, and the king arrived in the Thames with one hundred and sixty ships. Proceeding to Cricklade, they destroyed Warwickshire with sword and flame. King Æthelred issued an edict that every able-bodied Englishman should go with him to war. But when an innumerable people had assembled, the king was told that his own men wished to betray him. Therefore, dismissing the army, he returned to London.

Edmund went to Uhtred, ealdorman of Northumbria, and together they plundered Staffordshire, Shropshire, and Chester. Cnut, on the other hand, went through Buckinghamshire into Bedfordshire; then into Huntingdonshire; [Col. 0915C] then beside the marshes to Stamford; then into Lincolnshire; then into Nottinghamshire; and so into Northumbria toward York. Hearing this, Uhtred abandoned his raid, returned to Northumbria, and by necessity submitted himself to Cnut, together with all Northumbria. He gave hostages, yet was killed there. Edmund returned to London to his father. But Cnut appointed Hirc as ealdorman over Northumbria in Uhtred’s place and returned to his ships before Easter; after Easter he set out with his fleet for London.

Æthelred, having reigned for thirty-seven years, died in London after many labours and anxieties of his life, before the hostile fleet had arrived.

After him his son Edmund was chosen [Col. 0915D] king. He was called Ironside, that is, “iron side,” because in military affairs he possessed the greatest strength and remarkable endurance. King Edmund went into Wessex, and all the people submitted to him. Meanwhile the Danish ships came to Greenwich and from there to London; making a great ditch on the southern side, they drew their ships round from the western side of the bridge and dug around the city, so that no one could enter or leave. They often and severely attacked the city, but its citizens resisted them shrewdly and bravely. Are not Edmund’s wars and his courage recorded with the highest praise in the histories of the ancients?

Edmund fought his first battle against the Danish army at Peonna near Tillinges, and the outcome fell more openly in Edmund’s favour. [Col. 0916A] He fought his second battle against King Cnut at Sherston, where the struggle was most fierce. Ealdorman Eadric and Almer Derling were in the battle against King Edmund. Many therefore fell on each side, and the armies separated from one another. Thirdly, with a chosen band of warriors, he came to London and, having driven the army besieging the city back to its ships, most bravely liberated it and entered it in due triumph.

Two days later he fought the fourth battle against the same army at Brentford. Many of his men, hurrying over the crossing too rashly, were drowned in the river; nevertheless, he gained the joyous honour of victory. King Cnut, seized by the greatest fear, strengthened his own force with many troops summoned by messengers. King Cnut and Ealdorman Eadric also devised how they might overcome by treachery the man whom they could not defeat by arms. Thus Ealdorman Eadric made an agreement with him to betray Edmund. By his counsel Edmund went into Wessex to lead a great army against Cnut. Meanwhile Cnut besieged London and fiercely attacked it by land and water, but the citizens resisted him bravely.

For the fifth time King Edmund crossed the River Thames again at Brentford and went into Kent to fight the Danes. But at the very encounter an immense terror seized the advancing Danish standard-bearers, and they turned to flight. Edmund pursued them with great slaughter as far as Aylesford [variant: Eilesford]. Had he continued the pursuit, [Col. 0916C] that day would have been the last for the war and for the Danes. But Ealdorman Eadric, by most wicked counsel, made him halt. No worse counsel had ever been given in England.

Edmund fought the sixth battle with a very great host, and Cnut with all the Danish armies assembled, in Essex at Ashingdon. A most fierce and decisive battle was fought, and both sides, invincible and scorning slaughter, held firm. There Edmund’s youthful valour was displayed. For when he saw the Danes fighting more fiercely than usual, he left the royal position—which, by custom, was between the dragon standard and the emblem called the Standard—and rushed terribly into the foremost line. Brandishing a chosen sword worthy of the arm of young Edmund, he split the battle-line like lightning; breaking through the middle, [Col. 0916D] he passed across it and exposed himself to be overwhelmed by those following him. Then he flew upon the royal battle-line. When dreadful shouting and clashing began there, Ealdorman Eadric, seeing the Danes’ ruin at hand, cried to the English people: “Flet, Engle, flet, Engle: dedis Edmund.” This means: “Flee, English, flee, English: Edmund is dead.” Thus crying out, he was the first to begin flight with his followers, and the entire English nation followed him into flight.

There a terrible slaughter of the English was made. There Ealdorman Eadnod was killed, and Ealdorman Ælfric, Ealdorman Godwine, Ulfketel ealdorman of East Anglia, Ailward son of Ealdorman Ælfsi, and the whole flower of Britain’s nobility. King Cnut, relying on so great a victory, took London and the royal sceptres. Yet for the seventh time the armies were assembled in Gloucestershire. [Col. 0917A] On the one side they feared King Edmund’s strength, and on the other that of King Cnut; the nobles said to one another: “Why do we madly expose ourselves so often to the danger of death? Let those who seek to reign alone fight one another alone.” The kings approved the decision, for King Cnut was a man of no ordinary courage. The kings were placed at Molania and began their duel. When the missiles and spears on both sides had been broken, they took up the matter with swords, weapons surpassing all other weapons. Each people heard and saw the dreadful ringing and fiery collisions with groaning and shouting, until at last Edmund’s incomparable strength began to strike like lightning.

King Cnut resisted him with great vigour, yet feared for himself, and said: “Bravest of all young men, what necessity is there that one of us should perish by the sword for the sake of reigning? Let us be adoptive brothers and divide the kingdom: let me rule in your affairs, and you in mine. Denmark too shall be ordered under your authority.” [Col. 0917B] These words soothed the generous mind of the young man, and they gave one another the kiss of peace. When the people assembled and wept for joy, Edmund received the kingdom of Wessex, while Cnut, receiving the kingdom of Mercia, returned to London.

A few days afterwards King Edmund was killed by treachery at Drineford. This was how he was killed. While the king, terrible and most feared by his enemies, flourished in his realm, he went on one night to the privy for the necessities of nature. There the son of Ealdorman Eadric, lying concealed in the secret pit by his father’s design, struck the king in his private parts with a double-edged dagger; thrusting the blade into his entrails, he fled and left him. Eadric therefore came to King Cnut and greeted him, saying: “Hail, sole king.” When he disclosed what had been done, the king answered: “In reward for so great a service, I shall make you higher than all the nobles of the English.” He therefore ordered him beheaded and his head fixed upon a stake on the highest tower of London. Thus perished the strong King Edmund after reigning one year; he was buried beside his grandfather Edgar at Glastonbury.

King Cnut of the English married Emma, daughter of the duke of the Normans and wife of King Æthelred. Afterwards the king gave the English a fitting recompense for their wickedness. He himself held Wessex in his lordship; Hyrc held Northumbria; Turchil, East Anglia; and Eadric, Mercia. [Col. 0917D] King Cnut killed Eadric, exiled Turchil, and compelled Hyrc to flee. Moreover, he attacked and killed the greatest nobles: he killed the Norman ealdorman; exterminated Edwi Ætheling; mutilated Æthelwold; exiled Edwi Cheorleging [variant: Edwiceorleking]; and deprived Bridric of life by the sword. He also caused an extraordinary tax to be paid throughout England, namely eighty-two thousand pounds, besides the eleven thousand pounds paid by the Londoners.
