Thus the just Lord imposed upon the English a fitting exactor [variant: *exauctorem*, perhaps “author”].

In the third year of his reign Cnut went to Denmark, leading an army of English and Danes against the Wends. As he approached and was to fight the enemy on the next day, Godwine, earl of the English, leading [Col. 0918A] the army, set out by night against the enemy without the king’s knowledge. He fell upon them unprepared, killed and routed them. At first light the king thought that the English had fled or had treacherously gone over to the enemy; he sent battle-lines in formation against the enemy, but found in their camp nothing except blood, corpses, and plunder. Therefore thereafter he held the English in the highest honour, no less than the Danes. Having accomplished these things, he returned to England.

About this time, after the death of Archbishop Leving, his successor Athelnold went to Rome. Abbot Lefwin of Ely went with him and, by Pope Benedict’s command, recovered the abbey unjustly taken from him. On his return from Rome the archbishop translated the body of St Ælfheah from London to Canterbury.

In the eighth year of King Cnut, Richard II, duke of the Normans and father of Emma queen of the English, did not remain alive. [Col. 0918B] His son Richard ruled after him for almost one year, and after Richard his brother Robert for eight years. In the following year the king went with an English army into Denmark against Ulf and Eilaf, who brought against him by land and sea a very formidable multitude from the people of Sweden. There many English and Danes on Cnut’s side perished, and the Swedes were victorious.

In the twelfth year of King Cnut, he went from England with fifty ships into Norway, drove out Olaf, king of the Norwegians, in battle, and received that kingdom into his subjection. When King Cnut had returned to England, Olaf returned to Norway and was killed by the people [Col. 0918C] of that country. Cnut retained that kingdom while he lived. About this time Henry, son of Robert king of the French, succeeded his father.

In the fifteenth year of King Cnut, Robert duke of Normandy died while on pilgrimage to Jerusalem; his illegitimate son William succeeded him while still a boy. King Cnut went magnificently to Rome and permanently assigned to the Roman Church the alms called Romscot, which his predecessors had given. Who could number his alms, his liberality, and the great deeds which the great king performed on that pilgrimage? No king within the western world had sought the holy places at Rome so splendidly and so famously. In the same year, [Col. 0918D] returning from Rome, he went into Scotland; Malcolm, king of the Scots, submitted to him, as did two other kings, Melbeath and Jermarc.

After reigning twenty years, King Cnut died at Shaftesbury and was buried at Winchester in the Old Minster. A few points concerning this king’s power should be touched upon. No king of such greatness had existed in England before him. He was lord of all Denmark, all England, all Norway, and also Scotland. Apart from the innumerable wars in which he shone most brilliantly, he performed three deeds elegantly and magnificently. First, he married his daughter, with unspeakable riches, to the Roman emperor. Second, as he travelled to Rome, he caused all the oppressive dues along the road leading through Gaul to Rome—called [Col. 0919A] tolls or transit-dues—to be reduced by half through payment from his own money. Third, in the full vigour of his imperial power, he ordered his seat to be placed on the shore as the tide rose. He said to the rising sea: “You are subject to my dominion, and the land on which I sit is mine; nor has anyone resisted my command without punishment. I command you, therefore, not to rise onto my land, nor presume to wet the clothing or limbs of your lord.” But the sea, rising as usual, without reverence wetted the king’s feet and legs. The king sprang back and said: “Let all who inhabit the world know that the power of kings is empty and trifling, and that no one is worthy of the name of king except him to whose will heaven, earth, and sea obey by everlasting laws.”

[King Cnut thereafter never placed the golden crown upon his head, [Col. 0919B] but set it for ever upon the image of the Lord fixed to the cross, in praise of God the great king:] through whose mercy may the soul of King Cnut enjoy rest.

Harold, son of King Cnut and Ælfgifu [variants: Alwina or Alina], daughter of Ealdorman Ælfhelm, was chosen king. A great council was held at Oxford, where Earl Leofric and all the nobles north of the Thames, together with the Londoners, chose Harold to preserve the kingdom for his brother Harthacnut, who was in Denmark. But Earl Godwine, father of the later King Harold, and the nobles of Wessex began to oppose this, but to no effect. They therefore reached an agreement that Queen Emma, with the household of the deceased king, should preserve Wessex at Winchester for the benefit of her son; and Earl Godwine should be their military leader.

King Harold exiled Queen Emma, his stepmother; she went to Baldwin, count of Flanders, who gave her the castle of Bruges, where she might live and from which she might act. Since William, lord of the Normans, was still a boy and remained with the king of France, Normandy was a royal possession. In the following year, on the death of Atelnod [variant: Athenold], archbishop of Canterbury, Eadsi succeeded him.

After King Harold had reigned four years and four months, he died at Oxford and was buried at Westminster. In those days, [Col. 0919D] eight marks of silver were rendered from every port for sixteen ships, as in his father’s time.

Harthacnut, son of King Cnut and Queen Emma, came from Denmark to Sandwich, where he was immediately received and chosen king by English and Danes alike. In his second year the payment for the Danish army was made, namely 21,000 pounds and 89 pounds; afterwards, 11,000 pounds and 48 pounds were paid to thirty-two ships. In the same year Edward, son of King Æthelred, came from Normandy to King Harthacnut, his brother; for both were sons of Emma, daughter of Count Richard.

King Harthacnut was snatched away by death after reigning two years, in the very flower of his youth, at Lamhuthe [variant: Lambhite]. He had been a youth of distinguished character and kindness toward his own people. [Col. 0920A] He is said to have been so liberal that four times a day he had royal meals set before his entire court, preferring prepared dishes to be left by those invited rather than dishes yet to be served to be demanded by those not invited. In our time, by contrast, it is customary—whether through avarice or, as they themselves say, because of satiety—for princes to set food before their men only once a day. King Harthacnut was buried in the Old Minster at Winchester beside his father Cnut.

The English nobles, now freed from Danish domination, joyfully sent messengers for Alfred [variant: Alured], Æthelred’s eldest son, that he might be raised to the royal crown. Since he was English by his father and Norman by his mother, he brought with him into England from Normandy some of his mother’s kinsmen and many companions of his own age, fellow-soldiers. [Col. 0920B] But Godwine, although a most powerful earl, was also a most savage traitor. He planned that he might give his daughter as queen to Edward, the younger and more simple brother. He foresaw, however, that Alfred, being the elder son and a man of great worth, would never deem his daughter worthy of him. Godwine therefore announced to the English nobles that Alfred had brought with him an excessive number of Normans, promised them English lands, and brought a people most strong and crafty; it was unsafe, he said, for the English to uproot them among themselves. These men, he said, had to pay the penalty, lest others afterwards dare to impose themselves upon the English because of royal kinship.

The Normans who had come with [Col. 0920C] Alfred were therefore seized and bound. As they sat in a row, nine were always beheaded and the tenth was left alive at Guildford. When all except a tenth part had been killed, it seemed to the English that too many had survived; so they had the tenth part itself decimated, and thus very few escaped. Alfred himself was captured and taken to Ely; his eyes were put out, and he died. They then sent messengers and hostages to Edward the younger in Normandy, telling him to bring with him only very few Normans and promising to establish him most faithfully as king. Edward obeyed, came to England with a few men, was chosen king by all the people, and was consecrated by Archbishop Eadsi at Winchester on Easter Day [variant: “And before his brother was buried, Edward was chosen by all the people and consecrated by Archbishop Eadsi at Winchester on Easter Day”].

Archbishop Eadsi relinquished the archbishopric because of illness, and Siward was consecrated in his place. Stigand was also then made bishop of East Anglia.

King Edward took under the protection of his kingdom the daughter of the very powerful Earl Godwine, named Edith [variant: Edieva], sister of the future King Harold. About this time so great a famine overwhelmed England that a measure of wheat, ordinarily a single horse-load, sold for five shillings and even more. Afterwards Stigand, who was bishop in East Anglia, was also made bishop at Winchester. The king exiled Earl Sweyn, son of the aforesaid Earl Godwine. [Col. 0921A] He withdrew to Baldwin, count of Flanders, and wintered there at Bruges.

In the sixth year of King Edward, a battle was fought at Val-ès-Dunes between Henry, king of France, and the nobles of Normandy, because they did not wish to receive William as their lord. When Duke William overcame them victoriously, he exiled some and mutilated others. At that time two Danish nobles, Lothen and Hirling, came to Sandwich. Having taken countless spoil there, including abundance of gold and silver, they sailed around and plundered Essex. Then they directed their course to Flanders; after selling their plunder, they returned whence they had come.

In the following year Earl Sweyn returned to England, having obtained peace from the king. When his brother Harold and Earl Beorn had gone aside, Sweyn later came to his father Godwine at Pevensey and humbly begged him and his brothers Harold and Tostig, and Earl Beorn, until he obtained from them that Earl Beorn should go with him as far as Sandwich to seek the king’s friendship. [Col. 0921B] Beorn therefore entered Earl Sweyn’s ships in order to help him, and was wickedly killed by them. His friends buried his body at Winchester beside King Cnut, his uncle. Sweyn returned to Flanders. In the following year Sweyn was reconciled to the king through the stratagem of his father Godwine.

At that time Pope Leo held a synod at Vercelli, where Ulf, bishop of Dorchester, was present; and his episcopal staff was nearly broken unless he paid a higher price. For he did not understand his office as befitted a bishop. Archbishop Eadsi departed this life. Siward, his successor, had also died.

In the tenth year of Edward’s reign, he gave Robert, bishop of London, the archbishopric of Canterbury. It was reported to the king that his son-in-law Godwine, Godwine’s son Sweyn, and Harold intended to betray him. When summoned to answer the charge, they refused to come without hostages; the king therefore exiled them. Thus Godwine and Sweyn went to Flanders, while Harold went to Ireland. The king, moved to anger, dismissed the queen and took from her her treasure and lands. He gave Odo the earldom of Devonshire, Somerset, [Col. 0921D] and Dorset; and he gave Algar, son of Earl Leofric, Harold’s earldom.

In the second year of King Edward, Emma the Norman, wife of kings and mother of kings, underwent the common fate of death. Earl Godwin and his son Sweyn, sailing with full-spread sails from Flanders to the Isle of Wight, also plundered Portland. Harold, coming from Ireland, plundered at Pordocan [otherwise Portlocan]; and thence, joining his father on Wight, they proceeded to Pevensey, then to Ness, Kumene, Hythe, Folkestone, Dover, Sandwich, and Sheppey, everywhere taking hostages and ships. Some men, coming out, burned the royal vill of Widdeltune; while the fleet, making for London by way of the North Mouth, encountered fifty ships in which the king was present. [Col. 0922A] Then, through envoys and by the counsel of Bishop Stigand, hostages having been exchanged, the king and his son-in-law were reconciled; and the king restored to him and his followers their lands and everything they had formerly possessed, and received his queen back again. Archbishop Robert, however, and all the Frenchmen by whose counsel the king had exiled the earl, were banished. Stigand was made Archbishop of Canterbury.

About this time Earl Siward, the mightiest man of Northumbria, almost a giant in stature and most hardy both in hand and mind, sent his son to conquer Scotland. When it was reported to the father that he had been slain in battle, he said: “Did he receive his mortal wound on the front or the rear of his body?” The messengers replied: “On the front.” And he said: “I rejoice indeed; for I deem no other [Col. 0922B] death worthy of either myself or my son.” Siward therefore marched into Scotland, defeated the king in battle, devastated the whole kingdom, and subjected the devastated land to himself.

In the twelfth year of King Edward’s reign, while he was dining at Windsor, where he was accustomed to reside most often, Godwin, his son-in-law and traitor, reclining beside him, said: “Often, O king, it has been falsely reported to you that I have plotted treason against you; but, if the God of heaven is true and just, may He grant that this morsel of bread may not pass my throat if I have ever even thought of betraying you.” But God, just and true, heard the traitor’s words, and immediately, choked by that very bread, he tasted beforehand eternal death. Harold his son received [Col. 0922C] his father’s earldom. But Ælfgar, Earl of Chester, received Harold’s earldom.

In the thirteenth year of King Edward, the nobles of Normandy fought the French people at the castle called Mortemer; Ralph the chamberlain, commander of the French army, was killed; and victory fell to the Normans. King Henry of the French and Duke William of the Normans were not themselves present in the battle. In the following year Earl Siward, most stern of men, was afflicted by flux of the belly and perceived that death was near. He said: “What shame, that I could not die in so many battles, but should be reserved with disgrace for the death of cattle! At least clothe me in my impenetrable coat of mail; gird me with my sword; raise me with my helmet; put my shield in my left hand and my gilded axe [Col. 0922D] in my right, that, bravest of soldiers, I may now die the death of a soldier.” He had spoken; and, as he had said, honourably armed, he breathed out his spirit.

But because his son Waltheof was still a little child, his earldom was given to Tostig, son of Earl Godwin. In the same year Ælfgar, Earl of Chester, was banished because he had been convicted in council of treason against the king. Going to Gruffydd, king of North Wales, he returned with that king, burned Hereford and the church of Saint Eilbricht [otherwise Athelbricht]. Afterwards Edward, son of Edmund Ironside, came into this land and immediately died; he was buried in London, in the church of Saint Paul. He was the father of Margaret, queen of Scots, and of Edgar Ætheling [otherwise Atheling]. Margaret was the mother of Matilda, [Col. 0923A] queen of the English, and of David, the most cultivated king of the Scots. Likewise Leofric, most noble Earl of Chester, died at that time. His wife, named Godiva, worthy of everlasting remembrance, flourished in much virtue and built the abbey at Coventry, which she enriched beyond comparison with gold and silver. She also built Stow Church beneath the Lincoln promontory, and many others. Her son Ælfgar received the earldom of Chester.

In the twenty-second year of King Edward, when King Henry had died and his son Philip was reigning, William, Duke of Normandy, subjected Maine to himself. Harold, crossing into Flanders, was driven by a storm into the province of Ponthieu. The Count of Ponthieu captured him and delivered him to William, Duke of Normandy. [Col. 0923B] Harold swore to William upon many and most choice relics of saints that he would marry his daughter and preserve England, after King Edward’s death, for William’s use. He was therefore received with the highest honour and enriched with lavish gifts; but when he had returned to England, he chose the guilt of perjury.

In the following year Harold and Tostig went on an expedition into Wales. The people of that country submitted to them and gave hostages. Afterwards they killed their own king Gruffydd and brought his head to Harold. Harold appointed another king there. It happened in the same year that, in the royal hall at Windsor, Tostig seized his brother Harold by the hair before the king himself while Harold was serving wine to the king. For this had supplied fuel [Col. 0923C] for envy and hatred: although Tostig himself was the first-born, his brother was more dearly loved by the king. Thus, driven by a rush of fury, he could not restrain his hands from his brother’s hair. The king foretold that their destruction was now drawing near and that God’s anger would no longer be delayed. For those brothers were guilty of such cruelty that, whenever they saw a well-appointed estate belonging to anyone, they ordered its owner to be killed by night, and obtained for themselves the whole of his family and the dead man’s possessions. Yet these were the justiciars of the realm. Tostig therefore, departing from the king and his brother in a frenzy, went to Hereford, where his brother had prepared a very great royal provisioning; there, having mutilated all his brother’s servants, he placed in each vessel [Col. 0923D] of wine, mead, ale, spiced wine, mulberry wine, or cider, a human leg, head, or arm. And he sent word to the king that, when hastening to his farm, he would find sufficiently salted provisions, but should take care to bring other food with him. The king therefore ordered him to be stripped of his office and exiled for so boundless a crime.

In the twenty-fourth year of King Edward, the Northumbrians, hearing this, drove out their earl Tostig, who had inflicted many slaughters and disasters upon them. Having killed all his household, English as well as Danes, they seized his treasure and weapons at York. They then appointed Morcar, son of Earl Ælfgar, as earl over them. With that people, and with Lincolnshire, Nottinghamshire, and Derbyshire, he advanced as far as Damtune; and his brother Edwin [Col. 0924A] came against him with the men of his own earldom, with many Britons also accompanying him. Then Earl Harold came to them. They sent him to the king, together with messengers, begging that Morcar might be their earl. The king granted this, and sent Harold back to them at Hamtune, where he confirmed it to them. Meanwhile, though burning, plundering, and killing, they spared not that province; after obtaining their request, they carried many thousands of persons away with them and for many years made that part of the kingdom worse than before. Tostig and his wife, turning aside to Baldwin, Count of Flanders, spent the winter there.

In the year of grace 1066, the Lord who rules fulfilled upon the English people what He had long [Col. 0924B] intended. He delivered them to the fierce and crafty people of the Normans for extermination. For, when the basilica of Saint Peter at Westminster had been dedicated on the feast of the Holy Innocents, and afterwards King Edward had departed this world on the eve of Epiphany and had been buried in the same church which he had built and enriched with many possessions, some of the English wished to raise Edgar Ætheling [otherwise Atheling] to the kingship. But Harold, relying on his strength and lineage, seized the royal crown.

William, Duke of Normandy, was spurred and inwardly provoked by three causes. First, because Godwin and his sons had dishonoured and killed his kinsman Alfred. Secondly, because Godwin and his sons had by their contrivance exiled from England Bishop Robert, Earl Odo, and all the French. [Col. 0924C] Thirdly, because Harold, falling into perjury, had seized without any right a kingdom which by right of kinship ought to have been William’s. Summoning the Norman nobles, he asked their help in conquering England. When they came together to deliberate with him, William, son of Osbern, the duke’s steward, was present. Declaring that the undertaking of crossing to England was most arduous and that the English people were exceedingly strong, he argued most vigorously against the very few who wished to go to England. Hearing this, the nobles rejoiced greatly and pledged their faith to him that all would agree to whatever he should say. Entering before them in the duke’s presence, he said: “I am prepared to set out devoutly on this expedition [Col. 0924D] with all my men.” Therefore all the Norman nobles were obliged to follow his proposal. A very great fleet was accordingly prepared at the harbour called Saint-Valery.

When King Harold, a man most vigorous in war, heard this, he put out to sea with a naval force against Duke William. Meanwhile Earl Tostig came into the Humber with sixty ships; but Earl Edwin came with an army and drove him away. Fleeing to Scotland, Tostig encountered Harald, king of Norway, with three hundred ships, and gladly submitted to him. Then both came into the Humber as far as York, and, near the city, Edwin and Morcar the earls fought against them; the place of battle is still shown on the southern side of the city. Harald, king of Norway, [Col. 0925A] and Tostig won it, under the glorious omen of Mars. When Harold, king of England, heard this, he met them at Stamford Bridge [otherwise Steinfordesbrige] with a strong force.

A battle then began, than which none had been more severe. Fighting from early morning until noon, and continuing their terrible assaults from both sides, a great number of English forced the Norwegians to yield, though not to flee. Driven beyond the river, the living marched over the dead and resisted courageously. One Norwegian, worthy of everlasting fame, stood upon the bridge and, striking down more than forty chosen Englishmen with an axe, alone held up the whole English army until the ninth hour of the day; until a man entered a boat and, through openings in the bridge, struck him from beneath with a javelin. [Col. 0925B] The English then crossed over, killed King Harald and Tostig, and either laid the whole Norwegian battle-line low by arms or burned those caught by fire.

Harold, king of the English, returning that same day to York in the highest joy, heard while dining a messenger say to him: “William, Duke of Normandy, has occupied the southern shore and has built a castle at Hastings.” The king, without delay, hastened there and drew up his line on the Hastings plain. William splendidly led five companies of cavalry against the enemy; and, after arranging them in a formidable formation, he made this speech:

“I address you, Normans, bravest of peoples, not because I doubt your valour [Col. 0925C], nor because I am uncertain of victory—a victory which no chance or obstacle has ever been able to wrest from you. If you had ever been unable to conquer, perhaps you would need exhortation, so that your valour might shine forth. But what is inborn and, as it were, necessary to you—what exhortation does it require? O strongest of mortals, what could the king of the French accomplish by war, with every people from Lorraine to Spain, against our forefather Hasting? He acquired as much of France as he wished; as much as he wished he left to the king; as long as he pleased he held it, and, when satisfied, yearning for greater things, he left it.

“Did not Rollo, my father, the first duke and founder of our people, with our fathers defeat the king of the French in battle at Paris, in the midst of his own kingdom? Nor could [Col. 0925D] the French king hope for safety unless, as a suppliant, he offered both his daughter and the land called Normandy after you. Did not your fathers capture and hold the king of the French at Rouen until he restored Normandy to your duke Richard, then a boy, on this condition: that whenever the king of France and the duke of Normandy met, the duke should be girded with a sword, while the king might carry neither sword nor even knife? Your fathers imposed this everlasting ordinance upon a great king.

“Did not that same duke lead your fathers as far as Mirmande near the Alps, and in battle compel the duke of that city—namely, his son-in-law—to obey his bride? And lest it seem too little for you to have conquered men, he himself also conquered the devil, wrestling with him bodily, overthrowing him, binding his hands behind his back, and leaving him ashamed, as a victor of the English [Col. 0926A].

“But why do I recount ancient things? When you fought at Mortemer in our own time, did not the French in their panic prefer flight to battle, their spurs to their weapons? You, after killing Ralph, the chief commander of the French, won glory and spoils and maintained your native excellence by its accustomed necessity. Let some Englishman come forth—men whom our forefathers, the Danes, and the Norwegians have conquered in battle a hundred times—and show that the people of Rollo from his time until now have once suffered shipwreck in war; and I will depart defeated. Is it not shameful to you that a people accustomed to defeat, a people destitute of war, a people who do not even possess arrows, should march against you, bravest of men, as though arrayed for battle? Are you not ashamed that King Harold, a perjurer against me, dared show his face before you? [Col. 0926B]

“Yet it amazes me that you have seen with your own eyes those who, by infamous treachery, beheaded your parents together with my kinsman Alfred, and that their heads still remain upon their shoulders. Raise the standards, men; let there be neither limit nor moderation in the wrath they have deserved. From east to west let the lightning of your glory be seen; let the thunder of your onset be heard, you most noble avengers of blood.”

Duke William had not yet finished his speech when all, inflamed with anger beyond belief, rushed upon the enemy in an irresistible charge according to their battle-lines, leaving their duke speaking now to himself alone.

A certain man named Taillefer, long before the combatants came together, played by tossing swords before the English [Col. 0926C] host; while all marvelled at him, he killed one English standard-bearer. He did the same a second time. Doing the same a third time, he himself was killed; and the battle-lines clashed. A joyful cloud of arrows begins. The thunder of blows follows. The fiery collision of helmets and swords leaps forth.

Since Harold had placed all his people in one exceedingly compact line and had, as it were, made a castle of them, they were impenetrable to the Normans. Duke William therefore taught his men to feign flight. As they fled, they came to a great pit artfully concealed, where a large number of them, falling in, were crushed. While the English persisted in pursuing, the main Norman line passed through the middle of the English force. Seeing this, those who were pursuing [Col. 0926D] through the aforesaid pit were forced to return and there perished in great part. Duke William also instructed his archers not to shoot directly at the enemy but to send their arrows high into the air, blinding the hostile wedge with arrows. This was greatly detrimental to the English.

Twenty most valiant knights pledged their faith to one another that, breaking through the English force, they would seize the royal ensign called the Standard. While doing this, many of them were killed. But part of them, having cleared a way with their swords, carried off the Standard. Meanwhile the whole shower of archers’ arrows fell around King Harold, and he fell, struck in the eye. Then a mass of cavalry broke in and killed the wounded king, and killed Earl Gyrth, Earl Leofwine, [Col. 0927A] and their brothers with them. Thus the English army was crushed.

William, having gained so great a victory, was peacefully received by the Londoners and crowned at Westminster by Aldred, bishop of York. And there occurred a change of the right hand of the Most High, which a great comet at the beginning of that year had signified. Hence it was said:

> In the year one thousand, sixty also, and six,  
> England’s boundaries felt the comet’s flames.

The battle was joined in October, on the feast of Saint Callixtus. At that place King William afterwards built a noble abbey for his dead, and aptly called it by the name of Battle.

In the following year King William crossed the sea, taking hostages and treasures with him; and, returning in the same year, he divided the land among his soldiers. But the young Edgar went with many soldiers into Scotland and gave his sister Margaret in marriage to the king of Scots. When the king had granted the earldom of Northumbria to Count Robert, the provincials killed him and nine hundred men with him. Then the young Edgar came to York with all the people of Northumbria, and the townsmen made peace with him. But the king came with an army, plundered the city, and inflicted a great slaughter upon the faithless people. Edgar returned to Scotland. [Col. 0927B]

In the third year of King William, two sons of Sweyn, king of the Danes, and Earl Osbern, his brother, came with three hundred ships into the Humber. [Col. 0927C] Earl Waltheof and the young Edgar came to them; and, united together, Danes and English captured the castle of York, killed many Frenchmen, carried their leaders in chains and their treasures to the ships, and wintered between the Ouse and the Trent. But the king came, put the Danes to flight, and devastated the English of that province. Earl Waltheof, however, was reconciled with the king.

In the following year Baldwin, Count of Flanders, whose daughter King William had married, died, and his son Arnulf succeeded him. King William of England and Philip, king of France, supported him. But his brother Robert the Frisian, fighting in battle, killed Earl Arnulf, William son of Osbern, of whom we have spoken above, and many thousands of the men of both kings. [Col. 0927C]

In the fifth year of King William, Earls Morcar and Edwin began to plunder through fields and woods. Edwin was killed by his own men. Morcar, Hereward, and Bishop Æthelwine came to Ely [otherwise Eli]. The king, leading an army by land and sea, besieged the island, built a bridge, and skilfully constructed a siege-house which remains to this day. Entering the island, he captured the men named above, except Hereward, who, bravest and most vigorous of men, led his followers out. In the next year the king led an army by land and sea into Scotland; King Malcolm became his man and gave him hostages. In the year following, the king led an army of English and French into Maine. The English devastated that land by burning villages and cutting down vineyards, [Col. 0928A] and subjected it to the king. In the next year the king went into Normandy; the young Edgar was reconciled with him and remained for a long time at the king’s court.

In the ninth year of King William, Ralph, to whom the king had given the earldom of East Anglia, planned to expel the king from his kingdom with the counsel of Earl Waltheof and of Roger, son of William son of Osbern. Earl Waltheof had married Roger’s sister, and it was at that very wedding that they discussed this treason. But the nobles of the kingdom resisted him courageously; therefore he embarked on ships at Norwich and withdrew into Denmark. On returning to England, the king sent Earl Roger, his kinsman, to prison. He caused Earl Waltheof to be beheaded at Winchester; he was buried at Crowland. Of the others who had taken part in the wicked wedding, [Col. 0928B] he drove many into exile and deprived many of their eyes.

Earl Ralph, bringing with him Cnut, son of Sweyn, king of the Danes, and Earl Hakon, returned to England with two hundred ships. But, because they did not dare fight against King William, they crossed the sea into Flanders. In the same year Queen Edith died and was buried beside her husband King Edward at Westminster. In the following year the king crossed the sea and besieged Dol; but the Bretons held the castle bravely until the king of France came and delivered them. Afterwards the king of France and King William were reconciled.

King Malcolm of Scots plundered Northumbria as far as the Tyne, bringing back a very great booty and many people in chains. King William, likewise, while conducting a military operation against his son Robert at Gerberoi, a castle in France, was thrown by his horse; his son William was wounded, and many of his men were killed. The king cursed his son Robert. Moreover, the Northumbrians treacherously killed Walcher, bishop of Durham, at a peacefully appointed assembly beside the Tyne, together with one hundred men. [Col. 0928C]

In the fifteenth year of King William, he led an army into Wales and subjected it to himself; afterwards he put his brother Bishop Odo in prison. When these things had occurred, Queen Matilda died. At that time the king exacted six shillings from every hide in England. Turstan, abbot of Glastonbury, committed a shameful crime. He caused three monks who had taken refuge beneath the altar to be killed and eighteen to be wounded, so that their blood ran from the altar over the steps and from the steps onto the sand. [Col. 0928D]

In the eighteenth year of King William—during which year Urban became pope of Rome—he returned from Normandy to England with so great an army of French, Normans, and Bretons that it seemed astonishing how this land could feed them. For he had learned, as report spread abroad, that Cnut, king of Denmark, and Robert the Frisian, Count of Flanders, intended to bring England beneath their dominion by the steps of Mars. But when, by God’s will, their preparations failed, he dismissed great portions of the armies to their native soil.

Thereafter the most powerful king sent justiciars through every shire—that is, province—of England, and caused inquiry to be made under oath how many hides (that is, acres sufficient for one plough in a year) were in each village, and how many animals; he also caused inquiry to be made what each city, castle, hamlet, village, river, marsh, and forest yielded each year. All these things were written on charters and brought to the king, and are preserved among the treasures to this day. In the same year Maurice became bishop of London and began the very great church which is not yet completed. [Col. 0929A]

In the nineteenth year of his reign, King William the Strong, after holding his court as was his custom at Christmas at Gloucester, at Easter at Winchester, and at Pentecost at London, clothed his younger son Henry in the arms of manhood. Then, receiving the homage of all landholders in England, whatever their fief, he did not delay to receive also their oath of fidelity. Afterwards, having accumulated great stores of treasure from all upon whom he could find any charge, whether justly or unjustly, the king went into Normandy.

In the twenty-first year of King William’s reign, after the Normans had fulfilled the Lord’s just will upon the English people, and scarcely any prince of English descent remained in England [Col. 0929C], while all had been reduced to servitude and sorrow, so that even to be called English was an insult, William, the author of this vengeance, ended his life. For God had chosen the Normans to exterminate the English people, because He had seen them surpass all peoples in the prerogative of singular cruelty. For it is their nature that, when they have so oppressed their enemies that they can add nothing further, they oppress themselves and reduce themselves and their lands to poverty and desolation. And Norman lords, whenever they have crushed their enemies, since they cannot refrain from acting cruelly, crush their own people also in hostile fashion. This appears ever more clearly in Normandy, England, Apulia, Calabria, Sicily, and Antioch—the finest lands which God had subjected to them.

In England, therefore, unjust tolls and most wicked customs flourished in these times. All the great men were so blinded by greed for gold and silver that this might truly be said of them [Col. 0929D]: no one asks whence a man has it, but he must have it. The more they spoke of right, the greater the wrong became. Those called justiciars were the fountainhead of all injustice. Sheriffs and reeves, whose office was justice, were more cruel than thieves and robbers and more savage than all the most savage men. When the king had leased his lands to farm for the highest sum possible, he gave them to another who offered more, then to yet another; always disregarding the agreement and striving after a greater sum. Nor was there any concern for how much wrong the reeves inflicted on the poor.

Therefore, in this year God sent upon England the plagues of sickness and famine, so that one who escaped fever died of hunger. He also sent storms and thunderbolts, by which He killed many persons; nor did He spare animals [Col. 0930A] or cattle. In this year King William was in France and ravaged the kingdom of King Philip, putting many of his people to death. He also burned the noble castle called Mantes [otherwise Anaante], together with all the churches within it, a great multitude of people, and two holy anchorites. For these causes God, angered, gave the king, as he returned from there, first to sickness and then to death. Of the life of this most powerful king, both good and evil things must be briefly recorded, that examples may be taken from the good and caution learned from the evil.

William was stronger than all the earls of Normandy and more powerful than all kings of the English; he was more worthy of praise than all his predecessors. He was wise, but cunning; wealthy [Col. 0930B], but greedy; glorious, but devoted to fame. He was humble toward those serving God, harsh toward those who resisted him. He had put earls and princes in prison, deprived bishops and abbots of their possessions, and spared not even his own brother; nor was there anyone who could resist him. He took thousands of gold and silver pieces even from the most powerful men, and wearied everyone with building castles for himself. If anyone captured a slave or a boar, he tore out his eyes, and there was none to murmur. He loved wild beasts as though he were their father; accordingly, in the hunting forests called the New Forest, he caused churches and villages to be uprooted, the people to be extirpated, and the place to be inhabited by beasts.

When he took from his own people what was theirs, not from any necessity but from excessive greed, they were embittered [Col. 0930C] and wasted away in their hearts; but he set their anger at nothing. Everyone had to obey the king’s will if they wished to enjoy his favour, money, lands, or life. Alas, how grievously it must be lamented that any human being, though he is ash and worm, should be so proud as, forgetful of death, to exalt himself alone above all others.

Normandy had come to the aforesaid king by inheritance. He had acquired Maine by arms and made Brittany subject to him. He had ruled all England alone, so that there was not a single hide there of which he did not know to whom it belonged and what it was worth. He had also subjected Scotland to himself and had received Wales into his power. He had been so great an author of peace that a maiden laden with gold could pass through the kingdom of England uninjured. If anyone killed another for any cause whatsoever, he was subject to capital sentence; if he violated anyone by force, he was deprived of his sexual organs. He built the abbey of Battle, mentioned above, and that at Caen [otherwise Chaam] in Normandy, in which he himself was buried. His wife, named Matilda, built there a nunnery in which she herself was buried. May He who alone heals after death have mercy upon their souls. You therefore who read and see the virtues and vices of so great a man: follow the good, turn from the evil, and proceed by the straight way which leads to perfect life. [Col. 0930D]

In the same year pagans plundered the Christians in Spain and occupied large parts of the kingdom. [Col. 0931A] But King Alfonso, a Christian, having received aid from Christians on every side, rose up, killed and drove out the pagans, and repaired the losses of the land taken away. It also happened in Denmark that the Danes, never before faithless to their lord, treacherously killed their king Cnut in a monastery.

King William had left Normandy to his eldest son Robert, the kingdom of England to his second son William, and an abundance of treasure to his third son Henry. Robert, however, after selling Henry part of Normandy, took the land from him when he had received the treasure. This greatly displeased God, though He deferred vengeance to its proper time.

William went to Winchester and divided his father’s treasure according to his command. There were in that treasury sixty thousand [Col. 0931B] pounds of silver, apart from gold, jewels, vessels, and vestments. From it he gave ten marks of gold to certain churches, six marks of gold to others, and five shillings to every village church; and he sent one hundred pounds into every county to be distributed among the poor. By his father’s command, he also released every prisoner from his bonds.

The new king held his court at Christmas in London. Present were Archbishop Lanfranc, who had consecrated him king; Thomas, archbishop of York; Maurice, bishop of London; Walkelin of Winchester; Geoffrey, bishop of Hereford; Wulfstan, the holy bishop of Worcester; William of Thetford; Robert of Chester; William [Col. 0931C] of Durham; Bishop Odo of Bayeux, justiciar and chief of all England; and Remigius, bishop of Lincoln, concerning whom the subject requires a few words.

King William had given Remigius, formerly a monk at Fécamp, the bishopric of Dorchester, which lies upon the Thames. Since that bishopric, greater than all others in England, extended from the Thames to the Humber, it seemed burdensome to the bishop that the episcopal see should be at the very edge of his diocese. He was also dissatisfied because that city was small, whereas the most illustrious city of Lincoln, within the same bishopric, seemed more worthy of an episcopal seat. Having therefore purchased [Col. 0932A] estates on the summit of that city, beside the castle which rose in a strong place with very strong towers, he built a strong church in a strong place, a beautiful church in a beautiful place, a church for the Virgin of virgins; pleasing to those who served God and, as the times required, invincible against enemies.

Yet the archbishop of York claimed the province of Lindsey by ancient succession of times. But Remigius, thinking little of his challenge, completed the work he had begun without delay and, when it was complete, adorned it with clergy most approved in learning and morals. He was small in stature but great in heart; dark in complexion but handsome in deeds. He had indeed been accused of treason against the king; but his servant, clearing his master by the ordeal of hot iron, restored him to royal favour and wiped the stain from episcopal dignity. At this time, through this founder, and for these reasons, the modern church of Lincoln was begun. [Col. 0932B]

But now that events have been brought down to our own times, a new book must be devoted to new matters. If a clarifying recapitulation of the foregoing is required here too, I shall not seem burdensome to the reader on that account, since it will be brief. Behold, then, a mirror of the kings in the completed book:

Æthelred ruled over all the bounds of England for thirty-seven years, always with hardship.

Edmund, bravest of youths, reigned one year and was killed by treachery.

Cnut, greatest of all his predecessors, reigned gloriously for twenty years.

His son Harold reigned four years and sixteen [Col. 0932C] weeks.

Harthacnut, the generous son of King Cnut, having reigned two years less six days, was snatched away by death.

King Edward, good and peaceable, reigned in peace for twenty-four years.

King Harold, the perjurer, reigned one year, though not a full one; his own injustice destroyed him.

William, greatest of all those named above, shone gloriously for twenty-one years, of whom it was said:

> Caesar, if nature denied you flowing hair,  
> The comet-star bestowed it upon you, William.

## BOOK SEVEN

[Col. 0931]

[Col. 0931D] Thus far we have treated of those matters which we have discovered by reading the books of the ancients, or have learned through common report. Now we must deal with those which we ourselves have seen, or have heard from persons who saw them. It is plainly shown how the Lord, in accordance with their deserts, took salvation and honour away from the English people, and decreed that they should no longer be a people. From this point it will appear how He also began to afflict the Normans themselves, indeed their avengers, with various disasters. For all the more eminent nobles, making war upon William the Younger, not without perjury, and summoning his brother Robert [Col. 0932D] to the kingdom, each raged through his own province. Odo, bishop of Bayeux, chief and governor of England, beginning a rebellion in Kent, invaded and burned the estates of the king and the archbishop. Roger, count of Mortain [variant: Moretvil], began the same around Pevensey. Bishop Geoffrey, advancing from Bristol, destroyed the town of Bath, Berkeley, and the surrounding district. Roger, in the castle of Norwich, began the same work of wickedness no less vigorously through East Anglia. Hugh acted no more gently in the counties of Leicester and Hampshire. William, [Col. 0933A] bishop of Durham, perpetrated like acts in the neighbouring districts. The lords of Herefordshire and Shropshire, raiding with the Welsh, burned the county of Worcester up to the city gates. But when they were preparing to assault the church and the castle, the holy bishop Wulfstan invoked, in this extreme need, a certain intimate friend—namely God Most High. By His aid, lying before the altar, he sent out a few knights and slew or captured five thousand of the enemy, while the rest he miraculously put to flight.

The king, having assembled the English people, restored hunting-rights and woods, and promised desirable laws. He then advanced to the castle of Cambridge, from which Gilbert was rebelling against him. But when the royal army was already tightening its siege of the castle, Gilbert made peace with the king. [Col. 0933B] The king then proceeded to Pevensey and besieged Bishop Odo and Count Roger there for six weeks. Meanwhile Duke Robert of Normandy, hastening to come to England and gain it with the aid of those mentioned above, sent ahead part of his army to assist his supporters, intending to follow with great forces. But the English, guarding the sea, killed and drowned innumerable men among them. Therefore those at Pevensey, when food failed, surrendered the castle to the king. Bishop Odo swore that he would depart from England and surrender Rochester Castle; but when he had gone there with the king’s men in order to surrender it, Count Eustace and the other nobles in the city treacherously seized the bishop and the king’s officers and threw them into prison. [Col. 0933C] On hearing this, the king besieged Rochester until the stronghold was surrendered; Bishop Odo crossed the sea, never to return. The king also sent an army to Durham and besieged the city until it was surrendered to him. The bishop and many traitors were driven into exile. The king distributed their lands among his own faithful followers. Lanfranc, archbishop, illustrious teacher of clerics and most loving father of monks, passed from temporal things in the following year, the year in which there was a terrible earthquake.

In the third year of his reign, William the Younger, preparing to avenge the wrongs inflicted upon him by his brother, secured for himself, by gifts, the castles of Saint-Valery and Aumale; and, sending out his knights, began to plunder and burn his brother’s land. [Col. 0933D] In the following year the king himself pursued them and made peace with his brother, on the condition, however, that those castles which his brother had wrongfully acquired from him should remain with the king. The king was also to assist him in recovering everything that their father had possessed. They further agreed that, if either should die before the other without a son, the survivor should become his heir. Twelve nobles swore this compact on behalf of the king, and twelve on behalf of the duke.

Meanwhile Malcolm, king of the Scots, came to plunder England and grievously ravaged it. The king and his brother Robert therefore came into England and led their forces into Scotland. Malcolm, overcome by excessive fear, became the king’s man and submitted to him by an oath of fealty. But Duke Robert, [Col. 0934A] having remained for a long time with his brother and finding in him more feigned affection than true, crossed the sea back to his own lands. In the succeeding year the king rebuilt Carlisle and transferred settlers there from the southern parts of England. Bishop Remigius, when he was about to dedicate the now completed church of Lincoln, was seized by illness and died one day before the ceremony.

William the Younger fell ill at Gloucester in Lent, in the sixth year of his reign, and gave the archbishopric of Canterbury to Abbot Anselm, a holy and venerable man. He also gave the bishopric of Lincoln to his chancellor Robert, surnamed Bloet, than whom there was none fairer in appearance, more serene in mind, or sweeter in speech. The king also promised to amend the evil laws and establish peace in the house of God. [Col. 0934B] But once recovered, he regretted it and became worse than usual. Grieving therefore that he had not sold the bishopric of Lincoln, he conspired with the archbishop of York against Bishop Robert, maintaining that the city of Lincoln and the province of Lindsey ought to be subject to that archbishop. The case could not be settled until Robert had agreed to pay the king 5,000 pounds for the liberty of his church—an act reckoned simony for the king but justice for the bishop.

In the same year Malcolm, king of the Scots, while plundering in England, was unexpectedly intercepted and killed, along with his son Edward, who would have been his heir had he lived. When Queen Margaret heard this, she was troubled in spirit by a twofold grief unto death. [Col. 0934C] Going to church, she received confession and communion; commending herself to the Lord in prayer, she yielded up her soul. The Scots chose Duneval [variant: Duvenal], Malcolm’s brother, as king. But Duncan, son of King Malcolm, who was a hostage at the court of King William, came with the latter’s assistance, expelled his uncle, and was received as king. In the following year, however, the Scots, at Duneval’s counsel, treacherously killed their king Duncan.

In the seventh year of his reign William the Younger, provoked by his brother because he had not kept his oath, crossed to Normandy. When the brothers had met, the arbiters placed all blame upon the king; but the fierce king disregarded this, departed angrily, and invaded and captured the castle of Bures. In return, [Col. 0934D] the duke took Argentan Castle, capturing there Roger of Poitou, the king’s count, with seven hundred knights, and afterwards the castle of Houlme. Meanwhile the king ordered twenty thousand English infantrymen to be summoned to Normandy; but when they came to the sea, he took from each of them ten shillings for provisions and sent them home. Duke Robert brought with him King Philip of France and a large army, to besiege King William at Eu [variant: Ou]. But through the ingenuity and money of King William, the king of France returned home, and thus the whole army, darkened by the shadows of money, vanished away.

King William ordered his brother Henry, who was at Domfront, to be in England to meet him at Christmas. [Col. 0935A] Henry was therefore at London at Christmas; the king was at Wissant, whence he landed at Canterbury. In the following year he sent his brother Henry into Normandy with much money, to conquer it in the king’s stead by continual attacks.

When Robert, count of Northumbria, puffed up with pride because he had overthrown the king of the Scots, refused to attend the king’s court, the king led an army into Northumbria. Immediately, in a certain stronghold called Newcastle, he captured all the foremost counts and nobles. He then gained Tynemouth Castle and the count’s brother within it. Afterwards he besieged the count at Bamburgh [variant: Bebanburh]. Seeing it to be impregnable by arms, he built another castle before it, which he called Malvoisin; leaving [Col. 0935B] part of the army there, he withdrew. One night, when the count had left Bamburgh, the royal army pursued him as far as Tynemouth. There, while trying unsuccessfully to defend himself, he was wounded and captured and placed in prison at Windsor. Bamburgh Castle was therefore surrendered to the king; the count’s supporters, however, received harsh terms. William of Eu was deprived of his eyes; Count Odo of Champagne and many others were disinherited.

In the same year the energetic king led his standards into Wales, for the following reason. In the preceding year the Welsh had killed many Frenchmen, destroyed the strongholds of the nobles, and invaded the borderlands with sword and fire. In the present year also they had overthrown Montgomery Castle and killed its inhabitants. [Col. 0935C] The king therefore traversed all the borders of Wales; but since he could not pursue them through the mountain and forest retreats, he achieved little or nothing and returned. At that time stars were seen falling from heaven in such abundance that they could not be counted.

In the year 1096 the Jerusalem expedition was set in motion by the preaching of Pope Urban. Duke Robert of Normandy, setting out for it, mortgaged Normandy to his brother King William. Duke Robert of Flanders went with him, as did Count Eustace of Boulogne. From another quarter went Duke Godfrey, Count Baldwin of Mons, and another Baldwin, men who would become kings of Jerusalem. From a third quarter went Count Raymond of Saint-Gilles and the bishop of Le Puy. Who could pass over Hugh [Col. 0935D] the Great, brother of the king of France, and Stephen, count of Blois [variant: Blesis]? Who would fail to mention Bohemond and his nephew Tancred? This was a great miracle of the Lord, performed in our own times and unheard of in all ages: that peoples so diverse, so many most valiant nobles, leaving splendid possessions, wives, and children, should all with one purpose seek lands utterly unknown, despising death. Because of the magnitude of this event I ask the reader’s pardon for this digression. For even if I wished, I could not be silent concerning such wondrous works of God, nor am I without occasion, since the duke of the Normans provides it.

While Alexius ruled at Constantinople, all the aforesaid nobles, with the emperor’s agreement—whether willing or compliant—assembled there. Crossing the very narrow sea, formerly called the Hellespont but now the Arm of Saint George, they besieged the city of Nicaea, the capital of Romania. [Col. 0936A] At the eastern gate Duke Robert of Normandy was stationed, beside him the count of Flanders; at the northern gate Duke Bohemond, beside him Tancred; at the western gate Duke Godfrey, beside him Hugh the Great and Count Stephen; at the southern gate Count Raymond, beside him the bishop of Le Puy. There was an innumerable host from England, Normandy, Brittany, Aquitaine, Spain, Provence, France, Flanders, Denmark, Saxony, Germany, Italy, Greece, and many other lands. From the first day of their creation the rays of the sun had not surveyed [Col. 0936B] so great, so splendid, so awe-inspiring, so numerous a host, with so many and such warlike commanders. Let Troy be silent; let Thebes cease to name, in its own excuse, the leaders and princes of its destruction. Here were present the shining chosen sons of every age of the West, all marked with the sign of the cross, all the bravest among those remaining in their own kingdoms.

Accordingly, on the Day of the Ascension of the Lord, with trumpets sounding on every side, the city was attacked. Heaven was filled with shouts; the air grew black with arrows; the earth bellowed beneath the assaults; the waters resounded with the whistling; the wall was reached, and the work was done by sappers. Neither arrows nor javelins, wood nor stones, fragments nor masses, fire nor water, skill nor strength, nor strap-hurled missiles [*amentata missilia*] helped the pagans. [Col. 0936C] And behold, an army of Turks appeared from the southern region in terrifying battle-array, standards raised. Count Raymond and the bishop of Le Puy, protected by divine power and resplendent in earthly arms, joyfully met them with their army. When our men charged them fiercely, the enemy, suddenly stricken with dread, melted away and, at the Lord’s command, broke up. A great part of the fugitives were deprived of their heads; these were hurled by slings into the city, causing no small terror among its inhabitants. Thus, immeasurably terrified, they surrendered the city to our men, who, as they had agreed, surrendered it to the emperor.

After they had remained there seven weeks and three days, they set their route toward Antioch. On the third day the army was divided in two. [Col. 0936D] In one division were the leaders: Robert, duke of the Normans; Bohemond; Richard of the Principate; Tancred; Everard of Le Puiset; Achard of Montmerle; and many others. Three hundred and sixty thousand Parthians—now called Turks—Persians, Paulicians, Medes, Cilicians, Saracens, and Angulans [variant: Augulans] surrounded them, apart from the Arabs, whose number was beyond counting. The aforesaid leaders therefore sent a messenger to the other army. Meanwhile a dreadful battle was fought. For while the Turks, Persians, and Medes dealt death with arrows; the Cilicians and Angulans with missiles; the Saracens and Arabs with lances; [Col. 0937A] and the Paulicians with iron-studded clubs and swords, the Christians were fiercely struck down. Their horses, unable to bear the unfamiliar shouting, the blare of trumpets, and the beating of drums, would not obey the spurs. Our men too, stunned by such a din, did not know what was happening. When therefore the servants of Christ were already either contemplating or beginning flight, Robert, duke of Normandy, came up crying: “Where are you going, knights? Where are you fleeing? Their horses are swifter than ours; flight offers no protection. Here rather we must die. Think as I do; follow me.” He had spoken, and directed his lance-point at a certain pagan king; it pierced wood, bronze, and body alike, and in an instant laid low a second and a third man.

Then the tireless Tancred, warlike Bohemond, Richard of the Principate, and Robert of Ansa—a duke and a most valiant knight—were no less lavish with their blows. [Col. 0937B] Courage returned to our men and a most severe and horrendously protracted battle began. Then behold, Hugh the Great and Anselm of Ribemont [variant: Ripemont], riding ahead of the other army with only one hundred knights, cut through the weary pagans while still fresh themselves. Hugh’s lance flew like lightning; Anselm’s sword was like a cleaving flame. Then two of our leaders were slain, while the Arabs, the more of them were killed, pressed on in ever greater numbers. William, Tancred’s brother, having transfixed a king with his lance, was himself pierced by that king’s lance. Godfrey of Mont-Scabieux likewise, as he cut off an Arab’s head, had his body pierced by a Parthian arrow, his heated mail no longer resisting. [Col. 0937C] The Franks could no longer bear the weight and number of the enemy; but behold, opposite them appeared the forest of standards of the other army. The battle had lasted until the ninth hour; innumerable men in the first army had been killed, and none of them would have escaped had not the other host arrived. Never afterwards did the pagans fight so fiercely.

The foremost division of the arriving army was that of Godfrey; on his right each Baldwin led a division. On the left were Count Stephen and Useward of Nulsion [variant: Osward of Nulsion]. Raymond the count followed Baldwin’s division at a distance with his men, and Robert, the very powerful count of Flanders, followed Stephen’s division with his. But behind Godfrey’s division came the division of the nobles and innumerable crowds. [Col. 0937D] The bishop of Le Puy appeared from another hill with an unconquered army. When the fighting pagans unexpectedly beheld so many enemies, they lost heart as though heaven were about to fall upon them, and gave themselves to flight with their leader Soliman. The Christians won a costly victory and innumerable spoils on the first day of July.

The Franks, continuing their purpose of seeking Antioch, came to Heraclea; thence to Tarsus, which was subjected to the admirable Count Baldwin. Athens and Mamistra were subjected to the most valiant Tancred. The most noble duke of the Normans gave a certain Turkish city [Col. 0938A] to Simeon. Count Raymond the Great and Bohemond, the light of war, gave another city to Peter of the Alps. Thence the Christians came as far as Coxan, a city which submitted to them. A certain lord, Peter of Rosa, captured Rusa and many castles. The Christian people came to Marasim, which surrendered to them. Thence they came to the Iron Bridge. Afterwards they besieged Antioch, the capital of Syria, on 21 October.

When Bohemond heard that Turks had gathered in a castle called Areg, he went with his army to fight them. By God’s will, with few men he overthrew many, and brought many to be beheaded before the city gate in order to embitter the citizens. When Christmas had been celebrated by the Christians during that same siege, [Col. 0938B] Bohemond and the count of Flanders went with twenty thousand warriors into the land of the Saracens. Many had assembled from Jerusalem, Damascus, Aleppo, and other kingdoms to relieve Antioch; attacking them unanimously, our men put some to flight and killed others. The aforesaid leaders then returned with immense spoils and were received by our men with the triumph due to them.

Meanwhile those shut within the city fought back most fiercely against the besiegers and killed the standard-bearer of the bishop of Le Puy and many others. In February a remarkable pagan army gathered beyond the Iron Bridge near the castle of Areth. Leaving all the infantry at the siege, the leaders advanced with all the knights to battle and drew up six divisions of cavalry. [Col. 0938C] The first was led by the unconquered duke of the Normans; the second by Duke Godfrey of the Germans; the third by the distinguished Count Raymond; the fourth by Robert, glory of Flanders; the fifth by the most noble bishop of Le Puy; the sixth, the largest, by Bohemond with Tancred. As they clashed most bravely with the enemy, the cry resounded to heaven, showers of missiles darkened the day, and every man struck and was struck.

After the greatest force of Parthians, which had been in the rear, attacked our men so fiercely that they were gradually giving way, Bohemond, arbiter of wars and judge of conflicts, hurled his still untouched wedge into the midst of the enemy. Then Robert, son of Gerard, a most excellent knight and his standard-bearer, rushed among the ranks of the Turks as a lion among the ranks of a flock; [Col. 0938D] and the tongues of his banner always fluttered above the heads of the Turks. Seeing this, the others recovered courage and attacked the enemy as one. The duke of Normandy with his sword split a man’s head, teeth, neck, and shoulders down to the breast. Duke Godfrey cut another in half. When one part fell to the ground, the horse bore the other part of its master on among the fighting pagans; terrified by this portent, all alike fled away into the wrath of damnation. The heads of many were brought joyfully to Antioch. This battle took place at the beginning of Lent.

Meanwhile many men of the people of the emir of Babylon had come to Antioch. When our men were building a castle before the gate [Col. 0939A] where the bridge and the *mahumeria* [mosque?] stood, and Raymond and Bohemond had gone to the harbour of Saint Simeon for provisions, the army of the city boldly came out to fight, charged our men, put them to flight, and pursued them to their tents after killing many. On the following day, attacking Raymond and Bohemond, they killed a thousand of their men. The fleeing leaders rushed back to our forces. The Franks, wounded twice and driven to fury, then drew up terrifying battle-lines in the plain before the city gates. The pagans, likewise arranging their divisions without delay, attacked our men; but the Christians, crying out the sign of the cross, struck and drove back the enemy so fiercely at the first charge that they immediately took flight. Reaching the narrow bridge, they were either cut down by swords [Col. 0939B] or drowned in the river; for few could escape across the bridge. The water of the river, reddened and swollen with blood, raged onward. Thus twelve emirs were slain there, and the Lord gave His people a most glorious victory.

But on the next day, after the citizens had buried their dead, our men dug them up and took the gold, silver, and garments around them, then threw their heads into the city. All hope and pride of the citizens had now vanished. For Tancred, guarding the aforementioned castle before the gate, deprived them of hope of supplies. A certain emir named Pirrhus, of the Turkish people, repeatedly invited into friendship by Bohemond and foreseeing that his own side would perish, surrendered to Bohemond three towers which were under his authority. [Col. 0939C] Standards having been raised above the towers, the Franks broke down the gates and rushed into the city. Some Turks who resisted were killed; others fled outside the city; while certain men occupied the upper citadel. Cassian, lord of the city, fled but was seized by Syrians, and his head was brought to Bohemond. Thus Antioch was captured on 3 June.

Kerbogha, commander of the army of the sultan of Persia, and the king of Damascus and king of Jerusalem brought with them to besiege the Franks Turks, Arabs, Saracens, Azimites, Kurds [variant: Curtos], Persians, and Augulans. But why should I count the sand of the sea? They besieged the city. Kerbogha placed part of his army in the upper citadel, which fought against [Col. 0939D] us day and night. The rest besieged the city so that supplies could not enter.

On the third day the sons of God went out against the sons of the devil. They thought that, with battle prepared, they could hold out; but such was the strength and number of the unbelievers that our men were compelled to re-enter the city, many enemies having been killed by arms and many crushed at the entrance to the gate.

On the next day, four nobles of the army—namely William, another William, Alberic, and Lambert—secretly fled to the harbour of Saint Simeon; at their urging the entire supply fleet fled with them. Since our men could not endure the repeated sorties of those in the citadel, they built a wall between themselves and them. Thus the pagans’ hope increased and the Christians’ famine increased. For while they awaited the arrival of the emperor, which he had promised, [Col. 0940A] they bought a hen for fifteen shillings, an egg for two shillings, and a single nut for one penny. Moreover, they ate cooked leaves of trees and thistles; they also boiled and devoured the hides of horses and asses. Count Stephen, fleeing womanishly, met the emperor and, reporting that all the Franks had already perished, made him turn back in tears. Thus no hope remained to God’s people, who, overcome by famine, could no longer carry their weapons.

But fire appeared from heaven and fell among the army of the Turks. The Lord appeared in a vision to His servant, and God said: “Say this to the sons of the West: I delivered to you the city of Nicaea, all the wars of the foreigners, and the most strong city of Antioch; yet, when you possessed it joyfully and unharmed, you committed deeds with Christian and pagan women, from which a stench rose to heaven.” The man of God, falling at His feet, said: “Lord, help in so great an oppression.” And the Lord said: “Give help, and I will give help. Say to My people: Return to Me, and I to you; and within five days I Myself shall be present to fight for you.”

Saint Andrew the Apostle also appeared to a certain man, revealing to him the lance by which the Saviour had been struck, as he himself confirmed to the people by oath. [Col. 0940B] Therefore, after three days’ fasts had been completed, processions held, masses solemnly celebrated, alms given, and six divisions arranged, they advanced, with the Lord as their leader, tearfully to battle against the enemy. Hugh the Great and the count of Flanders led the first division; Duke Godfrey and Baldwin the second; brave Robert of Normandy the third; the bishop of Le Puy and William of Montpellier, with Count Raymond’s army which had remained to guard the city, the fourth; Tancred with Prince Richard the fifth; Bohemond with the count of Rusinole the sixth. Having gone out, they set up a seventh [division] in honour of the Holy Spirit, over which Rainald presided. Bishops, priests, clerics, and monks, dressed in sacred vestments, sang hymns to God upon the city walls. They saw a heavenly army, on white horses and in shining arms, whose commanders were George, Mercurius, and Demetrius. [Col. 0940C] Kerbogha, never more joyful than at that time, after arranging his innumerable companies, had abundant hay set alight on the opposite hill so that our men might be blinded by smoke. But the Lord, ruler of the winds, turned the wind, and the pagans were blinded by smoke and fled headlong. The Christians pursued them with great slaughter, and never in any battle had such spoils been taken. Seeing this, the emir who guarded the upper citadel surrendered it to the Christians and became a Christian. The Lord wrought this battle on the vigil of Peter and Paul, and His name alone was exalted on that day. The servants of Christ then remained joyfully in that kingdom until 1 November.

Meanwhile one of the nobles, named Raymond Pilet, gathering an army, captured a castle called Talamannia. From there he came to a city called Maʿarra, full of Saracens who had come [Col. 0941A] from Aleppo. At first the barbarians, fighting our men, were forced to flee; in the end, however, they won, and a great slaughter of Franks took place there. In November the leaders and armies of the Christians assembled to take the road to Jerusalem. On the fourth day before October [uncertain date as printed], they came to Maʿarra and attacked it; with a wooden tower drawn on four wheels and other engines they subdued it on 11 December. Remaining in that city at Christmas, they stayed there one month and four days, because the road to Jerusalem was obstructed by the dispute between Bohemond and Raymond over possession of Antioch. There such famine seized the Christians that they cooked and ate pieces of pagan corpses.

But on 14 January they departed and captured two castles filled with every good thing. [Col. 0941B] Afterwards they took the city called Zaphaila; thence a most wealthy castle in the valley of Desem. In the middle of February they besieged the castle of Arqa for nearly three months, and Easter was celebrated there. But Anselm of Ribemont [variant: Anselius of Ribemont], a most valiant knight, perished there from a stone cast; so too did William the Picard and many others. The king of the city of Camela had made peace with the army. Meanwhile part of the army captured the city of Tortosa and the town of Maraclea. The emir of Gibel made peace with the army. Afterwards, before the city of Tripoli, they killed such a multitude of citizens that all the waters of the city, even its cisterns, ran red. Afterwards the king [Col. 0941C] of Tripoli gave the Frankish leaders three hundred pilgrims, fifteen thousand bezants, and fifteen valuable horses, so that they would depart from Tripoli and from Arqa Castle, which belonged to him.

The Franks then passed through Betelon Castle and arrived, on the Day of the Ascension of the Lord, at the coastal city called Barat; then at Sidon; then at Tyre; then at Acre; then at Haifa; then at Caesarea at Pentecost; then at the village of Saint George; then at Jerusalem. They besieged it on 6 June: the most excellent duke of the Normans to the north, Count Robert to the east, Duke Godfrey and Tancred to the west, and Count Raymond to the south, namely on Mount Zion. Often assaulting the city, they raised a very high wooden tower. When the pagans built stone towers against it, [Col. 0941D] our men dismantled the wooden tower and erected it in another part of the city, which was unfortified. Then, pressing the city and climbing the walls by ladders, they captured it; they killed many who resisted in the Temple of the Lord, and the sons of God cleansed the holy city of unclean nations.

They offered the kingdom of Jerusalem to Robert, duke of the Normans. Because he refused it on account of the labour involved, God was offended with him, and afterwards nothing prosperous befell him. He himself, the count of Flanders, and Count Raymond returned to their own lands. Duke Godfrey reigned in Jerusalem; after him his most energetic brother Baldwin; then Baldwin the Second, their kinsman; then Geoffrey, duke of Anjou; and after him [Col. 0942A] Geoffrey’s son. Waging many and most severe wars, they subjected provinces and neighbouring cities to Christ, except Ascalon, which still persisted in its wickedness.

In the tenth year of his reign, William the Younger, having disposed at his pleasure of Normandy—which he had received in mortgage from his brother Robert when the latter set out for Jerusalem—returned to England on the vigil of Easter and landed at Arundel. Having been splendidly crowned at Pentecost at Windsor, he afterwards went with a great army into Wales. He often overthrew many Welsh companies; often he lost many of his own men in the narrowness of the terrain. Seeing that they were more impregnable through the situation of their land than through strength and arms, he ordered castles to be prepared near the Welsh borders and [Col. 0942B] returned to England.

Archbishop Anselm departed from England because the wicked king allowed nothing right to be done in his kingdom. He harassed the provinces intolerably with taxes which never ceased; with labour on the wall surrounding the Tower of London; with work on the royal hall at Westminster; and with plunder which his household practised in hostile fashion wherever the king went. But at the feast of Saint Martin the king crossed the sea to Normandy and sent the young Eadgar with an army into Scotland. Eadgar routed King Duvenal in a great battle and set up as king his kinsman Edgar, son of King Malcolm. In the same year a comet appeared.

In the eleventh year of his reign William the Younger was in Normandy, [Col. 0942C] always devoted to hostile disturbances and the concerns of war, meanwhile not merely scraping but flaying the English peoples with taxes and the most grievous exactions. In summer blood was seen bubbling from a pool at Finchamstead in Berkshire. Afterwards the sky appeared almost throughout the whole night as though it were burning. In the same year Walkelin, bishop of Winchester, died; and Hugh, count of Shropshire, was killed by the Irish, and was succeeded by his brother Robert of Bellême.

In the twelfth year of his reign William the Younger returned to England and held his first court in the new hall at Westminster. When he first entered it to inspect it, while others said it was sufficiently large, or even more than large enough, the king said that it lacked half its proper size. This saying brought great honour to a great king, though it was of small cost. Again, when hunting in the New Forest, he suddenly received a messenger from Maine, saying that his household there was under siege. [Col. 0942D] The king immediately hurried to the sea and boarded ships. The sailors said to him: “Why, greatest of kings, do you challenge the deep amid an intolerable storm, and not fear the imminent danger of death?” The king replied: “I have never heard of a king drowned by the waves.” Crossing the sea, therefore, while he lived he did nothing that gave him such fame and such a glory of renown. Going to Maine, he drove out Count Helias and ordered it to be under his own authority; then he returned to England. In that year the king gave the bishopric of Durham to Ranulf, a pleader but a perverter of justice, an exactor but a burner-out of all England. In this [Col. 0943A] same year Osmund, bishop of Salisbury, died.

In the year of grace 1100, in the thirteenth year of his reign, King William ended his cruel life by a wretched death. For, after he had magnificently and with ancestral honour held his court at Christmas at Gloucester, at Easter at Winchester, and at Pentecost at London, he went hunting in the New Forest on the day after the Kalends of August [2 August]. There Walter Tirel, aiming an arrow at a stag, unknowingly struck the king; the king, pierced in the heart, fell and uttered no word. A little earlier blood had been seen bubbling up from the earth in Berkshire; and rightly, in the midst of his injustice, he was snatched away. For he was more savage than a man, and, by the counsel of the worst men—which he always chose—[Col. 0943B] wicked toward his own people and most wicked toward himself, he harassed his neighbours with war and his own subjects with most frequent armies and continual gelds. England, miserably suffocated, could not draw breath.

While all who served the king plundered and overthrew everything, even violently and with impunity committing adulteries, whatever wickedness had previously sprouted grew to full maturity, and whatever had not previously existed sprang up in these times. This most wicked king, hateful to God and people, either sold bishoprics and abbeys or retained them in his own hand and farmed them out; indeed, he strove to be heir of all. On the day on which he died, he held for himself the archbishopric of Canterbury, the bishoprics of Winchester and Salisbury, and eleven abbeys leased out at farm. Finally, whatever displeased God [Col. 0943C] and those who loved God pleased the king and those attending him. Nor did he practise the crime of lust secretly and shamefully, but brazenly before the sun.
