He was buried on the day after his destruction at Winchester; and there his younger brother Henry was chosen king and gave the bishopric of Winchester to William Giffard. Proceeding to London, he was consecrated there by Maurice, bishop of London, after promising the desirable improvement of the laws and customs. Hearing this, Archbishop Anselm returned to England and betrothed Matilda, daughter of King Malcolm and Queen Margaret, to the new King Henry.

After Jerusalem had been taken, as has been said, and after the great battle victoriously fought against the army of the emir of [Col. 0943D] Babylon, Duke Robert returned to Normandy in August and was received with joy by all the people. Thomas, archbishop of York, a man of flourishing intellect and a confidant of the Muses, ceased to appear among men.

King Henry, after holding his court at Christmas at Westminster and at Easter at Winchester, found the princes of England stirred against him on account of his brother Robert, who was arriving with an army. The king sent a naval force to fight at sea against his brother’s arrival; but some of them submitted to Robert as he came. When Robert landed at Portsmouth before the Kalends of August [1 August], and the king advanced against him with very great forces, the nobles on both sides, unwilling to endure a war between brothers, established a treaty of peace between them [Col. 0944A], on the condition that Robert should receive three thousand marks of silver annually from England, and that whichever lived longer should be the other’s heir if the latter died without a son. Twelve of the foremost magnates on each side swore to this. Robert therefore remained peacefully in his brother’s kingdom until the feast of St Michael and returned home.

Ranulf, the perverse bishop of Durham, whom King Henry had put in chains on the counsel of the English people, escaped secretly from prison and went to Normandy, where by his advice and instigation he stirred Robert against his brother.

[Col. 0944B] King Henry, acting lawfully against a most wicked and faithless count, Robert of Bellême, exiled him. He first besieged the castle of Arundel. Since it was exceedingly difficult to take, after castles had been built before it, he went and besieged Bridgnorth until the castle was surrendered to him, and Robert of Bellême, lamenting, departed for Normandy. In the same year, at the feast of St Michael, Archbishop Anselm held a council at London, in which he forbade wives to English priests, though they had not previously been forbidden. This seemed most pure to some, dangerous to others: lest, while seeking a purity beyond their strength, they should fall into horrible impurity, to the utter disgrace of the Christian name. At that council many abbots, who had acquired their abbeys in a manner God had not willed [Col. 0944C], lost them as God willed.

In the following year Robert, count of the Normans, came to England; and, for various intervening reasons and through the king’s shrewd cunning, he remitted to him the three thousand marks which the king owed him annually. In the same year blood was seen bubbling from the ground in Berkshire at Hamstead. In the course of the next year the king and his brother fell out for intervening reasons. The king accordingly sent soldiers to Normandy; received by traitors of the count, they inflicted no small devastation upon the count’s territories by plundering and burning. But William, count of Morteuil [al. Moretuil], deprived of his English inheritance by the king for treachery, departed for Normandy and, a man of excellent courage and vigorous action, declared and inflicted upon the royal forces a war full of calamity. In this year four white circles appeared around the sun at midday.

In the fifth year of his reign King Henry went to Normandy to fight against his brother. He acquired Caen by money, Bayeux by arms and with the aid of the count of Anjou; he also took many other castles, and nearly all the nobles of Normandy submitted themselves to the king. These things done, he returned to England in August. In the following year the duke of the Normans came to his brother the king at Northampton, amicably asking him to restore in brotherly favour what had been taken from him. But since God did not assent to their reconciliation, the duke angrily went to Normandy, and before August [Col. 0945A] the king followed him.

When the king had besieged the castle of Tinchebray, the duke of the Normans came, with Robert of Bellême, the count of Moretuil, and all his supporters. The king, however, prudently had with him all the nobles of Normandy, the strength of England, and men of Anjou and Brittany. Thus, when the horns had sounded with their harsh clamour, the duke of Normandy, with few men, most boldly attacked many. Experienced in the wars of Jerusalem, he vigorously and terribly drove back the royal line. William, count of Mortain, likewise advanced, throwing the English line into confusion from place to place. But when the mounted line of the Bretons—for the king, the duke, and the other lines were on foot, that they might fight more steadfastly—suddenly charged the duke’s line from the opposite side, the duke’s force, overwhelmed by the mass of its size, broke apart and was defeated [Col. 0945B]. Robert of Bellême, as soon as he saw this, secured his safety by flight.

Thus Robert, the most valiant duke of the Normans, and William, count of Mortuil, were captured. And the Lord repaid Duke Robert: for though He had made him glorious in the deeds at Jerusalem, Robert had refused the kingdom of Jerusalem when it was offered him, choosing rather to serve ease and idleness in Normandy than to toil for the Lord of kings in the holy city. Therefore God condemned him to perpetual idleness and everlasting imprisonment. A comet had appeared in the same year as a sign of this event. On Maundy Thursday two moons were seen, one in the east and the other in the west.

[Col. 0945C] In the seventh year of his reign, after King Henry had destroyed or subdued his enemies and arranged Normandy as he pleased, he returned to England and cast his brother, the distinguished duke, and the count of Mortuil into the darkness of prison. Victorious, and then for the first time a mighty king, he held his court at Easter at Windsor; the nobles of England and Normandy alike attended it with fear and trembling. For earlier, both while he was young and after he had become king, he had been held in the greatest contempt. But God, who judges far otherwise than the children of men, who exalts the humble and brings down the mighty (Luke 1), deposed Robert, most celebrated in everyone’s favour, and commanded the renown of the despised Henry to shine throughout the world. The omnipotent Lord freely gave him three gifts [Col. 0945D]: wisdom, victory, and riches. Prosperous in all things through these, he surpassed all his predecessors; consequently he enriched all his own people.

In this year Maurice, bishop of London and founder of the church of London, died, as did Edgar, king of Scotland. He was succeeded by his brother Alexander, with King Henry’s permission.

In the eighth year of his reign, after Philip, king of the French, had died, Henry crossed into Normandy, waging a very great war against Louis, Philip’s son and the new king of France. In the same year, after the death of Gerard, archbishop of York, Thomas succeeded later. In the following year envoys from Henry, emperor of the Romans, outstanding in bodily stature and splendid apparel, were sent to seek the king’s daughter in marriage for their lord [Col. 0946A]. Holding his court at London, the most splendid court he had ever held, the king received at Pentecost oaths concerning the marriage of his daughter from the emperor’s envoys. Archbishop Anselm, the philosopher of Christ, had died in Lent. In the following year the king’s daughter was given to the emperor, as was fitting, to put it briefly. The king then took three shillings from every hide in England.

In the same year, after the king had held his court at Pentecost at New Windsor, which he himself had built, he disinherited those who had harmed him: Philip de Braose, William Malet, and William Baynard. Helias, count of Maine, who had held it under King Henry, was deprived of life [Col. 0946B]. But the count of Anjou received Maine with Helias’s daughter and held it against King Henry. In this year a comet appeared in an unusual manner. Rising from the east and ascending into the firmament, it seemed to move backward.

In the same year Nicholas, father of him who wrote this history, yielded to the law of death and was buried at Lincoln. Of him it was said:

> The star of the clergy falls; Nicholas’s splendour fades.  
> May the fallen star of the clergy shine in God’s high citadel.

The writer inserted this in his work in order to obtain from all readers a reciprocal return for his labour, so that they might deign, with an affection of piety, to say: “May his soul rest [Col. 0946C] in peace. Amen.”

In the eleventh year of his reign King Henry went to Normandy against the count of Anjou, who held Maine against Henry’s will; he steadily exercised the laws of war against him with sword and fire. Robert, count of Flanders, died; he had taken a most distinguished part in the Jerusalem expedition, and therefore his memory should not pass away for ever. His son Baldwin succeeded him as count, a young man altogether vigorous in arms. In the next year the king expelled the count of Évreux [al. Ebreux] and William Crispin from Normandy. He captured Robert of Bellême, that most wicked man of whom we have spoken, and, returning to England in the following year, placed him in perpetual prison at Wareham.

In the succeeding year the king gave the archbishopric of Canterbury to Ralph, bishop of Rochester. Then, after Thomas, archbishop of York, had died, Thurstan succeeded. A great dispute arose between Archbishops Ralph and Thurstan because the archbishop of York would not submit to that of Canterbury according to custom. The case was frequently argued before the king and frequently before the Apostolic See, but was not yet decided. In this year the king led an army into Wales; the Welsh submitted to him according to the grandeur of his will [Col. 0946D]. A great comet appeared at the end of May. The king crossed into Normandy, and in the following year made all the nobles of the country swear the fidelity owed to their lord William, his son; he then returned to England.

In the sixteenth year of his reign King Henry attended at Christmas [Col. 0947A] the dedication of the church of St Alban, which the venerable Robert, bishop of Lincoln, dedicated through the memorable Richard, abbot [al. knight] of that place. When the king crossed the sea to Normandy at Easter, a very great quarrel arose between him and the king of France. Its cause was this: Theobald, count of Blois, nephew of King Henry, had taken up arms against his lord, the king of France. In aid of Theobald, the king of the English sent his dukes and his soldiery, and sorely afflicted King Louis. In the course of the following year a most grievous burden arose for King Henry. For the king of France, the count of Flanders, and the count of Anjou swore to take Normandy from King Henry and give it to William, son of Robert [Col. 0947B], duke of Normandy. Many of the king’s nobles also deserted him, to his great loss. Yet the king prudently had as allies the aforesaid Theobald and the count of the Bretons.

The king of France and the count of Flanders therefore came with an army into Normandy. After spending one night there, fearing the arrival of King Henry with English, Normans, and Bretons, they returned home without battle. In this year England was oppressed by exceedingly frequent gelds and various exactions for the king’s need. Thunder and hail occurred on the Kalends of December [1 December], and in that same month the sky appeared red, as if it were burning. At the same time a very great earthquake in Lombardy destroyed churches, towers, houses, and people, throwing them down [Col. 0947C].

In the course of the following year the continual warfare of the aforementioned rulers grievously harassed the king, until Baldwin, the most valiant count of Flanders, was fatally wounded at Eu in Normandy in a military disturbance and withdrew home. Moreover Robert, count of Meulan, wisest of all men occupied in secular affairs as far as Jerusalem, and counsellor of King Henry, proved foolish in the end. For, having taken lands at the instigation of priests, he would neither restore them nor make the confession he ought; poor in heart, he perished, as it were, of his own accord. Thus it was well said: “All the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God” (1 Corinthians 3).

Then [Col. 0947D] Queen Matilda also lost the light. Of her wit and excellence of character it was said:

> Prosperity did not make her glad, nor adversity sad;  
> adversity brought her laughter, prosperity fear.  
>
> Beauty did not make her frivolous, nor the sceptre proud;  
> powerful only in humility, becoming only in chastity.  
>
> The first day of May, the night of our days,  
> made her who was snatched away present in everlasting day.

In the fifty-second year since the Normans obtained England, and in the nineteenth year of his reign, King Henry fought gloriously against the king of France. The king of France had placed in the front line an army commanded by William, son of Robert, brother of King Henry; he himself stood with very great forces in the following division. King Henry placed his nobles in the first line; in the second [Col. 0948A] he himself rode with his household; and in the third he placed his sons with the chief forces, on foot. Thus the first French line immediately drove back and scattered the mounted division of the Norman nobles. It then collided with the line in which King Henry stood, and that too was scattered.

The royal lines then struck against one another, and the fighting was exceedingly fierce: all lances were broken, and the matter was decided by swords. Meanwhile William Crispin struck King Henry’s head twice with a sword. Though the mail-coat was impenetrable, the violence of the blows nevertheless drove it somewhat into the king’s head, so that blood burst forth. But the king struck his attacker back with such a blow of the sword that, although his helmet was impenetrable, the force of the stroke threw down both rider and horse; and he was immediately captured before the royal feet [Col. 0948B]. But the infantry division, in which King Henry’s sons stood, had not yet struck but was about to strike; with lowered lances, they rose up opposite the enemy. Seeing this, the French, shattered by unexpected terror, turned their backs.

King Henry remained victorious on the field until the captured leading men of the enemy were brought and laid before his feet. Returning to Rouen amid the sound of standards and the chants of clergy, he blessed God, the Lord of hosts. Concerning the magnificence of his victory, one writer composed these heroic verses:

> Henry, king of kings and glory of rulers, took away  
> the lofty spirits of the French; for on the field at Noyon  
> a greater king overcame the great King Louis.  
>
> The French, headlong, preferred flight to battle, spurs to weapons;  
> the Normans won fame and spoils,  
> and everlasting praise crowns them with laurel [Col. 0948C].  
>
> Thus this glory of commanders crushed their swelling hearts  
> and compelled the proud mouths of the French to cease their boasting.

In the same year Pope Gelasius died and was buried at Cluny. Then Guy, archbishop of Vienne, was elected pope, called Calixtus; he held a council at Reims. From there he proceeded to Gisors to meet King Henry, and the great priest and the great king conversed. Baldwin, count of Flanders, also died from the wound he had received in Normandy. He was succeeded by his kinsman Charles, son of Cnut, saintly king of the Danes.

In the year of grace 1120, after all matters in France had been subdued and pacified, King Henry returned joyfully to England. But in the passage across the sea the king’s two sons, William and Richard, a daughter and a niece of the king, as well as many nobles, royal stewards, chamberlains, cup-bearers, and Richard, count of Chester, were shipwrecked [Col. 0948D]. All or nearly all of them were said—and were—to be entangled in the stain of Sodom. Behold the flashing vengeance of God! They perished, and nearly all were denied burial. Thus death unexpectedly swallowed up those who had completed their service, though the sea was utterly calm and without winds. Of them the poet wrote:

> While the Norman-born, renowned for overcoming the French,  
> seek the kingdoms of England, God himself opposed them.  
>
> As they crossed the grim sea in a frail boat,  
> He brought dense clouds upon the stirred-up sea.  
>
> And while the wandering sailors were carried along a blind course,  
> hidden rocks broke open the ships’ deep hulls.  
>
> Thus, as the conquering sea crept over the upper decks,  
> it drowned the king’s offspring and slew the glory of the world.

[Col. 0949A] King Henry was at Christmas at Brampton with Theobald, count of Blois; afterward, at Windsor, he married Adeliza, daughter of the duke of Louvain, because of her beauty. When the king was at Berkeley at Easter, he was crowned with his new queen at Pentecost in London. In summer, while he advanced with an army into Wales, the Welsh met him submissively and made peace with him according to the grandeur of his will. But on the eve of the Nativity of the Lord an extraordinary wind threw down not only houses but stone towers. Concerning the beauty of the aforesaid queen, one writer said in elegiac verse:

> Adelina [al. Adelida], queen of the English, while the Muse prepares  
> to recount your beauties, she grows rigid with astonishment.  
>
> What need have you, most beautiful one, of a diadem? What need of gems?  
> Before you the gem grows pale, nor does the diadem shine.  
>
> Put away adornment: nature supplies adornment;  
> blessed beauty cannot be made better.  
>
> Beware of ornaments; you receive no brightness from them:  
> they gleam, made brilliant by your light.  
>
> I was not ashamed to speak small praises of great things;  
> do not, I pray, be ashamed to be my mistress.

In the following year King Henry was at Christmas at Norwich, Easter at Northampton, and Pentecost at Windsor; then he went to London and Kent, and afterward to Durham in Northumberland. In the same year Ralph, archbishop of Canterbury, and John, bishop of Bath, died. In the spring of the next year the king was at Christmas at Dunstable and then went to Berkhamsted. There [Col. 0949C] God showed a noteworthy event. A certain royal chancellor, Ranulf, had been worn down by illness for twenty years, but at court was still readier than a young man for every crime, oppressing innocents and plundering many lands for himself. He considered it a great achievement that, although sick in body, he was so vigorous in mind. As he was taking the king to lodge with him, on the very summit of the hill from which his castle could be seen, he fell from his horse in pride of heart; and a monk rode over him, crushing him so badly that after a few days he died. Behold how great a pride perished most shamefully, by God’s will!

From there the king went to Woodstock, a notable place where he had made a dwelling-place together for men and beasts. There [Col. 0949D] Robert, bishop of Lincoln, ended his final day. His epitaph is this:

> Robert, honour of bishops, whom surviving fame  
> will make everlasting, dies, never to die.  
>
> Here was a humble rich man—strange thing!—powerful, devout, avenging;  
> compassionate and gentle when he endured wrong.  
>
> He would not be lord to his own people; he strove to be a father,  
> always a wall and weapon for his people in adversity.  
>
> On the tenth day of false Janus he left the dreams of the world,  
> and, awakened, beholds the true things that endure.

Afterward, at the feast of the Purification, the king gave the archbishopric of Canterbury to William of Corbeil, formerly prior at Chich. At Easter at Winchester he gave the bishopric of Lincoln to Alexander, a venerable man, who was [al. is] nephew of Roger, bishop of Salisbury. Roger was [al. is] justiciar of all England and second after the king [Col. 0950A]. The king also gave the bishopric of Bath to Geoffrey, the queen’s chancellor. Around Pentecost he crossed the sea, and the count of Mellend [al. Meslend] broke with him in open disagreement. The king besieged and took his castle called Puntaldemer [al. Pundaldemer].

In the following year the king was gloriously successful. William of Tancarville, the king’s chamberlain, fighting with the battle-lines drawn up, captured the aforesaid count, his brother-in-law Hugh of Montfort, and Hugh son of Gervase, and delivered them to the king; the king put them in prison. In the same year Theulf, bishop of Worcester, and Ernulf, bishop of Rochester, died. During the entire following year the king was in Normandy, where he gave the bishopric of Worcester to Simon [al. Simeon], clerk of the queen [Col. 0950B]. He gave the bishopric of Chichester to Seffrid, abbot of Glastonbury. Archbishop William, moreover, gave the bishopric of Rochester to his archdeacon John.

At Easter John of Crema, Roman cardinal, came down to England. Passing through bishoprics and abbeys, not without great gifts, he celebrated a solemn council at London on the Nativity of St Mary [8 September]. But because Moses, God’s confidant, wrote in sacred history the virtues as well as the faults even of his own forebears—the offence of Lot, the crime of Reuben, the treachery of Simeon and Levi, the inhumanity of Joseph’s brothers—it is fitting that we too should follow the true law of history concerning good and evil. If any Roman or prelate should dislike this [Col. 0950C], nevertheless let him keep silent, lest he seem to wish to imitate John of Crema.

For, after he had dealt most severely in the council with priests’ wives, declaring it the greatest crime to rise from the side of a prostitute in order to consecrate Christ’s body, he himself consecrated Christ’s body that day and after vespers was caught with a prostitute. So manifest a matter could not be denied, nor ought it to have been concealed. The highest honour everywhere shown him was turned into the deepest disgrace. He therefore went back to his own country, confounded and dishonoured by God’s judgement.

In the same year Emperor Henry, son-in-law of King Henry, died. It is worth hearing how severe the king was toward wrongdoers. He caused nearly all the moneyers of all England to be castrated and their right hands cut off, because they had secretly debased the coinage. This was the most expensive year of all in our time, when a horse-load of grain was sold for six shillings [Col. 0950D]. In this year also William, archbishop of Canterbury, Thurstan, archbishop of York, and Alexander, bishop of Lincoln, went to Rome. Of Alexander’s praiseworthy generosity and inexhaustible fame, one writer said in heroic verse:

> Alexander’s splendour does not shine so much by honour  
> as honour shines through him, for he is the flower of men.  
>
> Thinking that he possesses riches by giving, he compels honour to be his treasure,  
> and hastens to give freely before gifts are requested.  
>
> What he has not yet given, he does not yet believe that he possesses.  
>
> O glory, O guide of character! With his coming  
> sure faith, cheerful mercy, prudent power,  
> a gentle yoke, pleasing instruction, sweet correction,  
> becoming liberty, and graceful modesty come.  
>
> [Col. 0951A] Lincoln, once a great people, now always greatest:  
> may this man long remain to us the guardian of such honour.

In the twenty-sixth year of his reign, King Henry stayed in Normandy at Christmas, Easter, and Pentecost. After confirming with the princes of France terms worthy of a most victorious king, he returned to England about the feast of St Michael. He brought with him his daughter the empress, widowed, as has been said, by so great a husband. Robert, bishop of Chester, died. In the following year the king held his court at Christmas at Windsor and then went to London. In Lent and at Easter he was at Woodstock, where a messenger told him: “Charles, count of Flanders, greatly beloved by you, has been killed by his nobles in wicked treachery in the church at Bruges [Col. 0951B]; but the king of France has given Flanders to William, your nephew and enemy, who, now greatly strengthened, has punished all Charles’s traitors with various torments.”

Troubled by this, the king held a council at Rogationtide in London; William, archbishop of Canterbury, held one likewise in the same town at Westminster. When the king was at Winchester at Pentecost, he sent his daughter to Normandy to be betrothed to the son of the count of Anjou, and the king himself followed her in August. Richard, bishop of London, had died; the king gave his bishopric to Gilbert, a most learned and accomplished man. Richard, bishop of Hereford, also died.

[Col. 0951C] King Henry, most wise [al. most valiant], spent the entire following year in Normandy and went in hostility into France because the king of France supported his nephew and enemy. Staying at Épernay for eight days as securely as if he were in his own kingdom, he compelled King Louis not to bring aid to the count of Flanders. When King Henry inquired into the origin and course of the kingdom of the French, a learned man answered him thus:

“Most mighty of kings, like most peoples of Europe, the Franks derive their origin from the Trojans. Antenor, fleeing with his followers from the destruction of Troy, built in the region of Pannonia a city named Sicambria. After Antenor’s death, however, his people appointed Turgot and Francio as their leaders, from whom the Franks receive their name. After these men died, they chose Marcomir as their leader [Col. 0951D]. Marcomir begot Pharamond, the first king of the Franks. King Pharamond begot Clodio the Long-Haired, from whom the kings of the Franks are called ‘the long-haired.’ After Clodio’s death, his kinsman Merovech reigned, and from him the kings of the Franks are called Merovingians. Merovech begot Childeric; Childeric, Clovis, whom St Remigius baptized; Clovis, Clothar; Clothar, Chilperic; Chilperic, Clothar II. Clothar II begot Dagobert, the most famous and beloved king; Dagobert begot Clovis; and Clovis begot three sons by his holy queen Bathild: Clothar, Childeric, and Theuderic.

“Theuderic the king begot Childebert; Childebert, Dagobert; Dagobert [Col. 0952A], Theuderic; and Theuderic, Clothar, the last king of this lineage. After him reigned Childeric, who was tonsured and confined in a monastery when Pippin became king. From another line of descent, Ausbert begot Arnold through the daughter of King Clothar; Arnold begot St Arnulf, later bishop of Metz; St Arnulf begot Ansegisel; Ansegisel, Pippin, mayor of the palace; Pippin, Charles Martel; Charles, King Pippin; and King Pippin, the Emperor Charlemagne, who shone like a star above those who preceded and followed him.

“Charles begot the Emperor Louis; Louis, the Emperor Charles the Bald; Charles, King Louis, father of Charles the Simple; Charles the Simple, Louis; Louis, Lothar; and Lothar, Louis, the last king of this lineage [Col. 0952B]. After Louis died, the Frankish nobles set over themselves as king Duke Hugh, son of Duke Hugh the Great. King Hugh begot the most devout King Robert; King Robert begot three sons: Hugh, the most beloved duke; Henry, the most beloved king; and Robert, duke of Burgundy. King Henry begot King Philip, who became a monk at the end of his life, and Hugh the Great, who in the movement toward Jerusalem went to Jerusalem with many dukes of Europe to fight for it against the pagans in the year 1095 from the Lord’s Incarnation. King Philip begot Louis, who now reigns. If he followed in the footsteps of the ancient kings’ virtue, you would not rest so securely in his kingdom.”

After these words and deeds, King Henry returned to Normandy. There came [Col. 0952C] from the regions of Germany a certain Duke Theoderic, claiming Flanders and bringing with him certain Flemish nobles, and this at King Henry’s instigation. William, count of Flanders, drew up his forces and came against him. The battle was fierce. Count William, though his men were few, supplied their number by inexhaustible valour. Covered with blood, and with all his arms bloodied by the blood of the enemy, he split the enemy’s ranks with his lightning sword. The terrified enemy, unable to withstand the dreadful force of his youthful arm, gave themselves to flight. While this most victorious count besieged an enemy castle which was to surrender the next day, when the enemy were nearly annihilated, he was, by God’s will, wounded by a slight wound in the hand and died [Col. 0952D].

This most noble young man won eternal fame in a brief lifetime. Walo the versifier said of him:

> Mars dies on earth; the paired stars mourn their fellow star,  
> the gods their fellow god, splendours their equal splendour.  
>
> A new thing! In our times gods die;  
> henceforth it is credible that gods can die.  
>
> That unique man fell—his back never knew an arrow,  
> nor could his feet know flight.  
>
> Whenever the matter itself demanded it, he was nothing but lightning;  
> and, if not lightning, he was like lightning.  
>
> Flanders boasts of his tomb, Normandy of his cradle:  
> here was the setting of the star, there its rising.

In this year also Hugh of Payns, master of the soldiers of the Temple of Jerusalem, came to England and took many with him to Jerusalem. Among them went Geoffrey, count of Anjou and future king. Ranulf Flambard, bishop of Durham, and William Giffard, bishop of Winchester, died [Col. 0953A].

In the following year Louis, king of France, caused his son Philip to be raised as king. King Henry, having pacified everything in France, Flanders, Normandy, Brittany, Maine, and Anjou, returned joyfully to England. On the Kalends of August [1 August] he held a great council at London concerning the prohibition of priests’ wives. Present at that council were William, archbishop of Canterbury; Thurstan, archbishop of York; Alexander, bishop of Lincoln; Roger, bishop of Salisbury; Gilbert, bishop of London; John of Rochester; Seffrid of Sussex; Geoffrey of Bath; Simon of Worcester [Col. 0953B]; Everard of Norwich; Bernard of St Davids; and Hervey, the first bishop of Ely. For the bishops of Winchester, Durham, Chester, and Hereford had died. These were the pillars of the kingdom and the rays of holiness at that time.

But the king deceived them through the simplicity of Archbishop William. They granted the king authority concerning priests’ wives and were judged imprudent; this later became evident when the affair ended in the utmost disgrace. For the king took infinite money from the priests and redeemed them. Then—but in vain—the bishops repented of their concession, when the deception of the prelates and oppression of their subjects became plain before the eyes of all peoples.

In the same year those whom Hugh of Payns, mentioned above, had taken to Jerusalem met with misfortune [Col. 0953C]. For the inhabitants of that holy land had offended God by lust, robbery, and various crimes; but, as is written in Moses and in the books of Kings, crimes do not long go unpunished in those places. On the eve of St Nicholas, many Christians were defeated by a few pagans, although previously the opposite had usually happened. During the siege of Damascus, a large part of the Christians went out to seek provisions. The pagans were astonished that more numerous and very valiant Christians were fleeing from them like women; pursuing them, they slaughtered countless numbers. God himself pursued that night in the mountains, with a storm of snow and cold, those who had sought safety in flight, so that scarcely anyone escaped [Col. 0953D].

It also happened that Philip, son of the king of France, who, as has been said, had been adorned with the royal diadem, while playfully riding a swift horse, encountered a pig in his path. When the horse’s running feet stumbled, the new king fell and, his neck broken, died. Behold a sad, unprecedented, and most astonishing event! Behold how great a height was so quickly, so lightly reduced to nothing!

In the thirtieth year of his reign, King Henry was at Christmas at Worcester [otherwise Winchester], and at Easter at Woodstock, where Geoffrey de Clinton was accused and falsely charged with treason against the king. At Rogationtide he was at Canterbury for the dedication of the new church. At the feast of Saint Michael he crossed into Normandy; in that same year [Col. 0954A] Pope Honorius died.

In the following year the king received Pope Innocent at Chartres, refusing to submit to Anacletus. The Romans, divided into two parties, had elected both of them. Innocent, having been expelled from the city by the force of Anacletus, who had formerly been called Peter of Leves, was received throughout all Gaul with the aid of King Henry. After this, in summer, he returned to England, bringing his daughter with him. Thus, on the Nativity of Saint Mary, a great assembly was held at Northampton. When all the princes of England had gathered, it was resolved that his daughter should be restored to her husband, namely the count of Anjou, who was demanding her. After this, the king’s daughter was sent to her husband and received with magnificence worthy of so great a lady. After Easter Reginald, abbot of Ramsey and founder of this new [Col. 0954B] church, died. At the beginning of winter Hervey, the first bishop of Ely, died.

In the following year King Henry was at Christmas at Dunstable, and at Easter at Woodstock. After Easter there was a great assembly at London, where several matters were discussed, especially the dispute between the bishop of Saint Davids and the bishop of Glamorgan concerning the boundaries of their parishes. Baldwin, king of Jerusalem, died, and Geoffrey succeeded him.

In the thirty-third year of his reign King Henry was at Christmas at Windsor, ill. At the beginning of Lent an assembly was held at London concerning the bishops of Saint Davids and Glamorgan, and concerning the dispute between the archbishop and the bishop of Lincoln. At Easter the king was at Oxford, in the new hall, and at Rogationtide there was again [Col. 0954C] an assembly at Winchester concerning the matters mentioned above. After Pentecost the king gave the bishopric of Ely to Nigel and the bishopric of Durham to Geoffrey the chancellor. The king also established a new bishopric at Rarlot [reading uncertain], and crossed the sea. An eclipse of the sun occurred on the fourth day before the Nones of August.

In the following year King Henry remained in Normandy because of his delight in his grandchildren, whom the count of Anjou had begotten by the king’s daughter. Gilbert, bishop of London, died, and the bishop of Lavand [otherwise Lavandensis] died on his way to Rome concerning his case, which had been pursued for so long. In that year Archbishop William and Alexander, bishop of Lincoln, crossed to the king because of the dispute between them concerning certain customary rights of their [Col. 0954D] parishes.

In the thirty-fifth year King Henry remained continually in Normandy and often intended not to return to England; but his daughter detained him through the various disputes that arose for several reasons between the king and the count of Anjou—through the contrivances, that is, of his daughter. By these provocations the king was stirred to anger and bitterness of spirit, which some said had caused the natural chilling of his body and afterwards his death.

When the king had returned from hunting at Saint-Denis in the forest of Lyons, he ate lamprey flesh, which always harmed him, although he always loved it. Although his physician forbade him to eat it, the king would not yield to sound advice, as it is said:

> [Col. 0955A] We always strive for what is forbidden, and desire what is denied.  
> *(Ovid, Amores* III.4.17*).*

This meal, bringing on the worst humour and violently arousing similar humours, fatally chilled his aged body and caused a sudden and extreme disturbance. Nature, resisting it, raised an acute fever to dispel the assault of the most grievous matter. But when no strength remained to resist, the great king died on the first day of December, having reigned thirty-five years and three months. And now, at the end of so great a king, we shall bring the present book [Col. 0956A] to its end; yet, if he deserves it, let us pray that the Muse may grant him a memorial:

> King Henry dies: once the world’s glory, now the world’s grief;  
> The gods weep that their own divinity has perished.  
>   
> Mercury mourns, lesser in eloquence; Apollo, in force of mind;  
> Jupiter, in command; and Mars, in strength.  
>   
> Janus mourns, lesser in prudence; Hercules, in uprightness;  
> Pallas, in conflict; Minerva, in art.  
>   
> England, which by this god’s cradle and sceptre  
> Had shone in lofty splendour, now falls darkened.  
>   
> She languishes with her king; Normandy with her duke:  
> The one nourished the boy; the other has lost the man.

## To the Reader

[Col. 0955]

Between the seventh book and this one, which is now the eighth, some manuscript codices insert two other books. The beginning of the first is: “This is the year that encompasses the writer”; that of the second: “Concerning the illustrious men of the English, and the things accomplished through them.”

The first book contains three letters: the first, to Henry, the first king of that name, concerning the succession of the most powerful kings who existed throughout the world down to his own time; the second, to Warin the Breton, concerning the succession of the kings of Britain from Geoffrey Arthur; the third, to Walter, archdeacon of Oxford, his companion, concerning contempt for the world. The latter book is *On the Miracles of the English*, taken almost wholly from Bede.

These books, therefore—although unquestionably written by the historian of Huntingdon—have seemed best omitted, both because their subject is different, because they are absent from many manuscripts, and because they add nothing new that cannot be found more fully in Bede, Monmouth, and others.

# Book Eight

[Col. 0955]

[Col. 0955B] After the death of the great King Henry, the people uttered free judgments, as they commonly do concerning the dead. Some declared that he had shone with three outstanding splendours: supreme wisdom, for he was deemed most profound in counsel, conspicuous in foresight, and brilliant in eloquence; victory, because, besides the deeds he had performed with distinction, he had overcome the king of the French by the law of war; and riches, in which he had surpassed all his predecessors far and wide.

Others, in a contrary spirit, charged him with three vices: excessive greed, by which, like all his forebears, while wealthy he ensnared the poor with taxes and exactions, greedily using the hooks of informers; cruelty, by which he put out the eyes of his kinsman the count of Moretoil while he was held prisoner. So horrible a crime could not become known [Col. 0955C] until the king’s secret death disclosed it; nor did they fail to offer other examples, which we pass over. They also charged him with lust, because, in the manner of Solomon, the king was continually subject to the dominion of women. Such were the varying utterances of the free common people.

But through the course of that most terrible time which later blazed up through the mad treacheries of the Normans, whatever Henry had done, whether tyrannically or royally, seemed, by comparison with worse men, altogether excellent.

For without delay Stephen came there, the younger brother of Theobald, count of Blois, a man of great energy and boldness. Although he had sworn an oath of fealty to the daughter of King Henry concerning the kingdom of England, yet, trusting in vigour and shamelessness [Col. 0956B] [otherwise, imprudence], he tempted God and seized the royal diadem.

William, archbishop of Canterbury, who had first sworn the oath to the king’s daughter, alas, blessed him as king. God therefore decreed against him the judgment that he had decreed against the great priest who struck Jeremiah: namely, that he should not live beyond a year. Roger, the great bishop of Salisbury, who had been the second to swear that oath and had urged it upon all the others, supplied him with the diadem and the strength of his assistance. By God’s just judgment, he was afterwards seized and tortured by the very man whom he had made king, and suffered a wretched ruin.

But why delay? All who had sworn the oath—prelates, counts, and princes alike—gave their assent to Stephen and did him homage. It was indeed an evil sign that all England was subjected to him so suddenly, without delay or effort, as if in the twinkling of an eye. Having been crowned, he held his court at Christmas in London, [Col. 0956C] while King Henry’s body still lay unburied in Normandy.

King Henry had died on the first day of December. His body was brought to Rouen, where his entrails, brain, and eyes were buried. The remainder of the body was cut apart all around with knives, heavily sprinkled with salt, and enclosed in oxhides to prevent the stench, which was already infecting those standing nearby in great and unending measure. Thus the very man who had been hired for a great price to split the king’s [Col. 0957A] head with an axe, so as to extract the most foul-smelling brain, died from that cause, although he had wrapped his own head in linen cloths, having rejoiced vainly in his payment. This was the last of many men whom King Henry killed.

His household then carried the royal body to Caen. There it lay for a long time in the church where his father had been buried. Although it was filled with much salt and enclosed in many hides, a continual flow of liquid and horrible corruption nevertheless streamed from the body; it was collected in vessels beneath the bier by attendants who were wasting away from stench and horror, and then cast out.

See, therefore, whoever reads this, what became of the body of that most powerful king: a neck once crowned with gold and the finest gems, as though flourishing with divine splendour; hands gleaming with [Col. 0957B] sceptres; the rest of his person altogether shining with woven gold; a mouth accustomed to feed upon the most delicious and refined foods; one before whom all were wont to rise, all to tremble, all to rejoice, and all to wonder. See, I say, to what that body came, how horribly it was concealed away, and how miserably it was cast aside. Observe the outcome of things, upon which judgment always depends. Learn to despise whatever is thus brought to an end, whatever is thus annihilated.

At last the remains of the royal corpse were brought to England and buried, within the twelve days of the Nativity of the Lord, in the abbey of Reading, which King Henry had founded and enriched with many possessions. There King Stephen came from the court which he had held in London at that very Christmas, to attend [Col. 0957C] the body of his uncle; and William, archbishop of Canterbury, with many prelates and nobles, buried King Henry with the reverence due to so great a man.

Stephen then went to Oxford, where he recalled and confirmed the agreements he had granted to God, the people, and holy Church on the day of his coronation. These were as follows.

First, he vowed that when bishops died, he would never keep their churches in his own hand, but would at once consent to canonical election and invest bishops in them.

Secondly, he vowed that he would keep in his hand none of the forests of clerics or laymen, as King Henry had done, who every year had brought them to court if they had either taken game in their own forests or cleared or diminished [Col. 0957D] them for their necessities. This accursed kind of legal action was so detestable that, if men saw from afar any grove from which they thought money might be obtained, they at once asserted that it had been laid waste, whether it had been or not, in order that its owner might redeem it without cause.

Thirdly, he vowed that he would remit forever the *danegeld*, that is, two shillings per hide, which his predecessors had customarily received every year. These and other things he chiefly vowed to God; but he kept none of them.

In the first year of his reign, when King Stephen came to Oxford at the close of Christmas, he heard a messenger saying to him: “The king of Scots, pretending that he was coming peaceably to visit you as a guest, has arrived at Carlisle and deceitfully seized both it and the New Castle.”

To him King Stephen said: “What he seized deceitfully, I shall recover victoriously.” [Col. 0958A]

The energetic king therefore led against David, king of Scots, an army so great that no one could remember a larger force in England. Meeting him near Durham, King David made an agreement with him, restoring the New Castle; Carlisle, however, he retained by King Stephen’s grant. Yet King David did not become King Stephen’s man, because he had, before all laymen, sworn the oath to the daughter of King Henry—his own niece—that he would hold England in her hand after King Henry’s death.

But Henry, the son of King David, became King Stephen’s man, and King Stephen gave him the borough called Huntingdon as an addition. Returning from there, King Stephen held his court at London during Lent, at the Easter solemnity; never had a court [Col. 0958B] in England been more splendid in multitude, magnificence, gold, silver, jewels, garments, and every kind of lavish provision.

But at Rogationtide it was announced that the king was dead. On hearing this, Hugh Bigod entered Norwich Castle and refused to surrender it except to the king in person, and even then most unwillingly. Thus the aforesaid Norman madness began to spring up in perjury and treachery.

The king then took Bathampton Castle, whose lord, a certain traitor Robert, had revolted from him. He next besieged the city of Exeter, which Baldwin de Redvers [otherwise Rivers] held against him. Staying there a long time and constructing many siege engines, he expended much of his treasure. Yet the castle was surrendered to him only late, and, acting on the worst advice, he did not punish his traitors; for if he had [Col. 0958C] done so then, so many castles would not later have been retained against him.

The king then went to the Isle of Wight, took it from Baldwin de Redvers, of whom we have spoken above, and banished him from England. Elated by these successful achievements, he came hunting at Brampton, one mile from Huntingdon. There he held pleas concerning the forests of his nobles—that is, their woods and hunting rights—and broke his vow and agreement with God and the people.

In the second year King Stephen was at Christmas at Dunstable. In Lent he crossed into Normandy. Alexander, bishop of Lincoln, and many nobles crossed with him. There, while settling affairs by contests under Mars’s leadership, he brought all that he undertook to a distinguished conclusion: he drove back the enemies who surrounded him, overthrew hostile castles, shone gloriously among the greatest, made peace with the king of France, and his son Eustace became the king of France’s man for Normandy, which lies adjacent to the dominion of the French. [Col. 0958D]

Seeing this, the count of Anjou, Stephen’s chief enemy—who had, to be sure, married King Henry’s daughter, formerly empress of Germany, and who had received oaths concerning the kingdom of England, so that husband and wife laid claim to England—nevertheless made a truce with King Stephen. For he saw that for the moment he could not withstand the royal forces, so great was their store of valour and money, which still remained from the abundance of the late king’s treasure.

All things having gone prosperously, King Stephen returned in glory to England at the very [Col. 0959A] threshold of Christmas. These two years, therefore, were most prosperous for King Stephen; the third, of which we shall speak, was middling and interrupted; but the last two were ruinous and precipitous.

In the third year the energetic King Stephen, immediately upon entering England, hurried to Bedford and besieged it on the eve of the Nativity of the Lord and throughout Christmas. This also seemed displeasing to many before God, because he valued little or nothing the solemnity of solemnities. When Bedford had been surrendered, he led an army into Scotland.

For the king of Scots, because he had sworn an oath to the daughter of King Henry, acted abominably through his men, as though beneath a veil of holiness. They slit open pregnant women and tore out their prematurely delivered offspring; they tossed children [Col. 0959B] upon the points of spears; they cut priests to pieces upon altars; they placed the severed heads of crucified persons upon the bodies of the slain, and, taking the heads of the dead in exchange, set them upon crucifixes. Whatever the Scots touched was wholly full of horror and savagery. There was the cry of women, the wailing of old men, the groaning of the dying, and the despair of the living.

King Stephen therefore rose up and burned and destroyed the southern parts of King David’s realm; David himself did not dare to meet him. After Easter the accursed fury of traitors flared up. A traitor called Talebot held against the king a castle of Herefordshire in Wales, but the king recovered it by siege.

Robert, the bastard son of King Henry, held against him the very strong [Col. 0959C] castle called Bristol, and another called Slede. William [otherwise Ralph] Lovel held the castle of Cary; Paganellus, the castle of Ludlow; William de Moun [otherwise Moiun], Dunster Castle; Robert de Nichole, Wareham Castle; Eustace, son of John, the castle of Melton; and William, son of Alan, the castle of Shrewsbury. The king took the last by force of arms and hanged some of those captured. Hearing this, Walkelin, who held Dover Castle, surrendered it to the queen when she besieged him.

While the king was occupied in the southern parts of England, David, king of Scots, led an innumerable army into England. Against him the nobles of northern England, at the exhortation and command of [Col. 0959D] Thurstan, archbishop of York, resisted manfully, setting up the standard—that is, the royal banner—at Allerton.

Since the archbishop could not attend the battle because of illness, he sent in his place Ralph, bishop of Orkney, who, standing in the midst of the battle line on a high position, delivered this exhortation:

> Most illustrious nobles of England, Norman-born: remember your name and lineage, for it is fitting that you should fight with them in mind. Consider who you are, against whom, and where you wage war. No one has resisted you with impunity: bold France, having experienced you, has slunk away; fertile England, conquered by you, has submitted; rich Apulia, assigned to you, has flourished again; famous Jerusalem and renowned Antioch have each placed themselves beneath you.
>
> Now, however, Scotland, rightly subject to you, attempts to repel you while unarmed, preferring rashness—[Col. 0960A] more suited to brawling than battle. Among them there is no knowledge of military affairs, no experience in fighting, and no capacity for discipline. Therefore there is no ground for fear, but rather for shame: those whom we have always attacked and conquered in their own country have rushed, drunk and mad, into our country in a perverse fashion.
>
> Yet I, a bishop placed here in the stead of our archbishop, declare that this has been brought about by divine providence: so that those who in this land have violated God’s churches, stained the altars with blood, killed priests, and spared neither children nor pregnant women, may in this same land pay penalties worthy of their crime. Today God will accomplish the most just judgment of his ordering by our hands. Raise your spirits, therefore, noble men, and rise against this most wicked enemy, trusting in the valour of your country—indeed, in the presence of God.
>
> Let not their rashness move you, when even so many marks of our valour do not deter them. They do not know how to arm themselves for war; you train in arms in peace, so that in war you may not feel the uncertain chances of battle. Your head is protected by a helmet, your breast by mail, your legs by greaves, and your whole body by a shield; the enemy finds no place [Col. 0960B] to strike one whom he sees surrounded by iron. As we advance against unarmed and naked men, what do we hesitate over? Their number? Yet war is accomplished not so much by the number of many as by the valour of few; a multitude unaccustomed to discipline is an obstacle to itself—in success, to victory; in adversity, to flight. Moreover, your forefathers, though few, often conquered many. What then will ancestral glory, habitual training, and military discipline avail you, unless you, fewer in number, conquer many?
>
> But the enemy’s disorderly rush, and its scattered convergence—which greatly pleases my spirit—now [Col. 0960C] counsels an end to speaking. Therefore, in the place of your archbishop, since today you are to avenge offences committed against the house of the Lord, the priests of the Lord, and the little flock of the Lord, if any of you falls fighting, we absolve him from every punishment for sin, in the name of the Father, whose creatures they have foully and horribly destroyed; and of the Son, whose altars they have defiled; and of the Holy Spirit, from whom, having been exalted, they have madly fallen.

All the people of England replied, and the mountains and hills echoed: “Amen, amen.” At the same time the Scottish army shouted its national cry, and the cry rose up to heaven: “Albani, Albani!” But the cry was extinguished by the savagery of the blows and the dreadful crash.

The battle began when the line of the men of Lothian, who had snatched from the unwilling king of Scots the glory of striking first, [Col. 0960D] attacked our armoured cavalry line with javelins and very long spears. As if striking an iron wall, they found it impenetrable. Archers mingled among the horsemen darkened them with arrows and pierced them, since they were plainly unarmed. For the entire people of Normans and English stood motionless, massed into one battle line around the standard.

Then the chief leader of the men of Lothian was struck by an arrow and fell, and all his people turned to flight. For God Most High was offended by them, and all their strength was destroyed like a spider’s web.

Seeing this, the great [Col. 0961A] line of Scots, which was fiercely fighting elsewhere, lost heart and gave itself to flight. The royal line, which King David had formed from many peoples, saw this at once and began first to flee singly, then in groups, while the king was left almost alone. When the king’s friends saw this, they compelled him to take a swift horse and turn his back.

But the king’s most energetic son paid no attention to what he saw his own men doing. Intent only upon glory and valour, while the rest fled he attacked the enemy line most bravely and struck it with wondrous force. His line alone remained mounted, composed of English and Normans who belonged to his father’s household. Yet cavalry could not long hold out against armoured soldiers standing on foot [Col. 0961B] and packed together without moving. Their lances broken and horses wounded, they were forced to flee, though they had achieved a glorious deed.

Report says that eleven thousand Scots were killed in that field, besides those found and slain in the crops and woods. Our men triumphed happily with very little bloodshed. The leaders in this battle were William, count of Aumale; William Peverel of Nottingham; Walter Espec [otherwise Espech]; and Ilbert [otherwise Gilbert de Lacy] de Lacy, whose brother was the only man of all the cavalry killed there.

When the outcome of this battle was reported to King Stephen, he and all present rendered the greatest thanks to God. This battle was fought in August. But at Advent [Col. 0961C] Alberic, legate of the Roman Church and bishop of Ostia, held a council at London. There, through the support of King Stephen, Theobald, abbot of Bec, became archbishop of Canterbury.

In the fourth year, after Christmas, King Stephen took Slede Castle by siege. Afterwards he went to Scotland, where, while he conducted affairs under the leadership of Mars and Vulcan, the king of Scotland was compelled to make peace with him. Taking Henry, son of the king of Scots, with him into England, he besieged Ludlow. There the same Henry was nearly captured when he was dragged from his horse by a hooked iron; but the king himself splendidly drew him back from the enemy.

Then, with the matter unfinished [otherwise, completed], he made for Oxford, where an affair remarkable for its infamy and wholly foreign to all [Col. 0961D] custom occurred. Having received peacefully Roger, bishop of Salisbury, and Alexander, bishop of Lincoln, Roger’s nephew, the king violently seized them in his court, although they refused no justice and most dutifully sought the equity of a judgment.

He put Bishop Alexander in prison there, while he took the bishop of Salisbury with him to the latter’s castle called Devizes—than which there was none more splendid within the bounds of Europe. He maltreated him by the torment of fasting and by fastening a noose around the neck of his son, who had been the king’s chancellor, in order that he might be hanged. In this way he extorted the castle from him. Forgetting evilly the benefits which, at the beginning of his reign, the bishop had heaped upon him above all others, he returned such a reward for his devotion.

In the same way he seized [Col. 0962A] Sherborne, which was scarcely inferior to Devizes in splendour. With the bishop’s treasure he obtained Constance, sister of Louis, king of France, for his son Eustace.

Returning from there, the king took with him to Newark Alexander, bishop of Lincoln, whom he had left imprisoned at Oxford. The bishop had built there, over the River Trent in a most pleasant place, a most flourishing castle of splendidly varied design. When the king arrived there, he imposed an unlawful fast upon the bishop, asserting on pledged faith that he would be deprived of all food until he surrendered the castle. The bishop could scarcely obtain from his own men, with tears and prayers, that they should place his castle out of his legal possession and into the custody of strangers.

Likewise another of his castles was surrendered, called [Col. 0962B] Sleaford, second to the aforementioned neither in form nor situation.

Not long afterwards, when Henry, bishop of Winchester, the king’s brother and now legate of the Roman Church, held a council at Winchester, he, Theobald archbishop of Canterbury, and all the bishops present cast themselves at the king’s feet. In the most devout supplication they asked him to restore their possessions to the bishops mentioned above and graciously pardon them all that had been done against him. But the king, following the counsel of wicked men and despising the reverence due to so great a prostration, allowed them to obtain nothing.

For this reason the house of King Stephen was laid open to its approaching condemnation. For immediately the daughter of King Henry, who had been empress of Germany and to whom England had been dedicated by oath, came into England. When the king besieged her at [Col. 0962C] Arundel, he allowed her to go to Bristol—whether trusting treacherous counsels or because he saw that the castle was impregnable.

In the same year the aforesaid Bishop Roger withered away, worn down by grief as well as old age. Let all readers, then, be astonished at so great and sudden a reversal of circumstances. From the beginning of youth so many blessings had come to that man, and they had increased without interruption to such a height that we should all have said Fortune had forgotten her own changeableness in his case. No adversity could affect him throughout his whole life, until such an accumulation of misery converged upon him all at once at the end and choked him.

Let no one, therefore, trust in the constancy of good fortune. Let no one presume upon the stability of Fortune. Let no one maintain that a firmly fixed seat can long survive upon her turning [Col. 0962D] wheel.

In the fifth year of his reign King Stephen drove Nigel, bishop of Ely, from his bishopric because he was the nephew of the aforesaid bishop of Salisbury, from whom he had inherited hatred toward his family. Where he was at Christmas or at Easter is not worth recording. For the ceremonial courts and the royal splendour, descending from the ancient succession, had now entirely vanished. The immense abundance of treasure had already been lost; there was no peace in the kingdom; everything was being destroyed by killings, burnings, and robberies; everywhere were outcry, lamentation, and horror. Hence this elegiac poem:

> Who will give me a fountain—for what better—of tears,  
> That I may weep for the shameful deeds of my country?  
>   
> A Stygian darkness, released from the deep, has come,  
> And, gathered thickly, covers the [Col. 0963A] face of the kingdom.  
>   
> Behold: frenzy, tumult, fires, thefts, plunder,  
> Disaster [otherwise, slaughter], and no fidelity come rushing together.  
>   
> Now they rob wealth and the owners of wealth; even in their own  
> Sleeping camps they oppress them—O new kind of theft!  
>   
> To forswear oneself, to betray one’s pledged faith, is a noble deed;  
> To betray even one’s lords, an action worthy of men.  
>   
> A band of robbers breaks into cemeteries and churches;  
> For, grievous to say, it carries off priests.  
>   
> They torture the Lord’s anointed, and women also—  
> Shame!—seeking to torment them for ransom.  
>   
> Famine therefore flows in; their flesh consumed, groaning  
> Bones and skin breathe out their wandering souls.  
>   
> Who could bury such crowds of the dying?  
> Behold the face of the Styx and a plague like it!

In the sixth year King Stephen besieged the city of Lincoln shortly before Christmas; Ranulf, Earl of Chester, had deceitfully seized its fortifications. He remained there until the Purification of the Holy Virgin Mary, Mother of God. Then the aforesaid Earl Ranulf brought with him Robert, son of King Henry and his own son-in-law, and other very powerful magnates, to raise the king’s siege. When the exceedingly bold earl had with difficulty crossed an almost impassable marsh, he attacked the king in battle that very day, his battle-lines having been arranged. He himself, with his own men, formed the first division; the second consisted of those whom King Stephen had disinherited; the great duke Robert, with his followers, formed the third; and at the side stood a troop of Welshmen, equipped more with audacity than with weapons.

[Col. 0963B]

Then the Earl of Chester, a warlike man glittering in splendid armour, addressed Earl Robert and the remaining magnates as follows:

“Most unconquered duke, and you, my magnates and fellow-soldiers, I render you most heartfelt thanks, because you have nobly shown me the affection of your love even to the peril of your lives. Since, therefore, I am the cause of your danger, it is fitting that I should first expose myself to danger and first dash against the battle-line of that most faithless king, who, after granting a truce, broke the peace. Trusting both in my own courage and in the king’s injustice, I shall presently split the royal wedge; with my sword I shall make myself a path through the midst of the enemy. It is for your valour to follow one who goes before and imitate one who strikes. Already, in the foreknowledge of my mind, I seem to fly across the royal lines, tread the magnates beneath my feet, and run the king himself through with my sword.”

He had spoken. Duke Robert answered the young man thus, and, standing upon an elevated place, delivered the following speech:

[Col. 0963C]

“It is not unfitting that you seek the honour of the first blow, both because of the nobility and the courage in which you excel. Yet, if you contend on the ground of nobility, I, the son of a most noble king and grandson of the supreme king, am not surpassed; if on that of courage, here are many most excellent men, before whom no living person can be preferred in worth. But a very different consideration moves me. The king, contrary to the oaths which he swore to my sister, has cruelly usurped the kingdom; throwing all things into turmoil, he has caused the deaths of many thousands; and, following his own example, he has distributed lands to men with no right to them and despoiled those who held them by right. Therefore he must be attacked first by those wickedly disinherited men themselves, with the supreme Judge aiding them and furnishing vengeance.

“He who judges peoples in equity shall look down from the lofty dwelling-place of heaven and shall by no means abandon, in this great necessity, those who justly attack an unjust man.

[Col. 0963D]

“But there is one thing, most valiant magnates and all you soldiers, which I wish firmly to impress upon your minds: through the marshes which you have scarcely crossed, there can be no return for fugitives. Here, therefore, you must either conquer or die; there is no hope of flight. One thing alone remains: make yourselves a road into the city with your swords. If my mind truly forebodes anything, the fact that you can flee nowhere is precisely what, with God’s help, will grant you victory today. For he who has no other refuge must needs take refuge in courage. You shall see the citizens of Lincoln, who stand nearest their city, their spirits melting at the gravity of the attack, flee to their homes—while you are victorious.

[Col. 0964A]

“Yet consider against whom you wage war. Alan, leader of the Bretons, advances armed against us—indeed, against God: an accursed man, stained with every kind of crime, knowing no equal in wickedness; one to whom the desire to harm has never been lacking, and to whom it seems the sole and greatest reproach not to be incomparable in cruelty. The Earl of Mellent likewise advances against us: cunning in deceit, an artificer of fraud, with inborn wickedness in his heart, falsehood on his lips, and sloth in his actions; proud in heart, high-minded in speech, faint-hearted in deed; last to join battle, first to depart; slow for fighting, swift for flight.

[Col. 0964B]

“Earl Hugh advances against you, to whom it seemed too little merely to have broken faith with the Empress, unless he should openly perjure himself a second time, asserting that King Henry had granted the kingdom to Stephen and disinherited his own daughter. He certainly regards deceit as a virtue and calls perjury elegance. The Earl of Albemarle advances, a man of singular constancy in crime: changeable in committing it, immovable in abandoning it; his own bride left him as a fugitive because of his intolerable filthiness. That earl also advances against you who snatched away the bride of the aforesaid earl: a most manifest adulterer and pre-eminently impure, devoted to Bacchus, unknown to Mars, reeking of wine, ignorant of war. Simon, Earl of Northampton, advances: whose action is mere speech, whose gift is mere promise; who, when he says something, has done it, and, when he promises, has given it. The other magnates advance, like their king: accustomed to robbery, smeared with plunder, fattened on homicide, and, in short, all defiled by perjury.

[Col. 0964C]

“You, then, most valiant men, whom the great King Henry raised up, and this man has cast down; whom he equipped, and this man has ruined: raise your spirits. Trusting in your own courage—indeed, in God’s justice—undertake the vengeance offered you by God against these criminals; set before yourselves and your descendants unfading glory. Now, if you possess the same spirit to carry out this judgment of God, vow advance, renounce flight, and raise your right hands unanimously to heaven.”

He had scarcely finished when all, with hands stretched toward heaven, renounced flight with a terrible cry; gathering themselves in their armour, they advanced splendidly against the enemy.

Meanwhile King Stephen, heaving amid great waves of anxiety, had heard Mass on so solemn an occasion. When, according to custom, he placed in Bishop Alexander’s hands a wax taper worthy of a king to offer to God, it broke. This was a sign to the king of brokenness. Moreover, before the bishop, the pyx containing the Body of the Lord fell upon the altar when its cord snapped: this was a sign to the king of downfall.

[Col. 0964D]

Accordingly, the most vigorous king went out and, with the greatest confidence, arranged his battle-lines. Fighting on foot, he placed all the armoured multitude around himself in a close formation, their horses having been led away. He ordered the earls with their men to fight on horseback in two divisions; but those mounted divisions proved very small. For the false and factional earls had brought only a few men with them. The royal army, however, was very large, marked by the single banner of the king himself.

Since King Stephen lacked a festive voice, Baldwin son of Gilbert, a man of great nobility and a most valiant knight, was charged to deliver an exhortation to the whole assembly. Standing in an elevated place, with every eye raised toward him, when he had stirred their attention by restrained silence, he began thus:

[Col. 0965A]

“All who, after arranging your battle-lines, are about to fight must take account of three things: first, the justice of the cause; then, the number of soldiers; lastly, the valour of those present. The justice of the cause, lest the soul incur peril; the number of soldiers, lest one be overwhelmed by the enemy’s multitude; the valour of those standing by, lest an army relying on its number but supported by weak men be overthrown. In all these respects we see the undertaking to which we are bound as secure.

[Col. 0965B]

“The justice of our cause is this: that, keeping faith with the king before God, we stand by him in the danger of death against his own perjured enemies. Our number is not inferior in cavalry and is denser in infantry. Who could adequately praise in words the worth of so many earls, so many magnates, and soldiers always accustomed to war? The boundless courage of the king himself shall stand among you in the place of thousands.

[Col. 0965C]

“Since, therefore, your lord, the Lord’s anointed, to whom you pledged fidelity, is in your midst, fulfil your vow to God. You will receive from God a gift all the greater in proportion as you fight more faithfully and steadfastly for your king—loyal men against faithless, lawful men against perjurers. Indeed, secure and filled with the utmost confidence, consider against whom you wage war. Duke Robert’s strength is known. As usual, he threatens much and accomplishes little: a lion in speech, a hare in heart; conspicuous for eloquence, obscure through idleness.

[Col. 0965D]

“The Earl of Chester, a man of irrational boldness, is ready for conspiracy but unreliable in carrying it through; impetuous for war, heedless of danger; plotting schemes too great for himself, panting after impossibilities; bringing few regular followers and gathering a scattered crowd of adventurers. He possesses nothing which ought to be feared: whatever he has begun manfully, he has always abandoned effeminately. In all his deeds, undertaking matters unsuccessfully, he has either fled defeated from encounters or, if he has rarely emerged victorious, suffered losses greater than those of the defeated.

“Let the Welshmen whom he alone has brought with him be objects of your contempt. They prefer unarmed rashness to war and, lacking both skill and experience of warfare, rush upon spears like cattle. The rest, both magnates and soldiers, are deserters and wanderers. Would that more of them had been brought: the greater their number, the worse their effect.

[Col. 0966A]

“You earls and men of consular rank ought to remember what befits your courage and nobility. Today raise your abundant virtues to their most flourishing height; as imitators of your fathers, leave eternal splendour to your sons. Your continual victories are an incentive to fight; their continual misfortunes will be an incentive to flee. Already—unless I am mistaken—they regret having come; already they are considering flight, if the roughness of the terrain permits it. Since they can neither fight nor flee, what have they done except offer themselves and their baggage to you by God’s nod? You see, therefore, their horses, their arms, and their very bodies subject to your power. Raise your spirits, then, and, warlike men, stretch forth your unconquerable right hands to seize with the greatest rejoicing what God Himself has offered you.”

But before he could conclude the course of his speech, there arose the enemy’s shout, the blare of trumpets, the neighing of horses, and the rumbling of the earth.

[Col. 0966B]

### Beginning of the Battle

The line of the disinherited, which led the advance, struck the royal line. In it were Earl Alan, the Earl of Mellent, Earl Hugh of Estangle, Earl Simon, and the Earl of Warenne. With such force was it struck that immediately, as in the twinkling of an eye, it was scattered and split into three parts. Some were killed, some captured, and some fled.

The division commanded by the Earl of Albemarle and William of Ypres struck the Welshmen advancing on the flank and forced them to flee. But the Earl of Chester’s division struck the troop of the aforesaid earl, and it was scattered in a moment, like the first division. Thus all the king’s horsemen fled, and William of Ypres, a native of Flanders, a former earl and a man of great worth. Being highly experienced in war, and seeing that it was impossible to aid the kings, he deferred his assistance to better times.

King Stephen, then, with his infantry division, was left in the midst of the enemy. They surrounded the royal division on every side and attacked it all around as a castle is ordinarily assaulted. Then throughout the circuit of the royal line one might have seen the terrible face of war: fire flashing from the clash of helmets and swords, dreadful screeching, terrifying shouting. The hills resounded; the city walls resounded. Charging into the royal troop with their horses, they cut down some, overthrew others, and captured many whom they dragged away. No rest, no breathing-space, was granted them, except in the place where the most valiant king stood, while his enemies dreaded the incomparable violence of his blows.

[Col. 0966C]

When the Earl of Chester learned this, jealous of the king’s glory, he rushed upon him with the full weight of his armed men. Then the king’s strength appeared: with a great battle-axe flashing like lightning, he struck down some and hurled others to the ground. A new cry arose: all against him, he against all. At length the royal battle-axe was broken through the frequency of its blows. Drawing his sword, a weapon worthy of the king’s right hand, he acted marvellously until that sword too was broken.

[Col. 0966D]

Seeing this, William Dekains, a most powerful knight, rushed upon the king, seized him by the helmet, and cried loudly: “Here, all of you, here! I hold the king.” Everyone rushed up, and the king was captured. Baldwin also, who had delivered the persuasive speech, was captured, pierced by many wounds and crushed by many blows; by resisting nobly, he earned everlasting glory. Richard, son of Urse, was also captured; he appeared brilliant and glorious alike in giving and receiving blows. Even after the king was captured, the royal division continued to fight; for, being surrounded, they could not flee, until all were either captured or slain. The city, therefore, was plundered by the law of war, and the king was brought into it miserably.

[Col. 0967A]

Thus, after God’s judgment had been executed upon the king, he was led to the Empress and imprisoned in the tower at Bristol. The Empress was received as lady by all the English nation except the people of Kent, where the queen and William of Ypres resisted her with all their strength. She was received first by the Roman legate, the Bishop of Winchester, and then immediately by the Londoners. But she rose to intolerable pride because the uncertain fortunes of war had prospered for her, and she alienated from herself almost every heart. Therefore, whether through the prompting of treacherous men or by God’s ordinance—indeed, whatever men do, they do by God’s ordinance—she was expelled from London.

Irritated with feminine anguish, she ordered the Lord’s anointed king to be put in fetters. After some days, gathering forces with her uncle, the King of Scots, and her brother Robert, she came and besieged the tower of the Bishop of London [or: Winchester]. The bishop sent for the queen, William of Ypres, and nearly all the magnates of England. Thus a great army was formed on each side. They fought daily, not in pitched battle-lines, but through circuits and manoeuvres of military detachments. Events, therefore, were not confused, as in the blindness of war; each person’s worth was apparent, and glory attended merit, so that this delay seemed delightful to all because of the exalted brilliance of illustrious deeds.

[Col. 0967B]

At last the London army arrived, and those contending against the Empress, having been increased greatly in number, compelled her to flee. Many were captured in the flight. Robert, the Empress’s brother, in whose tower the king was imprisoned, was also captured; only through his capture could the king escape. Both were released. Thus the king, miserably captured through God’s justice, was marvellously set free through God’s mercy, and was received by the English magnates with great joy.

[Col. 0967D]

In the seventh year King Stephen built a castle near Wilton. Then an unexpected multitude of enemies came upon the royal soldiers while they had begun manoeuvres of war; unable to resist, they forced the king to flee. Many of his men were captured, including William Martel, the king’s steward, who gave the notable castle of Sherborne for his ransom.

In the same year the king besieged the Empress at Oxford from after the feast of Saint Michael until the coming of the Lord. During that period, not far from Christmas, the Empress escaped across the frozen Thames, wrapped in white garments which, by reflecting the snow and resembling it, deceived the besiegers’ eyes. She fled to the castle of Wallingford, and thus Oxford was at last surrendered to the king.

[Col. 0968A]

In the eighth year King Stephen attended a council at London in mid-Lent. Because no honour was accorded by plunderers either to clerics or to the Church of God, and clerics were seized and ransomed just like laymen, the Bishop of Winchester, legate of the Roman see, held at London a council necessary for the clergy in those times.
