It was decreed that no one who had laid violent hands upon a cleric could be absolved by anyone but the pope himself and in his presence. Thus a slight serenity scarcely dawned for the clergy.

[Col. 0968B]

In the same year the king seized Geoffrey de Mandeville in his court at Saint Albans, more in requital for the earl’s wickedness than in accordance with the law of nations, more from necessity than from honour. Had he not done this, he would have been deprived of the kingdom by that earl’s treachery. Therefore, in order that the king might release him, Geoffrey surrendered to him the Tower of London, the castle of Walden, and that of Pleshey. Deprived of his possessions, the aforesaid earl invaded Ramsey Abbey, expelled the monks, installed plunderers, and made the Church of God a den of thieves. He was a man of the highest merit, but of the utmost obstinacy toward God; greatly diligent in worldly affairs, greatly negligent toward God.

That same year, before Christmas, the Bishop of Winchester and afterwards the Archbishop of Canterbury went to Rome to deal with the legation. Pope Innocent had already died, and Celestine succeeded him.

[Col. 0968C]

In King Stephen’s ninth year he besieged Lincoln. While he was constructing a fortification against the castle which the Earl of Chester held by force, nearly eighty of his workmen were suffocated by the enemy. The undertaking being unfinished, the king withdrew in confusion.

[Col. 0968D]

In that same year Geoffrey de Mandeville grievously harassed the king and shone with great glory in every respect. In August God’s radiant justice displayed a miracle worthy of itself. Two men who, tearing away monks, had turned churches of God into castles—sinning alike—were punished with like penalties. Robert Marmion, a warlike man, had wickedly done this in the church of Coventry. Geoffrey de Mandeville, as we have said, had committed the same crime in Ramsey church. When Robert Marmion charged the enemy, amid the great ranks of his own men and before the monastery itself, he was killed alone; and, excommunicated, he is consumed by eternal death. Likewise Earl Geoffrey, among the dense battle-lines of his own men, was struck alone by an arrow shot by a most insignificant foot-soldier. Though he laughed at the wound, after some days he died from it, excommunicated.

Behold the same vengeance for the same crime, worthy to be proclaimed through every age in praise of God. While that church was held as a castle, blood bubbled from the walls of the church and the adjoining cloister, manifesting divine indignation and foretelling the destruction of the wicked. Many men, indeed I myself, saw this with our own eyes. Since wicked men said that God slept, God was awakened both in this sign and in the thing signified.

[Col. 0969A]

In that same year Ernulf, son of the earl, who after his father’s death retained the fortified church, was captured and thereby banished. The commander of his cavalry fell from his horse in his lodging, his brains spilled, and died. Reimer, the commander of his infantry, whose office had been to demolish or burn churches, was crossing the sea with his wife when, as many reported, the ship became motionless. As the sailors marvelled at this prodigy and cast lots to discover its cause, the lot fell upon Reimer. Though he opposed it with all his strength, when the lot was cast a second and third time it again fell upon him. He was therefore placed in a small boat, together with his wife and the money most wickedly acquired; immediately the ship ploughed the sea at the swift pace at which it had previously travelled, while the small boat, with its most wicked occupants, was whirled into a sudden abyss and swallowed up for ever.

In the same year, Pope Celestine having died, Lucius was appointed in his place.

[Col. 0969B]

In the tenth year King Stephen was first occupied with operations against the incursions of Hugh Bigod. But in summer Earl Robert and the whole body of the king’s enemies had built a castle at Faringdon. The king, no sluggish man, gathered forces and flew to the attack, bringing with him a terrible and numerous army of Londoners. Assaulting the castle day after day, while Earl Robert and his supporters waited not far from the king’s army for greater forces, they captured it by most laborious courage and not without much shedding of blood. Then at last fortune began to change for the better for the king and to extend his success on high.

[Col. 0969C]

In the same year Alexander, Bishop of Lincoln, again went to Rome and displayed the same lavish generosity as before. He was received with the greatest honour by Pope Eugenius, a new man fully worthy of such high dignity: his mind always kindly, his judgment always fair, his expression always not only cheerful but pleasing. Returning in the following year, with the fullest favour of the pope himself and of the whole curia, he was received by his own people with the greatest reverence and joy. He restored his church, which fire had disfigured, with such refined workmanship that it appeared more beautiful than in its first newness and yielded to no building anywhere within the bounds of England.

[Col. 0969D]

In the eleventh year King Stephen, assembling a great army, built an impregnable castle opposite Wallingford. Ranulf, Earl of Chester, now reconciled with the king, was present with large forces. Afterwards, when that earl came peacefully to the king’s court at Northampton, the king seized him, though he feared no such thing, and thrust him into prison [variant: confined him], until he restored the famous castle of Lincoln—which he had deceitfully taken from the king—and every other castle that had been under his control. Thus the earl, released from prison, was restored to free discretion.

[Col. 0970A]

In the twelfth year King Stephen was royally crowned with the diadem at Christmas in the city of Lincoln. No king had dared enter it because of the prohibition of certain superstitious persons; this reveals how great was King Stephen’s boldness and his spirit’s lack of fear before dangers. After the king’s departure, the Earl of Chester came to Lincoln with military forces to assault it. His commander, a strong and utterly unconquered man, was killed at the entrance of the North Gate, and the earl himself, having lost many men, was compelled to flee. The victorious citizens, filled with the highest joy, paid notable praise and thanks to the Virgin, protectress of virgins.

[Col. 0970B]

At Pentecost Louis, King of France; Theodoric, Earl of Flanders; the Earl of Saint-Gilles; an innumerable army from all the kingdom of France; and many Englishmen who had taken the cross, set out for Jerusalem to attack the pagans who had taken the city of Rohais. Yet the emperor of Germany, Conrad, led a larger army. Both armies passed through the territory of the emperor of Constantinople, who afterwards betrayed them.

In August Alexander, Bishop of Lincoln, set out for Auxerre to Pope Eugenius, who had previously been staying at Paris and was then residing there. Though the bishop was honourably received by the pope, he carried back to England the seed of illness through the untimely excess of heat. Therefore he soon yielded first to sickness, then to languor, and finally to death.

[Col. 0970C]

In the thirteenth year of King Stephen, Bishop Alexander died and was buried at Lincoln on Ash Wednesday. According to Moses’s custom, true things must therefore be said concerning the man’s character. Reared in the greatest luxury by his uncle Roger, Bishop of Salisbury, he acquired greater ambitions than were suitable for him. Wishing to surpass other princes in the lavishness of gifts and the splendour of entertainments, and since his own revenues could not suffice for this, he eagerly exacted from his own people whatever might fill the poverty produced by the aforementioned excess. Yet he could not fill it, since he always scattered more and more. He was, however, a prudent man and so lavish that the Roman curia called him “Magnificent.”

[Col. 0970D]

In that same year the armies of the German emperor and the King of the French, distinguished by the greatest leaders and advancing with the utmost pride, came to nothing because God rejected them. Their incontinence, which they practised in open fornications and also in adulteries—very displeasing to God—finally in plundering and every kind of crime, had risen before God’s sight. First laid low by hunger and by the treachery of the emperor of Constantinople, they afterwards withered beneath the enemy sword. The King of France and the German emperor fled disgracefully with very few men, first to Antioch and afterwards to Jerusalem.

[Col. 0971A]

Then the King of France, as though to perform some deed that might repair the injury to his reputation, besieged Damascus with the aid of the Knights Templar at Jerusalem and forces gathered from every side. But lacking God’s grace and therefore accomplishing nothing, he returned to Gaul.

Meanwhile a certain naval army of men who were not powerful and relied upon no great leader except Almighty God succeeded exceedingly well because they had set out humbly. With God’s help, a few of them won from many, through wars, a city in Spain called Lisbon, another called Almeria, and the neighbouring regions. Truly, “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” [James 4]. The army of the King of the French and the German emperor had been more splendid and larger than that which had previously conquered Jerusalem; yet they were crushed by very few and dispersed and destroyed like spiders’ webs. But no multitude could withstand [variant: resist] those poor men of whom we have spoken; whenever more men rose against them, they became weaker. The greater part of this force had come from England.

[Col. 0971B]

In the same year, as Christmas approached, Robert, surnamed de Querceto (“of the Oak”), Archdeacon of Leicester [variant: of Legrecestria], a young man worthy of every praise, was elected Bishop of Lincoln. All judged him worthy of so great an honour; with the king, clergy, and people assenting in the greatest joy, he received episcopal consecration from the Archbishop of Canterbury. At Lincoln, awaited with great expectation and greater still in his arrival, he was welcomed devoutly by clergy and people. May God prosper him in evil times, cherish his youth with the dew of wisdom, and gladden his face with spiritual joy.

[Col. 0971C]

In the fourteenth year David, King of Scots, gave manly arms to his nephew Henry. When they had gathered for the ceremony—the King of Scots with his forces and his nephew with the magnates of western England—King Stephen, fearing that they would invade York, came into the city with a very great army and remained there throughout August. Eustace, son of King Stephen—for in the same year he too had assumed manly arms—raided the lands of the magnates who were with Henry, son of the Empress. No one opposing him, with Mars and Vulcan as companions, he inflicted no small damage upon them. The King of England and the King of Scots, one of whom was at York and the other at Carlisle, wary of one another and afraid to strike, separated of their own accord and returned to the residences of their kingdoms.

[Col. 0971D]

In the fifteenth year King Stephen, having assembled his forces, magnificently assaulted the city of Worcester; after capturing it, he disfigured it with fire, though he could not take the castle within the city. That city belonged to Waleran, Earl of Mellent, to whom King Stephen himself had granted it, to his own harm. Enriched by the spoils of the plundered city, the royal troops returned through the lands of their enemies and brought away immeasurable booty, no one resisting.

[Col. 0972A]

In the sixteenth year Theobald, Archbishop of Canterbury and legate of the Apostolic See, held a general council at London in mid-Lent, where King Stephen, his son Eustace, and the magnates of England were present, and the whole council raged with novel appeals. For appeals had not been customary in England until Henry of Winchester, while legate, cruelly introduced them to his own harm. At this council an appeal was made three times to the hearing of the Roman pontiff.

In the same year King Stephen again attacked Winchester. Since he had not been able to take the castle in the preceding year, he laboured with all his strength for its capture. But when the besieged held out manfully, he built two castles to reduce it. Leaving some of his magnates there, he returned home. Yet because the king’s habit was to begin many things vigorously and carry them out sluggishly, by the skill of the Earl of Leicester the king’s besieging castles were demolished and the besieged were cleverly freed. The aforesaid earl was brother of the Earl of Mellent. Thus the king’s endeavour and labour withered and vanished.

[Col. 0972B]

In the same year the Count of Anjou, son-in-law of King Henry and son of the King of Jerusalem, a great and renowned man, yielded to the law of death. He therefore gave Anjou and Normandy to his eldest son Henry, and granted him the hereditary right which he held, though deprived of the kingdom, in the realm of England. It happened that Louis, King of the French, was separated from his wife, the daughter of the Count of Poitou, on grounds of kinship. Henry, therefore, the new Duke of the Normans, married her and through her possessed the County of Poitou, enlarged with the highest honours. Yet this marriage was the incentive and kindling of the greatest hatred and discord between the King of the French and the duke himself.

[Col. 0972C]

Accordingly Eustace, son of King Stephen, together with the King of the French, attacked Normandy in no small assaults. The duke resisted both of them and the entire French army with the greatest vigour. The king, however, having assembled all his forces, assaulted a certain castle called New Market and captured and held it powerfully and almost irresistibly; he then returned it to Eustace, son of the King of England, who had married his sister.

[Col. 0972D]

In the seventeenth year King Stephen wished to adorn his son Eustace with the royal diadem. He therefore asked Theobald, Archbishop of Canterbury, and the other bishops whom he had assembled there, to anoint Eustace as king and confirm him with their blessing, but he was refused. The pope had by his letters forbidden the archbishop to elevate the king’s son to kingship, namely because King Stephen seemed to have seized the kingdom contrary to his oath.

Thus father and son, consumed with inward grief and burning with excessive anger, ordered all the bishops shut up in a certain house and, harassing them severely, compelled them to carry out their demands. Although terrified by the greatest fear—for King Stephen had never plainly loved clerics and had formerly imprisoned two bishops—they nevertheless resisted, fearing no danger to their lives [variant: fearing danger]. Yet all withdrew unharmed, though despoiled of their possessions, which they later recovered when the king repented.

[Col. 0973A]

In the same year the king besieged and attacked the castle of Newbury, not far from Winchester, and at last took it. From there he besieged Wallingford Castle and built a siege-castle at the very entrance to the bridge, which deprived the besieged of free passage for bringing in provisions. Then, pressed very severely for the first time, they asked their lord, the Duke of Normandy, either to send assistance or to permit them to surrender the castle into the king’s hands.

[Col. 0973B]

In the eighteenth year of King Stephen, the Duke of Normandy, compelled by so great a necessity, unexpectedly came in haste to England. Then wretched England, ruined indeed but now seemingly about to recover life through his arrival, burst forth in these tearful words:

> Duke Henry, grandson of Henry the greatest of the great,  
> I, exalted England, fall—and now I do not fall in total ruin.  
> I can scarcely say, “I was”; for “I am” has departed.  
> If any hope remained for me who am miserable,  
> I would cry: “Have pity; come; help; stand firm.  
> For by right I am yours; you can raise me when fallen.  
> But now my lips grow stiff; now voice and life depart.  
> Yet what cry is this? He comes—again they cry, ‘He comes!’  
>
> What leader of leaders is this, a boy in years but old in mind?  
> Jewel of men—man, hail! While hope remains to me, my hope, hail!  
> You come too late: I have perished. Yet cry, ‘England, arise—  
> rather, arise again: though dead, I restore your life to you.’  
> Revived at your voice, after death I shall rise again.  
>
> Therefore, coming back to life, I see what I shudder to be seen:  
> how great the battles Stephen stirs! Let him stir them: I wish it; for  
> no glory would exist if he stirred no battles.  
> How many have you led against Stephen, who possesses such a multitude of men?  
> Few. Why few? Greater glory  
> lies in conquering many with few than many with many.  
> When the King of the French, the earls, the magnates—indeed all—  
> rise against you, the loss is slight. I resist the gods while absent;  
> I fight for you while present. Why should I at once bring forth [cur simul, edam: reading and sense uncertain],  
> if the struggle is not twofold and my glory will not be twofold?  
> “Kings shine much more brightly than to conquer kings” [reges … reges, as printed; syntax uncertain].  
> Who bears your standard? The grace of Christ Himself,  
>
> which my own conduct wins for me, no less than the king’s conduct wins it.  
> For peace alone pleases me; discord pleases the king.  
> Too late, too late, I seek peace for you with blood,  
> sweet foster-child of mine, for whom I have endured such dangers.  
> May I possess you, if yet you possess peace through me;  
> otherwise I shall die, lest I see you dying.”

When, therefore, the glorious duke, driven by a storm, had gained the shores of England, the land roared at once, stirred by sudden reports, like a reed-bed beaten by a quivering west wind. Flying abroad, Fame, as she is wont, scattered her seeds on swift wings: for some, of exultation and joy; for others, of fear and sorrow. Yet those who had long been anxiously awaiting his arrival were somewhat troubled because he had brought so few men with him. The enemy’s confusion, on the other hand, was greatly relieved by that same smallness of number. Both sides, however, [Col. 0974A] wondered at this. Some judged it magnanimity, others rashness, that in the very bosom of winter he had entered a stormy sea.

But the most energetic young man, gathering his followers—both those whom he found and those whom he had brought—hating delay above all things, besieged the castle of Malmesbury. Since the virtues of so great a man were great and many, they must be touched upon briefly, lest a fuller elucidation of the abundance of his deeds should produce excessive prolixity. He therefore immediately assaulted the besieged castle—for he never interposed delay in action—and at once captured it. Yet, though the town had been stormed, Jordan’s very lofty tower, which he held under royal command, remained, to be subdued by hunger alone. Jordan therefore hurried out with the utmost speed and disclosed what had happened to King Stephen.

Harassed by adverse news, King Stephen changed the dignity of his countenance by the veil of grief drawn over it. Nevertheless, without delay he gathered all his forces and pitched his tents not far from Malmesbury. On the day after his arrival he elegantly drew up battle-lines crowded with most select cavalry and distinguished according to the rules of war. His army was indeed immense, packed with a multitude of nobles, gleaming with golden insignia, exceedingly formidable and splendid; but God, in whom alone lies all salvation, had withdrawn far from them. For, opening the floodgates of heaven, He sent upon their faces such torrents, such relentless assaults of bitter cold, such blasts of a windy tempest, that God Himself seemed to be conducting the affair on the duke’s behalf.

Yet [Col. 0974C] they advanced in ordered ranks, as though contending against God’s power, tormented by dreadful sufferings. Opposite stood the young man’s army, relying more upon strength than numbers, but above all strengthened by God’s grace, which they possessed through the justice of the cause for which they stood, namely, mercifully. They stood not far from the walls of the aforesaid town, near the waters of a river which the flooding of rains and snows bore onward with such force and such vastness that it struck terror into those who would enter it and denied an exit to those who had entered.

The most noble young man went before his men, clad in arms worthy of so great a leader; his bodily appearance expressed the fullness of his spirit. Such was the distinction of his beauty that, if it may be said, arms did not so much become him as his own splendor made the arms shine. The storm was behind him and his men, but in the faces of the king and his men; they could neither bear their arms nor handle their rain-drenched lances. And because God had foreseen that He would hand over the land to His servant without the shedding of blood, since none of them could cross the river and the king could no longer endure such inundations, he turned back to London, his effort futile and exhausted by hardship.

The tower which he had besieged having therefore been surrendered to the duke, he hastened joyfully to the purpose for which he had come: namely, to relieve Wallingford Castle, already perishing from hunger. A force of soldiers was assembled to carry provisions into Wallingford Castle; and God prospered this undertaking also, granting them a peaceful result. There were indeed numerous castles [Col. 0975A] round about, filled with the king’s soldiery; yet, by the Lord’s will, they could not hinder those coming or returning. Only a short interval passed, and the most powerful duke, having united all the soldiery attached to him, besieged the castle of Craumers [alternatively, Crawemerse]. Laudably undertaking a difficult and immeasurable task, he enclosed the king’s castle and his own army with a very great rampart, so that an outlet lay open to his own men only through Wallingford Castle, while no escape was allowed to the besieged.

When the king heard this, he gathered together all the forces subject to his authority and came upon the duke in terrifying strength. But the duke was moved by no fear. Though inferior to the king in forces, he at once ordered the rampart which had protected his army to be thrown down; and, abandoning the siege, he advanced magnificently against the king with his battle-lines drawn up. Thus, when the royal army unexpectedly saw the enemy’s ordered ranks rising up before them, they were greatly afraid. The king, however, oppressed by no fear, ordered his own troops, drawn up in fearsome ranks, to advance.

But the nobles—indeed, the traitors of England—rose up and treated between themselves for peace, though loving nothing more than discord. They did not wish battle to be joined because they wished neither side to be exalted: lest, when one had been subdued, the other should rule freely, while the one always fearing the other could not exercise royal power over them. Thus king and duke, each discovering the treachery of his own followers, made a truce between themselves, constrained though unwilling.

Yet God, as was His custom, bestowed honor upon His young servant. For the royal castle which the duke had besieged was uncovered under the terms of that treaty. Afterwards the king alone and the duke alone spoke, with a river between them, about establishing perpetual peace between themselves, anxiously complaining to one another of the treachery of their nobles. That business of peace was tasted beforehand, but deferred to another time.

Discord had not yet been lulled when they returned to their own places; nevertheless, a bright dawn of happiness appeared most serenely to the great duke. For by God’s providence, without anticipating anything of the kind, he destroyed at the same time his most savage enemies, endowed with the greatest power—namely Eustace, the king’s son, and Simon, Earl of Northampton. By this unforeseen event the strength and hope [Col. 0975D] of all who rebelled against him suddenly withered away: both young men perished of the same illness in the same week.

Earl Simon was buried at Northampton, full of everything unlawful and everything unbecoming. The king’s son was buried at Faversham, in the abbey which his mother had founded: approved indeed in military matters, but obstinate in matters of God; most harsh toward the rulers of churches and most devoted to those persecuting them. Thus, after the strongest enemies of His beloved Henry had been uprooted, God Himself was now most graciously preparing the tranquillity of his kingdom.

He then brought his third siege against Stamford Castle. The town having been immediately captured, those rebelling against him [alternatively, fighting him] who were within the tower sent messengers to the king, [Col. 0976A] asking help for the enclosed men. But the king was besieging Tipeswig Castle, which Hugh Bigot held against him. Since he would neither abandon that siege nor give help to those shut in, the castle was surrendered to the great prince Henry; yet the castle which the king was besieging was also surrendered to the king. Departing from Stamford, the Duke of Normandy made for Nottingham and immediately captured the town. But those within the town’s castle burned the town itself.

Meanwhile Archbishop Theobald was working most earnestly with the king to arrange concord with the duke. He frequently spoke with the king in person, and with the duke through envoys. His helper was Henry, Bishop of Winchester, who had earlier disastrously [Col. 0976B] disturbed the kingdom by conferring the royal diadem upon his brother Stephen. But now, moved by repentance when he saw everything devastated by plunder, burnings, and slaughter, he worked to make the beginning of concord the end of such great evils.

Above all, God’s ordinance—He who makes peace and creates good—setting an end to England’s deserved scourges, granted them the success of their undertaking; and through them, peace’s serenity shone forth from Him, concord being confirmed by oaths. O joy beyond measure! O blessed day! In the city of Winchester, amid a brilliant procession of bishops and nobles and the rejoicing throng of an innumerable people, the most illustrious young man was gloriously received, with the king himself leading him. [Col. 0976C] The king adopted him as his son and appointed him heir to the kingdom.

Thereafter the king brought the duke with him to London, where he was received, with no less joy, by an innumerable assembly of people in most splendid processions, as befitted so great a man. Thus God’s mercy bestowed upon the ruined kingdom of the English the dawn of peace and the end of its grievous night. These things having been done, King Stephen and his new son departed in the greatest joy and affection, soon to meet again; for this concord was confirmed before the Nativity of the Lord.

At the octave of Epiphany they met again at Oxford, after the duke had remained in England for a year, engaged in the conquest—or rather, the resurrection—of England. There, at the king’s command, the princes of the English jointly rendered homage and the fidelity owed to a lord to the duke; and they undertook to preserve for the king the honor due to him and their fidelity so long as he lived. After that magnificent assembly, enjoying their new peace, they departed joyfully to their own homes.

Not long thereafter they assembled once more at Dunstable. There the brightest day was somewhat clouded. For the duke was displeased that the castles constructed everywhere for the worst purposes after the death of King Henry were not being demolished, as had been confirmed and settled between them in their concord and most binding treaty. A great part had indeed already been destroyed; yet, as the king’s clemency or cunning spared some castles belonging to his men, he seemed to weaken the fellowship of the agreement. The duke, pressing the king upon this matter, [Col. 0977A] met with a rebuff. Yet, yielding to his new father, he reluctantly deferred the matter, lest he seem to extinguish the light of concord. Thus they parted in peace; but not long afterwards, having received leave from the king, the most victorious duke returned to Normandy.

These are the deeds of Henry, that most splendid young man, in his second arrival in England. Let no one be angry with me because I have committed only a few of his many deeds to writing. For I could not weave a complete history either of so many and such great kings, or of deeds performed through so many centuries; that would require many volumes. Rather, I have brought together abridgments of histories into one work, lest deeds performed should be wholly hidden from posterity. Now let us return to our subject.

Thus the glorious duke, returning to the French lands, was received by his mother, by all the people of Normandy, and by those of Anjou, Maine, and Poitou, with the joy and honor due to him. King Stephen, meanwhile, now at last in peace, obtained very powerfully, for the sake of his adopted son, the honors due to royal dignity.

O dreadful madness of mortals! O accursed perversity! Certain sons of men, whose teeth are weapons and arrows and whose tongue is a sharp sword, were zealously striving to sow the stimulus of discord between the king who was present and the duke who was absent. The king could scarcely withstand their persuasions; and as time went on, as some supposed, he no longer withstood them. He listened to the counsels of the wicked—not unwillingly, but pretending as though unwilling—[Col. 0977C] with undue indulgence.

But the sons of men judged one way, God another. As befitted Him who brings begun works to completion, He reduced the counsels and perverse schemes of the wicked to nothing. For when the king had besieged and finally taken the castle called Drake, near York, and had victoriously gained many other places and demolished castles, he made for Canterbury to speak with the Count of Flanders. There, overtaken by illness and finally by death, [Col. 0978A] he died eight days before the feast of All Saints and was buried in Faversham Abbey beside his wife and son, having reigned for almost nineteen years, with excessive labor and without happiness.

Archbishop Theobald and very many of the nobles of England then sent hurrying messengers for their lord, the Duke of Normandy, that he might come without delay to receive the kingdom. Delayed, however, by winds and sea and very many other causes, he landed at New Forest a few days before the Nativity of the Lord, with his wife and brothers, many powerful men, and great forces. England was therefore without a king for about six weeks; yet, through God’s prevenient grace, it did not lack peace—whether through love or fear of the king who was to come.

But, as has been said, when he landed and made for London, he was, as befitted so great and so blessed a man, received with the utmost joy, many weeping for gladness; he was blessed as king and placed most splendidly on the throne of the kingdom. Of the blessedness of that time we have spoken thus in heroic verse:

> The king has died; yet England, bereft of its king, is not bereft of peace.  
> Henry, you first in the world create these miracles.  
> Not yet king, not yet present, yet you accomplish  
> what the king, though present, could not accomplish—most worthy of the sceptre.  
> How well you will bear the sceptre, you who guide the reins of the realm  
> while not yet bearing the sceptre, as you linger beyond the deep sea.  
> Through you, yet without you, England nevertheless enjoys peace.  
> This dawn, O Phoebus, has preceded your splendors.  
> Behold, you come radiant: the rays of your coming  
> are sure faith, cheerful clemency, such great [alternatively, prudent] power,  
> [Col. 0978C] a gentle yoke, fitting vengeance, sweet correction,  
> chaste love, measured honor, restrained pleasure.  
> While with these rays you adorn the splendid sceptres,  
> you adorn the diadem more than the diadem adorns you.  
> England, long numb with deadly cold,  
> now revived and growing warm in the heat of a new sun,  
> raises her head pressed down to earth; and, her tears of sorrow spent,  
> she weeps tears of joy.  
> With tears she pours forth these words to her foster-son:  
> “You are spirit; I am flesh. Now that you enter, I have revived.”

[Col. 0977]

## Letter of Henry, Archdeacon of Huntingdon, to Warin, on the Kings of the Britons

(See *Patrologia*, vol. CLX, col. 423, in Robert of Torigni’s continuation of Sigebert.)

[Col. 0979]

## Letter of the Same Author to Walter, on Contempt for the World [Note: Another manuscript reads “desire” (*appetitu*).], or on the Bishops and Illustrious Men of His Own Time

(*Anglia Sacra*, vol. II, p. 694, edited by Henry Wharton, who presents this letter from both Lambeth manuscripts, with variant readings appended.)

[Col. 0979A] Walter, once the glory of young men, once the delight of the world, now—alas!—you are wasting away in long illness [Note: “weakness” (*langore*)]; now you are being consumed by lamentable pain. In the pleasant flower of our summer I poetically composed for you a book of epigrams; I also wove a pleasing poem on love [Note: “love” in the accusative, *amorem*]. But a young man sends youthful things to a young man; now an old man sends old men’s things to an old man.

Accordingly, I have written certain things on contempt for the world for you and for myself, in which you may exercise yourself while sick, and to which I myself may return especially by frequent reading. I do not speak rhetorically or treat the matter philosophically. Every page of Scripture proclaims this one thing, and all the abilities of philosophers labor over it. But I speak altogether simply, so that it may be clear to more people—that is, the less learned—and so that, concerning matters which you and I have seen, we may now, in old age, learn to despise things contemptible. Therefore we add nothing from histories, nothing from earlier reports, but what we know by seeing, because the law admits no testimony of this sort other than such testimony. If the names of our time seem barbarous to posterity, or if they are weary of the harsh and winding discussion because so many names are introduced, will it not at least benefit you and me?

Let the first chapter, then, be on matters which have happened in our Church. From childhood almost every vice springs up except lust, [Note: “among which”] because excessive love of present things raises its most rigid head and assumes mastery. But when, by the natural good of advancing age, childhood is emptied of many evils—such as frivolity, instability in learning, and others—this aforesaid evil, which is more pleasant than the rest and seasoned with poisoned honey [Note: “is seasoned” (*conditur*)], remains and grows. Yet, as age greatly advances, what once caressed seems to sting, and what once sweetened seems to embitter. Nevertheless, minds captured by the habit of evil as by an inextricable hook are held fast by fleeting riches and pleasures. This I learned from myself.

For when, as a little boy, an adolescent, and a young man, I beheld the glory of our bishop Robert—namely, most handsome knights, most noble youths, most costly horses, vessels of gold and gilded vessels, the splendid array of attendants bearing numerous dishes, purple [Col. 0980A] and fine linen garments—I could think of nothing more blessed. Since everyone [Note: “all”], even those who read in schools about contempt for the world, obeyed him; and since he himself, reckoned as the father and lord [Note: “God”] of all, greatly loved and embraced the world—if anyone had then told me that these most beautiful things, which we all admired, ought to be despised, with what expression and what feeling would I have borne it? I should have judged him madder than Orestes and more importunate than Thersites. I thought that nothing could impair the felicity of so great a man.

Yet when I became a man, I heard an account of utterly disgraceful insults spoken to him. Had they been spoken to me, who had nothing, before so great an audience, I should have thought myself half dead. Thus I began to value that immeasurable blessedness less highly. Since very bitter things commonly happen to many worldly men before death, I shall explain what happened to him before his end.

He, who had been justiciar of all England and most greatly feared by everyone, was twice summoned to judgment by the king during the final year of his life through an obscure justiciar, and twice afflicted with most serious loss and disgrace. Such a shock of mind harassed him that, when I was already his archdeacon and reclined beside him at dinner, I saw him shed tears. Asked the reason, he said: “Once, those who stood beside me were dressed in costly clothing. Now the fines imposed by the king, whose favor I have always sought [Note: add “most earnestly”], have compelled them to wear lambskins.”

Thereafter he despaired so greatly of the king’s friendship that, when the outstanding praises which the king had uttered about him in his absence were repeated to him, he sighed and said [Note: “will have said”]: “The king praises none of his men except one whom he wishes utterly to injure [Note: “destroy”].” For King Henry was, if it is permitted to say so, of the utmost vindictiveness and exceedingly [Note: “of mind”] inscrutable.

A few days later, at Woodstock, where the king had appointed an assembly of men and beasts, while the bishop was speaking with the king and the Bishop of Salisbury, who were the greatest men in the kingdom, he was struck by apoplexy. Still alive but speechless, he was carried to his lodging and at once expired in the king’s presence. The great king whom he had always served, whom [Col. 0981A] he had greatly loved and feared, whom he esteemed so highly, in whom he had placed such confidence, was no more valuable to him in his utmost need [Note: add “than”] than a beggar. Observe, therefore, that it was not said without reason: “Cursed is the man who trusts in man and makes flesh his arm” (Jeremiah 17).

Therefore, when boy, adolescent, or young man sees persons who seem blessed, let him consider beforehand [Note: “consider”] how uncertain their end is, and that even in this world they are beginning to wither amid miseries. Bishop Robert was gentle and humble, raising many and casting down no one, father of orphans, delight of his own people; yet he met this end.

I ought also to have dealt with his predecessor Remigius, who came into England with King William and took part in the war; who afterwards received the bishopric of Dorchester [Note: “Dorkecestria”] by the gift of the aforesaid king; who finally transferred the episcopal see from Dorchester [Note: “Dorkeceastria”] to Lincoln; who founded our church, enriched it when founded with various possessions, and made it flourish when enriched with most honorable persons. We speak, to be sure, only of things heard and seen; we did not see him, but we saw all the venerable clerics whom he first installed in the church. [Note: Added: “Of these we shall mention a few briefly.”]

He appointed the reverend priest Ralph dean. He made Reiner, in whose place his nephew Geoffrey still lives, treasurer. Reiner was so devout a man that he often practiced psalmody in the tomb which he had prepared for his own death; becoming accustomed to the house of eternity, he prayed there at length, so that, when he could not pray, he lay there and was visited by God’s mercy. A blessed example of a most illustrious man.

Nor must the priest Hugh, a man worthy of memory, the beginning and as it were the foundation of the Church, be passed over. Osbert succeeded him, a man altogether gracious and beloved. In their place William now stands, a young man of great promise. Guerno became cantor; Ralph now lives as cantor in his place.

Nor do I pass over Albinus of Anjou, my master. His brothers, most honorable men and my companions, possessed a threefold excellence: deepest learning, most conspicuous chastity, and supreme innocence. Yet, by God’s hidden judgment, they were struck by leprosy; but they have now been cleansed by the purgation of death.

Remigius placed seven archdeacons over the seven districts subject to him. He appointed Richard archdeacon of Lincoln; Albert the Lombard succeeded him, William of Bayeux succeeded Albert, and now Robert the younger succeeds them, the richest of all archdeacons in England. Over Cambridge, Huntingdon, and Hertford he set Nicholas, than whom no one was more beautiful in body; nor was his character very unlike his body. When, around the time of his death, the district of Cambridge was separated from our bishopric and received a new bishop, I myself succeeded him as archdeacon of the two remaining districts.

He appointed Nigel archdeacon of Hampshire; Robert [Col. 0982A] succeeded him, and now William, the distinguished nephew of our bishop Alexander [Note: add “nephew”], succeeds them. At Leicester he appointed Ralph; Geoffrey succeeded him, and Walter, a man altogether worthy of praise, succeeded them; now Robert de Querceto, a man worthy of fame, holds the office. At Oxford he appointed Alfred [Note: “Alwred”], whom Walter, a supreme rhetorician, succeeded. At Buckingham he appointed little Alured; Gilbert succeeded him, a most courtly man in verse, prose, and manner. Roger succeeded Gilbert and has now become Bishop of Chester; afterwards came Richard, and now David, brother of the venerable Bishop Alexander, fifth from the first. As seventh archdeacon, at Bedford, he appointed Osbert. Ralph succeeded him and was miserably slain. Hugh succeeded them [Note: third from the first], and now Nicholas, fourth from the first, succeeds him.

Let the other most honorable clerics be left unmentioned, lest I be accused of prolixity. Consider [Note: “it would be considered”], therefore, how the aforesaid venerable persons have been emptied away and will shortly be swallowed even by oblivion [Note: “eternal”]. Indeed, recall in your mind all whom we formerly saw in the right choir and all whom we saw in the left choir. Not one [Note: “now”] remains. They loved what we love, desired what we desire, hoped for what we hope for; death has given them all to oblivion. Let us therefore consider that the same oblivion likewise awaits us. Let us strive with every effort to seek what endures, what is stable, what differs from a dream—indeed, what is something, since these things are nothing.

The second chapter on contempt for the world [Col. 0982C] concerns those whom we have seen reared in the height of pleasures and at last destroyed by the height of miseries. I write by chapters so that, since names and deeds of different persons are scattered and intermingled throughout, the discussion may thereby become more suitable [Note: “more open”] and clear.

We saw William, the king’s son, clothed in silken garments sewn with gold, surrounded by a crowded throng of attendants and guards, shining with an almost heavenly glory. He was the only son of king and queen, and he did not doubt that he would be exalted with the diadem. Indeed, I do not know what gave him a surer hope of future rule than the very possession of the kingdom gave his father; for the father had already passed through a great portion of his reign, while the whole remained yet reserved for the son. The father already thought, in mental anguish, about losing it; the son, wholly intent on possessing it, thought only with joy of having it.

His excessive refinement, however, displeased me and in my mind [Note: “my”] portended his coming ruin; and my mind said: “This one, so delicately nourished [Note: “is nourished”], is being fed for the fire.” Yet he was always swelling with proud thought about his future kingdom and exalted rank. But God said: “Not so the wicked, not so” (Psalm 1).

It therefore happened to him that, instead of a golden crown, his head was split upon sea-cliffs; instead of gilded garments, he rolled naked in the sea; instead of the height of a kingdom, he was buried in the depths of the sea, in the bellies of fishes. This was the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High.

Richard, Earl of Chester, the only son of Earl Hugh, reared in the highest splendor, the excellent heir expected so greatly by his father, still beardless, perished in the same ship and received the same burial. Richard also, the king’s illegitimate son, was splendidly reared by our Bishop Robert and honorably treated by me and others in the same household in which I lived. We admired his character and expected every great thing of him. Yet, when the ship was dashed against rocks while the sea was free of winds, he was snatched away by sudden death and swallowed by the sea.

When William, the king’s nephew—the son, namely, of Robert, Duke of Normandy—had become the sole royal heir and was judged worthy of everyone’s expectation; when by incomparable merit [Col. 0983B] he had acquired the county of Flanders and by unconquerable vigor had defeated Thierry in battle, he perished from a slight wound [Note: “in the hand”]. All who had confidently awaited him as future king and had prejudged anyone at their pleasure were deceived. If I followed individual examples, this letter would become a large volume.

But I do not pass over Simon, our dean, son of our Bishop Robert, whom Robert had fathered while he was chancellor to King William the Great. As befitted him, he was reared royally and, still a boy, became our dean; he was soon advanced to the highest friendship of the king and to courtly dignities. He was quick in intellect, distinguished in speech, handsome in appearance, radiant in favor, young in years, old in prudence—but tainted by the vice of pride. From pride grew envy; from envy, hatred; from hatred, slanders, quarrels, accusations.

Thus he aptly prophesied of himself, saying: “Among courtiers I am introduced like salt among living eels.” For as salt tortures eels, so by his accusations he twisted all who served the king. As the salt upon eels is dissolved by moisture, so he himself was brought to nothing by the breath of all men [Note: “was brought to nothing”]. He understood the first part of this prophecy but did not foresee the second. Yet unknowingly he spoke of himself.

Thus, being at the highest pinnacle of court and kingdom, after some days he fell into the king’s greatest hatred; placed in prison, he is said to have escaped through a latrine and entered, while still young, into exile and misery. Thus in him was plainly fulfilled the prophetic saying: “Those who were reared in saffron have embraced dung” (Lamentations 4). Therefore, when we see noble boys or young men shining in appearance, riches, and favor, let us not value it highly; for they are very often reduced to the greatest miseries. Now [Note: “then”] all the expectation of fools has been dissolved, and that which was nothing will be reduced [Note: “is reduced”] to nothing.

The third treatise will concern contempt for this passing life—would that it could be despised by me as much as my mind desires and its own worth requires—and the wisdom of this world, that is, what is most esteemed in the world. For it is more precious [Col. 0984A] than all the riches of the earth, and all things desired in the world cannot be compared with it. Yet it is written: “The wisdom of this world is foolishness with God” (1 Corinthians 3). I shall pursue [Note: “pursues”] the Apostle’s declaration with examples which we have seen.

Robert, Earl of Meulan, was the wisest of all men engaged in worldly affairs from here to Jerusalem. He was renowned for learning, charming in speech, penetrating in cunning, shrewd in foresight, versatile in intellect, invincible in prudence, profound in counsel, and great in wisdom. By these means he acquired great and various possessions—commonly called “honors” [Note: omitted]—and cities and castles, hamlets and villages, rivers and forests. His honors lay not only in England but also [Note: “but also”] in Normandy [Note: “in”] and France.

Thus, at his pleasure, the kings of France and England were now joined in concord, now fought in discord. If he rose against anyone, that person was crushed and humbled; if he wished to benefit anyone, that person was gloriously exalted. Hence an incredible abundance of treasures flowed to him: gold and silver, gems and costly cloths.

When he was living at the summit of his glorious estate, it happened that another earl seized his betrothed by faction and deceitful force. Therefore, in his old age, his mind disturbed and darkened by distress, he fell into the darkness of grief and did not feel himself cheerful or glad until his death. After days devoted to sorrow [Note: omitted], he fell into the illness that foretold death. The archbishop and priests, when performing for him the purgative office of confession, asked him penitently to restore the lands which he had taken from many by force or trickery and wash away his fault with tears.

He replied: “If I divide in many ways the lands which I have amassed, what will I, miserable man, leave my sons?” The ministers of the Lord replied: “Your former inheritances and the lands you acquired justly will suffice for your sons. Restore the rest, or else you have devoted your soul to Gehenna.” But the earl answered: “I shall hand over everything to my sons; they themselves shall mercifully act for their dead father’s salvation.” After his death, his sons strove more to increase unjustly what had been unjustly amassed than to distribute anything for their country’s [Note: “father’s”] salvation.

It is therefore plain that at the end—where praise is sung—the supreme wisdom of this man came not merely to supreme folly but to blind madness. What should I say of Gilbert, surnamed “Universal,” Bishop of London? In learning he had no equal as far as Rome. He was most learned in the arts, singular and unique in theory, and thus famous and illustrious. Accordingly, while he directed schools at Nevers in France, he was called to the supreme priesthood of London and came at their entreaty [Note: “yielded”]. Received amid great expectation, he began to serve the vice of avarice, seeking much and giving little. At his death he distributed nothing; but King Henry found an infinite abundance of treasure among his possessions. Even the bishop’s boots, [Col. 0985A] filled with gold and silver, were brought into the royal treasury. Thus a man of the highest learning was regarded by all the people as most foolish.

What also of Ranulf [Note: “Randulf”], the king’s chancellor? He was an exceedingly shrewd, astute, and cunning man; yet he turned all the force of his wisdom to disinheriting [Note: “disinherits”] the simple and extorting money. But during these activities he fell into unending illnesses. Then, as though resisting God and conquering nature, he did not cease to pile crime upon crime and to devour those he could. His greed grew with his torment, his deceit with his pain [Note: “pains”], until, when he fell [Note: “would fall”] from his horse, a monk rode over him and he was destroyed by an unusual death.

From the forest of innumerable examples, these instances already given are sufficient for discerning the world’s wisdom—or rather, its deceit.

[Col. 0985B] In the fourth place will be set the prosperity of men of great name, which the Lord Himself declares that He gave to King David in these words: “I have also made for you a great name, like the name of the great men who are on the earth” (2 Kings 2). David, therefore, possessed this prosperity happily; our contemporaries, unhappily. For in these times one does not attain a great name except through the greatest crimes. Thomas, a great prince ruling near Laon in Gaul, was great in name because he was supreme in wickedness. Hostile, therefore, to the surrounding churches, he had reduced them all to his own treasury. If he held anyone prisoner by force or deceit, that person could truly say: “The pains of hell surrounded me” (Psalm 114 [Vulgate]). Human slaughter was his [Col. 0985C] pleasure and glory. Contrary to custom, he put a countess in prison. Cruel and filthy man that he was, by day he inflicted fetters and tortures in order to extort money; by night, rape, in order to mock her. The most cruel men carried her from prison to Thomas’s bed almost every night. From the bed they brought her back to prison every day. Speaking peacefully to his neighbour, he would in his heart, and not without laughter, pierce him with the sword. Thus he more often carried a naked sword beneath his cloak than a sheathed one. All men, therefore, feared, revered, and adored him. His fame spread throughout all Gaul. Day by day his possessions grew, his treasure grew, and servitude grew.

Do you wish to hear the end of this criminal? Mortally wounded by the sword, refusing repentance, and turning his neck away from the body of the Lord, [Col. 0985D] he thus perished, so that one might rightly say:

> This death of yours was fitting to your life.

You have seen Robert of Bellême, who, when this Norman prince was put into prison, was Pluto, Megaera, Cerberus—or whatever more horrible thing can be written. He did not care to ransom captives, but to kill them. As though in play, he put out the eyes of his little son, placed beneath his cloak, with his thumbs. He impaled men and women upon stakes from anus to mouth. The horrible slaughter of human beings was for him food delightful to his soul. Thus he was on everyone’s lips, so that people said proverbially: [Col. 0986A] “The marvels of Robert of Bellême.” At last let us come to the end—that is, to a desirable outcome. He who had tormented others with prison was himself placed by King Henry in perpetual prison; the criminal perished under a long punishment. Though fame had celebrated him so greatly while he lived, no one knew whether he lived or had died in prison, and in silence they remained ignorant of the day of his death. I have described these two among many. I have judged that no further speech should be made concerning a race more dreadful than demons themselves.

Fifth, there shall be a treatment of the highest of men, who stand in human affairs as the most universal genera do in the categories. The kings of the nations are, as it were, God to their subjects. To them all have bound themselves by oath; the stars of heaven seem to serve them. Such is the exaltation of these summits of the world that [Col. 0986B] others cannot be satisfied with looking upon them, and those who live with them are judged to be above other men. Nor is it surprising if crowds of women, of young men, or even frivolous men rush forth to look at them. Yet even wise and sober men of discernment are driven by some enticing grace to behold those whom they have often seen.

What then is it? What can be more pleasant? What more blessed? Yet I should like one of them to speak with you and reveal completely the secrets of his mind. You would judge very differently. While others judge them blessed, they themselves are consumed by pain and racked by fear. No one in their kingdom is their equal in miseries, their equal in crimes. Hence the saying: “A royal estate is criminality.”

King Henry placed his brother and lord Robert in perpetual [Col. 0986C] prison and held him there until he died. He caused the eyes of his nieces to be torn out; he seized many by treachery, killed many deceitfully and covertly, acted often against his oath, and always served greed and avarice. What terrors did he feel when his brother Robert led an army against him from Normandy into England? Terrified, he indeed made peace with him; but during it he caused the foremost nobles to commit perjury, because he broke the peace and seized his brother. What terrors did he suffer when the count of Anjou plundered his castles, while he himself did not dare to advance? What terrors did he suffer when Baldwin, count of Flanders, set Normandy on fire in his very presence, while he himself did not dare to advance? How crushed in spirit was he when his sons, daughters, and [Col. 0986D] nobles were swallowed by the sea? By what anxieties was he destroyed when his nephew William was gaining Flanders and he believed with certainty that he would lose the crown of his kingdom? Yet he was accounted the most blessed of kings. But assuredly he was the most miserable.

What of Philip, king of the French, and his son Louis, who reigned in our own times, “whose god was their belly” (Philippians 3)—or rather, whose belly was their deadly enemy? For they devoured so much that they lost themselves in fatness and could not support their own weight. Philip once died of fatness. Louis, still a young man, is nevertheless already dead through fatness. But what of their prosperity? Was not Philip often defeated by his own people? Was he not often put to flight by persons of the lowest station? Was not Louis driven from the field of March by King Henry, and, as is clear, very frequently routed by his own people?

The king of Norway recently captured his own royal brother in war; he tore out the captive’s eyes, cut off his penis, removed his right foot, beheaded his infant son, and hanged his bishop with a noose. Both kings were equally unhappy.

But you will object: “Why then do you extol King Henry with such great praises in your *History*, whom here you overthrow with such grave accusations?” To this I answer: I called the king great in wisdom, profound in counsel, distinguished in foresight, eminent in arms, exalted in achievements, and singular in riches; [Col. 0987B] and nevertheless all that I have here added is entirely true—and would that it were false. But perhaps you will still say: “He has now reigned thirty-five years, and, if you count them, has experienced far more prosperity than adversity.” Against this I say: indeed, not even a thousandth part of his fortune can be counted as prosperity. For those things which seemed prosperous were always mingled with sorrows. When he defeated the king of France in battle, at the cost of what prolonged disturbance of mind did he gain that brief joy? I say brief, because another army immediately rose up and disturbed him with further fevers of the mind. And if you marvel at the length of his life and reign, a man of God has foretold that he will not reign for two more years. You will therefore soon see the wretched end of a wretched life. Would that, if possible, this might not occur! Yet it will not fail to occur. Do not, then, marvel at these unhappy kings; but regard God alone as blessed, and as the giver of blessed kingdoms to His own.

The sixth and final treatise shall concern the great men of the king’s kingdom, who were recently most powerful and now are powerless. Indeed, they are now nothing; they are nowhere; and, by an almost excessive expression, one may say that they never were. For now scarcely anyone remembers them. All memory of them has begun to perish; soon there will be none; they will come to nothing like running water.

Listen then, dearest Walter, my companion, to this discourse about illustrious men—tedious to hear, although we have seen them with our own eyes. In our time Archbishop Lanfranc shone forth, [Col. 0987D] a philosopher and a man of clear intellect. Anselm succeeded him, philosopher and most holy man. After them we saw Ralph, thought worthy of so great an elevation. Afterwards William sat at Canterbury, whose praises cannot be spoken, because they do not exist. At present Theobald is there, a man worthy of every praise.

In our time there was also Walkelin, bishop of Winchester, whom William Giffard, a most noble man, succeeded. These too have been emptied out and come to nothing. Now Henry, nephew of King Henry, sits in their place; he will become [Col. 0988A] a new kind of monster, composed wholly of integrity and corruption—namely, monk and knight.

In our time Ingulf was bishop of Rochester; after him Ralph; after him Arnulf; then John. All these have been emptied out. Now Ascelin sits there, soon to perish. In our time Maurice, bishop of London, died; after him Richard; after him Gilbert, a great philosopher. Now Robert, a man great in spirit, is there. And these too have been emptied out.

At Bath there were John the physician and Geoffrey. Now Robert sits there; and these are already nothing. At Worcester I saw the most famous Samson; after him Leulf. Now we see Simon there. At Chester we saw Bishop Robert; then another Robert, who was surnamed “Sin.” Now Roger sits there, soon to become nothing. At Norwich Herbert sat, a kindly and learned man whose writings survive. Everard succeeded him, a most cruel man, and for that reason now deposed. William now sits there.

The first bishop of Ely was Hervey, succeeded by Nigel. Osmund was bishop of Salisbury; Roger succeeded him, a man great in secular affairs, now the king’s justiciar. At Exeter Robert, lately dead and long since blind, sat; now his nephew Robert is there. At Chichester Ralph sat; in his place sits Pelochin, a Gnathonian—that is, fawning or parasitical—man, and therefore now deposed. At Durham William sat, who was killed; after him Ranulf, the plunderer who [Col. 0988C] set all England ablaze. Geoffrey succeeded them; William is there at present. We saw Gerard, archbishop of York; after him Thomas; after them Thurstan, wholly praiseworthy; but now William, treasurer of that same church. In our time Remigius was bishop at Lincoln. Robert, a most merciful man, succeeded him. Alexander, a faithful and generous man, succeeded them. So much for bishops.

Did you not see Hugh, count of Chester, and his son Richard, and their successor Ranulf, and now another Ranulf? All these too have been emptied out. You saw the most wicked and most wise man in secular affairs of whom I spoke above, namely Robert, count [Col. 0988D] of Meulan, and now his son Robert, small in praise. Did you not see Henry, count of Warwick, and his son Roger, who is now alive, ignoble in spirit? You saw William, count of Warenne; Robert, count of Bellême; Robert, count of Mortain—of whom we have spoken in the *History of the English*—Simon, count of Huntingdon; Eustace, count of Boulogne; and many others. Their very remembrance is tiresome. Though they appeared most powerful and most worthy of fixed attention, they are now not even worthy to be named. Even the sheep-skin on which their names are painted seems wholly lost, [Col. 0989A] and we cannot find eyes willing to read it through.

This letter is witness: although it concerns the names of men most powerful and most deserving of universal rising in their presence, no one—or scarcely anyone—can read it through. Why should I mention my lord Aldwin, abbot of Ramsey, and his successor Bernard, then Remald, a shrewd but unmerciful man, and now Walter, a refined man? Where are they too? Turald, abbot of Peterborough, Ernulf, Matthias, Godric, John, and Martin—all of whom we saw—have been emptied out and come to nothing.

But you ask why I insert among the dead, and at the end, those who are living, and say that they have already come to nothing. The reason is this: just as the dead have come to nothing, so these too will soon come to nothing; indeed, to speak more freely, they have already done so. For this life of ours, as Cicero says, is death. From the moment you begin to live, you begin to die. I pass over the most distinguished men, namely Ralph Basset and his son Richard, justiciars of all England, Geoffrey Ridel, justiciar of all England, and countless others, to whom not long ago it seemed pleasant to me to devote the service of great diligence; now, however, it seems worthless to devote even the briefest labour of writing to men who are dead.

Consider then, Walter, how much of a nothing this present life is. Since we see that the most powerful men, who have fully attained its riches, have accomplished nothing, let us, lest we too accomplish nothing, seek another path of life, in which we may hope for and attain blessedness. Rise, brother, rise and seek; for in this life you have never found what you sought.

Was not King Alexander, a man, so to speak, more than most powerful, at last destroyed by a little poison? He did not find what he sought. Was not Julius Caesar, a man equally or more powerful, when he had subdued all things, emptied out by daggers? He did not find what he sought. Seek, therefore, that which you may find; seek life after life, for life is not in this life.

O great God, how rightly are we called mortals! For from the moment we live, our death is continuous. That which is called death is the end of our [Col. 0990A] death. Whatever we do, whatever we say, from the moment it has been done or said, immediately dies. Its memory, indeed, like that of a dead person, lives for a while. But when that too has perished, a kind of second death has completely annihilated all our deeds and words. Where is what I did yesterday? Where is what I said? They have come to nothing. Where too is what I did or said on this day last year? They have been swallowed by the eternal death of oblivion.

Let us therefore desire death amid this death, because we shall not escape this death of living except through the death of the body, which is the middle boundary between death and life. But before I had finished this letter, news came that my friend to whom I was writing had yielded to the law of death. O degraded lot of mortals: wretched in being born, miserable in living, harsh in dying! O death, how swiftly you rush down! [Col. 0990B] How unexpectedly you attack! How magnificently you overthrow! May He who is physician after death grant you, Walter, the antidote of His mercy, to attain a life of unbroken health. Now a letter can no longer be sent to you, but only an epitaph: a brief memorial must be written with tears.

> I, Henry, bearing garlands for you, first brought epigrams,  
> Then the contests of Venus, then shoots of grass.  
>
> Now, Walter, I bring you an entire funeral song—  
> Another garland from Henry, who brought three garlands.  
>
> I am half destroyed: my beauty too has perished, and my light;  
> The form and mind of a man, a mind equal in affection.  
>
> [Col. 0990C] A mind accustomed to give great things to men, yet modestly,  
> Seeing that it had bestowed things lesser than its own mind.  
>
> A man’s mind accustomed to prepare things however lofty;  
> Yet, though it prepares much, it fears small gifts.  
>
> A man’s mind accustomed to give with festive countenance,  
> And to double the gift with equal joy.  
>
> A man’s mind accustomed so to give that gifts need not be requested,  
> Anticipating the spoken request, with both hands bearing them.  
>
> That supreme man had nothing middling, nothing equal to great things.  
> May God’s highest grace and welcome rest be his.

### Textual and editorial notes to the foregoing Latin text

- [Col. 0985] After “King David,” *suo* means “his own.” At “Thomas’s bed,” the reading is *Thomae* (“of Thomas”); *referebatur* means “she was brought back.” At “All men, therefore,” the variant is *ergo omnes* (“therefore all [men]”); at “his possessions,” *ei* means “to him / his.”
- [Col. 0985] At Robert’s imprisonment, *carcerem* is “prison”; at the blinding of his son, *extraxit* is “drew out [the eyes],” rather than merely “put out.” At the conclusion, *ipsis* means “themselves”: “more dreadful than the demons themselves.”
- [Col. 0985–0986] The note *desunt* at the reference to the crowds looking upon kings means that words are absent in the witness. At “their equal in crimes,” *nemo* is “no one.”
- [Col. 0985–0987] Before “killed many,” *desunt* again records omitted words; *sacramenta* is the plural “oaths.” At the question concerning Baldwin, *deest* records an omission. At “To this I answer,” *quod* means “which / to which.”
- [Col. 0987] *Enim* means “indeed”; *inspexerimus* means “we may have seen.” The spelling *Walkelinus* is retained for Walkelin. After “Henry, nephew of King Henry,” *deest* records missing text.
- [Col. 0987–0988] The Rochester bishop’s name also appears as *Ernulfus*; the successor “soon to perish” is *Ascelinus*. At Bath the place-name also appears as *Badae*; at Worcester the name is *Teulfum* rather than *Leulfum*. At Salisbury, the note gives *Jocelinus* in place of Roger as the king’s justiciar. At Exeter, *item Robertus* means “likewise / another Robert.” The Chichester place-name also appears as *Siceastria*.
- [Col. 0987–0989] Eustace is explicitly *consulem*, “count,” and Meulan appears as *Mellent*. After Bernard, *deest* records an omission; *autem* means “however / now”; and *desunt* records omitted words in “Where are they too?” Ralph’s surname also appears as *Basseth*. The supplementary reading is: “and Geoffrey Ridel, justiciar of all England.” *Constamenti* means “of great constancy” (the main text has the corrupt-looking *custamenti*); *deest* records omitted words after “seemed.”
- [Col. 0989] The alternative *dicimur* means “we are called,” rather than *dicimus*, “we call [ourselves].” *Morte* is “by / through death,” rather than *mortem*, “death.” *Inopinate* means “unexpectedly.”
- [Col. 0989–0990] In the poem, *gramina* means “blades or shoots of grass,” in place of *germina*, “shoots / buds”; *viri* means “of a man,” in place of *viris*, “to men”; and *pudibunde* means “modestly,” in place of *pudibunda*, “modest.”

## In the Year of the Lord 1168: Odo of Deuil, Abbot of Saint-Denis

[Col. 0991]

## Historical and Literary Notice

(*Literary History of France*, by the Benedictine religious, XII, 614)

[Col. 0991A] Odo, or Eudes, was born at Deuil, in the valley of Montmorency. [Note: *Gallia Christiana*, new edition, vol. VII, col. 377.] Having become a monk at the abbey of Saint-Denis, he distinguished himself there by his good conduct, prudence, and talents. His abbot Suger introduced him at court and secured for him the honour of accompanying King Louis the Younger to the Holy Land as secretary and chaplain. The monarch had every reason to be pleased with this choice, as one of his letters to Suger, written during the journey, testifies. [Note: Félibien, *History of Saint-Denis*, documents, no. 138.] On his return, Odo was placed at the head of the new community which the abbot of Saint-Denis established in 1150 at the abbey of Saint-Corneille at Compiègne. Suger having died in the following year, every vote fell upon Odo to replace him. Shortly after his election, [Col. 0991B] he became the target of calumny and needed the support of Saint Bernard to repel it. [Note: St Bernard, Letters 285, 286, 287.] The holy man wrote three letters on his behalf to Pope Eugenius III, whom Odo himself, as is probable, went to see in person. He was known to the pope from two journeys that he had already made to Rome: the first in 1149, on returning from the Holy Land in the retinue of the king of France; the second in 1150, to obtain confirmation of the reform of the abbey at Compiègne.

After overcoming the enemies of his reputation, he had to contend with those who attacked the property of his monastery. [Note: Doublet, *History of Saint-Denis*, p. 194.] Among them was the archbishop of Bourges, whose enterprises [Col. 0991C] obliged our abbot to take the road to Rome again at the beginning of 1153. Henry of France, bishop of Beauvais, raised against him a new dispute on similar interests; Pope Adrian IV referred its judgment to the bishop of Paris. [Note: *Gallia Christiana*, ibid.]

Odo’s firmness in defending the temporal possessions of his house did not arise from avarice and [Col. 0992A] greed. When occasion demanded, he gave proofs of disinterestedness and generosity; witness his donation of the land of Froyères to the abbeys of Ourscamp and Châalis. [Note: *Ibid.*] The king continued to show him the favour that he had bestowed upon his predecessor, although he does not appear to have admitted him to the affairs of government. There survives a charter of that prince in which he calls him his friend, while granting the abbey of Saint-Denis the right to hold an annual market at Saint-Clair-sur-Epte in the French Vexin. [Note: Félibien, *History of Saint-Denis*, documents, no. 141, p. 109.] Scholars, among whom Odo could take his place, likewise sought his friendship. John Sarrazin dedicated to him his translation of the works of Saint Denis. [Note: *Catalogue of English Manuscripts*, part I, no. 3614.] He died in [Col. 0992B] 1162 and was succeeded by Eudes of Taverny.

During the journey to the Holy Land, Odo did not confine himself to the duties he performed beside the king. A witness on the road to many memorable events, he hastened, as soon as he arrived at Antioch, to transmit their memory to posterity. He did this in an account divided into seven books or booklets, which he addressed in the form of a letter to his abbot Suger. [Note: Chifflet, *Saint Bernard, Gallic Illustrious Men*, pp. 9–77.]

The first book contains what occurred from the proclamation of the Second Crusade to the king’s departure. The second describes the march of the crusaders until their entry into Bulgaria. The third brings them from there to Constantinople. [Col. 0992C] The crossing of the arm of Saint George and their entry into Romania form the subject of the fourth book. The fifth recounts the disasters that befell the army of the German crusaders on the road from Nicomedia to Antioch, and its forced return toward Constantinople. The sixth concerns the various adventures experienced by the army of Louis the Younger from Nicomedia to Satalia. Finally, [Col. 0993A] the seventh presents the reasons which led that prince to embark, the circumstances of this embarkation, and his arrival at Antioch. The work ends there.

Here are now circumstances of this account that have escaped our modern historians.

When Louis undertook the expedition to the Holy Land, he wrote letters to the emperor of Germany and to the emperor of Constantinople, requesting passage through their territories, markets along the road for provisions, and banks for exchanging coined money. The Greek emperor sent the king of France a basely flattering answer: lavishing upon him the most excessive praises, he promised more than had been requested. When this response was read in the parliament at Étampes, the ambassadors of the king of Sicily, who were present, declared that no faith should be placed in it, since, they said, experience and history had shown them the deceitfulness of the Greeks. The assembly paid no heed to this warning, supposing that it was prompted by the Sicilians’ aversion to the Greeks, with whom they were then at war. Thereupon the ambassadors withdrew, groaning and predicting the misfortunes that occurred.

When the king had reached Worms with his army, he crossed the Rhine there on a great number of boats which Emperor Conrad had prepared for him. They halted on the other bank of the river to await the [Col. 0993C] English and Norman troops, led by Arnulf, bishop of Lisieux.

> “It was there,” says our author, “that the folly of our people began to show itself. The city sent us abundant provisions by the Rhine, and our people traded continually with those of the country. Unfortunately, this good understanding did not last. A quarrel arose on the water between the former and the latter. Our men threw a local merchant into the Rhine. Immediately the inhabitants of Worms ran to arms; among several of ours whom they wounded, they killed one. This outrage spread fury among the crusaders: they shouted that the city must be set on fire, without considering that this [Col. 0993D] disaster would involve several of our merchants and money-changers established at Worms. But the prudent persons in our army restrained these madmen. The townsmen, however, still seized by fear, withdrew their boats and thereby cut off all commerce with us. But the bishop of Arras, Alvise, having with difficulty found a boat, went to the city with several barons and succeeded in calming their minds. Then, having brought back their boats, they restored abundance to our camp.”

On leaving Worms, the crusaders divided because their excessive numbers had caused food to become costly. Some went toward the Alps; others, led by the king, took the [Col. 0994A] road to Regensburg in order to cross the Danube there. Ambassadors of the eastern emperor awaited the French monarch in that city, near which he pitched camp. Odo thus describes the ceremony of the audience he gave them:

> “When the tents had been pitched and the king lodged, the ambassadors were summoned. After greeting him and delivering the letters of their master, they awaited the reply standing; for they would not have dared sit down unless ordered to do so. When they had received the order, therefore, they took their places on seats which they had brought with them. We then noticed a Greek custom: whenever their masters sit, all their retinue remains standing. There you might have seen young men with legs tensed, heads bent, and eyes silently fixed upon their masters, showing by this posture their readiness to obey at the first sign. They wear no sashes, but rich silk garments, short and closely fitted, with narrow sleeves; this makes them nimble and unencumbered like athletes. The clothing of the poor has the same form, differing only in cost. As for the letters which they presented, two reasons—shame and inability—prevent me from giving their translation here. For the first and greatest part was devoted to winning the prince’s favour in so base and cringing a manner that its affectionate and wholly insincere expressions, far from befitting an emperor, would have dishonoured the vilest buffoon … The king nevertheless, though not without blushing, permitted his interpreter to render it all to him.”

Odo then discusses the second part, which contained the terms upon which the emperor offered passage through his lands and the necessary assistance to the crusaders.

Having arrived in Bulgaria, the French crusaders were not slow to perceive the perfidy of the Greeks. Their ill-treatment of them is well known.

> “Yet it appeared to some of our people,” says Odo, “that the Germans who went before us had given occasion for it, since, not content with plundering everything they encountered on their march, they had even, as we observed, burned certain villages and suburbs. Here is an example of their brutality, which I report with grief. Near the walls of Philippopolis the Latins occupied a considerable borough, where foreigners could obtain provisions in abundance for their money. The Germans made the stay they made there memorable to their shame. As they were scattered through the inns, a juggler came in; and although he did not know their language, he sat down among them, drank, and paid his share. Afterwards, wishing to entertain the company, he drew from his breast a snake that he had charmed, placed it in a cup upon the pavement, and performed several conjurer’s tricks around the reptile. At sight of this marvel, the Germans [Col. 0995A] rose in fury, seized the juggler, and massacred him.
