At the same time they cried that the Greeks were trying to destroy them by poison, attributing the crime of one man to all. This disturbance spread alarm throughout the suburb. The commander of the city arrived to calm the tumult, with an unarmed escort. The eyes of the Germans, clouded by fury and wine, saw only men running toward them and did not perceive that they were unarmed. In anger they went out to meet these peacemakers, imagining that they had come to avenge the murder which the Germans had committed. The officer and his troop immediately withdrew and returned to the city. But after taking up their bows, they came back against these madmen, put them to flight, wounded and killed [Col. 0995B] several of them, and did not stop until they had driven them all from the suburb. The slaughter took place especially in the inns. Care was taken of the corpses because of the money with which they were furnished, and they were thrown into caverns to be searched at leisure. Nor did the quarrel end there. The defeated men, having recovered their wits, returned in force to the attack, in turn put the townsmen to flight, ravaged the countryside around the city, and reduced the suburb to ashes.” [Note: Nicetas relates much the same thing: book I of the *History of Emperor Manuel*, chapter 5.]

> “Moreover, it was not only to their hosts that the Germans made themselves unbearable; our people had almost equal cause to complain of them. The following fact proves it. One day several Frenchmen, to avoid the crowd surrounding the king, went ahead and lodged near the Germans. Both sides went to market; but the Germans would not allow our men to buy anything until they themselves had obtained what they wanted. This gave rise to a dispute. There was much shouting on both sides; and, as they did not understand one another, blows soon followed. The French, who were fewer in number, suffered the worse treatment. The fighting ended only at nightfall. The next day they were ready to begin again; but the leaders, throwing themselves at the soldiers’ knees, calmed the disturbance by their prayers and moderation. Thus the Germans disturbed everything along their route and disposed the Greek nation [Col. 0995D] against our king, who was following them in a spirit of peace.”

Shortly afterward, Odo reports another example of their brutality.

> “After overcoming various obstacles, they arrive,” he says, “at the gates of Constantinople. Near that city was a vast and magnificent park enclosed by walls, containing a great quantity of game, ponds, and other waters. Several caverns had been dug there as shelters for the animals. Within this park rose splendid houses, where the emperors came to rest during the fair season. [Col. 0996A] The emperor of Germany, instead of respecting this abode of delights, threw himself into it at the head of his men, slaughtered the game, and destroyed nearly everything before the eyes of the Greeks. For the imperial palace, which commands the walls of the city, has this place beneath it; and by the continual gaze of its master it enlivens and encourages those who inhabit it. Nevertheless, the Greek emperor, to whom this strange spectacle had caused the greatest astonishment, had enough command of himself to conceal his indignation. He sent a delegation to the German emperor to ask for a conference. But the latter feared to enter the city, while the former feared to leave it—or did not wish to do so; each refused to make the first advance [Note: There was nevertheless an interview between these two [Col. 0996D] princes, which was rather cold, although they were brothers-in-law.] or to relax his customary magnificence [Col. 0996B] for the other’s sake.”

Louis was not so scrupulous concerning ceremony.

> “When we approached Constantinople,” says Odo, “the nobles and the most distinguished persons among clergy and people came to meet the king and received him with fitting honours. They begged him to condescend to visit the emperor, in order, they said, to satisfy his eagerness to see and speak with him. Louis, taking pity on his fear, granted this request. Having therefore chosen a small number of his own men, he advanced with them toward the imperial palace. There he found the emperor waiting under the portico and giving him a reception of which he could only be pleased. These two princes were nearly equal in age and stature, differing only in character and dress. Finally, after embracing and kissing one another, they entered the inner hall of the palace, where they sat upon two seats prepared for them. Surrounded there by their retinues, they began conversation through their interpreters. The emperor asked the king what his purpose was, made a thousand wishes for its success, and promised him assistance in everything within his power. Would to God that his speech had been as sincere as it was courteous! If ease of bearing and gesture, serenity of countenance, and gentleness of speech always revealed the dispositions of the heart, [Col. 0996D] all those present would unanimously have said that the emperor felt the tenderest affection for the king. But it is only too well known how equivocal such demonstrations are. Afterwards the two princes parted, and the nobles conducted ours to the palace in which he was to lodge.”

The description our author gives of the city of Constantinople deserves to be placed before our readers. “Constantinople,” he says, “distinguished by its renown, and still more by its riches, has in its layout the form of a triangle or a ship’s sail. At the inner angle [Col. 0997A] rise the church of Holy Wisdom and the palace of Constantine, where there is a chapel adorned with a great number of relics. The sea washes the city on two sides. As we approached this capital, we had on our right the arm of Saint George, and on our left a channel issuing from it and extending for about four thousand paces. There stands the palace of Blachernae, situated indeed in a low place, but raised in distinction by the magnificence, elegance, and grandeur of its buildings. The threefold variety of its surroundings affords a threefold pleasure to the eyes of its inhabitants, recreating them in turn with the sight of fields, sea, and city. The magnificence of its exterior scarcely admits comparison. But whatever I might say [Col. 0997B] of the splendour within would fall far short of the truth. Gold and paintings gleam everywhere. The court is paved with marble in marvellous workmanship; and, to speak truly, I do not know whether the subtlety of the art or the richness of the materials gives it greater worth and beauty. The third side of the triangle formed by the city borders upon fairly pleasant countryside. It is enclosed by a double wall, extending from the sea to the palace, about two miles in length. Yet this wall is not strong, nor are the towers defending it lofty. I think the city places its chief confidence in the multitude of its inhabitants and in the peace it has long enjoyed.

[Col. 0997C] “The ground adjoining the ramparts is unoccupied and divided into arable land and gardens, which supply every sort of vegetable. On this same side subterranean aqueducts bring an abundance of fresh water to the citizens. But the city itself is ill-kept, filthy, foul-smelling, and in many quarters condemned to perpetual night. For the rich overhang the streets with their buildings, leaving the poor and strangers nothing but refuse and darkness. Murders, thefts, and other crimes that shun the light are frequent there; and this must be so, since there are nearly as many masters as rich men, and as many thieves as poor men. Every villain has cast off all fear and shame, because crime is [Col. 0997D] unpunished there and darkness conceals it from public vengeance. In short, Constantinople exceeds the bounds of moderation in everything; and as it surpasses all other cities in wealth, so too it surpasses them in vices.

“It has many churches which, though inferior to Holy Wisdom in size, perhaps do not yield to it in beauty. Those among our people who could do so entered them, some out of curiosity, others to satisfy their devotion. The king himself visited them, accompanied by the emperor; and upon his return, overcome by the latter’s entreaties, he agreed to dine with him. The display of the meal, the delicacy and variety of the dishes, the pleasures of the music—all befitted the dignity of the guests, and all delighted at once [Col. 0998A] the eyes, ears, and palate. Several of our people feared for the king. But he, entrusting himself to Providence, was perfectly secure. For he who has no evil design does not readily believe that anyone wishes him harm . . . Yet the Greeks concealed the vengeance they were preparing for us until we had crossed the arm of Saint George.

“As long as we were in the neighbourhood of Constantinople, we had no cause to complain of them. For they were not blamed for shutting their gates against the multitude of crusaders, since the latter had burned several of their houses and olive trees, whether through lack of firewood or through drunkenness. The king often had the guilty men’s noses, ears, and even [Col. 0998B] feet cut off; but this was incapable of restraining the insolence of our people. In brief, one of two things had to be done: either thousands of them had to be put to death at once, or many of their outrages had to be tolerated.”

After crossing the strait, the imprudence of the French soon gave the Greeks an occasion to make their ill will against them plain. “We have crossed over,” says our author. “Ships laden with provisioners and money-changers follow in our wake. The bank is open on the shore. The treasures are displayed; gold and silver vessels which the Greeks had bought from us gleam upon the counters. Several men from [Col. 0998C] our army come to make the necessary exchanges; and others join them who covet what does not belong to them. One day it happened that, at the sight of these immense riches, a certain Fleming, deserving the whip and fire, allowed himself to be blinded by an unbridled desire to carry them off. Suddenly, crying, ‘Havo, havo!’ he rushed upon the treasures and carried away what had most tempted him. Men like him, emboldened by his audacity and attracted by the worth of the booty, were not slow to imitate him; and, as fools thrust themselves everywhere—for I count as such all who perished in the affair of the money-changers—those with money in hand were seen falling under blows from every side. The cries redoubled; fury increased; the [Col. 0998D] counters were overturned; gold was trampled underfoot and plundered. The poor, stripped money-changers sought safety in flight; the ships received the fugitives and brought back to the city those who had been buying provisions for us. These were beaten and despoiled by the Greeks. In the city itself, all foreigners found there suffered a like outrage and were treated as enemies.

“The king, informed of these disorders, summoned the count of Flanders and angrily demanded from him the culprit, whom he had hanged in sight of Constantinople. Then he set about recovering what had been lost, promising pardon to those who restored it; and, lest anyone be deterred by fear or shame from appearing before him, he ordered [Col. 0999A] that everything be handed over to the bishop of Langres. On the following day those who had fled were recalled and recovered all that they swore they had lost. Several of them demanded much more than was due to them. But Louis preferred to restore it from his own resources rather than disturb the tranquillity of his army. After this he sent two eminent men as envoys to the Greek emperor: Arnoul, bishop of Lisieux, distinguished for eloquence and piety; and Bartholomew, his chancellor. Their purpose was to demand the return of his people detained at Constantinople, together with the goods taken from them.

“Since the monarch’s orders were urgent, the two ambassadors crossed over very early in the morning and, through the favour of the ushers, [Col. 0999B] entered the palace; but they could not obtain an audience with the idol. That day all their consolation was conversation with one another, their food the feasting of their eyes upon the paintings; and when night came, the palace steps and pavement served them as pillow and mattress. On the following day, when this profane man—the emperor—had risen about the third hour, they appeared before him by his command and discharged their mission, setting before him the satisfaction that had been made to his people and that which he owed to ours. The bishop’s wise and gentle eloquence might have made him tractable, if that dangerous serpent had been susceptible to enchantment. But, deaf and swollen with poison like an asp, he appeared altogether different from what he had formerly been; or rather, he lifted the [Col. 1000A] mask under which he had hitherto concealed his malice. Nevertheless, the bishop pressed him and at last gained something: markets for the army were promised, and our detained pilgrims were permitted to rejoin the army, though without restoration of what had been taken from them. The emperor said that he wished to confer once more with the king and that he would send him an embassy concerning this as soon as possible. Thereupon the bishop and chancellor resolved to return, so as not to keep a fast for three whole days.” The rest is known.

These are the chief anecdotes we have found in this account. One might blame modern historians who have treated the crusades expressly for failing to collect these facts, or for touching on them too lightly. Most of them, it is true, do not redound to the crusaders’ praise; but history is not a legal pleading in which one speaks only in exculpation of one party and accusation of the other. Our author understood better the impartiality essential to this kind of writing. His account is almost a model in this respect. It is moreover composed with much order, good judgment, and clarity. Its style is vigorous, easy, and even elegant, as far as it could be in the twelfth century.

We owe the publication of this work to Father Chifflet, a Jesuit, who placed it at the head of his book entitled *The Noble Lineage of Saint Bernard Vindicated*.

[Col. 0999]

**THE WORK OF ODO OF DEUIL, WHO HIMSELF TOOK PART, ON THE EXPEDITION TO THE EAST OF LOUIS VII, KING OF THE FRANKS, SURNAMED THE YOUNGER, DIVIDED INTO SEVEN BOOKS.**

(See *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXXV, col. 1201, among the Appendices to the Works of St Bernard of Clairvaux.)

**A.D. 1168. BERTRAND DE BLANCFORT, MASTER OF THE TEMPLARS**

[Col. 0999]

**[LETTERS TO LOUIS.]**

(His letters to Louis the Younger appear in *Patrologia*, vol. CLV, col. 1269, among the *Documents concerning the Holy War*.)

**A.D. 1167. WOLBERO, ABBOT OF ST PANTALEON AT COLOGNE, OF THE ORDER OF ST BENEDICT.**

[Col. 1001]

## NOTICE

(R. P. Henry Gravius, Prolegomena to Wolbero, from a very ancient tablet preserved in manuscript in the monastery of St Pantaleon within Cologne.)

Wolbero was chosen twelfth abbot of the monastery of St Pantaleon in the year 1147, after the Reverend Father Gerard, worn out by old age, had resigned the pastoral staff in the presence of the Right Reverend Arnold, the first archbishop of that name, and the priors of the monastery. He was distinguished for talent and eloquence, being a man most devoted to the study of the divine Scriptures and, in secular learning, the most learned of his age. He wrote for sacred virgins of the Benedictine observance, serving God and blessed Mary on the island of the Rhine, four books on the *Song of Songs*, by which he left the memory of his name to posterity. He died in the year of the Lord 1167, on 9 April, under Alexander III, Roman pontiff of that name, Rainald, archbishop of Cologne, and Emperor Frederick I, after presiding for twenty-one years. He was buried beneath the chapel of St Margaret, virgin and martyr, as this epitaph attests:

> Here I have laid down the remains of my body for burial,  
> And beneath the sheltering protection of gracious Mary I hope for aid,  
> At whose shrine I built the sacred roof;  
> May there be rest for my soul; may there be full remission of guilt.

[Col. 1001]

## MOST ANCIENT AND PROFOUND COMMENTARIES ON SOLOMON’S SONG OF SONGS, CALLED IN HEBREW *SHIR HA-SHIRIM*, DIVIDED INTO FOUR BOOKS

By the Reverend Lord Wolbero, Abbot of St Pantaleon within Cologne, of the Order of St Benedict; now for the first time arranged in a better order for the benefit of preachers, and illustrated with notes and a copious index, through the work of the Reverend Father Henry Gravius, Bachelor of Sacred Theology, of the same Benedictine Order.  
(Cologne, at the expense of Michael Demen, bookseller under the sign of the Name of Jesus, 1630, with the permission of superiors.)

> Those who work through me shall not sin, and those who make me known shall have eternal life.  
> —Ecclesiasticus 24

## DEDICATORY EPISTLE

[Col. 1001] To the most reverend Father in Christ, the venerable Lord Henry Spichernagell, abbot of St Pantaleon and [Col. 1002] most worthy principal president of the Holy Bursfeld Union; and likewise to the most reverend and eminent [Col. 1003A] Lords Henry Libler, John Munch, Paul Vrechen, Henry Goermann, and Gabel Scaffen, most worthy abbots of the monasteries of the Order of St Benedict of the same observance at St Martin’s, Brauweiler, Deutz, Gladbach, and Grafschaft—his honoured lords and prelates.

Your most reverend and eminent Lordships will not without reason wonder why this commentator on Solomon’s *Song of Songs* lay hidden so long under a bushel and now sees the light for the first time. To this I might perhaps reply with the Jew Mordecai addressing his beloved Esther: “And who knows whether you have come to the kingdom for such a time as this?”—that this Wolbero might be brought forth at such a time. Therefore I judged that it was not enough for my soul alone if such an author, written in the house of St Pantaleon, merely lay concealed [Col. 1003B], unless, brought to the anvil and made available for the benefit and spiritual delight of very many, he should emerge opportunely into the light on some new occasion.

“And what,” you will say, “is this occasion?” It is now the third year since, at the annual chapter held in the monastery of St Pantaleon on the Kalends of September, sacred to blessed Abbot Giles, your consecrated heads also were newly adorned with the pontifical mitre. I can surely neither express nor set down in writing how much joy this brought your dearest brethren; nor how much gladness I myself felt, both personally and on the public’s behalf, and how earnestly I wished to congratulate you once I had learned that our most holy lord [Col. 1003C] Urban VIII had added this episcopal authority to your most reverend Lordships, and that the Right Reverend bishop of Cyrene had, in solemn rite, placed pontifical mitres upon your heads. For why should I not congratulate your Lordships upon so holy, honourable, and new a glory? A glory, I say, with which you have been endowed and honoured, beyond all ambition, as I am persuaded, solely by the merit of your most illustrious virtues—for you are numbered among the chief pillars of our holy Bursfeld Union, and by your steadfast support make it firm.

[Col. 1003D] What was I to do? Filial love demanded that I go down to acclaim this new honour of my reverend lord prelate; gratitude required that I come forth likewise to reverence the mitres of your most reverend Lordships; the examples of others urged me on. But I did not wish to appear empty-handed before the presence of the chief priests, nor did I have at hand a gift to offer. Then suddenly, by God’s inspiration, I remembered this commentator Wolbero, your fellow abbot; and I was delighted. Since many religious had previously been drawn by reading his most delightful interpretations and had deeply grieved with me that such devout and profound commentaries should lie hidden among the other furnishings of our library, and that so great a treasure should not be shared with more persons, I confidently undertook, in order to attest my readiness [Col. 1004A] and desire to merit the favour of your most reverend Lordships—a desire I had long cherished—to publish it. I not only revised the commentaries of our Wolbero, but also arranged them, once revised, in a better order; and, having thus arranged and renewed them, I left no stone unturned to have them printed and dedicated to the names of your most reverend Lordships.

Yet, since, as Solomon himself testifies, there is no end to making many books, and since the minds of this age usually favour new works more than old, I perhaps had cause to fear that either the antiquity of this commentator or, rather, the insignificance of my own person—by whom the book had been somewhat renewed—might be an obstacle to its successful circulation among many hands. [Col. 1004B] But encouraged by the authority of your most reverend Lordships, I judged that I should readily free myself from such fear, indeed from the detraction of all Zoiluses, who are never absent from good undertakings: both because the Lord’s storehouse and granary do not always receive the hundredfold or sixtyfold fruit, but more often the thirtyfold; and because, protected by your Aaronic horns, it may return from the prelate after the same period of the year has elapsed in which your abbatial hoods were changed into pontifical mitres.

Therefore, most reverend lord president, my most honoured prelate, receive this undertaking of your least client, added to my pastoral cares and hitherto prolonged by the obstruction of various military incursions; and, because according to the saying [Col. 1004C] of the Wise Man, “A man who loves wisdom gladdens his father” (Prov. 29), gladden through this effort of mine your spirit in the wisdom and spiritual song of this book, and refresh your weak and aged limbs, wearied though not broken by the many labours you have borne for the monastery and our Bursfeld Union. Receive it also, venerable prelates, as a slight token of my devotion toward you: your fellow abbot Wolbero, humbly dedicated by me to your most reverend Lordships. May he share in your new honour, since he was an outstanding transmitter of the ancestral monastic observance. I shall continually pray God, best, greatest, and most holy, our lawgiver Benedict and the patrons of his Order that it may grow and spread under you as prelates, increasing the spiritual discipline you have begun. [Col. 1004D] May He also deign, in His most patient goodness, to preserve your most reverend and eminent Lordships, with all committed to you, alive, safe, and well for as long and as happily as possible. Thus he cherishes and prays from the pastoral charge of Laugel, in the very year of Blessed Abbot Giles, 1629.

Of your most reverend and eminent Lordships, humble servant and brother,  
**Henry Ersmers of Gravius, Pantaleonite, of the Order of St Benedict.**

## EPIGRAM TO THE AUTHOR AND READER OF THESE COMMENTARIES

[Col. 1005]

[Col. 1005A]

> That you, most learned writer, may outlive the years of Nestor,  
> And that your fame may be known in every place,  
> It seemed fitting to many, not without praise to you,  
> To commit this excellent work to the press.  
>
> Therefore come forth without fear, Wolbero; it is not fitting  
> That writings so devout, born of your genius, should lie hidden.  
> Whoever is now touched by sweet love for composing songs  
> [Col. 1006A] Has, behold, Wolbero as his guide in composing them.  
>
> The Theban poet did not compose such songs  
> When the boar leapt at the touch of his lyre.  
> You deserve praise, Wolbero: he sings of a chaste life  
> When he recounts the mystical words of bridegroom and bride.  
>
> Go now, whoever loves the union of the soul and Christ:  
> Behold, here is the paranymph, the bridegroom’s friend, by whom you may be joined.

## BROTHER HENRY GRAVIUS TO THE BENEVOLENT READER

Although the commentaries of the venerable Lord Abbot Wolbero were once written and dedicated by their author at the request of devout virgins consecrated to God, and although he wished them to remain concealed with nuns alone and not come into public view unless someone had corrected them into a finished and masculine work, I would not have you, kindly reader, suppose that through my labour you have obtained precisely this result. For this is the great and splendid virtue of those who think humbly of themselves: to do or write great things while nevertheless holding a low and modest opinion of themselves and their works. Our abbot Wolbero shines forth in this kind of virtue in no ordinary degree. Although his commentaries are very ancient and were compiled through the unremitting study of nine years, I found nothing in them that was unformed, feminine, or in need of a more polished file—though in his dedication addressed to his religious sisters and in other prefaces to this work he seems to suggest this very thing. Rather, this little work ought deservedly to appear conceived by a divine rather than a human spirit and traced with the pen.

Therefore I would not have any future reader of this work remain unaware that I have added or mixed into these commentaries very little of my own, except where ambiguity of sense, disruption of periods, or the separation of verses seemed to require something of the kind. These were perhaps points that might have offended a fastidious reader in ancient Wolbero. Although my labour and effort have sufficiently remedied them, some errors have crept in here and there through the carelessness or haste, I know not which, of printer or corrector. They may be seen corrected at the end of this book. Receive this labour of mine, such as it is, favourably; while you enjoy it, accept it for your own benefit, and kindly accept this enduring memorial of its author. Farewell.

[Note: [Col. 1005] This new edition, purged of many errors of typography and correction, may be consulted with confidence and profit. —Editor.]

## DEDICATORY EPISTLE OF ABBOT WOLBERO

[Col. 1005B] To his most beloved sisters, serving God and blessed Mary on the Island of the Rhine, Wolbero, a sinner.

As I often considered with myself and repeatedly pondered in an uncertain mind what sweet, pleasant, and useful thing I might sing into the inward ears of your holy charity, O most holy sisters—something whose sweetness and encouragement might raise your minds to greater love of the heavenly life—there suddenly occurred to me that sung marriage-song of bridegroom and bride which, because of its excellence, is called the *Song of Songs*. For this kind of song is particularly suited to the dignity of your profession, because your vocation surpasses every order of profession just as that song surpasses every kind of song.

[Col. 1006B] There are indeed three kinds of profession: one of married persons, another of widows, and a third of virgins. We read of a song of praise, a song of joy, and a new song. Let us therefore assign, as it were by certain steps, the song of praise to married persons, the song of joy to widows, and the new song to virgins—the song which no one can sing except those who follow the Lamb wherever he goes (Rev. 14). Married persons sing the song of praise when they have embraced some beginning of religion and good conduct but have not yet escaped the tribulation of the flesh. Widows, however, sing the song of joy, since they have attained something higher, excel in greater religious devotion, and, having already experienced and been freed from the tribulation of the flesh, can therefore [Col. 1007A] sing both praise and joy. Virgins, moreover, sing the new song: they retain the highest degree, never having experienced the aforesaid tribulation of the flesh, and therefore are able to sing praise, joy, and a singular newness inexpressible to others.

But those called virgins must give very careful attention to which division they belong. For the Lord divided this profession into two parts: wise and foolish virgins (Matt. 25). This new song can be sung only by those belonging to the wise; and wise are those who are virgins both in body and mind, whereas foolish are those who, although virgins in body, nevertheless live with corrupted minds. Such women plainly cannot sing [Col. 1007B] the new song, nor even the song of the final profession; they do not attain its merit, because they have no oil in their vessel. Indeed, because of this neglect of themselves, they do not enter the bridegroom’s chamber.

Therefore your charity must pay close attention and be watchful: you who are virgins in body must also be virgins in mind. Virginity of the flesh profits you nothing if you have already married in mind. If, then, you maintain the right rule of the virginal profession, you sing a singular song—indeed, as I may say, not simply a song, as married women and widows do, but the *Song of Songs*. It is possible for those alone to sing it who stand before God’s throne without stain, because they have not defiled their garments (Rev. 14), that is, [Col. 1007C] their bodies.

The authorities for these three professions are found in sacred Scripture: marital chastity is commended in Elizabeth, widowed holiness in Anna, and virginal perfection in blessed Mary, Mother of God. The Lord himself shows the merit of each in the Gospel, where the seed is said to have fallen on good ground and borne fruit—some thirtyfold, some sixtyfold, and some a hundredfold (Luke 8).

The thirtyfold fruit belongs to married persons living chastely. The counting of the fingers signifies this number when the index finger is placed over the thumb, indicating the burden of their tribulation and abasement, deprived of the manly support and consolation of widows. [Col. 1007D] The hundredfold number, however, which stands for perfection, signifies the perfection of holy virgins: transferred from the left hand to the right, with the tip of the index finger joined to the tip of the thumb, it forms the crown of virginity.

Consider, then, the excellence of this profession: its reward is a hundredfold fruit; its merit is to sing the new song; and to its dignity, on account of its special union with divine grace, most fittingly belong these *Songs of Songs* which we intend, according to our measure, to sing to you. Yet I cannot with you, whoever among you are truly virgins, not merely sing but not even whisper these songs, since I differ far from your holiness. But as someone may be able to indicate verbally the knowledge of some art yet cannot express it in practice, so I too, though prevented by sin from singing these things with you, shall nevertheless try with God’s help to say something by which you may in some measure recognize the excellence and singular dignity of these Songs.

Therefore, as the pagan poet says:

> I shall perform the office of a whetstone,  
> Which knows how to make iron sharp, though itself incapable of cutting.  
> —Horace, *Art of Poetry*, 304.

And since I am not permitted to sing, let it at least be permitted me to give counsel for singing. For holy Moses, with whom God spoke face to face, listened to and acted upon the counsel of Jethro, his kinsman, a Gentile; Moses himself was full of wisdom [Col. 1008B] and holiness, whereas the other was far beneath him in Gentile status and manner of life. But since God has given the willing, may He also give the ability.

I know, indeed, that this will seem unworthy to many who accept only the writings of the ancients:

> He marvels at nothing except what Libitina has consecrated.  
> —Horace, *Epistles* II.1.49.

They may wonder that after the sayings of the elders, which charity has confirmed, I have shamelessly exposed my own trifles; yet your love will excuse me before those whose desire alone I have proposed to satisfy. If they criticize the language as too simple for the majesty of the subject, let them remember that in constructing the tabernacle not only gold, silver, fine linen, [Col. 1008C] and purple, but also goats’ hair was offered (Exod. 25); and that the widow’s two small coins were more highly praised by the Lord than the immense gifts of the rich (Luke 21). If they find fault with the arrangement of words, let them nevertheless reverence the subject-matter; and let both the dignity of the matter and the obedient charity of devout entreaty excuse the slenderness of the language or composition. For we have in the Church many books composed in metrical art, concerning the Gospels and the deeds of saints, in humble style and simple speech; yet, because of the dignity of their subject, they have already acquired authority.

Thus Arator, about to write the *Acts of the Apostles*, says:

> Though in lean speech, we have written rich deeds,  
> And a drop flows with the weight of the sea.  
> —Arator, *Epistle to Florus*, v. 7. *Patrologia*, [Col. 1008D] vol. LXVIII, p. 64.

Therefore let no one despise our simplicity, “for our conversation is with the simple” (Prov. 3); rather, let him more readily pardon us sinners for choosing to write something, however simply, rather than lie idle in vain leisure and sloth. We do not even wish this work to go anywhere abroad, but only to remain hidden with the holy sisters to whom it is sent—unless perhaps someone, out of kindness, should be willing to undertake its correction and fashion from its unformed and soft composition some beautiful and masculine work.

Receive, then, this labour of my small ability, in which I have not begrudged exertion for the sake of your love: for your benefit indeed, but as an enduring memorial of myself; so that when you behold [Col. 1009A] and read it, [Col. 1010A] you may remember me and pray to our common God for me, whether I live or die.

## JUDGMENT OF THE ABBOT OF GERODE CONCERNING ABBOT WOLBERO’S COMMENTARIES ON THE SONG OF SONGS

[Col. 1009]

[Col. 1009A] To the venerable and most dearly beloved Lord Wolbero, abbot of St Pantaleon, the one called abbot of the monastery of Gerode: may he be introduced not merely into the bridegroom’s cellar but also into his chamber, to be made drunk, in perfect charity, from the abundance of God’s house and to drink for ever from the torrent of His delight (Ps. 35).

For you write, with humility familiar to all who use the wisdom of the Spirit; in asking you exhort, and in exhorting you ask, that, with every attempt to win your goodwill entirely put aside, I should examine more carefully your work on the *Song of Songs* and inform you in writing what I think—whether I judge that it should be brought to light, or understand that it should be hidden and laid aside. You say that you trust no one more than me, since both kinship binds me to goodwill and the wisdom of correction does not refuse a judgment. Now, just as every discerning person recognizes that all judgments are contained in these two things alone, prudence and goodwill, so, when I reflect with sorrow that goodwill is certainly present but prudence absent, following him who prayed, “That I may know what I lack” (Ps. 38), I rightly shrink from bearing the burden you impose.

Yet since this is an excuse belonging even to all those benumbed by idleness, and since your charity, trusting me and hoping that I can do it, urges me to act—not as a judge, but as the bridegroom’s friend, gladly fulfilling your desire—I hear the voice [Col. 1010A] of the bridegroom supplying his doctrine to your heart in freedom of spirit. At the voice of the bridegroom, who uses you as an instrument, I rejoice with the truth in charity; and I judge that this work ought not to be suppressed, but rather, for the glory of God—for “it is glory to reveal a saying” (Tob. 12)—and for the benefit of God’s Church and the instruction of those to whom it is written, should by every means be made known. Indeed, every Christian intending to live well in the house of God will judge it wholly Catholic in faith and most fitting [Col. 1010B] for the instruction of morals.

I have learned that you were somewhat displeased because I did not immediately return the manuscript once I had finished; but certain things prevented me. First, no work done in haste can also be examined—a truth I learned from you, since you pressed me almost into a new year. What has been written with care ought not to be read and judged carelessly. Further, our brothers, contrary indeed to your will but with mine and to my great pleasure, eagerly seized this work, read it attentively and diligently, and made it esteemed through their zeal for reading; yet in this way they withheld its reading even from me, unwilling though I was, for a time. But now, having read it through carefully, I return it to you to be shared in Christ with all who are to read it. It remains that you do not deny a share in the fruit to him whom you judged worthy to share in the labour. Farewell.

## WOLBERO’S GENERAL PREFACE TO SOLOMON’S SONG OF SONGS

[Col. 1009]

[Col. 1009D] In Holy Scripture many songs are mentioned, differing by the various reasons for which they were sung, now generally and now specifically according to place and time: according to place, because they were sung either in their homeland or in a foreign land; according to time, because they were sung either in peace or in captivity. Thus there is called the Song of Moses, the Song of Anna, the Song of the prophet Habakkuk, and others of that kind; but all these are simply “songs.” Here, however, they are called the *Song of Songs*, because they surpass every kind of song by the majesty of their mystical meaning.

And the other songs indeed have a reason why they were sung [Col. 1010D]: thus Moses sang a song of praise for the victory won when Pharaoh, with his chariots and horsemen, was drowned in the Red Sea. Hannah likewise sang a song to the Lord because fertility had been granted her and the reproach of barrenness removed. Hezekiah too sang a song because his health had been restored. Thus each of these songs was an act of thanksgiving for a benefit bestowed upon its singer by God. This song, however, represents the harmony of that supreme and perfect charity by which, when every care for worldly things has been lulled, each faithful soul [Col. 1011A] is united to its Creator as a bride to her bridegroom in the ineffable sweetness of love. In his embrace it abides in such sweetness of peace and rest that there is nothing besides him which it desires, nothing which it prefers to so great a grace. For assuredly there is nothing that can resist the spirit which, having trodden down the warfare of the flesh and brought the flesh into subjection, keeps the Sabbath in Christ in that same blessed concord.

For a great share of, and a desirable, Sabbath—that is, rest—exists when the flesh does not lust against the spirit; but, when the tumult of vices has been calmed, the mind enjoys such sweetness of inward tranquillity that, desiring nothing but the Lord, it both wishes and is able to utter the Song of Songs—that is, to possess true and perfect charity. For charity surpasses all virtues, just as the Song of Songs [Col. 1011B] surpasses every song. Ascents, therefore, must be set in the heart, so that one may arrive, as by certain steps, at singing the Song of Songs. Just as one who enters the holy place still requires many things before being able to enter the Holy of Holies, and one who celebrates Sabbaths needs far higher things if he is to arrive at the Sabbath of Sabbaths, so one who sings songs must always advance to greater things, in order to be able to sing the Song of Songs.

For seven songs are found in the divine page; the occasions on which they were sung mystically indicate to us, as by certain steps, the soul’s advances, which are governed by the grace of the sevenfold Spirit. One must leave the Egypt of this world and pass through the Red Sea by baptism, or by tears of repentance, so that, when the attendant of vices has been drowned, we may first sing with Moses: “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously magnified; horse and rider he has cast into the sea” (Exod. 15). Then, abandoning the tumult of secular affairs, we must traverse the spiritual wilderness until we find the well which the fathers dug. Formed by their teaching and examples, we may then, according to the manner of right living, sing the second song, which the children of Israel sang because the well was found: “Rise up, O well,” they sang, “the well which the princes dug and the leaders of the multitude prepared, by the giver of the law and with their staffs” (Num. 21). And when we have come near the land of promise [Col. 1011D], preparing ourselves to possess that blessed land and inviting spiritual and carnal persons alike with us, let us sing the third song with Moses: “Give ear, O heaven, and I shall speak; and let the earth hear the words from my mouth” (Deut. 32).

But if we are to inhabit this land spiritually, the enemies of the soul must be fought, against whom we must wage war with our whole intention, so that, when they have been put to flight, we may sing the fourth song with Deborah: “The remnant of the people was saved; the Lord fought among the mighty” (Judg. 5). When the enemies have then been overcome, let us sing to the Lord the fifth song with David, for our escape and deliverance: the song which David sang when he was delivered from the hand of all his enemies and from the hand of Saul, saying: “The Lord is [Col. 1012A] my rock, my strength, and my saviour” (2 Sam. 22), and the rest. Once the motions of spiritual adversities have been checked and every concern for secular things set aside, and we have at last attained the desired repose of mind, we must rise and hasten onward in the soul’s progress, to merit the embraces of that heavenly Bridegroom. We shall sing, in the sixth place, with Isaiah, this song of intention: “I shall sing for my beloved the song of my kinsman concerning his vineyard” (Isa. 5).

When, in the progress of this angelic manner of life, we have flown on the wings of holy contemplation to such a height that, now abiding in the Bridegroom’s own embraces, we can say with the Apostle, “But our commonwealth is in heaven” (Phil. 3), then at last we shall sing the seventh song [Col. 1012B], which is called not merely a song but the Song of Songs, when, resting from every secular work, we begin to keep Sabbath with the Bridegroom himself in unceasing repose.

Three matters must be considered in this book: its subject matter, its intention, and its final cause. Its subject matter is the espousals of Christ and the Church, or of each faithful soul; these consist in true and perfect love for him—a love demonstrated by the mortification of vices, delight in virtues, and observance of his commandments. Its intention is to exhort readers and hearers to strive so to be united with Christ through charity that they may be worthy to be called a bride. Its final cause is that from this they may attain the highest good, which is God, of whom it is written: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man, are the things which God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Cor. 2) [Col. 1012C].

It must be observed that in this book nothing is to be understood carnally according to the letter; rather, everything must be referred to a spiritual meaning, because “the letter kills, but the spirit gives life” (1 Cor. 3). Since God, speaking by himself to the human heart, could not be comprehended, he mercifully moves and recalls it through enigmas; by things known he secretly instils into it love for things unknown. Thus, while he speaks allegorically through external things which it knows, it may understand inward things which it must love and observe.

For here words seemingly belonging to bodily love are set forth, where kisses, breasts, cheeks, and thighs are named, so that the soul, shaken from its torpor by customary expressions, may grow warm again and, through words of the love that is below, be stirred to the love that is above [Col. 1012D]. In this, sacred description is neither to be rejected nor despised; rather, the mercy of God must be considered—indeed, all the greater in this respect, because, in order to kindle us toward the embraces of sacred love, he stoops even to the language of our weakness. Yet where he humbles himself in speech, there he exalts us in understanding, because from the discourse of this love we learn how we ought to serve in the love of the Godhead.

We must look very carefully, however, lest, when we hear external things, we remain fixed upon those same external things in our understanding, and the device which is provided to lift us up instead oppresses and weighs us down more heavily. Therefore, in outward words we must seek whatever is within; and, though speaking of the body, we must become outside the body [Col. 1013A]. We must come to the marriage of Bridegroom and bride with the understanding of charity—with the wedding garment—lest, if we lack it, we be cast into the outer darkness (Matt. 22), into the blindness of ignorance.

Moreover, it should be known that Solomon composed three books: first Proverbs, second Ecclesiastes, third the Song of Songs. Each is assigned to one of the three branches of philosophy, namely physics, ethics, and logic—that is, natural, moral, and rational knowledge. In Ecclesiastes he discusses the natural condition of things; in Proverbs he speaks concerning moral integrity; in the Song of Songs he sings of the rational ordering of divine mysteries. By these three modes, as by certain steps, the progress of the mind is led: namely, by naturality, morality, and rationality. Naturality is the observable diversity of things created in an ordered fashion; morality is the formation of an upright life; rationality is the desirable attainment of spiritual and divine knowledge.

Indeed, from consideration of naturality—when one observes how beautiful and useful created things are, how fittingly, rationally, and orderly they have been established, and how unchangeably they observe their appointed alternations of place and time—one can sufficiently discern what kind of being, and how great, how much more beautiful, exalted, and powerful, and therefore how justly to be worshipped and worthily adored, is God, the Creator of creation itself. Hence the Apostle says: “His invisible things, from the creation of the world, are understood through the things that have been made, even his eternal power and divinity, so that they are without excuse” (Rom. 1) [Col. 1013C].

Thus no one will be able to excuse himself, because by such consideration he is led to knowledge of the Creator and to faith, which believes true the things God promises to the just and threatens to the unjust. From this he is first pierced by fear, and afterwards by love.

For by fear he first rises to the integrity of morality, until, through progress in his manner of life, morality itself is taken up by charity, which “casts out fear” (1 John 4). Since a human being is more excellent than every earthly creature, while creation itself possesses the beauty of which we have spoken, he can certainly perceive how much more beautiful he will become if, through the adornment of morality, he cleaves to his Creator. For man was made in the image [Col. 1013D] and likeness of God (Gen. 2), formed of two substances, namely soul and body. He possesses God’s likeness in that he lives and is called very good among the rest of creatures; and by the very disposition of his body he has from the beginning been raised up to receive heavenly things and tread down earthly ones. But just as God himself neither increases when creatures increase nor decreases when they decrease, though he is in all things, so the soul neither diminishes when limbs are diminished nor increases when they are enlarged, though it is in all of them.

Furthermore, man possesses the image of God in his better part, namely the soul, which flourishes in natural ability, reason, and understanding. In these, indeed, the image of God is displayed; through moral integrity the soul is conformed to him, so that, just as it has borne the image of the earthly man by loving earthly things, it may also bear [Col. 1014A] the image of the heavenly one (1 Cor. 15), by ardently seeking and practising heavenly things. For we must not childishly suppose that God, who is incorporeal and incomprehensible, can be grasped in bodily outlines, as though he possessed an image after which man was made. Rather, his image is the reason implanted in the human mind, by which man differs from irrational creatures; by which he distinguishes the just from the unjust, the honourable from the dishonourable, the useful from the useless; and by which, finally, he restrains the beastly impulses of the soul lest they corrupt the integrity of the mind. If some prompting of frailty should corrupt that integrity, he can again, under the guidance of that same reason, reform it through devotion to holy morality.

When a person has been formed morally by this devotion, grace of rationality graciously advances him, so that he receives knowledge both of himself [Col. 1014B] and of God. He knows himself insofar as he considers what he is and whence comes the gift he receives: that he is saved not by his own merit but by God’s grace, having been taken up into “the freedom of the glory of the children of God” (Rom. 8). He knows God insofar as he understands that nothing is better, nothing more powerful, nothing higher than God, whom alone he must know, fear, revere, love, and worship with all the strength of his soul. This is that wisdom which “will not enter a malicious soul, nor dwell in a body subject to sins; for the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit, withdraw himself from thoughts without understanding, and be rebuked by the approach of iniquity” (Wis. 1).

Therefore the virtue of morality receives the grace of rationality, because the mind which draws near to God through the integrity of discipline considers more deeply the subtlety of his knowledge, in accordance with the saying of James, who exhorts his hearers: “Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you” (Jas. 4) [Col. 1014C].

The Psalmist prays for this threefold progress of the soul, saying: “Teach me goodness, discipline, and knowledge” (Ps. 118). For he sets goodness first, then discipline, and knowledge in the third place. Since God is good by nature, he created man naturally good, because he made him in his own image and likeness, giving him reason by which he could distinguish good and evil. But man, understanding that he can know one of these, namely good, not from himself but from God, asks to be taught goodness, so that through the goodness of his natural constitution he may, with the affection of holy morality, seek discipline [Col. 1014D], through which he may advance to the incomprehensible and divine knowledge of rationality. Always desiring with his whole mind this order of progress, he cries: “Teach me goodness and discipline and knowledge.” As if he said in other words: “Because you, Lord God, created me naturally good, teach me how the good of that nature may not be corrupted by my fault but increased by your grace, so that in this way, with your help, I may wish and be able to live rightly, and, living rightly, penetrate with the citadel of my mind into the hidden things of your mysteries.”

This book is therefore assigned to that third part which we have called rationality, because of the excellence of the mysteries which are sung therein concerning Christ and the Church, or concerning any soul beloved of God. It is deservedly entitled *Song of Songs*, because, marked out above all songs as more perfect and exalted by a certain privilege of spiritual harmony, it gives utterance to mystical themes. For if you consider it more closely, you will understand that nearly all the mysteries of Christ and the Church are sung in it.

For example, at the very beginning of the song, when the Church says, “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth,” the coming of Christ in the flesh is desired. It is as though the Church said in other words: “You who once spoke to me through the mouths of your prophets and other Fathers, now present yourself to me in person, born according to the flesh, and offer me from your own mouth the decrees of your commandments.” It also denotes Christ’s passion and resurrection where the beloved says: “My beloved is to me a bundle of myrrh; he shall abide between my breasts”; and shortly thereafter, “My beloved is to me a cluster of henna” (Song 1) [Col. 1015B]. By myrrh the bitterness of the passion is expressed; by the cluster, the sweetness of the resurrection. Elsewhere she says: “Flee, my beloved, and be like a gazelle or a young stag upon the mountains of spices” (Song 8), signifying through the gazelle and young stag the power of the Lord ascending into heaven.

In “a flock of shorn sheep coming up from the washing” (Song 4, 6) is understood the people of the baptized laying aside the burdens of sins; in their twin offspring, the twofold charity; and in the eyes, teeth, cheeks, hair, and the arrangements of the other members named there, the spiritual adornment and ordering of the holy Church or of any holy soul is described. There the perversity of heretics and the sweetness of teachers are indicated; and, to embrace all in one statement, whatever is generally or particularly done or celebrated as accomplished in the holy Church is sung through most beautiful allusions. Thus this book is deservedly called the *Song of Songs* because of its excellence [Col. 1015C].

Our purpose in this work, then, is to investigate, insofar as we can, the rational meaning of these mysteries; but above all, holy sisters, to consider morality for your edification and to stir your minds to love for your Bridegroom, the Lord Jesus Christ.

We have divided the whole book into four volumes because of the four subdivisions marked by recapitulating sections [periochae], indicated by the third repetition of this verse: “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the gazelles and the hinds, that you do not rouse or awaken the beloved until she herself wills.”

The first of these sections runs from “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” to “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem.” The second runs from “The voice of my beloved! Behold, he comes, leaping upon the mountains, skipping over the hills,” likewise to “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem.” The third, longer section begins, “Who is this who comes up through the wilderness?” and continues to the third adjuration, “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem.” The fourth begins, “Who is this who comes up from the wilderness, abounding in delights?” and continues to the end [Col. 1015D].

We have divided the expositions of these four parts into four little books, whether on account of Aminadab’s evangelical—or moral—four-horse chariot, consisting of the four cardinal virtues, at which the troubled bride was afraid; or in order that a mind devoted to morality may be warned that it ought to be square in virtues. For just as any square object remains standing when it is set upon one of its sides, so such a mind should neither be lifted up by prosperity nor cast down by adversity; but, like a squared stone set in the building of the Lord, it should be conformed by the mortification of the carnal life to Christ’s passion, bearing its own cross, so that it may comprehend with all the saints “what is the length and breadth and height and depth” (Eph. 3) [Col. 1016A].

The power of this comprehension belongs only to the perfect, who, “rooted and grounded in charity” (*ibid.*), cleave so firmly to their Creator that they unceasingly sing the Song of Songs in the amplitude of charity. This fourfold dimension of charity consists in them as follows: charity in the saints is long, because it is not momentary but persevering and continuous; broad, because it extends even to enemies; high, because it is held on account of the hope and reward of eternal life; and deep, because it penetrates even the secrets of God. “For no one has known the things of God except the Spirit of God” (1 Cor. 2), through whom charity itself is poured out in the hearts of the saints (Rom. 5).

In our Lord Christ himself, the archetypal head, the beauty of this fourfold dimension also shines forth delightfully, figured in the manner of his passion, namely the form of the cross. From the top of the cross downward is expressed the length of his charity, of whom John says that, “having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them unto the end” (John 13) [Col. 1016C]. The breadth stretched from right to left extends to the love of enemies, for whom he prayed: “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke 23). The height is seen in the inscription of the title: scarcely can one comprehend the height of his goodness, by which he governs, cherishes, and guards us. The depth, through the portion fixed in the earth which supports the rest, conceals the abyss of God’s judgments; for, although God did and suffered so much for human salvation, why he receives this person and rejects that one is inscrutable and beyond investigation.

Therefore, beloved sisters, crucified to the world with the Lord, learn to comprehend with all the saints the length, breadth, height, and depth of charity, so that, brought into the chamber of our Lord, your Bridegroom, with lamps burning—that is, with good works—you may be able unceasingly to sing before the throne of God that new song which virgins alone may sing, truly the Song of Songs [Col. 1016D].

But now let us proceed to the sequence of the book itself, first warning that, if anyone is troubled because the discourse extends beyond measure and the exposition overflows the proper bounds of speech, he should know that we undertook this work not only in order to expound it. Rather, our intention was thereby to provide ourselves material with which we might satisfy, at least in writing, the devout desire of the holy sisters, whom we could not satisfy in speech.

## Of Lord Wolbero, Abbot of the Order of Saint Benedict, on the Song of Songs of Solomon

[Col. 1017]

## Book One

### [Chapter One]

[Col. 1017]

**2. Verse 1.—“Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.”**

If the Son of God is the Word of God, of whom John says, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was [Col. 1017B] with God, and the Word was God” (John 1), then the Son of God is certainly, and quite fittingly, understood also as the mouth of God, because a word is uttered by the mouth. We may not unfittingly understand the kiss as the Holy Spirit, because peace and charity, signified by a kiss, are given through the Holy Spirit. In him forgiveness of sins takes place; through him we are reconciled to God; through him is given the distribution of gifts by which we are united to God (Rom. 5).

But as the substance of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is undivided, so also is their operation undivided; and although in the whole Trinity there is distinction of persons, there is nevertheless one and the same will and operation. Therefore the one kissing, the mouth, and the kiss accomplish three things as one: namely, charity in the hearts of those who share this kiss. For, as we have said, the operation of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is one; and the kiss of the mouth—that is, of the Word, who is the Son—is both the kiss and that of the one kissing, namely the Father, because the Holy Spirit is of the Father and the Son. The kiss is the grace, peace, and charity of this undivided Trinity.

Therefore, through the kiss of the mouth of the one kissing—that is, through the Holy Spirit of Father and Son, whose substance, majesty, strength, power, will, and operation are one—there is first given forgiveness of sins, the kiss of peace, the reconciling kiss; then the distribution of gifts, the kiss of charity, the contemplative kiss [Col. 1017C].

This kiss of twofold grace, in its proper order, is sought from her Lord and Creator by the holy Church universally, or by every holy soul individually. It reflects and considers that the creating Trinity, though present everywhere through the power of divinity, is not present everywhere through the grace of indwelling; for it is present in this latter manner only through love. Through love the indwelling of divinity is known, and conversely through the indwelling of divinity, love. Therefore it asks that the kiss be offered to it: first, as we have said, the reconciling kiss through forgiveness of sins, so that it may then merit the contemplative kiss through the grace of gifts.

But since the proof of love is the performance of a work, the grace of the indwelling divinity is certainly recognized through the performance of a work; for working love and loving action are the kiss of the mouth of the one kissing—that is, the whole grace of the Trinity dwelling in the mind. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him; and we shall come to him and make our dwelling [Col. 1018] with him” (John 14).

She says, then: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.” As if she said in other words: “May my Creator himself, by his grace, so kindle my heart that I may love him; that, loving him, I may please him by action; and that, pleasing him, I may be made worthy of his indwelling.”

Or, if we refer the mystery of his incarnation to the person of the Son alone, the Church desires to hear him speaking in person, whom until then she had heard through the mouths of the Fathers. For the Word destined to become incarnate first promised the hidden meanings of his precepts and sacraments in the Law and the Prophets; afterward, when he came, he himself fulfilled them and, as it were by the impression of his own hand, sealed them as things to be observed unchangeably. Hence he says through the prophet: “Therefore my people shall know my name in that day, because I who spoke, behold, am present” (Isa. 52) [Col. 1018C].

That speech by which he spoke through the Law and the Prophets, as through an instrument, was obscure and indeterminate. But when he himself came and spoke in person, it became determinate and plain, because with truth present the shadow necessarily had to cease. Yet because the preceding speech, whether through an angel, a human being, or any other creature, was made in many ways—by voice, sign, action, vision, or the mere touch of the heart—the blessed Apostle says concerning the later speech through the Mediator of God and human beings himself: “God, who at many times and in many ways formerly spoke to the fathers in the prophets, has in these last days spoken to us in the Son” (Heb. 1) [Col. 1018D].

Surely, just as an artisan is far superior to an instrument, so this final speech, because the Son of God himself uttered it in his own person, is far worthier and more desirable than that speech in which he used the Fathers as instruments. It is final because after it nothing firmer or more certain could or can be said or written.

Burning with all the ardour of its soul for the sweetness of this utterance—the true truth of truth—to be revealed to its understanding, the holy Church cries: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.” A kiss is a sign of peace or love; and it is written of this truly peace-giving Lord Jesus Christ that, when he came, “he preached peace to those who were far off and to those who were near” (Eph. 2). What peace? Clearly, that peace which dissolves the enmities between God and humankind, which the holy prophets indeed announced but could not give. But he, the Angel of Great Counsel and Prince of Peace (Isa. 9), both announced it and gave it.

Therefore the holy Church, sighing for his presence, address, and gracious speech, desires with all its prayers to enjoy through his discourse, as though through the kiss of a peace-giving mouth, the true and complete peace which he sows and gives. It says: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of your mouth,” as though to say: “May he himself show me in person what the holy Fathers long ago confirmed by words, writings, and signs as something to be shown” [Col. 1019A].

And it adds the reason why it desires this more: “For your breasts are better than wine.” That is, the nourishment of evangelical gentleness provides for my salvation better and more swiftly than the austerity of the legal sentence or the swollen and empty talkativeness of philosophers. This will be treated more fully in the second verse [Col. 1019B].

In the moral sense, however, the soul beloved by God, now having attained that noble and incomparable celibacy and been admitted into the hidden, inaccessible-to-the-human-mind Holy of Holies of her Bridegroom, Creator, and Redeemer, rejoicingly says: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.” But whence comes this proclamation, so great and such, so confident and exalted? Certainly from “a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith” (1 Tim. 5). For this is the method of attaining perfection: to know what, how, and why—that is, the matter, intention, and usefulness—one acts. One must carefully consider what one does, with what intention, and for what fruit. Every action is conceived in the heart, nourished by intention, and perfected by faith.

Indeed, if you begin some good work, the intention of that good itself will be its judge. For “if your eye is single, your whole body will be full of light; but if it is evil, it will be dark” (Luke 11). Moreover, faith either destroys or advances the work itself. For one either believes or does not believe God, who promises his worshipper those things “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have entered into the heart of man” (1 Cor. 2). The unbelieving person acts unbelievingly, and the believing person acts faithfully.

Faith may be divided in three ways, and called dead, feigned, or tried. Dead faith may be called that which, according to the Apostle, is without works (Jas. 1); it is insensible, as though it had no soul—that is, charity—and is not enlivened or moved toward any good work. Feigned faith is that which, not rooted in charity, according to the Lord’s saying, “believes for a time and in the time of temptation falls away” (Luke 8). Tried faith is that which fails under no tribulations or adversities, because it has been firmly rooted in charity [Col. 1019D].

Therefore let the faithful and prudent soul strive, through unfeigned faith, to preserve charity from a pure heart and good conscience (1 Tim. 1). This is the perfection of the inward disposition, a disposition produced by charity alone—charity which, being perfect, casts out fear (1 John 4). It is attested by these three things: a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith; yet they themselves proceed from charity. Who keeps his heart with all diligence (Prov. 4), so as to possess a good conscience, except through charity? Who preserves firm and unshaken faith except through charity? Therefore these three are proofs of charity, while true charity itself produces them.

These are the oil, vessels, and lamps of the Gospel, with which the virgins—not foolish but prudent—adorned themselves while awaiting the coming of their Bridegroom, our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they might enter with him into the marriage of marriages. For what is oil but a good work? What are the vessels but the receptacles, namely the consciences, of these works? And what are the lamps but the fervour and brightness of the works themselves? For if holy persons burn with charity, they shine in performance, so that they are an example to those who see them and a light to those who act [Col. 1020B].

Therefore they carry oil in their vessels together with lamps who keep a good work in a joyful and secure conscience, with this intention: both that they may not seek human praise and that they may furnish their neighbours an example of right action.

Therefore, from a pure heart, good conscience, and unfeigned faith (1 Tim. 1), let the soul beloved by God raise for itself a ladder upon which it may set ascents, by which it may advance “from strength to strength” (Ps. 83) toward that highest good which is God, through charity. Let it take its pattern from its Bridegroom, Jesus Christ himself, who, though the exalted Lord above all nations (Ps. 112), came humble among the nations, in order to teach us to ascend by his humility, from which our first parents had descended through pride. For humility leads the soul through charity to that vision of the Godhead, as it were to the third heaven, to which the Apostle declared that he had been caught up and heard unspeakable words which it is not permitted for a human being to utter (2 Cor. 12) [Col. 1020C].

Let us suppose humility to be, as it were, the first heaven, charity the second, and the sublimity of contemplation the third. When the mind, then, lifted up to the virtue of humility as to the first heaven, has already despised and trampled down all worldly pleasures, it rises through charity—to which “many waters cannot quench,” for “love is strong as death” (Song 8)—to the second heaven. And when it has progressed so far that it thinks of and desires nothing but God, it is raised by contemplation to the third heaven, where, set above itself and marvelling at the hidden things of divine wisdom, it says: “My secret is mine; my secret is mine” (Isa. 29). There, already intoxicated by the torrent of that ineffable delight, its face washed and its lips purified by desolating coals (Ps. 119), it lingers in the desired embraces of its Bridegroom, saying: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” [Col. 1020D].

But what is this confidence, that it seeks so suddenly the kiss of its Lord’s mouth, as though reason did not permit it, without any order or stage, to approach something so eminent and supreme?

One must therefore consider that certain lower kisses preceded it: first the kiss of redemption, then the kiss of reconciliation, and finally the supreme kiss of love. The kiss of redemption is, as it were, a kiss of the Lord’s feet; the kiss of reconciliation, a kiss of his hands; and the kiss of love, a kiss of his mouth. By the feet, with which we move from place to place, the Saviour’s humanity is signified. The dispensation of that humanity—namely, that he was crowned with thorns, suffered, died, was buried, and rose again—was in movement and transition. For “Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him” (Rom. 6). Through this humanity he passed from the captivity of the devil into Christ’s freedom, and, according to the prophet, “the yoke was rotted away because of the oil” (Isa. 10).

For the Greek *eleos* (ἔλεος) is called *misericordia* (“mercy”) in Latin; and since it is the nature of oil to rise above all liquids, while “the mercy of the Lord is over all his works” (Ps. 144), when God looked upon the world with mercy, its yoke of captivity rotted away at the coming of the Saviour [Col. 1021B].

We kiss the feet of our Redeemer when we embrace, with faith and devotion, the mysteries of his humanity and imitate, insofar as we can, the traces of his humility, patience, and obedience. But when captivity had been removed, did the human being immediately merit union with God? By his own fault and free choice he had fallen into the devil’s captivity: though created good by nature, he had fallen into evil through his own fault. Therefore, because by will and action he had rebelled against God, and thus had withdrawn far from his grace, he needed reconciliation.

The holy Fathers, ministers of God, went before, advancing the cause of this reconciliation by preaching, exhorting, teaching, and frequently announcing his commandments. They were able indeed to free man from error, but could not grant him perfect freedom. His Creator himself then came, taking on man’s mortality in order to give him his own immortality; and, destroying the middle wall, abolishing enmities in his flesh through his blood (Eph. 2), he granted him freedom through the kiss of redemption. Then immediately he joined that same person to himself by the kiss of reconciliation. Stooping down from the height of his divinity, he tore up the old bond of sin and wrote upon the earth the new testament of peace and reconciliation through the sacrament of baptism [Col. 1021D]. In it, having bestowed grace as though of manumission, he restored perfect freedom; and, adopting as a son the one whom he had formerly not even deigned to have as a servant because of the voluntary yoke of sin, he gave him the written title to such an inheritance as “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man” (1 Cor. 2).

This testament or written title is now held, and will continue to be held, by the holy Church or by every faithful soul, so that, if it does not cease to know, possess, and love God as its true Father, it may always be secure of such an inheritance.

Therefore we offer the Lord a kiss upon his hands when we observe, in faith and action, the covenant or decree of this reconciliation; when, throughout the course of this life, agreeing with our adversary—that is, with the word of God—we maintain perpetual peace with him by living justly and devoutly [Col. 1022A].

7 But after reconciliation, as though security had been received, man began to draw nearer to the Godhead more freely and joyfully. And, as James says, “Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you” (James 4), the more he drew near to God through the pursuit of good works, the nearer he made God to himself through contemplation. Thus, setting aside all worldly business and trampling down earthly desires, he ascends the mountain with Moses and says: “Lord, show me your face” (Exod. 33). Abiding delightfully in that vision, he advances with such ardour of divine love that he seeks the kiss of His mouth, saying: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.”

Therefore he arrives not suddenly, but gradually, and as if by certain [Col. 1022B] steps, at the ineffable sweetness of that supreme love, as it were at the kiss of the Lord’s mouth. The first step is the redemptive kiss; the second, the reconciling kiss; the third, the contemplative kiss. For this is also the third heaven, to which the Apostle declares that he was caught up: there he received, from this chief kiss of the Lord’s mouth, the grace of special knowledge; and he came to proclaim the sweetness of this same kiss to churches throughout the world and to exhort them to the perfection of such holiness.

That woman in the Gospel indeed prefigured the grace of this threefold kiss by her dutiful service. First, falling devoutly at the Lord’s feet, kissing them, watering them with tears, and wiping them with her hair, she obtained forgiveness of sins, as though she had been given the [Col. 1022C] redemptive kiss, when she heard: “Your sins are forgiven you” (Luke 7). Then, having received, as it were, from the Lord’s hand the prescribed tablets of liberty, she is granted the reconciling kiss when, reconciled to God through remission of sins, she is told: “Go in peace” (ibid.). Thereafter, through progress in good conduct, she clung to the Lord with such ardour of love—as though with the kiss of His mouth, the contemplative kiss—that she was praised by the Lord Himself, who said: “Mary has chosen the better part, which shall not be taken away from her” (Luke 10).

We may also, not inappropriately, understand this threefold kiss as faith, hope, and love: faith as the kiss of the Lord’s feet, hope as that of His hands, and love as that of His mouth. For by faith we are saved; by hope we are sustained; [Col. 1022D] by love we are glorified. By faith we embrace the Lord’s feet—that is, the mysteries of His humanity—which pertains to salvation. By hope we touch the Lord’s hands, by which we are led to hope for heavenly promises, which pertains to patience; for “if we hope for what we do not see, we await it through patience” (Rom. 8). But by love we offer, as it were, a kiss to the Lord’s mouth, when He grants us eternal blessedness, which pertains to reward.

8 Let, then, the whole Church speak universally, or every holy soul particularly: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth”—with the kiss, he says, of His mouth, not, as formerly, by that of prophets or any other teachers, but His own. For He Himself, by His teaching and example, established for me a pattern of life, through which, with His help, all the obstacles of this world having been repelled [Col. 1023A] and cast away, and perfect liberty now attained, I may cling continually to Him in the kiss of love, until, having at some time assumed the immortality and incorruption of body and soul, I may be joined to Him unchangeably and inseparably, and may truly say: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth”; so that what I now see “through a mirror, in an enigma,” I may then see “face to face” (1 Cor. 13), when “God will be all in all” (1 Cor. 15). These things, then, I desire; this I seek; this I long for with all my prayers. Why?

**VERSE 2.—“For your breasts are better than wine, fragrant with the finest ointments.”**

What are these breasts of yours? The remission of sins and the distribution of gifts. They console me while weeping; they nourish me while small and bring me forth into manly strength. [Col. 1023B] They call, attract, and soothe me, because through your Gospel they cry to me: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand” (Matt. 3). But the wine of the biting Law frightens, turns away, and exasperates me by its authority, because it cries: “Eye for eye, tooth for tooth,” and, “Whoever has done this or that shall surely die” (Exod. 21). These breasts of yours, I say, greatly invite, encourage, and strengthen me because of the exceeding abundance of your mercy and the prerogative of your gifts. Yet, since from one of these breasts flows remission of sins, and from the other the distribution of gifts, the order is that remission of sins should first be given, and then the distribution of gifts. But the greatness of His mercy sometimes causes that which comes later—that is, the distribution of gifts—to precede, in certain persons, that which comes first—that is, remission of sins—for this reason: that they may be more strongly stirred up and labour more earnestly in response to your calling grace, in order to receive remission of sins.

This may be seen, for example, in Cornelius the centurion, in whom the gift of your grace in kinds of tongues came first, so that, more encouraged and as if assured, he might approach more readily to receive the sacrament of faith for the remission of sins. The same gift of your grace also came beforehand in the Apostle Paul, in the gift of understanding and discernment. When Ananias had been sent to him, he said: “Brother Saul, the Lord Jesus, who appeared to you on the road by which you came, has sent me, that you may see and be filled [Col. 1023D] with the Holy Spirit” (Acts 2). Did this seeing of his pertain only to the illumination of bodily eyes, rather than to the illumination of the mind, by which he might see and know the truth that he was attacking? Was not this also to be filled with the Holy Spirit?
