For you gave him the Holy Spirit while he was not yet baptized, so that he might know how to distinguish between the shadow of the Law which he defended and the truth of the Gospel which he attacked; and, leaving the shadow, might come more eagerly and fervently, with the assistance of that same Holy Spirit, to receive the truth in remission of sins. Therefore these evangelical breasts of yours, which draw people to salvation by their gentleness, are better than those legal ordinances which deter from salvation by their severity.

[Col. 1024A] But, to consider something more deeply: what, O Beloved, are these breasts of yours, if not the ineffable sweetness and glory of those heavenly secrets of yours, of which the Psalmist says: “I shall be satisfied when your glory appears” (Ps. 16)? Therefore, after I have ascended by the gift of your grace through contemplation into this wonderful inner chamber of yours, neither the allurements of enticing prosperity nor the blows of frightening adversities will be able to tear me from your embraces, because your breasts are better than wine. Better—indeed incomparable—are that paradise of your delight and the manifestation of your glory than the pleasures and passing honours of this age. But what sort are these breasts of yours? “Fragrant with the finest ointments.”

For these ointments are signs not of just any breasts, [Col. 1024B] but of yours; they give off such sweetness that by their very scent it becomes known what they are and whose they are. But what are these ointments? Surely those which that most excellent perfumer or maker of fragrances of yours, the Holy Spirit, has composed and continues to compose. And what are the ingredients from which these ointments are made? Certainly those which the Apostle, enumerating them in one place, calls spiritual fruits: “The fruits of the Spirit,” he says, “are peace, patience, goodness, kindness, faith, gentleness, obedience, self-control, chastity” (Gal. 5).

What a good and useful tree in the Lord’s garden, producing such kinds of fruit and rejoicing in its own fruitfulness, cries out: “But I am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of the Lord” (Ps. 51). The Holy Spirit is indeed the cultivator of this tree. He takes such fruits for Himself in order to compose the ointments by which the Beloved’s breasts are fragrant; these are bestowed on those anointed with such ointments, who can say with the Apostle: “We are the sweet savour of Christ to God in every place” (2 Cor. 2), because remission of sins and the distribution of graces are given to such persons.

Yet no human reasoning, without the assistance of grace, advances to the sweetness of ointments of this kind, compounded from the aforesaid varieties of virtues. For a human being, though capable of reason, begins or completes nothing holy or rational unless the maker of those very ointments, the Holy Spirit, accomplishes it by His inward anointing. as John says of Him to his hearers: [Col. 1024D] “His anointing will teach you concerning all things” (1 John 2).

Indeed, such an anointing is the true medicine of the inner person and the strongest antidote against the soul’s diseases. It heals and restores the soul wounded by the wound of sin; enlightens the mind; rouses it to earn the gifts of divine grace; and finally illumines it with such power of sweetness that, forgetting what is behind and stretching forward, it raises itself above itself, saying with the Apostle: “But our commonwealth is in heaven” (Phil. 3). There, having obtained freedom from every misery, it is satisfied from the breasts of God’s consolation and feasts at the entrance of His glory (Isa. 66).

The Beloved’s breasts may also fittingly be understood as the teaching and action of our Lord [Col. 1025A] Jesus Christ, through which, in His humanity, He made Himself known to the world, fragrant with the finest ointments of virtues. At first He nourished it with the milk of the teaching of the first fruits of the new faith and strengthened it by the power of His works; but now He strengthens the fullness of that faith, as with solid food, through teaching, and shapes it to the perfection of an honourable life by the example of His works.

These breasts, certainly fragrant with the ointment of such great mercy and grace, are far better than wine—that is, than the severity of royal ceremonies or historical acts—since truth surpasses shadow and the life-giving Spirit surpasses the killing letter. For, as the Apostle says, “the Law added nothing to perfection”; but “all these things happened to them in figure, and were written for our correction, upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (1 Cor. 10). Or they are better, or rather incomparable, to wine—that is, to the pleasure of worldly teachings—which infect their hearers with the ointment of carnal delight and drag them to the death of the soul. Thus, by contrast, as much as, O Beloved, a soul advances to your grace through the consolation of your breasts, so much does it fall away from that grace through the destructive compound of those teachings.

“Your name is oil poured out; therefore the young maidens have loved you.”

Those who observe me, O Beloved, marvel that I praise you so, proclaim such great grace of your mercy and sweetness, and desire your face and embraces with such eagerness. They wish to know what your name is and what your rank may be—you whom I esteem and judge so highly. Lest they excuse themselves on grounds of ignorance, saying that [Col. 1025C] your name has not been announced to them, I say that your name is not hidden or concealed, but rather manifest and like oil poured out, whose nature is to spread more widely when it is poured out.

How, then, has your name been poured out and spread abroad? Not merely as once you were known in Judaea and your name was great only in Israel (Ps. 75), but, as you say through another prophet: “From the rising of the sun to its setting, your name is great among the nations” (Mal. 1). It is the name above every name, so that “at your name every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Phil. 2). And “there is no other name under heaven given among men [Col. 1025D] by which we must be saved” (Acts 4).

And so that I may draw them with me to higher things, that they may understand and know why I so greatly desire your kiss and delight in the sweetness of your breasts, let them hear something further and consider why I have called your name “oil poured out.” For oil surpasses all liquids. What, then, is signified by oil except love, which surpasses all virtues? Indeed, no virtue can be called or be virtue without love; for where love is not, no virtue is. For “though I speak with the tongues of men and angels, but have not love, I have become like sounding brass or a clanging cymbal; and though I have prophecy, know all mysteries and all knowledge, and have faith so as to move mountains, but do not have love, it profits me nothing; and though I distribute all my possessions as food to the poor, and though I give my body to be burned, but do not have love, I am nothing” (1 Cor. 13).

See how great in power and excellence you judge love to be: without it neither prophecy, nor any knowledge, nor faith, nor almsgiving, nor martyrdom is anything. But what is this love? Surely it is you, O Beloved, as your beloved witness testifies—the one who clung to you in your holy kiss and, reclining upon your breast, drew in the sweetness of your breasts; that heavenly eagle, I say, who flies into your very secrets on the wings of holy contemplation and fixes the eye of his mind upon you, the Sun of righteousness. And what does he say? “God is love” (1 John 4). [Col. 1026B] Therefore you, O Beloved, are called and are love, because love made you take flesh, come into this world, and humble yourself for human salvation even to the death of the cross. And because of His exceeding love, with which God loved us (Eph. 2), He sent you, His Son, in the likeness of sinful flesh, that you might condemn sin through sin (Rom. 8), becoming a curse for us in order that you might free us from the curse (Gal. 2).

But how was this your name—the name of love—poured out and spread abroad? “Like ointment upon the head, which came down upon the beard, the beard of Aaron, which came down upon the hem of his garment” (Ps. 132). You are Aaron—that is, the mountain of strength—in whom, namely in our head, this outstanding love especially abounded, by which “God, your God, anointed you with the oil of gladness above your fellows” (Ps. 44; Heb. 1): that gladness by which you rejoiced, showing the abundance of your love and fulfilling the order of our redemption.

The apostles or apostolic men were the beard of this head. The grace of this ointment so flowed into them that, like a beard [Col. 1026C] upon the head, they clung firmly to you with the ardour of holy love even unto death.

“It came down upon the hem of your garment”: this garment your faithful know from the first age of the world to this one in which we now are, upon whom the ends of the ages have come (1 Cor. 10). We are the hem—that is, the end—of this garment of yours. In all of these, namely former, present, and future persons, the strength of this ointment, that is, of love, has laboured, labours, and will labour even at the very end of the age, under the persecution of Antichrist, for your name. Your name, therefore, is oil poured out because “your love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5).

“And therefore the young maidens have loved you exceedingly.” Because, he says, the sweetness of your breasts and the abundance of your love are so great that in you gentleness is found more than severity, and cherishing mercy more than a punishing sentence; therefore the young maidens have loved you exceedingly.

But who are these young maidens? Surely faithful souls, removed from the milk of infancy but not yet having attained the firmness of perfection. Therefore they are still weak and need to be sustained by divine help. And for this reason they have greatly loved, O Beloved, and do love you, because they perceive in you that from which they do not flee, but through which they may become stronger and stronger, at last rising to the height of perfection.

Holy Scripture is accustomed to signify growths of the mind through the stages of bodily growth. For just as human beings naturally advance to greater ages, so the faithful advance by grace to greater virtues of soul. Thus Peter exhorts his hearers to infancy—that is, innocence of life—saying: “Like newborn infants, desire the reasonable milk without deceit, that by it you may grow unto salvation” (1 Pet. 2). In the Gospel too, the Saviour, exhorting His disciples to purity [Col. 1027B] and simplicity of life, says: “Unless you are converted and become like little children, you shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 18). And the Apostle says: “Be little children in malice, that you may be perfect in understanding” (1 Cor. 5). Likewise the Psalmist, desiring the youth of his soul to be renewed after the eagle’s example, says: “Your youth shall be renewed like the eagle’s” (Ps. 102), so that, putting off the old man with his deeds, he may put on the new (Col. 3), who “was created according to God in righteousness and holiness” (Eph. 4). And in the Book of Wisdom the gravity of character is expressed by old age of mind, when it says: “Venerable old age is not long-lasting, nor is it counted by the number of years; for a person’s grey hairs are understanding, and a spotless life is the age of old age” (Wis. 4).

[Col. 1027C] Growth may therefore be divided in two: natural growth and affective growth. Natural growth is attributed to every bodily creature that, by vital animation, moves naturally according to its own nature. But affective growth is bestowed, in this present life, only upon the rational creature according to the measure of imparted grace; with the help of that grace, it advances by the strength of the spirit against the vices of the flesh, from good things to better things.

In divine Scripture, natural growth often signifies affective growth, as when the Psalmist says: “It shall please God more than a young calf producing horns and hoofs” (Ps. 68). For, if you understand this literally, what concern has God for an irrational animal naturally producing [Col. 1027D] horns and hoofs? But if you consider more deeply in the mystical sense, you may understand the young calf as a mind newly converted to the Lord and budding with the flower of good action. The Apostle calls it “the new man,” saying: “Put on the new man, who is renewed in knowledge according to the image of him who created him” (Col. 3). Enumerating the constituent parts of this person, he says: “Put on, therefore, as God’s elect, bowels of mercy, kindness, humility, modesty, patience, bearing with one another and forgiving one another” (ibid.).

But the horns of this young calf—that is, of the new person—may, not unreasonably, I think, be understood as steadfastness of mind and strength of spirit, or the spirit of fortitude [Col. 1028A] resisting vices and sins and driving away the adversaries of this new person.

Further, nothing prevents you from understanding its hoofs, with which it stirs up the earth, as contempt for the world and love of God. By these it casts away all earthly things and reduces its body to servitude, subjecting it to the spirit, so that it may cooperate and labour with it by consent in the discipline of good works; so that, in the future renewal, it may share in reward as it has shared in labour. This is precisely for the new person to be endowed with a double robe: the blessedness, namely, of body and soul.

Or understand the horns and hoofs of this calf as the exalted and distinctive transcendences of the contemplative life. For just as horns and hoofs proceed from flesh, yet surpass flesh, so the contemplative man, though he is in [Col. 1028B] the flesh, nevertheless transcends carnal affections in his mind, saying with the Apostle: “Though we walk in the flesh, we do not walk according to the flesh” (2 Cor. 10); and again: “But our commonwealth is in heaven” (Phil. 3); and elsewhere: “Whether we are sober-minded or beside ourselves, it is for God” (2 Cor. 5).

But this calf, still without horns and hoofs yet producing them, is young and has not yet advanced to the strength of a bull. For the soul of each believer, already taking hold of the rudiments of holy newness but not yet attaining the perfection of the holy Fathers, is called not an adolescent but, diminutively, a young maiden, because in its weakness it cannot rise to the height of perfection. Yet it produces, so far as it can, the first little flowers of good action, [Col. 1028C] until, gradually growing, it displays full and ripe fruits of virtues.

Let the bride, then, say: “Therefore the young maidens have loved you exceedingly,” because the minds of believers, still advancing daily in faith through grace, greatly love the sweetness of your mercy, O Beloved, since, through its sweetness, they can attain it by your gift. By your gift, I say, because without you we can do nothing. Therefore I cry out and invite all who love you to cry out with me: “Draw me; we shall run after you,” etc.

**VERSE 3.—“Draw me: we shall run after you in the fragrance of your ointments. The king has brought me into his inner chambers; we shall exult and rejoice in you, mindful of your breasts above wine: the upright love you.”**

But whence comes this cry or petition of a believing soul which longs for God? Surely from consideration of its own weakness, by which it recognizes that without assisting grace it can in no way suffice for itself. For, according to the Apostle, “it is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy” (Rom. 9). This statement does not destroy free choice; rather, it shows that divine grace’s help is altogether necessary to free choice, without which every will to work well always lies ineffective. Indeed, from free choice everyone has the will to come to God; not, however, because this very willing comes from oneself, since “we are not sufficient of ourselves to think anything,” which is less than willing, “as from ourselves” (2 Cor. 3). [Col. 1029A] These are the words of the Apostle, who attributes to God—not to his own choice—everything that can be good: thinking, willing, and accomplishing, “for good will” (Phil. 2).

If, therefore, God works these three things in us—thinking good, willing good, and accomplishing good—then He does the first without us, the second with us, and the third through us. For, by putting a good thought into us, He goes before us; by changing even an evil will, He joins it to Himself through voluntary consent; by providing the consent with ability or facility, the inward craftsman becomes known outwardly through our manifest work. Thus “it is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy” (Rom. 9), when, through the free gift of inwardly working grace, we have the will. But we cannot be moved to run without that assisting grace; and, once we are in the course, it will again be the work of merciful grace that we are able to arrive.

This drawing, therefore, which the bride asks for, is not the compulsion of a soul unwilling to follow God, but rather the leading of one that is willing. The Prophet prays for this in the Psalm: “Lead me in the path of your commandments, for I have desired it” (Ps. 118). It is as if he said in other words: Because by the gift of your grace I have the will to work well, lead me by the help of that same grace into action, so that I may arrive at the promise.

Such drawing occurs in four ways: through preaching; through weakness or adversity; through most evident miracles; through persecution or chastisement. This kindly Father intends thereby to make persons willing, [Col. 1029C] not to save them unwillingly, so that, in changing the will from evil to good, He may transform it rather than take it away. For no one is saved unwillingly. Thus there is no difficulty in what is read in the Gospel: “No one comes to me unless my Father draws him” (John 6), and likewise elsewhere: “Compel them to come in” (Luke 14). For although the merciful Father, who wills all to be saved (1 Tim. 2), may seem to draw or compel ever so many, He nevertheless judges no one worthy of salvation whom He has not first found willing.

The Creator has distinguished the rational creature in a singular way by this prerogative of divine dignity: just as He Himself was His own master and good by His own will, not by necessity, so that creature too might in some manner be its own master in this respect, so that only by its own will it might either become evil and be justly condemned, or remain good and be deservedly saved. This does not mean that its own will could suffice for salvation, but that no one could attain salvation without his own will.

The soul tending toward God, therefore, desires and prays to be drawn spiritually, not as someone is dragged unwillingly, but as a blind or weary person, when led, is not distressed but rather gives thanks to the one leading him, as to one lifting and helping him. So this soul too, giving thanks to God, asks that He who gave willing may also give power, so that with His assistance it may arrive at that toward which it tends, saying: “Draw me after you; we shall run in the fragrance of your ointments.”

Or, if it is pronounced: “Draw me after you,” and a pause is made there, then add: “We shall run in the fragrance of your ointments”; or if it is pronounced: “Draw me,” and a pause is made there, then add: “After you we shall run in the fragrance of your ointments.” The sense has the same force: to be drawn by Christ, or to run after Him, is to follow His footsteps by believing and acting.

“We shall run,” she says. What sort of running is this, and what ought it to be? Certainly not of the body but of the mind; not the movement of feet but of character. Of this progress, when the Psalmist spoke of the blessed who dwell in the Lord’s house and who, in this valley of tears, arrange ascents in their hearts, he said: “They shall go from strength to strength” (Ps. 83). And what is the fruit of this running or progress? “The God of gods shall be seen in Zion” (ibid.). [Col. 1030B] For what is the reward of this running except true and eternal blessedness? And what is true and eternal blessedness except contemplation of that supreme, eternal, and consubstantial Trinity? Therefore I shall not run alone; but as you, O Lord Jesus, hold my right hand, draw and lead me, and as it were run with me, we shall run.

By what way? Surely by you yourself, who said: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14). Through you I shall run to you for your sake: through you, who are the way, I shall run eagerly; to you, who are truth, I shall run securely; for your sake, who are life, I shall run joyfully. For I shall run eagerly because I have you as helper; securely because I do not doubt the reward; joyfully because I acknowledge and believe that to know and possess you is my reward.

[Col. 1030C] Thus I shall run not “as uncertainly” (1 Cor. 9), but so that I may obtain. The gift you have promised to those who run in this course of life through you, to you, and for your sake is of inestimable worth—what you proclaim through your prophet to be such that “eye has not seen, ear has not heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man” (Isa. 64).

“We shall run,” then, she says; but how? “In the fragrance of your ointments.” Since the Bridegroom’s ointments have many and diverse scents, and therefore do not all give off fragrance in one and the same way, why does she use the singular “in the fragrance,” and then the plural “of your ointments,” when she might rather have said, “in the fragrances of your ointments”? I think she has given some attention to this, because she has carefully considered how and by whom the ointments themselves are diffused. For what is this chief and singular fragrance except love? Every virtue, however, if it is without love, is no longer virtue, but rather a damnable vice, since all virtues ought to proceed from the root of love. Thus the Lord shows in the Gospel, where He instructs how the virtue of abstinence is to be maintained: “But when you fast, anoint your head and wash your face, so that you may not appear to men to be fasting, but to your Father who is in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you” (Matt. 6). What is it to anoint the head, except to cherish the ruling part of the mind in a good work by the sweetness of love? And what is it to wash the face, except to display the disposition of the inner [Col. 1031A] person as festive and joyful from delight in good works, through the sweetness of love?

Therefore neither abstinence, chastity, humility, obedience, nor any virtue is or can be anything without love. For although it may put forward the appearance of virtue, unless it proceeds from love of God or neighbour, it is not only not a virtue but even a detestable vice before God. And hence, when someone receives only human praise from it, he is at once deprived of the reward of divine recompense. But the disclosure of this ambiguous virtue will occur in the last judgment, when, according to the voice of Truth, in the night of that judgment—that is, in tribulation—there will be two in one bed, two women grinding together, and two in the field; of the two, one will be taken to life and the other left to death (Matt. 24; Luke 17).

By these names of things—bed, millstone, field—three kinds of vocations are denoted. Some rest with the Beloved in repose of mind, keeping sabbath; many are occupied with the labours of the active life; and others cultivate the hearts of hearers with the word of life. But in every vocation, an outcome of differing intention often appears. For in one bed—that is, in the repose of contemplative life, which especially belongs to those separated from worldly cares and devoting themselves to God alone through prayer or sacred meditation—this twofold intention is sometimes found: some perform it only for human favour [Col. 1031B] or fear, while others practise it solely for love and fear of God. So too in the active life, worldly favour compels some to labour, while the love of God compels others; and for many, either the vice of vainglory or the love of eternal life leads them to devote themselves to the word of preaching. Hence blessed Augustine, speaking of love, which “does not behave improperly” (1 Cor. 13) and is the judge of this twofold intention, says:

> “See how great are the works done by pride, how similar they are, and how nearly equal to those of love. Love feeds the hungry; pride also feeds them. Love does so that God may be praised; pride, that it itself may be praised. Love clothes the naked; pride also clothes them. Love fasts; pride fasts. Love buries the dead; pride buries them too. Whatever good works love desires to do and does, pride also sets in motion against it and, as it were, drives its own horses; but love is inward and removes the place occupied by wrongly directed pride.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Do not attend to what blossoms outwardly, but to what root is planted within. If covetousness is rooted there, there may be an appearance of good deeds, but they cannot truly be good works. If love is rooted there, be secure: nothing evil can proceed.”

In every good work, therefore, each person’s mind must burn with the fire of love, so that, with virtues kindled from it like aromatic spices, it may emit the sweetest smoke of fragrance. The Psalmist burned with such a fire of love when he said: “My heart grew hot within me, and in my meditation a fire shall blaze” (Ps. 18). Thus the Law also commands that fire should burn continually upon the altar (Lev. 6). For what is the altar except our heart, upon which we offer to God by intention whatever [Col. 1032A] good we do, or upon which we sacrifice ourselves by mortifying vices and practising virtues? On this altar, then, fire must burn continually, because no good work has any strength unless it proceeds from the ardour of love. Elsewhere too it is commanded that oil should always be in the house of the Lord for preparing lamps (Exod. 35; Lev. 24). By oil, which excels all liquids, love is understood, which surpasses all virtues. By lamps, however, good works are understood, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “Let lamps be burning in your hands” (Luke 12). The house of the Lord, or temple, is the body or mind of every holy person, concerning whom and which the Psalmist says: “Your holy temple is wonderful in righteousness” (Ps. 64). And elsewhere: “Holiness befits your house” (Ps. 92). The Apostle also says to believers: “The temple of God is holy, which you are” (1 Cor. 3). And elsewhere: “Do you not know that your bodies are the temple of the Holy Spirit?” (1 Cor. 6).

[Col. 1032B] Therefore oil for preparing lamps ought to be in the house of the Lord, because every faithful person, who is God’s house or temple, ought to possess love as the material by which he is kindled to pursuits of devotion.

The Beloved therefore fittingly speaks to her Bridegroom, saying: “We shall run in the fragrance of your ointments,” because surely in the course of good works each person labours in vain if he does not breathe forth the fragrance of love.

Yet in such a course four things must be considered: namely, measure, quality, intention, and usefulness. [Col. 1032C] This course [18] is nothing other than the life of each holy person. The perfect manner of running—that is, of living—ought to be such for each person that there is nothing excessive, nothing deficient, but that all things are paved with the love that lies between (Cant. III), following in the footsteps of the Fathers who went before, as Scripture commands: “Do not overstep the boundaries which your fathers have set” (Prov. XXII). Of these the Psalmist says that “the Lord knows the way of the righteous” (Ps. I), as though to say: because their way is known to God and pleases him, who, doing nothing outside discernment, sustain their lives by the even balance of justice. For those who wish or do something beyond and more than is right, the Apostle commands “not to think more highly than one ought to think, but to think soberly” (Rom. XII). But of those who fall short or grow lukewarm it is written: “Cursed is everyone who does the work of the Lord deceitfully” (Jer. XLVIII). Those have their pursuits paved with the love that lies between who, like those four living creatures, “having eyes before and behind,” whose feet were straight feet and were raised by the two wings (Ezek. I) of the twofold love of God and neighbor, also diminish their bodies—that is, their works—so that neither through the contemplative life do they withdraw from love of neighbor, nor through the active life fail in the love of God. In both they maintain so discriminating a manner of life that the perfect rule of justice admits nothing above or below it. Hence a wise man of this world says:

[Col. 1033A]

> There is a measure in things; in short, there are fixed limits,  
> Beyond and short of which the true cannot stand.  
> (Horace, *Satires* I.1.107)

Therefore, since every greater and lesser weight displeases God, each person’s life must be weighed with such equality that he neither collapse under excessive weight nor appear negligent and slothful under too slight a burden.

The quality of this course, or of the runner, must likewise be observed: namely, that it should be such as the Apostle describes: “In everything let us show ourselves as ministers of God: in much patience, in tribulations, in necessities, in distresses, in beatings, in prisons, in tumults, in labors, in vigils, in fastings, in chastity, in knowledge, in long-suffering, in kindness, in the Holy Spirit, in unfeigned love, [Col. 1033B] in the word of truth, in the power of God, through the weapons of righteousness on the right hand and on the left, through glory and dishonor, through ill repute and good repute; as deceivers and yet truthful; as unknown and yet known; as dying, and behold, we live; as chastened and not put to death; as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; as needy, yet making many rich; as having nothing, and possessing all things” (II Cor. VI).

See by what dispositions of soul this course is expressed. It is accomplished by the labor of the twofold human being, that is, body and spirit, so that, after the course has been completed, as there was labor and suffering in both, so there may one day be rest and consolation in both: this is the blessedness of the double robe.

The sages of this age, however, say that there are four species [19] [Col. 1033C] of quality. The first is habit and disposition. Although these belong to one species of quality, they differ in this: disposition is a habit easily changed; habit is a disposition remaining for a very long time. The second species of quality is that which arises from capacity and incapacity: capacity, indeed, when something can naturally be bent easily toward any occurrence; incapacity, when it cannot easily be bent otherwise. The third species is that which they call passive quality and passion. They distinguish the two within one species by saying that passion arises temporarily and is easily changed, whereas passive quality, by which we are called such-and-such, remains permanently. [Col. 1033D] This species seems similar to, and almost identical with, the first; but it differs in that passion is the momentary reception of something, whereas disposition, which they also call affection, is an intensified passion of that accident itself. Further, habit, since it is perfected through many things and in a certain order, is called an increased affection; while passive quality is a suddenly inborn and enduring passion. They placed the fourth species in figures and forms, calling figure certain outlines of things, but forms the beauty and shapeliness of those outlines. These kinds of quality are considered in the course of each person’s life according to the diversity of will and purpose, wherein lies the quality of applying one’s mind in whatever way to some work.

[Col. 1034A] Through disposition or affection, some pass into habit when, from opportunity or necessity, they turn certain good works, once begun, into custom through the progress of their manner of life; and, captivated by a certain delight in virtues, continually make advances, as is said of the saints: “They shall go from strength to strength” (Ps. LXXXIII). Further, as regards capacity and incapacity, there is no one who, in this course of rightly ordering life, does not possess the ability through the good of reason granted to him and grace assisting free choice; and he cannot be unable to assent to and labor with that grace.

According to the third species—that is, passion and passive quality—there are many who, when they hear a word concerning the punishment of the wicked and the glory of the good, are for a time pierced with compunction [Col. 1034B] and grow warm with love for good work; but because this love is not rooted in them, they grow cold in time of temptation. Yet there are some who, once they hear the word of God, are kindled to the practice of good work; and because they are “rooted and grounded in love” (Eph. III), they do not fall away from the love once conceived, but continually direct their steps in good work until the end of life.

Or we may call it passion when the mind suffers, as it were, for an hour through humility, patience, and obedience, resisting its own rather than another’s will—but this very rarely happens. Passive quality [20], however, occurs when by the enduring suffering of voluntary mortification, through the aforesaid or any other virtues, it is daily worn down, consenting to none of this world’s pleasures. But according to the fourth species, which they place [Col. 1034C] in figures and forms, this quality of life may be considered when it is ordered according to the example and form of some life, just as James exhorts the disciples: “Take, brothers, as an example of labor and patience the prophets who spoke to you in the name of the Lord” (Jas. V). And Paul says: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (Phil. III).

Therefore that quality by which affection passes into habit; by which, through God’s grace, willing and being able are at hand; by which one is constant in good work—not momentarily or hourly, but perpetually; or which receives the model of the Fathers who went before—must be most carefully attended to by everyone wishing to run well, so that according to it there may be made a kind of mirror of uprightness and discipline, by which he may gain both the reward of his own labor and the salvation of those who imitate him, as well as the benefit [Col. 1034D] of his neighbors.

The intention in running in this manner—that is, in acting rightly—will be this: that no desire for empty glory creep into the mind, but that love of God or love of eternal life be the cause of such labor and watchfulness.

Intention itself is, as it were, an eye of the mind. Of it the Savior says in the Gospel: “If your eye is single, your whole body will be full of light; but if it is evil, your body also will be dark” (Matt. VI). And in this same Song of Songs the bridegroom says to the bride: “Behold, you are beautiful, my friend; behold, you are beautiful; your eyes are those of doves” (Cant. V). Sometimes works are done which those ignorant of the intention from which they proceed interpret badly; [Col. 1035A] just as, conversely, some things are regarded favorably which are disapproved by the heavenly Inspector because they are brought forth with an evil intention. Such things are not only unrewarded but rather condemned, while those which the ignorant judge worthy of condemnation are more richly rewarded by the just Judge. Hence the Lord says of the reprobate through the prophet: “This people honors me with its lips, but its heart is far from me” (Isa. XXIX). Therefore all good things are directed according to this eye of intention, so as to be worthy either of reward or condemnation: reward, if done for God; condemnation, if carried out for human favor.

What the usefulness of this course or labor is, the Apostle explains, saying: “The sufferings [Col. 1035B] of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory which shall be revealed in us” (Rom. V). And the Lord cries to those running in this way in the Gospel: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will give you rest” (Matt. XI). Likewise the Apostle, knowing that he had not run in vain, after announcing the course of his labor—“I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith” [21]—confidently adds the fruit of that labor promised to himself: “Henceforth there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness, which the just Judge will render to me on that day” (II Tim. IV).

Great and beyond estimation, then, is the usefulness: the very fruit of eternal life, which is granted eternally in the life to come, without any defect, to those who labor for God. [Col. 1035C] But because the Church, or any faithful soul, is permitted even in the present life to taste beforehand the fruit of this usefulness, she continues, saying: “The King has brought me into his storerooms.”

This entrance possesses no small dignity, if one rightly considers the person who brings her in, the place, and the manner of the entrance. For it is not just anyone, but a king; and not merely a king, but the King of kings, who brings her in. Nor is it merely into a house, but into the storerooms; nor is this entrance made abruptly, but in a manner appropriate to reason. Many enter the house of this King—that is, the Church—but very few indeed can gain entrance into the storerooms. Some may keep watch before the doors of these storerooms and are able to look in, but cannot enter [Col. 1035D] unless he brings them in, he who “has the key of David, who opens and no one shuts, shuts and no one opens” (Apoc. III).

We must consider what these storerooms of so great a King are. All divine Scripture, divided into the two Testaments, namely Law and Gospel, is the treasury, or storehouse, of this King’s riches. It is divided threefold: into history, allegory, and moral instruction. For this King, wise and merciful, ruling and nurturing in his great kindness and providence, established the arrangement of his riches in such a way that they should contain what the strong might seek according to the capacity of their differing understandings, while the weak would not recoil.

Many delight in history; most are nourished by allegory; some are instructed by moral teaching. But those whom this King deems worthy by so great a favor as to grant them entrance into all these storerooms—so that they pass from historical knowledge into allegorical knowledge, and from allegorical into moral knowledge—by what sweetness, think you, are they fed? By what torrent of the Lord’s delight are they made drunk? (Ps. XXXV). [Col. 1036A] To such people the Lord promises through the prophet: “Behold, I shall send you grain, wine, and oil, and you shall be filled with them” (Joel II).

Desirable indeed are such storerooms, in which the delights of these kinds are contained: that bread may strengthen the human heart, wine gladden the human heart, and oil make the face cheerful (Ps. CIII). We receive grain from the Lord when, in more obscure sayings, [Col. 1036B] the covering of the letter having been drawn aside, we inwardly perceive the inner things of the Law through the marrow of the Spirit. The Lord gives us his wine when he makes us drunk with the lofty proclamation of his Scripture; he also grants us his oil when, through more open precepts, he orders our life with gentle mildness.

[22] It is pleasant further to consider reverently why these rather are the kinds contained in the divine storehouse. For if you consider that single grain of wheat which, having died in the earth, “brought forth much fruit” (John XII), and observe the glorious magnitude of the abundant harvest springing from it, you will see how magnificent examples of notable works shine forth from the historical storehouses; how sweetly the marrow of mysteries [Col. 1036C] gives fragrance from the allegorical storerooms; and how useful are the lessons of commandments that shine forth from the moral repositories.

The comparison of Christ to a grain of wheat is most beautiful. For in a grain the kernel is covered by its husk. What, then, is signified by the husk but Christ’s flesh? What by the kernel but his divinity? Thus, in the grain the kernel is covered by the husk; in Christ divinity is hidden by flesh. Husk and kernel make one grain; flesh and divinity constitute the one person, Christ, God and man. Therefore, when you have examined all that was done concerning this grain of wheat—that is, Christ, God and man—namely, how this grain descended from the heavenly granary, fell into the earth and died, then rose again [Col. 1036D] and ascended into heaven, and, multiplied in the apostles and other believers by the grain of faith and righteousness, filled the whole world; how, with the wine of preaching overflowing, he restrained offenders by the severity of correction; and how with the oil of love and mercy he soothed the penitent—for in this way the man who fell among thieves was healed by that evangelical Samaritan (Luke X)—when, therefore, you read and understand all these things, some historically, others allegorically, still others morally, at times separately and at times together, in this same threefold manner; and when by God’s grace you can administer the same things to others in the same way, may you not gratefully say, for so great a benefit bestowed on you: “The King has brought me into his storerooms”?

What more excellent and perfect distinctions of virtue [Col. 1037A] shone than in this grain—that is, in this man of the Lord? Whatever saints draw from the depths of compassion, from gentleness of spirit, from the heavenliness of uprightness, from the guarding of humility, from the fervor of love, they draw from that very fountain of mercy, that very root of gentleness, that very power of justice—that is, from the very mediator of God and human beings, the Lord God.

These three kinds, then, are found more especially and as it were principally in the Lord’s storehouses. Whatever gives forth fragrance from the abundance of the Old and New Testaments is either wheat, strengthening and confirming the perfect in faith and the exercise of virtues; or wine, which either caresses the saints with the sweetness of heavenly promises or frightens sinners with the severity of divine judgment; [23] [Col. 1037B] or oil, which is poured into the hearts of saints through love or consoles penitents through mercy. Hence holy Church, or every faithful soul beloved by God, contemplating in mind such treasures of her Bridegroom, King, and Lord—better than every precious furnishing of all kings and princes—and understanding what mysteries or sacraments they contain, can rightly sing with a joyful voice of soul: “The King has brought me into his storerooms.” Such an entrance is sufficiently commended by the person and the place. The manner of this entrance is that it is not for an hour, but with the right of possession and, as it were, under a deed of dowry: an assignment of a spiritual and most holy dowry granted with such great grace, by which the union of the divine and human mind may be confirmed. [Col. 1037C]

When this wonderful entrance has been celebrated, a fitting thanksgiving for the gift bestowed follows. It is offered to God by the soul joined to him and, through the movement of both parts of the human being, sharing in the good things appointed to her by him: “We shall exult,” she says, “and rejoice in you.”

Exultation and joy appear in some manner to differ from one another. Their distinction is said to be this: joy is a movement of the soul alone, whereas exultation is a movement of body and soul.

Therefore the holy soul, sensing in herself the gifts of divine grace, ought to receive and preserve them with joy and exultation, and to exercise in deed what she senses in mind. [Col. 1037D] For “the proof of love is the showing forth of a work” (Gregory). Thus the mind joined to God through love, while inwardly rejoicing in the grace of understanding bestowed upon it, ought also outwardly to exult in works of virtue. Hence, in the parable of children playing in the marketplace, the apostles cry to those who were unwilling to perform any good works in response to their preaching: “We sang to you, and you did not dance” (Luke VII). They wished their hearers to have the dance of the spirit, in order to show that faith without works is idle (Jas. II).

King David prefigured this religious dance when he played and leaped before the ark of the Lord. For in the spirit he saw far ahead that, through Christ to be born from his flesh, that sacrifice of the Lord—not made by hands but [Col. 1038A] heavenly—would one day be established by faith and works. That wonderful Prophet appropriately and fittingly set forth this most beautiful play of holiness by his own prelude; for the grace of so great a future righteousness, to be administered and confirmed through Christ, his son according to the flesh, he rejoiced and exulted before that typological sacrifice of the Lord. And because he was ruler and leader of God’s people, by this act he instructed beforehand rulers of churches, who ought to preside over those subject to them in word and example, that they must dance before the ark of the Lord—which is his Church—with a spiritual dance, namely a movement of soul and body; so that, according to the Apostle, they may “present their bodies as a living sacrifice, holy, [24] pleasing to God” (Rom. XII): a sacrifice indeed through the mortification of vices, but living through the performance of good works. [Col. 1038B] And this before the ark of the Lord, so that people may see their good works and glorify their Father who is in heaven (Matt. V).

Because “with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. X)—which is to move in soul and body—it is certain that one cannot exist without the other. Hence the prophet exhorts: “Lift up your hearts with your hands to God” (Lam. III). To lift up hearts with hands is to believe and work. For one who believes and does not work lifts up the heart indeed, but not the hands; while one who works but does not have faith lifts up the hands indeed, but not the heart.

Therefore, for that gracious admission, by God’s grace, into the ineffable subtlety of divine mysteries, [Col. 1038C] the holy soul and Bride of Christ ought to render God due thanksgiving through the jubilation of heart and mouth and through the performance of works. This is to take oil with lamps and go out to meet the Bridegroom, saying: “We shall exult and rejoice in you,” because we bear in our conscience the joy of good works, and this “in you,” when we ascribe every good that we do not to our own powers but to your grace. After that entrance, gloriously celebrated and for which she gives thanks by exulting and rejoicing, she adds the cause of this exultation and joy: namely, remembrance of the desirable divine breasts, better than wine. For what exultation or joy worthy of a religious mind thinking and working for God would there be if it did not retain [Col. 1038D] the remembrance of these breasts—breasts sweeter than wine, that is, than every pleasure of the world? But whose breasts? Surely either those of the two Testaments, of which all divine Scripture consists, or those of the two commandments of love, on which the whole Law and the Prophets hang (Matt. XXII). Certainly meditation upon the divine Scriptures produces remembrance of the divine commandments; in them consists the rule of right living, to whose rectitude each person’s life is directed. “I shall meditate,” says the Psalmist, “on your ordinances; I shall not forget your words” (Ps. CXVIII).

For how can anyone be or be called righteous unless he remembers what God commanded—especially these breasts, namely the two commandments of the love of God and neighbor? Without this love, as the Apostle says, neither kinds of tongues, nor prophecy, nor knowledge of all mysteries, nor faith, nor almsgiving, nor martyrdom (I Cor. XII), [Col. 1039A] nor any virtue can benefit anyone. For whoever keeps the whole Law but stumbles in one commandment of love has become guilty of all (Jas. II).

Therefore, wishing to show that the whole rectitude of her life rests upon such remembrance, Christ’s Bride continues: “The upright love you.” It is as though she said: love is the proof of uprightness [25]. For if they are upright, they love you; if they do not love you, they are not upright. But because they conceive this uprightness from the remembrance of your commandments and receive it perfectly from love of you, it may rightly be said [Col. 1039B] that “the upright, mindful of your breasts better than wine, love you.”

This middle phrase of the sentence—“mindful of your breasts better than wine”—may without absurdity be joined, by a minor division, to the parts placed on either side. Thus it may be read: “We shall exult and rejoice in you, mindful of your breasts better than wine.” Or thus: “We shall exult and rejoice in you”; and, after making a minor division here, let this follow: “Mindful of your breasts better than wine, the upright love you.” For those who retain remembrance of God’s commandments and order their way of life according to them become upright; and only the upright can love, nor are they upright unless they love.

Moreover, it gives no small delight to the eyes of our [Col. 1039C] inner person to consider the most beautiful progression of this song, from the place where it says, “Draw me after you,” up to this brief utterance, “The upright love you.” For the order of this progression is a certain consequence of the kiss requested.

Here that kindly sevenfold Spirit, by certain ascents of the heart, indicates the sevenfold graces of his condescension, through which the holy soul, Bride of Christ, gradually rises until she advances to the inestimable bridal chamber of her Lord, Bridegroom, and King, there to be joined to him in eternal love. First she is drawn by God’s mercy; then, as though moving her foot to run, she offers the first fruits of good intention; soon, applying diligence, she merits [Col. 1039D] to be brought into God’s storerooms; and, once she has entered, she exults by understanding and rejoices by believing and working.

Then from this active life she passes to a certain beginning of the contemplative life through meditation upon and remembrance of God’s commandments. Directing whatever strength she still has to their line, she attains the perfection of uprightness; and thus at last, having set aside all cares and business, clinging to God through contemplation, she becomes so near to him in ardent love that she can say: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.”

**VERSE 4.—“I am black, but beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem, like the tents of Kedar, like the skins of Solomon.”**

Universally, the whole Church; particularly, individual churches; and singularly, every soul beloved of God has endured and endures adversity [Col. 1040A] from the opposing party, because good and evil qualities are set over against one another and are divided into diverse and contrary pursuits. One of these parties is called the heavenly city, the other the earthly; one belongs to God, the other to the devil.

These two parties were typified [26] by two women: one free, Sarah; the other a slave, Hagar, mother of Ishmael, whose son was Kedar, a name interpreted “darkness.” To this darkness is compared the blackness which the Church, or every holy soul, says she possesses according to the judgment of those who live badly, although by right judgment she considers it not blackness but rather beauty. What, then, is this blackness? Clearly, persecution inflicted by the sons of the slave woman. It is thought black by the perverse, [Col. 1040B] who do not believe in future goods, because it is grievous and distressing and appears to make those who endure it rejected and miserable. Yet they become more glorious, and inwardly, through hope of future rewards, beautiful and fair with spiritual joy. For the sons of that city signified by Sarah, who was free, are persecuted by the sons of the other city, represented by Hagar the slave woman: at one time by inflicting bodily evils, at another by spiritually afflicting the soul through malice.

Accordingly, the Apostle calls that play enacted between the son of the free woman and the son of the slave woman persecution: “He who was born according to the flesh persecuted him who was born according to the Spirit; so it is now also” (Gal. IV). [Col. 1040C] For the sons of the slave woman persecute the sons of the free woman not only by carnal persecution, but also by spiritual persecution, through which they endeavor to deprive them of that true freedom by which Christ set them free (ibid.), lest they serve sin, as these sons of the slave woman do. This persecution is indeed more grievous than every bodily persecution by as much as the spiritual portion—that is, the soul—is better than the bodily.

Hence, angered by such persecution, that free woman and mother of free children says: “Cast out the slave woman and her son, for the son of the slave woman shall not be heir with the son of the free woman” (Gen. XXI). For slaves of sin do not belong to that heavenly inheritance to which those free in righteousness belong. Therefore the Church, or any holy soul, makes little of persecution of this kind. Firmly established upon the rock of faith, she is often shaken by storms of outward persecution alone, but is not cast down, possessing patience and awaiting glory, honor, and incorruption unto eternal life. [Col. 1040D]

Let her therefore say: “I am black, but beautiful”: black indeed in the estimation of those who judge me because of temporal affliction; but beautiful to you, daughters of Jerusalem, who know and believe future goods, because the more I am humbled by temporal affliction, the more I am exalted in a greater beauty of virtues. But how am I regarded as black? “Like the tents of Kedar.” Kedar was the son of Ishmael, concerning whom the divine voice says: “He shall be a servile man, and every man’s hand shall be against him; he shall pitch his tents opposite the region of his brothers” (Gen. XVI).

[Col. 1041A] Why, however, did she not say “like the tents of Ishmael,” but “of Kedar”? Because Ishmael is interpreted “God hears,” whereas Kedar means “darkness”; and this name of darkness [27] better fits the opinion of those who call light darkness and darkness light (Isa. V), and who, after the likeness of his father Ishmael—who was a slave and pitched his tents not among his brothers but opposite the region of his brothers—consider the rejection of this world and the labor of true philosophy to be a kind of savagery and opposition.

But in what way beautiful? “Like the skins of Solomon”: beautiful, she says, like skins—not those of any other mighty man, but Solomon’s. For as Solomon was wiser and richer than all people of his time, so he also possessed more beautiful and more ornamented tents, made from choice and elaborately worked skins.

Skins are those of dead animals. But what are the skins of dead animals except the virtues and examples of the Fathers who went before? From the virtues and examples of the holy Fathers who preceded us—shining like skins with varied beauty—I, compacted as though into one skin, am the laboriously wrought tent of my King, the true Solomon, that is, our Lord Jesus Christ, the Peaceful One, who through his blood makes peace with all things in heaven and on earth (Col. I). Thus may it worthily be said of me through God’s grace: “This is the tabernacle which God has pitched, and not man.” [Col. 1041B]

**[Col. 1041C] VERSE 5.—“Do not look upon me because I am dark, because the sun has discolored me. The sons of my mother fought against me; they made me keeper of the vineyards; my own vineyard I have not kept.”**

I am beautiful as I am, and I am the beauty of the skin of the true Solomon, as you, daughters of Jerusalem, well know, since you daily proclaim this same beauty of mine to the praise of God, whose grace is beauty itself.

Therefore, do not look upon me because I am dark, because the sun has discolored me. Do not, I say, judge my outward disposition and condition, which I have acquired through the scorching of the sun—that is, through the heat of worldly temptation and affliction—or through the burning love of the true Sun, of whom it is written: “For you who fear my name, the sun of righteousness shall arise” [Col. 1041D] (Mal. IV). He has, through the inseparable accident of his love, as it were scorched me with such fervor that neither tribulation, distress, persecution, famine, nakedness, danger, nor sword can separate me from his love (Rom. VIII). Such discoloration is indeed a great and glorious beauty and adornment of my inner person.

Further, a holy person sometimes does things which those who judge badly interpret unfavorably, because they do not know the intention of the doer, which God alone judges. For “there are ways which appear upright to people but are crooked” (Prov. XVI); and, conversely, crooked ways which appear upright, because they do not attend to that eye of intention according to which every work is either [28] made upright or distorted. Therefore, in this sense, let the faithful soul say: “I am black, but beautiful.” As though she said: I indeed seem black in some action of mine to those who, not possessing a single eye, construe it in the opposite sense; whereas I am more beautiful because of my single eye, through which my whole body is full of light (Matt. VI). So too you, daughters of Jerusalem, judge, you who look upon me with a single and dove-like eye. Therefore, do not look upon me because I am dark, because the sun has discolored me: that is, do not suppose that my body—that is, my work—is dark; for what proceeds from the radiant grace of the true Sun is wholly light, having no part of darkness. [Col. 1042A]

Further, any soul converted to the Lord through penitence appears, through the severity of penitence, [Col. 1042B] as though black because of a sad and mournful condition. But because this sorrow is according to God and “works a steadfast repentance unto salvation” (II Cor. VII), and because “blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. V), she is beautiful. In hope she possesses that, according to the prophet, she may receive from the Lord a crown for ashes, oil of joy for mourning, and the garment of praise for a spirit of grief (Isa. LXI). And as a certain wise man says: “A heart which knows the bitterness of its own soul shall not have a stranger mingle in its joy” (Prov. XIV). Let such a soul therefore say: “I am black, but beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem, like the tents of Kedar, like the skins of Solomon.” For through the blackness of penitence I seem at first to have belonged to the sons of the slave woman, whose works are works of darkness; [Col. 1042C] but afterward penitence itself has bestowed on me such beauty that I now belong to the sons of the free woman, who know both how to fashion and how to be the tents of the true Solomon by mortification of the carnal life. Therefore do not look upon me because I am dark, because the sun has discolored me: that is, do not despise my penitence, because the true Sun made me undertake it, he who penetrated and illumined my heart with the rays of his grace and mercy, so that I might recover through penitence that most universal good, God himself, whom I had lost by sinning.

The present singing of the Song suitably concerns you, most holy sisters, who are and ought to be Brides of Christ, in view of the character of your vocation and order. For you display a despised [Col. 1042D] outward dress, yet preserve an inward disposition beautiful to God because acceptable to him, as we believe. Therefore let the whole body of your holy community proclaim with one harmonious and sweet accord of heart and voice: “I am black, but beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem, like the tents of Kedar, like the skins of Solomon; do not look upon me because I am dark, because the sun has discolored me.” This is more explicitly to say in other words: “We have become a spectacle to this world, and to angels, and to men” (I Cor. IV). The children of this age judge us black and ugly, like the tents of Kedar—that is, like the nations dead in the blackness of evils, both to God and to the world. But we seek neither the favor nor glory [29] [Col. 1043A] of the world; rather, bearing “oil in our vessels” (Matt. XXV), that is, the joy of good works in our consciences, we are lovely and beautiful in the eyes of our Bridegroom, like the skins of Solomon. That is, carrying about in our bodies “the mortification of Jesus” (II Cor. IV), we build in our hearts tabernacles beloved by him, of which he may say: “I will dwell in them and walk among them” (II Cor. VI). Therefore do not look on us because we are dark, because we do not have the fleeting and ugly beauty of this age. For this was effected by the true Sun, who has shone upon us by his grace with the strong fervor of his love, so that, despising all the pomp of this corruptible life, we may choose rather to please him in action and manner of life than the world. “The sons of my mother fought against me; they made me keeper of the vineyards; my own vineyard I have not kept.”

[Col. 1043B] After the Church, or any holy soul, has set forth her outward discoloration and its cause—for “all who desire to live godly in Christ will suffer persecution” (II Tim. III)—she now adds the aggravation of her persecution: that she has suffered and suffers it not only from strangers but also from brothers, which is more grievous. For the evils inflicted by strangers cause less pain; but those torments rage more fiercely which are inflicted by persons from whose minds
was presumed.

The chanting of this passage, however, seems not to require a single straightforward sense, because the Synagogue, the Church, and the heavenly Jerusalem—as well as the goodness or power of the Creator—may equivocally be called by the name of Mother. [Col. 1043C] The same equivocation under the name of sons includes the apostles and their successors, Jews, heretics, and hostile powers. Likewise, the conflict of such sons is not of one kind, since it is understood both in a good and in an evil sense. Each aspect, however, ought to have its own exposition.

For the primitive Church, which was composed of Jews, suffered persecution from those Jews who did not believe. Thus we read in the Acts of the Apostles that, “filled with zeal, they laid hands upon the apostles and put them in the public prison”; and elsewhere: “After they had beaten them, they charged them not to speak in the name of Jesus” (Acts 5). And concerning the persecution in which Stephen suffered, it is written that “a great persecution arose [Col. 1043D] against the Church which was at Jerusalem, and they were all scattered throughout the regions of Samaria except the apostles” (Acts 8).

Therefore, since both parties—the believers and the unbelievers—were sons of the Synagogue by nature or descent, while the unbelievers persecuted the believers on account of faith in Jesus Christ, that believing party which was then the Church of Christ could rightly say: “The sons of my mother fought against me; they made me a keeper in the vineyards; my own vineyard I did not keep” [Song 1:5/6]. As if it said in other words: Since the Lord commanded, saying, “Do not go into the way of the Gentiles, and do not enter the cities of the Samaritans; but go rather to the lost sheep of Israel” (Matt. 10), I, desiring to fulfil this command, preached to the sons of my mother the faith which I received from the Lord and through which they [Col. 1044A] ought to have been saved. But they despised my preaching, fought against me in word and deed, and drove me from their borders; they made me a keeper in vineyards—that is, in the churches of the Gentiles, who received the word of faith with joy. While I devoted the diligence of my labour and guardianship to them, I neglected to keep my own vineyard—that is, my own nation—because they despised my care and refused to receive the word of salvation. As one of my own said to them: “It was necessary that the word of God should first be spoken to you; but since you reject it and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13). For, as the same man says elsewhere: “By their offence, salvation has come to the Gentiles, that they may emulate them” (Rom. 11); and shortly thereafter: “I do not wish you to be ignorant, brethren, of this mystery, lest [Col. 1044B] you be wise in your own eyes: that blindness has happened in part to Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter; and thus all Israel shall be saved” (ibid.).

On account of this contempt, the prophet foretold that this vineyard would be left without protection: “The daughter of Zion shall be left,” he says, “like a shelter in a vineyard, like a hut in a cucumber-field, like a city under siege” (Isa. 1). The primitive Church, whose mother was the Synagogue, could indeed say these things, as could the opposite party of which it says that the sons of its mother fought against it.

Moreover, the universal Church could, and can, say of the apostles and their successors: “The sons of my mother fought against me; they made me a keeper [Col. 1044C] in the vineyards; my own vineyard I did not keep.” For the heavenly Jerusalem is the mother of believers because of the faith, hope, and charity which they have toward her. Since they hope and believe that they may become sharers in that blessedness of which the saints who preceded them have become sharers, they act and labour through the charity by which they love so great a good, so that they may attain that heavenly homeland. For what is to live holy and just lives for its sake except to be spiritually begotten from it and unto it?

The apostolic men too were her sons. While they suffered many labours and were worn down even to death in order to merit this most glorious homeland, assuredly, by believing, hoping, and loving, they themselves were being born unto it; [Col. 1044D] and no less were they begotten, with a kind of maternal affection, by her who was the cause of this labour of theirs.

Such sons, therefore, fought against the Church when they strove to overcome it in its error, just as even now they daily overcome every faithful soul from vices to virtue by words and examples. Did not one of them fight in this manner against churches when he said to one of them: “What do you wish? Shall I come to you with a rod, or in a spirit of gentleness? It is altogether reported that there is fornication among you, and such fornication as is not even among the Gentiles, so that one has his father’s wife” (1 Cor. 4). See how he first fought against these persons; after he had overcome them from this sin by rebuke, he raises them up by a consoling letter: “If I made you sorry,” he says, “in [Col. 1045A] the letter, I do not regret it; although I did regret it when I saw that that letter, even if only for an hour, made you sorry. Now I rejoice—not because you were made sorry, but because you were made sorry unto repentance. For you were made sorry according to God, so that you suffered no loss from us in anything” (2 Cor. 7). Writing also to another Church, he says: “O foolish Galatians, who has bewitched you not to obey the truth?” (Gal. 3). While he fights against it in this way, he conquers it away from unbelief.

But what does it mean that these sons appoint as keepers in vineyards those whom they assail in this manner and conquer away from vices, except that they teach and exhort them to guard the shoots and fruits of virtues? Yet these persons do not keep their own vineyard, because, by the struggle directed against them, they have advanced to such vigilance in virtue that they now neglect to preserve the errors of their former habit; indeed, through God’s grace, they drive those errors far away from themselves by the spirit of fortitude. Hence the prophet speaks in the person of such persons: “I will stand upon my watch” (Hab. 2). He stands upon his watch who, by the diligence of discipline, does not yield to earthly desires but rises above them, so that, while he seeks the eternity that ever stands, everything passing lies beneath him.

In yet another way the Church cries out concerning false brethren—heretics and schismatics—who rebel against her. So long as they were in the Church and shared the same sacraments, they were thought to be sons of that heavenly Jerusalem, which is mother of the faithful, and to belong to the city of God. But after they were seen to blaspheme against [Col. 1045C] Christ’s divinity and humanity and to divide the holy unity, they were cast out of the inheritance of sons; and it was proved that they had not truly been sons, but rather adulterous children. To such people the Apostle says: “But if you are without discipline, of which all sons have been made partakers, then you are adulterous children and not sons” (Heb. 12). John also says of them: “They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would surely have remained with us” (1 John 2). And the Lord says through the prophet: “My sons went out from me and do not remain” (Jer. 10).

Therefore, at the time when these sons, illegitimate rather than true sons, attacked those who were of rightful sonship because of the assertion of a differing faith—when heretical leaders favoured defenders of perverse belief—the holy Catholic men were driven from their sees and suffered losses, exiles, and many dangers [Col. 1045D] because they preached the correct doctrine of faith and refused communion with heretics.

Since, therefore, both parties were distinguished by ecclesiastical offices and held the same sacraments, and on this account were believed to belong to the bosom of one Mother, they were divided solely by diversity of faith; and that society of the wicked persecuted the Catholic society. Scorched by the heat of this persecution, the latter calls itself black and says that it was darkened by the sun for which it contended: namely, that in divinity Christ should be said to be equal to the Father and of one substance, power, and will with him; and that in humanity he should be believed to be a true [Col. 1046A] human being—something which the opposing party blasphemously denied.

The Catholic party therefore gives the reason for its darkening: “The sons of my mother fought against me.” And because, while such sons—not legitimate sons but adulterous children, that is, heretics—were persecuting it, the party of sound faith was compelled to move to other places and leave its own cities, it adds: “They made me a keeper in vineyards; my own vineyard I did not keep.” For many churches at that time, deprived of their own pastor, were stained by heretics with perverse doctrine; and holy priests, exiled, scattered the word of faith in foreign places, which the exigency of the times prevented them from doing in their own.

Otherwise. Since the goodness and [Col. 1046B] power of the Creator are the mother of every creature—for it belonged to his goodness that he created us when we did not exist, and to his power that “he did all that he willed” (Ps. 113)—and since among all creatures there are two rational kinds, angel and human being, they seem, because of their share in reason and because both were created by that same goodness and power, to possess a certain fellowship of brotherhood, so that they may be called sons of the same mother. But because that part of the angels which fell saw—and envied—the human creature rising through God’s grace to the glory from which it had fallen, it persecuted and laboured in every way to destroy it. Let the human being therefore say, in the person of the weak: “The sons of my mother fought against me; they made me a keeper in vineyards; my own vineyard he does not [Col. 1046C] keep.”

“While,” he says, “these rational spirits, the sons of my mother, fought against me, they compelled my frail mind to love earthly occupations and to abandon the guardianship of my soul.” For by vineyards, whose work is carried on in the open air, may be signified occupations in outward actions. The more the mind is scattered abroad through the external senses around earthly activities, the more the soul within neglects its own custody.

For since the soul is invisible, it is in no way touched by pleasure in bodily things except because, being joined to the body, it has, as it were, certain outlets through the senses of that same body. Sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch are, as it were, certain paths of the mind through which it goes outside and desires those things [Col. 1046D] that are beyond its substance. Through these bodily senses, as through windows, the soul looks upon outward things, and, looking upon them, desires them. Hence Jeremiah says: “Death has ascended through your windows and entered your houses” (Jer. 9). For death ascends through the windows and enters houses when concupiscence comes through the bodily senses and enters the dwelling-place of the mind.

Thus hostile powers cause a mind occupied with earthly activities to neglect itself, when, through the dissipation of outward works, they compel it not to stand fast in the keeping of its soul. It may thus deservedly say: “The sons of my mother fought against me; they made me a keeper in vineyards; my own vineyard I kept.” But because in every adversity [Col. 1047A] or danger inflicted upon it not so much by strangers as by brethren, the universal or particular Church, or any faithful soul, is troubled by a certain heat of uncertainty—because many hold the faith only in name, and it is not easy to discern who are truly faithful—it turns to the Lord, its Bridegroom. Seeking his assistance for the grace of such discernment, it continues with the following prayer of entreaty: “Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you pasture, where you lie down at noon.”

**VERSE 6.—**“Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you pasture, where you lie down at noon, lest I begin to wander after the flocks of your companions.”

God is said to make known in three ways: by deed, by understanding, and by voice. By deed, indeed, when, to a mind in doubt, he manifests by some sign of his power what ought to be chosen or held. In this way, in order to restrain a seditious people from murmuring, when among twelve rods which he took from the individual tribes and commanded to be placed in the tabernacle of the covenant, Aaron’s rod alone, for the tribe of Levi, had flowered and borne fruit (Num. 17), he showed by this sign that he had chosen Aaron and his offspring for the priesthood, to approach especially for offering sacrifices to God and to enter the Holy of Holies. This was a foreshadowing of the most noble future succession through which that unique birth was to be brought about by the Virgin Mary. [Col. 1047B]

He makes known by understanding when, touching someone’s mind by hidden inspiration, he reveals to that person’s understanding what ought more rightly to be done. Thus, when King David, whose name was prophetic, thought of building a house for the Lord, this did not displease God but rather pleased him. Although God forbade him to do it in his own time because he was a man of blood (2 Sam. 16 [probably 2 Sam. 7; materially uncertain citation]), he did not disapprove the motive; indeed, he judged it worthy of so great a reward and honour that he promised to raise up a Son who would be exalted by such a prerogative of peaceful innocence and wisdom as to be fit to complete such a work. Moreover, desiring to reward this good will of David, which pleased him, God says: “I declare to you beforehand that the Lord will build you a house” (1 Sam. 7 [probably 2 Sam. 7]). Thus, in order to show that what David had conceived pleased him, and that he had made it known [Col. 1047C] to him by understanding, God not only did not forbid what he had thought, but also visited it with his grace so that that house might become of great renown and excellence throughout the world.

God makes known by voice, now by himself and now through others: by himself, as he spoke to Abraham, Moses, and the other prophets; through others, when first through the prophets themselves, then through the apostles and other believers to whom he entrusted the proclamation of his message to others, he made known what was his will and what concerned their salvation.

Again, according to these modes, God is said to make known in four ways: sometimes by deed and understanding; sometimes by deed and voice; most often by understanding and voice; and sometimes all at once, by deed, understanding, and voice. He makes known by deed and understanding when he foreshadows something by showing things, and at once makes known through understanding to the person to whom he shows it what he has foreshadowed. Thus, when the differences and qualities of future kingdoms were shown to Daniel through various likenesses of beasts, he understood some things only when an angel taught him; but he understood other things by himself immediately after seeing them. Thus, after the likenesses of things had been shown to him, he immediately adds in one place, “And I understood”; and elsewhere: “A word was revealed to Daniel, whose name was Belteshazzar; and the word was true, and of great strength; and he understood the saying” (Dan. 8 and 10). [Col. 1048A]

He is said to make known by deed and voice when he foretells something by an act and declares by voice what it means; as when he granted Peter the astonishing catch of fish and immediately disclosed the meaning of this miracle: “Do not fear; from now on you shall catch human beings” (Luke 8 [probably Luke 5]).

He makes known by understanding and voice when he gives someone to understand his will and, by an explicit voice, confirms that the person understood this through his inspiration. Thus, when Jacob was about to go down into Egypt and understood that Joseph had been sent ahead not without God’s will and ordering, without having consulted God concerning this, As Scripture relates: “He departed with all his household and came to the well of the oath; and, having offered victims there to the God of his father, he heard him saying to him in a vision: ‘Jacob, Jacob.’ [Col. 1048C] He answered, ‘Here I am.’ And he said: ‘Go down into Egypt; do not fear, and I will make you there into a great nation’” (Gen. 31 [probably Gen. 46]). See: what this man had understood to be God’s will, the divine voice likewise attested—that God had judged it so for him through understanding.
