But God seems to make known simultaneously by deed, understanding, and voice when he intimates something by a preceding sign, the meaning of which sign the understanding of the beholder, made capable by the Spirit, weighs; and the author of the very matter subsequently confirms it also by voice. Finally, when Isaiah, fearing to undertake the office of preaching, said: “Woe is me, because I have been silent; for I am a man of unclean lips and dwell in the midst of a people having unclean lips” (Isa. 6), he understood the condescension of the grace that called him, from the sign given him by God, which he describes thus: “One [Col. 1048D] of the seraphim flew to me, and in his hand was a coal which he had taken from the altar with tongs; and he touched my lips, saying: ‘Behold, this has touched your lips; and your iniquity shall be taken away, and your sin cleansed.’” When the Lord said, “Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?” Isaiah reverently attended to the divine will, and immediately, humbly and dutifully offering himself for the office, said: “Behold, I am here; send me” (Isa. 6). Then the Lord confirmed by voice what he had foreshadowed by deed and disclosed through understanding, instituting the prophet in the office of preaching: “Go,” he says, “and say to this people: ‘Hear, you who hear me, and do not understand; see the vision, and do not know’” (ibid.).

By one of the foregoing modes, therefore, the Church—or any soul pleasing to God—asks that the grace of necessary discernment be made known [Col. 1049A] to it, so that it may recognize where it can and ought to find the dwelling pleasing to divine favour. “Tell me,” it says, “you whom my soul loves.” “O Lord,” it says, “this making known of yours must not be received casually, lightly, or as though it were of little importance. Therefore grant the gift of this grace not to just anyone, but to me who love you; for only the power of contemplative charity avails for perceiving this subtle matter.”

And what will you make known? Namely, “where you pasture, where you lie down at noon.” Who are those whom God feeds except those whom he himself leads and sets forth in the green pastures of virtues, where they may gather the different kinds of holiness? Their healthfulness gives health to the soul, drives away diseases, and makes a person effective [Col. 1049B] for every good work. But what are these kinds, of such vigour that they produce a human being so strong, so beautiful, and so glorious? It is clearer than light: humility, patience, obedience, chastity, purity of body and soul, incorruption of mind and mortification of flesh, contempt of the world and fear of God, and finally the very charity of God and neighbour, without which the practice of all these kinds will have no efficacy.

For one who desires to know which and what kind of persons God feeds—that is, which persons are the sheep of that true Shepherd—this is the criterion. Of these he himself says: “My sheep hear my voice, and I the Lord know them” (John 10). Thus he proves those who hear his voice to be his sheep, and they are sheep because they hear; their hearing and being such sheep is his knowing them. Conversely, those who do not hear are not sheep; rather, beneath sheep’s clothing they are ravening wolves, concerning whom he says: “You will know them by their fruits” (Matt. 7). Their not hearing and not being sheep is his not knowing them, as he says to such persons: “I do not know you; depart from me, you cursed, into eternal fire” (Matt. 25). [Col. 1049C]

The place where God feeds those whom he feeds, then, is the meadows or green pastures of virtues, and the spiritual pastures of doctrines. There it is found and recognized who are the Lord’s sheep and who are not, because those who are according to the Spirit savour the things of the Spirit; but the natural person does not receive the things that are of the Spirit of God (1 Cor. 2).

These pastures in which God feeds whomever he feeds are not uniform, owing to the twofold manner of living and teaching, although in themselves they are the same in both respects. One is called good life and the other good knowledge; but in the subjects in whom they exist and of whom they are predicated, they differ because of the different distributions of graces. For one person is described as humble, another as gentle or mild; this one as patient, that one as obedient; another as chaste, yet another as merciful or generous, or by some other such quality pertaining to the manner of living well. In the other sphere, which is good knowledge, one subject is described as a good speaker or preacher; another as a good interpreter or expositor; another as skilled in the liberal arts, or by some other quality that pertains to the manner of teaching well. [Col. 1049D]

These qualities, individually predicated, also admit of more and less: on the one hand, one person is more patient or more chaste than another, or differs in any other respect that can attach in greater or lesser degree to an honourable life; on the other, one is more learned, eloquent, or educated than another, or differs in any other respect that can attach in greater or lesser degree to the soul’s capacity for knowledge. [Col. 1050A]

Therefore, although in such pastures, in which God feeds what he feeds, there is not a simple but a manifold diversity, and although more and less occur within that diversity, those who are fed, though not fed equally because of the diversity and measure of gifts, are nevertheless all the Lord’s sheep and are called such. For just as star differs from star in splendour, yet all stars are contained under one firmament, so there are indeed many differences among the saints because of the differing virtues that are in them, yet all are known to belong to the one kingdom of God. Hence, when the Lord said through the prophet, “Behold, I myself will seek my sheep and visit them, as a shepherd visits his flock on the day when he is among his scattered sheep,” he adds shortly afterwards: “Their pastures shall be by the streams, and in all the habitations of the land, and on the mountains of Israel” (Ezek. 34). Streams proceed from fountains; the pastures of the earth are lowly, but those of mountains are lofty. [Col. 1050B]

What, then, are the streams except certain deeds and sayings flowing from the great Fathers as from fountains? What are the pastures of the earth except the more elementary teachings of the divine commandments? And what are mountain pastures except the lofty mysteries of the divine sacraments? God therefore set before his sheep—great and small, weak and strong—pastures suitable for both according to the capacity of each, so that the small and weak might have nourishment and strengthening for eternal life, while the great and strong might have what enables them to advance and be satisfied.

In such sheep of his, whom and in whom God feeds in this way, he prepares rest for himself, so that he may lie down and rest in them for the sake of his own wrath. He is said to lie down and rest in them when he delights in their devout acts. Hence, through the prophet: “Upon whom shall I rest, except upon the humble and quiet person, and one who trembles at my words?” (Isa. 66). Conversely, he is said to labour in the minds of the reprobate when he is, as it were, wearied by their wicked acts. Thus, when the prophet said to certain perverse people, “You have made the Lord weary with your words,” and they replied, “How have we made him weary?”, he said: “By saying, ‘Everyone who does evil is good in the sight of the Lord, and such persons please him’” (Mal. 2). [Col. 1050C]

The Godhead, then, driven away from wicked hearts, exasperated and in some sense wearied by their perverse deeds—for, as it is written, “the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee from the deceitful and withdraw from thoughts devoid of understanding, and will be rebuked when iniquity comes upon it” (Wis. 1)—is rejected by them in this repulsion. But in the minds of the saints, invited and received by their devout acts, it lies down and rests sweetly and, as it were, delightfully; their reception of it is their election. [Col. 1051A]

The Church, therefore, or the holy soul asks to be told where the Bridegroom pastures and where he lies down, and this not at any time whatever but at noon. Since in this place “noon” ought to be understood only anagogically, it is first worthwhile to consider what “day” is said to mean, in what ways it is so said, and how many and what parts of a day there are. Once these matters are known beforehand, we shall leave it to another’s judgement which of the diverse significations contains the more ready meaning.

For “day” seems not to be said simply, because of the various forms of its signification; rather, by the community of its name and the diversity of its definition, it has the force of equivocation.

[Col. 1051B] Let us therefore posit four forms of day. The first is called the natural day; the next, established according to the form of the first, may not unfittingly be called the day of action. The third, consisting solely in the light of reason, may appropriately be called the intellectual day. Finally, the last, which never fails, alone lacks time, and remains fixed in its own immutability, is most suitably termed the eternal day. The first is the support of human life; the second an example for ordering life; the third a mirror for discerning life; the fourth and last the reward of a life well completed.

Let us suppose that each of these is divided into three parts—morning, noon, and evening—except the last alone, which was, is, and shall be always without time; for its being and incomparable splendour are God himself. [Col. 1051C]

The first day, the natural day, is not relevant to the present passage except insofar as the other two—for the last, as we have said, is without time—are formed according to its pattern.

In the natural day, then, morning is the sun’s first rising. As it gradually climbs and increases, it brings about noon around the middle of the day, at the point beyond which the sun does not advance but is, as it were, fixed at the centre. Then, descending and diminishing again, it brings about evening around the end of the day, which is the complete setting of the sun.

According to the form of this day, there is established the day which we have called the day of action, extending from the beginning of the world to its end. Its morning was the time before the Law, when the human being used only the natural law; its noon was under Law and grace, when one was instructed by both natural and written law; its evening is the time of the Last Judgement, when one will be judged, whether unto life or unto death, both for the natural and for the written law. [Col. 1051D]

Before the Law, through the natural law, the human being had morning—that is, a certain beginning of discernment. Reason guided him so that he could see and know by how much he excelled brute animals, because he could distinguish good and evil; and, at the highest level, could consider and understand that no creature can create itself, but that there is an Uncreated One who commanded all things that have been made to come into being. From the beauty and usefulness of creation, he could perceive how much more excellent and glorious that One is than all created things, and consequently that he would be without excuse if he rendered to the creature the honour owed to the Creator. [Col. 1052A]

But when this natural law was buried in some persons by the habit of sinning, the written law was given to prohibit and restrain sinners. By it the merit of each person might be established, since its observance was a cause of reward, and its transgression a cause of condemnation. Yet in some persons the natural law itself was so strong that they did not need the written law, since they were a law unto themselves, showed the work of the law written in their hearts, and, though without law, did the things of the law; their own conscience bearing witness to them on the day when God would judge the hidden things of human beings (Rom. 2; the printed text reads “Num. II”).

But where the written law was added to the natural law, after morning there came, as it were, noon, because those upon whom the sun of righteousness had already risen, being given the commandment either of truth or of the new law, were inflamed in both respects with such fervour of charity toward God that they chose rather to die than to transgress the honourableness of the law prescribed to them by God. [Col. 1052B]

This may be seen in those most fervent champions of either Law, who possessed a most steadfast zeal either to defend or to uphold the holy law. By way of example, one under the old Law was Phinehas son of Eleazar, who vindicated the law by killing those who had become transgressors of it; so also Mattathias and his sons, who defended the law, and the seven brothers, who chose rather to die while keeping the law than to live by transgressing it.

What, then, shall we say of those most glorious and valiant fighters under the new Law—the apostles and their followers? So great was their fervour of divine charity and their zeal for righteousness that they did not hesitate, for faith, justice, and truth, to endure every adversity, undergo every kind of death, and finally fall in death itself. Of them the Apostle says: “The saints endured mockings and scourgings, moreover also chains and prisons; they were stoned; they died by the slaughter of the sword” (Heb. 11). Were not all these persons, under Law or under grace, at noon, when they endured such burning trial in body and heart—the great heats of that doubly burning noon? For their minds burned with the fervour of holy charity, while their bodies were afflicted by the heat of much tribulation. [Col. 1052C]

The evening too, which is the time of the Last Judgement, must assign refreshment and rest after the heat of their labour to such distinguished recruits. From the heavenly King, for whose love they toiled, they shall receive the bounty of eternal recompense: that most universal, unfailing, and unchangeable good which is God of gods himself. For God’s rewarding is this: to give himself to his elect.

Moreover, that intellectual day is fittingly composed of the same parts set out above. In the mind of everyone who flourishes in the splendour and warmth of virtues, the beginning of a good work is, as it were, morning; the perfection of a work well begun, through the increase and progress of holiness, is noon; and the best completion, unto the end, of a work well begun and better perfected is evening. This day in every wise person is understanding itself, which judges and discerns the things around it both in thought and in action, because it is in the light and can see what it ought to do and what avoid. But one who walks in darkness does not know where he goes (John 12; Isa. 29, 50), because darkness has blinded his eyes. Therefore that person’s works are works of darkness; and because that person does not possess this day—that is, understanding—he is said to differ little from irrational creatures on account of the irrational and almost beastlike movements of wicked deeds. [Col. 1053A]

The first honourable works, still small and slight, are like the first beginnings of light in this intellectual day. But when they have grown through constancy and the mind has conceived a certain warmth from them, then, as this warmth gradually increases, it kindles into the full flame of divine charity, as into the noon of this day. The brighter light of understanding is then opened, so that earthly things no longer give delight, but the whole person burns with love of God. Hence the Psalmist, describing the morning and noon of this day, says: “My heart grew warm within me, and in my meditation fire blazes forth” (Ps. 38). As if he plainly said: My mind was long ago warmed by the desire for a good work; but because through meditation on God’s commandments it is daily led from things below to things above by contemplation, it is no longer merely warm, but wholly burns in love of its Creator with the fire of charity. [Col. 1053B]

The evening of such a day is the completion of a good work to the end of life; nor can the preceding parts avail anything if this final part is lacking. “For whoever perseveres to the end shall be saved” (Matt. 24). Hence the Psalmist says: “The lifting up of my hands is an evening sacrifice” (Ps. 140). As if to say in other words: The beginning or progress of my works becomes a sacrifice to God when I close my final day in their pursuit. And by the precept of the Law, the tail of the victim is commanded to be offered in sacrifice. For the tail is at the end of the body. One offers well who brings the sacrifice of good work to the end of the action required. Hence Joseph is described as having a long robe among his other brothers; for a robe reaching to the ankle is a good work extended unto completion. [Col. 1053C]

Therefore, the morning of the intellectual day is initiating virtue; noon is perfecting virtue; evening is contemplative virtue. Such a day admits of greater and lesser degrees according to the threefold condition of temporal growth in a person: in childhood understanding is less, in youth greater, and in old age greatest. Yet in many persons what remains declines, as in the decrepit, who sometimes seem to become childish again in understanding. Childhood or adolescence is a kind of morning, like the sun’s rising; youth is a kind of noon, like the sun’s highest ascent and most burning time, just as that age has the greatest heat and strength; old age is a kind of evening, like the sun’s descent from the high sky and the failing of heat, just as at that age a person declines from the warmth of youth. [Col. 1054A]

Whether, therefore, understanding is distinguished by the stages of life or is distinguished in itself by the growth of works, it may not unfittingly be called the intellectual day. Thus this is what the Psalmist says: “At evening, morning, and noon I will recount and declare” (Ps. 54). As if he said: In childhood, youth, and old age—or in the morning, noon, and evening, as it were, of age or understanding—I shall declare, by teaching and acting, the rule for right living.

The final form of the day, which we have called eternal, has of these three parts the noonday alone. For it has no morning in itself; but in those who [Col. 1054B] participate in it, it has some sort of morning: before the resurrection, indeed, in the soul alone, when by dying happily they are born into it; but at the resurrection, both in soul and body, when by rising again most happily they are reborn into it. Sacred Scripture calls this blessedness of body and soul the double robe; but the blessedness of the soul alone, the single robe.

Therefore, whatever blessedness has some beginning—even now in the soul, and then in body together with soul—has in its participants a certain morning, as has been said. But in its own nature and property, which immutably was, is, and shall be, there never was morning, because blessedness itself is God, in whose immutability those made immutable participate.

[Col. 1054C] But evening neither could nor can in any way exist, either in itself or in its participants, because they shall stand eternally fixed with him, to whose natural eternity they are joined by grace. Yet it has always had, and shall always have, noonday both in itself and in its participants: in itself, because of its singular excellence in beauty, brightness, and repose; in its participants, because of the most ardent fervour of divine charity. That charity is as much more fervent in that life than they can possess it in this life as that life is plainly far happier and beyond comparison with this one. Hence the prophet says: “The Lord lives, whose fire is in Zion and whose furnace is in Jerusalem” (Isa. XXXVI). To be a furnace is more than to be fire, because fire may be small; but in a furnace a broader flame [Col. 1054D] is kindled. Zion is called contemplation, but Jerusalem the vision of peace. Here, meanwhile, we contemplate our peace, so that there we may afterward see it fully. Therefore, from love of the Lord there is fire in Zion and a furnace in Jerusalem: here we burn somewhat with the flames of his love, where we contemplate something of him; but there we shall burn fully, where we shall fully see him whom we love.

This eternal day, then, has noonday alone, far brighter and more fervent than the noons of the formal or natural days described above. Yet it receives more and less according to the merits of those who participate in it, because, although it is in itself one and the same, those participating in it participate unequally. For in the Father’s house are many dwelling-places [Col. 1055A] (John XIV), because within one reward the glory of the elect is diverse, just as the misery of the reprobate is according to the merit of each.

In this passage, therefore, we must consider not the noon of the first or the last day, but that of the intermediate days—namely, the active and the intellectual—because the purpose of everyone living rightly ought to rest upon zeal either for the active or for the contemplative life.

Therefore, since many appear to be in the fervour of divine charity, whether living the active or the contemplative life, who do not have the single eye because they do good things without right intention, displaying them not for God but for empty glory or earthly gain, and since it is very difficult to distinguish such persons from those who truly [Col. 1055B] love God, the Church, or some holy soul, asks her Bridegroom to make known to her, by the spirit of discernment and in some manner of the modes set forth above, which are those who love and follow him not falsely but truly; among whom he feeds them with the sweetness of his commandments, and among whom he lies down and rests in the delightful repose of virtues at noonday—that is, in the fervour of his charity—as he himself says: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we shall come to him and make our dwelling with him” (ibid.). For whoever keeps the words of God proves that he loves God; and whoever loves God is worthy of God’s indwelling. He then adds the reason why she asks for this gift of discernment, saying: “Lest I begin to wander [Col. 1055C] after the flocks of your companions.”

Some are companions of Christ, and some are merely thought to be; and because they differ in the quality of their lives, they are rightly called not one flock but flocks. Those who truly are such are spoken of differently from those who are merely thought to be so. For those who are such truly imitate Christ, whether they are prelates teaching and instructing their subjects by word and example, as Christ did his disciples; or subjects listening and questioning one another, as it is written of Christ that “they found him in the temple, listening to them and questioning them” (Luke II). But those who are only thought to be such, though they are not, pretend to follow Christ: they preside in name alone, and preside over their subjects neither by word nor by example. Their subjects are joined together among themselves as brothers by a counterfeit [Col. 1055D] charity, and therefore are not recognized. Such persons, then, both are and are thought to be companions of the Bridegroom: they are so because they are true; they are thought to be so because they are false.

Accordingly, she asks for discernment as necessary to her, so that, since she had earlier promised that even the sons of her mother had fought against her, and it is therefore uncertain who are faithful and who unfaithful, she may, through the grace of discernment granted to her, recognize with whom she ought to unite herself, which teachers she should believe, and from whom she should receive the rule of right living, lest she be compelled to wander about aimlessly and perhaps unknowingly fall into the errors of some band of pretenders.

To one making such a request, the Lord replies as though reproaching her for distrusting his aid in some temptation, although for her great consolation he had bestowed upon her the diverse gift [Col. 1056A] of his grace: “If you do not know yourself, O fairest among women.”

**VERSE 7.—“If you do not know yourself, O fairest among women, go out and follow the tracks of the flocks, and pasture your kids beside the tents of the shepherds.”**

A little above, where we described the fourfold intellectual or active day, we located it particularly in some wise person: intellectual, indeed, because of reason and light rightly distinguishing among darkness—that is, virtues and vices; active because of discernment, bringing into works of light those things which it has rightly perceived. But now nothing prevents us from locating the intellectual day universally in every human being, on account of the vitality of reason naturally implanted within him.

[Col. 1056B] Let us therefore posit, by analogy with the natural day, which in its entirety is divided into day and night, two portions also of this intellectual day in the universal human being, according to privation and possession: that is, self-knowledge and self-ignorance. Let the former be reckoned as day and the latter as night.

For this is a certain disposition of the mind toward righteousness: when, from full knowledge of itself, it takes on a certain form of honourableness, toward which it is inclined or disposed; through grace assisting it, it advances so far that this inclination or disposition passes into a habit, and from this the whole person is called righteous. The privation of this habit is unrighteousness, when the mind itself either has never admitted any [Col. 1056C] form of godliness, or, if it had it, has lost it through the withdrawal of divine grace; or has drawn to itself the vice of some deformity, whose inclination or disposition in like manner passes into a habit contrary to the former, so that, as one is called righteous by participation in righteousness, so one is called unrighteous by participation in unrighteousness. This is according to possession; but according to privation, either the person lacks righteousness or unrighteousness itself is the privation of righteousness, according to the definition of evil, which says that evil is nothing other than the privation of good. Now righteousness is a species of good, just as, conversely, unrighteousness is a species of evil.

But because this species of good arises from the part that is self-knowledge, and the species of evil from the part that is self-ignorance, we must say what it is to know and to be ignorant of oneself.

[Col. 1056D] Whoever truly knows himself carefully considers, by subtle inquiry, how greatly he excels every visible creature in that he was created in the likeness of God. This likeness is not to be understood in the body but in the mind, according to the prerogative of reasoning intelligence, which discerns how even creation itself, serving his usefulness, is subject to him. He considers that his bodily substance is stretched upward, as a kind of reminder to the mind that it ought to despise earthly things and raise itself to heavenly things; that God loved his nature so greatly that he deigned to shed his blood for its redemption; and finally that he predestined that same nature to such glory that he decreed one day to make it a participant in his own immortality, immutability, and eternity [Col. 1057A]. Therefore he made it capable of every honourableness, virtue, and discipline. Thus, through this self-knowledge, as through the light of a certain day, a person is said to be led to desire and attain righteousness. Conversely, he is drawn toward unrighteousness by a certain blindness of mind, as by the darkness of a certain night, when he neither knows nor can consider within himself all the things set forth above; and this is to be ignorant of oneself. Self-knowledge, then, is a certain good disposition toward righteousness, just as self-ignorance is a certain evil privation of righteousness itself.

Therefore the Bridegroom—Christ—rebukes his bride, that is, the Church or any holy soul, which had complained that it suffered persecution not only from strangers but even from brethren, and that it was consequently very difficult [Col. 1057B] to discern among the Bridegroom’s companions which were true and which false. He rebukes her for such faint-heartedness and because, as though abandoned, she did not display the abundance of God’s grace within herself: “If you do not know yourself,” he says, “O fairest among women, go out. If you do not take any account of yourself, and do not know that you were made in my likeness; that I made you capable of reason, so that you may understand what you ought to seek and what you ought to flee; that I redeemed you by my blood; and that, among the synagogues of diverse doctrines or other souls, I made you alone beautiful, without spot or wrinkle, by the washing of baptism, the special gift of my sacraments, and also the distribution of diverse graces; if you do not know that I made you such that you ought deservedly [Col. 1057C] not to be troubled but rather strengthened and to glory in me, since it is altogether impossible that you should be forsaken when I have consecrated you to myself by so great a condescension of my grace and mercy—if you do not know this and refuse to know it, go out; that is, leave my fellowship and the communion of my secret place. For everyone who is ignorant shall be ignored, and there is no participation of light with darkness” (I Cor. XIV; II Cor. VI). “And follow the tracks of the flocks”: that is, imitate the actions of peoples who are not one flock nor one fold, because they do not have one shepherd; for, cutting themselves off from the unity of faith, they follow diverse teachers of manifold errors. “And pasture your kids”: that is, nourish and cherish those known to you who are carnal and lustful; or, “your kids,” that is, sinners, foul through your word and example [Col. 1057D] and to be set at the left hand in judgment, beside the tents of the shepherds—that is, beside the gatherings of erring teachers. They have many tents because they establish diverse synagogues for the various sects of their teachings, departing from that one tent of mine in which there is “one Lord, one faith, one baptism” (Eph. IV), and in which there is no schism in catholic unity.

This utterance of the Bridegroom is not a command but a prediction, because, according to his own saying, “No one can serve two masters” (Matt. VI), that is, God and the world; nor can anyone love God and the world at the same time. And John says: “Everyone who loves the world does not have the charity of the Father within him” (I John II). Therefore, if loving the world is not loving God, while [Col. 1058A] loving God is being righteous, then certainly loving the world is being unrighteous. But two contraries cannot at one and the same time exist together in one and the same thing, so that someone can be righteous and unrighteous at once. Again, in one and the same person, though at different times, two contraries can exist: someone doing something good may now be called righteous, but at another time, when sinning, unrighteous. But no one can definitely be called righteous and unrighteous at the same time, as we have already said. This is taught from the words of the Gospel, where certain persons are told: “Either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make the tree bad and its fruit bad” (Matt. XII). It is as though he said: Since you cannot definitely be called both good and bad at the same time, it is necessary that one of these existing in you destroy the other—that is, either goodness destroys wickedness, or wickedness goodness.

[Col. 1058B] This has been said with respect to the state of the inner person, who is always established either in good or in evil. But if you consider the whole person, who consists of soul and body, this rule of the dialecticians fails, because two contraries can at one and the same time exist together in one and the same person. Good and evil are contraries; but “human being” and “sinner” are two things. A human being, according to substance, is something good, for “all things which God made were very good” (Gen. II); but a sinful human being is a certain evil which the human being himself made. These two contraries exist at one and the same time, because that whereby he is human is good, while that whereby he is a sinner is evil.

[Col. 1058C] The Bridegroom therefore addresses the bride more sternly, as wandering, uncertain, and insufficiently confident. By the one proposition in which he says, “If you do not know yourself, O fairest among women, go out and follow the tracks of the flocks,” he shows an immediate consequence and teaches that one of two things must necessarily be chosen: either, by self-knowledge, taking on the good of righteousness, she must cleave especially to God by contemplative charity; or, falling through self-ignorance into the evil of unrighteousness, she must depart from him by loving the world. For the evil of unrighteousness deprives a person of the good of righteousness.

Thus the Bridegroom says to the bride—that is, Christ to every faithful soul—that if she should sink herself into such blindness of heart that she neither wishes nor is able [Col. 1058D] to recognize how graciously God has endowed her above others with beauty of mind, in order to consider and understand the purpose of divine goodness within her, she should leave the secret place of her mind and go by the broad and spacious way of erring peoples. There she would feed carnal impulses according to the teaching of masters who teach contrary doctrines and do not wish to possess the Lord’s tent, in which are the golden urn containing manna, Aaron’s rod, and the tablets of the covenant; for in it are preached and venerated Christ’s divinity and humanity, his priestly dignity, and the sublimity of the divine commandments.

For heretics and schismatics have many tents on account of the diverse teachings by which they deceive their followers, and they think their own assembly to be the Church, although they are the synagogue of Satan. But there is no place of salvation outside the catholic Church, and no churches other than this one are to be called churches. Although it is divided into many particular churches, nevertheless, because of the unity of faith, it is the one holy universal Church. Thus, in this same Song, when the Bridegroom had said that there are sixty queens, eighty concubines, and maidens without number, he added: “My dove, my perfect one, is one; she is the one of her mother, chosen by her who bore her” (Song VI).

[Col. 1059A] Hence, when that first Shepherd of the same Church, not yet having acquired perfect knowledge, beheld the glory of the Lord on the mountain and said, “Lord, it is good for us to be here; let us make three tents here, one for you, one for Moses, and one for [Col. 1059B] Elijah” (Matt. XVII), he was not heard, nor was such a plan approved for him. For no Church was to be established separately either in the Law or in the Prophecy; rather, the sole and one holy universal Church throughout the whole world was to be received and venerated under the New Testament, in which the Law and the Prophets are recapitulated. For the Gospel is nothing other than what the Law and the Prophets announced in things to come by deeds and words, while the Gospel presents it as already accomplished. Hence Ezekiel, in the vision of God’s glory, says: “The appearance of the wheels and their work was as though a wheel were in the midst of a wheel” (Ezek. I). The New Testament is a wheel in the midst of a wheel, within the Old Testament, because what the Old Testament prefigured, the New Testament [Col. 1059C] presented; and the New Testament is the exposition of the Old Testament. For the Old and New Testaments are one and contain one judge, because what the former represents in figure, the latter presents in truth; and what the former declares is to be done, the latter declares already accomplished, so that they may be the one tent of God.

Therefore the Church of God neither ought nor is able to be ignorant of itself, since it is adorned with such great beauty of mysteries and sacraments, and its whole glory is the very fitting diversity of venerable ordinances.

Likewise, any individual soul ought not to be ignorant of itself, lest, when it takes no account of its Creator’s gifts within it, it become estranged from him by descending into unlawful things. But if it considers within itself any goods by his grace, [Col. 1059D] it ought to attend to them gratefully and fittingly, and give attention to them by zeal for good action, lest it be rebuked for a buried talent; rather, it should be rewarded for a multiplied talent with the prize of eternal recompense. Therefore you also, O most holy sisters, who are gathered together in the house of discipline, do not be ignorant of yourselves. Rather, look carefully around you and consider what and how great your Bridegroom has made you: how he has separated you from other people as wheat from chaff; how he has specially fitted you to himself by the beauty of your distinctive manner of life; how he has adorned you with the manifold ornament of virtues, when, by your alternating exercises on every side, now chastity, now continence, now obedience, now humility, now frequency of prayers and vigils, you make a spectacle pleasing to God and his saints.

[Col. 1060A] Therefore, when you see yourselves to be such by the grace of God, do not cast your pearl before swine for them to trample upon it. That is, do not leave that contemplative and most safe inner chamber of your Bridegroom, and go after the clamour of worldly activities, where you would fulfil carnal desires according to the teaching of ungodly people. You ought to flee from their tents, lest the earth of worldly conduct swallow you up. Rather, when you have rightly recognized yourselves, render thanks for the divine condescension whose gift you are, and strive in every way to advance daily from good things to better, so that you may be able to pass from this present tent to that heavenly one, saying with the Psalmist: “How beloved are your tents, O Lord of hosts! My soul longs and faints for the courts of the Lord” (Ps. LXXXIII).

**VERSE 9.—“I have compared you, my beloved, to my cavalry among Pharaoh’s chariots.”**

After the Lord has generally rebuked the Church, or particularly a soul devoted to him, because in some adversity it doubted his aid, though by his grace it had received the benefits of many good things and ought rather to have been made stronger by trials, he proceeds to show that it ought to know itself, so that the good of God’s grace which it does not recognize within itself may, through his own showing, become manifest to it [Col. 1060C] and it may thereby be more steadfast amid all adversities. He says, therefore: “I have compared you, my beloved, to my cavalry among Pharaoh’s chariots.”

We must first say what this cavalry of the Lord was, and what Pharaoh’s chariots were; then what is the significance of these two opposites, and also what is the proportion between the things signifying and the things signified. The Lord’s cavalry was that army of the Israelite people, once pleasing to God, which he led out of Egypt with mighty hand and uplifted arm, after Egypt had been struck with ten plagues. The terrible manifestation of the tenth plague, together with the slaughter of the paschal lamb in the evening, brought about the people’s swift deliverance. For Scripture says that when the Lord was about to strike Egypt with that final plague, namely the death of all the firstborn, he commanded the children of Israel to sacrifice a lamb in the evening, family by family, and to put its blood on each doorpost and on the lintels [Col. 1060D] of the houses in which they ate it, so that, seeing this sign, the destroying angel might pass over and no one in that house be harmed. When they had done this, and in that night the Lord struck every firstborn in the land of Egypt, every house sprinkled with the blood of the lamb was preserved. Then all that cavalry of the Lord departed from the land of Egypt; and when Pharaoh pursued it with his chariots and horsemen, he was drowned in the Red Sea, while that cavalry crossed the same sea on dry ground (Exod. XII–XV).

If we apply the eyes of the mind, it is very beautiful to consider what mystery is contained in the departure from Egypt, the sacrifice of the evening lamb, the sprinkling of blood on the doorposts and lintels of houses, Pharaoh’s pursuit and his drowning, [Col. 1061A] the people’s deliverance, and finally their introduction into the promised land; and how greatly the analogy of all these things pertains to the universal Church. At the same time, it is pleasing to begin with how the Lord himself went before that people by a pillar of cloud in the day and a pillar of fire in the night, and how he bore before them that rod which, by divine command, wrought so many signs.

According to the likeness of that cavalry which went before in figure, that wonderful cavalry of the Lord has been ordered, or is being ordered, in which first the apostles and martyrs, then priests and orders of diverse professions, and thereafter their successors, have served and do serve, clothed in the armour of God: that is, the breastplate of righteousness, the shield of faith, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God (Eph. VI).

[Col. 1061B] What, then, is this cavalry? Surely it is the holy universal Church, in which whatever then went before only in outward fact is now performed daily in sacrament and in the reality of the sacrament. For what is the sacrifice of the lamb in the evening except Christ’s passion at the end of the ages? The blood of this Lamb is placed upon each doorpost when the sacrament of Christ’s passion is received by the mouth for redemption and held in the attentive mind for imitation. To place the lamb’s blood also upon the lintels of houses is to direct the mind’s intention—in which we dwell through thought—to the imitation of the Lord’s passion, and to fortify with the sign of that passion the forehead of the body in which we dwell while living.

That ancient cavalry of the Lord, then, delivered from Egyptian slavery through the sacrifice [Col. 1061C] of the lamb, crossed the Red Sea, saw its enemies drowned, received and accepted the Law in the wilderness, and entered the promised land. But this new cavalry of the Lord, after Christ’s passion, having cast off the yoke of diabolical condemnation, receives the land of the promised eternal inheritance through the washing of baptism, after the enemies of the soul—that is, vices and sins—have been drowned, through faith and observance of the Gospel. The Lord goes before this cavalry of his: by day in a pillar of cloud, and by night in a pillar of fire. To the saints, understood by day, he shows himself gentle and meek in the mildness of mercy; but to sinners, understood by night, he shows himself terrible in the terror of judgment.

[Col. 1061D] Indeed, in that cavalry the bearing of the rod was wonderful and glorious in mystery, through which God is remembered to have shown prodigies and signs of his power among his people. Could the wood of the Lord’s passion, which is the one hope and sum of all our salvation, not fittingly have been prefigured by this rod?

Certainly the Church of the Lord, which is compared by his own utterance to this cavalry, reverently sets this wonderful sign of the cross before all the arrangements of her offices, the doctrines of all sacraments and mysteries, and every administration of sacred things. Nothing in them can be valid or holy unless it has been confirmed by the prior invocation of this sign.

[Col. 1062A] Christ crucified is, as it were, the standard-bearer of this Church itself, which is not unfittingly called the Lord’s cavalry. By this victorious sign of his death he continually goes before her against Pharaoh’s chief horsemen and chariots, and against every assault of his perverse suggestion and every attack of his wicked contrivance. For this chief Pharaoh, as we call him, who is the head of the wicked and whose members are all wicked persons, stands opposed and contrary to Christ the Lord, the chief leader and author of this cavalry, who is head of all the elect and whose members are all the elect. Therefore these two cavalries, of God and of the devil, always fight each other, as citizens of two opposing cities.

[Col. 1062B] The City of God is the congregation of the faithful, extending from righteous Abel to the last elect person; they “have no abiding city here, but seek the city to come” (Heb. XIII). But the city of the devil is the synagogue of the unfaithful, bounded from reprobate Cain to the last of the reprobate. Like Cain, who first built a city, they seek and love earthly things and hold heavenly things cheap. They are called cities by that mode of speech in which what contains is put for what is contained: not because they are enclosed in buildings, but because they are local and circumscribed. The one is arranged for the reception of blessedness, the other for misery; and in each, one and the same thing—either blessedness or misery—is apportioned with manifold inequality of recompense according to the differing quality of merits.

This city, however, which is understood as the present Church, is mingled with good and evil persons, but it will itself be separated by the certainty of the future judgment. Thus two cities are said to exist in this one, because the portion of the good belongs to that receptacle of blessedness, which is interpreted as the heavenly Jerusalem, that is, “vision of peace”; while the portion of the evil belongs to that receptacle of misery called Babylon, that is, “confusion.”

[Col. 1062C] That city which is the congregation of the righteous is God’s cavalry and chariots, of which it is said: “The chariots of God are many tens of thousands, thousands of those rejoicing in them” (Ps. XLVII). Among these chariots are also those concerning whom it is said to God through the prophet: “You ride upon your horses, and your cavalry is salvation” (Hab. III). For his horses are the saints, over whom he presides. When the first seal was opened—that is, when the mystery of the Incarnation was revealed—he went forth on a white horse, namely a body white and spotless, conceived and born of a Virgin, not in human fashion but by the power of the Holy Spirit. In time, he was the leader of this cavalry of his by word and example; when their warfare has been completed, he will be their rewarder beyond time, with the prize of ineffable good and participation in his eternal kingdom.

Surely the glory of this procession is celebrated throughout the whole world to the praise of its advancing leader: how, as the trumpet of the Holy Spirit sounded while the leader himself gave the signal, these horses, placed in God’s chariot, went boldly to meet those armed with perversity and unbelief, so that “their sound went out into all the earth.” At the sound of their preaching, persons daily assemble from every quarter of the world, come to the end, join themselves to this cavalry, and cry with the prophet: “From the ends of the earth we have heard praises: glory to the righteous” (Isa. XXIV).

[Col. 1063A] Conversely, that opposing city which is the synagogue of the unfaithful is the chariots and cavalry of Pharaoh, that is, of the devil. Under his chariot are those red, black, white, and dappled horses: red with the blood of the saints whom they killed; black through the ugliness of sins; white through counterfeit faith and practice; and dappled through the diversity of doctrines and sects. Over all these presides the one who, when the fourth seal was opened—that is, when the Lord’s passion was at hand—went forth on a pale horse, the sign, namely, of persecution or death, to fight through those who were dead to God against those who lived [Col. 1063B] to God. As is added there: “Hell followed him, and power was given him over four parts of the earth, to kill and slay by sword, famine, death, and the beasts of the earth” (Apoc. VI). Hell is rightly compared to his cavalry because of its insatiable cruelty, which after the Lord’s passion raged through the four regions of the world by the four aforementioned kinds of affliction: sword, famine, death, and beasts of the earth.

In this wretched cavalry, the first and best-known followers of its present leader were, at the passion of that leader who came above on the white horse, Herod and Pilate, and after them many Roman emperors, who slew by diverse kinds of death, throughout all parts of the world, the most holy cavalry of the glorious leader. After them will come the greatest [Col. 1063C] of all, Antichrist; against him madness will be stirred, because in him especially the rider of the pale horse will preside, in order to deceive those dwelling on earth, and even, if possible, the elect (Matt. XXIV).

For concerning this person who exalts himself above everything called God or worshipped (II Thess. II), it must be understood that, just as incarnate Truth chose from his cavalry poor, unlearned, and simple people to preach, so conversely that one will choose to preach his falsehood shrewd and double-minded persons who possess the wisdom of this world. Hence Isaiah says: “Woe to the land of the cymbal of wings, which is beyond the rivers of Ethiopia, which sends envoys by sea and in vessels of papyrus upon the waters” (Isa. XVIII).

[Col. 1063D] The land to which “woe” is spoken is chiefly that condemned person, who is called a cymbal of wings because those who fly upward into lofty thought through pride sound forth that same perverse person by preaching him. That land is rightly said to be beyond the rivers of Ethiopia. For Ethiopia produces a black people; and this world, because it brings forth sinners, as it were gives birth to a black people of Ethiopia in every human being. But the land to which “woe” is spoken is said to be beyond the rivers of Ethiopia because that condemned person is so wicked in perversity that he surpasses the sins of all sinners. He sends envoys into the sea because he scatters his preachers throughout the world. How they are sent is rightly added when it says: “in vessels of papyrus upon the waters.”

[Col. 1064A] Paper is made from papyrus. What, then, is signified by papyrus but worldly learning? Vessels of papyrus are therefore the hearts of worldly teachers. To send envoys in vessels of papyrus upon the waters is to place one’s preaching in the minds of carnally wise men and call peoples who are drifting down toward guilt.

Ezekiel the prophet indicates by what leader and what company this cavalry is arranged, when he says: “There is Assur and all his multitude, and his graves round about him” (Ezek. XXXII). For what is expressed by the name Assur, a proud king, except him of whom it is written: “He himself is king over all the children of pride” (Job XLI)? But where Assur is, there is all his multitude, because the whole body of the reprobate surely cleaves to its head when, binding itself by his perverse laws, [Col. 1064B] it presents itself for his service. “And his graves are round about him”: graves cover the bodies of the dead. What, then, are his graves except the hearts of the perverse, which receive him, dead to the blessedness of eternal life, to be buried within themselves through carnal desires? Therefore his graves are around him because those in whose minds he now buries himself through desires, he afterward joins to himself as a tomb through punishments.

The same prophet announces shortly afterward what fruit belongs to such cavalry, saying: “They go down to hell with their weapons” (Ezek. XXXII). The weapons of sinners are the limbs of the body by which they carry out the evil desires that they conceive in the mind. Hence Paul says: “Do not present your members as weapons of unrighteousness to sin.” To go down into the lower regions with their weapons is to endure the torments of eternal judgment with those same limbs by which they fulfilled desires of pleasure.

[Col. 1064C] In opposition to this Pharaoh-like cavalry, then, the Lord’s cavalry is recognized. For if there has never been a good person whom the perversity of evil people did not test, those who, cleaving steadfastly to their leader, fight against that cavalry opposed to them, or against that contrary city, with patience and the spirit of fortitude, will deservedly be judged to belong to this cavalry of the Lord, or to this city of the Lord. They adorn themselves with such beauty of humility, patience, long-suffering, and other virtues that the whole universal Church [Col. 1064D] and each individual holy soul may fittingly be proclaimed the Bride of their Lord.

Concerning this universal Church, John says in the Apocalypse: “I saw the holy city Jerusalem coming down from heaven from God, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband” (Apoc. XXI). Therefore the Lord says to this his bride that she ought deservedly not to fear the devil’s city or cavalry opposed and contrary to her, because he has compared her to his cavalry among Pharaoh’s chariots. Thus, as that cavalry of old, delivered from Egypt after the sacrifice of the lamb, after crossing the Red Sea, after the drowning of its enemies, and after celebrating a hymn of praise for the victory, entered the promised land after the Law had been given and observed in the wilderness; so she, to be delivered from the Egypt of this world, [Col. 1065A] after the grace of baptism or compunction, after receiving the body and blood of the Lord, after the mortification of vices and the observance of the divine law, and after finally triumphing over every cavalry of diabolical oppression, shall enter from the solitude of this life into the inheritance of eternal promise, with thanksgiving for the abundance of so great a gift bestowed upon her.

It is not irrelevant, however, for stirring the minds of spiritual warriors, in considering such cavalry, to consider what proportion or comparison there is between truth and figure; then between the battle of each and the cause of the battle; between victor and vanquished. For according to the resemblance we seek between sign and thing signified, there can indeed be some comparison; but according to the dignity of the thing, absolutely none. The proposition among those we have set forth is this: as truth stands to figure, so victor stands to vanquished, and likewise the cause of battle to the battle itself—so that the proportion may be, as it were, that of a hundred to one, namely, a hundredfold. For this is the Lord’s promise in the Gospel: whoever has left house, or father, or mother, or children, or fields for my name’s sake shall receive a hundredfold (Matt. 19); not that he receives the very things he abandoned multiplied a hundred times, “but that, by comparison and according to their worth, they are as though the number one hundred were compared with a small number” (Jerome). Yet one hundred is also commonly taken for perfection. Thus, as we have said, truth has such dignity in relation to figure, the cause of battle in relation to battle, and victor in relation to vanquished, that there is absolutely no comparison between the perfection of the better part and the imperfection of the other. For the battle is the life of man upon earth; the cause of the battle is eternal and unchangeable life, for which one must fight and labor in the present life with all the strength of one’s soul. The vanquished one is the devil and his cavalry; the victor is he who triumphs over the devil and his cavalry. A figure is a reality apart from the sacrament; truth is a reality with the sacrament. For that ancient circumcision of God, the passage through the Red Sea, the food of manna, the giving of the law, and the flight and victory of those who fought carnally were figures of those things now performed in the sacrament of baptism, in the body and blood of the Lord, in the observance of Gospel precepts, and in the warfare of the Lord’s warriors who fight spiritually against the enemies of the soul.

Let us therefore compare the two cavalries of the Lord: the signifying and the signified, that which is according to the spirit; and let us say that the proportion between them is that between flesh and spirit, corruption and incorruption, temporality and eternity. Truth exceeds figure by as much as spirit exceeds flesh, incorruption corruption, and eternity temporality. Yet on both sides—that is, in figure and in truth—battle and its cause, victor and vanquished, are very unlike. There, namely in the figure, the struggle was fought carnally for a carnal, corruptible, and temporal thing; here, namely in truth, it is fought spiritually for a spiritual, incorruptible, and eternal thing. There a carnal victor overcame a carnal vanquished foe; here a spiritual victor overcomes a spiritual foe. There it was by bodily strength; here by strength of mind.

The proportion of truth to figure, by comparison and according to its worth, can therefore be as that of one hundred to one, that is, a hundredfold—either because of its own perfection, signified by the number one hundred, or because one hundred, transferred from the left to the right, represents the crown of blessedness, the most mighty reward for the warriors in this cavalry of the Lord.

Since the opposed battle and cause of battle have been set forth in the intent of this twofold cavalry, we must consider by what power and strength each side is armed, so that from such a disposition an argumentative topic may be drawn, should the question arise who is to be counted in the Lord’s ranks and who in the adversary’s. We have said that the battle is the life of every human being, as is written in Job (ch. 7): “The life of man is warfare”; but life itself is constituted according to the disposition by which the mind is affected, on which the whole power and strength of the combatants depend.

Let us suppose, then, that the power by which the mind of one fighting in the Lord’s cavalry is affected is love of God. For everyone who labors and fights for justice and truth labors and fights for that which he loves; but justice and truth are God; therefore he loves God. Further, one who labors and fights to obtain eternal life loves the thing which he desires to possess; but eternal life is God himself; therefore he loves God. And because he loves him, he desires to possess him, and therefore labors and fights for him.

[Col. 1066C] Therefore, if we ask what it is to love God, we recognize it from this definition: to love God is to labor and fight with one’s whole soul for the attainment of justice, truth, and eternal life. The definition is coextensive with the thing it defines; for it is convertible: to labor and fight with one’s whole soul for justice, truth, and the attainment of eternal life is to love God.

Let an argument therefore be drawn from the definition to prove that he belongs to the Lord’s cavalry whose mind has, by grace, been affected with such love of God that he does not shrink even from dying for justice, truth, and the attainment of eternal life. For the major proposition is: where the definition is present, that which is defined is also present. What is defined is this: to love God is to labor and fight for justice, [Col. 1066D] truth, and the attainment of eternal life; and that which is defined is also present, namely, love of God. Love of God and the Lord’s cavalry are therefore inseparably joined, since it is established that no one serves as a soldier for God unless he is shown to love him, and that no one is shown to love God unless he is shown to serve as his soldier.

Opposed to this cavalry of the Lord is the cavalry of the devil, in which the power affecting the mind of one serving on that side is envy, which likewise adheres inseparably to its subject. For envy is always on this contrary side, and conversely, where envy is, there is this contrary side. Here too, then, let an argumentative topic be drawn from the definition, if it is asked who may rightly be assigned to this side. [Col. 1067A] For to envy is to be tormented by another’s happiness; and conversely, to be tormented by another’s happiness is to envy, so that the definition is coextensive with the thing it defines. The argument therefore runs thus: everyone who envies does not love his neighbor, because he would not wish another’s good to exist; but not to love one’s neighbor is not to love God. Since loving God is known to be in his cavalry, not loving one’s neighbor, as has been said, is not loving God. To envy, therefore, is to be on the contrary side, that is, in the devil’s cavalry. Thus, just as the cavalries are opposed, so are the disposition and the cause of the cavalry itself: in one side the disposition is love, in the other envy; the cause for which they fight is eternal life in one side, transitory life in the other.

Neither side can so pass over into the other that one and the same person can belong to both at one and the same time. For it does not follow that one wasting away with the disease of envy can be in the Lord’s cavalry, or that one impelled by love of God can be counted in the devil’s cavalry. Rather, one who fights for transitory life also wishes to draw his neighbor with him, to whom he does not desire eternal goods: “Through the envy of the devil death entered into the world” (Wis. 2). But one who fights for eternal life wishes to lead his neighbor with him, to whom, as one truly loving, he desires eternal goods as for himself, in order to fulfill what is said: “Let him who hears say, ‘Come’” (Rev. 22). For one who hears and understands something concerning eternal goods, and shares the same things with his neighbor by teaching and exhorting him, shows that he truly loves the person whom he invites with himself to understand and earn those goods.

[Col. 1067] **56. FIGURE**

[Col. 1067]

[Col. 1069A] Thus four contraries are considered: two goods opposed to two evils. In order that their arrangement may appear more clearly, let them be set out in a square diagram, so that the upper line contains two items opposite each other and the lower line likewise contains two. Thus, in both lines their opposition appears directly; on the two sides are found items that follow one another: on the one side, two goods by grace—above, love; below, the Lord’s cavalry; on the other, two evils—above, envy; below, the devil’s cavalry. Diagonally, however, they conflict on both sides in such a way that they cannot exist together.

**VERSE 9.—“Your cheeks are beautiful as those of a turtledove; your neck as necklaces.”**

By a yet fuller manifestation of his grace, the bridegroom leads the bride to knowledge of herself, when he now praises her beauty, whose strength he had earlier praised, in order to suggest such a union of this twofold virtue that one cannot exist without the other: one is the safeguard of life to be preserved; the other, the ornament of the life preserved. For strength of spirit is needed to preserve the integrity of life itself; beauty, to adorn that integrity with good works. “For chastity is nothing without a good work, nor is any work good without chastity” (Gregory).

Therefore, after the virtue of strength has been set forth, the necessary virtue of beauty follows, in order to show that no one has acted courageously in all the endeavors of a dutiful mind if it is still clear that he has not advanced beautifully through purity [Col. 1069C] of mind and body. This beauty, however, is extended in a twofold grace: under the one general name of beauty, but specifically with one beauty of the cheeks and another of the neck. Their difference is inferred from the character of the things to which they are compared.

For although in this statement there are two subjects and one predicate—the subjects being the cheeks and the neck, and the predicate, “are beautiful”—yet the nature of an accidental predicate cannot in this place belong equally to two subjects in one and the same manner. Through God’s grace, one predicate can indeed belong to several subjects: the cheeks may be beautiful and the neck beautiful. But, as we have said, the beauty of the cheeks is described in one way and the beauty of the neck in another, although beauty is predicated of both. Thus in this place the two subjects receive one predicate, but not in the same way.

But if we wish to ascertain the varieties of this beauty, we must examine the things whose likeness is introduced—namely, the turtledove and the necklaces—so that a distinction may be drawn from their natural or material character. Natural beauty belongs to the turtledove; material beauty, to necklaces.

**58.** The natural historians (*Physiologi*) report three notable traits of the turtledove’s nature. One is that it possesses such chastity that, when it has lost its mate, it does not thereafter seek another. The second is that it has groaning in place of song. The third is that, seeking secluded places, it delights in its beloved solitude, building its nest and rearing its young where there is no injury from foes, since its retreats can scarcely or never be found. What, then, is expressed by the turtledove that loves chastity, groans instead of singing, and seeks secluded places, except the beauty of chastity, compunction, and contemplation? This remarkable beauty of the cheeks is distinguished in this threefold manner according to the threefold nature of the animal. Though there is one subject, there are three predicates; all three are in the subject and predicated of it when, through God’s grace, the cheeks are beautiful by the virtue of chastity, compunction, and contemplation. Each of these adornments of the cheeks has credible signs of its beauty. The cheeks blooming with the rosy blush of modesty, and fixing their gaze upon the ground with bowed head, signify the loveliness of chastity. Cheeks moistened by the healing fountain of tears speak of the grace of compunction. Cheeks made pale by the zeal and labor of fasts, vigils, and holy meditations proclaim the virtue of contemplation.

But since, as we have set forth above, the beauty of the cheeks differs from that of the neck, and since we have divided the beauty of the cheeks into three kinds—chastity, compunction, and contemplation—we may, having set down these as subordinate genera, make a further subdivision. Thus chastity is of one kind in virgins, another in widows, another in married persons; compunction is one kind reconciliatory and another loving; contemplation is one kind natural, another intelligible, and a third intellectual.

[Col. 1070C] Virginal chastity is the perpetual integrity of mind and body. Widowed chastity is a devotion of mind to continence, praiseworthy in the beauty of self-restraint. Conjugal chastity is the union of mind and body, commended by the grace of faithfulness and modesty. Reconciliatory compunction occurs when someone, visited by heavenly grace, is pierced with sorrow through recollection of sins, and while he is afflicted by the lamentations of repentance, is reconciled to God whom he had offended. For the mind is first pierced by fear, afterwards by love. Hence the other kind may fittingly be called loving compunction: when the mind is so inflamed with love for God that, having first wept lest it be brought back to punishment, it later begins to weep most bitterly because it is delayed from the kingdom. The grace of this twofold compunction is well described in sacred and true history under a figurative narrative, where Achsah, daughter of Caleb, is remembered to have asked her father, while sitting upon an ass, for the lower spring and the upper spring (Judg. 1).

**59.** [Lacuna.] Achsah sits upon the ass when the soul presides over the irrational movements of its flesh; sighing, it asks the Father for watered land, because the grace of tears must be sought from our Creator with great groaning. The soul receives the upper spring from him when it afflicts itself in tears through desire for the heavenly kingdom; it receives the lower spring when it fears the punishments of hell by weeping.

Although these are two kinds of compunction, compunction itself is distinguished by four qualities. For the soul of a just person is grievously afflicted in compunction either when it recalls its evils, considering where it has been; or when, fearing the judgment pronounced by God and seeking security, it reflects where it will be; or when, diligently considering the evils of the present life, it sorrowfully considers where it is; or when it contemplates the good of the heavenly homeland and, grieving because it has not yet obtained it, sees where it is not.

The first part of the third kind, that is, contemplation or speculation, is called natural: it concerns bodies and their scientific knowledge and understanding, which the Greeks call *physiologia*, and explains the natures and affections of bodies. The second part is intelligible: it comprehends by thought and understanding all the works of the heavenly divinity, whatever has worth beneath the lunar sphere by a more blessed mind and purer substance, and finally the wondrous ordering of human souls. The third part is called intellectual: when the mind is led beyond visible things and above itself to another, invisible reality, which, one and the same, abiding always in its own divinity through itself, is apprehended by no senses but by mind and intellect alone. This belongs to the contemplation of God, the incorporeality of the soul, and the inquiry of true philosophy; the Greeks call this branch *theologia*.

Certainly, among these divided subdivisions, one must consider that, if they are compared with one another, one exceeds another according to the higher dignity of its corresponding beauty. Virginal chastity surpasses widowed and conjugal chastity, because the merit belonging to that profession alone is to sing the new song and follow the Lamb wherever he goes (Rev. 14).

Further, the compunction generated by love is more excellent than that generated by fear, although the former is reached through the latter, just as the son takes precedence over the servant: for fearing belongs to servants, loving to sons. But that part of contemplation called intellectual is incomparable with the other two, because the speculation of the latter concerns creation, whereas the former, raised beyond creation by the eye of the purified mind, is fixed upon the Creator himself, though not perfectly, yet so far as may be possible through his grace. By it, a holy man, as it were, is separated from the flesh as fat; he seeks or desires nothing outward, but thirsting for God with ardent longing, cries with the Psalmist: “As the deer longs for springs of water, so my soul longs for you, O God. My soul has thirsted for the living God: when shall I come and appear before God’s face?” (Ps. 61).

The Apostle calls this part the third heaven, into which he says that he was caught up and heard things unspeakable, which it is not permitted for a human being to utter (2 Cor. 12).

Most beloved sisters, your holy community possesses, we believe, this threefold kind of beauty, you whom blessed solitude has placed apart from every tumult of secular disturbances, so that the farther you are from the world, [Col. 1072A] the more freely you may preserve the beauty of chastity, seek the grace of compunction, and stand at the summit of holy contemplation. Indeed, your very solitude is the delightful garden of the Lord, where the rose and lily breathe forth—the testimony of virginity and martyrdom; that martyrdom, namely, which may exist without the shedding of blood, and exists in the mind through the exercises of virtues. There are the springs of holy contemplation; there the little trees of heavenly contemplation rise, bloom, and bear fruit; there all these honorable things are so arranged that in them are pleasing and chosen walks for the Holy Spirit, who says: “I will dwell in them and walk among them; and they shall be my people, and I will be their God” (Lev. 26; 2 Cor. 6). But you must take heed with very cautious watchfulness lest you lose the privilege of so great a good through some worldliness or empty frivolity, lest your most sweet and mighty indweller and walker, angered, flee from you, saying that he has nowhere to lay his head (Luke 9).

Since, then, we said above that the beauty of the cheeks differs from that of the neck, and have now described the beauty of the cheeks according to our measure, it remains to speak of the beauty of the neck. This too is divided into two: preaching and incorporation. We must speak first of preaching and then of incorporation. In the neck is the throat; through the throat the voice is expressed, and food, once chewed by the teeth, is conveyed through the throat into the stomach. Therefore holy preachers are not unfittingly understood through the neck, for in them is this twofold beauty: preaching and incorporation. The beauty of preaching is considered in the adornment of the neck because the neck contains the voice, and preaching is performed by the voice. And as voice is the sign of the mind and the expression of the silent heart, so the preaching of the saints is a presentation, desirable for every person, of the honorable commonwealth.

By “commonwealth” here I mean that which, because of its goodness, can and ought publicly to be undertaken: knowledge, will, and action—namely, every good whose privation is evil.

**61.** For it is evident that to be chaste, humble, patient, modest, or anything else designated by the name of virtue, is good; and it follows that the negation of this good—that is, not to be chaste, humble, patient, or modest—is evil. Since one or the other of these must obtain, namely being or not being, the simple negation that says “not to be” follows the simple affirmation which proposes being chaste, humble, or patient; and the privative affirmation says that one is unchaste, proud, or impatient. For to say “not patient” is the same as to say “impatient,” and that evil which is impatience is the privation of that good called patience; likewise in the remaining cases. There is, therefore, a certain commonwealth, an array of virtues; and the ruler and administrator of this commonwealth is that eternal Emperor from whom all goods proceed and without whom nothing can be called or be good.

The preaching of the saints teaches and displays this commonwealth. Through it the other part, which we have called incorporation, is accomplished; for just as food is conveyed through the throat into the stomach, so through the preaching of the saints a sinner, broken from the grossness of his perversity by conversion, is incorporated into the Church.

But since, as we have said, the beauty of the neck is twofold—preaching and incorporation—each is distinguished by subdivision in a threefold manner. Preaching occurs in one way by word, in another by example, and in a third by word and example. Of those incorporated, some are incorporated by conversion, some by satisfaction, and some by conversion together with satisfaction.

[Col. 1073B] Preaching occurs by word alone because there are some in the Church who have received from God the gift of being able to edify others by exhortation in word, but because of obstructing weakness cannot give equally strong examples of virtue. It also occurs by example alone, because many do not possess the gift of public speaking in the Church; although they have understanding, they cannot express it openly. Nevertheless, they strive by such proofs of spiritual works that, by wondrous examples of virtues, they invite the minds of those who admire them to imitate them. What the former say in words, these say in deeds; and these philosophize better by silence than the former by declamation. Of this twofold quality of preaching the Apostle says: “To one is given the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge” (1 Cor. 12). For, as we have said, some are wise in understanding the discourse of divine commands and observing them through rational understanding, but are not eloquent in expressing it because of slowness of talent; while others, grasping through the capacity of a ready intellect the very discourse to be sown, pour it forth powerfully with abundance of eloquence.

Again, preaching occurs in both ways, [Col. 1073C] namely by word and example, when holy teachers have by divine grace both the ability to show by deeds what they preach with the mouth and, in their own conduct, to indicate that the things they teach should be avoided are not to be done. In their person the Psalmist, speaking to God, after first saying, “I spoke of your testimonies before kings and was not ashamed,” adds: “And I lifted up my hands to your commandments, which I loved, and I exercised myself in your justifications” (Ps. 118). It is as if he openly said: “The law of your commandments which I proclaimed publicly and confidently by preaching, I also proved by the performance of works, so that my hearers might hear in my words and see in my deeds what they ought to do for their own benefit and salvation.”

This third category of the beauty of preaching is certainly necessary for the teachers of the Church, because the preaching of those whose life is known to be alien from the good which they preach is frequently despised. And they grievously sin before the eyes of almighty God who, through silence, gain no profit of souls from the grace of preaching granted to them. Hence in the Old Testament it is commanded that, when the priest enters the tabernacle, bells be attached to the hem of his garments, lest he die (Exod. 28), because it is a great danger for a teacher if he enters God’s Church without the sound of preaching. But the priest’s garments are works of righteousness, as the Psalmist says: “Let your priests be clothed with righteousness” (Ps. 131); bells adhere to these garments, so that the priest’s works themselves may proclaim the way of life with the sound of the tongue.

The other part of the beauty in the neck, which is incorporation, occurs through conversion. For some, converted from Gentile life to God, are incorporated into the Church by faith and the grace of baptism, as we read of Cornelius, who, through the merits of good works brought about by God’s grace and preceded by the gift of the Holy Spirit, was shown worthy to be joined to the body of the Church (Acts 10).

For when he was rejected as though unworthy by those who had believed from the circumcision, the Holy Spirit necessarily came forward as his advocate; it pleased the Spirit’s condescension to show that God wished this man too to be incorporated into his Church through faith and baptism.

Others are incorporated into the Church through satisfaction: though at first they belong to the body of the Church through the unity of faith, nevertheless, as their sins require, they are at times cut off from the body of the Church by a condemnatory sentence. But when they come to their senses, they are again joined by a reconciliatory sentence, through satisfaction, to the body from which they had been cut off.
