Thus the Apostle, writing to the Corinthians, commands that the man who committed the crime be handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, [Col. 1074C] so that he may be saved on the day of the Lord (1 Cor. 5); afterwards, when he has been corrected by satisfaction, he commands that he be incorporated again into the Church, lest he be swallowed up by excessive sorrow.

Some are incorporated by conversion together with satisfaction: they receive faith by believing and, confessing their crimes, are joined to the body of the Church through repentance and baptism. Hence Peter, preaching to Christ’s killers, says: “Repent and be converted, that your sins may be blotted out” (Acts 3), showing that the remission of sins follows upon the prior conversion and satisfaction, a remission which occurs only in the Catholic Church, because that remission is precisely incorporation into the Church. But although in the earlier modes, which we have above set down separately—saying that incorporation occurs now by conversion and now by satisfaction—both conversion and satisfaction may be present in either case, we have distinguished them because one or the other element is more fully and evidently displayed. For although any saint is adorned not with one virtue but with many, a virtue is especially predicated of him according as it is recognized to be more predominant in him. Thus, when the Apostle described the divisions of graces, he said: “To one is given the word of wisdom; to another the word of knowledge; to another faith; to another the grace of healings; to another prophecy; to another discernment of spirits; to another kinds of tongues; to another interpretation of words” (2 Cor. 12). He did not mean that one who possesses one grace possesses none of the others, [Col. 1075A] but that a person is said especially to have that grace which is known to be stronger and more abundant in him. And in Cornelius we read of no satisfaction for a former life; but because an angel told him that his prayers and alms had been heard, and he was therefore commanded to send for Peter, he was formed in faith by Peter’s teaching and became a member of the Church through conversion (Acts 10). But one converted to faith who is separated from the Church through excommunication on account of some fault needs satisfaction in order to deserve readmission, although satisfaction itself may be called a conversion from a former error.

Since we have distinguished beauty in two ways and subdivided those modes further, it remains now to say why beauty itself is compared to necklaces.

A necklace is an ornament worn upon the breast by matrons, so called from *munire*, “to fortify,” because it fortifies their breast lest some adulterer violate the blush of chastity in any respect. A necklace, however, is not just any ornament: it is fashioned by the laboring hand of a careful craftsman out of gold and gems, so that a larger gem set in the middle [Col. 1075B] is encircled by smaller gems equally distant from it.

What, then, is represented by gold but wisdom, and by gems but virtues? A necklace is therefore composed of gold and gems because from the understanding of wisdom and the beauty of virtues there is produced a certain spiritual and necessary ornament of the soul, which so fortifies [Col. 1075C] the secret places of our breast that the ancient enemy does not dare to lay upon it any hand of his malice.

Certain settings are made in this crafted ornament in which the gems are enclosed. What are these settings but our external senses, which are, as it were, instruments of our actions? The lowering of the eyes and an honorable, disciplined composure of countenance are a most beautiful gem shining with the virtue of humility. The ear, obedient to the commands of God and of prelates, bears the gem of obedience. In the nostrils gleams the gem of holy discretion. The mouth displays a gem radiant with three virtues: abstinence, silence, and speech uttered honorably and profitably. The hands conspicuously show a gem sprinkled with twofold splendor, namely continence and generosity.

Amid these, placed in the middle, the greater and more splendid gem of holy charity shines chiefly in the breast. It so supplies the beauty of this ornament that no beauty can be proved to exist without it. For without charity no virtue can either exist or be called a virtue, because the whole Law and the Prophets hang upon the two commandments concerning God and neighbor (Matt. 22).

Thus the neck of the holy Church or of the faithful soul is fittingly compared to necklaces composed of gold and gem-material, because through the preaching and unanimity of the saints we ought so to order our senses by the brightness of wisdom and the holiness of virtues that we establish within ourselves an ornament of the soul in which that heavenly bridegroom may delight. But because the preachers of this same Church require the writings of both Testaments, from which they receive the order and manner of their preaching, the following words are added in the person of the bridegroom himself, or of those through whom the Scripture of the Church was issued at his inspiration—some of whom lived at the same time as Solomon spoke these words, and some of whom were yet to come.

**VERSE 10.—“We will make for you golden chains, variegated with silver.”**

A *murenula* is a kind of ornament, like a little chain woven of gold and interspersed with silver rods in the form of little worms. It is called a *murenula* because, like a moray eel (*muraena*), it is flexible, winding, or coiled. For when a moray eel is caught, it bends and coils itself in different directions. By the golden *murenula* variegated with silver, therefore, we understand Holy Scripture. Its inward sense is compared to gold because of its excellence and dignity; the speech by which that sense is expressed is designated by silver because of its brightness and clarity. Holy Scripture is golden because it shines with the splendor of wisdom; it is silver because it gleams with the clarity of expression. But because this same Scripture is divided in two, namely into the Old and New Testaments, it is said in the plural: “We will make for you golden chains, variegated with silver,” so that both Testaments may be shown to be golden with the splendor of inward meaning and silver with the brilliance of eloquence.

These two Testaments are called *murenulae* because they may be bent into diverse modes of exposition, being folded in many meanings, provided that they give forth nothing contrary to faith. Though, as we have said, they are golden through the value of their surpassing knowledge, they are said to be variegated with silver, distinguished by the clarity of expression, because with the brightness of that very knowledge they sound now humbly, now at a middle level, now sublimely; now they unfold history, now allegory, now moral teaching, not simply but in many ways. Hence Ezekiel says that when the living creatures went, the wheels following them went also; and when they stood, the wheels stood; and when they were lifted up, the wheels were likewise lifted up (Ezek. 1). For Holy Scriptures stand or move according to the understanding of the one investigating and comprehending them. They stand when they are understood simply according to the letter; they move when they are expounded according to the spiritual sense, whether allegorically or morally. And the more subtly they are considered, the more highly they are raised with the understanding of the interpreter.

Therefore, because they are bent by the preachers of the Church, not uniformly but with the beautiful variety of diverse senses—now allegorically, as we have said, now morally—and because they are presented according to the hearers’ capacity, now humbly, now sublimely, the bridegroom fittingly promises the Church golden *murenulae* variegated with silver. They hang, as it were, from her neck when they adorn the learning and eloquence of holy preachers.

It is not without reason to recapitulate briefly what has preceded and to consider how these later matters are connected with them. Above, when the bride said, “I am black, but beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem,” she did not recognize that same beauty perfectly. Hence she complains that so great a heat of temptations had affected her that even her brothers had fought against her. But the bridegroom rebukes this faint-heartedness, teaching that she had not rightly attended to the grace of beauty bestowed upon her: she called herself beautiful, indeed, but did not perfectly recognize the quantity and quality of that very beauty. Therefore it could happen that, when she began to be at variance, she would depart from the fellowship of her bridegroom and pursue the manifold errors of the world. Thus the bridegroom, with his customary mercy, brings her back to herself and strengthens her by enumerating the parts of the beauty granted her, so that, recognizing herself, she may perfectly know how and how greatly beautiful she is, and through this may cling more ardently to her betrothed.

This beauty, to define it thus, is the disposition of a well-ordered mind. Its parts are strength, beauty, and knowledge of the Holy Scriptures, which the bridegroom himself has now enumerated: strength, where he said, “I have compared you, my beloved, to my cavalry in Pharaoh’s chariots”; beauty, not uniform but, as we distinguished above, where he says, “Your cheeks are beautiful as those of a turtledove; your neck as necklaces”; and knowledge of the Scriptures, where he says, “We will make for you golden chains, variegated with silver.”

In the major and principal proposition, whatever belongs to the parts must necessarily belong to the whole. Taking his argument therefore from the parts, he proves her to be truly beautiful: for if the kinds of beauty—that is, fortitude, loveliness, and knowledge of the holy Scriptures—are dispositions of a well-ordered mind, the genus also, namely beauty, must necessarily be present. Consequently, since she has called herself beautiful, she ought not to fear adversities, she whom the Bridegroom’s grace has made such. But if through grace she fails to recognize herself as such, she will not belong to the Bridegroom’s fellowship; for ignorance will cause her, going out through sloth and negligence, to wander away from the Bridegroom’s companionship. And this is an argument [Col. 1077D] from the efficient cause: everyone who does not understand the good of the grace bestowed upon him is, through ignorance, negligent of that good within himself; but one who is negligent is not near to God. Therefore the bride, ignorant of herself, departs from the Bridegroom’s fellowship and must necessarily seek external things. Restored therefore to herself, once she has recognized herself and profitably attended to the grace granted her, he demonstrates this by adding: “While the king was at his table, my nard gave forth its fragrance.”

**VERSE 11.—“While the king was at his table, my nard gave forth its fragrance.”**

The King’s reclining is the dispensation of all Christ’s temporal acts: for he deigned to humble himself from that ineffable height of his divinity and, for human salvation, to bend himself down to the weakness of humanity: first, by being born into the Virgin’s womb; then by dying on the cross, lying in the tomb, and descending to the lower world; afterwards, raising himself up from that very bending down by rising again and ascending into heaven.

During the time of this dispensation, the Church especially grew in the increase of virtues. Taught also by Christ’s command and example, she learned to share his sufferings through patience, having so advanced in love for him that she did not set even life itself above his love, saying: “While the king was at his table, my nard gave forth its fragrance.”

Nard is an aromatic shrub, with a heavy, thick, short, black, and brittle root, and a small, dense leaf. Its tops spread out into spikes; consequently perfumers prize both the spikes and the leaves of nard for their twofold excellence. Hence the Gospel recounts that a woman brought for the Lord’s anointing “an ointment of costly spikenard” (John 12).

What, then, is signified by nard except the virtue of good work? The root of good work is love; for just as all the strength and vigor of herbs arise from the root, so every virtue of good work is generated from love alone.

Various natural qualities, however, are said to reside in the root of nard; these may be referred to the manifold virtues of love. Love is weighty, because it outweighs all virtues; the Apostle calls it a more excellent way, saying: “I show you a still more excellent way” (1 Cor. 12). [Col. 1078C] It is thick, as having a more living sap in accordance with the inward vigor of the mind; it supplies the other virtues with their effect of holiness, whereas without it every virtue remains, as it were, dry and barren. Considering its richness, the Psalmist, who declared that he watched with thirsting desire for God, says: “Let my soul be filled as with marrow and fatness” (Ps. 62).

It is short, because it is written of it that “the Lord will make a word completed and shortened upon the earth” (Rom. 9). The completed and shortened word is love, because in it consists the perfection of all virtues, and this one expression is the conclusion of this whole holy order: the word of love is completed, because “love is the fullness of the law” (Rom. 13); concerning it the Psalmist says: “I have seen the end of all perfection” (Ps. 118). This is not an end that makes what exists cease to be, but one that brings into being what does not yet exist and leads it to perfection. It is shortened because all the commandments of the Law are summed up in this one: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and your neighbor as yourself; on these two commandments hang all the Law and the Prophets” (Matt. 22). How short a word, consisting of three syllables and seven letters, yet containing all the fullness of holiness! For “God is love” (1 John 4): [Col. 1078D] he is three in the distinction of persons, one in equality of majesty; and the grace of the Holy Spirit is sevenfold, through whom love itself is poured into the hearts of the saints. Therefore, if God is love, and no good can exist without God, whoever is proved not to possess love, which is God, is beyond doubt concluded not to be good.

The root of nard is also called black, because love, which, as we have said, is the root of all virtues, willingly endures for God and for the salvation of the brethren the blackness of persecutions and every adversity; for, as it is written, “Love is patient” (1 Cor. 13). It is brittle because of the excessive tenderness of brotherly compassion, because it is compelled by the bowels of mercy to suffer with those who suffer, to be weak with the weak, to weep with those who weep, to grieve with those who grieve, and to be sorrowful with the sorrowful. For it is written: “Love is patient, love is kind” (ibid.). Love abounds with such sweetness of kindness that it regards every need of its neighbor as its own. It has a small [Col. 1079B] and dense leaf, because love always displays humility while it abounds in the rich density of all virtues. It spreads into spikes because the holy mind, increasing in divine love, is lifted to heavenly things by the sharpness and subtlety of understanding.

These seven natural properties of the root of nard may therefore not improperly be understood as the praises of love proceeding from the sevenfold grace which we have set forth. For just as, from the root of nard and the addition of leaves and spikes, a most precious ointment is prepared, so from love, which is the root of all goods, and from diverse kinds of virtues, with the Holy Spirit as the craftsman, there is prepared the choicest composition of holiness. Anointed with it, the holy Church, or any holy soul, sends forth from itself a most fragrant odor: the good repute and fame of good conduct. Of such an odor the Apostle says, “We are the sweet fragrance of Christ to God in every place” (2 Cor. 2); and a certain wise man says, “A good reputation fattens the bones,” because every virtue of the soul is enfeebled unless it is filled with the richness of such a composition.

The Church, therefore, or the holy soul, says that she gives forth such a fragrance from this *pistic* nard—that is, faithful nard—by which that heavenly King and Bridegroom may be delighted while reclining: that is, in that ineffable secrecy of the Father’s bosom. For his reclining in the Father’s bosom is his being there through the same essence and the same power of divinity. His reclining also is, as we have stated above, his bending down to the nature of human weakness through the wonderful order of the completed [Col. 1079D] dispensation. His reclining is likewise his dwelling in the thought of the holy mind through the most abundant condescension of his manifold grace.

That Gospel woman, who is written to have anointed the Lord, displayed the fragrance of this precious *pistic* nard both in fact and in sacrament: in fact according to history, and in sacrament according to moral interpretation. For to anoint the Lord’s feet was to contemplate, though through a mirror and in an enigma, the height of his divinity through the uplifting of the mind. Therefore, to anoint the Lord’s head and feet is to believe and proclaim his divinity and humanity. Hence it is written concerning the power of that anointing with which Mary anointed the Lord that “the house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment” (John 12).

The house, indeed, is the Church, which is filled with the fragrance of this anointing because it believes and confesses Christ as God and man, and through the rightness of this faith and confession is spread throughout the whole expanse of the world. Through this house—that is, through the universality of the Church—John the Evangelist scatters the sweetness of this fragrance from the Lord’s head and feet: from the head, when he says, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God”; from the feet, when he says, “And the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1).

The anointing of the Lord’s head and feet may also be understood in this way: whoever follows Christ’s footsteps through devotion to the active life falls at his feet by living well; and thus, advancing day by day to better things, he raises himself, through the virtue of the contemplative life, as it were to Christ’s head, by constantly cleaving to God. The anointing of the feet, then, is the active virtue; the anointing of the head is the contemplative virtue. For good conduct and the exercise of holy meditation are an offering of most sweet fragrance, in which that heavenly King and Bridegroom delights while reclining, awaiting and desiring to place with himself in the eternal resting-place of his own reclining those who are fragrant with such an odor.

But in order that the holy Church or faithful soul may attain his eternal reclining, she must, in this reclining of his temporal dispensation—in which he chose to recline by being born and dying for her salvation—follow the examples of his humility, patience, and obedience, and prepare for him a resting-place in her mind, fragrant with virtues. Thus he may afterwards introduce her, like a bridegroom his bride, spotless to spotless, into the bridal chamber or reclining-place of his kingdom; so that, as he now rests in her temporally through the diversity of graces, she may thereafter rest in him eternally through everlasting glory. Hence, in what follows, the same bride indicates that this is the fixed decree of the gracious Bridegroom: whoever shares his sufferings through patience shall also share his eternal kingdom through consolation.

**VERSE 12.—“My beloved is to me a bundle of myrrh; he shall dwell between my breasts.”**

For by myrrh is expressed the bitterness of the Passion; by the cluster, the sweetness of the Resurrection. “While,” she says, [Col. 1080D] “my Bridegroom and my King—under whose rule I have both the willing and the ability for good—reclined in the suffering of the cross, and, having become obedient unto death, was now laid in the tomb: I, who had formerly complained that I was black because not only strangers but even my brothers fought against me, being prepared, as it were, with a most precious nard from his most ardent love and from the example of his humility, patience, and obedience, scattered the fragrance of good reputation throughout the whole world, ready to succumb, for love of him, not merely to one death but to a thousand kinds of death. Thus my beloved is not to me merely myrrh, but a bundle of myrrh; for in return for the one kind of death which he underwent for me, I desire to gather a bundle of many and diverse deaths.”

[Col. 1081A] What is this bundle? “Dangers from rivers, dangers from robbers, dangers from the Gentiles, dangers in the city, dangers in the wilderness, dangers at sea, dangers among false brethren; labor and hardship, many sleepless nights, hunger and thirst, many fasts, cold and nakedness; mockery and beatings, chains and prisons, stoning, sawing asunder, and finally death by the sword” (2 Cor. 11; Heb. 11). Behold, the bundle of myrrh.

But because martyrdom is twofold—one in the body, the other in the mind—let us divide this bundle and say that one is the bundle of myrrh, that is, of bodily suffering, and another the bundle of myrrh of the mind. We have enumerated above the bundle of bodily suffering. But the bundle of mental myrrh, that is, suffering, is virginity of the flesh, renunciation of the world and of every worldly pleasure, or the manifold labor of continence. “My beloved,” says the Church or holy soul, “is the cause of this twofold bundle for me, because for his name and love I have set the shoulders of mind and body beneath the burden of bearing this bundle: the mind through the mortification of vices, the body through endurance of diverse sufferings.” Why is this? Because the Beloved himself also became for me a bundle of myrrh, when, for me, in his body he accepted scourges, spitting, blows, mockeries, a drink of gall, the cross, the piercing of hands, feet, and side, and finally death itself; thus he gathered, as it were, a bundle of manifold sufferings. Such a bundle, my Beloved, shall dwell between my breasts, because I daily [Col. 1081C] recall in my mind all these marks of his Passion; and while I keep their memory, I too gather more ardently, for love of him, the bundle of my own sufferings.

In the arrangement of the body, the chest is situated between the breasts placed on either side; rightly, therefore, we understand the remembrance of the bundle of myrrh between the breasts as that remembrance of the Lord’s Passion which ought to be in the heart.

Or let us take the breasts to be the two Testaments, Old and New, and observe that the Beloved dwells in them by the commemoration of his Passion: the earlier Testament foretells the Passion itself as future; the latter presents it as already accomplished. “He shall dwell between my breasts,” she says, because in the two [Col. 1081D] Testaments set before me for my knowledge of him and for my salvation, I gather his bundle of myrrh: in the Old Testament through figures of the Passion foretold, and in the New through the saving sap of eternal redemption offered to the whole world. For the sap of myrrh is said to cure many diseases, and the sap of this Lordly myrrh has driven away every sickness of the soul and established throughout the world the medicine of perpetual health.

Or, “He shall dwell between my breasts,” that is, between the two peoples constituted in my body from Jews and Gentiles, who receive this bundle of myrrh by the Lord’s faith, follow it in their conduct, commemorate it daily in sacrament, recollect it in mind, and receive it continually with their mouths.

[Col. 1082A] Or, “between my breasts,” that is, between the two thieves, among whom my Beloved, suspended, gathers the bundle of his Passion. These prefigured the same two peoples: the one believing, the other crucifying; the one chosen, the other rejected. They were my breasts: the former because of natural and written law, the latter because of natural law alone—thus both possessing the nourishment of reason, so that they are without excuse. The latter, indeed, through my Beloved dwelling in their midst and displaying the bundle of his myrrh, received in addition a new law illuminating natural law. The former, however, by God’s hidden but just judgment, after the Law had been given, lost even natural law because of unbelief.

Therefore, when the Beloved himself hung on the cross, it offered him [Col. 1082B] wine mingled with myrrh; its bitterness was poured into him when it said: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 27).

**VERSE 13.—“My beloved is to me a cluster of Cyprus, in the vineyards of Engaddi.”**

And because it chose to receive the bitterness of this remedy, it lacked the sweetness of the cluster; and so it neither died with the Beloved to sin nor rose with him to righteousness. But to me, in the other people coming to faith, who receive, venerate, and adore the mysteries of the Passion, he became a cluster of Cyprus; for when he rose from death, he also enlivened me by the hope and sweetness of the future resurrection.

For he is the cluster brought from the land flowing with milk and honey by the two scouts, signifying the two peoples. Born of Mary his mother, with the sweetness and richness of the Holy Spirit flowing, he was suspended on the cross for the salvation of both peoples. But just as it is the custom of bearers that one should go before and the other follow, so the Jewish people was first known to God through observance of the Law, while the following Christian people was received through the religion of the new Law. As the one going before does not see what it carries and puts it behind itself by a certain turning away of the back, whereas the follower always has it before his face, continually watches it with his gaze, and possesses it through bodily nearness, so the Jewish people, carrying Christ in the Law, does not understand him but, as though turning away, despises him. The Christian people, however, understands him, bears him on forehead [Col. 1082D] and mind, guards him by worshipping him, and obeying his commandments.

That people abhors and despises this cluster hanging on the cross on account of the curse of the Law. This people receives the saving covenant of his blood, pressed out in the winepress of the cross, drinking with spiritual sweetness the sole remedy of body and soul; and in hope it awaits, after the general resurrection, the desirable and incomparable joy of the same twofold substance—body and soul.

Therefore, in this people—for I am this people, the bride of God, the Church of God—my Beloved is to me a cluster of Cyprus: for he who was a bundle of myrrh in the bitterness of Passion will be a cluster in the sweetness of Resurrection; and he for whose sake I have gathered a bundle of many sufferings, [Col. 1083A] both in body and mind, will be for me a cluster in the eternal refreshment of the soul and the most sweet recompense for this labor.

For this reason he is rightly called a cluster of Cyprus. Cyprus is interpreted “sadness” or “mourning”; therefore he is called a cluster of Cyprus because he himself is the true and sweet consolation of all my mourning and sadness. And just as the cluster of Cyprus surpasses the clusters of all lands in size, so my Beloved, “the Father of mercies and God of all consolation” (2 Cor. 1), surpasses all things in heaven and on earth in his dignity and grace.

But where did the Beloved become a cluster of Cyprus? In the vineyards of Engaddi. Engaddi is said to be a very large village in Judaea, near the Dead Sea, where there are vineyards, not of wine but of the balsam shrub; these are called vineyards because they grow upward in the manner of vines. From balsam mixed with olive oil chrism is made, through which certain greater rites of ecclesiastical consecration are performed. For by it the font of baptism is consecrated, and priestly and royal dignity is confirmed; and a special sanctity is assigned to churches, altars, and sacramental vessels. In a figurative sense, however, the gifts of spiritual charisms are signified by anointing with such liquid; by the grace of the Holy Spirit they make the hearts of believers fit for divine ministries.

Engaddi, moreover, is interpreted “the spring of the kid.” [Col. 1083C] But what is the spring of the kid except baptism or the grace of tears? The kids are sinners to be placed at the left; all the righteous are to be set at the right. The vineyards of Engaddi—that is, of the spring of the kid—are spiritual gifts, granted only to those who have been washed from the filth of sins in sacred baptism or through tears of repentance. For the spring of the kid is baptism, by which sinners, that is, kids, are washed and become righteous, that is, Christ’s sheep. Or, if they have fallen into sin after baptism, they are restored to their former state through the grace of tears, as through a second baptism.

“My beloved is a cluster of Cyprus to me in the vineyards of Engaddi,” because in them he is certainly for me food and drink of consolation and salvation: in those who, through baptismal grace, have been made worthy to receive knowledge of the divine sacraments [Col. 1083D] and the abundance of spiritual gifts; or for those who, through the spring of tears, merit absolution from sins and, dead to sins, rise to the life of eternal salvation. Thus, if according to the Apostle they have been planted together in the likeness of Christ’s death, they may likewise be in the likeness of his resurrection (Rom. 6).

The order of these four predicates is certainly to be observed: the fragrance of nard, the bundle of myrrh, the cluster of Cyprus, and the vineyard of Engaddi. In the same order in which they follow one another here in the sequence of words, they are related as fulfilled in the Lord Jesus Christ: before his Passion, Mary anointed him with precious spikenard, and the house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment (John 12); in his Passion he was given wine mingled with myrrh (Mark 15); and after the Passion he was anointed with myrrh and other kinds of spices [Col. 1084A] and laid in the tomb (John 19). Therefore, rising after three days (Mark 16), he offered believers the sweetness of the spiritual cluster in the chief joy of the Resurrection. Shortly thereafter he poured into them the grace of the Holy Spirit, possessing every power, like balsam in the vineyards of Engaddi, granting them authority through water and Spirit (John 20), or through the laying on of hands, to forgive sins and make Christ’s sheep out of kids.

But what thus took place beforehand in himself according to history, in the Head, may also be displayed in his members according to moral interpretation in a corresponding order: first comes the fragrance of virtues, then follows the mortification of vices, because bodily affliction and contempt for worldly glory are instruments of this mortification. Are not hunger, thirst, nakedness, vigil, and continual prayers the instruments or material of this mortification? (Rom. 8.) The principal and greatest proposition is that where the instrument is lacking, the cause of the instrument is likewise lacking; where the material is absent, that which is made from the material is likewise absent; and thus it follows that where virtues are lacking, vices rule, because after the antecedent steadfastness of virtues comes the downfall of vices. [Col. 1084B] Hence the Apostle, describing two things opposed to one another, namely flesh and spirit, first declares: “Walk in the Spirit,” and then, “you shall not fulfill the desires of the flesh” (Gal. 5), to show that the flesh is subjected by the strength of the Spirit and that vice cannot be overcome unless virtue comes first.

In this order, therefore, in imitation of the Head—that is, Christ—his members, namely the saints, first offer nard and then myrrh, because they must first have works of holiness, by whose strength the works of the flesh may be mortified. But because the same Apostle says, “If by the Spirit you mortify the deeds of the flesh, you shall live” (Rom. 8), spiritual resurrection fittingly follows spiritual mortification: those who have died with Christ by dying to sins rise with him by living to righteousness, saying with the same Apostle: “If we die with him, we shall also live with him” (2 Tim. 2). For just as death is twofold, of soul and body, so also is the resurrection of each twofold: those who now rise from the death of the soul through justification will, in the future resurrection, [Col. 1084D] rise from the death of body and soul through incorruption. Hence John says in the Apocalypse: “Blessed and holy is he who has a part in the first resurrection; over these the second death has no power” (Rev. 20).

This resurrection is signified by the name of a cluster, so that those who suffered a certain bitterness for a time by spiritually mortifying the flesh may afterwards receive eternally the ineffable sweetness of joy: here, resting spiritually from corruption of mind; there, from corruption both of mind and body.

This order also pleased the ordering grace as fitting and becoming: when they are fragrant with the nard of holy reputation, and have become a living sacrifice through the myrrh of inward mortification; when, through the cluster spiritually intoxicating them, they have been gladdened by the newness of the soul rising from the death of sin; and when, through the Spirit, they have been made superior to the flesh—then it has shown them worthy of the coming of the Holy Spirit, through the balsams of diverse graces which Engaddi has spiritually produced. Engaddi is the spring of the kid: namely, the twofold baptismal washing of the font and compunction, by which kids—that is, sinners—are washed and made Christ’s sheep.

Therefore, after the Bridegroom rebuked the bride for ignorance of herself, on account of which she deserved to undergo rejection from the Bridegroom’s fellowship, and after the bride, at last recognizing herself through his saving rebuke—she who formerly despaired of being able to persevere by herself—had learned, now full of faith, not to fail in tribulations even unto death for love of him, the Bridegroom rejoices in such [Col. 1085B] progress and, judging her now beautiful, flatters her with this praise, so that she may thereby be provoked to greater works of virtue.

**VERSE 14.—“Behold, you are beautiful, my friend; behold, you are beautiful; your eyes are doves’ eyes.”**

“Because,” he says, “when you first considered yourself, you called yourself black and swarthy because of the various surges of temptations, and, still of little faith, cried out concerning my help—though the following clause is textually uncertain (‘which nevertheless had not said to you’)—but afterwards, recognizing yourself as I revealed you to yourself, you advanced with such strength of spirit that you did not hesitate to offer me not merely the myrrh of Passion but a bundle of myrrh: behold, I declare to you that you are so beautiful; and because you are beautiful, you are my friend, and conversely, because you are my friend, you are beautiful. You are not beautiful once only, but beautiful again; for repetition is confirmation. You are so perfectly beautiful that you please me with a twofold beauty: that of faith and action, or of soul and body.”

In a beautiful order, between the two predicates of beauty placed on either side, a single subject is formed in the middle, because this middle receives its being from the two, so that if either of the twofold beauties, disposed on both sides, is lacking—namely, if there is faith without works or works without faith; or chastity of body without chastity of mind, or of mind without chastity of body—no soul is united to God by the covenant of spiritual friendship.

For since it is written, “Faith, if it has not works, is dead in itself” [Col. 1085D] (Jas. 2), and likewise the Lord calls foolish the soul which carries lamps without oil while going out to meet the Bridegroom (Matt. 25), it is clear that these twofold parts of beauty on either side constitute this most holy friendship. It is no slight honor in the judgment of almighty God to be so perfect by God’s grace that he deems one worthy of his friendship, and that one is called God’s friend as a special reward of virtues. It is indeed a great commendation. Hence the Lord says to the Apostles: “I will no longer call you servants, but friends, because all things whatsoever I have heard from my Father I have made known to you” (John 15). For the sign of this friendship is the revelation of the Father’s secret; and the excellence of contemplative dignity is bestowed especially upon those who love him and preserve the fidelity of this friendship.

But because above the bride calls them “companions,” where she says, “Lest I begin to wander after the flocks of your companions,” whereas now the Bridegroom himself calls the bride “friend,” we must consider what difference there is between a friend and a companion. A companion is one associated with us in doing something together; a friend is one joined to us by a devout and faithful love through likeness in the practice of life. The Bridegroom’s companions, therefore, are those who appear to be associated with him through certain good works; but events prove with what intention they did these things, when, desiring human praise, they show themselves far removed from his love, whom they seemed to imitate not simply and devoutly but for their own temporal advantage. His friends, however, are those who are faithfully joined to him solely in hope of eternal goods, and who, since neither prosperity nor adversity separates them from him, show how fervently they burn with love for him, before whom they take care to prefer absolutely nothing. Because of such a quality of life, the Church, or any holy soul that follows Christ’s footsteps, deserves to be called friend when this beauty is proclaimed of it. But since this beauty shines forth from the contemplation of the mind as from a kind of face, he gives the reason why he called her beautiful: “Your eyes,” he says, “are doves’ eyes.”

The eyes of the Church are holy teachers, because just as eyes guide us on our way, so holy teachers, showing us the way of life, go before us, as it were, with a double eye: word and example.

Morally, too, every soul—that is, the inner human being—has two eyes in its head: understanding and discernment. It understands and sees what it ought to do; then it discerns how that action ought to be ordered, so that in one eye it considers the quality of its act, and in the other its measure. For one sees well where one ought to tend if one considers both the quality of the life to be pursued and how that quality should, according to place and time, now be intensified and now relaxed, instructing the strong and the weak, provided that the very intensification or relaxation is fixed by a definite and fitting end. The reason, therefore, that he calls her beautiful is that her eyes are doves’ eyes; this comparison is rightly made because of the sevenfold virtue of the dove’s nature and simplicity.

For the dove lacks gall; it harms no one; it selects the better grains; it feeds other birds’ young; it nests in the holes of the rock; it has groaning instead of song; and it is accustomed to sit over waters so that it may foresee the coming of the hawk. Because of these seven marks of nature the bride is compared to a dove, so that, if she applies these things possessed by the dove’s eye to moral form, she may worthily be called beautiful, striving through grace to possess what the dove possesses by nature.

It lacks gall. Spiritually, Christ’s bride too must lack this, so that, according to the Apostle, “Let all bitterness, wrath, anger, clamor, and blasphemy be put away from her, with all malice” (Eph. 4). It harms no one: Christ’s bride likewise ought to harm no one, either by word or deed, but, according to the Apostle, be at peace with all [Col. 1087A] (Rom. 12). It selects the better grains: likewise, one who loves Christ ought to gather from divine Scripture the better sayings, by which one may know how to order one’s own life honorably and profitably and, by teaching and acting, form the lives of neighbors according to one’s example. It feeds other birds’ young: the Church likewise gathers in her bosom, as though they were her own children, those who are not of her body—such as heretics and perverse Christians—and strives to unite them to her body by admonishing, correcting, and drawing them through kindness. Every soul truly the bride of Christ must do this: it must love and cherish strangers and opponents for Christ’s sake as much as members of its household, so that it may always overcome evil with good (ibid.).

It nests in the holes of the rock in order to escape the bites of serpents. Likewise, the Church or the soul united to God ought to seek refuge in Christ’s Passion, for “Christ is the rock” (1 Cor. 10), and the openings of his Passion are his wounds, most powerful defenses against the snares of malignant spirits. It has groaning instead of song: in this temporal life, groaning ought to be song for one who loves God—that is, in place of worldly comfort and joy, the sorrow according to God which works steadfast repentance unto salvation (2 Cor. 7). For it is written: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. 5); and conversely: “Woe to you who laugh now, for you shall weep” (Luke 6). It is accustomed to sit over waters in order to foresee the arrival of the hawk: likewise the faithful soul ought to dwell in mind over the streams of divine Scriptures [Col. 1087C] so that from them it may understand and learn how it can guard against the snares of the ancient enemy.

The bride is declared beautiful on account of these seven parts of dove-like simplicity. Because she exercises them with the simple eye of the mind, as with a dove’s eye, she so pleases the Bridegroom’s eyes that he declares her beautiful not once but twice, as it were confirming it; and in these parts he intimates the twofold love of God and neighbor. For not becoming angry, hoping in the mysteries of Christ’s Passion for one’s sins or for the delay of the heavenly kingdom, and directing one’s mind to holy Scripture are signs of divine love. On the other hand, harming no one, receiving and cherishing strangers as one’s own, are the judgment of brotherly love.

But because the Holy Spirit, through whom God’s love is poured into our hearts, is that same love (Rom. 5), consisting in a twofold part of love—for John says, “God is love” (1 John 4)—let us consider in these seven parts of innocence the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit: namely, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and godliness, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord (Isa. 11).

It belongs to wisdom to restrain the movements of the mind, when it wisely considers that “the anger of man does not work the righteousness of God” (Jas. 1). Hence Solomon says: “The fool immediately reveals his anger, but he who overlooks an injury is prudent” (Prov. 12); and again: “A stone is heavy and sand weighty, but a man’s wrath is heavier than both; wrath has no mercy, nor does bursting fury” [Col. 1088A] (Prov. 27). Hence a certain pagan says:

> He who does not govern his anger will wish undone whatever pain  
> and the mind’s counsel urge upon him,  
> while in unavenged hatred he hastens by force toward punishment.  
> (Horace, *Epistles* I.2.59)

And, to show that it belongs to wisdom to know how to govern the mind, he adds:

> Anger is a brief madness: govern your mind; unless it obeys,  
> it commands. Restrain it with reins; restrain it with a chain.  
> (Horace, *Epistles* I.2.62)

Therefore, through the spirit of wisdom, the disordered movement of the mind must be restrained, because thereby the evils which commonly arise from it—often so grave that they are scarcely, or never, allayed—are wisely avoided.

The spirit of understanding also consists (Isa. IX) in harming neither oneself [Col. 1088B] nor others, and in understanding through the discernment of reason that it is just not to do to another what one does not wish done to oneself (Matt. VII). But because the wrong of every injury is inflicted in two ways by the one causing it, namely by word and by deed, and received in two ways by the sufferer, that is, in mind and body, a twofold remedy of understanding must likewise be applied, so that one may consider that both the integrity of brotherly charity is corrupted and the severity of divine mercy is provoked by harming both oneself and others. For true innocence is that by which one harms neither oneself nor others, because “he who loves iniquity hates his own soul” (Ps. X), and no one sins first against another rather than against himself. Great indeed is the gift of this understanding, by which a person establishes for himself such a manner of life as to please both God and human beings; and this is [Col. 1088C] the mark of true innocence: to love God and one’s neighbour, which brings all holiness to perfection.

Moreover, by the spirit of counsel, whoever has zeal for a holy intention gathers together the better and more useful sayings of the holy Scriptures. From their meaning, as from a kind of assistance in taking counsel with himself, he discovers a manner of life suited to his condition; and this collection of diverse sayings becomes counsel for rightly ordering one’s life.

But the spirit of fortitude greatly strengthens the mind that trusts in the power of Christ’s Passion, when, by the seal of that Passion, it is both fortified outwardly in the body against every assault of diabolical attack and inwardly made firm in the mind. By this spirit of fortitude Moses defeated the Egyptian enemies (Exod. [Col. 1088D] VII–XIV), when he cast them down by the rod through manifold plagues and delivered the people of God from their slavery, signifying that the Lord himself, “mighty and powerful in battle” (Ps. XXV), ought by the wood of his cross to bring aid to the whole world, after the universal enemy—that is, the devil—had been overthrown by the power of his Passion. By this same spirit of fortitude Gideon also overcame his enemies with three hundred men (Josh. VIII), bearing before them the form of the cross in the figure of that number, which is denoted by the letter TAU; and in Ezekiel (ch. IX) no one is struck who is found marked with this letter, as with the form of a cross.

The spirit of knowledge is to commit to a tenacious memory the sequence of the holy Scriptures, by which one may spread abroad the streams of sacred teaching, and to know how to divide them [Col. 1089A] with such discernment that the simple may have wherewith to be instructed and the learned wherewith to be exercised.

To offer equal charity to all—to love enemies as much as friends for God’s sake, and, according to the Apostle, “to become all things to all, that we may gain all” (I Cor. IX)—is surely the spirit of piety. By this spirit, certainly, is led whoever zealously strives to assist his neighbour in every necessity, whether of body or soul, according to his ability and beyond his ability.

Moreover, to groan by a twofold manner of compunction—that is, either by remembrance of sins or by the inward longing of a soul thirsting for God—belongs to the spirit of the fear of the Lord, by which one fears either to be condemned for sins or to be deprived of the inheritance of the merciful Father.

But since there are four fears—one servile, another [Col. 1089B] worldly, a third initial, and a fourth filial—the latter two are referred to the spirit of the fear of the Lord. One of these, namely initial fear, is not without charity—not, I say, perfect charity, but charity begun. Hence John, when he said in his Epistle, “Perfect charity casts out fear” (I John IV), showed that, although charity is not yet perfect, it is nevertheless present in initial fear. In the other fear, which is filial, charity alone, steadfast in perfect love, is present; concerning this the Psalmist says: “The holy fear of the Lord endures for ever and ever” (Ps. XVIII). Initial fear is that of which it is said: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Eccles. I), when a person begins to be wise and to taste God; there fear and the spirit accompany one another, [Col. 1089C] as it is written, “fear is not without hope.” And the more good will—that is, charity—increases, the more fear almost diminishes, so that from that initial fear, by which one fears punishment, which is the mark of imperfection, one may someday advance to filial fear, by which one does not fear punishment but separation, which is the mark of the perfect.

But the two fears mentioned previously, namely servile and worldly fear, do not belong to the spirit of the fear of the Lord, because they are separated from chaste fear. Servile fear is abstaining from evil because of a punishment threatening from a human being, while the evil will is nevertheless retained. Worldly fear is abstaining from good because of a punishment feared from a human being. Christ prohibits these fears, namely servile and worldly fear, when he says: “Do not fear those who kill the body but have nothing they can do to the soul” [Col. 1089D] (Matt. XX). Then he adds concerning initial fear: “But rather fear him who can destroy both body and soul in Gehenna” (ibid.); he would not command this unless charity, though not yet perfect, were in it.

And it should be noted that in divine Scripture this fear is sometimes called servile because it is akin to servile fear: for there too evil is abandoned through fear of punishment, and here likewise. But that fear causes one to abstain from an evil deed and not from an evil will; this one causes abstention both in deed and in will. Therefore, in the spirit of the twofold fear of the Lord—that is, initial or filial—every holy soul has groaning instead of song, because amid the joy of the present life it groans with a sorrowful mind, either because it fears condemnation for sin or because it fears 80 being separated from God. Thus, as we have said, because of the sevenfold quality of dove-like virtue and innocence, the bride is said by the bridegroom to have dove’s eyes [Col. 1090A], since in action she displays what, judging it useful and honourable by the grace of the Holy Spirit, she sees with right intention. But because she understands that whatever good she has, she has not from herself but from God, she ascribes every grace of beauty bestowed upon her to her Creator and Redeemer, saying: “Behold, thou art fair,” etc.

**VERSE 15.—“Behold, thou art fair, my beloved, and comely. Our bed is flourishing.”**

“Thou,” she says, “O beloved, art essentially fair and comely; but whatever beauty I possess, I possess accidentally, through participation in thee, according to the measure of grace bestowed upon me by thee. For thou, as Creator, art capable through indwelling grace; I, as [Col. 1090B] creature, am capable by participating in that grace as thou hast granted it. And this is according to the power of thy divinity. But according to thy humanity, in respect of the outward person, thou wast ‘fairer in form than the sons of men’ (Ps. XLIV); while according to the inward person, God gives the Spirit not by measure to thee alone, his only-begotten Son (John III), whereas thy participants receive him by measure, one in this way and another in that.”

They possess all beauty and comeliness from thee, who art truly and naturally fair and comely; for whatever meekness, whatever piety, whatever justice, whatever patience, humility, or, finally, whatever virtue or holiness ever could be or can be, they behold and receive in thee alone, [Col. 1090C] the holy man, as in the highest exemplar.

Having therefore first spoken the words, “Behold, thou art fair and comely,” she goes on to set forth certain parts of that beauty and comeliness, adding: “Our bed is flourishing,” etc.

The first of these parts, namely “our bed is flourishing,” can be referred both to the head and to the members of the head; but the two remaining parts refer only to the members, yet depend upon the head itself through participation in his beauty and comeliness. But first it must be said how the first part is to be understood of both the head and the head’s members: of the head, indeed, either according to the good pleasure of the divinity that rules all things, or according to the mystery of the humanity [Col. 1090D] redeeming the world; of the members, according to participation, as we have said, in divine grace, which indwells the mind of every holy person and works there the gifts of its gracious condescension.

By the name “bed,” rest is signified in two ways, namely bodily or spiritual rest. For just as the body seeks rest after labour, so also the mind, wearied by certain labours of disturbances, desires rest. But in this place “bed” must be understood as spiritual rest, because, as we have said, it is to be referred both to the head and to the members of piety.

Nevertheless, we must first consider the rest of the head. It must by no means be thought necessary or advantageous to that substance which is subject to no accident and with whom there is no change nor [Col. 1091A] shadow of alteration (James I); rather, the rest of the head is the salvation of the body. For just as God says that he labours when he endures the perversities of evil people, so he says that he rests when he delights in the virtues of good people. Concerning his labour, by which he endures those still living perversely, he says through the prophet: “I have laboured in bearing them” (Jer. VI). The Lord does not labour by bearing, for no weariness can touch the power of his majesty; but, speaking in human terms, he calls his own patience toward us “labour.” Yet concerning the rest by which he delights in the good he says: “Upon whom shall I rest, but upon the humble and quiet person who trembles at my words?” (Isa. LXVI). As though he said in other words: “That person prepares rest for me in himself who keeps, in humility and quietness, [Col. 1091B] the rule of my commandments.” Therefore God’s rest is our advantage, just as, conversely, his labour is our loss.

Accordingly, the signification of this bed—that is, the rest of which we have spoken—is fittingly applied to a member of this head, namely some faithful and holy person. For just as, conversely, the rest and delight of the reprobate in this world become perpetual labour and weariness of the soul in the future, so for the elect the labour and weariness of this world become eternal rest and consolation of the soul in the future. The bed of a holy person is the silence and worship of the contemplative life: the farther it is from the world, the nearer it is to God; and the more it labours in observing the divine commandments, the greater rest it has in the contemplation of divinity. As though upon one bed are God, inspiring, moderating, [Col. 1091C] and preserving by grace, and the human being, willing, acting, and bringing to completion through grace that inspires, moderates, and preserves: God, grace capable of being participated in; the human being, a participant in grace.

Therefore the members of this head say, “Our bed is flourishing,” because, while they are, as it were, in one rest with the aforesaid—the participable and the participant, that is, head and member—the unfading shoots of virtues spring forth, so that that bed is rightly called flourishing, that is, adorned with the varied beauty of good works. Thus the bride speaks to the bridegroom: “The bed is not thine but ours; flourishing,” because to cleave to God in thought, will, and action through the honourableness of a life flowering in holiness is as though to rest with him in one chamber. Otherwise the soul profits nothing without grace resting with it [Col. 1091D].

Moreover, according to the mystery of the beloved’s humanity, his bed is the womb of the blessed Virgin Mary, because it is wonderfully flourishing both in the beauty of virginity and in the inestimable and ineffable operation of the Holy Spirit in that singular birth. But “our bed,” she says, because it is thine through the election of the Incarnation and mine through faith in that Incarnation itself; thine because of the many proportionate gifts of thy grace dwelling in the mind of the Virgin and Mother, mine because I am to imitate, insofar as I can, the example of her magnificent holiness and to adore the unparalleled excellence of the novelty of novelties.

The bed of the beloved is also the tomb in which he was laid after the Passion; and it is flourishing because from [Col. 1092A] that burial sprang forth the marks of the glorious Resurrection. “This bed too,” she says, “is not only thine but ours, because thou didst rise from this bed, that is, from the tomb, and gavest me hope of rising again. The certainty of this hope is to me like a bed in which I rest securely, through the whole effort of thy grace working with me, because I do not doubt the future joy of the resurrection and the eternal reward of transitory labour.”

**VERSE 16.—“The beams of our houses are of cedar; our ceilings, of cypress.”**

The beauty and comeliness of the following parts, by which the beloved is proclaimed fair and comely by the bride—namely, “The beams of our houses are of cedar; our ceilings, of cypress”—belong especially to his members. Yet the virtues [Col. 1092B] and graces of those members are ascribed to his beauty and comeliness, whose is all that is called good and honourable.

First, however, it must be considered whose houses these beams and ceilings are. In their universality, the great house of this beloved—that is, of our Lord Jesus Christ—is the holy universal Church; but in a particular sense, the individual churches contained within this universality are also called his houses. The beams and ceilings of these houses are the angels—that is, the rulers and teachers—of the individual churches that have existed in time and place, for their defence and adornment by word and example. Spreading far and wide the fragrance of their holiness and teaching, they have fortified and adorned, [Col. 1092C] fortify and adorn, and will fortify and adorn the universal Church itself; their memory is in blessing for ever and ever.

But these beams are said to be cedar, while the ceilings are cypress. Cedar has three noteworthy natural properties: height, fragrance, and incorruptibility. These rightly suit holy teachers, because they are raised up by the contemplation of Divinity, diffuse on every side the fragrance of teaching and good action, and are not corrupted by any rottenness of unbelief or perversity. There is also a fourth notable feature of cedar nature: by its fragrance it is said to drive away serpents. This shows the corresponding power of the teachers whom it signifies: by their teaching they are able to repel evil thoughts that creep secretly in hearts [Col. 1092D], and to put to flight, together with those thoughts, the ancient serpent who suggests them, that is, the devil.

Cypress likewise has the two aforesaid graces in its nature, namely fragrance and incorruption; and these too suit teachers because of the fragrance of life and teaching and the incorruption of faith.

Yet beams and ceilings may suitably be understood differently: the beams as prelates in the Church and the ceilings as those subject to them. For beams support ceilings, just as prelates support their subjects by providing for their necessities; so that, as a house is clothed in beautiful adornment from the joining of beams and ceilings, so the Church of God is ordered with fitting and reasonable arrangement through the religious unanimity of prelates and subjects.

[Col. 1093A] And both are rightly described as fragrant and incorruptible, like cedar and cypress, because prelates are exalted by the good fragrance and incorruption of life, teaching, and faith, while those subject to them are daily stirred by their instruction toward the same graces of virtues. Hence cypress, which is placed on the side of the subjects, naturally has this quality: when worked by the hand of the craftsman, it presents a graceful appearance. For this is characteristic of good subjects: when they have been touched by the hand of holy admonition or rebuke from their prelates, they do not recoil insolently, but submit themselves obediently to their warnings with cheerful countenance and patient mind.

But if we consider all these matters generally in the universal Church as well, which is a kind of commonwealth of bridegroom and bride [Col. 1093B], these notable ornaments of the house of the Lord are daily venerated and proclaimed. It contains principally the head, namely Christ, in his deeds and commandments; and after him his members, among whom the blessed Virgin Mary, pre-eminent above all and of singular merit, is most beautiful, as is signified by the flourishing bed. Then come the apostles or apostolic men, and their hearers and followers, set within the very house of the Lord as beams and ceilings. By their whole life, learning, instruction, and authority this entire commonwealth of God is reverently strengthened and adorned, so that to those who rightly behold it nothing more honourable, nothing more pleasant, nothing certainly sweeter can be judged in this pilgrimage of life. For it is a kind of way and foretaste [Col. 1093C] of future blessedness, and a distant contemplation, in faith, hope, and charity, of that great and incomparable commonwealth.

But that this glorious condition of the nobly constituted Church stands by the will of him who said, “Without me you can do nothing” (John XV), the same bridegroom and ruler himself acknowledges, Truth confirming truth—not because he needs our testimony, but in order to instruct us in greater faith and teach us that no one should presume upon his own righteousness in any good thing.

## CHAPTER TWO

**VERSE 1.—“I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys.”**

“Rightly,” he says, “O beloved, dost thou perceive, who ascribest all thy beauty to me; for I truly am [Col. 1093D] the flower of the field—that is, the honour, beauty, and adornment of the whole universal Church, spread throughout the world as through a most delightful field, and springing and flowering in diverse forms of holiness and grace from my gift. I am also the lily of the valleys—that is, the cleansing, refreshment, and remedy of those who are humble, or who are cast down by any sorrow and affliction in this world for the sake of my name.”

For the nature of the lily has three delightful qualities: whiteness, fragrance, and a remedy against burning. Thus whoever in this valley of tears mourns his transgressions with humbled spirit and contrite heart, acknowledging himself infirm and ever imploring my aid, will without doubt obtain cleansing and whiteness of soul; and then, inspired and assisted by me, he will be refreshed by the fragrance [Col. 1094A] of good conduct and cooled against every incitement of the flesh, against the burning of affliction, and against the world as it were on fire, through the consolation of my love and hope set before him.

In another sense also, O beloved, I am the flower of the field, namely that flower of which Isaiah says: “A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root” (Isa. XI). For thou didst say above that our bed was flourishing, namely the womb of my mother, from which I chose to be incarnate; but I say that it is flourishing because I am its flower, from which flower proceed many other flowers, namely the spiritual graces enumerated by the prophet just mentioned. “And the Spirit of the Lord,” he says, “shall rest upon him”—without doubt, upon the flower—“the spirit [Col. 1094B] of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (ibid.). Therefore I am the flower of the field, namely of that earth of which it is said, “Truth has sprung up from the earth” (Ps. LXXXIV). It is called a field because it is not rough, twisted, or uneven, but level and smooth, having been made, by the power of the Most High, like a calm sea, flat from every inequality of character. It brought forth me, the flower of flowers—that is, the Holy of Holies—without male seed, just as a field without seed produces shoots of diverse flowers and herbs.

I am also the lily of the valleys: that is, the whiteness, fragrance, and salvation of those who imitate the humility of my mother and do not glory in the merit of chastity. For those who boast and restrain themselves only for human favour do not possess [Col. 1094C] the lily of virginal whiteness, the sign of inward purity; rather, they are unclean with the blackness of vain glory before the sight of my purity. Therefore I neither am nor can be called their lily; but I am the lily, by the gift of grace, of those who imitate me and her, while she is a lily by example, so that they too may become lilies by imitation. Hence follows: “As a lily among thorns.”

**VERSE 2.—“As a lily among thorns, so is my friend among the daughters.”**

“Just as I,” he says, “shone among the Jews—whom I expected to produce grapes, but they produced thorns instead (Isa. V)—with humility, meekness, patience, and manifold grace of virtues, while they, existing against me like thorns, pierced me with many barbs of words and deeds, so thou, O my Church, my bride, or any soul that loves me, ought to be among the daughters [Col. 1094D] of this age—that is, souls thorny with malice and unbelief—with humility and patience. When thou hast imitated me in this way, thou shalt truly be proved my friend; and such imitation of me is the proof of true friendship.

“Or, just as Mary, my mother according to the flesh, who is a lily in the whiteness of virginity and the fragrance of holiness, walked with humility and patience among the daughters of the Synagogue, who pierced her as thorns by laying upon her the stain of infamy because they did not believe in God’s power and might—since by the Spirit she recognized God’s dispensation and felt fulfilled in herself what she had once heard through the prophet and afterward through the angel—so also, by her example, every soul that is my friend through faith and love ought, among the daughters whom the corruption of malice and impiety has begotten, [Col. 1095A] to preserve humility, patience, and uprightness, and never to fail in these because of hope for future recompense.”

Or, more simply, let us say that the soul which desires to show itself worthy of God’s friendship ought always to remain among wicked people as a lily among thorns. Just as a lily set among thorns does not lose the dignity of its whiteness and fragrance, so that soul should not lose its integrity of faith and patience, or of any holiness granted to it, amid corrupt habits; but rather, through endurance, it should learn that the more it is afflicted by their perversity, the greater merits of virtues are accumulated for it. For, as blessed Gregory says, whoever does not tolerate evil people is himself, by his intolerance, a witness that he is not good. Thus blessed Job speaks of himself, saying: “I am brother to dragons and companion to ostriches” (Job XXX); and the Lord says to Ezekiel: “Son of man, unbelievers and destroyers are with thee; thou dwellest with scorpions” (Ezek. II). Peter too commends Lot’s life, saying: “And he delivered righteous Lot, oppressed by the injury and licentious conduct of the wicked; for he was righteous in sight and hearing, dwelling among those who from day to day tormented the righteous soul with their wicked deeds” (II Pet. II). Thus John writes to the Church at Pergamum: “I know where thou dwellest, where Satan’s seat is; and thou holdest my name and hast not denied my faith” (Rev. II). Paul also praises and strengthens [Col. 1095C] the disciples, saying: “In the midst of a crooked and perverse nation, among whom ye shine as lights in the world, holding fast the word of life” (Phil. II).

From these authorities it is sufficiently evident how great a virtue it is to tolerate the wicked ways of human beings, since the greater the malice of the reprobate, the greater the gains of merit that increase for the elect. For it is written: “The more Pharaoh oppressed the people of God, the more they multiplied” (Exod. I).

What the daughters are, among whom the Church or holy soul is said to dwell as a lily among thorns, is gathered from the comparison itself. For those who are compared to thorns plainly are understood in the adverse sense; and they are called daughters because [Col. 1095D] they are begotten from the evil seed of perverse doctrine or from an evil conception of the mind. But the Church, or every faithful soul that is Christ’s bride through faith and works, in order that it may be as a lily among thorns, comes before him who governs and protects it with gracious praise through another comparison, saying: “As an apple tree among the trees of the woods,” etc.

**VERSE 3.—“As an apple tree among the trees of the woods, so is my beloved among the sons. Under his shadow, whom I desired, I sat; and his fruit was sweet to my throat.”**

“My beloved,” she says, “compared me to a lily among thorns because I preserve his virtue. Although he granted this to me by his gift, he nevertheless taught me to become this by his own example. For just as the apple tree, a fruitful tree, has three useful things by which it refreshes—namely fruit, fragrance, and shade—and is deemed incomparable among the trees of the woods, which are certainly fruitless, so my beloved refreshes, teaches, and defends those who believe in him by the fruit and fragrance of holiness, justice, and teaching, and by the shade of his protection. He stood among the sons, that is, the Jews, [Col. 1096A] who were indeed sons at first and now wish to be so, but are not, because God said of them: ‘I have nourished and exalted sons, but they have despised me’ (Isa. I); and elsewhere: ‘Strange sons have lied to me; strange sons have grown old and limped from their paths’ (Ps. XVII). They boast that they are sons of Abraham, but are not, because they do not have his works (John VIII); and therefore they are fruitless and useless trees, and for this reason are to be cut down and cast into the fire.

“For among such trees, destined for eternal burning, he hung upon the tree of the cross, from which he poured out to me the sweetest fruit of his body and blood, by which he daily refreshes those who believe in him. But they, like wild trees, not only bore no fruit of good work, but also poured forth the most bitter sap of their malice and impiety, crying, ‘Crucify, crucify’ (John XIX), and, ‘His blood be upon us and upon our children’ (Matt. XVII).

“Therefore beneath the shadow of this tree—that is, beneath the refreshment and consoling protection of the New Testament—which I had long desired in the ancient fathers, who with great longing sighed for the times of grace that would soothe and refresh them, I at last sat after Christ’s coming, Passion, resurrection, and ascension [Col. 1096C], with unwavering and steadfast faith. For the Law had long afflicted me with a certain heat of severity and incurable punishment, when it said: ‘If anyone does this or that, let him die the death’ (Exod. XIX); but grace removed such heat by the shade of mercy and the remedy of repentance. Under this desirable shadow I did not walk or stand, but rather sat and rested, because I undertook to hold immovably this decree of mercy, confirmed by the authority of my Lord himself.

“This tree is indeed the tree of life, whose shade and divine protection its branches cast forth—the branches of honour and grace, namely the opposing virtues set against the heats of worldly temptations: against pride, [Col. 1096D] the necessary opposition of humility; against anger, patience; against lust, chastity and continence; against obstinacy, obedience; against avarice, generosity and mercy; against disputes and quarrels, peace and concord; against envy and hatred, love. And, to put it briefly, against all the pleasures and temptations of this world must certainly be set the remembrance of the future misery of the wicked and the glory of the just.

“The outpourings of such shadows protect the soul from the heat of carnal suggestions and pleasures. Beneath them, because I desired them, I sat—that is, I rested—because I found in them the pleasant and health-giving refreshment of protecting grace.

“And his fruit”—without doubt that of the apple tree, namely Christ, my bridegroom and Lord—“is sweet to my throat,” because the usefulness and sweetness of his commandments are sweet and pleasing to the palate of my heart and to the capacity of my mind. Or the fruit of this apple tree hanging on the tree of the cross is sweet to my throat, because the reception of Christ’s body and blood pours sweetness and healing into my breast and is plainly the perfect refreshment of my body and soul.”

In another sense, the sons among whom the bridegroom is said to dwell as an apple tree among the trees of the woods are understood as the elect, who are called sons of God by adoption because of their observance of his commandments, for which they will receive the inheritance of eternal life from their heavenly Father. Christ dwells among them as an apple tree among the trees of the woods because, as the apple tree [Col. 1097B] surpasses all the trees of the woods in beauty and in the fragrance and sweetness of its fruits, so Christ surpasses all the saints in the beauty of virtues and sweetness of teaching. As it is written of him: “Fairer in form than the sons of men, grace has been poured upon thy lips; therefore God, thy God, has anointed thee with the oil of gladness above thy companions” (Ps. XLIV).

Under whose shadow the Church is wonderfully protected and consoled from every heat of sorrow and disturbance, remaining secure and immovable through hope of future recompense, since the branches of his sacraments, commandments, and gifts are spread over the whole breadth of the world. Its fruit is sweet to her throat, because all the mysteries of his sayings and the venerable institutions of his sacraments, which [Col. 1097C] he brought forth from the hidden wisdom of his divinity, are sweet and welcome to the mind that devoutly embraces and venerates them, because of the salvation thereby granted to it, which gives life and refreshes without end.

He then makes clear, by what follows, what effect the sweetness and pleasantness of this fruit has and what more sublime and perfect thing it brings forth.

**VERSE 4.—“The king brought me into the wine-cellar; he ordered charity within me.”**

The effect of this introduction proceeded from the cause of a fruit well pleasing and therefore received with great zeal of mind. For the more God’s commandments are desired, the more people are brought by divine love to desire ever greater things.

Not all receive equally that fruit which flowed forth and still flows forth from that glorious and most excellent tree, the Lord Jesus Christ: for one receives this and another that, according to what he understands and loves.

To one the virtue of patience is more pleasing and delightful; to another, obedience; to one, humility; to another, continence. One is more delighted by diligence in prayer, another by reading or fasting; and through the divine gift they acquire diverse kinds throughout the whole range of the graces of virtues.

There is a certain special storehouse, as it were, standing apart in a secret place, which is called a cellar because of a certain narrowness, since it admits few into its recesses. There is hidden the sweetness and pleasantness of that fruit which gladdens the human heart (Ps. CIII) and dries up every moisture of vices: namely, the Gospel commandment concerning the benefit of charity. It is rightly called by the name of wine, because just as wine, in purifying itself, rejects every harmful thing from itself and, by its natural colour, dries up every noxious moisture, so the commandment of charity drives every plague of vices from the heart and expels every passion of the mind. For no one can both have charity and be evil; and therefore the full understanding of this commandment is rightly called the wine-cellar.

Those, therefore, who delight in resting beneath the branches of that saving tree and in gathering without weariness the sweetest fruit of holiness will at some time arrive at this perfection, so as to enter the wine-cellar without obstacle. For this path is not narrow to those for whom the broad and spacious path of worldly pleasure has been utterly closed. For the path of this commandment is narrow, because it seems difficult and laborious to many when it says: “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you” (Matt. V).

But because we read that it has been observed by many saints, this commandment is difficult only to those who have not yet perfectly tasted the sweetness of the fruits, that is, of the divine commandments. This wine-cellar, therefore, is the perfection—and, for those freely entering the narrow way, the sweet and thus perfecting understanding—of the divine commandment concerning the excellence of charity.

But because charity itself has diverse objects, it is necessary to observe order within it, so that one may know in what place every affection is to be put, and which is to be received first and which afterward. Therefore, after saying, [Col. 1098C] “The king brought me into the wine-cellar,” he adds, “and he ordered charity within me.” For this is the order of holy love: first to love God, then one’s neighbour, and lastly even one’s enemy. This order is necessary, for it is impossible for anyone to love his neighbour—or, what is more difficult, his enemy—unless he loves God, since love of God is the cause of loving them; and in this way what was impossible becomes possible. For what necessarily is, cannot fail to be; and what necessarily is not, cannot be. The love of God must be where love of neighbour is, because no one loves his neighbour for God’s sake unless he loves God. And the love of God must not be where there is no love of neighbour, according to John’s saying: “He who does not love his brother whom he has seen, how can he love God whom he has not seen?” (I John IV).

But the love of God need not always be absent where there is no love of an enemy, because it may happen that one who loves God has no enemy whom he may love for God’s sake. But if he has one, then the love of God must be absent where the love of an enemy is absent, because whoever does not wish to love an enemy for God’s sake proves that he does not love God.

This order, therefore, as has been said, appears necessary when it is determined that love of neighbour is impossible unless love of God precedes it—yet this applies to the love that is according to God, not that which is according to the world.
