For worldly love [Col. 1099A] is without love of God, because the former is according to the flesh, the latter according to the spirit.

There is a twofold mode of love according to the flesh. One is wholly opposed to God, as is the mutual love of evil people based on their shared wrongdoing. The other is not opposed to God, as is the love of parents, relatives, and friends; yet the love of God, and love for every neighbour for God’s sake, must always be preferred to that love. But the first carnal mode is altogether foreign to the present passage, because it is wholly disordered and contrary to God. The other, which is not contrary to God, does not conflict with the present passage if it is ordered; for if a human being is loved in God more than God himself, it is then disordered.

[Col. 1099B] It may also reasonably be understood that there is a twofold order of charity: one in God, the other in one’s neighbour. For it is written: “God is charity” (1 John 4). In this charity, which is God, the Church, or any holy soul, ought to learn, know, and understand an order: that it may name the Father first, as it were the voice; the Son second, as it were the Word from the voice; and the Holy Spirit third, as it were the understanding proceeding from voice and Word. Yet it should not speak thus as though there were any rank within the Trinity—which it is impious to say—but so that it may distinguish in persons, in this order of names, that charity, that is, God, whom it ought to love with all its heart, all its soul, and all its strength, one and the same in substance.

[Col. 1099C] This love itself is distinguished in this order: God is to be loved first with the whole heart, then with the whole soul, and finally with the whole strength—by believing with the whole heart, confessing with the whole soul, and acting with the whole strength.

But in the love of one’s neighbour, charity is ordered through each of the legal commandments which follow. For not committing adultery, not committing murder, not bearing false witness, honouring father and mother, and so forth, in the order of the Decalogue, are also charity ordered in their proper places. Charity also orders how, and with what affection, the different persons in the Church ought to be loved: a faithful friend in one order, a most dear son in another, parents in another, a full brother in another, [Col. 1099D] a spouse in another, a servant by his lord in another, a lord by his servant in another, a stranger in another, an acquaintance in another, a priest in another, and a relative or neighbour in another. For giving necessities to those in need, visiting the sick or those consigned to prison, consoling the needy and those oppressed by an unjust judgment, burying the dead, correcting those who act wrongly, helping brethren in some labour, instructing the less knowledgeable, or providing whatever else is necessary for the benefit of neighbours—all these are surely duties capable of being ordered by holy charity.

Rightly, then, is the holy mind led by its king and bridegroom into the wine-cellar, that is, into the understanding of divine commandments, when, intoxicated by the sweetness of his grace, it understands how manifoldly ordered is the diligence required in bestowing charity. Accordingly, [Col. 1100A] when it is affected with such strength by this intoxicating wine that it remains almost insensible to every worldly delight, and through its immense desire for charity so ordered not only grows astonished but even languishes, it asks for a certain consolation in this languor, adding:

**VERSE 5.—“Support me with flowers; surround me with apples, for I languish with love.”**

What are flowers but souls bringing forth the first beginnings of good work and beginning to give fragrance through heavenly desire? And what are apples but souls which, nourished by divine grace from the beginnings of good works, now possess perfection, advancing as it were from flowers to fruit? Therefore she who languishes with divine love [Col. 1100B] asks to be supported by flowers and surrounded with apples, because, although she is not yet able to see him whom she loves so orderly with all her heart, all her soul, and all her strength—that is, by faith, confession, and action—as he is, she nevertheless finds great consolation in rejoicing at the devout progress of neighbours, some just beginning and others already perfected.

92 For holy Church has within herself certain lesser members whom she instructs by word and example, that they may be like flowers taking hold of the first fruits of holiness. She also has certain greater members by whom she is instructed and through whose teaching and examples she is daily built up; they are like apples, already pleasing in the ripeness and perfection of good works. Such lesser and greater persons, growing by this zeal of devotion, [Col. 1100C] greatly console holy Church. For with great gladness of heart she sees that her children—small and great, untrained and perfect—love what she herself loves intensely; and it is a great consolation in her languor, during the exile of this pilgrimage, that they strive with her in desire toward that to which she believes she will someday attain as a reward.

In this way also any saint who languishes with love for God may say, “Support me with flowers; surround me with apples,” when he judges it a great remedy for such languor that he sees the progress in good works of those whom he loves in God: some of these springing up toward devout pursuits, and others bearing fruit in those pursuits themselves. Was not he who [Col. 1100D] languished with such love when he said, “I desire to depart and to be with Christ,” yet desired his neighbours’ benefit when he said, “But to remain in the flesh is necessary for your sake” (Phil. 1)? He regards seeing their progress in the meantime as a great consolation, while he is not yet able perfectly to attain the sight of God’s face which he so greatly desires to see. Though he greatly desires to depart and be with Christ, did this man, who languished with divine love, fear that he might never obtain what he loved? Certainly not. Rather, this came about by God’s dispensation: the postponement of this reward became a greater exercise of virtues and also a more abundant recompense for his labour, for the benefit of those whom he loved. For he who desired to depart was certainly sure of the reward, as he himself says elsewhere: “We know [Col. 1101A] that if our earthly house of this dwelling is dissolved, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens” (2 Cor. 5).

Therefore he bore the pain of this delay more lightly because he rejoiced that those whom he loved were pressing onward with him to receive the same reward.

Thus he sends consoling words to some of his disciples, saying: “I give thanks to my God always for you, for the grace of God which has been given you in Christ Jesus, because in all things you have been made rich in him, in every word and in every knowledge, just as the testimony of Christ has been confirmed in you, so that you lack no grace as you await the revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Cor. 1). Behold: he who desired to depart [Col. 1101B] and be with Christ rejoiced and gave thanks so greatly that, because he could not yet attain this, the progress of the children whom he had begotten in Christ greatly relieved the hardship of the delay.

93 In another way, too, the Church desires the benefit and progress of her children through faith and action. Thus she is said to be supported with flowers when she is adorned by the faith of believers, which is the beginning of religion and, as it were, the first flower of holiness to arise. But because “faith without works is dead” (Jas. 2), she is said to be surrounded with apples when she rejoices at the devout works of those believers, who bear fruit in many ways, as though in fruits now mature.

And since these two are so joined together that one cannot be useful [Col. 1101C] without the other—for it is written that “without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. 11), but “faith, if it does not have works, is dead in itself” (Jas. 2)—it is certainly a great consolation to the soul languishing in the love of God when it sees its neighbours advancing in faith and action.

But because this bride of Christ, made weak and languishing by that love so magnificently ordered, as we have said, is sustained not only by the progress and benefit of her neighbours but also by the possession of present goods and the hope of future ones, she adds:

**VERSE 6.—“His left hand is under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me.”**

[Col. 1101D] Christ’s left hand—that is, his left—is temporal goods; his right hand is eternal goods. God grants certain temporal goods in this world to his elect in expectation of future goods, so that, while they receive his present gifts, they may prepare themselves more ardently and securely to desire eternal things.

But Christ’s left hand is under her head, because she presses down these temporal goods by the purpose of supreme love, regarding them as lower things while always fixing her attention upon eternal goods as higher things. For all these temporal things ought to be beneath the head—that is, beneath the mind—not above it: namely, so that she may never prefer them to divine love, but may use them in such a way that, not for pleasure but rather for necessity, she moderates them with the rational balance of her mind, [Col. 1102A] while continually admiring in love and longing those things which ought to be above the mind. This is his right hand which shall embrace her: those everlasting goods, which, once she has obtained them, will enable her to rest in secure blessedness and blessed security.

She therefore says, “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me,” because I shall hold in thought, for thanksgiving, all things which he has arranged in created things for my benefit; but those things for which these have been granted to me for a time, I shall strive to love and desire with all devotion of mind, since they will remain with me eternally.

Or, “His left hand is under my head,” because his birth and suffering, his resurrection and ascension into heaven, [Col. 1102B] shall be in my memory; “and his right hand shall embrace me,” because the remembrance of these things will encourage me to love and seek the splendours of the future resurrection and glory.

Or, God’s left hand is a certain small knowledge of him in this present age; his right hand, after this life, is the full and true knowledge of him. But his left hand is under our head, and his right hand shall embrace us, because “now we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face” (1 Cor. 13). The left hand is under the head because in this life we are granted to think and perceive something of God with the mind; but his right hand shall embrace us because in the future life he will fill and surround us with so great a vision of himself that what it is like can neither be seen by eye, [Col. 1102C] heard by ear, nor enter into the human heart (1 Cor. 2).

Thus charity, by the gracious condescension of the ordering grace in the bride, places the left hand beneath her head and embraces her with its right hand, so that, with all temporal gifts assigned a secondary place, she may rest principally in the desire of eternal life. In this way the granting of present things becomes also the assurance of future things, and a consolation to the mind weak and languishing in the love of God.

And you, sisters beloved in Christ, who languish in the love of God by despising the world, ought to give such a sign of this love: that you may be supported with flowers by believing, and surrounded with apples by acting. Let Christ’s left hand be under your head, and let his right hand embrace [Col. 1102D] you, so that you may always regard temporal goods, somehow granted you by God, as lower things, but eternal goods as higher things. “Length of days is in his right hand; in his left are riches and glory” (Prov. 3), because in this present life he sometimes grants his elect a foretaste of the riches of his goodness, but in the future life grants them to possess them eternally without end. “Delights are at his right hand unto the end” (Ps. 15), and you can surely attain them if you languish in his love in such a way that you persevere in him steadfastly and firmly unto the end. For his right hand shall embrace you, because he will grant you knowledge of himself not in part, as now, but whole and perfect; and for brief and passing labour he will grant you rest and life and length of days for ever and ever. Amen.

## BOOK TWO

[Col. 1103]

### 95 PREFACE

[Col. 1103A]

“How,” says the Psalmist, “shall we sing the Lord’s song in a foreign land?” (Ps. 136). But what is the Lord’s song? First, to speak simply: the Lord’s song is whatever we compose, write, and say in harmonious modulation of thought and words according to the manner of ecclesiastical teaching or ordinance. The Lord’s song is the whole page of the Old and New Testaments, which we sing well when we proclaim it with right and full faith, expounding now the sequence of events, now the meaning of the events themselves, in praise of the Lord. But anyone may sing such a song by way of knowledge, not only in his own land but also in a foreign land; for bodily location does not take away the power of singing, though it may take away the will and pleasure because of some experience of sorrow. Thus it was with that people placed in the grief of captivity, who, when they were told, “Sing us a hymn from the songs of Zion,” answered: “How shall we sing the Lord’s song in a foreign land?” Indeed, understood figuratively, their inability to sing the Lord’s song in a foreign land was our inability perfectly to praise the Lord in the place of our pilgrimage, which is for us like a foreign land: “For here we have no lasting city, but we seek the one to come” (Heb. 13), which is our homeland and the land of our eternal inheritance. For recounting God’s works, declaring his commandments, writing and expounding them, is, as we have said, a kind of singing of the Lord’s song. This too is possible in the place of our pilgrimage, as the Psalmist says: “Your statutes were songs to me in the place of my pilgrimage” (Ps. 118).

[Col. 1103C] But, to consider something more deeply, there is another song of the Lord which cannot be sung in a foreign land. What, then, is it? It is undoubtedly that which the Holy Spirit modulates through his sevenfold grace, as though through seven distinctions of voices; for the voice of the inner person sounds in one way through the spirit of wisdom, in another through the spirit of understanding, in another through the spirit of counsel, and in another through the spirit of fortitude; in another manner through the spirit of knowledge, in another through the spirit of piety, and again in another through the spirit of the Lord (Isa. 11).

[Col. 1103D] By these distributions of graces, as by diverse voices, the whole modulation is formed of the Lord’s song—that sweetest song which an upright, holy, God-pleasing, and perfect life sings upon the strings of virtues.

96 For there is no discord there between flesh and spirit, because the flesh sings so harmoniously in accompaniment to the spirit that they form the perfect harmony of the spiritual [Col. 1104A] song, which is the best kind of divine song in the place of our pilgrimage. But this song cannot be sung in a foreign land, that is, in a body subject to sins. It is then a foreign land when, being in sin and in the devil’s power, it is unworthy of Christ’s dwelling; or it is alienated from us when, by acting wickedly, it resists the spirit and the reason of the mind. The land is foreign: the human being, always loving earthly things, is thereby alien from God and therefore unable to sing the Lord’s song, because “the natural person does not receive the things of the Spirit of God” (1 Cor. 2).

But why say these things? Plainly in order to show you, most holy sisters, that the task you have imposed upon me exceeds my powers. Since I am little or not at all suited to sing the Lord’s song, I shall be far less suited to sing the Song of Songs. For such a subject belongs to orators who declaim eloquently and wisely, whose office is to speak fittingly in order to persuade, and whose end is to persuade by speech. But since I possess neither wisdom nor eloquence, and lack the office of speaking fittingly, I am surely still less capable of attaining the end of persuading by speech. I would write usefully to you only if I said what I say or intend to say so fittingly that I could persuade you toward uprightness of life and the good of the soul. For my land is foreign, resisting the spirit and serving the lordship of sin; and therefore I am unfit to sing the Lord’s song in it, much less [Col. 1104C] the Song of Songs. Yet, as someone has said, “Let one who fears be permitted to hope”: though I fear, because of the smallness of my understanding, to pursue such an exalted subject, let me nevertheless hope that through your prayers I may be helped, out of regard for the divinity, to carry out what I have begun.

## CHAPTER II FOLLOWS

**VERSE 7.—“I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes and the stags of the field, that you do not rouse or awaken the beloved until she herself wishes.”**

Therefore the beloved, delighting in the sleep of his beloved, beneath whose head—that is, mind—he had placed his left hand, that is, temporal benefit, and whom he had embraced with his right hand, that is, love of eternal life, addresses the daughters of Jerusalem, that is, faithful souls, in this way: “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes and the stags of the field, that you do not rouse or awaken the beloved until she herself wishes.”

[Col. 1104D] What is this sleep, so sweet and so salutary, that such an adjuration of the beloved should be made on its account? Is it not that sleep in which the beloved, resting in sweet and desirable tranquillity, had said above: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me”?

97 For she had set aside all temporal things, [Col. 1105A] while she fixed the contemplative eye of her desiring soul upon eternal and unfailing goods; and she slept delightfully, as it were, in this desirable vision of the mind. Such sleep cannot readily arise in a mind already freed from all activities and laid out in great repose in the love of God. Hence the Lord admonishes through the Psalmist: “Be still,” he says, “and know that I am God” (Ps. 45). These two expressions are inseparable in this matter, because no one can see the essence of the Godhead with the eye of inward contemplation unless he has first endeavoured to be free from every outward hindrance. Therefore, after first saying, “Be still,” he adds, “and know,” thereby indicating that the mind must first be freed from every thought of worldly things, so that, when its eye is closed to earthly matters, it may become possible to sleep in the love of the divinity with a clearer and subtler vision.

But since the grace of this sleep does not come and remain equally for all, and since one person is clearly raised by a greater power of contemplation and another by a lesser—for Mary advanced further in divine vision than Peter or John, and these further than any other saint—it is certain that each saint has, in a different manner, the holiness of this sleep, manifold because of the unequal degrees of repose. Thus each, in his own place, according to the grace of repose bestowed upon him, has a special sleep in the contemplative life. Hence the prophet says, in the person of every faithful person sleeping in this manner: “I will rest and consider [Col. 1105C] in my place” (Isa. 18), as though plainly to say: Because this is the order of sleep—that one may not sleep before having repose—I will rest, that is, I will remove from myself every cause of earthly anxiety; and then at last, sleeping to these things in mind, I shall cleave to divine contemplation in the place of the special grace granted to me. Therefore, whatever the manner or place in which the beloved sleeps, the daughters of Jerusalem are adjured by the beloved not to rouse or awaken her until she herself wishes.

But what are the daughters of Jerusalem except souls tending toward the vision of heavenly peace, though still unable fully to attain it because of the hindering weakness of the mind?

And what is the beloved’s adjuring except binding by a written decree of his commandments? And what are those commandments but, like the roes and stags of the fields, teachings of the holy Scriptures, lifting souls to heavenly things and making them vigorous and strong in good works?

[Col. 1105D] Or by the roes and stags we may understand the Fathers of the Old and New Testaments, whose natural characteristics signify their gifts, virtues, and pursuits. For the roe is said to have four notable natural traits: when wounded, it is healed by tasting dittany; it distinguishes health-giving herbs by the sharpness of its sight; it chews the cud; and it grazes in mountainous places and always seeks higher ground. Such too are the life and teaching of the saints: to heal their failings by humble confession; to distinguish the better judgments of holy Scripture by the sharpness of their understanding; to receive the food of divine commandments by reading and to take it up again by committing it to a tenacious memory; and daily to rise in progress from virtues [Col. 1106A] to virtues.

Three praiseworthy natural qualities are also observed in the stag: namely, that after swallowing a serpent it drinks from a spring and sheds every poison from its whole body together with its hairs; that, pursued by dogs in the densest woods, it opens a path of escape for itself with its antlers; and that, when changing pastures, they move in a line, each resting its head upon another’s back and mutually supporting one another because of the weight of their antlers.

These things likewise befit the faithful in action and teaching: whoever has been infected by some poison of sin should run to Christ, the fountain of mercy, so that through the infusion of his compassion and grace he may be free both from that sin and from the other vices of the soul. If he is harassed in spirit by evil spirits, as though by dogs, in the forests of worldly affairs, which are full of sins and vices, he should make for himself a way of escape through a strong rebuff of the spirit; or, renouncing all such occupations, he should strive to devote himself to God alone in the love of contemplative life. This too is to open for oneself the way of salvation with antlers. For an antler, although it grows from flesh, rises above flesh; and the person who cleaves to the contemplative life, although in the flesh, is nevertheless raised in mind beyond the flesh. Let them strive to endure one another’s weaknesses of character or body with equanimity and to serve one another in dutiful charity, as [Col. 1106C] the Apostle says: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ” (Gal. 6).

Therefore the daughters of Jerusalem are adjured by the bridegroom—that is, souls wishing to pursue peace are bound—by the roes and stags of the field, that is, by the precepts and teachings of the holy Fathers, not to rouse or awaken the beloved, that is, not to disturb her from her purpose of inward rest and sleep, until she herself commands it: that is, until her inward indweller, to whom she is joined by love, breathes upon her so that she wishes at times to condescend to the weakness of her neighbours and provide for their necessary needs. For this willingness is in the ordering of him who provides for all things, who by hidden inspiration reveals to her [Col. 1106D] when it is useful and fitting to cleave to contemplation and when, according to place and time, to provide for the needs of neighbours.

Finally, the force of this adjuration is such that the children of obedience are bound to render the honour of reverence to their superiors, because it is written: “Obey your leaders and submit to them, for they keep watch as those who will render an account for your souls” (Heb. 13). Hence they do not dare to awaken them as Christ’s vicars in office and bridegrooms in zeal for holy conduct, lest they disturb them by forcing them, through some impropriety or importunity of their own, to be torn from the secret of inward repose and occupied too frequently with outward affairs. Those subject to them should also receive among themselves the word of this adjuration, so that they do not disturb the devout pursuits of their brethren, whether in reading, prayer, or any spiritual office, so long as divine inspiration keeps them there.

[Col. 1107A] But the beloved woman, ever ardently desiring that the repose of this contemplative sleep be confirmed and defended by such an adjuration of her beloved, and that she should, as it were by right, not be disturbed, becomes more secure and proclaims: “The voice of my beloved.”

**VERSE 8.—“The voice of my beloved! Behold, he comes, leaping upon the mountains, bounding over the hills.”**

“The voice,” she says, “of the aforesaid adjuration is not the voice of any prophet, lawgiver, or teacher, as though announcing or teaching something of himself; but rather the voice of the beloved himself, establishing through himself [Col. 1107B] and through them the decrees of his mysteries and commandments. For all Scripture is the voice of my beloved, uttered by the spirit of his mouth and inscribed in our hearts by the finger of his divinity. Therefore you, daughters of Jerusalem, ought not to regard this voice lightly, so as to awaken me and compel me to be awake frequently because of outward matters.

For this too is a kind of the beloved’s voice, a voice of adjuration and, as it were, of legal authority: ‘Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things shall be added to you’ (Matt. 6). Thus, with the beloved himself declaring it, it ought to be just that the necessary use of creation should subsequently serve those who cleave to God. The beloved himself plainly taught and confirmed this by his own testimony when he extolled with such praise Mary, my companion [Col. 1107C] in this pursuit: ‘Mary has chosen the best part, which shall not be taken from her’ (Luke 10). This too is indeed the beloved’s voice: that I ought rightly to prefer this pursuit of my sleep to all the wakeful activity of business. But what is it that I heard and learned from this voice of my beloved—that is, from holy Scripture—when I slept in his contemplation through the repose of the mind? It is surely what I shall now tell you, daughters of Jerusalem, about the power of my beloved himself: ‘Behold, he comes, leaping upon the mountains, bounding over the hills.’ “Behold,” she says, “he comes.” His coming is spoken of not according to his divinity but according to his humanity. For how could he who in his divinity is uncircumscribed and without place be said to come, since he remains immovable and unchangeable, ever one and the same in himself, neither changing place nor being borne in diverse directions by any variation? But whenever he is said to come into the hearts of the saints, this is not referred to any changeability in him, but to their disposition, according as they apply themselves more or less to his love: he is said to come through his inspiration. Therefore he came according to his humanity, when, made passible for us, he willed to undergo the local movement proper to human life. For in order to become visible he came down from heaven and assumed human nature, in which he suffered and died, rose again, and ascended into heaven; all this involved movement and, as it were, coming from one place to another. In this manner of coming [Col. 1108A] the beloved came, leaping upon mountains, when in the time of the dispensation he shone forth in many great leaps upon the mountains of sublime virtues.

For the mountains are certain chief and eminent virtues, in which this beloved made leaps when he advanced from virtue to virtue. The God exalted above the heavens came humbly to earth by being born; from that mountain of humility he ascended to another mountain, that of obedience: for “he became obedient to God the Father unto death, even death on a cross” (Phil. 2). By undergoing this he made a leap to the mountain of patience; from this he finally climbed to the mountain of glory, where by rising again and ascending into heaven he established the triumph of his victorious death.

[Col. 1108B] Thus this beloved came leaping upon the mountains, bounding over the hills, because whatever wisdom and understanding, whatever counsel and fortitude, whatever knowledge and piety, whatever fear of God, and indeed whatever uprightness, justice, and holiness there ever could have been or can be, shone forth in this beloved, as in the head, more sublimely and gloriously than in all his members—that is, the saints, who are called hills. Any intelligent person can see in part in the books of the Gospels how this beloved leapt upon mountains, that is, in virtues of word and example, surpassing all saints’ examples and teachings by the singular and incomparable excellence of his action and teaching. “He rejoiced as a giant to run his course, his going forth is from the highest heaven, and his circuit unto its height” (Ps. 18).

**101 VERSE 9.—“My beloved is like a roe or a young stag. Behold, he stands behind our wall, looking through the windows, gazing through the lattices.”**

Why is he said to be like a roe and a young stag? For it is natural to the roe always to seek ascents; and although the distribution of graces is granted to the saints in different ways—“to one indeed thus, but to another thus”—God gives the Spirit to the only-begotten Son not by measure, because “in him dwells all the fullness of divinity bodily” (1 Cor. 7; John 3; Col. 2). The saints, in the pursuit of virtues, now ascend and now do not ascend, because the grace which they possess now works and now rests in their merits, so that it may preserve their humility that they do not always have ready at hand the grace of the virtue bestowed on them. But the grace of virtues belongs to this beloved not for a time or at intervals, but without interruption, as is written of him: “The Holy Spirit descended in the form of a dove and remained upon him” (Luke 3; John 1).

[Col. 1108D] He is also likened to a young stag because of swiftness. For as a young stag, because of the lightness of its youthful body, is much swifter than a stag, so this beloved, as a young stag of the stags—that is, a son of the patriarchs, from whose stock he sprang—is far superior and more agile in the effectiveness of virtues and the wisdom of words than the pursuits and teachings of those ancient Fathers themselves.

Therefore, since this beloved invites everyone to the pursuit of virtues by exhorting them and surpassing them; and since some follow according to their ability, others despair of being able to follow because frailty hinders them, and still others, weighed down by the burden of sins, distrust their power to rise to them, she removes from them every occasion for despair by setting before them the ineffable mercy of this beloved, who mercifully invites all to his grace, and adds: “Behold, he stands behind our wall,” and so forth. One wall is general: namely, original sin; but this wall spreads out into many particular walls of actual sin. For from original sin, as from a certain mass, many diverse actual sins have arisen, because after the first parent fell through original sin, the condition of this weakness was passed on to his descendants: namely, that they are always inclined to sins. But this general wall began to be destroyed when the Son of God came in the flesh, and was at last removed and scattered by his blood, when, destroying the enmity between God and humankind, he reconciled us to God (Eph. 2). And lest it be rebuilt, it is daily destroyed in the Church by the grace of baptism.

[Col. 1109C] But a particular wall is established differently in different persons: in one is the vice of pride, in another greed, 102 in this one lust, in that one shamelessness, in someone disobedience, in another impatience, or whatever other vice it may be. According to the character, degree, and number of the vice itself, it makes some sort of wall between a human being and God; and the greater, more frequent, or more numerous the vice in a person, the heavier and more immovable is the weight in the wall.

But this beloved stands behind this wall, whether the general wall of original sin or the particular one of actual sin, because he is ready mercifully to receive anyone who, having removed such a wall or having laboured through repentance to destroy it, strives to draw near to him. For standing belongs to one who helps, sitting to one who judges. He stands behind the wall because, when he prepares to come to us by his grace, the wall of sin standing in his way seems to compel him to stand. First, indeed, he stood for a long time without coming to remove that wall of original sin, because many things delayed his coming: the many afflictions and adversities with which he pursued those who desired and awaited his coming, knowing that, when he came, this wall would be destroyed by his blood and that they would be reconciled to God.

[Col. 1109D] For this reason, then, he stood and delayed his coming, meanwhile looking through the windows and gazing through the lattices. What, indeed, were the windows in the wall but the prophets and other teachers of the divine law? Through their teaching and preaching God found, as it were, certain openings for looking, through which he might pour forth some light of his grace, so that the human race, illuminated and admonished thereby, might cease to delay the coming of this beloved, which would profit its salvation, by interposing so great a wickedness as though it were a wall.

But the lattices—that is, the front part of a building—were the ancient fathers who came before: namely, the patriarchs before the Law who announced Christ. Through them he, who was to come long afterward, gazed in part through signs, wonders, and certain demonstrations of reason, admonishing people not to hinder by the wall of their evils the future time of so great a salvation.

[Col. 1110A] Therefore he stood behind our wall for so long, mercifully gazing upon us and providing counsel by word, law, signs, and miracles, until at last, moved by the distress of his people frequently crying, “Come, Lord, and do not delay; forgive the sins of your people,” when the disturbances of all lands had been restrained under Caesar Augustus and a most firm and true peace had been arranged by God’s ordinance, this beloved began, as though the wall of obstructing wickedness had already been shaken, to show the long-desired face by being born. Thereafter, by preaching, dying, rising again, ascending into heaven, and thus spreading the law of his Gospel throughout the whole world, he daily destroyed through the grace of baptism the wall of original sin that had long stood opposed.

Moreover, the windows and lattices in the wall of actual sin, through which this Beloved looks daily, [Col. 1110C] are the examples and teachings of the Gospels, the apostles, and the other holy Fathers. They are windows where they pour into our hearts the light of knowledge and understanding, so that we may see how to remove the wall of each sin set between us and God. They are lattices where, from their writings, we know in part God looking toward us through the power of contemplation, and prophesy in part (I Cor. XIII), so that, while we consider the glory or punishment of the life to come, we may labour daily to destroy the wall of sin that separates us from God.

Further. The Son of God, coming in the flesh, stood behind the wall of our mortality, looking toward us through the windows and lattices of his divinity. [Col. 1110D] He shone forth as God through the power of miracles, yet lay hidden through the nature of human passibility. For one who looks through windows and lattices is neither wholly seen nor wholly unseen. Thus our Redeemer also, coming in the flesh, showed himself to be God by miracles, but concealed this through sufferings. He therefore stood behind the wall of human passibility, because, hidden among human beings by his humanity, he did not come as God; yet he looked through windows and lattices, because by divine mercy he bestowed upon the whole human race the everlasting gifts of salvation. And because he had drawn his beloved inwardly by the gaze of his mercy and also instructed her outwardly by the word of preaching, he makes this clear by adding:

VERS. 10.—My beloved speaks to me: “Arise, hasten, my friend, my dove, my beautiful one, and come.”

[Col. 1111A]

This utterance of the Beloved is distinguished by a threefold beauty: of address, exhortation, and reason. The address is when he says, “my friend, my dove, my beautiful one”; the exhortation, when he says, “Arise, hasten, come”; the reason, when he says, “For now winter has passed, the rain has gone and departed, flowers have appeared, the time of pruning has come.” The beauty of the address is to call her friend, dove, beautiful; the beauty of the exhortation is “arise, hasten, come”; and the beauty of the reason is that winter and rain have withdrawn, flowers appear, the time of pruning is present, the voice of the turtledove has been heard, the fig tree has put forth its unripe figs, and flowering vines have given forth fragrance.

[Col. 1111B] 104 The order of this address, exhortation, and reason is not arranged without consideration. In the address, he says first “friend,” then “dove,” and lastly “beautiful”; in the exhortation, first “arise,” then “hasten,” and lastly “come.” In the reason, moreover: first, winter has passed; second, rain has withdrawn; third, flowers have appeared; fourth, the time of pruning has come; fifth, the turtledove’s voice has been heard in our land; sixth, the fig tree has produced its unripe figs; seventh, the flowering vines have given forth fragrance. The reasons for this exhortation, by which the beloved is urged to arise, hasten, and come, are the retreat of winter and rain, the appearance of flowers, and the time of pruning; the turtledove’s voice, the fig trees producing their unripe figs, and the flowering vines.

[Col. 1111C] But we must see whence this utterance proceeds. Above she had said, “the voice of my beloved,” which voice we called Holy Scripture; for the entire divine page is God’s voice. By reading it, the beloved hears the one clothed in the wall of our mortality leaping, and speaking to her through the windows and lattices of miracles and teachings. For whenever we see or read the Holy Scriptures, God speaks to us or with us. In this manner, then, the beloved—that is, the Church or any faithful soul—perceives the Beloved speaking to her when she hears, reads, or understands the order of the divine dispensation, the sacred character of the sacraments, and the usefulness of the divine commandments.

But the Beloved himself, as though solicitous for the salvation of his beloved, [Col. 1111D] in an utterance of this kind assumes the office of a good orator, so as to draw the hearer in three ways: that is, to make her attentive, teachable, and well disposed. For when he calls out not once but three times, saying, “Arise, hasten, come,” as though he said, “Offer yourself not sluggishly but quickly and earnestly,” he makes her attentive, as one about to hear something weighty and unusual. When, moreover, he repeatedly calls her by terms of love and grace—“my friend, my dove, my beautiful one”—he makes her well disposed, so that she may have a greater willingness to prepare and listen.

Further, by distinctly stating the reason for this summons in a numbered sequence—“For now winter has passed, the rain has gone and withdrawn, flowers have appeared, the time of pruning has come, the turtledove’s voice has been heard, [Col. 1112A] the flowering vines have given fragrance”—he makes her teachable, so that she may recognize the time of great salvation and grace which she ought to receive with great reverence and joy.

And this is an indication of great compassion: this Beloved often looks toward us through windows and lattices, standing, in his infinite clemency, behind the wall of our evils—like a cloud set in place so that prayer may not pass through (Lam. III)—and daily speaking and warning us to shatter this wall or cloud by the battering-ram of virtues and by the breath of the Holy Spirit.

What, therefore, does the Beloved say to his beloved? “Arise,” he says, “hasten, my friend, 105 my dove, my beautiful one, and come.” Arise through faith; hasten through hope; [Col. 1112B] come through charity. Or: arise through intention, hasten through action, come through contemplation. For this is the perfection of all your worship and religion: to believe, hope, and love. The other three—intention, action, and contemplation—are constituted from these. For if you believe rightly, you also rightly direct your intention toward good actions. You act because you hope to obtain a reward; and you contemplate more subtly in proportion as you are more lifted up to God through charity.

And you will be able to do this if you are my friend—that is, if, casting aside the error of unbelief, you are reconciled to me through faith; if you are a dove—that is, if you live simply, injure no one, and are content with what is yours in hope of future recompense; or if, compelled by some frailty, [Col. 1112C] you leave the ark—that is, the Church—by acting wrongly, you do not remain in the world, but return quickly, bringing an olive branch in your mouth: that is, having hope of mercy through confession and a measure of penance.

If you are beautiful—that is, if, through the love of God alone, you set aside all worldly cares, or anything that may stain the beauty of your mind—then, having not Leah’s bleary eyes but Rachel’s fair and lovely countenance, you may fix the purified eye of your mind upon that majesty of heavenly blessedness which is God.

VERS. 11, 12.—For now winter has passed; the rain has gone and departed.

[Col. 1112D] Flowers have appeared in our land; the time of pruning has come; the turtledove’s voice has been heard in our land.

Why, then, does he invite her so earnestly to these things? Because the coldness of unbelief and the storm of blindness and ignorance which had covered the whole face of the world have withdrawn; flowers have appeared—that is, the beginnings of good works have now begun to sprout; and the time of pruning has come—that is, in the time of grace counsel and a rule for cutting away vices and sins are now available. The turtledove’s voice too has been heard: that is, the sound of preaching, from which resound counsels, commandments, and examples of chastity, solitary life, heavenly contemplation, and penitence. The chaste and mourning turtledove, lover of solitude and [Col. 1113A] nesting on high, expresses all these things. At the very beginning of the Gospel voice, the turtledove cries out in words and conduct: either the Lord Jesus Christ himself, the son of virginity; or his own mother, the blessed Virgin Mary; or his forerunner, the blessed John the Baptist.

Finally, the Lord himself, born of a Virgin, is the herald of chastity; led into the wilderness, he consecrates solitude; praying on the mountain, he urges the pursuit of contemplation; and he exhorts to penitence, proclaiming as in the mournful voice of a turtledove: “Do penance, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matt. X). The blessed Mother of God also is a singular mirror of chastity: solitary and placed in divine contemplation, she is greeted by an angel and instructed beforehand that she is to become Christ’s mother; and immediately, with penitence transformed, she proclaims the sentence of divine regard, when she declares that his mercy shall be from generation unto generations (Luke II). [Col. 1113B] Saint John the Baptist, the son of chastity and a virgin in mind and body, was nearer to God in contemplation in proportion as he was more remote from human beings. For he was in the wilderness preaching a baptism of penitence (Matt. III), and crying in the mourning voice of the turtledove: “Produce fruits worthy of penitence” (ibid.).

VERS. 13.—The fig tree has put forth its unripe figs; the flowering vines have given their fragrance. Arise, hasten, my friend, my beautiful one, and come.

“The fig tree,” he says, “has put forth its unripe figs”: that is, hitherto barren carnal Judaea has begun to understand the ceremonies [Col. 1113C] spiritually; and, believing in its heart unto righteousness and confessing with its mouth unto salvation (Rom. X), what it formerly understood carnally it now understands spiritually and eagerly strives to show through faith and works.

The flowering vines too have given fragrance, because the Gentiles, having heard the word of faith, are now beginning everywhere to diffuse the fragrance of good works.

Therefore the order of this utterance is not without reason, in which are considered those three things—faith, hope, and charity—or the other three—intention, action, and contemplation. For these follow one another: whoever believes should hope and love; and no one can hope and love unless he has believed. Neither does anyone act unless he first directs his intention to what, how, when, and why he acts; nor can anyone attain the subtlety of contemplation [Col. 1113D] unless he has advanced to it by the loftiness of good works.

Nor, as we believe, will it be inappropriate to note the sevenfold number of the reasons, in order to show that the effect of this reason has always been the gracious favour and good pleasure of the sevenfold Spirit. For the passing of winter—that is, of unbelief; the passing of rain—that is, of persecution; the appearing of flowers—that is, of good works; the cutting away of vices; the proclamation of the turtledove—that is, of the Gospel; the putting forth of the fig tree’s unripe figs—that is, the revelation of legal observances into the truth of mysteries; and the sweetly fragrant activity of the vines—that is, of the Gentiles converted to faith—what are they but the good pleasure and gracious favour of the sevenfold Spirit?

For from the beginning the Spirit of God worked, and still works daily, such causes and what was, [Col. 1114A] or is, effected by them—namely, believing, hoping, loving—because the removal of every unbelief and evil and the bestowal of faith and salvation depend upon the gift of him who provides for, orders, and arranges every condition of fairness, honour, and usefulness in the holy Church. Thus too, when the Bridegroom says to the bride, “The turtledove’s voice has been heard,” he adds, “in our land,” to imply that there is no effect of the sacraments and no hope of salvation outside the Catholic Church. Rather, every voice of Gospel preaching must be maintained within the holy Church in the observance of commandments and in the order and reverence of the sacraments; within it the Holy Spirit himself is given and received.

For in the beginning, as it is written, [Col. 1114B] “the earth was void and empty,” because before the human mind was made fruitful by the divine Spirit, it was adorned by no flower or shoot of virtues. But after “the Spirit of God moved over the waters” (Gen. I)—that is, over the flowing and unstable hearts of human beings—then at last the light of truth and the fruit of righteousness were poured out throughout the world, so that the earth, formerly void and empty, might become God’s Church, in which he himself might dwell through his grace. Thus he made it his own land, now flowering and fruit-bearing and displaying, through the indwelling grace, a living and rational likeness, as it were, of a human being in uprightness and discipline.

Therefore, when the Beloved has made his beloved attentive to her own salvation, he warns her not to be negligent of the salvation of her neighbours also, [Col. 1114C] so as to commend that charity which, with the zeal of devotion, provides for neighbours as for itself. Thus she may deservedly be honoured by the grace that calls and justifies with the title of friend, dove, and beautiful one.

For the Beloved continues, repeating the earlier numerical sequence of address: “Arise, hasten, my friend, my beautiful one, and come.” “Because,” he says, “you have advanced by my grace to the point that you can care for yourself, by despising the world and adhering to my love through the pursuit of the contemplative life, you ought also sometimes to benefit your neighbours through the labour of the active life, by word and example. For since I have made you such that you possess the grace of teaching and acting, you will render an account, not without danger to yourself, for the talent buried in the ground. Therefore arise at times to this labour [Col. 1114D] from that sweetest sleep of your rest, for the sake of a brother’s need; hasten by teaching and by drawing your neighbours back from love of this world, so that you may lead them also with you into that solitary dwelling of your rest. You will do this as my friend through faith, my beautiful one through action, my dove through the outpouring of the Holy Spirit.”

VERS. 14.—My dove in the clefts of the rock, in the hollow of the wall: show me your face; let your voice sound in my ears, for your voice is sweet and your face beautiful.

Because I have compared you to a dove. 108 A dove has its refuges in the clefts of the rock, in the hollow of the wall. What, then, shall be your refuges, [Col. 1115A] in which you may place all hope of your salvation and flee from the manifold temptation of this world? Surely, in the clefts of the rock, of which it is written: “And the rock was Christ” (I Cor. X). These clefts are the wounds of my Passion, which are for every Christian certain refuges in all adversities. For my five wounds are safe refuges for your five senses, so that when you set before yourself the sign of my Passion in this number, you may remain secure in the wholeness of all your senses.

For this integrity of the senses will be necessary to you in teaching and acting. If you bring forth what you teach and do in my name with honour and usefulness, reasonably, orderly, and moderately, you will be more able to attract the minds of hearers or observers. For often an honourable kind of cause, if presented unworthily, offends; just as a humble kind of cause, if presented reasonably, will sometimes obtain a share of honourableness.

Thus in my Passion you have become friend, beautiful one, and dove, because I laid down my soul and shed my blood for you, that I might present you to myself as a glorious bride without spot or wrinkle (Eph. V). Since you were foul, you were not sufficient for yourself through yourself, nor could the whole creation suffice for you; but my Passion, to which the whole world is not equal, made satisfaction to God for you. Hence, reconciled and joined to me, you are called friend, beautiful one, and dove.

[Col. 1115C] Or the clefts of the rock are the four Gospels, in which my deeds and sayings are seen; or they are also the pursuits of virtues—namely humility, patience, obedience, prayers, vigils, holy readings, and the rest—which are like certain entrances by which one comes to me and enters the kingdom of heaven. You ought to preach and show all these things to your neighbours, because without them they cannot attain salvation.

“My dove in the clefts of the rock, in the hollow of the wall.” Christ is the rock (I Cor. X); Christ is also the wall. He was a wall before the Passion, because in his human weakness he was still fragile and passible; but a rock after the Resurrection, when, all corruption laid aside, he became impassible through the strength of his glorified body. [Col. 1115D] The beloved ought to be a dove in the clefts of the rock, in the hollow of the wall, because when she considers the many signs of virtues and deeds, and the displays of power which were in Christ by his divinity, she ought especially to consider that outstanding token of charity which he displayed in his flesh, delivered to death for her salvation. For he showed the greatness of this love toward humankind when, in order to redeem it, he was able to offer nothing other than himself.

The hollow of the wall, therefore, is the charity of Christ dying in the flesh. In this charity the Church generally, and each holy soul particularly, is a dove, because through charity it finds a place to remain in Christ, where it may spiritually [Col. 1116A] nourish the young of good works and escape the snares of the ancient serpent. For it is written: “God is charity; and he who remains in charity remains in God, and God in him” (I John IV).

The dove too is in the clefts of the rock, in the hollow of the wall. A dove has groaning in place of song; and the faithful soul ought to groan when it recalls the Passion of the Redeemer, considering what God has done for it: when he “committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (I Pet. II), yet chose to die for sinners, and God made man paid what humanity owed. Let it groan also for its transgressions in the clefts of the rock, in the hollow of the wall, because it has with the Father Jesus Christ the righteous as advocate; “and he is the propitiation for its sins” [Col. 1116B] (I John II). Every day he grants salvation to everyone who repents, through the sacrament of his Passion and the singular example of this charity.

For each day our Redeemer renews for us his clefts—that is, the signs of his Passion—in the offering of his body and blood; and, in the manifestation of such great charity, he shows the hollow in which we are protected from the enemies’ snares.

The wall may also be understood as the teaching of the apostles or apostolic men. For as a wall is built from many stones, so the teaching of the saints is constituted from very many lessons in virtue. In it is a hollow for every faithful soul—that is, a safeguard of life—because from their sayings and writings it learns how, by fleeing sins and nourishing the young [Col. 1116C] of good works, it may escape the snares of malignant spirits.

The beloved is therefore warned sometimes to leave the repose of contemplation and go out to the labour of the active life for the sake of her neighbours, so that she may bring to her neighbours’ minds by preaching what she herself has learned in quiet from the divine commandments and examples of the saints; and so that, as she herself has been moved to a continual practice of contemplation by their sweetness, she may likewise move the souls of her neighbours to desire it through the power of preaching.

Therefore the Beloved adds in warning her: “Show me your face.” For what is the beloved’s face but a shining image of holiness, issuing from fellowship with the Beloved? For the more diligently anyone adheres to divine contemplation, [Col. 1116D] the more beautifully the face of the mind gleams with the radiance of holiness. Hence Moses, who spent forty days 100 with the Lord on the mountain, is written to have brought forth a shining face from fellowship with the Lord’s speech (Exod. XXXIV).

Whoever remains on the mountain of heavenly contemplation produces from the very Spirit of God, with whom he is one, a certain countenance of holiness. Hence the Apostle says: “With unveiled face, beholding the Lord’s glory, we are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord” (II Cor. III). Therefore those who are led by the Spirit of God are transformed by that Spirit into Christ’s image according to the inward person, from glory to glory. Those who have drawn some brightness from him into the face of the inward person, by which they may know him more clearly, draw yet more brightness from him as they approach him more closely [Col. 1117A] through contemplative brightness, so that through it they may know him ever more clearly and truly.

Thus Ezekiel, when describing the vision of the holy living creatures, said: “The likeness of a human being was in them” (Ezek. I). Whatever justice and gentleness, whatever moderation and humility, whatever patience and devotion, whatever holiness at last the chosen of God have been able or may be able to possess, they drew from that unique human being, the Lord Jesus Christ. Enlightened by that chief countenance of holiness, they too received, each in their own manner, a countenance of holiness.

“Such a face,” says the Beloved, “spiritually formed from my grace, O beloved, show me: [Col. 1117B] that is, come forth publicly for the praise of my name with the fair appearance of deed and speech, so that your neighbours, seeing your works, may glorify your Father who is in heaven (Matt. V), and may themselves shape the countenance of their own mind and intention according to the rightly ordered countenance of your conduct and speech.”

“Let your voice sound in my ears.” The voice of the preacher sounds in the ears of the Lord when it accords with my voice, so that what sounds outwardly through a voice in human ears may speak through faith in God’s ears. And fittingly, after saying, “Show me your face,” he adds, “Let your voice sound in my ears,” in order to show that one believes with the heart unto righteousness, but confession with the mouth is unto salvation (Rom. X). Through the face, knowledge of faith may be expressed; [Col. 1117C] through the voice, the sound of preaching.

Further: “Show me your face; let your voice sound in my ears”: that is, come forth from that angelic dormitory of your holy solitude into public action and preaching with such an intention that you admit me alone as witness to your conscience—not exposing yourself for human favour, but seeking to please my gaze alone. “For your voice is sweet and your face beautiful.” You ought therefore to come forth, because your neighbours can observe in the beauty of your conduct and the sweetness of your speech that by which they may correct the perversity of their own conduct and receive the integrity of right faith.

111 Often, moreover, the very display of countenance and dress is a kind of voice of the mind, as someone says:

> Often, though silent, the countenance has voice and words.

Thus it is written of the woman who displayed sorrow of mind by the altered expression of her face, after the reproach of barrenness had been removed: “Her countenance was no longer changed in different ways” (I Sam. I). [Col. 1117D] For the variation of the face showed variation of mind; but once the cause of that variation had been removed, an upright and ordered countenance likewise spoke of an upright and ordered mind.

But this voice of honourableness, established in the countenance and bearing of the outward person, sounds in God’s ears when one keeps it unchangeably for the sole purpose of earning the glory of eternal life. “Your voice,” he says, “is sweet, and your face beautiful.” Your voice, he says, which is the interpreter of the mind and speaks either through conduct or through the tongue—for it preaches and teaches both by acting well and by speaking well—this sweet voice, he says, should sound in my ears. For that life greatly pleases me which both acts and teaches what is good, with love of God and neighbour working in it, so as to please God and edify its neighbour. [Col. 1118A] And your face is beautiful because your intention and faith—both known to me alone—bring it about that what you do or say is worthy of the praise of my approval.

Therefore attend to yourself in this appearance and beauty; go forth prosperously and reign, so that, since you are joined to me by such a dowry of virtues, you may fittingly be called the queen of your Bridegroom who is King, when, under my rule and instruction, you know both how to govern yourself reasonably and how to exercise the governance of souls for others.

[Col. 1118B] But because heretics often corrupt this sweetness and beauty of right faith and right preaching by perverse teaching, in order to pervert simple hearts, the voice of the Beloved turns to the teachers of this faith and preaching when it adds, “Catch for us the little foxes.”

VERS. 15.—Catch for us the little foxes that destroy the vines, for our vineyard has flowered.

Foxes are heretics, because of the deceit and cunning by which they deceive the unwary with arguments of words. They always seek hiding places in which to teach; they think perversely and form separate gatherings, lest the holy and Catholic Church should discover their perversity. They are called little foxes [Col. 1118C] either because of the feigned humility of the heretics themselves or because of the subtlety of their most ingeniously devised opinions. By these they especially compel the minds of those who are astonished but less discerning to favour their perverse teachings.

“Catch for us,” he says. For heretics are caught for God when, by the assertion of sound reason—which they cannot overthrow by any arguments—Catholic teachers, with divine grace going before, lead them back to the bosom of their mother, the holy Church, from which they had departed in error. Then they confirm by words and examples the faith which they had formerly attacked. “Catch for us the little foxes”: that is, convict the subtle and crafty corrupters of the right faith by their own propositions, and compel them by a plausible argument which they cannot possibly refute [Col. 1118D] to pass over into fellowship with our party. “I will catch the wise in their own craftiness; I will destroy the wisdom of the wise and reject the prudence of the prudent” (I Cor. I, III), so that, once they have recognized the manner of living or teaching rightly, their own wisdom may displease them; what they previously strove to establish through it, they may destroy once truth is recognized; and they may become one with my faithful people.

“For our vineyard has flowered”: that is, either the universal or a particular Church, or some individual and single believer, has undertaken the beginning of right living or believing. Therefore those who arise among them while not living or believing rightly must be removed or caught, lest they choke the tender faith and works of devotion by evil doctrine and evil examples.

[Col. 1119A] Nor, we believe, is it absurd for us to call every faithful soul the Lord’s vineyard, just as we call the universal or particular Church so, because of the similar propagation of virtues and the spiritual wine that gladdens the human heart (Ps. CIII), which can abound by the grace of the Holy Spirit in each individual believer as in the universal or particular Church.

For each person ought to cut away the secret things [sacramenta] of vices with the knife of spiritual discipline; turn up the soil of the heart with the hoe of inward consideration; and, if anything earthly or unclean has entered through thought or deed, lay it around the root of the heart by retaining it in memory, and water it in penitence with frequent streams of tears. One should bind every intention of one’s good purpose to Christ, who is the tree of life, [Col. 1119B] lest it again flow down to earthly things; always hope in his help and support; or cling to the wood of Christ’s cross, carrying his mortification in one’s body. In this way, when the mind is continually cultivated and tended by the grace of the Holy Spirit, it may become ever more fruitful and be called, with the prophet, a vineyard of Sorec, a name meaning “chosen and beautiful.”

Hence the Lord’s teaching in the Gospel concerning the barren and fruit-bearing vineyard, where he calls himself the vine, his disciples the branches, and the Father the husbandman: “Every branch in me that does not bear fruit, the Father will take away; and every one that bears fruit he will cleanse, that it may bear more fruit” (John XV). If, therefore, the Saviour is the vine, we are the branches, and God the Father the husbandman, then so long as we keep God’s commandments we are always cultivating; and our cultivation is purification, that we may bear more fruit. [Col. 1119C] “For it is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy” (Rom. IX), whose help we always need in order to arrive at the end of our good purpose.

113 VERS. 16, 17.—My beloved is mine, and I am his, he who feeds among the lilies until the day breathes and the shadows decline.

Divine and human love are not established in a similar manner or on equal grounds. Though they are called by the same name, they are very different in the logic of their definition, since there is absolutely no comparison between such affections of flesh and spirit. Divine love always has a certain correlate; human love, however, does not always have one, because often one who loves is not loved, and the consequence is not the same in both cases.

For it follows that a human being loving God is loved by God, since to love God is nothing other than to live justly and devoutly; and it follows that the just and devout are loved by the just and devout God, because such affection comes from the gift of his own grace. But it does not follow that a person who loves is always loved by another person, because, although carnal affection often produces this correlate, it does not always do so. Divine affection, however, always produces it, according to the saying of the Saviour: “He who loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and reveal myself to him” (John XIV).

For the correlate of this love is reciprocal: because it loves, it is loved; [Col. 1120A] and because it is loved, it loves. Prevenient grace works this in the hearts of the elect, so that by divine love they may see the gifts which it loves in each person as its own. Hence the beloved here speaks of the Beloved: “My beloved is mine, and I am his.” For it is characteristic of relatives to be spoken of reciprocally: what is predicated of the beloved is conversely predicated of the beloved woman. For a beloved man is someone’s beloved, and a beloved woman is someone’s beloved. This relation is therefore formed in this way: the beloved of the beloved woman, beloved man and beloved woman, the beloved woman of the beloved man. Let her then say, “My beloved is mine, and I am his,” as though she said: “Because the Beloved has bestowed his grace upon me so that I may please him by right faith and action, he is therefore my beloved; and because, when he has given me free will, I obey calling grace by keeping his commandments, I am therefore beloved by him. [Col. 1120B] Unless he loved me in mercy, I could not love him by grace; he would not love me in mercy. Indeed, whatever good is available to me—to will, to be able to act, to accomplish—I have wholly from his gift” (Rom. IV).

“He feeds among the lilies.” Behold the reason why I am beloved by him: for he feeds—that is, delights—in the brightness, namely the purity and chastity, of mind and body, and in the most sweet fragrance of virtues. Because these breathe forth from me through his grace and my love, he has made me worthy of his love.

“Until the day breathes and the shadows decline”: that is, until that true and eternal day of future blessedness shines forth, and the night of this worldly misery and tribulation withdraws. 114

[Col. 1120C] When “God shall be all in all” (I Cor. XV), he will give me the full, perfect, and unchangeable reward of his vision, where he himself will feed in me on the beauty of his gifts, and I in him upon the eternal incorruption of body and soul.

Since, moreover, this mutual love which we have set forth always applies to every father and son, this is characteristic of things said in relation: that what they are is spoken in relation to others, or in whatever way something is related to something else. Whatever is recognized in the nature of relation must necessarily be considered with another. For when “father” is said, there must necessarily be a son of whom he is called father; and the same must be said conversely concerning a son. Therefore, if holy persons are God’s sons through love and observance of his commandments, God himself must necessarily be called their Father through grace, creation, and governance; and conversely, if God is Father, they are sons. Hence it is not absurd to say here: “My beloved is mine as Father, and I am his as son or daughter.” For God himself says in one place concerning his own: “I will be to them a Father, and they shall be to me sons and daughters” (II Sam. VII).

[Col. 1120D] Or let us state it in another way: the relation appears to have a nearly similar sense, so that when “my beloved is mine” is said, “he is helper and protector” is understood; and when “I am his” is said, “I am obedient” is understood. These too correspond to one another: because he is my helper and protector, I am obedient to him; and because I am obedient to him, he bestows his help upon me.

“He feeds among the lilies,” because he delights in the brightness of virtues and the purity of thoughts and deeds, as he says elsewhere: “And I dwell among pure thoughts” (Prov. VIII). And, as it is written, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. V), he works the effect of his grace in me until the day of spiritual understanding and knowledge shines out, the darkness of ignorance or carnal understanding having been driven away. For the more the mind is joined to God in progress in virtues, the more highly it is raised into the subtlety of divine contemplation.

[Col. 1121A] Or “until the day breathes” means: until the light and splendour of good works, which has shone in my mind through the indwelling of divine grace, shines by word and example upon the hearts of others and removes from them every shadow or night of perversity and evil. “For the fruit of light is in all goodness and righteousness and truth.”

“Return; be like, my beloved, the roe or the young stag upon the mountains of Bethel.”

While the Beloved was feeding among the lilies of the soul, white and fragrant with virtues, he refreshed that soul with the sweetness of his love so greatly that, despising earthly things, it was wholly suspended upon heavenly things; yet it could not comprehend the uncircumscribed Godhead as it is. Therefore, when it pursues with all the effort of its mind the Beloved who surpasses every understanding and who, as it were, flees from it—because he is incomprehensible and ineffable—it is struck back by the radiance of such immeasurable brightness [Col. 1121C], and judges that it must pursue him no further, since it perceives that he can in no way be comprehended. For it is written of the holy living creatures that, when a voice came from above the firmament, they stood and lowered their wings (Ezek. 1).

By the name of the firmament, indeed, the higher powers are denoted, which, when other companies of angels fell from heaven, themselves remained steadfast in the love of God. A voice in the mind is a certain sound of understanding. But one voice is made beneath the firmament, another from the firmament, and another above the firmament. For in holy minds raising themselves from earthly to heavenly things, a voice is made beneath the firmament when they subtly understand something concerning the nature, order, and quality of visible things. But a voice is made from the firmament when they reflect upon the ineffable and eternal joys of those heavenly [Col. 1121D] spirits. A voice is made above the firmament when, in contemplation, they think something concerning the height of the Godhead. Since they can comprehend nothing of it fully as it is, they stand still, unable to advance further; humbly they lower the wings of contemplation, and are astounded at him whom they understand to be incomprehensible. Astounded, they venerate and fear him; fearing, they love him; loving, they at times behold him as he is.

Therefore, because the beloved fails in the contemplation of the Godhead and cannot long pursue the Beloved as though he were already flying away, she calls him back and implores him to deign somehow to reveal at least the mysteries of his humanity, saying [Col. 1122A]: “Return, my Beloved; be like a roe or a young stag upon the mountains of Bethel.” As though in other words she said: “Since I cannot perfectly grasp the sublimity of your Godhead—for now we see through a glass, darkly (1 Cor. 13)—grant me at least to examine and understand the truth of your humanity: the reason of that truth, and the usefulness of that reason; the truth in faith, the reason in its cause, the usefulness in the end of the cause. For we believe that you became man for this reason: that you might save the human race, whose end is eternal life.”

But in accomplishing such a work you were like a roe or a young stag, because, born from the stock of the patriarchs, like a swift fawn of stags (*cervorum*; the printed *servorum* is evidently corrupt), you quickly ordered the economy of human salvation. For [Col. 1122B] after you began to preach, in three and a half years you completed the universal good of so renowned and wonderful a work; having suffered, you quickly rose after three days; and after forty days you ascended into heaven. Such was your going forth and return, like that of a roe or young stag leaping upon the mountains.

**116** But this going forth and return of yours was upon the mountains of Bethel, that is, the house of God, which is the Church. Its advancement and establishment were being accomplished in this going forth and return. Upon its mountains—that is, upon the apostles and the other holy preachers—you ran, like a swift young stag, with the ready gift of your grace, when by the sudden coming of the Holy Spirit you taught them so that what others can scarcely grasp through long periods of time, these men might attain in one moment. [Col. 1122C] For what swifter leap could you have made upon these mountains than to give, in one hour, knowledge of every language?

Grant, therefore, that I may understand the mysteries of all these things; that, understanding them, I may be able to meditate upon them; and that I may not depart from them in faith and deed—by believing in faith and by imitating according to my ability in deed. For you are like a roe or a young stag in my heart when I reflect upon these mysteries of your dispensation: namely, how, to establish these things, you ran in a series of leaps from heaven into the Virgin’s womb, from the womb to the cross, from the cross to the tomb, and from the tomb again into heaven. This likeness appears to me upon the mountains of Bethel, that is, in the Scriptures which the holy Church holds [Col. 1122D] and venerates. These Scriptures are mountains because of the height of meaning contained in them, derived from the usefulness of the divine commandments or from the mysteries and realities of the sacraments.

But because the whole force of this love between the Beloved and the beloved rests upon faith in the sacraments and observance of the divine commandments, she set aside that intention of inquiry by which she had wished to comprehend God in his own nature but could not at all do so. She began instead to direct her attention to how she might comprehend God through faith and righteousness. For if, according to John’s utterance, God is love (1 John 4), and to possess faith and righteousness is to love God, then surely to possess this love is to possess God.

[Col. 1123A] But what do we call this love except every good which can be conceived by the mind, believed in the heart, confessed by the mouth, and exercised in deed? Certainly no one attains all this good unless one perfectly loves God, and no one loves God unless one attains this good, as was set forth a little above: “My Beloved is mine, and I am his.”

For this good is a kind of way that leads to the apprehension of better things; its limit and conclusion is eternal life. But because there is no small difficulty in finding such good, since very few possess perfect love of God, the beloved continues, recounting the order of this inquiry and discovery which is not easily achieved.

## CHAPTER THREE

[Col. 1123B] **117 VERSE 1.**—“Upon my bed by night I sought him whom my soul loves; I sought him, and did not find him.”

By “bed” may be denoted rest and tranquillity of mind, because, when through reflection we rest from worldly noise, we can more subtly investigate the quality and manner of the good we seek. To understand the end of this good is to find God. By “end” we mean not that at which he ceases to be, but that at which he begins to be perfectly. Therefore the beloved seeks the Beloved upon her bed when, in the repose of her mind, she desires to understand the right rule of goodness, discipline, and knowledge.

But she seeks by night because, in considering subtle matters, the eye of the mind grows dim, so that it is not immediately able [Col. 1123C] by itself to see what it seeks. Hence she does not find the Beloved whom she seeks, because the very difficulty of understanding creates a certain delay in finding.

**VERSE 2.**—“I will rise and go about the city; through the lanes and streets I will seek him whom my soul loves. I sought him and did not find him.”

**118** What, then, must be done? Surely she must rise from that repose of mind in which she lies relying only upon her own understanding, and turn to the task of seeking also the understandings, actions, and writings of others, so that what she cannot understand by herself, she may perceive from their words and writings.

For this is to go about the city and seek the Beloved through lanes and streets: to traverse the Church [Col. 1123D] and examine the opinions of holy teachers; to investigate those who walk by the broad and the narrow way; and to consider whether there are any traces of holiness in them. For sometimes secular people possess something of good conduct that ought to be imitated, and indeed imitated according to one’s ability. The broad way is that of secular persons; the narrow way, that of the saints, because many walk by the broad way, but few by the narrow way (Matt. 7).

**VERSE 3.**—“The watchmen who guard the city found me: Have you seen him whom my soul loves?”

As she goes about the city and the lanes and streets, the watchmen find her. For when a diligent mind investigates the teachings of the Church—examining history also, which is like a broad way because it is open and easy to understand; examining allegory also, which is like a narrow way because [Col. 1124A] it is subtle and difficult to understand; and seeking out whatever in these is useful and necessary for faith and conduct—the holy teachers meet it with their sayings and authorities, and show the Beloved whom it sought to one who desires to understand and imitate him.

They are called watchmen, concerning whom the Lord says in the Gospel: “Blessed are those servants whom the Lord, when he comes, shall find watching” (Luke 22). For holy teachers, while established in the body, kept watch—and still keep watch—by their teaching and practice, for the benefit of themselves and their neighbours.
