Stripped of the body, they keep watch and will keep watch by their writings and examples: for their own reward indeed, and for their neighbours’ salvation. These watchmen guard the city because holy teachers establish and protect the holy universal Church by the arguments and authorities of their testimonies and [Col. 1124B] examples, and make it impregnable against the enemies of the holy faith.

The hesitant beloved, then, is awakened by such watchmen, saying: “Have you seen him whom my soul loves?” “Can you,” she says, “in your writings and deeds show and prove that you have loved God in such a way that, by imitating your life and teaching, the Beloved may be found?”

**VERSE 4.**—“A little while after I had passed by them, I found him whom my soul loves. I held him, and will not let him go, until I bring him into my mother’s house, and into the chamber of her who bore me.”

**119** But because perseverance in inquiry does not delay the result of finding, she adds: “A little while after I had passed by them, I found him whom my soul loves.” For when she passes for some time over the deeds and writings of the holy Fathers by reading or hearing, she at last finds the Beloved by understanding and desiring to imitate him.

And because here she resolves to preserve by faith and deed what she has understood, as the Beloved whom she has found, she continues: “I held him, and will not let him go, until I bring him into my mother’s house and into the chamber of her who bore me.” What is eagerly and diligently sought with desire is, once found, held more dearly and more firmly. Therefore, after the beloved—that is, the holy soul—has gone about the Church and frequently examined the sayings and deeds of the holy Fathers, she finds the standard of right living and teaching, as though understanding God himself as the Beloved. [Col. 1124D] For to live and teach rightly is to possess God. She holds him firmly in memory and does not let him go until she also makes him known to others by teaching and acting, and introduces him into their understanding through faith and love. This does not mean that after such introduction she ceases to hold him, but that she desires that a share in this grace may also be bestowed on others and, through the power of love diffused in her by the Holy Spirit, be conferred upon herself together with them eternally.

For this expression, “until,” must be understood as used not for a limitation but for eternity; as though she said: “I shall commend him to their tenacious memory for so long, mercifully giving him to my own understanding and to that of others, until he is so established in us through faith and action that he can no longer fall away from our mind.”

[Col. 1125A] Nor should it be thought without reason that the places of this introduction are set forth so distinctly and differently: the mother’s house and the chamber of her who bore her. Since the whole Church, because of the diversity of understandings and pursuits, is divided into three groups—little ones, those of middle rank, and great ones—the house receives all, but the chamber does not receive all: only the great, and those who attain some special distinction beyond others. For every house is a more evident and spacious place, into which not only the Lord but the whole household enters: it is the public, universal place of the Church. But the chamber is a particular and, as it were, private place in the Church, to which access and entry are open only to those raised to ecclesiastical dignity and order, whose profession it is specially to cleave to God.

Relative names, moreover, such as “father” and “mother,” which are always said in relation to others, are understood in three ways: [Col. 1125B] **120** by nature, affection, and adoption. Leaving aside the first, the remaining two meanings can be applied to the mother or she who bore one in this passage. For the holy Church is the mother of every believer by affection and adoption, because she always manifests her affection to one whom she has adopted to herself in faith as a son, while he lives holily and justly. And, to make a distinction here, let us say that she is also his begetter insofar as she begets him by forming him toward the honour and usefulness of a holy life, or by instructing him through the pages of sacred Scripture, and so rearing him into a perfect man in virtue and knowledge according to the measure pleasing to assisting grace.

The beloved, therefore, introduces the Beloved into her mother’s house when she shows to the children of her holy mother the Church—that is, to little, middle, and great ones—the God whom she knows by faith and deed. She does so through examples of holy deeds and the teachings of the divine Scriptures, which she now sets forth according to the letter alone, now interprets according to a mystical sense, so that all may attain them according to their capacity: the little ones indeed only according to the letter; those of middle rank according to both the letter and the mystical sense, but partially and not perfectly; the great according to both letter and mystical sense, not partially but perfectly, and such as can still investigate and understand [Col. 1125D] other matters, virtually inscrutable to others. Therefore the Beloved is shown only to these in the chamber of her who bore her, because from the secret instruction of the Church they learn the subtlety and discernment of the commandments and a certain hidden examination of the divine mysteries.

After this, the beloved’s inquiry, finding, and introduction may also be understood in this way: in some respects differently and in others uniformly with the preceding interpretation. For by “bed” may be understood the secure dissolution of carnal pleasure and the dissolute security of such pleasure. Since this is the night of sin, Christ is not found there. Therefore let the sinner rise with eager resolve from this useless and wretched repose, and, to speak uniformly with the preceding sense, let him traverse the holy Church with devout intention. Passing by its watchmen—that is, its teachers—through reading [Col. 1126A] and hearing, let him learn how to correct his ways. Let him find in the city of virtues the God whom he could not find upon the bed of evil security; and let him grow in progress until he introduces him into his mother’s house. This may otherwise be called this world, which is the place and dwelling of the human race, like the universal mother who brings forth humankind. For he openly preaches to all how great things God has done for him, and, urging them by his example, exhorts them, after despising carnal pleasure, to forget the house of this mother by leaving the world.

And when, through the active life, he has in this manner introduced the Beloved into his mother’s house, **121** he makes such progress at last that through the contemplative life he introduces him into the chamber—that is, into the hidden seclusion of solitude [Col. 1126B] or the desert or the monastery. This, in a uniform sense, is the chamber of her who bore him: that is, the Church, which begets, nourishes, and forms him toward the honour of monastic life. He subsequently excels in that life with such excellence of virtues that by his example and teaching the Church herself profits more than he formerly profited by her instruction. This is to introduce the Beloved into the chamber of her who bore him.

The Beloved lovingly approves and praises this pursuit and purpose, and addresses the daughters of Jerusalem—that is, the simple souls in the Church. They are called daughters rather than sons because, through weakness of mind, they are not yet able to rise to those things to which the perfected have attained by manly strength of mind. “I adjure you,” he says, “daughters of Jerusalem,” etc.

[Col. 1126C] **VERSE 5.**—“I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes and stags of the fields, that you do not awaken or rouse the beloved until she herself wishes.”

For those resting in mind and body in the chamber of monastic life often encounter circumstances that make it necessary to lay aside for a while the contemplative eye and provide in some matters for their neighbours’ benefit or need. But there are certain weak minds that wish this to occur more frequently through their superiors, and more insistently demand that they be aroused and awakened to outward things. They are, as it were, prohibited by certain adjurations—the sayings and authorities of the Fathers ranging through the wide expanses of the holy Scriptures—and are instead to leave this to the judgment [Col. 1126D] of those who, through the spirit of discernment, understand at what place and time they ought to awaken for this duty.

For the sayings of the holy Scriptures, or the authors of those sayings themselves, are like certain roes and stags. In proposing that earthly things are to be left and heavenly things desired, they show certain leaps from earth to heaven; and, in commanding people to be fervent and diligent in good works, they indicate that they must possess a certain agility of mind. For it is written: “Set your minds on things above, not on things upon the earth; seek things above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God.” And elsewhere: “But our citizenship is in heaven.” And in another place: “Hasten to enter into that rest.” And again: “Hastening and making speed to meet the Lord.” And elsewhere: “Run in such a way that you may obtain.” And the Lord in the Gospel: “Run while you have the light, lest darkness overtake you.” And elsewhere: “Lift up your heads, because your redemption draws near.” And in the Psalm: “Blessed is the man whose help is from you; he has set ascents in his heart in the valley of tears” (Col. 3; Phil. 3; Heb. 4; Amos 4; 1 Cor. 9; John 12; Luke 21; Ps. 83).

[Col. 1127A] Behold the roes and stags of the divine **122** fields, which show that it is more useful to sleep in the chamber of contemplation than to keep wakefulness in outward business. This does not mean that such matters should be omitted altogether when the benefit or need of neighbours requires them, but that Mary’s part is better than Martha’s.

With these and similar sayings, then, as with certain incantations, the Beloved adjures the daughters of Jerusalem not lightly and without cause to compel their neighbours to descend from inward repose and pass over to outward actions. Therefore, O daughters of Jerusalem, who see the vision of peace—yet only if you walk in the Spirit and have mortified the deeds of the flesh (Rom. 8), for the flesh desires against the Spirit and the Spirit against the flesh (Gal. 5), and to be free from their wars is to see the vision of peace—always love the secret place of holy contemplation; always strive to introduce this Beloved, that is, the Lord Jesus Christ, into the chamber [Col. 1128A] of your mind. Thus, when the Spirit of divine love has taken you up and taught you to despise all earthly things, you may hear after you, with the prophet, the voice of a great commotion: “Blessed be the glory of the Lord from his place” (Ezek. 3).

For you are the place of God’s glory when you receive him in your hearts through love of holiness. And if through humility, patience, obedience, chastity, and other works of piety you shed abroad anything of virtue and grace, it is the glory of God, from whom and through whom you possess it. He himself is blessed, to whose praise and glory all that appears in you of honour and discipline contributes.

For this is the voice of a great commotion, because those who are raised by the Spirit are moved by such grace of compunction [Col. 1128B] that they afflict themselves with grievous lamentations, whether because they are still bound by their sins or because they are delayed so long from the joys of heavenly life.

You also hear after you the voice of a great commotion when you consider the tumults and fleeting joys of this world, yet set them aside in your mind out of love for eternal joys; and, forgetting what lies behind and stretching yourselves forward, you press toward the prize of the heavenly calling. Thus the hearing of this voice is no small consolation to you when it is said: “Blessed be the glory of the Lord from his place.”

**123 BOOK THREE**

[Col. 1127]

## CHAPTER III—Continuation

[Col. 1127C]

We read in the history of Kings that, when Elisha the prophet was questioned by the king of Israel, who said, “Why has he assembled these three kings, to deliver them into the hands of Moab?” after some further words he said: “Bring me a minstrel.” And when the minstrel played, the hand of the Lord came upon him, and he said: “Make this valley full of ditches” (4 Kings 3). In this matter it is clear that the spirit of prophecy was not always present to the prophets. Therefore, when the spirit was resting within him, the prophet had a minstrel brought, so that, as the minstrel played, the spirit which in a certain manner rested within him might be roused—*concessus* (“having yielded”), perhaps *concussus* (“shaken”), an uncertain reading—and he might see the answer to what had been asked of him.

But to what end is this example brought forward? Surely [Col. 1127D] it concerns both your purpose, beloved sisters, and mine. For because it seemed to your humility that the Spirit of holy love rested in you and was, as it were, idle, you judged it useful and necessary to bring in a minstrel, so that by his playing the spirit that had, as it were, fallen asleep in your minds might be awakened. This, I think, was for a twofold reason: either that, just as David by singing soothed Saul’s frenzy, so, if any sudden unevenness should steal into your minds, it might be composed by the sweetness of song; [Col. 1128C] or that, if your mind possessed too little fervour in divine love, it might be kindled by some inward power of song.

Since this was your purpose, I do not know by what spirit you brought in my littleness, which knows how to sing nothing of the sort, and imposed upon me the office of this minstrel. What was I to do? On one side your affection impelled me; on the other, the danger arising from my own lack of talent repelled me. At last, trusting in God’s help and in the assistance of your prayers, I did not refuse to be your minstrel, though unlearned; for I judged that my failing would readily be pardoned by your love. And, according to the saying of the great orator, a virtue attended by love must not be rejected. But what is my virtue? Certainly a small one, [Col. 1128D] and one almost without strength for the arduous work of so great an office. Yet if love can do anything at all, it renders this service.

That indeed was your purpose; mine, however, was to obey those who asked and to sing something by which your spirit might be awakened. But now inexperience stands in the way of goodwill, since it belongs to a skilled singer to know how both to profit and to delight, according to that saying of Flaccus:

> He wins every vote who mingles usefulness with sweetness.

[Col. 1129A] **124** Secular literature reports that a certain Orpheus softened tigers and lions by his song; that is, figuratively, because he tamed brutal and savage human manners by the rational force of his discourse. Amphion likewise was said to move stones by the sound of his lyre and to lead them where he wished by gentle entreaty, because he rightly composed harsh and unformed human manners by a sweet manner of reasoning. Great, therefore, is the skill of the singer who changes the minds of hearers by the manner of his song. But I do not think that the manner of this song I have begun has had such effect upon your holiness—not because of any slowness in your intelligence, but because of the density of my ignorance. For an unskilled singer is one who does not know the proper character of voices and modes,

[Col. 1129B]

> And the lyre-player  
> who always strikes the same wrong string  
> is laughed at.  
> —Horace, *The Art of Poetry*, v. 356.

Therefore, after singing some part of this most excellent song, I had resolved rather to be silent than to expose any further my great ineptitudes.

But because a skilled craftsman sometimes laboriously remakes a form fashioned from the same material by an unskilled craftsman, making it, as it were, another form; and because a skilled singer restores to a discordant and, as it were, discoloured song its proper, wholly pure, and integral colour: encouraged by this, I too, for the sake of your love, shall gird myself again with God’s help for the things I had thought to leave behind. Thus, if I make any work distorted and ill-composed, some learned and skilled person may find material in it upon which to exercise his talent, producing for it a better, more useful, or more vivid form and colour—provided that the work itself escapes the scraper or the flame it deserves.

**VERSE 6.**—“Who is this that comes up through the wilderness like a column of smoke from spices of myrrh and frankincense and every powder of the perfumer?”

The beloved has now entered the Beloved’s chamber; she has now begun in some measure to draw near to his kiss, because she has flown away from the allurements and cares of secular life. Fleeing them, she has withdrawn far off and has remained in the solitude of her body and soul. Solitude of body is to remain quietly in one’s appointed place and not to wander through the outward senses amid the business of this world, whether in [Col. 1129D] speech or action. Solitude of soul is to be occupied by no outward thing, either in thought or in will.

This solitude is certainly a great ascent of the mind. The daughters of Jerusalem marvel at the beloved’s wonderful ascent through the wilderness, because weak minds greatly wonder at and praise the singular life of those devoted to God alone and having no care for worldly honour or advantage. Therefore it says: “Who is this that comes up?” But before describing this ascent, let us consider what and what kind of wilderness it is through which this ascent takes place. First, let us understand that both “ascent” and “wilderness” are equivocal terms, since a single name may signify different things. For there is an ascent of the body and an ascent of the heart.

[Col. 1130A] **125** The wilderness may be the Church of the Gentiles; the wilderness may be the synagogue of the Jews; the wilderness may be the world; the wilderness may be a place set apart; the wilderness may be a mind withdrawn from all worldly cares.

“Wilderness” is said from forsaking, because it forsakes and is forsaken: it forsakes the continent person, and is forsaken by the continent person. For the world forsakes one who practices continence because, by its attraction, it cannot in any way attach itself to a holy soul that regards all things of this world as nothing. It is forsaken by the continent person because the holy soul by no reasoning consents to share in the world’s pleasures or actions, lest, perhaps held fast by it, it should escape only with difficulty or never.

We call this continence according to [Col. 1130B] the general state of the body, which belongs to good and bad alike, and according to the state of the mind, which belongs particularly to the good and particularly to the bad, in accordance with an inclination to good or evil.

The state of the body is an outward place; the state of the mind is an inward place. And sometimes an outward place benefits or harms the inward place. We said a little above that the wilderness is the world, a place set apart, or a mind withdrawn from worldly cares. To a mind withdrawn from worldly cares, the world is harmful not according to its substance, but according to its inclination toward evil; and a secluded place is beneficial not according to its nature, but according to the tranquillity it affords and its removal from noise. Thus an outward place, in this respect, benefits or harms the inward place. Let us therefore say why each of the things set above is called by the name of wilderness.

For the Church of the Gentiles, as long as it remained in Gentile life, was a kind of wilderness, because it did not yet possess the worship of any religion or the abundance of sacred laws and ordinances. It was, as it were, a den of beasts because of the beastly manners of men, in whom reason itself and natural law were so deeply asleep that they could not discern what honour they owed to their own life, or what reverence and submission to the Creator. Of this wilderness the Psalmist says: “The lovely places of the wilderness shall grow rich” (Ps. 64). For what are the lovely places of this wilderness except the most healthful and fitting institutions of venerable sacraments and ordinances? These began then to grow rich when, by the teachings and authorities of the holy Fathers, they advanced to greater increase in honour and reverence. Concerning this wilderness the Lord says through Isaiah: “I will make the wilderness a pool of water, and the pathless land streams of water” (Isa. 41). For he made the wilderness a pool of water and the pathless land streams of water when he gave the streams of preaching to Gentile life, which, through the dryness of its mind, bore no fruits of good works; and when he afterwards caused streams of teaching to flow forth for that land, to which, because of the harshness of its dryness, no way lay open for preachers. In another place through the same prophet he promises it, saying: “The wilderness and pathless places shall rejoice, and the solitude shall exult and bloom like a lily” (Isa. 35): [Col. 1131A] **126** it shall rejoice in faith, exult in action, bloom with the beauty of virtues, so that, like a lily, it may be fragrant with the scent of a good life, shine with the whiteness of purity, and have power as a medicine of inward salvation.

Judaea too is called a wilderness, for from it the covenant and the giving of the law and every rite of sacrifices and ceremonies have departed. Thus, with the Temple destroyed and the city laid waste, all royal and priestly dignity and every solemn rite among them have ceased; while they themselves, scattered through different regions, bear the sign of this desolation. The Lord foretold this would happen to them in the Gospel: “Your house shall be left to you desolate” (Matt. 23). And it is written in Jeremiah: “The Lord has cast down and has not spared; in his fury he has destroyed all the lovely places of Jacob” [Col. 1131B] (Lam. 2).

The world also may be called a wilderness, not bodily but spiritually, because the more it is heaped with the filth of sins, the more it is desolated of the presence of divine grace. For it is written: “The earth shall be reduced to solitude” (Jer. 50). The earth is in solitude because a mind occupied with earthly cares and pleasures is desolated of the assembly of virtues.

A secluded place is also called a wilderness, because where there is no approach of secular business or public affairs, it is not unfittingly called a kind of solitude. Thus, when the Psalmist had set forth such tribulations from enemies, vexations from iniquities, and disturbances of heart that he feared even death, he at last turned away from them and said: “Who will give me wings like a dove, that I may fly away and be at rest?” (Ps. 54). Then, having found a healthful counsel, he said: “Behold, I have withdrawn in flight and remained in solitude; I waited for him who saved me from faintness of spirit and from the tempest” (ibid.). And after his baptism the Lord was led into the wilderness to fast, where he was tempted by the devil (Matt. 4). In himself he triumphed over our temptations, showing that those who love the quiet life will indeed be wearied by temptations but will be delivered by God’s help through fasts and prayers.

The wilderness is also the mind removed from all worldly cares, because the less it thinks upon worldly things, the more solitary it keeps the heart from carnal desires. Therefore the Lord says in the Gospel: “When you pray, enter into your chamber, and, having shut the door, pray to your Father” (Matt. 6). For in praying we enter the chamber when, in the secret of our heart, we stand alone and disclose without voice only to God what we ask. We also shut the door when we close the entrance of our outward senses, lest through them anything be introduced into the heart that might hinder our prayers. This is the solitude of soul, most necessary for everyone seeking and wishing to find God.

We said above that there is an ascent both of body and mind, but here we must consider only the ascent of the mind, which does not occur except through the wilderness.

**127** For as long as the mind is entangled in the cares and [Col. 1132A] tumults of this world, it cannot ascend to the height of virtues. Rather, solitude of body and mind must first be sought, so that, when the mind is drawn away by no outward or inward disturbance, it may more freely be raised to the pursuit of good works.

Thus the holy Church, gathered from two peoples coming from uncircumcision and circumcision, ascends through the wilderness of unbelief when, while unbelievers from both peoples remain in unbelief, she herself grows among them in faith, hope, and love to admirable heights of virtue. And the more grievously she is crushed and, as it were, ground down by their persecutions, the more highly she sends forth from the fire of the Holy Spirit the smoke of holiness through the uprightness and rigour of life and teaching. Hence it follows: “Like a column of smoke from spices of myrrh [Col. 1132B] and frankincense and every powder of the perfumer.”

Like a slender rod, because it remained upright and firm in its end and in its action; but it was a rod of smoke, because that very uprightness and strength gave forth smoke from the fire of divine love. What, then, was the material in which this divine fire grew hot? Surely faith, hope, and charity, which are signified by the kinds of spices—myrrh, frankincense, and every powder of the perfumer.

Myrrh has a bitter juice, and with it the bodies of the dead are also preserved lest they decay; frankincense, however, is offered to God in sacrifice; and from every powder of the perfumer is made a most precious ointment. When the Nine, for preserving the integrity of orthodox faith, suffered many and various persecutions and deaths from unbelievers and heretics, corruptors of that very faith [Col. 1132C], they sent up, as it were, myrrh of smoking faith into heaven. For throughout the whole world this smoke of faith and sufferings rose up; by the severity of miracles it blinded and put to flight unbelievers and persecutors, while it illuminated and strengthened believers with a most sweet fragrance.

But when, fervent in the worship of God and in the religious life, they continually persisted in prayers for the condition of the Church and for attaining the eternal blessedness for which they hoped, did they not also offer frankincense of smoking and fragrant hope? For unless they possessed a firm hope of future goods, they would never continually beseech God to obtain them. And when, strong in faith and hope, they could say with the Apostle: “I am certain that neither life nor death, nor angels, [Col. 1132D] nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, nor strength, nor height, nor depth, nor any creature shall be able to separate us from the charity of God” (Rom. VIII), did they not scatter aloft the fragrance of every powder of the perfumer?

For what is charity but every powder of the perfumer? Charity is indeed a universal virtue, because all virtues spring from its root; and therefore, wherever any virtue is found, there is charity.

And who is this perfumer except the Holy Spirit, since by His grace He compounds this universal powder? “For the charity of God is poured abroad in our hearts by the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. V).

**128.** Let us see to what fineness the Apostle reduced charity, as though into powder, when [Col. 1133A], enumerating its parts, he says: “Charity is patient, is kind; it does not envy, does not act perversely, is not puffed up, is not ambitious, does not seek its own interests, is not provoked, thinks no evil, does not rejoice at iniquity, but rejoices together with truth; it bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things” (I Cor. XIII). See into how many parts he divides charity, so that by these determinate parts he may indicate that whatever virtue is last and most strongly fortified out of the whole body of goodness is an atom of charity.

But where “all” is said, nothing is excepted. Therefore every good is charity. Thus, just as every powder of the perfumer is composed from every precious spice, so charity is composed from every virtue of the soul, so that it is not inappropriately marked by the signification of every [Col. 1133B] powder of the perfumer. For where any virtue is lacking, perfect charity is not present.

Every soul beloved by God also ascends through the desert of this world when, despising and setting aside all its cares, business, and pleasures, it ever tends toward heavenly things through progress in the virtues; and although it is held in the world in body, it nevertheless dwells in heavenly things in mind. It also makes ascents through the desert of the soul, because the more the mind is occupied with outward things, and the more it is deserted by a multitude of useless thoughts, the more it is borne upward by love of divinity and delight in good deeds. And this is like a rod of smoke from the spices of myrrh and frankincense and every powder of the perfumer: according to the preceding sense, it also has [Col. 1133C] the rod of equity itself, through faith, hope, and charity, by the grace of the Holy Spirit.

In this valley of tears, moreover, may myrrh of labor and patience smoke before the sight of God, considering that “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory which shall be revealed in us” (Rom. VIII). Let it also kindle the purest frankincense by persistence in prayers, so that God, delighted by its sweet fragrance, may confer upon it the grace of His blessing, through which it may increase and multiply in offspring of virtues. And let it be fragrant with every powder of the perfumer, so that with a spirit of humility and a contrite heart it may render to God every service of holiness; for “a contrite spirit is a sacrifice to God” (Ps. L). For it is as though sifted into the minutest powder [Col. 1133D] when, through the breaking of a deeply humbled heart, one who is established in the highest virtues is made small before the eyes of God.

For David, kindled by the fire of the Holy Spirit with the finest powder of this breaking and humility, gave forth smoke when he said: **129.** “I am a worm and no man” (Ps. XXI), and when elsewhere he called himself a dead dog and a flea (I Kings XXIV, XXVI). And in the Psalm Moses is said to have stood “in the breaking” before God, to turn away His wrath (Ps. CV). For with how great contrition of spirit and strength of compassion was he broken when, praying to God for the sin of the people, he said: “Either forgive them this offense, or, if you do not, blot me out of your book which you have written” (Exod. XXXII). Paul likewise, crushed by the abasement of humility, calls himself the least of the apostles [Col. 1134A] (II Cor. XV); but broken by piety and compassion, he wishes for his brethren that he himself might become accursed (Rom. IX).

This ascent, moreover, is said to have been like a rod of smoke. When smoke rises, it gradually fails as it rises, until it can no longer be seen at all. So great is the subtlety of the contemplative life in the saints, so great the loftiness of holy conduct through the desert of inward solitude, that it escapes the minds of those who marvel at it rather than being retained for imitation by reflection; so that, unable to grasp it by following, the mind fails in the very act of contemplating it.

**VERSE 7.—“Behold, Solomon’s bed: sixty mighty men surround it, of the mightiest of Israel.”**

It does not, I think, conflict with reason if we understand this bed of Solomon [Col. 1134B] in three ways: as the universal Church, as the soul of each saint, or as the holy Scripture of the two Testaments. This is not because He who is without spatial limits is enclosed in places, but because the bestowal and preservation of graces and saving effects in one of the aforesaid things is His rest: a rest that saves, guards, and governs.

The universal Church is the bed of this Solomon, that is, of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Man of Peace, because He rests in it through its saving observance of His commandments and its life-giving incorporation with His sacraments. The Church presents this to Him under the form of sacramental realities, as He makes peace between the things in heaven and on earth, so that there may be, as it were, one commonwealth of this magnificent emperor: one Church, namely, both that which rejoices in its homeland and that which still journeys on earth.

[Col. 1134C] For Christ is the head of the Church, while the Church itself is the body of Christ (I Cor. XI). And just as the body does not live or accomplish anything without the head, and just as the head is not living without the body, so Christ gives life to no one apart from unity with the body of the Church. Therefore Christ and the Church are one. Since the head is indivisible from its body, whoever does not possess the peace and unity of the Church does not possess Christ either. Hence, even in the body of the sacraments themselves—namely, the body and blood of Christ—the body is made co-sacramental and co-corporeal with the head; that is, **130.** the Church is made one sacramentally and corporally with Christ, by its own mystery and His, when the mystery of Christ, received in the reality of His body [Col. 1134D], benefits no one unless that person has also received, by the same sacrament, the mystery of the Church—that is, ecclesiastical fellowship.

For, as we have said, Christ is indivisible from His body, that is, the Church. Thus Christ is not said to be truly received in His sacrament unless He is received whole, joined to that same Church by the mystery both of Himself and of the Church. For He Himself says: “He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him” (John VI).

Where, then, does Christ rest more fully than in the Church, which daily, by sharing in His body and blood, is incorporated into Him and made, as it were, one with Him? Hence those who cut themselves off from the unity of the Church by evil living or false teaching do not abide in the Church; and since Christ and the Church are one, they do not abide in [Col. 1135A] Christ. Therefore, when they partake of His body, they indeed receive Him in the reality of His substance, but do not receive Him to the saving effect of their own salvation.

This is what it means not to receive Him truly: He is not received whole. For since, at the altar, the Church—as has been said—is co-corporeal and co-sacramental in Christ, one who is outside the Church does not receive the whole body of Christ, namely the head together with its members, because he does not unite himself to Christ and the Church in the sacrament of both. He indeed receives the sacrament itself according to its essence, which comes to some unto life and to others unto ruin; but he does not receive the power and reality of the sacrament. For its power and reality are that all who partake [Col. 1135B] of it should belong to the unity of the body of the Church by loving one another—a unity which brings ruin to none, but benefits every believer unto salvation.

Whoever, therefore, has not truly been a participant in so great a fellowship, Christ conforming and uniting him, does not truly receive Christ, since he is shown to receive Him not for his salvation but for judgment. For Christ Himself commands, saying: “If you offer your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar and go first to be reconciled to your brother; and then, when you come, you shall offer your gift” (Matt. V). He shows that a gift is not to be accepted where the mind of the offerer lacks the bond of peace and charity. If failure to preserve this unity, even particularly among fellow-members, causes the offerings of worshippers to be rejected, how much more will one who abandons the unity of the entire body of the Church be unable either to offer a gift or to share in what has been offered? [Col. 1135C]

But this is the bed of Solomon—that is, of the Man of Peace who said, “I give you my peace; I leave you my peace” (John XIV)—who joins together the things in heaven and on earth. For since the Church is the one body of Christ, partly reigning in heaven with Christ and partly still journeying in the body, whoever departs from the unity of this pilgrim part does not deserve fellowship with that heavenly part. For although they are not yet joined in one place, they are one in the power and reality of the sacrament—that is, of ecclesiastical unity—and are so joined in spirit that whoever does not have the one does not have [Col. 1135D] the other.

Therefore, in this bed of the Man of Peace—that is, in the Church, in which Christ still rests beneath the veils of the sacraments—whoever has recovered through repentance the unity he lost also deserves to be joined to that Church which is above, when He comes who reincorporates and reconciled us to God through His blood.

The soul of every saint likewise is the bed of this our true Man of Peace. Since the soul of the righteous is called the seat of wisdom (Wis. VII), God surely rests there sweetly, where the place of that rest is ordered wisely, reasonably, and honorably under the governance of Wisdom itself; where the mind is so joined to God through grace that it becomes one spirit with Him. The sacrament of this unity confers every saving effect, as the Savior Himself says: “He who abides in me, and I in him, bears much fruit; because without me you can do nothing” (John XV).

[Col. 1136A] For since the mind is powerless for every fruit of goodness and instruction without cooperating grace, such power is conferred upon it by this union that, because He to whom it is joined through unity of spirit is omnipotent, it too is made omnipotent through grace, as He Himself says: “All things are possible to the one who believes” (Mark IX). For if saints joined to God are called gods—He essentially, they only by designation—it does not seem inconsequent that, when they are made co-corporeal with the Omnipotent through the sacrament of unity, they too are made participants in His omnipotence in their own manner. They can say with the Apostle: “He has given us all things with Him” [Col. 1136B] (Rom. VIII). For to those to whom He has given all things with Him, since they possess the Omnipotent, there is nothing that they cannot do in Him and through Him.

But such a mind is specifically called the bed of the Savior—that is, of the Man of Peace—because wherever this Man of Peace rests and makes His dwelling through the condescension of His grace, every hostile force of carnal affection that resists the spirit is put to sleep.

Further, this bed of Solomon may also, without absurdity, be understood as divine Scripture, because in it Christ rests through the teachings of His commandments and the examples of virtues. There is preached the testament of this Man of Peace, which He confirmed in His death: namely, the commandment of peace and love, when [Col. 1136C] He says, “I give you a new commandment: that you love one another as I have loved you” (John XIII). The fullness of this love consists in a twofold relation, namely to God and to neighbor, “on which hang the whole law and the prophets” (Matt. XXII).

Since every page of both Testaments contains this love, and discerns nothing useful or honorable apart from it, sacred Scripture may rightly be called the bed of this Man of Peace. There the reader and meditator finds Christ; there he can understand what he ought to believe, what he ought to hope, and what he ought to love. To possess this threefold virtue is to possess God, whom one is led and strengthened to possess eternally through faith, hope, and charity. There Christ, hidden and as it were resting, is recognized and awakened: after He has been understood in the minds of readers, if the mind is moved by the steps of faith and good works, Christ who was resting is, as it were, awakened.

For it is written in the Gospel that Christ, who lay hidden in the form of a traveler, was recognized in the breaking of bread (Luke XXIV), because divine Scripture, which is that heavenly and living bread, Christ, is alien to those who do not understand it. But when it has been distributed through the breaking of exposition, Christ who was hidden in it is recognized in the mind of the one who understands.

But we must consider what it means that sixty mighty men from among the mightiest of Israel are said to surround this bed of the Man of Peace, all holding swords and most skilled in war. Many have attempted to destroy this bed and take away this Man of Peace: some by vain and irreligious observances, some by perverse morals, others by the errors of corrupt doctrines. These mighty men resisted them most courageously in deeds, words, and writings, holding the swords of the word of God and highly skilled in defeating enemies of this kind: first, indeed, the holy apostles and apostolic men; then the holy martyrs; and finally priests. All were among the mightiest in mind, seeing God and drawing from Him the strength of unconquerable courage. Each in his own time and place surrounded and guarded this bed—not because they were necessary to this Man of Peace, but because He was exceedingly necessary to them, and they feared to lose Him through the perversity of evil people who labored in every way to overthrow the Catholic faith. [Col. 1137A]

[Col. 1137B] Why, however, is the multitude of these mighty men, or mightiest men, fixed at the number sixty? It is not without reason that, although the multitude of these mighty men was innumerable, it is comprehended by this finite number. It may indeed have been that the historical Solomon had more guards for his body, or appointed certain designated guardians for his possessions stored in various places. But since God granted him such great peace that no wars were stirred up in his time, it seems strange, if this is to be understood literally, that so many mighty men should have been assigned merely to guard his body.

But since reason requires that these matters be referred rather to a spiritual sense, let us see what this number sixty signifies. [Col. 1137C] For sixty is composed by multiplying six and ten one by the other. Six, because it is neither diminished nor enlarged when its parts are gathered together, is said to signify perfection. Ten, composed by doubling five, indicates the Decalogue of the Law. According as that Law is observed or despised, through the five bodily senses, by whose service the mind is led either to good or to evil, the whole human race is either rewarded or condemned in the order of the ten virgins, five prudent and five foolish.

Six, then, signifying perfection, and ten, displaying the Decalogue, multiply one another and produce sixty. They show that these sixty mighty men adapted their outward senses so perfectly to keeping the divine commandments [Col. 1137D] that they are deservedly counted in the lot of the five prudent virgins.

Those who possess knowledge of the art of arithmetic are accustomed to call a number such as sixty “superabundant.” Since there are certain numbers which are equal to the sum of their parts, so that they receive neither less nor more than the whole body, and are therefore called perfect; and since some, because the sum of their parts amounts to less than the whole body, are called deficient; so those which, when their proper parts are gathered together, exceed the whole body by some quantity are called superabundant.

But we, who interpret the number of these mighty men in a favorable sense, ought to understand this excess not as superfluity but as the increase of spiritual gain, which advances from virtue to virtue [Col. 1138A]. Thus we may say that these mighty men worked so magnificently with the five talents of the senses entrusted to them for their own benefit and that of their neighbors that, as their zeal in good works continually increased, they became from mighty men the mightiest.

Let us see, moreover, what parts this number sixty yields, so that we may know whether they belong to the perfection of these mighty men of Christ. The half of sixty is thirty; its third, twenty; its fourth, fifteen; its fifth, twelve; its sixth, ten; its tenth, six; its twelfth, five; its fifteenth, four; its twentieth, three; its thirtieth, two; and its sixtieth, one. When these parts are collected together, they make one hundred and eight, exceeding the whole number sixty by forty-eight [Col. 1138B].

And what is the reward of all the perfect except a recompense a hundredfold better than all their labor in the future regeneration, when they are reborn into the immortality of their bodies for that life of the eighth age which shall never end?

Therefore the assembly of these mighty men, or mightiest men, is fittingly comprehended by the number sixty, whose parts, brought into one, grow to one hundred and eight, so that we may refer this not to superfluity but to an increase of virtues. By acting and teaching rightly, they gained progress for themselves and for others; in return for this they attain perfect blessedness, signified by the number one hundred, and completed in the eighth age, which, as we have said, shall endure without end.

[Col. 1138C] **VERSE 8.—“All holding swords and most skilled in war; each man’s sword upon his thigh because of fears in the night.”**

What do these sixty mighty men from among the mightiest of Israel do as they surround Solomon’s bed? “All,” he says, “holding swords and most skilled in war.” He does not say “having,” but “holding,” because they might indeed possess within some hidden treasury of a soul that knows and understands, but not hold forth publicly in the voice and active bearing of one who preaches. Therefore they hold swords because they always bear ready the teachings of knowledge and action by which they may instruct those who see and hear them for spiritual conflicts.

[Col. 1138D] But what are these swords except the words of God? “For the word of God is true and effective and more penetrating than any two-edged sword, reaching even to the division of soul, joints, and marrow, and discerning thoughts” (Heb. IV). God sent such a dividing and separating sword into the earth when He came to separate a man against his father, a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law; and “a man’s enemies shall be those of his own household” (Matt. X).

The renowned warriors of God, whose purpose is to surround by teaching and action the bed of this Man of Peace, must use this sword of the word of God, by which separation and complete discernment are commanded between good and evil, virtues and vices—whether we refer this bed to the Church or to the mind of each saint, [Col. 1139A] in which divinity is believed to rest through the condescension of His grace. Thus in both cases they may defend the Church from the perversity of unbelievers and protect themselves from the suggestion or deception of malignant spirits.

What, then, are the wars in which such men ought to fight and for which they are called most skilled? Surely the great strife and discord of virtues and vices, where the opposition of two adversaries is at issue—namely, flesh and spirit. “For the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Gal. V). And rightly they are proclaimed most skilled not in “war” but in “wars,” in the plural; for one is the war of humility against pride, another of chastity against lust, another of patience against anger, another of obedience against stubbornness, another of sobriety against luxury, [Col. 1139B] another of avarice against generosity, or that of any virtue which struggles against its opposed vice.

These sixty **135** mighty men are called most skilled for happily waging these wars because in their deeds and writings is found reason and counsel for preparing and honorably completing these conflicts.

Hence it follows: “Each man’s sword upon his thigh because of fears in the night.” For the method of repressing different vices differs: pride is checked in one way, lust in another, and avarice in another; and individual vices demand individual and contrary remedies, so that one fights against each opposite, as it were, with a different sword. The sword, however, is the vigilant guarding of the mind, concerning which Scripture commands: “Keep your heart with all vigilance” [Col. 1139C] (Prov. IV). This sword is placed upon the thigh when the suggestion of delighting flesh is repressed by the vigilant guard of a resisting mind.

Let us speak by analogy. In the thigh is the seed-bed of offspring; from it, after conception has been given, a human being is formed. Its limbs are individually distinguished in the womb; at length it is brought forth in birth and gradually, through the stages of age, is led to a perfect human being. What is the suggestion of delighting flesh in each person except a kind of conception of suddenly assailing vice? If it is not immediately crushed by the sword of a mind strongly resisting, it takes form in the mind through delight; then, through consent, it is as it were born; [Col. 1139D] and thus gradually growing through action, it becomes a damnable and deadly vice through habit.

For in the propagation of every vice there are these stages of progress: suggestion, delight, consent, action, habit—just as in a human being there are these stages of natural development: conception, formation, birth, growth of the body, and fullness of age. Therefore the sword of each person ought to be upon his thigh, so that when the head of evil suggestion has been swiftly cut off, and the seed-bed, as it were, of malice about to be conceived has been weakened, the whole body of the vice that would be born may be driven away.

And why is this? “Because of fears,” he says, “in the night.” What do those who guard a city or house fear at night except sudden enemies or thieves—except malignant spirits [Col. 1140A] that endeavor to plunder or steal the treasures of our soul? For these rush upon and creep into the mind through the night of evil suggestion or delight, with which they envelop each person’s mind so that it cannot discern the danger of the evil itself. They wound the mind with such arrows of temptations that they sometimes cast it down from the state of its uprightness.

But they can do this only at night: when, as the warmth of devout zeal departs, the cold of torpor and negligence occupies the soul; when the sun of righteousness has set in it through sloth and has not shone with the light of His grace. For then “they prepare their arrows, to shoot the poor in secret” (Ps. X).

Because of these fears in the night—that is, the hidden snares of temptations—each person ought to stand girded with the weapons of righteousness and watch every entrance to the inner house of the soul so vigilantly that no place of entry can lie open to the enemy. Such diligence shows who are the mighty or mightiest men who, surrounding, guard or are able to guard the bed of the true Solomon; and who, girded for a holy purpose, are most skilled, always holding the swords of foresight and ready vigilance because of the sudden fears of vice creeping in by night. [Col. 1140B]

But the following words indicate where and by what means these mightiest men receive the knowledge and courage for this spiritual warfare. For it follows: “King Solomon made himself a litter,” etc.

**VERSE 9.—“Solomon made himself a litter from the woods of Lebanon.”**

[Col. 1140C] From where do they receive the means to be mighty except from the teachers of the holy Church, whose deeds and words they desire to imitate, or from the testimonies and authorities of the canonical holy Scriptures?

The litter of this true King Solomon is the holy Church, or the entire canonical Scripture of the Church itself, or individually the soul of any righteous person. For since *ferculum* (“litter”) is so called from *ferre*, “to carry,” each of these may suitably be called a *ferculum* in the same sense: the Church, because it bears the divine sacraments contained in it; holy Scripture, because it receives divine utterances and commandments, whose mysteries and benefit it contains; and the soul of the righteous, because it receives divine knowledge, through which it becomes capable of uprightness and instruction. All these are delights of spiritual banquets. [Col. 1140D]

We shall endeavor to explain how the individual parts may belong to each of the things we have proposed; that is, how the silver columns, golden couch, purple ascent, and the middle paved with charity may suit the Church, canonical Scripture, and the soul of the righteous.

First, however, we must consider how each of these litters is said to have been built from the woods of Lebanon. Lebanon is interpreted “whitening.” What then are the woods of Lebanon, which are said to be naturally incorruptible, except the saints and elect, who through strength of spirit and the brightness of a worldly life have kept and keep holiness uncorrupted in thought, speech, and work? [Col. 1141A]

Therefore King Solomon made Himself a litter from the woods of Lebanon because Christ most fittingly ennobled His Church and composed His holy Scripture from the venerable and incorruptible deeds and teachings of His saints; and He instructed the soul of every righteous person, so that each might be a heavenly litter of banquets and refreshment for faithful souls.

**VERSE 10.—“He made its columns silver, its couch gold, and its ascent purple; He paved the middle with charity for the daughters of Jerusalem.”**

Silver and gold are suitably understood in each case because of the brightness and purity of utterances, and the majesty of the meanings that shine in those utterances. If you refer this to the Church, its columns are silver because the holy patriarchs and prophets, the apostles also and apostolic men, in their preaching or exposition of the two Testaments, by which they raise and support the Church, proclaim what they say or write in speech that is faithful and clear. [Col. 1141B]

In this speech the couch is golden because their preaching or exposition itself gleams with the precious splendor of meanings. In it anyone who formerly labored in ignorance and inquiry, now understanding, may refresh himself as though resting, and may lean his mind, wearied by ignorance, upon the feasts of inward refreshment.

[Col. 1141C] The ascent of this litter is also purple because, in the peace of the Church, the profession is most lofty that prepares a purple ascent through contempt for the world, mortification of the flesh, rejection of one’s own will, and martyrdom of the mind, when the mind offers itself to God as “a living sacrifice, a sweet-smelling offering” (Eph. V). For no one, unless free from every care and desire of the world, can ascend through contemplation to the highest degree of divine charity. Although the saints ascending in virtues have many and varied degrees, as it is written of them, “They shall go from virtue to virtue” (Ps. LXXXIII), nevertheless, as we learn, the highest ascent is where the mind raises itself above itself in contemplative charity.

In this purple ascent there are different degrees, because one is higher than another. It is more to pray, fast, and keep vigil than merely to meditate and read; it is more to endure insults, reproaches, or any sort of persecution for righteousness than merely to abstain from injustice. Yet in all ascents of this kind the labor of body and soul and restraint of life are like a certain precious purple of the mind. [Col. 1141D]

But King Solomon paved the middle of this litter with charity for the daughters of Jerusalem, because in the midst of such lofty merits in the Church many minds are laid down, as it were, because of their frailty and weakness. Although they cannot perfectly leave the world, they nevertheless love and reverence those who despise the world. Although they cannot labor for God by fasting, keeping vigil, praying, or mortifying the flesh, yet, because they love these things in those who perform them, they make them, as it were, their own; and what they do not have in themselves through weakness, they have in others through charity. Such persons belong to this litter and are refreshed in it in their own way, because what the saints and perfect possess in deed and virtue, these attain by charity alone. [Col. 1142A]

Further, if you consider the whole body of canonical Scripture, its silver columns and golden couch are the sayings and authorities of divine utterances: clear in the brightness of their words and radiant in the singular excellence of their meanings. Their reading is a most sweet refreshment for the soul, because there faith supports, hope raises up, and charity reclines through contemplation. Hence the couch is golden, because contemplative charity is greater than faith and hope, just as gold is more precious than silver.

For when any believer, by reading or hearing from this litter, has learned what he ought to believe and hope, then, setting aside all transient things, he is fed and nourished for eternal life in the love of God alone, as though on a golden couch of contemplation, through the rest of the mind. [Col. 1142B]

In this litter the ascent is purple because there are recounted there the Passion of the Redeemer and the glorious triumphs of martyrs who die for love of the Redeemer himself; and in these sufferings there were ascents. For, as we can see in the chief of martyrs himself, He was first scourged, then smeared with spittle, struck with blows, crowned with thorns, and finally fastened to the cross. Thus, as it were, in His Passion He made a purple ascent. Following in His footsteps, the martyrs had ascents of manifold labor: “they suffered mockings and scourging, moreover also chains and prisons; they were stoned, sawn asunder, tempted, and finally died by the sword” (Heb. XI), so that through these ascents of suffering they might reach the highest degree of eternal blessedness.

When devout minds read and hear this ascent, they strive to imitate it, so that as they share temporal sufferings, they may also share eternal consolations. [Col. 1142C]

The middle of this litter is likewise paved with charity because in the whole divine page charity holds, as it were, the central place. All the sayings of holy Scriptures look toward it as toward a certain best and sure end. As the Apostle says, “the end of the commandment is charity from a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith” (I Tim. I). And when the Lord set forth the two commandments of love, namely love of God and neighbor, He said: “On these two commandments hang the whole law and the prophets” (Matt. XXII). But that upon which all other things depend seems in some way to hold the highest and principal place. Therefore King Solomon paved the middle of this litter with charity because He established the primacy of charity in the midst of the holy Scriptures. [Col. 1142D]

And why was this done? For the daughters of Jerusalem—that is, for souls belonging to the heavenly Jerusalem, that is, to the vision [Col. 1143A] of peace—so that they may understand that neither silver columns, nor a golden couch, nor a purple ascent possesses any virtue without the virtue of charity; rather, all things must proceed from charity as many branches from the one root of a tree.

For the Apostle says: “Though I speak with the tongues of men and of angels,” which is to have silver columns, “but have not charity, I have become as sounding brass or a tinkling cymbal. And though I have prophecy and know all mysteries and all knowledge,” which is to be a golden couch, “and though I give my body to be burned,” which is to have a purple ascent, “but have not charity, it profits me nothing” (I Cor. XIII).

[Col. 1143B] See how our king Solomon paved the middle of this his litter with charity: throughout the whole body of holy Scripture he placed charity, as it were, at a certain centre, so that all things might revolve around it and toward it. And just as the sun is at its highest when it is fixed at the centre and proceeds no further, so holy Scripture, when it treats of virtues, reaches its summit in the proclamation of charity and advances no further, to the prejudice of any virtue beyond it.

Thirdly, if you consider the soul of any righteous person, its silver columns are the four cardinal virtues, of which all the rest are appendages: prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance. But in what sense are they silver? They are tested by purity of faith and by the true proclamation of evangelical doctrine, purged of every dross of heretical falsehood; concerning this it is written: “The words of the Lord are pure words, silver tried by fire” (Ps. 11). Hence the Lord says through the prophet concerning heretics: “I gave them silver and gold; but they made Baal out of the silver and gold” (Hos. 2). Gold pertains to the mind, silver to speech. For God grants gold and silver to the holy soul when he allows it both to possess divine understanding and wisdom, and to express with the beauty of speech what the mind conceives. Since heretics corrupt this understanding and proclaim it in corrupted teaching, they fashion idols of falsehood, as it were, from gold and silver.

Therefore, whoever wishes the virtues which he possesses to be columns supporting the structure of the soul must take care that they are silver. For unless they shine with purity of faith and doctrine, there is great danger that, unable to bear the structure itself, they will collapse through the weakness of their crookedness. But he whose columns are silver has also a golden couch, because “out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks” (Matt. 12): wherever wisdom abounds in understanding, there praiseworthy eloquence flows outwardly. It is written: “Wisdom rests in the heart of the righteous, and prudence in the speech of his mouth” (Prov. 19). For when the mind shines with the radiance of wisdom, it follows that it prudently expresses that by which it understands something. But why is the mind of the righteous called a couch? Surely because in a mind pleasing to itself, by the beauty of humility, patience, chastity, and obedience, the divinity is said to recline through the gold of the gift of its indwelling grace; [Col. 1144A] whereas, on the contrary, it is said of the minds of the reprobate that “the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (Matt. 8).

But what is the purple ascent of this litter? It is faith and remembrance of the Lord’s Passion: to believe in it, to establish in it every hope of one’s salvation, and, in conformity with it, to crucify oneself also to the world, to vices, and to desires, so as to be able to say with the Apostle: “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. 6). Without doubt, this is to ascend by the purple ascent of the mind.

How the middle of this litter is paved with charity for the daughters of Jerusalem, the Apostle shows when he says: “I became weak to the weak, that I might gain the weak” (1 Cor. 9). Whence came this, if not from charity? For since love is twofold—love of God, namely, and of neighbour—and one depends upon the other, whoever is endowed with the highest virtues ought to have this as his middle: when fraternal need or benefit requires it, he should descend a little from that height of his strictness and provide for his neighbours’ weakness by condescending to it.

For unless he loves his neighbour in this manner, he is in no way proved to love God, since one love is constituted from the other: “For he who does not love the neighbour whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see?” (1 John 4).

Whether, then, the Church, holy Scripture, or the soul of any righteous person is called the litter of this true Solomon, what follows is not inconsistent, so that the members may suitably adhere to each head. But if the gaze of the mind is applied carefully, it will not, I think, be tedious to consider how beautifully the final member of this litter is marked by the conclusion of charity. For what in the Church belongs to religion, what belongs to sacramental reality, what in the whole divine page belongs to knowledge or eloquence, what in the holy soul belongs to holiness and justice, does not establish its whole beginning or end in relation to charity? Further, what are the sacraments of the Church, what are the utterances of all holy Scripture, and what is it that the soul of the righteous ought to believe, hope, and love, except the incarnation, Passion, resurrection, and ascension of Christ, and the manifestation of all the deeds which he performed for human salvation? And what are the holy proclamations of all these things except signs of divine charity? For because of his exceeding charity, by which God loved us, he sent his Son in the likeness of flesh, who was made a curse for us, that he might redeem us from the curse (Eph. 2). Whether this litter, therefore, is called the Church, holy Scripture, or the soul of the righteous, this charity occupies the middle place everywhere, because all things proceed from it and all things look to it. For the whole sum of this charity is that God became man; and this is the whole teaching of the saints in the Church through divine Scripture: that we should give the fullest attention to the greatness of this divine charity and mercy, [Col. 1145A] because through it we have been freed from death and restored to the eternal life which we had lost by sinning.

Accordingly, in what follows the daughters of Zion are now admonished carefully to consider the grace of divine goodness, not only in the event itself but also in the bringing about of that event, and to observe the wondrous ordering of their salvation.

**VERSE 11.—“Go forth and see, daughters of Zion, King Solomon in the diadem with which his mother crowned him, on the day of his espousal and on the day of the joy of his heart.”**

Zion means “contemplation.” What, then, are the daughters of Zion—that is, of contemplation—but the souls of believers, who through the grace of contemplation subtly survey the hidden mysteries of heavenly things? They are told to go forth because those who desire to be occupied with the spiritual things perceived by the eye of the mind ought by no means to be occupied with carnal things. “Go forth,” he says, “and see”; for you cannot see unless you first go forth. Go forth, therefore: that is, depart from the consideration of bodily and visible things, fix the gaze of your mind upon the glory of divine magnificence, upon the very cause of universal redemption, and upon the wholly incorporeal reality of human salvation. Why? Namely, that you may see King Solomon in the diadem with which his mother crowned him. But with what eye ought you to see? Surely with the inward rather than the outward eye; for by faith you must pass from corporeality to corporeality [reading uncertain], and you must understand spiritually rather than carnally the things which you see or hear. Thus “see” is said as though it meant “understand.”

Therefore you daughters of Zion, who are called not sons because of strength but daughters because of weakness, since you have not yet progressed to the strength of spiritual understanding—seeing that King Solomon has made for you a litter, at whose banquet you daily sit by examining the sacraments of the Church, reading and hearing canonical Scripture, and searching out the judgments of holy doctors—go forth in a loftier understanding and see King Solomon himself in the diadem with which his mother crowned him.

What or what kind of diadem is this of King Solomon, with which his mother crowned him? We can indeed say, in a particular sense, that it is the one sign of the Passion—namely, the crown of thorns with which his mother, the Synagogue, who bore him according to the flesh, crowned him in mockery. But it seems better to understand this diadem as the whole sum of his twofold Passion, which, just as a diadem is composed of many kinds of precious stones, is composed of many signs of diverse sufferings. [Col. 1145D] After he endured it in his body, he was crowned, as it were, with a diadem of glory and honour, as the Apostle said: “We see Jesus, because of the suffering of death, crowned with glory and honour, that by the grace of God he might taste death for all” (Heb. 2). Therefore, O daughters of Zion, do not consider only the outward and contemptible signs of these sufferings—scourges, spittle, blows, the crown of thorns, the cross, and burial—but go forth from this consideration and see with the eyes of your mind what glory and honour, remedy and healing, have thereby arisen for the whole world. For this is the diadem which you ought to admire and venerate, and this is that pre-eminence of charity which he placed in the middle of his litter; by such a diadem shines the excellence of his mercy toward you. Was he not crowned with glory and honour when, rising from the corruption of this passible body into impassibility and incorruption, he placed upon his body, which is the Church, the crown of this glory and honour, when he confirmed in it for ever a share in the future incorruption together with himself?

Or, if we call this diadem generally the whole order of the human dispensation with which his mother—namely, the blessed Virgin Mary, from whose womb he received this same humanity—crowned him, this does not appear contrary to reason. For in the composition of this diadem, with which Christ was crowned as man, the birth, circumcision, baptism, fasting, temptation, Passion, resurrection, and ascension are like ornaments of distinguished gems; all these are enclosed in the gold of his mercy. For gold is more precious than all metals, and “the mercies of God are over all his works” (Ps. 144). Thus this diadem of King Solomon, that is, of the true peaceful Lord Jesus Christ, was fashioned out of the most shining gold of God’s infinite mercy and from the works and signs of that mercy which we mentioned above: he who, reconciling us to God, “made peace in all things in heaven and on earth” (Col. 1). Therefore the daughters of Zion, who possess the grace of divine contemplation, are admonished to perceive all these things with inward understanding and to know how great a salvation has flowed to them from them.

But when was he crowned with such a diadem? “On the day,” he says, “of his espousal, on the day of the joy of his heart.” What was the day of Christ’s espousal except the time of the Incarnation, when he came forth from the Virgin’s womb “like a bridegroom coming out of his chamber” (Ps. 18), to join the Church to himself, for whose redemption he deigned to become incarnate? Or rather, the day of his espousal was the time of his Passion, when at the price of his blood he presented to himself the Church, redeemed as a glorious bride “without spot or wrinkle” (Eph. 5). For he gave her an earnest by this price of inestimable weight; for her he caused the kingdom of his Father to be inscribed as an eternal dowry; and from her he in turn demands bridal gifts—namely, the merits of faith and virtues, without which no soul can be joined to God. He enumerates some parts of these shortly afterwards in what follows.

What, then, was the day of the joy of his heart? Certainly the time of the resurrection, when, all sorrow of Passion and corruption overcome, he showed himself triumphant, crowned with glory and honour, bearing the trophy of completed redemption. Yet this affection of the heart did not come upon him in such a way that he was previously uncertain and did not know what was to happen, then conceived joy in his mind as though uncertainty had been removed—for no time is ascribed to the Godhead. Rather, such a manner of speaking belongs only to his humanity: he is said to have had a day of joy on account of the glory of the resurrection and the completed purpose and order of redemption. Although this may more properly be referred to the Church, which is his body, according to that manner of speaking whereby, frequently in holy Scripture, what is said of the head is referred to the body, and conversely what is said of the body to the head, because of the co-bodily union and unity by which Christ and the Church are made one. For Christ’s Passion, resurrection, and ascension are the Church’s greatest and special joy, when she remembers that through this wondrous aid she has passed from captivity into freedom, from death to life, and from corruption [Col. 1147B] to incorruption.

Since this whole epithalamium of bridegroom and bride, which is here called, because of its excellence, the *Song of Songs*, looks toward the wondrous spectacle of this espousal, let us see how beautifully and delightfully the bridegroom and bride sing in responsive alternation the praises of holy love. Above, the bride explained the dignity and excellence of the bridegroom to whom she is spiritually joined: in the splendour of the bed, in the abundance of litters, in the brilliance and glory of ornaments, and, greater than all these, in the singular prerogative of charity. She was exhorting the daughter of Zion to go forth in order to behold and admire the beauty of these nuptials, so that they too, striving according to their ability to be joined to these nuptials, might afterwards see face to face the King in his beauty, whom they now see “through a glass, in an enigma,” once the eye of the mind had been wholly purified.

The bridegroom immediately meets her with a song-like testimony to her beauty, and enumerates many parts of that beauty as bridal gifts offered by the bride to himself. Yet they are from the grace of that same bridegroom, who gives so that he may in turn receive. Thus he shows that she deserves to be joined to him, since by his gift he has made her glorious through so many praises of beauty; he has also applied to her the name of the previously signified bed and litter, and has brought about the cause of the ornaments placed upon her. He says, then: “How beautiful you are, my beloved!”

## CHAPTER IV

[Col. 1147D] **VERSE 1.—“How beautiful you are, my beloved! How beautiful you are! Your eyes are doves’, apart from that which lies hidden within; your hair is like flocks of goats which have come up from Mount Gilead.”**

Since every blessing of virtues flows by the grace of the Holy Spirit in the field of the Church, the bridegroom fittingly now exalts her with sevenfold praises of beauty, which he observes in the beauty and grace of her eyes, hair, teeth, lips, cheeks, neck, and breasts. For Christ judges the Church worthy of his fellowship, commending her, because of her abundance of graces, through the elegance of all the members of her face.

For the face of the Church is its public assembly, in which matters always necessary and useful for the instruction of its members and their formation in the beauty of unity are considered, arranged, and commanded, so that no stain of deformity may appear among them, whether in faith, conduct, or the establishment of any canonical enactment. This public assembly of the Church is distinguished by the varied character of professions, dignities, and orders. For the profession of monks is one thing, that of clerics another, and that of laypeople another. Among these, again, the profession of virgins is one, of the continent another, and of married persons another. Of dignities, the imperial is one, the pontifical another, the prefectural another, or whatever else may be called by the name of dignity. Likewise, of orders, one is priestly, another Levitical, another sub-Levitical, or any other ecclesiastical order. All these are signified by those previously described features which the bridegroom’s testimony commends as placed in the bride’s body. For the Church’s eyes are the guardianship and prudence of its rulers; its hair, the multitude of subjects; its teeth, the interpreters of holy Scripture; its lips, the elegance of preachers, or of readers reciting divine Scripture; its cheeks, the modesty of those under discipline; its neck, the lofty eloquence of doctors; its breasts, the diligence of teachers instructing the younger. Praising the distinct variety of all these in the body of the Church, the Psalmist says: “The queen stood at your right hand, in gilded raiment, surrounded by variety” (Ps. 44). But each of these must be discussed more fully in its proper place.

“How beautiful you are,” he says, “my beloved; how beautiful you are!” The one whom he calls beautiful he also calls beloved, in order to indicate that each produces the other. For she who is adorned with so many kinds of beauty, as he goes on to describe, is deservedly made beloved; and she who is proved beloved is certainly declared beautiful. For he would not make her, as beloved, the confidante of his secret unless he had joined her to himself by grace as one pleasing to him in the beauty of virtues. The repeated praise of beauty approves the twofold virtue of faith and action, which are so inseparably joined to one another that either without the other is always proved useless.

Setting forth the first feature of sevenfold beauty, he says: “Your eyes are doves’, apart from that which lies hidden within.” As noted above, the Church’s eyes are the guardianship and foresight of rulers for the benefit of their subjects. For just as the eyes are, as it were, guides and guardians to the body subject to them—“the blind man walks in darkness and does not know where he goes” (John 12)—so prelates guard those subject to them by their care and vigilance, and lead them into the chosen way by preaching and conduct, placed as watchmen for both the needs and benefits of souls and bodies. But these eyes are doves’ eyes, apart from that which lies hidden within, because innocently and simply they provide for bodily things, while prudently foreseeing and avoiding the dangers of their subjects by administering spiritual things. For when they are sometimes occupied with earthly things for the benefit of their subjects, they view those earthly things not with a raven’s eye but a dove’s: without greed and carnal desire, they seek and possess them simply for necessity alone. Of these the prophet says: “And as doves to their windows” (Isa. 60). For what are our windows but the outward senses, through which we look out upon visible things, either desiring them or despising them? But the saints are like doves at their windows, because whatever they apprehend externally through their bodily senses, they employ simply and innocently for their own uses. They seize nothing in these things with greed or delight, but attend only to their own common need and that of those dependent on them.
