To maintain devotion to the active life in this way is praiseworthy; but far more praiseworthy is that which lies hidden within—namely, the virtue of the contemplative life. For outwardly they administer external things honourably, but only divine knowledge perceives with what intention they do this, while some religious persons, handling outward things, are often judged by human eyes that do not see hearts.

The second portion of sevenfold beauty follows: “Your hair is like flocks of goats which come up from Mount Gilead.”

As noted above, hair signifies the multitude of subjects. Although they cannot attain the perfection of their superiors, they nevertheless adorn the assembly of the Church as hair adorns the head, cleaving, according to their manner and ability, to their heads—that is, to their superiors—by obeying them and observing the rule established for them. Each adorns and embellishes every profession in its own place and order, according to the rule set by the Fathers for common observance, though in different ways. For although in the universal or particular Church not all live equally, and not all equally observe the rule assigned to them in their own private office—often even exceeding it—they are nevertheless covered by the public and common ornament of religion and order. Conversely, the devotion of one person adds no honour or dignity to the whole body of the Church if the institution as a whole is disfigured by irreligion. In short, its religious community is its beauty and nobility, just as its irreligious unanimity is its ugliness and ignobility.

Therefore it is said that this hair is like flocks of goats, because in each profession there are certain flocks, united multitudes: flocks indeed with respect to the diversity of orders or particular Churches, but one flock with respect to unity of faith and the universal Church. These are flocks of goats because all ecclesiastical professions, although differing among themselves because of the diverse character of their orders, nevertheless always look with equal intention to one end: all seek heavenly things and each, in its own manner, cleaves to God.

But what kind of goats? “Which have come up,” he says, “from Mount Gilead.” Gilead means “heap of testimony.” And what is this heap of testimony except a certain collection and sum of the divine Scriptures or of institutions written by the holy Fathers for the benefit and dignity of the Church? For what is holy Scripture but a heap of testimony everywhere proclaiming and testifying concerning Christ? Of this testimony the Psalm sings: “The testimony of the Lord is faithful, giving wisdom to little ones” (Ps. 18). For little ones—that is, the humble—understand the testimony of holy Scripture; when by believing and living well they obey it, they are wise, for the highest philosophy is the best manner of life. The institution of the holy Fathers is likewise a heap of testimony, because, when it is lawfully observed, it provides its observers with assurance for an honourable life.

The hair of holy Church, therefore, is like flocks of goats which have come up from Mount Gilead, because multitudes of subjects daily advance through the testimonies of holy Scripture and the institutions of their rulers toward the common order of life prescribed for them.

[Col. 1150B] **VERSE 2.—“Your teeth are like flocks of shorn sheep which have come up from the washing, all bearing twins, and none among them is barren.”**

Third is set forth: “Your teeth are like flocks of shorn sheep which have come up from the washing, all bearing twins, and none among them is barren.”

As stated above, teeth may not unfittingly be understood as interpreters of holy Scripture. For just as teeth crush food, so holy interpreters in the divine Scriptures reduce the coarseness of the letter to the subtlety of spiritual meaning, so that what could not be understood on the surface, once ground by these teeth, may pass more easily into the stomach of understanding.

But why are these teeth like flocks of shorn sheep which have come up from the washing? Namely, because their mind is free from worldly business and washed from the dust of earthly action by the fountain of the divine Spirit. For they cannot advance to the subtlety of such great understanding unless they have laid aside these cares as burdens and, with the whole body of the inward person, have been washed in that whole fountain of divinity of which the Psalmist says to God: “You will give them drink from the torrent of your delight, because with you is the fountain of life” (Ps. 35). And what benefit this washing or drinking confers he indicates when he adds: “And in your light we shall see light” (ibid.); as if plainly to say: when you pour into us the light of knowledge, we shall understand the obscure things of divine Scripture.

The teeth of holy Church, then, are like flocks of shorn sheep which have come up from the washing, because the more free interpreters of holy Scripture are from earthly activities, and the more cleansed by the washing of divine inspiration, the more powerfully they can break and the more subtly grind the entire literal solidity of the Old and New Testaments.

For the allegorical or moral meaning, flowing fittingly and profitably from the literal surface of holy Scripture, is the becoming brightness and, as it were, attractive beauty of these teeth.

Therefore it is added: “All bearing twins, and none among them is barren.” What are the twin offspring of these teeth but either the twofold meaning of holy Scripture which is, as it were, crushed by exposition—namely, the allegorical and moral senses—or knowledge of the two Testaments, or the display of twofold charity? For since the whole body of divine Scripture has a threefold sense—historical, allegorical, and moral—wherever the historical sense is expounded, it is resolved into one of these two branches, allegory or morality. Often the interpretation of one and the same history is brought into the sense of both branches, so that sometimes what the history says ought to be understood only mystically. Of this threefold sense of divine Scripture it is said: “Write them threefold in your heart” (Prov. 22). They are enriched, as it were, with twin offspring of the two Testaments because whatever they expound they take either from the Old or from the New Testament. Moreover, they multiply in the offspring of twofold charity, because love of God—whom they delightfully taste in Scripture itself—draws them to the labour of expounding holy Scripture; and likewise love of neighbour, for whose benefit they willingly undertake this occupation.

Among them there is no barrenness of any of these twin offspring, because all whom the weight of earthly activity does not burden and whom the most health-giving fountain of the divine Spirit washes can delightfully devote themselves to the business of expounding books with this twofold intention and motherly love: looking by intention to allegory and morality, by material to the Old and New Testaments, and by love to God and neighbour.

[Col. 1151C] **VERSE 3.—“Your lips are like a scarlet ribbon, and your speech is sweet; your cheeks are like a piece of pomegranate, apart from that which lies hidden within.”**

Among the praises of this sevenfold beauty is: “Your lips are like a scarlet ribbon, and your speech is sweet.” The lips may be understood as preachers of the divine word, or as those who elegantly pronounce the divine utterances by reading or singing them and kindle God’s people to divine fear and love by sweetness of meaning or voice. Hence they are compared to a scarlet ribbon: just as a ribbon binds and arranges hair so that it is not scattered, so holy preachers—or those who sweetly sing or read in the Church—join the listening people by the bond of peace and unanimity, and make them sound in harmony with one another in faith and love. For the ribbon of subjects, as it were, clashes and is discordant with the ribbon of holy preachers when they neither believe rightly nor act rightly. But when they are led by the preachers’ proclamation to truth and rectitude, they are, as it were, joined to them in faith and love, since they believe and love what the preachers themselves believe and love, and agree with them in the law of God. When they hear and heed the same truth proclaimed either in beautiful harmony or with the assertion of convincing reason, through the grace of compunction they bind themselves more firmly in the love of God.

Hence the ribbon to which they are compared is said to be scarlet. Scarlet is fiery in colour; and what is charity but fire? For when people, hearing of that highest good which is God, are moved to act well in order to attain that good itself, they are surely kindled by the fire of divine charity.

The Church’s lips, therefore—that is, holy preachers, or those dutifully arranging the preaching itself—are like a scarlet ribbon, because through the dignity and sweetness of the things which they preach they inflame the minds of their hearers with love for eternal life.

Hence it is added, “Your speech is sweet.” For the weak are drawn by gentler precepts and repelled by harsher ones. Under the Law sinners were commanded to be punished and wrongdoers received retaliation, when they were ordered to give “eye for eye, tooth for tooth” (Exod. 21). But in the time of grace the Church’s speech is sweet, because mercy rather than punishment is promised to sinners confessing their sins; and wrongdoers, if they look back, are not punished by retaliation but are absolved by repentance. Or holy preachers are a scarlet ribbon for this reason: by their preaching they restrain superfluous thoughts and actions, so that through devotion to holy action they may burn with the fire of divine charity and, through contempt of the world, may become red by a kind of martyrdom of the mind. For scarlet is both fiery and red, and those who burn with divine charity do not fear to suffer every adversity for God.

Further, how great is the beauty of the seventh-fold comeliness that proclaims the modesty of the disciplined in the Church, when it is said: “Your cheeks are like a piece of pomegranate, apart from that which lies hidden within.” The pomegranate is called *malum Punicum* because its kind was brought from the Punic region; it is also called *malum granatum*, “seeded apple,” because it contains a multitude of seeds. A piece of pomegranate is red outwardly, white inwardly, and smells more fragrant when broken than when whole. Thus the cheeks of the Church are said to be like a piece of pomegranate because the discipline of religious people, outwardly displaying the habit of honourable conduct in the house of discipline, bears modesty externally in the beauty of a rosy face; this proceeds from the gracious activity of a mind inwardly shining white. For the brightness of chastity that shines in the mind produces the blush of modesty in the face when a religious soul fears to commit something which would detract from its honour or discipline. Hence, conversely, the prophet says to a reprobate mind, unashamed to sin boldly: “You have the forehead of a harlot; you refused to blush” (Jer. 3).

A downcast countenance, therefore, and a dignified composure of the eyes are the sign of a religious and modest mind. Accordingly, those honourably composed in conduct are fittingly said to be like a piece of pomegranate, since they reverently show outwardly in bearing and conduct the beauty of holiness which they bear inwardly in intention and thought. And although outward gesture, religiously composed, is praiseworthy, that inward disposition of the soul known to God alone is far more praiseworthy, since the holy soul scarcely or never suffices outwardly to display how greatly it burns inwardly with divine charity.

Therefore, when the bridegroom said beforehand of the bride, “Your cheeks are like a piece of pomegranate,” he added: “Apart from that which lies hidden within.”

For what is that which lies hidden within except the power of charity, which appears to God alone and produces whatever honour or holiness it works outwardly?

The disciplined hearts of holy Church, therefore, are like a piece of pomegranate, apart from that which lies hidden within. For they outwardly exhibit, through the form of patience and modesty, the brightness of virtues which they inwardly possess through God’s grace. But they leave to God’s judgment that very power which contains, through the operation of the Holy Spirit, the whole efficacy that gives life and strength within them. Thus they stand indeed in great hope, but they are not without fear even in their hope. They feel within themselves the power of divine charity, but they do not know by what weighing in God’s judgment the conduct and life which they proclaim from that charity will be assessed.

[Col. 1153B] **VERSE 4.—“Your neck is like the tower of David, built with battlements; a thousand shields hang from it, all the armour of the mighty.”**

In the sixth place, the praise of the enumerated beauty is set forth thus: “Your neck is like the tower of David, built with battlements; a thousand shields hang from it, all the armour of the mighty.” Above we observed that the neck signifies the lofty eloquence of doctors, and is compared to a tower because it rises to height through the profundity of words and meanings. But this is called David’s tower—that is, the tower of “strong hand”—because whatever beauty or loftiness the utterances of doctors contain, whether spoken or written, is surely due to the grace of him who is spiritually called strong of hand, because it belongs to him

> To spare the conquered, and subdue the proud.  
> (Virgil, *Aeneid* IV.654)

As it is written of him: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (Jas. 4). For he rests in the hearts of the humble and fittingly distributes to them the gifts of his knowledge, as pleases him: to one in this way, to another in that.

But what are the battlements by which this tower is built, except the fortifications of strong and lofty maxims? For by the authorities of the maxims which doctors thunder forth, the Church is fortified and strengthened against the doctrines and deeds of the perverse, so that, founded upon the rock of faith, it need not fear any assaults of a contrary and hostile party. In this tower are seen the counsels and precepts of virtues, and the wondrous deeds and miracles of the holy Fathers.

Hence it is added: “A thousand shields hang from it.” For what does the number one thousand, which is used for perfection, signify except universality? A thousand shields are all the teachings of virtues, which defend us against the attacking devices of vices. For if

> Avarice boils within you, and you are tormented by wretched desire,  
> there are words and utterances by which you may soothe this pain  
> and cast off a great part of the disease.  
> Are you swollen with love of praise? There are sure remedies  
> which can restore you after a little book has been read through three times with care.  
> [Col. 1154A] Envious, angry, sluggish, drunken, amorous—  
> no one is so savage that he cannot be softened,  
> provided only that he lends a patient ear to cultivation.  
> (Horace, *Epistles* I.1.39)

If the glory of this world delights you, hear the apostle John saying: “Do not love the world or the things that are in the world; if anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him” (1 John 2). If you are tempted by the vice of vainglory, hear the Apostle saying: “Let us not become desirous of vainglory” (Gal. 6). If you are tempted by avarice, hear the same Apostle saying: “For God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Cor. 9). If you are tempted by lust, hear him again saying: “Do you not know that your bodies are the temple of the Holy Spirit? If anyone violates this temple, He will destroy [Col. 1154B] him; for the temple of God is holy, which temple you are” (1 Cor. 6). 146 If anger assails the mind, hear what is said: “Be angry, and do not sin”; and, “the anger of a man does not work the righteousness of God” (Ps. 4). If the sin of disobedience corrupts the mind, hear it written: “Obedience is better than sacrifices, and hearkening than offering the fat of rams; for resistance is like the sin of divination, and refusal to comply like the crime of idolatry” (1 Sam. 15). If impatience weighs down the mind, attend to what is written: “The patient man is better than the conqueror of cities” (Prov. 16). If pride presses upon the mind, hear it written: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (1 Pet. 5).

Behold, these are the shields which hang from the tower and fortifications [Col. 1154C] of the most eloquent doctors, whose judgments and authorities are the Church’s strongest defense. Their precepts and counsels, moreover, are for every soul both instruction and protection against vices and sins. Therefore a thousand shields hang from it, because there is no vice against which a defense cannot be found in the whole body of sayings and writings of the holy Catholic Fathers. But because these same writings recount the mighty deeds of the saints and the precepts of the divine law most steadfastly kept by them, it is fittingly added: “all the armor of the mighty.” There you will find how bravely those fought against vices and sins with the weapons of spiritual warfare, whose armor was the observance of the divine commands and [Col. 1154D] the imitation of the Fathers who went before them. Thus a thousand shields and all the armor of the mighty hang from it, because whatever strength one desires to seek against the enemies of the soul may be found in the most learned judgments and magnificent deeds of the Fathers.

But although fortifications and shields have the same office of defense, they nevertheless differ in this: fortifications stand immovably, whereas shields can be held and moved by the hand. What, then, may the fortifications be called except the miracles of the saints? And what are the shields but the eminent practice of holy virtues? In Holy Scripture, therefore, which the utterances of doctors set forth and commend, are related the wondrous miracles of the saints—things which we cannot perform and, as it were, move. Yet we can carry out works of virtue [Col. 1155A] and, as it were, holding them in the hand, set them in motion by our various efforts, each according to his measure, if we burn with the love of God.

Therefore from the neck of holy Church hang a thousand shields and all the armor of the mighty, because in Holy Scripture, which the eloquence of doctors unveils and adorns, she finds defensive protections and weapons of repulsion against the darts of vices in general.

**VERSE 5.—“Your two breasts are like two twin fawns of a roe, which feed among the lilies until the day breathes and the shadows decline.”**

147 The seventh commendation of the beauty already proclaimed is as follows: “Your two breasts are like two twin fawns of a roe, which feed among the lilies until the day breathes and the shadows decline.” As was shown above [Col. 1155B], the two breasts may signify the diligence of teachers in instructing the less advanced, through the twofold teaching of piety and knowledge: of piety, when they form them in the uprightness of the active and contemplative life, or in love of God and neighbor; of knowledge, when they instruct them by reading the Old and New Testaments, or by the historical and allegorical exposition of that same Scripture.

These two breasts are like two twin fawns of a roe, because those who instruct the less advanced in the Church are small in their own eyes. They act and teach in accordance with the doctrine of their elders, presume nothing from their own knowledge, follow the holy Fathers in life, conduct, and teaching—as children follow mothers—and so tend upward; daily progressing in these things in talent and understanding, they lead with themselves those whom they teach toward higher [Col. 1155C] things to be understood and desired. They are fittingly compared not simply to fawns, but to twins, on account of the two teachings of piety and knowledge which cling to one another inseparably, so that, as though born at one moment, neither is prior to the other in any respect.

For Christ’s Church has always had disciples of both lives, that is, the active and the contemplative; she has always flourished in love of both God and neighbor; she has always shone with knowledge of both Testaments. The two Testaments are so inseparably joined that one signifies or explains the other: the Old signifies the New, and the New expounds the Old. Likewise, love of God can in no way exist without love of neighbor, nor love of neighbor without love of God, [Col. 1155D] because each proves the other. For one who loves the neighbor is shown to love God, since love of God moves him to love his neighbor. Nor can one be a lover of the contemplative life who does not know the active life; nor does one possess the active life who does not desire the contemplative.

Thus the two, doing one and the same thing at the same time, are mutually entailed by the consequence of their existence. It follows that one who understands the Old Testament understands the New, since they are one—the former in figure, the latter in truth—and that one who loves the neighbor loves God, and conversely; for these must always exist together. Moreover, one cannot contemplate God who does not know how to act rightly. Therefore these two, being undivided in either case, are said to be twins, as though under one birth; [Col. 1156A] and they are proclaimed in the Church’s two breasts as the seventh and final element of beauty.

Historical and allegorical exposition, however, are not always joined so inseparably. Often pure history alone must be retained; sometimes allegory alone, when many things can stand according to the letter 148 which cannot stand at all according to the spirit, and some things are understood according to the spirit which can in no way be taken according to the letter.

But where they suitably concur, the aforementioned likeness of twins is not inappropriately observed, so that in the Church’s two breasts they may be proclaimed indivisibly, like two twin fawns of a roe. But because every pursuit of piety looks to a definite end—for nothing good is taught or learned except for the attainment of eternal life [Col. 1156B]—there follows:

“Which feed among the lilies until the day breathes and the shadows decline.” For the qualities of all the forms set forth above, which were proclaimed in the beauty of the Church’s breasts, feed among the lilies; that is, they are nourished in the brightness and fragrance of virtues. For no one advances in the uprightness of the active and contemplative life, or in love of God and neighbor, without the page of both Testaments, except through purity of mind and the exercise of good action.

And for how long? “Until the day breathes and the shadows decline”: that is, until the day of eternal blessedness dawns and the night of this mortality fails; and then what was here seen through [Col. 1156C] a mirror in an enigma shall be perfectly seen in truth, and what was here held in hope shall there be held in reality. There those two breasts, which we above distinguished in four ways, shall be seen on that eternal day, not in labor but in reward. The breathing of the day and the declining of the shadow signify this, for shadow signifies labor and day signifies reward.

The word *until*, however, is used not to establish a limit but in the sense of eternity, so that we may understand that in this life we must labor in good works until we attain eternal life in blessed rest.

**VERSE 6.—“I will go to the mountain of myrrh and to the hill of frankincense.”**

After the Beloved, in the body of the beloved—that is, [Col. 1156D] the Church—has enumerated the kinds of beauty marked by outstanding variety, he adds the general beauty which all members must possess who wish to belong to her body. This beauty is attained in two ways: by mortifying the flesh and by the petition of a devout spirit. For one who walks according to the flesh and does not mortify the deeds of the flesh by the Spirit does not belong to that beautiful body of the Church which has neither spot nor wrinkle; for those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires (Gal. 5). The petition of a devout spirit, moreover, springs from the most merciful breathing of the divine Spirit, because the Spirit himself intercedes for us with inexpressible groanings (Rom. 8). Indeed, he is said to “intercede” because he causes intercession: for the mind [Col. 1157A] which he fills he moves into the grace of compunction, 149 so that it groans either from consideration of its sins or from the delay of the kingdom to come; groaning, it prays; praying, it sometimes receives either forgiveness of sins or the crown of the desired blessedness.

Thus mortification of the flesh is expressed by myrrh, on account of the bitterness of toil and suffering. The petition of a devout spirit, however, is understood by frankincense, because of the, as it were, smoking sorrow of slight compunction or penitence, or the burning of love, from which the pure prayer of a supplicating mind rises to God. But although both virtues—namely, mortifying the flesh and praying frequently—are of the highest worth and usefulness in the body [Col. 1157B] of holy Church, that is nevertheless shown to be more excellent which is acquired by greater labor of mind and body.

Accordingly, in order that their merit may be distinguished, myrrh is named a mountain and frankincense a hill. He therefore says, “I will go to the mountain of myrrh and to the hill of frankincense”; that is, to express the matter more plainly in other words: I shall go, through grace which cooperates with and bestows grace, to the minds of those who labor with the intention of mortifying themselves against vices and sins and who strive to achieve this through continual prayers, so that by my indwelling I may prove worthy those whom the beauty of these virtues delights; for I am ready both to assist those who labor and to grant the petitions of those who pray.

[Col. 1157C] **VERSE 7.—“You are wholly beautiful, my beloved, and there is no blemish in you.”**

Since, he says, I have above extolled you with praises of sevenfold beauty, and then have graciously observed in you the mountain of myrrh and hill of frankincense—for the submission of mortified flesh is a great elevation of the mind, from which arises the contemplative intercession of a free spirit to God—by mortification of the flesh vices and sins are so lulled to sleep that nothing remains which resists the spirit. Rather, there is such purity and serenity of mind that you can admit no stains in your body which might blot out the grace of your beauty.

Therefore, “You are wholly beautiful, my beloved, and there is no blemish in you.” There is no blemish [Col. 1157D] in you, I say—that is, it has no abiding existence; for even if some blemish should arise briefly through human frailty, it is quickly driven away by compunction of heart, humble confession, and daily prayer.

**VERSE 8.—“Come from Lebanon, my bride; come from Lebanon, come. You shall be crowned from the summit of Amana, from the peak of Sanir and Hermon, from the lairs of lions, from the mountains of leopards.”**

Therefore, “Come from Lebanon, my bride; come from Lebanon”: that is, because every lust of the flesh has now been conquered and mortified, you have been made white through purity of heart and body. “Come from Lebanon”—that is, from this your whitening; for Lebanon is interpreted “whitening.” Come not once only, but again, because you ought not merely to please in thought [Col. 1158A] but also in deed. Come, I say, from this your whitening; for you cannot come unless you are white. And, as my Bride, now made worthy through this whitening of my embraces, enter also into partnership in my kingdom, so that henceforth you may possess an unchangeable state and condition of a whitened soul.

Come a third time, because it does not suffice merely to please in thought and deed unless you also please by perseverance in that good work itself, which is the present assurance of future blessedness.

Or: in order that you may proclaim faith in the holy Trinity, come by preaching the Father, come by preaching the Son, come by preaching the Holy Spirit; distinguish one God in these three persons, establish the holy sacraments of religion, and strengthen the whole world in the unchangeable truth of this faith.

Or: come in faith, come in hope, come in love; that is, by faith undertake every perfection of good work, by hope lay it up, by love embrace it. Or, with respect to the sacrament of my body and blood and the reality of the sacrament: come by believing faithfully, come by administering it reverently, come by receiving it beneficially, so that, incorporated into me through this remedy for the soul, you may truly be called my bride and beloved.

But you cannot come to such incorporation except from Lebanon—that is, either made white by baptism, or, if through your fault you have been cut off from my body, restored to your former whiteness by the fountain of penitence.

[Col. 1158C] Spread all these teachings of truth and faith through every region of the whole world, so that through you my praise may be proclaimed to the ends of the earth. Let those who seek my sacraments seek, recognize, and receive them, and let their conversion become your reward. For this is what follows: “You shall be crowned from the summit of Amana, from the peak of Sanir and Hermon, from the lairs of lions, from the mountains of leopards.”

By these three mountain-names are denoted three kinds of worldly heights. By destroying them holy Church attained perfect peace; by humbling them she deserved an everlasting crown.

The first height was found among worshipers of idols. Though through the good of reason implanted within them and the beauty of visible things they had known the Creator of all those things, [Col. 1158D] they did not glorify him as God or give him thanks. Instead, they became vain in their reasonings, and their foolish heart was darkened, because they exchanged the truth of God for a lie and served the creature rather than the Creator (Rom. 1). In this way, to despise God was a certain height of pride.

The second height was the persecution carried out by the reprobate. Opposing God by their perverse conduct, they persecuted the heralds of truth and justice with great injuries, afflicting them with many punishments and driving them even to death. Thus to resist God himself in his elect was likewise a certain height of pride.

151 The third height, moreover, was the perverse speech or writing of heretics, by which they tried to destroy the true faith through human reason and labored to corrupt the simplicity of Holy Scripture with a certain arrogance of dialectical speech. While seeking to appear wise, they became foolish, desiring in a kind of pride of mind merely to display their own knowledge.

[Col. 1159A] Now *Amana* is interpreted “night-bird,” *Sanir* “tooth of watchfulness,” and *Hermon* “anathema.” These meanings of the names may first be applied to the very head of all the wicked, of whom it is written: “He himself is king over all the children of pride” (Job 41), so that he may be called night-bird, tooth of watchfulness, and anathema. The night-bird, which is also called an owl or a light-shunner, rightly signifies the devil, who hates the light—that is, good works—and loves sins, which are works of darkness. As it is written, “He sleeps in the shadow, in the secret place of his chamber” (Job 40), because, when he subjugates by consent the minds around which he flies in temptation, he makes for himself, as it were, a resting-place in the shadow of sin.

He is also called a tooth of watchfulness because it is written of him that, “like a roaring lion, he goes about seeking whom he may devour” (1 Pet. 5); his wakefulness is never resting from an evil will. He is not inappropriately called anathema also, because he has been separated and, as it were, excommunicated from the fellowship of good spirits; and he hastens to drag others with him to destruction, so that, as he himself is, they too may become anathema—accursed or set apart—from God.

[Col. 1159C] What belongs to the head, therefore, may not inappropriately belong also to the members. We said a little above that these three mountain-names can signify three types of worldly heights, which we have located in three classes of perverse persons: worshipers of idols, persecutors of saints, and heretics.

But it must be considered how the interpretations of these names suit such persons. Idol-worshipers may certainly not absurdly be called a night-bird, on account of the blindness and fickleness of their minds: blindness, because, just as this bird flees the day and wanders more by night, so they, refusing to receive the light of truth and faith, embraced rather the darkness of unbelief, until they were delivered from this unbelief by the grace of God. They are compared to a bird also because of fickleness, [Col. 1159D] for they wandered in such uncertainty of error that they could grasp nothing true, nothing stable, in their worship.

Persecutors of the saints, however, may be called a tooth of watchfulness on account of the savagery and cruelty of their persecutions: the tooth itself being the savagery, and the watchfulness the persecutions that know no rest. For it is written in Jeremiah that, when the Lord said, “What do you see, Jeremiah?” he answered, “I see a wakeful rod”; and the Lord said, “You have spoken well, for I shall watch over my word to perform it” (Jer. 1). Therefore, just as in this passage the wakeful rod signifies correction which does not rest because of the people’s sins until it is fulfilled, so the tooth of watchfulness may signify the savagery of persecutions, wakeful in the punishment and killing of the saints.

[Col. 1160A] Heretics, however, are called *anathema*, that is, separated from God, because, when on account of the perversity of their faith they are separated from communion with the Church by the sword of cutting-off—that is, excommunication—they are surely separated from the Head, that is, Christ. The Apostle says: “If anyone should preach to you anything other than what you received from us, let him be anathema” (Gal. 1). But heretics preached something other than what had been preached by the apostles; therefore they were anathema, and so they went forth anathematized and excommunicated from the Church.

Accordingly, the Bridegroom cries “Come” three times to the bride, to show that she is to be crowned threefold from their head or summit: “You shall be crowned,” he says, “from the summit of Amana, from the peak of Sanir and Hermon.” But how shall you be crowned?

First, from the summit of Amana—that is, from the worshipers of idols, who, converted through your preaching, grew in faith and action like good trees. Their conversion and progress were surely an ornament upon your head. Then you shall also be crowned from the peak of Sanir—that is, from the persecutors of the saints, who, through your exhortations and the terror inspired by miracles, laid aside their savagery and submitted themselves to Christ’s yoke. Their conversion and humbling likewise increase your crown as the recompense for your labor.

[Col. 1160C] Thirdly, you shall be crowned from the peak of Hermon—that is, from the proud eloquence of heretics. After they have been turned from the perversity of their false knowledge by your reasonable eloquence joined with the wisdom of sound teaching, they defend with the strongest assertion of truth the faith which they formerly attacked. Their reformation to the right faith is your crown and the recompense of your labor.

And since, conversely, just as the soul of a righteous person is the dwelling-place of God (Wis. 7), so the soul of the perverse is the habitation of an unclean spirit, there follows: “From the lairs of lions, from the mountains of leopards.” Those whom we distinguished under the names of the three mountains may rightly be called lairs of lions because, when evil spirits have subjected them to themselves through wickedness, those spirits, nourishing that very wickedness in them through their suggestion and the persons’ consent, rest as it were in certain lairs. Lions are evil spirits, which roar in every direction in order to deceive the human race, thirsting for the soul’s blood—that is, desiring to take away from the soul the nourishment of virtues. [Col. 1160D] For just as a person’s life is in the blood, so the soul’s life is in the nourishment of virtues.

The mountains of leopards, moreover, are the same hearts of the reprobate set upon pride; and leopards are likewise the evil spirits, because of their ferocity and the manifold forms—like variegated colors—of their countless deceits. Therefore the Church is crowned from the lairs of lions and the mountains of leopards because, by her preaching, she makes dwellings of divine grace out of the minds of those who, devoted to earthly and perverse acts, had been lairs of demons. She likewise makes worthy of divine indwelling in a spirit of humility the hearts of those who, claiming a proud and, as it were, singular life or knowledge, have produced the varied colors of sects and heresies. From [Col. 1161A] their conversion and progress, assuredly, the fruit of her pious labor is increased.

**VERSE 9.—“You have wounded my heart, my sister, my bride; you have wounded my heart with one of your eyes and with one lock of your neck.”**

Still more does the Bridegroom—Christ, that is, speaking to the Church or to the soul of each believer—approve and marvel at the zeal and progress of the bride, and at the beauty and merit of that progress. Above he first enumerated seven parts of her beauty, as it were in her outward adornment; then he expounded a twofold quality of inward adornment; and thirdly he offered a threefold crown in the progress of others. In all these things he showed the great pleasure of his condescension. Now he introduces a more eminent and, as it were, supreme part of beauty, divided in two, by which the sister and bride, through the greatness of her worth, has not merely moved but wounded the Bridegroom’s heart in that same good pleasure: sister through faith, bride through holy and true love.

But what is this twofold part: “one of the eyes” and “one lock of the neck”? If in each person’s perception we consider the two eyes as in one body, we place one on the right and the other on the left. The eye on the left side is wonder at all visible things, marvellously and orderly disposed. From considering them, it gathers, though only through a mirror and in an enigma, something of the Creator’s greatness, beauty, and power, and of his wisdom and goodness in their ordering and governance. [Col. 1161C] But the eye on the right side is drawn beyond these visible things when it is freed from every contamination of this worldly desire and fixed, with the gaze of contemplative love, upon the very face of the Creator.

The Bridegroom’s heart is wounded by this one of the bride’s eyes because, when a holy mind by the force of divine love so joins itself to heavenly grace that it receives the name *Seraphim*, that is, “burning one,” then by its very ardor it inflicts upon the divinity joined to it, as it were, a wound of love.

By the one lock of the neck we understand the subtlety of preaching. But though there are many subtleties of preaching, what is its one and singular subtlety, as it were one lock of the neck? It is according to the articles [Col. 1161D] of faith, both in the divinity of the Trinity and in Christ’s incarnation. What, then, is the one lock in the divinity of the Trinity? One God in three persons, whose incomprehensible rationale of divinity we are commanded to believe and are not permitted to investigate. And what is the one lock of the neck in Christ’s incarnation? God made man. For who can possibly investigate how the Word is embodied, how the supreme and life-giving Spirit is animated within the mother’s womb, or how he who has no beginning comes to exist and is conceived?

But in this one lock of the neck in both cases the Beloved’s heart is wounded, because, when each person believes what human reason cannot grasp, he is strongly joined in the love of almighty God through the merit of faith. For faith has no merit where human reason provides proof. [Col. 1162A] Faith is not contrary to reason, but above reason; therefore one who wishes to believe nothing except what he comprehends by reason—like the philosophers—has no merit in his faith. But one has faith who believes what is not contrary to reason and yet is above reason. Hence the Apostle says: “The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart; this is the word of faith” (Rom. 10). Christ likewise is not contrary to reason, but above reason. Thus in one of the eyes love is expressed, and in one lock of the neck faith.

But because faith working through love is the foundation of all good, while without love there is no virtue even in faith—for the demons believe and tremble (Jas. 2)—these two cannot be separated where they unite to God a mind of perfect virtue. Therefore the Beloved’s heart is wounded by the one eye of contemplative love and by the one lock—that is, the subtlety of faith, which is established chiefly in two things, namely the mystery of divinity and the sacrament of the incarnation—because by the force of a mind abounding in faith and love it is, as it were, penetrated toward fuller knowledge. Hence, repeating the words not once but twice, he says: “You have wounded my heart, my sister, my bride; you have wounded my heart.” [Col. 1162B] For both faith working through love and love advancing through faith are highly commendable in the eyes of almighty God. Faith is the foundation of every good thing; love, building upon that foundation, is its beauty and adornment.

“One of the eyes” and “one lock of the neck” may also be understood in another way: as identity and immutability in the mind’s state of commitment to good. In one of the eyes is the same, unfailing intention in spiritual actions; in one lock of the neck is the same, enduring disposition of humility and lowliness of mind. Hence it is written: “A holy man abides in wisdom like the sun, but a fool changes like the moon” (Sir. 27). And it is written of the cows carrying the ark of God that they went straight ahead and walked by one road, turning neither to the right nor to the left (1 Sam. 6).

What is the ark of God except the mind of a saint, in which divinity is contained through the gifts of diverse graces? But one who bears it must not turn aside from the way of righteousness, lest, walking on a crooked path, the divine grace depart from the mind and he no longer be said to bear the ark of God. “One of the eyes,” then, is the one way of those who walk rightly before themselves, as is written of the holy creatures that each went forward before its face. “One of the eyes” is the same countenance of the mind, always forgetting what lies behind and stretching toward what lies ahead (Phil. 3). [Col. 1162D] One lock of the neck is the same constant smallness and slenderness of humility, so great that, though a holy person is of great merit before God, he so despises himself before men that he scarcely permits what he is to be seen in himself—just as one lock, though it is something, is scarcely seen or held.

One lock of the neck is the constancy of a mind humbling itself to God through obedience, persisting so in the condition of this resolve that it is neither raised up by prosperity nor dissolved by adversity. Conversely, it is said of a reprobate mind that it “walked with outstretched neck and uplifted head” (Isa. 3); and of the Jews, who did not humble themselves to God through obedience, that they were stiff-necked and obstinate of heart (Acts 7). Thus the Beloved is wounded by one of the eyes and one lock of the neck, because he is greatly pleased by one and the same persevering spiritual intention and discretion in actions, and likewise by a single, stable humility of the mind bowed to God through obedience.

[Col. 1163A] **VERSE 10.—“How beautiful are your breasts, my sister, my bride! Your breasts are more beautiful than wine, and the fragrance of your ointments than all spices.”**

We must carefully consider what this praiseworthy beauty of the bride’s breasts means—that is, of the Church’s breasts, or those of any holy soul. For just as breasts provide nourishment for the bodies of little children and those newly born, so there can be certain spiritual nourishments by which souls still tender and weak receive some growth in holiness, either from themselves or from others: they themselves from themselves through exercise; others from them through instruction.

First we must consider what these breasts are; then what their beauty is, so praised by the Bridegroom. I do not think it contrary to reason if we call these breasts knowledge of truth and love of virtues. But since there are two creatures, one spiritual and the other bodily, we believe it not unfitting if we assign to each two qualities of growth, as it were two breasts. For as there are two creatures, as we have said—one spiritual and the other bodily—so there is also a twofold good of the creature: one spiritual, the other bodily. The good of the spiritual creature consists especially in the two things set forth above under the signification of breasts, namely knowledge of truth and love of virtue.

[Col. 1163C] The good of the bodily creature is either in itself or outside itself. Its good in itself is the soundness of its senses and affections according to the five senses; its good outside itself is an ordered distribution among creatures. For whatever is corrupted or amended is for humanity, and whatever is good or evil is good or evil for humanity. Since all goods, whether inward or outward, are gifts of almighty God, the deprivation of either is God’s wrath and humanity’s punishment; conversely, their bestowal is God’s grace and humanity’s salvation.

Knowledge of truth and love of virtue, however, must be considered in a particular way. In each soul they continually receive increase, as though from certain breasts and udders of exercises, because the exercises themselves admit of more and less: more if they continue, less if they cease; that is, according as persons know truth and love virtue more or less. These two are joined to one another as naturally as two breasts in one body, because no one can love virtue unless he has known truth, and one who knows truth cannot but love virtue.

[Col. 1164A] But if we consider the whole body of the Church universally, as regards herself she does not receive more and less in knowing truth or loving virtue, since she possesses imperfect knowledge of truth and love of virtue. Yet with respect to the others whom she believes to be in Christ, their growth in holiness is increased daily from knowledge of truth and love of virtue.

In both cases there are first breasts and then udders: for just as breasts belong to girls who cannot yet provide the nourishment of milk but nevertheless hold the hope of providing it, while udders belong to women who have an abundance of such nourishment, so the Church in those whom she nourishes—or each soul in itself—first has a certain hope through the aptitude of a mind applying itself to good things and always advancing toward better things. Then, grown as it were mature through faith and love, it begins to possess such full knowledge of truth and love of virtue that it can nourish all its senses, inward and outward, and through God’s grace lead them to perfection.

By outward senses here we mean senses to be nourished not so that they may function better bodily, but spiritually, lest, if badly guarded, they become instruments of sin, as the prophet rebukes sinners concerning them, saying: “Death entered through your windows” (Jer. 9).

[Col. 1164C] The Church offers the nourishment of these her breasts in three ways: through things, deeds, and words. Through things, as in the sacraments, without which no salvation can come to the soul; through deeds, as in the acts of the saints, by whose examples it is stirred and invited; through words, as in the precepts and admonitions of Holy Scripture, by which it is daily nourished unto eternal life.

We have stated what the bride’s breasts are; now we must say what their beauty is, thus praised by the Bridegroom. This beauty is not accidental, such as may be present or absent without corruption of the subject, but essential, consisting in the property of its own nature. For what is it for knowledge of truth and love of virtue to be beautiful except for them to exist? To know truth and love virtue is beautiful, just as it is beautiful to be chaste, just, humble, patient, or obedient. Chastity, justice, humility, patience, and obedience are a kind of beauty; and these, as we have said, are not beautiful accidentally in the subjects which participate in them, but essentially in themselves. For if they exist, they are beautiful; if they are not beautiful, neither do they exist, because when they are corrupted, they are no longer beautiful, since they cease to be what they were.

[Col. 1164D] For when chastity, or any other virtue, is corrupted, how is it beautiful, since that whose corruption is evil no longer exists?

Since, therefore, the good of the soul consists especially in two things, by which it is nourished as from breasts unto eternal life—knowledge of truth and love of virtue—the corruption of knowledge may be called ignorance, of which the Apostle says: “Whoever is ignorant shall be ignored” (1 Cor. 14); the corruption of love is cupidity, which is the root of all evils (1 Tim. 6). And the more this ignorance and cupidity increase, the more the soul’s good is corrupted. For the soul, being an incorporeal substance, cannot be corrupted in its substance, but only in the good which it participates in; and this is worn away and diminished in it all the more as it is increasingly deformed by sins.

The breasts or bosom, therefore, of the holy Church in general, or of each holy soul in particular, are beautiful, because the former shines forth to her children and the latter within herself with so abundant a fertility of good perceptions in the knowledge of truth and love of virtue that from them flow the nourishment of all spiritual goods; the natural goods also—such as reason, intelligence, and memory—flourish more vigorously, and thus the whole beauty of the soul is formed by participation in these things. [Col. 1165B]

But what is meant by these breasts being called more beautiful than wine, when “in wine is excess” (Eph. V), whereas in these breasts there is holy and sober delight of soul, and consequently no proper comparison between the two can possibly exist? Certainly, by the figure of *tapeinosis*, which is the humbling of a great thing, these are called more beautiful than wine—not because there is any praiseworthy beauty in wine, but because the aforesaid things, namely the knowledge of truth and the love of virtue, are better and more beautiful to the rational soul, on account of their usefulness and sweetness, than all the delights of the world signified by wine: for these corrupt the soul by participation in them, whereas those restore it.

In the same way, moreover, concerning what follows: “And the fragrance of your ointments above all spices”—if by the fragrance of ointments we understand the good reputation of virtues, what comparison can there be between spiritual and corruptible things? For there can be corruption of the good found in a spiritual creature, and corruption of the good found in a bodily creature. Since there are two creatures, spiritual and bodily, as we have already said above, there are likewise two goods: one in the spiritual creature and the other in the bodily creature. The good of the spiritual creature is virtue; the good of the bodily creature is an ordered distribution among creatures. The corruption of the good that occurs in the spiritual creature—as sin and fault in the soul—is either punishment, or tends toward punishment. Therefore, by the incorruption of spiritual good we are united to God; but by the incorruption of bodily good we are not only not united to God, but are very often separated from him, when through delight in it we often forget ourselves and are led away from the good of our purpose; while by the corruption of that bodily good, when we are afflicted, we are sometimes brought back to good things. What comparison can there be amid such dissimilarity? [Col. 1165C–D]

But in this comparison there is an argument from the lesser to the greater, in this manner: if bodily goods—that is, the fragrance of spices—have such sweetness, how much more spiritual goods, that is, the fragrance of virtues: incorruptible good is incomparable with corruptible good, just as the incorruptible soul is incomparable with the corruptible body.

**159.** I call the soul incorruptible, however, according to the substance of its nature, which is simple and incorporeal; just as the incorruptible good consisting in the soul is said to be so according to substance, not according to an addition. For “good” can be said in two ways, substantively and adjectivally. Good in itself is not corrupted, but is said to be corrupted by the privation of good, when it departs from the soul and is changed into evil; just as the soul itself is not corrupted in itself, but is said to be corrupted by the privation of good, because the privation of good is evil. [Col. 1166A]

Therefore it is said: “The fragrance of your ointments is above all spices,” as though it said: “The renown and reputation of your virtues are better and more beneficial to you than all the delights of this world, because these kill, whereas those give life.”

[Col. 1166B] But if in another way we wish to refer both parts—namely, the fragrance of ointments and all spices—to a spiritual meaning, we must consider what this special fragrance of the beloved’s ointments is, and what are all the spices to which that fragrance is so greatly preferred. For if we take all spices to mean all virtues, what will be those particular virtues that are preferred to the entire body of virtues? It does not seem unreasonable to us if we call these virtues faith, hope, and charity. For without these virtues all other virtues are, as it were, idle; for it is written that “without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. XI). Since no one can please God without faith, it is clear that no good works can bring salvation without faith. But whoever, believing, does good works, undoubtedly does so in hope of future goods; and each person loves those things which he hopes to obtain, and whatever good he does, he does through love, because unless he loved, he would not labor to obtain them. [Col. 1166C]

Therefore, since no good works can exist without these—that is, faith, hope, and charity—these are rightly preferred to all virtues. Thus it is said: “The fragrance of your ointments is above all spices,” as though it said: “Above all virtues, faith, hope, and charity give forth fragrance in you; they make you perfectly a bride and beloved.”

But why are these called ointments? Because, just as many kinds of herbs, when gathered into one in order to make a certain compound ointment, take the name of the ointment itself from that ingredient from which they have greater power, so the ointments of the Church, or of any holy soul, are principally said to be whatever good works have been compounded with the seasoning of faith, hope, and charity. For they are not otherwise effective unless they have been named through the addition of these, so that one may say: “This ointment is a compound of faith, hope, and charity.” For example, someone possesses humility, chastity, patience, obedience, and certain other virtues, whose combination can be called a kind of spiritual ointment. But it will be entirely ineffective unless faith, hope, and charity are there. Again, someone may not possess all the virtues just mentioned, but has others; yet even this person cannot have from them an approved ointment without [Col. 1167A] the addition of these three virtues. Whatever virtues, therefore, or however many virtues anyone possesses, he must never lack these three if he desires to possess what suffices for his salvation. Since, then, in the Church some are endowed with these virtues, others with those, some with more and some with fewer, while faith, hope, and charity always adhere to them, it may rightly be said not in the singular, “the fragrance of your ointment,” but in the plural, “the fragrance of your ointments.” Yet this fragrance is above all spices, because virtues mixed with these give forth fragrance and have power; those lacking them, even if they give forth fragrance, remain ineffective. It follows: “Your lips are a dripping honeycomb.”

**VERSE 11.—**“Your lips, bride, are a dripping honeycomb; honey and milk are under your tongue, and the fragrance of your garments is like the fragrance of incense.”

[Col. 1167B] What should we understand by the lips of the bride, except the preaching of the two Testaments? For just as lips are arranged in the body so that one is upper and the other lower, so the Old Testament is earlier and the New later. And because speech is expressed through the lips, the preaching of these two Testaments is fittingly understood through the lips. But what does it mean that these lips are called a dripping honeycomb? A honeycomb, indeed, is honey in wax. And what is honey in wax except divinity in humanity? What else does the preaching of the two Testaments proclaim than God made man for the redemption of the human race—one signifying this by figure, the other presenting the thing signified in truth? Whatever the Church preaches concerning Christ concerns both his divinity and his humanity. [Col. 1167C]

Who does not know that honey is sweet and wax is soft? Christ, through his miracles and preaching, was sweet by reason of his divinity; through the passion of his body, he was soft and pliable by reason of his humility. Hence he could be seized and killed, because God—immeasurable, incomprehensible, and invisible—through humility made himself visible and humble, like wax, soft and pliable. He was, as it were, honey in wax, because by bending down from heaven to earth and dispensing the light of his truth, he poured throughout the whole world the sweetness of his mercy and compassion. Therefore the lips of the holy Church are called a dripping honeycomb, because through her preaching the sweetness and grace of the whole divine dispensation carried out for the human race—and now daily carried out in the sacraments and in the realities of the sacraments—is made known. [Col. 1167D]

Concerning this it is further added: “Honey and milk are under your tongue,” that is, both in voice and in heart. For honey is the food of the strong and milk of infants; and the Church declares these in preaching, whether speaking or writing, so that the strong may be strengthened and the weak nourished. And because she confirms her preaching by good works, instructing her children by word and example, it is added:

“And the fragrance of your garments is like the fragrance of incense.” That garments should be understood as good works is taught by the authority of Holy Scripture. For it is written: “Blessed is he who keeps his garments, lest he walk naked and they see his shame” (Rev. XVI). [Col. 1168A] And in Solomon’s Proverbs: “Let your garments be white at all times” (Eccl. IX). To keep one’s garments is to possess good works, lest one suffer a shameful rejection at judgment if one appears naked, without the covering of virtues to conceal the ugliness of one’s sins. To have white garments is not to defile one’s works with the stains of vices, because works of virtue that are befouled by a mixture of vices are foul in God’s sight.

What, then, is the fragrance of garments except the renown and reputation of good actions? But this fragrance of garments is like the fragrance of incense, because no good work has any effectiveness unless it gives forth fragrance from the fire of charity. For just as burned incense smokes and gives forth fragrance, so the mind of a holy person, kindled by the fire of the Holy Spirit, smokes with the grace of compunction, whether lamenting its sins or longing for the heavenly homeland. And when through the grace of compunction it has recalled past fault, or through hope of future goods has wished for the brief duration of this life, it pursues the gains of piety more ardently, when it burns more inwardly through charity and gives forth fragrance more outwardly through good reputation. [Col. 1168B] For while its neighbors advance by its example, it makes their gains its own as well, because in its actions they learn how to acquire for themselves the merits of good works.

Therefore the bridegroom says to the bride—that is, to the Church or the faithful soul—**“The fragrance of your garments is like the fragrance of incense,”** as though he said: “The good fragrance of your virtues pleases me because, kindled from the fire of my charity, it gives forth fragrance; and so that fragrance is directed to me like a kind of prayer, just as incense is burned and offered to me alone in the devotion of prayers.” [Col. 1168C]

**VERSE 12.—**“A garden enclosed is my sister, my bride; a garden enclosed, a fountain sealed.”

Through the metaphorical figure, which occurs in four ways—namely, from animate to animate, from inanimate to inanimate—the bridegroom continues to proclaim the beauty of the bride, mingling the two modes of speech mentioned above, namely from animate to animate and from inanimate to inanimate. For when above he had declared the bride’s various beauty through eye and hair, breasts or bosom, and lips, which are parts of an animate body, and also through the fragrance of garments, which is a property of an inanimate body, he now, by the single mode that is from inanimate to animate, enumerates other praises of the beauty of her dignity through the likenesses of a garden, a fountain, and the outpourings of that garden, which are described by seven kinds: namely, cypress, nard, crocus, reed, cinnamon, myrrh, and aloe. Each of these must be discussed. [Col. 1168D]

Why, then, is the Church called a garden? Surely because of the shoots of virtues that continually spring up in her. Just as it is called a garden because something always arises there, so the Church is called a garden because works of virtues always arise in her through the progress of her children, whom she acquires daily in baptism, nourishes in faith, and advances in works of faith. [Col. 1169A]

But why is this garden enclosed? Either because of the invisible power and singular dignity of the sacraments; or because of the wonderful depth of Holy Scripture; or because of the impregnable strength of divine protection. For though the salvation of believers daily springs up from the invisible power of the sacraments, it is not open to everyone how the Holy Spirit works inwardly through each sacrament, both the power and the reality of the sacrament; why the sacraments themselves were instituted; how and by whom these same sacraments ought to be administered and received; what faith is required; what is the merit of faith; what order is required; what is the reason for order; finally, what reverence is due to the sacraments themselves, and what and how great is the fault of irreverence. Since all these things are so hidden and enclosed that they are not open to anyone except those who can say with the Apostle, “But God has revealed them to us through his Spirit” (I Cor. II), the Church in which these sacraments are contained is rightly called an enclosed garden. Hence even the ministers of the sacraments themselves are not admitted into such a garden unless they enter through him who says: “If anyone enters through me, he shall be saved” (John X). [Col. 1169B]

But because many obtain the offices of those sacraments through ecclesiastical ranks purchased for money, although before human eyes they seem to enter this garden, it is altogether closed against them before the eyes of God. And although they are called Christ’s ministers, they are not so, because they have not entered through the door but have climbed up another way. The Savior teaches what they are when, having said that he is the door, he adds: “He who does not enter through the door but climbs up another way, that one is a thief and a robber” (ibid.). [Col. 1169C]

See how enclosed this garden is: no one is granted access to it except through the door—that is, as it is written; but whoever does not approach through it is proclaimed a thief and robber. Hence Gregory says: “Why is it not considered that a blessing is turned into a curse for one who is promoted for this purpose, that he may become a heretic? I do not think that priesthood remains there.” Therefore this garden is truly enclosed to such persons. Though they possess the sacraments, they do not possess the reality of the sacraments, because they are shown to possess them not for salvation but for their own condemnation; and thus what they seem to possess before human eyes they lose before the eyes of God. [Col. 1169D]

Further, because of the depth of Holy Scripture, the Church of God is called an enclosed garden, because full entry into its meaning lies open to no one except by the guidance of him who has the key of David, “who opens and no one shuts, shuts and no one opens” (Rev. III). But those who have deserved entry into this garden through God’s grace—how many, how great, and how health-giving kinds of spiritual herbs do you suppose they will find in it, by which they can repel the diseases of the soul and restore a wounded mind? This garden is enclosed to Jews and heretics, because they do not understand the sacraments hidden within it but attend only to the letter. To them belongs that saying of Isaiah: “And the book shall be given to one who knows letters, and it shall be said to him: Read; and he will answer: I cannot, for it is sealed” (Isa. XXIX). [Col. 1170A]

This book—that is, the whole sequence of divine Scripture—is contained in this enclosed garden, that is, the Church: written within and without, that is, in literal and mystical sense; sealed with seven seals (Rev. V), that is, with the seven sacraments contained in the faith of the Church: namely, the Lord’s nativity, circumcision, baptism, passion, resurrection, ascension, and future judgment.

Therefore this garden is enclosed because of the sealed depth of this book, which no one can open except the Lamb who was slain, who alone was found worthy to unfasten this book and open its seven seals (Rev. V), because it belongs to his grace alone to open to human understanding the mysteries of divine Scripture that proclaim the power of those seven sacraments. [Col. 1170B]

The Church may also be called an enclosed garden because of the impregnable strength of divine protection, because, always fortified by divine aid, it cannot be shaken by the assault of evil spirits or of human beings. Though they make many and frequent attacks upon her, no power of their evil will enters into her, because she is enclosed by such a hedge of divine protection that they find absolutely no means of entering her from the opposing side. Hence, having received great security, she confidently cries aloud in the Psalm: “The Lord is my illumination and my salvation; whom shall I fear? The Lord is the protector of my life; of whom shall I be afraid?” (Ps. XXVI). “The Lord is my helper; I shall not fear what man may do to me. The Lord is my helper, and I shall look down upon my enemies” (Ps. CXVII). [Col. 1170C]

Therefore the Church is an enclosed garden under divine protection, because God has so strengthened her by his grace that the perverse cannot corrupt her faith, remove the institutions of the sacraments, or cast her down from the state of her inward peace. If they are permitted for a time to try her by outward affliction, this trial comes to her not for condemnation but for a crown.

And the garden is called enclosed not once but again, because God has enclosed her not only outwardly but inwardly as well, sanctifying and guarding her in every respect so that she may be preserved whole in body and soul until the day of our Lord Jesus Christ (I Thess. V): here indeed temporally, but afterward eternally. [Col. 1170D]

The Church is called not only an enclosed garden but also a sealed fountain, both because of the uniformity of baptism and because of the purity of holy preaching. For just as bodily filth is washed away by a fountain, so the filth of the soul—that is, sins—is washed away by baptism; and just as a weary body is refreshed by a fountain, so a soul failing in relation to God is raised up by holy preaching. This fountain is said to be sealed; but we must consider from what, by whom, and why it is sealed.

From what, therefore, is it sealed? In the sacrament of baptism: by form, reality, and intention; in preaching: by truth, sweetness, and usefulness. Thus the Church is rightly called a sealed fountain in these two things, baptism and preaching, because baptism helps nothing unless there are present both the form of the sacrament—that is, the invocation of the Holy Trinity—and the reality of the sacrament—that is, the power and efficacy of the sacrament—as well as intention, that is, the will to baptize in a catholic manner. Preaching, moreover, conveys nothing unless it is true so as to awaken faith, sweet so as to attract, and useful so as to instruct. [Col. 1171A] By these elements of the sacrament, as by certain seals, this fountain is opened, so that its special power, purity, and health-giving quality may be made known.

But by whom is it sealed? Surely by the Holy Spirit, who has marked it with the seal of his sevenfold grace. For from the institution and power of the sacraments, and from the usefulness of holy preaching, flow in the Church the streams of all spiritual gifts. There the holy mind receives what and how it ought to taste and understand, by what counsel and strength it ought to be strengthened, by what knowledge and piety it ought to be adorned, and with what fear of the Lord it ought to be filled. Indeed, by these spiritual gifts the fountain of the Church is so sealed that no one can partake of this fountain who possesses none of these seven graces. [Col. 1171B]

But why is it sealed? Because the sacraments of the Church must be entrusted to no one unless he has faith and works: faith, so that he may understand and believe that what he sees visibly performed outwardly in the sacraments works salvation invisibly within; works, so that in participating in those sacraments he may show himself worthy. Nor is the office of preaching entrusted to anyone unless he is proved to possess the grace of this knowledge, as the Apostle says: “How shall they preach unless they are sent?” (Rom. X). He receives the grace of the office from God. [Col. 1171C]

**VERSE 13.—**“Your outpourings are a paradise of pomegranates with the fruits of orchards.”

What, then, do this enclosed garden and sealed fountain, guarded with such divine providence, send forth? “Your outpourings,” he says, “are a paradise of pomegranates with the fruits of orchards.” The outpourings of this garden must be wonderful indeed, since it is made fruitful by the irrigation of a fountain flowing so sweetly and healthfully, and so carefully sealed. For it is constituted, as it were, a paradise through the glorious outpourings of diverse virtues, or of flowers and herbs, that spring forth spiritually. Although the very many kinds of aromatic plants, displaying the whole body of virtues, are enumerated below, they are nevertheless divided into two final causes because of the twofold condition of the times, namely persecution and peace. For every consummation of the saints has either been celebrated in persecution through martyrdom or accomplished in peace through confession. [Col. 1171D]

Therefore the outpourings of this garden—that is, of the holy Church—are aptly called a paradise of pomegranates with the fruits of orchards, because the holy proclamations of her glory in martyrdom or confession everywhere flourish and give forth fragrance. For what is signified by pomegranates except the glorious purple of martyrs, and what by the fruits of orchards except the life of confessors made bright by good actions? [Col. 1172A] O what delights of this paradise! What abundant and happily flowing outpourings of virtues, where both the strong are nourished and the weak refreshed! There those who desire to imitate marvel at, proclaim, and venerate the constancy of martyrs; there those who cannot be martyrs observe, approve, and emulate the commendable life of saints who live gloriously in peace.

**VERSE 14.—**“Cyprus with nard; nard and crocus; reed and cinnamon with all the trees of Lebanon; myrrh and aloe with all the finest ointments.”

Accordingly, the designated beauty, healthfulness, and usefulness of this enclosed garden, or sealed fountain, follows through seven kinds of aromatic herbs—not only because the sevenfold grace of the Spirit brings about these outpourings of its holiness, but also because the totality of virtues is expressed through this sevenfold number of kinds. For no virtue can be lacking in the whole body of the Church, because, since Christ is the head of the Church and the Church is the body of Christ, whatever holiness, honorableness, and usefulness ever could or can exist may be perceived in the whole Christ, that is, in head and members. [Col. 1172B]

Let us therefore examine the kinds themselves by which, as we have said, the whole body of virtues is denoted, and understand in the whole what we understand in the parts. “Cyprus,” he says, “with nard; nard and crocus; reed and cinnamon with all the trees of Lebanon; myrrh and aloe with all the finest ointments.”

*Cyprus* is an aromatic tree, signifying the blessing of spiritual grace, and it is interpreted as grief or sorrow. Therefore *cyprus* in the Church is any holy soul, like an aromatic tree, which has from God’s grace the power to despise the transitory joys of this world, possessing that sorrow which is according to God and “works steadfast repentance unto salvation” (II Cor. VII), mindful of that saying of the Gospel: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. V), and of that apostolic saying: “Be wretched and mourn; let your laughter be turned into mourning and your joy into sorrow” (Jas. IV). [Col. 1172C]

Nard is said to repel cold, whereas crocus brings refreshment to those who burn. What, then, is represented by nard except charity, and by crocus except chastity? For charity rouses those who are lukewarm in good work and makes them fervent; chastity, however, moderates and restrains the mind from the heat of evil desire. [Col. 1172D]

Reed is a short and small aromatic tree, but of hard bark; when this is crushed, it is drunk and heals the internal organs. By the reed, therefore, which, as we have said, is short and small, humility is fittingly understood. When its hard bark is crushed and drunk, the internal organs are healed, because when the swelling of hard and proud flesh is broken by the virtue of humility, the wound of the soul is healed by the medicine of a contrite and humble heart.

Cinnamon, however, has an ashen color and retains its power for a long time. By cinnamon, therefore, which is ash-colored and long retains its strength, is signified the lowly condition of penitents, who can say with the Prophet: “I ate ashes like bread” (Ps. CI), and with blessed Job: “Therefore I condemn myself and do penance in dust and ashes” (Job XLII). But this lowliness retains its power for a long time, because that repentance is true which so preserves the uprightness of a converted heart that it afterward admits nothing needing repentance. [Col. 1173A]

“With all the trees of Lebanon,” that is, with all the virtues of a life made white by baptism, strengthened by right faith, and exalted by good works. For having first set forth individually the virtues named above through the aforesaid kinds of trees, he adds universally, through all the trees of Lebanon, all virtues. Thus we understand that the garden of the Lord—that is, the Church—does indeed send forth every virtue from itself through the diverse lives of saints, but that the virtues named above are the heads of all virtues, so that the other members of virtues lie weak without them. [Col. 1173B]

“Myrrh and aloe with all the finest ointments.” He further adds two kinds of the seven virtues: namely, mortification of the flesh and patience. By myrrh, through which dead bodies are preserved unharmed from the corruption of worms and decay, should be understood that mortification of the flesh by which the decay of vices and fleshly pleasures is restrained. By aloe, which indeed has a sweet fragrance but a bitter taste and cleanses the stomach, we may understand patience. Since patience endures the evils of the world for the future goods of everlasting life, it gives forth a good fragrance because of the cause for which it suffers, but is bitter because of the cause through which it suffers. If some sickness of sin weighs down the soul, the bitterness of the evil which it suffers cleanses it. [Col. 1173C]

“With all,” he says, “the finest ointments,” that is, with the precious and approved gifts of spiritual graces, which the Apostle enumerates, saying: “To one indeed is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom; to another the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit; to another faith in the same Spirit; to another the working of miracles; to another prophecy; to another discernment of spirits; to another kinds of tongues; to another interpretation of sayings” (I Cor. XII). Behold, these may be called the finest ointments, prepared by divine grace. Not without reason are the two kinds of virtues designated above through myrrh and aloe—namely mortification and patience—placed before them, so that we may understand that only those are to be imbued with these spiritual ointments who “have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires” (Gal. V), who can say with the Apostle: “We glory also in tribulations” (Rom. V). [Col. 1173D]

It is pleasant, therefore, here to observe and marvel that the garden of the Lord is truly, through these its outpourings, like a most beautiful paradise—that is, a garden of delights—where the eternal salvation of the soul and every sweetness flourish, where every beauty and spiritual delight flower, where everlasting life and eternal rest abide. This does not mean that these are conferred here in the present life, but that through the outpourings of virtues and graces mentioned above one arrives at them, and the temporal exercise of those is the eternal bestowal of these. Therefore this garden, or paradise, is most rightly said to be enclosed, because the holy Church, strengthened by the grace of the spiritual outpourings of this garden, is overcome by no hostility of evil spirits. [Col. 1174A]
