But since the Church in general is called the garden of the Lord, so also every holy soul in particular, which flourishes with the shoots of virtues and the beauty of manifold graces, can be called the same. Yet we must consider, since the Church is a certain whole whereas one soul is a part of the whole, how much the part differs from the whole. For what is present in the part must be present in the whole; but the converse does not follow, so that what is present in the whole must likewise be present equally in the part. The universal Church, in its parts—that is, in the individual and particular human beings from whose gathering it is constituted—is a certain whole. Since many flourish in diverse virtues, and in this diversity all kinds of virtues are contained, the whole contains all things in its parts, but a part contains not all, only some. [Col. 1174B]

The whole and the part differ in this, that the whole is far more comprehensive than the part: all things flow together in the whole, whereas in the part there are not all things but only some. Therefore, while the holy universal Church is generally called the garden of the Lord because within her the shoots of all virtues are displayed, any holy soul that bears forth some shoots of virtues can also be called the garden of the Lord, according to the particular measure granted to it by divine grace.

**VERSE 15.—**“A fountain of gardens; a well of living waters, which flow with force from Lebanon.”

But since whoever is instructed is instructed either by word or by example, and the part has what it has from the whole, while words and examples are universally in the whole, it reasonably follows that that principal garden of the Lord, namely the universal Church, is called the fountain of particular gardens, namely of individual souls. For whence comes what they say, do, and teach, except from the teachings and institutions of the holy universal Church? And whence come those teachings themselves except from the words, writings, and examples of the holy Apostles and apostolic men? Therefore the Church is rightly called the fountain of these gardens—that is, of holy souls. **169.** For whatever holiness or integrity they possess, [Col. 1174C–D] they conceive and bring forth it all from the irrigation of ecclesiastical preaching; every aspect of their progress follows the rule and order of ecclesiastical discipline.

For a fountain (Gen. II) goes forth from the paradise of the Lord—that is, from the Church of God—and is divided into four rivers, that is, into the four Gospels. These water the whole face of the earth, that is, every inclination of the dry mind, so that, inebriated by their teaching through God’s grace, it may say with the Psalmist: “The Lord will give goodness, and our land shall yield its fruit” (Ps. LXXXIV). For unless God’s goodness visits the human heart, it will be unable to bear any fruit of good works.

But although the same Church is commonly called a fountain to all these gardens, which bear fruit in diverse ways because of their differing kinds of knowledge and works, since she waters them all by the infusion either of knowledge or of devout zeal, she is nevertheless called, in a special sense, a well of living waters to some because of the hidden depth of divine knowledge especially present in them, which flows from the fountain of the Church herself. A fountain flows openly above the ground, but the water of a well is hidden within the earth, because one kind of knowledge is easily attained by the simple and weak because of its accessibility, while another is scarcely explored by the learned and strong because of its subtlety. Therefore the Church is a fountain to all the elect, but she is not a well to all, because all read, hear, and understand the literal surface, but very few discern the hidden depth of the spiritual sense within. [Col. 1175A–B]

But this well has living waters because, when the Church opens the depth of the divine utterances to those who read or hear, she both corrects them from perversity and kindles them to good works. Thus she refreshes, as by living waters through life-giving teaching, those who ought to have died in sins.

But of what kind are these waters? “Which flow,” he says, “with force from Lebanon.” What is the force of these waters except the vehement current of Holy Scripture flowing with great authority? And what is expressed by Lebanon except the knowledge and virtue of exalted teachers? Therefore waters flow with force from Lebanon because Holy Scriptures display the great power of their authority from the knowledge and virtue of the holy Fathers. This force was indeed necessary for the Church, because the course of faith and sound teaching would have been hindered by heretics and perverse persons unless the torrent of utterance from holy teachers had driven back the obstructing devices of falsehood by the force of true reasoning and eloquence. [Col. 1175C]

But because the adversary has always stood against the holy Church, or against any holy soul, in a twofold battle—he tempts it either by threats or by blandishments in order to cast it down from the uprightness of its condition—the bridegroom, wishing to show how much it advances through this temptation, adds in a permissive manner of speech, saying: “Arise, north wind,” and so forth.

[Col. 1175D] **170. VERSE 16.—**“Arise, north wind; and come, south wind; blow upon my garden, and let its spices flow.”

By the north wind, which is harsh and cold, is understood the harshness of threats, descending from the coldness of a perverse mind; by the south wind, which is warm, is understood the gentleness of blandishments, proceeding as though from a certain sweetness of a deceitful heart. Therefore, when the Church or some holy soul is wearied by these two modes, it is trained for greater exercises of virtue, so that the more strongly it resists the enemy, the more gloriously it is joined after victory to the embraces of its bridegroom. By this twofold warfare the constancy of martyrs has been tested; by it also the conduct of the faithful is daily tested and crowned. For what mind is not tempted by this world’s prosperity and adversity? But that mind is tested and crowned which is neither lifted up by prosperity nor cast down by adversity. Hence John is commended by the Lord in the Gospel because he is said not to have been a reed shaken by the wind (Matt. XI). For when a reed is driven by wind, it bends in whatever direction; but he is not a reed shaken by wind who is bent toward neither side, namely neither right nor left, because he is neither shaken by terror nor deceived by blandishment. The north wind rises when one is assailed by detraction or some harshness; the south wind comes when one is tempted by favor or some prosperity.

With these winds blowing through the Lord’s garden, its spices flow forth; for the more the Church, or a holy soul, is touched by adversity or prosperity, the more it is filled, through progress, with the good fragrance of virtues. For this quality of life is a test of holiness and righteousness, so that the one adorned with such virtue of patience, humility, and long-suffering is rightly called the Lord’s garden; but where this good is lacking, the designation of spiritual good cannot exist.

Further: by the north wind the devil is often signified, and by the south wind the Holy Spirit, because the former constricts with cold, while the latter loosens with warmth. For the devil is reported, with the prophet bearing witness, to have said: “I will sit on the mountain of the Covenant, on the sides of the north” (Isa. XIV). But as the devil suggests and blows, iniquity and malice have abounded in the world. For Truth itself bears witness: “Where iniquity has abounded, the charity of many will grow cold” (Matt. XXIV). And the prophet says of Judaea: “As a cistern makes its water cold, so it has made its malice cold” (Jer. VI). But the Holy Spirit is understood by the name of the south wind, because by his grace the numbness of the mind is loosened, as the Psalmist testifies: “Restore, O Lord, our captivity like a torrent in the south” (Ps. CXXV). For our captivity, which had remained sluggish in following God through the cold of numbness, is loosened by the warmth of the Holy Spirit, so that it may run into the love of God.

Therefore the heavenly Bridegroom, graciously visiting his bride—that is, the Church or a holy soul—commands the north wind to depart and the south wind to come. For it is a just and fitting order that, once the cold of unbelief and malice has first been expelled, the mind should receive, through the coming of the Holy Spirit, the warmth of faith and good action. “Arise,” he says, “O north wind, and come, O south wind; blow through my garden, and its spices shall flow”: as though he were saying in other words: “Since the grace of the Holy Spirit cannot enter the minds marked out for me until the cold of unbelief has been driven away, whatever numbness or sloth you have settled in those minds, whether through ignorance or negligence, arise and depart. And come, Holy Spirit, that by the warmth of your breath you may loosen these minds bound by torpor, so that, having conceived the strength of good will and devout intention, they may overflow with fruits and fragrances of holiness, spreading far and wide and drawing many around them into their fellowship.”

[Col. 1177A] Moreover, at this voice of the Bridegroom, the bride, now as though given life and in some manner raised again, rises eagerly in spirit to meet the grace that breathes upon her. And since it follows that, when the Holy Spirit blows, she produces the fruit of good action, she shows this when she says: “Let my beloved come into his garden,” etc.

172 CHAPTER V.

VERSE 1.—“Let my beloved come into his garden, and eat the fruit of his trees. I have come into my garden, my sister, my bride; I have gathered my myrrh with my spices; I have eaten my honeycomb with my honey; I have drunk my wine with my milk. Eat and drink, friends, and be intoxicated, dearly beloved.”

She rightly says that the beloved comes into his own garden, because the reason for his coming is that he is beloved, and that the garden is his own. Unless he were loved, he would not come. “If anyone loves me, he will keep my commandments; and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John XIV). But one who says that he loves God must prove it by works; for this is what it is for the garden to be his. Where diverse flowers of virtues bloom and fruits abound, it is not improperly called, in a spiritual sense, the Lord’s garden; and to be such a garden is to love God.

The beloved therefore comes into his garden when he illuminates, by the grace of his visitation, a mind devoted to good deeds. In this garden he eats the fruit of his trees, because he delights in and is nourished by the fragrance and sweetness of virtues in the mind which he has filled with his grace. Hence the beloved himself, as though rejoicing with his beloved, replies: “I have come into my garden, my sister, my bride; I have gathered my myrrh with my spices” [Col. 1177C]. What is understood by myrrh but the mortification of the flesh? Yet because vices are nourished by the pleasure of the flesh, just as virtues are generated by its mortification, he rightly places myrrh first in particular and then adds spices in general. For unless the flesh is subjected to the spirit through the mortification of vices, the mind does not rise to virtues, because, in its own prompting, the spirit does not oppose the flesh. But when the spirit always resists the flesh, the mind, once the flesh has at length been made subject, advances to the heights of virtues; and when, through daily progress in good work, it has reached a certain maturity of perfection, the time of harvest has, as it were, come for it.

[Col. 1177D] The beloved therefore harvests her good works when, having cut her away from the field of earthly dwelling by the sickle of death, he gathers her to be rewarded in the granaries of the heavenly kingdom. This harvest is either the separation of the soul from the flesh or the separation of the elect from the reprobate. He who harvests takes one part and leaves another: in the separation of the soul from the body, the soul is taken and the body left behind. Moreover, when the elect are separated from the reprobate, they themselves, like a good crop, are taken up to life, while the reprobate, like the remaining stubble, are left for eternal fire.

But the beloved harvests myrrh when he says: “Come to me, all you who labour and are burdened, and I will give you rest” (Matt. XI); he harvests spices when he says: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. XXV). Therefore he harvests myrrh with spices when he separates from the company of the wicked those who, through contempt for the world and affliction of the flesh, have advanced to works of virtue, and lays them up in the storehouse of his kingdom.

He aptly calls them his myrrh and his spices, because whatever good they possess, they possess through the gift of his grace. This harvest, as has been said, takes place by the sickle of judicial sentence, in this present time both by dissolution and by predestination. By dissolution, indeed, when the soul, as the higher and worthier part, is taken up to heaven, while the body, as the lower and baser part, is left in the earth. By predestination, because those whom he knows beforehand will persevere in good, he chooses as a crop by predestining them to eternal life; but those whom he knows will remain in evil, he leaves, like stubble fixed in earthly actions, by predestining them to eternal death.

[Col. 1178B] Let the beloved therefore say: “I have come into my garden; I have gathered my myrrh with my spices,” because, after by my grace visiting the Church or the faithful soul I caused it to put forth the shoots of virtues, I made especially fit for myself those dead to the world and devoted to devout actions; and because I separated them from the reprobate by election, I numbered them among the fellowship of my kingdom. Hence he immediately adds: “I have eaten my honeycomb with my honey; I have drunk my wine with my milk.”

The beloved further rejoices in the progress of his budding garden, which the pursuits and virtues of the elect wonderfully adorn. In the honeycomb are honey and wax: honey is sweet; wax is soft and pliable, and serves light. In wine there is austerity, but in milk whiteness and gentleness. What can be signified by these kinds of things except the diverse character of words in holy preachers, corresponding to the diverse dispositions of their hearers? For just as the Apostle says to one whom he was instructing for preaching, “Reprove, entreat, rebuke” (II Tim. IV), holy teachers temper the force of their preaching when they consider person, place, and time, and carefully judge where, when, and whom they ought profitably to reprove, entreat, or rebuke.

For according to the diversity of minds, there are some who gladly receive the word of holy preaching as soon as they hear it; there are others who wish neither to hear nor receive it; and there are many who do not wish, or cannot, receive and hear it in one place or time, but hear and receive it in another. Likewise, some minds are corrected by gentle and sweet preaching; others are restrained only by harsh rebuke; while still others are stirred to greater works of virtue by devout entreaty. Because of these diverse dispositions of souls, teachers of souls ought to be very discerning in their preaching, since they must carefully consider what they preach, and when, where, and to whom, lest they appear to cast forth words to no purpose.

[Col. 1179A] Therefore, when they correct sinners whom they see to be soft and pliable, they ought to reprove them with gentle and sweet admonition, according to the saying of the wise man: “A gentler answer breaks anger” (Prov. XV). But those whom they see to be hard and unyielding they ought to strike with harsh rebuke and the terror of divine punishment; while they should entreat those devoted to good works that they may always advance to what is better.

Therefore, since prelates ought to instruct their subjects in these three ways, when they cherish the good with the sweetness of pious exhortation and console them by preaching the pleasantness of the heavenly kingdom, they are honeycomb with honey. But when they restrain sinners now with moderate speech, now expose them by harsh rebuke, declaring the punishments of hell, they are wine with milk.

Thus the beloved eats his honeycomb with his honey and drinks his wine with his milk, because he makes into his own members, incorporating them into himself, the rulers of the holy Church whom his grace orders in preaching in the manner described; he delights in their efforts and progress and is, as it were, refreshed by them. Having shown that they belong to his body by the conformity and unity through which he has incorporated them into himself, he addresses those who can be instructed by their teaching and examples, saying:

“Eat and drink, friends, and be intoxicated, dearly beloved”: as though he were openly saying: “Because I have prepared refreshment for your souls in the deeds and words of teachers whom I have filled with my Spirit, you who ought to be instructed by their teaching, lay up in the stomach of memory what you hear and see from them; and fill your minds with such sweetness of virtues that you may remain insensible to every movement of vice—my friends through faith and action, and my dearly beloved through inward love.”

For this eating and drinking is the full reception of the divine commandments. Hence the Psalmist says of those intoxicated by this fullness: “We are intoxicated from the abundance of your house” (Ps. XXXV). What is the house of God except the Church, or the mind of any righteous person? And what is the abundance of this house except a certain fullness of divine commandments and sacraments, by which the holy Church, or the soul of some holy person, is filled and enriched? But all who receive full knowledge through the instruction of the Church or the teaching of some holy person are filled and intoxicated by this abundance, through the necessary usefulness and worthiness of those very commandments and sacraments.

[Col. 1179D] He was filled with this abundance who said: “Though unskilled in speech, yet not in knowledge” (II Cor. II). The Psalmist desired the fullness of this abundance when he said: “Let my soul be filled as with fat and richness” (Ps. LXII).

But because the bride had heard the exhorting voice of the Bridegroom and tasted upon the palate of her heart the sweetness of his commandments, and had been intoxicated by hearing, reading, believing, and doing, through the fullness of this good, she declares the effect this complete outpouring had produced, and what profit she had gained from it, saying: “I sleep,” etc.

VERSE 2.—“I sleep, and my heart keeps watch. The voice of my beloved knocking: Open to me, my sister, my friend, my dove, my undefiled one; for my head is full of dew, and my locks with the drops of the night.”

If you consider the outward aspect, the acts of this sleeping and waking cannot at the same moment and time exist together in one and the same person, because no one can simultaneously sleep and, while awake, think something at one and the same instant or time. But if you consider inward things and attend to the character of this sleeping and waking, these two adhere to each other so inseparably that at one and the same time they must either both be absent or be together.

What is this sleep except freedom from all the cares and activities of the world, and a certain rest and pause of the mind? What is the wakefulness of the heart except a contemplative love—or loving contemplation—continually directed toward God with sincerity? Yet since it is certain that no one can possess the virtue of holy contemplation unless he has endeavoured to be free and unencumbered from all worldly affairs, and conversely that no one can free himself from worldly affairs unless he begins to love and desire God with pure and simple intention, it is evident that these two, as has been said, cling to one another in such a way that in one and the same person they must either both be wholly absent or both be present at one and the same time.

In this manner, then, it is possible to sleep and wake at the same time; nor is there any contradiction where, in the mind’s disposition, these states are one and the same. For in this sense to keep watch is the same as to sleep, and to sleep is the same as to keep watch: to cling to contemplation is to sleep to the world and to keep watch for God; and unless one sleeps to the world, one does not keep watch, nor does one sleep to the world unless one keeps watch for God.

[Col. 1180C] But one may ask why the bride says, “I sleep, and my heart keeps watch,” as though the whole person were said to sleep while a part of the person, namely the heart, keeps watch. The answer is that the whole person is called body and soul, while the heart is a part of the whole. This part pertains only to the inward person, that is, the soul; but the whole person concerns both the outward and inward person together. The whole person ought to sleep when this part, namely the heart, endeavours to keep watch in contemplation: that is, body and soul—will and action—must cease from all outward things and, as it were, rest, so that they may be freer to attend to inward things.

Therefore, because the bride recognized that she could not perfectly cling to the vision of the heavenly Bridegroom unless she possessed all her inward and outward senses free and unencumbered, she rightly says: “I sleep, and my heart keeps watch”: as though she were saying forcefully in other words: “Because I rest utterly, in thought and deed, from the noise of earthly things, I therefore keep watch more keenly in mind in divine contemplation.”

This should be connected to what precedes as follows. Since the Bridegroom had said of his preaching that he had filled them with such sweetness and authority of sound doctrine that no one ought to doubt that they were incorporated into himself, and that it was consequently both very useful and fitting to be intoxicated by their preaching, the bride, as though aroused by this admonition and greatly benefited by the preaching, words, and examples of the saints, replies: “Because, O beloved, I obeyed your counsels, you breathing upon me, coming to me, and helping me onward, and because I applied my mind by faith, hope, and charity to the teachings of your preachers, I have not merely, as it were, eaten and drunk, but have been wholly intoxicated. My bodily senses have been put to sleep by this intoxication, so that, behold, I now sleep entirely to all the cares and desires of the present life, while my heart keeps watch by intimate love in contemplation of divinity alone.”

[Col. 1181B] “Although,” she says, “instructed by the sayings, writings, and deeds of the holy Fathers in how I ought to advance in both the active and the contemplative life, I have nevertheless chosen the better part, since I have resolved in the contemplative life to devote my whole heart and body to God alone. But because my beloved by his grace has fed me with the bread of life and understanding, and given me to drink the water of saving wisdom (Ecclus. XV), so that I may be fit for the office of preaching, he knocks and rouses me, commanding that I care not only for myself, resting in contemplation, but also for my neighbours, labouring in preaching.

“Open to me,” he says, “for foxes have dens and birds of the air nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (Matt. VIII; Luke IX). For apart from a few by whose faith I am received, almost the whole world rejects me either through unbelief or through the perversity of faith: Jews and pagans do not believe, while heretics corrupt the orthodox faith. Hence, as I stand beneath the open sky, my head is drenched with dew, because my divinity is dishonoured by the perverse opinions of heretics, which fall as though from heaven because of their elegance of expression, yet are cold in their opposition to truth and right faith. My locks too are full of drops of the night, because the faithful, who ought by faith and action to adhere to me as to their head, are infected by their perverse doctrines, falling in the nights of distorted thoughts, and grow cold toward the love of truth.

“Or: ‘My head is full of dew, and my locks with the drops of the night,’ because the hearts of unbelievers are cold toward the love of God and neighbour. By the head God may be understood, and by the locks one’s neighbours. Open therefore to me, because unless you preach and teach, I shall not be able to enter their hearts. Therefore arise at times from that sweet bedchamber of your inward solitude and undertake the office of preaching, so that after they have been taught by your preaching, renounced their former errors, and prepared in their minds a lodging for me by right faith and action, I may gladly enter and bestow upon them the saving gift of my grace.”

[Col. 1181D] “My sister, my friend, my dove, my undefiled one”: what is the force of this enumeration of four names? Does the Holy Spirit intend nothing in this very distinct placing of four terms? Certainly not. For if you apply the eyes of the inward person, you will perceive in this number of names a reason—and a usefulness of that reason—not to be despised. The form of a spiritual square is necessary to every soul wishing to stand at the height of perfection; for a square stands whichever way it is turned. This ought to be the constancy of the perfect: that they be neither lifted up by prosperity nor cast down by adversity, but always persist in one and the same order and position of holy purpose.

But what is this spiritual square? Clearly, faith, hope, charity, and action. For faith, as the Apostle says, works through love (Gal. V), and “faith, if it has not works, is dead in itself” (Jas. II). The proof of charity is action. He who does not believe does not hope; and he who does not hope has nothing to love. Moreover, one who neither believes, nor hopes, nor loves has nothing for which to act. This is the intention of every good work in each person: that he may deserve at some time to attain what he believes, hopes, and loves.

[Col. 1182B] In the measure of a square one side is not greater and another smaller, but all four sides alike extend over an equal space. So too, so long as we live this life, we shall find within ourselves these same virtues—faith, hope, charity, and action—to be equal. For everyone engaged in the exercise of the active life believes as much as he hopes; he acts and loves as much as he believes; he loves as much as he believes, hopes, and acts; and he acts as much as he believes, hopes, and loves.

Let us also say that this square of the soul consists in the four principal virtues: prudence, fortitude, justice, and temperance. These virtues form a square such that one does not exceed another. Prudence indeed may be great; but if one is less brave in dangers, less just in actions, and less temperate from pleasures, one is certainly less prudent.

Fortitude is great; but if one understands less well what goods to preserve and what evils to resist; if one maintains the works of justice less firmly and is sometimes overcome by the rule of injustice; if one controls appetite less from pleasures but is conquered by delight—then one is less brave.

Justice is great; but if one discerns less well than one should between just and unjust actions, strengthens oneself less against adversities, and restrains the flesh less in pleasure, one is less just.

Temperance is great; but if one understands less well from what one ought to restrain oneself; if one is less able through fortitude to endure adversities and lets fear cast down the mind; if one through rashness sometimes rushes into works of injustice—then one is less temperate.

[Col. 1182D] Therefore, if the life of perfect believers is measured by a square, one side is as great as each of the others. For each person is as prudent as he is brave, just, and temperate; as brave as he is just, prudent, and temperate; as just as he is prudent, brave, and temperate; and as temperate as he is prudent, brave, and just. But because the Teacher of the Gentiles says, “I chastise my body and bring it into slavery, lest perhaps, after I have preached to others, I myself should become reprobate” (I Cor. IX), the preacher must always endeavour to show in his own actions the things which he rightly preaches with his mouth.

This fourfold configuration of the virtues we have set forth is therefore necessary to every preacher: that he himself possess faith, hope, charity, and action, and preach that others must possess them; and that he shine in prudence, fortitude, justice, and temperance, and instruct others in these things also by teaching.

179 Therefore, because this beloved arouses his beloved, resting securely in contemplation, to the office of preaching, he calls her by the name of fourfold grace, so as to indicate that one sent to preach must always be squared by these four virtues. He calls her sister because of faith, friend because of hope, dove because of charity, undefiled because of action. For the holy Church, or any holy soul, which has received the name of bride and beloved by believing in the Almighty, attains the eternal inheritance so as to become an heir of God and co-heir of Christ, because it merits by grace the divine sonship which he possesses by nature.

Thus this heavenly Bridegroom calls his beloved soul, redeemed at the price of his blood, his sister, because what he is essentially, she may be called so by name. For John says in his Gospel that “to all who received him, he gave power to become children of God—to those who believe in his name, who were born not of bloods, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God” (John I). Of these the Lord himself also says: “Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven, that person is my brother and sister and mother” (Matt. XII).

[Col. 1183C] He calls her friend because, when he reveals to her certain secrets of his knowledge and the immensity of his ineffable goodness, he raises her to great hope of future blessedness. For it is a mark of true friendship to make someone privy to one’s secret. Thus the Lord said to the disciples to whom he had revealed the mysteries of the divine will: “I shall no longer call you servants, but friends, because I have made known to you everything which I heard from my Father” (John XV).

He calls her dove because he approves her as simple, innocent, peaceable, and endowed with love of God and neighbour, just as the dove is a simple creature, harmless, abstaining from every act of tearing, and sometimes tending the young of others as though they were its own.

For one who is truly innocent is known to possess charity toward God and neighbour, because true innocence is defined thus: “True innocence is that which harms neither itself nor others.” It harms itself when, by acting wickedly, it offends God; it harms others when it provides examples of evil action. Thus the person who avoids evil action proves that he loves God, because in striving not to lose God he thereby preserves himself as well; and he proves that he loves his neighbour, because in preserving himself from offending God he thereby invites that neighbour to act well.

[Col. 1184A] The definition of true innocence is therefore correct: it harms neither itself nor others, because through it love of God and neighbour is expressed, and in this love the whole fullness of the law consists.

For what the fullness of the law is is beautifully declared by the fifth kind of definition, which in Greek is called *kata antilexin* (κατὰ ἀντίλεξιν), in Latin *ad verbum* (“by a word”), when what is sought is shown by one word, in this way: “The fullness of the law [is] love” (Rom. XIII). Therefore, if the fullness of the law is charity, and charity “does not act perversely” (I Cor. XIII), then surely one known to possess charity is shown to keep the entire law. And because charity itself is poured into the hearts of the elect through the Holy Spirit (Rom. V), it follows that one who possesses the gift of charity confirms that he has been illumined by the gifts of the Holy Spirit. For if no virtue has worth without charity, and charity is conferred through the Holy Spirit, then one who has charity is shown to have the Holy Spirit, in whom the gifts of all virtues are bestowed.

Accordingly, the Bridegroom rightly calls the bride whom he invites to preach a dove, so that he may indicate to her that she ought to possess the charity given through the Holy Spirit, who is asserted to have appeared in the form of a dove.

He calls her undefiled so that she may remember to do whatever she displays in action with pure intention—not to receive human praise from it, but to please divinity alone—for those works are filthy before God which have been performed for the favour of the world.

Or he calls her undefiled in order to indicate that purity of mind and body is to be cherished, or to warn her carefully to avoid every stain of heretical perversity in her preaching.

[Col. 1184C] Moreover, because of the four principal virtues in which the most beautiful square of the mind consists, the beloved addresses his beloved by these four names, to show that she whom he urges to rise for preaching must be prudent, brave, just, and temperate—as sister, friend, dove, and undefiled one.

For the person who hastens through integrity of faith to the inheritance of the highest Father wisely understands what, and of what kind, that which he believes is. The person who, God revealing it, knows the mysteries of divine commandments and sacraments, who courageously endures adversities for God, and courageously despises the enticing pleasures of the world, surely shows what he hopes for. But the person filled with the grace of the Holy Spirit, who embraces the good of simplicity and innocence because he strives to be just, speaks by that very justice of his love for God. And the person who adopts such a manner of life that in all actions he knows how to keep the restraints of holy discernment, tempering himself from worldly pleasures through the pursuit of virtues and treating the good of justice without indiscretion, demonstrates how pure and upright he is in all his activity.

181 The Bridegroom therefore rightly calls the bride whom he raises to the office of preaching sister, friend, dove, and undefiled one, thereby indicating how steadfastly squared in mind she ought to stand in all her duties and actions. But she replies to his knocking and refuses to rise from the chosen leisure of inward rest, saying: “I have taken off my tunic,” etc.

VERSE 3.—“I have taken off my tunic; how shall I put it on? I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them?”

“I have cast out from my mind,” she says, “the hindrances of the world and the cares of the active life, in which I was hitherto entangled, that I might attend more freely to divine contemplation. How then do you now urge me, through the office of preaching, to rise again from this rest and serve the pursuits of the active life? I have washed my feet—that is, I have washed away with the water of compunction arising from divine charity the negligences of my works, which I contracted from the dust of worldly thoughts and things. How shall I contract them again from the filth of earthly commotion? For it is very difficult to live among the people of this world and not be stained by some contagion of human frailty. Material externally applied to the bodily senses readily infects the inward beauty of the soul.”

But while I was considering these things with myself and thought that I ought not entirely abandon my purpose, I shall tell you, O daughters of Jerusalem, what my beloved did.

VERSE 4.—“My beloved put his hand through the opening, and my inward parts trembled at his touch.”

What are his hand, the opening, and his inward parts? You must surely understand the hand of the beloved as the power of his omnipotence and secret inspiration. But when the human mind, devoted to worldly pleasures, thinks nothing of God and nothing of the soul’s salvation, it is as though enclosed and overgrown by a certain wall of perversity; it has no entrance or opening through which the light of divine grace may deign to enter.

[Col. 1185C] But because divine power sometimes comes beforehand by its breath to such persons, so that they are pierced with compunction for their sins, the wall of the condemned mind is, as it were, broken open, and an opening and a certain fissure is made, from which flow tears of compunction, stirred by the grief of a repentant and, as it were, torn heart. Of such a fissure the prophet warns: “Tear your hearts and not your garments” (Joel II).

And since there are two kinds of compunction—because a mind converted to God is first pierced by fear and then by love—when someone, fearing the punishments of Gehenna, renounces worldly desires and laments the sins he has committed, divine grace has, as it were, made an opening and fissure in his heart. But through progress in a good manner of life, once he has conceived some assurance from divine mercy, he burns with such love for God that he who once wept lest he be led to punishment afterwards begins to weep most bitterly because he is delayed from the kingdom.

Then, through the opening which grief has made in the repentant heart, the most merciful Lord puts forth the hand of his soothing grace and mercy, and refreshes the mind by a touch so sweet that, wholly kindled in the love of God, it seeks and desires nothing earthly, counts all visible things as little, and strives with its whole mind to attain heavenly and eternal things alone.

[Col. 1186A] At the sweetness of this touch the inward part trembles, because a mind drawing in the sweetness of the contemplative life is moved by the power of grace breathing upon it, so that it understands that love of God cannot exist without love of neighbour. Rather, this is the fullness of perfect love: that one who loves God for God’s own sake should also love one’s neighbour for God’s sake.

“In this manner, then, O daughters of Jerusalem, my beloved put forth his hand—that is, the help of his power and grace—through the opening of my contrite heart, indicating and warning that, since I have made an entrance for him in my heart by clinging to his love, I should not doubt that through the office of preaching I must likewise prepare an entrance for him in the hearts of my neighbours. For he is always at hand through assisting grace, and is accustomed both to grant me what, or in what manner, I should teach, and to open the ears of the mind in those who hear.”

The same sense which I have applied to myself may also, without absurdity, be applied to my hearers: the beloved is said to put his hand through the opening whenever, sounding through the outward ears of hearers by the voice of preaching, he enters the inward ears by inserting the hand of assisting grace. At this touch my inward part trembles, because the weaker among my people, who before did not understand through weakness of intellect, come to understand; and, trembling as they hear the terror of divine judgment, they also learn to be moved toward the fruit of good work.

VERSE 5.—“I arose, therefore, to open to my beloved; my hands dripped with myrrh, and my fingers were full of finest myrrh.”

Because he promised me his assistance, by which I should obtain the fruit of my labour, it was fitting that I should not shrink from the office of preaching. Rather, just as I had opened my heart to him through his grace, so through the same grace I should open to him the hearts of my neighbours by preaching.

[Col. 1186D] My hands dripped myrrh because, according to the word of the Teacher of the Gentiles, “I chastised my body and subjected it to slavery, lest perhaps, while preaching to others, I myself should become reprobate” (I Cor. IX). My hands are my works, which must always drip myrrh, because they must always give off the fragrance of mortification of the flesh, abstinence from vices, and abundance of virtues.

My fingers were full of finest myrrh because my works of virtue, such as they are, ought indeed to possess great restraints of discernment; but that discernment itself ought to abound in divine and brotherly charity. For what is finest myrrh except charity, the choicest of all virtues? And why myrrh, except because “love is strong as death, and zeal hard as hell” (Song VIII)? For “no one has greater charity than that one should lay down one’s life for one’s friends” (John XV).

[Col. 1187A] My fingers, therefore—that is, my acts, distinguished in one mind as in one body by the ten commandments—are full of the myrrh of charity, because, loving my beloved strongly, I do not refuse to labour even unto death to keep and preach his laws.

For the salvation or need of my brethren, I also endeavour to have this discernment: although I desire more to be absorbed in divine contemplation, brotherly charity nevertheless sometimes compels me to descend and gather the myrrh of labour for their benefit.

Therefore, having now arisen at my beloved’s exhortation so as to open to him also the closed hearts of my neighbours by preaching to them the word of life, with my hands dripping myrrh and my fingers likewise full of finest myrrh, I girded myself for the office of preaching.

### Verse 6

“I opened the bolt of my door to my beloved; but he had turned aside and passed on. My soul melted when my beloved spoke. I sought him and did not find him; I called him and he did not answer me.”

I relaxed for a time, I say, the strictness of my resolve, or the enclosure of my silence; and, going forth in public, I opened my mouth and drew in the spirit: “I opened my mouth and drew in breath” (Ps. 118 [119]). Having also cast away from myself every obstacle of the mind, I began more diligently to investigate the wonderful testimonies of my beloved, so that I might show them in action and set them forth in speech. But when I desired that he might enter wholly into me, and say to him with Moses, “Lord, show me [Col. 1187C] your face” (Exod. 33), he had already turned aside and passed on, leaving only his back parts to be seen in some measure.

184 For what was his turning aside and passing on? Certainly, his turning aside was his descent from that height of heaven to our weakness through birth and death; and because he did this in time, this was his passing on. For all those things occurred in passing: “Christ, having risen, dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him” (Rom. 6). Therefore, when I endeavoured somehow to comprehend him as he is and to show him, as best I could, to others who desired to hear, he withdrew, turned aside, and passed on, because he is incomprehensible, and in this life no one can perfectly grasp that divine [Col. 1187D] substance by the mind. Yet when he had passed on, I saw only his back parts, because I was able to understand and preach certain things concerning his humanity.

And while I thus preached the words and deeds of my beloved and stirred the minds of my hearers to keep his commandments and follow his footsteps, a greater force of compunction dissolved me, so that I wholly poured myself out in his love. For he who spoke outwardly from me to others through the voice of preaching also spoke inwardly to me through the grace of inspiration. For whenever we preach him, he himself speaks in us and through us, as he says in the Gospel: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. 10). But where the Spirit speaks to the Father, the Son also speaks, because those whose substance is one have one operation also.

I was seized by such sweetness of his speech that, in hearing him inwardly, my soul not only softened from all hardness but even melted; and, strengthened by deliberate resolve for the daily exercises of good works, I said with the Psalmist: “I will hear what the Lord God speaks in me” (Ps. 84 [85]). For he rightly attends to God speaking within him who readily obeys inspiring grace and free will going before it. Likewise, whoever understands, by grace’s own revelation, the things that he reads in Holy Scripture hears God speaking within himself. And when he seeks God more frequently by meditation upon it, the more subtly he investigates him, the more highly God is lifted up in his heart. Hence the Psalmist says: “Man shall approach the lofty heart, and God shall be exalted” [Col. 1188B] (Ps. 63 [64]); and it is written in Ezekiel that, “when the living creatures were lifted up from the earth, the wheels beside them were lifted up at the same time” (Ezek. 1). For the more attentively one applies oneself to Holy Scripture, the more sublimely it is raised into spiritual meaning for the person who considers it subtly.

Therefore, while my soul melted through the fire of love at such speech from my beloved, I sought him more intensely by reading, meditating, and preaching, and desired to know what he was like. I sought him by prayer, fasting, vigils, and mortification of the flesh; but in this life I could 185 not find him as he is. I therefore sought him and did not find him, because I could neither perfectly know him by reading nor show him to others by preaching; for “we see through a mirror in an enigma” [Col. 1188C] (1 Cor. 13). “I called, and he did not answer me”: when I thought that he was already, as it were, present to me, though in some sense set at a distance and seemingly about to be grasped, I called to him by some utterance of subtle understanding. Yet he did not answer me, because, as I reconsidered the things which I thought I had perfectly understood, he did not fully disclose them by the answering voice of his grace.

For it is written in the vision of the prophet Ezekiel that, “when a voice came over the firmament, the living creatures stood still and lowered their wings” (Ezek. 1). They had already spread the wings of inward contemplation; already, flying in mind, they had conceived whatever knowledge of divinity they could, although still in an enigma. But when the voice came not beneath the firmament, nor from the firmament, but above the firmament, they stopped, unable to go farther; and, lowering the wings of their begun contemplation, they perceived that to comprehend the incomprehensible was beyond them. For, thinking him so near that they could grasp him, they called; but he did not answer them, because he did not show by the inward voice of address that what they thought they had understood about God was indeed so. Thus I called and he did not answer me, because, when I wished to attempt something above myself, I recognized how far below it I was, since I could attain no perfect knowledge of the incomprehensible substance.

### Verse 7

“The watchmen who go about the city found me; they struck me and wounded me; the watchmen of the walls took my cloak from me.”

[Col. 1189A] What then? I laid down the wings which I had vainly spread beyond my power, and, turning to the writings and sayings of the holy Fathers, I heard: “Do not overstep the boundaries which your fathers set” (Prov. 22). They indeed spoke by inspiration of the Holy Spirit (2 Pet. 1), and showed the way and measure both of believing and of reasoning concerning God. These, surely, are the watchmen of the city—that is, of the holy Church—of which it is written: “Glorious things have been spoken of you, city of God” (Ps. 86 [87]). For by words, examples, and the protection of their prayers, they guard her from the assault of evil spirits and human beings.

These therefore found me, because they found me withdrawing from my former intention and wishing to be content with their sayings and writings. They found me, I say, because they so drew me by the sweetness of their discourses that, putting every other intention aside, I fixed my attention upon the one final and heavenly end: eternal life, which is God himself. The vision of him is the complete and perfect rest and consummation of all our labour. Thus, while I read or heard their writings, they struck me with the dart of divine love; and they not only struck but wounded me, because they pierced my mind with the compunction of heavenly longing, so that a fountain of tears, like a kind of blood of the soul, flowed from it.

“The watchmen of the walls also took my cloak from me.” The walls here may fittingly be understood as the divine Scriptures, because, as a wall is built from many different stones, so divine Scripture is formed from the many and various teachings and pronouncements of the holy Fathers. And as walls fortify a city, so divine Scriptures protect the holy Church, because all her defence and ornament consist in knowledge and observance of the holy Scriptures.

Furthermore, the watchmen of these walls may be understood as the simple people in the Church, of whom it is written: “The simplicity of the righteous shall guide them” (Prov. 11). Although they have little or no knowledge of the Scriptures, nevertheless, by preaching through their deeds that the commandments of those Scriptures must be observed, they build up their neighbours [Col. 1189D] to no small extent. These guardians of the spiritual walls took my cloak from me because, through the example of good works, they removed from me the impediments of superfluous thought which had veiled my mind in the tangle of indiscriminate inquiry. They persuaded me “not to think high things, but to agree with the lowly” (Rom. 12), and to serve God in simplicity.

### Verse 8

“I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, if you find my beloved, tell him that I languish with love.”

Therefore, I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, if you find my beloved, tell him that I languish with love. But what does it mean for me to adjure? Certainly, to bind you by the sacrament of faith and action. Otherwise you are not daughters [Col. 1190A] of Jerusalem, because you do not belong to the vision of heavenly peace unless you please God by faith and deed. Therefore, if you find the beloved—that is, if you have advanced so far through my preaching that, by right belief and good works, you possess him—then I adjure you; that is, as I have said, I bind you by the sacrament of faith and action, to violate which is to lose salvation. Tell him, namely, by displaying the signs and, as it were, a certain mark of my zeal and labour, by which I toiled in preaching for the sake of your salvation. Thus the Apostle says to his disciples: “You are the signs of my apostleship among the Gentiles” (2 Cor. 12).

What, then, ought you to tell him? Namely, that I languish with love: that is, I am so held by his charity and love that I remain weak, languid, and almost insensible toward every worldly pleasure [Col. 1190B] and beauty. You, therefore, proclaim by your life and conduct how true, right, and useful my preaching has been, so that your progress may become also the fruit of my labour.

At this utterance of the beloved, obedient to her beloved and rising to preach, and proclaiming the zeal and usefulness of that preaching, the daughters of Jerusalem—that is, holy souls belonging to the vision of heavenly peace—ask into the reasons for so great an adjuration, and address the beloved in this manner: “What is your beloved more than another beloved?” and so forth.

### Verse 9

“What is your beloved more than another beloved, O most beautiful of women? What is your beloved more than another beloved, that you have so adjured us?”

[Col. 1190C] “We perceive,” they say, “no small force in this adjuration, in which we have learned that the whole sum of our salvation hangs; and therefore we desire to know the power and dignity of this beloved, for whose sake you have thus adjured us.

“What, then, is the beloved from the beloved—that is, the Son from the Father, God from God, light from light? For it is a great thing to know him whom you so earnestly endeavour to commend, and the height of wisdom to understand him for whose love you languish so greatly. But since the beloved from the beloved—that is, the Son from the substance of the Father, of one essence, one power, one will, and one operation—cannot be perfectly comprehended, for ‘we know in part and prophesy in part’ [Col. 1190D] (1 Cor. 13), nevertheless whatever may be thought, understood, or said about God, you, O most beautiful of women—that is, of souls that bear spiritual children to God—are able to teach it. For this your special prerogative of beauty has merited: because you are called the beloved of this beloved, you are able to approach him more closely with the eye of the mind.

“For all your glory and adornment are within” (Ps. 44 [45]), and the pure God, with whose purity nothing may be compared, is seen only by pure hearts; for “blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5).

The other women indeed are beautiful—that is, the faithful souls which, each in its own manner, place, and time, bear spiritual children to God—but you are more beautiful than all, universal Church, who daily beget children in the Spirit through the sacrament of baptism [Col. 1191A] and the teaching of holy preaching. Therefore tell us what the beloved from the beloved is like: that is, what ought to be understood and believed concerning his divinity according to human capacity.

Or again, what is the beloved from the beloved like? That is, he who was formerly made beloved to you by being born and dying for you: in what way is he now beloved, pouring into you the abundance of his grace and drawing you into the divine sweetness of his love? Or, he who in an earlier age was beloved among the ancient Fathers by displaying the majesty of his divinity through figures and enigmas and through very many miraculous signs: in what way is he beloved now, in the last age, by assuming flesh and accomplishing the salvation of the whole world? The repetition of the same word is the eager inquiry of a soul desiring knowledge.

The beloved, moreover, in order to kindle the questioning souls to greater love and reverence for her beloved, sets forth his qualities tropologically, singing the beauty of his divinity and humanity in ten praises, as though upon a ten-stringed psaltery [Col. 1191B] (Ps. 91 [92]). For the number ten is perfect and contains the mystery either of the Decalogue or of the four Gospels. Beginning from one, it reaches four in such a way as to complete the number ten: for if you add to unity the three succeeding numbers—that is, two, three, and four—you will have ten, and thus through the number four you complete the number ten.

The psaltery is a musical instrument shaped like the letter delta, which in Greek signifies four. Therefore the beloved fittingly sings the dignity and beauty of her beloved as though upon a ten-stringed psaltery, by the testimony of ten praises, in order to show that the Old and New Testaments resound with every mystery flowing to her from the grace of the beloved: the one prefiguring in figure what the other celebrates as already fulfilled in truth. She therefore says: “My beloved is white and ruddy.”

### Verse 10

“My beloved is white and ruddy, chosen from among thousands.”

If we draw near attentively with the ear of the heart, we shall be able to perceive by inward hearing that the chief theme of this harmony, which the beloved intends to perform upon this ten-stringed instrument, is the praiseworthy grace of a twofold beauty: namely, chastity and martyrdom. This is first seen in the Head himself; afterwards it is distributed through his members, now in alternating and now in mingled sweetness.

“My beloved,” she says, “is white and ruddy.” This twofold colour—whiteness and redness—appears chiefly, singularly, and fully in the Head of the Church, that is, Christ. For no whiteness can be compared with the purity of his most chaste and holy flesh, which he assumed from the most chaste Virgin by the ineffable operation of the Holy Spirit. And it is written of the Wisdom of God the Father, which he himself is: “Compared with light, she is found prior to all beauty of the stars; for she is the brightness of eternal light and the spotless mirror of God’s majesty” [Col. 1192A] (Wis. 7).

He is therefore white in divinity, because of the unspeakable splendour of the divine nature, by which he enlightens every human being coming into this world (John 1); and white in humanity, because of the assumption, as we have said, of flesh immaculate and free from every sin. Moreover, he was specially ruddy in his Passion, because no charity can be equal to his charity: he loved his creation so greatly that he chose to die for it, not disdaining to become sin of the flesh and the curse of the cross (Rom. 8; Gal. 3). Concerning this unique Passion, he himself speaks in the prophet: “I have trodden the winepress alone, and of the peoples there was no man with me” (Isa. 63).

[Col. 1192B] For no suffering is comparable with this Passion, which alone accomplished the salvation of the entire world, and alone led the captive servant from slavery to sin into the true freedom of the glory of the children of God (Rom. 8).

Therefore, after saying, “My beloved is white and ruddy,” she adds, “chosen from among thousands.” The number one thousand, because it stands for perfection, signifies universality. He is therefore called chosen from among thousands because he alone is set above the whole company of the faithful by the uniqueness of virtues and graces. For it is written of him that “God anointed him with the oil of gladness above his companions” (Ps. 44 [45]). And while all the elect receive grace in differing measure, “one indeed in this way, another in that” (1 Cor. 7), to the Only-begotten alone God gives the Holy Spirit not by measure [Col. 1192C] (John 3); and “from his fullness we all receive” (John 1), in whom “all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Col. 2), because he is the head above every principality, power, virtue, and dominion (Eph. 1).

This beloved, then, the Lord Jesus Christ, is uniquely white and ruddy in his own personal reality of divinity and humanity; he is chosen from among thousands. But among those thousands—that is, among the whole company of the elect—the whiteness of holiness and redness of Passion do not shine in one manner or to an equal degree. For in some both are found, and in others not both; now whiteness of purity and redness of martyrdom are bestowed together upon one, now either whiteness alone or redness alone upon another. Thus before God one is white and ruddy, another wholly white or wholly ruddy; one surpasses another in a greater, lesser, or sometimes equal measure of these virtues. Therefore, in his body—that is, the Church—Christ too is white and ruddy, according to the measure which his goodness and grace please to give to each of the elect.

### Verse 11

“His head is like the finest gold. His locks are like the raised branches of palm trees, black as a raven.”

Accordingly, in what follows, the gifts of his twofold beauty are enumerated member by member, now appearing together, now separately, in the same body of Christ. After the unique dignity of the Head above all saints has been set forth, the differing colours of dignities in his body are then introduced: those who, by grace uniting and incorporating them to him, advance each in its own manner and place. For she says: “His head is like the finest gold.”

What is signified by gold except his divinity? As gold is more precious than all metals, so Christ’s divinity surpasses all creatures; and whatever glory of dignity may exist in creatures is nothing in comparison with divinity. The Head of the beloved, therefore—that is, his divinity—is like gold, and not merely gold but the finest gold, because the substance of divinity is good: not merely good, but the highest and most universal good, and, if it may be so said, the good of goods, because he is the fount and origin of every good, from whom all good things proceed.

Or, because in Holy Scripture the chief part of the mind is called its head, while Christ is the power and wisdom of God the Father (1 Cor. 1), and the Word begotten from the Father’s heart, by which Word and Wisdom all things were made, and without which—or whom—nothing was made. The finest gold, therefore, is that very power and wisdom which is “the brightness of God’s glory and the image of his substance” (Heb. 1).

Whatever beauty and excellence are poured out upon the body of this Head flow from that divinity and wisdom, so that the grace of the locks, eyes, cheeks, and other members that will presently be enumerated may fittingly be proclaimed concerning this body.

The first of these is: “His locks are like the raised branches of palm trees, black as a raven.” [Col. 1193C] The locks of this Head may be understood in two ways: as the holy prophets and apostles, or as the holy Scriptures which flowed forth through them by divine inspiration. For they clung to God as to their Head in the sweetness of contemplative love, and therefore received from the power and wisdom of God a great subtlety of mind in discerning that divine Word.

191 Hence they are said to be “like raised palm trees,” because, while “their conversation was in heaven” (Phil. 3), their minds also were lifted into heaven by contemplation. They had conquered and trampled down every troublesome earthly delight; and the glory of this spiritual triumph is signified by the palm, the emblem of victory. But because they suffered no slight evils in gaining this victory—either by enduring adversity from wicked people, or by crucifying their flesh with its vices and desires within themselves (Gal. 5)—they are rightly called “black as a raven.” For despisers of worldly glory were considered lowly and obscure by lovers of the world; yet they were made all the more fitting, like subtle locks, for the glory and adornment of the divine Head, the more they were despised by worldly people for love of divinity.

The holy Scriptures drawn forth through them can likewise be called the locks of the divine Head, because, as locks grow from the head, so Holy Scripture proceeds from divine wisdom; and as locks adorn the head, so Holy Scripture adorns the preeminence and headship of God’s Church. They are said to be like raised palms because they raise the minds of believers, by their admonition or consolation, from earthly things to love and desire heavenly things; they equip them with spiritual armour against vices and sins, and promise the palm of eternal blessedness to those who fight well to the end. But these locks are called black as a raven because Holy Scripture is wrapped in many obscurities: “dark water in the clouds of the air” (Ps. 17 [18]), because knowledge in the holy Scriptures is profound. Yet because this blackness signifies either voluntary or imposed affliction, when some suffering of mind or body is perceived in it, the beloved is in this respect proclaimed wine-coloured—that is, ruddy—in his body.

### Verse 12

“His eyes are like doves beside streams of water, washed with milk, and resting beside abundant streams.”

What are the eyes of the beloved but the prelates or angels of the Churches, who are set over the house of God—that is, the holy Church—as watchmen? Thus God says to one of them: “I have appointed you a watchman for the house of Israel; you shall hear the word from my mouth and announce it to them from me” (Ezek. 3). A watchman looks out from on high, so that he may announce from as far away as possible the coming of enemies, against whom precautions must be taken. Therefore the Lord says through the prophet to such a watchman: “Let a trumpet be in your throat, like an eagle over the house of God” [Col. 1194C] (Hos. 8).

For a watchman has a trumpet in his throat when he preaches the word of God openly and publicly, far and wide, and with lofty voice and mind declares what end awaits virtues and vices. He is like an eagle over the house of God because, applying the keenness of subtle understanding to divinity, he summons those committed to him to the subtlety of the contemplative life. He spreads over them the wings of his protection, preserving them from the snares of evil spirits both through the diligence of teaching and through the aid of prayers.

But these eyes of the beloved are “like doves washed with milk,” because holy watchmen attending to the house of God, if they truly are God’s eyes, possess works of simplicity and innocence, together with chastity of heart and body, by which they nourish both themselves and those subject to them for eternal life. And whence is this? Because they dwell “beside streams of water” and “rest beside abundant streams.” It is, indeed, the natural habit of doves to sit beside streams of water in order to guard against the approach of hawks. Since these watchmen dwell beside streams of water—that is, the sayings of Scripture—they know how to provide for themselves and their subjects, by ordering or correcting conduct and by guarding against the snares of the ancient enemy. They also rest beside abundant streams because they daily keep before their eyes the teachings of both Testaments. These are truly not only full but most full of knowledge of every mystery: in the one Testament these are presented through figures and enigmas, [Col. 1195A] and in the other they are proclaimed as displayed in truth. In this third member, one of the two colours previously proclaimed in the body of the beloved must be observed: namely, whiteness, so that souls washed in milk-white colour may bear the badge of chastity and purity.

### Verse 13

“His cheeks are like beds of spices planted by perfumers. His lips are lilies, dripping the finest myrrh.”

The cheeks of the beloved may fittingly be understood as those who practise continence, adorning their resolve with a multitude of diverse virtues, as though with a crowd of hairs displaying manly strength of mind. Since, for God’s sake, they abstain from the pleasure of eyes and ears, from the other senses, from food and clothing, and from other delightful things of this world, they scatter from themselves as many fragrances of continence as they make beds of spices.

For example, the reverent restraining or turning away of the eyes is a beautiful bed in which as many merits of continence shine as fragrant spices exhale perfume. The ear, too, the mouth, nostrils, and hands may be called beds. Since they can receive good or bad things, and since certain things which are good by nature are often made bad through the abuse of those who partake of them, whenever the irrational appetites for those things are broken through love of virtue, these beds exhale the varieties of spiritual spices with which they are planted. Each spice gives fragrance according to the quality of continence that produces it: for the more a thing delights, the more continence from it commends a person to God.

But because these forms of continence ought, by the virtue of discernment, to have a fitting limit—so that neither a natural necessity may be turned into vice nor the rigor of virtue exceed the proper measure—these beds are rightly said to have been planted by perfumers. For such forms of continence are planted in their beds not casually, indiscriminately, or confusedly, but in an ordered, composed, and rational manner, by those who are proved to possess knowledge of such planting. These perfumers are the holy apostles and holy teachers, who in their sayings and writings show the kinds of virtues as so many spices. From these, against vices and sins as against diseases of the soul, they prepare a most health-giving antidote. Therefore the cheeks of the beloved are like beds of spices planted by perfumers, because those who give forth from themselves the diverse scents of continence gather from the sayings and deeds of the holy Fathers whatever diligence and excellence they fashion in their conduct.

It should also be considered that in this member the twofold colour of the previously mentioned beauty—redness and whiteness—shines forth, so that the inward state is indicated in outward appearance. For while these cheeks redden and whiten, they testify both to the modesty of chastity and to the labour of continence. It cannot easily be determined which colour is more eminent: redness in martyrdom or whiteness in virginity, since virginity is found in martyrs and itself makes martyrs. Certainly, two things are discerned as one in these cheeks, because in the virtue of each person’s continence and chastity the merit of martyrdom shines, and its reward is hoped for because of the labour.

“His lips are lilies, dripping the finest myrrh.” Behold the perfumers by whose labour the grace of chastity shines in the cheeks: namely, the holy preachers. They are designated by the lips because by their preaching they prepare the diverse spices of virtues. They are like lilies because they give instruction toward wholeness and purity of life, and counsel for the wounds of souls; and they can say with the Apostle: “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God among those who are being saved” (2 Cor. 2). For the nature of the lily displays both whiteness and scent, and brings abundant healing to wounds.

They are lilies “dripping the finest myrrh,” that is, the best myrrh, because, while they mortify vices and sins in themselves in order to preserve integrity and purity of heart and body, and unceasingly preach to others by word and example that they must do the same, they truly show how great is their love toward God and neighbour.

For charity may be called the finest myrrh, that is, the best and proven myrrh, because wherever it is true and perfect it extinguishes every incentive to vice in a person. Just as corpses are embalmed with myrrh so that they may not decay, so souls are strengthened by divine charity lest they fall into the decay of vices.

[Col. 1196C] In this member too of his body, the beloved is white and ruddy: in his holy preachers he is called white for the lily of chastity, but through the myrrh of suffering he is proclaimed ruddy. For “all who desire to live piously in Christ will suffer persecution” (2 Tim. 3).

### Verse 14

“His hands are rounded and golden, full of hyacinths. His belly is ivory, adorned with sapphires.”

If we look at the Head himself, his hands are surely rounded and golden, because it is written of him: “How magnified are your works, O Lord! You have made all things in wisdom” (Ps. 103 [104]). For one who works with a lathe works more swiftly, perfectly, and smoothly. And who has ever worked more swiftly, perfectly, or smoothly than God himself? He made what he chose to make exceedingly quickly, because he merely spoke and they were made (Ps. 32 [33]); and at one and the same time, though in different ways and forms, for him to speak was to make. No one has worked more perfectly than he, because he made all things not incomplete, or by parts, or still needing improvement, but perfect; and for him to make once was to make wholly and completely.

Nor was anything smoother than his work, because the nature of things could be delayed by no impediment; rather, it has kept as a perpetual law the course and measure which it receives once for all. There is nothing distorted or uneven, deficient or superfluous in his works, because he “ordered all things in measure, number, and weight” [Col. 1197A] (Wis. 2). His hands, therefore, were rightly rounded, because, as has been said, he made all things with such speed, perfection, and beauty that from his works the observer may see clearly how great is the beauty and majesty of the Creator himself. This consideration is not a full comprehension of his deity, but a contemplation of the Creator which proceeds from the dignity of the creature and shines forth as much as is possible for the human mind.

The hands themselves are called golden because their being, life, vigour, and flourishing are established by the ordinance of divinity; for by gold, which is more precious than all metals, divinity is signified, and nothing is higher than it.

But why are they said to be full of hyacinths, when other stones also are very suitable ornaments for hands and fingers? All visible things are, in some way, marvellous and beautiful ornaments of divine works; yet in these works are especially wonderful because they contain more subtle secrets of heavenly marvels. The contemplation of these belongs first to incorporeal creation: the heavenly spirits or holy minds, always intent upon heavenly things, whose manner of life is an operation of divine goodness. In the second place is the corporeal creation of higher things, which are in a certain sense nourishment for lower things; their rational ordering is likewise a marvellous operation of divine wisdom. The hyacinth is sky-coloured, and therefore the hands of the beloved are said to be full of hyacinths, because the works of the Creator are especially proclaimed in the beauty and adornment of heavenly things.

But if you look to the members of the Head, his hands are rounded, golden, and full of hyacinths, because those intent upon good works and always hastening to enter future rest run the way of the commandments not slowly or sluggishly but swiftly and diligently. Whatever crooked or uneven thing they see in their conduct, they remove and smooth through the turning-work of right action; and, in the sight of their Creator—yet by the work of that Creator himself—they render it perfect. The reason for this effectiveness is the understanding within them, corresponding to the gold of wisdom divinely bestowed and always directed, in the sweetness of the contemplative life, toward the blessedness of heavenly goods.

They are called his hands because whatever good they do belongs not to their own strength but to the grace of God. From him comes also their being rounded through the perfection of their conduct, golden through the brightness of their understanding, and full of hyacinths through the sublimity of angelic conversation.

Moreover, in considering these members, the twofold colour is seen in the body of the beloved with special praise. Their hands being rounded signifies labour or Passion, by which they are turned away from every superfluity and unevenness of conduct into a vessel of honour, pleasing to divine eyes. Their being golden and full of hyacinths signifies the shining virtue of the celibate life, by which they glow with the brightness of chastity and purity. Thus in this part too the beloved is sung as white and ruddy.

[Col. 1198A] “His belly is ivory, adorned with sapphires.” If we consider the person of the beloved distinctly, it is not unreasonable to take his humanity as signified by the name of belly, because the belly is the more fragile part of the body, and that humanity experienced every human bodily weakness except sin. But why is this belly called ivory? Ivory is the bone of the elephant, an animal said to be most chaste. And what is more chaste than Christ’s humanity, which was assumed from the most chaste Virgin without any male agency, through the operation of the Holy Spirit alone? The belly of the beloved is therefore ivory because, while all human beings are conceived in iniquities and sins, he alone was conceived in humanity without sin, uniquely from the most chaste Virgin, as has been said.

[Col. 1198B] Why, moreover, is this belly said to be adorned with sapphires? The sapphire is blue in colour. The belly of the beloved is said to be adorned with sapphires because, although according to his humanity he endured hunger, thirst, weariness, and the other things that a human being could suffer on earth, in suffering he showed heavenly miracles through his divinity by performing them.

If we consider the multitude of believers who, as members, cling by faith to that person as to their head, this multitude may be compared to the belly on account of its greater frailty. For in the Church some are bound by the bond of marriage, while others marvellously practise continence in the frail sex. Yet those who have wives “as though they had none” (1 Cor. 7) may rightly be called an ivory belly [Col. 1198C], because, although they seem frail outwardly, they are nevertheless strong through the honourableness of a holy and chaste life. Hence it is written of holy married persons that “they were walking blamelessly in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord” (Luke 3). For this is for the belly to be marked with sapphires: amid the cares of worldly affairs which marital frailty requires, they shine by devout observance of heavenly precepts.

Moreover, those who wonderfully practise continence in the frail sex show a more praiseworthy constancy in this resolution of theirs, because, although weak and frail in body, they nevertheless rise strongly to the merits of holiness through vigour of mind. Hence in them too the belly is called ivory, because the virtue of chastity is proclaimed all the more in the frail sex [Col. 1198D].

But it is said to be marked with sapphires because the virtue of chastity is adorned also with the ornaments of other virtues. Bodily chastity cannot otherwise be a virtue unless it is adorned by chastity of mind, which consists in humility, patience, sobriety, contempt for secular life, and observance of the remaining heavenly precepts. For, if the belly is to be ivory in the body of this beloved one, it must be marked with sapphires: “bodily chastity is of no benefit without good work, nor good work without chastity” (Gregory). Therefore, because the frail sex holds fast the virtue of chastity with a strong mind, the beloved’s belly is ivory; but because it also strives after other virtues for heavenly glory, it is marked with sapphires. For in the ivory belly the colour of chastity gleams; in the sapphire, although blue, the colour of suffering nevertheless reddens on account of the labour of virtues. Chastity itself, which shines outwardly in the pure body, inwardly reddens through the mind’s martyrdom; for to resist the natural movement of the flesh is certainly a kind of suffering of the mind.

The exposition of this present clause concerns in no small degree the rule of your profession, most beloved sisters, because, since you truly belong to the body of this beloved one, you can be such a most becoming member of him. For when you shine in the so frail vessel of your body with the bright garment of chastity and modesty, you may indeed be called and be the ivory belly of this beloved one. And because together with that chastity you also shine with the ornaments of other virtues, you clearly gleam as marked with sapphires [Col. 1199A]. But you must take the greatest care not to suppose that you can please God by chastity alone if you lack other good works. You must therefore always join chastity to good work, and good work to chastity, so that you may please God perfectly.

**VERSE 15.**—“His legs are columns of marble, founded upon bases of gold. His appearance is like Lebanon, chosen as the cedars.”
