In the eighth place, the attentive beholder of the beloved touches, as it were, the eighth string of the ten-stringed psaltery, rendering that *diapason* harmony whose proper characteristic is that its eighth note has the same pitch as its first. For, since on the first string above she sounded that the beloved’s head was finest gold, she now says that his legs are set upon golden bases [Col. 1199C], so that the same note, low and high, resounds with the beloved’s golden adornment at the highest and lowest points. But we must consider what the legs of this beloved are, and why they are compared to marble columns built upon golden bases.

Since God is immovable and unchangeable in his nature—for he is non-local, filling and containing all things, while himself contained by none, being wholly everywhere at all times—and since what moves from place to place is local, whereas God does not move and is therefore non-local because immovable, he is nevertheless said to move, not in himself, but in those whom he moves by his will and purpose, through the power that orders all things, whether according to justice or according to mercy: “he has mercy on whom he will, and hardens whom he will” [Col. 1199D] (Rom. 9). One of these belongs to mercy, the other to justice. Therefore, since he goes before all his creation, as it were, by this twofold path of his ordering—namely justice and mercy—justice and mercy may rightly be called his legs. For, as the Psalmist says, “all his ways are mercy and truth” (Ps. 24). Truth and justice are the same; for what is true is just, and what is just is true.

Why, then, are these legs called marble columns, except because they are upright and strong? For a column has uprightness, marble hardness. God’s justice is hidden, yet never unjust. Who can know why he mercifully chooses one person and judicially rejects another? Therefore the Apostle cries: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments, and unsearchable his ways!” [Col. 1200A] (Rom. 2).

But what are the golden bases upon which these columns—understood as those legs—are founded? Clearly, if you weigh the matter rightly, they are his wisdom and goodness, because he wisely and well orders and disposes all that he does. They are bases, indeed, because they contain and support all things; golden, because they shine wonderfully in the very workings of things. Thus the beloved’s legs, if you direct your attention to the head himself, are, as was said, mercy and truth. Founded upon bases—that is, upon the feet of his wisdom and goodness—they either stand or walk according to the measure and character [Col. 1200B] of the things that have been made. For all things that have been made are either eternal or temporal. They stand in those things which God himself has eternally predestined for his own according to grace and mercy; they walk in those things which he bestows or removes temporally, whether mercifully or judicially.

But if you look to the members of that head, what do you suppose are to be called the legs of this beloved? In that ancient people of God, among whom God was then known alone, God established two chief dignities by which that people might be defended and adorned: kingship and priesthood. In outward matters, it was armed with royal strength against those who, at the prompting of the devil, strove to destroy God’s purpose, which he held for the salvation of the whole world and prefigured in that people, so that throughout their commonwealth they might proceed in peace and honour, faithfully carrying out in figure the affairs of the divine promise. In inward matters, however, it was instructed by the office of priesthood to understand these affairs wisely through the figure and to handle them reverently, so that by faith and love it might labour toward the eventual fulfilment of God’s purpose, in hope of future salvation [Col. 1200C].

In these two dignities lay such the support of that people that, when God was later angry with that people for sinning and threatened many punishments, he finally proposed this ultimate punishment to a people refusing correction: that, once kingship and priesthood had been removed and destroyed, all their honour and religion would utterly pass away. Thus it is said through the prophet Jeremiah: “The Lord has consigned to oblivion in Zion feast and sabbath; and, in the reproach of the indignation of his wrath, king and priest” [Col. 1200D] (Lam. 2). For king and priest no longer existing meant that the entire ceremonial rite had failed.

Does not the holy Church also subsist in this present age, now that that promise has been fulfilled, through two such dignities? The power of royal judgment fights outwardly against unbelievers and faithless persons with the material sword; the majesty of the priestly office also fights inwardly against them with the spiritual sword. See how, when the Lord allowed the sword for defending the universal safety of this new commonwealth which now exists, and heard that two were ready, he answered that they were enough [Col. 1201A] (Luke 2), because he established two deadly sentences in the Church: one by the material sword, the other by the spiritual sword. For outwardly this is done through fear of royal power, so that the Church may serve God in peace and honour; inwardly it is instructed by priesthood, so that it may know how to serve God with reverence and love. What then? Since these two dignities are, as it were, a support for the Church of God in the propagation of all religion and, to speak properly, the strongest support of the entire body of this beloved, can kingship and priesthood not rightly be called the legs of this beloved?

And these, because of their strength and eminence, are called marble columns, since they themselves are raised by virtue and power and the whole house of the holy Church is supported upon them. But what are the golden bases [Col. 1201B] upon which these columns are built? Clearly, in kingship or priesthood itself, since the cause ought to serve the common good and honour, there must shine forth great force of reason and the virtue of discernment, so that in every administration and judgment there may always be reason and discernment. But since these must proceed from great clarity of understanding and wisdom, may they not rightly be called the golden bases of these columns?

Therefore these legs of the beloved are marble columns set upon golden bases, because in the holy Church kingship and priesthood flourish through reason and discernment in administration and judgment.

The prelude placed near the beginning of this ten-stringed song also answers the song of this eighth string, by which the beloved is praised as white and ruddy [Col. 1201C]. For this part of kingship acts amid labour and danger to life, so that in it this beloved may be proclaimed ruddy; while the other part, priesthood, acts in peace and tranquillity, so that in it the beloved may be proclaimed white—in holiness, chastity, manner of life, observance of God’s commandments, and preaching.

“His appearance is like Lebanon, chosen as the cedars.” As Mount Lebanon, he says, surpasses other mountains in splendour and beauty, and in the wonderful arrangement of the trees planted there, so my beloved surpasses all saints and is far more beautiful in the power of virtues, in wisdom and knowledge, in every beauty of worldly actions, and in every fullness of divine graces. “For God does not give the Spirit to him by measure” [Col. 1201D] (John 3). “But all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily in him” (Col. 2); and from this fullness of his the saints receive grace for grace (John 1). What he possesses universally, they obtain only partially; and they do not possess it always at the will of each, since at times this portion of grace is ready in them, while at other times it lies sluggishly, as though asleep, and must be awakened only with some labour. Hence Paul says to Timothy: “For this reason, I remind you to rekindle the grace that is in you through the laying on of my hands” (2 Tim. 1).

It is awakened in many ways, but especially by prayer and psalmody. For example, when the king of Israel said to Elisha, “Why has God assembled these three kings, to deliver them into the hand of Moab?” he replied: “As the Lord lives, in whose presence I stand, if I were not ashamed before the face of Jehoshaphat king of Judah, I would certainly neither attend to you nor look upon you. But now bring me a musician.” And it came to pass, while the musician was playing, that the hand of the Lord came upon him, and so forth [Col. 1202A] (4 Kings 3).

Therefore, except for this beloved one, of whom it is written, “Upon whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining, this is he who baptizes in the Spirit” (John 1), all other saints receive a divided or partial grace of the Holy Spirit according as it pleases the Holy Spirit himself, who breathes where and when he wills (John 3). Rightly, then, is the appearance of this beloved said to be like Lebanon, because he is “beautiful in form beyond the children of men” (Ps. 44), and no appearance can be compared with his appearance, no virtue with his virtue, no grace with his grace [Col. 1202B].

“Chosen as the cedars.” Why are cedars chosen above the other trees of Lebanon except because they possess certain special natural properties? Cedar is incorruptible, fragrant, and hostile to serpents. But who could be without corruption except this beloved one alone, who “commits no sin, neither was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Pet. 2)? No one could ever be so holy, so innocent, as not to have contracted some corruption, since it is written that God “found iniquity even in his angels” (Job 4). Sin is indeed a kind of rottenness, a kind of corruption; and although it is greater in one person and lesser in another, it cannot be absent, even in the holiest and most righteous person, however slight it may be. But in this beloved one alone, no stain at all, even the faintest, of such rottenness or corruption could exist [Col. 1202C].

Therefore he is rightly said to be chosen as the cedars, because he alone possesses by nature that which has been granted to no saints by grace. Let this be said of the head alone.

But if you look to the body, which is one with the head by incorporation because it is incorporated into that head through his grace, his appearance is fittingly compared to Lebanon when this whole beloved one is considered distinctly in himself and in his body. For what can be considered in the face or appearance of the Church except the presence of divinity in the administration of sacraments, in the proclamation of divine utterances, and in the ordering and arrangement of suitable and rational affairs? And what is this Lebanon, to which the appearance of this beloved in his whole body is compared? If you consider the thing as it is, Lebanon is a mountain of Phoenicia, abounding in cedars rooted in it and stretching upward. And just as this mountain is adorned by a multitude of cedars, thereby presenting great beauty to those who behold it, so this beloved, in his body, adorned by the multitude of his elect rooted in him by faith and cleaving to him in love, offers to the whole world a truly wonderful spectacle of holiness and honourableness [Col. 1202D].

If, however, you understand it metaphorically, this is the Lebanon of which the prophetic utterance cries: “Open your gates, Lebanon, and let fire consume your cedars” (Zech. 2). For the temple of God, built in that earthly Jerusalem and having inner chambers round about made of the wood of Lebanon, of cedar wood, was called by the name Lebanon because in it was the Holy of Holies. This was a certain glory and eminent beauty not only of that city but also of all its people spread over many territories. Thus the beloved’s appearance is like the appearance of Lebanon, because, just as that temple was once the chief and singular monument of religion for that ancient people of God, so now the assembly of the Church, where Christ is honoured in his body, is a chief point and a certain eminence of holiness for the entire Christian people. For in it is discerned a way and an approach to the sublimity of that highest good and to the eternity of future salvation [Col. 1203A].

Even now the faithful people daily run to the assembly as to a mountain of God, looking in hope toward that land of promise which God will give to his elect. In it is the temple of that heavenly Jerusalem, inhabited by the Holy of Holies himself, where the saints are multiplied like the cedars of Lebanon, made incorruptible by participation in that eternal blessedness and highest good which is God.

“Chosen as the cedars”: how is this beloved one, in his body—that is, the Church—said to be chosen as the cedars? If you consider the properties of cedar mentioned above, namely that it is incorruptible, fragrant, and drives away serpents, you can surely perceive how great is the usefulness of the unity of the holy Church, how greatly every soul ought to choose it, and how far it ought to be preferred above all other things. For there one attains incorruption of mind, smells the fragrance of virtues, and drives away vices and sins as poisonous serpents. What is more excellent than this? Christ is therefore rightly said to be chosen as the cedars in his body, because in every action of his, whether canonical or administrative disposition, he is the cause of every spiritual efficacy [Col. 1203C].

In this passage the beloved, who above, as we have often said, is presented as coloured in two ways, white and ruddy, shines only with bodily beauty in the countenance of his body—that is, of the Church—which he chose for himself “without spot or wrinkle” (Eph. 5). This is proved by the exposition concerning the appearance of Lebanon, a name interpreted as “whitening.”

**VERSE 16.**—“His throat is most sweet, and he is altogether desirable. Such is my beloved, and he is my friend, daughters of Jerusalem.”

In the throat is the voice; in the voice, sound; and in the sound, if the voice is articulated, a definite expression of some thing. What is understood by the throat except the sound of holy Scripture? We know that the whole sacred Scripture was composed either by the voice of the Lord himself or by the saints whom God himself used as certain instruments. For what do the divine Scriptures sound forth except God speaking either through himself or through his own servants? And what does he speak? Clearly, the character of the future promise, according to his purpose in predestining, calling, justifying, and glorifying his elect. He grants them now to taste beforehand the sweetness and pleasantness of this glorification through hope, which raises them up, makes them pant for it with their whole desire, and in some manner gives them already a kind of experience of that sweetness [Col. 1204A].

This very experience may also be called the throat of this beloved, because in the mind of every holy soul tasting beforehand the sweetness of divine goodness, that sweetness is delightfully savoured which it understands from the preaching of sacred Scripture. Of it it is said that “eye has not seen, ear has not heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love him” [Col. 1204B] (Isa. 54; 1 Cor. 2). Hence the Psalmist says to those advancing through experience of that very sweetness: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet; blessed is the man who hopes in him” (Ps. 33). Thus the beloved’s throat is either the voice of sacred Scripture declaring the sweetness of divine mercy, or the experience of that same mercy sweetly refreshing the mind of every faithful person.

The throat is most sweet because it pours forth the remembrance of such an abundance of divine holiness that, to the attentive helper, nothing seems sweeter to sound in the ear of the heart than not only to hope for the everlasting goods of future blessedness, but also to hold them with firm certainty, and therefore to desire them with the whole mind.

Accordingly, whereas the individual parts above are compared to particular things—the head, for example, to gold; the hair to the raised branches of palm trees; the eyes to doves; the cheeks to beds of spices; and the rest, as set forth above, to things suitable to them—this final part alone is compared to nothing, because that highest and most universal good is as incomparable as it is ineffable [Col. 1204C].

Having enumerated the praises of this beloved part by part, both in himself and in his body, as though each string in this ten-stringed instrument had been expended in such description, she sets forth, as it were, the final note of the praise she has sung: “And he is altogether desirable.” It is as if she said: Why do I proclaim his beauty and dignity part by part? There is nothing in him that I can except; for he is altogether desirable, whether you consider the height of his divinity or behold the humility of his humanity. This is the sum of the whole praise, sung at the end and expressing in itself, as it were, the colour of the whole song.

For what could be said more briefly and more definitively as the sum of praise concerning Christ, God and man, than that he is altogether desirable? For if everything in him, or that can be said of him, is desirable, he is blessed in every respect. It surely follows that the highest and final mode of praise is to call him altogether desirable [Col. 1204D].

“Such is my beloved, and he is my friend, daughters of Jerusalem.” “You asked me,” she says, “what sort of beloved mine was, on whose account I so earnestly adjured you. Behold, I have shown you what sort my beloved is, whose form I described through his individual members. But what is to be said about this form? Has this beloved acquired this disposition through arrangement or affection, and is he capable of increase and diminution? Certainly not in his own nature: he is essentially good, wise, beautiful, holy, and just. But in his body—that is, the Church—he passes into this disposition through arrangement or affection, receiving more or less according as his grace pleases to dispose it in each of his members. This quality or disposition is his nature, because he himself is goodness, wisdom, beauty, holiness, and justice [Col. 1205A].

And he is worthy of my seeking, not because I am necessary to him, but because he is greatly necessary to me. Why? Because he is my friend, O daughters of Jerusalem. For the disposition of my inward person is formed from him, as it were from image to image, through participation in the grace dwelling in my heart. By its illumination, those mysteries of invisible things are opened to me which are contained in the sublimity and significance of the divine precepts and sacraments, according as understanding and reason instruct and guide me; and these are the greatest beauty of this disposition of my inward person.

This friend of mine guards me in such knowledge through the grace of humility. For he says to the Father: “I confess to you, Father, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and have revealed them to little ones” (Matt. 11). Humility, indeed, is the guardian of virtues. He is called *friend* (*amicus*) as though “guardian of the mind” (*animi custos*). Therefore, in order that I may not lose this friend, I must possess him through humility as the guard of my mind [Col. 1205B].

For if a mind inclined or disposed toward divine knowledge at some time receives, through cooperating grace, a disposition—that is, a permanent possession in itself of such knowledge—it becomes, as it were, one with God through participation in him, so that the mind itself too is called God by fellowship with God. Hence a certain wise man says to his son:

> If the mind is God to us, as songs declare,  
> Let this above all be worshipped by you with a pure mind.

That is to say plainly: since the mind is God to us—that is, true and spiritual life—glorify it especially by living well. For a person who, through the inborn power of reason and understanding, discerns rightly and orders his life well, retaining God within himself, is God [Col. 1205C], not essentially but by designation, as the Prophet says of the saints: “I said, ‘You are gods, all of you sons of the Most High’” (Ps. 81). The force of such a designation is the bond of a great friendship.

But the daughters, not sons, of Jerusalem—that is, souls still weak and not yet able to attain perfection in virtues—considering the benefit of this friendship and seeing that the beloved has constituted this great beauty of spirit in his beloved, are themselves inflamed by the love of holy desire. They wish also to enjoy the benefit of this friendship, by which they may be able to attain the same beauty of spirit. For they say: “Where has your beloved gone?” and so forth.

**VERSE 17.**—“Where has your beloved gone, O most beautiful among women? Where has your beloved turned aside? And we will seek him with you.”

What is God’s going away or turning aside, when he is not contained in place and with him “there is no change nor shadow of turning” (Jas. 2)? God is said to go away or turn aside in two ways: by the approach and by the withdrawal of his grace, according to the perfection or deficiency of any mind, whether approaching God or departing from him. But in this passage, the beloved’s going away is the mercy of his goodness moving someone; his turning aside is his entering into a person’s mind through the gift of his grace [Col. 1206A].

“Tell us,” they say, “O most beautiful among women, in what person among your faithful has your beloved, by going away and turning aside through his mercy and grace, set before us an example of living well or of striving more earnestly in some virtue. Tell us—that is, show us—either by reading, by which you daily proclaim their life, or by action, by which you daily number them among your company. And we also, drawn by their example, will seek this beloved with you, calling him by prayer, fasting, and other good works, so that he too may deign to turn aside toward us by visiting us with the gift of his grace.”

For he says: “If you seek me with all your heart, you shall find me” (Jer. 29). To seek him is not by prayer alone, but also by good action, just as elsewhere he says concerning those who seek him: “They seek me day by day and desire to know my ways” (Isa. 38). For when he says that they desire to know his ways, he clearly shows that they seek him by good action [Col. 1206B].

Thus we will seek the beloved with you in this way, O most beautiful among women. But women of what sort? Certainly those who, in themselves, bring forth to God the fruits of good work as children of holiness through faith and love; or who bring forth others as children of light unto the day of eternal life by word and example. Therefore, because we admire in you so great a beauty, O most beautiful among women—a beauty which you have drawn to yourself by seeking and finding your beloved—we too, desiring to attain some trace of your so great and noble beauty, wish to know toward whom your beloved is moved or toward whom he turns aside through mercy and grace. Thus, seeking him also by your example, after we have found him, we may be thought beautiful to some extent, even if not most beautiful [Col. 1206C].

To this the Church, or the soul beloved by God, showing the place of this beloved’s movement or turning aside, at the same time indicates the action involved in his turning aside, saying: “My beloved has gone down into his garden,” and so forth.

## CHAPTER VI

**VERSE 1.**—“My beloved has gone down into his garden, to the bed of spices, to feed in the gardens and gather lilies.”

What, indeed, was it to seek the beloved except to ascend to him through the power of contemplation? Since in the hearts of the saints faith works through love (Gal. 5), and love always draws the mind upward, to do good is therefore to descend to God in one’s mind. But since every good is from God, without whom no good exists, for someone to be assisted by him in doing good is surely for God to descend to that person. For it is written in Exodus that Moses ascended the mountain and the Lord descended to him (Exod. 19). For as much as anyone ascends to God in thought, seeking him in action, so much does God descend to that person: either by opening his mysteries through understanding or by imparting the aid of his grace through strength of mind. Where anyone ascends to God by free choice, in will and work, there God descends to him through assisting grace, by his mercy and condescension [Col. 1207A].

Therefore the beloved fittingly replies here to those desiring to seek the beloved: “My beloved has gone down into his garden.” It is as though she said: “Because you desire to know where my beloved has gone or turned aside, behold, I tell you that my beloved has gone down into his garden.” What is the beloved’s garden except either the holy Church or any holy soul bringing forth diverse kinds of virtues? Into it the beloved descends because he bestows the aid of his grace upon it as it blossoms in good actions.

But after he has descended into the garden, where has he turned himself? “To the bed,” she says, “of spices.” What is the bed of spices [Col. 1207B] except a mind planted with diverse kinds of sweetly fragrant virtues, or sprinkled with the renown of different graces as with a sweet odour? For those who can say with the Apostle, “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God in every place” (2 Cor. 2), may each in his own way be called a bed of spices in the Lord’s garden—that is, in the holy Church—because through examples of good works they spread into the minds of their neighbours the fragrance of a good reputation.

Why does she say not a bed, but, by diminution, a little bed (*areola*)? Surely because the holy mind which shines with the loftiness of virtues ought to be small in its own eyes, and should earnestly show that “the Lord on high looks upon lowly things” and “will save the humble in spirit” (Pss. 112, 33). To this little bed the beloved, descending into his garden, turns aside, because he makes himself accessible and, as it were, manageable to the holy mind through increases of holiness and knowledge. Every pursuit seems difficult to the beginner but easy to one accustomed to it. The gate is narrow and the entrance difficult to one entering upon the way of God’s commandments or the knowledge of holy Scripture; but to one who treads it through long exercise and, as it were, drives back frequent obstacles, the broad and spacious way of holiness and understanding opens up, and thereafter entrance and exit lie open easily [Col. 1207C].

She then gives the reason why he descended: “To feed,” she says, “in the gardens, and to gather lilies.” He feeds in the gardens because he delights in the fragrance spread from the bed of spiritual spices—that is, of good works. For he himself says in the Gospel: “My food is to do the will of my Father” (John 4). The Father’s will is that all people should be saved (1 Tim. 2). But for people to seek salvation and attain it is his work. And whatever the Father does, the Son also does, because the Father and the Son will the same thing, and their will and operation are one.

He gathers lilies because he especially chooses those who shine in integrity and purity of heart and body, or receives for reward in eternal blessedness those perfect in faith and work [Col. 1208A].

**VERSE 2.**—“I am my beloved’s, and my beloved is mine, who feeds among the lilies.”

“My beloved,” she says, “previously commanded me: ‘Arise, open to me, my sister, my friend, my dove, my undefiled one’ (Song 5), and I obeyed him by opening the bolt of my door, preaching him to all and reasonably showing how great and what sort he is. But what did my beloved do in response? He surely repaid my rejoicing obedience by singing to me the praise of his condescension, celebrating as blessed in me not my grace but his own. For it was his doing that I willed, that I was able, and that I accomplished. He therefore proclaims his own gifts in me, in order to show me and all who obey his grace how great is the merit before God of a life obedient to holiness and honourableness [Col. 1208B].

But what sort of beloved is he? “Who feeds among the lilies,” she says: that is, he delights in pure thought and action. Not that anything grows in him incidentally, since he never receives increase or decrease; he always remains unchangeable in one and the same essence and property. Rather, by a manner of speech transferred from the creature, the affection of his goodness is expressed toward those whom he has deigned to honour with his love and grace. He is said to feed when the progress of virtues is increased in the mind of anyone whom his grace inhabits.

But with what song, or in what mode of song, did the voice of this beloved sound to me? Surely with a sweet song, a song to be attended to no lightly: in an eight-stringed mode indeed, but disposed in each string in a distinctive fashion according to the force of each sound, with its own proper theme.

**VERSE 3.**—“You are beautiful, my friend, sweet and lovely as Jerusalem, terrible as an army arrayed in battle.”

It is pleasing to observe attentively here how the modulation of the present song proceeds in eight parts, as though through eight notes, so that the character of that harmony which musicians call *diapason* may be perceived. Its last note is the same as its first, as may be seen in the arrangement of these parts: the first part is set down in this manner, “terrible as an army arrayed in battle,” and the last part likewise ends in the same manner, namely, “terrible as an army arrayed in battle” [Col. 1208C].

But the individual parts require individual explanations, which are distinguished as follows. The first is: “You are beautiful, my friend, sweet and lovely as Jerusalem, terrible as an army arrayed in battle.”

“You are beautiful,” he says, “my friend, sweet and lovely as Jerusalem”: beautiful in intention, sweet in speech, lovely in action, and therefore to be joined to me in the inviolable covenant of holy friendship. And how do this beauty, sweetness, and loveliness appear? “As Jerusalem.” What does Jerusalem mean except “vision of peace”? Three kinds of this vision are indicated under the name Jerusalem: one earthly, another spiritual, a third heavenly. The middle one is constituted in likeness to the outer two; yet it transcends the first and prepares for the last.

How, then, is the middle one constituted in likeness to the outer two? In the mind of each person there are virtues, like citizens and members of the household of the soul; against them are set vices and sins, like the soul’s bitterest enemies. The middle vision takes its likeness from the vision of earthly peace: just as a city, after its enemies have been conquered and expelled, flourishes, rejoices, and prospers in peace, so the mind, after overcoming vices and sins, rests sweetly in the delight of virtues and grows peacefully in God’s grace, with the flesh subjected to the spirit. And it is raised all the more toward contemplation of divinity the less it is attacked by earthly desires [Col. 1209B].

Moreover, it takes another likeness from the vision of the peace above, though not one wholly comparable; for this is in a mystery, whereas that is in truth. Thus, as there the soul, free from every misery and toil, ceaselessly beholds God in contemplative love, so here the mind, freed from every assault of the flesh, makes daily progress toward the sweetness of that same contemplative life. Therefore this middle vision may rightly, as has been said, be a preparation for that final and eternal one, because through this one we come to that; while it is a surpassing of the first, because, although there is some likeness between them in principle, there is nevertheless no comparison in dignity: the former is a momentary enjoyment of worldly peace, the latter an eternal contemplation of heavenly peace—one which indeed begins here but is perfected there.

To which, then, of these three visions of peace is the beloved’s beauty compared? If we say to the first, what comparison can there be between flesh and spirit, light and darkness, time and eternity? But if we say to the last, what comparison is there between that which is still held in fear and that which is granted free and secure from every fear without end? It may therefore be compared to the middle vision, so that this beauty, this sweetness, this comeliness are gathered from the vision of inward peace; and they arise, increase, and remain where no delights of temporal things weary the mind, but where, as the conflict of flesh and Spirit ceases, according to the Apostle, “May the peace of Christ, which surpasses all understanding, guard hearts and minds” (Phil. IV), resting in the love of contemplative life. Therefore you are beautiful, beloved, sweet and comely like Jerusalem: like the vision of a mind at peace, which no injury of disturbance and no vexation of adversity unsettles amid the delight of holy contemplation.

What effect, then, does the delight of this contemplation produce? Surely a great one: it kindles the whole mind in love of God and neighbour and makes it terrible to malignant spirits—the enemies, that is, of its own soul. For he adds: “Terrible as an army drawn up in battle array.” For when an army is so ordered that, by the unanimity and concord of the forces arrayed together, no opening for attack can be afforded to the enemy, then it surely presents itself as terrible to that enemy. But where, through the disorder of the army, an opening for assault is granted to the enemy, there it certainly appears terrible in no way.

Therefore, when the holy Church, or a soul beloved by God, sets the battle-line of spiritual warfare against malignant spirits, it is supremely necessary that it always be found united and bound together by love, never broken apart by discord. For even if it possesses every good thing, if love is absent, a place is opened in the battle-line through the evil of discord, by which the enemy can enter to strike. For the ancient enemy fears neither chastity nor abstinence nor the distribution of earthly possessions when these exist without love, since he is not weighed down by flesh, so that either its lust might weaken him or the necessity of taking food or acquiring the means of riches might constrain him.

But he greatly fears true love—that is, the humble love which believers mutually show one another—and he intensely envies their concord, because they possess on earth what he, refusing to possess it, lost in heaven.

Therefore it is well said, “Terrible as an army drawn up in battle array,” because malignant spirits fear the multitude of the elect all the more as they see them more closely united and massed against themselves through the concord of love.

[Col. 1210C] VERSE 4.—“Turn your eyes away from me, for they have made me fly away. Your hair is like a flock of goats that have appeared from Gilead.”

The second and third parts are contained in this verse. He says, then: “Turn your eyes away from me, for they have made me fly away.” Because, he says, the building of your mind rises honourably and profitably from the foundation of fraternal love within Jerusalem—that is, the vision of peace—displaying its beauty afar in thought, speech, and deed. This, indeed, is the summit and highest point, as it were the conclusion, of that same building: that it may be brought to completion in one cubit, namely by fixing your whole intention upon the love of God alone. Hence, O friend, you still possess this more abundantly from my grace: that through the subtlety of a purified mind you may be able to penetrate something of my power and splendour.

Yet, however much you strive and however greatly you exert the keenness of your mind, your labour is frustrated, because it is impossible for any ingenuity or reasoning to define that which is incomprehensible and unbounded.

For this reason, “Turn your eyes away from me”: that is, do not wish perfectly to know the substance of my divinity, which is granted to no one in this life. Rather turn to yourself, and remember human frailty. For your eyes—that is, the perceptions of your mind—too intently fixed upon me, have made me fly away; because the more you stretch yourself toward me, the more you will find me incomprehensible, according to what is written: “Man shall approach a deep heart, and God shall be exalted” (Ps. LXIII). For the more deeply and subtly you approach me in examining the proper character of my substance, the more sublimely I fly away, surpassing every consideration and subtlety of your understanding. Therefore, “Turn your eyes away from me,” because although your perceptions are indeed very penetrating in contemplation of the mind through the abundance of my grace, they utterly fail to comprehend me—who seem to fly away because of the depth of the reality. But if such is the grace of your eyes, what, likewise, is the grace of your hair?

“Your hair is like a flock of goats that have appeared from Gilead.” A little above, the beloved’s praise was sung in the same terms, which he now repeats either in order to show that she ought to possess the same beauty and comeliness of disposition and soul in preaching the word of God for the instruction of hearers as she had in the solitude of contemplation for her own benefit; or because the holy Church, whether universal or particular, is more commendable in the twofold order of which it consists, namely superiors and subjects. In these are considered all its beauty, grace, and dignity: in the former, through their life and teaching; in the latter, through obedience and reverence for discipline.

For just as hair, growing from the head, adheres to the head, so subjects adhere in faith and conduct to the prelates who have begotten them through the word of life. They ascend, as it were, from Gilead, because, while their teachers set before them a heap of testimony—that is, sacred Scripture—they raise their lives toward heaven by right conduct.

[Col. 1211C] VERSE 5.—“Your teeth are like a flock of sheep that have come up from the washing; all bearing twins, and none is barren among them.”

Here the fourth part is touched upon. By teeth, indeed, what are understood but teachers, who bring the coarseness of the letter into the subtlety of spiritual meaning? They are white through simplicity, as though washed in the laver of holy compunction. Hence they themselves are fruitful with a twofold love, or instructed by the twofold Testament; and they make those subject to them fruitful through the same love and the same Testament, teaching them so that none among them—that is, neither superiors nor subjects—may grow sluggish through barrenness of virtues.

But the hair of the individual soul, born from the governing faculty of the mind as from a head, are the subtleties of thoughts directed toward a heap of divine sayings. Its teeth, on the other hand, are the vigorous, studious applications of the same mind, repeatedly considering matters: they break down the hard and strong propositions or oppositions of the Scriptures and unravel their many entanglements. In these there is no barrenness, because the more diligently and continuously they apply the mind to the Scriptures, the more strongly they are pierced toward the love of God and neighbour, and the more fully they attain knowledge of both Testaments; or, while keeping the commandment, they add counsel. For the commandment is not to seize another’s property; the counsel is to give one’s own.

These, indeed, are the twin offspring by which the soul is made fruitful: love of God and neighbour, knowledge of the Old and New Testaments, observance of the commandment together with the addition of counsel. By the intention and study of these, every inward barrenness is driven away, so that the beloved is rightly declared beautiful, sweet, and comely in thought, action, and preaching.

VERSE 6.—“Like the rind of a pomegranate, so are your cheeks, apart from your hidden things.”

If we refer this universally to the whole Church, its cheeks may be called those who live spiritually within it. When they shine through memorable and wonderful words and deeds, and also through astonishing miracles, they appear venerable, as it were, upon the face of the Church. For the beauty of cheeks is seen in their redness. But if so great is the glory of its beauty in what appears, what will its pure glory be in those things that do not yet appear? Of these it is written: “Eye has not seen, nor ear heard, what God has prepared for those who love him” (I Cor. II).

Thus the cheeks of the Church are compared to the rind of a pomegranate; but its hidden things, because they are ineffable, are therefore incomparable.

But if we refer this particularly to the dignity of the holy soul, its inward beauty is often declared by certain outward signs. For when the modesty of virginal chastity reddens in the face, what is held within the mind is shown outwardly. Thus its cheeks are like the rind of a pomegranate apart from its hidden things: outwardly it produces, through modesty, a certain sign of holiness; but how greatly that holiness itself flourishes in the hidden part of its mind is known only to him from whom nothing can be concealed. And this is concerning the cheeks.

VERSE 7.—“There are sixty queens and eighty concubines, and maidens without number.”

The sixth and seventh parts are described in the present verse. For whereas in the preceding verses he had proclaimed the Church’s beauty part by part, in prelates, subjects, and those living spiritually, who were signified by hair, teeth, and cheeks, he now celebrates its perfect beauty as a whole in the unity of faith with illustrious praise. For although the holy Church seems in some way diverse because of the diversity of merits, nevertheless, on account of the one and same faith, it is not found diverse. Three classes of those living within it may be considered: there are in it the perfect, the less perfect, and the imperfect. The perfect are those who have left all that is theirs and have clung to God alone with their whole mind; the less perfect are those who have not left all that is theirs, but strive to minister to God in his members from what they are able to possess; the imperfect are those who indeed adhere to the former by faith, but who, as still in a tender manner of life, have not yet attained the good of perfect discernment.

Accordingly, the sum of three numbers is introduced here not inappropriately: namely, sixty, eighty, and ten. For ten multiplied by six rises to sixty, while eight multiplied by ten makes eighty. Six is called perfect by the rule of arithmetic, because, when all its parts—three, two, and one—are added together (three being its half, two its third, and one its sixth), it is restored to its original sum without any increase or decrease. Eight, on the other hand, is called deficient, because its half is four, its fourth two, and its eighth one; when these parts are added together, they make seven, namely a quantity less than the preceding total. But ten, which signifies the Decalogue of the Law, because it consists of seven and three, indicates the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit and the confession of faith in the holy Trinity; this number shows who are perfect and who imperfect. [Note: [Col. 1213D] Something is lacking.] For the Holy Spirit himself, in the effects of his gifts, shows who love God perfectly, who love him less, and who as yet have neither fear nor love of God.

For there are two things that make us wholly subject to God: fear and love. His power and wisdom especially instil fear, when we know that he exists, that he can punish all things according to his will, and that nothing is hidden from him. But his goodness particularly belongs to love, so that we should chiefly love him whom we know to be most good. From this it is also certain that he wishes to avenge impiety, because the more justice pleases him, the more iniquity displeases him, as it is written: “You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity” (Ps. XLIV).

Therefore, by the number sixty, which is produced by multiplying ten by six, the perfect number, is expressed the life of the perfect. They would not perfectly observe the divine commandments unless they first possessed initial fear and afterward filial love, which casts out fear itself. Such souls are rightly called queens, because, with divine grace cooperating, they know and are able to govern themselves by reason and understanding. They discern usefulness, glory, and honour in carrying out good; but loss, misery, and horror in perpetrating evil. Therefore they strongly pursue good and strongly shun evil.

But by the number eighty, produced by multiplying ten by eight, which is called deficient, is denoted the life of the less perfect. They observe the divine commandments indeed, but do not love God so perfectly as to be able to leave all earthly things. These souls are designated by the name of concubines because, although they are joined to God through good works, they have not yet attained that divine right of which it is said: “He who clings to God becomes one spirit with him” (I Cor. VI). For this is the full settlement of the spiritual dowry: that those who utterly renounce the world may never be separated from divine fellowship. But the number of maidens is not specified, because the number of the imperfect is infinite. Being still established in the first beginnings of faith, they need the instruction of their elders in order to conceive the fear of God, through which they may one day advance to his love.

Among them are some whose standing is often doubtful, since not all belong to the lot of the elect, according to the Lord’s saying: “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. XX).

VERSE 8.—“My dove, my perfect one, is one; she is one to her mother, chosen for her who bore her. The daughters saw her and proclaimed her most blessed; the queens and concubines praised her.”

Although, then, there are such diverse degrees of merit in the Church, is it therefore said to be diverse? By no means; rather, as follows: “My dove, my perfect one, is one; she is one to her mother, chosen for her who bore her.” In what sense one? Namely, because of the one and same reception of faith and sacraments, the worship of one God, and a like rite of religion. For “there is one faith,” as the Apostle says, “one baptism, one God and Father of all, who is above all and in all of us” (Eph. IV).

“My dove, my perfect one,” he says, “is one.” For she is not my dove unless, bearing in her mouth the sign of peace and mercy, she keeps the unity of the Spirit in her heart and exercises the virtue of mercy in deed. “Mercy and truth have met one another; righteousness and peace have kissed” (Ps. LXXXIV). For she ought always to sing of mercy and judgment (Ps. C), in the authority to bind and loose granted to her by me. Nor will she be my perfect one unless she possesses full knowledge of discernment, so as to know who ought justly and worthily to be bound or loosed. She is one dove and one perfect one of mine, because outside her there is no remission of sins and no distribution of gifts. Therefore those are excluded who do not confess the one, holy, catholic, and universal Church. For the lamb is eaten in one house and its flesh is not carried outside, because the sacraments have no efficacy except in the one catholic Church.

“She is one to her mother,” that is, to the heavenly Jerusalem, because she who here on earth is one in faith and in the dignity of the sacraments will there in heaven be one in the blessedness of eternal life. For the blessedness of the saints is one, although they do not enjoy it in one manner, owing to the differing qualities of their merits. “Chosen for her who bore her,” that is, for the Church of the ancient Fathers, namely the patriarchs and prophets, whose faith she imitated and whose promise she inherited. For she is the chosen one to whom that promise of God’s purpose was to be given—the promise made to the Fathers in the first days and fulfilled in the last days. The same faith justifies her concerning things past and future which justified the ancient Fathers only concerning future things.

For faith concerns present and future things as well as past things, although faith concerning present things is so called improperly and not strictly. For when the Apostle defines faith, saying, “Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen” (Heb. XI), it is clear that faith is evidence of those things which cannot appear. Things that are apparent do not have faith, but knowledge.

But since we are dealing with the Song of Songs, does musical speculation have any relevance to those two numbers set forth above, namely sixty and eighty? It does not seem at all irrelevant that, where songs are under discussion, we should sometimes consider the modes of singing. For since the whole constitution of our soul and body is joined together by a musical fitting-together, it is clear—and proved by examples on the authority of both divine and human writings—that the force of musical harmony has greatly availed to compose, stir, or calm minds. Should not, then, in this Song of Songs, which wholly aims to kindle minds in love for the heavenly bridegroom, some consideration of musical consonance avail for the composing or stirring of the soul? Certainly, in this place it may offer some small assistance to the imperfection of the concubines and maidens, so that they may in some degree be incited to attain the perfection which it is evident they do not yet possess.

But because every harmonious arrangement of numbers is assigned by proportions, we must see what consonance is contained in the proportional relation of these two numbers, sixty and eighty. The relation of eighty to sixty is therefore *epitrite* (ἐπίτριτα), or sesquitertian, because eighty contains the whole of sixty and its third part, that is, twenty. In music this proportion sounds as the *diatessaron* (διατέσσερον), the fourth; it is called *diatessaron*, “through four,” because it resounds through four notes, consisting of two tones and a semitone.

[Col. 1215C] If it is asked what relevance, in this place, consideration of this harmony has through the proportion of these numbers, we reply that there is a very fitting rationale for such consideration. For the whole universal Church, spread through the four quarters of the world and, as has been said, distinguished by three classes of those living within it—the perfect, the less perfect, and the imperfect—attains the whole sum of its salvation through the faith and sacraments of the New Testament, established in the perfection of the four Gospels. Thus, as it were, a sweet concord of the *diatessaron* harmony consists in the consonance of the four evangelists, in four books as in four voices, through which the mind of every Christian is stirred and ordered toward the worship of sacred religion.

“The daughters of Zion saw her and proclaimed her most blessed; the queens and concubines praised her.” Such a Church, he says—as has been stated, differing in the quality of merits but alike in unity of faith and sacraments—the daughters of Zion saw: that is, souls who direct their attention by the contemplation of the mind, not by bodily sight, and weigh the beauty and dignity of the whole Church in the excellence of spiritual dignities and the grace of virtues. They also consider the necessary benefit of that beauty, since within her are found a more abundant and more salutary bestowal of temporal things and an incomparable, never-ending grant of eternal things. Therefore they proclaimed her most blessed, because nothing is more blessed than always to possess God: here, using him temporally in his gifts; there, enjoying him eternally.

The queens and concubines likewise praised her, because holy souls that know how to govern their inner and outer senses by reason greatly delight in this dignity of the holy Church and in the benefit of that dignity. They greatly praise—that is, approve—her spiritual marks of action and the pious aids of sacramental things.

VERSE 9.—“Who is this that comes forth like the rising dawn, beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun, terrible as an army drawn up in battle array?”

Thus these daughters of Zion, or the beloved himself, proclaiming her beauty, ask not interrogatively as though ignorant, but affirmatively in wonder at what they know well. In such a proclamation they raise, as it were, an eighth voice and say:

“Who is this that comes forth like the rising dawn, beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun, terrible as an army drawn up in battle array?” For those who look here not cursorily but attentively find, in the measure of this praise, a noteworthy modulation of the aforementioned harmony which we called *diatessaron*. It suggests the confirmation of faith, hope, love, and the sacraments; the preaching of the Gospel through the four parts of the world; and likewise the useful and necessary attainment of the four principal virtues. Why should we not discern here a distinction of four voices and a fourfold comparison of diverse things: the advance of dawn, the beauty of the moon, the excellence of the sun, and the strength of an army in battle array? For what more belongs to the beauty of the whole Church? Indeed, if faith, hope, love, and the sacraments are lacking; if the preaching of the Gospel is not received; if the four foundations of virtues are absent, from which the edifices of all other virtues arise—what beauty will remain to the Church or to any holy soul?

But we must see what these likenesses signify and how they correspond to the foregoing: namely, faith, hope, love, and the sacraments. Dawn is the beginning of day; faith, moreover, is the beginning of holiness and religion, as it were of a certain day. For holiness is understood by the name of day and light, just as sin is understood by the name of night and darkness. Therefore the Church, or any holy soul, advances like dawn, because, called first to faith by divine grace, it receives daily increase in that same faith through the same grace.

The moon always receives light from the sun and, placed in the other half of the hemisphere opposite the sun, pours the full light of its disk upon the earth. But when it begins to wane, it returns toward the sun in order to be rekindled by it, and then again supplies the world through the fullness of its light. From whom, then, does the holy Church, or any holy soul, receive the light of knowledge, the light also of holiness, righteousness, and holy hope, except from that true Sun of righteousness, the Lord Jesus Christ, “who enlightens every person coming into this world” (John I)? But because its beauty differs greatly from the beauty of him from whom it receives its beauty, it is not called beautiful absolutely, but beautiful by comparison, like the moon. For just as the moon, compared with the sun—or shining with the sun—does not shine, yet whatever light it has it has from the sun, so the saints, compared with the Holy of Holies, are nothing; yet whatever holiness they possess, they possess from him. And what is the Church but the gathering of saints?

When, because of fraternal love or because of the obstacle of their own frailty, they often depart from divine contemplation and decline somewhat from the light of subtle understanding, they at times gather themselves back to themselves and return with their whole mind to him of whom it is written: “Draw near to him and be enlightened” (Ps. XXXIII). Looking upon him, as it were, through a certain opposition of the mind, they receive from him whatever fullness they have, from him of whom it is said: “And from his fullness we have all received” (John I).

What, then, do those advancing in faith and in the works of faith conceive except hope? For who would not hope for future goods when their works are full of light? Thus the Church is rightly said to be beautiful as the moon in them.

But since faith is like dawn advancing—that is, pouring forth the first light of its religion and holiness—through faith one surely comes to hope, because we hope that we shall one day obtain what we believe. Hence the Apostle says: “Through faith we have access to this grace in which we stand, and we glory in hope of the glory of the children of God” (Rom. V). It is as if he said in other words: Through faith, which is the beginning and, as it were, an entrance to every good work—as dawn is to day—we come and advance into the grace of full light, that is, holiness, according to the measure granted us by grace itself. In the grace of this light we stand, that is, persevere, because through it we have hope of being joined to the future glory of the children of God.

Immediately he adds: “And not only”—understand, “do we glory in this hope”—“but we also glory in tribulations, knowing that tribulation produces patience, patience testing, testing hope, and hope does not disappoint.” To show the efficient cause of the certainty of this hope, he adds: “Because love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.” For this is the anchor of all good intention and action, because, as the same Apostle says, “Love never fails” (I Cor. XIII).

This is what follows: “Chosen as the sun,” namely because of love. For as the sun is brighter than all the stars, so love is more excellent than all virtues, although in relation to divinity it is altogether incomparable. But the holy Church, in those who burn with perfect love and shine in action, is called chosen as the sun. For although “star differs from star in glory” (I Cor. XV), that part of the saints which is found brighter than the rest in holiness is compared with the sun. Thus in those who are still weak and tender in faith and action, she advances like dawn; in those who have already made some progress through the course of their manner of life, she is called beautiful as the moon; but in those who are perfect, and through love—which casts out fear perfectly—pass beyond the highest spirits, called seraphim, that is, “burning ones,” and are joined more closely to the true sun, she is rightly called chosen as the sun.

Or “chosen as the sun” means predestined for adoption, so that by grace she may be what that true Sun is by nature, who “gave power to become children of God to those who believe in his name” (John I).

But, someone may ask, what does the fourth member—the fourth voice, as it were, of the aforesaid *diatessaron* harmony—have to do with the sacraments: “Terrible as an army drawn up in battle array”? Certainly, I say, it has much to do with them, as is evident from the effects of the sacraments themselves. For what is more terrible to the enemies of the soul, that is, malignant spirits, than the powers of the sacraments, by which their power is weakened and all their authority and audacity put to flight?

Wherever any sacrament is so performed that the reality of the sacrament may also be present—that is, in the peace and unity of the Church, outside which there is no place for saving sacraments—there the effect of that sacrament is surely exceedingly terrible and unbearable to evil spirits. This is so whether it be in baptism, in the Lord’s body, in the conferral of orders, or in the ordering of any matters performed according to ecclesiastical institutions. This seems to be suggested by the comparison in which she is called “terrible as an army drawn up in battle array.” For just as a well-bound and orderly compacted battle-line suffers no breach, so the Church, joined by the sacrament of unity, is not scattered by any assault of malignant spirits.

But heretics, who have cut themselves off from this unity, are not contained within this battle-line. Being placed outside, they cannot repel any adversities from those spirits, since the Church’s sacraments, which they seem to possess, they do not possess in reality but only in outward form. Nevertheless, if sacraments are rightly celebrated by them and received by believers, those believers receive both the sacrament and the reality of the sacrament—that is, its inwardly operative power. The heretics themselves, however, are shown to receive the sacrament but not the reality of the sacrament. Therefore their assembly is not terrible as an army drawn up in battle array, because, so far as they are concerned, the sacraments do not produce that effect and confer upon them no remedies.

VERSE 10.—“I went down into the garden of nuts, to see the fruits of the valleys, and to observe whether the vines had flowered and the pomegranates had budded.”

After the beloved has graciously pursued the beauty of the holy beloved—that is, the Church—with praise, although that praise itself derives from him who by his grace has presented her to himself “without spot or wrinkle” (Eph. V), he shows in what follows that, through the unbelief of the Jewish people, she obtained this gift and merit of faith. As the Apostle says: “Through their transgression salvation came to the Gentiles; and their transgression is the riches of the world, and their diminution the riches of the Gentiles” (Rom. XI). He who exalted the one in an admiring manner depresses the other in the same manner, because while the former believed and received the word of God, the latter was unwilling either to believe or to receive that very word. Hence it is written of her in the Gospel: “And Jesus marvelled at their unbelief” (Mark VI).

He says, then: “I went down into the garden of nuts.” What was his going down except to come into this world by being born from the height of his divinity, and then to endure every weakness of humanity? Were not all these things, fulfilled in their proper order, a kind of descent? And where were these descents enacted? Was it not in Judaea? Indeed, the Lord himself says: “I was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matt. XV). This is what he says here: “I went down into the garden of nuts.” For the Jewish nation may not inappropriately be called a garden of nuts. Just as the kernel of a nut is covered beneath rind and shell, so among the Jews the sweetness of spiritual understanding lies hidden beneath the hardness of the literal surface.

That nation, then, is called a garden of nuts because, although it is called a garden on account of the usefulness of legal commandments and observances—which flourished in their own time and benefited their observers until the time of grace—nevertheless all the future sacraments of the Church lay hidden in it under a figure, as beneath the rind of a nut. Therefore the Lord went down into this garden because he first showed the Jewish people the presence of his flesh by preaching and performing miracles.

Why, then, did he go down into this garden? “To see,” he says, “the fruits of the valleys”: that is, to make known whether any had produced the fruit of faith and righteousness, and whether, as reason showed them, they understood that they could not be justified by works of the Law, but by the faith which I set before believers through the grace of the New Testament. But when I say “to know,” I do not mean that I, who am everywhere and to whom all things past and future are present, had not eternally possessed in my presence this or any other knowledge. Rather, speaking in a human manner, I would show their works to the world, whether they were to be followed or not.

Why do I say “of the valleys”? Because of the lowliness of the letter which they carry out carnally, or because of the shadow of the Law by which they are surrounded, lest they be illuminated by the light of its truth.

“And to observe whether the vines had flowered”: that is, whether they had conceived even some taste of spiritual understanding, whether they had applied themselves through some beginning of a good work of faith. For the houses of Israel, distinguished by twelve tribes, are called vines. Though called vines because of the distinction of tribes, they are nevertheless called one vine because of the one observance of the Law; just as many churches are now spoken of because of difference of places, but one Church because of unity of faith. The Prophet testifies that the whole people is called the Lord’s vine: “The vineyard of the Lord is the house of Israel” (Isa. V). The Psalmist also says of it: “You brought a vine out of Egypt” (Ps. LXIX). But when I expected this vine to flower and produce grapes, it produced wild grapes (Isa. V); for after the Gentiles believed, they themselves remained in unbelief.

“I went down also, to observe whether the pomegranates had budded”: that is, whether they would not only believe in me but also possess the willingness to suffer for me. But they were unwilling either to believe or to suffer anything for me; indeed, they killed me as I preached to them and showed them the way of salvation.

In another way also, it does not seem burdensome to expound this passage of the present song through the likeness of the nut, so that the reader may choose what seems better and more correct to him in these matters. It is not absurd to understand the garden of nuts as the whole human race. For in a nut three things are considered: the outer husk, the shell, and the kernel; [Col. 1220B] and in humankind, man consists of flesh, bone, and soul. The substance of flesh is like the husk; the strength of bone is like the shell; and the sweetness of the soul is like the kernel. And just as the kernel is covered by husk and shell, so the soul is clothed with flesh and bones. Hence Job, considering that man consists of these three things, says: “You have clothed me with skin and flesh; you have compacted me with bones and sinews” (Job 10). And to show the third thing which gives life and vigor to those two, namely the soul, he adds: “You have granted me life and mercy” (ibid.). Therefore Christ descended into the garden of nuts when, by coming into this world, he assumed human nature.

And why? “That he might see the fruits of the valleys,” 222 that is, that he might visit the humble who bear the fruit of righteousness, [Col. 1220C] and choose them for himself. For his seeing is his choosing, so that, coming in humility, he might signify that he receives the humble and obedient, as it is written: “And he will save the humble in spirit” (Ps. 33). He descended also “to see whether the vines had blossomed and the pomegranates had budded,” that is, whether the Churches of the faithful had begun the endeavor of right living or teaching, and whether they strove to persevere in his love unto death, so that, by granting them his aid, he himself might be both inspirer and fellow-worker, as he says in promising them: “Behold, I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28).

[Col. 1220D] VERSE 11.—“I did not know; my soul troubled me because of the chariots of Aminadab.”

The Jewish people allege as the cause of their ignorance and blindness that, after the law had been given—which was to justify and save them—and after God had confirmed it by many signs and by the great authorities of the holy Fathers, it would be impossible for it to be set aside by any novelty, since God is immutable and does not, after the manner of men, say, command, and establish something at one time which at another time he prohibits and destroys. “For,” they say, “if what now pleases him displeases him in the future, he is changeable”—a most absurd thing to say, and something which cannot be maintained on any rational ground: that God is changeable. But if he himself is unchangeable, then his words and commandments also are unchangeable. Since he is altogether unchangeable, whatever [Col. 1221A] he has said or established must necessarily be fixed and unchangeable. Therefore he did not establish a second and new law in order to destroy the first and ancient one.

They are answered that what they have proposed must be granted: namely, that God is unchangeable; hence in the new law he established nothing that derogated from the former. Rather, the new law and the old are the same law: the former in the letter, the latter in the Spirit; the former in figure, the latter in truth. That this is so was foreshown long ago in the vision of Ezekiel the prophet, where “a wheel in the midst of a wheel” is said to have appeared (Ezek. 10). For the wheel in the midst of the wheel is the New Testament within the Old Testament, because what the Old Testament signified, the New displayed. Therefore the unchangeable God altered nothing in this, since he placed one [Col. 1221B] beneath the other in such a way that one was the signifier and the other the thing signified.

This, then, that people first did not know: they read what signified, but did not understand what was signified. But after being visited by divine grace, they began to know and believe that “the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life”; 223 and, repenting of their error, they were alarmed, saying: “I did not know; my soul troubled me because of the chariots of Aminadab.” As though saying: “I could not believe because I had not yet at all understood the grace of the Gospel. For my soul troubled me, because I wondered what it meant that I must now receive the four books of the Gospels, whereas formerly I received the five books of Moses—as though such a change could occur in God, so that what had formerly pleased him no longer pleased him, [Col. 1221C] and he should establish a new law after transferring the old one. But after I understood the wonderful providence of God, who instructed me through bodily things unto spiritual things, so that I might more easily and truly comprehend, ‘not first that which is spiritual, but that which is animal, then that which is spiritual,’ I laid aside every doubt and afterward defended the truth which I had formerly opposed—not only by believing and teaching the truth itself, but also by dying for it.”

But why do I say “the chariots of Aminadab”? Clearly because of the four books of the Gospel, in which are preached the four sacraments of this same Aminabad, whose name is interpreted “the willing one of my people.” And who is this Aminadab, unless Christ, who willingly laid down [Col. 1221D] his life in order to make me a willing people for himself and acceptable to God? And what are his four sacraments but his incarnation, passion, resurrection, and ascension? Therefore the chariot of this Aminadab is the book of the four Gospels, containing and imparting knowledge of the four aforesaid sacraments, with the Holy Spirit as charioteer, by whose inspiration such chariots were composed and ordered.

And when the gracious Father received that same people which had believed from among the circumcised, having cast off the thick darkness of ignorance and returned to itself, he meets it, as it were, with a consoling and exhortatory voice, urging it to repentance, saying: “Return, return, Shulamite,” etc.

[Col. 1222A] VERSE 12.—“Return, return, Shulamite; return, return, that we may look upon you.”

“Behold,” he says, “the voice of my chariot comes to meet you, proclaiming the cause, order, and necessary benefit of my sacraments—namely, my birth, passion, resurrection, and ascension. Though formerly, in your ignorance, you would neither hear nor receive that voice, now, O Shulamite—that is, captive, who are still held captive because you have not yet laid aside the bonds of original or actual sin through the washing of baptism and participation in my body and blood—return, because you have hope of pardon. For you withdrew from me through unbelief and ingratitude, forgetting the benefits which I wrought for you: when I freed you from the slavery [Col. 1222B] of Egypt; when I fed you with heavenly bread; when I gave you my law; and when, before all nations, I chose you as my own peculiar people. But now return to me through the voice of my chariot, through the four Gospels, which cry out to you as through four wheels and exhort you four times to repentance: return, return, return, return. Return through faith; return through action; return through right intention; return through love. For first you must believe, then act, since ‘faith without works is dead’ (Jas. 2). Moreover, your action must proceed from a good intention: that is, so that faith may work through love. For if your action does not arise from divine love, it is subject to vainglory [Col. 1222C] and therefore lacks reward, because it has not the merit of holiness.

“Return, moreover, that we may look upon you,” that is, that we may approve the beauty of your soul which you received through faith, and set you before others as an example to be followed. For this is your praiseworthy beauty, pleasing to our eyes: that, having laid aside error, you may follow truth; and that you who, through error and the shadow of the law, seemed ugly and dark, may through your return, through the truth and light of the Gospel, be seen as beautiful and bright. For as long as you lay hidden beneath the shadow, you were contemptible; but after you came out into the light of truth, you appeared worthy to be seen. And now ‘the king has desired your beauty’ (Ps. 44): namely, that heavenly King [Col. 1222D] who made you his bride through the grace of the Holy Spirit, after you returned to him by faith, action, right intention, and love.” These things have indeed been said particularly concerning that ancient people of God, which, the less it first understood the chariot of our Aminadab, the more abundantly, once it understood, received it with reverence.

But, to return to the moral sense, the signification of this chariot may not unprofitably be referred to the whole human race, so that we establish two parts of the whole and assign to one of them that chariot whose driver is the devil. For man, consisting of four elements, four humors, and likewise four stages of life, seems to possess, as regards the body, a kind of material chariot; [Col. 1223A] while as regards the soul, since it consists of four affections and also of four virtues by which it is led toward the good, the power and progress of the soul appear to possess a spiritual chariot.

Let us therefore first consider whatever bodily constitutions, arranged according to a fourfold scheme, may occur to the mind; then also the qualities of the affections, marked fourfold according to the soul. From these, as we have said, let us establish 225 two chariots: the material and the affective. Both, looking respectively to two charioteers—namely Christ and the devil—are subject to one or the other, since they cannot serve two masters (Matt. 6). Thus, if through God’s grace the spiritual chariot runs rightly and happily, it is called Christ’s chariot; [Col. 1223B] but if, through the deprivation of that same grace, the fleshly chariot runs perversely and unhappily, it is called the devil’s chariot.

There are, then, as we have said, four elements of which man consists: fire, air, water, and earth. These four are intermixed with the qualities of heat, cold, moisture, and dryness. Fire is hot and dry; air hot and moist; water cold and moist; earth cold and dry. Man himself, consisting of these four elements and their qualities, has heat from fire, breath from air, blood from water, and flesh from earth; and through the four stages of life, in the four seasons, he is changed by four humors.

[Col. 1223C] Spring, which is, as it were, the first flower and beginning of the year—for then the earth begins to bloom and bud—is hot and moist; it represents childhood, which is hot and moist, because blood in a child is hot and moist. Summer, which is hot and dry, represents adolescence, which is hot and dry, having red choler, abundant in adolescents, dry and hot. Autumn, which is cold and dry, signifies youth, which is cold and dry, having melancholic matter, that is, black choler, which in young people is cold and dry. Winter, however, which is cold and moist, signifies old age, which is cold and moist, with phlegm flowing, which abounds in old people and is cold and moist.

When such constitutions flourish in a person [Col. 1223D] well and in due order, they show the person to be healthy; but when they wander disorderly, they disturb the person and render him infirm. Yet because this fourfold constitution is materially present in the human body, by which man himself is drawn toward love of the flesh and desires of this world—desires contracted through the transmission of original sin—there also arise from this material constitution four affective qualities, which principally derive their power and nature from four internal members: namely, the gall bladder, spleen, liver, and heart. Thus, from the gall bladder man has the capacity for anger; from the spleen, the capacity for laughter; from the liver, the capacity for desire; and from the heart, the capacity for reason. Moreover, from the heart itself—whether called mind or soul—proceed, as it were, four conceptions, which [Col. 1224A] precede every action: thought, intention, will, and deliberation. 226 For when about to do something, we first think; then we intend why and how we shall do it; afterward we resolve in the will to do it; and finally we deliberate how to accomplish it. The power of reason itself is also diffused fourfold. Whoever possesses natural ability, memory, understanding, and discernment possesses the ability, through natural ability, to discover unknown and hidden things by seeking and investigating; through memory, to retain what has been discovered; through understanding, to order prudently, courageously, and honorably what has been retained; and through discernment, to assign what has been well ordered modestly to the places appropriate to it.

The rational soul also has four affections implanted in it: fear, hope, joy, [Col. 1224B] and sorrow. Of these the poet says:

> …They fear, desire, rejoice, and grieve.

And the philosopher says to one of his pupils, whom he wished to free from the stirrings of these passions:

> Drive out joys;  
> Drive out fear;  
> Banish hope;  
> And let no pain be present.

Those who treat of natural philosophy say that these affections rule more in some persons and less in others according to the constitutions of the material qualities set forth above. But [Col. 1224C] over all these presides the mind, vigorous in reason, which, when they intrude disorderly, composes them and, under the guidance of the divine Spirit, turns them toward some measure of honorableness or usefulness. For such an endeavor or discipline, four principal virtues must necessarily be employed and sought from God: prudence, fortitude, justice, and temperance. Since in every structure of the spiritual building they are laid, as it were, as cornerstones by which the other virtues are enclosed and held together, greater gifts of divine grace are recognized in them.

Since, therefore, we have established two chariots—the material and the affective—let us also set over each, as it were, two rulers: spirit and flesh; and let God and the devil be their charioteers. For the affective chariot [Col. 1224D] is moved toward reason and virtue more or less according as it is impelled more or less by the material chariot, through care for the flesh, toward love of temporal life.
