And according as the one ruling each is higher or lower—namely, spirit or flesh, which always oppose one another, because “the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Gal. 5)—so it is moved. Indeed, we say that spirit and flesh preside over both because in them are certain parts which tend from the flesh toward the spirit, or lapse from the spirit toward the flesh.

For in that material chariot there are often some who, stirred by the natural 227 heat and moisture of the flesh, contend with such strength of spirit through God’s grace that they break every natural impulse of the flesh through the fire of divine love and the force of the spirit, and sometimes burn it out utterly; thus they grow warm toward God and remain wholly cold toward the world. Conversely, some of cold nature are cold inwardly in God’s love, as toward every action, and therefore do not labor zealously for any good work. In that affective chariot also there are those who grow angry over a temporal injury, and those who grow angry for justice; there are those who desire good things, and those who desire evil things; there are those who laugh and rejoice because of the wretched prosperity of this life, and also those who rejoice and laugh amid adversities because of hope and assurance of future blessedness. There are likewise those who make good use of the good of reason, act rightly, and think wisely; and those who [Col. 1225B] use it badly, think perversely, and act perversely. There are nevertheless some who use natural ability for good, and some for evil; some who understand good rightly, and some wrongly; some who make a correct offering but do not divide rightly—that is, do not discern—and some who both make a correct offering and divide rightly—that is, discern. Conversely, some neither make a correct offering nor divide rightly—that is, discern.

Accordingly, four forms adhere to both these chariots, leading each of them into the full motions of its own pursuit: suggestion, delight, consent, and habit. For each person’s mind is led either to good or to evil in these four ways: toward good, by the suggestion of the Holy Spirit, as is said of him, “For he himself will suggest to you [Col. 1225C] all things whatsoever I have said to you” (John 14); by the delight of the soul; by the consent of the spirit; and by the habit of good itself. Toward evil, however, it is led by the suggestion of the devil, the delight of the flesh, the consent of the spirit, and the habit of evil itself.

Therefore, in the midst of these chariots, formed from the material of the flesh and the affection of the mind, it is necessary that the four principal virtues which we set out above—prudence, fortitude, justice, and temperance—be established, so that through a certain surrounding disposition of them the whole mass of the body placed within may be governed and ordered into some measure of rational form. For, as someone says:

> “Virtue is the mean between vices, and withdrawn from either extreme,”  
> [Col. 1225D] (Horace, *Epistles* I.18.9),

that is, removed from both sides. For example, to be dull or wickedly crafty is vicious; but between these vices, namely dullness and wicked craftiness, the virtue of prudence is established, by whose moderation this inequality is corrected. Fortitude likewise is placed between timidity and rashness, so that the truly brave person is one found neither timid in good nor rash in evil. The same may be seen in the other virtues: by considering the vices placed beside them, their character is understood.

From all this material, then—both fleshly and spiritual, distinguished fourfold—there arises a single composite thing, which bears within itself, as it were, a double chariot of flesh and spirit, over which [Col. 1226A] either God or the devil presides as charioteer. But God governs, saves, and gives life; the devil overthrows, condemns, and kills.

The name is indeed equivocal: though it is called a chariot in both cases, it differs in definition. For to depart from God through the suggestion of the devil, the delight of the flesh, the consent of the spirit, and the habit of evil action is to be the devil’s chariot. Conversely, to advance toward God through the suggestion of God, the delight of the soul, the consent of the spirit, and the habit of good action is to be God’s chariot. Likewise, God’s chariot is the mind squared by the four virtues stated above—prudence, justice, temperance, and fortitude—whereas [Col. 1226B] the devil’s chariot is opposed to it: namely, the mind weakened by the four vices contrary to those virtues, that is, foolishness, injustice, luxury, and fearfulness.

Therefore the Church—or the Bridegroom himself through the Church—cries to the Shulamite: “Return, return, return, return,” so that she who had sinned in these four ways may, by returning to God, offer the four fruits of repentance and mortify these things within herself through God’s grace and the strength of the mind. “Return,” he says, “through repentance and satisfaction for past evils; return through contempt for the world; return through mortification of the flesh; return through steadfastness in virtues. Return, moreover, that we may look upon you,” that is, that after you have done penance we may have mercy on you. For God’s seeing is his having mercy; hence the Psalmist says to [Col. 1226C] God: “Look upon me and have mercy on me” (Ps. 85). Conversely, the turning away of his face is his anger, as the same Psalmist says: “You turned your face away from me, and I became troubled” (Ps. 29).

That he says in the plural, “that we may look upon you,” is that manner of speech used of God when elsewhere he says, “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. 3), a manner introduced because of the plurality of persons in the Holy Trinity.

229 CHAPTER VII.

VERSE 1.—“What will you see in the Shulamite, but the choirs of camps? How beautiful are your steps in sandals, daughter of a prince! The joints of your thighs are like necklaces fashioned by the hand of an artisan.”

As long as Judaea was held captive by the bond of its error, or any soul by the yoke of sin, no delight but misery could be seen in it. For the former, amid the conflict of letter and Spirit, and the latter, amid the conflict of flesh and spirit, was always inferior in its better part: Judaea followed the letter alone, and the soul the flesh. But when, through repentance, the former recognized and received the spiritual sense, and the latter, trampling underfoot the love of the flesh, began to live according to the spirit, the gracious Father mercifully received both and showed that he would give them his aid, so that, having now attained true and complete freedom and, as it were, won victory over the opposing part, they might joyfully offer him devout praises in flesh and spirit. For he himself promises this through the prophet, saying: [Col. 1227A] “Return to me, and I will return to you” (Mal. 5). Hence, rejoicing also in their conversion, he says to the Church: “What will you see in the Shulamite, but the choirs of camps?” In choirs is displayed the harmonious alternation of a resounding melody; in camps the company of warriors is assembled for defense. What, therefore, are the choirs of camps but the praises of warriors? And the meaning is: “Because this Shulamite has returned to me from the captivity in which guilt held her, I will grant her such grace of freedom and security that you, O beloved, should see and admire nothing else in her but joyful thanksgivings and daily proclamations of praise for the conquered and suppressed movements of vices and for the granted advances in virtues.”

Now, as the two walls approaching from opposite directions have been joined into one—the Jewish people and the Gentile people, by which he shows the whole universal Church to consist—the discourse is again directed to her praise, so that in one body it may proclaim the notably established and diverse graces of his condescension, and consequently the thanksgivings justly and fittingly due to him. Therefore he says: [Col. 1227B] “How beautiful are your steps in sandals, daughter of a prince!”

What is expressed by steps except the course of actions? What is signified by sandals, made from the skins of dead animals, except the examples of preceding fathers who have departed from this life? For just as feet are protected by sandals, so the conduct of those who follow them is defended by the examples of the holy fathers.

And who is the daughter of a prince except either the Church or any holy soul devoted through the grace of adoption to him who is the prince of the kings of the earth? Therefore the Church, or any holy soul, has beautiful steps in sandals because it has beautiful and reverent actions derived from the deeds and teachings of the holy fathers. Hence he fittingly adds: “The joints of your thighs are like necklaces fashioned by the hand of an artisan.”

By the jointing of the thighs is understood the harmony of the two Testaments, because the Old and New Testaments are joined so equally that what one announces in figure the other presents in truth. [Col. 1227D] But why are these Testaments compared to necklaces? A necklace is composed of gold, silver, and precious stones, and is worn upon the breasts of matrons, serving both for protection and adornment. Both Testaments are constructed from the radiance of divine meaning and the brilliance of speech, as though from gold and silver, and from the declarations of diverse virtues, as though from precious gems. And just as a necklace protects and adorns a matron’s breast, so both Testaments spiritually protect and adorn the breast of the holy Church or of any holy soul: they protect it indeed from the hostility of vices, and adorn it with the beautiful variety of virtues.

Therefore her jointing of the thighs is like necklaces, because [Col. 1228A] the harmony of the two Testaments, by which the holy Church or any holy soul is daily instructed, brings it great protection and adornment: protection indeed against the perversities of heretics, and adornment because of the beauty and loveliness of meanings and expressions, or because of the power of the sacraments celebrated in it and the honorable order of the Church.

And who is this artisan, by whose hand these necklaces—that is, the Testaments—were fashioned, except almighty God? By his will, power, and operation these were honorably composed, profitably expounded, and happily received. Therefore the dignity of these Testaments is highly commendable, since they were established by such an author, whose craftsmanship is not human but divine—not devised, but voluntary and sovereign. For “he has done all things whatsoever he willed” (Ps. 13), and his willing has always been also his doing.

Therefore the holy Church, or any holy soul, gathers all the beauty and loveliness of its inner person from consideration of these Testaments, which set before it the necessary benefit of what it ought to believe, hope, and love. Why, moreover, is the jointing of her thighs praised by the Bridegroom? Because the harmony of the two Testaments, or of the two peoples, or of the twofold love, establishes the greatest and entire rule of good living, and stores up the glory of reward as most certain for one who has kept the rule. And he fittingly said the jointing not of “thighs” (*femora*) but of “women” (*feminae*), because from these are conceived, born, and advanced all the honorableness and usefulness of the holy Church or of any faithful soul.

VERSE 2.—“Your navel is like a rounded bowl, never lacking cups. Your belly is like a heap of wheat surrounded by lilies.”

The navel is the middle of the belly. What, therefore, is the navel of the Church except the holy preachers and teachers, who move among the people, gathering that same people to themselves by teaching and conduct? For just as all the internal organs adhere to the navel, so the people adhere to their preachers, always looking to their words and examples as to a kind of central point [Col. 1228D] placed among them, so as to establish in their character and discourses a certain foundation for good living.

But this navel is called like a rounded bowl, because, in order to cut away superfluous and uneven elements of conduct, holy teachers always turn toward that same thing when, to attain that which is ever unchangeable and remains the same in its nature, they run, labor, and hasten to draw others with them. This bowl is said never to lack cups, because the same preachers always abound in the sayings of divine utterances, by which they themselves are made drunk through the grace of the Holy Spirit and endeavor sufficiently to refresh the thirsty hearts of the peoples. 232

In another sense, if we direct our attention to the soul of each believer, holy charity may spiritually be called the navel of the mind. Placed, as it were, at a center, it touches all the virtues as through a circumference, because, since no virtue can exist without charity, all virtues, looking to it, seem to be appendages of charity.

But how is this called a rounded bowl? The Apostle says that “the end of the commandment is charity unto righteousness for everyone who believes” (1 Tim. 1). Therefore all perfection consists in charity, because it is rounded, retaining in itself no superfluity or obstructing vice, and is thus perfect and smooth. For perfect charity casts out fear, because fear is not in charity (1 John 4). This perfection, indeed, is the end—that is, the completion—of the commandment, as the prophet says: “the consummated word which the Lord has made upon the earth” (Isa. 10; Rom. 9).

How, then, is it never lacking cups? The apostles were said to be full of new wine when they burned with the Holy Spirit, that is, with the fire of divine charity. For they were drunk with that cup of the spiritual chalice of which the Psalmist says: “And my inebriating cup, how splendid it is!” (Ps. 22). Therefore those filled with divine charity always flow and burn with that unfailing cup of the Holy Spirit. Conversely, the earth is said to wither in thirst when it is not sprinkled by the infusion of divine charity. Hence the Lord cries to those parched by this thirst: “Whoever thirsts, let him come to me and drink; and from his belly shall flow living waters” (John 7). Therefore this rounded bowl never lacks a cup, because perfect [Col. 1229C] charity never lacks the heavenly dew and the desire of that highest good.

But because in the Church there are prelates and subjects, strong and weak, prudent and simple, after Christ praised his Church in the virtues of the prelates, he also adds commendable testimony from the obedience and discipline of the subjects, saying: “Your belly is like a heap of wheat.” Since the belly is a fragile and soft part of the body, the belly signifies the frailty of subjects, who cannot yet attain the perfection of teachers. But because they too belong to the Church and are among the lot of the elect, whom that supreme householder calls his wheat and commands to be gathered into his barn, they are not unfittingly compared to a heap of wheat. A heap is broad below and pointed above; the whole mass consists of grains, as though mutually embracing and supporting one another.

233 What, therefore, is expressed by a heap of wheat except the multitude of faithful people obedient to their prelates? Although, through the weakness of the flesh and cares of worldly affairs, they are somewhat pressed down around the broad and spacious way, nevertheless through obedience, humility, and brotherly charity they are raised upward by faith and hope. For, embracing and helping one another, and bearing the weaknesses of character and body, they fulfill that saying of the Apostle: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Gal. 6).

[Col. 1230A] But this heap of wheat is said to be surrounded by lilies because, through the fragrance of right faith and the confession of sins, it makes great progress toward the brightness of eternal life. For lilies possess fragrance, whiteness, and healing: fragrance is in faith and action; healing in confession of sins; whiteness in the reward of eternal life.

VERSE 3.—“Your two breasts are like two twin fawns of a doe.”

By the two breasts may fittingly be understood the two commandments of charity, by which the soul of every believer is nourished through the tenderness of inward milk and brought to the strength of spiritual exercise, so that it can say with the Apostle: “I can do all things in him who strengthens me” (Phil. 4). For “love is strong as death” (Song 8), and no tribulation separates the saints from charity (Rom. 8). By it they “go from strength to strength” (Ps. 83). Hence he rightly compares the commandments of charity to two twin fawns of a doe, which by nature always seeks high places.

But why twin? Clearly because of the harmony and unity of the twofold charity itself—love of God and love of neighbor. They are so conceived and grow together in the minds of the saints that neither can be prior to the other: when one loves God, one loves the neighbor, and when one loves the neighbor, one loves God. Each is also proof of the other, because, as John says: “He who says that he loves God and does not love his brother is a liar” (1 John 4). Therefore these two commandments of charity are like two twin fawns of a doe, because they are borne in one place and at one time [Col. 1230C] and always advance to higher things through the daily increase of virtues.

Or the two breasts are the two Testaments, by which the holy Church is daily nourished unto works of piety. They too are like two twin fawns of a doe, because they are so one as signifier and thing signified that, although they were not presented at the same time, they nevertheless are at one in their signification. So great is the majesty of the Testaments that ever greater and loftier subtlety occurs to those who dispute concerning them.

[Col. 1230D] 234 VERSE 4.—“Your neck is like a tower of ivory; your eyes like pools in Heshbon, which are at the gate of the daughter of the multitude. Your nose is like the tower of Lebanon, which looks toward Damascus.”

Because the voice comes forth through the channel of the neck and food is conveyed to the stomach, holy preachers are rightly signified by the neck, since through the office of preaching they administer the food of teachings to their fellow servants. But it must be considered why it is called a tower, and why an ivory tower. First, it is a tower because the preaching of the saints is lofty through the sublimity of its meanings. Secondly, because from the lofty contemplation of the mind, as from a tower, the enemy’s approach is observed in order that its snares may be guarded against; and this contemplation of the mind is taken from the teaching of holy preachers. It is ivory because of the whiteness of wisdom shining within, and because of the chaste utterance of eloquence resounding without, as is sung in the Psalm: “The words of the Lord are chaste, and the commandment of the Lord is bright, enlightening the eyes” (Ps. 18).

Therefore the neck of the holy Church, or of any holy soul, is like a tower of ivory because its preaching is lofty, firm, and beautiful; while it raises the mind to God, it defends it from the snares of enemies and permits no stain of heretical perversity to corrupt it. Conversely, the Synagogue is called through the prophet “a misty tower” (Mic. 4), because the carnal knowledge of the Jews is dark and obscured. It is indeed a tower because of the containment of the lofty sacraments hidden within it, but misty because of the carnal understanding of the letter alone. “Your eyes are like pools in Heshbon, which are at the gate of the daughter of the multitude.”

The eyes of the holy Church, or rather of the soul of each faithful person, may suitably be understood as two contemplations in the mind, as it were in the head, directed to right and left: namely, toward the smallness and misery of temporal life, and toward the eternity and blessedness of perpetual and unchangeable life.

These are rightly called “pools in Heshbon,” which is interpreted “girdle of sorrow,” because from sorrow and grief for sins, or from longing for eternal goods, fountains of tears flow forth through compunction, like pools. These pools indeed flow from a twofold compunction born from the consideration of these two eyes: for while the mind weighs future punishments and remembers its own evils, it is pricked to repentance, as though watered from one of the pools.

[Col. 1231C] But these pools are in Heshbon, because by this double compunction it is girded with sorrow—on one side by repentance, on the other by love—so that it may neither fall back into former vices through remembrance of future evils, nor fail firmly to bind itself to the pursuit of virtues through desire for future goods, fulfilling the Lord’s command: “Let your loins be girded” (Luke 12).

Moreover, these pools are said to be “at the gate of the daughter of the multitude.” But what is this gate? Surely, the departure from this life and entrance into the life to come. Hence it is said in the Psalm concerning the blessed man: “He shall not be ashamed when he speaks with his enemies in the gate” (Ps. 126 [127]). For no shame will come upon the holy man at his departure from this life, [Col. 1231D] when the adverse party wishes to oppose and harm him, because during his life he served Him in whom the prince of this world found nothing of his own.

And what is the daughter of the multitude, of whom that gate is said to be the gate, unless it is the holy soul of every believer—the daughter, that is, of that multitude whose heart and soul were one (Acts 4)? At that time the Church was indeed rudimentary and primitive upon earth; yet it prefigured the unity of that Church which now reigns with Christ in heaven in true and perfect concord through ineffable and unchanging love.

The daughter of this multitude has those pools of twofold compunction at her gate, because, through repentance for past evils and desire for future goods, she departs confidently and blessedly from this [Col. 1232A] life and enters the kingdoms of heaven. Thus the eyes of the Church, or of the holy soul, are fittingly said to be like pools in Heshbon at the gate of the daughter of the multitude: because, while they are wet with a fountain of tears through a double compunction arising from the remembrance of sins or love of eternal life, they open for themselves the entrance to the heavenly kingdom at life’s departure.

In another sense, the eyes of the Church may suitably be called her overseers and teachers, to whom this comparison may likewise be applied: just as the pools in Heshbon surround and fortify the city, so these surround and fortify the Church with the girdle of sorrow—for this is the meaning of “Heshbon”—while by their teaching and preaching they summon people, as by a saving spring, to compunction, confession, and satisfaction, [Col. 1232B] saying the Gospel words: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand” (Matt. 3).

For repentance may rightly be called a girdle of sorrow, because the life of the penitent must be girded and fortified on every side, so that he may grieve over what he has committed and admit no further causes for grief. For that is true repentance in which past sins are so regarded that future ones are feared: it has sorrow from the past and fear from the future. But because this fear entails punishment, while it draws the soul into grief through remembrance of the past and fear of the future, the penitent rightly constricts his life with a girdle of sorrow.

But these pools in Heshbon are at the gate of the daughter of the multitude. Who then is the daughter of the multitude, or what is this multitude? Did not the apostles and their successors, the apostolic men, beget the holy Church? Beholding their dignity, the Psalmist says: “How exceedingly honored are your friends, O God; how greatly strengthened is their dominion” (Ps. 138 [139]); and considering that they were not few but many, he says: “I shall number them, and they shall be multiplied beyond the sand” (ibid.). [Col. 1232C] The holy Church is the daughter of this multitude, whom, as we have said, they begot by their teaching. She has a gate, namely the door of discernment, through which she distinguishes whom, and what sort of persons, she should reject from her body. For since tares are always mixed with wheat, she incorporates the good into herself as sweet food, tolerates the wicked within her body as harmful humors, but wholly removes heretics from herself as deadly poison.

At this gate of discernment the overseers or teachers of the holy Church stand daily. Like eyes in the head, they know by the spirit of wisdom how to discern who belongs, and who does not belong, to the body of the Church; which fish are to be chosen and which rejected on the shore of the final station. Thus they show the faithful the open gates of life; they open gates that had been closed to repentant sinners; but for the impious and unrepentant they close them eternally.

Or, the gate of the daughter of the multitude is called faith, which is the beginning and, as it were, an entrance upon the way of salvation. Without it, it is impossible to please God (Heb. 11). Holy teachers set it first before those seeking the way of life and desiring to reach the heavenly homeland, [Col. 1233A] because each person must first believe rightly and then, believing rightly, act well.

But because we have said that this gate of the daughter of the multitude is the grace of discernment, by which the holy overseers and teachers of the Church know how either to admit the repentant or to exclude the unrepentant, the nature of that discernment—what it is or ought to be—is set forth when it is said: “Your nose is like the tower of Lebanon,” etc.

For by the nose, through which we distinguish fragrances and stinks, is signified the discernment of the saints, through which they know how to distinguish the fragrances of virtues and the stinks of vices, so that they understand what they should choose and what they should reject. This nose is said to be like the tower of Lebanon [Col. 1233B] because the discernment of prelates must always be fortified by watchfulness and must always stand upon the height of life—that is, it must not lie in the valley of feeble conduct. For just as a tower is placed upon a mountain as a lookout so that approaching enemies may be seen from afar, so the life of the preacher must remain fixed on high, in order that, after the manner of nostrils, it may discern the stinks of vices and fragrances of virtues, foresee from afar the attacks of evil spirits, and render the souls entrusted to it cautious through its prudence. And because discernment itself is said to be the mother of virtues, it is rightly compared with the tower of Lebanon, a name that signifies whiteness, so that through it the beauty of all virtues may be understood to be preserved.

But this tower is said to look toward Damascus, [Col. 1233C] because the life of the saints is fortified by strong vigilance against the temptations of vices through the lofty consideration of discernment. Damascus is interpreted “drinking blood,” and by it this world is rightly signified, since it is daily made drunk with vices and sins. For the prophet indicates that sins are signified by blood, saying: “Blood has touched blood” (Hos. 4), that is, sin has been added to sin; and the Psalmist says: “Deliver me from bloodguiltiness, O God, God of my salvation” (Ps. 50 [51]).

Therefore this tower is directed against Damascus, because the life of the saints, lofty and fortified with virtues, is strengthened beforehand against the pleasures of this world by firm and discerning consideration.

**VERSE 3.**—“Your head is like Carmel, and the hair of your head like royal purple, bound to the channels.”

[Col. 1233D] By the head is signified the ruling principle of the mind. Carmel, however, is interpreted “knowing circumcision” or “a soft river.”

Therefore the holy mind is rightly compared with Carmel, because it is lofty in divine contemplation; it knows how to cut away from itself carnality of conduct or thought by spiritual circumcision; and, as divine grace is poured in, it strives to water the hearts of hearers with sweet teaching, as with a gentle river. “And the hair of your head is like royal purple, bound to the channels.”

The hair of the head may be understood as the thoughts of the mind. They are called like royal purple, bound to channels, because the more they are joined and directed to the Scriptures, as to certain channels, the more they are kindled to imitate Christ’s passion, mortifying [Col. 1234A] their flesh with its vices and desires; or, if need be, offering even the flesh itself to persecution for Christ, sacrificing to God the precious purple of heart and body in martyrdom.

We may also apply this portion of the speech in another way to the very Head of the Church, that is, the Lord Jesus Christ, so that he may be introduced as speaking in his own person to the Church, his bride: “Your head is like Carmel, and the hair of your head like royal purple, bound to the channels.” “I,” he says, “O bride, who am called and am your head, may be compared to Mount Carmel because of its height and the interpretation of its name. For, since I am the highest good, there is nothing that can be more excellent than my nature according to divinity; and according to humanity, [Col. 1234B] nothing is holier than my life and conduct. In my teaching true and perfect circumcision of heart is learned; and all my preaching truly runs as a soft river, refreshing the minds of hearers by its health-giving quality and forming them for the pursuit of good work.

“The hair of this your head is my apostles and likewise all my other saints, who cling to me in love as hair clings to the head. Purple fittingly corresponds to them, because, as purple nearer the channels is dyed more deeply, so the more a person’s mind is made near to my words or to the words and instructions of my prophets, the more it is kindled by power toward love of me. And in my tabernacle—that is, in my Church—it strives to shine as precious royal purple, namely as scarlet twice dyed (Exod. 28), in love of God and neighbor.”

Therefore, since “the head of man is God” (1 Cor. 11), if any believer desires through strength of soul to be hair of this his Head, he must cling as a diligent searcher to the sacred channels of Scripture. There he finds the means of being dyed, so that through inward love he may become the purple of his heavenly King by mortification of the carnal life. It should be noted, moreover, that the beloved fittingly answers the beloved’s proclamation of praise of this sort in ten parts, as though on ten strings, sounding spiritually upon one ten-stringed instrument. This is suitably set over against the earlier ten-stringed instrument which the bride had sung in praise of the bridegroom: the former imposes the measure of a most pleasing melody from the higher parts, the latter from the lower. Since the bride must always ascend to the bridegroom with right intention and perfect [Col. 1234D] love, it is fitting that she rise from lesser things to greater; and therefore the bridegroom graciously sings the praise of her soul as it advances and, as it were, grows in virtues. This advance, virtue, and power, however, are not the recipient’s own, but rather the praise belongs to the bridegroom who gives and grants her this virtue and power by his gift.

But the bride, reverently directing her attention to the immeasurable kindness of the bridegroom, who descends from heaven and humbles himself for us to our weakness, begins the proclamation of his praise with praise of the highest part of his body, that is, his head, as though from the higher string. Thus she shows that, being set below, she ought always to look upward toward the life and teaching of her bridegroom, set before her above and opposite her, and by imitation [Col. 1235A] ascend to him whom she knows has descended to her through the compassion of mercy.

**VERSE 6.**—“How beautiful you are, and how lovely, dearest one, in delights!”

After the bridegroom has praised in the bride, member by member, the diversity of features well and honorably composed by the disposition of the mind, he shows that one complete whole has thereby been produced, calling the totality of virtues by the name of stature and indicating abundance of teaching by the signification of breasts. For what beauty of conduct or speech is lacking in the whole body of the holy Church? Since this person shines in one virtue, that person in another, and another in yet another; since some possess more and some fewer kinds of virtues: what beauty of form and loveliness can there be that the holy Church does not have in her body? And since different persons are distinguished by different instruction in holy doctrines, what knowledge of truth or holiness can there be in which the holy Church does not abound? For, according to the Apostle, “to one is given the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge, to another faith, to another gifts of healing, to another the working of miracles, to another prophecy, to another discernment of spirits, to another kinds of tongues, to another interpretation of words” (1 Cor. 12): surely every beauty and adornment of works or words shines spiritually in the inward stature of the holy Church.

Therefore she is deservedly declared beautiful, lovely, and most dear in delights, because [Col. 1235C] abundance of virtues and the saving teaching of wisdom are indeed great delights of the soul. Yet the more the soul delights in these, the more fully it is filled with the sweetness of divine love.

**VERSE 7.**—“Your stature is compared to a palm tree, and your breasts to clusters.”

Why is such a stature compared to a palm tree? The palm is a sign of victory; and what victory is greater and more glorious than triumph over vices and sins? From what does so wondrous and glorious a stature arise except from the victory of virtues and destruction of vices? Thus the stature of the Church is suitably compared to a palm, because all her honorable and upright conduct proclaims conspicuous victories.

[Col. 1235D] Moreover, her breasts are compared to clusters because her doctrine and preaching abound in the sweet and pleasant savor of wisdom and spiritual understanding, and so intoxicate her hearers as to render them insensible to the pleasures of this world. But in order to show that the beauty of this stature grows and increases chiefly and principally from mortifying the carnal life, the bridegroom sets before her the example and benefit of his own passion: “I said, I will climb the palm tree.”

**VERSE 8.**—“I said: I will climb the palm tree and seize its fruit; and your breasts shall be like clusters of the vine, and the fragrance of your mouth like the fragrance of apples.”

As though he plainly said to his bride: “Whence do you have power to conquer, whence do you have power to advance? Is it by your own strength and industry that you can obtain for yourself the splendor of such great beauty? If you consider rightly, you will by no means ascribe the merit of any good to your own strength or prudence. For I said—that is, before the ages of the world I decreed and determinedly ordained—that because you fell through the transgression of the tree, you began to be powerless and, by sinning, found the enemy within yourself. Afterwards you were unable to prevail against him, but lay subject, as a captive, under his dominion. Therefore, through the counter-position of the wood, I might recover for you the good you had lost, rescue you from the enemy’s power and the captivity in which you were held, restore your freedom, lay your enemy beneath you, and, by providing against his snares, give you prudence and power [Col. 1236B] to resist. For this reason I said: ‘I will climb the palm tree,’ that is, the cross. After I have triumphed over the enemy upon it, seized the fruit of this my passion, and brought it forth in rising again as a sign of victory, I will proclaim this oracle of consolation to all who obey me and hope in my power: ‘Take courage; I have conquered the world’ (John 16).

“You therefore must fight; and because you are secure of victory through me, who have already gained victory, climb the cross with me by mortifying the flesh, so that the entire stature of your soul may be compared to a palm tree and be devoted, under the title of perseverance, to eternal victory.”

But this ascent of the palm tree is worthy of the reverence and adoration of every soul. Why? Because its fruit is truly great and incomparable. What then? Was not the whole human race refreshed and restored through this fruit? And what sort of fruit was and is it? Surely, redemption of the human race; reconciliation of its enmity toward God; daily forgiveness of sins; firm defense against the enemy’s snares; release from worldly misery; and entrance into the heavenly kingdom. For all the advancement of the Church began from the time of Christ’s passion and resurrection, and thence the proclamations of her holiness and the gifts of the Holy Spirit flowed forth in greatest abundance. Hence it follows: “And your breasts shall be like clusters of the vine, and the fragrance of your mouth like the fragrance of apples.” For after the removal of the shadow by the manifestation of truth, her preaching and teaching flowed more sweetly and abundantly; and [Col. 1236D] after Christ’s passion and resurrection they made many so drunk with divine love that the heat of the Holy Spirit dried up in them all moisture of worldly pleasure and kindled them toward love of the heavenly life.

The voice comes forth from the throat; consequently, by the throat is suitably understood the memory of the divine commandments, and by the voice the preaching of those commandments. Unless they are first retained inwardly in the mind through memory, they can by no means be brought forth outwardly in speech. But this voice of speech is compared to the fragrance of apples, because, as by fragrance a thing is perceived not only when present but even when absent, so from the time of Christ’s passion and resurrection, through the preaching of the Church, not only the deeds and words of the Lord himself and of his saints when present, [Col. 1237A] but also those of the past have been made known and are daily made known by reading and hearing. Future goods and evils likewise are inferred from them, when the rewards of the just and punishments of sinners are considered from afar, as though by the fragrance of an inward touch. This voice is not compared with the fragrance of flowers but of apples, because the Church’s preaching, which now resounds throughout the whole world, shows those who believe one faith that is not immature or tender, but ripe and perfect.

**VERSE 9.**—“Your throat is like the best wine, worthy for my beloved to drink, and for his lips and teeth to chew.”

The throat is called like the best wine because memory of the divine commandments intoxicates the mind with its sweetness; and what it drinks sweetly within through meditation, it pours out beneficially without through speech. “Worthy for my beloved to drink.” Christ is said to be refreshed and given drink in his body—that is, in the Church, which becomes one spirit with him—by righteousness, faith, and holiness; just as, conversely, he is proclaimed to hunger and thirst for righteousness, faith, and holiness among unbelievers. For when he hung upon the cross and said, “I thirst” (John 19), he thirsted for the faith and holiness of the unbelieving people, for whom he had been wearied, as it were, by a certain heat of labor: the people whom he had led out of Egypt by many signs and wonders; before whose face he had crushed nations; with whom he had established the covenant of his testament and law; to whom he had assigned the land of promise, a city, and a temple; [Col. 1237C] and for whose salvation he had finally not disdained to undergo death itself.

Therefore, when the holy Church, or any holy soul, meditates upon the law of the Lord day and night, Christ drinks in that mind a certain sweet wine of meditation, and its holy meditation is like a sweet and worthy drink for God. Hence, when the bridegroom praised the throat of his beloved—that is, meditation upon God’s commandments—as the best wine, she interrupts the voice of her praise-giver and rejoices in cooperating grace: “Worthy,” she says, “for my beloved to drink”; that is, worthy for him himself to advance by his grace and bring to completion.

How? “For lips and teeth to chew.” What she understands by frequent meditation within herself, she ought to dispense to others by teaching, treat by expounding, and reconsider by discussion. This is like the peculiar act of a clean animal: chewing the cud. For in the one body of the Church, understood as the whole Christ, the throat is meditation upon divine Scripture, the lips are the utterance of that Scripture, and the teeth are its exposition—the breaking down, as it were, of the coarse letter and its reduction to the subtlety of spiritual understanding. Why is it called worthy for the bridegroom himself to drink or chew? Because all advancement of the Church or of any holy soul is the result of his gift and grace.

**VERSE 10.**—“I am for my beloved, and his turning is toward me.”

“Since,” she says, “I please my beloved through meditation upon the holy Scriptures, with the grace of that beloved himself going before me, therefore I desire and rightly ought to draw nearer to him by obedience, striving in good acts, and proclaiming his commandments to others, so that what is written may come about: ‘Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you’” (James 4). For if I turn to him, then his turning is toward me, as he himself said: “Turn to me, and I will turn to you” (Zech. 1). There is, however, no changeableness in God, such that he may be said, in human fashion, to turn away or turn back; rather, the movement of grace coming or departing in a human being is called a certain turning toward or away by God. His turning toward us is the merciful action of grace calling, justifying, and glorifying, through which free choice is assisted and the intention of a good will is led [Col. 1238B] to the effect of a good purpose. Thus she fittingly says first, “I am for my beloved,” and then, “his turning is toward me,” because it belongs to us first to undertake the intention of a good will in the pursuit of good work; it belongs to him, through cooperating grace, to bring the work conceived with good intention all the way to a good end. Therefore, feeling a ready will within herself, she takes confidence from the help cooperating with her and immediately girds herself for the pursuit of action, saying: “Come, my beloved.”

**VERSE 11.**—“Come, my beloved; let us go forth into the field; let us dwell in the villages.”

“Let us go forth,” she says, “because after your turning toward me has taken place through cooperating grace, I can freely and securely go forth both to the office of preaching and to the pursuit of good action, so that all my work may always begin from you and through you bring to completion what has been begun. For without you we can do no good.

“But where shall we first go forth? Into the field, namely, that is, to the Jewish people, who are now fit to receive the seed of God’s word. For their hearts have already been ploughed by written law and also natural law, and therefore they can better understand from the law and prophets the purpose of divine goodness by which he decreed to restore the human race. ‘It was necessary that the word of God should first be spoken’ to them (Acts 13), ‘whose are the adoption as sons, the glory, the covenants, the giving of the law, the worship, and the promises; whose are the fathers, and from whom is Christ according to the flesh, who is God blessed forever’ (Rom. 9). [Col. 1238D] Let us then go forth through the office of preaching into this field, to scatter the seed of the divine word; and because the oracles of God were first entrusted to them (Rom. 3), let us also cast among them the first seedbeds of faith and divine mysteries.

“Then, proceeding onward, let us dwell in the villages—that is, among the Gentiles, who are distant from the city of God, namely the Church. Since they are slower to believe because the preaching of faith is unfamiliar and unheard-of to them, it will be necessary to remain for a time, and by more frequent proclamation of the word of life to bring them to the refinement of civic custom—that is, to observance of the ecclesiastical law. Let us dwell among them, you, O beloved, inspiring by grace, and I assisting by preaching, so that by frequent instruction we may wear down their inborn ignorance and the simplicity of an unformed mind, and instill our civic uprightness and true wisdom, through which they may deserve to be enrolled as blessed inhabitants of that heavenly city.

“When we have joined these two walls coming from opposite directions, namely Jews and Gentiles, in one faith, there will not be two peoples but one people, one vineyard of the Lord of hosts, cultivated by the work of the Holy Spirit; it will produce no longer wild grapes but sweet ones.”

**VERSE 12.**—“Let us rise early to the vineyards; let us see whether the vine has flowered, whether the flowers bear fruit, whether the pomegranates have flowered. There I will give you my breasts.”

To these vineyards, planted from circumcision and uncircumcision, [Col. 1239B] let us rise early—that is, at the rising of faith, when the true sun begins to rise in the hearts of believers, shining upon them with the love of his wisdom and kindling them with the heat of virtue. Let us see whether the vine has flowered: that is, whether the now unified people of Christians has produced beginnings of good works; whether the flowers bear fruit: that is, whether those beginnings themselves are striving to rise into some completeness and perfection; whether the pomegranates have flowered: that is, whether they burn with so great a love of God that they desire to suffer for him not only in mind but also in body.

“There I will give you my breasts.” For after we have made these two peoples one by unity of faith and advanced them to the pursuit of good work, then, to the praise of your name, O beloved, we shall entrust to them also the mysteries which, by your gift, we have come to know from [Col. 1239C] the subtle profundity of the two Testaments. Thus they may always be nourished in them for greater works of virtue, strengthened against the temptations of the world, and more ardently kindled to desire the future goods of blessedness. For I shall preach confidently and disclose the commandments of your precepts [as printed], because I have hope of bearing fruit and attaining the effect of good work. Whence? Because “the mandrakes have given forth their fragrance.”

**VERSE 12.**—“The mandrakes have given forth their fragrance at our gates. All fruits, new and old, I have kept for you, my beloved.”

This very fragrance brings me hope of preaching, because I believe that from that fragrance there will consequently arise the benefit of receiving fruit. But we must carefully consider what this mandrake is, and what the fragrance of this mandrake is. If you look to the letter, the mandrake is an aromatic herb, formed in the likeness of human members but lacking only a head. Its power is that, when given in drink to those oppressed by wakefulness, it brings sleep and rest; moreover, when barren women use it, it makes them conceive.

But if you attend to the spiritual sense, the mandrake may not unsuitably be understood as the conversion of the Gentile world. So long as it persisted in the perversity of its error, it was wearied not merely by vain but by ruinous labor. But after it was converted and began to know God, it learned to remain less awake—or rather more asleep—to the cares and pleasures of worldly things, and to rest from the perverse [Col. 1240A] labor of this world. And what had formerly been barren of good work afterwards became fruitful in virtues, fulfilling the prophecy which says: “Rejoice, barren woman who does not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who do not travail, because the children of the desolate woman are many more than of her who has a husband” (Isa. 54; Gal. 4).

As we have said, the mandrake has the likeness of a human body but lacks a head, because although the Gentile people naturally possessed reason for discerning good and evil, that power of reason was dulled in them insofar as they were unable to know their Creator. Since they did not possess him in their knowledge, they were as though without a head. The Jewish people likewise may be signified by the mandrake: although it used reason in its observance of the law, it nevertheless had no head because it refused to receive Christ. But this mandrake later gave forth fragrance, because what had previously been barren through unbelief afterwards, by believing, bore many children for God. Therefore “the mandrakes have given forth fragrance at our gates,” because the Jewish and Gentile peoples, when you, O beloved, ascended to heaven, received the mysteries of faith through your grace and my preaching.

But what are these gates at which the beloved says that the believing people gave forth fragrance? Surely, if you consider carefully, you will recognize through which gates the soul desiring to find God gradually advances even to the secrets of the bedchamber. First, there is in a person a conception in the mind, by which the person conceives that whose fullness he desires to attain; having conceived it, he investigates what it is and of what sort, until he has knowledge of it. Having known it, he embraces it, and so uses it for his benefit that he endeavors at last to draw its whole integrity to himself. Thus in every person who is to believe there is a certain gate and, as it were, a first entrance to God: the first conception of faith in the mind, by which he receives the will to believe. Then comes the investigation of that faith itself, in order that he may know what or how he ought to believe. After this second gate of investigation, a third gate is opened to him, namely knowledge of faith. After knowledge follows action, without which faith is declared idle; and contemplation with a pure heart unites to God the one who acts well.

[Col. 1240D] Therefore, as they strive to come to God through these gates, at the entrance of the gates themselves they spread the fragrance of good will. But this fragrance passes through the second gate of faith investigated, reaches also the third gate, now that of faith known, then passes through the fourth gate of action, and finally through the fifth gate of contemplative sweetness flows into the very inner secrets of the heavenly bridegroom. Therefore, when the mandrakes give forth fragrance at these gates, it is evident that souls seeking God are already ripening for the fruit of good work. Thus the bride fittingly speaks in congratulation to her beloved: “The mandrakes have given forth their fragrance at our gates,” because, when the Church attends to the advancement of her children, she offers God fitting acts of thanksgiving. Therefore she girds herself more earnestly for preaching, because she hopes to advance in the hearts of those whom she sees to have turned wholeheartedly to God.

She attributes this advancement not to her own labor and industry but to divine grace, saying: “All fruits, new and old, etc., I have kept for you, my beloved.” “For your honor, O beloved, I have kept every fruit of holiness that I have learned from the instruction of the Old or New Testament; or that I have learned from the formation given by your commandments; or that I have gathered by forming myself from the life and flowers of the Fathers. For it is your gift, not the result of my labor, both that I myself have advanced by living and teaching well, and that others have been able to advance through my example or teaching.” Or, to put it another way: “I have kept for you all fruits, new and old,” because I have taught and expounded that everything read as done and said mystically in [Col. 1241B] the Old Testament, but exhibited in reality in the New, was written concerning your birth, passion, resurrection, and ascension; and I have shown all readers and hearers in them the fruit of faith and good action.

## CHAPTER VIII

**VERSE 1.**—“Who will give you to me as my brother, sucking the breasts of my mother, so that I may find you outside and kiss you, and no one may now despise me?”

If we consider the allegorical sense, this voice may be referred to those saints who before the Lord’s coming burned with great desire to see what they knew had long been foretold by the patriarchs and prophets, and what they themselves foresaw in the Spirit would come to pass: namely, Christ’s incarnation, through which they did not doubt that the salvation of the whole world would come. Therefore let that ancient people of saints speak in the language of longing: “Who will give you to me as my brother, sucking the breasts of my mother?” My brother, I say, because of your assumption of human flesh and kinship with the human race; sucking the breasts of my mother—that is, born and nourished in the synagogue of the Jews. And why this desire? “So that,” he says, “I may find you outside and kiss you”; that is, that I may openly see and embrace you in the flesh, whom I cannot see in the hiddenness of divinity. “And that no one may now despise me,” but rather honor and love me because of the special nobility of so noble an offspring born from my flesh. “And I shall take hold of you [Col. 1241D] and lead you into my mother’s house,” because it pleased your condescension to show forth the presence of your flesh and demonstrate the power of your miracles only among the Jewish people. There you will teach me both by words and deeds what I ought to understand figuratively and what in truth, and that you yourself are “the end of the commandment unto righteousness for everyone who believes” (Rom. 10).

But how greatly I shall advance through the sweetness of your teaching! “I will give you a cup of spiced wine,” because you will, as it were, drink the delight of my faith and action, which I shall offer to you in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and in the power of faith, hope, and love. For just as spiced wine consists chiefly of three things—wine, honey, and spices—so my mind is seasoned by the teaching of your words with faith in the holy Trinity or, as has been said, with the power of faith, hope, [Col. 1242A] and love. “I will also give you must from my pomegranates,” because your preaching and action will bring forth in me a newness and sweetness of a soul cleansed from vices, through the fervor of love and the pursuit of manifold virtues.

But if we consider the moral sense, we shall apply this voice to every faithful soul that, attentive to holy Scripture, builds up itself by knowledge and others by a word of exhortation. For one who desires to possess the knowledge of sacred Scripture cries out to God with the whole eagerness of the soul in these words: “Who will give you to me as my brother, sucking the breasts of my mother?” Why do I call you brother? Surely because both of participation in humanity and of the grace of adoption, by which you yourself call yourself brother, saying: “Go, announce to my brothers” [Col. 1242B] (Matt. 28), and: “Whoever does the will of my Father is my brother, sister, and mother” (Matt. 12). Who then will give you to me as my brother, so that you may be with me and labor with me through cooperating grace—I mean you “sucking,” that is, causing the breasts of my mother to be sucked? For this is said in the same manner of speech that Scripture uses elsewhere: “He himself makes intercession for us with unutterable groanings” (Rom. 8): “makes intercession” meaning “causes intercession to be made.”

What, then, are the breasts of my mother, and of what mother are they mine? Surely the breasts of my mother are the doctrines of holy Church, which nourish the infancy of my mind from the pages of both Testaments and bring it forward to the strength of mature understanding. But why do I so greatly desire [Col. 1242C] that you be with me? “That I may find you outside and kiss you.” What does this mean? For where are you hidden when you are not outside? Surely in the cloud by day—that is, in the obscurity and subtlety of spiritual understanding. Once I have received this through the illumination of your fire, that is, of the Holy Spirit, I surely find outside you who were hidden within; and when I have found you, I kiss you—that is, I embrace you with all the powers of my mind—because I take such delight in the gift of understanding received that I am pleased to say with the Prophet: “How sweet are your words to my palate, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth!” (Ps. 118).

Indeed, when I cling thus to your embraces and wisely expound the mysteries of Holy Scripture, [Col. 1242D] no one will despise me, because, as it is written: “The wise person shall be filled with blessings, and the living shall praise him” (Ecclus. 37); and: “The wise person shall inherit honour among the people, and his name shall live for ever” (ibid.); and again: “The mouth of the prudent is sought in the Church, and they shall ponder his words in their hearts” (Ecclus. 21). Therefore no one will despise me, because they hear that the anointing of your Spirit teaches me concerning all things (1 John 2); indeed, falling to the ground, they have worshipped the Lord, declaring that God is truly in us (1 Cor. 14).

**VERSE 2.**—“I will take hold of you and lead you into the house of my mother. There you will teach me, and I will give you a cup of spiced wine and the new wine of my pomegranates.”

[Col. 1243A] 249 This sweetness is so pleasing to the palate of my heart that, having found you in this manner, I do not wish to keep you for my own benefit alone. Rather, I will take hold of you and lead you into the house of my mother—that is, the household of holy Church—so that I may graciously share with my brothers, who desire to hear and learn, what I understand by your grace.

There, then, you will teach me, because the more I teach others, the more I learn with them; for discussion contributes more than reading. And I will give you a cup of spiced wine, because by teaching or discussing in this way I shall expound the figure of the Law seasoned with the truth and grace of the Gospel, or the historical sense seasoned with allegory and moral meaning; and I shall give you this cup because I shall devote all this knowledge to your honour and grace.

[Col. 1243B] I shall also give you the new wine of my pomegranates, because while I preach the patience of the saints and their manifold labour in virtues, I myself also take their example of labour and patience. Yet I ascribe all these things neither to their power nor to mine, but to your mercy and grace.

Accordingly, carried away as though from all the pleasures and cares of this world by the presence, sweetness, and grace of my beloved and my brother dwelling with me, I turn to you, daughters of Jerusalem, and declare openly what I possess within myself and show how great is the charity by which I cling to him. “What,” they ask, “is this?” “His left hand,” she says, “is under my head.”

[Col. 1243C] **VERSE 3.**—“His left hand is under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me.”

For I set every temporal good granted me by him below the love of eternal goods; but eternal things I desire with all my mind, and with all the strength of my soul I resolve to attain them. Although riches and glory are in his left hand (Prov. 3), insofar as they concern the usefulness and beauty of creation by which a human being is led to knowledge of his Creator and is thus without excuse, yet length of days is in his right hand (ibid.): not a length that comes to an end, but one that unchangeably abides in its own blessedness.

Therefore his left hand shall be under my head, but his right hand shall embrace me, because the remembrance of temporal things will hold me, though not for the sake of delight in them and [Col. 1244A] a single perpetual object; whereas the desire for eternal things will surround me wholly, so that it turns all my senses toward its pursuit and compels me to forget the things behind and stretch myself wholly toward those before me (Phil. 3).

250 But because the bridegroom does these things—he who rejoices in the devout pursuits and progress of the soul and delights in the sweetness of its devotion and pure intention—he says: “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem,” etc.

**VERSE 4.**—“I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, do not awaken or rouse the beloved until she herself wills it.”

Do not, daughters of Jerusalem, he says, draw the beloved away from so useful and honourable a purpose by importunately suggesting to her some concern with passing things—your own necessity or her own in exterior matters—which do not permit the mind to remain free for seeking and perfectly preserving the repose of holy contemplation. Rather, leave this to her judgment, she who is taught by the anointing of my Spirit (1 John 2). Exercise this discernment: let her know when it is useful to devote herself to divine things and when to condescend to your weakness.

Or: do not in any way awaken or rouse the future beloved by compelling her with threats or promises, for God does not approve forced service. Rather, leave her to her own will, because it is written: “I will sacrifice to you willingly” (Ps. 53), and “Those who offer themselves willingly to the Lord are blessed by the Lord” (Lev. 22). “No one comes [Col. 1244C] to me unless the Father who sent me draws him” (John 6). For if one is drawn, one comes; if one does not come, one is not drawn. Therefore do not compel her until she herself wills it. For then the sacrifice of a good work will be acceptable to God, if it is supported by the seasoning of good will.

But you, most beloved sisters, whom this section of the Song has held somewhat more slowly and at length in its melody, heed this as it were final utterance in its conclusion. Consider how welcome to God and sweet to the soul it is to rest in the resolve of holy conduct and to sleep in the pursuit of divine contemplation; and conversely, how dangerous and contrary to God it is to draw yourselves away from this resolve on some occasion and divert yourselves to the care of temporal things.

# BOOK FOUR

[Col. 1243]

[Col. 1243D] 251 If the endeavour of my smallness in this preeminent genre of the Song had so advanced among your charity that, stirred with your whole spirit and laying aside the cares of temporal things, you could say with the Apostle: “I will pray with the spirit; I will pray also with the understanding; I will sing with the spirit; I will sing also with the understanding” (1 Cor. 14), then my heart would surely greatly rejoice in the Lord. For it would be no small cause of rejoicing for me to say with the Apostle: “You are my joy and crown in the Lord” (Phil. [3:1; citation printed as V]). If [Col. 1244D] you are now beginning somewhat to flourish in the Lord according to the manner of my singing, you fittingly praise the Song; for this, indeed, is to praise the Song: to experience the Song and its mode.

But what is the power of this Song? In accordance with its title, “Song of Songs,” it bears the mind more excellently and sublimely toward love of its Creator and perfectly strips away from it whatever among worldly things may hinder such contemplation. Therefore, if you have experienced this even somewhat, let the concord and harmony of flesh and spirit—which do not oppose one another—tell you that this is to sing beautifully and make melody rightly. If the handmaid serves the free woman—that is, if the flesh consents to reason—there is no better or sweeter harmony to please the supreme Divinity. This, indeed, is to sing a new song, and such praise is in the Church of the saints (Ps. 149).

For the praise of God is the devout life and conduct of the saints, because they have such a manner of living from God’s grace and kindness. Thus God must be praised, not the human being, because this is not the work of a human being but the work of God himself, who justifies the human being.

What, indeed, is the new song but the venerable commandment of the New Testament? What is it to sing the new song but to put off the old human being and put on the new? “Put off,” says the Apostle, “the old human being, and put on the new, which has been created according to God in righteousness and holiness” (Eph. 4). Therefore to be righteous and holy is surely to sing the new song, for every perfection of holiness is known from the instrument of evangelical instruction. For when the Law says, “You shall not kill,” the Gospel teaches that one must not be angry without cause; and when the Law [252] says not to commit adultery, the Gospel teaches that one must not sin even in desire (Exod. 20; Matt. 5). Such perfection of holiness is certainly the melody of the new song.

The Church of the saints sings this new song, and by frequently chanting it comes to chant [Col. 1245C] the Song of Songs. For what is it to sing the Song of Songs but to love the Lord with all one’s mind, all one’s soul, and all one’s strength? Just as that song is called the Song of Songs which surpasses all other songs in its dignity, so charity may be called the virtue of virtues, because it surpasses all virtues by its excellence.

Therefore, if you, beloved sisters, truly and sincerely love the Lord, you surely sing the Song of Songs. And because praise is in the Church of the saints, the praise of God will certainly be in you, who, as we believe, are the Church of the saints. Therefore bless the Lord in his works and sing to him with songs of your lips and with harps (Ecclus. 39). For whatever marks of religion and holiness are in you are surely his works; in them you bless him when you ascribe all these things not to your own diligence but to his grace.

Therefore you must sing to him with songs of lips and with harps, lest it be said of you: “This people honours me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isa. 29). What is it to sing with songs of lips and with harps? Is it not when voice and life praise the Lord? Then lips and harp sound together well.

On a harp are stretched strings made from the entrails of dead animals, and these are fitted to the wood in diverse ways so as to produce diverse sounds according to the tension and variety of their measures. What, then, can be signified by the harp except the mind of the righteous person? In it strings made from the entrails of dead animals are stretched, because there are set forth within it mortifications of vices which it has learned from the sayings, writings, and deeds of the holy Fathers who have departed this life. By these it disciplines its inward and outward senses so that it may offer to the ears of the Lord of Hosts, in sweet melody, the harmony of flesh and spirit.

A certain diversity of sounds is also thereby denoted: so long as the mortification of pride is performed in one manner, that of lust in another, that of anger in another, and that of avarice in another, the mind rightly seems to sound forth delightfully to the Lord its God a new song—indeed, the Song of Songs—in a most beautiful harmony. Therefore you sing with songs of lips and harps when by voice and deed you offer to the Lord God the service of your holiness. If, then, your mind has for some time been stirred by the sound of this Song, as we believe, toward love of the heavenly bridegroom, and if you have an attentive ear of heart for such harmony, your devotion will all the more encourage us toward what remains. For no one gladly speaks to an unwilling listener.

Therefore I shall begin to strike, with the Holy Spirit guiding the fingers of my mind, the final string, as it were, of this Song; and upon it, with the Lord’s help, I shall set forth the whole harmony of the promised tetrachord.

**VERSE 5.**—“Who is this who comes up from the wilderness, abounding in delights, leaning upon her beloved? Under the apple tree I raised you up; there your mother was corrupted, there she who bore you was violated.”

If I attribute this utterance to the Church, marvelling at the conversion [Col. 1246C] of Judea, it will not be absurd. For it was surely astonishing that a people stiff-necked and of untameable heart, after the passion of the Lord—whose divinity they refused to believe despite the many signs testifying to it, and whom they instead fastened to the cross after inflicting many injuries upon him—should suddenly, at the preaching of the apostles, embrace the way of salvation and receive the doctrine of the new Law.

And she marvels, not without cause, because she closely observes that it comes up from the wilderness, that it abounds in delights, and that it comes up leaning upon the beloved. The Synagogue was a kind of wilderness, abandoned by God on account of unbelief, as he threatens concerning it through the prophet: “The daughter of Zion shall be left like a shelter in a vineyard, like a hut in a cucumber-field, like a city being laid waste” (Baruch 6 [cf. Isa. 1:8]). And the Lord says in the Gospel: “Your house shall be left to you desolate” (Matt. 23). Thus Judea, when it believed, ascended from this wilderness through faith, because it passed from that lowly and feeble understanding of carnal observance to the spiritual and lofty pattern of evangelical instruction.

But it could not ascend except while abounding in delights, because it could not attain that sublimity of new understanding and grace except through abundance of virtues and fullness of holy charity. Yet it could not abound in these delights of virtue unless it leaned upon the beloved of holy Church—that is, Christ—because without the cooperation of his grace no glories of holiness and faith could come to it.

[Col. 1247A] Moreover, if you turn to each holy soul, understand the preceding words in another way. Attend carefully to the place where the beloved adjures the daughters of Jerusalem not to awaken or rouse the beloved until she herself wills it. What, do you suppose, has the beloved attained in this sleep of hers, that the beloved so strongly forbids her now to be awakened or roused? What, I say, does almighty God behold in this sleep of hers that is so beautiful, delightful, and pleasing to him? Surely, if you consider rightly, this most sweet beloved gazes with the gracious countenance of his favourable condescension upon something great, honourable, and worthy of admiration. For he marvels at the one ascending, at the place of her ascent, at the condition of the one ascending, and at the aid by which she ascends.

What is this ascent, as it were, of one sleeping and resting, except a contemplative elevation from earthly things to heavenly things, from the world to the Lord? But since the solitude of mind and body greatly aids this ascent—for each helps the other, inasmuch as the solitude of the mind is guarded by the solitude of the body, while bodily solitude profits little if the mind is occupied with the noise of the world—almighty Father marvels, with the serene gaze of mercy, at the soul ascending from the wilderness, saying: “Who is this who comes up from the wilderness?” “Who,” he says, “is this who has set ascents in her heart, in the valley of tears” (Ps. 83), ascending from the wilderness—that is, from the solitude of a mind despising the noise [Col. 1247C] of this world, sleeping in the peace of the Spirit, and choosing only the observance of my commandments?

From this it follows that she takes on the disposition by which she seems to abound in delights, because the observance of my commandments grants this: that she may abound in the delights of virtues. Nor is there anything else in abounding in virtues than keeping my commandments. For whatever can be or be called a virtue is wholly contained in the catalogue of my precepts. But from where does she have this ability—to ascend and abound in delights? From herself? Not at all, because every soul is weak and feeble without cooperating grace. And who is this beloved? My Son, I say, concerning whom I told you: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. [3:17]). Therefore, because she leaned on him, because she followed his footsteps by keeping and, as far as she could, imitating the things that he displayed in the flesh and taught in deed and word, she was able to ascend in mind and abound in the delights of virtues.

It will not be absurd to understand it in yet another way: namely, to take the wilderness as the present life, and the delights in which the beloved ascends abounding as Holy Scripture. For why should Holy Scripture not be called delights, when it contains such diversities of understanding for the soul’s progress, like the various courses of food on a single table? For just as, among varied dishes, one food is more delicate than another, so in Holy Scripture, among different understandings, one meaning is subtler than another. There, while reading, at one time bare history nourishes like coarser food; at another, under the covering of the letter, moral allegory refreshes deeply like a subtler food; at another, contemplation, raising the mind to higher things, sweetly affects it like singular and choice food.

For whoever abounds in delights is relaxed into a certain release from oneself and, as though through weariness, is eased from the pursuit of labour. Thus, when the soul begins to abound inwardly in delights, it by no means consents to brood over earthly desires; rather, captured by love of its Creator, free in a sweet captivity, it sighs in faintness for the contemplation of his beauty and, as it were, grows strong by growing weary. For while it can no longer carry filthy works, it hastens through repose to him whom it loves inwardly. Thus the soul comes up from the wilderness of the present worldly life, abounding in delights, because while it is nourished by the mystical understandings of Holy Scripture, it is daily lifted up to contemplate heavenly things.

[Col. 1248B] Yet it is described as leaning upon the beloved, because unless it clings to him by diligently investigating Holy Scripture, it cannot lift the step of its ascent to grasp those lofty things of spiritual understanding. For the mind intent on Holy Scripture leans upon its beloved, because God is found and known in Scripture; and the mind that knows and loves him is, as it were, inclined upon God himself.

Therefore this may be the voice of the Church rejoicing in the progress of each holy soul and saying: “Who is this who comes up from the wilderness, abounding in delights, leaning upon her beloved?” As if it said in other words: “Who is this who clings with such zeal to my beloved, the Lord Jesus Christ, by meditation on Holy Scriptures, that, abounding in their mystical understandings as in certain delights, she is able to ascend through contemplation to love of eternal life?”

It immediately adds: “Under the apple tree I raised you up; there your mother was corrupted, there she who bore you was violated.”

After the beloved has approved his beloved—that is, the faithful soul—for the state and disposition of virtue granted to her, he suddenly turns directly to her, recalling the victory of her good condition so that she may grow into a greater grace [Col. 1248D] of divine charity. “Under the apple tree,” he says, “I raised you up.” As if he said: “If you observe what you were in the first parent, from whom you contracted guilt, as though by propagation, together with the whole human race, you will not without reason cling to me more earnestly when you consider what I have now made you and how great a grace I have bestowed.”

For under the apple tree I raised you up, because, so that you might persevere in my grace, I set before you the pattern of your condition and bound you by the law of obedience so that you might learn to be under my power. For when I said to Adam, “Eat of every tree of Paradise, but of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil do not eat” (Gen. 2), I raised you up while you were still immature and ignorant, and I admonished you to the duty of using reason well, so that you might learn to adapt yourself to the pursuit of discipline and obedience. But what happened? He transgressed the command and despised the good of discipline and obedience.

[Col. 1249A] Therefore there your mother was corrupted; there she who bore you was violated. How? Eve was deceived and violated; she persuaded the man, and both presumed to take from the forbidden tree. Therefore under the apple tree your mother—that is, she who gave you birth—was corrupted and violated: corrupted through the lack of restraint of the external senses, violated through the consent of spirit and soul in the fault of disobedience. For she saw and desired, obeyed the serpent’s persuasion, touched the forbidden fruit, ate it, and offered it to the man to eat (Gen. 3).

256 After this sin had been completed, it brought forth death (Jas. 1); and the penalty of this death, as though proceeding from this root of your first parents, was spread throughout the posterity of the whole human race.

Accordingly, I raised you up in your first parents and urged you toward the pursuit of virtues; but you, in those very parents of yours, turned rather toward vices and did not fear to become subject to death.

But when you had been lost in such a manner, who restored you to salvation? Who made you such as you now appear? Was it not I who underwent death for you and redeemed you from that death? Was it not I who again raised you up under the apple tree—that is, beneath the wood of the cross—and lifted you to such honour and beauty of life?

But in order that you may preserve this honour and beauty of life inviolate, you must persevere with a strong mind in my charity.

[Col. 1249C] **VERSE 6.**—“Set me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm; for love is strong as death, jealousy is harsh as hell; its lamps are lamps of fire and flames.”

Here the beloved proposes two seals to the beloved: one to be placed upon the heart, the other upon the arm. What are these two seals—of heart and arm—but the guarding of the heart and the guarding of one’s work? For concerning a seal, that is, the guarding of the heart, it is written: “Guard your heart with all vigilance, because life proceeds from it” (Prov. 4). But concerning a seal, that is, the guarding of work, it is written: “In all your works remember your last things, and you will never sin” (Ecclus. 7).

[Col. 1249D] These two things are rightly necessary to a person throughout one’s life; and if the first guarding is neglected, the second perishes. For just as a good person brings forth good from the good treasure of one’s heart, so an evil person brings forth evil from the evil treasure of one’s heart (Luke 6). Whatever proceeds outwardly into action was first conceived in the heart.
