Therefore, if the guarding of the heart is neglected so that it is not governed by reason, whatever is shown outwardly in deed is judged irrational. If the heart is ordered by reason, what it brings forth into action is honourable, because every action of an agent, good or bad, is understood in accordance with the state or quality of the mind.

What, then, does the bridegroom say to the bride: “Set me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon [Col. 1250A] your arm”? What guarding can be safe and secure without God? “Unless the Lord guards the city, the one who guards it watches in vain” (Ps. 126). Therefore the Psalmist prays: “Guard me, Lord, as the pupil of the eye; protect me beneath the shadow of your wings” (Ps. 16).

And because, just as no good work can be begun without him, so it cannot be completed without him, the same Psalmist says: “Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labour in vain” (Ps. 126). Therefore it is also necessary that the seal of God be placed upon the arm, lest the building of good work be destroyed.

Thus the bride is rightly told: “Set me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm,” because she cannot think or do rightly unless divine grace inspires and guides her; nor can she bring these things to their completion by perseverance unless the same grace guards her. For when works of holiness are closed and, as it were, sealed, lest they be corrupted by some perversity, then the seal of God may indeed fittingly be understood as placed upon the heart and arm of each soul.

Or let us call the seal of God the imprint of holiness, which must be placed upon the heart and arm of every soul that desires to live holily and justly. For when the life, conduct, or teaching of the Lord Jesus Christ is set before a holy soul for imitation or observance, his seal is rightly impressed upon its heart and arm, so that just as it bore the image of the earthly one, it may bear also the image of the heavenly one (1 Cor. 15).

[Col. 1250C] When the Lord said to his disciples, “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. 11), did he not seem to say: “Set me as a seal upon your heart”? For there he wished to leave impressed on their hearts the image, as it were, of meekness and humility. But when he said, “I have given you an example, that as I have done, so you also should do” (John 3 [probably 13]), did he not seem to say: “Set me as a seal upon your arm”? For there he wished to leave them a kind of pattern and image of good action and dutiful charity, which they themselves would later impress upon their hearers by teaching and acting.

Thus also the Apostle, writing to the Philippians and desiring to impress upon their minds the seal or stamp of holiness from his own mind, says: “Brothers, whatever things are true, whatever chaste, whatever just, whatever holy, whatever lovable, whatever of good report; if there is any virtue, if there is any praise of discipline, think on these things. What you have learned, received, heard, and seen in me, do these things, and the God of peace will be with you” (Phil. 4).

[Col. 1250D] Therefore the bridegroom, that is Christ, says to his bride, that is, the faithful soul: “Set me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm.” As if in other words he said to her: “Store in your mind whatever you read in my teaching and works, and fulfil it in your actions, so that from them you may receive the pattern and image of holiness through which you may lay aside every image of the old human being which it assumed by sinning beneath the apple tree.” And why? “For love is strong as death.”

The beloved appropriately adds immediately, after having said, “Set me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm,” “For love is strong as death; jealousy is harsh as hell.” Since God himself is charity, as John says (1 John 4), to place God upon the heart is to have his charity; and to place him upon the arm is to perform good work through that same charity, because, as it is written, “Faith works through love” (Gal. 5).

Charity is the root of all virtues, because just as many branches grow from one root, so many virtues are generated from one charity. Therefore, if charity alone generates many virtues, and no one nourishes virtues within oneself except one who loves God, surely to have charity is to have God. Thus, with his seal placed upon heart and arm, action through love is good and honourable.

[Col. 1251B] But what made God become incarnate and die, except charity? “For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life” (John 3). Thus each faithful soul sets God as a seal upon heart and arm when, in imitation of him—as he laid down his life for her—it does not hesitate to labour for him and, if the cause demands it, even to undergo death.

Therefore love itself is rightly called strong as death, because it kindles the mind that truly loves God with such force that it does not hesitate to die for him whom it fears to offend by any love of a worldly thing. For charity, when it possesses someone perfectly, utterly kills in that person the love of worldly things. Therefore love is strong as death, because just as death destroys temporal life, so the love of God kills in the mind of the righteous the love of this world; and it renders one whom charity has thoroughly imbued inwardly as though insensible to the carnal desire of all external things.

Jealousy too is harsh as hell, because imitation of Christ’s works is as powerful to absolve and justify a human being from sins as hell is powerful to torment sinners. Yet this jealousy proceeds from the ardour of charity, which brings such force of pain from desire for heavenly [felicity], as hell brings to the sinners whom it torments from the remembrance of their evils.

[Col. 1251D] It is therefore added: “Its lamps are lamps of fire and flames,” so that charity itself may be understood in the hearts of the elect not merely as warmth, but as fire and flame.

**VERSE 7.**—“Many waters could not quench love, nor shall rivers overwhelm it. If a man were to give all the substance of his house for love, he would regard it as nothing.”

For its force is so great in the mind of every saint that, just as waters cannot quench an immense fire, so the many tribulations of the world cannot take the fervour of charity away from the saintly mind. [Col. 1252A] Therefore one who burned with this fire of charity says: “Who shall separate us from the charity of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword? But in all these things we overcome through him who loved us. For I am certain that neither life nor death, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor virtues, nor dominations, nor any creature will be able to separate us from the charity which is in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Rom. 7 [cf. 8:35–39]).

It is therefore rightly added that, if a man were to give all the substance of his house for love, he would regard it as nothing.

For why should a holy soul not despise all its substance for love of God, when it despises itself so much that it does not fear death for that same love of God? If it despises for the sake of his love all things that are not God, what can it set above that love? And since it sets nothing in heaven above charity, which is God, then it is surely not merely a small thing but nothing if it despises all its substance for it. It follows, therefore, that charity is the highest good, if no good can be set above it.

**VERSE 8.**—“Our sister is little and has no breasts. What shall we do for our sister on the day when she is to be addressed?”

Above, the beloved commended the eminence of charity and showed what and how great a good charity is. He now intends to show how it may be attained. For, since it is of such excellence and dignity, the way of grasping it and keeping it in the peace of perpetual security is not easy. Constancy or strength of mind, knowledge of the Scriptures, and perseverance in good work are therefore necessary for obtaining it.

Accordingly, the beloved says of the beloved—that is, the Church, or any holy soul, whom he calls sister because of faith and good works—that she is little and has no breasts; and he immediately gives counsel as to what must be done for this imperfection.

“Our sister,” he says, “is little.” In what respect is she little? Because she is still tender in faith, in understanding, in speech and reason, in strength of mind, and in the practice of a good life. “And she has no breasts.” How does she have no breasts? She does not yet possess the understanding of Holy Scripture contained in the two Testaments. Although she reads and hears what the letter displays and sounds forth, she has not yet received the knowledge of spiritual understanding, in which all the force and method of right speaking and disputing consist. Without it, no capacity for teaching or preaching can be obtained.

Therefore she must first put away the things of a child (1 Cor. 13) and tend toward perfection in faith and action, so that, after she has breasts through an entire knowledge of the two Testaments, she may finally undertake fittingly the office of teaching and preaching.

[Col. 1253A] “What, then, shall we do,” he says, “for our sister on the day when she is to be addressed?” Although our sister is still little and therefore cannot yet be addressed, let her nevertheless grow daily and desire to attain perfection. When the time comes to address her, so that it may be said to her, “Arise, hasten, my friend; show me your face; let your voice sound in my ears” (Song 2), what counsel shall we find on the day when she has acquired discernment, understanding and knowledge, and an honourable life?

**VERSE 9.**—“If she is a wall, let us build upon her silver battlements; if she is a door, let us fasten it with boards of cedar.”

There are two kinds of prelates. One kind consists of those devoted to the office of public preaching, who set themselves like a wall before the house of Israel—that is, the Church—against heretics and all reprobate persons (Ezek. 13). The other consists of those who exercise only the office of teacher and cleave to the contemplative life, kindling their subjects to the pursuit of good action by word and example. They are like a door to their subjects when, by right teaching and good conduct, they show them the entrance to the kingdom of heaven.

What, then, shall we do for our sister on such a day, when she is to be addressed and urged now to begin preaching or teaching? She must have two things necessary for this office: a wall and a door, so that she may be steadfast and learned, resisting heretics and instructing the people of God. For she will have a wall for defence and a door for admission.

[Col. 1253C] If, then, she is a wall, what shall we do? “Let us build,” he says, “silver battlements upon her.” Battlements are necessary against the snares of enemies. But why of silver? Because “the words of the Lord are silver tried by fire” (Ps. 11). Thus silver battlements are the defences of the divine sayings, which must be built in the preacher’s mind through knowledge of Holy Scripture.

“If she is a wall,” he says, “let us build silver battlements upon this wall.” If amid adversities and prosperities she has strength of spirit and such constancy that she stands like a wall for the defence of righteousness, let us also give her knowledge of Holy Scripture. From its sentences, as from battlements, [Col. 1253D] she may be able to fight against the perversities of heretics and evil persons and defend the cause of truth.

Moreover, if it is a door, and she diligently keeps watch for this purpose, to instruct her hearers by the word of life and to introduce them to a good manner of living, what shall we do? “Let us,” he says, “fasten that door together with cedar boards”; for painting serves in place of reading for those who do not know letters. What, then, is the material of this painting to be set upon this door, if not the life and conduct of the saints? For whenever any prelate, for the sake of edification, sets before those subject to him the examples of the saints, he surely paints, as it were, in their minds what they ought to love, what to fear, and how they ought to order their life in imitation of them.

[Col. 1254A] Hence this painting is also said to be composed of cedar boards; for cedar is by nature incorruptible, and therefore cedar boards rightly signify the saints, because they are corrupted by no rottenness of vices. Rather, they fill the Church with a good fragrance, because they are the good fragrance of Christ in every place (II Cor. II).

Therefore the door is fastened with cedar boards when any preacher confirms his preaching by the virtues of the saints whom he adduces as examples, so that he may either open the gate of eternal life to those who imitate them, or shut it against those who despise them.

Thus the holy Church, or any holy soul that strives toward love of her bridegroom, while she is still little and tender in faith and knowledge, in character and discipline—if she desires to attain that perfection [Col. 1254B] which brings forth within her the full love of God—must possess, along with steadfastness of mind, the bulwarks of the divine utterances, and must stand with blessed perseverance in teaching and in good life. For when she has breasts of preaching and teaching, so that she may also nourish others and bring them to perfection, she seems, as though by obligation, bound to communicate to her neighbours what she has by God’s grace. As the Apostle says: “I am debtor both to Greeks and to barbarians, both to the wise and to the unwise; so, as far as lies in me, I am ready to preach the Gospel also to you who are at Rome” (Rom. I). Therefore, immediately after obtaining the grace of knowledge, freely presenting herself at the door of preaching, she answers her bridegroom steadfastly: “I am a wall, and my breasts are like a tower.”

[Col. 1254C] 262 VERSE 10.—“I am a wall, and my breasts are like a tower, from the time when I became before him as one finding peace.”

For she shows the reason for the grace bestowed upon her: namely, the finding of peace, through which she strives, by steadfast preaching and working, to advance both herself and others. Since “the life of man upon earth is a warfare” (Job VII), when a person is in battle and suffers the violence of opponents, how could one stand in defence of others who is still labouring for his own sake? He must therefore first experience peace and rest within himself, attain inward security, and only then become a wall for the defence of others. He must first know how to instruct, govern, and teach himself, and then extend the breasts of his teaching for the advancement of others. [Col. 1254D] This too is a sign of a certain peace: for when the mind labours through ignorance and struggles with itself to acquire knowledge, once knowledge has been gained, after long warfare with itself, it is proved surely to have attained the fruit of great peace and rest.

What peace, then, does she say that she has found, and where? Undoubtedly that peace which surpasses all understanding (Phil. IV), which the bridegroom himself left to his lovers, saying: “Peace I leave with you; my peace I give unto you” (John XIV). What peace can be preferred to this peace, which indeed begins here but remains there eternally? For Christ himself is peace, of whom the Apostle says: “For he is our peace, who made both one” (Eph. II). Hence she says that she found this peace before him: “From the time when I became before him as one finding peace.” For there she finds peace, where she recognizes as present him who is true peace.

But how did she find and recognize him as present? And how, with him present, did she find peace? Surely in the way taught by him who says to his own: “Have salt in yourselves, and have peace among yourselves” (Mark IX). For when he was about to teach concerning the possession of peace, not without reason he first said, “Have salt in yourselves.” No one can attain this peace unless his mind is seasoned with the salt of wisdom. For, as someone says, wisdom is the absence of folly; since, as salt removes decay from flesh, so wisdom removes folly from the heart. Once folly, which produces the rottenness of vices, has been removed from the heart by the seasoning of wisdom, it quickly reaches this peace, [Col. 1255B] by which every conflict between flesh and spirit is stilled, and the flesh desires nothing that opposes the spirit. Thus, once this peace has been found on earth, it shall one day attain that peace which can never be taken away.

But how is this conflict removed so that peace may be granted, unless before him, unless in the presence of him who consoles his own as they fight, saying: “Take courage; I have overcome the world” (John XVI)? As though he said: “Because I have overcome, through me you also shall overcome.”

Rightly, then, the bride says: “From the time when I became before him as one finding peace, I am a wall, and my breasts are like a tower.” For from the time when, by his grace, I conquered fleshly desires and was strengthened with spiritual peace, I can [Col. 1255C] also stand for the salvation of others and steadfastly proclaim words of exhortation. “My breasts are like a tower,” because through divine grace I have grown so greatly in the word of exhortation that, according to the prophet, I can ascend a high mountain and lift up my voice with strength in order to proclaim good news to Jerusalem (Isa. XL). Indeed, I am a wall, to defend and protect the people of God; and my breasts are like a tower, that I may look out from on high and announce future things from afar.

VERSE 11.—“The Peaceful One had a vineyard in her who has peoples; he entrusted it to guardians; a man brings a thousand silver pieces for its fruit.”

It must be considered very carefully who this Peaceful One is; what the vineyard of the Peaceful One is; who indeed are the peoples, who the guardians, and what is the fruit of this vineyard.

This Peaceful One is the Lord Jesus Christ. He is called Peaceful on account of the reasons for peace stated above: “his place is made in peace” (Ps. LXXV); and he called us in peace, dissolving enmities in his flesh, abolishing the law of commandments in decrees, in order that he might create the two in himself into one new human being, making peace, that he might reconcile both to God in one body through the cross, killing enmities in himself; and, coming, he preached peace to those who were far off and peace to those who were near (Eph. II).

With the enlightened eye of the inward human being, one must diligently consider how fittingly, truly, and uniquely this one is Peaceful—he who dissolved in his flesh such enmities, so great and so long-lasting. The wonderful and adorable majesty of reconciliation is recognized all the more when the character and magnitude of the enmity are weighed. For how great an enmity did the first human contract against God through the evil of disobedience, so that he not only lost the happiness of the paradise in which he had been placed, but also incurred death, the avenger of transgression? Yet the weight of this enmity increased through the succession of humankind, by the growth of wickedness and depravity, until the Creator himself, as Scripture says, inwardly touched by grief of heart, said: “It repents me that I made man” (Gen. VI). Therefore, after judicial sentence was pronounced, the whole world was consumed by the avenging water, except Noah, who alone at that time was saved with his wife and sons.

[Col. 1256B] But who could remove the weight of so great an enmity? Could an angel? Yet an angel, no less than a human being, is a creature of God and needed God’s grace; and a creature could not free a creature from such necessity. Therefore the Creator of the creature came—needing nothing, omnipotent, and in every respect sufficient, without any obstacle, both to destroy the wall of this enmity and to establish the eternal covenant of reconciliation and true peace. Since he could not be seen in his divinity, he came through humanity in order to become visible. At his birth the whole world met him with the sign of temporal peace, announcing and proclaiming the emblem of that supreme and eternal peace to be established through him. Hence at his birth the angels cried: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke II).

[Col. 1256C] Who, then, is more truly Peaceful than this eternal maker of such great peace? Solomon indeed, who was called Peaceful from his name—for *Solomon* is interpreted “peaceful”—was a temporal king who, by God’s grant, possessed temporal peace, so that he might build a house for God with no one hindering him. But by his name, work, and time he preceded this true Peaceful One as night precedes day and shadow truth. For this true Peaceful One, in order to establish a house for himself, namely the holy Church, placed as it were in its foundation the sign of this wondrous peace which must be preserved, saying: “Peace I leave with you; my peace I give unto you” (John XIV).

This Peaceful One had a vineyard, namely the holy Church. It is not inappropriately called a vineyard because, if one considers either its cultivation or its nature, it appears to draw no small benefit for its own advancement from the likeness. What, then, is the method of cultivation applied to a vineyard? At pruning time it is cleansed, as it were, by cutting away useless shoots; then it is dug around, raised up, and tied to stakes. Further, if you consider the quality of its nature, you will see that it first puts down a living root; then, because it is pliant and prone to fall, it grasps and binds whatever it embraces with what are, as it were, little arms—namely, its tendrils—and by these it raises and lifts itself. What is pruning in the Church or in any soul except the cutting away of vices from hearts? What is digging around except bringing one’s deeds to mind through compunction and confession of sins? [Col. 1257A] For the mass of earthly deeds is brought to remembrance, as though by a hoe of compunction, so that the mind, relieved through confession and satisfaction, may bear fruit more effectively in good works.

And what does the minister of this office do, when he receives a penitent and lays upon one who confesses a measure of penance? He raises the person by the hand of assured consolation and the hope of divine mercy; and by setting before him the examples of the saints, he shows what purpose of life he ought thereafter to maintain, by which he should support himself, as if tied to stakes, lest he fall.

Further, according to the nature of the vine, the advancement of the Church or of any soul is considered. Once it has been planted and fixed by the root of faith, and its low-growing shoot has been checked lest it be bent or drawn aside by any storms or tempests of the world, it embraces every neighbour with the tendrils and coils, as it were, of charity, and rests in their compunction.

Such, therefore, was the vineyard of the true Peaceful One, our Lord Jesus Christ—not because it is not so now or ought not to be so in the future, but because “was” must be understood in accordance with his foreknowledge and predestination. Thus elsewhere it is written of every creature: “What was made in him was life” (John I), because in his foreknowledge all things already were and lived, just as the form or pattern of a thing to be made exists in the mind of an artisan, whose likeness the hands of the worker imitate in order to bring the thing into view.

The vineyard, moreover, was in her—that is, peace—“who has peoples,” [Col. 1257C] because the Church is gathered not from the people of the Jews alone but from the peoples of all nations into unity of faith, love, and peace, as it is written: “They had one heart and one soul” (Acts IV). It should further be noted that he does not say, “in that peace which the peoples have,” but “which has peoples,” so that one may attend more to the grace of the One who calls, justifies, and glorifies than to the labour and effort of one who wills, runs, and strives to attain. For, as the Apostle says: “It is not of him who wills nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy” (Rom. IX). For he is our peace, who made both one (Eph. II), and from him comes the peace which surpasses all understanding (Phil. IV).

When this peace has peoples, then no schism or dissension can break their unity of faith; rather, they adhere so firmly in that peace that they become a choicest vineyard for the true Peaceful One, our Lord Jesus Christ. For if they themselves possessed peace without being possessed by peace, they would not be held by a firm root, because they would not have been planted together in that peace in which they would sleep and rest in one and the same state (Ps. IV). This sleep and rest are given after this life in that same state, because “we shall see him as he is” (I John III), and “there is no change, nor shadow of turning” there (James I); but the peace which we have once received we shall preserve eternally without any alteration.

Yet although in the first place we must understand these peoples possessed by this peace as the universal Church gathered from Jews and Gentiles, in the second place [Col. 1258A] we may not inappropriately understand a particular Church, established within the universal Church through its various kinds of profession. This too may be called the Lord’s vineyard, and it ought to be bound together by the same peace and unanimity. If, further, we descend to individuals, some faithful soul serving God may without absurdity be called the Lord’s vineyard, whose cultivator is the Holy Spirit through grace. For, according to the pattern set out above, which we said suited the whole body, it also seems suitably to belong to the individual: namely, that its aim should be to cut away vices and sins like useless shoots by the hand of pious work through cooperating grace; to bring earthly works to mind through compunction and confession, as though through digging around; and thus, by repenting and doing good works, to offer fruit acceptable to God.

“He entrusted it to guardians.” The guardians of this vineyard—that is, of the holy Church—were the holy apostles and their successors, apostolic men. Their care and diligence consisted in instructing it in holiness and righteousness and defending it, by word and example, from the plague of evil works and perverse doctrines. This does not mean that whatever progress they attained in this guardianship was their own work; rather, they were ministers and servants of divine operation and efficacy. Thus the Lord says to Aaron in Numbers: “You shall place my name upon the children of Israel, and I, the Lord, will bless them” (Num. VI). That is, as if he said in other words: “Through the ministry entrusted to you, convey my grace to people by word and deed; it will be mine to show in them the good of that grace itself and bring it to effect.”

[Col. 1258C] The word “entrusted,” however, which is set forth in this statement, must be considered with no little fear by all prelates of churches and by those subject to them, because it warns both the former to be careful and diligent in the virtue of prudence, and the latter in the virtue of obedience. The Apostle speaks to prelates: “Take heed to yourselves and to the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit has placed you as bishops, to rule the Church of God, which he acquired with his blood” (Acts XX). And to subjects: “Obey your leaders,” he says, “and be subject to them. For they keep watch as those who will render account for your souls, that they may do this with joy and not groaning; for this is not profitable for you” (Heb. XIII). Therefore this word of entrusting, “He entrusted it to guardians,” ought to make you—that is, prelates—attentive with concern and foresight, and these—that is, subjects—attentive with humility and patience.

If, then, God entrusted his Church to guardians, it is greatly to be feared that, if the guardians neglect their custody and those who are to be guarded despise the guardians, or resist and speak against the guardianship, they will grievously offend him who appointed the guardians and established the guardianship. God calls these guardians watchmen, as the prophet himself says: “I have made you a watchman to the house of Israel; what you see, you shall announce to them from me” (Ezek. III). [Col. 1259A] “What you see,” he says, “you shall announce to them from me”: that is, whatever you understand with the eye of the mind or observe with the bodily eye as requiring correction or amendment, you shall announce to them by exhortation, counsel, and command, “from me”—that is, according to the method and measure which I shall indicate to you by inspiration.

In this entrusting of guardianship, God also set before the guardians, or watchmen, both the danger and the means of escaping it, saying: “If, when I say to the wicked, ‘You shall surely die,’ you do not announce it to him, he indeed shall die in his iniquity, but I will require his blood from your hand.” Behold the danger. The way of escaping this danger follows in what he says: “But if you announce to the wicked that he should turn from his iniquity, and he does not heed you, he indeed shall die in his iniquity, but you have delivered your own soul” (ibid.). Thus to guardians—that is, to prelates in the Church—danger for negligence and security for vigilance are set forth; hence they ought to be held to greater care and concern for the office entrusted to them.

But for private persons or subjects the danger arising from contempt and disobedience is no less—indeed, it is more serious. For prelates commonly sin through weakness and negligence, whereas these offend through pride and recklessness; and contempt and irreverence toward the former are contempt and irreverence toward God. So he himself says: “He who hears you hears me, and he who despises you despises me” (Luke X). And to the prophet, whom he says he made a watchman for the house of Israel: “Therefore,” he says, “they do not hear you, because they are a provoking house” (Ezek. III). It is an evil and fearful designation for a house of undisciplined and disobedient persons to be called a provoking house; and elsewhere they are said to be stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart because they resist the Holy Spirit (Acts VII). For those who resist the word of discipline and uprightness resist the word of God. The words of God are spirit and life (John VI), and therefore they resist the Holy Spirit. Hence, because the Prophet saw that resisting God’s word was damnable, he asked God to teach him goodness and discipline, because he had believed and obeyed his commandments (Ps. CXVIII).

[Col. 1259D] In the sacred law, moreover, the divine word commanded concerning a stubborn, unruly, and disobedient son that his parents should seize him and bring him to the elders of the city and to the gate of judgment (Deut. XXI), so that they might not hastily pronounce their own sentence but call wise persons as witnesses. For they should know that the first fault of our race, which we all pay for, is disobedience; and that God’s justice stores up no pardon for the stubborn and unruly. Rather, as it is written: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (I Pet. V).

Such persons must always be examined at the gate of judgment, so that, if they remain in their stubbornness or recklessness and refuse to obey, they may be expelled from the fellowship of the brethren; but if they repent and become humble and peaceable, they may be received again. This too is the gate of judgment in the city of God—that is, the holy Church: that stubborn and rebellious persons, if they refuse correction, may be cut off with the sword [Col. 1260A] of excommunication like rotten members from the body of the Church. Of these it is written: “They went out from us, but they were not of us” (I John II). But those who repent and put an end to their wickedness may be restored to the body of the Church like healed and holy members. Therefore other sins must indeed be tolerated in the house of God, but the severity of wise fathers crushes stubborn and unruly children, in order to remove evil from its midst, by the authority of the Lord’s law which we have mentioned; indeed, by the example of God himself, who expelled the first disobedient humans from paradise (Gen. III).

The word of entrusting which is spoken concerning the lord of the vineyard must therefore be pondered and weighed, not negligently but diligently and with fear; for when it is neglected or despised on either side, whether by prelates or by subjects, it brings one under the judgment of the one who entrusted it.

“A man brings a thousand silver pieces for its fruit.” The diligent and attentive student of this chapter must consider what or of what sort, or how great, is the fruit of this vineyard, which is valued at such a price that, to obtain it, not ten or twenty or thirty, but precisely a thousand silver pieces must be brought. And one who would purchase this fruit with them must be called—and must truly be—not merely any powerful, rich, official, or private person, but simply a *man*.

What, then, is this fruit? Surely it is that which is depicted as though in three colours of beauty: power, wisdom, and goodness—power than which nothing is more effective; wisdom than which nothing is more rational; goodness than which nothing is sweeter. For power is constrained by no law of impossibility or weakness; wisdom admits nothing lacking the force of reason; goodness abounds with such fullness of sweetness that there is nothing beyond it. Moreover, the touching and enjoyment of such fruit affords the whole person an effective and most health-giving experience of well-being. But where is this found among creatures and visible things? Is it found in angels? Yet it is written that God “found iniquity even in his angels” (Job IV). A creature can be subject to corruption and change; but what cannot be so subject must necessarily be immutable and incorruptible.

[Col. 1260D] We have said that the three beauties of this fruit are such that they can admit nothing above themselves. Yet something below them can, through their influence or participation, be called in some manner powerful, wise, and good, but not substantially power, wisdom, and goodness. For that which can receive and be participated in is not the same as that which receives and participates. For that which receives and participates is so when it neither receives nor participates, and therefore is subject to change and can be corrupted. But that which is receivable and participable, always abiding immutably in its own essence, can never be corrupted; and no creature is receivable and participable. Therefore it is God.

When, therefore, we inquire what is the fruit of this vineyard and consider every circumstance of its power and beauty, [Col. 1261A] we conclude beyond doubt that it is God. By receiving and participating, however, the rational creature attains this: that it may someday pass into incorruption and immutability, not by nature but by grace. Thus, from the human being’s working and God’s cooperating, this fruit is, as it were, born and grows. It is the reward of all who belong to God’s kingdom, and is called true blessedness. True blessedness, however, is God himself: to possess him and enjoy him eternally is truly to be blessed. This fruit, therefore, is God.

But what shall we say of the quality of such fruit, when it is written of it that “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man” (I Cor. II)? Nevertheless, above we distinguished the same fruit by three colours, which belongs more to quality—not because diversity of colours makes the fruit diverse, but because this diversity adheres so inseparably to the one substance that it in no way removes the force and efficacy of any property. For example, in some one subject three colours may occur: one is named red, another white, and a third green; yet the substance which contains them is one and the same. So in this fruit, although power is not one thing, wisdom another, and goodness another, the fruit is nevertheless one and the same, and everywhere possesses one and the same power and efficacy: namely, to be able, to know, and to give life. These, however, bring it about that no good is lacking from its fullness.

[Col. 1261C] What, moreover, can be said of the magnitude of this fruit, since it is of such immensity that it is circumscribed by no place and enclosed by no boundary? Yet it seems to have certain dimensions, not in itself but according to that which participates in it. Nothing, however, can participate in this thing except a rational creature. Now the rational creature is either spiritual, like an angel and a soul, or bodily, like the elements and things composed from them. But since this is not the place to discuss the dimensions of bodily things, constituted by line, surface, or solid body—and since this fruit of whose magnitude we have begun to speak is not bodily but spiritual, for “God is spirit” (John IV)—no one can either conceive or express its magnitude, since it is incomprehensible and uncircumscribed. Yet let us now see what dimensions it can have, not in itself but according to that which participates in it.

For whatever goodness, uprightness, holiness, discipline, or knowledge a participating soul can possess, it receives into itself, as though flowing from the participable God, the strength of grace. Thus the participant seems to possess something longer or shorter, broader or narrower, higher or lower, according as it pleases him to distribute who gives each person grace according to the measure of faith (Rom. XII). Hence the Apostle, speaking to those whom he exhorted to receive such dimensions, says: “Rooted and grounded in charity, that you may be able to comprehend with all the saints what is the length, [Col. 1262A] breadth, height, and depth” (Eph. II).

But because this fruit of which we speak is born and grows from the root of charity, and comes to maturity, as it were, to perfection—not in respect of God, who is always perfect, but in respect of the human mind capable of receiving him, which is subject to increase and decrease—so that by advancing in this way it may someday comprehend God and become, in its own manner, perfect and unchangeable with him, let us first see how our Lord Jesus Christ himself, according to his humanity, received in himself from the root of charity all these dimensions: length, breadth, height, and depth. For who had greater charity than he who laid down his life for his sheep? (John XV).

[Col. 1262B] If we direct the eyes of the mind to the kind and character of his passion, we shall see all these dimensions contained in it in a venerable manner, and by this example every Christian soul is vigorously advanced. For in the form of the cross these four dimensions must be observed: length, height, breadth, and depth. From the root of Christ’s charity they extend throughout the whole world, signifying and warning every soul redeemed by his passion that, if it wishes to obtain the aforesaid fruit—that is, eternal blessedness—it must reach it through the dimensions of that same charity, according to the measure and nature granted to it.

For charity must be broad, because it must extend even to love of enemies, as Christ, hanging upon the cross, prayed for his enemies, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they do” (Luke XXIII). It must be long because it must not last merely for an hour, but until the end of life, as is written of Christ: “Having loved his own, he loved them unto the end” (John XIII). Charity must have such perseverance that it fails under no tribulation or distress. It must be high because of its final cause: it must attend to why it acts or suffers, that is, for eternal blessedness, the fruit of which we speak, for whose sake it is always urged to reach upward and to have its citizenship in heaven. It must have depth because it must never be without fear, but must always consider [Col. 1262D] that whatever it attains through breadth, length, and height, it possesses not from its own merits but from God’s mercy. And therefore, because it does not know the hidden and deep judgment of God—why he chooses one and rejects another—and because the end is always uncertain while many are called and few chosen (Matt. XX), it must never be without fear.

Accordingly, since in Christ “all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Col. II), and God gives him the Spirit not by measure (John III), while all the saints receive from his fullness, grace for grace (John I), they seem, each according to his own mode or measure, to reach the dimensions of these spaces according as he gives to them who possesses fully and can give from his fullness as much as he wills.

[Col. 1263A] Moreover, since charity, placed like a centre in the middle, touches all virtues, as it were, through a circumference—for every virtue descends from the root of charity—and since every movement has six forms, namely forward and backward, upward and downward, to the right and to the left: wherever the human mind directs its intention in pursuit of such fruit, it always derives the source of every good movement from the force of charity. And because man himself is called a lesser world, and, after the likeness of the greater world, consists of four elements, he is likewise measured by four parts by which he is wholly contained, if he has been established to preserve the likeness of God: prudence, justice, temperance, and fortitude.

With these four parts extending at equal distance from the centre of the mind—that is, charity—you touch and enclose, as it were, in a circle everything that can be virtue in the soul.

This, then, can in some manner be the measure or dimension that this fruit has in its participant, not in itself, as was said; so that when it has someday been attained by the participant as it is, it may thereafter take away every capacity for increase and change of dimension, and bestow perfect, eternal impassibility, immutability, and immortality. [Note: [Col. 1263D] An obscure passage.]

Thus this fruit is true blessedness, and true blessedness is God, whose quality and immensity are incomprehensible. But since we have now learned what the fruit of the aforesaid vineyard is, let us consider [Col. 1263C] the offerer: who he is, since he is said to be a man and cannot offer unless he is a man.

For *vir* (“man”) is derived from *virtus* (“virtue”), and one who must offer for so great a fruit ought to shine with the beauty and grace of virtues; for an offering commended by no brightness of virtues will not be accepted. In the relationship of giver and receiver there ought to be such order that the disposition and grace of uprightness and discipline in the giver produces favour and gladness of countenance in the receiver and makes the gift more acceptable. If mortal people seek and approve this good of discipline and uprightness among themselves, what do we suppose almighty and immortal God seeks and desires from us, whose nature is singular goodness, holiness, uprightness, and discipline?

Therefore one who offers to such a Lord must be clothed with strength and girded with power (Ps. XCII): with strength of mind, to restrain and repel vices and sins; with vigour of spirit, to perform and practise good works. For an offering darkened by the stain of sin is not right. Thus the Lord said even to Cain: “If you offer rightly, but do not divide rightly, you have sinned” (Gen. IV). He offered rightly who gave God fruits of the earth, but did not divide rightly because he kept his heart in evil and defiled his offering with the plague of envy. He ought to have separated good from evil, because light has no fellowship with darkness, nor can truth and falsehood, justice and wickedness, be together in God’s sight.

He offered rightly because he offered to God, to whom he ought to offer; but he did not divide rightly because he rightly withheld from God what was better and gave what was inferior. For the person who offers God his possession but keeps himself for himself is not sufficiently dear to God; indeed, he is unworthy of God.

Such a man the Prophet describes in the first psalm, where he sets forth the disposition and purpose of this kind of man. Since that psalm is known to those who understand, whoever wishes to take up this man should meditate upon it continually and put it into practice. Elsewhere too he briefly recalls this same man, saying: “Blessed is the man who fears the Lord, who greatly delights in his commandments” (Ps. CXI), and the rest. For this is what makes him a man and blessed: it belongs to virtue to fear God and to consider and keep his commandments; and it belongs to blessedness that, because of this, his seed shall be mighty on earth and his righteousness shall remain for ever and ever (ibid.).

273. Having described what kind of man the offerer ought to be, we must now consider what fruit such a man brings and ought to bring. “A thousand pieces of silver,” he says. The number one thousand is used for perfection; silver signifies the pure and shining meaning of chaste utterances, as it is written: “The utterances of the Lord are chaste utterances, silver tried by fire” (Ps. 11). But what can we call a silver coin fashioned and inscribed from this silver? If we examine carefully, what fashions or inscribes in the human mind the image of God, the image of holiness and righteousness [Col. 1264C], except “the bright commandment of the Lord, enlightening the eyes” (Ps. 18)—that is, the eyes of the inward person? But where do we hear the Lord’s commandment, and from where do we know it, except from Holy Scripture, which is the utterance of the Lord? Scripture, then, when rightly understood, fashions the mind of a person and makes in it, as it were, a certain inscription. Thus, when from the reading of Holy Scripture one has perfectly embraced charity “from a pure heart and a good conscience and an unfeigned faith” (2 Tim. 2), one receives the stamp of a certain silver coin, inscribed thus: “after the image and likeness of God.” For the Creator of all things himself appointed this form to be impressed upon humankind in creation when he said: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1) [Col. 1264D]—that is to say: Let us make a living, rational human being, like God. For the condition of human beings surpasses all living creatures by a twofold honour, when it is said, “in our image and likeness”: in the image, namely, that the person may be rational; in our likeness, that the person may be upright in following God’s righteousness. Of one of these, namely rationality, a person cannot be deprived; the other, that is, the likeness of divine uprightness or righteousness, cannot be attained except through grace. Yet the faculty of rationality, of which a person cannot be deprived, is an instrument—or a kind of eye—for seeking the likeness of God. Therefore one is without excuse when one has not attained God’s likeness [Col. 1265A], since one refused to use for the purpose for which it was given the good instrument granted for that purpose.

But when God first made man, he made him not merely rational but also endowed with the honour of his likeness. For, Scripture says, “God made man upright, but he entangled himself in many inquiries” (Eccles. 7). Now, deceived, he has indeed lost the honour of God’s likeness; yet the power of reason has remained in him, by which he may hear the one calling him back and be able to follow the guide and teacher of his restoration. Therefore that divine and supreme banker inscribed such silver in the human soul when he made it rational and a participant in his holiness.

274. Therefore a human being is indebted to God: because God [Col. 1265B] distinguished him with this twofold honour, he ought to understand his obligation—namely, that, being capable of reason, with reason itself as guide, he may always advance through holiness toward the likeness of God. Otherwise, if he does not understand, “he shall be compared to senseless beasts and become like them” (Ps. 48). The Lord shows in the Gospel that a human being owes this debt to God. When he was tested by scribes and Pharisees who said, “Is it lawful to pay tribute to Caesar or not?” he answered, “Show me the coin of the tribute.” When they showed it, he said, “Whose image and inscription is this?” They replied, “Caesar’s.” “Render,” he said, “the things that are Caesar’s to Caesar, and the things that are God’s to God” (Matt. 22).

By this saying the Lord shows, and by showing teaches, that just as it is right for a mortal human being [Col. 1265C] to render, in tributary submission, to another mortal the things that belong to him and have been given by him, so it is right—indeed, most right—for a human being to offer to almighty and immortal God, with the highest devotion and humble submission, the things that are God’s and have been granted by him. Reason and understanding have been granted to human beings by God; they ought to use them so as to advance by good living toward the likeness of God, and so receive in their soul and mind, from the splendour of holiness, this inscription of the silver coin: “after the image and likeness of God.”

Thus a faithful person offers one, two, three, or more such silver coins, according to the measure of God’s gift, so as to acquire that fruit [Col. 1265D]—that is, eternal life—which works through love and tends and advances toward the likeness of God. But one brings a thousand silver coins who has attained the image and likeness of God in the brightness of perfect holiness.

Or the thousandfold unity signifies one faith, one baptism, one God, “who works all things in all” (1 Cor. 12). Whoever desires that fruit, namely eternal life, must hold and teach the true and right faith; have and worship one God and one man; adorn with faith and works the name of Christianity received in baptism; and read, teach, embrace, and follow the true, catholic, and one divine Scripture. Therefore, when the beloved woman says these things about herself for the grace and glory of her beloved [Col. 1266A], she immediately replies: “My vineyard,” etc.

### Verse 12

“My vineyard is before me. A thousand are for you, O peaceable one, and two hundred for those who guard its fruit.”

“My vineyard,” he says, “is before me”: that is, I know and approve my vineyard, because I find in it the grace of my planting. If I did not find it, it could not be before me, nor could it be called my vineyard. For concerning you, who can be called and be my vineyard, I spoke through the prophet: “I will look upon you and make you grow; you shall multiply, and I will establish my covenant with you” (Lev. 26). For those who are before me in such a way as to be worthy of my presence and gaze, shining with the brightness of good works, I acknowledge and guard; for “the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous” (Ps. 33). Conversely [Col. 1266B], those who put me behind them in contempt, I also put behind me in rejection, and therefore do not bestow the assistance of my grace upon them.

“A thousand are for you, O peaceable one, and two hundred for those who guard its fruits.” The meaning of this passage will appear more clearly from the contrast with the vineyard that was turned to evil, of which it is said: “I expected it to produce grapes, but it produced wild grapes” (Isa. 5). For the Lord says of it through Hosea under the figure of a harlot: “I dug her out for myself for fifteen pieces of silver, and a cor of barley and a half-cor of barley” (Hos. 3). A most beautiful mystery lies hidden in these numbers: here, in the thousand pieces of silver; there, in fifteen pieces of silver, a cor of barley, and a half-cor of barley. Its point is this: this woman is both a virgin and joined to a husband, whereas that one [Col. 1266C] is neither a virgin nor joined to a husband. For the thousandfold unity signifies this one’s virginity, while the binary hundred signifies her union or marriage. Mathematicians, or reckoners on the abacus, know better what is meant and have in their treatises the rationale by which unity is called a virgin: when multiplied by itself, it creates nothing, because one times one is one—a property belonging to no other number. For other numbers, multiplied into themselves, produce others: twice two is four, and three times three is nine. Moreover, the binary hundred signifies this one’s marriage; and this is most blessed, because this beloved woman, who is of faith, is always united to her husband and yet always remains a virgin: she always bears offspring, yet always remains a virgin.

[Col. 1266D] On the other hand, the fact that her price neither remained in unity nor reached the binary number signifies at once that other woman’s widowhood and corruption, when it is said: “I dug her out for myself for fifteen pieces of silver, and a cor of barley and a half-cor of barley.” If you consider the silver pieces, they are neither ten silver pieces, which would be decimal unity, nor twenty, which would be the binary decimal; rather, they are fifteen, a number greater than unity and less than the binary number. Likewise, there is neither one cor of barley alone nor two cors, but a cor and a half of barley: greater than the monad, less than the binary number. Thus it is most unhappy for her as well, because she is neither a virgin nor has a husband. Therefore your thousand peace-making silver coins, that is, all utterances harmonious in one faith—for this number is a thousandfold [Col. 1267A] unity—make or obtain peace for you, that is, forgiveness of sins. For to have one Lord, one faith, and one baptism is to be in the catholic Church, where forgiveness of sins is given through peace, that is, through Christ, “who is our peace, who made both one” (Eph. 2).

For Holy Scripture, which sounds forth and teaches these three things, contains within itself the whole sum of this peace. Whatever you read concerns God, faith, or the religion of Christianity; all the Church’s sacraments are constituted from these, and whoever possesses them as one ought to possess them obtains that peace which experiences the wars of vices. And when, having been given forgiveness of sins, one has advanced with this peace to an abundance of virtues, one will attain that perpetual and never-ending peace, where there will be no labour, no pain [Col. 1267B], nothing whatever able to oppose it.

These three things, then, are the instruments of this peace, because every soul tending toward it must always consider whom it believes, what it believes, and how it believes. If you ask whom, or in whom, you ought to believe, God is set before you; if you ask what you ought to believe, the sacraments of the Church are shown to you; and if you ask how you ought to believe, the religion of Christianity is prescribed to you. For “faith without works is idle—indeed, dead” (Jas. 2); and “without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. 11). Accordingly, as we have said, because of the unity of these three things, which establish and obtain true and eternal peace, it is rightly said that this vineyard has a thousand peace-makers.

[Col. 1267C] But why are there said to be two hundred for those who guard its fruit? First we must see who these guardians of the fruit are; then what this binary hundred, of which we spoke a little above, means when given to them. In the first place we may call guardians of this fruit those who preside in God’s Church by word and deed, and who strive to resist with tongue and hand—that is, by teaching and action—lest this fruit be snatched from the minds of believers by heretics and other perverse people. They must never be barren, but always bring forth offspring of virtues in themselves and in others. In the second place, all Christians generally ought to be guardians of this fruit, because the Christian religion requires this of them: that they may not lose eternal life by evil living, but, always being one spirit with God [Col. 1267D], may be enriched with the fruitfulness of good works from this spiritual union; and thus at last, in the virginal marriage of the heavenly nuptials signified here by the binary hundred, may enjoy God forever. The dowry of this marriage will be the twofold robe, namely, the blessedness of body and soul. The binary hundred may also signify this, because the number one hundred, on the right hand, represents the crown of that same blessedness.

### Verse 13

“You who dwell in the gardens, your friends listen; make me hear your voice.”

After the many and varied, beautifully and praiseworthily spoken exchanges of the beloved and the beloved woman, the same beloved, as though uttering the concluding and final voice of this epithalamium, proclaims to her as now instructed and fully taught through companionship in his discourse [Col. 1268A], and declares that through the grace and beauty she has acquired from this instruction she is to go forth as an example to others. “You who dwell,” he says, “in the gardens.” What are the gardens but the loveliness of the Scriptures or the delight of virtues? Nothing flowers more pleasantly, or smells more sweetly, than the streams and flowing waters, or the shoots, of the holy Scriptures, and the beautiful, delightful, and health-giving variety of virtues. In both places the discipline is praiseworthy and heavenly: here in speaking, there in acting. What does it mean to dwell in these gardens except to rest in frequent meditation upon the holy law and in the exercise of virtues? For one “whose delight is in the law of the Lord, and who meditates on his law day and night,” dwells simply at home with Jacob (Gen. 25): that is [Col. 1268B], one remains with secure constancy in the tranquillity of one’s mind, admitting nothing unstable or changeable into the unity of faith or morals. Conversely, one does not dwell in these gardens who, like Esau, intent upon hunting worldly things (Gen. 25), wanders amid the noise of the world through forests of thoughts, preserving neither unity of faith nor integrity of morals.

Therefore, O beloved, you who dwell simply and wholesomely in these gardens, make me hear your voice. What sort of voice? The voice of godly speech; the voice of virtue; the voice of one who teaches well and rightly; the voice of one who lives justly and piously. For just as true and right preaching is a great voice, so a godly and holy manner of life is a great voice. Humility is a great voice; obedience is a great voice; chastity is a great voice; patience is a great voice; charity is a great and resonant voice. And by however many virtues a holy soul shines, it cries to God as though with so many great voices.

[Col. 1268C] And why do I wish to hear your voice? Namely, that I may hear you crying out by word and deed, as it is written: “The children who shall be born and arise shall hear and recount them to their children, that they may place their hope in God and not forget the works of God, but seek his commandments” (Ps. 77). And what is my hearing? Surely, approving, accepting, and judging you worthy of my help. When I hear, I approve; when I hearken, I help. But do you make me hear your voice. How will you do this? By living honourably and piously, by teaching what is true and devout. For I have granted you reason and understanding [Col. 1268D], memory and intelligence, so that you may be without excuse and may not say that you neither know nor can do it. I have removed from you every necessity arising from impossibility, so that you may possess and perform what is owed. Yet I wish to be your debtor, so that when you have done what you are bound by right to do, “I may be overcome when I am judged” (Ps. 50). I wish, I say, to be overcome by your judgment, because I take great delight when you use my gift well; and therefore it is yours to make me wish to hear your voice. Yet your doing is not yours but mine, because your willing and being able are gifts of my grace.

“Make me hear your voice,” he says. Why? “Because your friends listen.” Whose friends? Both mine and yours: mine through charity, because they love me by keeping my word [Col. 1269A]; yours because they love you by desiring your salvation. There are friends whom you do not see with bodily eyes, who rejoice over your progress and salvation, or over your conversion. Of them it is written: “There is joy among the angels of God over one sinner doing penance” (Luke 15). These are the ministering spirits sent throughout the whole earth for those who shall receive the inheritance of salvation (Heb. 1). They are concerned and act for human salvation, as one of these invisible friends says to one of the visible friends: “At that time Michael shall arise, who stands for the children of your people” (Dan. 12); and soon after: “There is none to help me in all these things except Michael, your prince” (Dan. 10).

These friends therefore listen, because they take great delight in hearing your voice crying to me, whether in prayer, psalmody, preaching, or desire. There are also other friends whom you have before your eyes, who likewise delight in hearing this fourfold harmony of songs, like a beautiful *diatessaron* (a fourth) harmony [Col. 1269B], and therefore lend their ears, listen, and desire to hear you singing and saying: “But I, like a fruitful olive tree in the house of the Lord, have hoped in the mercy of my God, and I shall wait for your name before the presence of your saints” (Ps. 51). These holy friends, I say, listen in a wishing and longing manner, that you may become like them. Thus one of them wished himself to become accursed for his brothers (Rom. 9), whose salvation he desired. And because he himself already dwelt in the gardens of virtues, wisdom, and knowledge, he was concerned so to modulate his voice in my ears that he might please both God and human beings, and might show by life and teaching what was fitting for human salvation. Hence this is his voice, resounding from the gardens of wisdom and virtue and audible to me: “I chastise my body and reduce it to servitude, subjecting it, lest perhaps, after preaching to others, I myself should become reprobate” (1 Cor. 9).

In this way, when the flesh is so subjected to the spirit that it desires nothing below itself and seeks only what is above it, this is the voice that sounds delightfully in my ears. Indeed, this is the Song of Songs, than which no mortal and passible human being can sing anything sweeter in this mortal life. By such a voice and song one is always drawn toward the apprehension of that ineffable sweetness “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard” (1 Cor. 2), the attainment of which will make the human being immortal and impassible. While angels and all my saints listen to and desire to hear this voice and song, they do not doubt that those saints—that is, human beings—will attain by faith, hope, and charity the same glory that those others—that is, the angels—have attained. They earnestly desire that you too, who have not yet attained it, may attain it with them, and for this they pray to me without ceasing. What, finally, does the beloved woman answer to this voice? “Flee, my beloved,” etc.

### Verse 14

“Flee, my beloved, and be like a roe or a young stag upon the mountains of spices.”

If we consider attentively, this is the great voice of one humble in heart [Col. 1270A], whether we refer it to the whole Church or to any soul devoted to God. For why should the holy Church, or any holy soul, not use this voice to God in the present life? One of the saints says: “We know in part and prophesy in part; but when that which is perfect has come, that which is in part shall be done away” (1 Cor. 13). What did he perceive, who declared the imperfection of knowing and prophesying in this present life? That what is in part is not perfect. But he says that this imperfection will be done away when that which is perfect comes in the future life. If you consider rightly what kind of imperfection this is, it is surely the flight of this beloved.

[Col. 1270B] Whatever is done in the Church’s sacraments contains great and profound mysteries, all of which proclaim the power, virtue, and grace of this beloved; but who can fully discuss them? Hence the beloved woman, astonished by such greatness, knows in part and prophesies in part. Yet because she cannot comprehend fully, she fails and calls for the beloved to flee—not because she neglects him, but because of her deficiency. For this beloved’s flight consists in the examination of the sacraments of subtle things. When we cannot fully explain or examine their force and efficacy, this beloved flees us. Likewise, when we direct our gaze toward the face of Holy Scripture but cannot fully see it through or enter into the hidden treasures of its mysteries, this beloved certainly flees [Col. 1270C] us.

280. But let us not rashly hold back the fleeing one. Rather, whatever we cannot comprehend in a sacrament or in the subtlety of the holy Scriptures, let us “burn with fire”—that is, reserve it for the Holy Spirit—and, lest through excessive examination we fall into heretical understanding, let us allow the beloved to flee. According to the example of blessed Jacob, who wrestled with the angel, we are indeed instructed to wrestle with the Word of God; but once we have received the blessing and have been made lame by the touch of the sinew, let us permit the Word of God to flee. For what is it to wrestle with the Word of God except tirelessly to investigate the meaning of Holy Scripture? And what is it for the victor to ask and receive a blessing from the vanquished, except to seek and find understanding of that meaning itself? But the victor, after receiving a blessing from the vanquished, limps as his thigh withers, because one who, through God’s inspiration, has rightly understood Holy Scripture, with all carnal pleasure extinguished, advances in the active and contemplative life. He conquers with great profit to the spirit but with great loss to the flesh [Col. 1270D].

Finally, the one who conquered limps because the one who was conquered touched the sinew of his thigh, and it withered. How does he limp? He rests one foot on earth while holding the other suspended from the earth: that is, he does not wholly abandon the active life because of care for those subject to him, but clings with all his strength to the contemplative life because of its sweetness.

This lame man leaps or climbs like a stag, and scarcely deigns to touch the earth, for “his manner of life is in heaven” (Phil. 3). Yet he does so only in part, for now he is suspended there for the time being with but one [Col. 1271A] foot, until that which is perfect comes. Therefore, because he cannot yet comprehend perfectly, he rightly says: “Flee, my beloved.” When, then, speaking with the Lord on the mountain, we perceive in the mind the meaning of God’s word, let us heed the Apostle’s saying: “Do not be high-minded, but fear” (Rom. 11), lest, while heedlessly pursuing the fleeing beloved, we fall into the pit of perverse doctrine. We also call the beloved’s flight this: he is always incomprehensible. For this must be granted to his majesty, that he cannot be comprehended; he must always be desired and desirable, and it must remain hidden from us, while we are in this body, how great is “the multitude of his sweetness, which he has hidden for those who fear him” (Ps. 30).

[Col. 1271B] Therefore let us say to him: “Flee, flee, being cautious and provident toward us, lest while we live we ever suppose that we have comprehended, though we follow in order to comprehend.” Or in this way let every faithful and wise soul say with a humble and devout mind to God: “Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof” (Matt. 8); I am not worthy that you should show in me any frequent miracle of your presence or visitation. “Flee,” she says, “my beloved: in the present life I do not seek glory, but desire grace; I do not seek the splendour of miracles, but long for forgiveness of sins. Flee, my beloved, and make leaps like the leaps of a roe or a young stag—not over me, but over the mountains of spices, over the lofty merits of saints and the perfect. It is not for me [Col. 1271C] to treat or dispute concerning the secret of your divinity, the loftiest teachings of your commands, or the profound mysteries of your sacraments, but rather for those who may be called lofty mountains because of their eminence in wisdom and virtues. Touched by your Holy Spirit, they emit your sweet fragrance, so that with the Apostle they may say: ‘We are the sweet fragrance of Christ [Col. 1272A] to God in every place’” (2 Cor. 2), and therefore they are rightly called mountains of spices.

And what wonder if I, conscious of my own weakness, bid you flee, when those great and learned mountains themselves are astonished when they consider your works, commands, and sacraments, and at times allow you to flee? For one of those mountains, who had been raised to the third heaven and had heard things not permitted for a human being to speak (2 Cor. 12), fearing to pursue you, the fleeing beloved, said: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments and unsearchable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counsellor? Or who has first given to him, and shall be repaid? For from him [Col. 1272B] and through him and in him are all things; to him be honour and glory for ages of ages” (Rom. 11).

Therefore, my beloved, flee—not so as to abandon me altogether, but so that what I cannot attain here, where you are incomprehensible, you may grant me in the future life in true and eternal blessedness without end. Be like a roe or a young stag upon the mountains of spices. That is, surpass even the understanding of perfect saints through the incomprehensible knowledge of your divinity; or make such leaps in their hearts that they may advance “from virtue to virtue” (Ps. 83). For whenever the elect advance from good things to better things, from virtues to virtue, God makes, as it were, certain leaps in their minds, so that by these gradual steps or leaps they may attain that highest and perfect [Col. 1272C] state in which “the God of gods is seen in Zion” (Ps. 83). There they may without ceasing speak and sing in the ears of the Lord of Hosts, not simply a song but the Song of Songs: that is, know and apprehend that highest and best good for ages of ages. Amen.

## An Exhortation of the Author in Place of an Epilogue

To the sacred virgins for whom he wrote and to whom he dedicated these commentaries.

[Col. 1271]

[Col. 1271D] Behold, beloved sisters, we have sung to you as we could, and according to what that supreme teacher of ours has granted, under whose instruction are all who seek the knowledge of singing rightly and well. But because the art of singing rightly and well consists of a threefold instrument—namely heart, mouth, and work—I am convicted of not being a skilled singer. I can sing with my mouth; but if the other two are lacking, every appearance of my song will be empty before the Lord. For singing with heart and work can please God even if one does not sing with the mouth; but singing with the mouth alone [Col. 1272D], and not with heart and work, cannot possibly please God. Moreover, whoever wishes to possess the perfect art of singing and to know its highest dignity must always have the capacity for all three of these. Showing that he knew and possessed this, the Apostle says: “I will sing psalms with the spirit; I will sing psalms also with the mind” (1 Cor. 14). For to sing psalms with the spirit is both to utter spiritual words from memory, which is to sing with the mouth, and to proceed to works conceived by the spirit, which is to sing by work. To sing psalms with the mind is to apprehend in the mind the life-giving meaning of the words, which is to sing with the heart.

[Col. 1273A] But once the instrument for attaining the knowledge of singing rightly and well has been given, we must also know what is first to be learned in singing, and what kind of song leads us to the Song of Songs. First we must learn and sing that new song concerning which the Holy Spirit exhorts us in the Psalm: “Sing to the Lord a new song; his praise is in the Church of the saints” (Ps. 149). If you consider the nature of correlatives, where “new” is said, “old” necessarily follows. But first let us see what the old song is, that by recognizing it we may understand the new one better.

That old song was sung and taught by the old man Adam, but it is utterly opposed and contrary to the new song later heard, and differs from it by the distance that separates what kills from what gives life. What is that song? Surely that by which the old man cried out against his Maker and shouted against righteousness and piety: namely, pride, disobedience, and the excusing of his sin. For it was right that he should be subject and obedient to his maker and ruler. But it was grievous that, after his fault, he neither acknowledged himself [Col. 1273B] nor trusted in God’s mercy; rather, despising his sin, he transmitted the punishment of exile from paradise to all his posterity. The more many people sing the mournful tragedy of this song by imitating his presumption and negligence, the greater is the penalty of the death imposed upon them that they pay.

But opposed to this song is that new song: the song of peace and joy, the song of life and righteousness, the song of virtue and salvation, which that new man sang before us—not merely a human being, but God and man. With such a precentor, who said, “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble in heart, and you shall find rest for your souls” (Matt. 11), we are instructed to sing the new song of profit. Moreover, following the example of the Lord himself, of whom the Apostle says, “Christ became obedient to God the Father unto death” (Phil. 2), we are instructed to sing the song of sweet obedience. And at the voice of the same new precentor who says, “Do penance, for the kingdom of heaven will draw near” (Matt. 4), we are instructed not “to incline our heart to words of malice, to make excuses for [Col. 1273D] sins” (Ps. 146). For that is the most grievous—indeed, the most miserable—voice of the impenitent old man: the voice, I say, of the old song full of sorrow.

Rather, with such a song reversed and changed into a new one, let us sing to God the melody of a contrite spirit—laborious indeed with respect to the body but wholesome with respect to the soul—in four modes: contrition, confession, satisfaction, and perseverance. And in each of these four modes, let us daily lay aside its final element: thought, speech, action, and habit.

For these are the final elements of both songs, the old and the new: thought, speech, action, and habit; and they take on a mode of laying aside corresponding to the nature of the preceding song—[Col. 1274A] elegiac in the case of the old, sweet and musical in the case of the new. A musical laying aside is one accomplished by a rational conjunction, ordering, and sustaining of voices or tones. The new song receives this more especially—indeed, always—because of the rational movement of a mind singing well and beautifully, and always tending toward a good end in thought, speech, action, and habit. Conversely, elegiac laying aside is sad and wretched, occurring through an irrational and unequal movement of the mind; and because the form of such singing is confused, it produces a harsh and unmelodious quality of ending.

[Col. 1274B] There is therefore between these two songs the same distance as between life and death, because the old song kills, whereas the new gives life. This is illustrated by a comparison: certain sea creatures are called sirens; while they entice and attract sailors by the sweetness of their song, they suddenly drown the unwary and negligent. So, when carnal persons, as though sailing upon the sea of this world, are held by the sweetness of carnal life and the delight of sin, they suddenly neglect the salvation of their souls, refuse conversion through penance, and are snatched away by unclean spirits to eternal death. This is the manner of the old song: beginning from the spirit of pride and disobedience, it brings forth its final note, through the most grievous and wretched sound of an impenitent heart, into the abyss of eternal damnation.

On the other hand, there is the comparison shown to us in divine and human literature. In divine literature it is written that David with his harp calmed Saul’s frenzy (1 Sam. 16); in human literature it is written that Orpheus softened tigers and lions by his song, and Amphion moved stones by the sound of his lyre. This signifies that the power of the new song is to calm the beast-like minds of people raging against their own salvation, and to shape the hard hearts of mortals, by the rational movement of words and meanings, toward a good manner of life and the rational uprightness of morals [Col. 1274C]. This is the manner of the new song: beginning from the spirit of humility and obedience, it brings forth its final voice, through the lofty and joyful sound of an innocent or penitent heart, into the joy of eternal blessedness.

[Col. 1274D] Therefore, just as life and death are contrary to one another, so too are the old and new song contrary to one another, according to the qualities of the persons from whose authority each song receives its beginning and end. The author of the old song is the devil; the author of the new song is Christ. Therefore, despising the author of death, let us follow the author of life. Constantly attending to the delightful and most sweet harmony of his holiness, let us pass by with deaf ears the foolish voices of the sirens—that is, the foolish persuasions of malignant spirits.

The workshops and dwellings in which the instruments of this new and health-giving song are prepared and preserved, in which we hear and learn the song itself, and in which through the custom and practice of singing [Col. 1275A] we come to that Song of Songs whose sweetness and delight will never fail, are the beloved tabernacles of the Lord. Concerning them, that divine man of old, who said that he heard the words of God and beheld the vision of God, who falls and yet has eyes thus opened, asks:

“How beloved are your tabernacles, O Jacob, and your tents, O Israel: like wooded valleys, like gardens watered beside rivers; like tabernacles fixed by the Lord, like cedars beside abundant waters” (Num. 24).

The tabernacles of true Israel and spiritual Jacob, journeying or fighting in this present age, are religious orders well arranged according to Christ’s discipline: namely the orders of married persons, continent persons, widows, and virgins of both sexes. Each of these tabernacles is plainly beautiful in its own calling [Col. 1275B].

How beautiful are the tabernacles, how beautiful the tents! “Like wooded valleys, like gardens watered beside rivers.” This comparison is clear from other places in Scripture.
