In Isaiah, the Lord promises to the Gentile world, once forsaken, the merits of spiritual virtues like shrubs in a desert: “I will give in the wilderness the cedar and thorn, the myrtle and olive tree; I will set in the desert the fir tree, elm, and box tree together, that they may see, know, consider, and understand alike” (Isa. 41). Therefore the tabernacles are beautiful like wooded valleys: valleys because of humility, wooded because of the beauty of diverse virtues.

[Col. 1275C] For in these tabernacles of God, that is, holy professions, there are cedars: that is, saints incorrupt and unrotting in faith and works, fragrant with the scent of virtues. There are thorns, pricking others by word and example and provoking them to good works. There are myrtles, tempering their neighbours’ tribulations by compassion with a word of consolation. There are olive trees, abounding in acts of mercy and piety. There are fir trees, ever rising on high through the virtue of contemplation. There are elms, which, although secular and less fruitful, nevertheless sustain and assist others who live well with their resources. There are box trees, which, though they do not rise to the heights of virtues or bear fruit, nevertheless are ever green through the faith of their parents. [Col. 1275D] Therefore these tabernacles of the Lord are like wooded valleys, because they acquire this from a humble heart and likewise from lowly action and condition, so that they may grow green and flower with so great an abundance of virtues.

They are also like gardens watered beside streams, as it is said elsewhere: “You shall be like a watered garden, and like a spring of waters whose waters shall not fail” (Isa. LVIII). And in the same Song: “A locked garden, a sealed spring, a fountain of gardens, a well of living waters flowing in a rush from Lebanon” (Cant. IV). Behold, the tabernacles are beautiful like gardens watered beside streams, because through the moisture of the Holy Spirit they are ever green and flowering in speech and action, and in continual meditation upon the divine commandments.

They are likewise cedars beside waters, as the Psalmist [Col. 1276A] shows, who, after saying, “Watering the mountains from his upper chambers,” etc., immediately adds: “The fields and the cedars of Lebanon which he planted shall be filled” (Ps. CIII). Therefore the tabernacles are beautiful like cedars beside waters, that is, beside waters in which sparrows make their nests (Ps. CIII); when these are wealthy persons, their abundance supplies the need of the poor.

Thus these tabernacles are 286 like the tabernacles which the Lord has pitched, because all their beauty, adornment, and arrangement are the work of almighty God, who by his grace establishes, advances, adorns, and sustains them.

“Water shall flow from his bucket, and his seed shall be in many waters” (Num. XXIV). What is his bucket? Or rather, what is his water? Surely, that of the true Jacob, that is, the supplanter, [Col. 1276B] or of the true Israel, that is, the mind beholding the Lord. Some of these dwell in these tabernacles, that is, professions. His bucket is Christ, from whom water is drawn, that is, Holy Scripture. For through him Holy Scripture is opened; indeed, by him thirst is stirred up so that this water may be desired; by him understanding is opened so that the Scriptures may be understood. Therefore water shall flow from his bucket: that is, true understanding of the Scriptures shall issue forth from his Christ. What follows? “And his seed shall be in many waters.” What the water from his bucket is, that is the multitude of waters from his seed. For his seed is the seed of his father Abraham (Gen. XVII), namely, of him who is truly Christ, the “Exalted Father,” or “Father of many nations.”

This his seed shall be in many waters: that is, this [Col. 1276C] seed pours forth many waters. By drinking, we have experienced that his seed truly is in many waters. “He who believes in me,” he says, “from his belly shall flow rivers of living water” (John VII). Likewise: “Whoever drinks of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst; but the water that I shall give him shall become in him a spring of water leaping up to eternal life” (John IV). This, I say, we have experienced by drinking his grace. For behold, from this bucket, which is Christ himself, we have received many gifts of the Holy Spirit in the one Church, and in our minds possess many and most abundant meanings of the Scriptures.

Therefore in these tabernacles of the Lord that new song always resounds, which the inhabitants of these tabernacles sing with seven distinctions of voices, [Col. 1276D] the Holy Spirit directing the song through his sevenfold grace: namely wisdom and understanding, counsel and fortitude, knowledge and piety, and the fear of the Lord. Moreover, from these seven distinctions of voices arise diverse beatitudes, as it were forms of eight modes: namely humility, meekness, mourning—or the three according to the Lord—peace, mercy, purity, desire for righteousness, and patience.

And this song, or praise of God, exists only in the Church of the saints, because what the saints are, and what they know and are able to do—the source of their sanctity—is the gift of the grace of God alone. And such persons, daily departing from the Egypt of this world, holding through contempt of their own will the harps of God, that is, mortification of the flesh, not only sing a new song but also [Col. 1277A] the Song of Songs; for in this manner they advance to that ineffable love of God, which is the virtue of virtues, from which proceeds and in which is contained the fullness of all virtues.

Therefore, beloved sisters, because you are a tabernacle of God, or dwell in the tabernacles of God, always sing this new song through humility, chastity, patience, obedience, mortification of the flesh, and love of God and neighbour. Let the just ordinances [Col. 1278A] of the Lord be songs for you in the place of your pilgrimage (Ps. CXVIII), so that one day, departing from the Egypt of this age, arriving at the land of promise, and eternally enjoying the goods of that land, which “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man” (I Cor. II; Isa. LXIV), you may sing with all delight and sweetness, without interruption, not only the new song but also the Song of Songs, through all ages of ages. Amen.

## The Mirror of Charity

501 Letter of Gervase, Abbot of Park, urging Aelred to publish the following books.  
503 Preface of Blessed Aelred.  

### Book I: Demonstrating the Excellence of Charity

505 Chapter I.—That nothing is more fitting than that the Creator should be loved by His creature.  
506 Chapter II.—On nature, form, and use, bestowed in common upon all creatures.  
507 Chapter III.—That man was made in the image of his Creator and is capable of blessedness.  
508 Chapter IV.—That through love—in which he had a fuller taste of blessedness—man fell away from God; and, thus made wretched, corrupted but did not abolish God’s image within himself.  
509 Chapter V.—That after the Savior’s coming God’s image is renewed in man; and that the perfection of this renewal is to be hoped for not here but in the future.  
510 Chapter VI.—A disputation against the fool who said in his heart: “There is no God.”  
511 Chapter VII.—That man fell away from God through the inclination of his mind.  
512 Chapter VIII.—That through the disposition of charity man is re-formed into God’s image.  
513 Chapter IX.—That our love toward ourselves is divided, through charity and cupidity, by contrary desires.  
513 Chapter X.—That free choice occupies a middle place in the soul, yet is not equally sufficient for good and evil.  
514 Chapter XI.—That grace does not take away free choice.  
515 Chapter XII.—That free choice is not taken away either from the saved or from the damned, and that grace works only in free choice.  
517 Chapter XIII.—The reason why free choice is not equally sufficient for good and evil.  
517 Chapter XIV.—What difference there is between the grace which the first human beings possessed in paradise and that possessed by the predestined in the world; and that an evil will is justly imputed to man, although free choice lacks the power to attain a good will.  
518 Chapter XV.—That even the condemnation of little children is altogether just.  
[Col. 1291] 519 Chapter XVI.—That charity lacks nothing of perfection.  
520 Chapter XVII.—On the spiritual circumcision contained in charity.  
521 Chapter XVIII.—That the true and spiritual Sabbath is in charity.  
521 Chapter XIX.—How greatly the seventh day is preferred to the others, and that on it God’s charity is commended.  
523 Chapter XX.—Why the number six is commended in God’s work and the number seven in His rest.  
524 Chapter XXI.—That in all creatures a certain trace of divine charity appears, and that therefore all things tend, as it were, toward the Sabbath—that is, toward rest.
